Article.Title: A Unified Framework for Self-Recognition Across Monkeys, Infants, and Robots
Article.Authors: Zhang, W.; Chen, K.; Zhang, T.; Sun, Q.; Sun, Y.; Jia, Y.; Chang, L.; Liu, J.; Qian, H.; Qin, P.; Jiang, F.; Wang, G.; Gong, N.
Article.Abstract: Self-recognition is a basic cognitive ability that indicates self-consciousness in humans. However, whether non-human agents such as monkeys and robots can possess a similar sense of self remains debated. Here, we develop a multi-scenario apparatus to examine self-recognition from different perspectives across macaque monkeys, human infants, and simulated robots. Monkeys trained for mirror-perspective (MP) self-face recognition were able to spontaneously recognize themselves when viewing video images of their back from a third-person perspective (3PP); however, this generalization required a few minutes of "exploration". In contrast, monkeys trained for 3PP self-back recognition spontaneously demonstrated MP self-recognition within seconds. Meanwhile, first-person-perspective (1PP) self-hand recognition represented a more basic ability that naive monkeys could achieve naturally. Interestingly, human infants aged 1 to 2 years exhibited a stepwise developmental sequence of 1PP, MP, and 3PP self-recognition abilities, consistent with the hierarchical levels of self-recognition in monkeys. Furthermore, we constructed world-model-based simulated robots and found that robots equipped with a body schema exhibited the emergence of self-recognition ability following multisensory integration training, along with the spontaneous generalization of self-recognition across different perspectives. Notably, the formation of internal self-body maps was identified as a key factor enabling this generalization. The convergence of findings across humans, monkeys, and robots not only redefines the evolutionary continuity of the self but also provides an operational framework for designing artificial systems capable of locating themselves in the world.

Article.Title: Cerebellar transcranial AC stimulation produces frequency and phase-dependent changes in Purkinje cell complex spike waveform
Article.Authors: Mourra, D.; Sloane, J.; Sahin, M.; Lang, E. J.
Article.Abstract: Cerebellar transcranial alternating current stimulation (ctACS) can improve motor learning and may speed rehabilitation. The mechanisms by which ctACS induces long-term changes in brain function that underlie these effects are not known, and knowledge of them could greatly improve the application of ctACS. One potential mechanism is alteration of Purkinje cell (PC) complex spike (CS) activity, as CS activity is a key regulator of cerebellar synaptic plasticity. Thus, we investigated how ctACS modifies CS firing rates and waveform. Extracellular recordings were obtained from cerebellar PCs in anesthetized adult rats while ctACS (250 A) was applied across a range of frequencies (0.5 - 50 Hz). The effect of ctACS on CS waveform was quantified via measuring changes in the overall size of the CS and in the number and amplitude of the spikelets that comprise a CS. ctACS produced phase-dependent modulation of the CS waveform in a majority of PCs at most tested frequencies, with 1 Hz stimulation causing modulation in all PCs tested at the frequency. The modulation reflected changes within the normal range of CS waveforms rather than an expansion of that range. Analysis of individual spikelet periods (windows) revealed that ctACS modified discrete portions of the CS, with 93.8% of PCs showing significant modulation in at least one window. Notably, the strength of phase-dependent CS waveform modulation was relatively consistent across frequencies, in contrast to the frequency dependence of simple spike (SS) entrainment. Significant modulation of spikelet amplitude was found more often than that of spikelet number; however, the relative strength of the modulation when present was similar for the two parameters. CS waveform modulation was correlated with SS entrainment strength and was strongest in PCs located near the cerebellar surface (i.e., near the apices of the folia). Together, these findings demonstrate that ctACS exerts phase-dependent control over CS waveform. Moreover, the differing frequency dependence of the waveform effects and SS firing modulation suggests that it may be possible to target CS-related plasticity selectively, providing a potential strategy for selectively modulating cerebellar learning with ctACS.

Article.Title: Variable penetrance of schizophrenia in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is associated with impaired, but reversible, neuronal mitophagy.
Article.Authors: Stronati, E.; Rossano, A. J.; Li, J.; Stoesser, A. R.; Wallace, D. C.; Giulivi, C.; Anderson, S. A.
Article.Abstract: The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22qDS) is a major genetic risk factor for schizophrenia (Sz). We found that iPSC-derived neurons (iNeurons) from 22qDS +Sz individuals exhibit weaker mitochondrial energetics, whereas iNeurons from individuals with the same deletion but no psychosis (22qDS -Sz) upregulate expression of mitochondrial biogenesis-related genes. Here, we investigated why the +Sz group fails to undergo this compensation, finding that 22qDS +Sz iNeurons have older and more depolarized mitochondria than 22qDS -Sz or controls. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed downregulation of mitophagy-related pathways, and live imaging revealed elevated lysosomal pH. Restoring lysosomal acidity with acidifying nanoparticles improved mitophagy and, remarkably, increased the expression of mitochondrial biogenesis-related transcription factors in the +Sz neurons. We conclude that lysosomal dysfunction and impaired mitophagy differentiate 22qDS individuals who develop schizophrenia from those who do not. Mitophagy could be a novel therapeutic or preventative opportunity for Sz in the context of genetic neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Title: Early visual experience contributes to the calibration of higher-order body representations
Article.Authors: Liu, Y.; Wang, Y.; Ma, Y.
Article.Abstract: Higher-order body representations, including representations of body shape and size, play an important role in maintaining perceptual constancy in touch. However, whether the development of these representations depends on early visual experience remains unclear. Here, we investigated tactile distance perception in congenitally blind, late-blind, and sighted individuals. A given tactile distance is typically perceived as longer on the finger than on the forearm, reflecting distortions in cortical topography that is partially rescaled by higher-order representations of body size and shape. Congenitally blind participants showed a greater tendency to perceive identical tactile distances on the index finger as longer than those on the forearm. A similar bias was observed when comparing the forehead and face, suggesting that altered tactile distance perception in congenital blindness is not limited to body regions with extensive sensory-motor experience. Furthermore, within the late-blind group, the similarity of perceptual patterns to sighted controls, relative to congenitally blind participants, was associated with blindness duration. Together, these findings suggest that both early visual and post-blindness experience contributes to the calibration of tactile distance perception across the body, with its influence potentially extending beyond body regions extensively engaged in sensory-motor activities.

Article.Title: Partially shared representational space for vision and language across objects, scenes, and visual events
Article.Authors: Zou, Q.; Jozwik, K.
Article.Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) and behavioural similarity judgements of visual stimuli predict neural responses in visual cortex. Recent work shows that large language model (LLM) embeddings and similarity judgements of language descriptions also predict visual brain activity. These predictors were examined separately across modalities (vision vs language) and types (models vs human behaviour). It remains unclear to what extent these predictors explain shared or unique aspects of visual brain responses, how these contributions vary along the visual hierarchy and category-selective regions, and whether vision-language convergence depends on the stimulus type. We used three fMRI datasets progressing toward naturalistic visual experience, from objects (THINGS) to scenes (NSD) to dynamic events (BMD). For each dataset, we collected similarity judgements of visual stimuli and of their language descriptions from human participants (N = 21-35), extracted vision DNN features and LLM embeddings, and related similarity judgements and model representations to visual brain responses using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and variance partitioning. Vision-language convergence was higher within behaviour than within models. From objects to dynamic events, LLM alignment with vision-based similarity judgements increased, whereas vision DNN alignment remained stable. A shared, predominantly cross-modal component increased along the visual hierarchy and dominated explained variance in high-level visual cortex. LLMs made their largest unique contributions in face- and body-selective regions (FFA and EBA), where shared representations of vision- and language-based human similarity judgements also explained variance beyond the models. In summary, we find a partially shared representational space for vision and language in high-level visual cortex, most clearly in regions representing social information related to people and their actions. As each predictor retained unique variance, combining computational models and human behaviour across vision and language may offer a more comprehensive account of high-level visual representations.

Article.Title: Distal inhibition is recruited for action but not sensation in the primate superior colliculus
Article.Authors: Bourrelly, C.; Yang, F.; Gandhi, N. J.
Article.Abstract: Sensorimotor transformation requires neural circuits to coordinate excitation and inhibition, but how and whether this organization changes as the circuit transitions from processing sensation to action remain unresolved. We recorded laminar local field potentials across superior colliculus (SC) layers in four male macaques and computed current source density to resolve transmembrane currents during saccades to a target at one of eight isoradial directions. During the visual response, excitation was spatially confined to the receptive field, with little modulation at distant sites. During saccade generation, local excitation remained strongest for movements toward the receptive field, while inhibition extended across the SC map, including locations where spiking remained at baseline. Because the same recordings detected distal inhibition during movement, its absence during vision cannot reflect insufficient sensitivity, indicating that distal inhibition is selectively recruited during action. After saccade completion, excitation emerged regardless of saccade direction, potentially reflecting a rebound from, or release of, the preceding inhibition. These patterns were only partly reflected in spiking activity, which primarily captured local excitation, unmasking circuit dynamics largely invisible at the level of neuronal output. Together, our findings reveal a striking reconfiguration of SC population dynamics across sensorimotor transformation, spanning from spatially restricted excitation during sensation, to local excitation coupled with distal inhibition during movement generation, then to global post-movement excitation. Thus, fixed circuit architecture can express a sequence of behaviorally gated excitation-inhibition states largely invisible to spiking output.

Article.Title: Hormone therapy attenuates menopause-related impairments in motor cortical spike-timing-dependent plasticity
Article.Authors: Ansdell, P.; Spillane, P.; Nedelec, E.; O'Hanlon, M.; Inns, T.; Piasecki, M.; Hausmann, M.; Goodall, S.; Vincent, K.; Stagg, C. J.; Piasecki, J.
Article.Abstract: The menopause marks the permanent cessation of menstruation via a decline in endogenous hormone production. This transition influences brain health, yet its effects on motor cortical excitability and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) are poorly understood. Across two sites, 46 females were categorised as pre-menopausal (PRE, age 28{+/-}7 years), perimenopausal (PERI, 50{+/-}3 years), post-menopausal (POST, 60{+/-}8 years), or combined continuous hormone therapy users (HT, 52{+/-}3 years). Transcranial magnetic stimulation was used to measure corticospinal excitability (MEP/Mmax), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and intracortical facilitation (ICF) before, then 10 and 30 min after a paired associative stimulation (PAS) protocol (25-ms interstimulus interval). Serum hormone concentrations were quantified from venous blood. Resting corticospinal excitability and SICI were not different between groups before the PAS protocol. However, a group x time interaction (p=0.0152) for MEP/Mmax revealed distinct STDP responses. PRE showed a significant increase in corticospinal excitability following PAS (+48%, p=0.0045), whereas PERI and POST showed no facilitation (p[≥]0.2079). Between groups, both PRE and HT exceeded PERI, and HT also exceeded POST; however, HT users showed a smaller, non-significant increase (+32%, p=0.0666) that collectively distinguished them from the blunted responses of PERI and POST. The magnitude of STDP was not associated with any single hormone or chronological age across the whole sample of participants. These findings provide the first evidence that motor cortical STDP is influenced by menopause stage. With blunted responses in PERI and POST, yet preserved responses in HT users, these data have implications for motor learning and rehabilitation across the female adult lifespan.

Article.Title: Scalable construction of near-wild-type brain atlases enables variability-aware neuronal identification in C. elegans
Article.Authors: Yu, Z.; Yang, W.; Moon, Y.; Liang, J.; Moon, S.; Yang, Z.; Lee, H. J.; Parra Arroyo, L.; Ge, M.; Calhoun, W. A.; Kumar, S.; Zhang, Y.; Lu, H.
Article.Abstract: Matching cells across individuals is essential for comparing cellular data but becomes challenging when cell positions vary between animals. Here we introduce a framework for constructing probabilistic neuronal atlases by integrating partially overlapping observations from sparsely labeled, near-wild-type strains to reconstruct cellular organization from incomplete observations. Using five strains imaged without compression in a microfluidic array, we built an atlas of 129 head neurons (55 classes) that captures positional variability and infers spatial relationships even between neurons never observed together. We find that variability is spatially structured with neurons in compact regions being more stereotyped, while neuronal relative positions are more stable than their absolute positions. Exploiting these statistical relationships, variability-weighted identification improved top-1 accuracy to 86.3%, approaching human inter-annotator agreement, with the correct identity among the top three candidates in 98.2% of cases. Relationships stitched across strains reproduced observations in a held-out strain, and the atlas supplied correct identities in males and in pan-neuronal calcium imaging in vast majority of cases. Our extensible framework enables community-built atlases and offers a strategy for cell identification when anatomical variability limits template-based registration.

Article.Title: Restoring Marcenko-Pastur noise estimation and denoising of diffusion MRI under common image reconstruction
Article.Authors: Mordhorst, L.; Mohammadi, S.; Tabelow, K.
Article.Abstract: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging can reveal microstructure in the living brain, but the measurements are inherently noisy. Marcenko-Pastur denoising is a widely used remedy, helping to separate signal from noise under a simplified noise covariance model. However, we find that the model breaks under common image reconstructions across 28 public in vivo datasets, resulting in weaker denoising than intended. We restore the intended denoising behavior with a noise covariance model estimated from the reconstructed images, and validate the estimated model on repeated ex vivo and in vivo scans. The method requires no additional measurements or knowledge of the reconstruction, opening headroom for microstructure analyses in both existing and newly acquired data.

Article.Title: "The self" as shifting coalitions of brain systems in a continuous configuration space
Article.Authors: Skipper, J. I.; Blackburne, G.; Cooper, G.; Jaglinska, M.; Jedlovszky, K.; Kuc, J.; McAlpine, R.; Timmermann, C.
Article.Abstract: Philosophers and psychologists distinguish many forms of self, yet neuroimaging results often implicate a shared core in the cortical midline or insula. We propose self-related processing arises from shifting coalitions of distributed brain systems, without a core. In a meta-analysis of 912 neuroimaging publications, titles and abstracts clustered into ten forms, including autobiographical memory, body ownership and interoception. No single location was significant in all ten associated brain maps, although each occupied different parts and amounts of midline and insular territory. Their differences were distributed across the brain. Regional patterns varied with study context, corresponded selectively with aspects of consciousness and resembled maps of general functions. Brain patterns combined at continuously varying strengths predicted regions reported in held-out publications better than single patterns or on/off combinations. Self-related processing therefore has no core and arises from shifting coalitions of distributed brain systems whose graded contributions define a continuous configuration space.

Article.Title: Generalized hippocampal replay exhibits memory recall-like dynamics
Article.Authors: Cai, G.; Lustig, B.; Lee, A. K.; Mattar, M. G.; Gershman, S. J.
Article.Abstract: Hippocampal replay has been intensely studied for theorized roles in memory consolidation, credit assignment in reinforcement learning, and online planning. Much work in the field assumes that replayed trajectories traverse states smoothly and sequentially, in either forward or reverse order of experience. In a synthetic setting, we demonstrate that incorrect transition priors lead to systematic decoding error and show how model comparison addresses this issue. We compare a diverse set of transition models, including recall-like transition dynamics, and show how they can capture qualitatively different replay structures. Applying model comparison to three neural recording datasets from adult male rats, we find that the recall transition dynamics offer a statistically superior description of spiking during population burst events compared to a commonly used heuristic model of smooth trajectories. We propose a generalized conception of replay events through this theoretical connection to human free recall dynamics. Furthermore, our theory suggests that generalized replays may be a neural instantiation of online planning through generalized rollouts. We find preliminary evidence that generalized replays are more prevalent in settings where planning is beneficial. Overall, the proposed theory has implications for decoding methodology and the normative interpretation of hippocampal replay.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: hippocampal replay; online planning; decoding errors; memory consolidation; free recall

Article.Title: Non-canonical subthalamic nucleus projections regulate motor variability
Article.Authors: Oladunni, O. A.; Elvig, S. K.; Bennis, H. C.; Elzaree, L. A.; Nandy, S.; Liu, Y.; Chatterjee, S.; Mathur, B. N.; Wolff, S. B. E.
Article.Abstract: Regulation of motor variability is a key hallmark of motor skill learning, balancing motor exploration with optimization of identified task solutions. Nevertheless, the underlying circuit mechanisms in the mammalian brain remain largely unknown. Subnuclei of the dorsal striatum in the basal ganglia promote stereotyped or variable behavior, respectively, and deep brain stimulation of the downstream subthalamic nucleus (STN) can alter motor variability. We therefore tested whether the STN regulates motor variability via non-canonical projections to striatum. We discovered that silencing STN neurons projecting to dorsolateral striatum impaired motor variability reduction in rats developing complex stereotyped movement patterns. In contrast, silencing STN neurons projecting to the anterior thalamic nuclei, or neurons in these nuclei that receive STN input and project to dorsomedial striatum, accelerated variability reduction. These results deepen our anatomical and functional understanding of subcortical motor circuits and reveal unknown roles for STN's non-canonical striatal projections in motor variability regulation.
Article.Topic: Deep Brain Stimulation and Movement Disorders

Article.Title: Selective Gut-Related Biomarker Profiles Define Parkinson Disease Trait and State
Article.Authors: Keshavarzian, A.; Alam, M. S.; Engen, P. A.; Voigt, R. M.; Shaikh, M.; Naqib, A.; Villanueva, M.; Bonfanti, A. P.; Giron, L. B.; Joshi, N.; Green, S. J.; Abdel-Mohsen, M.; Luo, S.; Goetz, C. G.
Article.Abstract: Objective: Gut-brain-axis abnormalities are increasingly implicated in Parkinson disease (PD), but most studies examine individual biological compartments of this axis. We asked whether readily accessible stool and plasma-based biomarker profiles show broad or selective gut abnormalities in PD and whether the profiles associated with PD diagnosis (Trait) are the same as those associated with clinical severity (State). Methods: This cross-sectional study included 211 participants with PD and 204 healthy controls. Twenty-four stool and plasma biomarkers were organized into an overall profile, three parent domains (microbiome/dysbiosis, gut barrier/inflammation, systemic inflammation/immune activation), and eight more focused mechanistic profiles. Rank-based Global Statistical Tests (GSTs) compared PD Trait and State. Results: The overall profile showed no evidence of a PD vs. control difference (GST P=0.607; permutation P=0.521), whereas the domain of microbiome/dysbiosis differed (GST P=0.017; permutation P=0.013). Four of eight focused profiles differed nominally: microbial functional-groups, microbial functional-ratios, epithelial injury/bacterial translocation, and myeloid activation. Across PD clinical severity, overall-profile results differed (GST P=0.053; permutation P=0.037); both categories of microbiome/dysbiosis (GST P=0.023; permutation P=0.016) and microbial alpha-diversity (GST P=0.027; permutation P=0.031) differed. Interpretation: The analyses detected differences associated with PD Trait and State in selected gut-related profiles rather than a detectable overall PD-control difference. Microbiome-related profiles showed the most consistent domain findings across PD Trait and State, but they are sufficiently different to suggest that causation and progression of PD follow distinctly different gut processes. These findings refine the concept of the Parkinson gut and prioritize the microbiome for mechanistic and interventional studies.

Article.Title: Restrictive eating is linked to weaker recollection of food in young adults
Article.Authors: Zhao, C.; Wildes, J. E.; Bakkour, A.
Article.Abstract: Affective significance often enhances episodic memory, with stronger effects on recollection than on familiarity, but prior research has focused primarily on within-person manipulations of emotional valence. Here, we tested a novel question: whether stable individual differences in the personal significance of food were associated with long-term memory across individuals, given that food ranges from highly appetitive to strongly avoided. Across two experiments, we examined familiarity-based memory (using an image recognition task) and recollection-based memory (using a spatial source recognition task) for food and nonfood stimuli as a function of eating-related individual differences in young adults. In Experiment 1, familiarity-based recognition memory was largely unrelated to eating behavior. In Experiment 2, however, greater restrictive eating and fear of negative consequences from eating were associated with poorer recollection-based memory for food when compared to nonfood stimuli. Together, these findings suggest that individual differences in the affective significance of food do not correlate with episodic memory uniformly but instead are selectively associated with reduced recollection, but not familiarity, of food relative to neutral stimuli.

Article.Title: Preserved cognitive control with altered ventromedial prefrontal activity in lichen simplex chronicus: an fMRI study during the Multi-Source Interference Task.
Article.Authors: Valenzuela, L.; Valdes, J.; Domic-Siede, M.; Curi, M.; Solis-Avaca, M.; Crossley, N. A.; Zamorano, F.; Sandoval, M.; Ossandon, T.; Medel, V.
Article.Abstract: Lichen simplex chronicus (LSC) is a chronic pruritic skin condition, and one of its central features is the itch-scratch cycle. It has been hypothesized that resisting the urge to scratch, and thereby stopping this cycle, may depend on mechanisms of cognitive control. Here, we used the Multi-Source Interference Task (MSIT) during fMRI to examine whether patients with LSC (n = 9) differ from healthy controls (n = 11) in interference control or in the brain activity that supports it. Our results show that both groups had the expected interference effect, with no statistically significant group differences in behavioral performance or in cingulo-frontal-parietal BOLD activity. Whole-brain analysis revealed a greater interference-related decrease in ventromedial prefrontal cortex activity in patients than in controls. These exploratory findings show distinct patterns of brain activity in LSC while preserving interference control, warranting further investigation in larger samples.

Article.Title: The role of shape and local features in human object recognition and learning
Article.Authors: Schneider, A. R.; Maltz, O.; Ayzenberg, V.
Article.Abstract: An object's shape is an important visual cue, critical for both perception and cognition. However, the current best models of human vision, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), do not prioritize shape, but instead, they rely on texture-like local visual features. This raises the question: Could shape be less important for human perception than previously believed? In seven experiments with both adults (N = 300) and 5-year-old children (N = 100), we tested the role of shape and local features in visual object recognition and learning. We found that humans could identify common objects as accurately using local visual features as they could using shape. This finding suggests that, like DNNs, local features may be sufficient for everyday visual recognition and that shape may not be necessary. However, we found that shape played a crucial role in novel object learning, allowing participants to even accomplish one-shot object categorization. Together, these findings force us to reconsider the role of shape in visual recognition and suggest that DNNs, despite not using shape, may nevertheless capture an important aspect of human visual processing.

Article.Title: Constrained Geometric Approach for Robust Local Optic Axis Estimation with Single Input Polarization Sensitive Optical Coherence Tomography
Article.Authors: Wan, J.; Clickner, C. R.; Sheft, M.; Jones, G. L.; Wang, H.
Article.Abstract: Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PSOCT) enables label-free, depth-resolved microstructure mapping in biological tissues, making it a powerful tool for studying myelinated fiber structures in the brain. Conventional single-input PSOCT measures cumulative retardance and apparent optic axis, which become inaccurate when fibers cross over depth. In single-input PSOCT systems, local optic axis estimation is challenging due to high noise levels, limiting the reliability of depth-resolved orientation estimation. In this work, we present a robust framework for local optic axis estimation in single-input PSOCT that incorporates physical constraints and polarization super-pixels. Polarization super-pixels serve as a preprocessing step to cluster spatially connected pixels with similar polarization states, increasing the effective signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and reducing instability in recursive matrix inversion. In addition, a physical constraint based on the mirror state of the input polarization is enforced during geometric fitting, significantly improving robustness and accuracy under noisy and low-SNR conditions. Experimental validation on ex vivo human brain tissue and phantoms demonstrates substantially improved stability and robustness of local optic axis estimation. This work enables reliable depth-resolved fiber orientation mapping in sophisticated fiber crossing scenarios and extends the potential of single-input PSOCT for analyzing structural connectivity at high depth resolution.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography; structural connectivity; myelinated axons; signal-to-noise ratio; fiber orientation mapping; white matter; physical constraints; crossing fibers

Article.Title: Image-grounded encoding models reveal distinct temporal profiles of naturalistic object and scene processing in the human brain
Article.Authors: Müller, N.; Scholte, H. S.; Groen, I. I. A.
Article.Abstract: In real-world vision, the human brain needs to process large amounts of information to effectively interact with its environment. It is well established that our visual system has specialized regions to process information efficiently, such as scene-, face-, and object-selective areas, which can be uncovered using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). However, functional localizers typically use artificially separated stimuli (e.g. scene backgrounds vs. object cutouts), and fMRI signals are insensitive to potential temporal processing differences. Here, we identify temporal signatures of object and scene processing in real-world visual environments by building image-grounded brain-predictive encoding models of human electroencephalography (EEG) responses. In a large set of high-resolution natural images, we first separate object-bound from scene-bound features on a per-image basis, and then used these features to train separate deep neural network-based encoding models to predict EEG responses to the full, intact images. We find that encoding models trained on object-bound features consistently exhibit a delayed temporal encoding profile compared to models trained on scene-bound features. Control analyses confirm the robustness of this delayed object encoding, showing that a consistent separation of objects from scene parts is needed to achieve a temporal distinction. Using these distinct encoding profiles as processing templates, we reveal the typicality of individual image elements as objects or part of the scene. These findings demonstrate that object and scene processing in the human brain unfold differentially over time and indicate that image-grounded encoding models are helpful tools for isolating components of naturalistic visual perception.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: scene processing; object processing; naturalistic images; EEG responses; visual perception

Article.Title: The ANKLE2-VRK1 pathway promotes neuronal resilience by preserving proteostasis during aging
Article.Authors: Link, N. L.; Dietze, M.; Mambou, E.; Primavera, S.; Newlin, H.
Article.Abstract: ANKLE2 is a key regulator of neural stem cell division through inhibition of the kinase VRK1, and mutations in either ANKLE2 or VRK1 cause rare neurodevelopmental disorders that impact brain growth and development. Recent evidence showing that reduced ANKLE2 activity promotes Tau aggregation in vitro suggests that ANKLE2 may also contribute to age-related neurodegenerative processes; however, its role post-development remains unknown. Using Drosophila, we show a novel role for the Ankle2-ballchen (VRK1) pathway in maintaining neuronal resilience and proteostasis. Pan-neuronal and motor neuron reduction of Ankle2 in adult animals shortens lifespan, impairs motor function and accelerates neuronal loss. Lifelong reduction produces more severe phenotypes including an upright wing posture reminiscent of Drosophila Parkinsons disease models. Mechanistically, loss of Ankle2 causes the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins throughout the central nervous system, indicating impaired protein clearance. Ankle2 mutants have reduced proteasome activity with activation of compensatory degradative pathways, supporting this hypothesis. Loss of Ankle2 behavioral and protein accumulation phenotypes are rescued by expression of human ANKLE2, indicating neuronal ANKLE2 function is conserved between flies and humans. Importantly, VRK1/Ballchen reduction also rescues ubiquitin accumulation and behavior phenotypes caused by loss of Ankle2, demonstrating that the developmental Ankle2-VRK1 pathway is preserved and remains functionally important in aged neurons. More broadly, our findings reveal that a conserved developmental ANKLE2- VRK1 pathway is repurposed in aged neurons to maintain proteostasis and neuronal resilience, providing a mechanistic framework linking neurodevelopmental disease genes to age-associated neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Automated behavioral profiling reveals baseline phenotypes in marmosets
Article.Authors: Menegas, W.; Corbett, E.; Beliard, K.; Xu, H.; Parmar, S.; Desimone, R.; Feng, G.
Article.Abstract: Recent advances in genetic engineering have accelerated the production of nonhuman primate models for brain disorders. To use these models for preclinical drug testing, behavioral screening methods will be necessary to determine how the model animals for each disorder deviate from controls, and whether treatments can restore typical patterns of behavior. In this study, we collected a multimodal dataset from a large cohort of marmoset monkeys and described typical patterns in their behavior and responses to stimuli. We found that these behavioral measurements varied substantially across days, and that behavioral state usage was consistently correlated to the behavior of cagemates and to the total vocalization rate in the housing room. To elicit acute behavioral responses, we presented animals with a panel of stimuli including novel, appetitive, neutral, aversive, and social stimuli. Some stimuli elicited strong and consistent responses, while others failed to elicit large responses. By splitting each animal's recordings into two halves, we found that stable individual traits could be used to divide animals into groups with test-retest consistency. We found that these groups tend to be shared within families. Finally, we found that some stimulus responses were correlated with baseline behavior in the absence of stimuli, while others were not. This data will help guide the use of marmosets for the preclinical testing of therapies for brain disorders.

Article.Title: Re-emergence of orientation coding in primate IT cortex and deep networks reveals functional hubs for visual processing
Article.Authors: Karami, B.; Nigam, T.; Plewe, S. S.; Schwiedrzik, C. M.
Article.Abstract: The primate visual system is a hierarchical network of brain areas that transform retinal inputs into rich percepts. According to efficient neural coding principles, basic visual features such as orientation, which are already represented in early visual areas, should not be redundantly encoded in higher areas like V4 and inferotemporal (IT) cortex. We tested this hypothesis by quantifying orientation representation throughout the entire visual stream using functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) and multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) in macaque monkeys watching full-field gratings. Contrary to predictions from efficient coding, we found robust orientation information along the entire visual ventral stream from V1 to IT cortex. Orientation information was distributed in cortical and representational space, especially in IT. Voxels with multivariate responsiveness to faces, objects, and bodies carried more orientation information than highly category-selective voxels. They also displayed stronger connectivity within IT and with upstream areas V1-V4. These finding suggests the existence of functional "hubs" that integrate low- and high-level features through enhanced connectivity. This phenomenon generalized to deep convolutional neural network models with high brain similarity, underscoring the importance of hub-like units in hierarchical processing of complex inputs. Together, our results show that orientation re-emerges in IT cortex not through redundancy but as a computational byproduct of functional diversity and connectivity, propounding the existence of "hub" neurons that may support flexible, integrative visual processing beyond object recognition.

Article.Title: Engineered post-transcriptional regulation of Scn10a by Pumilio ameliorates neuropathic pain in mice
Article.Authors: Garcia, G.; Shapiro, J. B.; Mikesell, A. R.; Falese, J. P.; Bartol, K. A.; McKenney, K. M.; Ruhly, S.; Goldstrohm, A. C.; Pearce, R. A.; Tanaka Hall, T. M.; Campbell, Z. T.
Article.Abstract: Post-transcriptional control of mRNA permeates biology, yet its contribution to sensory neuron physiology and pain remains unclear. The mammalian Pumilio proteins PUM1 and PUM2 (collectively referred to as PUM) are RNA-binding proteins that bind Pumilio response elements (PREs), typically situated in 3' untranslated regions. PUM recruits the CCR4-NOT complex to promote mRNA deadenylation and decay. Several mRNAs that encode voltage-gated sodium channels that regulate action potential generation in pain sensing neurons harbor PREs. Here, we explored whether PUM plays a role in pain signaling. PUM1 and PUM2 were enriched in TRPV1-positive dorsal root ganglion neurons, where PUM2 physically interacted with Scn9a, Scn10a, and Scn11a transcripts, which encode Nav1.7, Nav1.8, and Nav1.9, respectively. Depletion of PUM in sensory neurons produced mechanical hypersensitivity and enhanced inflammatory pain. These effects were reversed by blocking Nav1.8 but not Nav1.7, raising the possibility that repression of Scn10a by PUM can be harnessed using synthetic biology to diminish neuropathic pain. To this end, we generated a chimera comprising the RNA-binding domain of PUM2 and a repressive domain, which we dubbed "super-PUM". Expression of AAV-encoded super-PUM in sensory neurons reduced Nav1.8 abundance, diminished tetrodotoxin-resistant and suzetrigine-sensitive sodium currents, and prevented mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity following spared nerve injury. These results demonstrate that optimization of an endogenous post-transcriptional regulon provides a means to ameliorate neuropathic pain.

Article.Title: The social conditioned place preference assay is sensitive to drug dose, training regimen, and social context
Article.Authors: Dolen, G.; Wilkinson, M.
Article.Abstract: Beginning in the 1960s, researchers have understood that one of the unique properties of psychedelic drugs is that their effects are modified by the context in which they are taken (also known as their set and setting dependence). To date, 7 different studies have shown that critical period reopening is a shared property across psychedelic drugs, including ketamine, MDMA, psilocybin, LSD, and ibogaine. Moreover, the context dependence of psychedelics effects has been recapitulated for both MDMA and ketamine. Recently, Lu et al., Nature Neuroscience 2026 (PMID: 42972049) have claimed that psilocybin does not reopen the social reward learning critical period, which the authors interpret as a failure to replicate previously published results. Here, we re-analyzed results across three published datasets (Nardou et al., Nature 2019; Nardou et al., Nature 2023; Lu et al., Nature Neuroscience 2026) in order to compare the impact of dose, training regimen, and social context on the social conditioned place preference (social CPP) assay. Our analysis reveals that methodological modifications likely account for Lu and colleagues inability to reopen the social reward learning critical period with psilocybin. Nevertheless, because their results recapitulate previous findings that psychedelics effects are context dependent, they support rather than challenge the growing literature demonstrating that psychedelics reopen critical periods.

Article.Title: Geometric analysis of postnatal maturational transformations in brain's functional connectome
Article.Authors: Karolis, V. R.; Hajnal, J. V.; Jbabdi, S.; Edwards, D.; McAlonan, G.; Arichi, T.
Article.Abstract: Birth marks a profound shift in sensory experience, posing a question: does postnatal brain function represent simply a protracted continuation of prenatal developmental programmes or reflect system-level reconfiguration in response to the demands of the postnatal environment? To answer this, we first characterised functional hierarchies of the newborn human brain, separating sensorimotor from visual, unimodal from associative, and parietal from auditory systems. We then implemented a geometric framework to map global transformations that shape functional connectome hierarchies. We show that greater postmenstrual age at birth was associated with emergence of the frontoparietal and salience networks at the tip of the unimodal-associative hierarchical axis; in contrast, greater postnatal age was associated with increasing polarisation of primary perceptual and sensorimotor systems across functional hierarchies. Sex differences in the neonatal connectome recapitulated patterns associated with postmenstrual age at birth and postnatal age, suggesting more advanced maturation of functional architecture in females than in males. Together, the contrasting effects of prenatal and postnatal age support a model of postnatal reconfiguration of brain function, thereby indicating that birth could mark a transition between distinct modes of the functional organisation.

Article.Title: Harmonizing amyloid PET tracers at the local level: evaluation of regional Centiloid equations
Article.Authors: Silvestri, E.; Chaggar, P.; Gobbi, S.; Aldea, R.; Klein, G.; Tonietto, M.
Article.Abstract: INTRODUCTION: The Centiloid (CL) framework standardizes global amyloid-PET across radiotracers. While global scaling remains essential for participant selection, amyloid-targeting therapies require quantifying localized plaque removal. However, applying global equations regionally introduces systematic bias, particularly in subcortical structures where off-target binding alters non-specific background. METHODS: We extended the Centiloid framework regionally and voxel-wise using GAAIN datasets: Level-1 ([11C]PiB) and Level-2 paired [11C]PiB and fluorinated head-to-head cohorts ([18F]florbetaben, [18F]florbetapir, [18F]flutemetamol, and [18F]NAV4694). Level-1 defines the regional Centiloid scale using region-specific intercepts while fixing the global slope. Level-2 calibrates fluorinated tracer uptake to reference [11C]PiB SUVR using linear equations. We compared three slope-intercept models (Global, Regional-Intercept, and Regional) using information criteria and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). RESULTS: Regional-Intercept model was identified as optimal across all four radiotracers. In neocortical regions, Global and Regional-Intercept models showed high agreement across canonical lobes. In deep gray matter, global equations introduced large systematic offsets, with mean absolute conversion errors in the pallidum reaching 27.7 to 45.6 CL. The Regional-Intercept model eliminated this bias, reducing subcortical MAE on average below 15 CL while preserving a unified biological scale. DISCUSSION: Applying global Centiloid equations directly to regions introduces substantial bias in subcortical regions. With the Regional-Intercept model, the same Centiloid value corresponds to the same amyloid concentration across brain regions and radiotracers. This provides a reliable basis for cross- sectional regional evaluation, multi-tracer cohort pooling, tracking regional clearance, and mapping regional progression in clinical research.

Article.Title: A frequency-tagged fMRI platform for accessing spatiotemporally resolved cortical computations
Article.Authors: Rafeh, R. W.; Ngo, G. N.; Muller, L. E.; Khan, A. R.; Menon, R. S.; Schmitz, T. W.; Mur, M.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how the human cortex resolves competition between concurrent sensory inputs requires access to stimulus-specific responses, their temporal coupling, and nonlinear interactions at fine spatial scales. Conventional non-invasive neuroimaging cannot resolve these signals. We introduce multiplexed frequency-tagged fMRI (ft-fMRI) to resolve responses to simultaneous visual stimuli within individual cortical vertices. Across 3T and 7T, we identify fundamental, multiplexed, and intermodulation BOLD responses. Population receptive field mapping localizes multiplexed and intermodulation signals to visual-field locations where stimulus representations overlap, while response phase distinguishes positive and negative coupling to each stimulus drive. These signatures replicate across sessions, field strengths, and frequency pairings. To investigate their computational origins, we develop a population receptive field model incorporating divisive normalization between spatially intermingled neural subpopulations. The model accurately predicts vertex-wise frequency-response patterns, including intermodulation signals and their dependence on receptive field overlap. These findings establish ft-fMRI as a means to directly test cortical computations underlying sensory competition in the human visual cortex.

Article.Title: Schizophrenia-Linked 3q29 Deletion Produces Hyperdopaminergic Signaling in the Dorsal Striatum
Article.Authors: Sriramoji-Virdi, S.; Pollak, R.; Tischer, A.; Michaelides, M. M.; Mulle, J. G.; Bocarsly, M. E.
Article.Abstract: Dopamine dysregulation has long been recognized as a central feature of schizophrenia (SZ), yet the mechanisms linking genetic risk to dopaminergic dysfunction remain poorly understood. While pharmacological models have historically been used to induce hyperdopaminergic states and recapitulate select clinical features of SZ, these approaches do not model the underlying disease biology. In contrast, genetically informed models enable investigation of dopaminergic abnormalities as emergent consequences of bona fide disease-associated mechanisms. Here, we examined a mouse model of the 3q29 deletion. In humans, this 1.6 Mb deletion is typically de novo and confers a greater than 40-fold increased risk for SZ, representing the single largest known molecular risk factor for the disorder. Using this model, we identified a robust hyperdopaminergic phenotype characterized by elevated evoked dopamine release selectively within the dorsal striatum. Mechanistically, this phenotype appears to arise from a PKC-mediated reduction in dopamine transporter (DAT) availability, impairing dopamine clearance and prolonging dopaminergic signaling. Together, these results establish a direct link between a high-risk SZ mutation and striatal dopamine dysfunction, while also highlighting PKC-DAT signaling as a potential therapeutic target for treatment-resistant neuropsychiatric symptoms associated with 3q29 deletion.

Article.Title: Parvalbumin interneuron circuit sharpens orientation tuning via the extraclassical surround in cat V1
Article.Authors: Foik, A. T.; Liu, Y.; Shao, H.; Lean, G.; Zhang, L.; Scholl, L. R.; Jappelli, R.; Lyon, D. C.
Article.Abstract: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV) inhibitory neurons are central to cortical gain control, yet optogenetic studies disagree on whether they sharpen orientation tuning or merely rescale responses. Because this work has been performed almost exclusively in rodents, which lack orientation columns and an orientation-matched extraclassical surround, the contribution of surround circuitry has remained untested. Here we combine cell-type-specific rabies-virus tracing with optogenetics to activate or suppress PV circuits in cat primary visual cortex, and measure single-neuron orientation tuning for stimuli confined to the classical receptive field or extending into the extraclassical surround. Activating PV circuits sharpened tuning progressively with illumination power for classical-receptive-field stimuli, but left tuning unchanged once the surround was engaged; conversely, suppressing them broadened tuning only for surround-engaging stimuli and left classical-receptive-field tuning unchanged. This double dissociation places PV circuitry in the causal path that sets tuning width and identifies surround suppression as the inhibition it supplies: where the surround is not recruited there is little PV-mediated inhibition to remove, and where it is, removing that inhibition widens tuning. PV-dependent sharpening is therefore bounded by the receptive-field architecture through which the population is recruited, not by a fixed property of the PV population itself.

Article.Title: Dynamic information sharing across frontal-basal ganglia neurons during cost-benefit decision-making and reward pursuit
Article.Authors: Härmson, O.; Grennan, I.; Perry, B.; Toth, R.; Walton, M. E.; Manohar, S. G.; Sharott, A.
Article.Abstract: Cost-benefit decision-making requires animals to integrate prospective rewards with the costs of obtaining them and translate these evaluations into motivated action. How population activity is coordinated across the frontal-basal ganglia network during these processes remains incompletely understood. Here, we recorded simultaneously from the anterior cingulate cortex, medial/ventral orbitofrontal cortex, dorsomedial striatum, ventral pallidum and subthalamic area in rats performing a cost-benefit decision task. Using canonical correlation analysis, we identified shared population activity across these anatomically distributed circuits and characterised its dimensionality, task-related information and relationship to behavioural sensitivity. The strength and dimensionality of inter-area coupling varied across task epochs and circuit classes, with frontal-basal ganglia interactions exhibiting particularly high dimensionality during reward pursuit. Shared activity represented reward and time on task (trial count) during decision-making, while movement-related information became increasingly prominent during reward pursuit. These representations also depended on subsequent choice: reward was more strongly represented on accepted trials, whereas time on task was more prominent on rejected trials. The strength of inter-area coupling was further associated with behavioural sensitivity across sessions. Stronger coupling between the subthalamic area and the dorsomedial striatum was associated with reduced reward sensitivity. By contrast, communication between the medial/ventral orbitofrontal cortex and dorsomedial striatal was associated with reduced effort aversion. Together, these findings reveal a dynamic, circuit-specific organisation of shared neural activity during cost-benefit behaviour and link inter-area coupling to variation in motivated choice. They suggest that distinct communication pathways may contribute to specific facets of motivated choice, with applications to targeted neuromodulation therapies for disorders of motivation.

Article.Title: Bullying Victimisation, Medial Occipital White Matter Development, and Psychotic-Like Experiences: A Longitudinal Diffusion MRI Study
Article.Authors: Connaughton, M.; Mitchell, O.; Healy, C.; O'Neill, A.; Dooley, N.; Agarwal, A.; Ogunmola, O.; Riaz, S.; Cannon, M.; Roddy, D.
Article.Abstract: Childhood bullying victimisation is robustly associated with psychotic-like experiences, but the neurodevelopmental mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. This longitudinal study examined whether childhood bullying victimisation was associated with altered maturation of medial occipital white matter and whether bullying victimisation moderated the association between fractional anisotropy (FA) and psychotic-like experiences. A total of 96 young people (38 bullied, 58 controls) from the Adolescent Brain Development study underwent diffusion MRI at approximately 14, 16, and 20 years of age. PLE and bullying victimisation group classification were determined by expert consensus interview. FA from bilateral calcarine-cuneus, cuneus-lingual, and calcarine-lingual connections was examined using mixed-effects models. Compared with controls, the bullied group showed significantly different age-related FA trajectories in the right calcarine-cuneus connection ({beta} = -0.40, p < .001) and the left cuneus-lingual connection ({beta} = -0.35, p = .003). Bullying victimisation significantly moderated the association between white matter FA and PLE ({beta} = -6.14, p = .004), indicating that the association between FA and psychotic-like experiences differed according to bullying victimisation status. This moderation effect also varied with age, as indicated by a significant bullying victimisation-by-FA-by-time interaction ({beta} = -6.80, p = .008). Specifically, the moderating effect of bullying victimisation on the association between right calcarine-cuneus FA and PLE changed across development. These findings suggest that bullying victimisation is associated with divergent maturation of medial occipital circuitry and identify right calcarine-cuneus development as a potential marker of vulnerability to PLE following childhood bullying.

Article.Title: Learning predictive latent structure from unclustered neural spike trains
Article.Authors: Bray, S. R.; Kay, K.; Li, C. J.; Denovellis, E. L.; Comrie, A. E.; Joshi, A. L.; Sun, X.; Kaplan, A. D.; Eden, U. T.; Frank, L. M.
Article.Abstract: Neural activity patterns enable perception, thought, and action. A powerful approach to understanding these abilities involves identifying low-dimensional, interpretable latent variables that capture the relationship between activity patterns, the information they represent, and the computations they support. Yet current methods often yield variables that are difficult to interpret and require data preprocessing that limits their accuracy and temporal resolution. Here we introduce Contrastive Prediction of Point Process Observations (C3PO), an unsupervised method that learns a predictive, interpretable latent variable representation directly from continuous time neural spiking without requiring spike-sorting or binning. C3PO recovers structure associated with known latent variables across a variety of data sets without access to those variables during training. It identifies dynamics on timescales from tens of milliseconds to hours and reveals previously unreported representations and their dynamics. These results establish C3PO as a powerful tool for uncovering interpretable structure in high-dimensional point-process data sets.

Article.Title: α-Synuclein structural heterogeneity associates with distinct cytopathologies in multiple system atrophy
Article.Authors: Xu, X.; Forrest, S. F.; Martinez-Valbuena, I.; Scramstad, C.; Rogaeva, E.; Kosteniuk, S. E.; Watts, J. C.; Kovacs, G. G.; Enomoto, M.
Article.Abstract: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is characterized by oligodendroglial -synuclein inclusions, although neuronal inclusions also occur. We investigated whether regional differences in -synuclein filament structure are associated with distinct cytopathologies in a neuropathologically confirmed MSA brain by comparing the medial temporal lobe, which showed prominent neuronal inclusions and limited oligodendroglial pathology, with cerebellar white matter, which contained exclusively oligodendroglial inclusions. Cryo-electron microscopy resolved filaments from these regions at 3.0 [A] and 2.0 [A], respectively. Medial temporal filaments contained a previously undescribed protofilament fold, PF-IIIA, paired with canonical PF-IIB2, whereas cerebellar filaments adopted the canonical MSA Type II structure. PF-IIIA exhibits extensive remodeling of its core while retaining the asymmetric doublet architecture. These findings reveal regional -synuclein structural heterogeneity within a single MSA brain and suggest a potential association between distinct filament conformations and neuronal versus oligodendroglial cytopathology, highlighting the importance of regional and cellular context in filament organization and disease heterogeneity.

Article.Title: A digital twin of freely moving mouse V1 learns a general visual code bridging classical physiology and active vision
Article.Authors: Schneider, M.; Hou, Y.; Niell, C.; Beyeler, M.
Article.Abstract: Decades of controlled experiments in passive, head-fixed animals have characterized the response properties of mouse primary visual cortex (V1) and their strong modulation by behavioral state. However, in natural vision the animal is active, continuously shaping its own visual input as it moves and coupling vision to behavior. To bridge this gap between classical controlled experiments and natural vision, we trained a multimodal digital twin to predict V1 spiking in freely moving mice from retinocentric video together with locomotion, pupil, and eye and head movements, then froze it and probed it in silico under controlled conditions. The representation it learned generalized across stimulus classes, animals, and recording regimes. Although never trained on parametric stimuli or given cell-type labels, the model recovered V1's canonical tuning for orientation, spatial frequency and contrast, including the systematic differences between putative excitatory and inhibitory cells. A single model transferred to new mice from a few minutes of recording. Without retraining, it matched the representational geometry of an independent head-fixed dataset of natural movies as closely as two recorded mice match each other. Behavior modulated most V1 neurons, and clamping each variable in turn showed that locomotion and pupil dilation share a gain increase, while only locomotion shifts sensitivity toward high spatial frequencies. By learning this representation from the freely behaving animal and probing it under controlled conditions, freely moving digital twins bridge classical visual physiology and active vision.

Article.Title: Structure learning and context inference emerge from next-state prediction in a cerebellar-medial temporal lobe circuit
Article.Authors: Bhatia, C.; Gershman, S. J.; Amematsro, E. A.
Article.Abstract: Humans learn many context-dependent behaviors; yet the contexts driving these behavior are rarely explicit and must instead be inferred. Further, we are rarely exposed to the same context multiple times, so we must learn how to generalize to new contexts from our experiences in prior ones. Motor learning relies on both. People can hold multiple conflicting visuomotor mappings and recall the appropriate mapping when needed. Much as cricket is easier to learn for someone who already plays baseball, experience with previous mappings accelerates learning of others. Indeed, human motor learning is well described by context inference, in which the learner infers the context and uses it to update and recall the appropriate memory. How the brain implements this inference, and which circuits perform it, however, is unknown. Here we introduce a circuit in which a cerebellar forward model predicts the next state conditioned on a latent from the medial temporal lobe. At the same time, the medial temporal lobe updates that latent from the cerebellum's prediction error. While we only trained the circuit to predict next state, it learns to infer context and represents contexts in a structured latent space. Coupled with this latent, a motor cortex module reproduces context-dependent retrieval, savings after washout, spontaneous recovery, and evoked recovery, and compensates for perturbations it has never experienced. The same circuit reproduces cerebellar-dependence of object-location memory and independence in object-recognition memory, loss of place-cell stability in the dark when cerebellar plasticity is blocked, and the abstract geometry of hippocampal activity in a reversal task. Cerebellar-medial temporal lobe interaction is therefore a candidate locus for context inference and structure learning in the brain.

Article.Title: Preparatory Bias Currents Alone Write Letters and Words in a Fixed Recurrent Circuit
Article.Authors: White, A. J.; Lo, C.-C.
Article.Abstract: We show that preparatory input currents, or bias currents, alone can make a recurrent circuit with fixed weights write all 52 cursive letters, and words built from them. Each letter is produced by its own bias pattern, ramped in as a preparatory drive and withdrawn at a go cue; the recurrent weights and the readout never change, and the readout's weights are random, with a single global gain picked on four letters (a-d). We take the stability-optimized circuits (SOCs) of Hennequin et al. and extend them with mutual inhibition: all inhibitory neurons inhibit one another through a single shared weight (MISOC, mutual inhibition SOC). With 200 units, the pen of the SOC stays on average 1.7% of a letter width from the target over all 52 letters, and that of the MISOC 0.9% (25 random circuits; R2 = 0.996 and 0.999). The other 48 letters are learned through their bias patterns alone, without changing a single synapse, so new letters cannot disturb old ones. Letters learned one at a time chain into words in one continuous run. Mutual inhibition improves the circuit: with a shared weight of 0.5 the MISOC writes with 16-48% less error than the SOC at every network size tested (50 to 200 units), and with fifty network-derived input channels instead of one bias per neuron it keeps its advantage. Bias currents and mutual inhibition let small, fixed circuits hold a large and growing motor repertoire and switch within it without any synaptic change.

Article.Title: Longitudinal examination of cerebellar morphometry across typical aging adults reveals nonlinear heterogenous trends
Article.Authors: Brodnick, Z. M.; Doron, N.; Turner, J. A.
Article.Abstract: Cerebellar structural integrity has been associated with cognitive capability in both neurodegenerative and healthy aging populations. The understanding of regional, longitudinal cerebellar structural changes is not well studied, and with an increasing aging population, there is an increasing need to fill this gap. Moreover, traditional modeling approaches apply linear techniques, which may fail to detect possible nuanced aging patterns. The present study investigates the nonlinear effect of age on subregional cerebellar structures in healthy adults (n = 1,371), aged 36 to 90+, from the Human Connectome Project in Aging and the follow-up continuation, Aging Adult Brain Connectome studies. Subject T1w images underwent cerebellar segmentation and volumetric estimation via the Automatic Cerebellum Parcellation using U-NET with Locally Constrained Optimization (ACAPULCO) algorithm. Cross-sectional, longitudinal, and sex specific volumetric differences were examined using generalized additive mixed models. Heterogenous atrophy patterns were observed across the cerebellum; however, the majority of effects were evident in the posterior cerebellum. Longitudinal models showed nonlinear negative trends for all regions surviving correction, while baseline age effects had a combination of linear and nonlinear negative trajectories after correction. Specific sex differences emerged, where men predominantly had higher regional volumes, as well as there being sex-related influences of longitudinal morphologic patterns. Furthermore, midlife appeared as a period of structural vulnerability, demonstrating escalated volume loss. Consistent with the literature, the identified volumetric reduction patterns suggest that age effects on the cerebellum are multifaceted, with region specific alterations, highlighting the complexity of this structure.

Article.Title: Circuit decoupling with surrogate compensation for baseline tuning in biophysically detailed neural models
Article.Authors: Novikov, N.; McElroy, S.; Chen, J.; Irby, E.; Dura-Bernal, S.; Neymotin, S. A.
Article.Abstract: The baseline regime of a neural circuit shapes its dynamical behavior. Establishing an appropriate baseline is therefore an important part of tuning a computational circuit model. This baseline can be specified in terms of target population firing rates and achieved by adjusting the background inputs to each population. Due to recurrent coupling, these inputs need to be tuned jointly, requiring a high-dimensional search that is especially costly for biophysically detailed circuit models. This remains a major bottleneck since current optimization methods are limited in their ability to tackle this problem. Decoupling the circuit by removing all the connections between its cells allows background inputs to be tuned independently, but the solution may not hold when the connectivity is restored. We developed a compensated decoupling method in which missing recurrent inputs are replaced by surrogate inputs from spike generators firing at the corresponding target rates. The resulting input approximates the recurrent drive expected at the target regime, so the background inputs tuned in this setup may remain valid after restoring connectivity. We applied the method to a 43-population biophysically detailed model of the macaque auditory thalamocortical circuit, which had previously proved challenging to fit closely to experimental data. First, we tuned the background input independently for each population in the fully decoupled setup. Next, we tested the solution in the isolated cortical and thalamic subcircuits, preserving recurrent connections within each subcircuit. The cortical subcircuit had two coexisting regimes and settled into the off-target one by default. A gradual transition from surrogate to recurrent self-excitation allowed it to reach the near-target regime. The thalamic subcircuit exhibited a single regime deviating from the target due to imperfect surrogate compensation. Jointly tuning a separate tonic input correction for each thalamic population substantially reduced the errors. Finally, we tested the solution in the full thalamocortical circuit, combining the tuned background inputs, thalamic corrections, and gradual restoration of self-excitation. The full circuit consistently reached a near-target regime across multiple random model realizations. The approach yielded an improved macaque auditory thalamocortical baseline model, providing a community resource for investigating the auditory thalamocortical system's dynamics. Together, the results demonstrate that our method can facilitate baseline tuning in a biophysically detailed model by enabling decoupled optimization and guiding subsequent refinement.

Article.Title: NeuroMASS v4: Geometry-Aware Neural Population Dynamics via Learnable Hyperbolic Latent Representations and Biologically-Calibrated Diagonal State Space Models
Article.Authors: Singh, R.; Cherukuri, J. V.; Somanna, A.
Article.Abstract: The geometry of neural population activity is a fundamental challenge in computational neuroscience. We present NeuroMASS v4, a novel architecture that introduces learnable hyperbolic latent geometry to spike-train co-smoothing on the Neural Latents Benchmark (NLB'21). Our central scientific claim is that the curvature c of a Poincar&eacute-ball--learned end-to-end from extracellular spike recordings--constitutes a biologically interpretable geometric signature: significantly positive for ring-manifold motor circuits (MC_Maze, MC_RTT) and near-zero for topologically unstructured frontal circuits (DMFC_RSG). The architecture unifies five principled components: (i) discrete spike-count embed- dings with learned neuron-identity vectors, (ii) permutation-equivariant attention-weighted neuron pooling, (iii) a diagonal S4D state space model initialised with a log-uniform frequency prior spanning 2-200 Hz, (iv) a Poincar&eacute-ball projection with learnable scalar curvature, and (v) a Frobenius-bounded session adapter. Training uses masked self-prediction of spike counts with an auxiliary behaviour decoding objective; all experiments use exclusively real DANDI/NLB recordings under a strict fail-stop data policy. We report results across four NLB datasets spanning motor, somatosensory, and cognitive cortices in rhesus macaque, and demonstrate that learned curvature statistically predicts circuit topology.

Article.Title: Visual Illusion: A Matter Of Disorder Between Retinal And Perceived images
Article.Authors: Paul, A.; Mukherjee, A.
Article.Abstract: Visual illusions reveal that perception is constructive rather than a faithful copy of the retinal image. This paper proposes that the brain supplements ambiguous or incomplete sensory input with virtual edges, filled-in surfaces, brightness and size cues, and illusory contours. Using gray-level Shannon entropy, we compared original and perceived images across five illusion classes: edge detection, surface filling-in, brightness perception, size perception, and the Hermann grid. In all cases, perceived-image entropy exceeded real-image entropy. These findings support a unified account of visual illusions as constructive inference: the brain introduces additional information to achieve global coherence, reflecting a trade-off between low-entropy processing and perceptual interpretation.

Article.Title: Tracking single neurons across days reveals acute and persistent effects of psilocybin in the mouse brain
Article.Authors: DeWeese, T. E.; Cheng, A.; Koukuntla, S.; Tamashiro, K. L. K.; Harris, T. D.; Graves, A. R.
Article.Abstract: The psychedelic psilocybin offers a novel approach to treat depression and other psychiatric disorders. A single dose of psilocybin induces rapid neuroplastic effects that persist for many weeks to months. However, psilocybin's effect on neural firing beyond its systemic presence, and the neural mechanisms linking these acute and sustained effects remain unknown. Using chronically implanted Neuropixels probes, we tracked 1,692 neurons spanning prefrontal and hippocampal regions following saline and psilocybin injections and 24 h later. Psilocybin bidirectionally modulated firing acutely in a cell-type and region-specific manner. Persistent firing (24 h post-injection) is net suppressed relative to saline, including in acutely activated neurons. The late acute response, but not early peak response, predicted a neuron's firing 24 h later. To our knowledge, this is the first evidence that directly reveals psilocybin's sustained impacts on neuronal firing, providing key insight into the circuitry accompanying its lasting cognitive and behavioral alterations.

Article.Title: Motor cortex facilitates visual action override through the superior colliculus
Article.Authors: Song, K.; Usseglio, G.; Feugas, P.; Morou, S.; Cui, P.; Mariatos-Metaxas, D.; Navarro, I.; Femenia, T.; Damoulas, T.; Reig, R.; Le Merre, P.; Lazaridis, I.; Kardamakis, A. A.
Article.Abstract: Unexpected visual events can leave goal pursuit undisturbed or trigger visual action override - an interruption that redirects behaviour towards the stimulus. Using a visual distraction task in freely moving mice, population calcium recordings and causal perturbations identified the lateral motor-related superior colliculus (lSCm) as a key node controlling distractor engagement. Retinal inputs to the sensory-related SC signalled distractors even when mice ignored them. Pre-distractor behaviour and motor cortical activity predicted subsequent engagement, while increased corticocollicular and decreased nigrocollicular activity before distractor onset were consistent with a permissive state for override. Suppressing corticocollicular transmission weakened override without detectably altering task engagement. Single-unit recordings in head-fixed mice revealed response amplification in subsets of lSCm neurons during combined retinal and motor cortical stimulation, despite weak responses to either input alone. Motor cortical input thus facilitates sensory recruitment of collicular action circuits, shaping the balance between action stability and action override during ongoing goal pursuit.

Article.Title: Inter-protocol reproducibility of multi-shell diffusion MRI metrics across major neuroimaging study protocols
Article.Authors: Wren-Jarvis, J.; Stepanov, V.; Ades-Aron, B.; Chen, J.; Mehrin, S.; Jeet, N.; Coelho, S.; Coronado-Leija, R.; Novikov, D. S.; Veraart, J.; Fieremans, E.
Article.Abstract: Diffusion MRI is a core component of large-scale neuroimaging initiatives, yet the reproducibility of quantitative dMRI metrics across different acquisition protocols remains unclear. We acquired seven multi-shell diffusion protocols representative of major consortia and clinical settings on a single scanner in 41 healthy adults, isolating protocol effects from hardware and site variability. A linear mixed-effects model was used to estimate the inter-protocol coefficient of variation (CV) and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), and standard model imaging (SMI) metrics across atlas-based white matter regions. Rank agreement was assessed with Kendall's W, and repeated scans of one protocol provided a reference for test-retest variability. Overall, inter-protocol variability was low, with median CVs of 2.9-6.1% for DTI, 3.7-5.0% for DKI, and 3.0-4.7% for SMI metrics. Protocols ranked subjects consistently (W = 0.73-0.86) but agreed less in absolute value (ICC = 0.31-0.66), with fractional anisotropy (FA) being the most stable metric. Acquisition parameters, including TE, b-values, and signal-to-noise ratio jointly explained 53-93% of the inter-protocol variance. Differences in the b-values used for DTI and DKI estimation were particularly important for the diffusivities: matching b-values across protocols reduced the median inter-protocol CV for MD from 5.0% to 1.8%, with smaller reductions for mean kurtosis (MK), axial kurtosis (AK) and the axonal water fraction (f). These findings demonstrate good reproducibility of quantitative higher-order diffusion MRI metrics across commonly used multi-shell acquisition protocols, which can be further improved by aligning b-values, providing a foundation for data pooling, harmonization, and normative modeling in large-scale neuroimaging studies.

Article.Title: State-dependent gating of sensory and cortical inputs by median raphe neurons
Article.Authors: Huang, W.; Wang, D. V.
Article.Abstract: The mesopontine median raphe (MnR) plays an important role in regulating brain states, hippocampal network activity, and memory processes. Recent studies have revealed that the MnR comprises three major neuronal populations: serotonergic (5-HT), glutamatergic (Vglut3-expressing), and GABAergic neurons. How these distinct neuronal populations may gate sensory and cortical inputs across different brain states remains largely unknown. Here, we combined in vivo electrophysiological recording, sensory or optogenetic stimulation, and transgenic approaches to characterize the response properties of 5-HT, Vglut3, and GABAergic MnR neurons during wakefulness and sleep. We found that MnR neurons exhibited pronounced state-dependent responses to both sensory and cortical stimulation, with response amplitudes significantly greater during slow-wave sleep than during wakefulness. Auditory and somatosensory stimuli elicited fast responses in the MnR: 5-HT neurons were primarily suppressed, whereas Vglut3 and GABAergic neurons were primarily activated, suggesting the presence of direct inputs from sensory thalamic or brainstem structures. Retrograde tracing identified several brainstem structures and, notably, the medial prefrontal cortex as sources of direct projections to the MnR. Optogenetic stimulation of prefrontal inputs to the MnR evoked inhibition of 5-HT neurons but robust excitation of Vglut3 neurons during slow-wave sleep, suggesting top-down control of MnR activity by the prefrontal cortex. Together, these findings reveal that the MnR exhibits enhanced sensitivity to both ascending sensory and descending cortical inputs during sleep, suggesting that it may integrate environmental and cortical signals to regulate hippocampal network activity and gate sleep-dependent memory processing.

Article.Title: An isogenic human stem cell model reveals NGLY1-dependent control of microglial development
Article.Authors: Zhang, H.; Xue, H.; Jin, M.; Wang, T.; Rauckhorst, A. J.; Jiang, P.; Wang, Y.-C.; Liu, Y.
Article.Abstract: NGLY1 is a cytosolic N-glycanase involved in glycoprotein quality control and proteasome-mediated protein degradation and is critical for normal brain development and function. Although neuronal alterations caused by NGLY1 deficiency have been extensively characterized in animal and human cell models, how NGLY1 deficiency affects human glial cells, particularly microglia, the brain-resident innate immune cells, remains largely unknown. Using patient-derived NGLY1-deficient human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) lines and their corresponding CRISPR-mediated gene-corrected isogenic lines, we found that NGLY1-deficient primitive macrophage progenitors (PMPs) exhibited increased GlcNAc-Asn (GNA) accumulation and elevated expression of RUNX1, a key transcription factor regulating myeloid lineage development, accompanied by abnormal proliferation. Following further differentiation, NGLY1-deficient human microglia exhibited reduced morphological complexity and impaired phagocytic capacity. In addition, NGLY1-deficient microglia showed increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1{beta}, IL-6, and TNF, under both basal and stimulated conditions, indicative of a heightened inflammatory state. Mechanistically, our data showed that RUNX1 upregulation induced by NGLY1 deficiency partially mediated impaired PMP proliferation and subsequent microglial abnormalities, implicating RUNX1 dysregulation in NGLY1-associated microglial dysfunction and identifying RUNX1 as a potential therapeutic target. Together, using patient-derived and gene-corrected isogenic hiPSCs, our study establishes a human stem cell platform for modeling NGLY1 deficiency and reveals that impaired deglycosylation alters human microglial developmental trajectories and ultimately compromises microglial homeostasis and function. These microglial abnormalities may contribute to the neurological deficits observed in patients carrying loss-of-function variants in NGLY1.
