Article.Authors: Kamenna, E.; Nemesh, K.; Cervenka, J.; Sekac, D.; Landles, C.; Kolesnikova, A.; Valekova, I.; Juhas, S.; Juhasova, J.; Osborne, G.; Kupcova Skalnikova, H.; Vodicka, P.; Motlik, J.; Klempir, J.; Ellederova, Z.; Klima, J.
Article.Abstract: Huntington's disease is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder with no disease-modifying treatment available. Preclinical trials of gene therapies rely on large animal models and the transgenic Huntington's disease (TgHD) minipig is one of them. Minipigs live more than a decade, so the effect of a single dose of gene therapy can be followed for years. The TgHD transgene carries a mixed CAG/CAA repeat that is not expected to expand somatically. However, its putamen, part of the striatum that degenerates first in patients, had not been examined by genome-wide methods, nor beyond 4 years of age. Seven genes were differentially expressed at 4 years and 3,324 at 8 years, and the pathway changes of the transcriptome and the proteome were concordant at that age. The D2 medium spiny neuron marker gene set was reduced at 8 years in both the transcriptome and the proteome. Mitochondrial and oxidative phosphorylation pathways were positively enriched at 4 years and negatively enriched at 8 years. Immune and complement pathways were positively enriched at 8 years, and the number of altered splicing events increased almost fivefold between 4 and 8 years. We detected no age-dependent accumulation of soluble mutant huntingtin. Since the repeat does not expand, these changes developed without somatic expansion, a major driver of progression in human Huntington's disease. We propose that the reduced neuronal markers reflect a loss of neuronal identity rather than neuronal death. The TgHD minipig would then recapitulate the slow early phase of the disease, when treatment is arguably most likely to help.

Article.Authors: Nunez, P.; Kumar, G.; Gotti, C.; Wang, P.; Martineau, L.; Bonaventure, P. L.; Hoyer, R.; Misic, B.; Albouy, P.; Laureys, S.; Tewarie, P. K. B.

Article.Title: Cerebellar transcranial AC stimulation produces frequency and phase-dependent changes in Purkinje cell complex spike waveform
Article.Authors: Mourra, D.; Sloane, J.; Sahin, M.; Lang, E. J.
Article.Abstract: Cerebellar transcranial alternating current stimulation (ctACS) can improve motor learning and may speed rehabilitation. The mechanisms by which ctACS induces long-term changes in brain function that underlie these effects are not known, and knowledge of them could greatly improve the application of ctACS. One potential mechanism is alteration of Purkinje cell (PC) complex spike (CS) activity, as CS activity is a key regulator of cerebellar synaptic plasticity. Thus, we investigated how ctACS modifies CS firing rates and waveform. Extracellular recordings were obtained from cerebellar PCs in anesthetized adult rats while ctACS (250 A) was applied across a range of frequencies (0.5 - 50 Hz). The effect of ctACS on CS waveform was quantified via measuring changes in the overall size of the CS and in the number and amplitude of the spikelets that comprise a CS. ctACS produced phase-dependent modulation of the CS waveform in a majority of PCs at most tested frequencies, with 1 Hz stimulation causing modulation in all PCs tested at the frequency. The modulation reflected changes within the normal range of CS waveforms rather than an expansion of that range. Analysis of individual spikelet periods (windows) revealed that ctACS modified discrete portions of the CS, with 93.8% of PCs showing significant modulation in at least one window. Notably, the strength of phase-dependent CS waveform modulation was relatively consistent across frequencies, in contrast to the frequency dependence of simple spike (SS) entrainment. Significant modulation of spikelet amplitude was found more often than that of spikelet number; however, the relative strength of the modulation when present was similar for the two parameters. CS waveform modulation was correlated with SS entrainment strength and was strongest in PCs located near the cerebellar surface (i.e., near the apices of the folia). Together, these findings demonstrate that ctACS exerts phase-dependent control over CS waveform. Moreover, the differing frequency dependence of the waveform effects and SS firing modulation suggests that it may be possible to target CS-related plasticity selectively, providing a potential strategy for selectively modulating cerebellar learning with ctACS.

Article.Title: Hybrid virtual reality object lifting matches real-world object lifting
Article.Authors: Sager, C. A.; Zenti, J.; Marneweck, M.
Article.Abstract: Object manipulation requires anticipatory force control and online force adjustments to accommodate variability in digit position. Appropriate force scaling is learned rapidly, but repeated manipulation can interfere with updating control when object dynamics change. Sensory feedback and prior experience support object manipulation, yet how proprioception contributes remains poorly understood. Hybrid virtual reality (VR), in which participants manipulate a physical object while viewing tracked virtual representations of the object and their digits, allows controlled visual-proprioceptive discrepancies to be introduced to examine visual and proprioceptive contributions to control. However, replacing direct viewing with virtual feedback could itself affect these control processes. We therefore compared manipulation of the same physical object under direct vision and hybrid-VR without experimentally imposed visual-proprioceptive offsets. Fifteen healthy young adults lifted a visually symmetric inverted T-shaped object with a concealed asymmetric mass distribution while preventing tilt toward the weighted side. After either one or five repeated lifts, the mass distribution switched to the opposite side. In both environments, anticipatory torque increased with repeated lifts, and five preceding lifts produced greater post-switch error than one, consistent with repetition-induced anterograde interference. Digit position and lift-force differences were negatively correlated during later pre-switch trials in both environments. We detected no significant differences between environments in the learning rate of anticipatory force control, position-force coordination, or switch-related interference. These findings characterize object manipulation under no-offset hybrid-VR and provide a baseline for future studies using controlled visual-proprioceptive discrepancies to examine how these signals support anticipatory control, learning, and online adjustment.

Article.Authors: Stringer, C.; Ki, C.; Del Grosso, N.; LaFosse, P.; Zhang, Q.; Zhong, L.; Pachitariu, M.
Article.Abstract: Neural recordings using optical methods have been steadily improving. For example, we demonstrate here recordings of over 100,000 neurons from the mouse cortex obtained with a standard commercial microscope. To process such large datasets, we developed Suite2p, a collection of efficient algorithms for motion correction, cell detection, activity extraction and quality control. We also developed new approaches to benchmark performance on these tasks. Our GPU-accelerated non-rigid motion correction outperforms alternative methods, while running over five times faster. For cell detection, Suite2p outperforms the CNMF algorithm in Caiman and Fiola, finding more cells and producing fewer false positives, while running in a fraction of the time. We also introduce quality control steps for users to evaluate performance on their own data, while offering alternative algorithms for specialized types of recordings such as those from one-photon imaging.

Article.Title: MRI-Based Glymphatic Markers and Their Associations with Polysomnographic Sleep in Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis
Article.Authors: Sharifpour, R.; Elands, S.; Hrabovecky, J.; Rovai, A.; Borrelli, S.; Debourgoing, G.; Perrotta, G.; De Tiege, X.; Strauss, M.
Article.Abstract: Background and Objectives: The glymphatic system is the brain waste clearance pathway. Although its dysfunction has been associated with several neurological disorders, its role in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains poorly understood. Glymphatic activity is thought to peak during sleep, yet its relationship with objectively measured sleep has scarcely been explored in humans. We assessed two MRI glymphatic proxies in patients with relapsing-remitting MS (PwMS) and healthy controls (HCs) and their associations with polysomnographic measures, structural MRI, and, in PwMS, disease burden. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, PwMS (Expanded Disability Status Scale [EDSS] [≤]4.0) and matched HCs underwent overnight polysomnography and 3T MRI. Glymphatic proxies were the diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index and coupling of the global blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal with CSF inflow (gBOLD-CSF coupling). We also assessed sleep micro- and macroarchitecture, EDSS, disease duration, lesion volume, mean diffusivity (MD), lateral ventricle (LV) and choroid plexus volumes. Analyses were adjusted for age and sex. Results: We included 22 PwMS (34.2{+/-}10.1 years; 16 female) and 26 HCs (32.2{+/-}5.7 years; 18 female). DTI-ALPS was lower in PwMS (adjusted difference: -0.12, 95% CI -0.22 to -0.02), but MD was higher, and adjustment for MD attenuated this difference (-0.11, -0.21 to -0.0002). gBOLD-CSF coupling did not differ between groups (-0.02, -0.08 to 0.05). In PwMS, stronger coupling was associated with shorter total sleep time (r=0.49, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.77) and higher arousal index (r=-0.48, -0.77 to -0.04), whereas DTI-ALPS was unrelated to sleep. Associations with clinical and structural measures were borderline for DTI-ALPS and EDSS (r=-0.44, -0.74 to 0.01) and for coupling and LV volume (r=0.44, -0.00 to 0.74), and weak otherwise. Analyses were exploratory and uncorrected for multiplicity. Discussion: In MS, the DTI-ALPS index is partly confounded by white matter damage and should not serve as a standalone glymphatic marker. Stronger gBOLD-CSF coupling was associated with shorter, fragmented sleep in PwMS, consistent with the proposed compensatory waking CSF dynamics. If confirmed longitudinally, gBOLD-CSF coupling may serve as a glymphatic-related marker in MS and sleep a potential target to improve brain clearance in PwMS.

Article.Title: Successful retrieval is its own reward
Article.Authors: Smith, D. E.; Long, N. M.
Article.Abstract: The ability to successfully remember past events is critical to our daily lives, yet the neural mechanisms underlying the motivation to retrieve is unclear. Although reward-system activity and feedback-related signals have been observed during memory retrieval, whether this signal reflects intrinsic reward or goal-attainment is unknown. Adjudicating between these two alternatives is crucial for understanding how individuals are motivated to engage in retrieval and how retrieval supports later remembering. To test these two accounts, we conducted between-subjects recognition memory tasks on human participants undergoing scalp electroencephalography and varied test-phase goals (recognize old vs. detect new items). We used an independently validated feedback classifier to measure positive feedback evidence. We find positive feedback following successful retrieval regardless of task goals. Together, these results suggest that successful retrieval is intrinsically rewarding. Such a feedback signal may promote future retrieval attempts as well as bolster later memory for the successfully retrieved events.

Article.Title: Dendrite-wide voltage and Ca2+ imaging reveals structures of dendritic excitations during behavior
Article.Authors: Wu, X.; Lee, B. H.; Park, P.; Wong-Campos, J. D.; Xu, J.; Plutkis, S. E.; Lavis, L. D.; Cohen, A. E.
Article.Abstract: The dynamic interplay of dendritic voltage and Ca2+ shapes neuronal integration and synaptic plasticity, but the voltage-Ca2+ relationship during behavior remains poorly defined. Using dual-color Patterned Illumination Spinning disk COnfocal (PISCO) microscopy, we simultaneously mapped voltage and Ca2+ dynamics throughout the dendritic arbors of hippocampal CA2 pyramidal neurons during spatial navigation. Fast Na+ spikes usually initiated near the soma and back-propagated throughout the dendritic tree. Simple spikes primarily drove somatic and proximal Ca2+ increases, whereas complex spikes also engaged branch-selective apical Ca2+. In contrast, the voltage signals varied relatively smoothly across the dendritic tree. Dendrite-restricted excitations without concurrent somatic events were rare. We developed a biophysics-inspired model that accurately predicted local Ca2+ amplitude from local voltage waveforms across subcellular compartments and event types. Locomotion and spatial context shifted the relative prevalence of simple and complex spikes, but the same compact biophysical model captured the local voltage-Ca2+ relationships across behavioral states and contexts. We further found that local subthreshold depolarizations in apical dendrites preceding a plateau potential correlated with local Ca2+ amplitude during the plateau. Our results support a model in which conjunction of voltage back-propagation and branch-specific inputs together recruit regenerative dendritic electrogenesis and somatic bursting.

Article.Title: Selective ultrasonic suppression of pathological brain hyperactivity via an endogenous CAV3-NCX1 axis
Article.Authors: Lee, K.; Lee, J. M.; Kim, H.-J.; Koo, M.; Lee, S.; shin, S.; Youn, W.; Phan, T. T.; Lee, C. J. J.; Park, J.; PARK, J. M.
Article.Abstract: Selective suppression of pathological hyperactivity is a major therapeutic challenge across brain disorders. Ultrasound stimulation can modulate neural activity, yet the molecular basis of its inhibitory effects and its ability to selectively inhibit hyperactive rather than basally active cells remain unclear. Here, we identify the caveolin-3 (CAV3)-sodium-calcium exchanger-1 (NCX1) complex as a previously unknown mediator of state-dependent ultrasound-induced neural inhibition. Prolonged ultra-low-intensity ultrasound stimulation engages NCX1-mediated Ca2+ extrusion in hyperactive neurons and astrocytes, sparing cells with basal activity. NCX1 is both necessary and sufficient for this inhibitory response, and disruption of the CAV3-NCX1 interface abolishes the ultrasound-induced effects. In vivo, targeted ultrasound stimulation suppresses fear-evoked hyperactivity and freezing in an NCX1-dependent manner and attenuates neuropathic pain-associated hyperactivity, allodynia, and hippocampal epileptiform activity. These findings establish a molecular mechanism for state-dependent ultrasound inhibition, providing a basis for a new approach to neuromodulation that selectively targets pathological hyperactivity.

Article.Title: Lysosomal Glycosaminoglycan Catabolism Regulates Microglial Cell State in the Developing CNS
Article.Authors: Hope, K. T.; Zhang, Y.; Basu, A.; Luo, B.; Chassie, K.; Weiss, R. J.; Yellajoshyula, D.
Article.Abstract: Microglia acquire their adult homeostatic identity during postnatal CNS development, a period of extensive extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, through mechanisms not fully understood. Here we show that lysosomal catabolism of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), major ECM components, is a microglial function required to establish homeostatic identity. Using mouse models of Mucopolysaccharidosis VII, we examined the consequences of deleting {beta}-glucuronidase (GUSB), a lysosomal enzyme required for GAG degradation. Loss of GUSB resulted in the accumulation of undegraded chondroitin sulfate within microglial lysosomes, confirmed by LC/MS analyses of cortical microglia. GUSB-deficient microglia failed to acquire homeostatic identity. Single-cell RNA sequencing identified them as a distinct population enriched for a core transcriptional program shared by immature and disease-associated microglia (DAM). Together, these findings identify lysosomal GAG catabolism as a pathway linking ECM remodeling to the acquisition of homeostatic microglial identity during CNS development.

Article.Title: Much stronger coarse-to-fine visual processing in primate superior colliculus than primary visual cortex neurons
Article.Authors: Yu, Y.; Bogadhi, A. R.; Baumann, M. P.; Malevich, T.; Zhang, T.; Trottenberg, C.; Hafed, Z. M.
Article.Abstract: The visual system optimizes its signal processing properties to efficiently encode natural scenes. The superior colliculus (SC) and primary visual cortex (V1) both play important roles in visual-motor processing, and they both exhibit qualitatively similar visual responses. However, it is not clear whether the SC simply inherits V1's efficient coding image processing optimizations or not, especially given that the SC receives a substantial amount of direct anatomical inputs from V1. Here, by performing matched experiments in the two brain areas, as well as with the same visual stimuli and in the same experimental animals, we show that the dynamics of coarse-to-fine visual image processing in the SC are much stronger than those in V1. In the SC, visual response latencies, being fastest for coarse patterns, are dictated by image spatial frequency, independently of the spatial frequency tuning curves of the neurons. On the other hand, V1 visual response latencies are largely dominated by visual response sensitivity, which is itself much more broadband than in the SC. These observations remain fundamentally unchanged in active vision gaze-shift scenarios eliciting visual reafferent responses in both brain areas. Our results suggest that coarse-to-fine visual image processing dynamics are most observable, and thus most relevant, in visually-responsive neurons driving foveating eye movements, like in the SC. Besides explaining behavioral evidence for saccadic facilitation by images that are consistent with the statistics of natural scenes, these results indicate that coarse-to-fine visual processing dynamics are much more of a collicular than a cortical visual phenomenon.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: primary visual cortex; superior colliculus; spatial frequency tuning; natural scene statistics; efficient coding

Article.Title: Interference Between Pavlovian Cues and Instrumental Control: A Stratified Comparison Across Alcohol Use Disorder and Smoking
Article.Authors: Thill, L.; Chen, H.; Bäuchl, C.; Krasniqi, S.; Born, M.; Marxen, M.; Friedel, E.; Pilhatsch, M.; Heinz, A.; Smolka, M. N.
Article.Abstract: Pavlovian cues can interfere with goal-directed behavior, particularly when they conflict with the required instrumental response. Previous research linked an increased susceptibility to such Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer (PIT) interference to risky drinking and alcohol dependence. However, it remained unclear whether the observed behavioral and neural alterations generalize to non-treatment-seeking individuals with mild-to-moderate alcohol use disorder (AUD) and to other substances like tobacco. We therefore studied 200 participants from the general population who were stratified by AUD and smoking status before completing a single-lever PIT task during functional magnetic resonance imaging. PIT interference was assessed as the difference in error rates between incongruent PIT trials, in which a Pavlovian conditioned stimulus conflicted with the required instrumental response, and congruent trials. Associations with AUD and smoking status, as well as dimensional associations of PIT interference and related neural activation with substance-related measures, were examined. As expected, participants with AUD showed greater PIT interference and reduced activation in the lateral prefrontal, dorsomedial prefrontal, and anterior cingulate cortices during PIT conflicts than participants without AUD. The magnitude of these behavioral and neural alterations also correlated with higher AUD severity and alcohol consumption, while being independent of smoking status and other smoking-related measures. These findings suggest that enhanced PIT interference generalizes to the broader AUD population but may not extend to smoking. They further implicate a reduced recruitment of prefrontal control networks during PIT conflicts as a potential mechanism underlying enhanced PIT interference in AUD and its association with clinically relevant outcome measures.

Article.Title: Attenuated gaze synchrony in autism and its non-additive modification by co-occurring ADHD: a transdiagnostic eye-tracking study of naturalistic viewing
Article.Authors: Di, X.; Biswal, B. B.
Article.Abstract: Background. Autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder co-occur frequently, but whether co-occurrence compounds or alters the visual-attentional differences associated with autism remains unresolved. Inter-subject correlation (ISC) during naturalistic viewing provides a model-free index of how closely an individual's gaze and pupillary responses track those of typically developing peers. Methods. We analyzed eye-tracking data from the Healthy Brain Network across four videos differing in social and visual content (N = 2476 children and adolescents; 1186-2042 per video). Gaze and pupil ISC were computed against a typically developing reference, gaze as a two-dimensional complex correlation. Dimensional models used parent-reported autistic (SRS-2) and ADHD (SWAN) traits; categorical models used a 2 x 2 (ASD x ADHD) analysis of covariance. All models adjusted for age, sex, tracker configuration and screen shape. Results. Autistic traits predicted reduced gaze synchrony in three of four videos, independently of ADHD traits. An autism diagnosis was associated with reduced gaze synchrony in all four videos ({beta} = -0.78 to -0.45 SD; q [≤] 0.009). The ASD x ADHD interaction was significant and positive in three videos ({beta} = 0.46-0.65; lower 95% confidence limits [≥] 0.16; q [≤] 0.005), indicating that the reduction associated with autism was smaller when ADHD co-occurred. The interaction was significant in all four videos within a single acquisition configuration and was robust to adjustment for co-occurring psychopathology and same-day stimulant status and to down-weighting of extreme observations. Ten stimulus-independent oculomotor measures from the same recordings showed no consistent group differences. Absolute gaze phase did not survive comparison with a magnitude-matched null. Limitations. The group with autism and without ADHD was small (45-78 children per video), so the interaction is estimated imprecisely. The findings were not tested in an independent cohort. Diagnoses were made without standard autism research instruments, eye-tracker settings varied, medication status was mostly unknown, and the design was cross-sectional. Conclusions. Co-occurring ADHD is associated with a smaller, not larger, reduction in gaze synchrony than autism alone, which argues against additive models of their co-occurrence. Inter-subject synchrony captures group structure that coarse summaries of eye movement do not.

Article.Title: α-Synuclein structural heterogeneity associates with distinct cytopathologies in multiple system atrophy
Article.Authors: Xu, X.; Forrest, S. F.; Martinez-Valbuena, I.; Scramstad, C.; Rogaeva, E.; Kosteniuk, S. E.; Watts, J. C.; Kovacs, G. G.; Enomoto, M.
Article.Abstract: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is characterized by oligodendroglial -synuclein inclusions, although neuronal inclusions also occur. We investigated whether regional differences in -synuclein filament structure are associated with distinct cytopathologies in a neuropathologically confirmed MSA brain by comparing the medial temporal lobe, which showed prominent neuronal inclusions and limited oligodendroglial pathology, with cerebellar white matter, which contained exclusively oligodendroglial inclusions. Cryo-electron microscopy resolved filaments from these regions at 3.0 [A] and 2.0 [A], respectively. Medial temporal filaments contained a previously undescribed protofilament fold, PF-IIIA, paired with canonical PF-IIB2, whereas cerebellar filaments adopted the canonical MSA Type II structure. PF-IIIA exhibits extensive remodeling of its core while retaining the asymmetric doublet architecture. These findings reveal regional -synuclein structural heterogeneity within a single MSA brain and suggest a potential association between distinct filament conformations and neuronal versus oligodendroglial cytopathology, highlighting the importance of regional and cellular context in filament organization and disease heterogeneity.

Article.Title: Cell-state mapping reveals a reversible neuroblast accumulation in the aging mouse hippocampus
Article.Authors: Rasetto, N. B.; Herrero, M.; Berardino, A. A.; Dibella, D. J.; Giacomini, D.; Trinchero, M. F.; Arlotta, P.; Chernomoretz, A.; Schinder, A. F.
Article.Abstract: Hippocampal neurogenesis supports learning and memory by generating new granule cells throughout life. However, both the rate and speed of this process have been shown to decline with age in mice. Currently, the molecular determinants underlying the effects of aging on neuronal development and differentiation remain unknown. To elucidate these mechanisms, we combined lineage tracing with single-nucleus RNA sequencing of adult-born granule cells (aGCs) in the aging mouse hippocampus. Employing this temporally-resolved transcriptional atlas of aGCs development, we observed that aging leads to a marked accumulation of postmitotic neuroblasts (NBs), revealing a stage-specific bottleneck in the neurogenic trajectory. Voluntary running reduced NB accumulation by restoring the progression through this developmental impasse, allowing neuronal maturation to be resumed. This shift was accompanied by a significant reduction in apoptosis at the NB stage. Together, these findings highlight postmitotic NBs as a developmental stage of increased vulnerability during aging and point to the restorative effects of exercise in reducing apoptosis and driving cellular transitions towards a neurogenic trajectory.

Article.Title: Prediction Dynamically Modulates Gain and Width of Population Frequency Tuning in Human Auditory Cortex
Article.Authors: van Haren, J. J. G.; Auksztulewicz, R.; de Lange, F. p.; Kotz, S. A.; De Martino, F.
Article.Abstract: During perception, the brain must veridically portray sensory representations while simultaneously highlighting unexpected events. According to two-process theory of predictive perception, this balance is achieved via complementary mechanisms: precision-weighted predictions sharpen sensory tuning around expected features, while momentary surprisal scales response gain, dampening expected inputs and amplifying unexpected violations. However, standard approaches to investigate these processes, such as categorical multivariate decoding, primarily capture shifts in overall signal-to-noise, making it difficult to disentangle changes in population tuning width from modulations in response gain. Here, we combine ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI) with population receptive field (pRF) modelling and a continuous Bayesian ideal observer to test how expectations dynamically modulate frequency tuning across the human auditory hierarchy. We first established static pRF preferences and tuning widths independently of predictive inference. We then separately compared this static pRF tuning against two dynamically modulated alternatives. The first model evaluated how tone-by-tone precision-weighted predictions dynamically sharpen and broaden pRF tuning width, while the second model evaluated how gain (by amplification and dampening) was modulated by tone-by-tone information-theoretic surprisal. Across primary, belt, and associative auditory cortices, both a sharpening model driven by precision-weighted predictions and a gain model driven by surprisal explained significantly more variance compared to a static baseline model. Counterfactual models inverting these driving features yielded no improvement, ruling out non-specific model mimicry. Additionally, contrasting local and global tonotopic implementations revealed a feature-selective dissociation: whereas precision-weighted predictions locally sharpened pRFs tuned to expected frequencies, surprisal acted as a global broadcast signal that multiplicatively scaled pRF gain across all frequency channels of the tonotopic map. Together, these findings demonstrate that the auditory system continuously balances selectivity for expected structure and responsiveness to surprising input through local sharpening and global gain modulation.

Article.Title: Personalized functional networks scale with brain size beyond anatomy and are altered in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
Article.Authors: Sun, K. Y.; Snyder, W.; Tong, T. T.; Jaskir, M.; Sevchik, B. L.; Horien, C.; Jung, B.; Meisler, S. L.; Cieslak, M. L.; Prem, S.; Kafadar, E.; Gardner, M.; Hansen, J. Y.; Levitis, E.; Cyr, K.; Karandikar, S.; Seidlitz, J.; Bagautdinova, J.; Ruparel, K.; Li, H.; Fan, Y.; Shinohara, R. T.; Keller, A. S.; Raznahan, A.; Roalf, D. R.; Schmitt, J. E.; Gur, R.; McDonald-McGinn, D. M.; Gur, R.; Satterthwaite, T. D.; Alexander-Bloch, A. F.
Article.Abstract: Anatomically, cortical regions scale differentially with total brain size: some show disproportionate contraction in smaller brains and expansion in larger brains, while others show relative stability. Whether personalized functional networks (PFNs) follow similar areal scaling principles, and how these principles shape functional reorganization in conditions that alter brain size, remain unknown. We investigated PFN scaling in typical development (ages 8-23; n=1,332) and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS), a neuropsychiatric genetic disorder with globally reduced brain size (62 cases, 153 matched controls; ages 10-24). In typical development, PFN scaling diverged from anatomy, deviating more from proportional scaling, particularly in association networks. In 22q11DS, accounting for expected scaling with brain size reduction revealed two robust network effects: relative peripheral visual reduction and relative cingulo-opercular enlargement. Vertex-level 22q11DS PFN reorganization beyond global cortical reduction showed spatial alignment with normative PFN changes associated with brain size, linking typical scaling principles to disorder-related alterations.

Article.Title: Confidence in global motion discrimination is better predicted by perceptual reliability than by stimulus-based heuristics
Article.Authors: Oluk, C.; Szinte, M.; Masson, G. S.; Mamassian, P.
Article.Abstract: Decision-making requires evaluating the reliability of perceptual estimates, but whether confidence reflects perceptual reliability or stimulus-based heuristics remains debated. We used a multiple-aperture global motion stimulus in which the global direction, and therefore motion coherence, is only available after integrating locally ambiguous signals, so that no simple stimulus statistic can serve as a shortcut. Observers reported the global direction in two successive intervals and then chose which decision was more likely to be correct. Confidence tracked accuracy beyond what coherence alone could explain: observers were more accurate in chosen intervals even at the same coherence level. Observers also frequently reported the direction opposite to the true motion, and, in direct comparisons, were more confident in these errors than in other large errors. We compared two image-computable models of motion integration. A standard motion-energy model failed to produce opposite-direction errors and the associated confidence pattern. A normalized motion-energy model, adding tuned inhibition among direction channels and an untuned gain control that increases overall activation with coherence, accounted for most of the variance in both perceptual decisions and confidence judgments. Tuned inhibition, which must be sharp if it is close to excitation in strength, produced the opposite-direction errors and reproduced the direction of their confidence advantage, and the untuned gain was needed for confidence to depend on coherence as strongly as observed. Confidence was read out from the same signal as the perceptual decision, and noise at the confidence stage, although probably present, added little to the fit beyond explaining the accuracy difference between chosen and unchosen intervals. These results suggest that confidence in this task relies on perceptual reliability. They also suggest that seemingly unusual metacognitive behavior can emerge from perceptual computations, which must therefore be modeled explicitly to identify genuine confidence mechanisms.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: perceptual reliability; motion coherence; metacognition; gain control; perceptual confidence; perceptual decision making; global motion; motion integration

Article.Title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory
Article.Authors: Su, H.; Knight, C.; Liu, P. R.; Lee, H.
Article.Abstract: Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.

Article.Title: Human tau compromises neuronal structural integrity in C. elegans independently of disease-associated modifications
Article.Authors: Joshi, M.; van Schijndel, V.; Tiggelaar, J.; van Falier, S. J. A.; Sinnige, T.
Article.Abstract: Tauopathies are a group of progressive neurodegenerative diseases amongst which Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent. They typically have a late age of onset and lead to cognitive decline. Tau is a highly soluble, intrinsically disordered microtubule binding protein that aggregates in these diseases. The mechanisms by which age-associated changes alter tau functionality and compromise neuronal structural integrity remain poorly understood. Here, we show with the use of single-copy gene insertion Caenorhabditis elegans models that human tau preferentially localises to neuronal processes in the nematode, consistent with its function of binding to microtubules. The expression of tau in the nervous system led to age-associated changes in the structural integrity of the ventral nerve cord, in agreement with previous reports in touch receptor neurons. However, expressing either the disease-related P301L mutant, phosphomimic tau or co-expressing human kinases did not worsen the observed buckling phenotype. On the other hand, kinase expression was associated with the formation of tau inclusions in a small proportion of animals at old age. These results suggest that human tau induces structural alterations in C. elegans neurons independently of pathological phosphorylation or aggregation. At the same time, the late-onset formation of tau inclusions upon kinase overexpression make this new model suitable to study the sequence of events leading to tau pathology.

Article.Title: A Latent Variable Perspective on EEG Measures of Attentional Control
Article.Authors: Sabo, M.; von Bastian, C. C.; Wascher, E.; Schneider, D.
Article.Abstract: Attentional control is a core cognitive function, yet there is still a significant debate revolving around its definition, factorial structure and underlying neural mechanisms. Research in this domain has largely developed along two largely disconnected traditions. Psychometric approaches assess individual differences using latent-variable models (e.g., structural equation modeling, confirmatory factor analysis), while cognitive neuroscience focuses on group-level behavioral and neural effects. This raises a critical question: can neural measures robust at the group level validly capture stable individual differences? Or more specifically, can some of the principles and analytical methods adopted in individual-differences research be directly applied to neural correlates of attentional control? The current study aims to address this question. Electroencephalogram data were recorded from participants as they completed four attentional control paradigms: a change detection task, the go/no-go task, the Simon task, and the Stroop task. From each task, we extracted the P3 component and a data-driven decoding accuracy measure as indices of conflict processing and tested whether these neural measures load onto a common latent factor of attentional control. Results revealed weak and largely non-significant correlations. Structural-equation modeling provided no evidence for a common latent factor, despite robust within-task effects at the group level reflected both in the behavioral and the EEG parameters. These findings suggest that EEG components may lack the construct validity needed to reliably capture individual differences in attentional control.

Article.Title: Loss of metabolic resilience underlies maladaptive responses to lipid overload in TDP-43 proteinopathy
Article.Authors: Godoy Corchuelo, J. M.; Garcia-Toledo, I.; Lopez-Carbonero, J. I.; Larrad-Sanz, A.; Gil-Moreno, M. J.; Fernandez-Hernandez, L.; Fernandez-Beltran, L. C.; Pena-de-Diego, L.; Jimenez-Coca, I.; Jimenez-Rodriguez, J.; Fernandez-de-la-Rosa, R.; Fernandez-Bernal, A.; Portero-Otin, M.; Casarejos-Fernandez, M. J.; Mansillo-Aparicio, A.; Baleriola, J.; Fisher, E.; Matias-Guiu, J. A.; Bascunana, P.; Cunningham, T. J.; Corrochano, S.
Article.Abstract: INTRODUCTION Altered eating behaviour is a hallmark feature of behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD). These changes may represent a compensatory response to an underlying metabolic disturbance. However, whether increased lipid availability restores metabolic homeostasis or instead accelerates disease progression remains unknown. TDP-43 proteinopathies, which account for approximately half of FTD cases, are associated with alterations in lipid metabolism, providing a mechanistic framework to investigate the cerebral response to lipid overload. METHODS We combined clinical observations in patients with bvFTD with mechanistic studies in the physiological TardbpM323K/M323K knock-in mouse model to determine how TDP-43 dysfunction modifies the response to chronic lipid excess. RESULTS In the bvFTD cohort, elevated cholesterol and triglycerides were associated with poorer cognitive performance, while mutant mice fed a lifelong high-fat diet showed worse cognitive impairment. Multi-omics analyses of the frontal cortex revealed maladaptive metabolic rewiring characterized by impaired mitochondrial and cholesterol metabolism, lipid accumulation, and widespread remodelling of TDP-43-dependent RNA processing. These alterations affected synaptic function and neuronal communication and were accompanied by reduced cerebral glucose utilization measured by 18F-FDG PET, neurotransmitter imbalance and enhanced neuroinflammation. DISCUSSION Increased lipid availability fails to compensate for TDP-43-associated metabolic dysfunction and instead promotes maladaptive molecular and functional responses. These findings identify impaired metabolic resilience as feature of TDP-43-mediated neurodegeneration and suggest that altered eating behaviour in bvFTD may represent an unsuccessful attempt to counteract an underlying metabolic deficit rather than a purely behavioural symptom. Thus, the biological context may determine whether increased energy intake is beneficial or detrimental during neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Correlated but distinct: VIP and NDNF interneurons implement dissociable inhibitory motifs for state-dependent gain control in visual cortex
Article.Authors: Jenks, K. R.; Ahrlund-Richter, S.; Celotto, M.; Sipe, G.; Sur, M.
Article.Abstract: VIP and NDNF positive interneurons are both found in layers 1 and 2/3 of the cortex, but have distinct patterns of gene expression, morphology, and connectivity. Despite this, their functional roles in the sensory cortices seem remarkably similar; their activity correlates with behavioral state, and they gate behaviorally driven increases in excitatory activity and sensory-driven responses. We sought to directly compare VIP and NDNF positive interneurons in the mouse visual cortex to determine if their activity was indeed functionally redundant or could be distinguished by their correlation to behavioral state, to excitatory activity, or to excitatory visual responses. Using simultaneous recordings of pupil diameter and running speed together with dual-population calcium imaging, we found that although the activity of both VIP and NDNF positive interneurons was more strongly correlated with behavior than was excitatory neuron activity, VIP positive interneuron activity was more strongly correlated with pupil diameter, whereas layer 2/3 NDNF positive interneuron activity was more strongly correlated with running speed. Excitatory-to-VIP pairwise correlation increased during locomotion, whereas excitatory-to-NDNF pairwise correlation decreased during locomotion. Intriguingly, although VIP-to-NDNF pairwise correlation was high, cortical depth significantly affected both VIP-to-NDNF correlation and the correlation of NDNF positive interneurons with pupil diameter and running speed. As expected, excitatory visual responses were significantly modulated by both pupil dilation and locomotion. However, we found that the level of VIP and NDNF activity preceding stimulus onset had a unique contribution to and was positively correlated with the amplitude of excitatory visual responses. Thus, while highly correlated to one another and to behavioral state, VIP and NDNF positive interneurons are functionally distinguishable in their relationship to both behavior and excitatory activity in the mouse visual cortex.

Article.Title: Drug Repurposing of Rapamycin Mitigates Amyloid-β-Associated Proteotoxicity in Caenorhabditis elegans Models of Alzheimer's Disease
Article.Authors: Alkhudaydi, S.; Alsulami, A.; Linfoot, M.; Terlouw, M.; Holzer, A.; Albalawi, F.; McGrath, S.; Moreno, J.
Article.Abstract: Background: Alzheimers disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia worldwide, affecting an estimated 55 million people and projected to exceed 130 million by 2050. AD is defined pathologically by extracellular accumulation of amyloid-beta (A{beta}) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles. Currently no therapy halts the underlying neurodegeneration in AD patients. Proteotoxic accumulation of A{beta} is a central pathogenic event therefore, strategies that enhance its clearance represent a compelling therapeutic avenue. Rapamycin (sirolimus), an FDA-approved allosteric inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) that relieves mTORC1-mediated suppression of autophagy, positioning it as an attractive drug-repurposing candidate for AD. However, it remains unclear whether rapamycins neuroprotection depends on directly reducing A{beta} burden or acts through A{beta}-independent mechanisms. This question, along with whether rapamycin alters specific A{beta} species, has not been systematically examined in a single, genetically tractable model. Methods/Results: Using two transgenic C. elegans models of human A{beta} expression a temperature-inducible, muscle-specific strain CL4176 and the pan-neuronal strain CL2355. We exposed C. elegans to 20 M rapamycin the lowest, nontoxic concentration to produce a protective effect. Rapamycin treatment delayed A{beta} induced paralysis in log-rank p = 0.0001) and improved crawling and swimming locomotion parameters. In the pan-neuronal CL2355 strain, rapamycin rescued the A{beta} induced chemotaxis deficit (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.008) without altering chemotaxis in the non-transgenic CL2122 control. Rapamycin also extended Kaplan Meier survival in CL2355 and preserved locomotor health span, delaying the trajectory of age related motor decline. At the molecular level, rapamycin did not significantly affect A{beta} burden. Conclusion: Rapamycin provides broad-spectrum and A{beta}-selective neuroprotection across muscle and neuron expressing C. elegans models of A{beta} proteotoxicity, extending from paralysis and locomotion to chemosensory behavior, longevity, and health span.

Article.Title: Slow but not fast theta tACS modulation of hippocampal-cortical connectivity compresses temporal distance judgments
Article.Authors: Wang, Y.; Jing, Y.; Ivacs, L.; Duecker, F.; De Weerd, P.; van de Ven, V.
Article.Abstract: The temporal organization of episodic memory is thought to depend critically on the hippocampus, potentially coordinated by theta-band oscillations. Here, we used concurrent transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine whether slow theta stimulation (3 Hz) applied over the left parietal cortex modulates hippocampal-cortical functional connectivity during memory encoding, and how this relates to subsequent temporal memory performance. Twenty-seven participants encoded sequences of object-scene pairs that were presented either within a single context or across a context boundary, under different tACS conditions (3 Hz, 8 Hz, and no stimulation), and afterwards judged the temporal distance between item pairs. Behaviorally, 3 Hz stimulation led to significantly compressed temporal distance judgments compared to 8 Hz, suggesting altered temporal memory reconstruction. Further, 3 Hz tACS selectively reduced hippocampal connectivity with occipital cortex, comprising left calcarine and lateral occipital clusters, and reduced hippocampal activity during encoding. In contrast, 8 Hz tACS reduced connectivity between the stimulation site and right early visual cortex. Neither frequency modulated hippocampal-cortical connectivity during retrieval. These results suggest that slow theta oscillations can shape hippocampal-cortical network dynamics in a frequency-specific manner, influencing the construction of temporal relations in memory.

Article.Title: Subtractive and Divisive Methods for Isolating Neural Oscillations From Broadband Activity Yield Different, Even Conflicting, Power Estimates
Article.Authors: Gyurkovics, M.; Cunningham, E.; Low, K. A.; Clements, G. M.; Kalamala, P.; Beck, D. M.; Voytek, B.; Fabiani, M.; Donoghue, T.; Gratton, G.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the role of oscillatory brain activity in cognition is a key objective in cognitive neuroscience. However, quantifying the power of narrowband neural oscillations is made challenging by the presence of non-oscillatory broadband activity in the signal. Recently, there has been a proliferation of methods designed to separate oscillatory from non-oscillatory (aperiodic) signals. To perform this separation, these methods must model the relationship between oscillatory and aperiodic components. Crucially, however, such methods rarely explicitly clarify whether they assume that this relationship is additive or multiplicative, an issue compounded by the common use of log-transformed data (i.e., subtraction in log space is equivalent to division in linear space). Here, we show the importance of justifying which assumption about component relations is applied. Using simulated power spectra with additive oscillatory and aperiodic components, we illustrate that methods that assume a multiplicative model, such as the popular specparam (formerly fooof) toolbox, systematically mis-estimate oscillatory activity in ways that can obscure real oscillatory differences between conditions, or even reverse their sign, creating an illusory effect. We then demonstrate these effects in two complementary empirical datasets: (a) a cross-sectional, between-subjects analysis of age-related differences in alpha power, showing how separation approaches impact effect size and detectability; and (b) a within-subjects analysis of pre-stimulus changes in alpha power in a detection task, showing how switching between approaches can greatly reduce the evidence for an effect, leading to different conclusions. These results highlight that researchers must explicitly report and justify assumptions about aperiodic and oscillatory signal combination, as these assumptions have implications not only for analyses of oscillatory activity and resultant conclusions, but also for integration of results across reports (which may implicitly employ different assumptions), and ultimately for the development of theories regarding electrophysiological features and their putative relations to cognition.

Article.Title: Switches in single-neuron excitability class can induce rich dynamical states in balanced networks
Article.Authors: Drangmeister, M.; Engelken, R.; Schleimer, J.-H.; Schreiber, S.
Article.Abstract: Network states with rich dynamics and highly variable firing rates of individual neurons are prominent in experimental observations and thought to benefit complex information processing and learning. Such states have been proposed to arise from properties of network coupling, like a strong connectivity or slow synaptic dynamics. Here, we identify an alternative mechanism based on weak synaptic coupling and intrinsic cellular dynamics. We show that a switch in the cellular excitability class of action-potential generation (via a switch in the underlying mathematical bifurcation) results in super-Poissonian spiking variability in random balanced networks, where the recurrent network reinforces rather than averages out the single-cell effect. Information encoding is shifted to higher frequency bands and collective chaos in the network is enhanced when intrinsic cellular dynamics follow a saddle homoclinic orbit (HOM) bifurcation. Entropy production and attractor dimension peak close to the saddle-node-loop point that separates the two excitability classes, pointing to the qualitative nature of the transition as the origin of the effect. Because such switches are induced by common physiological variables, like temperature or extracellular potassium, and leave synaptic weights untouched, they offer a route to setting a network's dynamical regime independently of plasticity. The robust effect links the biophysics of individual neurons to collective dynamics of large random networks, highlighting the relevance of single-cell dynamics for computation in physiological and artificial networks.

Article.Title: Characterising semantic prioritisation in visual working memory
Article.Authors: Kerren, C.; Gonzalez-Garcia, C.; Linde-Domingo, J.
Article.Abstract: Visual working memory preserves multiple features of recently encountered information, but these features are not necessarily equally available to guide upcoming behaviour. In particular, categorical semantic content can be prioritised over perceptual content when objects are retrieved from memory. Here, we asked what drives this semantic prioritisation in visual working memory, and whether it depends on the attentional state of the remembered information. Across a reanalysis of a previous dataset and two preregistered experiments, participants showed a prioritisation of semantic-category information over perceptual one. Drift-diffusion modelling suggested that such an advantage arose from multiple components of decision formation, including processes beyond evidence accumulation. Critically, when a retro-cue allowed the relevant memory item to be prioritised before the probe, the semantic advantage in processes outside evidence accumulation almost disappeared, whereas its advantage during evidence accumulation remained largely unchanged. In a separate experiment, extending the retention interval alone did not reliably increase semantic prioritisation, while an intervening task produced a larger absolute advantage in pre-accumulation processing. These findings show that semantic prioritisation is not simply a fixed advantage of semantic judgements and that the relative availability of meaning and perceptual format in working memory is dynamically shaped by attentional prioritisation.

Article.Title: Attenuated, Not Absent. Trusting Autonomous Systems Tracks Reliability More Closely, With Less Neural Engagement, Than Trusting Humans
Article.Authors: Rogers, D. A.; Weuthen, A.; Finn, A.; Schlesewsky, M.; Bornkessel-Schlesewsky, I.; Ullsperger, M.
Article.Abstract: Users of autonomous systems and AI assistants decide whether to accept a system's output, yet whether such active trust decisions engage the same evaluative architecture as trust between people remains unknown. Forty-four participants made trial-by-trial decisions to trust or distrust a human or autonomous system partner during fMRI, with identical prescripted accuracy for both partners across five difficulty levels. Despite equivalent performance, trust in humans exceeded their reliability. At the highest difficulty level, the estimated probability of trusting the human partner was 72% but only 51% for the system, despite both performing at 52% accuracy. Distrust decisions recruited a prespecified performance monitoring network of valuation, salience, social-perceptual and affective regions. On hard trials, this network remained functionally coupled for both partners. Across the task, trust and distrust were discriminable in every component for both, with greater distrust-related activation and discriminability for human partners. Discriminability differences were expressed on hard trials, where partner accuracy was uncertain and trust diverged between partners. These findings indicate that trust in humans and autonomous systems engages a shared evaluative architecture, but that engagement is attenuated during autonomous system interaction. Whereas our earlier passive monitoring study found the P3a to system errors absent with no behavioural difference, an active decision appears to impose a floor of engagement, so that technology-related cognitive economization, a reduction in cognitive and social-affective resources for non-human partners, takes the form of attenuation rather than absence. Alongside this attenuation, trust in the system tracked its reliability without exceeding it.

Article.Title: A multiscale map of the descending sympathetic innervation of the spleen
Article.Authors: Remedio, L.; Lewis, Z. R.; Thomas, E. D.; Rodrigues-Vaz, I.; Schmidt, C. R.; Tun, L. T.; Chen, T. X.; Fancher, K. A.; Greene, J. S.; Bertagnolli, D.; Goldy, J.; Rimorin, C.; Tieu, M.; Cardenas, T.; Torkelson, A.; Guzman, J.; Ferrer, R.; Chakka, A.; Vicente, A. M.; Yao, S.; Smith, K. A.; Tasic, B.; Peterka, D. S.; Costa, R. M.

Single nucleus transcriptomics resolved three CMG neuron types and a Cre line marking the Rxfp1+ neurons labeled spleen-projecting neurons. CMG-projecting sympathetic preganglionic neurons occupied the intermediolateral cell column, intercalated nucleus, and spinal nucleus of the thoracic spinal cord. A tracing strategy designed to identify neurons upstream of these preganglionic populations labeled neurons in the medulla, pons, midbrain, hypothalamus, and several areas of the cortex including motor cortex. Motor-cortex axons formed vGlut1-positive boutons in close apposition to retrogradely labeled CMG-projecting neurons, providing anatomical support for a descending cortical route to sympathetic spinal circuits. Article.Title: A neuronal atlas of neurexin isoform expression in Caenorhabditis elegans
Article.Authors: Frankel, E. B.; Henry, P. S.; Karmirantzos, N.; Leider, M.; Kurshan, P. T.
Article.Abstract: The Caenorhabditis elegans neurexin gene nrx-1 encodes both long () and short ({gamma}) isoforms, but how their expression varies across individual neurons remains unclear. The two {gamma} reporters collectively marked a broader set of neurons than the reporter, and most neurons expressing the reporter also expressed at least one {gamma} reporter. Among the ventral nerve cord motor neurons examined, reporter expression was restricted to cholinergic neurons, while one {gamma} reporter was detected exclusively in GABAergic neurons. The other {gamma} reporter was consistently detected in most cholinergic motor neurons and detected in only a subset of GABAergic motor neurons, often variably across animals. In two-fold embryos, this same {gamma} reporter was detected in more neurons than the reporter. Two upstream regulatory elements contributed to its expression in different neuronal populations. At dorsal nerve cord synapses, disruption of either isoform class reduced NRX-1 fluorescence, with a larger reduction after disruption of the short isoforms. Article.Authors: Grossmann, R.; Woo, S.; Knoesche, T. R.; Villringer, A.
Article.Abstract: Near-threshold somatosensory stimulation is traditionally applied to investigate the post-stimulus neural correlates of conscious perception as well as ongoing brain activity like alpha oscillations that precede stimulation and modulate perception. The precise role of pre-stimulus alpha oscillations requires deeper investigation in the electrical modality and is yet fully undiscovered in the mechanical modality. Contrary to previous findings, we found no differences between modalities in early perceptual correlates. Both modalities showed robust correlates of stimulus perception likely corresponding to the N80 and N140 components. The effect of stimulus perception was localised in the right contralateral precentral and postcentral gyri, with the left ipsilateral hemisphere contributing shortly afterwards. We found a negative relationship between the pre-stimulus alpha oscillation amplitude and stimulus perception. Moreover, greater pre-stimulus alpha phase coherence coincided with an increase in stimulus perception. There was no evidence that the alpha effects differed between stimulation modalities.

ACE-339 functionally rescues TDP-43 dependent mis-splicing and synaptic activity. Lastly, ACE-339 rescues disease associated phenotypes in two independent mouse models of TDP-43 pathology. In addition, we now have a catalog of TDP-43 disaggregating compounds that are being developed further to be tested in clinical trials in patients with ALS and other TDP-43 proteinopathies.

Article.Authors: Chang, D.; Song, D.; Rao, H.
Article.Abstract: Skilled action observation unfolds over time: viewers follow changing movements, coordinate what they see with prior experience, and form a response to the performance as a whole. After adjustment for local gray-matter volume, age, sex, and motion, dancers had higher static BEN in 32 parcels and six networks (FDR q < .05). Dynamic BEN was higher in control and default-mode networks. Dancer-dancer ISC exceeded novice-novice ISC in five networks. Dancers occupied one common CAP less often and another more often, while performer synchrony and acceleration tracked state occurrence across spectators. These converging observations show that dance experience is expressed in local temporal irregularity, shared spectator responses, and the distribution of brain states during naturalistic action observation.

Article.Authors: Mombeek, L. M. M.; Brosens, A.; Jehoul, R.; Leembruggen, A. J. L.; Neckel, P. H.; Hao, M. M.; Boesmans, W.; Wilson, D. M.

Aged neurons showed enlarged, less circular mitochondria and increased pPDH immunoreactivity, indicative of declining neuronal activity. Consistent with remodeling of myenteric plexus architecture, neuronal calcium responses increased upon electrical stimulation while decreasing after agonist application. DSS-induced colitis did not reproduce the DNA damage, heterochromatin, or p21 changes seen with age, implying a direct role in the latter. Human aged enteric neurons showed higher {gamma}H2AX and H3K9me3 intensities. Article.Authors: Ekambaram, S.; Axeen, E. T.; Kapur, J.; Goodkin, H. P.; Dokholyan, N. V.

Pathway mapping in the Reactome database revealed both shared and drug-specific biological processes. Furthermore, molecular docking studies elucidated the atomistic interactions between the drugs and the predicted targets. Specifically, the predicted target landscape varied from eslicarbazepine and licarbazepine (59 predicted targets each) to lacosamide (18). Pathway analysis revealed recurrent enrichment in rapid depolarisation and the interaction between L1 and ankyrins shared across all drugs, alongside predicted off-targets, including the cannabinoid CB1 receptor for phenytoin and the carbonic anhydrases for lacosamide. Molecular docking supported these predictions, with binding scores ranging from -24 to -31 kcal/mol. Article.Title: Age-associated skeletal muscle dysfunction with spinal cord pathology in an App knock-in model of Alzheimer's disease
Article.Authors: Nakai, T.; Urano, Y.; Sobue, A.; Henmi, M.; Asai, S.; Hitachi, K.; Nagai, T.; Watanabe, H.; Yamanaka, K.; Tsuchida, K.; Yamada, K.; Saito, T.; Saido, T. C.; Yamada, S.; Enomoto, A.; Mizoguchi, H.
Article.Abstract: Skeletal muscle dysfunction is increasingly recognized in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but its pathological basis remains poorly understood. We examined age-associated muscle dysfunction together with skeletal muscle and spinal motor system alterations in male AppNL-G-F/NL-G-F knock-in (App-KI) mice, which develop age-dependent amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) pathology without amyloid precursor protein (APP) overexpression. Middle-aged App-KI mice had higher percentages of centrally nucleated fibers in the gastrocnemius and quadriceps femoris muscles. Transcriptomic and targeted expression analyses further revealed alterations in molecular profiles related to muscle development and myosin, including reduced expression of factors involved in myoblast fusion and selected myosin proteins. Despite evident cerebral A{beta} pathology, no apparent A{beta} immunoreactivity was detected in skeletal muscle. In the lumbar ventral horn, App-KI mice had fewer choline acetyltransferase-positive motor neurons, greater A{beta} deposition, and increased immunoreactivity for glial fibrillary acidic protein and ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1; serum interleukin-6 levels were also selectively elevated in middle-aged App-KI mice. Together, these findings indicate that age-associated reductions in strength-related performance in App-KI mice occur without overt muscle atrophy and are accompanied by histological and molecular abnormalities in skeletal muscle and pathological changes in the lumbar spinal cord. Article.Title: Scaling up naturalistic narrative research: A reproducible large language model-based tool for evaluating contextual information gain
Article.Authors: Palsule, R. A.; Goeschel, A.; Yoo, J.; Chen, J.; Bornstein, A. M.; Khoudary, A.
Article.Abstract: Narratives are a universal part of natural human experience. As experimental stimuli, narratives allow scientists to study complex mental processes with direct relevance to everyday experience. These analyses typically require manual labeling of key event features. Such characterization of narrative stimuli are extremely labor-intensive and prone to subjectivity. Automated tools could reduce these difficulties and enable scaling to longer, varied stimuli by exposing the exact quantities computed. We address this by introducing a metric that uses open-weight LLMs to compute contextual information gain. Our metric correlates with human ratings of event importance and causal centrality, critically distinguishing the latter from semantic centrality, thus overcoming limitations of existing automated tools. The metric similarly captures shared coactivation in the default mode network, a network implicated in narrative comprehension. Taken together, these results validate an automated, empirically-grounded tool that researchers can use to identify behaviorally- and neurally-relevant computational quantities in naturalistic stimuli.

Article.Title: Age and Sex Differences in Lateral Ventricle Choroid Plexus Volume in a Large, Manually Segmented, Multi-Site MRI Dataset
Article.Authors: Zeng, V.; Wolock, C. J.; Estrada, S.; Huang, L.-Y.; Raymond, N.; Jammoul, M.; Cao, Y.; Keshavan, M. S.; Fried, P. J.; Kuegler, D.; Reuter, M.; Lizano, P.
Article.Abstract: Introduction The choroid plexus (ChP), which produces cerebrospinal fluid and forms the blood-CSF barrier, has drawn growing interest in psychiatric and neurodegenerative neuroimaging. Scanner manufacturer and image resolution were significantly associated with measured left LV volume but not with ChP volume, and the quality-control metric was not significantly associated with any outcome. Both ChP and LV volume were significantly associated with several cognitive domains, including emotion recognition, working memory, inhibitory control, and episodic memory. Conclusion These findings demonstrate meaningful differences in ChP volume across age and sex. DataPlex represents the largest demographically and technically diverse manually segmented ChP dataset to date, establishing reference benchmarks for future automated segmentation tools and underscoring the importance of accounting for demographic and technical covariates in choroid plexus research.

Article.Title: Delayed Reduction in Painful Sensations Evoked by Cervical tSCS Following High-Frequency Stimulation
Article.Authors: Makarova, A. V.; Starodubtseva, N.; Lebedev, M. A.
Article.Abstract: Objective: Transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) is a non-invasive neuromodulation technique with potential effects on pain perception. However, tSCS itself can evoke discomfort or pain at higher current intensities, and it remains unclear whether high-frequency tSCS alters the pain evoked by subsequent low-frequency stimulation. This study examined whether high-frequency cervical tSCS delivered at motor-threshold intensity is followed by changes in pain ratings elicited by low-frequency tSCS in healthy participants. Approach: Twenty-five healthy participants completed a single experimental session. Individual sensory, motor, and pain thresholds were determined using single-pulse tSCS at the C6-C7 spinal level. Pain was assessed using 1-Hz stimulation delivered for 1 min at an individually defined intensity corresponding to 6-7 points on a 0-10 Numerical Rating Scale. Participants then received 80-Hz tSCS for 10 min at motor-threshold intensity, followed by three repeated pain-assessment sessions separated by 5-min intervals. Surface electromyography was recorded from the flexor carpi radialis and extensor carpi radialis. Pain analysis included 25 participants, whereas EMG analysis included 18 participants. Main results: Pain ratings were significantly lower than baseline during the second and third post-stimulation assessments. In contrast, ratings obtained immediately after high-frequency stimulation did not differ significantly from baseline. EMG responses showed substantial inter-participant variability. No EMG metric showed a significant omnibus session effect after correction for multiple comparisons, although exploratory comparisons indicated transient increases in ECR AUC and mean rectified amplitude immediately after high-frequency stimulation. Significance: These findings indicate that high-frequency cervical tSCS can exert a measurable short-term influence on pain perception. Pain ratings and stimulation-evoked EMG responses showed different temporal patterns and represent complementary, non-equivalent outcomes of spinal stimulation.

Article.Title: Electrophysiological dynamics of empathy for self- and other-related pain
Article.Authors: Rahnama Lashkami, P.; Golbabaei, S.; Gharibzadeh, S.; Borhani, K.
Article.Abstract: Empathy requires the ability to generate shared representations of the self and others while maintaining a distinction between them. However, it remains unclear whether, and to what extent, the neural processes involved in sharing and understanding others' pain overlap with those involved in processing one's own pain, particularly with respect to their temporal dynamics. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying empathic processing of self- and other-related painful facial expressions. To this end, EEG signals were recorded from 42 female participants while they viewed self- and other-related painful and neutral expressions. During the early stage of processing, the difference in N2 amplitude between self-related and other-related stimuli was smaller in the painful than in the neutral condition. Nevertheless, self-related painful stimuli continued to elicit more negative N2 amplitudes and greater Alpha/Mu suppression than other-related painful stimuli. In contrast, during the late stage of empathic processing, no distinction was observed between self- and other-related painful stimuli. Instead, painful expressions, regardless of whether they were self- or other-related, elicited larger late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes. These findings suggest that empathic processing is characterized by an early self-other distinction followed by a later convergence in the neural representation of self- and other-related pain.

Article.Title: Brain Signal Variability and Brain-Behavior Coupling in Adults with Dyslexia
Article.Authors: Luo, J.; Keller, A. S.; Xia, Z.; Arrington, N.; Krishnamurthy, L. C.; Clement-Lam, S. S. Y.; Pugh, K.; Hoeft, F.
Article.Abstract: Background: Brain signal variability indexed by fMRI has emerged as a promising transdiagnostic biomarker for neurodevelopmental disorders, demonstrating better predictive utility than time-averaged metrics for diagnosis, yet it remains underexplored in adult dyslexia. The Neural Noise Hypothesis of dyslexia proposes that genetic risk disrupts cortical excitation/inhibition balance, elevating neural noise and affecting processes essential for reading. Here, we examine resting-state fMRI BOLD variability, a metric linked to neural noise, in adults with dyslexia and investigate its links with behavior. Methods: In 30 adults with dyslexia (DY) and 76 typical readers (TR), we computed three complementary BOLD variability metrics: standard deviation (SD) and mean squared successive differences (MSSD) to quantify BOLD amplitude fluctuations, and dynamic regional homogeneity (dReHo) to quantify local temporal coordination. Results: DY showed higher SD and MSSD in the left ventral occipitotemporal pathway and higher MSSD in the cerebellum, whereas TR showed higher dReHo in frontal and temporoparietal regions. SD/MSSD in visual, somatomotor, cerebellar, and subcortical networks significantly covaried with multi-domain behavioral profiles. Conclusions: Adults with dyslexia showed localized, metric-specific differences in brain signal variability and brain-behavior covariance, indicating region-specific rather than global alterations. These results suggest that brain signal variability is a promising candidate task-free phenotype that could potentially index target engagement in interventions for adult dyslexia.

Article.Title: Automated, high-throughput kinematic analysis of skilled reaching in rodent models of neurological injury
Article.Authors: Friedrich, L. S.; Mendoza, E.; Huie, J. R.; Rosas, J.; Wang, Z.; Mathew, S.; Schultz, C.; Chhikara, N.; Samburg, N.; Specht, R.; Antolak, I.; Tsoulfas, P.; Ferguson, A.; Blackmore, M. G.

Here we present a novel and efficient approach to collecting, analyzing, and interpreting kinematic data with high throughput. We automated a single pellet reaching task in mice and created a video analysis pipeline that scores task success and extracts kinematic features from reaches. Regularized regression was then applied separately to select reach qualities that best predicted task success. Article.Title: MK-6240
Article.Authors: Biju, A. P.; Herrera, J. M.; McNamara, C. C.; Hipolito, E. L. M.; Liang, C.; Mukherjee, J.
Article.Abstract: Flortaucipir and MK-6240 are two tau imaging agents currently in use for measuring neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) progression in Alzheimers disease (AD). The aims of this study were to use postmortem AD and Down syndrome (DS) brain sections to study three issues: (1) Measure binding affinity of flortaucipir and MK-6240 in AD brain sections by using [125I]IPPI; (2) Evaluate the binding characteristics of [18F]flortaucipir in AD, DS and cognitively normal (CN) brains sections and compare them with [18F]MK-6240, and (3) Assess the binding of [18F]flortaucipir in CN and Parkinsons disease (PD) brain sections to identify any off-target binding. The half-maximal inhibition (IC50) of [125I]IPPI bound to anterior cingulate (AC) in AD brain sections for flortaucipir was 2.91 nM and MK-6240 was 5.99 nM. Using frontal cortex (FCX) and temporal cortex (TCX) of AD, DS and CN brain sections, [18F]flortaucipir displayed high levels of binding in the gray matter (GM) of AD and DS. The average ratio of DSAD GM to CN GM was 15.7 in FCX, while DSAD GM to CN GM was 15.2 for the TCX. In the case of AD, average ratio of AD GM to CN GM was 12.4 in FCX, while AD GM to CN GM was 9.5 for the TCX. Binding of [18F]flortaucipir in brain section of AC from CN and PD cases did not exhibit any off-target binding to monoamine oxidase-A (MAO-A). Article.Title: Multisensory brain processing is associated with depressive symptoms in youth with chronic pain
Article.Authors: Martin-Herrero, L.; Sunol, M.; Pascual-Diaz, S.; Ting, T. V.; Dudley, J. A.; Jackson, C.; Kashikar-Zuck, S.; Coghill, R.; Lopez Sola, M.
Article.Abstract: Juvenile fibromyalgia (JFM) is a chronic pain condition marked by widespread musculoskeletal pain and often accompanied by physical fatigue, nonrestorative sleep, headaches, anxiety, and depression. Previous studies have found that adolescents with fibromyalgia report augmented unpleasantness and altered brain responses to non-painful multisensory stimuli. Likewise, research in major depression has shown altered neural processing of sensory stimulation. We examined whether augmented brain responses to non-painful multisensory stimulation is associated with depressive symptoms in adolescent girls with JFM. Neuroimaging results in chronic pain patients revealed that greater depressive symptomatology was associated with increased activation in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) (pFWE<0.05), a region implicated in self-referential processing and specifically rumination in adults with chronic pain. JFM patients showed increased PCC-left middle temporal gyrus task-dependent connectivity using psychophysiological interactions analysis (PPI). Furthermore, hyperconnectivity between the PCC and brain areas involved in cognitive-affective regulation, sensory integration, and memory processing was strongly correlated with depressive symptoms in JFM patients. These findings underscore the role of depressive symptoms in sensory processing and integration in JFM patients and highlight the complex interplay between sensory processing and emotional/self-referential brain function in patients.

Article.Title: Zona incerta drives a strategy of persistence during nocturnal predatory hunting in mice.
Article.Authors: Shallow, M. C.; Wright, A. L.; Weible, A. P.; Smear, M. C.; Wehr, M.
Article.Abstract: Prey capture in lab mice is a complex, ethologically relevant behavior that provides us with an opportunity to study how mice integrate internal and external cues to drive goal-directed behaviors. Previous research has established that key parts of this behavior, such as the approach, are visually guided, but it has remained unknown how mice would perform if given exposure to hunting without visual cues. Zona incerta, a potential key locus for the integration of external and internal information, has previously been shown in naive mice to improve prey capture ability by increasing appetitive drive through integrating prey-related sensory information. It remains an open question if this region plays the same role in mice experienced with hunting in both the light and dark. Therefore, we examined the behavioral strategies used by mice with prior experience hunting in both the light and dark, as well as how these strategies are modulated by zona incerta. In experienced mice, we found that mice adjust their strategies to maintain similar success rates with and without visual cues, and that zona incerta further refines these strategies, specifically in the dark. This suggests that the role of zona incerta in these experienced mice is to maintain successful hunting by shifting behavioral strategies under ambiguous sensory conditions.

Article.Title: Integrating multiple imputation with harmonization in multisite neuroimaging data: implications for site effects and biological inference
Article.Authors: Ren, Y.; Dong, Y.; Minhas, D.; Cohen, A. D.; Wu, Q.; Tudorascu, D. L.
Article.Abstract: Multisite neuroimaging harmonization in Alzheimer's disease research with missing data has received limited attention in the literature. Post-processing harmonization reduced site-level variability compared to the original data, with method performance varying across evaluation metrics, while overall harmonization quality remained comparable after MI. Disease group differences remained statistically significant across all combinations, exhibiting a consistent regional pattern, strongest in Braak I and weakest in Braak VI. MI modestly increased effect size and coefficient estimates, with improved precision reflected by median standard error ratios below 1 (0.89 for effect sizes and 0.93 for coefficients).
