Article.Title: Adaptation can explain cortical responses to sound deviance without requiring prediction
Article.Authors: Jarzebowski, P.; Bishnoi, A.; Bendor, D.
Article.Abstract: Sensory systems amplify what is rare, allowing animals to orient toward threats and opportunities hidden among regular events. Whether this deviance detection reflects neuronal adaptation or error against the brain's predictive model is debated. The two processes can contribute simultaneously because the context that enables prediction also drives adaptation. To dissociate them, we recorded from primary auditory cortex neurons in awake mice during a modified oddball paradigm that separated recent sound history from longer-term sequence statistics. Contextual effects ranged from suppression to facilitation of responses. Facilitation increased with deviance magnitude, as expected for prediction error. However, neither facilitation, suppression, nor stimulus-specific adaptation depended on these longer-term statistics. A normalization model in which a neuron's inputs adapt at different rates reproduced the range of contextual effects and their weakening in background noise. Adaptive normalization can therefore generate deviance signals, including facilitation, without requiring a predictive model.

Article.Authors: Ayoub, A.; Lu, L. X.; Haydar, T. F.
Article.Abstract: Three-dimensional culture systems have emerged as a bridge between in vitro and in vivo models. Here, we present a rigorous methodological framework for the longitudinal analysis of dorsal forebrain spheroids, beginning with gross spheroid morphology, extending to structural phenotypes in rosette morphogenesis, and culminating in cellular analyses of neural progenitor cell proliferation and cell cycle dynamics. This workflow integrates isogenic iPSC-derived spheroid culture, whole-mount optical clearing, high-resolution 3D imaging and reconstruction, and cumulative EdU-labeling assays. Testing the sensitivity of this approach in an isogenic Down syndrome model, we reliably detected new features of altered spheroid growth, delayed rosette emergence, reduced rosette density, and prolonged progenitor cell cycle progression. This approach provides a reproducible strategy for measuring complex developmental phenotypes in 3D culture models and can be applied to neurodevelopmentally altered cell lines beyond Down syndrome.

Article.Authors: Rodriguez-Gatica, J. E.; Jayakumar, J. I.; Gnanasekar, S. I.; Mohammadi, A.; Ackels, T.; Rothermel, M.; Roos, D.; Schwarz, M. K.

Article.Authors: Perez-Boyero, D.; Perez-Arevalo, J.; Valero, J.; Weruaga, E.; Diaz, D.

Treated WT mice showed early behavioural changes, including reduced novel-object discrimination. Article.Title: Social Connection: Resting-State Functional Connectivity Associations with Social Networks, and the Roles of Empathy and Sex
Article.Authors: Casburn, M. G.; Fernandes, A.; Ressin, L.; Sheerin, A.; Voulgari, T.; Laighneach, A.; Morris, D. W.; Cannon, D. M.

Article.Authors: Zhu, Z.; Cao, Z.; Song, D.; Rao, H.
Article.Abstract: Hearing loss changes how the brain processes sound, yet how chronic auditory degradation shapes the temporal organization of spontaneous cortical activity remains unclear. Six complementary measures of signal amplitude, local synchrony, symbolic sequence diversity, successive variation, and temporal persistence showed no corrected STG differences. The BEN-defined STG region showed stronger focal functional connectivity with MCC (FWE p = 0.031). Article.Title: Glutamate/GABA Resource Asymmetry Enables Bidirectional Activity Correction

Article.Title: No allocentric distractor-location learning following self-movement even with contextual anchors and explicit knowledge
Article.Authors: Chen, L.; Fatato, C.; Jia, S.; van Ede, F.; Slagter, H. A.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive behavior requires learning where relevant information can likely be found, but also where distraction is likely to occur. For such learning to be useful in everyday life, it must generalize across changing viewpoints as observers move through the environment. Recent work suggests a striking asymmetry in this regard: whereas target-location learning can be grounded in world-centered coordinates, distractor-location learning appears tied to the observer's current viewpoint. One possibility is that allocentric distractor-location learning requires stronger contextual support than allocentric target-location learning. Alternatively, distractor suppression may be fundamentally constrained by viewer-centered spatial coding. To distinguish between these possibilities, participants performed an additional-singleton search task displayed on a tabletop and continuously changed their standing position around the table, while the high-probability distractor location remained fixed in the external environment. Unlike previous studies using this paradigm, contextual anchors were embedded directly within the search display, allowing distractor locations to be encoded relative to a stable task-relevant allocentric structure. In a second experiment, participants were additionally explicitly informed about the distractor-location regularity. Despite task-relevant contextual structure and explicit knowledge, distractor-location learning failed to emerge in world-centered coordinates. Article.Abstract: Behavioral inhibition (BI) is an early temperament associated with higher risk for later anxiety. Article.Authors: Chan, K. Y. I.; Mouloudi, I.; Ben-Yakov, A.; Dubossarsky, H.; Hahamy, A.

These findings suggest that neural reactivation of past events at event boundaries reflects an unfolding inferential process that transforms shared experience into subjective understanding.

Article.Authors: Bulgarelli, C.; Pinti, P.; Bazelmans, T.; Hamilton, A.; Jones, E. J.
Article.Abstract: Empathy is crucial for social interactions across all cultures, and is foundational to establishing social cooperation and group ties in human societies. Importantly, we showed an effect of age on network specialisation with brain activations of cognitive empathy stronger in younger compared to older preschoolers, and brain activations of affective empathy stronger in older compared to younger preschoolers. These results may provide the first evidence that cognitive empathy is engaged early and develops alongside or ahead of affective empathy in preschoolers, challenging existing models and suggesting a new framework for understanding the development of empathy.

Article.Authors: dos Santos Correa, M.; Vido Lopes, L.; Quintiliano dos Santos, A. C.; Castro, J. C.; Boscariol Lourenco, W. T.; da Costa Silva, A. C.; Ferreira, T. L.; Tiba, P. A.; Fornari, R. V.
Article.Abstract: Contextual fear memories can lose specificity as they age, modeling fear overgeneralization seen in post-traumatic stress disorder. Glucocorticoid receptor (GR) signaling in the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) during the immediate post-learning period may govern both endocrine recovery from an aversive experience and the eventual specificity of the resulting memory, but this link remains untested. We infused vehicle or the GR antagonist mifepristone into the dmPFC of rats immediately after contextual fear conditioning, then assessed corticosterone dynamics, behavior and c-Fos coactivation networks at recent and remote time points. Mifepristone accelerated corticosterone recovery without changing hormone release, spared recent memory, and produced stronger, generalized defensive behavior at the remote time point. This behavioral shift coincided with denser remote retrieval networks and greater default-mode-like than salience-like connectivity. These findings identify post-learning dmPFC GR signaling as a regulator of endocrine recovery and remote defensive expression, constraining fear memory specificity as memories undergo systems consolidation.

Article.Title: Personalized functional networks scale with brain size beyond anatomy and are reorganized in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
Article.Authors: Sun, K. Y.; Snyder, W.; Tong, T. T.; Jaskir, M.; Sevchik, B. L.; Horien, C.; Jung, B.; Meisler, S. L.; Cieslak, M. L.; Prem, S.; Kafadar, E.; Gardner, M.; Hansen, J. Y.; Levitis, E.; Cyr, K.; Karandikar, S.; Seidlitz, J.; Bagautdinova, J.; Ruparel, K.; Li, H.; Fan, Y.; Shinohara, R. T.; Keller, A. S.; Raznahan, A.; Roalf, D. R.; Schmitt, J. E.; Gur, R.; McDonald-McGinn, D. M.; Gur, R.; Satterthwaite, T. D.; Alexander-Bloch, A. F.
Article.Abstract: Anatomically, cortical regions scale differentially with total brain size: some show disproportionate contraction in smaller brains and expansion in larger brains, while others show relative stability. Whether personalized functional networks (PFNs) follow similar areal scaling principles, and how these principles shape functional reorganization in conditions that alter brain size, remain unknown. We investigated PFN scaling in typical development (ages 8-23; n=1,332) and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS), a neuropsychiatric genetic disorder with globally reduced brain size (62 cases, 153 matched controls; ages 10-24). In typical development, PFN scaling diverged from anatomy, deviating more from proportional scaling, particularly in association networks. In 22q11DS, accounting for expected scaling with brain size reduction revealed two robust network effects: relative peripheral visual reduction and relative cingulo-opercular enlargement. Vertex-level 22q11DS PFN reorganization beyond global cortical reduction showed spatial alignment with normative PFN changes associated with brain size, linking typical scaling principles to disorder-related alterations.

Article.Title: Brain Signal Variability and Brain-Behavior Coupling in Adults with Dyslexia
Article.Authors: Luo, J.; Keller, A. S.; Xia, Z.; Arrington, N.; Krishnamurthy, L. C.; Clement-Lam, S. S. Y.; Pugh, K.; Hoeft, F.
Article.Abstract: Background: Brain signal variability indexed by fMRI has emerged as a promising transdiagnostic biomarker for neurodevelopmental disorders, demonstrating better predictive utility than time-averaged metrics for diagnosis, yet it remains underexplored in adult dyslexia. The Neural Noise Hypothesis of dyslexia proposes that genetic risk disrupts cortical excitation/inhibition balance, elevating neural noise and affecting processes essential for reading. Here, we examine resting-state fMRI BOLD variability, a metric linked to neural noise, in adults with dyslexia and investigate its links with behavior. Methods: In 30 adults with dyslexia (DY) and 76 typical readers (TR), we computed three complementary BOLD variability metrics: standard deviation (SD) and mean squared successive differences (MSSD) to quantify BOLD amplitude fluctuations, and dynamic regional homogeneity (dReHo) to quantify local temporal coordination. Voxel-wise group comparisons and partial least squares correlation analyses examined brain-behavior associations across a comprehensive behavioral battery spanning reading (e.g., word reading, phonological processing), math, oral language, working memory, and executive function domains. Results: DY showed higher SD and MSSD in the left ventral occipitotemporal pathway and higher MSSD in the cerebellum, whereas TR showed higher dReHo in frontal and temporoparietal regions. SD/MSSD in visual, somatomotor, cerebellar, and subcortical networks significantly covaried with multi-domain behavioral profiles. Conclusions: Adults with dyslexia showed localized, metric-specific differences in brain signal variability and brain-behavior covariance, indicating region-specific rather than global alterations. These results suggest that brain signal variability is a promising candidate task-free phenotype that could potentially index target engagement in interventions for adult dyslexia.

Article.Title: Long-lasting chromatin and transcriptional states shape the maintenance of memory ensembles
Article.Authors: Vogel, I. R.; Kruettner, S.; Guzikowski, N. J.; Liu, H.; Koren, S. A.; Xu, L.; Sanalidou, S.; Griffith, E. C.; Greenberg, M. E.; Traunmueller, L.
Article.Abstract: Memories of recent events are stored within minutes in neuronal ensembles in the hippocampus. Over days to weeks, these memories undergo consolidation, and later retrieval depends on reactivation of a subset of neurons within the ensemble. However, how transient experiences produce lasting molecular and cellular changes in hippocampal ensemble neurons remains unknown. Here, we profile the functional, transcriptional, and gene regulatory states of hippocampal memory ensemble neurons at single cell resolution across multiple remote timepoints following single trial contextual fear conditioning. We uncover long lasting, cell type specific chromatin and gene expression changes after learning that coincide with sustained shifts in synaptic plasticity. Within dentate gyrus granule ensembles, we identify a persistent chromatin transcriptional program that emerges in a subset of ensemble neurons and is marked by sustained expression of many synaptic genes. This transcriptional signature predicts which neurons will be reactivated during memory recall, suggesting that only a fraction of initial ensemble neurons maintains a molecular state supporting later reactivation. Regulatory elements associated with this persistent state are highly enriched for AP1 motifs, the cognate binding sites for Fos family transcription factors, even though FOS protein has long since decayed away. Instead, we detect long lasting FOSB binding at these elements, suggesting a mechanism by which the effects of immediate early gene driven transcription are extended beyond the initial induction window. FOSB is particularly enriched in ensemble neurons that maintain enduring gene expression changes, suggesting it sustains chromatin accessibility and prolonged transcription in neurons reactivatable during memory retrieval. Together, these findings identify molecular mechanisms underlying the maintenance, maturation, and evolution of hippocampal memory ensembles over time.

Article.Title: Transcriptomic and Lipidomic Profiling of Human iPSC-Derived Microglia Reveals TREM2-Dependent and -Independent Processes
Article.Authors: Cardona, C. L.; Patel, R.; Finan, G. M.; Kim, T.-W.; Sproul, A. A.; Teich, A. F.
Article.Abstract: TREM2 has been implicated in AD as a critical regulator of microglial functions and loss of function mutations in TREM2 increases one's risk of developing AD. Given the diverse functional roles of TREM2, we sought to unravel how it affects downstream pathways using human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs) derived from TREM2 knockout (KO) and isogenic control lines and assessing the response to oligomeric amyloid-{beta} 42 (oA{beta}42). While previous studies have primarily used fibrillar A{beta}, we focused on microglial responses to oA{beta}42 given their disease relevance and potent cytotoxic effects. At baseline, we identified a set of TREM2-dependent genes, which corresponded to the DAM signature in mice and disease-associated signatures in humans. Additionally, loss of TREM2 resulted in increased expression of cholesterol biosynthesis genes. In response to oA{beta}42, we found that the transcriptional response was largely TREM2-independent and corresponded to a strong induction of inflammatory pathways, with TREM2 also being downregulated in control iMGLs. We identified subsets of genes and pathways that were unique to either control, such as mitochondrial DNA and RNA degradation, or TREM2 KO iMGLs, such as the senescence-associated secretory pathway and adipogenesis, suggesting some differences in gene expression driven by TREM2 in response to oA{beta}42. Given that the inflammatory response was TREM2-independent, we sought to identify signaling pathways that contributed to inflammation. Inhibition of toll-like receptor signaling significantly reduced the expression of pro-inflammatory genes and modestly increased expression of TREM2 and TREM2-dependent genes. Consistent with our transcriptional data, cytokine production and secretion in response to oA{beta}42 was significantly increased to similar levels in both controls and TREM2 KO iMGLs. Lipidomic profiling of microglia revealed that triglycerides and lactosylceramides were significantly increased in both control and TREM2 KO iMGLs in response to oA{beta}42. TREM2 KO iMGLs had decreased levels of BMPs and increased levels of cholesterol esters across all conditions, further highlighting a role for TREM2 in maintaining lipid homeostasis in microglia. Taken together, we describe genes, pathways, and lipids that are associated with TREM2 expression that likely influence microglial responses to oA{beta}42.

Article.Title: Pathogenic human autoantibodies target the soluble CASPR2 ectodomain to induce network hyperexcitability
Article.Authors: Serrenho, D.; del Villar, N.; Bueno, V.; Fernandes, D.; Tutor-New, Q.; Kanekiyo, T.; Wing, E.; Williams, R.; Steinke, S.; Ribeiro, L. F.; Pinheiro, P.; Coutinho, E.; Irani, S. R.; Carvalho, A. L.
Article.Abstract: The mechanisms by which autoantibodies contribute to antibody-mediated neurological diseases remain poorly understood. Autoantibodies targeting the extracellular domain of CASPR2 are found in patients with clinical features consistent with hyperexcitability, including neuromyotonia and seizures. These antibodies are reported to disrupt the functions of membrane-embedded CASPR2. However, given that CASPR2 is also detected in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which contains CASPR2 autoantibodies, targeting of CSF-shed CASPR2 may represent an additional pathogenic mechanism, introducing a novel paradigm of soluble antigen modulation by autoantibodies. Here, we found that patient-derived polyclonal and monoclonal CASPR2 antibodies enhanced neuronal network excitability and selectively amplified excitatory synaptic transmission in human and rat primary cortical neurons. In addition, CASPR2 antibodies impaired calcium homeostasis and altered the intrinsic properties of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Notably, these antibodies depleted CASPR2 from both neuronal culture medium and patient CSF, suggesting targeting of the shed CASPR2 ectodomain. Knockdown of plasma membrane calcium ATPase 2 (PMCA2), a reported target of the CASPR2 ectodomain, abrogated the observed effects of CASPR2 antibodies. Together, our findings identify shed CASPR2 as a underrecognized pathogenic target of CASPR2 autoantibodies and demonstrate that its neutralization disrupts PMCA2-mediated calcium regulation, driving neuronal network hyperexcitability. More broadly, we identify the neuronal sheddome as a source of autoantibody targets and soluble protein neutralization as a novel disease mechanism, highlighting shed CASPR2 as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target.

Article.Title: Opposing sleep and feeding phenotypes across development in desert flies
Article.Authors: Li, S.; Szuperak, M.; Nave, C.; Tang, S. H.; Donlea, J. M.; Kayser, M. S.
Article.Abstract: Sleep is essential for adaptation and survival across the lifespan, yet the ecological pressures shaping sleep ontogeny remain poorly understood. We investigated sleep across early developmental stages in Drosophila mojavensis, a stress-resilient, desert-adapted species. While adult D. mojavensis exhibit prolonged and consolidated sleep, along with enhanced starvation tolerance and survival compared to Drosophila melanogaster, the developmental trajectory of these phenotypes is unknown. In contrast to adults, D. mojavensis larvae sleep less than D. melanogaster but exhibit deeper sleep. They also consume more food and survive longer under starvation, linking reduced larval sleep with increased nutrient intake and starvation resistance. Metabolic analyses demonstrate elevated triglyceride accumulation across the D. mojavensis lifespan, consistent with enhanced energy storage capacity. Together, these findings reveal a reversal of sleep and feeding phenotypes across development in D. mojavensis, raising the possibility that the balance between sleep and other behavioral and metabolic demands is shaped by distinct ecological pressures across life stages.

Article.Title: Developmental emergence of cue-specific fear memory parallels maturation of prefrontal-amygdala circuitry in mice
Article.Authors: Martina, V.; Desa, Z. R.; Lewis, T.; Campos-Cardoso, R.; Sun, H.; Cummings, K. A.
Article.Abstract: Fear memories formed in early life are forgotten rapidly, but the circuits that delay stable memory expression are not well defined. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) projects to the basolateral amygdala (BLA), and both regions mature late, yet the behavior, anatomy and physiology of this pathway have rarely been examined together across development. We trained mice in cued auditory fear conditioning at postnatal day (P) 14-15, P20-21 or P59-70 and tested tone-evoked freezing 1, 7 and 14 days later. Early juvenile mice showed no cue-specific freezing at any memory retrieval time points, late juvenile mice showed it at 7 and 14 days but not at 1 day, and adults showed it at all retrieval time points. In separate mice, mPFC axons were low in the BLA at P11 and more abundant at P38 and P90, and light-evoked prelimbic synaptic responses in BLA principal neurons were not detectable at P11 but were robust at P35 and P70. Spontaneous synaptic currents and intrinsic excitability of BLA principal neurons, and excitability of prelimbic principal neurons and interneurons, also changed between P11 and adulthood. These data identify a protracted period of mPFC-BLA circuit maturation that overlaps the emergence of cue-specific fear and define the ages at which candidate mechanisms can be tested.

Article.Title: Endothelial VCAM1 links oncogenic KRAS signaling to myeloid inflammation and hemorrhagic instability in brain arteriovenous malformations
Article.Authors: Park, E. S.; Park, J.; Park, H.; Myint, O.; Kang, S. W.; Chen, X.; Zhao, Z.; Choi, J. M.; Jung, S. Y.; Huang, S.; Körbelin, J.; Choi, H. A.; Aronowski, J.; Chen, P. R.; Kim, E.
Article.Abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic conversion is the most devastating complication of brain arteriovenous malformations (bAVMs). However, endothelial mechanisms promoting macrophages (M{varphi}) recruitment, microglia (MG) activation, and bAVM lesion instability remain unclear. We investigated vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM1) as a mediator linking oncogenic endothelial signaling to myeloid cell responses and hemorrhagic progression in bAVMs. METHODS: We performed integrated transcriptomic analysis of human bAVM and epilepsy-control brain tissues, with validation in local bAVM specimens. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of bAVM lesions and intact brain tissues from mutant KRAS-induced bAVM mice were followed by histological validation. Using AAV-BR1-KRASG12V-injected Cx3cr1-gfp;Ccr2-rfp mice, we performed intravital imaging to assess M{varphi}/MG responses to VCAM1 neutralization. Hemorrhage and myeloid cell responses were also evaluated following endothelial-specific VCAM1 deletion. Plasma soluble VCAM1 (sVCAM1) was measured in patients with unruptured and ruptured bAVMs and unruptured aneurysm controls. Effects of sVCAM1 on MG activation were examined in vitro. RESULTS: Integrated human endothelial bulk and single-cell RNA-sequencing and tissue validation identified VCAM1 upregulation in bAVMs, including unruptured lesions. Plasma analyses showed increased sVCAM1 in unruptured and ruptured bAVM patients compared with unruptured aneurysm controls. In mutant KRAS-induced bAVM mice, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses demonstrated increased VCAM1 expression, with endothelial localization confirmed histologically. In vitro, mutant KRAS increased sVCAM1 production, while recombinant sVCAM1 stimulated inflammatory mediator expression in MG. Both MG and M{varphi} expressed VLA-4, a major VCAM1 receptor. Intravital imaging showed that VCAM1 neutralization reduced M{varphi} accumulation and MG activation, while early VCAM1 neutralization reduced hemorrhagic burden. Consistently, endothelial-specific VCAM1 deletion reduced M{varphi} accumulation, MG activation, and hemorrhage volume in bAVM mice and improved behavioral performance. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify endothelial VCAM1 as an upstream mediator linking mutant KRAS signaling to myeloid cell responses and hemorrhagic progression in bAVMs. This study establishes endothelial VCAM1 as a potential therapeutic target for attenuating hemorrhagic progression.

Article.Title: Within-Subject Precision Measurement: Theory and Utility of Assessing Change Scores and Their Variance
Article.Authors: Buckner, R. L.; Barch, D. M.; Mair, P.; Nichols, T. E.; Satterthwaite, T. D.; Yeo, B. T. T.
Article.Abstract: Within-subject studies gain statistical power by removing stable between-subject differences from the comparison. However, the metrics commonly used to select measurement instruments and anticipate their within-subject performance are often based on between-subject correlations of raw scores from test-retest designs. Measuring each subject's change directly -- after an intervention, and ideally more than once -- provides a firmer basis for evaluating measurement precision and planning studies of within-subject change. Here we describe the statistical theory behind estimating measurement properties from change scores. In one instantiation, the pre- and post-intervention measurements are each made twice, yielding the duplicate change-score design. Such a design provides an estimate of the mean signal change and enables the decomposition of the total observed variance of change scores into true between-subject response heterogeneity and measurement noise. In extended designs, where multiple measures are collected within and across days, measurement noise can be further decomposed to distinguish within-session from between-day measurement variability. These estimates supply the inputs needed for within-subject study design, including providing a basis for selecting among alternative measurements and comparing processing pipelines, performing power calculations, and estimating the precision limits of detecting change within individual subjects.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: change scores; statistical power; measurement precision; day-to-day variability; heterogeneous reactions; measurement noise

Article.Title: Neural rosettes emerge from an interconnected tubular network in human cortical organoids
Article.Authors: Trovo, L.; Gomez, G.; Einhorn, A.; Muotri, A. R.; Iakoucheva, L. M.
Article.Abstract: Cortical organoids generate multiple neural rosettes, self-organizing and radially arranged structures that resemble ventricular zones of the developing brain. Here, we show that these rosettes, commonly considered as discrete entities, originate from an interconnected tubular network. We demonstrate that the formation of this continuous structure involves neuroepithelial folding, invagination, and internalization, resembling aspects of neural tube formation. Using fluorescently labeled polyethylene nanoplastics as extracellular tracers, we further show that they accumulate within the developing tubular lumen, consistent with its formation through neuroepithelial folding and internalization. These findings provide new insights into early human brain morphogenesis and suggest the potential utility of cortical organoids for investigating developmental processes relevant to neural tube defects.

Article.Title: Can rat cortical cultures predict what comes next, unpredictable or learned?
Article.Authors: Cannard, C.; Reid, W.
Article.Abstract: In humans, physiological activity recorded before an unpredictable stimulus reportedly varies slightly with what the stimulus will be, an effect termed predictive anticipatory activity. Whether reduced neural preparations show it is unknown. We re-analyzed a public dataset in which twelve dissociated rat cortical cultures on high-density multi-electrode arrays performed a hidden-source inference task (DANDI 001611: 27 experiments, 691,200 trials). Two features of the dataset limit what it can test. Each experiment replays one fixed 256-trial source sequence in all 100 sessions, so the upcoming source is unpredictable only in session 1. One stimulation volley per trial arrives on an exact 1-s clock, so every pre-stimulus window lies in the previous trial's after-effects. Two questions were fixed before a confirmatory run on held-out experiments. Q1 asked whether, in session 1, a stimulation-free 250-ms window before each trial's volley carries information about the upcoming sources beyond what trial history explains. Q2 asked whether this information grows over the 100 repetitions, as learned expectation would predict. Q1 (13 experiments, 9 cultures): decoding above a shifted-label null, {Delta}AUC +0.003, 95% CI -0.026 to +0.033, randomization p = 0.73, equivalent to zero within +/-0.059 (the human effect expressed as AUC) and narrowly within +/-0.03. Q2 (12 experiments, 8 cultures): growth {Delta}G +0.004, 95% CI -0.006 to +0.013, p = 0.29, equivalent within +/-0.02. Pre-stimulus activity thus carried no detectable information about the stimulus, and none emerged with repetition.

Article.Title: Disentangling tonic and phasic dopamine in fiber photometry from single recordings to cohorts
Article.Authors: Peytral, G.; Tariq, Z.; Essmann, A.; Garcon-Poca, Z. M.; Garcia Ortiz, D.; Crook, C.; Bonaventura, J.; Abante, J.
Article.Abstract: Fiber photometry signals combine fast neurotransmitter transients with slower changes in baseline. However, current pipelines separate the two before measuring either, so errors in one carry over into the other. Here we present PhotoSVI, a multi-scale statistical model that splits a recording into a slow tonic signal and discrete release events, estimated together. For each recording, PhotoSVI returns event probabilities over time, the drug effect on event rate with its uncertainty, and the time course of the tonic response, and it pools recordings across a cohort. In simulations matched to experimental recordings, PhotoSVI detected transients and recovered the shape of the tonic response more accurately than existing methods. In mouse dopamine recordings, it revealed an effect that count-based analyses largely missed: a nociceptin receptor agonist enhances the phasic response to morphine while reducing the tonic one, consistent with lower tonic dopamine relieving phasic release from autoreceptor inhibition.

Article.Title: Rank Deficiency in Parameter Estimation for Hodgkin-Huxley Type Current Models
Article.Authors: Heinkenschloss, M.; Namazifard, S.; Gabbiani, F.
Article.Abstract: The Jacobians of nonlinear least squares residuals play a central role when simultaneously fitting parameters of Hodgkin--Huxley (HH) type models to ionic currents measured through voltage clamp experiments. Their rank deficiency is tied to parameter degeneracy, i.e., the ability to produce the same current response with different parameters, and the Jacobians' null spaces provide insight into the structure of the parameter degeneracy, as well as into which additional experiments can reduce or even remove it. This paper analyzes Jacobian rank structure across HH-type models used for H-, A-type, fast sodium, and delayed rectifier currents. The Jacobians are rank deficient to varying degrees, depending on experimental conditions. Analytical representations of the Jacobians' null spaces are provided. In all models, one source of rank deficiency is the multiplication of the peak conductance and state variables, such as activation and inactivation, inherent to the HH-type model structure. H-current models derived from either whole cell, or cell-attached patch recordings exhibit additional rank deficiencies, implying the local existence of manifolds of parameters that lead to the same current responses. For A-type, fast sodium, and delayed rectifier models there is no additional rank deficiency, although their Jacobians may exhibit characteristics associated with ill-conditioned parameter estimation problems. Descriptions of the null spaces of these Jacobians are used to prove that the rank deficiency can be reduced or even be removed by fixing certain parameters, or by adding additional experiments. The analytical results are illustrated numerically, using data from voltage clamp experiments described in the literature.

Article.Title: PreSMA population dynamics keep the beat atop the primate audiomotor hierarchy
Article.Authors: Marquez, P.; Ayala, Y.; Prado, L.; Mendoza, G.; Merchant, H.
Article.Abstract: Humans move in time with musical beats, yet how the brain builds the internal beat that guides movement is unknown. We recorded 4,719 neurons in six nodes of the audiomotor circuit while monkeys tapped in synchrony with auditory metronomes at different tempos. We found a clear functional dissociation in the temporal-frontal axis. Auditory cortex detected metronome clicks and contained local clocks that tiled each interstimulus interval, whereas parietal, striatal, and motor areas, most strongly the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA), generated movement-aligned neural sequences that rescaled with tempo. Only in preSMA did population activity formed a cone-shaped manifold that jointly encoded tempo in its height, the produced interval in its width, and the timing of each tap relative to the beat in its position along the trajectory. During timing errors, preSMA activity kept conical shape but drifted toward shorter or longer tempos, revealing a hierarchical neural clock for beat synchronization.

Article.Title: CortexDecoder: Efficient fMRI-to-Image Reconstruction from Cortical Flatmaps
Article.Authors: Imoto-Tar, T.; Fung, M.; Gurha, A.
Article.Abstract: Recent brain decoding work has shown the potential of Vision Transformers (ViTs) to learn mappings from neural representations to visual features. Here we present CortexDecoder, a framework that reconstructs viewed images from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) flatmaps, which are neural responses projected onto the cortical surface and unfolded into 2D images. We show that a frozen, pretrained cortical foundation model is sufficient for competitive reconstruction. A frozen CortexMAE encoder turns flatmap patches into brain tokens, and two lightweight cross-attention bridges map these tokens to semantic CLIP embeddings and low-level image features. The final image is generated using a frozen SDXL-unCLIP model which takes a low-level image reconstruction as an initial image and a predicted CLIP embedding used to condition the image generation. On Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) Subject 1 reconstruction benchmarks, CortexDecoder is competitive with prior methods and the best for cortical flatmap methods without multi-subject pretraining. CortexDecoder achieves this performance while training far fewer parameters compared to prior methods.

Article.Title: A multimodal arrayed Perturb-seq platform for dissecting microglial state dynamics and target identification
Article.Authors: Ju, L.; LaBranche, M. C.; Hromadka, S.; Li, J.; Kwak, Y. D.; Chen, X.; Yu, J.; Sukumaran, B.; Worringer, K. A.; Freyre, C.; Hsiao, J. S.
Article.Abstract: Microglia are highly dynamic immune cells of the central nervous system that can adopt diverse functional states in health and disease, making them both emerging therapeutic targets and challenging systems for target identification. Here, we developed TF-iMG, a human pluripotent stem cell-derived transcription factor-induced microglia model generated by inducible expression of SPI1 and CEBPA in Cas9-expressing stem cells. TF-iMG rapidly acquired microglia-like transcriptomic, morphological, inflammatory, and phagocytic features while remaining compatible with efficient lentiviral CRISPR knockout workflows that can be completed within one week. We next established an arrayed multimodal Perturb-seq platform that integrates lentiviral CRISPR knockout, multiplexed single-cell RNA sequencing, cytokine profiling, and live-cell imaging. Single-cell analysis showed that TF-iMG recapitulates intrinsic microglial heterogeneity and captures homeostatic, activated, inflammatory, and proliferative signatures. Stimulation with IL1B and IL4 reproducibly induced distinct pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory states, respectively, providing a framework for perturbation-based interrogation of microglial state regulation. Targeting IL1B and IL4 pathway components validated the platform by attenuating expected stimulus-driven state shifts. Profiling of putative microglial regulators and Alzheimer's disease-associated genes further revealed perturbation-specific transcriptional signatures, altered state occupancy, and multimodal phenotypes spanning cytokine release, morphology, and trajectory. Together, this platform enables scalable target identification in microglia.

Article.Title: Mathematical model for visual cortical development based on molecular mechanisms underlying the generation and elimination of dendritic spines
Article.Authors: Tanaka, S.; Miyashita, M.
Article.Abstract: In the developing brain, neural circuits are elaborated by the activity-dependent rewiring of synaptic connections. The current view of synaptic rewiring in early development is that filopodia spontaneously generated along dendrites transform into spines by establishing contacts with neighboring axonal boutons to form synapses whereas spines of inappropriate synapses are eliminated in an activity-dependent manner. In this theoretical study, we mainly focus on the processes of spine generation, maturation, and elimination to build a mathematical model of synaptic rewiring, incorporating experimental findings on actin polymerization and depolymerization under the activation of Rho-GTPases mediated by the binding of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) to neurotrophin receptors such as tropomyosin kinase receptor B (TrkB) and the low-affinity-nerve growth factor receptor (p75NTR). TrkB receptors are dephosphorylated by chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans (CSPGs) mediated by protein-tyrosine phosphatase {sigma} (PTP{sigma} in an age-dependent manner. The model describes the generation or elimination of dendritic spines of visual cortical neurons under actin polymerization and depolymerization to establish appropriate synaptic contacts on afferent fibers of cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus. The simulations based on the model reproduced not only simple-cell-like receptive fields and orientation-direction maps but also a characteristic profile of the total number of synapses, which shows an early increase and a delayed decrease during the critical period. It is also demonstrated that the formation of direction selectivity is delayed behind the formation of orientation selectivity, which is likely promoted by the pruning of inappropriate synapses.

Article.Title: The Cost to Scroll: Short-form Video Use and Episodic Memory
Article.Authors: Chen, K. K.; Miller, D. S.; Nguyen, K. K.; Wagner, A. D.; Tran, T. T.
Article.Abstract: Short-form video platforms expose users to rapid streams of novel content; these features are posited to place heavy demands on cognitive processes. In a preregistered online study, we used device-reported screen time (TikTok and total Instagram app use) to examine whether short-form video use is associated with sustained attention and episodic memory in participants aged 18-24 yrs (N = 497). During a sustained attention task, participants made indoor/outdoor decisions on scene stimuli, with 90% frequent trials (indoor images) and 10% infrequent trials (outdoor images); the subsequent surprise recognition test assessed memory for these items. Among participants with device-reported TikTok or Instagram use (N = 395), short-form video use was not significantly associated with attention performance. By contrast, greater short-form video use was associated with poorer episodic memory ({beta} = -0.15, p = .004); this relationship was strongest for infrequent-category items. These observational findings connect heavier short-form video consumption with poorer episodic memory in young adults, showing how daily digital habits co-vary with memory function.

Article.Title: A toolkit to identify parameter degeneracy and solution manifolds of Hodgkin-Huxley type current models
Article.Authors: Namazifard, S.; Gabbiani, F.; Heinkenschloss, M.
Article.Abstract: Countless studies have fitted Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) type models of active currents to voltage clamp data using nonlinear least squares. Yet, little is known about the uniqueness of parameter solutions and the interdependence of HH-type model parameters. Here, we show that considerable insight can be gained from the singular value decomposition (SVD) of a matrix closely related to the objective function used in the fitting procedure. After fitting all model parameters simultaneously using synthetic data originating from a representative range of experimental cases, this reveals that a manifold of solutions is possible depending on the type of voltage clamp data available and on the selected HH-type model. In such cases, we use the SVD to determine which parameters are least identifiable. Next, we develop an SVD-based manifold tracing technique that can efficiently unveil the structure of the manifold of equivalent solutions in the parameter space of the model. Our methods also identify parameter interdependencies and their impact on joint parameter confidence regions. The most salient one consistently observed across our experimental examples was between the peak conductance and reversal potential of active HH-type current models. The SVD-based strategy presented here is expected to be generally applicable to investigate parameter degeneracy and solution manifold structure in biophysical models of single neurons. Thus, our results should prove valuable for understanding the constraints imposed by the biophysics of ion channels on single neuron computation.

Article.Title: Structure learning and context inference emerge from next-state prediction in a cerebellar-medial temporal lobe circuit
Article.Authors: Bhatia, C.; Gershman, S. J.; Amematsro, E. A.
Article.Abstract: Humans learn many context-dependent behaviors; yet the contexts driving these behavior are rarely explicit and must instead be inferred. Further, we are rarely exposed to the same context multiple times, so we must learn how to generalize to new contexts from our experiences in prior ones. Motor learning relies on both. People can hold multiple conflicting visuomotor mappings and recall the appropriate mapping when needed. Much as cricket is easier to learn for someone who already plays baseball, experience with previous mappings accelerates learning of others. Indeed, human motor learning is well described by context inference, in which the learner infers the context and uses it to update and recall the appropriate memory. How the brain implements this inference, and which circuits perform it, however, is unknown. Here we introduce a circuit in which a cerebellar forward model predicts the next state conditioned on a latent from the medial temporal lobe. At the same time, the medial temporal lobe updates that latent from the cerebellum's prediction error. While we only trained the circuit to predict next state, it learns to infer context and represents contexts in a structured latent space. Coupled with this latent, a motor cortex module reproduces context-dependent retrieval, savings after washout, spontaneous recovery, and evoked recovery, and compensates for perturbations it has never experienced. The same circuit reproduces cerebellar-dependence of object-location memory and independence in object-recognition memory, loss of place-cell stability in the dark when cerebellar plasticity is blocked, and the abstract geometry of hippocampal activity in a reversal task. Cerebellar-medial temporal lobe interaction is therefore a candidate locus for context inference and structure learning in the brain.

Article.Title: Neural processing of linguistic speech features and their modulation by selective attention in users of hearing aids and cochlear implants
Article.Authors: Jehn, C.; Schueller, A.; Vavatzanidis, N. K.; Hahne, A.; Reichenbach, T.
Article.Abstract: Understanding speech relies on the neural processing of acoustic and linguistic features, which can both be analyzed using Temporal Response Functions (TRFs). While both types of features have been the focus of numerous studies in typical-hearing individuals, much less is known about the neural processing of continuous speech for people with hearing loss, particularly how hearing-impaired listeners process word-level features in noisy environments, where they typically struggle. We recorded EEG from hearing aid (HA, n=29) and cochlear implant (CI, n=24) users, and an age-matched typical-hearing (TH) control group (n=29), while participants listened to audiobook segments in quiet and with a competing speaker, using their personal hearing devices (CI and HA). A hierarchical encoding framework incrementally added word onset, word frequency, and word surprisal as predictors of the EEG signal. Attentional modulation was assessed by comparing encoding scores for attended versus ignored speech. All three groups showed clear neural responses to word onset, frequency, and surprisal for speech in quiet. Surprisal tracking emerged at 400~ms in TH participants, 500~ms in HA users, and 600~ms in CI users, weakest in the CI group. All three groups exhibited attentional modulation of surprisal tracking. Word frequency yielded significant encoding gains in quiet only for TH and HI listeners, not CI users. We show for the first time that CI users exhibit significant, attention-modulated neural responses to word surprisal. More broadly, surprisal tracking was present across all hearing-impaired groups but weakest in CI users, the cohort with the greatest difficulty understanding speech in noise.

Article.Authors: Kozawa, R.; Sawada, S.; Kiumi, H.; Hamada, S.; Kitamura, M.; Yamamoto, M.; Wakazaki, M.; Sato, M.; Toyooka, K.; Ohno, N.; Takemura, H.; Ohtsuka, T.; Hagiwara, A.
Article.Abstract: integrates sensory and motor information and transmits signals to the muscles via motor neurons. The sole cerebellar output neurons, Purkinje cells (PCs), receive two main inputs from climbing fibers (CFs) and parallel fibers (PFs), which are the axons of granule cells (GCs). The serine/threonine kinase liver kinase B1 (LKB1) regulates GC migration; however, its role in PF synapses remains unclear. Conventional electron microscopy showed a slight increase in the PF terminal area in LKB1 cKO mice, whereas three-dimensional reconstructions revealed no significant differences in bouton morphology except for an increased mitochondrial volume ratio. In contrast, the proportion of PF boutons forming multiple synapses with PC spines was higher in LKB1 cKO mice than in controls, potentially altering synaptic inputs to PCs and contributing to downstream changes in cerebellar output and reduced presynaptic occupancy at neuromuscular junctions. These findings highlight the importance of LKB1 in GCs for maintaining PF-PC synaptic remodeling and cerebellar circuit integrity, which may contribute to motor coordination.

Article.Title: A plasma proteomic atlas of rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders reveals convergent molecular signatures, neurodegenerative overlap, and a cross-disorder severity index
Article.Authors: Ramirez, R. N.; Aumann, M.; Wieczorek, L.; Elmizadeh, S.; Misko, A.; Weiss, Y.; Szobota, S.; Powers, B.; Sasaki, S.; Rizzo, M.; Jagadish, S.; Laranjo, M.; Davis, N.; Manry, J.; Cattin Messaoudi, M. E.; Hipp, J.; Hawtin, R.; Younginger, B.; Miller, N.; Wright, K.; Viggiano, G.; Poliquin, S.; Morris, T.; Yavarow, Z.; Aguilar, N.; Terala, A.; Keener, W.; Hatcher, K.; Ricupero, C.; Bain, J.; Kravis, E. Article.Abstract: Rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders are individually too small for well-powered biomarker studies, and each is typically studied alone. We present a harmonized plasma proteomic resource that treats them together: over 10,000 proteins measured across 27 rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders and unaffected family members, 26 of them with enough participants for differential abundance analysis, paired with standardized adaptive behaviour phenotypes and released with the full analysis pipeline. Aggregating across disorders makes shared biology visible that single-disorder studies cannot resolve. Genetically distinct disorders converge onto two proteomic clusters separated along a single dominant axis, distinguishing cytoskeletal and vesicle-trafficking proteins from metabolic and hepatic ones; the grouping is independent of gene function and of clinical classification, indicating convergence on shared downstream biology rather than gene-specific pathology. Epilepsy leaves a reproducible plasma signature detectable across disorders and largely independent of genotype, identifying candidate markers of seizure burden that are shared rather than syndrome specific. These proteomes also overlap those of adult neurodegenerative disease: most disorders are enriched against at least one signature of Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, frontotemporal dementia or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, more often inversely than concordantly, placing early-life monogenic disorders on a shared axis with late-onset degeneration. A multivariate severity index built from plasma proteins tracks adaptive communication ability in disorders held out entirely from model training and distinguishes severity among individuals who share a diagnosis rather than only separating disorders from one another. Twenty-four of the prioritised cross-disorder proteins have a recorded drug interaction, several with agents already approved for other indications. Recruitment was concentrated at single sites for a subset of disorders, and results for those disorders are reported separately and descriptively throughout. Collectively, these findings support a shift from single-gene to pathway-based, cross-disorder trial strategies that leverage convergent biomarker panels and mechanistically informed, potentially repurposed interventions.

Article.Title: Electrophysiological correlates of placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia during the anticipation and delivery of pain
Article.Authors: Baumgarten, A.; Schlitt-Nguyen, F.; Hartmann, H.; Schmidt, K.; Rose, M.; Timmann, D.; Nio, E.; Kruithof, E. S.
Article.Abstract: Positive and negative expectations can substantially shape pain and analgesic treatment outcomes, highlighting the need to elucidate neural mechanisms underlying placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia. The primary aim of this feasibility study was to assess adaptations to an established placebo-nocebo conditioning pain paradigm in the context of electroencephalography (EEG). The secondary aim was to assess EEG correlates of placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia during the anticipation and delivery of experimental heat pain in healthy volunteers. Placebo and nocebo effects as well as positive and negative pain expectations were successfully established, demonstrating paradigm effectiveness. EEG results showed increased theta, alpha and beta power in the placebo compared to the control condition during pain delivery, and in the nocebo compared to the control condition during pain anticipation and delivery. Additionally, gamma-band power was increased in the nocebo compared to the placebo condition as a function of a higher perceived pain intensity. Taken together, feasibility of the EEG-compatible placebo-nocebo conditioning pain paradigm was demonstrated. Furthermore, our EEG results are in line with previous findings that, in the context of placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia, link theta-, alpha- and beta-band activity to top-down processing, and gamma-band activity to expectation-modulated sensory processing.

Article.Title: Implication of the amyloid precursor protein expressed in GABAergic interneurons for CA3 neuronal dynamics
Article.Authors: Erhardt, A.; Moreira de Sa, A.; Deforges, S.; Ferreira Rodrigues, E.; Kees, A. L.; Mulle, C.
Article.Abstract: The amyloid precursor protein (APP), a key player in Alzheimers' disease (AD, is ubiquitously expressed in a large majority of neurons, including GABAergic interneurons (INTs) in the hippocampus. We selectively deleted APP, and its homolog APLP2 to prevent compensatory mechanisms, in CA3 INTs. We categorized INTs into different clusters based on morphological and electrophysiological properties, and detected only subtle differences in intrinsic excitability and dendritic complexity between control and conditional KO INTs. In contrast, the selective deletion of APP/APLP2 in CA3 INTs impaired the amplitude and kinetics of spontaneous inhibitory currents in CA3 pyramidal cells (PCs). We further performed in vivo silicon probe recordings within CA3 in head-fixed awake mice to investigate the impact of APP/APLP2 deletion on CA3 circuit activity. By analysing oscillations and the spiking activity of putative CA3 PCs and INTs we revealed alterations in the cross-frequency coupling at oscillatory frequencies in the low gamma range, as well as in the strength of connections specifically between INTs. Our work helps better understand the physiological contribution of APP to network activity and to excitatory/inhibitory balance within hippocampal circuits, which are impaired in AD.

Article.Title: Probe-assisted Structural Topography Reveals In-tissue Lesion Heterogeneity in Alzheimer's Disease
Article.Authors: Wang, F.; Sun, X.; Zhao, Q.; Hu, Y.; Xu, L.; Zhang, S.; Cui, B.; Li, D.; Zhang, J.; Chen, W.; Liu, C.; Piatkevich, K. D.; Yang, D.
Article.Abstract: Disease lesions are typically defined by morphology, yet this classification often masks underlying structural heterogeneity. Leveraging PASTA, we quantify plaque maturity via the Protofibril Index (PFI) at sub-lesion level, and resolve the three-dimensional (3D) in-tissue architecture of A{beta} plaques at ~30 nm resolution, identifying radially extended A{beta} branches as fundamental structural units. PASTA enables structural mapping across plaque developmental stages to reconstruct their dynamic growth trajectories, resolving two distinct assembly lineages (dense and loose) with divergent growth paths that converge to a mixed terminal subtype and share a common transition point. We further applied PASTA for mapping microglial engagement, linking interdigitated microglial contacts to dense plaque compaction and uncontacted fibril branches to loose morphology. Together, PASTA provides an unprecedented framework for understanding A{beta} heterogeneity, nanoscale architecture, and microglial-mediated remodeling in AD.

Article.Authors: Maddipatla, R.; Guo, E.; Bartuzel, M. M.; Cai, Y.; Zhang, A.; Moussa, K.; Yiu, G. C.; Zawadzki, R. J.; Jonnal, R. S.

Article.Title: Torsion in motion: the visual system as a three-axis gimbal
Article.Authors: Mendez, A. H.; Otero-Millan, J.; de la Malla, C.; Lopez-Moliner, J.
Article.Abstract: Eye movements are usually characterized by where we look and represented using the two rotational degrees of freedom that direct the line of sight onto a target. The third, torsion about the line of sight, is often regarded as a limited response and has rarely been measured outside the laboratory. Yet the conditions producing the largest torsional responses, looking at a target straight ahead, are the ones that dominate natural walking. Here we tested whether torsion is present during this pervasive behavior and measured its impact on the visual input. Ten participants walked toward a distant target wearing a mobile eye tracker fitted with an iris camera to estimate torsion. Comparing iris feature rotations in the eye camera with simulated projections of candidate three-dimensional eye rotations, eye rotations were poorly explained without torsion and best explained by substantial torsional counter-rotation to head roll (gains .6-1). In the reconstructed retinal flow, this torsion cancelled the rotation added by head roll, leaving flow dominated by the observer's translation through the scene. Together, these results reveal that torsion is a substantial component of eye movements during locomotion and show that realistic models of oculomotor control and visual input during self-motion must account for all three of the eye's rotational degrees of freedom.

Article.Title: Beyond morphometry: Adolescent brain microarchitecture reflects sex differences in pubertal timing and hormones
Article.Authors: Christensen, E.; Dhamala, E.; Herting, M.; Bottenhorn, K. L.
Article.Abstract: Puberty is a sensitive neurodevelopmental period characterized by dramatic increases in adrenal and gonadal hormones, yet how these changes relate to human brain microarchitecture remains unclear. At ages 9 to 11 years, microarchitecture differences explained 11-13% of pubertal hormone variability in female youth and 4-6% in male youth. Further, microarchitecture features were differentially associated with pubertal hormones. Younger male youth exhibited widespread pubertal hormone-related differences in neurite density that consolidated into fewer, stronger associations with age, while female youth exhibited age-related expansion in pubertal cellular density differences. Anatomically, hormone-relevant microarchitecture consistently included reward processing hubs (e.g., pallidum, accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex). Because animal models suggest that DHEA and testosterone metabolites have opposing effects on GABAergic signaling, we hypothesize that future research should investigate gray matter microarchitecture for insight into pubertal hormone contributions to adolescent refinement of excitatory-inhibitory balance. Ultimately, these findings provide a starting point for investigating how pubertal endocrine changes shape reward circuitry and neurotransmitter systems, with potential implications for the pubertal emergence of sex differences in adolescent psychopathology.

StaGIC thus provides a differentiable framework for inferring multiscale cortical organization from non-invasive functional imaging.

Article.Title: Stage-Dependent Requirement for SETX in Human Motor Neuron Maturation and Survival
Article.Authors: Hosain, M. A.; Islam, M. K.; Duan, Y.; Cui, H.; Shen, X.; Ko, T.; Li, S.; Ding, B.
Article.Abstract: Senataxin (SETX) is an RNA/DNA helicase involved in transcription, RNA processing, R-loop resolution, and genome maintenance. Concordant decreases in selected RNAs and proteins supported disruption of neuronal structural and synaptic programs. Together, these findings reveal a stage-dependent requirement for SETX and identify SETX as an important regulator of transcriptional programs governing human MN maturation, function, and survival, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding the selective MN vulnerability associated with SETX-linked neurological diseases.

Article.Title: Biological Embedding of Social Experience Over Genomic and Neural Time Scales
Article.Authors: Peng, T.; Cash Ahmed, A. C.; Flores, M. E.; Legarra-Marcos, N.; Hernaez, M.; McLane-Svoboda, A. K.; McLane-Svoboda, S. B.; Saha, D.; Robinson, G. E.

Article.Title: Modeling CNS inflammatory demyelination using myelin-directed CAR T cells
Article.Authors: Cordano, C.; Gupta, S.; Guglielmetti, C.; Shepherd, C.; Heady, M.; Duecker, J.; Abdelhak, A.; Ng, B.; Zhu, R.; Yu, W.; Sagan, S.; Stefanoff, D.; Sin, J.; Beaudry-Richard, A.; Montevirgen, A.; Kozanno, L.; Hauser, S.; Wilson, M.; Zamvil, S.; Green, A.; Lim, W. A.; Simic, M.
Article.Abstract: Multiple sclerosis therapies remain confined to immunomodulatory agents that reduce inflammatory activity; none restores lost myelin, and disability can continue to accumulate independently of relapses. Development of remyelinating therapies has been hindered by models that incompletely reproduce the persistently inflamed lesions in which remyelination fails. Here we show that chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells targeting myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) build such lesions on demand. Human CD4+ CAR T cells transferred into immunodeficient mice infiltrated the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerve, producing perivascular demyelinating lesions, with reproducible optic nerve involvement. Within these discrete optic nerve lesions, treatment with the remyelinating compound clemastine reduced lesion size and improved optic nerve conduction, despite persistent inflammation. Thus, this MOG CAR T model reproduces key features of inflammatory demyelinating disease and enables testing of remyelinating therapies; more broadly, it introduces CAR T cells as programmable perturbative agents for building defined pathology in vivo.

Article.Title: Two co-occurring dynamics explain the organization of a natural movement repertoire
Article.Authors: Rubinstein, Y.; Moshkovitz, M.; Tishby Tamari, S.; Tiomkin, S.; Avitan, L.
Article.Abstract: Natural movements vary across multiple kinematic features, making it difficult to identify the dynamics shared across movements that generate a behavioral repertoire. Here, we provide a low-dimensional, interpretable generative account of the larval zebrafish hunting repertoire that links tail dynamics to behavioral outcomes. Analysis of thousands of movements spanning classically defined bout types revealed that repertoire diversity arises from continuous combinations of two simultaneously expressed dynamics: a slow, non-oscillatory bending component and a fast, oscillatory undulatory component. An analytical model captured these dynamics with six interpretable parameters and accurately reconstructed movements across the full repertoire and at two developmental stages. Different parameters predicted distinct aspects of movement outcome: maximum tail bend predicted change in heading angle, maximum tail curvature and movement duration predicted distance traveled, and oscillatory asymmetry predicted displacement direction. Relationships among the dynamical parameters constrained the movements and outcomes available to the animal. Key parameters could also be recovered directly from empirical tail kinematics, establishing them as experimentally accessible movement variables rather than model-dependent latent dimensions. Together, these results explain both the diversity and limits of a natural movement repertoire through constrained combinations of co-occurring dynamics.

Article.Title: Shared-Encoder Residual Task-Bridging Network for Motor Execution to Motor Imagery EEG Transfer in Brain-Computer Interfaces
Article.Authors: Wang, P.; Zhu, Y.; Xie, T.; Shen, W.; Zhou, Y.; Zhang, X.
Article.Abstract: Motor-imagery brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) hold promising application prospects in the fields of limb motor rehabilitation and human-computer interaction. However, the reliability of MI calibration data is limited by the difficulty of verifying participants' engagement during motor imagerywhereas motor execution (ME) provides a more readily supervised source of motor-related information.To investigate the potential of ME-derived knowledge for assisting MI decoding, we propose a Shared-Encoder Residual Task-Bridge Network (SE-RTBNet) to achieve accurate intra-subject cross-task knowledge transfer from ME to MI. The proposed framework consists of two major components: a shared encoder and a residual task-bridge module. The shared encoder extracts stable general motor representations from multi-band EEG signals and explores the shared feature patterns underlying ME and MI tasks. The residual task-bridge module is equipped with a performance-aware routing mechanism. It adaptively compensates for task-specific discrepancies between the two tasks, enabling precise cross-task feature alignment and knowledge transfer. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed model, experiments are conducted on three public datasets. The proposed method achieves average classification accuracies of 69.39%, 74.61%, and 98.94%, respectively, and outperforms existing transfer-learning algorithms in overall performance. Our model provides an effective strategy for reducing dependence on extensive MI calibration data through intra-subject cross-task knowledge transfer.The source code of the proposed SE-RTBNet is publicly available at https://github.com/Daisyzyx2002/SE-RTBNet

Article.Title: TDP2 couples PKA-CREB signalling to genome stability in human cerebellar development
Article.Authors: Wang, W.-P.; Ma, G.; Wang, F.; Deng, Y.; Zheng, Y.; Qiu, Z.; Lou, M.; Zhan, W.; Tao, J.; Tao, K. T.; Li, H.; Xie, J.; Liang, Z.; Zhou, L.; Sun, Y.; Wang, W.
Article.Abstract: Transcription and neuronal activity in the central nervous system generate abundant DNA damage, particularly DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), rendering neural cells - and cerebellar neurons especially - vulnerable to genome instability. Tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase 2 (TDP2, also known as TTRAP) resolves topoisomerase-2-linked DSBs, and biallelic TDP2 mutations cause spinocerebellar ataxia autosomal recessive 23 (SCAR23), yet how DNA repair shapes human cerebellar development is unknown. Here we model SCAR23 in cerebellar organoids derived from patient induced pluripotent stem cells carrying TDP2 c.650del and from prime-edited isogenic TDP2 c.400C>T lines. TDP2 inactivation caused organoid hypoplasia during FGF8b-dependent cerebellar specification, which was reversed by TDP2 complementation. TDP2 inactivation upregulated PKIB, a cerebellum-enriched inhibitor of protein kinase A, lowering PKA and CREB phosphorylation. Whole-genome sequencing showed excess de novo deletions in mutant organoids, enriched at candidate cis-regulatory elements of neurodevelopmental genes. Pharmacological activation of the cAMP-PKA cascade restored CREB phosphorylation, reduced DNA damage and rescued organoid growth. These findings link developmental signalling to genome maintenance in the human cerebellum and identify the cAMP-PKA-CREB axis as a candidate therapeutic target in DNA-repair-deficient cerebellar disease.

Article.Title: Innate development of cognitive functions and motor programs by chemoaffinity
Article.Authors: Schuessler, F.; Ciceri, S.; Sprekeler, H.
Article.Abstract: Humans and animals possess a rich repertoire of innate cognitive and behavioral abilities, yet the developmental mechanisms that establish the underlying neural circuitry remain unclear. Here, we show that a simple chemoaffinity-based connectivity rule, combined with stochastic cell-autonomous expression of cell adhesion molecules, can establish neural networks for a broad range of cognitive functions. We derive expression patterns that support the development of continuous attractor networks for path integration with toroidal grid-cell topology, networks with exponentially many discrete Hebbian assemblies, and circuits generating innate motor trajectories. Expression patterns can be combined in a modular way to encode recurrent networks for increasingly complex functions. Our results suggest that chemoaffinity may determine not only the anatomical organization of neural circuits, but also the structure of innate cognition and behavior.

Article.Title: Robustness of cortical distortion metrics to unmodelled OPM errors
Article.Authors: Mariola, A.; Mellor, S.; Bonaiuto, J. J.; Tierney, T. M.; Ashburner, J.; Balbastre, Y.; Lopez, J. D.; Barnes, G. R.
Article.Abstract: The estimate of cortical current flow from magnetic fields measured outside the head is an ill-posed problem. Recent work using head casts to minimise co-registration errors in conventional cryogenic magnetoencephalography (MEG) has shown that ground truth anatomy can be used to judge between different inversion schemes and metrics. Inversion algorithms or metrics that are insensitive to anatomical distortion are unlikely to reflect correct assumptions about the underlying current distribution. Here we aim to identify constraints when using this approach to validate current flow estimated from recordings made with optically pumped MEG (OP-MEG). To do so, we used simulations contaminated by different sources of (typically unmodelled) error. For example: error in the estimate of the true sensor positions or orientations and the effects of unmodelled gain changes. In accordance with previous work, with no unmodelled errors, distortion was minimized when the simulation and the inversion assumptions matched. We then quantified the amount of error (in mm) relative to the true cortical mesh that one might expect in empirical recordings (given gain, position and orientation errors). We found that the approach was tolerant to independent sensor position errors of less than 2 mm (per axis); orientation errors of less than 5 degrees; fixed array displacements of less than 10 degrees and to random sensor gain errors of less than 10%. Additionally, we tested this approach using two empirical OPM datasets. We found that source reconstructions based on both minimum norm and beamformer assumptions were sensitive to the underlying anatomy.

Article.Title: False-negative assessment of NanoNewron's NewroBus blood-brain barrier delivery platform in the JAX apical-domain-humanized TfR1 mouse
Article.Authors: Chakraborty, I.; Yin, T.; D'Adamio, L.
Article.Abstract: Humanized transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) mice are frequently used to evaluate blood-brain barrier (BBB) delivery, yet available strains differ in the extent and design of receptor humanization. Thirty mice received intravenous injections and were evaluated 24 h later. Brain parenchymal-fraction signals were reported in all 12 Cyagen mice, but in none of six JAX or 12 wild-type animals. Serum concentrations were measurable in every group and followed the same rank order for both constructs: Cyagen-CDS>Cyagen-HU>wild type >JAX. Mean CDS-to-JAX serum ratios were approximately 13--fold for both constructs. Compared with the Cyagen-HU strain, the CDS strain showed higher parenchymal concentrations; the ratio of mean parenchymal to mean serum concentration increased prominently for NN-841, but only modestly for NN-843. These findings indicate that model choice influences 24-h circulating concentrations and apparent BBB delivery. Circulating soluble human TfR1-mediated stabilization and endothelial TfR1-dependent transport are plausible, untested explanations for strain-dependent differences. A negative brain-delivery result in JAX #038212 alone cannot be taken as evidence that NewroBus lacks BBB delivery activity

Article.Title: Children become accurate years before they become fast: electroencephalography dates the separate maturation of decision components
Article.Authors: Cui, H.; Zhu, Y.; Li, B.; Huang, S.; Xu, T.
Article.Abstract: Perceptual decisions, a hallmark of cognitive development, become faster and more accurate from early childhood to adulthood, but whether the underlying components mature together, as a single global gain in processing speed would predict, or on separate timetables remains unclear. Behaviour alone cannot distinguish whether age-related improvement reflects clearer sensory encoding, more efficient evidence accumulation, fewer attention lapses or shorter non-decision processes, and prior direct measurements have typically come from small samples spanning limited age ranges. We analysed electroencephalography from 1,534 participants aged 5 to 21 years in the Healthy Brain Network during a contrast-change discrimination task. On the same trials, we measured the visual response and an evidence-accumulation signal, while a decision model estimated accumulation efficiency, attention lapses and non-decision time. We found that the visual response did not grow with age and retained 77% of its strength on missed targets. Instead, accuracy improved through fewer lapses and more efficient accumulation, both reaching half of their developmental change by about 9 years, whereas speed improved later: non-decision time shortened between 11 and 14 years and was longer in children whose accumulation signal rose later. These findings show that perceptual decision-making matures through dissociable stages rather than a single global increase in processing speed: mechanisms supporting accuracy mature in middle childhood, whereas those supporting the fastest responses continue to develop into early adolescence. This framework links developmental theories of processing speed to neural mechanisms of decision-making and provides a reference for identifying which component is disrupted in children who struggle.

Article.Title: Heterogeneous short-term plasticity reformats latent temporal information into an explicit population clock
Article.Authors: Buerkle, N. P.; Jeanne, J. M.
Article.Abstract: Short-term plasticity (STP) supports diverse synaptic-level computations, but how its organization across a circuit shapes emergent, network-level dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we first characterize STP across sparse inputs to Kenyon cells in the Drosophila mushroom body, revealing an unstructured and near-random organization that could not be explained by either pre- or postsynaptic cell identity. Rather than representing biological noise, an experimentally constrained network model instead shows how this heterogeneous organization reformats temporal information embedded in presynaptic spike rate trajectories into a behaviorally relevant population clock. Although an ideal observer could recover the same degree of temporal information from most alternative models, only the STP-mediated transformation made that information accessible to a biologically realistic decoder. Together, our results identify heterogeneous STP as a distributed biophysical mechanism that collectively functions as a temporal basis set to support circuit computations across variable input statistics.

Article.Title: Spinal Recurrent Inhibition Shapes the Dynamics of TMS-induced Motor-Evoked Potentials: A Computational Modeling Study
Article.Authors: Chien, V. S. C.; Bernasconi, E.; Müller, E.; Wang, P.; Lowery, M.; Liegey, J.; Wendt, K.; O'Shea, J.; Denison, T.; Ranieri, F.; Lazzaro, V. D.; Hlinka, J.; Knösche, T. R.; Weise, K.; Schmidt, H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) elicited by TMS reflect the integrity of the corticospinal pathway, yet the contributions of spinal and peripheral mechanisms to the shape of individual MEP waveforms remain poorly understood. Motor unit action potentials were derived from a finite-element hand model informed by diffusion tensor imaging of the first dorsal interosseous muscle. Models with (RC+) and without (RC-) recurrent inhibition were fitted to MEPs across TMS intensities in 10 healthy participants and compared with a phenomenological benchmark. Results: The RC+ model explained approximately 90% of waveform variance (mean R2 = 0.89), comparable to the benchmark (0.91; p = 0.32). Removing RC inhibition reduced waveform goodness-of-fit in every participant (mean R2 = 0.79; p = 0.002 vs. RC+), although input-output curve fits of MEP amplitude did not differ significantly between the two variants (p = 0.49). Conclusions: RC recurrent inhibition was required to reproduce the temporal structure of TMS-evoked MEPs. MEP waveforms thus carry more information than amplitude-based measures. Fitted to individual waveforms, the model can estimate unobservable spinal and peripheral activity, such as motor unit firing times, as well as participant-specific pathway parameters.

Article.Title: Persistent light-induced reduction of neuronal excitability in cortical neurons
Article.Authors: Lightning, A.; Ghersi-Egea, J.-F.; Di Rocco, F.; Guenot, M.; Kuczewski, N.
Article.Abstract: Visible light is widely used in neuroscience, yet its direct effects on neuronal activity in the absence of optogenetic manipulation remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated whether light stimulation can induce sustained changes in neuronal excitability. Using electrophysiological recordings in brain slices, we show that repeated pulses of blue light (5 s, 430 to 495 nm, 19 mW) produce a robust and persistent reduction in evoked firing activity in cortical neurons from both male and female mice, with an average decrease of ~60% relative to baseline. This inhibitory effect persisted for more than 20 minutes following stimulation and was associated with changes in both passive membrane properties and active ion channel conductance. To assess the potential translational relevance of visible-light stimulation as a future therapeutic approach for brain pathologies, we examined its effects in human cortical neurons where the , responses were more heterogeneous. While a subset of neurons exhibited similar inhibitory effects, others showed increased excitability, with this response occurring more frequently in neurons from female patients, suggesting a potential sex-dependent effect, which ultimately remains exploratory in the present work. In addition, a transient depolarizing response to light was observed in a minority of human neurons but not in mice. Because the contribution of light-induced heating was not experimentally isolated, the relative roles of photochemical and thermal mechanisms in these effects remain unresolved. These findings indicate that visible light exposure, independently of exogenous opsins, can induce long-lasting modulation of neuronal activity without evidence of acute cytotoxicity under the conditions tested. This raises the possibility that visible light may provide a previously underappreciated, opsin-independent mechanism for modulating neuronal activity, with potential relevance for disorders characterized by neuronal hyperexcitability. We outline a framework for future investigations, including validation in human systems, in vivo studies, optimization of stimulation parameters, and assessment of therapeutic potential in pathological models.

Article.Title: Timing and meaning in spoken thought relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics
Article.Authors: Song, D.; Rao, H.
Article.Abstract: When people think aloud, their reports vary in duration and in how closely successive thoughts are related in meaning. We asked whether these two dimensions relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics. Using 10-minute think-aloud fMRI scans from 75 adults, we quantified timing as variability in sentence-event duration and semantic continuity as similarity between adjacent grouped thoughts. In models including both measures, greater duration variability was associated with lower relative brain entropy (BEN), estimated from BOLD time series, in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (voxel wise FDR q < 0.05). This association persisted after adjustment for speech coverage, pause duration, articulation rate and event count. Semantic continuity was associated with differences in BOLD amplitude and synchrony across bilateral sensorimotor regions. These voxel wise associations fell below the FDR threshold after adjustment for speech coverage or pause duration. In a secondary atlas-based analysis, semantic continuity remained positively associated with local synchrony in Default C after adjustment for speech timing ({beta} = 0.517, P = 0.003). These findings link the timing of spoken reports to dorsolateral prefrontal brain activity irregularity and show how the sensorimotor correlates of semantic continuity covary with speech timing.
