Article.Title: Stability and flexibility in the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task emerge from goal-directed inference and planning under the free-energy principle
Article.Authors: Goto, D.; Idei, H.; Ogata, T.
Article.Abstract: In goal-directed behavior, the brain has to balance stability and flexibility. Stability means keeping the current recognition of environmental context, whereas flexibility means switching to a new one. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (WCST) is a standard task for studying this balance. In this task, stability is keeping the category estimate after correct feedback, and flexibility is switching it after incorrect feedback. Computational models have been proposed to elucidate the mechanism behind this balance. However, most models are given a variable for each category in advance, and every model treats correct feedback as desirable from the start. These models cover neither the category learning process nor the goal-directed process that adjusts the card selection to get correct feedback. To explain both processes under one principle, we modeled the WCST with a hierarchical recurrent neural network based on the Free Energy Principle (FEP). The model first infers the environment from observations and then plans the card selection to reach the goal. In both steps, the model minimizes prediction error based on the FEP. For inference, the error lies between the predicted signals and the received signals. For planning, it lies between the predicted feedback and the correct feedback. As a result, the latent states formed category-related clusters during learning. In the testing phase, the model kept the estimate after correct feedback and switched it after incorrect feedback. Removing the goal-directed process degraded the keeping and the switching. This implies that the two processes and this balance emerge from the FEP.

Article.Title: Spectral and complexity-based signatures of advanced concentration absorption meditation: A high-density EEG study of jhana
Article.Authors: Skov-Andersen, P. M.; van Lutterveld, R.; Paludanus, S.; Cahaly, T. J.; Potash, R. M.; Canales-Johnson, A.; Yang, W. F. Z.; Sacchet, M. D.
Article.Abstract: Advanced meditation provides structured and reproducible alterations of consciousness that are increasingly used as model states for the neuroscience of consciousness. Between practitioners, lower power and higher entropy accompanied more visual and auditory but less bodily content, a redistribution rather than an enrichment of experience; within practitioners, only reduced low-frequency power tracked wider attention and less narrative thought. ACAM-J thus emerges as a non-pharmacological model state at the high-complexity end of the spectrum of altered consciousness, and reveals a previously unquantified dissociation between neural complexity and experiential richness for specific ACAM-J states.

Article.Title: Distinct developmental organization of intrinsic brain dynamics supports different components of inhibitory control during adolescence
Article.Authors: Chang, D.; Song, D.; Rao, H.
Article.Abstract: Adolescent inhibitory control develops within a changing organization of intrinsic brain activity, yet the signal properties and cortical systems associated with different control demands remain unclear. Spatially standardized ALFF showed age associations in somatomotor and salience/ventral-attention networks. Contextual control, assessed with the AX Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT), showed the broadest age-dependent coupling: all four spatially standardized measures yielded voxelwise interactions surviving permutation-based cluster false discovery rate correction, and the frontoparietal BEN interaction survived network correction. Better action cancellation was associated with higher frontoparietal BEN without a corrected network age interaction. Independent cortical references further differentiated these patterns: raw BEN age-effect evidence was stronger toward association cortex, whereas the ALFF-AX-CPT age interaction was stronger toward sensorimotor cortex. Additional task interactions aligned with the second and third connectivity gradients. Core voxelwise AX-CPT findings persisted after age trimming. These findings link the differentiation of inhibitory-control demands to the developmental organization of complementary intrinsic signal properties across cortical systems, highlighting contextual control as a prominent locus of age-dependent brain-behavior coupling.

Article.Title: Neuronal activity regulates glycolysis to sculpt synaptic transmission
Article.Authors: Theisen, E. K.; Borden, P. M.; Clandinin, T. R.
Article.Abstract: Neuronal computation imposes rapid, localized changes in energy consumption, yet how energy production is regulated at such fine spatiotemporal scales is incompletely understood. Using two photon imaging of neuronal activity and energy metabolism in Drosophila , we show that neurons recruit glycolysis in less than a second, with cell-type and subcellular specificity. This coupling scales with neuronal activity and is regulated by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). Activity-induced glycolysis is tightly correlated with presynaptic sites in cholinergic neurons, and is required for cholinergic but not glutamatergic neurotransmission. In cholinergic neurons, glycolysis supports both energetic demand and acetylcholine biosynthesis, with ATP citrate lyase linking these functions by both activating acetylcholine biosynthesis and disinhibiting glycolytic flux. These findings establish glycolysis as a previously unrecognized regulator of cell-type specific computation.

Article.Title: Oligodendrocyte Development and Myelination in the 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome
Article.Authors: Hutchin, A.; Lokhandwala, M.; Rock, C.; Yee, A.; Baldemor, M.; Lara, R.; Turner, Z.; Sidhu, S.; Cocas, L.
Article.Abstract: The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is associated with a high risk of neurodevelopmental disorders, including a 25% chance of developing schizophrenia (SCZ). SCZ is prevalent in 0.4-0.7% of the population. Evidence suggests that the cognitive deficits of SCZ may be caused by neurodevelopmental disconnection due to impaired oligodendrocyte (OL) maturation and myelination. We hypothesized that the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome impairs OL life cycle progression, halting oligodendrocytes in their immature phase and preventing advancement to the mature stage. This in turn creates myelination changes, demonstrated by a decrease in myelin. To test this, we utilized a 22q11.2 deletion mouse model focusing on the prefrontal cortex (PFC), a late-myelinating brain region. We evaluated PFC regions (mPFC, dlPFC, mOFC, lOFC) in adolescent (P14 and P28) mutant mice and controls. Additionally, we examined the two-hit hypothesis of schizophrenia using a maternal separation model. At P28, mutant mice displayed a significant increase in immature OLs and mature OLs in the PFC, and a decrease in myelination and myelin process length compared to controls. At P14, mutant mice showed subtle reductions in oligodendrocyte precursor cells and subtle myelination alterations in the mPFC. When considering the two-hit hypothesis, we saw equivalent reductions in myelination in the genetic-only, environmental-only, and two-hit groups. Together, these data demonstrate that the 22q11.2 deletion impairs OL maturation and functional myelination between P14 to P28, a critical window for neurodevelopment. Examining the impact of SCZ on OLs could reveal key intervention targets before SCZ symptom onset, and may determine the role of OLs and the 22q11.2 deletion in neural disconnectivity in schizophrenia.

Article.Title: Precision of sensory representations in cortex is indexed by alpha power and pupil dilation, and tracks the dynamics of correlated noise
Article.Authors: Chekroud, S. R.; Kolling, N.; O'Reilly, J. X.
Article.Abstract: Sensory representations fluctuate in precision from moment to moment, shaping the fidelity of perception and memory. Population-coding theory proposes that these fluctuations are constrained by correlated variability within neural populations, yet linking these mechanisms to behaviour and brain state in humans has remained challenging. Here we combined EEG with an encoding-decoding framework to reconstruct orientation-selective population responses and quantify representational precision dynamically over time. Precision predicted subsequent working-memory performance and evolved in close correspondence with the dynamics of correlated variability between decoded orientation channels. Following stimulus onset, correlated variability was selectively suppressed among similarly tuned channels, the pattern predicted to maximise coding fidelity. Prestimulus alpha power and pupil size independently predicted representational precision, linking these dynamics to endogenous cortical and neuromodulatory state. Together, these findings identify candidate mechanisms and accessible physiological markers of representational precision in humans.

Article.Title: PROGMF: Progressive Multimodal Fusion and Representation Learning for Incomplete Neuroimaging Data
Article.Authors: Solomon, V.; Calhoun, V. D.; Adali, T.; Silva, R. F.; Angryk, R. A.; Liu, J.
Article.Abstract: Multimodal neuroimaging studies often involve cohorts with partially overlapping data modalities. Many conventional multimodal fusion methods rely on participants with complete observations across the selected modalities. We introduce Progressive Multimodal Fusion (ProgMF), a novel fusion framework for learning multimodal source representations from incomplete neuroimaging data without imputing missing observations. ProgMF integrates modalities sequentially through independent vector analysis (IVA), cross-stage component alignment, and anchor-guided representation transfer, allowing information learned from earlier-stage cohorts to inform subsequent multimodal decompositions. We evaluated ProgMF on four neuroimaging-inspired synthetic modalities, while varying subject overlap, observation noise, modality relatedness, and fusion orders. ProgMF generally achieved lower source-recovery errors than complete-case IVA and the evaluated imputation-based methods, with larger improvements as multimodal subject overlap decreased. We further applied ProgMF to structural MRI gray matter, resting-state functional network connectivity, and 18F-florbetapir (AV45) amyloid positron emission tomography data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. ProgMF achieved higher mean cross-modal fusion scores than the imputation-based baselines and a modest improvement over complete-case IVA. Among the 293 participants with complete multimodal observations, two recovered source component vectors showed significant associations with clinical diagnosis across cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia groups. Both sources were also significantly associated with cognitive performance and dementia severity. The recovered sources exhibited diagnosis-related structural and amyloid PET patterns involving regions such as the hippocampi, precuneus, and cingulate cortices. Our findings support progressive representation transfer as an effective approach for recovering coherent, interpretable multimodal sources from participants with incomplete modality coverage.

Article.Title: Counterfactual aging in individual digital twin brains uncovers a latent dimension of resilience to aging
Article.Authors: Takahashi, Y.; Idei, H.; Tomita, H.; Yamashita, Y.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive reserve concerns why the same aging causes less decline in some individuals than others, a question that digital twin brains can address by aging each individual in silico. Here we present Brain-VRNN, a connectome-constrained variational recurrent neural network trained on longitudinal multitask functional MRI. Its regenerated brain signals reproduced four functional aging markers of unseen individuals (r = 0.93-0.96) and identified each person (accuracy 0.98). Without cognitive scores, its global latent learned a trait dimension stable within each person, which helped predict future cognition. Crucially, when every individual underwent the same counterfactual aging, those with a lower trait value declined more, yet recovered up to 1.6 times as much with a reduction in body mass index, a modifiable dementia risk factor. Aging single regions showed that different markers decline through different regions, with a lateral temporal-angular region shared by all. Brain-VRNN brings within-person simulation to cognitive reserve.

Article.Title: Aging remodels the neuronal activity-dependent transcriptome
Article.Authors: Um, J.; Lei, H. C.; Nakamura, K.; Tycksen, E.; Adelman, J. W.; Pollina, E.
Article.Abstract: Experience-driven neuronal activity induces coordinated transcriptional programs in neurons and glia that support plasticity and memory. How aging reshapes these activity-regulated gene (ARG) programs, and whether activity mitigates or exacerbates aging phenotypes, remain open questions with implications for cognitive decline. Here, we develop novel-environment and chemogenetic paradigms to characterize age-dependent remodeling of ARG transcriptomes in the mouse hippocampus at single-cell resolution. Aging contracts youthful ARG programs in both gene number and dynamic range, a contraction that persists under controlled chemogenetic stimulation independent of behavior. In parallel, novel experience in older mice reveals a latent transcriptional competence. First, distinct sets of genes respond to neuronal activity selectively in older cells. Second, enhancing activity in older animals partially reverses, or buffers, basal aging-associated changes across the transcriptome. Novel experience counteracts aging-associated changes in the target genes of the memory regulator CREB1 and the ER-stress sensor ATF6 across cell types. These data constitute a resource for neuronal activity-dependent transcription across the lifespan and identify a basis for the benefits of cognitive engagement: novel experience buffers age-related transcriptional drift.

Article.Title: Thrombin cleavage of circulating osteopontin in the lung drives hippocampal neuroinflammation and acute delirium-like neurologic dysfunction after acute kidney injury
Article.Authors: Weerasinghe Mudiyanselage, P. D. E.; Ojha, R.; Ning, L.; Celorrio Navarro, M.; Tolby, L.; Suresh, A.; Morser, J.; Leung, L.; Honda, M.; Kon, S.; Friess, S. H.; Herrlich, A.
Article.Abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common clinical problem with high morbidity and mortality due to frequently occurring secondary organ complications, including acute neurologic dysfunction, such as delirium. Specific mechanisms responsible for this kidney-brain crosstalk are unknown but hypothesized to include uremic toxins and neuroinflammation secondary to systemic inflammation. Here we show that uremic mice with AKI show hippocampal monocytic neuroinflammation associated with acute delirium-like neurologic dysfunction only in the presence of circulating osteopontin fragments. Mechanistically, circulating osteopontin (OPN/Spp1) released by the injured kidney was cleaved by thrombin in the lung into OPN-N and OPN-C-terminal fragments. Both OPN fragments were required to drive upregulation of the monocyte chemoattractant chemokine-ligand-2 (CCL2) in hippocampal endothelial cells. AKI mice lacking OPN or unable to activate OPN by thrombin cleavage showed kidney injury and serum uremic toxin elevations like wt controls but were protected from hippocampal CCL2 upregulation, monocyte recruitment, and delirium-like symptoms. Systemic application of an OPN or CCL2 neutralizing antibody was protective. Our results suggest that a specific kidney-released circulating factor, osteopontin, drives acute neurologic dysfunction after AKI and challenge the widely held hypothesis that uremic toxins play a dominant role. They also identify thrombin cleavage of OPN as a potential therapeutic target and critical switch for the remote functions of circulating OPN.

Article.Title: Molecular analysis of 55 dopamine transporter variants from psychiatric patients reveals convergent mechanisms of dysfunction
Article.Authors: Campana, A.; Alves da Silva, L.; Degrandmaison, J.; Stoier, J. F.; Kastner, N.; Paggi, L. A.; Kooti, F.; Klein Herenbrink, C.; Newman, A. H.; Sitte, H. H.; Werge, T.; Herborg, F.; Stockner, T.; Gether, U.
Article.Abstract: Rare genetic variants are increasingly recognized as contributors to neuropsychiatric disease and may reveal underlying pathobiological mechanisms. The dopamine transporter (DAT), encoded by SLC6A3, regulates dopaminergic neurotransmission through rapid dopamine (DA) reuptake. Although disease-associated DAT variants have been linked to disorders ranging from infantile parkinsonism to neuropsychiatric disease, the molecular basis of DAT dysfunction remains poorly understood. Here, we systematically investigated 55 DAT missense variants identified in the iPSYCH2012-nested case-control cohort. By assessing transport activity, inhibitor binding, cell-surface expression, subcellular localization, amphetamine responsiveness and constitutive DA efflux, we resolved the variants into seven phenotypic classes. These reflected distinct molecular defects, including impaired substrate and ion coupling, destabilized intramolecular interactions, and defective folding, trafficking or surface expression. Molecular dynamics simulations provided structural insight into representative variants. Collectively, our findings reveal mechanistic convergence of genetically diverse DAT variants and establish a framework for interpreting the pathogenicity of newly identified SLC6A3 variants.

Article.Title: Cask dysfunction in inhibitory neurons reveals distinct synaptic and epileptic phenotypes in mouse models of CASK-related disorder
Article.Authors: Jiang, K.; Lee, D.; Yang, L.-T.; Luo, Z.; Karatayev, S.; Menon, N.; Vaidya, B.; Medico, S.; Xue, M.
Article.Abstract: Epilepsy is a major neurological manifestation of genetic neurodevelopmental disorders, yet how genetic disruptions produce distinct seizure phenotypes remains poorly understood. CASK-related disorder is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder frequently accompanied by epilepsy. It is caused by pathogenic variants in CASK, which encodes calcium/calmodulin-dependent serine protein kinase, a protein with diverse molecular functions. Here, we establish sex-specific mouse models of CASK-related disorder and identify epileptic phenotypes in both sexes. Cell type-specific Cask deletion identifies inhibitory neurons as a critical cellular locus of distinct forms of epileptic activity. Cask deficiency in parvalbumin- or somatostatin-expressing inhibitory neurons primarily causes spike-wave discharges or motor seizures, accompanied by reduced spontaneous or evoked inhibitory synaptic transmission, respectively. Thus, Cask dysfunction in different inhibitory synapses and circuits produces distinct seizure phenotypes. These findings reveal how cell type-specific synaptic dysfunction shapes epilepsy in CASK-related disorder and may provide insights into diverse neurological phenotypes of neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Title: Modern speech recognition systems exhibit human-like word recognition but superhuman use of statistical dependencies between words
Article.Authors: Magaro, A.; Elbanna, G.; Shook, E.; Kell, A.; Saddler, M. R.; McDermott, J. H.
Article.Abstract: Advances in machine learning have yielded machine systems that approach human performance on real-world perception tasks. For speech recognition, it remains unclear whether such models' behavior resembles that of humans. We addressed this question by measuring word recognition abilities in humans and models across 272 speech distortions, providing a detailed behavioral fingerprint. Three recent industry speech recognition models trained on hundreds of years of speech outperformed humans. However, in conditions where linguistic context was removed, they matched human performance well, suggesting that the models are superhuman in their ability to leverage statistical dependencies between words. Experiments manipulating model training data suggest that training data variability and realism contribute to the match to human perception. Overall, the results show that superhuman performance is now possible with systems that are optimized over enough data and suggest that accurate models of human speech recognition require optimization over appropriate tasks and amounts of speech.

Article.Title: The global geometry of optimal neural representations
Article.Authors: Tian, G. J.; Doiron, B.
Article.Abstract: Efficient coding hypothesizes that neural activity optimally represents information under resource constraints. The global structures of such optimal population codes are difficult to study theoretically, and previous works have usually resorted to either focusing on local properties like fine discrimination or placing restrictions on the parametric forms of neural tuning. We address the general problem by analytically deriving the neural representation that minimizes the all-pairs average classification error of a one-dimensional circular variable under various forms of neural response noise. Our method is based on formulating the space of neural response distributions as a statistical manifold whose geometry can be simplified through a generalized version of variance-stabilizing transformations. The theory fully characterizes the complete family of optimal population codes and allows us to make two novel predictions. First, an optimal code should allow the existence of oppositely peaked bimodal tuning curves. Second, there should be a correlation between spike count variability and tuning sharpness. We validate both of these predictions in the mouse head direction system.

Article.Title: Region-Specific Changes in the Aging Enteric Nervous System
Article.Authors: Marciano, J. H.; Druckmann, S.; Becker, L. S.; Kaltschmidt, J. A.
Article.Abstract: As human life expectancy increases, understanding the physiological changes that accompany aging becomes increasingly important. Gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction is common with age, and age-related changes in the enteric nervous system (ENS), which regulates GI motility, may contribute to this decline in function. Studies of the aging ENS have reported contradicting results, potentially reflecting the substantial regional heterogeneity of the ENS and the fact that most studies focus on only one or two areas of the GI tract. Neurons in the myenteric plexus, which regulate intestinal contractions and motility, are organized into ganglia that form circumferential stripes along the length of the gut. Here, we systematically compare neuronal and glial density and organization across all five regions of the small and large intestine in young (3-4 month-old) and aged (22-26 month-old) mice. We find that neuronal density remains unchanged with age across all regions, despite localized changes in ganglia organization. Although the overall stripe-like arrangement is preserved, ganglia are less aligned with stripes in the duodenum and ileum, while those in the ileum and distal colon are smaller, contain fewer neurons, and have a greater proportion of neurons located outside the ganglia. Glial cell numbers vary regionally with age, increasing in the duodenum and distal colon but decreasing in the proximal colon. The proportion of Calretinin+ neurons, meanwhile, remains stable across the small intestine. Together, these findings reveal that aging is associated with selective, region-specific remodeling of myenteric plexus cytoarchitecture rather than uniform structural decline across the GI tract. This comprehensive regional analysis may help reconcile conflicting reports of age-related changes in the ENS.

Article.Title: Optogenetic RNA relocalization reveals causal neural function in vivo
Article.Authors: Cai, S.; Deng, B.; Fu, M. L.; Alusa, A.; Prakhar, P.; Wu, G.-H.; Choi, A. A.; Han, D.; Situ, Y.; Han, M.; Zhu, Y.; Wu, X.; Chiu, W.; Hong, G.; Wang, S.; Qi, L. S.
Article.Abstract: RNA localization dictates where translation occurs, yet its disease role is unclear because most assays manipulate abundance, not position. We develop an optogenetic CRISPR-dCas13 system (Opto-CRISPR-TO) that repositions endogenous RNAs with subcellular precision, second-scale kinetics, and reversibility, enabling causal tests in vivo. In cells, Opto-CRISPR-TO routes diverse RNAs to organelles and ribonucleoprotein granules with multiplex, bidirectional control, revealing distinct RNA behaviors in centrosomes and P-bodies. In mouse retina, acute (4-hour) mislocalization of Actb mRNA redirects {beta}-actin protein, remodels synaptic architecture and cell positioning, and persistently impairs vision. Thus, RNA location governs proteome topology and neural circuit output, and brief mislocalization drives lasting dysfunction. The approach generalizes across targets, compartments, and cell types, establishing a framework for probing RNA localization mechanisms in development, plasticity, and degeneration.

Article.Title: Alpha-synuclein and neuromelanin converge to promote Parkinsons disease pathology
Article.Authors: Nicolau-Vera, A.; Gonzalez-Sepulveda, M.; Cladera-Sastre, J. M.; Cuadros, T.; Parent, A.; Roch, G.; Marongiu, J.; Huynh, B.; Mahabadian, A. A.; Su, F.; Chatterton, Z.; Hoyo, J.; Laguna, A.; Fu, Y.; Halliday, G.; Vila, M.
Article.Abstract: Parkinsons disease (PD) is defined by the preferential degeneration of neuromelanin (NM)-containing dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra (SN), accompanied by intraneuronal inclusions rich in alpha-synuclein (aSYN). However, the mechanistic relationship between NM accumulation and aSYN pathology remains unclear. Here, we reveal a bidirectional pathogenic relationship between aSYN and NM. In a rat model that recapitulates age-dependent, human-like NM accumulation via targeted tyrosinase (TYR) expression, co-expression of aSYN accelerates NM buildup, enhances aSYN oligomerization, and aggravates nigrostriatal degeneration. Mechanistically, aSYN oligomerization in NM-producing rats decreases vesicular dopamine storage and impairs vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane, increasing cytosolic dopamine availability for oxidation into NM. Together, these findings support a pathogenic feedback loop in which elevated aSYN accelerates NM synthesis through disrupted dopamine compartmentalization, while NM accumulation further promotes aSYN aggregation and neuronal loss. This aSYN-NM axis may underlie the preferential vulnerability of pigmented nigral neurons in PD and provide a mechanistic framework for the development of future targeted therapeutics.

Article.Title: Membrane voltage multistability in coupled glial cells
Article.Authors: Janjic, P.; Solev, D.; Zhou, M.; Kocarev, L.
Article.Abstract: Growing interest to describe the electrical behavior of glial cells, mainly astrocytes, in intact brain tissue poses more and more challenges to commonly accepted belief they only respond in a linear manner in uptake of the excess of extracellular potassium and maintenance of their network equipotentiality. Their highly conductive mutual interconnections via gap junction (GJ) connections introduce yet another class of nonlinear elements. As more studies report nonlinearities in membrane voltage V_m dependence of both, the membrane and junctional conductances, the need to formulate minimal dynamical models of their transient behavior is getting more acute. Since ODE models of coupled cells, even in simplest 1-d arrays, require simplified descriptions and small set of parameters, rare quantitative studies on glia makes the task even more difficult. This study attempts to qualify a self-coupled cell, or a glial cell coupled to fixed voltage as useful system for detecting the nature of instabilities and transitions coming from coupling. In a novel biophysical model of coupled astrocyte, we introduce nonlinear kinetics of deactivation for large junctional voltages for the first time. We found that N-shaped nonlinearities and corresponding fold structure in the vector field of isolated cell serves as a baseline on top of which coupling nonlinearities enrich the bifurcation picture. Numerical simulations of 1-d array of coupled astrocytes show that coupling increases the propensity of astrocytic V_m to bistability and front propagation. We believe that presented illustrations of possible effects of coupling nonlinearities will motivate neurobiologists to further explore their impact in disease.

Article.Title: How can brain-like dynamics and phonetic generalization emerge in speech representations? A study using self-supervised models
Article.Authors: Liu, O. D.; Tang, H.; Feldman, N. H.; Goldwater, S.
Article.Abstract: Speech representations in the human brain do not simply mirror the instantaneous speech signal; rather, they display several properties that are hypothesized to facilitate the integration of speech sounds into words. In particular, neural encodings of speech maintain information that has dissipated from the acoustics, and have also been argued to abstract over variability in how individual speech sounds are produced. Here, we investigate how such characteristics could arise. We introduce a computational framework that uses modern neural network models from speech technology to examine two factors in particular: the learning mechanism and the learning input. We find that self-supervised models trained without lexical or semantic feedback developed temporal dynamics similar to brain representations, regardless of whether they were trained on speech or non-speech audio. In contrast, only models trained on speech learn to abstract over variability due to word position and phonetic context. Overall, our results suggest that domain-general learning mechanisms can lead to several important properties of speech representations, but in some cases require domain-specific input in order to do so.

Article.Title: A nonlinear inhibition pathway underlying cortical responses to tuned holographic optogenetic perturbations
Article.Authors: Chau, H. Y.; Oldenburg, I. A.; Miller, K. D.; Palmigiano, A.
Article.Abstract: Optogenetics enables causal manipulation of cortical activity. Theory is essential for predicting network-mediated perturbation responses, which are often counterintuitive. Existing approaches have relied on linear approximations, which can fail for multi-neuron holographic perturbations. We develop a nonlinear theory of responses to such perturbations in networks with cell-type-specific structured connectivity. We apply our theory to mouse V1 data, which shows cotuned-ensemble suppression: perturbing spatially clustered neurons with similar preferred orientations yields stronger short-range suppression than perturbing untuned ensembles. We show that cotuned-ensemble suppression requires a nonlinear inhibition pathway, and predict a mediating inhibitory cell type that is feature-tuned and suppresses excitatory neurons. Indeed, recent data show that somatostatin-positive (SST) interneurons have both properties. We further predict that, relative to untuned ensembles, cotuned ensembles suppress parvalbumin-positive but facilitate SST neurons, and link both effects to SST response variance. This framework reveals how nonlinear inhibition sculpts cortical dynamics and establishes a predictive theory for targeted optogenetics.

Article.Title: Torsion in motion: the visual system as a three-axis gimbal
Article.Authors: Mendez, A. H.; Otero-Millan, J.; de la Malla, C.; Lopez-Moliner, J.
Article.Abstract: Eye movements are usually characterized by where we look and represented using the two rotational degrees of freedom that direct the line of sight onto a target. The third, torsion about the line of sight, is often regarded as a limited response and has rarely been measured outside the laboratory. Yet the conditions producing the largest torsional responses, looking at a target straight ahead, are the ones that dominate natural walking. Here we tested whether torsion is present during this pervasive behavior and measured its impact on the visual input. Ten participants walked toward a distant target wearing a mobile eye tracker fitted with an iris camera to estimate torsion. Comparing iris feature rotations in the eye camera with simulated projections of candidate three-dimensional eye rotations, eye rotations were poorly explained without torsion and best explained by substantial torsional counter-rotation to head roll (gains .6-1). In the reconstructed retinal flow, this torsion cancelled the rotation added by head roll, leaving flow dominated by the observer's translation through the scene. Together, these results reveal that torsion is a substantial component of eye movements during locomotion and show that realistic models of oculomotor control and visual input during self-motion must account for all three of the eye's rotational degrees of freedom.

Article.Title: AutoMorphoTrack: A modular framework for quantitative analysis of organelle morphology, tracking, and image colocalization
Article.Authors: Bayati, A.; Schumacher, J. G.; Chen, X.
Article.Abstract: AutoMorphoTrack is an open-source Python framework for analyzing organelle morphology, centroid tracking and colocalization in multichannel fluorescence microscopy. Steps in the analysis are connected by means of shared masks and persistent identities. Fifty synthetic sequences and eight publicly available microscopy studies were used in evaluation. A lack of sufficient vesicle coverage with the original, revised configuration motivated the development of a separate frozen particle pipeline. Six movies were used in parameter estimation and six were set aside for validation within a previously assessed study containing 284 manually tracked trajectories across all 12 movies. The mean accepted-link recall on the validated movies improved to 0.696 from 0.212, when fixed top-hat preprocessing was changed to the particle pipeline. For the 50 synthetic sequences, the mean Dice coefficient improved to 0.877 with the particle pipeline from 0.532 with the original revised configuration. External masking of mitochondria yielded mean Dice of 0.369 for seven MoDL SIM patches and 0.060 for thirteen Myofibril confocal patches. Reproducibility tests using source-pinned command-line and interactive notebook routes recovered defined outputs on named fixtures. However, further validation for other organelles and membranes is warranted. Colocalization describes fluorescent overlap, and does not establish membrane contact or functional interaction.

Article.Title: The ANKLE2-VRK1 pathway promotes neuronal resilience by preserving proteostasis during aging
Article.Authors: Dietze, M.; Mambou, E. A.; Primavera, S.; Newlin, H.; Link, N.
Article.Abstract: ANKLE2 is a key regulator of neural stem cell division through inhibition of the kinase VRK1, and mutations in either ANKLE2 or VRK1 cause rare neurodevelopmental disorders that impact brain growth and development. Recent evidence showing that reduced ANKLE2 activity promotes Tau aggregation in vitro suggests that ANKLE2 may also contribute to age-related neurodegenerative processes; however, its role post-development remains unknown. Using Drosophila, we show a novel role for the Ankle2-ballchen (VRK1) pathway in maintaining neuronal resilience and proteostasis. Pan-neuronal and motor neuron reduction of Ankle2 in adult animals shortens lifespan, impairs motor function and accelerates neuronal loss. Lifelong reduction produces more severe phenotypes including an upright wing posture reminiscent of Drosophila Parkinsons disease models. Mechanistically, loss of Ankle2 causes the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins throughout the central nervous system, indicating impaired protein clearance. Ankle2 mutants have reduced proteasome activity with activation of compensatory degradative pathways, supporting this hypothesis. Loss of Ankle2 behavioral and protein accumulation phenotypes are rescued by expression of human ANKLE2, indicating neuronal ANKLE2 function is conserved between flies and humans. Importantly, VRK1/Ballchen reduction also rescues ubiquitin accumulation and behavior phenotypes caused by loss of Ankle2, demonstrating that the developmental Ankle2-VRK1 pathway is preserved and remains functionally important in aged neurons. More broadly, our findings reveal that a conserved developmental ANKLE2- VRK1 pathway is repurposed in aged neurons to maintain proteostasis and neuronal resilience, providing a mechanistic framework linking neurodevelopmental disease genes to age-associated neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Spinal Recurrent Inhibition Shapes the Dynamics of TMS-induced Motor-Evoked Potentials
Article.Authors: Chien, V. S. C.; Bernasconi, E.; Müller, E.; Wang, P.; Lowery, M.; Liegey, J.; Wendt, K.; O'Shea, J.; Denison, T.; Ranieri, F.; Lazzaro, V. D.; Hlinka, J.; Knösche, T. R.; Weise, K.; Schmidt, H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) elicited by TMS reflect the integrity of the corticospinal pathway, yet the contributions of spinal and peripheral mechanisms to the shape of individual MEP waveforms remain poorly understood. Objective: To develop a biologically grounded model of the spinal and peripheral motor pathway that can be fitted to individual MEP waveforms across TMS intensities, and to test whether Renshaw cell (RC) recurrent inhibition is required to reproduce them. Methods: Corticospinal volleys (D- and I-waves), reconstructed from published epidural recordings in humans, drove 100 conductance-based leaky integrate-and-fire alpha motor neurons coupled to an RC population. Motor unit action potentials were derived from a finite-element hand model informed by diffusion tensor imaging of the first dorsal interosseous muscle. Models with (RC+) and without (RC-) recurrent inhibition were fitted to MEPs across TMS intensities in 10 healthy participants and compared with a phenomenological benchmark. Results: The RC+ model explained approximately 90% of waveform variance (mean R2 = 0.89), comparable to the benchmark (0.91; p = 0.32). Removing RC inhibition reduced waveform goodness-of-fit in every participant (mean R2 = 0.79; p = 0.002 vs. RC+), although input-output curve fits of MEP amplitude did not differ significantly between the two variants (p = 0.49). Conclusions: RC recurrent inhibition was required to reproduce the temporal structure of TMS-evoked MEPs. MEP waveforms thus carry more information than amplitude-based measures. Fitted to individual waveforms, the model can estimate unobservable spinal and peripheral activity, such as motor unit firing times, as well as participant-specific pathway parameters.

Article.Title: Unified CEBRA learns shared neural latents across recordings to map single-neuron contributions to population codes
Article.Authors: Benquet, C.; Mirzaeri, H.; Schneider, S.; Mathis, M. W.
Article.Abstract: Neural computation is thought to rely on distributed populations; however, most single recording samples capture only a fraction of them, and rare cell types may contribute only a small proportion of neurons per session. Pooling many recordings could reveal how these populations encode information, but each recording samples different neurons, so their contributions cannot be easily compared directly. Here we show that recordings can be combined into a single model of all recorded neurons by aligning them with a shared label, used at both training and inference, placing every neuron's contribution to the population code on a common scale. This approach, called Unified CEBRA, retained interpretable task information across recordings in the monkey and mouse sensorimotor cortex, rat hippocampus, and mouse visual cortex. Pooling thousands of excitatory and inhibitory neurons from hundreds of sessions from mouse visual cortex, we found that the neurons that contributed most to the model's readout of visual features were not only the most strongly tuned, but also those that responded more reliably and were less coupled to co-recorded neurons. Unified CEBRA, therefore, can unveil coding principles studied at the population scale with mappable features to individual neurons from sparse, multi-session recordings using our new approach.

Article.Title: Dissociable patterns of neurophysiological alterations during guided search in schizophrenia and autism: Evidence from fixation-related potentials, alpha modulation, and functional MRI.
Article.Authors: Gonzalez-Moreira, E.; Martinez, A.; Aburto-Ponce, M. B.; Greisberg, M.; Beggel, O.; Tobe, R. H.; Franco, A. R.; Dias, E.; Javitt, D. C.
Article.Abstract: Schizophrenia (SZ) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are associated with convergent differences in social perception relative to non-autistic, non-schizophrenia controls (NC), but divergent patterns of alterations in early visual activity. Here, we used multimodal imaging during the Guided Visual Search task to investigate the differential patterns of early visual alteration across SZ and ASD including superior colliculus (SC) and pulvinar nucleus. In Experiment 1, simultaneous eye tracking and EEG were obtained from 91 individuals (35 NC, 20 ASD, 36 SZ). Fixation-related potential (FRP) was time-locked to fixation onset. In Experiment 2, fMRI during Guided Search was obtained from a partly overlapping sample of 71 individuals (27 NC, 25 ASD, 19 SZ). In behavioral analyses, SZ was associated with significantly prolonged search time (d=.74, p=.003), which was attributable primarily to reduced mean saccade amplitude, whereas ASD was associated with a small advantage (d=.35), which was not statistically significant. In EEG analyses, SZ was associated with reduced amplitude of the FRP P1 (lambda) response (d=1.15, p<.0001) relative to NC that remained significant following control for saccade size (p<.0001), but with normal task-related modulation of background alpha activity. In contrast, ASD was associated with normal FRP amplitude and larger alpha suppression (d=.83, p=.007) that was attributable to increased alpha levels during pre-task fixation (at matched pre-onset alpha levels, d=.14, p=.66). Within SZ, P1 correlated with the MCCB composite (r=.56, p=.001). Within ASD, ADOS-2 Communication correlated with P1 (r=.51, p=.024) and with the broadband change from pre-onset to search (r=-.51, p=.030). In fMRI, SZ was associated with correlated activation reductions in the Visual1 (Sidak p<.001) and Visual2 (Sidak p=.022) networks and SC (Sidak p=.019), whereas activation was unaffected in the Dorsal Attention and Frontoparietal networks, Frontal Eye Fields and pulvinar. In ASD, activation was increased in pulvinar (Sidak p[≤].038), but unaffected elsewhere. Cortical activation patterns associated with SC activation resembled those associated with P1 generation across groups. Article.Title: The Computational and Neural Basis of Zero-Shot Control in Dynamic Pursuit
Article.Authors: Kim, D.; Lee, J. J.; Hayden, B. Y.; Yoo, S. B. M.
Article.Abstract: Biological agents flexibly adapt their behavior to novel goals and environmental demands without additional training, yet the computational principles enabling such control remain unclear. Here, we propose that three cognitive constructs constitute minimal computational motifs for such flexible control: relational structure, spotlight attention, and affordance computation. We examine whether these constructs underpin flexible control in an embodied dynamic pursuit task that requires continuous integration of inter-entity relations, reward, and action feasibility, making it a suitable testbed for real-time control. By implementing these constructs within a multi-module graph convolutional network, we show that the model achieves zero-shot transfer across novel pursuit scenarios that vary in physics, target properties, and interaction policies such as fleeing or chasing, without additional training. Although not explicitly trained to do so, the model also exhibits change-of-mind (CoM) behavior, or mid-course target revision, a hallmark of flexible control exhibited by biological agents. Neural recordings from the primate dorsal anterior cingulate cortex revealed population-level signatures that link these constructs to neural dynamics, providing biological support for the proposed computational architecture.

Article.Title: Whole Brain Cellular Activation After Mu and NOP Receptor Agonism: Shared Regional Targets with Divergent Network Consequences
Article.Authors: Martinez, M.; Ozawa, A.; Van Zant, D.; Thornberry, J.; Toll, L.
Article.Abstract: Rationale Mu and nociceptin/orphanin FQ peptide (NOP) receptors are both Gi/o-coupled and inhibitory, yet opioid agonists increase neuronal activation across the brain. How this occurs, and whether it differs between naive and dependent animals or between receptor subtypes, is unresolved. Objectives To map and directly compare whole-brain cellular activation after acute mu agonist treatment, in opioid-dependent animals and after NOP receptor agonism. Methods TRAP2/Ai9 reporter mice received acute morphine (10 mg/kg), an escalating twice-daily morphine regimen producing dependence, or the NOP agonist Ro 64-6198 (0.6 mg/kg). Brains were cleared and imaged intact by light-sheet microscopy; tdTomato-positive cells were quantified across 198 grey-matter regions registered to the Allen CCFv3, and interregional co-activation networks constructed. Results All treatments shifted activation upward relative to vehicle, significantly so for morphine in males; acute morphine engaged the most regions, all increased. Sex differences were confined to magnitude: the whole-brain increase was significant in males but not females, and no region showed a condition x sex interaction after correction. Ro 64-6198 produced a substantially weaker profile, smaller in magnitude rather than anatomically restricted, with no region surviving correction. Fewer regions were activated in dependent animals than after acute morphine, with no region distinguishing the two. Dependence substantially altered interregional co-activation and changed hub composition, while global network organization showed no detected change. Conclusions Mu and NOP agonism are distinguished by response magnitude and network role rather than by regional identity; dependence likewise acts principally on the coordination of activity rather than on which regions are recruited.

Article.Title: Attentional prioritization enhances the accessibility of neural representations during working memory maintenance
Article.Authors: Zhang, M.; Akyurek, E.; Kruijne, W.
Article.Abstract: Given the limited capacity of working memory (WM), prioritization is essential for efficient information processing. Whether prioritization acts primarily at encoding, or dynamically shapes representations during maintenance, is currently unclear. Here, we employed a delayed response task and compared prioritization conditions in which the testing order of items was either known in advance or not. Behaviorally, prioritization selectively reduced guess rates and had little effect on precision. Using multivariate pattern analysis, we decoded stimulus information from EEG voltage as an index of item specific representations, and used alpha power decoding as an index of internal attention. Prioritization did not alter decodable representations during encoding. During maintenance, however, prioritization enhanced both voltage-based decoding and alpha power-based decoding for the prioritized item. Mediation analyses further revealed an indirect association between alpha-based attentional signals and behavior via voltage-based representational strength, consistent with the idea that internal attention supports performance by maintaining prioritized representations in an accessible state.

Article.Title: Hippocampal representations of temporal structure increase in scale and symmetry across development
Article.Authors: Friend, O. W.; Dutcher, A. M.; Varga, N. L.; Coughlin, C. A.; Preston, A. R.
Article.Abstract: Learning which experiences reliably co-occur in time is fundamental to episodic memory and improves markedly across childhood and adolescence. Although children and adults both engage the hippocampus while learning predictable sequences, the nature of the neural representations supporting statistical learning across development remains unknown. Here, we directly quantified item-level neural representations before and after children, early adolescents, and adults learned predictable temporal relationships between items, providing a direct measure of learning-related representational change. We identified three developmental shifts in hippocampal representation. First, although posterior hippocampus integrated temporally adjacent sequence elements similarly across age groups, integration of non-adjacent sequence elements increased with age in anterior hippocampus, indicating developmental expansion in the temporal scale of neural integration. Second, hippocampal representations changed in their directional organization, with children showing hippocampal representations reflecting only forward associations between adjacent events, whereas adolescents and adults exhibited bidirectional integration of sequence relationships. Third, functional connectivity between anterior hippocampus and frontoparietal cortex tracked statistical transition probabilities during learning and predicted memory performance. Together, these findings show that improvements in statistical learning during development reflect reorganization of hippocampal representations and hippocampal-cortical interactions, revealing how the developing brain constructs increasingly flexible representations of predictive temporal structure.

Article.Title: Investigating the impact of adverse life events on neuroanatomy across adolescence
Article.Authors: Wiersch, L.; Brosch, K.; Christensen, E.; Dhamala, E.
Article.Abstract: Background Adversity during adolescence can increase vulnerability to neuropsychiatric disorders. However, how various factors of adversity and stress can shape these effects, and whether these effects vary by sex, developmental stage, or reporting source have not been established. Methods Here, we used multivariate brain-based predictive models to examine how the number, appraisal (positive or negative), and impact of adverse life events during adolescence (reported either by the youth or their caregivers) are reflected in neuroanatomy (cortical thickness, surface area, cortical and subcortical grey matter volume). We used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study at 2-year (N=6,366, age 11-12), 4-year (N=5,035, age 13-14), and 6-year (N=5,953, age 15-16) follow-ups to examine neural correlates of adversity. Results Descriptively, youth, compared to their caregivers, reported more adverse life events, higher impact, and were more likely to appraise events negatively. Multivariate associations between adverse life events and neuroanatomy were sparse at the 2-year and 4-year follow-ups but emerged at the age of 15-16 (6-year follow-up). Among the significant associations, positively appraised events were predominantly associated with higher measures of cortical thickness, surface area, and volumes, whereas negatively appraised events mapped predominantly negatively on neuroanatomy. Conclusions Our analyses suggest that associations between childhood adversity and the brain vary across adolescent development. Furthermore, our results illustrate important differences between youth and caregiver reports, highlighting the importance of differentiating between reporting sources when interpreting the impact of adverse life events on neurodevelopment.

Article.Title: State-Dependent Organization of Microscale Functional Circuitry in Visual Cortex
Article.Authors: Biswas, R.; Wickrama Senevirathne, H.; Wang, Y.; Zhang, J.; Mukherjee, S.; Abbasi-Asl, R.
Article.Abstract: Directed functional connections between individual neurons, inferred from recorded activity, reflect information routing in cortex. Yet their organization across brain states and relation to synaptic connectivity remain poorly understood. Here, we present one of the largest single-neuron-resolution directed functional circuit maps, across about 45,000 neurons in four mouse visual areas. We inferred connections from deconvolved two-photon calcium activity with CITS, a causal-inference method designed for neural time series. In co-registered electron microscopy, CITS-inferred pairs were 3.0-fold more likely to be synaptically connected than other pairs. The map's organization aligned with synaptic connectivity at areal, laminar, and cell-type levels. In low and high pupil-linked arousal, the anterolateral area (AL) had the highest intra-areal density. The strongest inter-areal pathway linked AL with the rostrolateral area. This organization held in both states, yet mean connection strength was higher in high arousal in every scan, by 9.4% on average. Finally, stronger connections linked neurons with more similar stimulus-driven predictive performance in both states.

Article.Title: Children and adults use distinct neurocognitive mechanisms to support successful memory-based inference
Article.Authors: Coughlin, C.; Schlichting, M. L.; Morton, N. W.; Sherrill, K. R.; Moreau, M.; Preston, A. R.
Article.Abstract: Reasoning depends on connecting information across distinct experiences to derive knowledge that was never directly observed. Behavioral work indicates this capacity improves into emerging adulthood. However, it remains unclear whether these developmental gains reflect the quantitative strengthening of a single inference mechanism or qualitative changes in the knowledge representations and computations that support inference decisions. Here, we tested whether improvements in inference are linked to maturation of the hippocampus and posterior parietal cortex, resulting in age-related differences in how inference decisions are computed. We predicted that neural engagement in children (7-12 years) would track a variable-speed process, consistent with an iterative retrieval mechanism wherein distinct memories are retrieved and combined during inference. In contrast, neural engagement in adults would track a fixed-speed process, consistent with a direct inference mechanism supported by structured representations of shared relations across experiences. Using functional MRI combined with computational modeling of response times, we show that hippocampal activity predicts inference through iterative retrieval in both children and adults. In contrast, angular gyrus activity shows significant developmental differences in its relationship to both inference computations, with stronger associations with variable-speed processing in children and fixed-speed processing in adults. Moreover, we showed stronger relationships between fixed-speed computations and activation in both hippocampus and angular gyrus in adults relative to children. Together, these findings identify a developmental shift in the neural mechanisms supporting inference, suggesting that maturation of posterior parietal cortex may facilitate access to structured representations that capture links across events to enable more efficient inference.

Article.Title: Comparative Evaluation of Deep Generative Models for Capturing Topological Features in Brain Structural Connectivity Matrices
Article.Authors: Kumada, C.; Hiroyasu, T.; Hiwa, S.
Article.Abstract: Structural connectivity (SC) data are crucial for brain network analysis, but SC-based machine learning often suffers from limited data availability, hindering model generalization and robustness. Although data augmentation using deep generative models has attracted increasing attention, it remains unclear how different models capture the complex topological features of SC data. To clarify the model-specific generative characteristics of deep generative models for ROI-level weighted SC matrix generation, this study compares three representative models: variational autoencoder (VAE), Wasserstein generative adversarial network with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP), and denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM). We systematically evaluated these models using both synthetic datasets as diagnostic benchmarks to isolate model-specific biases in reproducing graph properties and two real-world SC datasets. Generation quality was assessed using graph-theoretic metric comparisons and visual inspection of the generated adjacency matrices across four training runs. For the empirical SC datasets, we also evaluated inter-subject variability and sample diversity. WGAN-GP performed consistently across synthetic datasets and achieved the strongest results on most metrics for both SC datasets, most closely reproducing variability and diversity. VAE captured average characteristics but underestimated sample variability. DDPM reproduced stochastic connection patterns but struggled with coordinate-specific patterns and run-to-run consistency. Despite WGAN-GP's balanced performance, each model had distinct strengths and limitations, emphasizing the need to consider relevant graph properties when comparing generative models. All models struggled to reproduce strict global constraints, such as planarity. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating structural constraints alongside statistical similarity and accounting for graph-specific properties when developing generative models.

Article.Title: Using atorvastatin-induced vascular weakness to model brain haemorrhage in vascularised cerebral organoids
Article.Authors: Crilly, S.; Sundararaman, S.; Haley, M. J.; Segantin, E.; Campbell, N.; Lafarge, E. J.; Cheeseman, A.; Fumado Navarro, J.; McKernan, D.; Couper, K. N.; Lomora, M.
Article.Abstract: Intracerebral haemorrhage is the most severe subtype of stroke; however, pre-clinical investigation often fails to translate to the clinic. Cerebral organoids offer an adaptable, in vitro model of human brain tissue for pre-clinical investigation of disease. We recently demonstrated that the tissue can be successfully vascularised to mimic the cerebrovasculature. Cerebrovascular weakness was induced with atorvastatin to mimic damage observed in intracerebral haemorrhage and to replicate the disease's pathological features. We used atorvastatin to disrupt functional morphology in human brain microvascular endothelial cells in 2D and 3D model systems. Whole human blood was added to initiate damage to cerebral tissues. Vascularised cerebral organoids exhibited loss of vascular integrity when treated with atorvastatin. Tissue was vulnerable to injury from human whole blood, and an innate immune response was initiated, resulting in increased cell death. Here we show that vascularised cerebral organoids demonstrate a novel model platform for investigating pathology associated with human whole blood insult in intracerebral haemorrhage.

Article.Title: Structural basis of CO2 valence coding in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Javorski, D.; Bergkirchner, B.; Ensinger, G.; Lingl, A.; Navolic, J.; Batawi, A.; Hummel, T.
Article.Abstract: In the olfactory system, glomerular sensory channels of single receptor identity support reliable odor recognition for appropriate approach or avoidance behaviors. For many olfactory stimuli, the assigned sensory value is innate but weighted by the internal state and previous experiences. How context-dependent modulation of innate valence coding supports distinct behavioral responses is poorly understood. Here we show that CO2 sensory information in Drosophila, intrinsically aversive but modified by attractive food signals, diverges from the canonical glomerular channel already in the antennal lobe via the polarized local interneuron LN23. LN23 relays sensory input via an extraglomerular CO2 pathway and manipulation of LN23 activity revealed a dominant role in CO2-induced avoidance behavior. The extraglomerular CO2 pathway projects to the posterior lateral protocerebrum (PLP) adjacent to the canonical Lateral Horn (LH) olfactory processing center and segregates into anatomically distinct valence channels. Connectome data together with functional characterization showed the convergence of parallel CO2 channels onto two interconnected 3rd order neurons which integrate additional sensory modalities via distinct mechanisms: while the glomerular CO2 pathway converge with food relay neurons onto separated dendritic domains of the PD5 interneuron in the LH, the extraglomerular pathways integrating CO2 information with antennal humidity and temperature modalities establish antagonistic inputs onto the PLP interneuron PV9. This early anatomical divergence of a defined olfactory channel followed by separated multimodal integration provides a structural basis for context-dependent valence coding and appropriate behavioral responses.

Article.Title: Zhx2 expression in the mouse brain
Article.Authors: Miracle, S.; Hofmeyer, M. L.; Gorelik, A. G.; Glavine, A. B.; Conti, I. C.; Pavlidis, S. V.; Ajjawi, H.; Lynch, E. E.; Bryant, C. D.
Article.Abstract: Prescription opioids like oxycodone (OXY; the active component in OxyContin) continue to drive the ongoing opioid use disorder (OUD) epidemic due to their widespread prescription and distribution. Genetic factors influencing pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of opioids can have profound impacts on drug response and, in turn, influence risk for OUD. We previously used quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping and gene validation to identify zinc-finger homeobox 2 (Zhx2) loss-of-function as a quantitative trait gene and mechanism underlying increased brain concentration of oxymorphone (OMOR) following systemic administration of OXY in BALB/cJ females that was linked to increased OXY reward. To test whether we could rescue the behavioral phenotype, we overexpressed Zhx2 in the brain via retro-orbital injection of a brain-specific adeno-associated virus (AAV). We observed restricted Zhx2 expression (especially females), with more widespread expression in males. Consequently, we did not observe any significant effect of brain Zhx2 overexpression on OXY reward as measured via conditioned place preference (CPP). However, Zhx2 overexpression did protect against OXY-induced weight loss in females following a high-dose OXY regimen. Despite the effect on weight loss, Zhx2 overexpression had no effect on spontaneous or naloxone-precipitated withdrawal behaviors. We then examined native Zhx2 protein expression in the brains of the BALB/cByJ substrain (showing wild-type levels of Zhx2 expression) via immunohistochemical co-localization and found that Zhx2 is mainly expressed in neurons located in key reward, motivational, and emotion-related regions such as the hippocampus (HPC), amygdala, striatum (Str), and cerebellum. To summarize, Zhx2 overexpression via retro-orbital AAV administration was quite limited, yet had significant effects on opioid-induced weight loss. Furthermore, for the first time, we provide anatomical visualization of Zhx2 expression at the protein level in neurons vs. glia throughout multiple brain regions.

Article.Title: Investigating the effect of acute consumption of kiwifruit on cognitive function using functional MRI
Article.Authors: Asghar, M.; Eldeghaidy, S.; Poggesi, S.; Hort, J.; Francis, S.
Article.Abstract: Objectives: Acute nutritional interventions may modulate cognitive function and underlying brain activity. This study investigated the impact of consuming three kiwifruit varieties - green (Zespri Green), gold (Zespri SunGold), and red (Zespri RubyRed) - on cognitive performance and brain activation using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Cognitive function was assessed using an N-back working memory task during fMRI acquisition. Behavioural performance, psychometric measures (mood, fatigue, appetite), and blood biomarkers (vitamin C) were also collected. Behaviourally, task difficulty increased with N-back load, while psychometric measures indicated greater positive affect following kiwifruit compared to control. fMRI results showed that the maltodextrin condition elicited broader brain activation, suggesting reduced neural efficiency. In contrast, kiwifruit -particularly the red variety - showed enhanced differentiation between low and high cognitive load (2-back vs. 0-back), with increased activation in regions associated with working memory and cognitive control. Conclusions: These findings suggest that acute kiwifruit consumption may enhance cognitive efficiency and modulate brain responses, with effects varying by kiwifruit cultivar.

Article.Title: Nethobench: Forecasting design and conditioning shape the structural realism of generated neural dynamics
Article.Authors: Marion, B.; de Vicente, A.; Mahn, M.; Luthi, A.; Luithlen, L.; Mitelut, C.
Article.Abstract: Which properties of neural population activity does a forecasting model reproduce? Neural forecasts are commonly evaluated by how closely they follow a held-out recording. Yet in a stochastic, partially observed system, several future trajectories are consistent with the same neural history. A forecast that averages over these possibilities can achieve low pointwise error while suppressing fluctuations that characterize individual recordings. We introduce Nethobench, a benchmark that measures structural agreement between generated and recorded neural activity. Its five metric families compare activity distributions, temporal and spectral structure, dependencies among neurons or brain regions, latent geometry, and transitions between population states. We validate these measures in stochastic systems with known dynamics and apply them to mouse and human recordings to examine how model design and conditioning on sensory and behavioral inputs shape the dynamics that forecasts reproduce. Reporting these structural profiles alongside predictive accuracy can allow researchers to compare forecasters on the properties of neural activity most relevant to their scientific question.

Article.Title: NED-Net: open-source software for building and refining seizure detectors during rodent EEG experiments
Article.Authors: MIR, M. Y.; Ledri, M.
Article.Abstract: Long-term EEG is the main readout of rodent epilepsy models, and automated detectors are usually delivered as fixed models that a laboratory cannot adapt to its own animals. NED-Net is open-source software in which annotations, rule-based detections and model proposals share one file per recording, reviewed events train the next detector, and detection runs live during acquisition, so a detector can be refined while an experiment runs. A detector built in NED-Net on one kainate mouse cohort detected 64% of 221 video-adjudicated convulsive seizures in a second cohort as delivered, and 72% of its detections on held-out recordings were seizures. Retraining on annotations made in the app, a few seconds of review per event, raised recall to 88% at 74% precision. SeizyML, a published detector, reached similar recall with three times the detections and did not improve with the same annotations. Article.Title: Semaglutide quiets "food noise" in mice by impairing the wanting, but not the liking, of glucose
Article.Authors: Molina, O.; Ruiz-Huerta, L.; Caballero-Ruiz, A.; Gutierrez, R.
Article.Abstract: Semaglutide and other GLP-1 receptor agonists are transforming obesity treatment, and patients often describe a quieting of intrusive food thoughts that motivate overconsumption of ultra-palatable foods, referred to as "food noise," yet it remains unclear which components of feeding behavior they act upon. Here, we designed a battery of behavioral tasks that separate the perceptual, hedonic, and motivational components of glucose intake in mice. Semaglutide impaired sweet taste categorization (in a psychophysical task) and induced conditioned taste avoidance not aversion, and thus left palatability intact. Its largest effect, however, was on motivation: it selectively disrupted the active pursuit of glucose and, to a lesser extent, lipids, sparing passive intake. In a novel lick-triggered taste alternation task, two fixed sippers delivered either glucose or a second tastant (e.g., saccharin or lipids), with the tastants swapping positions after a set number of licks. This design separated effortless consumption, when the swap brought glucose directly to the mouse (passive hit), from effortful pursuit requiring crossing to the opposite sipper (active hit). A single dose of semaglutide left passive hits intact, but markedly reduced active hits: mice readily exploited glucose that came to them, yet often failed to go after it. As the drug's effect waned, mice regained body weight by selectively overconsuming standard chow over glucose, and glucose over lipids, a shift in diet choice that persisted through the end of the experiment. Thus, semaglutide impairs the wanting, but not the liking, of glucose, providing (in mice) a behavioral correlate of the quieting of "food noise" reported by patients.

Article.Title: Tonic dopamine regulates cell-type-specific PKA activity and motivated behavior
Article.Authors: Lodder, B.; Kamath, T.; Hartman, I.; Lopez, M. S.; Hoogendoorn, S.; van Kleef, A.; Man, K. N. M.; Opitz-Araya, X.; Raghubardayal, M.; Timmins, J.; Adan, R. A. H.; Ting, J.; Tian, L.; Sabatini, B. L.

Article.Title: Early life stress reduces prefrontal dendritic spine density in adult male mice
Article.Authors: Bansal, P.; Cote, E.; Alarcon, J. M.
Article.Abstract: Early life stress (ELS) is a major risk factor for anxiety, depression and substance use disorders later in life, and it is thought to act in part by changing how emotion-regulating circuits develop. The prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) cortices exert top-down control over the basolateral amygdala (BLA), and this circuit is still maturing during early postnatal life. Stress in adulthood removes dendritic spines from prefrontal neurons, but it is less clear whether ELS causes lasting spine changes across this circuit, and the IL in particular has rarely been studied. Here, we asked whether ELS alters dendritic spine density in the PL, IL and BLA of adult male mice. From postnatal day (PND) 10 to 17, ELS pups were separated from the dam for 3 h per day and individually isolated from their littermates, and their home cage had reduced nesting material until PND21. Control pups were separated together with their littermates for only 15 min per day and kept standard nesting. In adulthood, brains were processed for Golgi-Cox staining, and spines were counted on proximal apical and basal dendrites of layer II/III pyramidal neurons in the PL and IL, and on dendrites of principal neurons in the BLA. ELS reduced spine density by approximately 30% in the IL and PL dendrites, with the largest losses concentrated on proximal apical dendrites. The BLA showed a smaller reduction of about 12%. These preliminary findings suggest that ELS leads to an important and lasting loss of dendritic spines in prefrontal regions that regulate emotional responses.

Article.Title: Dissociated network and cellular remodeling in the hippocampal-cortical circuit after induction of neuronal hyperexcitability
Article.Authors: Varona-de la Hera, D.; Osejo-Ocampo, J. D.; Boveda-Altube, L.; Aguilera, M.; Encinas-Perez, J. M.; Llamosas, N.
Article.Abstract: Neuronal hyperexcitability (NHE) can leave lasting consequences in neuronal circuits. It is often assumed that hyperexcitable neurons give rise to hyperactive networks. CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons and CA3 interneurons exhibited increased evoked firing, whereas CA1 interneurons exhibited reduced evoked firing. Deep-layer entorhinal neurons, however, received less excitatory synaptic input and fired less. Thus, network and cellular alterations were dissociated after NHE. Finally, a pharmacological challenge with the GluK1 agonist ATPA revealed region-specific changes in network responsiveness, with a blunted response in CA3 and enhanced response in the non-entorhinal cortex, with no differences in DG, CA1 or entorhinal cortex. Article.Title: The mechanical nature of injury shapes the composition and temporal dynamics of inflammation after traumatic spinal cord injury
Article.Authors: Ahmanna, C.; Gaussot, A.; Boussion, K.; Kante, K.; KANAIE-ATRIAN, E.; Soares, S.; von Boxeberg, Y.; Nothias, F.
Article.Abstract: The pathophysiology of traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) is a complex, evolving process that begins with a mechanical trauma. Progressive secondary damage then occurs, in which neuroinflammation plays a pivotal role. Much has been learned about the persistent inflammatory response during the chronic phase of SCI. However, variations in lesion models, animal species, strains, and the post-lesion intervals investigated make it difficult to conclude on how inflammation contributes to recovery or to exacerbation of damage. The two models shared some inflammatory patterns, but specific cellular and molecular responses differed in magnitude, composition, and temporal evolution. These signature inflammatory dynamics were associated with differences in endogenous axonal plasticity, astroglial remodeling and progressive lesion maturation, and with distinct functional recovery rates. As the lesion gradually became chronic, inflammatory activity was remodeled, but persisted. These results reveal the interplay between the mechanical cause of SCI, the corresponding immune response, and the ensuing tissue remodeling processes. They highlight the importance of injury context and subsequent evolution. We discuss them as contributions to our understanding of the physiopathology of spinal cord lesions, with the broader goal of designing therapeutic strategies aiming to appropriately modulate inflammation

Article.Title: Constructing value on the fly from episodic memory supports flexible decision-making
Article.Authors: D'Alessandro, M.; Pezzulo, G.
Article.Abstract: Value-based decisions often require people to flexibly draw on and combine information from past experiences to evaluate novel stimuli and adapt to changing demands. Here, we introduce GENESIS-Value, a computational framework that constructs value on the fly by retrieving and integrating episodic memories, rather than relying on stable, precomputed value representations. The model combines generative stimulus representations with a flexible query-key-value retrieval mechanism, allowing the same memory store to support different valuation and choice strategies. Across five simulations, we demonstrate that GENESIS-Value can use episodic sampling to reconstruct the values of experienced stimuli, generalize to novel stimuli based on shared features, estimate feature values, guide both individual and sequential choices, and select among multiple offers involving different rewards and levels of risk. We further show that retrieval can be guided by stimulus features, temporal proximity, reminders, and reward outcomes, as well as combinations of these factors, enabling adaptation to different decision demands without requiring separate value functions. The model also captures qualitative behavioral signatures reported in empirical studies of episodic decision-making. Together, these findings establish a unified computational account of how episodic retrieval can support diverse forms of value-based inference and choice. Rather than replacing stable value representations, episodic retrieval may provide a complementary mechanism that allows decision-makers to flexibly address a variety of choice scenarios by reconstructing the value of available options on the fly.

Article.Authors: He, W.; Yang, Y.; Sha, Z.; Hu, Q.; Zhai, X.; Shi, J.; Yang, L.; Guo, Z.; Zhang, M.; Zhang, Y.; Li, W.; Tang, L.; Liao, Y.

Article.Authors: Choubdar Parvin, H.; Meador, K. J.; Razavi, B.

Projecting these connectivity patterns onto time-resolved BOLD activity revealed a common dominant latent space with graded regions of preferential occupancy across modalities. Overlap-adjusted event-related analyses further showed that auditory and visual targets were associated with a similar initial displacement along the first temporal latent dimension, followed by modality-dependent trajectories, particularly along the second dimension. This later divergence reflected different balances of regional contributions within a largely shared cortical architecture. By integrating dimensionality reduction of high dimensional functional connectivity with network and temporal analyses, our findings link the spatial organization of distributed cortical systems to their evolving responses, revealing how shared brain networks can support both common and modality-dependent aspects of sensory target detection.

Article.Title: The information architecture of the naturalistic human brain
Article.Authors: Blackburne, G.; Liardi, A.; Bacalum, A.; Levchenko, E.; Cooper, G.; Dick, F.; Luppi, A. I.; Skipper, J. I.; Mediano, P. A. M.

Article.Authors: Speer, S.; Lee, C.; Mwilambwe-Tshilobo, L.; Tsoi, L.; Burns, S.; Falk, E.; Baldassano, C.; Tamir, D.
Article.Abstract: Conversations among friends are often more dynamic, enjoyable, and wide-ranging than those between strangers. How do friends do this? We found that the more a dyad aligned neurally, the more they also explored. While both neural alignment and exploration predicted the breadth of conversations, only neural exploration predicted better perceived conversation quality. Friends were more neurally aligned, which was associated with more exploration. Thus, when friends brains represent the world more similarly to each other, they tend to embark on more diverse and far-reaching conversations spanning a broader range of topics, all while staying anchored in common ground.

Here we show analytically that this approach does not provide a valid test of whether the hypothesized compartment identifies the true substrate. To illustrate the empirical consequences, we conduct semi-synthetic simulations using 4119 ischaemic lesions, modelling behavioural deficits dependent on a global lesion attribute, on widely investigated distributed cortical networks and white matter tracts, or on a right frontal substrate of fluid intelligence previously identified by multivariate methods. We apply regionally weighted regression with each hypothesized compartment as the target over 5000 iterations spanning multiple realistic noise levels. Where the hypothesized target is not the true substrate, we find spuriously significant dependence despite definitionally absent anatomical specificity; adjustment for lesion volume attenuates or exacerbates the observed bias dependent on the chosen target. Conversely, where the target is the true substrate, lesion volume correction universally reduces already poor sensitivity. Our analysis potentially explains common discrepancies across localisation studies, and highlights the necessity of multivariate approaches that explicitly model lesion and substrate anatomy at finely resolved spatial scales.

Finally, AMUA based Granger analyses revealed sustained jitter specific directed influences from both dorsal and ventral MGB toward multiple cortical layers during the poststimulus period. Together, these findings demonstrate that temporal regularity robustly modulates auditory thalamocortical responses and is associated with changes in directed interactions between thalamus and cortex.
