Article.Authors: Li, C.; Brenner, J. W.; Ye, H.; du Pont, B.; Kudarauskas, M.; Aloor, J.; Duan, C. A.; Chen, J. A.; Erlich, J. C.

Here we show that simple networks with local, Hebbian-like learning rules, which have no reward objective, nonetheless reproduce hallmark features of animal reward-seeking when placed in closed-loop environments where rewards arrive as ordinary sensory input. Six canonical local learning rules were tested under these conditions, and despite most rules being designed for unsupervised representation learning, all rules learned to seek out signal. However, at the parameters tested, only one rule, prospective configuration, robustly captured all of a set of tested phenomena: reward-magnitude-dependent learning rates, probability matching, memory retention across contexts, and switching between exploration and exploitation with heavy-tailed statistics. In these networks, actions that produce input become self-sustaining states (attractors) of network dynamics. Attractors reside in an activity-weight space and mediate behaviors, and adapt to their environments rather than being fixed properties of the networks. These flexible geometries provide a parsimonious account of how heavy-tailed runs of repeated choices, which resemble Levy flights seen in foraging, also change with the environment. A single framework then makes predictions about behavior and neural population geometries that can be used to investigate the learning dynamics of the brain.

Article.Title: Sex-dependent gating of astrocyte-driven nociceptive plasticity
Article.Authors: Klinger, L.; Uhrik, L.; Ravagnan, E.; Holzinger, R.; Trofimova, L.; Kurija, D.; Siegert, A. S. M.; Ada, S.; Waidhofer-Soellner, P.; Schmidt, M.; Drdla-Schutting, R.
Article.Abstract: Sex differences in pain are well established, yet how nociceptive processing is differentially regulated across sexes remains poorly understood. Here, we show that spinal astrocytes provide pathway-specific control of acute nociceptive synaptic plasticity in rats. Chemogenetic activation of distinct astrocytic G-protein-coupled receptor pathways induced synaptic depression or potentiation at spinal nociceptive synapses in males, but failed to evoke detectable plasticity in females. Despite this lack of astrocyte-induced synaptic plasticity, females developed mechanical hypersensitivity comparable to males, revealing a dissociation between synaptic plasticity and pain-related behavior. Gonadectomy prevented astrocyte-induced plasticity in males, whereas testosterone treatment enabled Gq-dependent synaptic depression in ovariectomized females. Females exhibited more prominent perineuronal net labeling, and enzymatic degradation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components enabled Gq-dependent synaptic depression in females. Together, these findings identify hormonal status and ECM organization as important determinants of the susceptibility of spinal nociceptive circuits to astrocyte-driven synaptic plasticity.

Article.Title: Rage bait: a neurofunctional signature of moral outrage elicited by social media
Article.Authors: Gan, X.; Zhang, R.; Zhou, F.; Wagels, L.; Jiang, H.; Wang, J.; Qing, Y.; Yang, X.; He, J.; Zheng, Z.; Xu, T.; Mathiak, K.; Jiang, B.; Yao, D.; Becker, B.
Article.Abstract: Moral outrage is ubiquitous online, with powerful emotional and motivational consequences for social life. Combining naturalistic fMRI during exposure to short-form social-media videos depicting moral violations with predictive modeling, we developed a neurofunctional signature of subjective moral outrage (MONS) in discovery/validation (n=80/30) cohorts. MONS predicted experienced outrage and punishment tendencies across cohorts. Positive predictive weights encompassed regions implicated in mentalizing, threat detection and action initiation (precuneus, posterior cingulate, periaqueductal gray, hypothalamus, cerebellum), whereas negative weights involved valuation and behavioral flexibility systems (amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex). Across 11 datasets (n=478), MONS captured anger and disgust but was dissociable from general negative affect and affective arousal. Notably, MONS did not predict perceived moral wrongness in conventional moral judgment paradigms, suggesting that moral outrage is not reducible to more cognitive moral evaluation. Findings provide a moral outrage neurofunctional model that delineates its relationship to other affective states and distinguishes it from traditional moral judgment.

Article.Title: Expanded representation and function of PDF neurons in the mosquito circadian network
Article.Authors: Dong, L.; Plank, A. V.; Duvall, L. B.
Article.Abstract: Female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes can transmit pathogens when they bite humans, their preferred hosts, and this host-seeking drive is tightly gated by time of day. Daily rhythms depend on the molecular clock and communication among clock neurons, yet mosquito circadian network organization remains poorly understood. Using a mosquito-specific PERIOD antibody, we mapped the putative clock network of Aedes aegypti and found that neurons expressing the neuropeptide Pigment-Dispersing Factor (PDF) make up a much larger proportion of clock neurons compared to other insects, indicating a divergent network organization. PDF neurons are required for normal rhythms across insects, but whether their importance scales with their abundance in the network is unknown. We therefore tested the functional role of this expanded PDF neuron population in mosquitoes: we show that electrically silencing Aedes aegypti PDF neurons abolished the separation of daily activity into morning and evening peaks and led to misaligned clock protein rhythms across circadian neurons, even under entraining light-dark cycles. Thus, in a network built around an unusually large PDF population, PDF neuron activity plays an outsized role in behavioral timing and network synchrony.

Article.Title: Common organization of collective dynamics across divergent self-organized neural architectures
Article.Authors: Zhao, Z.; Yang, L.; Nemenman, I.; Levchenko, A.
Article.Abstract: Brain organoids and other model neuronal networks build synaptic circuits through self-organization, and different protocols yield markedly different architectures, letting us test how collective dynamics depend on large-scale organization. We compared organoids of layered cortical-like structure against networks of cell-body clusters joined by axonal cables, quantifying the reproducible patterns of population activity in each. Bursts occurred in both architectures and comprised several collective patterns in each, so no single recurring template describes them. Recurrent activation sequences capture only part of this organization, sequence participation is graded, and neurons that rarely join a sequence still contribute to the shared dynamics. The patterns also pick out overlapping neuronal groups with propagation-like spatial order. Although the patterns differed between tissue models, their organization was conserved, and remained unchanged under pharmacological increases in network activity. Recurrent sequences therefore represent one manifestation of a broader collective organization that emerges across distinct self-organized neural architectures.

Article.Title: Preprocessing Determines Whether Fractal Biomarkers Detect Neurodegeneration: A Systematic Evaluation Across Five fMRI Pipelines
Article.Authors: Chattopadhyay, T.; Cen, H. S.; Thomopoulos, S. I.; Volkov, A.; Maximov, Y.; Motter, A. D.; Tankesly, H.; Ruekgauer, A. H.; Khopade, A.; Gabitov, I.; Thompson, P.
Article.Abstract: Fractal analysis of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has been proposed for detecting altered neural dynamics in Alzheimers disease (AD), but the effect of preprocessing on these measurements is poorly constrained. We evaluated 229 ADNI3 participants (156 cognitively normal [CN], 60 mild cognitive impairment [MCI], and 13 AD) processed with five ENIGMA HALFpipe variants. Each scan contained 197 volumes (TR = 3.0 s) and 434 regional time series. The reported CN-AD effect varied 4.5-fold for the detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) Hurst exponent and 13.1-fold for Sample Entropy; both measures met p < 0.05 only after aCompCor. Under aCompCor, mean H was 0.812 in CN, 0.827 in MCI, and 0.872 in AD (d = -1.40, p = 0.0003), whereas the other four DFA effects were approximately d = -0.31 to -0.40. A variance decomposition attributed 41.5% of total H variance to pipeline, 44.5% to participant, and 0.3% to diagnosis. Whole-brain analysis found higher H in AD across 16 of 18 networks, with 36 cortical regions surviving false-discovery-rate correction. Synthetic fractional Gaussian noise experiments confirmed monotonic DFA estimation at the available scan length. The small AD group makes all disease-effect estimates exploratory. These results show that preprocessing choice can determine whether fractal group differences are detectable and should therefore be treated as part of the biomarker definition.

Article.Title: Prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling promotes maladaptive plasticity of direct pathway striatal projection neurons
Article.Authors: Martin, J. R.; Power, S. K.; Cavanagh, A. E.; Maltese, M.; Melani, R.; Sippy, T.; Dasen, J. S.; Kang, U. J.; Tritsch, N. X.
Article.Abstract: As Parkinson's disease (PD) progresses and nigrostriatal dopamine (DA) neuron degeneration worsens, DA replacement therapies shift from restoring motor function to evoking dyskinesia. How disease progression mediates this transition remains poorly understood. Here, we optimized a 6-hydroxydopamine (6OHDA) model that reliably generates multiple severities of DA axon denervation within the striatum of individual mice. We identify a critical denervation threshold at which direct-pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs), which are key drivers of dyskinesia become pathologically hyperresponsive to DA. Using slice electrophysiology, we establish that denervation-induced increase in intrinsic excitability is insufficient to explain the aberrant response of dSPNs to DA. We further demonstrate using genetic and chemogenetic manipulations that prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling drives the pathological transformation of dSPNs cell-autonomously, and that sustained Gs-coupled metabotropic receptor signaling in dSPNs is sufficient to both prevent and reverse it. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how PD progression renders striatal circuits vulnerable to DA-evoked motor complications and identify sustained signaling by Gs-coupled receptors as a potential avenue for preventing or reversing denervation-induced maladaptive striatal plasticity.

Article.Title: ASTEROID, A Validated Annotated Dataset of Analytical Decisions in Graph Theory Based fMRI
Article.Authors: Imam, S. H.
Article.Abstract: Graph theory-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies use complex analytical pipelines, but methodological decisions are often reported in unstructured text, limiting systematic comparison and the design of multiverse analyses. Here, we describe ASTEROID, a structured annotation dataset derived from 156 graph theory-based human fMRI study publications. Its schema contains 125 labels, comprising 61 methodological labels and 64 labels for study characteristics and experimental design. An LLM-assisted workflow generated initial annotations, which underwent automated quality-control checks and expert human review. The dataset captures preprocessing, functional connectivity, and graph-analysis decisions. Within these categories, steps and their sequence, software, algorithms, parameters, and supporting text spans are included where available. This accompanying paper provides prompt specifications, processing scripts, and documentation, and describes an interactive viewer that supports exploration of the annotation schema and the study records. ASTEROID enables comparison of reported analytical choices, the informed design of multiverse-based robustness analysis and supports the development and evaluation of automated methodological information-extraction tools and educational resources for fMRI data analysis.

Article.Title: Data-Driven Decomposition of Precisely Aligned Fiber-Orientation-Preserving Probabilistic Tractography Connectomes with Non-Negative Matrix Factorization
Article.Authors: Zhou, A.; Coalson, T. S.; Rosen, B. Q.; Rafipoor, H.; Lange, F. J.; Yoshida, N.; Yang, A.; Hayashi, T.; Sotiropoulos, S.; Jbabdi, S.; Van Essen, D. C.; Glasser, M. F.
Article.Abstract: The major goals of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) were to characterize the structural and functional connectivity of the human brain. Although there has been tremendous work done for functional connectivity, including application of a variety of data driven decomposition approaches, structural connectivity from the HCP has seen less attention. This work presents a collection of methodological advances that, in combination, enable similar approaches to be applied to diffusion tractography data. Here, we use multi-modal non-linear volumetric alignment with FSL's MultiMOdal Registration Framework (MMORF) to precisely align white matter tracts and globular gray matter nuclei, use the White matter Hierarchical Modelling (WHIM) method to align voxel-wise fiber orientations, enable efficient GPU-accelerated computation and storage of full resolution probabilistic gray matter x white matter x fiber sparse tractography matrices in precise alignment across individuals using the aforementioned MMORF and WHIM alignments together with areal-feature-based cortical surface registration. These tractography dense connectomes can be averaged across individuals and sparse, computationally efficient non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) can be applied to perform data-driven decompositions into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories. The primary outputs of this effort to date are 1) A set of HCP software pipelines enabling such analyses, 2) A new unbiased HCP-derived volumetric standard space that is representative of the young adult brain and follows ACPC orientation conventions across individuals. 3) Reproducible NMF decompositions of HCP young adult tractography data into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories, which could be projected using non-negative dual regression back to individuals. These data represent a starting point for a new generation of data-driven atlasing efforts for human white matter, and these methods can be applied to study the white matter in development, aging, and brain diseases.

Article.Title: Modelling vortex interactions reveals distinct patterns of brain reconfiguration following psilocybin and escitalopram
Article.Authors: Acosta-Gordo, A.; Dagnino, P. C.; Sanz Perl, Y.; Carhart-Harris, R.; Erritzoe, D.; Nutt, D. J.; Kringelbach, M. L.; Deco, G.
Article.Abstract: Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, yet how interventions reorganise brain dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how psilocybin and escitalopram reshape brain dynamics in depression using pre- and post-treatment resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) from a double-blind randomised controlled trial (NCT03429075). We compared two whole-brain modelling approaches: conventional signal-space modelling describing interactions between regional brain signals, and vortex-space modelling capturing interactions between evolving patterns of local synchronisation. This represents the first application of vortex-space modelling to a psychiatric disorder. Vortex space was more sensitive than signal space in most analyses, including distinguishing treatment-related brain states, relating baseline connectivity to clinical improvement and predicting response to escitalopram. Our results further revealed distinct patterns of reorganisation following the two interventions. Psilocybin produced widespread increases in vortex-space effective connectivity and reduced network modularity, whereas escitalopram showed no comparable changes. Despite these differences, greater increases in brain turbulence (i.e., spatiotemporal variability in local synchronisation) were associated with greater symptom reduction in both treatments, with a significant post-treatment increase in responders. These findings suggest that psilocybin and escitalopram may reorganise brain dynamics in markedly different ways and yet share dynamical features associated with clinical improvement. Overall, vortex-space modelling offers a promising framework for characterising brain dynamics in depression and its successful treatment.

Article.Title: Distinct Cerebellar Activation Patterns Separate Novelty, Movement, and Motor Learning
Article.Authors: Sholomiski, M.; Yon, V.; Mudlaff, F.; Suvrathan, A.
Article.Abstract: The cerebellum supports a wide range of motor and non-motor behaviors, yet the specific cerebellar regions and neuronal populations underlying this functional diversity remain poorly understood. Here, we mapped patterns of immediate early gene activation in the cerebellar cortex during the accelerating rotarod task, an established form of cerebellum-dependent motor learning. Using the immediate early gene c-Fos to identify cells active during the task, we found significantly greater activation throughout the vermis and in crus I of the hemispheres, specifically within the molecular and granule cell layers, compared to naive controls. However, a second control group, which was exposed to the rotarod apparatus but not placed on the rotating rod, revealed similar patterns of c-Fos expression, suggesting that novelty contributed substantially to the observed activation. To separate this potential novelty signal from the motor component of the task, mice were habituated to the apparatus prior to testing. This habituation resulted in an overall decrease in c-Fos expression across cerebellar lobules, with significant motor activity-related differences found in the anterior vermis. Finally, to determine how learning influences c-Fos expression patterns, mice were subjected to a multi-day motor learning paradigm in which genetic tagging of c-Fos-expressing neurons was performed on day 1, followed by c-Fos immunostaining on day 5. We found that, in mice that had learned the task, there was no significant increase in c-Fos signal above naive controls, indicating that rotarod task performance no longer recruited the same level of cerebellar cortical activity, consistent with a potentially reduced role for the cerebellar cortex once the task is well learned. Overall, these findings reveal distinct patterns of activation associated with novelty, motor behaviour, and learning, providing a framework for linking behavior to regional cerebellar function.

Article.Authors: Koch, S. P.; Perales, M.; Sil, T.; Hiew, S.; Hartig, J.; Weigl, B.; Muthuraman, M.; Lange, F.; Li, N.; Kuhn, A.; Breininger, K.; Tovote, P.; Ip, C. W.; Volkmann, J.; Reich, M.; Boehm-Sturm, P.; Peach, R. L.
Article.Abstract: Cross-species differences in brain organisation complicate the interpretation of mouse experiments and the selection of mouse regions from human imaging findings. Here we present OTTER, which combines functional and structural connectivity, spatial position and comparative anatomy through optimal transport to estimate probabilistic mouse-human brain correspondence. Assessment of the connectomes used to fit OTTER shows lower mouse-based reconstruction accuracy for human functional connectivity in the expanded association cortex compared to sensory and motor regions. The corresponding anatomical contrast increases over time in a separate longitudinal MRI analysis following alpha-synuclein fibril injection in mice. OTTER predicts human maps from mouse experiments and candidate mouse targets from human imaging.

Article.Title: Ketamine Modulates Endogenous Opioid Peptide Signaling and Reduces Heroin-Seeking in Male Long-Evans Rats
Article.Authors: Dawoud, A. M.; Gupta, A.; Gomes, I.; Shapiro, J. E.; Devi, L.; Hurd, Y. L.; Osman, A.
Article.Abstract: Ketamine, a non-competitive N-Methyl-D-Aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antagonist, has emerged as a promising therapeutic for numerous psychiatric illnesses due to its robust antidepressant properties and glutamate-mediated synaptic plasticity. Emerging evidence have implicated the endogenous opioid system in its actions, but few studies have investigated ketamine's potential as an intervention for opioid use disorder (OUD) which continues to be a pressing public health crisis, marked by high relapse rates and limited treatment options. This study investigated ketamine's effects on endogenous opioid and glutamatergic systems and heroin-seeking behavior in male Long-Evans rats. Using a multi-cohort design, we investigated ketamine's effects on opioid-related transcriptional, protein, and signaling properties in brain regions associated with reward and addiction, and on heroin-seeking during abstinence following heroin self-administration. We also quantified transcriptional changes to NMDAR subunits. The results showed increased expression of endogenous opioid system-related genes and endogenous opioid peptides at the protein level, elevated mu-opioid receptor protein levels, and enhanced G protein activity, suggesting increased receptor function. Notably, transcriptional changes were particularly prominent in the shell subregion of the nucleus accumbens (NAc). We also observed that ketamine increased NMDAR subunit expression in the medial prefrontal cortex and NAc, in line with perturbation of synaptic plasticity. Behaviorally, ketamine significantly reduced heroin-primed, but not cue-induced, seeking activity, that correlated with expression of opioid peptide levels in the NAc shell. Together, these findings suggest that ketamine reduces acute relapse vulnerability to opioids through coordinated modulation of opioid and glutamatergic systems, highlighting its potential as a potential intervention for OUD.

Article.Title: Maturation-associated ERG3 and timed regulation of circuit stability
Article.Authors: Watanabe, H.
Article.Abstract: Neural maturation remodels excitability, but how this supports stable computation remains unclear. In a layered network, unreliable transmission destabilised learning when forward and update perturbations differed. This motivated a developmental screen for conductances that could support reliable responses. Mouse Kcnh7 (human KCNH7), encoding K11.3 (ERG3), rose late postnatally. Adult single-cell data showed expression in excitatory and inhibitory populations. In a Purkinje-cell model, ERG3 raised tonic-firing threshold and broadened pre-tonic responses. ERG3-inspired adaptation prolonged effective learning but reduced associative recall at low sampling temperature. In recurrent models, ERG3 shaped history-dependent firing, and prediction depended on modulation timing and perturbation type. Clustered interruptions of receptor modulation increased departures from the maintained state in a wake-maintenance model, whereas cue-timed loss delayed value updating during sustained activity. Together with receptor expression and mouse orexin data, these findings motivate testing whether disrupted ERG3 modulation contributes to fragmented wakefulness or impaired adaptation to changed rules.

Article.Title: Resting Cortical Alpha and Beta Oscillations are Continuous Across Space and Frequency
Article.Authors: Wilson, I. S.; Flores-Alonso, S. I.; Wiesman, A. I.
Article.Abstract: Cortical alpha and beta oscillations are traditionally conceptualized as spatially distinct, with alpha rhythms constrained to the occipital cortex and beta rhythms to frontal cortices. Little work has tested this spatial separability empirically and explored whether the distribution of these cortical rhythms may be continuous in space and frequency. Using task-free magnetoencephalography of 604 participants and density-based unsupervised clustering of individual spatio-spectral peaks, we show that the distribution of cortical oscillatory activity across the alpha-to-beta frequency range is structured along a continuous spatio-spectral gradient from occipitotemporal to frontal cortices. Across individuals, the expression of this gradient decays with age. This work introduces a continuous spatio-spectral organizational structure linking alpha- and beta-band activity across all lobes of the neocortex, with a potential role in flexible segregation and integration of communication between sensorimotor regions of the brain.

Article.Title: Pitch motor areas contribute to the perception of prosodic categories in speech
Article.Authors: BAEK, S.-C.; Kim, S.-G.; Maess, B.; Sammler, D.
Article.Abstract: Prosody is a fundamental aspect of speech characterized by suprasegmental features such as pitch. Prosodic pitch contours convey speakers' intentions, for example, distinguishing statements from questions. Understanding these intentions requires abstracting continuous, variable pitch information into discrete categories. The perception of segmental speech features has been proposed to recruit motor areas according to the articulatory effectors used to produce them. However, whether this principle extends to vocal pitch and prosodic category perception remains unclear. To address this question, we collected magnetoencephalography data from 29 participants (15 females) while they identified the prosody (Statement vs. Question) of single words varying in pitch contour along a five-level continuum; 25 participants also completed a singing localizer involving simple five-tone melodies. Region-restricted searchlight decoding of singing versus rest identified two premotor regions relevant to vocal pitch production, anatomically corresponding to the putative ventral and dorsal laryngeal motor cortex. Perceived prosodic categories were decodable from these regions, with a stronger contribution from the dorsal subregion more closely linked to pitch modulation, particularly in the left hemisphere. Moreover, decoding performance mirrored behavioral discriminability across the prosody continuum before typical response times, but not later, suggesting functional relevance to perceptual categorization. Finally, bidirectional transfer of category-related information between pitch motor and auditory areas argued against these motor areas merely echoing processing in auditory regions. Together, these findings support effector-relevant motor area involvement in prosodic category perception, thereby broadening the scope of motor contributions to speech perception from vocal-tract articulators to the laryngeal sound source.

Article.Title: The transcriptional landscape of human microglia reveals strong conservation of miRNAs and preservation of function across vertebrate species.
Article.Authors: Stone, S.; Walsh, A. D.; Sol-Foulon, N.; Pennings, L.; Martin, E.; Baretto Arce, L.; Leventer, R. J.; Kilpatrick, T. J.; Lockhart, P. J.; zalc, B.; Ansell, B. R.; Binder, M. D.
Article.Abstract: The central role of microglia in CNS function in health and disease has resulted in large interest in targeting microglial as treatments for neurodegenerative disease; understanding the factors that regulate microglial gene expression will be crucial to this goal. microRNAs (miRNAs) are among the most abundant post transcriptional regulators of gene expression. miRNAs suggests miRNA were likely key to significant evolutionary events as regulators of gene expression. The miRNAome of microglia is critical to their correct functioning but the miRNA that define microglia identity and regulate key functions have not been fully defined. In this study we performed a detailed analysis of the microglial miRNAome to identify miRNA enriched in microglia that are conserved across species (human, mouse, and xenopus). We further characterised the expression of these conserved miRNAs during demyelination and remyelination and identified conserved function of a microglial enriched miRNA across species. These findings reveal evolutionary conservation of specific miRNAs, suggesting an important role in establishing and maintaining microglial identity. They also highlight miRNAs that may be critical for microglial function in the central nervous system in both health and disease. Overall, this work advances our understanding of the factors that regulate microglial gene expression.

Article.Title: Tonic dopamine regulates cell-type-specific PKA activity and motivated behavior
Article.Authors: Lodder, B.; Kamath, T.; Hartman, I.; Lopez, M. S.; Hoogendoorn, S.; van Kleef, A.; Man, K. N. M.; Opitz-Araya, X.; Raghubardayal, M.; Timmins, J.; Adan, R. A. H.; Ting, J.; Tian, L.; Sabatini, B. L.
Article.Abstract: Dopamine in the striatum fluctuates on fast "phasic" and slow "tonic" timescales. Although disruptions in tonic dopamine have been implicated in the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disease, the effect of slow, minutes-long fluctuations in dopamine on neuronal activity and behavior remain unknown. Here we use two-color fluorescence lifetime photometry at high temporal resolution (FLIPR) and calibrated optogenetic and chemogenetic manipulations to determine the impact of tonic dopamine on motivated behavior and downstream signaling in vivo. We establish a method for tracking tonic dopamine using FLIPR and determine that dopamine release fluctuates across short (100s of milliseconds) and long (10s of minutes) timescales. We find that dopamine type 1 (D1R) and type 2 (D2R) receptor expressing spiny projection neurons (SPNs) are differentially affected by changes in tonic dopamine in vivo, confirming long-standing hypothesis on tonic dopamine function in the striatum. Finally, we show that accumbal tonic dopamine levels predict and causally mediate an animal's motivation to work for reward by regulating the rate of reward-motivated actions and engagement in a progressive ratio task. Altogether, we show that tonic dopamine affects downstream signaling and motivated behavior, and establish a new set of methods that allows for careful capture and manipulation of tonic dopamine in vivo.

Article.Title: Lipidome of Compact Myelin from Cortical Regions of the Aging Murine Brain
Article.Authors: Liu, V. P.; Johnson, C. E.; Lakhani, S.; Furber, K. L.
Article.Abstract: Age-related cognitive decline has been associated with neurodegeneration in cortical white matter tracts. The trajectory of white matter degeneration over the lifespan follows a similar pattern in humans, primates and rodents including the loss of myelin integrity and concomitant loss in myelinated axonal segments. Previous studies suggest that biochemical alterations in myelin begin to occur well prior to myelin loss. To better understand these biochemical determinants underlying white matter degeneration, we investigated the lipid composition of myelin isolated from young adult, middle-aged and aged murine brain. Compact myelin was enriched from cortical regions using a refined density centrifugation protocol and profiled the lipidome using LC-MS/MS. Over 2000 lipid species were identified, with the relative expression of 414 species changing over the age-span. The myelin lipidome from young mice was biochemically distinct compared to the aging cohorts. Aging was characterized by an overall decrease in high abundant species of glycerophospholipid and sphingolipids, including phosphocholine, phosphoethanolamine, sphingomyelin and cerebrosides. Pathway analysis by LipidSig 2.0 and lipid ontology analysis by LION/web highlighted alterations to lipid metabolism and membrane biophysical properties related to bilayer stability and organization. These data support the concept that myelin lipid compositional changes are apparent by middle age which underly structural changes in myelin at later ages. The findings provide greater insight into age-related biochemical alterations in the myelin sheath and may aid in strategies to mitigate white matter degeneration over the lifespan.

Article.Title: Precision-Weighted Updating Explains Serial Dependence Across Sensory and Contextual Transitions
Article.Authors: Qu, C.; Shi, Z.
Article.Abstract: Serial dependence is influenced by sensory uncertainty and by the continuity of context, but it remains controversial whether these influences reflect separate mechanisms or different expressions of a shared updating process. Across two time reproduction experiments (N = 44), we examined how motion coherence and transitions between coherence levels modulated the attraction toward the preceding duration, while controlling for central tendency. In Experiment 1, low current coherence led to stronger serial dependence than high coherence, whereas central tendency did not change. In Experiment 2, in which abrupt coherence onsets and a color change marked each encoding interval, serial dependence was elevated when low coherence repeated across trials. A three-state Kalman filter, comprising a fast duration estimate, a slowly learned mean, and a slow response bias, captured these patterns. In the fitted models, coherence did not change how strongly the current duration was weighted. It changed how much of the trace left by the preceding trial was retained in the prior for the current estimate, and in Experiment 2 a change of coherence interrupted this retention. With all parameters fixed, the same model predicted how both biases change when the volatility of the stimulus sequence is manipulated, in the data of Glasauer and Shi (2022). These findings support a precision-weighted updating account in which current evidence quality and perceptual continuity regulate the use of recent history.

Article.Title: Real-time posterior probabilistic TMS motor mapping with robust individualized stopping criteria
Article.Authors: Qiu, R.; Feng, Z.-J.; Numssen, O.; Zang, Y.-F.; Wilhelmy, F.; Güresir, E.; Knösche, T. R.; Weise, K.
Article.Abstract: Background: Electric-field-informed regression provides high-resolution transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) motor maps, but conventional nonlinear fitting is too slow to update the map during acquisition, so sessions rely on predefined stimulation budgets, despite substantial inter-individual variability in the data required for stable localization. Objective: To develop a real-time analysis updating a posterior probability map between pulses and compare its hotspots with finger-tapping functional MRI (fMRI). Methods: We analyzed two independent cohorts (12 and 13 participants, one newly collected); each hand muscle was analyzed independently. We replaced the conventional per-element sigmoid fit with Spearman's rank correlation coefficient and transformed the resulting score map into a posterior probability map using Bayesian evidence. Acquisition stopped once posterior mass within 5 mm of the hotspot passed a preset confidence level. Results: The Spearman and linear scores updated the region of interest within milliseconds, versus tens of seconds for sigmoid fitting. Spearman more closely matched the full-data sigmoid hotspot in recorded sessions and converged faster and more precisely to the true source in virtual subjects. Across both fast scores, at a confidence level of 0.85 the stopping criterion was met after a median of 74-159 pulses. FDI hotspots lay 8.3 {+/-} 4.3 mm from the fMRI center of gravity, in the precentral hand region. Conclusions: Rank correlation reduces computation time without loss of accuracy relative to sigmoid fitting. The resulting posterior probability map provides a session-specific stopping criterion in place of a fixed pulse budget.

Article.Title: Local and network-level dynamics of alpha and beta rhythms during visuospatial attention in autism
Article.Authors: Polzer, L.; Boxhoorn, S.; Schütz, M.; Grossmann, A. M.; Mössinger, H.; Bast, N.; Luckhardt, C.; Freitag, C. M.
Article.Abstract: Visuospatial attention is altered in autism, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Neural oscillatory activity coordinates distributed processes supporting attentional selection and their flexible adjustment to changing environmental demands. Altered oscillatory organization may therefore provide a mechanistic basis for atypical attentional processing in autism. We tested this theory using EEG recordings from 80 autistic and neurotypical children and youth performing a spatial cueing task with valid and invalid cues. We quantified alpha- and beta-band measures of local power and inter-trial phase clustering (ITPC) together with power- and phase-based measures of posterior-frontal long-range connectivity. Across validity conditions, autistic participants showed a more frontal alpha distribution, reduced posterior alpha lateralization and posterior beta ITPC, and higher frontal beta power. Crucially, autistic participants also presented reduced neural adaptation across attentional conditions, reflected in attenuated validity-dependent modulation of alpha power and of posterior-frontal beta connectivity, with elevated beta connectivity particularly in the valid cue condition. This neural pattern was accompanied by greater reaction-time slowing in the invalid compared with the valid cue condition. Within autistic participants, beta dynamics showed nominal associations with restricted and repetitive behaviors that did not survive multiple-comparison correction. Together, these findings suggest that visuospatial attention in autism is characterized by altered local oscillatory organization, combined with reduced modulation of local and distributed dynamics as attentional demands change. Alterations in alpha and beta activity may reflect reduced spatially selective attentional gating alongside greater maintenance of established attentional states.

Article.Title: Music and speech dissociate local temporal irregularity from response strength in human superior temporal cortex
Article.Authors: Song, D.; Rao, H.
Article.Abstract: Speech and music engage overlapping auditory cortex. We asked whether they shape the timing of local activity in ways that regional response strength alone leaves unresolved. In intracranial recordings from 30 participants watching a film with alternating music and speech, 1-10-Hz activity in the superior temporal gyrus (STG) had higher sample entropy during music, indicating that similar short patterns were less likely to persist (mean paired difference = 0.02256, FDR q = 0.00753). The contrast persisted in comparisons of adjacent film blocks and was larger relative to surrogate signals matched for amplitude distribution and approximate power spectrum. Speech elicited higher STG high-frequency power in the intracranial subset and stronger bilateral STG BOLD responses in all 30 participants in the separately acquired fMRI recordings. Together, these findings show that the soundtrack category associated with stronger regional responses differs from the one associated with greater local temporal irregularity. The temporal organisation of local activity therefore adds a dimension to how shared auditory cortex responds to natural sounds.

Article.Title: Shox2 maintains thalamocortical neuron firing for whisker-based somatomotor responses and sleep spindles in mice
Article.Authors: Febbo, I.; Martinez, L. A.; Maroteaux, M.; Yu, D.; Anderson, A. E.; Galazo, M. J.; Schrader, L. A.
Article.Abstract: In the mouse thalamus, thalamocortical neurons (TCNs) relay sensory information to cortex and generate rhythmic activity, including sleep spindles, through precisely timed firing. TCNs switch between tonic and burst firing modes that depend on intrinsic membrane properties, yet what maintains these properties in the mature thalamus remains unknown. Transcription factors, which regulate the ion channel genes that shape firing, are natural candidates. Here, we investigate Shox2, a transcription factor implicated in rhythmic activity across multiple systems, in ventral posterior medial (VPM) thalamus. Using genetic labeling and optogenetic activation, we show that Shox2 expressing neurons form functional thalamocortical and thalamoreticular projections capable of driving cortical responses. Conditional knockout of Shox2 in VPM alters intrinsic membrane properties, reducing both tonic and burst firing without altering thalamocortical circuit organization or barrel field architecture. These firing deficits are accompanied by impaired whisker-dependent somatomotor performance and a reduction in sleep spindle density in cortical target regions, while overall sleep architecture remains intact. Together, these findings identify Shox2 as a transcriptional regulator required to maintain intrinsic firing modes in VPM thalamocortical neurons, linking a transcription factor to spindle deficits, an emerging neurophysiological biomarker for autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia.

Article.Title: Neonatal exposure to SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in mice is associated with localized changes in cerebral cortex cell proliferation
Article.Authors: Portela, D. M.; Andrade, B.; Lima, E. V.; Christoff, R. R.; Batista, C.; Araujo, S.; Castilho, L.; Carvalho, R. S.; Figueiredo, C. P.; Garcez, P. P.; Clarke, J. R.
Article.Abstract: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) can cause acute and persistent neurological manifestations, and evidence suggests these effects may be at least partly explained by direct effects of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) spike protein, which includes neuroinflammation, cognitive dysfunction, and persistent pain. Because the developing brain undergoes finely regulated processes of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and cerebrovascular maturation, exposure to SARS-CoV-2 or its components during this critical period may interfere with neurodevelopment. We therefore investigated whether neonatal exposure to the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein affects processes underlying brain development. To this end, we used a mouse model previously developed by our group, where Swiss mice received an injection (s.c.) of spike protein from the ancestral viral strain or vehicle at postnatal day 1 (P1). Body weight, body length, and the righting reflex were evaluated until postnatal day 20 (P20). At P10, mouse brains were analyzed for cell proliferation, neural cell populations, and cerebrovascular organization, while blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability was assessed at P20 using Evans Blue. Neonatal spike protein exposure did not affect body weight, body length, or postural righting reflex. At P10, cell proliferation in spike-exposed animals was comparable to control groups, whereas region-specific alterations in SOX2-positive cells and TBR1-positive neurons were observed. Spike protein exposure did not broadly alter cerebrovascular architecture or BBB permeability, although increased IB4 fluorescence was detected in the lateral dentate gyrus (DG). Our findings provide evidence that exposure to the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein during postnatal development can influence specific aspects of neural development, highlighting the importance of understanding how viral components may affect the developing brain during critical windows of vulnerability. Keywords: spike protein, brain development, coronavirus, COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, cerebrovasculature.

Article.Title: Evolutionarily conserved coupling of lysosomal response sensing and disease-associated microglial reprogramming scales with pathological timescales
Article.Authors: Liang, Y.; Yuan, H.; Zhao, Y.; Guo, L.; Wang, J.; Liyi, L.; Zhang, Y.
Article.Abstract: Background Microglia transition into disease-associated microglia (DAM) during central nervous system (CNS) injury and neurodegeneration, yet the upstream intracellular logic driving this state conversion in vivo remains unclear. The lysosome acts as a signaling hub, but whether physiological phagocytic load universally initiates and quantitatively couples to DAM reprogramming across different pathological timescales is unknown. Methods We established a rigorous, unit-corrected analytical framework to overcome pseudo-replication in public single-cell data, anchoring statistical inferences at the level of independent biological units (animals, sequencing plates, or donors). We integrated six transcriptomic datasets spanning three murine injury/amyloidosis models and three large-scale human neurodegenerative cohorts (>320,000 microglial nuclei), alongside human Alzheimer's disease (AD) GWAS summary statistics. Results We demonstrate that the MiT/TFE-regulated lysosomal biogenesis program temporally precedes DAM reprogramming and maintains an evolutionarily conserved baseline coupling even in uninjured homeostatic tissue. In human microglia, MITF and TFE3 transcripts closely track DAM activation, whereas post-translationally regulated TFEB mRNA does not. Genetic enrichment analysis (MAGMA) reveals that common AD risk does not act upon the upstream lysosomal program, but is strongly anchored downstream at APOE. Furthermore, Trem2-knockout models demonstrate that disease-induced coupling amplification retains roughly half its magnitude even when the mature DAM subpopulation collapses. Cross-system comparisons reveal a state-transition synchrony model: disease-driven amplification of lysosomal-DAM coupling ({Delta}) scales with pathological timescales, showing strong amplification in acute murine injury and aggressive amyloidosis (5xFAD {Delta} = +0.252), but manifesting primarily as steady baseline maintenance across decades-long asynchronous human AD progression (SEA-AD {Delta} = +0.072). Conclusions Our study establishes the lysosomal stress-DAM coupling as an evolutionarily conserved pacemaking module for microglial state transitions, providing a quantitative framework for therapeutically targeting neuroinflammation and tissue repair.

Article.Title: Universal barcoded connectomics for massively parallel single-neuron projection mapping in diverse vertebrate species
Article.Authors: Qi, H.; Wan, X.; Cheron, J.; Majeed, M.; Elorette, C.; Fan, A.; Yang, Z.; Anant, M. M.-G.; Faltine-Gonzalez, D. Z.; Shi, C.; Washington, C.; Lowman, M.; Bourne, J. A.; Horwitz, G. D.; Rudebeck, P. H.; Chen, X.; Long, M. A.; Sakata, J. T.; Kebschull, J. M.
Article.Abstract: Neuroscience relies on diverse model species to understand animal behavior and brain function. Yet, tools for rapid, high-resolution brain connectivity mapping remain unavailable in most vertebrate species, slowing progress in many neuroscience models and rendering cross-species circuit comparisons challenging. Here, we overcome this barrier by establishing sequencing-based barcoded connectomics for rapid single-neuron tracing in seven vertebrate species ranging from frogs to birds to non-human primates. We develop a general solution to viral tropism and barcode trafficking, validate our reagents by mapping the projections of thousands of neurons in the songbird HVC, and discover a single set of reagents that functions across highly divergent species. Together, we provide ready-to-use barcoding reagents for diverse species and a simple framework for further adapting them if necessary, enabling high throughput single-neuron tracing across vertebrates.

Article.Title: Neural correlates of neonicotinoid-induced impairment of olfactory long-term memory
Article.Authors: Cabirol, A.; Paoli, M.; Calliari, N.; Fayolle, M.; Bariselli, S.; Schloetel, J.-G.; Giurfa, M.; Haase, A.; Fehrman, A. L.
Article.Abstract: Reports of olfactory learning and memory deficits in honey bees exposed to neonicotinoid pesticides have been accumulating over the past decades. As agonists of the nicotinic receptors to acetylcholine, neonicotinoids target most of the projection neurons conveying olfactory information to the mushroom bodies, the brain centres involved in learning and memory. However, the neural mechanisms by which neonicotinoids interfere with memory formation are poorly understood. Here, we investigated the consequences of chronic exposure to the neonicotinoid imidacloprid on the number of projection neuron terminal boutons and on their plasticity in the context of long-term memory formation. Imidacloprid-treated bees exhibited a higher number of boutons in the mushroom bodies, which was associated with long-term memory deficits. Using super-resolution STED microscopy, we characterized synapsin-positive units within boutons and revealed their sensitivity to imidacloprid exposure. Altogether, our experiments suggest that, by altering the number of olfactory projection neuron boutons and their synaptic vesicle content, imidacloprid interferes with the recall of long-term memory.

Article.Title: FUSE: FUsing EEG-MEG in a Shared Embedding via self-supervised learning for BCI
Article.Authors: Messuti, G.; Scarpetta, S.; Sorrentino, P.; Corsi, M.-C.
Article.Abstract: Combining complementary neurophysiological modalities offers a promising strategy for improving motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), but learning shared representations across modalities remains largely unexplored. Here, we propose a two-phase deep learning framework for multimodal EEG-MEG decoding that explicitly decouples representation learning from downstream classification. In the first phase, a convolutional encoder-decoder learns a shared latent representation by predicting the power spectral density (PSD) of EEG and MEG signals directly from time-domain activity, rather than using the conventional objective of reconstructing the input signal. In the second phase, the encoder is frozen and its learned representations are reused, without further adaptation, to perform the classification of the downstream MI-BCI task. The framework was evaluated on simultaneous EEG and MEG recordings from 20 participants. The learned representations consistently outperformed conventional handcrafted spectral features, increasing median classification accuracy from 0.734 to 0.794. The multimodal framework also improved performance over MEG alone (median accuracy from 0.680 to 0.794) and yielded a modest increase over EEG alone (median accuracy from 0.765 to 0.794), providing a more robust decoding strategy than single-modality approaches. Furthermore, the learned latent representations were transferable across participants, with more than half of cross-subject models performing within 0.01 accuracy of their subject-specific counterparts. These findings demonstrate that task-agnostic representation learning can capture physiologically meaningful multimodal neural representations that remain transferable across individuals, offering a promising foundation for more robust and reusable BCI pipelines.

Article.Title: Neural Circuit Mechanisms of Representation Transformation in Sequential Economic Choice
Article.Authors: Gu, J.; Ni, K.; Vengerik, B.; Cai, X.; Lim, S.
Article.Abstract: Choices under sequential offers require the brain to encode a current offer, maintain its value, and compare it with a later offer before selecting an action. Prominent models explain choice through attractor dynamics that maintain stable, identity-preserving representations of offers and choices. However, recent recordings from monkey orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) during sequential-offer economic choices revealed strong order-based choice signals and weak identity-based signals. To identify the circuit principles underlying these representations, we trained recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to perform an order-based choice task and reproduce the observed psychometric behavior. The networks developed overlapping value representations across offer identities and dynamically reformatted the first offer across delay periods into a memory signal that could be compared with the incoming second offer. Low-dimensional latent-circuit inference revealed complementary roles for feedforward and recurrent connectivity: feedforward weights mapped different offer types onto a common value scale, whereas asymmetric recurrent interactions between sensory and decision variables generated order-based choice signals. Relationships among value coding across task phases and order-choice preference were qualitatively consistent with monkey OFC data. In a controlled comparison, RNNs trained for juice-based choice exhibited relatively stable, attractor-like representations, yet these could coexist with order-based transformations within individual networks. Together, these findings illustrate how recurrent circuits can flexibly reformat value representations across computational stages to support memory-guided decisions, linking this population-level reorganization to a specific dynamical circuit motif.

Article.Title: Diet-Induced Obesity is Associated with Sex-Dependent Cerebral Microvascular Changes and Cognitive Decline in Mice
Article.Authors: Sheppard, L.; Sawiak, S.; Riches, C.; Lundh, S.; Secher, A.; Nishimura, E.; Martis, L.-S.; Evans, M.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic diseases, including obesity and diabetes, are major risk factors for cognitive impairment and dementia, yet the underlying causal mechanisms remain unclear. Here we investigate whether this link is mediated by dysfunctional changes in cerebral microvessels. Using a multimodal longitudinal approach combining 3D light-sheet fluorescence microscopy, contrast-enhanced MRI and cognitive testing, we characterise structural, functional and behavioural changes to the brain microvasculature in a mixed-sex mouse model of diet-induced obesity (DIO). Our results reveal a striking sex-specific vulnerability to obesity-driven cerebrovascular dysfunction. Brains from male DIO mice exhibited reduced capillary diameter and volume in the frontal cortex, alongside decreased blood volume and accelerated cognitive decline over time in an object recognition task. Conversely, female DIO mice displayed compensatory capillary vasodilation and were protected against neurovascular and cognitive impairment. These findings link cerebral microvascular changes to obesity-associated cognitive decline, and identify sex-dependent differences in the cerebrovascular response to obesity.

Article.Title: MLE EEG Toolbox: A Personal AI Laboratory Assistant for Literature-Informed and Reproducible M/EEG Research
Article.Authors: Liu, X.; Chen, W.; Wan, B.; Wang, S.; Lin, Z.; Zhang, X.; Dong, L.; Hu, S.; Guo, X.; Cui, R.; Ge, R.
Article.Abstract: Electrophysiological research increasingly relies on complex analytical workflows, yet integrating methodological evidence, computational execution and reproducibility remains challenging. Here we introduce MLE EEG Toolbox, a framework for building a personal AI laboratory assistant for electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) research. The toolbox integrates locally deployed AI, natural-language-guided analysis, literature retrieval and methodological comparison, and reproducible computational workflows. A constrained language model translates research instructions into validated, researcher-approved operations, while literature-informed guidance supports parameter selection and protocol reconstruction. Computational provenance enables transparent inspection and replay of analytical workflows. The assistant achieved action-selection accuracies of 85.6% for EEG and 95.5% for MEG, while 142 cross-platform tests demonstrated close numerical agreement. Applications to public EEG and MEG datasets illustrated integrated spectral, network, decoding and source analyses. Running on standard personal computers without external AI APIs or token charges, MLE EEG Toolbox provides an accessible, researcher-controlled environment that connects methodological knowledge with reproducible electrophysiological analysis.

Article.Title: A CT-to-brain-atlas mapping framework using cranial base landmarks in marmosets
Article.Authors: Yagishita, H.; Kawabata, M.; Nagai, Y.; Hori, Y.; Hirayama, Y.; Ebina, T.; Sehara, K.; Oyama, K.; Matsuzaki, M.; Minamimoto, T.; Isomura, Y.
Article.Abstract: Objective. The common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), a small, experimentally tractable nonhuman primate, is increasingly used as a model for studying higher brain functions. However, substantial individual differences in its skull and brain limit the accuracy of stereotaxic coordinates. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of each animal improves accuracy but is costly. Computed tomography (CT) is easy to acquire and shows the skull and implanted devices, but not the brain. We therefore aimed to map CT images to a brain atlas without MRI of each animal. Approach. Six marmosets with both CT and MR images served as references. A target CT image was registered to a reference CT image and mapped to the atlas via the reference's MR image. For this CT-to-CT registration, we compared intensity-based registration with landmark-based registration using eight cranial base landmarks. We also averaged mappings across multiple references. Mapping error was measured against the mapping via the target's own MR image. Main results. With a single reference, landmark-based registration had a significantly smaller error than intensity-based registration. Averaging the mappings from five references improved the accuracy (0.45 mm), and five or more landmarks gave almost the same accuracy as all eight. Landmark-based registration also worked better on CT images from a different scanner and on postoperative CT images with implants (three and two marmosets, respectively). Using our new open-source software, Marmoset Atlas Mapper, we assigned Neuropixels recording sites to brain regions on postoperative CT, and the region boundaries were qualitatively consistent with boundaries in local field potential correlations. Significance. Cranial base landmarks and multiple references allow CT-to-atlas mapping with a submillimeter mean error without MRI of each animal, even with image artifacts or partly missing landmarks. This enables in vivo localization of implanted devices, including those in deep structures, facilitating studies of higher brain functions in marmosets.

Article.Title: Motor learning engages intrinsic plasticity in the human cortex
Article.Authors: Clennell, B.; Luo, B.; Lam, K. T.; Hu, Y.; Peterchev, A. V.; Hannah, R.
Article.Abstract: Learning is commonly explained by changes in synaptic strength. In animals, however, learning also engages intrinsic plasticity -- changes in how readily neurons convert synaptic input into firing. Its contribution to human learning has been unclear, because conventional non-invasive measures of cortical excitability primarily reflect synaptic strength. Here we used controllable-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation to estimate two biophysical indices of intrinsic excitability in human motor cortex, before and after motor training. Training produced signatures of increased intrinsic excitability, selectively in the cortical representation of the trained muscle, but not an untrained muscle. Individuals showing larger intrinsic excitability changes learned faster, independently of changes in motor-evoked potential amplitude, an index of synaptic excitability that increased following training but did not predict learning rate. An axon model reproduced the measured changes through small shifts in membrane excitability. These findings provide evidence that intrinsic plasticity is expressed in the intact human brain, and that it represents a behaviourally relevant component of learning-related cortical adaptation.

Article.Title: Distinct roles of microglial and neuronal P2X4 in persistent neuropathic pain
Article.Authors: Gilabert, D.; Sueur, B.; Nobili, P.; Linck, N.; Fossat, P.; Boue-Grabot, E.; Ulmann, L.
Article.Abstract: Neuropathic pain is a chronic, debilitating condition characterized by persistent sensory hypersensitivity and frequently associated with anxiety- and depression. Although microglial P2X4 receptors are well-established mediators of early neuropathic pain, their cell-specific contributions to pain maintenance and associated affective disturbances remains poorly understood. We investigated these contributions in male and female mice 30 and 60 days after spared nerve injury (SNI) using conditional P2X4 deletion in microglia (Cx3cr1CreERT2) or neurons (Synapsin-1-Cre), behavioral assessments, and in vivo recordings of spinal dorsal horn wide dynamic range neurons. Microglial P2X4 deletion before SNI completely prevented mechanical allodynia whereas deletion initiated 40 days after injury fully reversed established allodynia in both sexes. Notably, P2X4 immunoreactivity was undetectable in spinal microglia at the late time points examined, suggesting that the sustained contribution of microglial P2X4 may involve mechanisms outside the spinal microglial compartment. Neuronal P2X4 deletion partially attenuated mechanical hypersensitivity and reduced dorsal horn neurons hyperexcitability at day 60 after SNI, supporting a modulatory role in persistent spinal sensitization. Global P2X4 deletion prevented anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors that emerged by day 30 in males and day 60 in females. Whether this protection reflects a direct contribution of P2X4 to affective disturbances or an indirect consequence of reduced pain remains unresolved. Together, these findings identify distinct microglial and neuronal P2X4 contributions to established neuropathic pain and reveal sex-dependent differences in the onset of associated affective disturbances.

Article.Title: TSPAN10 Loss-of-Function in hESC-Derived RPE Reveals Critical Roles in Pigmentation, Polarity, and Antioxidant Defence
Article.Authors: Kaye, R. A.; Nazlamova, L.; Keeling, E.; Martinez, M.; Lakowski, J.; Lotery, A. J.
Article.Abstract: Expression quantitative trait loci studies have highlighted TSPAN10 as a gene that confers an increased risk of developing age-related macular degeneration (AMD). We report the generation of human embryonic stem cell derived RPE with TSPAN10 knockout using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing. This provided an in vitro model to investigate the functions of TSPAN10. TSPAN10 knockout cells were differentiated into mature RPE. Significant differences were observed in cell pigmentation, polarisation and cell body height, and the response to oxidative stress in comparison to wild type. These results demonstrate for the first time a role for TSPAN10 in the RPE, aligning with published data to support the importance of TSPAN10 for pigmentation, and adding to our understanding of the heterogeneous disease AMD.

Article.Title: 5-HT2A receptor deletion is associated with reduced hippocampal parvalbumin levels and anxiety-like behavior in BALB/c mice
Article.Authors: Dial, K.; Wonnenberg, P.; Ma, J.; Conant, K.
Article.Abstract: The serotonin 2A receptor (5-HT2AR) is a target of drugs used to treat anxiety and mood disorders, yet whether endogenous 5-HT2AR signaling constrains or promotes anxiety, and how the 5-HT2AR affects cell populations linked to anxiety, is not fully resolved. Here we report that constitutive deletion of the 5-HT2AR in male and female BALB/c mice is associated with robust anxiety-like and repetitive behavior across multiple paradigms. Unbiased proteomic analysis of male knockout hippocampal tissue revealed substantially reduced levels of parvalbumin (PV), a proxy of their activity. Consistent with the intense metabolic demands of fast spiking interneurons, proteins supporting energy metabolism were also downregulated, including those related to oxidative phosphorylation and the electron transport chain, glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid cycle, together with the cytoplasmic ribosome. In terms of how reduced 5-HT2AR signaling could lead to reduced PV expression, we examined key perineuronal net (PNN) components. The PNN constituents aggrecan and HAPLN1 were not significantly changed, whereas the link protein, HAPLN4 was substantially reduced. In a separate cohort, 7 days following a single dose of the selective 5-HT2AR agonist, 25CN-NBOH, many of the same energy metabolism proteins were shifted in the opposite direction. Together these findings indicate that constitutive loss of 5-HT2AR signaling is associated with coordinated reductions in parvalbumin and in the biosynthetic and bioenergetic machinery that supports fast-spiking activity, without a generalized loss of perineuronal net structural components.

Article.Title: How reliable is the link between effort and nucleus accumbens connectivity at rest? A psychometric evaluation of repeated assessments
Article.Authors: Karlocai, Z.; Kühnel, A.; Schulz, C.; Grahlow, M.; Kaduk, K.; Frick, A.; Derntl, B.; Kroemer, N. B.
Article.Abstract: Individuals differ in their willingness to work for rewards. Although effort-based behavior shows trait-like stability and motivational traits associate with functional connectivity (FC), it remains unclear how robustly individual differences in effort are reflected in intrinsic FC of reward circuits. Here, we investigated whether effort-based behavior and questionnaire scores are reflected in nucleus accumbens (NAcc) FC. Second, NAcc FC showed the highest reliability in subcortical regions (ICCs = 0.59-0.69), while cortical connections were heterogeneous and, overall, less reliable. Higher effort exertion was associated with stronger NAcc<>IFG FC (tmax(76) = 4.65, pFWE = .041, k = 141), while greater sensitivity to task difficulty was associated with stronger NAcc<>subcallosal gyrus FC (tmax(76) = -5.15, pFWE = .028, k = 155). Our findings show that identifying robust brain-behavior associations likely requires comparable multi-session approaches, at least in moderately sized samples. Beyond reliability, such approaches may also help reveal additional insights about the temporal profile of brain-behavior associations, which may differ markedly for new versus routine task performance.

Article.Title: Lightness illusions and saliency maps for reflectance estimation are similar across a wide range of deep neural network architectures
Article.Authors: Patel, J.; Flachot, A.; Vazquez-Corral, J.; Brainard, D. H.; Wallis, T. S. A.; Murray, R. F.
Article.Abstract: People perform many visual tasks that depend on having representations that remain correlated with surface reflectance despite large variations in illumination and context. This ability is known as `lightness constancy'. Here we extend this work by testing whether these findings are specific to the network architecture we used in our previous work, or whether they generalize broadly across architectures and training procedures. We compared networks where the initial, stimulus-encoding phase used pre-trained weights learned for other tasks, and networks where all weights were optimized for reflectance estimation. We found that all architectures and training procedures tested produced similar reflectance estimation performance on held-out images, and were susceptible to several classic lightness illusions. Furthermore, saliency analyses showed that all networks had broadly similar spatial sensitivity across input images. Together, these results suggest that lightness constancy and susceptibility to lightness illusions do not depend strongly on details of network architecture and training, but instead often emerge robustly in networks that have been optimized to infer surface reflectance from luminance.

Article.Title: Network-related variations of cerebrovascular status are correlated with cognitive control performance
Article.Authors: Quan, X.; Low, K.; Kałamała, P.; Karayanidis, F.; Sutton, B. P.; Gratton, G.; Fabiani, M.
Article.Abstract: Cerebrovascular health has emerged as a crucial factor in influencing cognitive decline in aging, including cognitive control and fluid intelligence. Previous studies have largely relied on peripheral assessments of vascular health due to the paucity of global and regional estimates of cerebrovascular status. For the first time, we integrate a network-based approach based on previous fMRI studies and pulse-DOT regional mapping of cerebrovascular status, to test whether the support provided by the cerebrovascular system to different brain networks may differentially impact cognitive control performance. To comprehensively assess how various mechanisms of cognitive control are influenced by the cerebrovascular health of different networks, we used a task-switching paradigm that simultaneously measures proactive and reactive control processes. After removing the global signal, we found that larger positive PReFx residual values in the Dorsal Attention and Visual Networks are linked to lower cognitive control costs. Conversely, larger positive residual values in the Default Mode and Fronto-Parietal Networks are associated with higher cognitive control costs. These results indicate that the relative balance of arterial elasticity across different brain networks impacts cognitive control, highlighting the importance of studying network-based cerebrovascular status for understanding cognitive performance.

Article.Title: Functional cell type diversity in the Drosophila lamina is established by a single transcription factor dFezf, controlling a large repertoire of ion channels and receptors
Article.Authors: Sporar Klinge, K.; Wagh, N.; Akhtar, J.; Santiago, I. J.; Ilic, M.; Pecot, M.; Silies, M.
Article.Abstract: Neuronal cell types in the brain can show remarkable diversity in their functional properties. In the visual system, neurons at different levels of hierarchy show diverse kinetics, leading to the encoding of different features of the visual scene. How this behaviorally relevant diversification is achieved is not understood. Here, we address this question in a simple system, studying two visual cell types in Drosophila that diversify their responses despite receiving the same photoreceptor input to encode two distinct basic visual features, contrast and luminance. We first show that this cell type diversity is mostly established by cell-intrinsic mechanism. While cell-type specific transcriptome analysis delivers promising receptor and channel candidates, genetic manipulation of these differentially regulated genes fails to identify individual channels or receptors that are necessary or sufficient for the functional differences between luminance-sensitive L3 neurons and contrast-sensitive L2 neurons. However, loss of the L3-specific transcription factor dFezf makes L3 neurons transient and contrast-sensitive. Interestingly, dFezf controls the cell-type-specific expression of several receptors and ion channels that we initially found to be differentially expressed between L2 and L3. Together, this argues for a degenerate system in which multiple genes jointly shape cell type-specific functional properties. Our finding that a single transcription factor regulates the expression of such a set of genes that can be relevant for function suggest that similar regulation might also be in place in other degenerate systems, which exist widely across cell types, brain regions, and species.

Article.Title: Speech and music organize neural activity differently over time in human superior temporal cortex
Article.Authors: Song, D.; Rao, H.
Article.Abstract: Speech and music engage overlapping auditory cortex. We asked whether they shape the timing of local activity in ways that regional response strength alone leaves unresolved. In intracranial recordings from 30 participants watching a film with alternating music and speech, 1-10-Hz activity in the superior temporal gyrus (STG) had higher sample entropy during music, indicating that similar short patterns were less likely to persist (mean paired difference = 0.02256, FDR q = 0.00753). The contrast persisted in comparisons of adjacent film blocks and was larger relative to surrogate signals matched for amplitude distribution and approximate power spectrum. Together, these findings show that the soundtrack category associated with stronger regional responses differs from the one associated with greater local temporal irregularity. The temporal organisation of local activity therefore adds a dimension to how shared auditory cortex responds to natural sounds.

Article.Title: Trial history and model-derived reward prediction errors in mousevisual decisions
Article.Authors: Mirabedini, A.; JanatAbadi, R.; Khanteymoori, A.
Article.Abstract: A reward prediction error (RPE) estimated from an animal's behavior can predict its next choice. Recent choices strongly improved prediction. An RPE based on a stimulus-dependent reward expectation added a small gain beyond the preceding choice and reward, and this gain fell to near zero once the model included the preceding stimulus. When the model also summarized choices and rewards over several earlier trials, an RPE trace with the same retention parameter as the history traces did not reliably improve prediction. In simulated agents with known decision rules, a simplified version of this comparison detected an RPE-based learning rule in which choices depended on accumulated prediction errors, and did not improve prediction for an agent that used trial history directly. Article.Title: PolyMorph3D: A flexible MATLAB-based tool for quantifying microglia morphology and multi-colocalization in three dimensions
Article.Authors: Yoblinski, A. R.; Pham, T. Q.; Dubey, J.; Seney, M. L.
Article.Abstract: As the principle immune cell of the central nervous system (CNS), microglia have been extensively studied throughout development and in a wide range of disease states. Of special focus have been their morphological features such as branching complexity, physical cell-cell interactions with surroundings, and gene expression readouts relating to phagocytosis and cytokine signaling. Each of these domains offers a window onto microglia function, and high-resolution confocal microscopy has long been a workhorse technique to visualize all three. A comprehensive view of microglia function requires both high-fidelity quantification with 3D resolution and colocalization of microglia with functional proteins such as those related to phagocytosis and with nearby structures such as synapses. Accordingly, a number of analytical tools have been developed to measure these features. However, existing open-source options lack either colocalization or 3D capability, while commercial solutions can be costly. Here, we sought to develop an open-source solution that addresses each of these limitations. PolyMorph3D is a MATLAB-based program capable of yielding individual cell-level data of microglia morphology and overlap with up to 4 other sources, all in 3D. The pipeline can be used effectively in mouse tissue and in human postmortem brain, thereby offering a flexible, low cost, and high-fidelity solution for the analysis of microglial morphology and function.

Article.Title: When spike sorting matters: single-neuron identity in the quantification of neural circuits
Article.Authors: Suarez-Barrera, D.; Encinas-Rodriguez, N.; Diaz, H.; Zainos, A.; Bayones, L.; Rossi-Pool, R.
Article.Abstract: Multiunit threshold crossings support high-performance brain-computer interfaces and preserve the low-dimensional trajectories that summarize population dynamics, raising the question of when spike sorting is still necessary. From the same spikes, we built three representations: putative single units obtained with nonlinear sorting (UMAP and HDBSCAN), intermingled units obtained with linear sorting, and unsorted multiunit activity. Nonlinear sorting resolved up to three times more units than multiunit activity. In area 1, mixing discarded the periodicity information carried by phase-locked neurons, lengthened intrinsic timescales by about 40%, increased trial-to-trial variability, and raised neurometric detection thresholds by 33%. In premotor cortex, mixing reduced the task-related information recovered from the population and hid significant dimensions of its dynamics. After geometric alignment, the overall shape of population trajectories was nearly identical across representations, but distances between population states were distorted, and the approximately linear representation of interval duration saturated for longer intervals. Multiunit activity is therefore sufficient for analyses that rely on the dominant, shared structure of population activity, such as decoding, whereas analyses of single-neuron coding, variability, timescales, dimensionality, and parametric representations often require spike sorting.

Article.Title: Implications of recursive Bayesian Sensory Inference
Article.Authors: Mortensen, E. S.; Ottenheijm, M. E.; Christensen, M. S.
Article.Abstract: During everyday life, we rely on proprioceptive feedback to inform us of the current position and velocity of our limbs. In a simulated reaching task with briefly presented offset visual feedback, such a system produces the classically observed shifted endpoint errors, while an Agent relying mainly on positional feedback is able to correctly update its inferred hand position after visual feedback is removed, thereby limiting this type of biased endpoint error. When biased visual feedback remains continuously available, or when muscle vibration is simulated, the two configurations can produce very similar behaviour. These findings underscore the importance of carefully considering the composition of proprioceptive signals when building computational models and when interpreting human sensorimotor experiments.

Article.Authors: Shirolkar, S. A.; Bueh, L. T.; Cerere, L. W.; Ahmed, N. E.; Some, G.; Awe, O. I.
Article.Abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a highly selective barrier that restricts the entry of many therapeutic agents into the brain. The lack of efficient methods for BBB permeability research and data management remains a significant challenge for central nervous system drug-development pipelines. Although BBB permeability data are available from multiple open sources, few platforms integrate these datasets with molecular exploration, predictive tools, and a structured process for community-supported data verification. Here, we present BrainRoute, an open platform for BBB molecular data collection, exploration, prediction, and community-supported verification. BrainRoute provides searchable and filterable molecular records, physicochemical and structural information, source-linked data, single-molecule and batch prediction, and a structured workflow through which users can submit additional evidence for review. The prediction tool model-development cohort contained 7,888 unique molecules, including 5,424 BBB+ and 2,464 BBB- molecules. Six machine-learning classifiers were evaluated using PaDEL descriptors, Morgan fingerprints, frozen ChemBERTa embeddings, and combined feature representations. The three selected models were integrated into the platform as a probability-averaged ensemble. The primary five-fold scaffold-grouped analysis achieved a best mean balanced accuracy of 0.783 {+/-} 0.026. On an independent external set containing 410 non-overlapping molecules, the deployed ensemble achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.659 (95% CI 0.600 - 0.712) and an AUPRC of 0.670 (95% CI 0.583 - 0.752). BrainRoute serves as a platform for exploring BBB-related molecular data and computational predictions while supporting the continued growth and verification of the underlying dataset. Article.Authors: Ajmera, S.; Husain, F. T.
Article.Abstract: Tinnitus, or ringing in the ears, is a hearing disorder that affects approximately 15% of human adults globally.
