However, with the increase in data sharing practices, data scarcity can be overcome with harmonization methods if scans from independent sites and studies are pooled successfully. To achieve data harmonization for limited data from a tinnitus neuroimaging study, we merged a modest fMRI dataset acquired in our lab (n=35) with age- and gender-matched samples from another large dataset, the Lifespan Human Connectome Project Aging (n=377). We assembled and trained neural network modules to purge dataset-identifying information from FC maps, and retained patterns that can characterize tinnitus-related FC. Hallmark artifactual information of the datasets was significantly reduced while reconstructing resting state FC data. Relevant relationships in brain connectivity that discern the condition of tinnitus from controls were well-preserved in the reconstructed resting state FC data. In agreement with existing literature on brain networks of tinnitus, connectivity related to default mode, ventral attention and frontoparietal control networks were identified to be crucial for distinguishing the condition, as masking these networks connections severely impacted downstream classification prediction on reconstructed FC. The data harmonization model was successful in merging FC matrices from independently acquired fMRI datasets, without losing out on meaningful functional connectivity patterns of interest for the neuropsychological disorder of tinnitus. Our findings demonstrate the potential of data harmonization by integrating independently acquired datasets on healthy controls to overcome neuroimaging data scarcity while preserving disorder-relevant neural signatures, advancing research on understudied neurological disorders.

Article.Title: When Velocity Becomes Position: Proprioceptive Contributions to State Estimation
Article.Authors: Mortensen, E. S.; Christensen, M. S.
Article.Abstract: In this study, we investigate the relative contributions of positional- and velocity-based proprioceptive feedback to state estimation when visual feedback of the hand is unavailable. In both cases, visual feedback of the hand position was withheld, except for a brief moment, during which an offset to the left or right was sometimes applied. By analysing the movement path following the offset visual feedback and comparing it to the non-offset condition, we can infer the extent to which the brain relies on rate-of-change information compared to absolute positional feedback for estimating the hand position. We compare and contrast our empirical data with simulated movements from a computational model based on Bayesian sensory integration under varied assumptions of the reliance on positional and velocity-based feedback. Our human and simulated data together indicate a substantial reliance on velocity-based information, as movement offsets induced by biased visual feedback decay slowly during both target-tracking and sequential reaching tasks. Article.Title: Early Life Shift in Fear Extinction is Driven by Prefrontal-Amygdala Engagement
Article.Authors: Wilkin, J.; Canella, A. E.; Khlaifia, A.; Cruz-Sanchez, A.; Premachandran, H.; Inayat, M.; Nacakli, M.; Varghese, S.; Arruda-Carvalho, M.
Article.Abstract: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) displays a delayed maturation long hypothesized to guide developmental changes in threat processing. Nevertheless, the mechanism by which ontogenetic changes in mPFC function guide the developmental emergence of behavior is unclear. Early life marks a shift between a permanent extinction phenotype typical of juveniles, toward the standard, more transient extinction seen in adult rodents. This shift coincides with developmental changes in mPFC-amygdala connectivity, a pathway necessary for extinction processing in adults. Here we used optogenetics and slice electrophysiology to show that, in contrast to adult animals, juvenile mice displaying permanent extinction fail to engage the mPFC-amygdala pathway at the synaptic, cell activity or behavioral levels. Consistent with a requirement of this pathway for the developmental transition in extinction types, optic potentiation of the mPFC-amygdala pathway accelerates the onset of adult extinction. Our findings show that the developmental onboarding of the mPFC-amygdala pathway drives a shift in extinction processing toward increased fear reemergence that persists throughout adulthood.

Article.Title: Velocity-dependent friction in a simple two-oscillator system. II. Regions of stability
Article.Authors: Luo, Y.; Priyadarshini, N. S.; Hsu, M.; Worrell, G.; Hsu, D.
Article.Abstract: In Part I, a gamma friction that follows theta velocity produced theta gamma phase amplitude coupling (PAC) whose strength is a closed-form function of one dimensionless number, kappa;. Here we ask when this coupling destabilizes the gamma oscillator. The friction on gamma is negative during part of every theta cycle, yet gamma stays bounded: as long as it keeps oscillating, the energy gained while theta rises is returned while theta falls, and Liouville' sformula fixes the growth over a theta cycle at the baseline decay, whatever the coupling. Instability arises only in rare large theta cycles in which the friction exceeds critical damping, so that gamma stops oscillating and the gain is no longer returned. The typical trajectory becomes unstable when such cycles, about one in a hundred, outweigh the decay in all the others. This gives a boundary g* {sigma}x = 10, where {sigma}x is the typical theta amplitude set by the fluctuation dissipation theorem; the prediction agrees with a direct Lyapunov scan to within 6% for damping ratios from 0.0005 to 0.0055. The distance to the boundary is set by the same number kappa that sets the PAC strength, so that stronger PAC means closer proximity to instability. The mean-square boundary lies far lower but is set by events of negligible probability. Stimulating theta at or below its own frequency raises gamma energy and PAC and can drive giant gamma bursts or divergence, but no self-sustained activity, suggesting that a transition to seizure requires memory.

Article.Title: Velocity-dependent friction in a simple two-oscillator system. I. Phase amplitude coupling
Article.Authors: Luo, Y.; Nayak, S. P.; Hsu, M.; Worrell, G.; Hsu, D.
Article.Abstract: Cortical gamma oscillations often arrive in bursts locked to the phase of slower theta waves, a pattern called theta gamma phase amplitude coupling (PAC). PAC is linked to memory and altered in epilepsy, but most models tie it to particular cells or circuits. We start from a generalized Langevin equation, an equation of motion for a few collective variables in which friction and random forces stand for the unobserved neural activity, and let its stiffness and friction depend on the state. Expanding them to first order in the theta and gamma variables yields ten possible interaction terms; only the two friction type terms change gamma energy and produce PAC, and depending on the term and its sign the gamma bursts sit at the peak, trough, rising or falling phase of theta. We study a gamma friction that follows theta velocity as a simplified example. Because the time integral of theta velocity is theta coordinate, the gamma amplitude rises and falls with theta coordinate as exp(gvvx{theta}/2). The fluctuation dissipation theorem turns noise and damping into a theta effective temperature, and the PAC strength becomes a closed form function of one dimensionless number, kappa , that combines the coupling with this temperature. Without fitted parameters, this prediction accounts for 51,095 simulated records (R2 = 0.993) and for the median PAC of 5,160 combinations of coupling and damping (R2 = 0.989). The coupling also drives gamma out of equilibrium: its kinetic temperature grows far above the one inferred from its response. All coefficients enter linearly so that they can, in principle, be estimated from recordings by linear regression. A companion paper shows that the same number sets the distance to a stability boundary.

Article.Title: Tetrodotoxin-resistant NaV1.8 contributes to action potential conduction in a population of mouse and human vagal nerve fibers
Article.Authors: Nair, S. S.; Taylor-Clark, T. E.
Article.Abstract: Axonal action potential (AP) conduction is dependent on voltage-gated sodium channels (NaV1s). AP conduction in the vagus nerve (which contains afferent and efferent fibers) is essential to its reflex regulation of most visceral organs. The nine isoforms of NaV1s show diverse expression patterns in vagal neurons. In rodent vagus nerves, multiple NaV1 isoforms contribute to AP conduction, with NaV1.7 playing an essential role in ~70% of fibers. Here, we investigated the contribution of tetrodotoxin-resistant (TTX-R) NaV1.8 towards vagal AP conduction ex vivo. We tested two structurally different NaV1.8-selective inhibitors, A803467 and PF01247324 and their effects on electrically evoked C-fiber compound action potentials (CAPs) along mouse and human vagus nerves. Tetrodotoxin completely abolished mouse and human vagal CAPs. Nevertheless, both A803467 and PF01247324 caused a concentration-dependent decrease in the C-fiber CAPs in mouse and human vagus nerves. The selectivity of both drugs was tested in NaV1.8 knockout mice. A803467 but not PF01247324 significantly decreased NaV1.8 KO vagal CAPs, indicating that PF01247324's inhibition of wildtype vagal CAPs was solely mediated by NaV1.8, and that A803467 caused inhibition via NaV1.8-mediated and non-NaV1.8-mediated mechanisms. In further studies of wildtype mice, NaV1.8 inhibition following incubation with NaV1.7-selective inhibitor PF05089771 showed no further decrease in mouse vagal CAP, demonstrating that NaV1.8-dependent inhibition affects fibers also sensitive to NaV1.7-dependent inhibition. These data suggest that TTX-sensitive NaV1.7 and TTX-R NaV1.8 cooperate to conduct APs along a select population of vagal nerves. Axonal NaV1.8 inhibition could be utilized to treat aberrant vagal nerve activity in visceral organ diseases.

Article.Title: An H3K9me3high epigenetic state constrains neuronal activation and synaptic remodeling in the aged dentate gyrus
Article.Authors: Moreno-Lopez, Y.; Rodriguez-Ortiz, C. J.; Fuentes-Ibanez, A.; Suarez-Rangel, C. A.; Butler, C. W.; Berchtold, N. C.; Prieto, G. A.
Article.Abstract: How epigenetic states shape neuronal responses to experience and memory remains poorly understood. Here, using a quantitative, single-event approach, our study identifies a subset of neurons that accumulate H3K9me3 (H3K9me3high neurons) via the methyltransferase Suv39h1, specifically in the dorsal dentate gyrus (dDG) of aged mice. FACS coupled to RNA-seq showed that dDG-H3K9me3high neurons express a transcriptional state that fails to induce plasticity machinery despite engaging memory-stabilization programs. Using our novel NucleuSynapse-Tag approach, we found that H3K9me3 accumulation interferes with neuronal activation and synaptic remodeling in response to behavioral stimulation in aged mice. Further, genetically inhibiting Suv39h1 to lower dDG-H3K9me3high numbers improved memory in aged mice. Together, these findings reveal a region- and cell-type-specific epigenetic mechanism linking impaired neuronal responsiveness to age-related memory decline, providing mechanistic insight into the therapeutic potential of targeting Suv39h1.

Article.Title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNS for Flexible Working Memory
Article.Authors: Lu, K.; Chu, T.; TUERHONG, A.; Sun, Y.; Luo, H.; Fang, F.; WU, S.
Article.Abstract: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

Article.Authors: Werner, G.; Schulte-Schrepping, J.; Rodde, R.; Gnaerich, J.; De Domenico, E.; Kislinger, G.; Nalbach, K.; Dinkel, L.; Schlachetzki, J. C. M.; Hummel, S.; Feiten, A. F.; Hoffelner, P.; Nuscher, B.; Reich, M.; Paris, I.; Parhizkar, S.; Colombo, A.; Mueller, S. A.; Willem, M.; Lammich, S.; Schrader, C.; Spintge, J. B.; Prtvar, D.; Ricci, A.; Roth, S.; J., M.; Logan, T.; Wefers, B.; Wurst, W.; Feederle, R.; Liesz, A.; Edbauer, D.; Beyer, M. D.; Grosche, A.; Kawahara, K.; Glass, C.; Di, G.; Tahirovic, S.; Lichtenthaler, S. F.; Simons, M.; Schifferer, M.; Brendel, M.; Haass, C.; Capell, A.; Schultze

Conversely, lysosomal rescue markedly reduced the GPNMB-associated program, demonstrating its reversibility. CSF proteomics identified a convergent lysosomal and microglial signature across models overlapping with alterations reported in human FTD. Article.Title: Distal inhibition is recruited for action but not sensation in the primate superior colliculus
Article.Authors: Bourrelly, C.; Yang, F.; Gandhi, N. J.
Article.Abstract: Sensorimotor transformation requires neural circuits to coordinate excitation and inhibition, but how and whether this organization changes as the circuit transitions from processing sensation to action remain unresolved. We recorded laminar local field potentials across superior colliculus (SC) layers in four male macaques and computed current source density to resolve transmembrane currents during saccades to a target at one of eight isoradial directions. During the visual response, excitation was spatially confined to the receptive field, with little modulation at distant sites. During saccade generation, local excitation remained strongest for movements toward the receptive field, while inhibition extended across the SC map, including locations where spiking remained at baseline. Because the same recordings detected distal inhibition during movement, its absence during vision cannot reflect insufficient sensitivity, indicating that distal inhibition is selectively recruited during action. After saccade completion, excitation emerged regardless of saccade direction, potentially reflecting a rebound from, or release of, the preceding inhibition. These patterns were only partly reflected in spiking activity, which primarily captured local excitation, unmasking circuit dynamics largely invisible at the level of neuronal output. Together, our findings reveal a striking reconfiguration of SC population dynamics across sensorimotor transformation, spanning from spatially restricted excitation during sensation, to local excitation coupled with distal inhibition during movement generation, then to global post-movement excitation. Thus, fixed circuit architecture can express a sequence of behaviorally gated excitation-inhibition states largely invisible to spiking output.

Article.Title: A Shared Neural Network for Highly Liked and Disliked Music
Article.Authors: Ripolles, P.; Belfi, A. M.; Kasdan, A.; Vessel, E. A.; Halpern, A. R.; Rowland, J.; Hopkins, R.; Starr, G. G.; Poeppel, D.
Article.Abstract: While the neural correlates of music-induced peak moments of pleasure (e.g., chills) have been well studied, data on other types of aesthetic responses, such as judgments of beauty, goodness, or liking, are sparse. Among these, liking is of particular interest given its complex nature and its ubiquity in everyday, and musical, experiences. In this fMRI study, 26 participants listened to musical excerpts while continuously rating how much they liked the music. In addition, subjects provided an overall liking judgment at the end of each musical piece. Participants' individualized musical preferences manifested remarkably early and were sustained over time, with the value of the continuous rating at the end of each piece showing the strongest correlation with the overall ratings. Most importantly, at the neural level, highly liked and disliked musical pieces activated a shared neural network previously associated with the processing of both positive and negative emotional stimuli. This network encompassed the anterior cingulate cortex, limbic system, basal ganglia, and precuneus. Interestingly, participants who reported greater responsiveness to artistic stimuli also showed stronger engagement of this network during music listening overall. Finally, the default-mode network showed more negative modulation by the slope of continuous liking ratings for highly liked than for disliked excerpts, potentially reflecting greater engagement with listening and evaluation as liking increased. In linking behavior and brain function to better characterize the way humans make aesthetic judgments of music, the data support a model in which preferences and aesthetic choices are modulated by brain circuits associated with emotion and reward.

Article.Title: From clusters to curves: A model-based alternative to cluster-based permutation tests for the analysis of time-resolved data
Article.Authors: Nalborczyk, L.; Buerkner, P.
Article.Abstract: Time-resolved electrophysiological measurements such as those obtained through magneto- and electroencephalography (M/EEG) offer a unique window onto the neural activity underlying cognitive processes. Researchers are often interested in determining whether and when these signals differ across experimental conditions or participant groups. The conventional approach involves mass univariate statistical testing across time and space followed by corrections for multiple comparisons or some form of cluster-based inference. While effective for controlling error rates at the cluster-level, cluster-based inference comes with a significant limitation: by shifting the focus of inference from individual time points to clusters, it prevents drawing conclusions about the precise onset or offset of observed effects. Here, we present a model-based alternative for analysing M/EEG time series, such as event-related potentials or time-resolved decoding accuracy. Our approach leverages Bayesian generalised additive multilevel models, providing posterior odds at each time point, while naturally accounting for between-participant variability. Using simulated data with known ground truth, we show that the proposed approach consistently provides accurate recovery of the overall temporal extent and onset of neural effects across a range of signal-to-noise ratios, although offset localisation is comparatively more variable. In an empirical MEG decoding dataset, the approach also yields the highest split-half temporal overlap among the methods considered and highly stable temporal segmentation across repeated participant splits. Together, these results illustrate the potential of model-based inference as a complementary approach to conventional cluster-based procedures when temporally localised inference and explicit modelling of between-participant variability are scientifically important. We provide an open-source R package implementing the method and describe how it can be integrated into M/EEG analysis pipelines using MNE-Python.

Article.Title: Cortical Stimulation Strength and sgACC Connectivity Shape Neuro-Cardiac Responses to Prefrontal TMS
Article.Authors: Feng, Z.; Martin, S.; Gerardos, G.; Weise, K.; Hartwigsen, G.; Knoesche, T.; Numssen, O.
Article.Abstract: Autonomic dysregulation is associated with major depressive disorder, yet how cortical stimulation strength and network connectivity shape autonomic responses to prefrontal transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) remains unclear. In linear mixed-effects models, electric-field strength provided better fit and explained more HBC variance than motor-threshold-based intensity. Adding sgACC connectivity further improved model fit and revealed site-specific electric-field-by-connectivity interactions. High-resolution mapping revealed spatial correspondence between regions of higher E-field-HBC explained variance and sgACC-anticorrelated cortex. Negative sgACC connectivity was associated with steeper predicted increases in HBC at several sites, while nonlinear models showed site-dependent differences in dose-response profiles between negative and positive connectivity. Together, these findings link acute cardiac responses to cortical electric-field exposure and sgACC connectivity, supporting HBC as a network-sensitive physiological readout for investigating frontal-vagal function. This framework provides a basis for testing individualized prefrontal TMS targeting and dosing in depression-related autonomic dysregulation.

Article.Title: What's in a Story? Studying Neural Narrative Engagement with Auditory Passages Using EEG Inter-Subject Correlation
Article.Authors: Bunderson, M.; Kaneshiro, B.; Hernandez, P. A.; Rajagopalan, N.; McCandliss, B. D.
Article.Abstract: Narrative engagement - a state implicating attention as well as emotional and sequential processing - is crucial in contexts ranging from social interaction to education. Yet we still lack an understanding of how narrative contents and listener perceptions relate to the neural responses they elicit. In this study, we investigate relationships between auditory narratives and listener responses using electroencephalography inter-subject correlation (EEG-ISC), a measure of neural synchrony that has been shown to correlate with narrative cohesion, attention, preference, and learning. We analyzed dense-array EEG recorded from 46 adult participants who listened to social and non-social narrated literary excerpts. The data were spatially optimized using Reliable Components Analysis, and ISC was calculated for each of the three maximally reliable components (RCs) on a per-stimulus basis. While we found no significant relationships between EEG-ISC and broad social/non-social categorizations of the excerpts, ISC for high sociocognitive word usage significantly exceeded that of medium and low word usage in the third spatial component, RC3. We further observed a significant positive correlation between participants' summed ratings of interest, compulsion, and enjoyment and ISC, both for RC2 and when summed across RC1-RC3. Interaction analyses suggest that passage content and behavioral responses contributed independently as additive effects to these relationships. Taken together, these findings extend previous research utilizing EEG-ISC in natural speech contexts and, importantly, suggest that the decomposition of EEG into maximally correlated spatial components can separate co-occurring neural processes engaged during story listening.

Article.Title: Retinal Vessel Volume Density and Intraoperative Cortical Vascular Phenotypes in Moyamoya Disease
Article.Authors: Zhao, L.; Lou, S.; Liang, H.; Morozova, A.; Liu, Y.; Gao, T.; Sun, Y.; Guo, G.; Liu, Z.; Li, Z.; Jin, S.; Yang, K.; Li, K.; Radovanovic, I.; Andrade-Barazarte, H.; Li, C.
Article.Abstract: Background Angiographic staging describes large-artery stenosis and collateral evolution in moyamoya disease but does not directly depict the cortical surface vasculature, which can vary among patients with similar Suzuki stages. We examined whether a side-matched three-dimensional retinal vascular measure was associated with intraoperative cortical vascular phenotypes after accounting for Suzuki stage. Methods This prospective single-center cohort included 52 patients with moyamoya disease who underwent combined direct and indirect revascularization; 48 had analyzable retinal vessel volume density (RVVD) in the side-matched eye. RVVD was defined as the percentage of the corresponding retinal tissue volume occupied by three-dimensional optical coherence tomography angiography vascular signal within the central 6 x 6-mm region from the retinal nerve fiber layer to the inner plexiform layer. After dural opening and before vascular manipulation, overall cortical vascular richness and arterial, venous, and small-vessel richness were graded from 0 to 3. Associations were evaluated with Spearman correlation and proportional-odds ordinal logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, and ipsilateral Suzuki stage. Results Mean RVVD was 12.92% (SD, 3.30 percentage points). Higher RVVD was associated with greater overall cortical vascular richness ({rho} =0.523; bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap 95% CI, 0.279-0.714; P<0.001) and arterial richness ({rho} =0.522; 95% CI, 0.261-0.714; P<0.001). Per 1-SD higher RVVD, the adjusted cumulative odds ratio for being in a higher richness category was 3.92 (95% CI, 1.82-8.44; P<0.001) for overall cortical vascular richness and 4.31 (95% CI, 1.92-9.70; P<0.001) for arterial richness. Conclusions In moyamoya disease, higher side-matched RVVD was associated with richer overall and arterial cortical vascular phenotypes at revascularization surgery, independent of Suzuki stage. Three-dimensional retinal vascular imaging may therefore provide a noninvasive, side-specific preoperative measure of cortical vascular remodeling.

Article.Title: Early locus coeruleus tauopathy features potassium channel dysfunction and is attenuated by Kv7 activation
Article.Authors: Zhang, Y.-C.; Wang, Y.-G.; Zhang, X.-T.; Chen, P.-Y.; Tan, K.; Zhou, Z.-Y.; Min, X.; Zeng, W.; He, Z.-H.; Xu, H.-T.; He, K.-W.
Article.Abstract: Background The locus coeruleus (LC) accumulates abnormal tau early in Alzheimer's disease, yet the mechanisms linking early tauopathy to neuronal dysfunction and the potential to modify subsequent pathology remain unclear. We investigated potassium-dependent excitability control, associated molecular 5 changes and Kv7-targeted intervention. Pharmacological channel modulation and glycogen synthase kinase- 3 (GSK- 3) inhibition assessed pharmacological modulation of the electrophysiological phenotype. Chronic retigabine treatment assessed pathological outcomes after unilateral locus coeruleus fibril inoculation in young PS19 mice. Exploratory single-cell profiling identified candidate expression changes in marker-defined noradrenergic neurons: increased stress-associated gene expression coincided with reduced expression of neurofilament, neuronal-maintenance and potassium-channel genes, including Kcnq3 and Kcnd1. Increased nuclear RE-1 silencing 20 transcription factor (REST) and reduced Kv7.2 and Kv7.3 immunoreactivity suggested a candidate transcriptional mechanism associated with channel dysfunction. Local fibril inoculation reproduced the physiological abnormalities in wild-type mice, with hyperexcitability depending on endogenous tau. Combined Kv4/Kv7 modulation attenuated hyperexcitability, while GSK- 3; inhibition reduced tau phosphorylation, increased low-threshold potassium currents and lowered tonic firing. Both models showed increased dark-phase wakefulness and state-dependent electroencephalographic power changes. Chronic treatment with the Kv7 opener retigabine reduced bilateral LC AT8-positive tau burden and was associated with higher tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive neuronal density after unilateral seeding. Conclusions Early LC tauopathy combines impaired potassium channel-dependent excitability control with transcriptional changes consistent with cellular stress and reduced neuronal maintenance. Kv7 activation attenuates seeded tau pathology, supporting excitability regulation as a candidate intervention strategy during early tauopathy.

Article.Title: Overexpression of α synuclein in Midbrain Dopamine Neurons Drives Learning Deficits in Mice
Article.Authors: Coutant, B.; Zhuang, X.; Seiler, J.; Nadel, J.; Romo, K.; Fu, Y.; Edwards, R. L.; Halliday, G.; Lerner, T.; Nelson, A. B.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson disease (PD) is diagnosed based on core motor features. However, changes in cognitive function are often already present. Cognitive symptoms include changes in executive function, including organization, planning, multi-tasking, and flexible decision-making. These early cognitive deficits have been difficult to model and remain understudied. Here, we investigated whether AAV-based overexpression of wild-type human alpha-synuclein (syn) in midbrain dopaminergic neurons can produce deficits in learning and behavioral flexibility. We found that syn mice develop progressive impairment in basic action-outcome learning. In addition, we found that syn mice show impairments in behavioral flexibility during probabilistic reversal learning. Together, these findings demonstrate that syn overexpression in midbrain dopaminergic neurons is sufficient to drive cognitive decline. Our early-stage PD model offers a temporal window to dissect cellular and circuits mechanisms underlying non-motor manifestations of PD.

Article.Title: Chronic stress reduces behavioural flexibility and autonomic adaptation when aversive outcomes are controllable
Article.Authors: Rajput, D.; Felmingham, K.; Sophie Lin, C.-H.; Garrido, M. I.
Article.Abstract: Chronic stress is associated with altered adaptation to threat, yet its effects on aversive learning under varying threat predictability and controllability remain unclear. Thirty participants with chronic stress and thirty healthy controls completed a task to learn how well visual cues predicted upcoming electric shocks (predictability) and whether correct predictions of shocks could reduce shock intensity (controllability). We found that, for controllable conditions, accuracy was similar across varying degrees of predictability in the chronic stress group, whereas accuracy in the healthy control group was highest in highly predictable blocks. The chronic stress group responded more slowly than controls and their skin conductance responses were generally lower and indistinguishable across predictability and controllability. We used a computational model to estimate subjective uncertainty and related these estimates to behavioural responses and skin conductance. Modelling showed that controllability shaped uncertainty differently across groups. In chronic stress, with control, subjective stress reflected uncertainty about likely outcomes, reaction time reflected changing outcome probabilities, and skin conductance reflected unexpected outcomes. Without control, subjective stress reflected unexpected outcomes, reaction time uncertainty about likely outcomes, and skin conductance both unexpected outcomes and outcome uncertainty. In healthy controls, subjective stress reflected changing outcome probabilities with control and outcome uncertainty without control, whereas skin conductance showed the reverse pattern, and reaction time reflected likely outcomes only under control. Together, these findings indicate less adaptation in chronic stress, reflected in reduced modulation of reaction time by controllability and skin conductance by predictability and controllability, alongside altered uncertainty associations across response domains.

Article.Title: Neural mechanisms of lightness constancy
Article.Authors: Didehvar, F.; Vanstiphout, R.; Cavanagh, P.; Franken, T. P.
Article.Abstract: Object-specific variables are entangled in sensory input. For example, lightness, whether a surface is white or black, not only depends on the surface reflectance but also on the incident illumination. The brain must thus perform inference to achieve a reliable percept of lightness irrespective of illumination (lightness constancy). Whether this results from simple luminance contrast operations early in the visual system or computations at higher levels remains unresolved. We find that neural lightness signals only appear in the extragranular layers of cortical Area V4, and dominate for shadow regions, as opposed to the comparison of local and surrounding luminance (simultaneous contrast). This suggests that lightness is computed downstream from simultaneous contrast, ruling out simple low-level mechanisms, and instead supporting mid-level anchoring theory.

Article.Title: Microglia and microglia activation are protective in an LSD1-induced model of neurodegeneration
Article.Authors: Bai, Y.; Gosrani, S. P.; Han, C.; Fix, C. E.; Katz, J.; Beddingfield, Z.; Jain, M.; Gouveia-Silva, A.; Engstrom, A. K.; Soares, M. L.; Katz, D. J.
Article.Abstract: Attempts to determine the function of microglia activation and the immune system in neurodegenerative diseases have yielded conflicting results, with some data showing a protective effect, while other data shows a detrimental effect. This discrepancy in the function of microglia activation and the immune system in neurodegeneration likely stems from differing functions during the build-up of pathological proteins versus later stage defects. Therefore, we investigated the function of microglia activation and the immune system in Lsd1 inducible deletion mice, which serve as a late-stage tau-associated neurodegeneration model without the build-up of pathological proteins. We found that loss of LSD1 causes the morphological and transcriptional activation of microglia, accompanied by astrocyte activation and a broader immune response. Blocking microglia activation by inactivating Trem2 inhibited the entire Lsd1-induced immune response, while pharmacologically inhibiting microglia via PLX3397 treatment eliminated microglia but did not block astrocyte reactivity or the broader immune response. Surprisingly, despite these effects, neither blocking microglia activation nor depleting microglia prevented Lsd1-induced neurodegeneration, paralysis and death. Instead, we found in both cases that survival was significantly reduced. These results suggest that microglia and microglial activation, independent of astrocyte reactivity and the broader inflammatory response, is neuroprotective in a late-stage tau-associated neurodegeneration model.

Article.Title: Neural competition predicts speech production advantages in congenital amusia
Article.Authors: Wang, Y.; Liu, M.; Jin, Z.; Huyang, S.; Guo, N.; Zhan, J.; Lian, Q.; Su, C.; Liu, Q.; Huang, S.; Ji, Y.; Wu, D.
Article.Abstract: Mental health research has traditionally been deficit-focused, and cognitive advantages in mental conditions have almost always been documented retrospectively. Here we propose and test an a priori pathway for predicting such advantages from a condition's impaired neural basis, neural competition and brain-mind associations. Using congenital amusia (CA), a neurodevelopmental disorder with a well-defined deficit in right frontotemporal circuit (FTC), as a model, we predicted that interhemispheric competition would release the left homologue from inhibition, conferring advantages in speech production. Two independent studies, multimodal neuroimaging and behavioral testing, confirmed this prediction: MRI revealed right FTC impairment alongside competitive-like benefits of the left FTC in CA; and CA showed speech production advantages with intact episodic memory and constrained music learning. These findings provide the first empirical demonstration that cognitive advantages can be predicted in advance and then verified, offering a principled, mechanism-based alternative to the deficit-focused paradigm.

Article.Title: Shared Fine-Scale Functional Organization in the Human Subcortex Revealed by Connectivity Hyperalignment
Article.Authors: Tu, J. C.; Feilong, M.; Zhang, Y.; Gobbini, M. I.; Haxby, J. V.
Article.Abstract: Subcortical structures are central to cognition, emotion, and social processing, and their dysfunction underlies a wide range of neurological and psychiatric conditions. Yet subcortical fine-scale functional organization has remained largely inaccessible to group-level fMRI analysis: nuclei are small and have low-SNR, and their functional topography varies idiosyncratically across individuals in ways that anatomical alignment cannot resolve. This idiosyncrasy carries real stakes. For example, deep brain stimulation targets with more variable functional connectivity across individuals show correspondingly less consistent clinical outcomes. Here we show that this seemingly idiosyncratic subcortical organization in fact reflects shared, fine-grained structure that can be recovered by modeling each individual's connectivity in a common functional space (connectivity hyperalignment, CHA), rather than relying on anatomical correspondence. Applying CHA to fMRI data collected during naturalistic movie viewing, we found that aligning subcortical voxels by their cortical connectivity, rather than their anatomical location, sharply increased cross-subject correspondence in both stimulus-evoked responses and connectivity profiles. Critically, this alignment sharpened rather than blurred local structure: neighboring voxels became more functionally distinct from one another, and cortical connectivity targets became substantially more decodable across subjects. These results indicate that human subcortical nuclei possess a common fine-scale functional architecture that is masked by anatomical variability but recoverable at the individual level. This reframes a central methodological constraint in subcortical neuroimaging: rather than trading spatial resolution for signal quality via smoothing, group-level analyses can achieve voxel-level precision by aligning function rather than anatomy, opening a path to studying cortical-subcortical circuit organization in greater detail.

Article.Title: Visualizing whole-head neuronal activity and information-sharing dynamics in Caenorhabditis elegans during the transition into the anesthetized state.
Article.Authors: White, H.; Bosinski, C.; Bogaert, H.; Gabel, C. V.; Connor, C.
Article.Abstract: General anesthetics, such as isoflurane, induce immobility and decrease responsiveness to external stimuli. Our previous studies used C. elegans to investigate recovery from anesthesia, and established information-theory metrics characterizing how system-wide neuronal dynamics differ under these conditions. This study develops a novel technique enabling the corollary experiment: visualization of neuronal activity throughout the transition into the anesthetized state. C. elegans worms expressing pan-neuronal nuclear RFP and cytosolic GCaMP6s were imaged with wide-field cameras (behavior), and a light sheet microscope (neuronal activity) in most neurons in the animal's head during isoflurane exposure. Stable concentrations were maintained by measured flow vaporization of isoflurane into a specially designed gas enclosure compatible with the imaging system. We analyzed ensemble neuronal activity, spectrograms of frequency over time, and metrics of shared information between neurons. Behavioral decline differed among tested isoflurane conditions and was most pronounced at 8% isoflurane. Spectrograms indicate loss of bulk signal power, with a somewhat greater loss in higher frequency bands. State Decoupling, Internal Predictability, and System Consistency were among the useful metrics for discriminating anesthetized state. The ratio of State Decoupling to System Consistency ("Disconnection Ratio") showed a prominent increase over time for the 8% condition. The induction of anesthesia produces progressive changes in neuronal activity and communication that can be quantified at single-neuron resolution. Information metrics (State Decoupling entropy, System Consistency entropy, and their ratio) demonstrate that the isoflurane anesthetization process results in altered entropy-derived information sharing, particularly at high anesthetic concentrations.

Article.Title: Neural representation of action grammar structure in primate frontal cortex
Article.Authors: Tian, L. Y.; Hanuska, D. J.; Garzon Gupta, K.; Liu, Y.; Wang, X.-J.; Tenenbaum, J. B.; Freiwald, W. A.
Article.Abstract: Humans and other animals rapidly solve novel problems, often on the first attempt. This capacity is hypothesized to rely on grammars, or internalized systems of abstract rules for recombining units of knowledge into novel composites. Yet, whether and how the brain realizes grammars remains unclear. Here we identify a neural population that represents the latent structure of a grammar. Macaque monkeys traced complex geometric figures with stroke sequences according to the action grammar AnBmCk, meaning "repeat A, then B, then C", where A, B and C are variables that take specific shape values (e.g., A=circle), and n, m, and k correspond to numbers of repetitions. Macaques used this learned grammar to solve unfamiliar problems, including ones more complex than those seen in training--evidence for immediate grammar-based generalization. Recordings across eight frontal cortical areas revealed a representation of grammar structure during drawing, strongest in the presupplementary motor area (preSMA). A, B, and C were represented as distinct states that abstract over specific shapes, resembling roles in hypothesized role-filler structures underlying symbolic cognition. Ordinal position during repetition was encoded along linear axes that were largely orthogonal across A, B, and C. Thus, preSMA represents the geometry of action grammar structure supporting the use of internalized rules to generate novel action sequences.

Article.Title: Movement refinement and cholinergic regulation of outcome-dependent updating during skilled reaching.
Article.Authors: Yeh, N.-H.; Prokop, L.; Marshall, J. J.; Contractor, A.
Article.Abstract: Motor skill learning transforms initially variable actions into precise and reproducible movements. Because conventional measures of task success obscure the distinct processes through which this refinement occurs, we combined detailed outcome scoring and kinematic analysis of single-pellet reaching in mice to resolve how individual components of the action change with repetition. Decomposing reaching into successive stages revealed improvements in targeting and retrieval, while grasp success-rate after pellet contact did not change detectably. Paw trajectories became more consistent across both successful and unsuccessful reaches, whereas changes in the mean speed profile were only detected in successful reaches. To examine how striatal cholinergic signaling contributes to movement refinement and the influence of recent outcomes on subsequent actions, we monitored acetylcholine (ACh) in vivo and inhibited cholinergic interneurons (CINs) during training. ACh was elevated before reach onset and declined during execution across all reach outcomes types. CIN inhibition had little effect on movement refinement across days but altered how recent outcomes influenced the next reach. In control animals, a failed attempt moved the reach away from the animal's practiced successful trajectory but this did not occur after CIN inhibition, most clearly when the pellet had been grasped and then lost. These findings distinguish refinement of the practiced movement from outcome-dependent adjustments to its execution. Together, they raise the possibility that the pre-reach ACh elevation plays a role in enabling the evaluation of recent outcomes to update the execution of the next reach.

Article.Title: Prefrontal cortical pathways mediating cognitive control enhancement from internal capsule stimulation
Article.Authors: Sretavan Wong, K.; Nagrale, S. S.; Pipia, V.; Sachse, E. M.; Dastin-van Rijn, E. M.; Kim, J.; Eiting, S.; McInnes, A. N.; Palnitkar, T.; Chandrasekaran, J.; Braun, H.; Brenny, S.; Seddighi, Y.; Patriat, R.; Harel, N.; Johnson, M. D.; Widge, A. S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) targeting the ventral internal capsule/ventral striatum (VCVS) is an effective treatment for several psychiatric disorders, but clinical responses vary amongst patients, likely reflecting an incomplete mechanistic understanding of the brain pathways mediating response. VCVS DBS may improve cognitive control, a core deficit in multiple psychiatric disorders. Here, we investigated which prefrontal cortical pathway(s) in the internal capsule are associated with improved cognitive control task performance during VCVS DBS. Methods: Four participants with bilateral VCVS DBS completed the Multi-Source Interference Task (MSIT) across 27 stimulation configurations varying by side (left/right lead), electrode, amplitude, and frequency. Each condition included 100 trials, and response time (RT) assessed task performance. Individualized pathway activation models quantified axonal recruitment across 11 segmented prefrontal cortical fiber bundles per hemisphere. Associations between pathway activation and task RT were analyzed to identify circuits linked to improved cognitive control task performance. Results: Right-sided VCVS stimulation was associated with greater reductions in MSIT RT than left-sided stimulation. Activation of right dorsal prefrontal cortical pathways connected to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) was associated with faster RT, whereas no left-sided pathways were significantly associated with changes in RT. Conclusions: Right-sided dorsal prefrontal pathways connected to the dlPFC and dmPFC are candidate pathways associated with improved cognitive control task performance during VCVS DBS. Pathway activation modeling may inform more precise stimulation strategies for psychiatric disorders characterized by impaired cognitive control, although whether this approach improves clinical outcomes remains to be established.

Article.Title: Next generation Human Neocortical Neurosolver model with biophysically realistic somatic, dendritic and synaptic dynamics
Article.Authors: Duecker, K.; Soplata, A.; Tolley, N.; Pugliese, S.; Jones, T. A. E.; Kandpal, C.; Waller, D. A.; Daniels, D. S.; Jones, S. R.
Article.Abstract: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN) is an open-source biophysical modeling tool for multiscale interpretation of human electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. HNN's foundation is a pre-tuned canonical neocortical circuit model consisting of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in supra- (L2/3) and infragranular (L5) layers. This model was originally developed based on studies in rodent and non-human primate cortices when dynamics of human neurons were poorly characterized. Yet recent advances in recordings from human tissue now provide unprecedented detail to update the model. Here, we present a significantly updated model for use in the HNN software, with electrophysiological properties and synaptic connections tuned to human tissue. Beyond reproducing biologically realistic somatic dynamics, the pyramidal cells simulate dendritic calcium (Ca2+) spikes in the L5 extratelencephalic-projecting (ET) neurons, and shorter dendritic spikes in the L2/3 pyramidal neurons. We demonstrate how the updated circuitry and new features in the HNN software can be used to disentangle somatic, synaptic, and dendritic contributions to human E-/MEG signatures. The model is distributed with workflows to simulate event-related responses and oscillations, and tutorials demonstrating how membrane potentials, Ca2+ dynamics, and synaptic currents can be recorded and visualized. These enhancements allow extensive model validations based on in vitro and in vivo electrophysiology, voltage and Ca2+ imaging, and provide users with novel insights on the mechanisms underlying E-/MEG signals.

Article.Title: Motor cortical signals predict finger velocity beyond task geometry
Article.Authors: Du, Z.; Lai, Z. Y.; Hu, L.; Ye, T.
Article.Abstract: Finger movements toward the same target can differ in speed. How much does motor cortical activity add to a velocity prediction once the decoder knows the starting position and the intended target? We compared predictions of finger velocity on held-out trials with and without spiking-band power from motor cortex. In 18 sessions from one macaque, neural activity reduced mean squared error by 4.92% relative to a baseline that used the target, starting position and time within the trial. The reduction was 4.63% in 20 additional sessions from the same animal, with improvement in every session. Giving the baseline the preceding 100 ms of measured finger position reduced the neural gain in every session. Mean error reductions fell to 2.75% and 2.05%, respectively. In all 20 additional sessions, neural activity from the same trial gave more accurate predictions than activity substituted from a closely matched trial. In simulations, an incomplete model of task geometry could also produce this pairing effect. Motor cortical activity predicts variation in finger velocity beyond the movement expected from task geometry, and part of that variation is also predictable from recent finger position.

Article.Title: Opposing signaling molecules exert cortical control over dissociable behaviors that tile an aggressive state
Article.Authors: Gatlin, R. E.; Du, Y.; Gagon, J.; Kwak, D.; Park, S.; Walker, H.; Rondem, K. E.; Liu, Y.; Kroheim, L.; Everett, T.; Covington, A.; Fluck, M. M.; Zickmund, T.; Zweifel, L. S.; Frost, N. A.; Zelikowsky, M.
Article.Abstract: Neuropeptides exert broad effects across the brain to influence behavior. However, the mechanism by which neuropeptide signaling exerts top-down, cortical control over complex behavior remains poorly understood. Prolonged social isolation induces sweeping changes to behavior, including increasing aggression. Here, we find that isolation-induced aggression engages Tachykinin-2 expressing (Tac2+) neurons in the mouse medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). Behavioral analyses and in vivo recordings reveal that mPFC Tac2+ neurons are tuned to two distinct phases of an aggressive encounter: an initial phase marked by increased investigatory behaviors and a second phase comprised of increased aggression. RNA sequencing and subsequent molecule-specific loss-of-function perturbations targeting the ability of Tac2+ neurons to release either the stimulatory neuropeptide Neurokinin B or the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA reveal that these signaling molecules exert dissociable control over increased investigation and aggression, respectively. Surprisingly, these findings reveal that the cotransmission of signaling molecules with opposing actions from the same population of cells is nevertheless able to exert coordinated control over distinct behaviors that tile an aggressive state, revealing an efficient, multiplexed neurochemical mechanism by which neuropeptidergic populations in the mPFC influence behavior.

Article.Title: Linking cross-species hemodynamics with neuronal activity in prefrontal cortex during abstract sequence viewing
Article.Authors: Conen, K. E.; Stewart, B.; Rivera Nunez, M. V.; Hyde, H.; Yusif Rodriguez, N.; Ahuja, A.; Basu, D.; McKim, T.; Desrochers, T. M.
Article.Abstract: Humans and other primates have a remarkable ability to identify and predict abstract patterns that evolve through time, but the neural mechanisms that support this capability remain poorly understood. Lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) has been implicated in abstract sequence tracking in both humans and macaques, but it is unclear whether underlying processes are shared across species. Further, most existing evidence relies on hemodynamic responses, which can have variable relationships with neuronal activity. We leveraged a combination of human fMRI, monkey fMRI, and electrophysiology to bridge these gaps. We found that humans and macaques show functionally homologous hemodynamic activation in LPFC during abstract sequence viewing, and neuronal responses within fMRI-targeted regions in macaques contain information about abstract and sensory variables in parallel. However, neuronal activity did not directly mirror hemodynamic responses, and abstract sequence responses were found both near and far from fMRI peaks. In contrast, distinct dynamics of spiking activity were selectively present near fMRI peaks, suggesting that temporal coordination across neurons may influence hemodynamic activity in prefrontal cortex. Together, these experiments establish a link between human brain activity, macaque fMRI, and single neuron responses, providing a window into the neural processes that mediate abstract sequence detection.

Article.Title: Competing routes back to firing shape population hyperexcitability and its selective suppression
Article.Authors: Kamaraj, A. K.; Szuromi, M. P.
Article.Abstract: Even within the same neuron, successive spikes can follow distinct trajectories, with afterdepolarization permitting early return to firing and depolarization block prolonging inactivity. Therefore, we propose that hyperexcitability involves changes in the opportunities to fire again from different points across the spike cycle, and not just from quiescence. The hazard of firing - the instantaneous propensity to fire again with time elapsed after a spike - isolates these opportunities. In bursting dopamine neurons, the hazard rises early due to burst-sustaining spikes, falls, then rises again due to burst-initiating spikes. Within a renewal framework, we represent each rise as a competing pathway back to firing and show that recruitment from quiescence and firing again before full recovery provide independent control over population activity. Changes in pathway engagement distinguish subclinical from overt hyperexcitability and allow neurons of the same type to respond differently to a common input. Adding a slower return pathway for drug-bound neurons shows how sodium-channel blockers such as phenytoin and carbamazepine can suppress pathological bursting while leaving physiological activity apparently intact.

Article.Title: NOTCH3 p.R544C Drives Early Neurovascular Unit Dysfunction through Blood-Brain Barrier Failure, Complement Signalling and Metabolic Dysregulation
Article.Authors: Lee, J. W. L.; Zhang, Z.-W.; Chauhan, M.; Teo, X. Q.; Tan, A. Q. L.; Lim, T. S.; Wee, H. S.-A.; Ngian, Z. K.; Sanders, L. H.; Cheung, C.; Zhong, P.; Ng, A. S. L.; Ong, Q.; Tan, E.-K.; Zeng, L.
Article.Abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease is a major cause of stroke and vascular cognitive impairment, yet the mechanisms that initiate neurovascular dysfunction before irreversible brain injury remain poorly defined. CADASIL, caused by cysteine-altering NOTCH3 mutations, provides a genetically tractable model to resolve these early events. Here, we investigated the Asian-enriched NOTCH3 p.R544C variant and tested whether early disease emerges through interconnected blood-brain barrier (BBB), inflammatory, and metabolic dysfunction. NOTCH3 p.R544C iPSC-derived endothelial cells showed impaired angiogenesis and migration, reduced barrier resistance, disrupted tight-junction organisation, and altered vascular, adhesion, and extracellular-matrix programmes. In multicellular BBB-like microtissues, these defects propagated across the neurovascular unit, producing disorganised vascular networks, enlarged luminal structures, and increased permeability, establishing BBB failure as an early disease layer. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed coordinated loss of endothelial BBB transport and efflux programmes with astrocytic complement, innate immune, and matrix-remodelling activation. Secretome profiling and patient-plasma measurements converged on complement- and matrix-associated mediators, including C1S and CLU, identifying complement-matrix activation as a second interconnected layer. Importantly, combined cilostazol and isosorbide mononitrate treatment improved barrier function and reduced selected complement- and matrix-associated proteins in mutant microtissues, supporting pharmacological reversibility of components of this early disease programme. Seahorse analysis further demonstrated reduced mitochondrial respiratory capacity associated with NOTCH3 p.R544C. In vivo, three-month-old mutant mice showed altered cerebral pyruvate metabolism and early microvascular abnormalities, whereas six-month-old mice developed more prominent extracellular-matrix, inflammatory, and gliovascular changes, supporting an age-dependent transition from early metabolic dysregulation to broader neurovascular remodelling. Together, these findings define NOTCH3 p.R544C CADASIL as an early multicellular neurovascular disorder organised across three interconnected mechanistic layers: BBB failure, complement-matrix signalling, and metabolic dysregulation, while identifying early BBB-centred dysfunction as a potentially tractable state before advanced cerebrovascular injury develops.

Article.Title: Detecting behavioural oscillations with increased sensitivity: A modification of Brookshire's (2022) AR-surrogate method
Article.Authors: Harris, A. M.; Beale, H. A.
Article.Abstract: A core challenge of cognitive neuroscience is to understand how cognition changes over time within individuals. For example, the tendency for behavioural responses to oscillate over time has been documented extensively in a range of cognitive domains. Recently, however, the phenomenon of behavioural oscillations has been called into question by indications that past findings might reflect aperiodic temporal structure rather than true oscillations. Brookshire (2022) proposed methods to control for aperiodic temporal structure while examining oscillations in behavioural time-courses and found no evidence of behavioural oscillations in reanalyses of four published datasets. However, Brookshire's (2022) method has been criticised for having low sensitivity to detect effects of realistic magnitude, so it is currently unclear whether these findings suggest that behavioural oscillations are not present in these and perhaps many other datasets, or whether they are false negatives. Here, we present a modification of Brookshire's (2022) method that uses an integrated moving average (IMA) model applied to the single-participant data, instead of the original auto-regressive (AR) approach applied to the group-level data. This method demonstrates increased sensitivity to detect effects of realistic magnitude, adequate control of false positives, and other desirable properties such as the ability to increase statistical power by adding more participants. Using this method, we reanalyse the same publicly available datasets and show significant behavioural oscillations in each of them, suggesting oscillations in behaviour are a robust phenomenon upon which to draw theoretical inferences. The participant-level IMA-surrogate method is currently the most sensitive method available for analysing behavioural oscillations while controlling for the contribution of aperiodic data fluctuations.

Article.Title: Unexpected Long Range Actions of AAV8
Article.Authors: Lahr, J. M.; Ly, J.; Erdem, E.; Williams, M. R.
Article.Abstract: Adeno-associated virus vectors (AAVs) have broad utility in neuroscience. A variety of features, such as titer, capsid, enhancers and promoters, coding and non-coding elements, can be utilized to pursue diverse experimental ends. The net effects of titer and capsid have been used experimentally to pursue retrograde and anterograde studies, such as through the monosynaptic spread of high-titer AAV1. The literature on AAV8 is conflicting, with evidence for and against its long-range action outside of the infected starter population. Using the mouse corticopontocerebellar tract, we report that AAV8, when used at high titers, can be associated with long range recombination outside of the starter population. This phenomenon depended upon the viral titer and was influenced by the presence of other experimental injections. Surprisingly, separate injections of high-titer AAV8 recombinase and recombinase-reporter AAV8s gave rise to recombination across long distances in populations not known to be monosynaptically connected. Given the possibility of long range and emergent effects, we suggest that investigators empirically determine titer, capsid, and injection designs that reduce false positives and/or indirect effects.

Article.Title: Astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D regulates hippocampal memory through extracellular matrix remodeling
Article.Authors: Kim, H.; Cha, S.; Ji, M.; Kim, G. H.; Shin, S. A.; Lee, S. E.; Lee, K. J.; Lee, S.-W.; Chae, S.; Park, H.
Article.Abstract: Astrocytes contribute to hippocampal cognitive functions, but how astrocyte-derived factors regulate memory formation remains unclear. Here, we identify astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D (CtsD) as a regulator of hippocampal learning and memory. Proteomic profiling of hippocampal astrocytes upon learning identified candidates predicted to be secreted, among which we focused on CtsD, whose extracellular brain functions are unknown. Neutralizing extracellular CtsD or astrocyte-selective CtsD knockdown (aCtsD-KD) impaired hippocampal long term potentiation (LTP) and memory acquisition, suggesting an extracellular role for astrocytic CtsD. In aCtsD-KD mice, these deficits were accompanied by alterations in excitatory transmission and synaptic structures. aCtsD-KD also caused abnormal extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation, and its partial digestion by chondroitinase ABC rescued the memory deficit, indicating that astrocytic CtsD-dependent ECM degradation contributes to hippocampal memory. Together, our findings suggest a CtsD-dependent astrocyte-matrix-synapse axis regulating hippocampal memory.

Article.Title: A latent tau amplifier in the neuronal proteome lowers the seeding threshold for Alzheimers disease pathology
Article.Authors: Tsaka, G.; Kolla, R.; Wiedmer, A. E.; Georgilis, A.; Kenis, S.; Van der Hoeven, G.; Claes, F.; Khodaparast, L.; Khodaparast, L.; Lahaije, B.; Tome, S. O.; Muwonge, K.; Duran, R.; Vandenberghe, R.; von Arnim, C. A. F.; Louros, N.; Thal, D. R.; Rousseau, F.; Schymkowitz, J.
Article.Abstract: The stereotyped spread of tau pathology through connected brain regions is accompanied by striking differences in the vulnerability of individual neuronal populations, pointing to cell-intrinsic determinants of susceptibility. Using a combination of computational APR analysis, in vitro and cellular aggregation assays, and quantitative proteomics of human postmortem brain, we identify the splicing factor TRA2B as an endogenous modifier of this susceptibility. TRA2B enhances the activity of patient-derived tau seeds, promotes tau pathology in vivo, and progressively redistributes from the nucleus into insoluble tau-associated material in Alzheimers disease brain. Mechanistically, TRA2B contains two aggregation-prone regions (APRs) homologous to tau nucleation sites that are required for tau interaction and seeding enhancement. Yet this activity is not constitutive: isolated TRA2B APRs promote aggregation, whereas the full-length protein can inhibit, amplify or have little effect on tau aggregation depending on protein state and seeding context. Perturbation of the regulatory RS2 region switches TRA2B away from its amplifying state, revealing that its sequence-encoded aggregation potential is regulatable. Thus, TRA2B acts as a latent tau amplifier, providing a mechanism by which the neuronal proteome can tune cellular susceptibility to the propagation of pathological tau.

Article.Title: Bayesian nonparametric identification of spectrally distinct neural states
Article.Authors: Yamada, S.; Nagel, S. E.; Kobeleva, X.; Schmidt, R.
Article.Abstract: Identifying neural oscillations is essential for linking fast brain dynamics to underlying cognitive processes. However, this is challenging because oscillatory events can be brief, embedded in 1/f-like background activity, and may comprise an unknown number of spectrally distinct states. Conventional approaches often apply narrowband band-pass filters to one or a few predefined frequency bands and then use amplitude thresholding to identify oscillatory events, but detection outcomes can be highly sensitive to these choices. Although recent unsupervised alternatives based on hidden Markov models (HMMs) address these limitations, they still require the number of states to be specified in advance and can underfit or overfit when this number is misspecified. We propose a Bayesian nonparametric method that identifies distinct oscillatory states while inferring an appropriate number of states directly from the data. This method combines time-delay embedding (TDE) with the Dirichlet-process Gaussian mixture model (DP-GMM). TDE augments the signal with time-shifted copies, enabling the DP-GMM to capture frequency-specific local autocovariance structures, while the Dirichlet-process prior adapts model complexity by pruning inactive components. We benchmarked the approach against a filter-based thresholding method and the time-delay embedded HMM using single-channel synthetic data designed to mimic neural time series (e.g., EEG, MEG, and local field potentials), with multiple frequency components masked by 1/f-like noise. In this setting, the proposed model reliably recovered multiple distinct frequency components under noisy conditions while also inferring the number of oscillatory states. Applied to a resting-state motor-cortex MEG dataset, the model identified multiple frequency-selective, short-lived oscillatory states alongside distinct aperiodic states with different spectral profiles. These states exhibited substantial inter-individual heterogeneity in peak frequency, occurrence rate, and power. Overall, this provides an unsupervised framework for discovering frequency-selective oscillatory states without predefining frequency bands or fixing the number of states.

Article.Title: CortexDecoder: Efficient fMRI-to-Image Reconstruction from Cortical Flatmaps
Article.Authors: Imoto-Tar, T.; Fung, M.; Gurha, A.
Article.Abstract: Recent brain decoding work has shown the potential of Vision Transformers (ViTs) to learn mappings from neural representations to visual features. Here we present CortexDecoder, a framework that reconstructs viewed images from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) flatmaps, which are neural responses projected onto the cortical surface and unfolded into 2D images. We show that a frozen, pretrained cortical foundation model is sufficient for competitive reconstruction. A frozen CortexMAE encoder turns flatmap patches into brain tokens, and two lightweight cross-attention bridges map these tokens to semantic CLIP embeddings and low-level image features. The final image is generated using a frozen SDXL-unCLIP model which takes a low-level image reconstruction as an initial image and a predicted CLIP embedding used to condition the image generation. On Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) Subject 1 reconstruction benchmarks, CortexDecoder is competitive with prior methods and the best for cortical flatmap methods without multi-subject pretraining. CortexDecoder achieves this performance while training far fewer parameters compared to prior methods.

Article.Title: How brain operation emerges from its nested recurrent circuitry extending into the body
Article.Authors: Szeier, S.; Jorntell, H.
Article.Abstract: Behavior and thoughts are dynamic processes driven by activity in a multitude of internal and external nested neuronal circuitry loops. This causes an unexplained complexity in neuron population dynamics. Pursuing an atomic principle of how brain operation emerges from these nested closed loops, here we show that the activity state space travel of a neuron population can be understood as a consequence of a vector field with an attractor point, which emerges from the intrinsic neuronal properties and the synaptic connections between them. Neuronal activity in the brain in vivo, however, indicates that attractor point continually moves along trajectories, which we show requires dynamic input from sensors and input-independent activity generation in neurons. In a spinal network-biomechanical system, the state-dependent intrinsic dynamical structures of the neural and the biomechanics systems drive each others activity trajectories to generate diverse behaviors. Similarly, independent self-generated thalamic neuron activity forms closed-loop thalamocortical subnetworks that continually shape each others trajectories to drive the dynamic global cortical activity also without dynamic sensory input. These high-dimensional attractor trajectories are susceptible to criticality effects that allow for a rich behavioral flexibility based on sensory inputs and intrinsic anticipative subnetworks, explaining why complex neural dynamics is foundational to brain operation. We argue that in this conceptual framework the contribution of each functional subsystem of the CNS to sensorimotor control and motor planning is given a natural, emergent, and scalable explanation, and the goal of synaptic weight learning partially becomes fundamentally different from most models in the literature.

Article.Title: The exocyst is an insulin-sensitive regulator of amyloid precursor protein trafficking and amyloid-beta generation in neurons
Article.Authors: Balaan, C.; Patwardhan, G. Y.; Sachs, R. K.; Kumasaka, H.; Sadagopan, S.; Aou, S.; Lee, A. J.; Nelson, L. T.; Hew, B. E.; Owens, J. B.; Polgar, N.; Ortega, M. A.; Nichols, R. A.; Fogelgren, B.
Article.Abstract: Intracellular trafficking of amyloid precursor protein (APP) critically influences amyloidogenic processing, yet the mechanisms regulating this pathway remain incompletely defined. The exocyst is a highly conserved, insulin-responsive, eight-protein Rab effector complex that directs intracellular transport vesicle targeting and docking. We identified APP in a proteomics screen of neuronal cell surface proteins altered following chemical inhibition of exocyst activity. In SH-SY5Y cells expressing an APP mutant that enhances amyloidogenic processing, RNAi-mediated silencing of exocyst subunits significantly decreased sAPP and A{beta} secretion, accompanied by intracellular APP accumulation. High-resolution microscopy revealed APP colocalization with exocyst subunits in the soma and neurites of differentiated SH-SY5Y neurons and primary mouse hippocampal neurons. Live-cell TIRF microscopy demonstrated coordinated movement of fluorescently tagged exocyst and APP proteins. Proximity ligation assays (PLAs) confirmed close (<40nm) APP-EXOC5 association in differentiated SH-SY5Y neurons, primary mouse hippocampal neurons, and histological sections of mouse brain. To examine whether insulin regulates neuronal exocyst activity, as in adipocytes and muscle, we generated SH-SY5Y cells expressing pHluorin-tagged GLUT4. Using this model, we found that chemical inhibition of exocyst activity prevented insulin-stimulated GLUT4 exocytosis to the plasma membrane. Furthermore, PLAs in both primary hippocampal and SH-SY5Y neurons revealed that insulin increased GLUT4-EXOC5 associations while markedly reducing APP-EXOC5 associations. These findings suggest that insulin signaling redirects the exocyst away from APP-positive vesicles towards GLUT-positive vesicles. Together, our data identify the exocyst as a novel insulin-regulated mediator of neuronal APP trafficking and A{beta} secretion.

Article.Title: An atlas of the aging glycoproteome reveals how glycosylation modulates autoantibody binding in the brain
Article.Authors: Schoof, M.; Reitenbach, J.; Abraham, K.; Tilton-Low, G.; Wu, D.; Chithrananda, S.; Freund, Y.; Channappa, D.; Pepi, L. E.; Dunn, J. E.; Wernig, M.; Han, M. H.; Iram, T.; Seeley, E. H.; Guldner, I. H.; Bertozzi, C. R.; Wyss-Coray, T.
Article.Abstract: Protein N-glycosylation generates substantial molecular diversity, yet how glycan composition varies throughout aging remains poorly understood. We mapped the N-glycoproteome of brain, liver, spleen, kidney, and plasma across nine ages spanning the mouse lifespan, identifying 79,517 unique N-glycopeptides at 9,217 glycosites on 4,397 glycoproteins, with matched proteomic trajectories (glycoproteinatlas.org). Brain aging increased short paucimannose glycans, driven partly by increased abundance of hexosaminidase B (HEXB). We identified MOG-reactive autoantibodies in aged individuals and patients with MOG antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) and showed that MOG glycosylation modulates autoantibody binding. Glycosylation changes associated with normal aging were also observed after experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a model of autoimmune neuroinflammation. These findings reveal N-glycosylation as both a marker of age and a regulator of disease-relevant molecular interactions.

Article.Title: Weberian interval discrimination and temporal pattern generalization in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Lo, T.-N.; Huang, C.-Y.; Lin, S.
Article.Abstract: Recognizing temporally structured signals, from human speech and music to the songs and calls of other animals, relies on comparing the durations of their elements. In vertebrates, interval discrimination often follows Weber's law: sensitivity depends on the ratio between intervals rather than their absolute difference. Such proportional scaling may enable efficient representation of a wide range of durations and support recognition of temporal patterns despite changes in their speed. Whether insect brains use the same computational principle, and which neural circuits support flexible temporal learning, remain unclear. Here, we developed an auditory learning paradigm in which fruit flies, Drosophila melanogaster, learn to associate temporal patterns of sound with a sugar reward. Flies discriminate tone durations ranging from subsecond to a few seconds and use this information to guide reward-seeking behavior. Their discrimination depends on the ratio between durations rather than their absolute difference, consistent with Weber's law. Flies also generalize learned temporal relationships to proportionally compressed durations and transfer them from auditory to visual stimuli, indicating a flexible representation of temporal structure. Finally, blocking mushroom body output impairs temporal pattern learning but leaves auditory pitch learning intact, identifying the mushroom body as a critical neural circuit for this form of learning. Together, these findings demonstrate that ratio-based and generalizable temporal computations can be implemented in a compact, genetically tractable brain, providing insight into the evolutionary origins of temporal cognition and establishing Drosophila as a powerful system for investigating its neural basis.

Article.Title: Access and local retention control neutrophil function in retinal regeneration
Article.Authors: Li, Y.; Xu, T.; Zhi, Y.; Zhao, R.; Lu, Q.; Xu, H.
Article.Abstract: Neutrophils are among the first immune cells to reach injured tissues, yet their contributions to regeneration range from essential to dispensable or even inhibitory across injury contexts. Whether this variability reflects differences in tissue access, post-entry function, or persistence remains unresolved. Here we show that neutrophils are required for regenerative responses in needle-poked, but not NMDA-injured, zebrafish retinas. In stab injury, where barrier disruption permits neutrophil entry, pharmacological neutrophil ablation suppresses Muller glia proliferation, progenitor formation, and neuronal regeneration. In contrast, in the NMDA injury model, neutrophils show minimal infiltration into the retinal parenchyma, and their depletion has no significant effect. We further show that Cxcl12-Cxcr4b signaling retains neutrophils at the stab injury site, and that manipulating retention correspondingly alters regenerative outcomes. At the injury site, neutrophils modulate microglial reactivity and inflammatory responses and provide Hb-egf as an early regeneration-promoting factor. These findings identify a previously unrecognized requirement for neutrophils in retinal regeneration and reveal a two-tiered control of their function: access to the injured tissue, and local retention that enables regenerative signaling.

Article.Title: Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C) Attenuates Dichlorvos-Induced Neurobehavioral and Oxido-Inflammatory Stress in Discrete Brain Regions
Article.Authors: Ogbuokiri, D. K.; Abugu, J. I.; Oladosu, O. B.; Unekwuojo, I. B.; Agufusi, N. P.; Kenechukwu, E. V.
Article.Abstract: Background: Dichlorvos is a widely used organophosphate pesticide associated with neurotoxicity through acetylcholinesterase inhibition, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation. Chronic exposure may cause neuronal dysfunction and structural brain alterations. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C), a potent antioxidant, may provide neuroprotection against oxidative damage. This study evaluated the protective effects of ascorbic acid against dichlorvos--induced neurobehavioral and oxido--inflammatory alterations in adult male Wistar rats. Methods: Thirty--six rats were randomly assigned into six groups (n = 6): control, dichlorvos (20 mg/kg), dichlorvos plus low--dose ascorbic acid (50 mg/kg), low--dose ascorbic acid, dichlorvos plus high-dose ascorbic acid (150 mg/kg), and high--dose ascorbic acid groups. Treatments were administered orally for six weeks. Neurobehavioral performance was assessed using the T--maze and hanging--wire tests. Oxidative stress biomarkers, including malondialdehyde, superoxide dismutase, and catalase, were evaluated in the hippocampus and amygdala. Histological examinations of the hippocampus, cerebellum, and prefrontal cortex were also performed. Data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test (). Results: No significant difference in brain weight was observed across groups. Neurobehavioral assessments showed no statistically significant differences between pre-- and post--treatment performances, although dichlorvos exposure produced a slight decline, while ascorbic acid--treated groups showed dose--dependent improvement. Dichlorvos significantly increased malondialdehyde levels and decreased superoxide dismutase and catalase activities compared with control (p < 0.05). Co--administration of ascorbic acid significantly reduced lipid peroxidation and improved antioxidant enzyme activities relative to the dichlorvos group (p <0.05). Histologically, the hippocampus remained largely preserved, while mild neuronal degeneration was observed in the prefrontal cortex of dichlorvos--treated rats. The cerebellum showed mostly normal architecture, with mild molecular layer degeneration in the high--dose dichlorvos plus ascorbic acid group. Conclusions: Ascorbic acid attenuated dichlorvos--induced oxidative stress and reduced associated histopathological alterations, with limited but observable improvements in neurobehavioral outcomes. These findings suggest its potential protective role against organophosphate--induced neurotoxicity. Keywords: Ascorbic acid, dichlorvos, oxidative stress, neuroprotection, hippocampus, cerebellum,
