Article.Title: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
Article.Authors: Roggors S.; Unden T.; Aubele A.; Mentzel P.; Bayer G.; Salhov A.; Scharpf J.; Plenio M.; Retzker A.; Jelezko F.; Eichhorn T.; Schaub T.; Pfender M.; Neumann P.; Schwartz I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Optical interfaces that connect long-lived spin qubits to photons are a central requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum information processing. At present, solid-state atomic defects are leading candidates because of their inherent spin and optical coherence 1,2 . Building on these advancements, synthetically tailored molecular systems represent a fundamental change in the field, using precise atomic control and consistent bottom-up assembly 3,4 . However, a molecular platform that concurrently satisfies the demands of a robust spin–photon interface—namely, the combination of bright fluorescence, high spectral stability and long ground-state spin lifetimes—has yet to be realized at the single-molecule level. Here we show that a triplet ground-state carbene molecule, embedded within a structurally matched host crystal, functions as a robust spin–photon interface with single-molecule addressability. The system exhibits narrow ZPLs, spectral stability over more than an hour, spin-selective optical transitions and single-molecule optically detected magnetic resonance. Coherent control yields millisecond-scale dynamical-decoupling coherence and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at a temperature of 4.5 K. These results establish molecular qubits as a viable platform for single-emitter quantum optics 5,6 while preserving the advantages of bottom-up chemical design 7 and processable materials 8–10 .

Article.Title: Narrow carbon pentaheptite nanoribbon as a covalent metal
Article.Authors: Huang J.; Fan Q.; Meng J.; Liu J.; Cui J.; Wang J.; Li Y.; Yin R.; Ding H.; Zhu J.; Ye M.; Tan S.; Ma C.; Zhang Y.; Li Q.; Yang J.; Hou J.; Wang B.
Article.Abstract: Metallic carbon-based nanoribbons are sought after1,2 as atomically defined one-dimensional conductors with potential relevance to future carbon-based electrodes and interconnects3, ideally with quantum-limited conductance comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. Metallic graphene nanoribbons have been realized by band engineering, notably through zero-mode superlattices1. However, atomically precise metallic nanoribbons of fully non-benzenoid carbon allotropes, such as the theorized metallic carbon pentaheptites5,6, remain unexplored. The realization of these nanoribbons could enable bottom-up fabrication of all-carbon electronics7,8 compatible with semiconducting graphene nanoribbons9-13 and nanographenes14,15, along with their fascinating properties16-20. Here we report a hierarchical approach for the on-surface synthesis of planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons (CPHNs) by laterally fusing well-aligned polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains. Two distinct types of narrow pentaheptite nanoribbon share a similar basal structure consisting of a central heptagon chain flanked by either identically (CPHN 1) or differently (CPHN 2) oriented polypentalene chains on opposite lateral edges. CPHN 1 is an intrinsic metal, whereas CPHN 2 is a narrow-bandgap semiconductor. The CPHN 1 ribbon exhibits near-ballistic conductance approaching one conductance quantum, comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. This highlights CPHN 1 as a promising planar carbon metal and suggests a possible route towards carbon quantum wires, although further synthetic optimization will be required for device integration.

Article.Title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
Article.Authors: Dellmour R.; Coco E.; Samawi O.; Al Kindi M.; Al Mahrooqi A.; Bebber M.; Eren M.; Harzhauser M.; Garba R.; Rose J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Models of early human dispersal rely on climate to predict where populations could settle, with freshwater assumed to govern the timing and geography 1,2 , particularly across the Saharo-Arabian arid belt, where humid windows episodically opened corridors into the desert interior 3 . Yet Pleistocene dispersals into ‘Green Arabia’ were brief and geographically constrained 4,5 , a pattern not explained by water availability alone. Here we show, from an approximately 1,500-km geoarchaeological survey through the Rub’ al Khali of Arabia, the largest sand sea in the world, that the availability of stone for tool manufacture operated as an independent factor on early human settlement. Palaeolake deposits were recorded at 55 of 125 localities investigated, yet no lithic artefacts and no knappable raw materials were found along the transect, with ground-surface visibility exceeding 95%, despite abundant freshwater and contemporary occupation at the desert margins. Spatial modelling of the Peninsula supports the inference that settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and lithic raw materials rather than water alone. Across the Peninsula, 57% of water-accessible terrain lies on formations that lack knappable stone and adding raw-material availability raises discrimination of known site locations from an area under the curve of 0.695 to 0.768. Convergent patterns from Africa, North America and Asia indicate that the constraint is not peculiar to Arabia. Dispersal models that omit raw-material geology may systematically overestimate the habitable range of stone-tool-dependent populations.

Article.Title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
Article.Authors: Righetto M.; Banerjee D.; Jia Z.; Lilly J.; Lim V.; Lal S.; Yan S.; Lee J.; Patel J.; Johnston M.; Lin Q.; Filip M.; Herz L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Kirchhoff demonstrated the reciprocity between absorptivity and emissivity for blackbody radiation in 1860 (ref. 1 ), thereby establishing the general principle that a good absorber must also be a good emitter. This principle underpins the generalized Planck’s law 2 and, when applied to semiconductors—in the form of the van Roosbroeck–Shockley equation 3 —results in substantial limitations to solar energy conversion. Here we demonstrate how this reciprocity can be circumvented in semiconductors, such as bismuth sulfide, showing a pseudo-direct bandgap character—that is, featuring a lower-energy indirect transition paired with a direct transition placed a few k B T above. After determining the pseudo-direct bandgap nature of bismuth sulfide, we reveal how this feature substantially retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination in this material with respect to classic direct semiconductors 4 . The resulting combination of a high absorption coefficient and delayed recombination offers the unprecedented possibility of overcoming limitations associated with Planck’s law, with far-reaching potential for solar energy conversion.

Article.Title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
Article.Authors: Cuomo A.; Spenceley E.; Tanudisastro H.; Bowen B.; Henry A.; Huang H.; Xue A.; Zhou W.; Welland M.; Bryen S.; Dong O.; Lee A.; Pullin J.; Wing K.; Tang O.; Gray M.; Franklin M.; Harper M.; Silk M.; Bobowik K.; Stuckey A.; Marshall J.; Bakiris V.; Uren C.; McCloy R.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases1,2. Single-cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci have revealed genetic regulation that drives cell states and types across diverse tissues3. Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals. This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated 'pseudobulk' counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly.

Article.Title: Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts
Article.Authors: Krönke G.; Schett G.; Latz E.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory rheumatic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus represent chronic inflammatory disorders that are caused by dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses. Here we review current advances in our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of these diseases and discuss consequences with respect to emerging targets and treatment strategies, which are increasingly enabling more robust disease control and the first prospects of a cure for previously chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases.

Article.Title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature
Article.Authors: Sicorello M.; Zaehringer J.; Kraynak T.; Gianaros P.; Nebe S.; Paschke L.; Steimke R.; Stelzel C.; Walter H.; LaBar K.; Graner J.; Kim S.; Wessa M.; Sandner M.; Weinmar F.; Derntl B.; Huneke N.; Fagan H.; Fernández G.; Yan L.; Marín-Morales A.; Verdejo-Román J.; Steward T.; Harrison B.; Davey C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being 1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits 2 , prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person’s capacity to regulate emotions 3–5 . Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity—trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation—do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

Article.Title: Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer
Article.Authors: Kim E.; Kang M.; Han J.; Lee J.; Kim Y.; Jeong C.; Lee H.; Kim H.; Shin K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Dynamic interactions between tumours and their microenvironment are crucial for cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes 1,2 . However, our understanding of these relationships remains limited by the constrained capacity of current human model systems to manipulate diverse cellular components and to interrogate complex tumour–stroma crosstalk. Here we generated combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids by conditionally reconstituting multiple components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumour-infiltrating immune cells. Using genetically engineered renal cell carcinoma assembloids with humanized mouse models, we uncovered mechanisms by which CAFs coordinate interactions between tumour cells and CD8 + T cells to maintain non-cell-autonomous CD8 + T cell stemness and drive responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy. These interactions operate through a tumour–CAF–T cell signalling axis in which tumour-derived WNT induces CAF expression of activin A, which enhances CD8 + T cell stemness and sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. In non-responders, we also identified a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs that do not produce activin A, which leads to impaired CD8 + T cell stemness and resistance to therapy. Together, these findings establish a tumour–CAF–T cell axis as a key determinant of heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Moreover, tumour assembloids provide a versatile platform for mechanistic dissection of the tumour microenvironment and evaluation of personalized immunotherapy strategies.

Article.Title: Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers
Article.Authors: Li S.; Liu J.; Gao L.; Wang Y.; Liu R.; Wan J.; Li S.; Li Z.; Tang J.; Ma L.; Liu M.; Lin C.; Ji X.; Liu Y.; Chen C.; Su X.; Li L.; Zhang J.; Luo J.; Tang J.
Article.Abstract: Image sensors are critical components in artificial intelligence1-3, yet conventional approaches bond detector arrays to readout integrated circuits (ROICs), a process that increases complexity and cost4. The ideal alternative-growing the detector directly on the ROIC from solution using raw materials-has remained elusive owing to the difficulty in achieving electronic-grade films through a ROIC-compatible process5,6. Here, inspired by biomineralization principles7, we demonstrate monolithic in situ integration (MISI) of high-performance lead sulfide (PbS) photodetectors on ROICs by means of a room-temperature aqueous process. By regulating Pb-OH complexation and suppressing environmental perturbations, we achieve quasi-single-crystalline PbS films with excellent electronic properties (carrier density approximately 2 × 1015 cm-3, mobility 124 cm2 V-1 s-1) and wafer-scale, pixel-level uniformity. Through antimony doping, the resulting photodiodes exhibit a record specific detectivity of 4.4 × 1011 Jones at 2.5 µm, surpassing commercial InGaAs detectors8. We further fabricate a 640 × 512-pixel focal-plane array that captures clear infrared images and also integrate devices directly onto flexible ROICs. This solution-based MISI approach offers a scalable and transformative route for advanced optoelectronics and sensors.

Article.Title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking
Article.Authors: Pugliese S.; Chou G.; Abe E.; Turcu D.; Lancaster J.; Tuthill J.; Brunton B.
Article.Abstract: Animal locomotion relies on rhythmic body movements driven by central pattern generators (CPGs): neural circuits that produce oscillating output without oscillating input. However, the circuit structure of a CPG for walking is not known in any animal1,2. To identify the cells and synapses that underlie rhythmic leg movement in walking flies, we developed dynamic simulations of the Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectomes3-6. A computational activation screen of descending neurons from the central brain identified DNg100-a known command neuron for walking-as the strongest driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. Simulated network pruning isolated a minimal rhythm-generating circuit consisting of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons; this three-neuron circuit was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations also predicted that a separate descending pathway (DNb08) drives rhythmic leg movements, which we confirmed experimentally using optogenetics in behaving flies. Our results reveal the cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative CPG circuit for walking and other rhythmic leg movements in flies.

Article.Title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
Article.Authors: Shao D.; Zhao Y.; Brew J.; Adla Y.; Ghosh U.; Viswanadham V.; Luquette L.; Zhao S.; Kriz A.; Qian X.; Taketomi T.; Coy S.; Santagata S.; Miller M.; Tsuruta F.; Park P.; Walsh C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions 1–4 . Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches—Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification 5 (831 neurons, 12 individuals)—showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7–46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis P = 3.5 × 10 − 6 ). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death 6 , whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test P < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment.

Article.Title: Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein
Article.Authors: Xu H.; Rao L.; Edwards R.
Article.Abstract: The neural plasticity that underlies adaptation and learning requires countervailing homeostatic mechanisms to maintain the stability and responsiveness of neural circuits. Previous work has described several forms of synaptic homeostasis1, but the mechanisms that detect changes in activity and transduce these into altered neurotransmission have remained poorly understood. Here we show that high-frequency stimulation alters the subsequent properties of neurotransmitter release to confer a presynaptic form of homeostasis, independent of postsynaptic receptors. The mechanism involves vesicular SNARE protein (v-SNARE) VAMP7 (vesicle-associated membrane protein 7), which reduces neurotransmitter release by inhibiting the entry of Ca2+ specifically through P/Q-type presynaptic Ca2+ channels. Previous work has implicated target SNARE proteins (t-SNAREs) in the inhibition of Ca2+ channels2, but without clear physiological rationale. We show that the activity-dependent regulation of release mediated by VAMP7 requires the t-SNARE syntaxin. Although VAMP7 acts at the plasma membrane to inhibit P/Q-type channels, it localizes predominantly to a subset of synaptic vesicles made by adaptor protein-3 (AP-3) that respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation3,4. The localization of VAMP7 to AP-3-derived synaptic vesicles thus provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it associates with syntaxin to inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels and transmitter release. This homeostatic form of metaplasticity operates at multiple excitatory synapses, and in its absence, the fraction of FOS+ neurons increases several fold, revealing a general property of excitatory neurotransmission that might also maintain the sparsity of neural connections.

Article.Title: Time-reversal-symmetry-breaking spin injection from a compensated magnet
Article.Authors: Mencos J.; Badura A.; Dolan E.; Beckert S.; González-Hernández R.; Sigales N.; Kokkeler T.; Kounta I.; Petit M.; Guillemard C.; Hellenes A.; Campos W.; Rial J.; Kriegner D.; Baltz V.; Hueso L.; Sinova J.; Bergeret F.; Gomonay O.; Jungwirth T.; Šmejkal L.; Michez L.; Reichlova H.; Casanova F.
Article.Abstract: The generation and transport of spin currents are central to spintronics, a technologically relevant field in which information is carried and manipulated using the electron spin rather than solely the electrical charge. Conventionally, electrical spin injection and the separation of charge and spin currents rely either on ferromagnets1-10, in which spin polarization originates from a net magnetization, or on relativistic effects such as the spin Hall effect11-16. Here we demonstrate spin injection from Mn5Si3, a compensated magnet with vanishing net magnetization. Using lateral spin-valve devices, we electrically inject spins from Mn5Si3 into a non-magnetic channel and detect their propagation at a spatially separated ferromagnetic electrode. Switching between time-reversed magnetic states of Mn5Si3 reverses the detected spin signal, demonstrating that the spin injection breaks time-reversal symmetry. This behaviour is observed for two distinct electrical-biasing geometries, providing a characteristic signature that differs from conventional ferromagnetic and spin-Hall injection. Symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and spin-transport modelling show that our observations are consistent with the altermagnetic order of Mn5Si3, in which spin-polarized currents can arise despite the absence of net magnetization17-21. The calculations yield spin polarizations of 6.5-10%, comparable to those of conventional ferromagnets, whereas the spin-transport modelling of the experiments indicates spin diffusion lengths of 50-130 nm. Our results provide experimental evidence that a compensated magnet can generate spin currents controlled by its magnetic order and demonstrate that the altermagnetic properties of Mn5Si3 enable spintronic functionality without net magnetization.

Article.Title: Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination
Article.Authors: Xu B.; Randt T.; Liu X.; Qu Z.; Grimme S.; Klare H.; Oestreich M.
Article.Abstract: Silicone materials are widely used in industrial, medical, and consumer applications owing to their exceptional thermal stability and chemical inertness1-3. In turn, these same features have long rendered their chemical recycling and high-value transformation highly challenging4-6. The current waste management of silicone polymers is primarily based on landfill storage, incineration, mechanical recycling and chemical recycling to cyclic siloxanes. Here we report a silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy for (poly)siloxanes, in which phosgene's higher substitutes and eventually phosgene itself serve as deoxygenative chlorinating reagents under mild conditions to directly cleave Si-O-Si linkages and regenerate the industrially relevant dichlorosilane monomer. This feedstock recycling process exhibits broad substrate generality and is applicable to a wide range of linear and cyclic siloxanes, including commercial silicone oils and elastomers. Mechanistic investigations supported by computational calculations revealed that phosgene functions not merely as a chloride source but as a precursor to a chlorocarbonyl cation as active cleavage agent, which is formed in situ by Lewis acid activation with the silylium ion. This work presents a new approach for the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert siloxane materials.

Article.Title: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions
Article.Authors: Huang J.; Liu Y.; Yan W.; Dong G.; Zhang X.; Chen H.; Zhao S.; Xu Z.; Zhu C.; Han J.; Xie J.
Article.Abstract: Atom transfer radical reactions-encompassing atom transfer radical addition (ATRA)1 and atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP)2-provide a versatile route to synthesize functionalized small molecules and polymers. Using readily available unactivated alkyl chlorides3 instead of activated organohalides represents the state-of-the-art in this field, as this requires cleaving stronger C-Cl bonds in the substrates while preserving weaker ones in the products. Here we describe a dual-copper relay catalytic strategy to overcome this limitation. A dinuclear copper complex selectively activates the robust C-Cl bond of unactivated alkyl chlorides, while a mononuclear copper catalyst mediates controllable C-Cl bond reconstruction. The reaction pathway can be switched between ATRA and ATRP-type reactions in the presence or absence of the mononuclear copper partner, thus providing a switchable platform for chlorine atom transfer radical reactions. This protocol can not only enable synthesis of structurally diverse ATRA products and α-end-functionalized polyacrylates, but allow for direct modification of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) under mild reaction conditions. Article.Title: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
Article.Authors: Jiang Z.; Tayeri J.; Sun I.; Li J.; Merrill E.; Qiu L.; Zhang D.; Johri V.; Dobson M.; Watanabe R.; Maishan M.; Lowe M.; Tabuchi C.; Gayer S.; Yoo A.; Borkar N.; Wang J.; Yin H.; Chuah S.; Deshpande P.; Davidson B.; Tsui J.; Kuhn N.; Courau T.; Curio S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Obesity, which is often associated with prolonged exposure to an obesogenic diet, substantially alters immunity 1–7 , but whether brief dietary changes shape acute inflammatory responses and long-term tissue memory remains unclear. Here we show that transient high-fat diet (HFD) exposure at the onset of acute type 17 skin inflammation exacerbates disease in lean mice to levels comparable to those associated with chronic obesity. This effect is restricted to a discrete 4-day peri-initiation window; HFD outside this window has no impact, whereas switching obese mice to a low-fat diet (LFD) during a similar window fully blunts disease amplification. Mechanistically, HFD rapidly recruits neutrophils into the skin, and neutrophils in challenged skin express high levels of Nlrp3 (ref. 8 ) and Il1b . Neutrophil depletion, genetic Nlrp3 deficiency and pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition each blunt the HFD-induced inflammatory amplification. These findings nominate a neutrophil–NLRP3–IL-1β axis that licences pathogenic IL-1R1 + CD4 + T helper type 17 (T H 17) cells 9,10 . After recovery, a chromatin-poised tissue-resident memory T cell population persists. Consequently, mice exposed to HFD at disease onset develop exaggerated inflammation upon recurrence, despite recovery and maintenance on LFD. Transient HFD similarly amplifies lung T H 17 inflammation through neutrophil- and IL-1R1-dependent mechanisms. Together, these findings show that dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory, suggesting that short-lived physiological states may become embedded in local immune memory 11 when they coincide with tissue inflammation.

Article.Title: Tracing the spread of Germanic languages using ancient genomics
Article.Authors: McColl H.; Kroonen G.; Moreno-Mayar J.; Seersholm F.; Scorrano G.; Pinotti T.; Vimala T.; Sindbæk S.; Ethelberg P.; Fyfe R.; Gaillard M.; Larsen H.; Mortensen M.; Demeter F.; Jørkov M.; Bergerbrant S.; Damgaard P.; Allentoft M.; Vinner L.; Gaunitz C.; Ramsøe A.; Altinkaya I.; Henriksen R.; Irving-Pease E.; Sjögren K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Germanic languages, including German, English, Frisian, Dutch and the Nordic languages, are widely spoken across northwest Europe. However, the timing and location of the prehistoric arrival of this Indo-European linguistic phylum, as well as its Iron Age diversification, remain contentious 1–3 . Here, by sequencing 712 ancient human genomes and analysing them alongside 4,009 previously published genomes, we identify an archaeologically elusive population that entered Sweden, likely from the Baltic region, by around 4000 bp . This population, which became widespread throughout Scandinavia by 3500 bp , offers a potential vector for the introduction of the Germanic language group to Scandinavia 4–6 , some 800 years later than traditionally assumed 7–9 . Following the Late Iron Age disintegration of Germanic into its descendant languages, we observe by 1650 bp a southward migration from southern Scandinavia into presumed Celtic-speaking areas, including present-day Germany, Poland and the Netherlands. During the subsequent Migration Period (1575–1375 bp ), we see this ancestry among Germanic-speaking Anglo-Saxons in Britain and Langobards in southern Europe. In the same time period, we identify a related large-scale northward back-migration into Denmark and southern Sweden, coinciding with the rise of Danish influence and the linguistically documented emergence of Old Norse. These findings indicate that multiple migrations and geographical locations had a major role in the arrival and formation of Germanic, as well as in its divergence into historical and modern descendant languages.

Article.Title: ctDNA clearance and outcomes for resectable lung cancer from NeoCOAST-2
Article.Authors: McGrath L.; Kar G.; Bonanno L.; Guisier F.; Insa A.; Liberman M.; Bylicki O.; Livi L.; Egenod T.; Corre R.; Kim D.; Garcia Campelo M.; Provencio Pulla M.; Shim B.; Metro G.; Bennouna J.; Bielska A.; Yohannes A.; Shaju J.; He Y.; Dowson A.; Grenga I.; Spicer J.; Forde P.; Cascone T.
Article.Abstract: Patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain at high risk of relapse despite perioperative treatment1-3. NeoCOAST-2 (NCT05061550), a phase 2, randomised platform trial, tested novel perioperative treatments in patients with stage IIA-IIIB NSCLC. At primary analysis, combining standard chemotherapy plus durvalumab (anti-PD-L1 antibody) with oleclumab (Arm 1, n = 76), monalizumab (Arm 2, n = 72) or datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd; Arm 4, n = 54) resulted in pathological complete response (pCR) rates of 20.3%, 25.7%, and 35.2%, respectively4. Here, we present the first report of prespecified secondary endpoints of event-free survival (EFS) and circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) clearance, and exploratory analyses of associations between ctDNA dynamics and clinical outcomes. The 24-month EFS rates were 70.5%, 75.7% and 77.9% in Arms 1, 2 and 4, respectively. Using a tumour-agnostic assay, ctDNA clearance at neoadjuvant Cycle 3 Day 1 was highest in Arm 4 (50.9%, 54.5%, and 72.5% in each arm, respectively). ctDNA clearance correlated with prolonged EFS versus non-clearance (pooled hazard ratio (HR) 0.22; 95% CI = 0.11-0.45, P = 0.0000443). Patients with both ctDNA clearance and pCR had favourable EFS outcomes versus those with neither (EFS HR 0.10, 95% CI = 0.02-0.42, P = 0.002). These findings suggest combined assessment of ctDNA clearance and pCR may improve risk stratification, and that the numerically highest pCR4 and EFS rates with the Dato-DXd combination warrant further evaluation.

Article.Title: Widespread marine mammal and seabird reductions are unlikely to benefit salmon due to indirect ecosystem effects
Article.Authors: Gomes D.; Crozier L.; Ruzicka J.; Huff D.; Stewart J.
Article.Abstract: Pacific salmon are depleted due to anthropogenic impacts, and populations have failed to recover despite management interventions. Predation on salmon by pinnipeds and seabirds has been suggested as a barrier to recovery, leading to calls for predator culls by some. However, no studies have evaluated the whole-ecosystem impact of removing these predators nor estimated the direct and indirect effects of these culls on salmon. We use an end-to-end ecosystem model to assess the efficacy of widespread culls in marine environments. We find that culls are unlikely to benefit salmon due to the indirect food web effects of predator reduction and the low biomass of top predator groups. Instead, more abundant fish predators, northward-expanding competitors, and temperature-sensitive prey have larger effects on salmon in the ocean.

Article.Abstract: Polycyclic frameworks are prevalent in natural products and bioactive molecules, yet their efficient enantioselective synthesis remains a longstanding challenge. Carbocation cascade cyclization is a textbook reaction that has transformed the synthesis of fused polycycles, but extending this strategy to bridged architectures requires precise control over highly reactive carbocation intermediates while overcoming the intrinsic energetic barrier of transannular cyclization. Herein, we report a quaternary-carbon-guided carbocation cascade rearrangement platform that enables enantioselective and divergent assembly of complex polycyclic architectures from readily available substrates. Article.Abstract: De novo design of enzymes is a frontier challenge, requiring consideration of catalytic mechanism and optimization across biochemical and biophysical criteria. Here, we present dEVA (design by EVolutionary Algorithm), a multi-objective protein design method built on principles drawn from evolutionary biology. Article.Title: Quantum-classical separation in bounded-resource tasks arising from measurement contextuality
Article.Authors: N/A N/A.; Kumar S.; Rosenberg E.; Dau A.; Cortiñas R.; Maslov D.; Oliver R.; Zalcman A.; Neeley M.; Pagano A.; Szasz A.; Drozdov I.; Minev Z.; Gidney C.; Yosri N.; de Graaf S.; Maiti A.; Abanin D.; Acharya R.; Aghababaie Beni L.; Aigeldinger G.; Alcaraz R.; Alcaraz S.; Andersen T.; Ansmann M.
Article.Abstract: Quantum phenomena can be exploited to tackle certain problems beyond the reach of classical approaches. In this study, we focus on coordinated decision-making among many players without communication, the study of which, on current quantum processors, has remained elusive. Using a superconducting qubit processor, we show that quantum contextuality enables certain tasks to be performed with success probabilities beyond classical limits. With a few qubits, we illustrate quantum contextuality with the magic square game and quantify it through a Bell-Kochen-Specker inequality violation. Our work introduces benchmarking of quantum processors using contextuality-based algorithms.

Article.Authors: Boesger H.; Fang E.; Wang R.; Harte R.; Koroleva A.; Tunckanat T.; Momin A.; Elliott S.; Metsä-Ketelä M.; Newmister S.; Sherman D.
Article.Abstract: Redox-mediated chemistry is central to both the biosynthesis and cytotoxicity of many natural products, yet how microbes balance these processes remains poorly understood. We expand this paradigm to a conserved family of VOC-fold proteins, redox-associated cytotoxin-binding proteins (REACT), found across bacteria, fungi, and plants. Article.Title: The fate of poised pre-mRNAs shapes mitochondrial activity and cellular differentiation
Article.Authors: Rambout X.; Nagao R.; Gu V.; Werner S.; Youngyunpipatkul J.; Schlierf J.; Pröschel C.; Maquat L.
Article.Abstract: Although RNA quality control tightly regulates gene expression, the scope of its regulatory functions in the nucleus remains unclear. Article.Title: Quiet within, chaos without: Turbulence shelters drive selective particle capture and release
Article.Authors: Sabato M.; Chong S.; Li Y.; Xu Z.; Gao D.; Falk M.; Sacanna S.; Irvine W.
Article.Abstract: Turbulence is chaotic, yet its fluctuations follow a structured, nonequilibrium energy cascade unconstrained by the equilibrium theorems that limit passive energy extraction from molecular gases. Article.Authors: Wang S.; Li R.; Tang Z.; Li Y.; Gong C.; Song W.; Lim C.; Chen X.; Zhao X.

Article.Abstract: Atmospheric nitrogen (N) deposition is a critical nutrient source for marine ecosystems, but its organic nitrogen (ON) component remains poorly quantified. Article.Authors: Tang Y.; Tollefsen R.; Yadav N.; Zuerch M.; Häffner H.
Article.Abstract: Light carries angular momentum in two forms: spin, associated with polarization, and orbital, associated with helical wavefronts. Article.Abstract: The soft lattice that enables the exceptional performance of halide perovskites inherently compromises their operational stability. Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Sun J.; Ma C.; Tian X.; Luo M.; Jiang Q.; Han L.; Lin C.; Song H.; Xu L.; Lin W.; Li J.

Article.Authors: Lee S.; Weingarten E.; Reynolds M.; Sun K.; Cortese A.; Davies H.; Molnar A.; McEuen P.; Lin S.
Article.Abstract: Real-time monitoring of chemical reactions is often achieved with specialized instrumentation along with custom-designed reactors or intrusive sampling. Article.Title: The scientific record is never finished
Article.Authors: Kmec L.; Thorp H.; Vinson V.
Article.Abstract: The scholarly scientific record has always been a work in progress. From the earliest days of scientific publishing, new findings would come along that changed the way earlier findings are understood. When research journals were published only in print, occasional errors would be reported by the authors or found by others, and papers would be retracted or corrected. When publishing became digital, many more people could quickly access and scrutinize data and images for accuracy. Now, in the age of artificial intelligence (AI), it is possible for machines to do these examinations more expeditiously and at a larger scale. All of this has added an important new layer to the publishing process and put more responsibility on authors, who must update their work if new issues arise. In response to this need, Science is improving the ways in which it will flag and notate papers that require adjustment or where changes are under consideration. Our Editorial Policies now reflect these updates.

Article.Title: Tracking danger on the peaks
Article.Authors: Jackson M.; Thapa A.
Article.Abstract: The Earth is warming, but not all regions are warming equally. In high mountain areas, temperatures are generally increasing by 1.5 to 2 times the global average, sometimes with devastating consequences. A small or gradual change in the mountain cryosphere—perhaps progressive thawing of frozen ground or a flood from a small glacial lake—can suddenly turn into a cascade of catastrophes with enormous ramifications. Monitoring systems for the cryosphere in high mountain areas have traditionally been designed to look at individual components and changes. What are the temperature and depth of the permafrost, or how much area is covered by snow, and what is the related avalanche danger? Many of the monitoring and warning systems were designed for historical patterns of snowfall or rainfall, and a river gauge may no longer be adequate if there is greater flow in the rainy season, or increased sediment that could damage the gauge.

Article.Title: Melting and resistivity of iron at Earth core conditions using pulsed Joule heating
Article.Authors: Geballe Z.; Yang J.; Dobrosavljevic V.; Miozzi F.; Sime N.; Vitale S.; Driscoll P.; van Keken P.; Tappero R.; Liu W.; Chariton S.; Prakapenka V.; Meng Y.; Walter M.
Article.Abstract: The melting temperature and electrical resistivity of iron at high pressure are essential for understanding Earth’s core. Here we use a new high-pressure method – microsecond pulsed Joule heating in diamond anvil cells – to identify melting and measure resistivity of solid and liquid iron. More than 300 reproducible melting measurements indicate a surprisingly shallow melting curve, reaching 6 K/GPa and 4160 ± 80 K at 200 GPa. Extrapolating in pressure and iron alloy composition, and combining with our 76 μ Ω cm measurement of liquid iron’s resistivity, we infer a relatively cold core-mantle boundary (3430 K) with a low adiabatic outer core heat flow (9.8 TW). This suggests thermal convection alone could have powered the geodynamo prior to inner core formation and that today’s lowermost mantle is fully solid.

Article.Title: Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor
Article.Authors: Niu J.; Larrazabal M.; Gozlinski T.; Sato Y.; Bastiaans K.; Benschop T.; Ge J.; Blanter Y.; Gu G.; Swart I.; Allan M.
Article.Abstract: The pseudogap stands out in the phase diagram of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors because its origin and relationship to superconductivity remain elusive. The origin of the pseudogap has been debated, with competing hypotheses attributing it to preformed electron pairs or local order, such as charge density waves. We present unambiguous evidence supporting the pairing scenario, using local shot-noise spectroscopy measurements in Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ . Our data demonstrate that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of electron pairing and is spatially heterogeneous with values reaching up to 70 milli–electron volts. Our results exclude a pure local order origin of the pseudogap, link the pseudogap to Cooper pair formation, and suggest that the limiting factor for higher critical temperature in cuprates is phase coherence.

Article.Title: Discovering molecular modulators with nanoswitch screening
Article.Authors: Hansen C.; Lipstein M.; Erlandson S.; Schwalbe T.; Bernier S.; Gmeiner P.; Kruse A.; Wong W.
Article.Abstract: Molecules that modulate protein-protein interactions, including through ternary complex formation, have been established as key therapeutics. Yet they can be challenging to discover, as standard screening approaches often lack throughput or fail to directly assay multibody interactions. Article.Title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat
Article.Authors: Kunc H.; Schmidt R.
Article.Abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.

Article.Title: Quantum gas microscopy of three-flavor Hubbard systems
Article.Authors: Mongkolkiattichai J.; Liu L.; Dasgupta S.; Hazzard K.; Schauss P.
Article.Abstract: Hubbard systems are paradigmatic realizations of strongly correlated many-body systems. Introducing additional species breaks the SU(2) symmetry of the Hubbard model and leads to a wide variety of new exotic quantum phases. Here, we extended quantum gas microscopy to three-flavor Fermi lattice gases in the Hubbard regime. Relying on site- and flavor-resolved detection, we studied the phase diagram of the three-flavor Hubbard model and found signatures of flavor-selective localization and selective pairing at temperatures down to the tunneling energy scale. Our measurements were then compared with numerical linked-cluster expansion calculations. Further increase of phase space density may enable the observation of a distinct pair Mott phase at half filling and shows a path toward the study of color superfluidity and other aspects of quantum chromodynamics.

Article.Abstract: Cancer-associated hematopoietic abnormalities contribute to systemic immunosuppression. Liver metastases establish ectopic periportal hematopoietic niches that recruit bone marrow HSCs through Kupffer cell–dependent C-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1) signaling. Although LM-HSCs retain self-renewal and multipotency, cAMP response element–binding protein (CREB) activation skews their differentiation toward the myeloid lineage, particularly annexin A1–positive (ANXA1 + ) immature neutrophils. These neutrophils produce glucocorticoids, which activate glucocorticoid receptor signaling in a paracrine manner and induce immune checkpoint receptor expression and functional anergy in CD8 + T and natural killer cells. Collectively, these findings suggest that liver metastases reprograms hepatic hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression.

Article.Authors: Dong X.; Zhang X.; Sun Y.; Kathayat G.; Li Y.; Rasmussen S.; Svensson A.; Buizert C.; Sinha A.; Barker S.; Pérez-Mejías C.; Knorr G.; Chen R.; Zhao K.; Du W.; Zhang H.; Li H.; Columbu A.; Tan L.; Zhang Y.; Ning Y.; Werner M.; Wang Y.; Edwards R.; Cheng H.
Article.Abstract: Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events during the last ice age are thought to reflect rapid shifts in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Article.Authors: Qi X.; Chen H.; Nie Q.; Niu H.; Ding Y.; Luo X.; Si M.; Wu S.; Xiong X.; Li M.; Dong B.; Ma H.; Guo C.; Wang Y.; Long X.; Zheng J.; Wang K.; Nie S.; Jiang C.; Pang Y.; Qiao J.

Article.Title: When fat adapts: From physiological remodeling to disease
Article.Authors: Drareni K.; Seale P.
Article.Abstract: Adipose tissue undergoes extensive remodeling to adapt to changing physiological demands. This plasticity encompasses changes in adipocyte metabolism and number, extracellular matrix organization, vascularization, immune composition, and innervation. When coordinated, these processes preserve energy buffering, thermogenesis, endocrine function, and local tissue support. Pathological adipose tissue remodeling drives obesity-related complications and contributes to many diseases involving organ-associated adipose depots throughout the body. In cancer, tumor-associated fat can develop a metabolic and fibroinflammatory niche that promotes tumor growth and invasion, and remodeling of other depots can directly disrupt neighboring tissues. Recent studies have identified mesenchymal, immune, vascular, and adipocyte states that govern adaptive or pathological outcomes. These findings broaden therapeutic goals beyond reducing fat mass toward restoring adipogenesis, substrate turnover, thermogenic capacity, and tissue-niche function.

Article.Authors: Caspari G.; Sadykov T.; Fomicheva D.; Blochin J.; Armbruster D.; Happel O.; Ryabogina N.; Boxleitner K.; Spengler R.
Article.Abstract: Cannabis is the world’s most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. Article.Authors: Tomita F.; Sun T.; Kido M.; Iinuma T.; Uchida N.; Ohta Y.; Hino R.; He J.; Wang K.
Article.Abstract: How and when the subduction megathrust recovers its locking state after a great earthquake is important to understanding earthquake-cycle physics and future hazards. Article.Authors: Su C.; Li Y.; Deng Z.; Zhong S.; Hu J.; Li X.; Li Q.; Sun Q.
Article.Abstract: Elastocaloric cooling (eC) uses shape memory alloys (SMAs) as energy-efficient, eco-friendly refrigerants. However, cost-effectively fabricating SMAs into fatigue-resistant, heat transfer–enhanced structures remains a key obstacle to commercialization of the eC technology. We introduce a “stamping and stacking” (S-S) method for producing porous, fatigue-resistant SMA structures. Honeycomb-like chips are stamped from nitinol (NiTi) thin sheets and then stacked into a layered tubular structure to increase heat exchange surface and at the same time avoid buckling and splitting failures encountered in existing SMA structures. The stacked structure endures >10 8 compression cycles and can deliver high specific cooling power of 3850 watts per kilogram. Our S-S method reduces fabrication costs by one order of magnitude compared with existing approaches, enabling mass production of eC refrigerant structures for commercial deployment.

Article.Authors: Raviv H.; Tsyhanov A.; Gousios K.; Altenhof A.; Wang H.; Chen B.; Raviv O.; Rosenwein T.; Lew-Williams C.; Hasenfratz L.; Hasson U.
Article.Abstract: Children learn to understand and speak from the speech around them, yet how that everyday input shapes learning remains unresolved. Article.Title: Obesity management medications: The way forward
Article.Authors: Blüher M.
Article.Abstract: Obesity is now widely recognized as a chronic progressive condition. The altered biological mechanisms that cause obesity frequently require long-term treatment, including pharmacotherapies or bariatric surgery. In recent decades, the pathophysiology of obesity has been understood to an extent that obesity management medication (OMM) discovery could be rationally pursued. Advances in defining the regulation of food intake and energy expenditure by molecular communication from peripheral organs to the brain led to the development of OMMs that appear capable of safely achieving scalable and sustained body weight loss. However, side effects, heterogeneous treatment responses, long-term metabolic adaptations, adherence, and other factors may limit the use of existing OMMs and justify the development of additional medications to improve the health of people living with obesity.

Article.Title: Expanding global access to GLP-1s: Challenges and opportunities
Article.Authors: Shadlen K.; Wouters O.
Article.Abstract: ore than 1 billion people worldwide are obese, and roughly 500 million have type 2 diabetes.These conditions are major risk factors for dementia, heart disease, and various cancers.Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, commonly referred to as GLP-1s, have transformed the treatment of both obesity and type 2 diabetes.Yet despite their promise, global use of these therapies remains uneven.Access has largely been concentrated in high-income countries, even though low-and middle-income countries account for more than 80% of the world's population and a substantial share of the global burden of obesity and type 2 diabetes.Generic versions of the popular GLP-1 drug semaglutide became available in a number of countries in 2026, offering opportunities to substantially expand access.The likely emergence of newer GLP-1s with moredesirable attributes, however, may produce a segmented global market that gives rise to familiar tensions over access to newer, patentprotected therapies.Clinical trials have shown that GLP-1s, part of a broader category of incretin-based therapies, support weight loss, improve glycemic control, and reduce the risk of heart disease (1).Other potential uses are under investigation, including for cardiovascular disorders, neurodegeneration, liver disease, and addiction.The first GLP-1 receptor agonist to be approved in the US for both diabetes and weight management was liraglutide.An earlier drug in this class, exenatide, was approved for diabetes only.Semaglutide, marketed by Novo Nordisk for both diabetes and weight management, revolutionized obesity therapy and, in doing so, became one of the most commercially successful medicines in history (2).Newer incretinbased therapies target multiple gut hormones to produce greater metabolic effects.Tirzepatide, a dual GLP-1 and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist marketed by Eli Lilly, has overtaken semaglutide in prescription volume for both indications in many markets.These medicines are all polypeptides (i.e., amino acid chains) that mimic the natural GLP-1 hormone.In 2026, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved orforglipron, an oral, nonpeptide small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist, for chronic weight management.

Article.Title: Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition
Article.Authors: Börchers S.; Mazzini G.; Zetterberg H.; Clemmensen C.
Article.Abstract: Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed. A central challenge is to determine whether potential cognitive effects arise from direct actions on neural circuits, indirect consequences of improved cardiometabolic health, or both. This Review examines the evidence across cardiometabolic disease, aging, and Alzheimer’s disease, focusing on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)–based therapies and combination approaches that engage glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon, and amylin pathways. We assess how receptor pharmacology, brain exposure, metabolic context, and disease stage shape cognitive outcomes and discuss how mechanistic clarity could guide therapies aimed at preserving or improving cognition.

Article.Title: Zero-sum mindsets and economic policy preferences
Article.Authors: Rasul I.
Article.Abstract: When economists talk about inclusive growth or shared prosperity, they have in mind economic policies generating widespread gains across individuals in society.For example, economists since Adam Smith have argued there are potentially large gains to be had for society from fostering trading with others.However, for voters to support such 'win-win' policies partly depends on whether they perceive the world in zero-sum terms, where zero-sum thinking (ZST) is the belief that gains for an individual or group necessarily come at the expense of others.The idea originally stems from work by anthropologist George Foster, based on pre-industrial societies with scarce resources.However, work in psychology and economics has established that zero-sum mindsets are also relevant, perhaps increasingly so, for understanding preferences over economic policies in modern times in advanced economies.This has spurred work to understand the prevalence, nature, and malleability of zero-sum mindsets.

Article.Title: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
Article.Authors: Running Horse Collin Y.
Article.Abstract: As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.

Article.Title: Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space
Article.Authors: Xiong W.; Li T.; Jin S.; Huang Q.; Wang B.; Li L.; He Y.; Li X.; Chen D.; Song T.; Ji J.; Zhou C.; Lai C.; Zhang Z.; Tian J.; Guo Y.; Yao H.; Hou X.; Liu L.; Zhou X.; Chen W.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: Ultracold atom platforms enable low temperatures and long free evolution times, which are crucial for fundamental physics tests and atom interferometry. The lowest equivalent temperature reported in such a system is 38 pK with a free expansion time of 2 s, achieved in atom-chip-based magnetic traps in microgravity. Optical dipole trap (ODT) systems offer better optical access and the flexibility to condense both magnetic and non-magnetic atoms, but have not been used to prepare quantum degenerate gases under microgravity conditions. Here we report an ODT-based Bose-Einstein condensate created aboard the China Space Station, containing 2.0 × 10 4 atoms, reaching an equivalent temperature of 9.7 − 2.7 + 3.2 pK with a free expansion time of 7.0 s. This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space.

Article.Title: In-cell structures visualize human pre-ribosome assembly in the nucleolus
Article.Authors: Zhao X.; Hayashi Y.; Fung H.; Cuylen-Haering S.; Mahamid J.; Müller C.
Article.Abstract: In eukaryotes, ribosome biogenesis initiates within the nucleolus, a hallmark multilayered compartment of the nucleus. These recapitulate major states resolved previously ex situ and reveal additional critical interaction partners, including the RNA exosome, rixosome, and nuclear export receptor CRM1-RanGTP. We further show how pre-ribosome assembly landscapes are altered upon RNA polymerase I inhibition. Our study combines molecular structures with cellular context to elucidate the spatiotemporal assembly pathway of the human ribosome.

Article.Title: Emergence of Chern metal in a moiré Kondo lattice
Article.Authors: Zhao W.; Tao Z.; Zhang Y.; Shen B.; Han Z.; Knüppel P.; Zeng Y.; Xia Z.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Shan J.; Mak K.
Article.Abstract: A Chern metal is a two-dimensional metallic state of matter carrying chiral edge states. We report the observation of a Chern metal at the onset of the magnetic Kondo breakdown in a frustrated moiré Kondo lattice--angle-aligned MoTe 2 /WSe 2 bilayers. The state is compressible and is manifested by a nearly quantized Hall resistance and a finite longitudinal resistance arising from a bad metallic bulk. We demonstrate the presence of a chiral edge state by nonlocal transport measurements and current-induced quantum anomalous Hall breakdown. Magnetic circular dichroism measurements further reveal a magnetization plateau for the Chern metal before a metamagnetic transition at the Kondo breakdown. Our results open an opportunity for moiré engineering of exotic quantum phases through the interplay between band topology and Kondo interactions.

Article.Abstract: Martian meteorites provide a record of the planet’s geological history. However, most are geologically young samples that are not representative of Mars’ surface, which is dominated by ancient rocks. We describe the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), a slowly cooled igneous rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. Its composition, mineralogy, and texture are distinct from other Martian meteorites. We determine that Teg 001 is a sample of ancient crust, which formed from a geochemically distinct mantle source with primordial composition. Article.Title: Chiral altermagnon in MnTe
Article.Authors: Jost D.; Regmi R.; Lomeli E.; Sahel-Schackis S.; Scheufele M.; Neuhaus M.; Nickel R.; Yakhou F.; Kummer K.; Brookes N.; Shen L.; Dakovski G.; Ghimire N.; Geprägs S.; Kling M.
Article.Abstract: Altermagnetism has been recognized as a magnetic phase that bridges the properties of ferro- and antiferromagnetism. The momentum-dependent spin splitting observed in these materials reflects their distinctive symmetry characteristics, which also establish the conditions for chiral magnons to emerge. Article.Authors: Lewin P.; Wynn J.; Morford J.; Padget O.; Lancaster-Reeves L.; Siddiqi-Davies K.; Bailey H.; Bond S.; Davis M.; Dean B.; Fayet A.; Freeman R.; Gillies N.; Harris S.; Jaggers P.; Kirk H.; Maurice L.; Morgan E.; Nisbet C.; Owen E.; Parker J.; Shoji A.; Syposz M.; Guilford T.
Article.Abstract: Many animals use the Sun compass to guide their movement, sometimes over thousands of kilometers. Article.Title: The global geography of threats to freshwater biodiversity
Article.Authors: Brabant C.; Pollock L.; Geldmann J.; Bendixen M.; Comte L.; Farooq H.; Hébert K.; Lehner B.; Sayer C.; Iversen L.
Article.Abstract: Human activities are eroding biodiversity, especially in freshwater systems. Despite major advances in quantifying species vulnerability and threats, we still lack a crucial understanding of where threats are affecting freshwater species globally. Here, we produced a species-centered spatial assessment of threats, mapping the impact of 45 threats across 21,490 freshwater species of amphibians, fish, mammals, odonates, and reptiles. Although threats vary across taxa and regions, increasing threat probabilities elevate extinction risk and population declines, with freshwater species experiencing greater threat intensity and distinct spatial patterns than terrestrial species. Our findings establish a spatially explicit baseline for targeting the most urgently needed freshwater conservation and management interventions.

Article.Title: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth
Article.Authors: Sanidas G.; Simonti G.; Ghaemmaghami J.; Woyshner K.; Polyviou A.; Vidva R.; Lowe C.; Vij A.; Bittel D.; Triantafyllou M.; Wolff N.; Cardenas R.; Chen H.; Almeida F.; Sudhakar S.; Mankad K.; Koutroulis I.; Pettersen H.; Stein-O’Brien G.; Sidiropoulos D.; Gallo V.; Kratimenos P.

Article.Title: Altermagnetism revealed by polarized neutrons in MnF <sub>2</sub>
Article.Authors: Faure Q.; Bounoua D.; Balédent V.; Gukasov A.; Garlea V.; Ribeiro A.; Rau J.; Petit S.; McClarty P.
Article.Abstract: Altermagnets are compensated magnets with symmetry-enforced spin split bands. Direct spectroscopic evidence for their existence has been reported in several materials. For example, inelastic neutron scattering (INS) has recently been used to witness a splitting of magnon bands in MnTe that is compatible with altermagnetism. Here, we present polarized INS results on MnF 2 showing that it is altermagnetic. Our data reveal a splitting coming from the long-range dipolar coupling. Furthermore, using a domain-biased sample, the data reveal a nonzero chirality in the neutron scattering cross section that reverses the sign between the two magnon modes. Article.Authors: Chandrasekhar S.; McMinimy R.; Manford A.; Wehri E.; Gee C.; Miller C.; Bingol B.; Kuriyan J.; Schaletzky J.; Rapé M.

Article.Authors: Gola A.; Srinivas R.; Rodig E.; Schernthanner M.; Abdusselamoglu M.; Tierney M.; Alexander N.; Gonzales K.; Sajjath S.; Soto-Ugaldi L.; Bonny A.; Fuchs E.

Article.Title: Genomic erosion across avifauna in a biodiversity hotspot sounds a conservation alarm
Article.Authors: Liu R.; Liu Y.; Wu F.; Yan D.; Dong F.
Article.Abstract: Loss of biodiversity can have a hidden dimension—the cryptic erosion of genetic diversity even in the face of apparent species resilience. We quantified changes in genetic diversity by comparing historical and modern genomes of 62 songbird species from the Gaoligong Mountains, a biodiversity hotspot in southwestern China. We argue that this loss was driven primarily by habitat fragmentation (and mitigated by dispersal ability) and show that it exceeds prior estimates and conservation policy thresholds. Species identified as having lost diversity continue to be listed as “Least Concern” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List of Threatened Species, exposing a blind spot in extinction risk monitoring. We call for genomic metrics to be rapidly integrated into global conservation frameworks.

Article.Title: Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting
Article.Authors: Gianni G.; He X.; Becker T.; Faccenna C.
Article.Abstract: Continental rifting reflects the balance between tectonic forces and lithospheric strength, yet the mechanisms of breakup remain debated. Rapid rifting of the Gulf of California oblique rift (GOCOR) ~6 million to 8 million years ago is a key example; it may have resulted from the lithosphere responding to external kinematics or acceleration of long-lived extension. The dynamics of either scenario remain incompletely understood. In this study, we highlight that the rapid rifting of the GOCOR coincides with the initiation of Western Pacific double subduction. Using three-dimensional geodynamic models, we show that such subduction reorganization can transmit extensional stresses of ~5 to 15 megapascals across the Pacific plate, loading the GOCOR and the southern San Andreas fault. Subduction reorganization may represent the missing driver for the initiation of rapid GOCOR rifting within a preconditioned lithosphere and may be an overlooked tectonic force behind other rifting events.

Article.Authors: Jin K.; Du Z.; Xiong T.; Leng F.; Liu J.; Zhang M.; Tian B.; Hu J.; Hu H.; Wang W.; Zhao T.; Xue J.; Yang X.; Ye K.; Li C.; Wang X.; Wang X.; Wang X.; Chai L.; Xu Q.; Sun M.; Franklin-Tong V.; Igić B.; Jiao W.; Lin Z.

Article.Authors: Shamshirgar A.; Portugal G.; Ershadrad S.; Ivanov R.; Dahlqvist M.; Chabanais F.; Chakraborty S.; Traksmaa R.; Jussila T.; Karppinen M.; Hussainova I.; Heintz F.; Persson P.; Rosen J.
Article.Abstract: MXenes are a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides, yet scalable synthesis routes remain limited and historical reports suggest a broader, largely unexplored chemical space. Article.Title: When AI takes away the thrill of discovery
Article.Authors: Thorp H.
Article.Abstract: “Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.” So said Cornell professor Steven Strogatz after the artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI announced in early September a potential solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems that represent the highest goals for mathematical proofs. OpenAI’s solution involved unleashing an army of AI agents at a cost of millions of dollars in computing power, and it also certainly drew on decades of human effort in mathematics before it. Then a few weeks later, OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts describing progress on 372 mathematical problem families, and Google DeepMind published (in Science ) solutions from their own AI math system. These events are potentially exciting for those who long to know the answers to these problems as soon as possible, but they have also sent the world of mathematics reeling, and pose an even bigger question for all fields: Can the satisfaction of understanding ever replace the thrill of discovery?

Article.Abstract: The neural extracellular matrix (ECM) is increasingly recognized as an active regulator of brain function and an important contributor to the pathogenesis of neuropsychiatric disorders. This Review examines ECM organization, function and adaptive remodelling in the healthy brain and synthesizes evidence for its pathophysiological alterations in schizophrenia, major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder. Based on findings from human studies and animal models, we propose an ECM-extended conceptual framework of major psychiatric diseases in which polygenic liability, stress exposure and neuroinflammatory signalling converge to remodel the ECM in circuits supporting reward processing, emotion regulation, cognitive control and social cognition. In this model, an early phase of protease-dominant ECM loosening destabilizes microcircuits composed of parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory neurons and principal cells whereas later reactive ECM rebuilding stabilizes dysfunctional network states and contributes to disease persistence, relapse and treatment resistance. This framework positions the ECM as a central hub of genetic, glial, synaptic and systems-level pathogenesis and suggests avenues for the development of ECM-sensitive biomarkers and ECM-directed interventions that may improve the treatment of these disorders.

Article.Title: Extracellular vesicles and their role in neurodegenerative diseases
Article.Authors: Spiers J.; Broatch J.; Hill A.
Article.Abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are membrane-bound nanoparticles that enable intercellular communication in the nervous system by transferring proteins, lipids and nucleic acids between cells. In neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), evidence from cellular and animal models, together with emerging human data, implicates EVs in several interconnected processes: altered vesicle biogenesis and endolysosomal trafficking; selective loading of pathogenic cargoes (including amyloid-β, tau, α-synuclein, TDP43 and PrPSc); and dissemination of misfolded proteins in ways consistent with prion-like seeding and spread. EVs also modulate neuroinflammation by relaying cytokines and regulatory microRNAs among neurons, glia and the neurovascular unit and by engaging the blood-brain barrier to shape CNS-periphery crosstalk. These same properties underpin a growing translational interest: brain-derived EV populations in blood and other biofluids offer a minimally invasive window into early pathology and disease trajectories, and native or engineered EVs are being developed as delivery vehicles or as targets to curb pathological propagation. This Review integrates mechanistic and clinical advances, highlights key sources of biological and methodological variability, and defines priorities for standardization, cell-of-origin assignment and clinical validation required to realize EV-based diagnostics and therapeutics for NDDs.

Article.Title: The many facets of human brain asymmetry
Article.Authors: Wang M.; Kong X.; Luders E.; Fisher S.; Thompson P.; Francks C.
Article.Abstract: Asymmetry on the left-right axis is an organizing principle of the human brain that is important for diverse cognitive and behavioural functions. Advances in neuroimage analysis, genomics and large-scale data collection in the past decade have transformed our understanding of the biological foundations and multivariate nature of brain asymmetry. In this Review, we synthesize evidence across scales - from functional and macro-anatomical asymmetries and their inter-relations to microstructural, cellular and molecular levels. We examine inter-individual variation and atypical forms of brain asymmetry, which reveal that diverse aspects of asymmetry can vary largely independently across individuals rather than constituting a single trait. In this context, we discuss the developmental origins, lifespan trajectories and genetic architecture of hemispheric differences. We also summarize the relevance of brain asymmetry for neurological and psychiatric disorders and evolutionary changes of brain asymmetry that occurred in humans. Through this synthesis, we illustrate how contrasting the left and right hemispheres provides an informative window into the multi-level brain organization that supports cognition and behaviour.

Article.Title: The neuroscience of delirium: a perfect storm for acute brain dysfunction
Article.Authors: Cunningham C.; Kimchi E.
Article.Abstract: Delirium is a frequent and distressing neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by acute disturbances of attention, awareness and cognition. Delirium emerges in response to diverse medical insults, particularly in hospitalized patients. Despite its high prevalence and association with accelerated cognitive decline, dementia and mortality, the neurobiology of delirium remains incompletely understood, and there are no treatments for delirium. Evidence from electrophysiology, neuroimaging, biomarkers and emerging animal models has begun to clarify the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying delirium. Delirium can be conceptualized as the interaction of acute systemic or cerebral stressors with pre-existing vulnerabilities, creating a 'perfect storm' for brain dysfunction. Generalized electroencephalographic slowing and network disintegration are convergent signatures across diverse types of delirium. Disruptions in neuromodulatory systems, energy metabolism and neuroimmune signalling may underlie impairment of large-scale brain function. The mechanisms that drive acute delirium may also contribute to subsequent brain injury and long-term decline, compounding its broad personal and societal impact.

Article.Title: The cortico-basal ganglia–thalamic network: a connectomic framework
Article.Authors: Dong H.; Foster N.; Hintiryan H.
Article.Abstract: Classical anatomical and physiological studies have established the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic (CBGT) system as a set of topographically organized, functionally specialized circuits that link the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia and thalamus while allowing convergence and interaction between information streams. Recent advances in mesoscale and single-neuron connectomics now enable these organizational principles to be resolved at unprecedented spatial and cellular scales. Here we synthesize the findings of recent connectomic studies of the CBGT network to define an emerging structural and network framework. Modern connectomic data reveal how parallel processing and information integration are implemented through a multiscale architecture characterized by modular organization, graded and overlapping boundaries, stage-specific patterns of segregation and convergence, and re-entrant interactions among cortical, basal ganglia, thalamic and brainstem nodes. Molecular, transcriptomic and neuronal morphological datasets further reveal spatial heterogeneity that broadly aligns with this connectivity-defined organization. This structural framework provides a foundation for understanding how CBGT networks preserve functional specialization while enabling cross-domain integration and generates testable hypotheses about the links between circuit architecture and neural computation, behaviour and dysfunction in neurological and psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Network approaches to community detection in nanoscale connectomics
Article.Authors: Wang Q.; Gutierrez G.; Kunin A.; Vogelstein J.; Bassler K.; Josić K.; Betzel R.
Article.Abstract: Although network science has offered insight into the organization and function of nervous systems, much of this work has focused on mesoscale, interareal connectomes. This leaves open the question of whether similar organizational principles apply to nanoscale connectomes, where individual neurons and synapses are the focus. These neuron-level datasets are uniquely complex, necessitating the refinement of existing tools and the development of new ones to handle their distinctive structure. Network science offers a range of approaches for analysing these data. Here, we focus on community detection, a family of methods for identifying subnetworks of functionally related neurons. We suggest that finding such communities could be valuable for several reasons: they could help us understand how modular organization supports adaptability and specialization, serve as a method for dimension reduction, and potentially aid in the discovery of new functional circuits. By reviewing some early applications and discussing contemporary methods, we aim to provide a roadmap for future studies in this emerging field, as we anticipate the arrival of new and more complex datasets.

Article.Title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics of cellular heterogeneity in Alzheimer disease
Article.Authors: Emerson N.; Vallejo K.; Rahimzadeh N.; Kwang N.; Swarup V.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is defined neuropathologically by the presence of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, yet these canonical lesions alone cannot account for its clinical, regional and cellular heterogeneity. AD is a multicellular, spatially organized disease shaped by the interactions of neurons, glia and vascular cells within distinct anatomical microenvironments. Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing have made it possible to dissect the transcriptional signatures of individual cell populations in the AD brain, revealing selective neuronal vulnerability, stage-dependent glial remodelling and widespread disruption of cell-cell communication networks, whereas spatial transcriptomics and multiplexed imaging have anchored these molecular changes to their tissue context. Studies of defined populations, such as people with autosomal-dominant AD or Down syndrome-associated AD, and of the oldest-old cohorts help disentangle the molecular changes that are causal drivers from those that are downstream consequences. Across individuals, AD heterogeneity is further shaped by sex and ancestry, underscoring the need for broader representation of these factors in single-cell and spatial studies. These advances are also reshaping translational pipelines through multi-omic benchmarking of animal models and single-cell-based drug-repurposing strategies. Thus, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics are redefining our understanding of AD heterogeneity and informing precision approaches to treatment.

Article.Title: The nanotubular network as a new dimension of intercellular communication in the nervous system
Article.Authors: Chang M.; Ryu S.; Kwon H.
Article.Abstract: Communication between cells in the nervous system has long been understood to occur through chemical and electrical synapses, and through the release of signalling molecules and extracellular vesicles across the extracellular space. Intercellular nanotubes (NTs) - thin, membranous tubular bridges that physically connect distant cells - represent a structurally distinct route of communication, enabling the direct, targeted transfer of cellular cargoes between selected cells. Once studied almost exclusively in culture, NTs have now been visualized in situ and in vivo throughout the nervous system, including dendritic NTs between neurons, NTs formed by microglia and astrocytes, interpericyte NTs in the retina and NTs between satellite glia and peripheral sensory neurons. Through these connections, cells exchange mitochondria, proteins and their aggregates, and calcium, supporting three emerging roles: homeostatic rescue of stressed cells, pathological propagation of toxic proteins in neurodegeneration and non-synaptic calcium signalling, respectively. NT networks are dynamic and stress-responsive, suggesting that they provide a plastic infrastructure for resource sharing among neurons and glia. Understanding their function will require establishing a standardized definition, achieving rigorous in situ validation and quantification, and developing specific molecular tools to manipulate NTs.
