Article.Title: A two-platform blueprint for modeling human brain development
Article.Authors: De Los Angeles A.; Chen C.; Tam T.; Xu S.; Deng H.; Huang C.; Li T.; Liu P.; Loh Y.; Lunshof J.; Ong C.; Pei D.; Theunissen T.; Trounson A.; Yu L.; Sugaya K.; Silva J.
Article.Abstract: No single experimental system spans human neural-plate induction through late-stage circuit maturation. Brain organoids have transformed human developmental neuroscience, yet a decade of progress has clarified their intrinsic limitations: they cannot fully recapitulate neural induction driven by embryo-scale developmental signals, nor achieve the degree of circuit maturation that requires an in vivo physiological context. Stem cell-based embryo models are positioned to provide mechanistic access to peri-gastrulation and early neurulation, whereas interspecies chimeras provide the physiological milieu to study myelination, pruning and circuit-level function. Here we propose a two-platform roadmap that integrates stem cell-based embryo models to decode developmental logic with interspecies chimeras to study functional maturation. We outline reproducibility and reporting standards, including rigorous benchmarks for neural-tube formation and closure, and present a milestone-based oversight framework anchored to verifiable developmental landmarks. Together, these complementary platforms enable causal interrogation of human neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease while remaining responsive to ethical and technical constraints.

Article.Title: Computational methods for cell–cell communication via single cells
Article.Authors: Li H.; Zhou X.; Sun X.; Nie Q.; Gao Y.; He J.
Article.Abstract: Cell-cell communication (CCC) analysis has become a cornerstone in dissecting single-cell and spatial omics data, having an indispensable role in high-throughput screening and comprehensive characterization of tissue communication landscapes. Computational models and analytical objectives have emerged continuously in recent years, propelling CCC methodology development and leading to unprecedented biological discoveries. Methodological varieties and differences in their characteristics underscore the urgent need for a coherent framework bridging between CCC biology and computational advances. Here, we systematically curate 161 published CCC methods, classifying them hierarchically into two primary categories and nine subcategories based on their functions and model features and highlighting the power of CCC methods using oncology examples. Four directions for future CCC methodology development are presented, emphasizing AI-biology integration. This Review aims to delineate the CCC algorithm-demand landscape, thereby fostering comprehensive, in-depth and reliable elucidation of CCC and facilitating broad applications in biology and disease studies.

Article.Title: Characterizing the solution space of migration histories of metastatic cancers with MACH2
Article.Authors: Roddur M.; Ramavarapu V.; Bunkum A.; Huebner A.; Mineyev R.; McGranahan N.; Zaccaria S.; El-Kebir M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Metastases arise when cancer cells disseminate from the primary tumor, or other metastases, and seed tumors at distant anatomical sites. Reconstructing migration histories from DNA sequencing data is key to understanding the cellular mechanisms underlying metastatic dissemination. While the data often support many equally plausible histories, current methods return a single solution or sample alternatives without guarantees of optimality or completeness. Here we introduce MACH2, which enumerates all optimal migration histories and summarizes them to identify high-confidence migrations. MACH2 combines existing parsimony criteria with a new criterion that minimizes the number of clones assigned to locations where they were not observed, and includes MACH2-viz, an interactive tool for exploring solutions. Using simulated tumors with known ground truth, we show that MACH2 outperforms existing methods. Across 145 lung, ovarian, breast and prostate cancers, MACH2 reveals extensive uncertainty in migration histories, infers histories consistent with orthogonal experimental data, and finds metastasis-to-metastasis seeding and linear progression to be common.

Article.Title: 4D ultrasound cerebral angiography reveals the hemodynamics of the circle of Willis in primates
Article.Authors: Haidour N.; Dizeux A.; Loayza J.; Bolliet L.; Mateo P.; Santin M.; Lehericy S.; Pernot M.; Tanter M.; Pouget P.; Papadacci C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Noninvasive imaging of hemodynamics in deep cerebral arteries is essential for understanding cerebrovascular regulation, yet remains technically challenging. Existing angiographic techniques provide structural information with limited hemodynamic characterization, whereas transcranial ultrasound is limited by skull-induced attenuation, sensitivity and restricted deep-brain coverage. Article.Title: Transforming molecular evolutionary analyses with protein foundation models
Article.Authors: Kumar S.; Alibutud R.; Allard J.; Mowlaei M.; Shi X.
Article.Abstract: Transformer-based protein foundation models (pFMs) are emerging as powerful tools for analyzing protein sequences. Their adoption in evolutionary analysis requires articulating their evolutionary foundations and their relationship to traditional models and workflows. We introduce primary products of pFM-based analysis and demonstrate that they are informed by neutral evolutionary patterns, without incorporating substitution matrices, phylogenies or even multiple sequence alignments. We suggest that analyzing individual sequences with pFMs will streamline many evolutionary and functional analyses, including those with few homologs. Development and integration of pFMs with traditional approaches will advance molecular evolutionary investigations from phenomenological modeling of primary sequence differences to models of residue dependencies. We discuss limitations, computational considerations and open questions regarding the routine use of pFMs in protein evolutionary research.

Article.Title: A zero-shot spillover denoiser for highly multiplexed images
Article.Authors: Lequyer J.; Nowlan F.; Hsu W.; Philip R.; Erpf A.; Chan A.; Tran C.; Wang B.; Maliga Z.; Jackson H.; Pelletier L.
Article.Abstract: Highly multiplexed imaging techniques are an important part of the biological analysis toolkit. However, the resulting images can suffer from considerable noise and spillover. SpillOT uses optimal transport theory to identify similar patches across channels and retain only the true signal. We demonstrate that SpillOT surpasses existing zero-shot image restoration techniques and markedly improves the reliability and precision of downstream analyses on Imaging Mass Cytometry, Tissue Cyclic immunofluorescence and Opal multiplexed immunofluorescence datasets. We also show that using SpillOT, we can find previously undetectable immune infiltration patterns in diabetes data. We release SpillOT as both a standalone script and a Fiji plugin.

Article.Abstract: Organoids are complex, miniaturized three-dimensional structures that replicate key biological features and functions of human tissues and organs. These characteristics make them powerful model systems for investigating tissue and organ development, homeostasis and regeneration; understanding disease mechanisms; and advancing drug development and personalized medicine. To fully harness their potential, it is essential to develop advanced tools capable of comprehensively profiling their intricate composition. In particular, cutting-edge technologies are needed to accurately characterize their genotypic and phenotypic profiles, including DNA, RNA, proteins and physiological functions. In this Review, we examine molecular and functional profiling methods for organoids, providing an overview of emerging techniques, recent advancements, future technologies, key knowledge gaps and challenges, and a framework for multimodal integration of methods. Additionally, we examine current barriers to progress and explore opportunities to refine organoid profiling methods with the aim of deepening our understanding of organoid biology.

Article.Abstract: Abstract Image-based single-cell transcriptomics can identify diverse cell types in intact tissues. However, in adaptive immunity, V(D)J recombination generates unique immune receptors in cells of the same type, leading to important functional variation that is not yet defined by these methods. Here we introduce B cell receptor multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (BCR-MERFISH), which measures plasma cell clonality based on V gene usage in combination with transcriptome profiling. We demonstrate that BCR-MERFISH accurately identifies V gene usage in cell culture and in mice with restricted or native plasma cell diversity. We then use BCR-MERFISH to elucidate the microbiota-dependent changes in plasma cell abundance, clonal diversity, and public clonotype usage in the mouse gut and the non-uniform distribution of plasma cell clones along the mouse ileum. Given that tissue context is an essential modulator of plasma cell dynamics, we anticipate that BCR-MERFISH may offer new insights into a wide range of immunological questions.

Article.Title: Deciphering the gene-centric spatial dynamics across tissue and time with GeneSPOT
Article.Authors: Zou Q.; Wang Z.; Li S.; Lin S.; Han C.; Cui Y.; Li S.; Wang L.; Zhang D.; Zhang W.; Qian B.; Gao R.; Yuan Z.
Article.Abstract: Spatial omics technologies provide unprecedented opportunities to investigate how molecular programs are organized within tissues. However, existing analytical frameworks primarily focus on identifying cellular states and characterizing differentially expressed molecular features across these states. The relational spatial organization of molecular features and its dynamics across biological contexts therefore remain largely unexplored. Here we present Gene SPatial Optimal Transport (GeneSPOT), a gene-centric computational framework for characterizing the spatial relationships among genes and quantifying their reorganization across biological conditions. Although gene-centric in design, GeneSPOT generalizes to other molecular features. Across diverse applications, GeneSPOT resolved tissue structures, integrated paired and unpaired spatial multi-omics data, unveiled the spatial convergence of gene programs during embryonic development and identified aging-associated spatial reorganization among genes whose expression did not change significantly with age. GeneSPOT thus complements conventional cell-centric analysis, providing a framework for deciphering how spatial relationships among molecular features are reorganized across biological conditions and over time.

Article.Title: Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC
Article.Authors: Xu C.; Liu S.; Heng Y.; Yang C.; Cao Y.; Gao J.; Wei S.; Jia D.; Liang D.; Ma Y.; Ng S.; Li H.; Zhang X.; Gong Y.; Shen H.; Deng H.; Chen A.; Xu X.; Liao S.; Jiang Q.; Liu B.
Article.Abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies measure multiple molecular layers within intact tissues. Two central challenges are vertical integration, which combines different molecular modalities, and horizontal integration, which aligns cell types across studies. Here we show domain invariant representation through adaptive calibration (DIRAC), a geometric deep learning model that unifies these tasks in a generalized domain adaptation framework. DIRAC learns task-discriminative features that are insensitive to domain shifts caused by batch effects, omic modalities or study sites, enabling a shared embedding space and automated cell-type annotation through label transfer from reference datasets. Across sequencing-based and imaging-based datasets, DIRAC identified a new microvascular proliferation domain in glioblastoma, corrected cortical-layer annotations in severe Alzheimer's disease, resolved subtle structures in mouse embryos and remained robust to missing data and unseen cell types. We generated mouse spleen and thymus Stereo-CITE-seq data and used DIRAC to reveal thymic T cell migration and splenic immune cell interactions. DIRAC is fast and scales to millions of cells.

Article.Title: Automated identification of individual birds by song enables multi-year recapture from passive acoustic monitoring data
Article.Authors: Lapp S.; Lyon R.; Wilson S.; Rhinehart T.; Czarnecki C.; Chronister L.; Fiss C.; Larkin J.; Bayne E.; Kitzes J.
Article.Abstract: Autonomous sensors and machine learning are transforming ecology by enabling large-scale observation of organisms and ecosystems. However, camera traps, audio recorders and other sensors currently produce species-level detections. Tracking individuals continues to require invasive, high-effort capture-mark-recapture. Here we introduce an automated, general approach that identifies individual animals in passive acoustic recordings based on individually distinctive vocalizations. We train a convolutional neural network to extract salient features from audio recordings using a location-prediction task, then apply dimensionality reduction and clustering on features to achieve song-based individual identification. We identify individuals not included in the training data with 96% accuracy. We apply this approach to track 405 male ovenbirds (Seiurus aurocapilla) from 126 locations across 4 years, then model abundance and apparent survival. We provide open-source code to facilitate applications of our approach to other species. Performing automated individual identification on passive acoustic datasets will support the study of population trajectories and inform proactive ecosystem management to prevent biodiversity loss.

Article.Title: abcFISH enables multiplexed, single-molecule visualization of circular RNA spatial heterogeneity
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Jiang B.; Liu K.; Yang L.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the subcellular localization of RNAs is critical for their functions, but visualizing circular RNAs (circRNAs) has been hindered by their sequence overlap with linear counterparts. We further applied abcFISH to validate therapeutic double-stranded circRNA aptamers, simultaneously visualizing AAV-delivered double-stranded circRNA aptamers and the resulting reduction in astrocyte infiltration around transduced cells. Article.Title: Limitations of de novo peptide sequencing in resolving sequence ambiguity
Article.Authors: van Puyenbroeck S.; Beslic D.; Suomi T.; Holstein T.; Muth T.; Elo L.; Martens L.; Bouwmeester R.; Van Den Bossche T.; Claeys T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract De novo peptide sequencing enables peptide identification from fragmentation spectra without relying on sequence databases. However, incomplete spectra create ambiguity, making unambiguous identification challenging. Recent deep learning advances have produced numerous de novo models that predict sequences and refine peptide-spectrum matches under such conditions. Yet, their relative strengths, weaknesses and ability to handle spectrum ambiguity remain unclear. Here we benchmark eight state-of-the-art models on three publicly available proteomics datasets, comparing performance using established metrics and quantifying inter-model agreement. We assess post-processing approaches, including iterative refinement, rescoring and reranking, for their ability to improve identification accuracy, and perform an error analysis to identify common mispredictions and their causes. Model performance varied, with considerable overlap of correct identifications. Post-processing yielded no or only modest improvements. Most sequencing errors were model-independent and driven by limited fragment ion coverage, a limitation also observed in database searches with large search spaces.

Article.Title: Head-mounted camera for reconstructing outdoor behavior in freely flying birds
Article.Authors: Voit K.; Sawinski J.; Klioutchnikov A.; Junker K.; Cheekoti A.; Wallace D.; Stahr P.; Matheson E.; Gill L.; Fischer D.; Kerr J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Capturing the fine details of behavior when animals perform complex tasks, such as prey pursuit and capture, in natural environments is a challenging endeavor. For birds of prey, commonly used tracking approaches, such as lightweight GPS and inertial measurement units, cannot simultaneously track the bird’s position and the fine details of body part motion or moving external objects. Here we designed a head-mounted, tetherless, 4π camera system which, combined with a high-resolution environmental scan, enabled detailed three-dimensional measurement of both head position and orientation in freely flying Harris’s hawks ( Parabuteo unicinctus ) performing aerial pursuit in the wild. Article.Title: Selective profiling of translationally active tRNAs and their dynamics under stress
Article.Authors: Monti M.; Yilmaz H.; Del Piano A.; Arnoldi M.; Bonomo I.; Llovera L.; Sarabando J.; Ribeiro D.; Soares A.; Clamer M.; Novoa E.
Article.Abstract: During translation, transfer RNAs (tRNAs) deliver specific amino acids to the ribosome in a coordinated manner with the sequence encoded by the messenger RNA. Despite their central role in protein synthesis, their precise contribution to the modulation of translation remains poorly understood, primarily due to lack of methods to characterize tRNA abundances and their modifications from actively translating ribosomes. Here we develop tRIBO-seq, a simple and robust nanopore-based method to selectively capture ribosome-associated native tRNA populations (ribo-tRNAs) from actively translating ribosomes, providing tRNA abundance, modification and fragmentation information from a single experiment. Using tRIBO-seq, we find that ribo-tRNAs, but often not total tRNAs, are significantly altered on stress. Notably, we find that tRNAome alterations strongly vary depending on the stress type; while viral infection and leucine deprivation leads to changes in ribo-tRNA abundances, methionine starvation causes a dramatic loss of methyl-based tRNA modifications. By contrast, we find that arsenite exposure does not alter tRNA abundances nor modification patterns, but rather causes major fragmentation events in selected subsets of ribo-tRNAs. Altogether, tRIBO-seq offers a robust and reproducible approach to map the full tRNA landscape-capturing tRNA abundance, modification and fragmentation patterns-across both total and actively translating tRNA populations, revealing the dynamics of the tRNAome with unprecedented resolution, in a single experiment.

Article.Title: RobPicker: a meta-learning framework for robust identification of macromolecules in cryo-electron tomograms
Article.Authors: Liang Y.; Hosseini R.; Rahmani H.; Singh D.; Zhang R.; Zhang L.; Guo H.; Choe S.; Lee J.; Xu M.; Segal E.; Zou J.; Williamson J.; Villa E.; Grotjahn D.; Xie P.
Article.Abstract: Accurate particle picking of macromolecules of diverse types, shapes and sizes in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is critical for understanding the molecular architecture of biological systems in their native state. Here, to address these limitations, we developed RobPicker, a meta-learning framework that effectively mitigates these issues by automatically learning to correct label errors and by placing greater emphasis on smaller and rarer macromolecule species. Article.Title: Nondisruptive 3D profiling of combinations of epigenetic marks in single cells
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Radda J.; Alderman M.; Jin S.; Cheng Y.; Zhang Y.; Liu M.; Xiao A.; Wang S.
Article.Abstract: Advances in single-cell sequencing and spatial omics technologies have enhanced our understanding of diverse cellular identities, compositions, architectures and functions. However, the single-cell three-dimensional (3D) organization of the epigenome is still not well understood, due to an absence of spatial single-cell methods that allow high-resolution, locus-specific detection of combinations of epigenetic marks while maintaining 3D genome organization. Here we develop epigenetic proximity hybridization reaction (Epi-PHR), a nondisruptive image-based single-cell spatial epigenetic profiling technology. Phased Epi-PHR combined with chromatin tracing reveals unexpected associations between epigenetic mark enrichment and chromatin folding of an imprinted gene cluster at the single-chromatin-copy level for the distinct alleles from different parental origins. We expect Epi-PHR will be broadly applicable in research requiring single-cell spatial epigenetic information, advancing our understanding of the combinatorial epigenetic code and its relationship with chromatin organization.

Article.Title: Spatial single-cell mapping of transcriptional differences across genetic backgrounds in mouse brains
Article.Authors: Hemminger Z.; Tam G.; De Ocampo H.; Wang A.; Underwood T.; Xie F.; Zhao Q.; Song D.; Li J.; Dong H.; Wollman R.
Article.Abstract: Genetic variation can alter organ structure and function. Here we introduce atlas-scale transcriptome localization using aggregate signatures (ATLAS), a scalable tissue mapping method that learns transcriptional signatures from single-cell RNA sequencing data, encodes them in situ with tens of thousands of oligonucleotide probes and decodes them to infer cell types and imputed transcriptomes. Article.Title: Enhanced cfDNA methylation profiling by detection and correction of jagged ends
Article.Authors: Wang R.; Hamilton E.; Almanza D.; Bonilla R.; Sugio T.; Hui A.; Tian F.; Phillips N.; Liu C.; Yoo C.; Alig S.; Rossi C.; Juul N.; Chen E.; Liu K.; Shen E.; Shi W.; Olsen M.; Kang X.; Nair V.; Wakelee H.; Shrager J.; Shi S.; Desai T.; Esfahani M.

Article.Title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain
Article.Authors: Santra K.; Barber K.; Logiacco F.; Frechou M.; Bellafard A.; Liou J.; Vaziri A.
Article.Abstract: Extending the depth reach of multiphoton microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an 'exponentially hard' problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain; however, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. TrUDI achieves a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photon yield at the same laser power as in previous approaches thereby enabling in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 × 230 µm2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

Article.Title: Aptamer-mediated multivalent endogenous ADAR1 recruitment for highly efficient RNA editing
Article.Authors: Zhu H.; Zhou Y.; Huang R.; Wang Y.; Hu Y.; Wang L.; Jin J.; Ye Q.; Liu X.; Wang Z.; Xie H.; Li J.; Pang D.; Liu S.
Article.Abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing mediated by endogenous ADAR enzymes represents a promising therapeutic strategy because it can correct mutations at the transcript level without inducing permanent changes to the genome. However, existing systems face challenges, particularly the limited editing efficiency, which limits their practical applications. Here we introduce MARRS (multivalent ADAR1-recruiting RNA editing system)-an efficient and specific RNA editing platform that leverages engineered multivalent RNA aptamers to robustly recruit endogenous ADAR1 enzymes. Operating without the need for exogenous enzymes, the MARRS system offers a safe, efficient and programmable platform.

Article.Title: Continuous mass photometry by single-molecule trapping
Article.Authors: Loewenthal D.; Asor R.; Thorpe S.; Peters J.; Zouboulis K.; Kaplan M.; Thiele J.; Bardzil J.; Helmi S.; Burnap S.; Tan T.; Struwe W.; Benesch J.; Kukura P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The dynamic choreography of biomolecular interactions underpins the processes of life, but its direct observation remains challenging. Here we introduce continuous mass photometry, enabling hour-long, mass-resolved observation of individual biomolecules tethered to supported lipid bilayers, their complexes and interactions, with up to sub-kilodalton mass precision and millisecond temporal resolution. Our approach represents a quantitative time-resolved single-molecule measurement modality for studying complex biomolecular mechanisms in action.

Article.Title: Neotenic expansion of adult-born dentate granule cells reconfigures GABAergic inhibition to enhance social memory consolidation
Article.Authors: Chung A.; Alipio J.; Ghosh M.; Evans L.; Miller S.; Goode T.; Mehta I.; Ahmed O.; Sahay A.
Article.Abstract: Immature adult-born dentate granule cells (abDGCs) show heightened synaptic and structural plasticity and preferentially contribute to hippocampal-dependent memory. Protracted maturation (neoteny) of abDGCs in higher mammals is posited to offset the decline in adult hippocampal neurogenesis by supporting increased plasticity. Here we found that selective, synchronous expansion of 4-week-old immature, but not 8-week-old mature, mouse abDGCs promotes recruitment of fast-spiking parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons (INs) in hippocampal CA3 and CA2, increases feed-forward inhibition, decreases social memory interference and enhances social memory consolidation. In vivo local field potential recordings in dorsal CA1 and CA2 revealed increased baseline power, amplitude and duration of sharp-wave ripples, as well as enhanced rate modulation by social experience. Inhibitory neuron-targeted chemogenetic manipulations implicate dorsal CA3 and CA2 INs, including parvalbumin-expressing INs, as necessary and sufficient for social memory consolidation following and sans neotenic expansion of abDGCs, respectively. Our findings suggest that neoteny of abDGCs supports cognition by increasing feed-forward inhibition in DG-CA3 and DG-CA2 and promoting network oscillations that underlie memory consolidation.

Article.Title: Microglia mediate motor memory decay through activity-dependent phagocytosis of myelin sheaths
Article.Authors: Hu Z.; Luo Y.; Zhou T.; Wu X.; Ma J.; Wang C.; Wang L.; Wang X.; Shen Y.; Gu Y.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: Experience-dependent changes in myelination are important for motor learning, with newly generated oligodendrocytes contributing to the formation of new myelin. However, motor memories decay over time and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here we show that motor memory decay is linked to changes in memory-associated myelin sheaths resulting from microglial phagocytosis in mouse brain. Mechanistically, reduced activity of motor memory engram cells lowers oligodendrocyte expression of the 'don't eat me' signal from Cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47), facilitating microglial phagocytosis and driving myelin loss. Knockout of CD47 from motor memory-associated oligodendrocytes increased microglial phagocytosis of myelin sheaths and accelerated the decay of motor memory, whereas overexpression of CD47 showed opposite results. Moreover, microglia phagocytose myelin sheaths and synapses independently. Our findings reveal that microglial phagocytosis of motor memory-associated myelin sheaths leads to the decay of motor memory. Since various types of memory require myelination in the brain, this mechanism may contribute to the decay of other memory types.

Article.Title: Distinct prelimbic microcircuits control sensory and affective dimensions of neuropathic pain
Article.Authors: Gan Z.; Oswald M.; Dou Y.; Naser P.; Wang L.; Tan L.; Beretta C.; Chen Y.; Kaushalya S.; Sonntag I.; Zheng H.; Kuner T.; Kuner R.
Article.Abstract: The microcircuit mechanisms underlying deactivation and altered output of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a common feature of several chronic pain conditions, are poorly understood. Here, using unbiased in vivo longitudinal multiphoton imaging in the mouse prelimbic cortex (PrL), we show that nerve injury induces sensitization of all classes of GABAergic interneurons and a phenotypic switch from unimodal to polymodal responses. Through circuit interrogation, we identified functions for caudal geminal eminence-derived Prox1+ interneurons and revealed that distinct classes of inhibitory and excitatory neurons in the PrL have different functions in promoting neuropathic pain. In addition, we show that the sensory and affective dimensions of neuropathic pain engaged two distinct microcircuits, PV+-Rbp4+ neurons and Prox1+-Cux2+/Ntsr1+ neurons, respectively, to control distinct projection outputs. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for how mPFC guides actions to avoid or overcome pain and how prefrontal deactivation exacerbates neuropathic pain.

Article.Title: Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism
Article.Authors: Chen G.; Nair G.; Osorio A.; Holley S.; Ghassemzadeh K.; Zhou Y.; Gonzalez J.; Martin J.; Lu C.; Sanjana N.; Cepeda C.; Geschwind D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect. We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A , and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation. Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology. These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Title: Gene discovery and pleiotropic architecture of multidimensional pain in a genome-wide association study of >1.2 million individuals
Article.Authors: Toikumo S.; Davis C.; Jinwala Z.; Khan Y.; Jennings M.; Davis L.; Sanchez-Roige S.; Kember R.; Kranzler H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chronic pain is highly prevalent worldwide, yet its genetic architecture remains to be fully elucidated. Here we leveraged data from 1,235,695 European-ancestry individuals across three biobanks. In a meta-analytic genome-wide association study of multidimensional pain (MP), we identified 343 independent loci, 92 of which were new pain associations. Sex-specific meta-analyses revealed 115 independent loci (12 of which were new) among males ( n = 583,066) and 12 loci (2 of which were new) among females ( n = 241,266). Multi-omic gene prioritization analyses highlighted 490 genes associated with MP through their effects on brain-specific and blood-specific regulation. Mendelian randomization analyses showed causal associations between MP and psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders and C-reactive protein levels. MP variants also showed pleiotropic associations with several brain imaging-derived phenotypes. This study expands our knowledge of the genetics of pain and its pathogenesis, highlighting the importance of its pleiotropy with multiple disorders and elucidating its multi-omic pathophysiology.

Article.Title: Information formatting in neuronal populations predicts differential functional contributions to behavior
Article.Authors: Ruff D.; Markman S.; Kim J.; Cohen M.
Article.Abstract: Neurons throughout the brain encode essentially everything, so why have distinct areas? We proposed that areas format different information sources differently, implying their computational role. Here we compared the middle temporal (MT) area, involved in visual motion perception, and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), implicated in decision-making and reward. In a task that required monkeys to combine motion and reward information, both regions encoded both motion and reward, but formatted differently. Area MT represented them separably, whereas the dlPFC combined them in a decision-related format. A recurrent network model trained to reproduce that formatting predicted a distinct effect of stimulating those areas. Consistent with predictions, MT stimulation biased choices whereas dlPFC stimulation produced 'winner-take-all' outcomes. Our findings suggest that a modular structure flexibly reformats information to enable complex behaviors.

Article.Title: Single-neuron encoding of rapidly learned visual information reshapes human perception
Article.Authors: Armendariz M.; Blumberg J.; Singer J.; Aiple F.; Kim J.; Domínguez-Iturza N.; Brandt A.; Reinacher P.; Schulze-Bonhage A.; Kreiman G.
Article.Abstract: Humans can swiftly learn to recognize visual objects after minimal exposure. Integrating new information with existing knowledge requires forming enduring neuronal representations to enable future recognition. Yet, the neuronal mechanisms in the human brain underlying such rapid perceptual changes remain unclear. Here we recorded single-neuron activity in occipital cortex (OC) and medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions as participants rapidly learned to recognize degraded images. OC and MTL neurons modulated their activity to encode newly learned visual information and reshape perception. Population decoding revealed that OC neurons required additional processing time to resolve the identity of learned images, with delayed neuronal responses in the MTL. Our findings suggest that OC supports recognition after rapid learning via extensive recurrent processing, potentially involving higher-order neocortical areas, without relying on feedback from MTL. These results provide mechanistic constraints for biologically plausible models of visual recognition and few-shot visual learning.

Article.Title: A multi-institutional investigation of psilocybin’s effects on mouse behavior
Article.Authors: Lu O.; White K.; Raymond K.; Liu C.; Klein A.; Green N.; Vaillancourt S.; Gallagher A.; Shindy L.; Li A.; Wallquist K.; Li R.; Zou M.; Casey A.; Perez N.; Asim M.; Metanat S.; Logas K.; Chhaya V.; Enos A.; Ho E.; Cameron L.; Pomrenze M.; Tucciarone J.; Sohal V.
Article.Abstract: Studies reporting the effects of psychedelic drugs on mouse behavior are rapidly emerging. However, the reproducibility and reliability of these effects remain uncertain. Here we implemented a multi-institutional collaborative approach to assess which effects of psilocybin on mouse behavior are robust and replicable. Five independent laboratories performed the same experiments to test the acute and persistent effects of psilocybin (2 mg kg-1, intraperitoneally) on various behaviors. Psilocybin acutely increased anxiety- and avoidance-related behaviors and decreased fear expression in a robust and replicable manner. Surprisingly, however, psilocybin did not have replicable effects 24 h after administration in terms of reducing anxiety- and depression-like behaviors or facilitating fear extinction learning. Additionally, we did not observe psilocybin-induced alterations in social preference or social reward learning. Our characterization of psilocybin's behavioral effects, using ~200 male and female mice per experiment across five laboratories, demonstrates several robust acute effects and suggests that some of psilocybin's reported persistent effects in mice may be modest and/or inconsistent.

Article.Title: Serotonin signaling enhances phagocytosis by brain macrophages through Htr2b and alleviates brain injury after stroke
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Chen Y.; Cheng Y.; Li R.; Chen W.; Li Y.; Fan Q.; Zhou Y.; Huang T.; Xie W.; Guo Y.; Liesz A.; Wan J.; Ginhoux F.; Li P.
Article.Abstract: Brain myeloid cells, including infiltrating monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) and microglia, play critical roles in ischemic brain injury, clearing debris and shaping neuroinflammation and neurological outcomes. Yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, using single-cell RNA sequencing and fate mapping with an MDM-specific Ms4a3creERT2-Ai14 mouse line, we identified serotonin receptor Htr2b+ MDMs as a crucial cell population involved in resolving neuroinflammation within the ischemic penumbra. Htr2b+ MDMs significantly accumulate in the peri-infarct region and exhibit enhanced phagocytosis and inflammation-resolving gene signatures. Mechanistically, Htr2b activation promotes nuclear translocation of Tfe3, a key lysosomal regulator, enhancing lysosomal biogenesis and supporting phagocytic activity. MDM-specific Htr2b ablation impairs debris clearance, exacerbates neuroinflammation and ischemic injury, whereas pharmacological agonism or Tfe3 activation restores lysosomal biogenesis in brain MDMs and improves post-stroke outcomes. Thus we demonstrate a previously unrecognized Htr2b+ MDM subset that integrates serotonin signaling to license intrinsic phagocytic function, alleviating ischemic brain injury.

Article.Title: Stimulus-specific recruitment of human amygdala neurons predicts episodic memory encoding success
Article.Authors: Xiao J.; Daume J.; Salimpour Y.; Kurilenko N.; Mosher C.; Anderson W.; Valiante T.; Mamelak A.; Rutishauser U.
Article.Abstract: Controlling whether an experience is encoded into long-term memory and thus later remembered is a crucial aspect of memory. Here we examined single-neuron activity in the human brain while participants formed memories for novel visual stimuli and later retrieved them with confidence ratings. Category-selective amygdala neurons exhibited elevated firing during encoding of later remembered items relative to later forgotten items. This effect was predictive of the episodic aspect of the memory, was restricted to the preferred category of each cell, emerged earlier and was stronger in the amygdala compared to the hippocampus, and did not depend on stimulus valence and arousal. Successful memory formation was accompanied by enhanced spike-field coherence between the activity of amygdala category cells and hippocampal field potentials. These findings demonstrate that stimulus-specific recruitment of the amygdala predicts memory formation and suggest category cells in the right amygdala as a target for interventions to treat disorders affecting episodic memory in humans.

Article.Title: Circuit mechanisms for disentangled representations and generalization in the hippocampus
Article.Authors: Tang W.; Chang H.; Liu C.; Perez-Hernandez S.; Zheng W.; Park J.; Karaba L.; Oliva A.; Fernandez-Ruiz A.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how the heterogeneous activity patterns of individual neurons give rise to coherent population dynamics and cognition is a central challenge in neuroscience. In the hippocampus, neurons are tuned to spatial location, yet their activity is also modulated by multiple external and internal variables and appears to drift randomly over time, making it difficult to link hippocampal computations to behavior. By analyzing hippocampal population dynamics in behaving mice, we reveal a structured organization underlying the diversity of single-neuron responses-the hippocampus encodes different aspects of experience as disentangled variables represented in the co-activity dynamics of cell assemblies. The temporal and contextual components of these representations are governed by local inhibitory interactions and input-driven cell-assembly dynamics, respectively. Our findings reveal the circuit basis of disentangled hippocampal representations, offering a unifying geometric principle of population coding that supports flexible memory representations and enables rapid generalization of prior knowledge to new situations.

Article.Authors: Berghoff S.; Spieth L.; Vitale S.; Schlaphoff L.; Zirngibl M.; Junker N.; Dean A.; Liu L.; Damkou A.; Roth S.; Hurler C.; Hosang L.; Perez Anderson K.; Besson-Girard S.; Reich M.; Feiten A.; Huber L.; Müller C.; Kislinger G.; Dinkel L.; Nkeh Y.; Groh J.; Williams A.; Liesz A.; Schifferer M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Dysfunctional immune responses impair remyelination and contribute to neurodegeneration. While immune and metabolic responses to acute myelin injury are well characterized, myeloid cell adaptations to chronic myelin damage remain poorly understood. Here we performed a comparative analysis of genetic and toxic mouse models of acute and chronic demyelination, which identified a distinct microglial state associated with chronic demyelination, characterized by sustained pro-inflammatory activation, lysosomal lipid sequestration and reduced lipid droplet formation. Transcriptomics profiling further revealed a metabolic program marked by upregulated cholesterol synthesis and diminished sterol efflux. Our findings uncover a pro-inflammatory microglial state characterized by lysosomal dysfunction and increased myelin reactivity, highlighting a novel therapeutic target for chronic demyelinating disorders.

Article.Title: Microglial NUS1 deficiency drives dopaminergic neurodegeneration through intercellular iron dysregulation in Parkinson’s disease models
Article.Authors: Liu L.; Hong Y.; Wang X.; Huang X.; Ma Y.; Wang R.; Sun Q.; Sun H.; Hao Z.; Mu C.; Lu X.; Hu L.; Guo J.; Tang B.; Wang G.; Ren H.
Article.Abstract: The selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta is a defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. NUS1, which encodes neurite outgrowth inhibitor-B receptor (NgBR), was recently identified as a PD risk gene. Here we show that NgBR is highly expressed in microglia, where its deficiency drives progressive PD-like motor deficits and dopaminergic neurodegeneration via the LCN2-SLC22A17 iron-transport axis in mice. NgBR deficiency in mouse and human microglia triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress and PERK-ATF4-NUPR1 signaling, which preferentially induces LCN2-mediated iron efflux over cytokine release. Subsequently, microglia-derived iron-loaded Holo-LCN2, but not iron-free Apo-LCN2, is internalized by SLC22A17, a receptor highly expressed in dopaminergic neurons, leading to iron overload and ferroptosis. Pharmacological inhibition of LCN2-SLC22A17 axis or ferroptosis alleviated dopaminergic neuron loss and PD-like symptoms caused by microglial NgBR deficiency in vitro and in vivo. Our findings identify disrupted intercellular iron homeostasis as a pathological driver of PD and highlight the LCN2-SLC22A17 axis as a potential therapeutic target.

Article.Title: Endolysosomal damage promotes intraluminal protein condensate formation that limits cytosolic leakage
Article.Authors: Li X.; Zhang Y.; Zhao K.; Chen G.; Cui D.; Nikan M.; Young S.; Li X.; Bennett C.; Seth P.; Ni T.; Gutierrez M.; Jiang H.
Article.Abstract: Endolysosomal membrane damage is a detrimental process in mammalian cells that results in leakage of the luminal contents into the cytosol. However, the nature and extent of the leakage during membrane damage are unknown. Here we show that endomembrane damage induces the rapid formation of intraluminal condensates in endolysosomes. A subset of resident luminal proteins undergoes spatially coordinated condensation on endomembrane damage. Electron microscopy reveals distinct luminal morphology, and cryo-electron tomography confirms the compact ultrastructure in their native state. Condensate formation occurs across mechanistically distinct modes of membrane injury, and the condensates are reversibly dissociated on lysosomal recovery. Remarkably, these condensates impose a barrier to endolysosomal escape of therapeutic oligonucleotides. Despite endomembrane damage, luminal oligonucleotide therapeutics are sequestered in damaged endolysosomes through condensate-mediated biophysical immobilization. Targeting condensate sequestration could represent a strategy to improve oligonucleotide-based therapeutics.

Article.Title: Low-order assemblies drive oncogenic RTK fusion signalling without condensation
Article.Authors: Gonzalez-Martinez D.; Mumford T.; Wilde D.; Wissert S.; Gao Y.; Brackhahn E.; Kriwacki R.; Rhoades E.; Bugaj L.
Article.Abstract: Receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) fusions are a large class of oncoproteins found in ~5% of cancers. Key questions remain, however, about how RTK fusions transmit oncogenic signals, including how these largely cytoplasmic proteins activate downstream pathways that originate at the plasma membrane. Fusions are often multimeric and can form mesoscale condensates in cancer cells, and condensation has been implicated as an essential mechanism to enable signal transmission from the cytoplasm. However, whether condensates play a causal role or whether smaller 'diffuse' assemblies are sufficient to transduce signals, has been challenging to establish. Here we apply advanced microscopy, single-cell analysis and synthetic fusions to determine the principles by which multimerization and condensation drive signalling from cytoplasmic RTK fusions. For EML4-ALK, a prominent fusion that forms condensates, we found poor correlation between condensation and signalling and abundant EML4-ALK activity in the diffuse phase. Synthetic RTK fusions showed that cytoplasmic dimers of ALK or RET domains-and even constitutively active monomers-were sufficient to induce strong Ras-Erk signalling despite the absence of condensates, and non-condensing fusions were sufficient to transform cells in vitro and in subcutaneous tumour models. A panel of various other cancer-driving RTK fusions showed that low-order multimerization was widespread across fusions, whereas mesoscale condensation was rare and did not correlate with signalling. Our results suggest that low-order multimerization is sufficient to drive fusion phosphorylation, which is necessary and sufficient to trigger downstream oncogenic signalling.

Article.Title: Mapping mammalian placental formation and implantation transitions with single-cell transcriptomics and live imaging
Article.Authors: Chen D.; Hu W.; Nakagawa S.; Williams B.; Readhead C.; Meglicki M.; Thomson M.; Wold B.; Zernicka-Goetz M.
Article.Abstract: Implantation remains the most inaccessible stage of mammalian development. Consequently, we know remarkably little about how the embryo coordinates the cellular transitions that establish the body plan and initiate placental formation, despite this being the period when most pregnancies are lost. Here we combine single-cell transcriptomics, live imaging and functional experiments to define these transitions at cellular resolution. Our results identify an intermediate state bridging naive and primed pluripotency in the embryonic lineage, trace anterior-posterior axis specification origins in the extraembryonic endoderm, and reveal trophectoderm bifurcation into distinct placental progenitors. Strikingly, we find that the placenta arises from two sources: the classically recognized polar trophectoderm and a previously unrecognized population of mural trophectoderm that migrates from the polar-mural border. Human mural trophectoderm shows similar region-specific behaviour and may include invasive-trophoblast-biased progenitors. These findings open new directions for improving stem-cell-derived embryo models and uncovering the early determinants of pregnancy success.

Article.Title: The optogenetic tool ASAP acutely inhibits autophagy
Article.Authors: Mondal P.; Cyril A.; Mamriev D.; Parham L.; Wierzbicki I.; Shen C.; Doglioni G.; Dufresne S.; Komarla A.; Gonzalez D.; D’Angelo M.; Towers C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Autophagy, a conserved recycling process, manages intracellular quality control to mitigate stress. To determine the rapid effects of autophagy perturbation, we developed an optogenetic tool to rapidly inhibit autophagy, termed ASAP. Our approach leverages light-induced proteolytic cleavage to selectively inhibit autophagy within 5 min of light exposure, providing a precise and dynamic approach to study autophagy regulation. Proteomic profiling with ASAP revealed the most tightly regulated autophagy substrates along with previously unidentified substrates, including nuclear pore complex proteins. Of note, autophagy regulates quality control of cytoplasmic complexes of nucleoporins via specific LC3-interacting regions, sparing nuclear pore complex proteins embedded in the nuclear envelope. Upon rapid autophagy inhibition, incomplete nucleoporin complexes accumulate and instead of undergoing autophagic degradation, cytoplasmic nucleoporin complexes aggregate in processing bodies (P bodies). Using ASAP, we demonstrate rapid and specific inhibition of autophagy, revealing that nuclear pore complex proteins are tightly regulated autophagy substrates.

Article.Title: TMEM192 is a calcineurin-regulated membrane receptor for ubiquitin-independent lysophagy
Article.Authors: Liu X.; Yang Y.; Li W.; Peng K.; Qiu X.; Xu Y.; Zeng S.; Neculai D.; Sun Q.; Zhou T.; Shen H.; Liu W.
Article.Abstract: Lysophagy is a selective form of autophagy responsible for clearing damaged lysosomes. Although existing models predominantly highlight ubiquitin-dependent mechanisms, here we identify the lysosomal membrane protein TMEM192 as a key ubiquitin-independent receptor for lysophagy. We demonstrate that lysophagy persists in cells even when protein ubiquitination is inhibited or autophagy adaptors are deleted. Following lysosomal damage, the efflux of calcium from lysosomes activates calcineurin, leading to the dephosphorylation of TMEM192 at Ser229. This exposes a latent LC3-interacting region and enables direct recruitment of autophagosomes. Depletion of TMEM192 or blockade of its dephosphorylation severely impairs lysophagy, resulting in the accumulation of damaged lysosomes. In a mouse model of acute hyperuricemic nephropathy, deficiency in TMEM192 exacerbates renal tubular injury. Our findings establish a ubiquitin-independent lysophagy pathway, which holds important implications for understanding and intervening lysosomal-related diseases.

Article.Title: Full-length RNA sequencing profiles intracellular and extracellular RNAs in euploid and aneuploid human embryos
Article.Authors: Sugimoto T.; Mariya T.; Kato T.; Hitachi K.; Furusato S.; Maruhashi Y.; Kishigami S.; Kawachiya S.; Sakurai A.; Saito T.; Nishizawa H.; Kurahashi H.
Article.Abstract: Cell-free RNA (cfRNA) in human embryo culture medium may provide molecular information about preimplantation development, but its origin and regulation remain unclear. Here we show, using full-length total RNA sequencing of individual human blastocysts and matched spent media, that extracellular cfRNA profiles differ according to embryonic chromosomal status. Euploid embryos showed relatively stable intracellular and extracellular transcriptomic programmes, whereas aneuploid embryos displayed disrupted transcriptional states with stress-associated signatures, including nonsense-mediated decay and TP53-mediated apoptosis. Analyses of stable non-differentially expressed genes and long non-coding RNA-mRNA co-expression modules linked cfRNA signatures to RNA processing, RNA export, vesicle trafficking, autophagy and RNA degradation pathways. Mouse perturbation experiments further supported a connection between autophagy-lysosome-vesicle pathway activity and embryo-derived cfRNA signatures. These data establish a transcriptomic resource for studying intracellular and extracellular RNA states in human embryos and support cfRNA as a biologically informative readout of embryonic state.

Article.Title: Tau monomers and fibrils escape microglial clearance via distinct cellular mechanisms
Article.Authors: Kulkarni V.; Fredrickson C.; Adrian M.; Town J.; Ho H.; Dutka P.; Shangguan J.; Reid D.; Hayne M.; Kschonsak M.; Ndoja A.; Jeong C.; Hoogenraad C.
Article.Abstract: Tauopathies, such as Alzheimer's disease, are neurodegenerative disorders characterized by the accumulation and propagation of toxic extracellular forms of the microtubule-associated protein tau across brain regions. Microglia, the resident macrophages of the brain, are known for clearing and degrading toxic proteins. However, emerging evidence suggests that microglia also enhance tau spreading. To dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying microglial responses to extracellular tau, we use high-resolution imaging and biochemical approaches to assess the trafficking dynamics of different extracellular tau species in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia. Here we find that tau monomers are internalized by microglia via cell-surface LRP1 receptors but fail to reach terminally degradative lysosomes; instead, they are persistently recycled back to the extracellular space. In contrast, tau fibrils are not internalized and primarily adhere to the cell surface through an HSPG-dependent mechanism, triggering TLR4-mediated microglial activation and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Heparin or anti-tau treatments dampen tau fibril-mediated microglial activation. In addition, disease-associated variants of the Alzheimer's disease-related protein APOE reduce microglia-tau interactions, further reducing tau uptake. Together, these findings demonstrate that microglia fail to efficiently clear extracellular tau monomers and fibrils through mechanistically distinct cellular processes, emphasizing the need for tailored therapeutic strategies to enhance extracellular tau clearance in neurodegenerative diseases.

Article.Title: Positional replication fork instability drives PARP inhibitor cytotoxicity
Article.Authors: Gupta D.; Ding X.; Zhang L.; Coleman K.; Tang G.; Lee W.; Oyer J.; Kang X.; Ramms D.; Yu Z.; VanArsdale T.; Fenyo D.; Huang T.; Rothenberg E.
Article.Abstract: Although poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) show promise for treating homologous recombination-deficient cancers, the observed PARPi hypersensitivity in additional genetic contexts expands their potential use in precision oncology. Yet, the DNA lesions driving PARPi-induced cytotoxicity remain poorly defined. Here we uncover distinct replication-fork lesions in specific genomic regions as key determinants of PARPi cytotoxicity. Using CRISPR screens, we identify that loss of replication-coupled cohesin acetyltransferase ESCO2 confers PARPi hypersensitivity independently of homologous recombination deficiency. Quantitative single-molecule imaging reveals that ESCO2 loss promotes accumulation of G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures at a subset of replication-associated sites, associated with PARP1 activation and engagement of fork protection factor TIMELESS to mitigate G4-induced stress. Notably, these G4 lesions localize to fragile pericentromeric regions and engage the G4 helicase DDX11. PARP inhibition disrupts this protective G4-processing response by preventing PARP1-dependent engagement of TIMELESS and DDX11, leading to G4 accumulation, DNA damage and chromosomal instability. Together, our findings define the G4-PARP1-TIMELESS-DDX11 axis as a critical safeguard of replication fork stability at hard-to-replicate loci and reveal ESCO2 as a therapeutic target for promoting synthetic lethality in PARPi-treated cancers.

Article.Title: STING-dependent TNF signalling promotes IKKβ-mediated ATG9A phosphorylation and autophagy
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Zhong Y.; Tian X.; Long M.; Lin S.; Wang S.; Hu Z.; Lu G.; Shang Z.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Chemotherapeutic drugs, either alone or in combination with immunotherapy, are routinely used in cancer treatment. However, cancer cells frequently develop resistance to chemotherapy, and the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using head and neck squamous cell carcinoma as a model, we show that chemotherapy activates the cGAS-STING pathway, leading to the induction of TNF. TNF mediates a paracrine signalling pathway in recipient tumour cells, leading to IKKβ activation and ATG9A phosphorylation at serine 654, thereby promoting autophagy. Moreover, IKKβ activation and ATG9A S654 phosphorylation are induced by TNF, nutrient deprivation and mTOR inhibition, suggesting that the IKKβ-ATG9A axis may represent a common regulatory mechanism of autophagy. Analysis of patient samples further reveals that chemotherapy induces autophagy, and elevated phosphorylation of ATG9A at S654 correlates with poor chemotherapy response. Of note, TNF blockade enhances therapeutic efficacy in both chemotherapy alone and chemotherapy combined with immune checkpoint inhibition. Together, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized TNF-IKKβ-ATG9A signalling axis that promotes autophagy and highlight TNF blockade as a promising strategy to overcome chemotherapy resistance.

Article.Title: Reconstructing the emergence of the human chorion via Hippo-mediated trophoblast induction
Article.Authors: Zhang M.; Lim R.; Reis A.; Piszker W.; Boyd W.; Pagon A.; Mahajan A.; Wu L.; Zhao C.; Petropoulos S.; Ronda C.; Simunovic M.
Article.Abstract: Differential Hippo-LATS-YAP signalling controls the first mammalian cell-fate decision, yet how human trophectoderm specification progresses to chorion formation remains unknown. Here we establish a developmentally informed model in which LATS kinase inhibition initiates the trophectoderm trajectory without exogenous morphogens. Stage matching to an integrated embryo-chorion single-cell reference revealed ordered progression from early trophectoderm to secondary chorionic lineages. Whole-genome bisulfite sequencing showed a naive-like hypomethylated state followed by remethylation, with key known placenta-associated imprinted domains retaining methylation and allelic bias. We then established a three-dimensional human chorion model by agitating induced-cell aggregates in suspension, yielding secondary chorionic lineages that self-organized with outward-facing trophoblast polarity and inside-out stromal-epithelial topology. Endogenous WNT signalling was dispensable for initial trophectoderm induction but regulated later chorionic lineage balance. Isolating CLDN6+ITGA6- cells identified a proEVT-like intermediate with villous and extravillous potential. Together, this framework connects human trophectoderm induction to three-dimensional chorion modelling and enables investigation of placental specification.

Article.Title: Phase separation of SMARCAL1 orchestrates epigenetic reprogramming and methionine metabolism to foster radioresistance and immunosuppression
Article.Authors: Zheng C.; Cui Q.; Li J.; Chen J.; He L.; Zhang X.; Liu Z.; Chen T.; Lyu Y.; Liang C.; Ma S.; Li M.; Shi X.; Jia Y.; Li Z.; Wang X.; Xu W.; Li B.
Article.Abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation has emerged as a key mechanism governing cellular organization and function, but its role in pathological processes and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely elusive. Here we show that SMARCAL1 forms nuclear condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation to enhance histone H4 lactylation and chromatin accessibility. This SMARCAL1‑driven epigenetic reprogramming not only facilitates the recruitment of DNA repair proteins, leading to radiotherapy resistance, but also regulates methionine adenosyltransferase transcription, thereby promoting the methionine cycle and inducing T cell exhaustion and immune therapy tolerance. Intriguingly, SMARCAL1 is identified as a biomarker for predicting therapy response and patient stratification. Importantly, pharmacological disruption of SMARCAL1 condensates by digoxin sensitizes tumours to both radiotherapy and anti-PD1 therapy in multiple models. These findings highlight the crucial role of condensates centred on SMARCAL1-histone H4 in governing DNA repair and immune microenvironment remodelling, as well as propose an innovative strategy to overcome radioimmunoresistance.

Article.Title: Methylated eEF1A selectively decodes mRNA to shape cancer proteomes
Article.Authors: Liu S.; Cruz-Navarrete F.; Hausmann S.; Szkop K.; Ikram S.; Brady R.; Lu X.; Dong R.; Vu J.; Flores N.; Zahn E.; Thompson J.; Garcia B.; Larsson O.; Topisirovic I.; Blanchard S.; Gozani O.; Mazur P.
Article.Abstract: Although mRNA decoding efficiency influences protein synthesis, it remains unknown whether the translation elongation machinery harbours intrinsic mechanisms that selectively modulate codon decoding to shape proteomes. Here we show that METTL13-catalysed dimethylation of the elongation factor eEF1A at lysine 55 (eEF1AK55me2) enhances decoding of select codons, preferentially increasing pro-oncogenic protein synthesis to promote tumorigenesis and targeted therapy resistance. Proteomic profiling and single-molecule imaging reveal that eEF1AK55me2 increases decoding efficiency, particularly for under-represented codons with weak wobble-position base pairing. In cancer cells, METTL13 knockdown reduced translation of oncogenic mRNA enriched in eEF1AK55me2-dependent codons, including KRAS; synonymous recoding with eEF1AK55me2-independent codons reversed this effect. METTL13 loss inhibited the growth of KRASG12C inhibitor (sotorasib)-resistant lung adenocarcinoma syngeneic tumours and patient-derived xenografts. In relapsed autochthonous KRASG12C-driven lung adenocarcinoma, METTL13 ablation mitigated sotorasib resistance and significantly extended survival in vivo. Among patients receiving a KRASG12C inhibitor, inferred METTL13 activity was associated with inferior clinical response. These findings identify an eEF1AK55me2-mediated mRNA decoding mechanism promoting selective oncogenic protein synthesis and suggest METTL13 targeting may counteract KRAS-inhibitor resistance.

Article.Title: Motile vesicles (MoVes) are a cancer cell migration-associated extracellular vesicle population
Article.Authors: Tsering T.; Nadeau A.; Ghasemi M.; Mousovich-Neto F.; Tobias G.; Chen Y.; Kienzle L.; Dickinson K.; Douanne N.; Serganova I.; Zappasodi R.; Matei I.; Lyden D.; Burnier J.
Article.Abstract: Migrating cancer cells release diverse extracellular vesicles (EVs) that carry cargo capable of influencing tumour progression and intercellular communication. However, the mechanisms by which intracellular components are incorporated into EVs remain poorly understood. Here we identify and characterize a previously undescribed population of large EVs (2-5 μm), termed motile vesicles (MoVes), that are generated during active cancer cell migration and associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Comparative analyses across EV populations show that MoVes display distinct ultrastructural features, molecular composition and sedimentation behaviour. Live-cell imaging and scanning electron microscopy reveal that MoVes arise from trailing-edge retraction during mesenchymal migration and are actively shed by cancer cells but rarely by non-transformed cells. MoVes contain genomic DNA spanning the genome of the parent cell, recapitulating its mutational landscape, as well as organelles and proteins associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Moreover, MoVes-associated mitochondrial cargo can enhance oxidative phosphorylation in recipient cells. Together, these findings identify MoVes as a cancer cell migration-associated EV population capable of disseminating genomic DNA and organelles.

Article.Title: Tubulin acetylation regulates nuclear shape fluctuations and DNA repair
Article.Authors: Wallis S.; Tse W.; Donker L.; Baxter A.; Dave N.; Weber A.; Gillespie E.; Chen B.; Burden J.; Friskes A.; Medema R.; Charras G.; Calado D.; Godinho S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Genome stability depends on the accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). While chromatin-based mechanisms have been well studied, emerging evidence reveals that nuclear mechanics actively shape repair outcomes, although the mechanisms remain unclear. Here we identify microtubule acetylation as a regulator of nuclear mechanics that promotes DSB repair via homologous recombination (HR). DNA damage induces progressive tubulin acetylation, leading to displacement of the perinuclear vimentin cage. Loss of the vimentin cage softens the nucleus and renders the nuclear envelope responsive to microtubule forces, which drives transient nuclear shape fluctuations, localized DSB mobility and repair. Inhibiting tubulin acetylation abolishes these fluctuations, restricts DSB mobility and negatively impacts the homology search during HR, leaving non-homologous end joining intact. Consequently, persistent DSBs coalesce and cluster at the nuclear periphery, triggering cell-cycle arrest and senescence and increasing sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents. Removal of the vimentin cage is sufficient to rescue these effects, with restored nuclear fluctuations and repair efficiency. Thus, we propose that nuclear fluctuations act as a mechanical strategy to accelerate error-free repair. These findings reveal how cytoskeletal forces shape nuclear function and establish nuclear fluctuations as a fundamental principle for maintaining genome stability.

Article.Title: A three-dimensional human co-culture system reveals reciprocal embryo–endometrial adaptation at implantation onset
Article.Authors: Bi Y.; Tu Z.; Zhang X.; Hu J.; Chen C.; Xu Y.; Zheng Y.; Song Y.; Chen Y.; Lin T.; Wang H.; Che X.; Li J.; Huang G.; Gao S.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Human embryo implantation begins with dynamic, tightly coordinated interactions between embryonic and endometrial compartments, yet the earliest trophoblast-endometrial interface dynamics remain poorly resolved in vivo. Here, using an endometrial assembloid-based three-dimensional co-culture system with human blastoids and natural blastocysts, we analyse implantation-like progression by time-series single-cell transcriptomics and functional perturbation. Importantly, we identify co-culture-induced trophoblast subsets marked by SDC1+MMP7+ and enriched for transcriptional features associated with extracellular matrix remodelling and cell migration. These subsets are reproducibly detected across independent implantation-like systems, emerge specifically within a decidualized stromal co-culture context, and are further linked to stromal-derived CSF3 signalling by intercellular communication analysis and targeted perturbation. In parallel, the endometrium displays transcriptional changes associated with enhanced decidualization and a glandular hypersecretory transition. Together, our study provides a tractable framework for dissecting reciprocal embryo-endometrial adaptation at the onset of implantation.

Article.Title: On the nature of GABAB receptors and their plasticity in the mammalian brain
Article.Authors: Booker S.
Article.Abstract: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter of the mammalian CNS, essential for circuit function and behaviour. In the brain, GABA activates GABAA and GABAB receptors to modulate circuit activity on behaviourally relevant timescales. GABAB receptor signalling in pre- and postsynaptic domains of neurons is often overlooked, despite the strong inhibition it produces. Importantly, GABAB receptors are diversely phosphorylated and interact with various auxiliary subunits to modify function. This review compares the evidence for the expression and modulation of GABAB receptors, their effectors, and regulatory mechanisms between cell types, brain areas, and mammalian species, particularly focusing on the plasticity of these mechanisms and their relationship to neurological diseases such as epilepsy and dementia.

Article.Title: When minds become data: brain–computer interfaces and the future of mental privacy
Article.Authors: Seymour K.; Ienca M.; Koenig-Robert R.
Article.Abstract: The rapid advancement of brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), particularly adaptive closed-loop systems, presents unprecedented opportunities for medical intervention and human augmentation. At the same time, the growing adoption of applications outside clinical settings also poses significant risks to mental privacy. In this article, we review the current state of neural decoding advancements and their projected trajectory to assess what current and foreseeable technologies can reveal about mental states and the implications for mental privacy. Drawing on a neuroscientific perspective, we clarify the scope and limits of emerging mental privacy risks and argue for a shift in responsibility from reactive regulation to proactive, privacy-embedded design.

Article.Title: Sleep-dependent microglial functions in Alzheimer’s disease
Article.Authors: Calafate S.; Mancuso R.
Article.Abstract: Sleep is a fundamental regulator of brain homeostasis, yet how distinct brain cell types contribute to this process remains poorly understood. Microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, actively regulate neuroinflammatory tone, metabolic waste clearance, and synaptic remodeling, thereby contributing to neural circuit maintenance and proteostasis. Delineating the different functions played by microglia during specific brain states, such as sleep, represents an active area of research. In this article, we review a growing literature supporting the notion that sleep dynamically shapes microglial functional outputs. We further suggest that the failure of the sleep-microglia axis may represent an important component of the molecular framework of Alzheimer's disease (AD), contributing to disease progression. Finally, we discuss preclinical and clinical evidence suggesting that sleep-targeting interventions may modulate AD pathology, and highlight the possibility that restoring sleep physiology could recalibrate microglial homeostatic functions and slow disease progression.

Article.Title: The mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome in aging and brain diseases
Article.Authors: Shawky A.; Huang H.; Parikh D.; Morris-Blanco K.
Article.Abstract: The mitochondrial genome is a dynamic regulatory platform that extends far beyond its protein-coding capacity. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) harbors epigenetic modifications and produces diverse noncoding RNAs that influence mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis. Evidence from animal models and human studies indicates that mtDNA methylation, mitochondrial-encoded noncoding RNAs, and cytosolic release of mitochondrial nucleic acids regulate transcription, metabolism, and stress signaling. In this review, we synthesize emerging insights into how the mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome shape mitochondrial function and serve as regulatory interfaces linking cellular stress and neuronal vulnerability in brain aging and disease.

Article.Title: Resilience and vulnerability in the midbrain dopamine system during aging
Article.Authors: McMurtrie G.; Mabry S.; Glausier J.; Rocha E.; Freyberg Z.
Article.Abstract: The midbrain dopamine system is integral to movement, reward, and motivation, and its dysfunction underlies a range of brain disorders. Age is a primary risk factor for many of these disorders, yet systematic analysis of how the dopamine system changes during healthy aging remains relatively understudied. In this review, we first examine the impact of healthy aging on the dopamine system across sexes and species, including flies, mice, rats, and humans. We next consider the neuroadaptive mechanisms that sustain dopamine neuron function with age. Finally, we contrast the molecular mechanisms of age-related neurodegenerative diseases with those of healthy aging, exploring the possibility that loss of neuroadaptive reserve drives dopamine neurodegeneration. Elucidating these neuroadaptive mechanisms could offer a path toward preserving dopamine neuron function across the lifespan and potentially preventing age-related neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Apolipoprotein E4 and immune dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease: mechanisms and therapeutic implications
Article.Authors: Shi H.; Zhao Y.; Zhu W.; Wang Y.; Bu X.
Article.Abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) functions as an organizer of brain-periphery immune crosstalk, coupling maladaptive microglial states with peripheral immune remodeling to establish a self-reinforcing neuroimmune loop that may accelerate the progression of Alzheimer's disease. In the central nervous system, APOE4 pushes microglia away from homeostatic surveillance toward metabolically stressed, inflammatory, and synaptotoxic phenotypes, thereby weakening pathological protein clearance and promoting neurodegeneration. In the periphery, APOE4 primes innate and adaptive immune cells toward a pro-inflammatory state, creating a reservoir that can communicate with the diseased brain and infiltrate it. In addition, APOE4 erodes the separation between central and peripheral immune compartments, enabling bidirectional immune crosstalk that amplifies neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. In this review, we synthesize evidence for APOE4-driven central and peripheral immune dysregulation; discuss therapeutic opportunities for targeting the APOE4 immune axis; and highlight the need for human-derived, longitudinal, cross-tissue studies to identify causal, stage-specific, and targetable immune nodes for precision intervention.

Article.Title: Tumor innervation in non-central nervous system tumors: origins, mechanisms, and phenotypic plasticity
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Ye Z.; Wang Y.; Tang S.; Chen G.
Article.Abstract: The peripheral nervous system has emerged as an important regulator of solid tumor biology. We synthesize recent advances in cancer neuroscience, focusing on three interconnected themes: the cellular origins of tumor-associated nerves, the molecular mechanisms that govern neural recruitment and remodeling, and the resulting phenotypic plasticity within the tumor microenvironment. Tumor innervation arises through axon extension from pre-existing nerves, recruitment of neural precursors, and neuron-like transdifferentiation of non-neuronal cells. These processes are driven by neurotrophic factors, axon guidance cues, extracellular vesicles, and stress-associated pathways. The functional consequences of innervation are context-dependent, with sympathetic, parasympathetic, and sensory inputs exerting distinct effects across tumor types and stages. We conclude by outlining key challenges and future directions for therapeutic translation.

Article.Title: Evolving perspectives on cardiac innervation: from relay to a complex regulated network
Article.Authors: Habecker B.; Montgomery J.
Article.Abstract: Neural control of the heart adjusts cardiac output to the functional demands of the body in order to maintain homeostasis. Sensory afferents monitor blood pressure, metabolites, and other parameters, sending information to the brainstem that then alters the balance of stimulatory sympathetic and inhibitory parasympathetic transmission to the heart. 'Autonomic imbalance' between sympathetic and parasympathetic efferent transmission in the heart is a characteristic of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases that contributes to pathology. We summarize data from induced pluripotent stem cells, small and large animal models, and human studies that reveal more complexity in peripheral components of this system than previously understood. We also discuss peripheral neuroplasticity in cardiovascular disease and the potential impact of neuromodulation therapies.

Article.Title: Constructing events across perception, action, and thought
Article.Authors: Kwon D.; Park J.; Shim W.
Article.Abstract: The brain organizes continuous experience into events that structure episodic memory and guide behavior. Traditional accounts have primarily focused on sensory discontinuities and prediction errors that trigger updates of event models. Here, we broaden this view to consider event boundaries arising during goal-directed behavior, spontaneous thought, and memory recall, including transitions generated in the absence of corresponding changes in sensory input. We propose that prediction error and uncertainty provide complementary signals for event model updating: prediction errors signal a violation of current expectations, whereas uncertainty may promote updating when upcoming states become difficult to predict. We further suggest that the hippocampus may serve as a candidate hub linking boundary-related representational changes across perception, action, and thought. Together, this framework offers an integrative account of how the brain detects and generates event structure in continuous experience to support memory and behavior.

Article.Title: Functional brain signatures of successful cognitive aging
Article.Authors: Behrenbruch N.; Fischer L.; Kirschner H.; Harrison T.; Maass A.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive aging trajectories vary markedly. While many older adults experience gradual decline in memory and executive function, some maintain high cognitive performance well into advanced age. Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying this variability carries important implications for early detection of unfavorable aging trajectories and the development of interventions. Here, we review functional brain signatures associated with successful cognitive aging in humans, integrating evidence from functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography within a unified conceptual framework of brain maintenance and compensation. Across both modalities, evidence increasingly links successful cognitive aging to the preservation of youth-like neural dynamics, while the contribution of compensatory neural recruitment remains empirically contested and methodologically difficult to establish.

Article.Title: Beyond memory strengthening: noradrenergic control of memory specificity
Article.Authors: Gulmez Karaca K.; Schwabe L.; Roozendaal B.
Article.Abstract: Emotionally significant events are typically remembered better and for longer than mundane experiences. This emotional memory enhancement critically depends on arousal-induced norepinephrine release within the brain. Beyond memory strengthening, recent work shows that noradrenergic activity also shapes the specificity, detailedness, and temporal precision of memories during both early consolidation and systems consolidation. In this review, we synthesize recent findings from human and animal research spanning molecular, circuit, systems, and behavioral mechanisms to propose an integrative framework for how emotional arousal-induced noradrenergic activity affects neural systems that regulate memory specificity and systems consolidation dynamics. The proposed framework refines current models of memory under emotional arousal and may have relevant implications for stress-related psychopathologies.
