Article.Title: The dark and light sides of dynorphin and enkephalin: from reward to aversion
Article.Authors: Węzik M.; Cunha-Macedo M.; Soares-Cunha C.; Rodrigues A.
Article.Abstract: The endogenous opioid system regulates reward and aversion through multiple peptides and receptor subtypes distributed across the brain. In this review, we focus on two opioids: enkephalins, classically linked to reward, and dynorphins, classically linked to aversion. We argue that this dichotomy oversimplifies a system defined by circuit specificity and context dependence. Methodological advances have enabled direct measurement and manipulation of endogenous opioid signaling in vivo at behaviorally relevant timescales, and evidence shows that endogenous opioid signaling is temporally dynamic, circuit-specific, and functionally heterogeneous, challenging simple reward-versus-aversion models. We discuss how these advances reshape our understanding of dynorphin and enkephalin function, using the nucleus accumbens-ventral pallidum-ventral tegmental area circuit as a framework, given its dense, interacting opioid systems and a central role in rewarding and aversive behaviors.

Article.Title: Episodic memory consolidation by reactivation of human concept neurons during sleep reflects contents, not sequence of events
Article.Authors: Niediek J.; Reber T.; Bausch M.; Schwimmbeck F.; Gast H.; Coenen V.; Boström J.; Elger C.; Mormann F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract How do our brains manage to store our everyday experiences into memory? Neurons in the human temporal lobe that respond to the concept of an individual person or object have been shown to provide the semantic building blocks for episodic memory. Recording from 1415 neurons in neurosurgical patients who learned a story involving specific concepts, we found reactivation of neurons representing these concepts during slow-wave sleep after learning. Concept neurons were conjointly reactivated, particularly during sharp-wave ripples, with time lags suitable for synaptic modification. However, the temporal sequence of reactivation did not reflect the sequence of concepts in the learned story. Unlike rodent place cells, which can acquire preferred firing locations during exploration of new environments according to their pre-existing preferred sequence of activation, human concept neurons are tuned to specific semantic contents before learning starts. Consequently, pre-existing firing sequences correlate with consecutive place fields in rodents, but not with sequences of events in human experience. Thus, in contrast to reactivation of rodent place cells, reactivation of human concept cells does not reflect sequences of events in human experience.

Article.Title: Chronically stable, frequency-selective auditory brainstem stimulation via ultra-flexible penetrating electrode arrays
Article.Authors: Pan J.; Liu B.; Wang Z.; Chen G.; Wang C.; Chen Y.; Jia H.; Wang Z.; Ren C.; Zhao Z.; Wu H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The auditory brainstem implant (ABI) targeting the cochlear nucleus (CN) can restore hearing in patients ineligible for cochlear implants. However, conventional ABI using surface electrode array yields highly variable outcomes, from poor to moderate, due to limited spatial resolution and restricted tonotopic access. Here, we developed a penetrating ABI based on a high-density, ultra-flexible implantable neural electrode array (uFINE). In normal-hearing rats, uFINE mapped frequency tuning from 0.5 to 32 kHz in CN and the inferior colliculus (IC). Selective CN stimulation via uFINE evoked IC responses closely matching acoustic tonotopy, with IC tuning widths comparable to tone-evoked responses, and these remained stable for over 136 days, with minimal gliosis observed. Daily sequential CN–IC microstimulation progressively shifted the location of the CN-evoked IC response peak toward the targeted IC stimulation site, consistent with use-dependent plasticity. Together, these findings demonstrate that uFINE enables high-resolution, tonotopically precise, and long-term stable CN stimulation across a broad frequency range with minimal tissue disruption, highlighting its potential to enhance ABI-mediated hearing restoration.

Article.Title: The genetic and proteomic determinants of pediatric stature development and their link to adult height and type 2 diabetes
Article.Authors: Fragoso-Bargas N.; Lupu A.; Campillo-Pereda I.; Huang Y.; Sundfjord J.; Karimi R.; Lind T.; Holm J.; Holm L.; Havdahl A.; Andreassen O.; O’Rahilly S.; Sole-Navais P.; Jacobsson B.; Bratland E.; Davey Smith G.; Juliusson P.; Ong K.; Hansen T.; Njølstad P.; Vaudel M.; Johansson S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Stature is a key indicator of pediatric health, yet the molecular and metabolic architecture governing childhood growth remains incompletely defined. We conduct genome-wide association analyses of stature from birth to childhood (574,580 measurements; 72,704 Norwegian children) and integrate UK Biobank data (age 10 and adulthood). We uncover life-stage shifts in the genetics of stature, identifying previously not identified childhood-specific effects including variants near GLP1R with BMI-independent effects, and reveal three temporal clusters - Infancy and Childhood clusters enriched for endocrine and metabolic pathways, and a Lifetime growth cluster enriched for skeletal biology. Proteome analysis reveals that prepubertal height is associated with widespread changes in the circulation, identifying 106 height-associated proteins and linking IGF1, IGF2, and IGFBP3 levels to childhood-height polygenic scores. Mendelian randomization shows that reduced fetal growth and taller prepubertal height increase type 2 diabetes risk, independent of adult stature. These findings uncover developmental stage-specific genetic and proteomic influences on child-growth and links to adult metabolic health.

Article.Title: Benzoxaboroles target CPSF3 for degradation through a SUMO-dependent pathway in trypanosomes
Article.Authors: Zhang N.; Zahedifard F.; Samad A.; Altmann S.; Ridgway M.; Wall R.; Tinti M.; Schirmer E.; Horn D.; Zoltner M.; Field M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Benzoxaboroles (BoBs) such as acoziborole feature a boron-heterocyclic core and are an important innovation in the development of drugs against a range of pathogens and other pathologies. A broad pharmacological spectrum is associated with chemically diverse BoB derivatives, including multiple modes-of-action (MoA) and molecular targets. However, a consensus MoA for BoBs targeting evolutionarily diverse protozoan pathogens has emerged, with identification of CPSF3 in the CPSF complex as a target in both apicomplexan and kinetoplastida parasites. Here, using comprehensive genetic screens in Trypanosoma brucei , we establish a functional connection between the boron-heterocyclic scaffold shared by all BoBs and protein sumoylation genes. We observe a rapid, transient increase in global protein sumoylation following BoB exposure. While we do not observe direct CPSF3 sumoylation, we find that acoziborole and other BoBs rapidly and specifically destabilise CPSF3 in a SUMO- and proteasome-dependent manner.

Article.Title: Foliar and floral frost damage reshape reproductive phenology with limited carry-over effects
Article.Authors: Lin J.; Delpierre N.; Rathgeber C.; Ren H.; Huang J.; Berninger F.; Li X.; Ma Q.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Late spring frost is an intensifying climatic disturbance, yet how frost damage to different organs (leaves and flowers) reshapes reproductive phenology and generates carry-over effects remains unclear. Using 259,732 phenological observations across eight European woody species spanning 1950–2024, we show that foliar frost damage shortened the fruit development period (FDP; the interval from flowering to fruit maturity) by 1.6 days, driven by delayed flowering and advanced fruit maturity. Conversely, floral frost damage prolonged FDP by 1.3 days through delayed fruit maturity, with both effects strengthening under greater frost severity. Accounting for anomalously warm conditions in the frost year substantially reduced the estimated delays in flowering and subsequent-year phenology, indicating that neglecting climatic context leads to overestimation of frost effects. These findings reveal organ-specific pathways through which frost damage reshapes reproductive phenology while generating limited carry-over effects, refining current understanding of phenological responses under climate change.

Article.Title: Heparan sulfate sulfatases are essential for the patterning of human stem cell-derived midbrain dopaminergic neurons
Article.Authors: Tremolanti C.; Abaurre C.; Chien Y.; Gamon L.; Mitchell C.; Gout E.; Agirre E.; Lyu G.; Karlsson R.; Davies M.; Castelo-Branco G.; Vivès R.; Saltó C.; Marklund U.; Miller R.; Turnbull J.; Arenas E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Midbrain dopaminergic neurons (mDA) are selectively lost in Parkinson’s disease, driving sustained efforts to generate bona fide mDA neurons from human-induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) for replacement therapy. While morphogen gradients and transcription factors have been extensively studied, extracellular regulators remain largely overlooked. Here, we identify the heparan sulfate-modifying enzymes SULF1 and SULF2 as essential for establishing mDA neuron identity in vitro. Using CRISPR/Cas9-engineered iPSCs, we show that loss of SULF1/2 increases 6-O-sulfated heparan sulfate species and disrupts patterning both at the anteroposterior and dorsoventral axes in human iPSC-derived mDA cultures. Double-knockout cells thus fail to acquire ventral midbrain fates and instead adopt hindbrain, spinal cord and neural crest-like identities as revealed by single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Mechanistically, we partially explain the changed patterning to aberrant FGF signaling and demonstrate that FGF inhibition redirects cells toward midbrain fates, however without restoring ventral identity. These findings establish a critical role for SULF1/2 in mDA neuron in vitro differentiation and uncover a previously unrecognized layer of extracellular control over neural patterning.

Article.Title: Desmin filaments extend along actin filaments within the mouse skeletal muscle sarcomere
Article.Authors: Joseph S.; Ko J.; Dahan N.; Dadosh T.; Pak H.; Kirk J.; Jhe W.; Shemer S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Although desmin intermediate filaments are critical for muscle architecture and homeostasis, their spatial 3D organization remains elusive. Their known localization to sarcomeric Z-lines delimits the periodic array of actin and myosin filaments. Here, using d STORM and SIM sub-diffraction resolution microscopy, we resolve the spatial 3D organization of desmin filaments within mouse skeletal muscle, and reveal they are not confined to Z-lines. Our reconstruction reveals that desmin intermediate filaments extend from Z-lines into the sarcomere interior, where they align with actin filaments. Functional assays show that disrupting desmin filament assembly in normal male mouse muscle using a dominant negative inhibitor of desmin selectively reduces active tension at longer sarcomere lengths, indicating a role for desmin in sarcomere mechanics. These findings expand the structural model of the muscle sarcomere and support a role for desmin in force production.

Article.Title: Plankton ecological complexity amplifies climate-driven weakening of the ocean biological pump
Article.Authors: Lin F.; Le C.; Chen Y.; Negrete-García G.; Luo J.; Henson S.; Dutkiewicz S.
Article.Abstract: The ocean biological pump regulates atmospheric carbon dioxide, yet Earth system projections may miss how plankton food-web complexity shapes its response to warming. Here we use a single Earth system model framework with three progressively more complex plankton ecosystems to show that ecological complexity amplifies the climate-driven weakening of future carbon export. Across historical and future emission scenarios, warming and stratification cause only modest changes in global net primary production but persistent declines in net community production and export fluxes. This weakening increases systematically with ecosystem complexity across scenarios. Under SSP5-8.5, late-century global net community production falls by 5.8% in the default configuration, compared with 8.8% and 12.8% in the more complex configurations. The amplification arises from climate-driven shifts towards smaller phytoplankton and stronger zooplankton grazing, retaining more fixed carbon in the upper ocean. Coarse plankton representations may therefore underestimate future biological-pump weakening and climate-carbon feedbacks.

Article.Title: Biosynthesis of iboga alkaloids
Article.Authors: Kang M.; Kamileen M.; Nakamura Y.; Hamilton J.; Kang G.; Huettel B.; Wurlitzer J.; Heinicke S.; Kunert M.; Buell C.; Caputi L.; O’Connor S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Tabernanthe iboga (iboga) is the source of voacangine, which is widely used as a semi-synthetic starting material for the anti-addiction agent ibogaine. Despite extensive investigation of voacangine biosynthesis, production of this compound cannot be reconstituted in a heterologous host, suggesting that one or more enzymes required for biosynthesis are missing. Additionally, T. iboga produces ibophyllidine, a pyrroloindole alkaloid that utilizes the same upstream precursor as voacangine, but is a member of a structurally distinct alkaloid class. Here we use bulk and single cell gene expression from leaf and root tissue to identify the unknown enzymes from these two pathways. We identify two additional enzymes that enable biosynthesis of voacangine in a heterologous host. The missing enzymes includes a pathogenesis-related (PR)10 family protein that likely catalyzes cyclization of a transient intermediate. Careful analysis of gene expression profiles in leaf and root also enabled the discovery of four additional enzymes that convert an upstream intermediate to ibophyllidine. This work reveals the chemical logic that generates two distinct alkaloid scaffolds in this important medicinal plant.

Article.Title: Visible light drives bright extreme-ultraviolet high harmonics
Article.Authors: Karst M.; Gebhardt M.; Eisenbach L.; Gierschke P.; Sidiropoulos T.; Klas R.; Rothhardt J.; Limpert J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Coherent extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) light is a central tool in modern photon science, probing the electronic, chemical and structural properties of matter. High-harmonic generation can extend the reach of laser sources into this spectral range, but the achievable photon flux falls sharply as photon energy increases. We show experimentally and theoretically that plasma-core-induced self-guiding of a visible-wavelength driver in helium sustains high intensity and favorable phase matching over an extended propagation length. We achieve a conversion efficiency of up to 10 −6 in a single high-harmonic line and phase-matched emission extending to 100 eV. With less than 10 W of average power at 516 nm from a frequency-doubled ytterbium laser, we generate 1.8 × 10 11 photons s −1 within 2 % bandwidth at 13.5 nm (91.8 eV), exceeding previous reports by more than an order of magnitude. These results establish a power-scalable XUV platform for actinic metrology, spectroscopy and coherent imaging.

Article.Title: G3BP1-induced retrograde transport blockade triggers HSC activation and liver fibrosis via COPI alternative splicing
Article.Authors: Wu E.; He M.; Song Y.; Liu M.; Cheng Y.; Leng Y.; Zhang Y.; Ye S.; Zheng Y.; Wang Z.; Kong L.; Zhang H.
Article.Abstract: The molecular mechanisms underlying hepatic stellate cell (HSC) activation and subsequent liver fibrogenesis remain incompletely elucidated. Here, Ras GTPase-activating protein-binding protein 1 (G3BP1) is identified a significant upregulation in liver specimens from patients with liver fibrosis and experimental murine fibrosis models. G3BP1 promotes HSC activation in human LX-2 cells, primary mouse HSCs, and CCl 4 -/BDL-induced fibrotic mouse models, acting independently of stress granules (SGs). Genetic ablation of hepatic G3BP1 attenuates HSC activation and fibrotic progression. Integrative transcriptomic and APEX‑mass spectrometry analyses in HSCs reveal that G3BP1 regulates alternative splicing of coat protein complex Ⅰ (COPI) subunits through functional interaction with the splicing factor heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein M (hnRNPM). The consequent accumulation of exon 2-deficient COPG1 and exon 8-deficient COPB2 isoforms impairs COPI-dependent retrograde transport and induces endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, which drives HSC activation and fibrogenesis. Further studies demonstrate that G3BP1 recruits SRPK1 to phosphorylate hnRNPM, thereby promotes alternative splicing of COPI subunits. Pharmacological intervention of G3BP1/SRPK1/hnRNPM improves liver fibrosis. In conclusion, these results uncover an unrecognized role of G3BP1 in HSC activation by promoting COPI alternative splicing, and provide a potential therapeutic target for liver fibrosis.

Article.Title: Structural basis for constitutive activation of oncogenic gp130 mutants found in human inflammatory hepatocellular adenomas
Article.Authors: Zhou Y.; Cao J.; Ramlall T.; McGoldrick L.; Jones J.; Cook A.; Leidich R.; Sleeman M.; Olson W.; Stevis P.; Franklin M.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory hepatocellular adenomas (IHCAs) are benign liver tumors primarily driven by somatic mutations in the gp130 receptor, resulting in its constitutive activation. To uncover the structural mechanisms underlying this activation, we employ cryo-electron microscopy and mutagenesis to study five representative IHCAs-associated gp130 mutants and two engineered mutants with ligand-independent activity. Most mutants form “X”-shaped dimers through a 3D domain-swapping mechanism, characterized by large separations between juxtamembrane domains and reliant on D1 domain-mediated “tip-to-tip” interactions for dimer clustering and activation. A rare mutant displays a distinct “Y”-shaped dimer conformation, with closely aligned juxtamembrane domains enabling direct activation independent of dimer clustering. These findings highlight the diversity of gp130 mutant activation mechanisms and provide a foundation for developing therapeutic strategies targeting aberrant gp130 signaling in IHCAs.

Article.Title: Localized strain-engineered 1D electron guides in 2D MoS2 devices with synaptic memory and high-mobility transistor functionalities
Article.Authors: Byeon J.; Harm O.; Pyo J.; Park S.; Kim B.; Cho E.; Lim J.; Kim T.; Yoo B.; Oh S.; Song C.; Jeong H.; Park K.; Pak S.; Cha S.
Article.Abstract: Local strain engineering has been studied as an effective strategy to modify the electronic band structure of two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors. However, using precisely controlled localized strain as a scalable tool for directing and controlling charge dynamics in 2D electronics remains largely underexplored. Here, we introduce wafer-scale localized strain engineering that applies periodically localized one-dimensional (1D) uniaxial strain to monolayer MoS 2 -based dual-functional electronics. By transferring MoS 2 onto a line-patterned HfO 2 substrate, we can deterministically generate a periodic localized 1D potential well. This approach creates a well-defined 1D potential landscape that facilitates dual functionality within a single material platform, depending on the alignment between the potential well orientation and the direction of carrier transport. Charge transport perpendicular to the 1D potential wells results in controlled charge trapping, thereby yielding a multibit synaptic memory device, whereas transport parallel to the potential wells experiences reduced lattice scattering and an effective mass with trap-free carrier conduction, leading to a high-mobility field-effect transistor. Systematic transport analyses elucidate how localized uniaxial strain modulates charge-trap density, lattice scattering, and effective mass, giving rise to direction-dependent charge transport. These findings highlight localized 1D strain as an effective design parameter for high-performance, scalable multifunctional 2D electronics.

Article.Title: [c2]Daisy-chain molecular turing machines with switchable fluorescence outputs
Article.Authors: Li W.; Liu C.; Rao Y.; Yang S.; Xia X.; Kwok R.; Sun J.; Qin Y.; Yang H.; Lam J.; Tang B.
Article.Abstract: Synthetic small-molecule machines capable of bidirectionally reading and writing information on molecular tapes with visual output remain elusive due to the challenge in amplifying molecular-scale motions into macroscopic signals. Herein, we report two [c2]daisy-chain molecular Turing machines that convert reversible mechanical motions into different fluorescence signals by developing novel aggregation-induced emission luminogens with an intramolecular charge transfer mechanism. Attributed to the collective and amplified shuttling motions triggered by anions or solvents, the [c2]daisy chains exhibit controllable and reversible fluorescence modulation in solution for up to 42 cycles. Moreover, incorporation of [c2]daisy chains into polymers yields fast-response macroscopic Turing machines capable of conformation-dependent fluorescence switching. Importantly, the [c2]daisy chains enable binary ASCII and nucleotide-base encoding, allowing visual representation of letters, digits, and 64 genetic codons. By mapping codons to fluorescence, they also enable visual decoding of DNA information, bridging molecular-scale motion to macroscopically readable information processing and advancing functional molecular computation. Synthetic small-molecule machines capable of bidirectionally reading and writing information on molecular tapes with visual output remain elusive due to the challenge in amplifying molecular-scale motions into macroscopic signals. Here, the authors report two [c2]daisy-chain molecular Turing machines that convert mechanical motions into fluorescence signals.

Article.Title: Greenhouse gas responses to coastal wetland land use change vary by ecosystem and conversion pathway
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Yan F.; Wang C.; Sun J.; Liu M.; Lin X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Land-use and land-cover change (LULCC) is altering greenhouse gas (GHG) dynamics in coastal wetlands, yet how these responses vary among ecosystems and conversion pathways remains uncertain. Here, we synthesized 276 studies and applied multilevel meta-analysis to paired LULCC comparisons. GHG responses varied with pre-conversion wetland type, destination land use, hydrology, and soil carbon and nitrogen status. Pooled sustained-flux global warming potential (SGWP) was ‒122.41 ± 81.99 mg CO 2 e m ‒2 h ‒1 for natural coastal wetlands and 250.60 ± 101.06 for LULCC sites, corresponding to 0.17 ± 0.06 Gt CO 2 e of cumulative emissions over two decades. The descriptive SGWP contrast with pooled LULCC sites was larger for vegetated wetlands ( + 309.32%) than for tidal flats ( + 165.02%). Ecologically restored wetlands showed negative pooled SGWP ( − 33.03 ± 114.70 mg CO 2 e m ‒2 h ‒1 ), contrasting with the positive pooled LULCC estimate. Our results indicate that GHG responses to coastal wetland conversion are ecosystem- and pathway-specific, underscoring the importance of conserving vegetated wetlands and targeting restoration.

Article.Title: Entropy-engineered polar heterogeneity enables near-decoupled polarization–strain behavior for high-density energy storage
Article.Authors: Yang Y.; Zhang L.; Huang Y.; Chen F.; Yang Y.; Jing R.; Chen Z.; He L.; Wang D.; Zhou B.; Chen X.; Zhang Y.; Wu H.; Tan H.; Zhang H.; Liu G.; Yan Y.; Yang J.; Zhang S.; Jin L.
Article.Abstract: Dielectric energy-storage (ES) ceramics are central to pulsed power technologies, yet excessive polarization–strain coupling in lead-free systems induces electrostrain, compromising ES density and device reliability. Here, we introduce configurational entropy ( S config ) as a quantitative design parameter to engineer polar heterogeneity and regulate polarization–strain interactions in lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics (RFEs). Entropy engineering generates chemical heterogeneity, local lattice distortions, strain-field fluctuations, and polar fragmentation, disrupting long-range polar coherence and reducing the spatial cooperativity of polarization-induced deformation while preserving large field-induced polarization. This entropy-mediated reconstruction of the polar landscape yields an ultralow electrostrictive coefficient Q 33 of ~0.010 m 4 C –2 in a (Bi 0.5 Na 0.5 )TiO 3 -based high-entropy RFE, enabling a near-decoupled polarization–strain response with high polarization and suppressed macroscopic electrostrain. Multilayer ceramic capacitors achieve a recoverable ES density of 21.5 J cm –3 at 1200 kV cm –1 , together with a low electrostrain of 0.073% at 300 kV cm –1 . Atomic-scale imaging reveals vortex and antivortex polarization configurations associated with entropy-induced structural heterogeneity and lattice distortions. Phase-field simulations demonstrate that heterogeneous polarization states redistribute elastic energy and reduce cooperative polarization-induced deformation. This work establishes S config as a quantitative descriptor for engineering weak electromechanical coupling and high-ES-density performance in lead-free dielectric capacitors.

Article.Title: Accelerating high-throughput catalyst screening by direct generation of equilibrium adsorption structures
Article.Authors: Huo S.; Cao X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The adsorption energy serves as a crucial descriptor for the large-scale screening of catalysts. Nevertheless, the limited distribution of training data for the extensively utilised machine learning interatomic potential, predominantly sourced from near-equilibrium structures, results in unreliable adsorption structures and consequent adsorption energy predictions. In this context, we present DBCata, a deep generative model that integrates a periodic Brownian-bridge framework with an equivariant graph neural network to establish a low-dimensional transition manifold between unrelaxed and DFT-relaxed structures, without requiring explicit energy or force information. Upon training, DBCata effectively generates high-fidelity adsorption geometries, achieving an interatomic distance mean absolute error of 0.035 Å on the dataset from Catalysis-Hub, which is approximately 70% lower than that of the current state-of-the-art machine learning potential models. Moreover, the corresponding DFT accuracy can be improved within 0.1 eV in 94% of instances by identifying and refining anomalous predictions through a hybrid chemical-heuristic and self-supervised outlier detection approach. We demonstrate that DBCata enables accelerated high-throughput computational screening for alloy catalysts in the oxygen reduction reaction, highlighting the potential of DBCata as a powerful tool for catalyst design and optimisation.

Article.Title: Shape conforming Janus hydrogel for preventing anastomotic leaks
Article.Authors: Song D.; Chen L.; Li Y.; Ni C.; Yang H.; Chen S.; Yang C.; Liao X.; Yu J.; Liu Y.; Hu Y.; Kong X.; Guo C.; Chen H.; Xiao Q.; Zhao Q.; Xie T.; Ding K.
Article.Abstract: Anastomotic leaks are severe complications following gastrointestinal surgery. The shape conformability of powder-based hydrogels makes them potentially suitable for leak-sealing, but they typically cause undesirable tissue adhesion, prohibiting clinical applications. Here we present a powder-based Janus hydrogel that forms in situ to simultaneously prevent anastomotic leaks and tissue adhesions. By rational regulation of dissolution and gelation kinetics, a powder mixture of chitosan lactate and oxidized chondroitin sulfate rapidly forms an adhesive porous scaffold in situ via amine-aldehyde condensation. A zwitterionic anti-adhesive layer is synthesized on the peritoneal side of the porous layer, creating a stable Janus structure via mechanical interlocking. The chemical and structural asymmetry between the serosal and peritoneal surfaces reconciles the conflicting demands of robust tissue integration, leakage prevention, and anti-adhesive safety. Further, the Janus hydrogel improves short- and long-term survival by reducing immune responses and perianastomotic adhesions, highlighting its potential for clinical translation in gastrointestinal surgery.

Article.Title: Landscape fire sourced PM2.5, cause-specific paediatric hospitalisations, and the role of tree cover
Article.Authors: Zhou S.; Xu Z.; Yang Z.; Yu W.; Huang W.; Lavigne E.; Abramson M.; Morawska L.; Coelho M.; Tantrakarnapa K.; Kliengchuay W.; Wu Y.; Wen B.; Xu R.; Chen G.; Yu P.; Ye T.; Zhang Y.; Ju K.; Liu Y.; Chen B.; Xing Y.; Li Z.; Huang J.; Tang L.
Article.Abstract: Landscape fire smoke threatens child health, but tree cover’s role is unclear. We analyse 67.9 million hospitalisations among children aged 0-19 years in 1012 communities across seven countries/territories during 2000-2019 using time-series models and meta-analysis. Here we show that each 10 µg/m 3 increase in daily landscape fire-sourced fine particulate matter is associated with a 1.4% increase in all-cause hospitalisation risk (95% confidence interval 1.2-1.6%) with low tree cover versus 0.5% (0.2-0.8%) with high tree cover. Under a counterfactual 10% increase in tree cover, attributable fractions decrease significantly for all-cause (−0.03%, 95% confidence interval −0.05% to −0.01%), respiratory (−0.05%, −0.09% to −0.01%) and infectious (−0.04%, −0.07% to −0.01%) hospitalisations, with significant reductions in communities with low gross domestic product. These findings support considering tree cover alongside broader smoke-protection strategies.

Article.Title: Influenza A virus orchestrates ciliated cell fate and injury during the mucociliary damage repair cycle
Article.Authors: Xiao B.; Zhao X.; Guo S.; Fan M.; Zhang H.; Yang X.; Zhang L.; Li Y.; Ma K.; Zheng Y.; Peng Y.; Liu L.; Chan R.; Wang S.; Qi W.; Ye Z.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Influenza A virus causes acute damage to airway epithelium, yet the damage–repair cycle and mechanisms underlying persistent mucociliary clearance (MCC) dysfunction long after viral clearance remain unclear. Here, using longitudinal in vivo quantitative micro-optical coherence tomography, we show that global MCC impairment persists for more than 14 days, marked by impaired ciliary activity and sustained mucus hypersecretion in male mice infected with the H1N1 influenza A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (PR8) strain. Through lineage tracing and multi-omics analyses, we identify an immune-mediated transdifferentiation program in which IFN signaling activates the IDO1–AhR axis to drive ciliated-to-mucous cell fate transition and chronic muco-obstruction after H1N1 PR8 infection in a reconstructed human bronchial epithelium model. In parallel, we identify the viral M2 protein as a key driver of ciliary loss, suppressing the host TP73–FOXJ1–RFX3 regulatory axis and promoting proteasomal degradation of FOXJ1. Together, these findings uncover host- and virus-driven pathways that cooperatively impair airway epithelial homeostasis and sustain MCC failure beyond active infection, highlighting therapeutic targets for post-influenza muco-obstructive disease.

Article.Title: A global atlas of digital dermatology to map innovation and disparities
Article.Authors: Gröger F.; Lionetti S.; Gottfrois P.; Gonzalez-Jimenez A.; Habermacher L.; N/A N/A.; Böhm M.; Cerminara S.; Nikolakis G.; Romswinkel A.; Amruthalingam L.; Groh M.; Pouly M.; Navarini A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence promises democratized access to dermatological care, but model reliability depends on the quality and comprehensiveness of the underlying data. Despite rapid growth in publicly available dermatology images, the field lacks quantitative indicators to measure whether new datasets expand clinical coverage or merely replicate what is already known. Existing collections are widely assumed to be biased, yet the scale and topography of these gaps have remained unquantified, leaving the community without a road map for strategic data acquisition. Here, we show, by unifying 1.1 million images from 29 public datasets into a queryable semantic atlas, that the global archive is markedly skewed and increasingly redundant: darker skin tones (Fitzpatrick V–VI) constitute only 11.0% of images, pediatric patients only 2.3%, and informational novelty has plateaued despite exponential growth, revealing where targeted data acquisition is most needed.

Article.Title: A highly distorted benzenium cation
Article.Authors: Tian B.; Chang J.; Sun Q.; Zhang Q.; Zhang S.; Huang H.; Xu X.; Sun Z.; Chen W.; Tan T.; Li S.; Pang S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract In contrast to the well-explored peripheral functionalization of benzene, its skeletal alteration remains underdeveloped. Here, we report a highly distorted benzenium cation, 2,3-dihydroxy-1,4,6-triamino-5-nitrobenzenium (TANBC + ), featuring a ring twist angle of 35.91° and a ring C-C bond length of 1.540 Å, both rank the highest among all benzenium cations. Such pronounced structural distortions endow TANBC + with unique electronic properties, including a highly positive electrostatic charge on the warped carbon, weak aromaticity, and a low ring bond dissociation energy. Consequently, instead of undergoing peripheral functionalization like typical benzenium cations, TANBC + participates in three distinct benzene ring reconstruction pathways or remains inert under standard electrophilic substitution conditions. Moreover, despite its distorted structure, TANBC + exhibits excellent ambient stability, stabilized by extensive hydrogen bonding, and can be synthesized readily without harsh conditions usually required for conventional benzenium cations. This work not only introduces a new strategy for benzene reconstruction but also redefines the role of benzenium cations from mediators of peripheral functionalization to promoters of skeletal alteration, thereby advancing the fundamental chemistry of benzene.

Article.Title: Deep ultraviolet gallium-oxide avalanche photodiodes reaching an impulse-response-derived gain-bandwidth record of 152 GHz
Article.Authors: Dong D.; Fu J.; Ren H.; Zhang Q.; Zhang T.; Liu X.; Cao Y.; Peng M.; Zhu X.; Tang Y.; Zhang F.; Zhang J.; Jiang Y.; Zhang Y.; Wu Z.; Qiu C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Solar-blind Ga 2 O 3 -based photodetectors, sensing deep ultraviolet (DUV) light (200–280 nm), offer unparalleled opportunities for secure non-line-of-sight optical communication. Yet their practical applications have been largely hindered by the relatively low gain-bandwidth product (GBP), due to the fundamental trade-off between response speed and photoelectric gain. Here, we report nanosecond-level-response solar-blind avalanche photodetectors based on β-Ga 2 O 3 /MgO/La 0.8 Ca 0.2 MnO 3 (LCMO) n-Barrier-p heterojunctions with high apparent gain over 2.6×10 6 , thereby achieving an impulse-response-derived record-breaking 152 GHz gain-bandwidth product — outpacing the state-of-the-art Ga 2 O 3 -based devices by 3 orders of magnitude. The MgO interlayer enables lattice matching and engineered conduction band offset to boost gain and suppress dark current, while the p-type LCMO layer introduces a large valence band offset and simultaneously establishes a hole-selective transport highway for ultrafast response. This work not only resolves the longstanding gain-bandwidth trade-off in DUV photodetection but also presents a universal band-engineering framework for next-generation optoelectronics.
Article.TopicFields: Materials Science > Electronic, Optical and Magnetic Materials > Ga2O3 and related materials; Materials Science > Materials Chemistry > 2D Materials and Applications; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Advanced Semiconductor Detectors and Materials

Article.Title: Mapping temperature using transmission Kikuchi diffraction
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Ling X.; Lodico J.; O’Neill T.; Regan B.; Mecklenburg M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract As electronic devices are engineered at increasingly smaller length scales, new nanoscopic metrologies are needed. Measuring nanoscale temperatures and pressures is challenging as physical contact inevitably perturbs the system, and collecting far-field thermal radiation limits the spatial resolution. Kikuchi diffraction thermometry (KDTh), a non-contact scanning electron microscope (SEM) technique, can sensitively map nanoscale temperatures. Local lattice changes measured by Kikuchi pattern fitting enable translating volumetric strain to temperature via the material’s coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE). Measurements on Joule-heated graphite come from rastering a 5.5-nm electron probe across the sample, achieving a ~ 0.01% fractional precision and 2.2 K/ $$\sqrt{{{\rm{Hz}}}}$$ Hz temperature sensitivity. KDTh offers superior sensitivity by fitting the entire Kikuchi pattern, instead of a particular Kikuchi band or interband angle. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) techniques can achieve a similar precision, but electron-transparency limits their applications. KDTh can operate in both transmission and reflection modes to cost-effectively accommodate a variety of samples.

Article.Title: Early-life skin molecular signatures are predictive of atopic dermatitis risk in an Asian preconception birth cohort
Article.Authors: Ta L.; Wearne S.; Lim S.; Chia M.; Duan K.; Loo E.; Shek L.; E. N. Goh A.; Chong K.; Goh S.; Van Bever H.; Teoh O.; Cheng Z.; Lee Y.; Yap F.; Tan K.; Chan J.; Chong Y.; Lee B.; Common J.; Nagarajan N.; Tham E.
Article.Abstract: Early identification of infants at risk of atopic dermatitis (AD) is critical for timely prevention, yet preclinical biomarkers remain elusive. In this nested study within the prospective Singapore Preconception Study of Long-Term Maternal and Child Outcomes (S-PRESTO) cohort (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03531658), we investigated whether early molecular signatures of infant skin could predict disease onset. The primary endpoint was physician-diagnosed AD by 18 months of age; secondary endpoints included AD severity and longitudinal trajectories of skin metagenomic, metabolomic, and proteomic profiles. Non-lesional skin tape strips were collected longitudinally from 119 infants (60 AD cases, 59 controls) at week 1 and months 3, 6, and 18. Here, we show that distinct microbial and host molecular alterations significantly precede clinical manifestation. Healthy infants exhibited progressive microbial diversity, transitioning from Staphylococcus epidermidis to lipophilic commensals, accompanied by butanoate fermentation and elevated natural moisturizing factors. Conversely, infants developing AD displayed early dysbiosis, driven by Pseudomonas stutzeri at week 1 and Staphylococcus aureus by month 3, alongside premature upregulation of antimicrobial peptides and uncoupled host-microbiome interactions. Predictive models showed strong performance in stratifying AD risk, shifting from microbial and peptide markers at week 1 to sustained inflammation at month 3. These preclinical signatures offer practical non-invasive tools for early infant risk stratification.

Article.Title: Hyperelastic microfibers as bioinspired proprioceptive artificial muscles
Article.Authors: Won J.; Jang J.; Kim H.; Choi I.; Jo K.; Lee Y.; Kang J.; Park S.; Lee G.; Park Y.; Yuk H.; Majidi C.; Park S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Skeletal muscles combine forceful contraction with built-in sensing of their own length and movement, known as proprioception. Reproducing this combination in soft artificial muscles remains difficult, because added sensors often reduce actuation performance, complicate fabrication or limit miniaturization. In natural muscle, specialized sensory fibers are embedded alongside, and mechanically coupled to, the force-generating fibers. Inspired by this arrangement, we pair a hyperelastic, highly stretchable fluid channel with a stiffer, off-center optical core inside a single thin fiber. When liquid is pumped in, the channel wall undergoes a shape bifurcation: a localized bulge forms and propagates along the fiber. Because the core resists stretching, the bulge bends the fiber into a contracting coil, while the core also reports the fiber’s shape through the light it transmits. Here we show that such fibers, produced continuously by a scalable drawing process, act as artificial muscles that sense their own contraction and stretching, supporting self-monitoring movement in soft robots.

Article.Title: Twist-engineered arbitrary polarization detection for intelligent polarimetric sensing
Article.Authors: Shi M.; Ye T.; Deng J.; Wang R.; Bu Y.; Cui T.; Fu L.; Huang J.; Ning J.; Guo X.; Shu H.; Chen X.; Zhou J.
Article.Abstract: Twist-photonics offers a powerful route to engineer light-matter interactions beyond conventional planar architectures. Although twist-photonic platforms, including twist-stacked metasurfaces, van der Waals (vdW) materials and photonic crystals have successfully engineered chiral optical responses, anomalous dispersion and high- Q localized modes, most platforms remain passive. Their translation into on-chip optoelectronic sensing is hindered by an intrinsic trade-off: photosensitive absorbers can quench twist-engineered resonances, whereas passive twist-photonic modes often couple inefficiently to active photocarrier-generation regions. Here, we report an emerging twist-photonic paradigm that integrates anisotropic metasurfaces with anisotropic black phosphorus (BP). Coupled to a vectorial cavity, this twisted stack produces quasi-pure circular-polarization photoresponses and enables arbitrary polarization selectivity across the full Poincaré sphere at multiple wavelengths. Then, we establish an ultra-compact on-chip full-Stokes polarimeter using only two metasurface-BP twisted stacks, achieving high-accuracy full-Stokes reconstruction with a root-mean-square error below 1.3%, and the highest responsivity among reported vdW material-based full-Stokes polarimeters. We further implement an in-sensor kernel matrix that directly maps polarization states into synaptic weights for polarization-programmable multimodal convolutional image processing, reducing electrical switching energy by 1 to 3 orders of magnitude and reconfiguration latency by 2 to 4 orders of magnitude, as the array scales from the 10k-pixel to megapixel level.

Article.Title: SMC5/6 safeguards chromatin compartments and TAD boundaries for genome stability
Article.Authors: Silva R.; Morea A.; Lembo G.; Nunomiya A.; Lucini F.; Iannelli F.; Crosetto N.; Ferrari F.; Branzei D.
Article.Abstract: SMC5/6, a member of the Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes family, coordinates 3D genome organization, chromatin states, and transcriptional regulation, yet its role in higher-order chromatin architecture remains poorly defined. Here, we investigate the impact of conditional SMC5 depletion in human B lymphoblastoid cells. Hi-C analyses reveal global rewiring of chromatin interactions, with increased long-range and reduced short-range contacts, leading to altered large-scale chromosome organization. SMC5 loss induces changes in 3D genome compartmentalization affecting ~2% of the genome and is accompanied by transcriptional upregulation of inflammatory and cancer-associated gene programs. SMC5 depletion also promotes double-strand break accumulation, preferentially in active compartments and following gene expression levels. However, regions undergoing architectural reorganization display comparatively fewer breaks, indicating that chromatin changes are not driven by DNA damage. Together, our findings establish SMC5/6 as a key regulator of chromatin compartmentalization and TAD boundary integrity, linking 3D genome organization to transcriptional control and genome stability.

Article.Title: Viscoelasticity of synthetic antigen presenting cells reprograms T cell metabolism for TCR-T cell manufacturing and therapy
Article.Authors: Yang Y.; Li Y.; Liu Z.; Zhou H.; Zhu Y.; Shen X.; Lai D.; Cen Y.; Miller E.; Nan H.; Zhang B.; Wang S.; Lin J.; Chen Y.; Raykowski B.; Zhu E.; Shen J.; Shen K.; Park J.; Li J.; Shen X.; Wang Z.; Yang L.; Li S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Adoptive T cell receptor (TCR)–based immunotherapy offers a powerful strategy to target solid tumors. However, how the physical properties of the antigen-presenting interface regulate T cell metabolic programming remains poorly defined. Here we develop synthetic viscoelastic activating cells (SynVAC), artificial antigen-presenting cells whose stress-relaxation kinetics are chemically tuned independently of stiffness and of peptide–MHC (pMHC) and co-stimulatory ligand density. SynVAC-pMHC provides a defined, scalable platform that outperforms monocyte-derived dendritic cells to enrich antigen-specific CD8 + T cells. Fast-relaxing SynVAC-pMHC amplifies TCR signaling and mTOR activity, drives metabolic changes, and programs antigen-specific T cells toward an energetically favorable state with improved memory-like features after expansion. TCR-T cells expanded using fast-relaxing SynVAC-pMHC exhibit superior persistence and durable antitumor activity in melanoma and ovarian cancer models. These results establish cell-mimetic viscoelasticity as a key biophysical cue governing T cell metabolism and differentiation and offer a fully synthetic strategy for manufacturing potent TCR-T cells.

Article.Title: Efficient n–i–p all-perovskite tandem solar cells enabled by interconnection layer engineering
Article.Authors: Jeong M.; Kim D.; Jeon S.; Woo M.; Kang S.; Lee S.; Choi Y.; Kim C.; Kim S.; Park J.; Oh O.; Kim D.; Kim J.; Noh J.
Article.Abstract: All-perovskite tandem solar cells promise ultrahigh efficiencies, yet monolithic devices have been realized predominantly in the p–i–n architecture because n–i–p integration imposes stringent materials constraints. The preformed wide-bandgap top subcell and its hole-selective contact must withstand bottom-subcell fabrication temperatures, limiting material choices. Here we address this challenge using a 2.0 eV Cs-based all-inorganic wide-bandgap subcell and an additive-free P3HT hole-selective contact whose molecular organization is reconfigured by MeO-2PACz. This interfacial modification enhances P3HT ordering and promotes efficient hole extraction, alleviating a transport bottleneck in monolithic n–i–p tandems. Coupled with PCBM modification of the ALD-SnO₂ electron-selective contact in the 1.55 eV bottom subcell, this architecture enables balanced carrier coupling across the interconnection layer, suppresses charge accumulation and voltage loss, and delivers efficiencies of 25.3% and 24.7% for 0.096 cm² and 1.045 cm² devices, respectively, with a stabilized power output of 24.4%. Additionally, combining the n–i–p double-junction device with a p–i–n narrow-bandgap subcell (1.25 eV) yields a four-terminal triple-junction device with 28% efficiency. To our knowledge, this is the first report of an n–i–p double-junction device exceeding 25% efficiency and an n–i–p-based four-terminal triple-junction device reaching 28%, advancing perovskite tandem technology.

Article.Title: var2csa transcription implicates variant surface antigen switching in cerebral malaria pathogenesis
Article.Authors: Stucke E.; Coulibaly D.; Lawton J.; Kapadia S.; Sobota R.; Courneya J.; Sebastian S.; Adams M.; Smith D.; Ventimiglia N.; Dwivedi A.; Dara A.; Nakajima R.; Jain A.; Koné A.; Traoré K.; Guindo B.; Tangara B.; Niangaly A.; Tolo Y.; Sissoko M.; Cummings B.; Laurens M.; Ouattara A.; Berry A.
Article.Abstract: Previous PCR-based gene expression studies linked severe malaria, including cerebral malaria (CM), to Plasmodium falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein-1 (PfEMP1) variants that bind endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR). Using RNA sequencing and de novo transcriptome assembly in a matched CM case-control study of Malian children, we quantify var gene transcripts encoding PfEMP1s in 13 matched pairs of CM cases and uncomplicated malaria controls and in 25 CM cases and 55 uncomplicated malaria controls. Contrary to earlier findings, PfEMP1s that bind EPCR alone are not associated with CM. Transcription of conserved gene var2csa is implicated in var gene switching in vitro. Here, its transcription is significantly associated with CM across study sites, suggesting that switching may contribute to CM pathogenesis. Importantly, this association is observed at the transcript level, but potentially not translation. We use a protein microarray to show a lack of antibody responses to the VAR2CSA antigen in cerebral malaria, supporting an association between CM and var2csa transcription rather than antigenic presence. CM is also associated with distinct var transcriptional profiles and dual ICAM-1/EPCR-binding PfEMP1 variants. These findings underscore the complexity of PfEMP1-mediated pathogenesis and highlight the need for deeper investigation of transcriptional and regulatory mechanisms underlying severe malaria.

Article.Title: Expert operating skills learning-based intelligent shared control method for a CT-guided percutaneous biopsy robot
Article.Authors: Wang S.; Zhang G.; Chen W.; Zhang H.; Zhang W.; Yang G.; Li Q.; Qu J.; Xie L.
Article.Abstract: Accurate and minimally invasive percutaneous biopsy is critical for early lung cancer diagnosis, yet conventional manual procedures suffer from repeated radiation exposure, high reliance on doctor expertise, and risk of tissue injury. This study presents a 5 degree-of-freedom robotic system combined with an intelligent shared control framework guided by expert skills learning. Expert skills were modeled using a variational autoencoder-hidden Markov model to segment latent procedural phases, and dynamic motion primitives reconstructed representative expert trajectories. These learned skills were integrated into a phase-adaptive shared controller, enabling online modulation of impedance and trajectory parameters. Both phantom and in vivo porcine experiments validated the system's feasibility, safety, and accuracy, with animal experiment studies confirming minimal tissue trauma and stable physiological responses. Compared with manual, leader-follower, and admittance control methods, the intelligent shared control substantially reduced force fluctuations and trajectory deviations.

Article.Title: Soybean Pb encodes a WD40 protein regulating pubescence tip morphology and seed size during domestication
Article.Authors: Cui L.; Jing Y.; Li Y.; Wang Y.; Zhang B.; Chen X.; Liu H.; Dong S.; Liu C.; Zheng M.; Zhao L.; Zhang E.; Wei C.; Zhi X.; Zhao Y.; Li P.; Zhang H.; Zhan W.; Sun C.; Chu S.; Xiong E.; Tian Z.; Jiao Y.
Article.Abstract: The classical soybean Pb locus controls pubescence tip morphology, with sharp ( Pb /-) and blunt ( pb / pb ) types. It associates with insect resistance and experiences strong negative selection during domestication, yet the causal gene remains unknown, leaving unclear whether Pb directly confers insect resistance and the selective mechanism. Here, we report the cloning of Pb , which encodes a seven-WD40-repeat protein. A 4.88-kb deletion in the pb allele causes premature translation termination. Transgenic Pb soybeans with sharp pubescence tips show unchanged antibiosis and antixenosis against leaf-chewing insects compared with blunt-tip wild-type plants, demonstrating pubescence tip morphology alone does not confer insect resistance. The Pb gene reduces seed size, likely explaining its near disappearance in modern cultivars. Pb promotes assembly and activity of the GmLEC1a/GmNF-YC2/GmbZIP67 complex to regulate seed development. These findings resolve long-standing questions about the Pb locus and advance our understanding of soybean domestication.

Article.Title: Optical observation of ultrafast carrier separation in InGaN photocatalyst nanostructures
Article.Authors: Shen Y.; Hanish J.; Navid I.; Pan Y.; Mi Z.; Norris T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Understanding carrier dynamics in semiconductor nanostructures is essential for optimizing their photocatalytic performance. We present direct optical evidence of ultrafast carrier separation in InGaN nanostructures used for water splitting. Two types of InGaN-based photocatalysts are studied: deepnano structures, which are a p-type InGaN micro-network, and nanowires incorporating an InGaN/GaN layered heterostructure. Here, we show that rapid lateral carrier separation in these nanostructures produces observable signatures in ultrafast spectroscopy. Using combined time-resolved photoluminescence and time-resolved differential reflectance spectroscopy, we observe photoluminescence exhibiting fast decay while differential reflection remains stable. This indicates rapid carrier separation. Studies of temperature and power-dependent photoluminescence confirm that carrier separation dominates over recombination-driven decay, and Mg doping studies reveal that stronger band bending enhances the carrier separation. The physical interpretation of the observations is supported by a numerical model including drift, diffusion, and thermal relaxation. The results provide critical insights into charge carrier dynamics in InGaN nanostructures, highlighting their potential for efficient photocatalysis.

Article.Title: High-κ bismuth molybdate single-crystalline dielectric for high-temperature two-dimensional transistors
Article.Authors: Qiao Y.; Tang Y.; An Y.; Zhang L.; Li Y.; Ma G.; Yan F.; Su C.; Zhou Y.; Li X.; Liu Q.; Hong Z.; Li D.; Gao W.; Xu H.
Article.Abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors represent promising alternatives to traditional silicon for next-generation electronic devices. However, there are still significant challenges in high-temperature 2D electronic devices integrated by existing high-κ dielectrics. Here, we report a BiOCl-assisted chemical vapor deposition method to synthesize high-quality bismuth molybdate (Bi 2 MoO 6 ) single-crystalline nanosheets with controllable thickness and good thermal stability. High-κ (54.2) nature is identified within as-grown Bi 2 MoO 6 nanosheets, with wide bandgap (∼3.85 eV) and large breakdown field strength (∼3.9 MV/cm) at room temperature. As results, Bi 2 MoO 6 top-gate MoS 2 transistor exhibits a negligible hysteresis and an average subthreshold swing less than 100 mV dec −1 within 3 orders of magnitude of current range, as well as excellent operational stability. Moreover, the transistor maintains a high on/off current ratio of > 10 4 and a hysteresis of less than 10 mV/(MV cm −1 ) at the high temperature up to 500 K, meeting the requirements of high-temperature electronic devices. The inverter with Bi 2 MoO 6 gate dielectric is also achieved, yielding a high gain of 86.1 at supply voltage of 5 V. This work enriches the high-κ gate dielectric family and provides considerable application potential in high-temperature electronic devices.

Article.Title: A renewable autologous biomaterial for reprogramming cellular metabolism
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Zhao D.; Chen Y.; Xiang L.; Saiding Q.; Ling S.; Tang Y.; Jiang Q.; Mutailifu M.; Ma Q.; Li G.; Wang H.; Lin Z.; Liu Y.; Wang L.; Lu M.; Zhao W.; Cui W.
Article.Abstract: Autologous blood-derived products are attractive for tissue repair because they are biocompatible, renewable and readily accessible, but their liquid form limits local retention and provides little structural support. Here we show that autologous serum can be transformed into an injectable hydrogel microsphere biomaterial using gas-shearing microfluidics combined with ionic and fibrin-based enzymatic crosslinking. Reconstruction of the fibrin network improves structural support, interfacial lubrication and local retention of serum-derived factors. Compared with citrate-anticoagulated PRP, anticoagulant-free autologous serum better preserves chondrocyte metabolic adaptation under hypoxic inflammatory conditions. Multi-omics analyses further indicate enhanced chondrocyte proliferation, migration and matrix maintenance, together with modulation of hypoxia-responsive metabolic pathways. In osteoarthritis models, the microspheres promote cartilage repair and reduce disease progression. These findings establish a renewable autologous serum biomaterial platform that integrates biochemical and mechanical functions and may support personalized regenerative therapies.

Article.Title: Endocrine, nutritional and metabolic diseases drive cancer risk through subtype-specific and shared proteomic mediators
Article.Authors: Wu J.; Yao Y.; Chu Y.; Chen L.; Chen L.; Chen L.; Zhang C.; Liao F.; He S.; Xu B.; Shi X.; Liu Z.; Song K.
Article.Abstract: Cancer is associated with metabolic disorders, yet the impact of endocrine, nutritional and metabolic diseases (ENMs) on cancer remains unclear. Here, we show the associations of 25 ENMs with cancer trajectories, from primary cancer incidence to multi-primary cancers and mortality, using a multi-state model in a prospective cohort of 405,023 participants. Our findings reveal heterogeneous associations of ENMs across cancer sites and types, identifying 8 cancer-related ENMs that define four subtypes: C1 (iron deficiency/metabolism disorders dominated), C2 (type 2 diabetes dominated), C3 (lipid/lipoprotein metabolism disorders dominated), and C4 (osteoporosis dominated). Subtype-specific and subtype-shared proteomic mediators are identified and their contributions are quantified, with RNASET2 emerging as the major shared mediator. Furthermore, a deep-learning model integrating ENM subtypes and mediators enables personalized prediction of cancer incidence (AUCs = 0.80-0.90) and performs better than conventional Cox models. Our findings highlight the relevance of ENMs to cancer risk, providing mechanistic insights into metabolism-associated tumorigenesis.

Article.Title: Local niche-derived immunosuppressive CXCR2+ cells impair antiviral immunity
Article.Authors: Satomi A.; Saito R.; Satou K.; Ding Y.; Morimoto N.; Abe S.; Yamada J.; Mizuno T.; Sugishita H.; Ukai H.; Shichino S.; Yanagisawa M.; Matsushima K.; Gotoh Y.; Okazaki T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Symptom severity after viral infection varies among individuals, yet its mechanism remains poorly understood. We categorize mice into recovering and non-recovering groups based on body weight after infection with the same titer of vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV). We reveal that in the olfactory bulb (OB) where VSV initially expands, non-recovering mice exhibit an anti-inflammatory environment, suggesting its detrimental effect. Importantly, CXCR2 + cells resembling immunosuppressive myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are more abundant in the OB of non-recovering mice than in that of recovering mice after VSV infection. Depleting CXCR2 + MDSC-like cells from the brain increases inflammatory responses and the animal’s survival after infection. Furthermore, site-specific labeling indicates that a significant fraction of these cells in the OB originate from the skull-bone marrow (skull-BM) as well as circulation. This study reveals the lethal effects of CXCR2 + MDSC-like cells on local immune responses to viral infection, highlighting their therapeutic potential for antiviral defense.

Article.Title: Genome-wide association study identifies a functional myostatin variant increasing lean mass in humans
Article.Authors: Larusdottir A.; Teitsdottir U.; Tragante V.; Palsson F.; Kristinsdottir A.; Hjorleifsson Eldjarn G.; Stefansdottir L.; Oddsson A.; Aegisdottir H.; Styrkarsdottir U.; Bustamante M.; Olafsdottir T.; Snaebjarnarson A.; Olafsdottir T.; Einarsson G.; Gudjonsson S.; Halldorsson G.; Ferkingstad E.; Sigurdarson Sandholt A.; Einarsson E.; Vaura F.; Pajuste F.; Ripatti S.; Palotie A.; Laisk T.
Article.Abstract: Muscle mass is central to physical function and metabolic health, but can decrease with disease, aging and weight loss interventions. As weight loss interventions become more widely used, agents that preserve or increase muscle mass are needed. To identify such therapeutic opportunities, we perform genome-wide association meta-analyses of arm, leg, trunk and total lean mass measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, a widely used method to estimate muscle mass. We identify 63 loci, including a rare missense variant in MSTN (p.Ile225Thr, rs143242500), which has the largest effect on leg lean mass (β = 0.28 SD [95% CI: 0.19, 0.37], P = 1.9 × 10-9). MSTN encodes myostatin, a negative regulator of skeletal muscle mass and a therapeutic target for muscle wasting disorders. Here, we identify a genome-wide significant association at MSTN in humans and characterize its functional consequences, providing genetic evidence that may inform the long-term systemic effects of myostatin inhibition.

Article.Title: Benefits and harms of antihypertensive treatment a modelling study in 5.5 million electronic health records
Article.Authors: Wang A.; Koshiaris C.; Gould N.; Archer L.; Banerjee A.; Bellows B.; Clark C.; Clegg A.; Hobbs F.; Mant J.; McManus R.; Payne R.; Stevens R.; Treadwell J.; Usher Smith J.; Sheppard J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Antihypertensive prescription is guided by cardiovascular risk prediction models. However, existing models often exclude individuals with prior cardiovascular disease or those prescribed statin treatment. Consequently, there is limited evidence regarding how the benefits and harms of treatment vary according to an individual’s baseline risk. This cohort study includes 5,578,002 patients aged≥40years (mean age 59; 52% women) from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink between 1998–2018. A cardiovascular risk prediction model is developed using the Clinical Practice Research Datalink GOLD dataset and externally validated using the Aurum dataset. The model demonstrates excellent calibration and discrimination. Antihypertensive therapy is more likely to prevent serious major cardiovascular events (eight events prevented per 1,000 patients over 10 years, 95% confidence interval = 1 to 14), than to cause serious falls (two events per 1,000 patients, 95% confidence interval = −4 to 10). The risks of other adverse events indicate more nuanced or potentially harmful trade-offs. Here we show that a cardiovascular risk prediction model developed using routinely collected primary care data accurately predicts risk across a broad population of patients eligible for antihypertensive treatment. These findings will enable clinicians to better communicate individualised benefits and risks of antihypertensive therapy.

Article.Title: Large language models' complicit responses to illicit instructions across socio-legal contexts
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Xie H.; Wang Y.; Xiao C.; Chen H.; Sargeant H.; Steffek F.; Shao J.; Liu Z.; Sun M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Large language models may facilitate unlawful activities, yet this risk remains underexplored in studies assessing illicit-content recognition or narrow categories of illicit scenarios. We define complicit facilitation as model guidance that assists users with illicit instructions. To assess it, we develop a legally-informed, automated pipeline grounded in real-world cases and legal frameworks, and introduce EVIL, a benchmark covering 269 illicit scenarios and 50 illicit intents across Chinese and United States legal contexts. Evaluations indicate that complicit facilitation is widespread across models, with legal warnings and lawful alternatives often omitted. Risks vary across socio-legal contexts and are elevated for crimes against societal interests, non-violent offenses, and intents involving subjective motives or deceptive justifications. Models provide more complicit assistance when instructions describe users as older adults, racial minorities, non-religious individuals, or workers in lower-prestige occupations. Existing open-source safety benchmarks and alignment datasets offer limited coverage and mitigation of these risks.

Article.Title: Cholesterol dysregulation contributes to hematopoietic failure in parn-mutant zebrafish with implications for dyskeratosis congenita

Article.Abstract: Germline mutations in PARN cause dyskeratosis congenita (DC), an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by multilineage cytopenia and progression to myeloid disease. The mechanisms underlying this malignant transformation have not been fully elucidated. Here we show, using a loss-of-function CRISPR-Cas9 zebrafish parn mutant, hematopoietic stem and progenitor (HSPC) expansion and reduced mature hematopoietic cells across various lineages. Cholesterol biosynthesis was transcriptionally activated; a finding recapitulated in patient-derived iPSCs with PARN mutations. Inhibiting cholesterol biosynthesis rescued HSPC expansion and anemia in parn mutants. Concurrent myeloid differentiation therapy or Wnt inhibition reduced HSPCs to varying degrees. We further demonstrate a role for activated Erk signaling in impairing erythrocyte differentiation and show robust rescue with trametinib treatment. Overall, our findings uncover unrecognized roles for Parn in regulating cholesterol metabolism and Erk signaling and provide preclinical evidence for targeting these pathways to restore hematopoiesis in DC.

Article.Title: Pathway-dependent chiral toroid self-assembly and topological transformations based on large π-conjugated dipeptides
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Lu J.; Hao A.; Xing P.
Article.Abstract: Rational introduction of large π-conjugated moieties to peptides is crucial for their assembly, luminescence, chiral expression, and functional applications. In this work, a series of dipeptides functionalized with large conjugated benzoperylene imide segments are designed and synthesized, demonstrating programmable chiroptical and self-assembly behaviors. Water as poor solvent is identified as a critical factor governing the self-assembly of these dipeptides, by modulating the balance of intermolecular interactions to produce diverse morphologies such as nanoparticles, helical fibers, toroids and supercoiled structures. The assembly pathway progresses through multiple stages governed by diffusion-limited kinetics, interfacial energy minimization, and chiral internal stress. By varying the concentration, aging time, and temperature, it is possible to achieve diverse chiral morphological transitions, thereby enabling the preparation of toroids with both high phase purity and pronounced chiroptical activity. Furthermore, enantiomeric excess transforms toroids into helical rods, with racemic mixtures undergoing spontaneous resolution. Structural evolution and pronounced chiroptical activity, including strong circularly polarized luminescence, are confirmed by spectroscopic and diffraction analyses. This work offers new insights into both the mechanistic understanding of supramolecular chirality and an engineering framework for designing π conjugated dipeptide-based functional materials with tailored chiroptical properties. Rational introduction of large π-conjugated moieties to peptides is crucial for their assembly, luminescence, chiral expression, and functional applications. Here the authors functionalize a series of dipeptides with large conjugated benzoperylene imide segments demonstrating programmable chiroptical and self-assembly behaviors.

Article.Title: Nanofriction strengthened mechanically adaptive electrolytes for safe lithium metal batteries
Article.Authors: Jiang Y.; Pan L.; Chen L.; Pan H.; Song C.; Yang L.; Su Y.; Lu Z.; Zheng Q.; Chen N.; Yang Z.; Song M.; Zhu X.; Yan Q.; Peng X.; Song J.; Lu J.; Zhao T.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: The expanding application of lithium metal batteries in emerging fields such as unmanned aerial vehicles and humanoid robots exposes them to heightened risks of mechanical abuse, which has become a critical factor contributing to safety failures. To address this predicament, we design a mechanically intelligent responsive multifunctional electrolyte using a “nano-friction-strengthening” strategy to dynamically reinforce its mechanical robustness. The high-polarity carbonate solvents spontaneously infiltrate the hydroxyl-rich poly(hydroxyethyl methacrylate-diethyl allyphosphonate) shell and induce a hydrogen-bond-driven, self-regulated swelling response that enables uniform nanoparticle dispersion. Consequently, the electrolyte attenuates impact forces by 73.1%, enabling single Li‖LiFePO 4 pouch cells to endure impact without short-circuiting. Article.Authors: Raich L.; Teze D.; Bidart G.; Fredslund F.; Hobusch M.; Kunstmann S.; Putkaradze N.; Noé F.; Welner D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract C -glycosides are valuable compounds containing hydrolytically stable C-C bonds, yet their scarcity in nature and synthetic complexity limit their availability. Here, we study the intricacies of the maize C -glycosyltransferase Zm UGT708A6 using X-ray crystallography, biochemical assays, and atomistic simulations. Structural and dynamical analyses reveal two flexible gates that control substrate access and reactive conformations. Complementary pH- and substrate-activity experiments, together with Quantum Mechanics calculations, indicate that substrate hydroxylation patterns, protonation states, and σ-complex energetics restrict the scope of C -glycosides. Our results provide a coherent mechanistic framework that reconciles experimental observations across diverse conditions and advances our understanding of enzymatic C -glycosylation.

Article.Title: Double-membrane-spanning RNA export pores are a conserved feature in nidovirus replication organelles
Article.Authors: Fronik S.; Wolff G.; Limpens R.; de Jong A.; Zheng S.; Agard D.; Koster A.; Snijder E.; Bárcena M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Upon infection, arteriviruses, coronaviruses, and other nidoviruses transform endoplasmic reticulum membranes into viral replication organelles. These include large numbers of double-membrane vesicles (DMVs) whose interior is considered the primary site of viral RNA synthesis. Early studies characterized nidovirus DMVs as sealed compartments, leaving it unclear how newly synthesized viral RNA could be exported to the cytosol. The discovery of DMV-spanning pore complexes in coronavirus-infected cells provided a plausible solution for this topological challenge. However, their structural organization, functional features, and evolutionary conservation across the nidovirus order, have remained unclear. Here, we investigate the macromolecular architecture of DMVs induced by two prototypic arteriviruses using cellular cryo-electron tomography. Despite the substantial evolutionary distance separating arteriviruses and coronaviruses, we observe DMV-spanning pore complexes with striking structural similarities to those previously described in coronaviruses. These pores may facilitate both export and encapsidation of viral RNA. In the absence of viral RNA synthesis, ectopic expression of the arterivirus transmembrane nonstructural proteins nsp2 and nsp3 suffices to induce the formation of pore-containing DMVs. Together, our findings reveal the conservation of key structural features of DMV pores across two distantly related nidovirus families and support a central role for these pores in nidovirus replication.

Article.Title: Intravenous phage therapy for difficult-to-treat infections: a systematic review and meta-analysis of individual patient data
Article.Authors: Arnaiz Guerrero F.; Schmiedel Y.; Gupta N.; Soentjens P.
Article.Abstract: Intravenous phage therapy enables systemic bacteriophage delivery in difficult-to-treat infections, but raises distinct pharmacokinetic, immunological and safety considerations, while evidence remains fragmented. Here in this systematic review we analysed 60 studies from nine high-income countries, predominantly case reports, case series and uncontrolled trials reporting intravenous phage therapy with or without local administration and mostly alongside antibiotics. We extracted and synthesised individual patient data both descriptively and through a meta-analysis using mixed-effects models, which estimated probabilities of reporting clinical improvement and microbiological eradication of 65.8% (n = 122) and 55.3% (n = 106), respectively, while the probability of reporting adverse reactions was 9.2% (n = 168), with reactions predominantly mild and self-limited. In exploratory analyses, combined intravenous and local administration was associated with more frequent reporting of clinical improvement than intravenous administration alone, raising questions regarding potential limitations of the intravenous route. However, the uncontrolled and heterogeneous nature of current evidence warrants cautious interpretation and underscores the need for rigorous research.

Article.Authors: Guan Z.; Xie Y.; Wang J.; Yu H.; Lin W.; Wang P.; Li W.; Qiu F.; Zhao G.; Li M.
Article.Abstract: Meeting the escalating demand for high-capacity optical communication requires electro-optic (EO) photonic integrated circuits (PICs) that combine terabit-scale capacity, energy efficiency and scalable manufacturing. We further demonstrate a monolithically integrated 16-channel wavelength-division multiplexing transmitter supporting 3.2-Tbps-class optical interconnects. These results establish PZT as a practical wafer-scale platform for multi-terabit photonic systems.

Article.Authors: Harpers N.; Storz D.; Fox L.; Ng A.; Gilgannon J.; Freitas D.; Eberhard L.; Rizzo R.; Cordonnier B.; Jayawickrama E.; Fusseis F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mineral dehydration can alter the mechanics and hydraulics of fault zones and affects even plate boundaries, yet direct observations of how mineral replacement reorganises the architecture of a shearing fault gouge remain limited. The dehydration reaction progressively reorganises the load-bearing grain framework during shear, producing a transition from distributed granular deformation of gypsum gouge to localised brittle faulting of hemihydrate. By direct correlation between evolving microstructures and macroscopic mechanical and hydraulic behaviour, our results show that dehydration can induce a rheological transition, driving strengthening, embrittlement, and shear localisation even under drained conditions. Article.Authors: Miao B.; Zhang Y.; Shao W.; Fu S.; Bartolomei M.; Walker C.; Coarfa C.; N/A N/A.; Zhang B.; Wang T.
Article.Abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are mobile DNA sequences that constitute a significant portion of mammalian genomes and are generally epigenetically silenced, yet can regulate gene expression and chromatin architecture. Article.Title: Fully stretchable moisture-electric generators with peak milliamp-scale output via conformationally adaptive ionic hydrogels for wearables
Article.Authors: Li J.; Shao B.; Lu H.; Gao T.; Lan T.; Li Y.; Xu C.; Du J.; Zhang Z.; Zhao T.; Tan S.; Lai Y.; Sun B.

We show its use as a self-powered, deep-learning-assisted skin-hydration sensing platform, achieving 98% classification accuracy during extended on-body operation with smartphone feedback. Article.Title: Linking human sources to antibiotic resistance genes in global surface waters
Article.Authors: Zhong G.; Li S.; Jones K.; Zhu Y.
Article.Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global public health threat driven by antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Yet global human ARG generation, environmental discharges and surface-water abundances remain poorly characterized, and their linkages remain unclear, particularly at gene-specific absolute abundances, given differences in antibiotic and pathogen associations among ARGs. Here, we compiled 464 absolute abundance measurement data of five key ARGs ( qnrS , ermB , tetA , tetM , and sul1 ) and intI1 in wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) influent covering 30 countries, and combined these data with machine learning, a WWTP removal framework and a spatially explicit dilution model to estimate these metrics. Per capita generation was highest in Africa, whereas total generation and discharges were greatest in Asia; surface-water hotspots clustered in water-scarce regions, highlighting hydrological constraints alongside discharge intensity. Raising WWTP coverage in below-average countries to the global mean and high-income standards could increase global removal from 12–29% to 53–60% and 72–76%, respectively. These findings quantitatively link human ARG sources to surface-water abundances, providing a foundation for surveillance and intervention to curb ARG dissemination.

Article.Title: VHSeek: biology foundation model-based virus representations revealing virus host associations
Article.Authors: Liu W.; Wang Y.; Fuhrman J.; Li H.; Song L.; Rao G.; Sun F.
Article.Abstract: Virus-host association prediction is fundamental to virus-related disease control and phage therapy, yet many existing tools require candidate-host genome sequences, which may be unavailable for some eukaryotic hosts or impractical to search at the scale of large virome studies. We present VHSeek, a supervised virus-host association predictor that integrates DNA- and protein-derived viral representations. VHSeek combines nucleotide representations from AIDO.DNA and protein representations from ESM2 to learn virus-host association patterns, and then transfers predictions through known host taxonomies from lower to higher ranks. During inference, VHSeek uses viral sequence data and known host taxonomies, without host sequence data. Compared with iPHoP, the state-of-the-art baseline evaluated in this study, VHSeek improves genus-level maximum F1 score (Fmax), Top-1 accuracy, and area under the precision–recall curve (AUPR) by 12%, 19%, and 27%, respectively. Confidence thresholding enables abstention and reduces false discoveries. On the processed IMG/VR v4.1 metagenomic collection, VHSeek expands effective host coverage from 36.5% to 64.5% using a validation-calibrated confidence threshold. VHSeek prioritizes candidate viruses and reservoir hosts with potential human health impacts, including multi-host hypotheses in which one virus may be associated with humans and additional hosts (e.g., Saboya virus with Homo sapiens and Culicidae) not currently captured in the dataset.

Article.Title: Chemical upcycling of mixed polyolefins via rapid C–H nitration
Article.Authors: Che Y.; Wang Y.; Li B.; Niu Z.
Article.Abstract: Non-degradative C–H functionalization provides a promising route to upgrade polyolefins into functional materials by installing polar groups onto the carbon backbones, but few methods are universally applicable to the diverse and mixed polyolefins commonly encountered in waste streams. Herein, we report a rapid, selective, and broadly applicable C–H nitration strategy for the direct upcycling of mixed polyolefins. Driven by the low steric hindrance and radical nature of NO 2 , diverse substrates are nitrated with high selectivity (87–97%), reaching functionalization degrees of up to 2.4 mol% in just 5 min while substantially maintaining their molecular weights. The functionalized polymers not only exhibit enhanced tensile and adhesion properties, but can also be formulated into a dynamic covalent polymer network that displays 23-fold higher toughness than the original polyolefin mixture.
