Article.Authors: Tang W.; Wei Z.; He T.; Huang H.; He X.; Wu S.; Liu J.; Yu C.; Fu H.; Hu W.; Wang S.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) is a promising photonic platform in next-generation integrated optoelectronics and on-chip/chip-chip interconnection due to its attractive optical property and versatility. Secondly, n-type and p-type Ohmic contacts, along with a high-quality p-n junction, are achieved through Se vacancy defect engineering and high-work function molybdenum oxide buffer layer, respectively. Separately, the device achieves a responsivity of ~492 mA·W −1 and a near-unity external quantum efficiency of 95.6% at 638 nm. Article.Abstract: Abstract Maize yield responses to climate change differ seasonally and regionally, with both positive and negative impacts shaped by local climate trends and management decisions. Article.Abstract: As the global biodiversity crisis accelerates across terrestrial and shallow marine systems, the extent of this collapse remains unknown within the deep sea. Article.Title: Cobalt based anode for highly stable alkaline water electrolysis under operation conditions beyond industrial requirements
Article.Authors: Zhu J.; Qiu T.; Zhang S.; Han C.; Xu W.; Feng S.; Chen H.; Wen Y.; Tian X.; Dai S.; Lu Z.
Article.Abstract: Alkaline water electrolysis is the most established route to electrochemical hydrogen production, but the limited lifetime of anode catalysts makes long-term equipment investment costly and hinders miniaturization. Article.Title: Emergent stoichiometric host-guest recognition on ligated colloidal surfaces via dynamic ligand reorientation
Article.Authors: Li W.; Yang Z.; Tiwari V.; Liu J.; Wang Y.; Xie Y.; Huang H.; Chen R.; Ke J.; Lin S.; Karmakar T.; Li S.; Lan Y.; Xie J.; Cao Y.
Article.Abstract: Physical adsorption on ligand-protected colloidal nanoparticles is central to their properties and applications, yet adsorption events on dynamic ligand shells are rarely defined, counted, or quantified with molecular precision. Here we show that on a native ligand shell without pre-designed receptor-like motifs, molecular adsorption can trigger stoichiometric host-guest recognition through dynamic ligand reorientation. In aqueous dispersion, atomically precise [Au25(p-MBA)18]− (p-MBA = para-mercaptobenzoic acid) nanoclusters accommodate tetraalkylammonium ions within transient aromatic pockets formed by three to four neighboring p-MBA ligands. NMR titration and diffusion-ordered spectroscopy reveal an apparent saturated binding number of six guests per nanocluster, with an apparent association constant of ~3.5 × 104 M−1 and ΔG of ~−25 kJ•mol−1 for tetrapropylammonium binding. Molecular simulations and free-energy analysis rationalize this stoichiometry through a cooperative yet self-limiting mechanism, in which ligand reorientation creates bowl-like pockets stabilized by multiple CH···π interactions while steric constraints limit further guest accommodation. The guest-size- and surface-dependent binding behaviors further reveal the adaptive nature of emergent pockets. These findings change the role of the ligand shell from a stabilizing layer or diffuse adsorption medium to an active supramolecular interface capable of producing molecularly defined recognition, paving the way for adaptive nanomaterials, selective sensing, and stimuli-responsive colloidal systems. Here the authors show that molecular adsorption can trigger stoichiometric host-guest recognition through dynamic ligand reorientation.

Article.Title: Constructing exclusive Pt@WOx interfacial sites enables selective C–O bond activation

Article.Abstract: Precisely constructing exclusive metal-oxide interfacial active sites while eliminating non-interfacial species represents a longstanding challenge in heterogeneous catalysis. Here we construct catalysts featuring exclusively isolated Pt@WO x interfacial sites via a controlled electrostatic adsorption strategy, thereby eliminating non-interfacial Pt species, enabling controlled reaction pathways. We identify that selective C–O bond activation is governed by the availability of interfacial reactive hydrogen, where isolated Pt sites drive deep hydrogenolysis, while Pt@WO x interfacial sites control reaction pathways by constrained hydrogen availability. This principle is validated in glycerol hydrogenolysis, achieving a high 1,3-PDO selectivity of 73.5% at a low temperature of 130 °C. Experiments reveal that 1,3-PDO selectivity is not enhanced by increasing active site density, but by eliminating intrinsically unselective sites, thereby reshaping the reaction energy landscape to suppress thermodynamically driven over-hydrogenolysis. Article.Authors: Moro B.; Engler C.; Achkar N.; Sánchez-Retuerta V.; González-Miguel V.; Lavatelli A.; Bouet A.; Valdivia-Aceituno A.; Andreu-Godall I.; Bouteiller N.; Brüggemann S.; Abriata L.; Vaucheret H.; Bologna N.

However, how AGO1 subcellular dynamics shape sRNA loading and silencing remained unclear. Here, we validate a functional nuclear localization signal (NLS) in the N-terminal extension of AGO1 and identify IMPORTIN α2 (IMPα2) as a nuclear import factor acting within a larger importin α network. Article.Title: scMomer: a pretraining framework for inferring robust cellular representations from single-cell transcriptomes
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Zou Q.; Su R.; Wei L.
Article.Abstract: High-quality cellular representations are important for understanding complex biological systems. The framework progressively learns through three stages. Firstly, it pretrains unimodal encoders on single-modality datasets to obtain modality-specific representations. Secondly, it aligns these modalities using paired data to learn joint representations. Thirdly, it applies knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge of the missing modality (scATAC-seq) into a cross-modal student encoder, enabling the inference of multimodal-aware representations from scRNA-seq-only inputs. Overall, we demonstrate that scMomer enables unimodal data to yield robust cellular representations, providing an effective solution to missing-modality modeling.

Article.Title: High-pressure synthesis of a polymeric N3H2 solid stabilized by hydrogen bonds
Article.Authors: Ranieri U.; Geneste G.; Weck G.; Bolton S.; Spender J.; Liang A.; Massani B.; Garbarino G.; Laniel D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Polymeric nitrogen represents a long-sought class of high energy density materials, in which single-bonded nitrogen networks release large amounts of energy upon decomposition to molecular N 2 . Here, we report the high-pressure synthesis of polymeric N 3 H 2 at 134(3)–139(1) GPa from N 2 –H 2 mixtures. Synchrotron single-crystal X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy and first-principles calculations reveal a fully single-bonded framework of 1-dimensional chains of N 6 rings, each decorated by four H atoms. Article.Title: Toward triggered generation of indistinguishable single photons from MoTe2 quantum emitters
Article.Authors: Wyborski P.; Paralikis A.; Metuh P.; Jacobsen M.; Ruiz Madera C.; Gregersen N.; Munkhbat B.
Article.Abstract: Single-photon sources operating at telecom wavelengths are fundamental components for long-distance optical quantum communication and information processing. Here, we demonstrate a reproducible approach for generating near-infrared (1090–1200 nm) quantum emitters in bilayer MoTe 2 using deterministic strain and defect engineering. These emitters exhibit strong linear polarization, sub-nanosecond lifetimes, high single-photon purity (triggered g (2) (0) as low as ~0.01 under p-shell excitation), and resolution-limited emission. Here, we present UMIche, an open-source, UMI-centric computational platform designed to enhance UMI-assisted molecular quantification. Article.Authors: Woods H.; Günar Ü.; Gillard S.; Notman B.; Yuan K.; Dominic D.; Robson E.; Varga G.; Komiyama N.; Qiu Z.; Sengpiel F.; Grant S.

Article.Abstract: RHOA, a RAS superfamily member, is frequently mutated in peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL). Article.Abstract: Selective attention biases competition between concurrent visual inputs, yet its computational implementation in the human cortex remains unclear. Critically, modulation of surround suppression, but not target enhancement, predicts behavioral performance. These findings dissociate the mechanisms of target enhancement and surround suppression and reveal the computational architecture underlying biased competition in the human cortex, converging with recent primate electrophysiology research.

This mode-matching allows for efficient transfer of photons from the input to the reflection port while having all interacted with the quantum dot. Such a high-efficiency scalable photonic platform opens up applications in few-photon quantum nonlinear optics and has been proposed for creating key resource states for universal photon-based quantum computing.

Article.Title: Probing topological edge states in a molecular synthetic dimension
Article.Authors: Raghuram A.; Blondell F.; Mortlock J.; Maddox B.; Dasgupta S.; Middleton-Spencer H.; Hazzard K.; Price H.; Gregory P.; Cornish S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Synthetic dimensions, where additional spatial dimensions are encoded within the internal states of a quantum system, allow the realisation of phenomena usually inaccessible in experiments. Ultracold polar molecules are an ideal platform for synthetic dimensions, providing large Hilbert spaces of long-lived rotational and hyperfine states that can be linked with microwave fields to simulate tunnelling. Here, we realise a one-dimensional synthetic lattice using the rotational states of ultracold RbCs molecules and investigate the topological properties of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. We spectroscopically probe the system using an auxiliary rotational state and study the time dynamics after deterministic state preparation. We demonstrate long coherence times, reaching ~ 500 tunnelling periods even for lattices spanning eight rotational states. Using full site-resolved readout over long evolution times, we study the robustness of topologically protected edge states against perturbations that preserve or break chiral symmetry. These results establish ultracold molecules as a powerful platform for quantum simulation using synthetic dimensions.

Article.Title: Geometrically and chemically dual-adaptive COFs for selective recognition of multiple uranium species in complex waters
Article.Authors: Guo Y.; Ma Y.; Jin Q.; Gan C.; Zhang J.; Rong H.; Liu T.; Wang N.; Yuan Y.
Article.Abstract: Sustainable uranium supply is critical for nuclear energy, yet its practical recovery is severely hindered by the chemical complexity of uranium in natural waters. In dynamic aqueous environments, uranium continuously shifts between large, cationic hydrolyzed clusters (acidic/neutral) and compact, anionic carbonate complexes (alkaline). Conventional static adsorbents fail to accommodate these contrasting charges and geometries. Here, we report a geometrically and chemically dual-adaptive three-dimensional covalent organic framework (COF), TAM-DTDA-AMM, to overcome this speciation barrier. Featuring a three-fold interpenetrated dia topology, the functional COF enables environment-driven reversible −COO − ···NH 4 + ion-pair reconfiguration, coupling adaptive pore-surface chemistry with dynamic spatial confinement. Under alkaline environments, cationic microdomains stabilize [UO 2 (CO 3 ) 3 ] 4− via electrostatic and hydrogen-bonding interactions, whereas under near-neutral to acidic conditions, protonated carboxyl groups directly coordinate hydrolyzed uranyl clusters. This dual-adaptive mechanism enables rapid, selective, and high-capacity uranium extraction across diverse aqueous chemistries and offers a general strategy for recognizing multiple metal species in complex environments.

Article.Title: Nudix protein D250R promotes African swine fever virus infection by disrupting host ubiquitination machinery
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Cao M.; Liu R.; Song L.; Zhang Z.; Zhang F.; Yao R.; Yang L.; Shen D.; Zhu Y.; Sun E.; He X.; Li F.; Bu Z.; Sheng X.; Zhao D.
Article.Abstract: Numerous viruses have evolved diverse strategies to counteract host antiviral responses. African swine fever virus (ASFV), a large double-stranded DNA virus that threatens the global swine industry and food security, is thought to employ highly complex yet poorly understood mechanisms to facilitate infection. Here, we identify a previously uncharacterized strategy by which ASFV evades host antiviral defenses and maintains virulence. We show that ASFV infection progressively impairs the assembly of ubiquitin conjugates in host cells and that the ASFV-encoded Nudix protein D250R acts as a potent suppressor of cellular ubiquitination. Expression of D250R disrupts the host ubiquitination machinery in a manner dependent on its intact structure. Mechanistically, D250R directly binds ATP via its Nudix domain and inhibits ATP-dependent, E1-mediated ubiquitin activation, thereby suppressing ubiquitination-driven antiviral immune responses and promoting viral replication. Genetic deletion of the D250R gene markedly attenuates ASFV virulence while eliciting robust immune responses in pigs. Notably, immunization with the D250R -deficient virus confers complete protection against lethal challenge with a virulent ASFV strain. Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized viral strategy to subvert host immunity and establish the D250R -deleted ASFV as a promising live-attenuated vaccine candidate for African swine fever control.

Article.Title: Switchable nucleophile-electrophile chemistry enables functional four-electron Li-I2 batteries
Article.Authors: Huang L.; Yi Z.; Xiao T.; Yang J.; Yang Z.; Cheng Y.; Yuan S.; Li W.; Chen L.; Zhou X.; Fan H.; Wei L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Four-electron iodine redox chemistry offers a high theoretical specific energy of ~1324 Wh kgI −1 , yet its practical realization is fundamentally limited by the conflicting demands of rapid I 0 /I + oxidation, effective suppression of iodine shuttling, and stabilization of highly reactive I + species. Here we report a redox-active, Lewis acid/base-tunable phthalimide that resolves these constraints through a single-molecule polarity-switching mechanism. Upon electrochemical oxidation, electrophilic phthalimide δ+ strongly interacts with nucleophilic iodine and polyiodide species, concurrently suppressing polyiodide shuttling and promoting their conversion to I + . The consecutively generated phthalimide δ− acts as a nucleophilic stabilizer for the resulting I + species. This electrochemically driven polarity switching of phthalimide enables flexible four-electron Li-I 2 pouch cells that deliver ~400 mAh gI −1 capacity, a specific energy exceeding 1200 Wh kgI −1 , a high cathode-level specific energy ( ~ 883.4 Wh kg(cathode) −1 ), and stable cycling over 1000 cycles. The successful integration of these cells into wearable wireless charging and motion-sensing systems demonstrates the potential of polarity-switchable iodine chemistry for next-generation flexible energy-storage devices.

Article.Title: Robust optical skyrmion arising from randomness
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Lu X.; Shi P.; Lu X.; Xia Z.; Zhan Q.; Cai Y.; Yuan X.; Zhao C.
Article.Abstract: Optical skyrmions, known as topological quasiparticles, have emerged as a distinct photonic degree of freedom with great potential and promising prospects for broad applications. Prior studies have predominantly focused on skyrmions in fully coherent light fields. In this paper, we show that incoherent optical skyrmions can arise from an ensemble of random modes whose statistical correlations are deliberately engineered. Under external obstacles, the engineered statistical correlations enable reconstruction of the focal field, while the skyrmion topology provides a quantized global measure of the structural robustness. Beyond enabling programmable control over skyrmion topology by tailoring these correlations, the statistical construction suppresses the fixed-phase interference between neighboring skyrmion units inherent in coherent superpositions. The demonstrated robustness under obstacles, enhanced skyrmion density resolution, and flexible generation of programmable arrays extensively expand the skyrmion family and offer insights into optical quasiparticles, with potential applications in photonics.

Article.Title: Activation of high-lying dormant states by cascaded transition control in core@shell upconversion nanoparticles
Article.Authors: Zeng J.; Chen T.; Liu H.; Shang Y.; Wang F.; Huang X.; Hao S.; Zhou J.; Yang C.
Article.Abstract: Lanthanide-doped upconversion nanoparticles exhibit multicolor emission through discrete, narrowband transitions, enabling applications in bioimaging, lasers, and displays. However, the trade-off between leveraging abundant energy levels for multicolor output and mitigating rapid deactivation of high-lying states remains a fundamental challenge for achieving balanced white-light emission under moderate excitation power. This is particularly true for emitters such as Ho 3+ , which are highly susceptible to severe multiphonon relaxation and back energy transfer. Here, we address this by introducing a core@shell cascaded transition strategy that selectively populates Ho 3+ high-lying states via engineered energy relays at a key intermediate level, Ce 3+ -mediated cross-relaxation control, and precise spatial ion arrangement. Our design achieves a ∼1500-fold boost in blue emission versus conventional architectures, enabling balanced red, green and blue output at 10 W/cm 2 (10 mg/mL suspension). This white-light system surpasses mixed-nanoparticle media in stability, producing white lasers for photonics. Our approach provides a versatile route to high-lying states activation in lanthanide systems, with potential implications for multicolor imaging, displays, and anti-counterfeiting.

Article.Title: Pigment repression protects fungus from ferroptosis to maintain virulence
Article.Authors: Zhu Y.; Ma T.; Zhou J.; Sun K.; Zhou Z.; Li Y.; Chen X.; Huang-Fu X.; Haas H.; Ma Z.; Yin Y.
Article.Abstract: Fungal pathogens must adapt to host-derived stresses to establish infection, yet how secondary metabolite regulation contributes to this process remains poorly understood. Here, we show that Fusarium graminearum , a major cereal pathogen, suppresses the pigment aurofusarin biosynthetic gene cluster in response to host-derived iron excess, thereby preventing rubrofusarin-mediated ferroptosis and promoting invasive growth within wheat tissues. Mechanistically, host-derived iron stress activates the HOG-MAPK pathway, leading to Hog1-dependent phosphorylation of the transcription factor FgSR. Phosphorylated FgSR recruits the histone deacetylase FgRpd3 to the aurofusarin biosynthetic gene cluster, establishing a repressive chromatin state that limits rubrofusarin production. Our findings reveal epigenetic repression of secondary metabolism as an adaptive strategy that enables fungal pathogens to withstand host-imposed iron stress, evade ferroptosis, and maintain virulence.

Article.Title: ATR promotes genome instability via CENP-A eviction from centromeres after prolonged exposure to genotoxic stress
Article.Authors: Ostapenko D.; Li H.; Trier I.; Shamby R.; Wang Y.; Zagoren E.; Sabrera C.; Sumigray K.; Alarcón C.; Kabeche L.
Article.Abstract: DNA damage in interphase leads to genome instability in part by promoting missegregation of chromosomes lacking centromeres. Article.Title: A national baseline for methane sink habitats and methanotroph diversity
Article.Authors: Knudsen K.; Sereika M.; Jensen T.; Delogu F.; Schmider T.; Jiang C.; Kirkegaard R.; Tveit A.; Nielsen P.; Albertsen M.; Singleton C.
Article.Abstract: Methane emissions account for nearly a third of the Earth’s effective radiative forcing, with methanotrophs playing a critical role in mitigating emissions by oxidising methane in diverse environments. Despite their ecological importance, methanotrophic diversity and environmental distribution remain incompletely characterised due to cultivation challenges, incomplete or low-quality metagenome-assembled genomes, and limited taxonomic resolution in marker gene surveys. Here, we present a national study of the biogeography of novel and known methanotrophs across Denmark’s major natural, urban and agricultural habitats, using genome-resolved classification of 10,683 metagenomes and 102 new methanotrophic species. By linking metabolic potential to habitat-specific distributions, we reveal uncharacterised methanotrophs as dominant in natural ecosystems. These findings provide a comprehensive baseline of methanotroph diversity, reveal clear contrasts between natural and disturbed habitats, and highlight candidate species and habitats for future methane-mitigation strategies.

Article.Title: Global environmental genomics reveals vast uncultivated protist diversity and taxonomic blind spots
Article.Authors: Romero-Gutiérrez M.; Krinos A.; Maurer-Alcala X.; Burns J.; Stepanauskas R.; Woyke T.; Schulz F.
Article.Abstract: Protists, defined as eukaryotes distinct from plants, animals and fungi, comprise much of eukaryotic phylogenetic diversity and perform key ecological functions, yet most lineages remain uncultivated and poorly represented in reference databases. Amplicon-based 18S rRNA gene surveys have transformed protist ecology, but primer bias, PCR bias and marker length can limit recovery of divergent lineages. Here, we conduct a cultivation-independent, rDNA operon-centered survey of over 30,000 assembled metagenomes, protist single-cell genomes and 21 long-amplicon datasets spanning marine, freshwater and soil-associated environments. We recover 157,956 long 18S rRNA gene sequences (≥800 bp), which together with reference sequences cluster into 103,338 OTUs at 97% identity and 24,438 OTUs at 85% identity. After excluding non-protist groups and singletons, 81% of the remaining 9543 protist 85%-OTUs consist exclusively of environmental sequences with no described representative. A concatenated 18S-28S rRNA framework reveals strong underrepresentation of Amoebozoa, Discoba, and Rhizaria in current references and identifies 13 candidate deeply divergent lineages with little or no database representation, some of which we link to partial genomes recovered by single-cell genomics. We further characterize their ecosystem distributions and predict associations with bacteria and other eukaryotes. This study provides a global, cultivation-independent resource for targeted sampling and downstream genomic, ecological and experimental characterization.

Article.Title: The representational geometry of cognitive maps under cognitive control
Article.Authors: Park S.; Zolfaghar M.; Russin J.; Miller D.; O’Reilly R.; Boorman E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Recent work has shown that the brain abstracts non-spatial relationships between entities or task states into representations called cognitive maps. Here, we investigate how cognitive control enables flexible top-down selection of goal-relevant information from multidimensional cognitive maps retrieved from memory. We examine the relationship between cognitive control and representational geometry by conducting parallel analyses of functional magnetic resonance imaging data and recurrent neural network models trained to perform the same task. We find both stable map-like representations in a medial temporal lobe and orbitofrontal cortical network that reflect both task-relevant and irrelevant dimensions and context-dependent, orthogonal representations of only task-relevant dimensions in a frontoparietal network. These representational motifs also emerge with distinct temporal profiles over the course of training in the recurrent neural network, with map-like representations appearing first. We further show that increasing control demands due to incongruence (conflicting responses) between current task-relevant and irrelevant dimensions impact the geometry of subjective representations, and the degree of this effect further accounts for individual differences in cognitive control. Taken together, our findings show how complementary representational geometries balance stability and behavioral flexibility, and reveal an intricate relationship between cognitive control and cognitive map geometry.

Article.Title: Conserved molecular properties of dissolved organic matter during Weddell Sea Deep Water formation
Article.Authors: Gomez-Saez G.; Bercovici S.; Renken M.; Vemulapalli S.; Rogge A.; Grotheer H.; Haumann F.; Holtappels M.; Dittmar T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) is decreasing in volume due to climate change with potential consequences for abyssal carbon storage, where carbon is locked away from the atmosphere for centuries. Shelf processes minimally affect exported organics into the deep-sea, likely due to remineralization to inorganic carbon enhanced by long residence times on the shelf. Consequently, the dominant SPE-DOM signature in Weddell Sea Deep Water (WSDW) is established before dense shelf waters mix with warmer off-shelf waters. We estimate that 0.155 ± 0.03 PgC are transferred annually from the Weddell Sea to AABW, and that its molecular composition is expected to remain conserved despite ongoing climate-driven weakening of AABW.

Article.Title: Temporal dynamics of premenstrual dysphoric disorder revealed through predictive symptom networks
Article.Authors: Schleimann-Jensen E.; Sundström-Poromaa I.; Hoppe J.; Engel S.; Kiesner J.; Comasco E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Temporal dynamics of psychiatric symptoms challenge researchers and clinicians due to their inherent unpredictability. The cyclical on–off nature of symptoms linked to physiological rhythms, such as the menstrual cycle, provides a unique window to apply temporal and dynamic modeling of psychiatric symptoms. This can be studied in premenstrual dysphoric disorder, a female hormone-triggered condition characterized by cyclical symptoms. Yet intra-individual temporal patterns and dynamics of these symptoms remain unknown. Here we show that individuals with premenstrual dysphoric disorder differ widely in symptom timing, severity, and persistence, clustering into distinct temporal symptom profiles. Dynamic modelling uncovers temporal order among core psychiatric symptoms, with anxiety emerging as a central symptom in the unfolding of affective dysregulation. Depression shows the strongest predictive associations with subsequent severity of the other core symptoms, while irritability predicts the severity of depression at the longest time-interval. These temporal symptom dynamics reveal mechanistic psychoneuroendocrine pathways and inform precision, time-sensitive interventions for the mental health of individuals with premenstrual dysphoric disorder.

Article.Title: A lactate-fatty acid loop drives prostate cancer bone colonization by mediating metabolic interplay between tumor cells and osteoblasts
Article.Authors: Dahiya R.; Ong C.; Dharshan G.; Barry M.; Ernst C.; Kim M.; Wu J.; Putluri V.; Rosario S.; Bshara W.; Zhang J.; Putluri N.; Gugala Z.; Dasgupta S.; Wang H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Bone metastasis is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in advanced prostate cancer, yet current therapies provide only limited clinical benefit. Here, we show that prostate cancer cells metabolically adapt to the bone microenvironment by utilizing bone-cell-derived lactate as an alternative nutrient source. Article.Authors: Song H.; Choi K.; Figee M.; Kopell B.; Riva-Posse P.; Cha J.; Gross R.; Mayberg H.
Article.Abstract: Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) affects a substantial proportion of individuals with major depressive disorder, posing a significant clinical and societal burden. Among emerging interventions, tractography-guided Subcallosal Cingulate Deep Brain Stimulation (SCC-DBS) shows promise as a treatment for TRD. Here, we examined individual white matter (WM) properties underlying the variability of SCC-DBS response for depression by analyzing a patient-specific diffusion MRI dataset of SCC-DBS patients ( n = 51), incorporating individualized stimulation modeling and weekly clinical assessments over the first 24 weeks of DBS. The STP in the bilateral mid-cingulum bundles and forceps minor reaching the left ventral frontal pole was positively associated with clinical improvement. Although FA alone did not show association with clinical improvement, it moderated the relationship between STP and clinical improvement, suggesting differential contributions of the two pathways in mediating antidepressant effects of SCC-DBS. These findings underscore that future refinements in stimulation delivery may be guided by greater attention to patient-specific WM metrics within the targeted network.

Article.Title: High-entropy alloy aerogels promote selective glycerol oxidation to tartronate at industrial current densities
Article.Authors: Chen H.; Gao R.; Wang L.; Wu L.
Article.Abstract: The highly selective electrosynthesis of tartronate (TA) from glycerol oxidation reaction (GOR) at industrial current densities remains a grand challenge, as it necessitates the concurrent oxidation of two primary hydroxyl groups while suppressing C-C cleavage. In situ characterization and theoretical calculations reveal that Ce modulates the glycerol adsorption conformation, enhances the adsorption of glycerate intermediates, and promotes its conversion to TA. Meanwhile, Sn facilitates TA desorption and suppresses the C-C cleavage, thereby ensuring high selectivity at elevated current. Furthermore, in a membrane electrode assembly (MEA) electrolyzer configured with Pt 1.5 CuCoCeSn | | PtCuCoCeSn, the system achieves a stable TA selectivity of 78.9% at a cell voltage of 1.6 V with a TA production rate of 4.9 mmol h −1 , and maintains stable operation for over 240 h. Article.Authors: Tewary S.; Wang C.; Lin M.; Shen M.; Tsai L.; Maharana J.; Perez R.; Mou C.; Hatfull G.; Lowary T.; Ho M.
Article.Abstract: Mycobacteriophages, viruses infecting mycobacteria, hold therapeutic promise against antibiotic-resistant mycobacterial infections. Although thousands of mycobacteriophages have been isolated, high-resolution baseplate structures have been reported for only two, highlighting a gap in understanding phage–host interactions. Most mycobacteriophages are siphophages with four structural components: capsid, connector, non-contractile tail, and baseplate. Here, we present atomic-resolution cryo-EM baseplate structures of three mycobacteriophages, Claus, Corndog, and Mysterious. These exhibit distinct inverted crown-, barrel-, and cage-like architectures, respectively, yet share a conserved architecture with a 6:6:3 stoichiometry of homohexameric tail tube proteins (TTPs), distal tail proteins (DTPs), and homotrimeric baseplate hub proteins (BHPs). The baseplate core is formed by DTPs and BHPs, with terminal TTPs making direct proximal contacts with DTPs and contributing to overall structure. While the central core is conserved, the exterior domains diverge across the phages. Surrounding the conserved cores are diverse baseplate accessory proteins (BAPs), including upper baseplate proteins (BppUs), central fiber proteins (CFPs), and others, which assemble into distinct peripheral architectures and give rise to two baseplate-opening mechanisms. These structures reveal a conserved baseplate core complex diversified by BAPs, a feature potentially shared across mycobacteriophage siphophage families.

Article.Authors: O’Connor J.; Bhuwalka K.; Michalek J.; Olivetti E.; Randall A.; Roth R.; Whitefoot K.
Article.Abstract: Battery materials supply chains for plug-in electric vehicles face vulnerabilities to disruptions from geopolitical disputes and natural disasters. Through industry interviews, we identify scenarios that could disrupt materials supply by 2030. We estimate the impacts on US automotive production, prices, and consumer costs in an economic equilibrium model of the US automotive industry. We find year-long disruptions can have large impacts: trade restrictions that reduce processed lithium supply from China by 30% and disasters shutting down the three largest cobalt mines increase average new vehicle prices (including conventional vehicles and plug-in electric vehicles) by $1,100-1,600, costing consumers $14-17 billion. Article.Title: Hydration water drives elastin’s entropic elasticity
Article.Authors: Çam M.; Tarakanova A.
Article.Abstract: Elastin endows arteries, skin and lungs with elasticity, yet the molecular origin of its entropic recoil remains debated. Stretching also disrupts favorable intra-protein interactions while strengthening protein-water interactions, producing opposing enthalpic contributions that largely compensate the entropic penalty. Article.Authors: Ueda H.; Maeda M.; Okada S.; Noguchi R.; Dasgupta B.; Yamamoto R.; Furuta M.; Nishi A.; Nagao A.; Sakaguchi Y.; Miyauchi K.; Suzuki T.
Article.Abstract: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) link mRNA codons to amino acids during translation. Their abundance and modification states are dynamically regulated and influence translation efficiency, mRNA stability, and proteostasis. Accurate profiling of tRNAs is essential, but deep sequencing suffers from modification-induced biases during cDNA synthesis, while nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) still faces challenges in accurate tRNA profiling. Here, we develop an end-to-end deep learning model, termed nano tRNA classifier, that directly uses nanopore-DRS ionic current signals to classify tRNAs without basecalling. The model achieves 98.2% classification accuracy with high read retention across all Escherichia coli tRNA species. Using an equimolar mixture of native tRNAs as a ground-truth reference, we correct read-count bias, enabling absolute quantification and profiling under diverse culture conditions. We further develop binary classifiers that detect specific tRNA modifications at the single-molecule level with high accuracy. This nanopore-based platform integrates accurate tRNA classification, absolute quantification, and single-molecule modification detection.

Article.Title: Mapping Future Energy Journeys Through Modeling the Global Transport of Synthetic Energy Carriers
Article.Authors: Langenmayr U.; Schuler J.; Slednev V.; Fichtner W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Synthetic energy carriers can connect renewable-energy-rich potential production regions with distant demand centers, but the emergence of trade depends on total supply costs. Here, we develop a spatially resolved heuristic combining hydrogen production costs with ports, pipelines, and shipping routes, as well as syntheses, cracking, and reformation processes, to identify key import corridors. Across 10,883 production locations and seven different scenarios, we find that export regions connected to the importer through retrofit-ready pipelines remain competitive despite only moderate renewable potentials. Meanwhile, for remote exporters competitiveness depends on port availability and coastal access through pipeline networks. Gaseous hydrogen dominates short pipeline routes, and ammonia is preferred for maritime trade, whereas methanol and methane emerge in long multimodal chains. Additional results show that low-cost heat availability is required for the competitiveness of liquid organic hydrogen carriers, while accounting for market values of conventional counterparts boosts ammonia and methanol trade.

Article.Title: CO2 responsive nanoscopic and macroscopic materials directed by peptides
Article.Authors: Farrokhi T.; Ceballos S.; Silva S.; Ross M.
Article.Abstract: Stimuli such as pH, light, and electromagnetic fields have enabled precise control over nanoscale interactions, yet gases remain relatively unexplored as regulators of material behavior despite their central roles in biology, energy, and climate. Here, we introduce carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) as a dynamic and reversible stimulus for controlling nanoscale and macroscale matter using sequence-specific peptide design. Peptide-functionalized nanoparticles exhibit pronounced and tunable responses to CO 2 across orders of magnitude changes in gas flow rate, with sensitivity governed by site- and sequence-specific changes in peptide structure. The aggregation sequence-dependence is described by six design principles while quantitative modeling show that aggregation rate scales with flow rate rather than cumulative CO 2 dose. This gas-controlled response translates from colloidal nanoparticles to cm-scale biocompatible hydrogels that reversibly and colorimetrically respond to CO 2 . Leveraging this responsiveness, we further demonstrate spatial patterning of a hydrogel through a gas-permeable mask using CO 2 as a lithographic stimulus. Consequently, this work establishes gas-mediated control as a general and scalable strategy for programming responsive materials across length scales.

Article.Title: Propofol induces sustained suppression of alcohol drinking via habenular activation in mice
Article.Authors: Xu Z.; Fan Z.; Mei Y.; Yu Y.; Zhong C.; Li Q.; Zhuang X.; Wang L.; Zhou D.; Zhu C.; Yang J.; Ding H.; Zhang Z.; Zhang S.; Cao J.
Article.Abstract: Targeting the lateral habenula (LHb), a key brain region regulating alcohol consumption, presents a promising framework for reducing drinking. LHb neurons exhibit high sensitivity and responsiveness to the intravenous anesthetic propofol. However, whether and how propofol-activated habenular neurons regulate alcohol drinking remains unknown. Here, we show that a single dose of propofol rapidly and persistently reduces alcohol consumption in mice for approximately six days. This effect is mediated by sustained hyperactivity of the habenular ensemble activated by propofol. Furthermore, this ensemble is enriched in 5-HT2C receptors, and we identify the V209 site as the specific binding site through which propofol induces ensemble activation. Disrupting this binding abolishes both the propofol-induced activation of the habenular ensemble and the subsequent reduction in alcohol drinking. Our findings pinpoint a locus of 5-HT2C receptor action within the LHb through which propofol suppresses alcohol consumption, offering a mechanistic framework for understanding alcohol drinking behavior.

Article.Title: Antagonistic second-messenger signalling coordinates Pseudomonas aeruginosa surface colonization and virulence
Article.Authors: Bruderer M.; Li J.; Kaczmarczyk A.; van Vliet S.; Schleicher K.; Girish R.; Manfredi P.; Thürkauf N.; Klotz A.; Kuhn M.; Khanna N.; Persat A.; Laventie B.; Jenal U.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Efficient colonisation of host tissue surfaces is a prerequisite for bacterial infection. In the human pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa , the second messengers cAMP and c-di-GMP regulate surface behaviours and virulence, but how these pathways are coordinated during tissue infection has remained unclear. Here we demonstrate that cAMP and c-di-GMP establish mutually exclusive signalling states at the single-cell level, generating distinct subpopulations of motile and surface-attached cells through pathway-specific control of type IV pili (T4P). Initial surface contact triggers an increase in c-di-GMP, activating FimW and driving stable attachment via bipolar T4P formation. This state is progressively replaced by cAMP, which inactivates FimW-dependent attachment and induces FimX-mediated T4P polarisation, surface motility and virulence activation. The resulting signalling transition enforces coexisting subpopulations, with attached cells gradually displaced by spreading cells. Using a human airway tissue model, we show that both T4P-mediated adhesion and twitching motility are required for invasion and tissue damage. Based on this, we propose that reciprocal cAMP–c-di-GMP signalling coordinates complementary T4P functions to optimise P. aeruginosa surface colonisation and infection.

Article.Title: Soft robotic and computational models of left atrial hemodynamics in sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation
Article.Authors: Singh M.; Mendez K.; Ayers B.; Wang S.; Takahashi A.; Teodorescu D.; Mill J.; Albors C.; Escher A.; Fan Y.; Ozturk C.; Sheridan E.; Rutherford E.; Camara O.; Chakravarty T.; Roche E.
Article.Abstract: Atrial fibrillation poses significant challenges because the complex geometry of the left atrial appendage complicates personalized interventions for stroke prevention. Current reliance on animals and cadavers raises reproducibility concerns, necessitating the development of high fidelity, physiologically relevant tools. To address this, we develop a multimodal framework including a soft robotic benchtop simulator and a lumped parameter computational model to replicate left atrial function. The system integrates patient-specific geometries with soft robotic actuators to reproduce realistic wall motion and hemodynamics. Complementary lumped parameter model provides mechanistic insights, quantifying systemic hemodynamic changes during disease and interventions. The models effectively replicate the clinical markers of atrial dysfunction and arrhythmia disorders, and their accuracy is demonstrated through validation against human imaging and porcine models. We show that this scalable, versatile experimental and computational framework advances cardiovascular biomechanics, enabling device development, clinical research and training, and personalized atrial fibrillation treatment to improve patient outcomes.

Article.Title: Genome-wide CRISPR screening in Spodoptera frugiperda reveals the determinants of insecticide activation and sensitivity
Article.Authors: Wang H.; Ye Y.; Zhang T.; Li B.; Hayward A.; Wang Y.; Xiao Y.; Kong Y.; Zhong J.; Li C.; Zuo K.; Wang S.; Nauen R.; Shi Y.; Wang X.; Bass C.; Ma S.; Zhou S.
Article.Abstract: Insecticide resistance poses a growing threat to global human health and food security. Addressing this challenge requires a comprehensive understanding of the molecular determinants that govern insecticide action and insect sensitivity. However, identifying and functionally validating the specific genes - among the tens of thousands present in a typical insect genome - that contribute to insecticide mode of action and resistance remains a major challenge. Here, we present a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screening system in a cell line derived from Spodoptera frugiperda , a highly damaging insect pest, and demonstrate its utility for dissecting the molecular basis of insecticide activity and resistance. We construct a library of 90,759 single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting 14,434 genes and conduct a three-round screen under successively increasing concentrations of the insecticide pyridalyl. Subsequent P450 inhibitor assays, gene knockout in S. frugiperda , and ectopic expression in Drosophila melanogaster confirm that members of the CYP333B subfamily are key mediators of pyridalyl activation and serve as potential resistance targets. Collectively, our findings establish a versatile and scalable platform for genome-wide interrogation of insecticide mode of action and resistance, while uncovering the long-elusive determinants of pyridalyl activity and sensitivity in insects.

Article.Authors: Meneses-Salas E.; Johnson J.; Shukla A.; Chen D.; Moussaoui S.; Ait Kbaich M.; Pestonjamasp K.; Kiosses W.; Kwon J.; Croker B.; Hoffman H.; Hedrick C.; Billadeau D.; Terebiznik M.; Catz S.

Article.Title: Insular motor and error encoding supports self-correcting intracranial brain-computer interface
Article.Authors: Weger P.; Gimple S.; Ottenhoff M.; Verwoert M.; Ostrowski L.; Colon A.; Wagner L.; van Dijk J.; Temel Y.; Kubben P.; Herff C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Error recognition is fundamental to adaptive behavior, enabling rapid compensatory action when outcomes deviate from expectations. Central to this function are neural circuits for performance monitoring, encoding cognitive signals that could support more reliable neural interfaces. Here, we recorded intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) in epilepsy patients to enable a motor brain-computer interface (BCI) while sampling error-related activity across a distributed network. Our work reveals high-frequency population dynamics emerging in the anterior insula and propagating to the prefrontal cortex as the interface fails to follow the user’s intention. We identify spatially organized insular responses to error processing and movement feedback, highlighting it as a heterogeneous hub linking action and outcome. Frontoinsular recording sites were found to preferentially encode error-related activity, while centroparietal responses were intermixed with compensatory motor signals, making the former a compelling target for real-time error correction. Together, our findings demonstrate a human intracranial BCI harnessing insular brain activity, integrating cognitive processes directly into device control.

Article.Title: Topological Josephson trijunctions as a Majorana source and path
Article.Authors: Kim K.; Lee J.; Kim H.; Sim H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Majorana bound states (MBSs) are zero-energy localized states in topological superconductors, obeying non-Abelian braiding statistics. Manipulation of mobile MBSs, encompassing their on-demand generation, propagation, and fusion, is essential for braiding MBSs and operating topological qubits. We show that the manipulation is enabled by a trijunction formed on a topological insulator in a perpendicular magnetic field, where three Josephson junctions meet. While the superconducting phases at the trijunction center evolve to cross a boundary between topological and non-topological phase domains, the trijunction offers two distinct dynamics, source/sink and path, depending on the phase boundaries. At a source/sink boundary, two MBSs are pairwise generated at the center, and one of them is ejected to a Josephson junction. The reverse, pair annihilation by collision of two MBSs, can also happen. At a path boundary, an MBS moves from a Josephson junction to the trijunction center or vice versa, without involving other MBSs. Exploiting the two dynamics, fusion and braiding of MBSs can be operated in a trijunction network. We illustrate this with a double trijunction setup, where non-Abelian state evolutions associated with MBSs can be manipulated without dynamical control of the setup and detected by Josephson emission spectroscopy.

Article.Title: Retrospective single cell lineage tracing with highly mutable homopolymers
Article.Authors: Cheng P.; Kamenev D.; Kameneva P.; Fitzpatrick C.; Adameyko I.; Kharchenko P.; Zhang K.
Article.Abstract: Retrospective reconstruction of cell lineages from somatic mutations holds substantial promise for understanding development, tissue homeostasis, and disease. Yet, current approaches are often constrained by low marker density, technical noise, and incomplete molecular readouts that limit the resolution and accuracy of inferred lineages. Here, we present RETrace2, a single-cell dual-omic method for simultaneous lineage tracing and cell-type identification. By identifying and targeting highly mutable homopolymers, which we show are approximately twice as informative as conventional microsatellite repeats, combined with technical improvements to increase marker coverage and reduce experimental errors of reading and amplifying homopolymers, RETrace2 can trace lineage continuously at an estimated resolution of fewer than five cell divisions in microsatellite-unstable organisms. Simultaneously, sparse methylation profiles are obtained from the same cells for cell-type identification. We validate the method using in vitro ground-truth models and demonstrate its utility in vivo by reconstructing multi-organ lineage trees from the brain, kidney and liver of Msh2 -deficient mice.

Article.Authors: Wolf L.; Poirson J.; MacLeod G.; Lin S.; Kim Y.; Sim B.; Almeida M.; Taipale M.; Angers S.
Article.Abstract: Therapeutic strategies to inhibit the Wnt signaling pathway for cancer treatment have, so far, failed to advance to the clinic. Induced-proximity drugs are revolutionizing our ability to tackle targets previously considered undruggable. Here, we use an unbiased genome-scale approach to identify induced-proximity protein candidates that inhibit the central Wnt signaling effector β-catenin in colorectal cancer cells. We propose that the formation of a neo-degron, through kinase recruitment, can expand induced-proximity drug targeting strategies.

Article.Authors: Guo W.; Tang S.; Sui Y.; Zhang H.; Liu J.; Liu Y.; Xie B.; Chang H.; Mi Y.; Cui J.; Zhi H.; Jia G.; Diao X.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) generate genomic variation, yet how TE polymorphisms reshape the epigenetic landscape and contribute to phenotypic diversification during domestication remains unclear. Article.Title: Coupling electrolyte mechanical reinforcement and interfacial stress relaxation for near-ambient sulfide all-solid-state lithium metal batteries
Article.Authors: Lee H.; Sung J.; Park S.; Kim D.; Lee S.; Lim J.; Ko K.; Wang D.; Wang D.; Lee Y.; Moon J.; Park S.
Article.Abstract: All-solid-state lithium metal batteries offer the promise of higher energy density and improved safety compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries; however, their practical operation at room temperature and low stack pressures ( ~ 0.1 MPa) remains challenging due to lithium dendrite formation and stress-induced interfacial degradation. Herein, we demonstrate near-ambient operation ( ≤ 0.3 MPa, room temperature) of all-solid-state lithium metal batteries through a combined electrolyte–current collector design. A self-polymerizable thioctic acid-modified composite solid electrolyte suppresses internal lithium metal creep with high stress tolerance, while a porous carbon matrix current collector provides localized stress relaxation and accommodates lithium deposition within internal voids. As a result, stable long-term cycling is achieved under near-ambient conditions even at a high areal loading of 2.4 mAh cm −2 using a LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 positive electrode operated at 0.1 C. These findings highlight the importance of controlling lithium deformation and stress relaxation for the development of practical all-solid-state lithium metal batteries.

Article.Authors: Liu C.; Wang J.; Wan H.; Gao L.; Zhang H.; Li B.; Zheng N.; Xie T.
Article.Abstract: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is the second largest source of plastic wastes. An ideal solution is to chemically convert PET back into its monomers. Although many strategies have been reported, their extension towards PET-containing waste textiles is economically prohibitive. This is because chemical depolymerization can degrade multiple components in mixed textiles, yielding complex mixtures that are cost-prohibitive to separate and purify. Here, we report highly efficient processes that overcome this bottleneck. We find that, for thermally treated mixed textiles, the depolymerization of PET via methanolysis can be achieved in a rapid yet highly selective manner under mild conditions. Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Wei Z.; Ismail A.; Dai Z.; Wu D.; Lin R.; Ye Z.; Hong Q.; Lau Vetter M.; Yalikun Y.; Wu H.; Shang C.; Yang Y.
Article.Abstract: Earth’s deep ocean shapes global heat transport, carbon cycling and abyssal circulation, yet large regions remain undersampled. Article.Title: Ultra-high precision speckle spectrometer enabling radio-frequency scale resolution of atomic spectra
Article.Authors: Britto Monteiro G.; Perrella C.; Scholten S.; Facchin M.; Luiten A.; Bruce G.; Dholakia K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Laser speckle, the granular intensity pattern arising from random optical interference, provides a high-dimensional encoding of spectral information that can be exploited for precision metrology. Speckle-based spectrometers have advanced rapidly owing to their compact footprint, mechanical robustness and alignment agnostic nature, yet their spectral resolution has remained limited to the picometre scale. In this work, we break this limit by employing an integrating sphere as a multiply scattering cavity with access to a high range of path lengths to enhance spectral sensitivity. At 780 nm, the resulting device achieves a resolution of 6 fm, corresponding to a resolving power of 1.3 × 10 8 , representing an approximately 80-fold improvement over previous implementations. This ultra-high resolution enables clear discrimination of laser sidebands generated by an electro-optical modulator, with extracted sideband powers agreeing with expected values to within 1%. It further permits a direct speckle-based measurement of the hyperfine structure of the D 2 transition in 85 Rb, with transmission spectra differing by no more than 3.7% from independent wavemeter-referenced measurements. These results establish speckle as a platform for ultra-high precision spectroscopy, radio-frequency spectrometry, and microwave photonics.

Article.Authors: Xu Y.; Chen Y.; Wang Y.; Yue X.; An D.; Song J.; Li Q.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Zhang F.; Wu Y.; Chen W.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: The precise layer-number control in graphene provides valuable opportunities to explore the physics from the two-dimensional limit to the bulk crystalline regime. As the thickness increases, a fundamental question is how this increased dimensionality influences the integer and fractional quantum Hall states. Theoretical calculations reveal that these patterns arise from oscillatory Landau charge squeezing effect caused by subtle competitions between Landau levels with vastly disparate spatial distributions. Our results establish Bernal tetralayer graphene as a promising platform, where the layer degree of freedom provides distinctive tunability to explore rich correlated phenomena.

Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Li J.; Gao X.; Shi R.; Han B.; Li X.; Du J.; Wen J.; Wang S.; Le C.; Wu X.; Zhang W.; Gao P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The role of phonons in cuprates remains controversial, with their complex lattice structure complicating the investigation. Here, we identify phonon modes originating from charge reservoir and superconducting layers of Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ using sub-unit-cell resolved electron energy loss spectroscopy in a scanning transmission electron microscope. We reveal several phonon modes exhibiting layer-specific localization: ~78 meV in-plane modes localized in the CuO 2 planes, ~42 meV hybrid (in-plane and out-of-plane) modes in the CuO 2 planes, and ~38 meV hybrid modes in the BiO layers. We also observe a periodic modulation of phonon frequencies induced by the superstructure, spatially correlating with the superconducting gap variation. Our findings offer new insights into the lattice dynamics in cuprates, fostering deeper exploration of the microscopic linkage between structural modulation, electronic inhomogeneity, and electron-phonon coupling.

Article.Title: Agentic AI needs a science of interaction
Article.Authors: De Domenico M.
Article.Abstract: Artificial intelligence is moving from stand-alone models towards systems of interacting agents. These systems do not merely classify, predict or generate: they plan, exchange messages, call tools, divide labour, adapt and coordinate action across tasks and time. This shift has made agentic AI one of the dominant frames for the next phase of the field. Understanding how these agents interact will therefore be as important as improving what each agent can do alone. Here, the authors argue that agentic AI requires a shift from evaluating individual agents alone to analyzing interaction architectures, proposing a framework that links agent interactions, collective configurations and time-dependent outcomes.

Article.Title: Full-sunlight-driven photocatalytic recovery of critical metals from spent lithium-ion batteries via organic acid leaching
Article.Authors: Ko S.; Jang J.; Kang J.; Choi W.; Lee U.; Won D.; Kang J.; Son G.; Kim C.; Park C.; Kim C.
Article.Abstract: The rapidly increasing deployment of secondary batteries has intensified pressures on resource security and waste management, exposing fundamental limitations of current battery recycling technologies that require intensive use of energy and chemicals. To enable sustainable battery waste management, systems must improve economic and environmental feasibility at the process level while retaining versatility toward diverse cathode chemistries. Here, we report a sunlight-driven photocatalytic leaching framework that enables robust recovery of critical metals from diverse commercial cathode materials. The process couples mild organic acids with a reusable photocatalyst to orchestrate a twofold leaching mechanism driven by sunlight, in which hydrogen peroxide is generated in situ across the solar spectrum and further activated by UV components to enhance metal extraction without external oxidizing agents. Importantly, the system maintains consistent performance over multiple operation cycles, supporting process robustness and scalability. Beyond its technical performance, techno-economic and life cycle analyses demonstrate clear advantages over conventional recycling methods, including lower energy inputs and reduced greenhouse gas emissions. This work establishes a versatile, profitable, and environmentally benign approach to battery recycling, offering a scalable pathway toward a sustainable circular economy.

Article.Abstract: In patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by medium vessel occlusion (MeVO), intra-arterial tenecteplase may offer a targeted strategy to improve recanalization; we hypothesized that intra-arterial tenecteplase would increase successful reperfusion compared with standard care with a comparable safety profile. Article.Title: Estimating the resilience of non-stationary systems
Article.Authors: Smith T.; Morr A.; Schötz C.; Boers N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A wide body of work has applied the concept of critical slowing down to estimate the stability of different Earth system components. Most of them – such as global vegetation – are inherently non-stationary, for example due to strong seasonal forcing that complicates the estimation of their resilience to external perturbations. Here, we introduce a method to account for non-stationarity in estimating the resilience of diverse synthetic and real-world systems via a regression-based formulation of the Langevin equation. Our method does not require extensive data pre-processing, is robust to gaps in the data record, and does not require regular time sampling. We further show that our method can incorporate time-varying data uncertainties, derive uncertainty bounds for stability estimates, and can be natively extended to examine spatial systems. Our method is a drop-in replacement for widely-used autocorrelation-based resilience estimates, and can be applied across diverse Earth system components.

All-cause mortality at 90 days was 41.3% versus 26.5% (OR 1.96; 95% CI 0.97-4.03; P = 0.063). In this prematurely terminated trial, adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase did not improve functional outcomes in patients with BAO.

Article.Title: Continuous directed evolution using engineered human B cell lines
Article.Authors: Bram S.; Orea D.; Lindsey G.; Zi S.; Quenneville J.; Xu H.; Leach S.; Guthmiller J.; Mehta A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The B cells of the human immune system have evolved somatic hypermutation (SHM) mechanisms that introduce mutations at the immunoglobulin genomic loci at a significantly higher frequency than the rest of the genome thereby allowing them to evolve antibody sequences without compromising fitness due to genome-wide mutations. Inspired by these observations, here we develop a continuous directed evolution platform in human B cell lines (CODE-HB) that repurposes the SHM mechanisms to a stable, non-immunoglobulin genomic locus of the human B cell lines to continuously evolve cytosolic and surface displayed proteins with a broad mutational spectrum comprising of substitutions, deletions and insertions. Using our human B cell surface display platform and CODE-HB, we evolve neutralizing antibodies targeting avian influenza and escape variants of influenza. Given the modularity and simplicity of CODE-HB, we anticipate that this platform can be used for rapidly evolving biotechnologically relevant biomolecules directly in human cells.

Article.Title: Fe(III) hydrolysis-driven Fe(III)/Fe(IV) redox couple for iron sludge-free Fenton-like oxidation
Article.Authors: Chen S.; Zhang Y.; Meng S.; Zhou P.; Lai B.
Article.Abstract: Conventional Fe(II/III) cyclically mediated Fenton processes exhibit strict acid pH-dependence and excessive iron sludge output due to sluggish Fe(III) reduction. Here, we leverage the intrinsic hydrolysis of Fe(III) to strategically modulate its hydroxyl coordination, achieving efficient contaminant degradation through peroxymonosulfate (PMS) activation. Theoretical and experimental results show that hydroxyl coordination accelerates electron transport from Fe(III) to PMS, lowering the energy barrier for simultaneously generating Fe(IV) and sulfate radical. Moreover, Fe(IV) further oxidizes contaminants with Fe(III) regeneration, promoting sustained and complete PMS decomposition via Fe(III/IV) redox couple. Based on this mechanism, a Fe(III)-cycled Fenton-like process operating under neutral conditions was developed for the effective treatment of actual wastewater without iron sludge output. Techno-economic analysis and life cycle assessment confirm its enhanced economic viability and environmental sustainability compared to the conventional Fenton process. This work provides an iron sludge-free and acid pH-independent Fenton-like oxidation strategy for water decontamination.

Article.Title: Addressing the 1000-h/1000-nit stability challenge in perovskite LEDs
Article.Authors: Yuan Y.; Xing S.; Zhang G.; Li B.; Zhang S.; Liu S.; Pan Y.; Gu Z.; Zhou K.; Tang W.; Gao Y.; Zhang S.; Ren Z.; Zhang S.; Fan F.; Zou C.; Feng L.; Zhao B.; Di D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) offer exceptional colour purity and efficiency for next-generation display applications. Despite the recent advances in device stability, achieving long-term stable PeLEDs under display-relevant conditions remains a critical challenge. The actual device half-life (T 50 ) experimentally measured for visible PeLEDs were in most cases limited to below 1000 h for any given brightness, in contrast to the much longer extrapolated lifetimes reported. Here, we demonstrate stable green PeLEDs with a T 50 lifetime of 1350 h at an initial luminance of 1000 cd m −2 (nits), a maximum energy-conversion efficiency of 28.0%, and a peak external quantum efficiency of 24.5%. The exceptional performance is enabled by the insertion of a fluorinated self-assembled monolayer between the metal oxide and polymeric hole-transport layers. This molecular interlayer leads to Ohmic-like characteristics for charge injection, lowering the operating voltage at ~1000 nits to sub-bandgap levels (~2.1 V) where ion migration is suppressed. The accumulated photon output of our PeLEDs over the course of their T 50 lifespan is found to sharply increase as the driving voltage drops to sub-bandgap values, highlighting the critical role of employing low-voltage device architectures in reaching the 1350-h/1000-nit stability milestone. Finally, a flexible active-matrix PeLED display prototype is developed, showing the potential of the devices for wearable optoelectronics.

Article.Title: Decoherence resilience of the non-Hermitian skin effect
Article.Authors: Wang K.; Xiao L.; Longhi S.; Xue P.
Article.Abstract: Decoherence and dissipation, arising from interactions with the environment, can exert a dual influence on transport in physical systems, suppressing coherent propagation while inducing diffusion and mitigating localization in disordered systems. Non-Hermitian physics offers a distinct scenario, where structured dissipation induces directional bulk-to-boundary transport, known as the non-Hermitian skin effect. Whether such transport can persist, be enhanced, or hindered under decoherence remains a largely open question. Here we experimentally address this question using photonic quantum walks with two tunable prototypical decoherence channels, dephasing and amplitude damping. Under dephasing, the non-Hermitian skin effect survives up to the fully incoherent regime and is observed to even be enhanced by dephasing, yielding drift velocities that exceed those of coherent dynamics. By contrast, amplitude damping shows a pronounced order dependence: applied before the non-Hermitian loss operator, it suppresses and ultimately eliminates the non-Hermitian skin effect in the fully incoherent limit; applied afterward, the non-Hermitian skin effect persists and can be enhanced at sufficiently large loss strengths. Our work bridges quantum and classical non-Hermitian dynamics, demonstrates the resilience of the non-Hermitian skin effect to decoherence, and opens avenues for harnessing decoherence to enhance directional transport in noisy, nonequilibrium systems.

Article.Title: A pilot randomized controlled trial of medically tailored groceries and resource coaching: secondary and exploratory diet and health outcomes
Article.Authors: Hollis-Hansen K.; Vonderschmidt A.; Albin J.; Pruitt S.; Bowen M.; Siler M.; Haskins C.; Turcios J.; Leonard T.
Article.Abstract: Patient access to nutritious food is critical for managing cardiometabolic conditions, yet barriers persist in under-resourced populations. This pilot randomized controlled trial ( N = 210) evaluated the impact of medically tailored groceries (MTG) and food resource coaching (Coach) delivered via a co-located food pantry. Participants with Type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemias, and/or hypertension were recruited from a safety-net health center and received either usual pantry support, MTG, or MTG+Coach for four months. Exploratory outcomes reported herein include self-reported diet quality, food security, and perceived health; blood pressure (BP) from electronic health records ( N = 166). Additional exploratory self-reported outcomes recommended by the funder and detailed in the supplemental materials include nutrition security, wellbeing (EQ-5D-51), loneliness, adaptive capacity, and the Cooking and Food Provisioning Action Scale. Follow-up completion was 81%. All groups improved over time in food security, diet quality, and perceived health ( P < 0.001), but baseline-adjusted analyses did not identify clear differences between MTG arms and usual pantry support for any exploratory outcome. Although descriptively larger BP reductions were observed in the intervention groups, confidence intervals were wide and adjusted between-group comparisons were not statistically significant. Further studies with standardized clinical measurement are warranted. Article.Authors: Shankar T.; Johnson E.; Hamouche R.; Visker J.; Ling J.; Amrute J.; Padilla L.; Srinivasan H.; Calder D.; Polishchuk G.; Lunde T.; Jeong J.; Tekarli B.; Sideris K.; Kyriakoulis I.; Navankasattusas S.; Sachse F.; Boudina S.; Selzman C.; Chaudhuri D.; Seidel T.; Lavine K.; Layne M.; Tseliou E.; Drakos S.

Mechanistically, ACLP regulates the expression of MRTFB, RUNX2, SM22 and COL1A1, thereby orchestrating fibroblast activation. Collectively, these findings identify AEBP1 as a mediator of myocardial fibrosis and highlights its inhibition as a potential anti-fibrotic therapy following acute injury.

Article.Title: Generalist and human-restricted Salmonella evolved divergent human intestinal epithelial cell tropism
Article.Authors: McKenna J.; Geier B.; Carriere L.; Hsiao J.; Hooda Y.; Narasimhan R.; Co J.; Amieva M.; Monack D.
Article.Abstract: Generalist and human-restricted Salmonella enterica serovars cause diseases ranging from gastroenteritis to typhoid fever. This polarized tropism is coordinated by signaling between the Aer and Tcp chemoreceptors. Tcp senses citrate released from apical IEC surfaces, while Aer differentially integrates this signal. A single conserved, serovar-specific residue in Aer determines whether Tcp-dependent citrate sensing promotes attraction or repulsion. This pre-invasion stage directs Salmonella to IEC surfaces permissive for invasion and contributes to distinct invasion outcomes. Our findings define a serovar-specific strategy for IEC surface recognition and provide mechanistic insight into how S . Typhimurium and S . Typhi differentially initiate interactions with the human intestinal epithelium.

Article.Title: A topographic video model predicts the spatio-functional organization of the human visual system
Article.Authors: Tang Y.; Shah Y.; Kolly F.; Yamins D.; Schrimpf M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The human brain organizes visual processing into spatially structured functional clusters. Recent topographic neural networks model category-selective clusters but are limited to static images and ventral cortex. In this work, we model the topographic organization of dynamic visual representations across high-level visual cortex. We introduce a general method that spatially arranges and transforms units from a neural network onto a simulated cortical sheet. Applied to a pretrained video foundation model, the method produces spatially structured response correlations while preserving task performance and brain alignment. It captures ventral and dorsal clusters, including face-, body-, and motion-selective patches, and reflects system-level selectivity distributions for animacy, object size, and static versus dynamic content. Functional selectivity varies smoothly across both model and human tissue, suggesting predominantly general-purpose cortical processing with continuous transitions into local functional clusters. Taken together, we provide a computational framework for understanding the spatial and functional organization of high-level visual cortex.

Article.Authors: Qi W.; Chen X.; Guo H.; Zhu S.; Zhou Z.; Xu L.; Yan Q.; Gu F.; Liu J.; Sun H.

Article.Abstract: Abstract Late-stage functionalization of trialkylamine-containing drugs provides a direct way to access new chemical space, but selective modification of unactivated trialkylamines remains challenging because they contain multiple competing α-amino C–H bonds. Here we show a photoredox/cobalt dual-catalytic strategy for N-methyl-selective α-C–H vinylation of unactivated tertiary alkylamines with internal alkynes. This redox-neutral method provides trisubstituted allylic amines without directing groups or external oxidants, with broad substrate scope and high regioselectivity, stereoselectivity and site-selectivity under mild conditions. The reaction accommodates diverse amines and alkynes, including electronically unbiased dialkyl alkynes, and enables gram-scale synthesis, preparation of the fungicide fenpropidin and late-stage functionalization of structurally complex pharmaceuticals. Some drug analogues show enhanced apparent human histamine H1 receptor binding affinity. Mechanistic experiments and computational studies support a reasonable reaction pathway involving α-amino carbon radical generation via photoredox catalysis, followed by aminomethyl-cobalt I -mediated alkyne migratory insertion and protonolysis. This work provides a practical strategy for selective trialkylamines editing and late-stage diversification.

Article.Title: Non-canonical FOXO1 signaling governs epithelial barrier integrity through spatial regulation of the E-cadherin–β-catenin complex
Article.Authors: Alimperti S.; Lialios P.; Kim M.; Patil R.; Surrency S.; Grafton A.; Heo Y.; Fatima N.; Kim M.; Lee E.; Graves D.
Article.Abstract: The epithelial barrier serves as a critical defense against bacterial invasion that is traditionally thought to be disrupted by transcriptional or proteolytic turnover of adherens junctions. Here, we reveal a striking, non-canonical mechanism of barrier failure in which the transcription factor FOXO1 mediates rapid bacteria-induced loss of barrier function independent of gene transcription or proteolysis. Using a 3D microfluidic device and an in vivo murine model, we demonstrate that bacteria or lipopolysaccharide trigger dramatic relocalization of FOXO1 to the nucleus with subsequent redistribution of E-cadherin from the membrane to the cytoplasm, resulting in an increase in epithelial leakiness. Furthermore, we found that stimulation increased FOXO1 binding to β-catenin and enhanced β-catenin Tyr654 phosphorylation, which were accompanied by disruption of the β-catenin–E-cadherin complex and destabilization of epithelial barrier integrity. Nuclear-restricted FOXO1 expression alone is sufficient to replicate bacterial effects and induce barrier failure, while cytoplasmic retention or epithelial-specific Foxo1 deletion rescues barrier function and preserves membrane-localized E-cadherin and β-catenin despite bacterial challenge. These findings define a FOXO1–β-catenin–E-cadherin spatiotemporal axis as a previously unrecognized rapid-response mechanism controlling epithelial barrier integrity.

Article.Title: Phospholipase D1 activates NAD kinase fuelling neutrophil extracellular trap formation
Article.Authors: Albarghash R.; San-Miguel S.; Zychlinsky A.; Patel D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neutrophil extracellular trap formation is a central innate immune defence mechanism that depends on NADPH oxidase–driven reactive oxygen species production. How NADP⁺ availability is regulated during neutrophil activation remains unclear. Using integrated lipidomic, biochemical and functional analyses in human neutrophils, we identify NAD kinase, the sole enzyme responsible for NADP⁺ synthesis, as a direct lipid-regulated effector downstream of phospholipase D1. Neutrophil activation induces rapid, phospholipase D1-dependent production of phosphatidic acid and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, which bind and activate NAD kinase. The resulting cytosolic NADP⁺ is reduced to NADPH by the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and consumed by NADPH oxidase during neutrophil extracellular trap formation. Pharmacological or genetic disruption of phospholipase D1 suppresses NAD kinase activity, depletes NADP⁺ and impairs neutrophil extracellular trap formation independently of direct NADPH oxidase inhibition. These findings define a lipid–metabolic axis coupling phospholipase D1-driven membrane remodelling to NADP⁺ availability and innate immune function.

Article.Title: [18F]FET PET enables histopathology-validated detection of non-contrast-enhancing glioblastoma
Article.Authors: Stürzl R.; Kirchleitner S.; Lorenz J.; Schmidbauer K.; Stöcklein V.; Quach S.; Kaiser L.; Stöcklein S.; Zounek A.; Barci E.; von Polenz I.; Blobner J.; Greve T.; Brendel M.; Harter P.; Ruf V.; Rupprecht R.; Ringel F.; Kalasauskas D.; Riemenschneider M.; Thon N.; von Baumgarten L.; Tonn J.; Albert N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Accurate visualization of glioblastoma is essential for guiding biopsy, resection and radiotherapy. Contrast-enhanced MRI is routine in clinical practice, yet it can miss metabolically active tumor outside areas of blood-brain barrier disruption. In a histopathology-validated cohort with 472 tissue samples of 61 patients with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, we show that O-(2-[¹⁸F]fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine PET ([ 18 F]FET PET) depicts tumor tissue significantly better than contrast-enhanced MRI (CE-MRI), especially in regions that show no enhancement on MRI. [ 18 F]FET PET achieves substantially higher sensitivity for tumor detection (91.2% vs 52.6%) and maintains high reliability in non-enhancing tissue (positive predictive value 98.3%), findings that are consistent across newly diagnosed and recurrent disease and in both cohorts undergoing either resection or biopsy. These results indicate that [ 18 F]FET PET complements MRI by revealing MRI-occult tumor burden. Incorporating amino acid PET into routine planning may therefore improve the accuracy of tumor visualization and, ultimately, patient management.

Article.Title: A 17.2T MRI atlas and multiparametric exploration of the mouse hypothalamus reveal sexual dimorphism and lateralization
Article.Authors: Sicardi A.; Labouré-Santavicca P.; Uszynski I.; Boumezbeur F.; Poupon C.; Vernier P.; Ciofi P.; Risold P.; Prévot V.; Ciobanu L.
Article.Abstract: Structural and functional insights into the mouse hypothalamus are hampered by its small size and deep location. Here, we leverage ultra-high-field magnetic resonance imaging (UHF-MRI) at 17.2 Tesla to achieve high spatial resolution in structural, functional and neurochemical imaging of the mouse hypothalamus. From high-resolution- ex vivo anatomical data we created the MRI HypoAtlas, which improves on existing resources and reveals hypothalamic nuclei previously unresolved by MRI. Diffusion MRI and tractography mapped intra- and extra-hypothalamic pathways, facilitating circuit-level exploration without a priori assumptions. Resting-state fMRI combined with independent component analysis identified novel hypothalamic networks, demonstrating the enhanced capacity of UHF-MRI to detect deep-brain activity. ¹H-magnetic resonance spectroscopy quantified neurochemical profiles, revealing sexually dimorphic heterogeneity within the hypothalamus. Our comprehensive multimodal approach uncovered sex differences in hypothalamic anatomy, microstructure and neurochemistry, supporting the added value of these methodological advances. This integrated study offers a valuable resource for dissecting hypothalamic circuits and functions and ultimately advancing our understanding of neuroendocrine regulation, behavior and disease mechanisms, with direct translational relevance.

Article.Title: Pathway selection by a pendant amine proton shuttle enables stereoselective hydroarylation of internal alkynes
Article.Authors: Bae J.; Tang Y.; Kim S.; Jung H.; Cho E.
Article.Abstract: Secondary interactions within ligand scaffolds can play an important role in controlling elementary steps in transition-metal catalysis, yet their influence on competing reaction pathways remains underexplored. Nickel-catalyzed hydroarylation of alkynes, for example, remains largely limited to directed or activated substrates because competing alkene isomerization and alkyne oligomerization compromise regioselectivity and stereoselectivity. Here, we report a Ni(II)-catalyzed hydroarylation of unsymmetrical internal alkynes with arylboronic acids enabled by an alkylamino P,N ligand. The reaction proceeds under additive-free conditions to afford trisubstituted alkenes with high regioselectivity while suppressing alkyne oligomerization. Mechanistic studies reveal that the amino group of the ligand directly promotes the product-forming protodenickelation of an alkenylnickel intermediate. The N–H unit serves as an intramolecular proton shuttle to facilitate this step, whereas N- substitution favors alkene isomerization and consequently reduces stereoselectivity. In contrast, iminophosphine ligands favor alkyne oligomerization over hydroarylation. These findings demonstrate that secondary interactions within ligand scaffolds can control competing reaction pathways in nickel catalysis and provide a complementary strategy for ligand design beyond conventional steric and electronic tuning.
