Article.Title: Evolutionary neuropharmacology of serotonergic psychedelics: a cross-species perspective on mechanisms, consciousness, and therapeutic potential
Article.Authors: Zhai H.; Wang H.; Wang Y.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Serotonergic psychedelics have revitalized psychiatric research by producing rapid and potentially sustained clinical benefits in selected neuropsychiatric conditions. However, the mechanisms linking receptor activation to neural plasticity, altered conscious experience, and clinical improvement remain incompletely understood, while the evolutionary origins of psychedelic signaling and the translational value of animal models continue to be actively debated. In this review, we integrate evolutionary biology, molecular pharmacology, comparative neuroscience, and computational psychiatry into a unified framework for understanding psychedelic action across biological scales. Building upon predictive processing and the Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS) framework, we discuss how serotonergic psychedelics transiently reshape hierarchical inference, providing computational principles that can be experimentally investigated across species despite profound differences in neural architecture and subjective experience. Comparative analyses from invertebrates to non-human primates further suggest that conserved receptor pharmacology coexists with species-specific circuit organization, highlighting that animal models should be interpreted as complementary platforms for investigating molecular, cellular, and computational mechanisms rather than direct proxies for human hallucinatory experiences. We further discuss preclinical and emerging translational evidence suggesting that biased receptor signaling and non-hallucinogenic psychoplastogens may partially dissociate plasticity-related therapeutic actions from hallucinogenic effects, providing new opportunities for mechanism-based drug development. By integrating evolutionary biology with molecular psychiatry, this review provides a mechanistic framework linking receptor pharmacology, neural plasticity, circuit computation, and therapeutic outcomes, thereby offering new conceptual and experimental strategies for developing next-generation psychedelic therapeutics.

Article.Title: Multivariate genome-wide association study of post-traumatic stress disorder, alcohol use, and alcohol use disorders
Article.Authors: Barr P.; Bountress K.; Chatzinakos C.; Hart J.; Neale Z.; Sheerin C.; Johnson E.; Atkinson E.; Nievergelt C.; Maihofer A.; Powers A.; Porjesz B.; Agrawal A.; Edenberg H.; Gelernter J.; Koenen K.; N/A N/A.; Nievergelt C.; Maihofer A.; Atkinson E.; Chen C.; Choi K.; Coleman J.; Daskalakis N.; Duncan L.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) commonly co-occurs with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Comorbid PTSD and AUD is associated with poorer outcomes including worse treatment prognosis and significant physical health consequences. Both PTSD and AUD are polygenic in nature and genetically overlap. Previous work showed negative or non-significant associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption but positive genetic associations between PTSD and AUD. This work highlights the need for more nuanced examination of the similarities and distinctions in the associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption versus AUD. We leveraged the latest large-scale GWAS data to perform a multivariate GWAS of alcohol consumption (ALCC), problematic alcohol use (ALCP), and PTSD using GenomicSEM. Partial genetic correlations revealed that ALCP and PTSD were associated with each other (rG = 0.39, p = 4.38 × 10-60) and with other psychiatric problems, medical conditions, and pain, while ALCC was only weakly correlated with PTSD (rG = -0.08, p = 2.03 × 10-4) and uncorrelated with most traits after accounting for its genetic overlap with ALCP and PTSD. We examined associations between GenomicSEM-derived polygenic scores (PGS) and their corresponding phenotypes in participants from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcoholism (COGA). PGS for ALCC were unrelated to PTSD diagnosis and PGS for PTSD were unrelated to drinks in a typical week. PTSD is more strongly related to alcohol problems, and much of the overlap in PTSD and consumption is accounted for by its overlap with alcohol problems. These results help demonstrate the complex partial overlaps of PTSD, AUD, and alcohol consumption.

Article.Title: Real-world associations of antipsychotic use with clinical outcomes in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Article.Authors: Yao H.; Peng Z.; Huang Y.; Wu R.
Article.Abstract: To systematically synthesize evidence on the association between antipsychotic medication use and diverse outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia, we searched PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, and Web of Science from inception to May 1, 2026. Eligible studies were observational studies reporting associations between antipsychotic use and clinical outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed study quality. Data was synthesized using multilevel random-effects models. Outcomes were categorized into mortality (including all-cause and cause-specific), somatic disorders, and other clinical outcomes. Sixty-eight studies comprising 1,424,455 individuals were included. Among individuals with schizophrenia, antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (pooled estimate, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.54-0.77) and lower relapse risk (pooled estimate, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.12-0.99) compared with nonuse. In contrast, compared with nonuse, antipsychotic use was associated with higher risks of cancer (1.41; 95% CI, 1.17-1.69), fractures (1.35; 95% CI, 1.17-1.56), and lung infections (1.25; 95% CI, 1.04-1.51), whereas evidence for other outcomes was non-significant. Overall, the evidence base was limited, with several pooled estimates derived from a small number of studies. Subgroup analyses suggested variation by region and study design. Antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality and relapse risk, alongside increased risks for some adverse outcomes such as fractures and lung infections. These findings should be interpreted cautiously, as residual confounding and bias may influence the observed associations and preclude causal interpretation. Further studies using rigorous designs are needed to clarify outcome-specific associations.

Article.Title: HINT1 in ventral hippocampal GABAergic neurons mediates depressive-like behaviors
Article.Authors: Li S.; Liu D.; Zhang H.; Wen R.; Hu H.; Xv J.; Cheng D.; Dang Y.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a complex psychiatric disorder with multifaceted etiologies, and its underlying molecular mechanisms are incompletely elucidated. Although histidine trimeric nucleotide-binding protein 1 (HINT1) has been implicated in major depressive disorders (MDD), its precise role and regulatory mechanism remain unclear. This study investigated the role of HINT1 in depression-associated phenotypes. In mice subjected to chronic social defeat stress (CSDS), stress-susceptible individuals exhibited significant upregulation of HINT1 in the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex. Targeted overexpression of HINT1 in ventral hippocampus (vHip) demonstrated that HINT1 directly induced depressive-like behaviors, whereas its knockdown exerted a robust antidepressant-like effect. Pharmacological inhibition of HINT1 with the selective inhibitor Tryptamine guanosine carbamate (TpGc) in vHip also reversed behavioral deficits and normalized neuronal activity in the CSDS-exposed mice. Cell-type-specific analyses demonstrated that HINT1 overexpression in vHip GABAergic neurons, including somatostatin-positive (SST+) and parvalbumin-positive (PV+) subtypes, exacerbated depressive-like phenotypes and disrupted neuronal activity. Proteomics analysis identified that HINT1 overexpression in the vHip significantly upregulated the small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) E3 ligases chromobox 4 (CBX4). Further overexpression of CBX4 in the GABAergic neurons of vHip induced depressive-like behaviors. Mechanistically, HINT1 interacted with and inhibited the phosphorylation of protein kinase C-β1 (PKCβ1), suppressing its downstream MEK1/2-ERK1/2 signaling and thereby increasing CBX4 levels. CBX4 promoted the SUMOylation of the glutamate N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor subunit 2 A (GluN2A) and affected its phosphorylation and trafficking. These findings demonstrated HINT1 as a key regulator of GABAergic signaling in vHip and highlighted its therapeutic potential for depression.

Article.Title: Genome-wide analysis identifies pleiotropic genes shared between severe mental disorders and biomarkers of cellular aging
Article.Authors: Pisanu C.; Nishioka M.; Manchia M.; Squassina A.; Kato T.
Article.Abstract: Severe mental disorders such as bipolar disorder (BD), major depressive disorder (MDD) and schizophrenia (SZ) are characterized by reduced life expectancy, premature mortality and alterations of aging biomarkers, leading to hypothesize that they might be associated with accelerated cellular aging. We quantified the genetic overlap between severe mental disorders and a comprehensive set of aging biomarkers including multivariate longevity and healthy aging (mvAge), brain age gap (BAG), leucocyte telomere length (gLTL), mitochondrial DNA copy number and epigenetic age acceleration (gEAA) using cutting-edge methods, and evaluated their functional enrichment and suitability as drug targets. All disorders were negatively correlated with mvAge. Further, MDD correlated negatively with gLTL and positively with gEAA. We identified several pleiotropic variants, with nine genes (AC068490.2, ASIC2, CNNM2, FURIN, GPM6A, HS6ST3, RP5-1043L13.1, SORCS3 and SP4) containing variants shared between aging biomarkers and all disorders. Functional analyses with summary-data-based Mendelian randomization showed that increased expression of the druggable gene CRHR1 in the prefrontal cortex was associated with increased risk of MDD and BAG measures. Our findings suggest that shared heritability might contribute to reduced longevity and healthy aging in severe mental disorders and identify pleiotropic genes involved in synaptic function and metabolic processes related to micronutrients such as folate and magnesium.

Article.Title: A specialized population of hair afferents dedicated to transmitting mechanical itch
Article.Authors: Fatima M.; Lee H.; Cha H.; Hor C.; Wang F.; Liu J.; Damblon J.; Zhang W.; Qu K.; Nagai Y.; Dinh A.; Wu Z.; Ajimal R.; Xiong A.; Chai M.; Asmar A.; Cai W.; Zhou X.; Balaji A.; Pan H.; Horwitz L.; Tsoi L.; Hu H.; Xu X.; De Koninck Y.
Article.Abstract: Hairs serve as sensory structures that are crucial for perceiving environmental cues through interactions with sensory endings. Depigmented and demedullated atypical hairs exhibit a limited distribution on mammalian skin and have not been extensively studied. In this study, we identify a specific type of hair, termed vellus-like hairs (VLHs), which are enriched in the postauricular region and on the hindpaws of mice. These hairs are innervated by Aβ low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs) that co-express Toll-like receptor 5 and Calbindin1 (TLR5Calb1). Genetic ablation or silencing of these hair afferents eliminated mechanical itch generated by gentle VLH stroking or indentation under both physiological and pathological conditions. Conversely, optogenetic activation of TLR5Calb1 hair afferents evoked itch behaviors. Mechanosensitive Piezo2 channels in TLR5Calb1 Aβ-LTMRs function as key mechanotransducers for mechanical itch signaling. Our study sheds light on the previously poorly understood somatosensory physiology of unique hairs, emphasizing the significant role of TLR5Calb1 Aβ-LTMRs in itch transmission.

Article.Title: Epigenetic control of microglial mitochondrial immunity by KAT7 drives Alzheimer’s disease pathogenesis
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Ye Y.; Fan M.; Cheng H.; Sun S.; Qiu Z.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)-driven innate immune signaling sustains chronic neuroinflammation in neurological diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet how this pathway is regulated in microglia remains poorly understood. Here, we identify the histone acetyltransferase KAT7 (HBO1) as a central epigenetic regulator that links chromatin remodeling to mitochondrial immune activation. KAT7 and its histone mark H3K14ac are elevated in microglia from 5×FAD mice and human AD brains. Integrative transcriptomic and epigenomic analyses reveal that KAT7 activates transcription of cytidine/uridine monophosphate kinase 2 (Cmpk2), a mitochondrial kinase essential for mtDNA synthesis. Loss of KAT7 reduces Cmpk2 expression, impairs mtDNA replication and release, and consequently suppresses cyclic guanosine monophosphate-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) and NLRP3 signaling. Importantly, both microglia-specific deletion and pharmacological inhibition of KAT7 mitigate cytosolic mtDNA-induced neuroinflammation, decrease β-amyloid burden, restore synaptic plasticity, and improve cognitive function in 5×FAD mice. Together, these findings uncover an epigenetic-mitochondrial axis sustaining microglial pathogenicity and establish KAT7 as a potential therapeutic target for AD.

Article.Title: Single-cell proteome atlas of aging mouse microglia reveals subpopulation-specific phagoproteome
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Liu Z.; Chen B.; Zhang G.; Wang L.; Wei C.; Zhang X.; Luo Y.; Peng T.; Fang Q.; Gu L.; Ge R.; Zhu J.; Yang R.; Shen W.; Jiang Z.; Sun Y.; Duan W.; Liu J.; Li T.; Wang J.; Gao Z.; Yu X.; Chen H.; Ye Z.
Article.Abstract: Microglia are brain-resident immune cells with complex physiological functions. Exploring their proteomic heterogeneity at the single-cell level has remained technically challenging. Here, we optimized a label-free single-cell proteomics (SCP) workflow using Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometry (MS) and applied it to fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-sorted microglia from the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex of young, middle-aged, and aged mice. This yielded one of the largest SCP datasets to date, comprising 3,085 single cells, with an average of 1,153 protein groups identified per cell. Compared with single-cell transcriptomic data, the SCP dataset showed higher expression completeness and moderate cross-modality correlation. This dataset revealed spatiotemporal proteomic heterogeneity of microglia during aging. Notably, we defined the microglial "phagoproteome," uncovering state-specific phagocytic preferences, and verified these results by imaging. This study underscores the potential of SCP to reveal subpopulation-specific proteomic dynamics and provides a new resource for studying microglial state transitions during aging.

Article.Title: Infraslow histaminergic dynamics govern priming states to gate moment-to-moment memory accessibility
Article.Authors: Morishita Y.; Takamura Y.; Nishimura K.; Yokoi Y.; Ishihama Y.; Idutsu R.; Ono M.; Matsumoto R.; Hitora-Imamura N.; Minami M.; Nomura H.
Article.Abstract: Memory expression fluctuates even in response to identical cues, which suggests that ongoing brain states bias memory accessibility. However, the cellular and circuit principles governing these state-dependent fluctuations remain unclear. Here, we show that spontaneous pre-cue activity of histaminergic neurons in the hypothalamic tuberomammillary nucleus (TMN) modulates the expression of reward-associative memory in mice. TMN histaminergic activity exhibited infraslow dynamics (0.05-0.1 Hz) that closely tracked an integrated brain-body state. Closed-loop cue delivery during high histaminergic states enhanced memory expression. Brief optogenetic activation or inhibition of these neurons before the cue bidirectionally modulated memory expression, and direct activation of histaminergic terminals in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) was sufficient to enhance memory expression. Furthermore, histaminergic inhibition before the cue impaired the cue-evoked BLA population response. Thus, ongoing histaminergic activity exerts an infraslow, state-setting influence that primes BLA circuits for robust cue responses and, in turn, modulates moment-to-moment memory accessibility.

Article.Title: Rapid strengthening and reversal of hippocampal-neocortical interplay mediates human memory formation
Article.Authors: Wang L.; Duan Q.; Song J.; Liang S.; Shi X.; Shen K.; Liu S.; Yang H.; Jia H.; Liao X.; Zhang C.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: Classical theories of systems consolidation highlight the importance of hippocampal-neocortical interplay for long-term memory formation. However, how this interaction evolves during multiple days of learning remains unclear. Using day-by-day multisite intracranial electrophysiology, we examined human subjects performing a repeated picture-learning task. From day 1 today 2, the ripple rates during picture learning and free recall significantly increased in the hippocampus and neocortex, which correlated with behavioral memory performance. These enhancements persisted throughout the remaining task days. Notably, from day 2 onward, the ripple coupling between the neocortex and hippocampus not only strengthened, but the temporal sequence of these coupled ripples also reversed-from hippocampus leading to neocortex leading. This rapid strengthening and reversal of hippocampal-neocortical information flow on the second day represents a key signature of human memory formation.

Article.Title: Objective quality assessment for precision functional MRI data
Article.Authors: Lynch C.; Chang M.; Elbau I.; Gordon E.; Laumann T.; Du J.; Ladwig Z.; Lueckel M.; Perez D.; Summerville I.; Chou J.; Johnson M.; Ho C.; Manfredi N.; Nilchian P.; Solomonov N.; Goldwaser E.; Ng T.; Moia S.; Caballero-Gaudes C.; Downar J.; Vila-Rodriguez F.; Gregory E.; Daskalakis Z.; Blumberger D.
Article.Abstract: Precision functional mapping (PFM) enables the individual-level characterization of brain network organization but requires substantially more and higher-quality fMRI data than is standard. Despite the growing use of PFM, the objective criteria for data sufficiency and the quality needed to ensure interpretable and replicable individual-level results remain unclear. Here, we introduce the network similarity index (NSI), an objective measure of the extent to which functional connectivity (FC) patterns express the large-scale network structure required for PFM. The NSI captures low-spatial-frequency, coherent network organization and denoising fidelity, and it aligns closely with blinded expert assessments of PFM usability. The NSI also accounts for the variability in the rate at which FC becomes reliable across individuals. This NeuroResource provides an open source framework for NSI-based data quality evaluation and models linking NSI values with expert-judged PFM suitability. This framework can inform expected returns from additional data collection, thus enabling principled decisions about data sufficiency and replication in precision fMRI research.

Article.Title: Fast-conducting mechanonociceptors uniquely engage reflexive and affective pain circuitry to drive protective responses
Article.Authors: Lezgiyeva K.; Liu J.; Nguyen K.; DeLisle M.; Ko F.; Fullam S.; Obeidat A.; Turecek J.; Alkislar I.; Lehnert B.; Martinez-Garcia R.; Sivakumar R.; Choi J.; Mazor O.; Garibyan L.; Sharma N.; Emanuel A.; Malfait A.; Miller R.; Ginty D.
Article.Abstract: Nociceptors detect damaging stimuli and evoke pain in healthy animals. We conducted an optogenetic activation screen to identify genetically defined nociceptor populations that elicit place aversion and nocifensive behaviors in response to stimulation. Smr2Cre- and Bmpr1bCre-labeled Aδ high-threshold mechanoreceptors (HTMRs) emerged as two of the few nociceptor populations, and we focused on investigating their physiological, morphological, functional, and synaptic properties. These neurons densely innervate skin and other organs, are activated only by intense, potentially damaging stimuli, and are necessary for protective responses to sharp mechanical stimuli. Centrally, Aδ-HTMR projections span multiple spinal segments and terminate across spinal cord laminae, forming strong, monosynaptic connections onto anterolateral tract projection neurons, including antenna cells of the deep dorsal horn. Aδ-HTMRs also engage a local spinal reflex circuit, enabling a remarkably rapid limb withdrawal. Thus, Aδ-HTMRs are myelinated nociceptors with unique properties that can be exploited for the development of new analgesics.

Article.Title: Inferring brain-wide interactions using data-constrained recurrent neural network models
Article.Authors: Perich M.; Arlt C.; Soares S.; Zhou S.; Beiran M.; Andalman A.; Benster T.; Young M.; Mosher C.; Minxha J.; Carter E.; Rutishauser U.; Rudebeck P.; Harvey C.; Deisseroth K.; Rajan K.
Article.Abstract: Behavior arises from the coordinated activity across anatomically and functionally distinct brain regions. Modern experimental tools allow unprecedented access to large neural populations spanning many interacting regions brain-wide. Yet, understanding such large-scale datasets necessitates robust, scalable computational models to extract meaningful features of inter-region communication and principled theories to interpret those features. Here, we introduce current-based decomposition (CURBD), an approach for inferring brain-wide interactions using data-constrained recurrent neural network models that autonomously produce dynamics consistent with experimentally obtained neural data. CURBD leverages the functional interactions inferred from such models to reveal directional currents between multiple brain regions simultaneously. We first show that CURBD accurately isolates inter-region currents in simulated, ground-truth networks with known connectivity and dynamics. We then apply CURBD to multi-region neural recordings obtained from many species-larval zebrafish, mice, macaques, and humans-to demonstrate the widespread applicability of CURBD in untangling brain-wide interactions and inter-area communication principles underlying behavior.

Article.Title: Hypothalamus-driven brain health through metabolic flexibility
Article.Authors: Horvath T.; Romanov R.; Matarese G.; Cota D.
Article.Abstract: Organismal physiology depends on continuous, non-hierarchical communication among cells, tissues, and organs. We argue that this communication rests on metabolic flexibility-the capacity of cells and tissues to adapt substrate use to changing energetic demands-and that the hypothalamus serves as the central hub coordinating this flexibility across the body. Using hypothalamic agouti-related protein (AgRP) and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons as a model, we show these melanocortin neurons do more than regulate hunger and satiety: by integrating metabolic, hormonal, and immune signals, they shape reward, learning, executive function, and social behavior, while imposing coordinated metabolic states on peripheral tissues. When this flexibility is lost, as with aging or overnutrition, body-brain communication becomes rigid, driving cognitive decline, chronic inflammation, and neurodegenerative disease. We propose that signals from the body are not peripheral modifiers of brain function but fundamental determinants of it, with direct implications for hypothalamus-centered strategies to preserve brain health across the lifespan.

Article.Title: Redox-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial nucleoids contributes to bioenergetic decline during neuronal aging
Article.Authors: Cheng X.; Gao Y.; Chan C.; Xie Y.; Dai Y.; Xiong G.; Sathler A.; Roney J.; Li S.; Li Y.; Wu L.; Sheng Z.
Article.Abstract: Why mitochondria progressively fail in aging neurons remains a fundamental question in neurobiology. Although bioenergetic decline and oxidative stress are hallmarks of aging, whether redox signaling remodels mitochondrial nucleoids (mt-nucleoids) to impair neuronal bioenergetics remains unclear. Using aged mouse neurons and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons, we demonstrate that redox-driven mt-nucleoid remodeling underlies reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and bioenergetic decline. Combining minimal photon fluxes (MINFLUX) nanoscopy with single-molecule transcription mapping, we identify distinct mt-nucleoid architectures governed by mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM)-mediated mtDNA compaction. Aging-associated oxidative stress drives mt-nucleoid remodeling from compact, transcriptionally active structures toward decompacted forms with reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and impaired mitochondrial ATP production. This remodeling involves species-specific TFAM redox mechanisms: cysteine oxidation promotes human TFAM polymerization, whereas methionine oxidation weakens mouse TFAM-mtDNA interactions. Notably, expressing an oxidation-resistant TFAM variant restores mt-nucleoid organization, mtDNA transcript abundance, and ATP production in aged neurons, identifying mt-nucleoid architecture as a potential target for preserving neuronal bioenergetics during aging.

Article.Title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy
Article.Authors: Bodart-Santos V.; Ravula A.; You Y.; Abdullah M.; Ruan Z.; Ellison J.; Radhakishun S.; Basu Ray N.; Melvin B.; Kurti A.; Liang Z.; Sakai Y.; O’Brien D.; Nguyen S.; Shaffer S.; Fiddes L.; Butovsky O.; Springer W.; Ikezu S.; Ikezu T.
Article.Abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

Article.Title: Opposing excitatory and inhibitory synaptic pathologies drive ZC4H2-associated intellectual disability
Article.Authors: Ma P.; Wan L.; Li Y.; Bu Y.; Li D.; Zhao S.; Zhang H.; Zhao S.; Yuan K.; Ding Y.; Li M.; Tao W.; Zhu J.; Tang A.; Bai G.; Mao B.; Sheng N.
Article.Abstract: Understanding genotype-phenotype correlations is critical for precision medicine, yet patients carrying mutations in the same gene are often classified under one disorder and treated alike, despite potentially opposite responses to therapy. ZC4H2-associated rare disorder (ZARD) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental condition caused by diverse mutations across ZC4H2. Here, we show that distinct ZC4H2 mutations drive intellectual disability through opposing synaptic mechanisms. The gain-of-function mutation ZC4H2L66H enhances GABAA receptor (GABAAR) degradation, impairing inhibitory synaptic transmission and plasticity. By contrast, the loss-of-function mutation ZC4H2R213W increases AMPA receptor (AMPAR) stability and dysregulates excitatory synaptic activity. Despite these diametrically opposed synaptic pathologies, ZC4H2L66H/y and ZC4H2R213W/y knockin mice exhibit comparable cognitive deficits. Importantly, muscimol, a GABAAR agonist, specifically rescues deficits in ZC4H2L66H/y mice, whereas the AMPAR antagonist perampanel rescues ZC4H2R213W/y mice. These findings demonstrate that opposing synaptic etiologies can underlie a single genetic disorder and highlight pathomechanism-based stratification for targeted therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: An astrocyte-microglia MFG-E8 axis promotes synapse engulfment in early amyloid pathology
Article.Authors: Sokolova D.; Puletti F.; Addington Ghansah S.; Georgiades T.; Zheng Y.; Wu L.; De Schepper S.; Lange J.; Ferreira L.; Sierksma A.; Rebejac J.; Crowley G.; Rueda-Carrasco J.; Geary B.; Nirujogi R.; Koutsiouroumpa A.; Muckett P.; Kittler J.; Gentry M.; Bourdenx M.; Freeman O.; Burden J.; Khakh B.; Hong S.
Article.Abstract: Region-specific synapse loss is an early hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, yet the upstream signals that render synapses vulnerable remain unclear. In a mouse model of amyloidosis, we identify an early astrocyte state that emerges in vulnerable brain regions before widespread plaque deposition and overt gliosis. These astrocytes exhibit bulbous-looking perisynaptic processes enriched in p62 and glycogen, impaired autophagic flux and calcium signaling, and diminished astrocyte-synapse coverage. Rather than exhibiting increased synapse engulfment, bulbous astrocytes show elevated milk fat globule-epidermal growth factor 8 (MFG-E8) and are associated with increased local microglial synapse engulfment. Astrocyte-specific gain- and loss-of-function experiments demonstrate that astrocyte-derived MFG-E8 is required for microglial synapse engulfment and acts through microglial β3 integrin signaling. Astrocytic Mfge8 deletion reduces microglial engulfment and synapse loss across amyloidosis models and is associated with reduced amyloid pathology, gliosis, and cognitive impairment. Together, these findings define an astrocyte-microglia MFG-E8 signaling axis that contributes to region-specific synaptic vulnerability during early amyloid pathology.

Article.Title: Antisense oligonucleotide silencing rescues neurodevelopmental deficits in AMPA receptor gain-of-function mice
Article.Authors: Chen C.; Huang Y.; Chung C.; Johnson R.; Tsai C.; Chen Y.; Tan H.; Hsiao F.; Huganir R.; Chiu S.
Article.Abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are essential for neuronal development and brain function. We investigated the role of a recurrent AMPAR GluA1 variant (GRIA1 p.A636T) identified in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using a Gria1-A636T knock-in mouse model, we show that this variant is sufficient to produce core ASD/ID-like behaviors and cause selective hippocampal vulnerability characterized by progressive dendritic atrophy and neuronal loss. Despite a reduction in GluA1-containing complexes, synaptic AMPARs exhibit hyperexcitability and fail to transition from calcium-permeable to calcium-impermeable AMPARs during development, resulting in persistent excitotoxicity. To explore potential therapeutic interventions, we developed an allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively silence the mutant transcript. A single neonatal ASO dose prevents hippocampal pathology and rescues behavioral deficits. These findings define a mechanism of developmental excitotoxicity driven by a GRIA1 gain-of-function channelopathy and support RNA-targeted precision therapy for AMPAR-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Title: Dissociable cerebellar pathways for reach correction and learning
Article.Authors: Dobrott C.; Nashef A.; Becker M.; Person A.
Article.Abstract: Sensory feedback can trigger rapid motor corrections, but how self-generated movement errors are corrected and influence subsequent behavior remains less clear. Here, we found that corrective submovements (CSMs), structured, feedback-driven adjustments, occurred either spontaneously or in response to neural perturbations during mouse reaching. Corrections were modestly encoded in the cerebellar anterior interposed nucleus (IntA) along with non-corrective reach kinematic correlates. Closed-loop perturbations directed to red nucleus-projecting neurons were readily compensated for with corrective movements and led to learned shifts in the timing of future submovements, while perturbations to IntA more broadly were not compensated for and produced no learning. Thus, subsets of IntA outputs differentially permit or corrupt accurate corrections and subsequent learning, respectively.

Article.Title: Slow-timescale regulation of dopamine release governs recovery of a motivational drive over days
Article.Authors: Sunkavalli P.; Madara J.; Singh Alvarado J.; Ventura B.; Baker J.; Zhu P.; Christenson L.; Diaz A.; Chen J.; Lazen E.; Ravotto L.; Patriarchi T.; Andermann M.; Zhang S.
Article.Abstract: The rise and fall of a motivational state can unfold over many days. We used mouse mating behavior to model how the brain orchestrates such slow-timescale changes in motivation. Male mice become sexually satiated after successful matings, and their motivation to mate recovers over a week. Using deep-brain fluorescence-lifetime imaging in the medial preoptic area (MPOA), we found that tonic dopamine transmission-which regulates mating drive-also declined after mating and gradually re-emerged across several days. First, successful mating transiently reduced the tonic firing of hypothalamic dopamine-releasing neurons, thereby inhibiting dopamine release and mating behavior for 1 to 2 days. Second, these neurons' ability to produce and release dopamine dropped after mating and recovered over the following week, paralleling the recovery of mating drive. Therefore, changes in neuronal firing rate and neurotransmitter composition cooperate to control the early and late phases of motivational dynamics, respectively.

Article.Title: Brain organoids: Experimental access to human-specific brain development
Article.Authors: Kastli R.; Andersen R.; Walsh C.; Arlotta P.
Article.Abstract: Human cerebral cortical development includes species-divergent cellular programs and unusually prolonged trajectories that remain difficult to investigate experimentally. These processes support human-specific cognitive abilities and are thought to be associated with vulnerability to neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain organoids provide a tractable system for studying these processes across developmental time and under controlled perturbation. Here, we review how cortical organoids model human-specific features of progenitor biology and cell diversification, as well as progressive cellular maturation and circuit formation. We consider the limitations that constrain later-stage maturation and how approaches including the addition of missing cell types, the use of assembloids, and transplantation can extend the developmental processes accessible to study. Finally, we examine how patient-derived, isogenic, chimeric, and perturbation-based organoid systems are being used to investigate neurodevelopmental disorders and, in turn, reveal mechanisms of typical human development.

Article.Abstract: As human neural organoid research advances, some key concepts in its ethical analysis need to be unbundled to keep pace with scientific developments. Article.Title: Advancing brain organoids from disease phenotypes to mechanisms and translation across developmental, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases
Article.Authors: Knoblich J.; Ming G.; Temple S.
Article.Abstract: Diseases of the central nervous system remain among the greatest unmet medical challenges. Human brain organoids provide 3D multicellular systems for investigating neurodevelopmental, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases in a human cellular context. Considering these distinct disease areas together highlights how organoid studies are moving beyond recapitulating disease phenotypes to define molecular and cellular mechanisms and trajectories: when pathogenic changes emerge, how they evolve, which cell types and states drive or resist disease, and how multicellular interactions shape progression. Integrating human genetics with longitudinal, single-cell, multi-omic, and functional analyses provides access to human-specific processes that are difficult to capture in animal models and enables identification of mechanisms and therapeutic targets anchored in human disease biology. Increasingly, well-characterized organoids offer human new approach methodologies (NAMs) for preclinical therapeutic evaluation. Advances in reproducibility, benchmarking, and appropriate validation will be critical to establishing their predictive value and supporting their use in drug development and regulatory applications.

Article.Title: Neural organoid models of human brain evolution
Article.Authors: Day C.; Pollen A.; Lancaster M.
Article.Abstract: The human brain has structural and functional differences to our closest living relatives, the other great apes. It is thought that these differences give rise to many of the traits we associate with being human, such as our prodigious capacity to learn and be creative. However, the molecular mechanisms that underpin these differences are mostly unknown. In this review, we describe how neural organoids, an in vitro model of brain development, enable questions of human brain evolution to be functionally investigated in evolutionarily relevant developmental contexts. We discuss new insights at the genetic, cellular, and developmental scales and highlight current challenges in organoid generation, in long-term culture, and in establishing multimodal phenotypic measurements. We anticipate expanding the application of organoid models across Mammalia to help us better define species- and lineage-specific traits and improve our understanding of how complex traits emerge and evolve across developmental and evolutionary timescales.

Article.Title: A coronavirus protease activates sensory neurons via TRPA1 to drive sneeze, cough, and pain
Article.Authors: Mali S.; Gong Z.; Silva R.; Flamm A.; Cook C.; Shallow L.; Souza J.; Cronce M.; Arp C.; Mousa A.; Vo U.; Vuong C.; Keasling J.; Moayedi Y.; Cox J.; Ramachandran R.; Stanley S.; Bautista D.

These responses are initiated by airway-innervating nociceptors that detect noxious stimuli, but how SARS-CoV-2 activates these neurons remains unclear. PLpro triggers sneezing, coughing, acute pain, and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release in the airways. Both the proteolytic activity of PLpro and the host ion channel transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) are required for neuronal activation and sneezing. Infection with the mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 or the murine coronavirus MHV-A59 also induces sneezing in mice, and MHV-A59-evoked sneezing is TRPA1-dependent. SARS-CoV-2 infection of the trigeminal ganglia altered transcriptional programs associated with nociception, including upregulation of the TRPA1-CGRP signaling pathway activated by PLpro. Together, these findings reveal a direct mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 triggers pain and airway reflexes and identify PLpro and TRPA1 as potential therapeutic targets for COVID-19.

Article.Title: Noncoding functions of FMR1 transcript in riboregulation of human neurodevelopment
Article.Authors: Sandoval S.; Méndez-Albelo N.; Chiang H.; Peters L.; Kaur H.; Raveendran N.; Knaack S.; Gao Y.; Sirois C.; Guo Y.; Dayley E.; Trygstad D.; Widicus A.; Lee J.; Yang P.; Ajit R.; Tan J.; Smith R.; Eckholm M.; Li L.; Skala M.; Zhao X.

Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Yang J.; Yu K.; Shrestha H.; Zhou Y.; Jiao Y.; Wang J.; Chen P.; Wang Z.; Ren X.; Sun H.; Liu D.; Yarbro J.; Wu Z.; Harper K.; He L.; Yuan Z.; Xu J.; Wang X.; High A.; Yu G.; Yu J.; Wen Z.; Peng J.

Article.Title: The neural mechanisms of fast versus slow decision-making
Article.Authors: Nashaat M.; Oraby H.; Krasniqi F.; Goh-Sauerbier S.; Bosc M.; Koerner S.; Lobova A.; Karayel S.; Kepecs A.; Larkum M.
Article.Abstract: One hallmark of intelligent behavior is the ability to optimize how much time is devoted to decisions. Yet the principles governing decision timing remain unclear. Article.Authors: Hakim R.; Jaggi A.; Heo G.; Matsumoto H.; Uchida N.; Watabe-Uchida M.; Datta S.; Musall S.; Sabatini B.
Article.Abstract: Animals use coordinated facial movements to sample the environment, ingest nutrients, and communicate. Article.Authors: Riedl Khursigara M.; Goss A.; Kost-Alimova M.; Keller K.; De Mata C.; Muraleedharan R.; Collantes E.; Brown M.; Grinkevich E.; Arines F.; Lin J.; Byrne P.; Bazua-Valenti S.; Morici E.; Roignot J.; Zavras J.; Silverman B.; Ignacio J.; Myung Y.; Kwon S.; Nelson A.; Yoo H.; Melanson M.; Racette M.; Padovano V.

Article.Title: TRIM28-mediated SUMOylation of ERG at K389 conveys PARP inhibitor resistance by inhibiting 53BP1 expression in CRPC
Article.Authors: Liu S.; Hong Z.; Wang Z.; Zhang Y.; Jiang C.; Jiang Y.; Zhang R.; Liu Z.; Shang Z.; Lin G.; Hong Z.; Dai B.
Article.Abstract: Both intrinsic and acquired resistance to poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPis) have emerged as a formidable challenge in clinical practice. ERG was posttranslationally modified by tripartite motif-containing 28 (TRIM28) as SUMOylation at lysine 389 (K389), which promotes DNA homologous recombination repair (HRR), thereby weakening the efficacy of PARPis. Mechanistically, the SUMOylation of ERG (K389) inhibited protein degradation mediated by the SPOP-mediated ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, thereby stabilizing the protein. Concurrently, this posttranslational modification increased HRR capacity by inhibiting 53BP1 expression, which in turn reduced PARPi sensitivity. These findings suggest that TRIM28-mediated ERG SUMOylation conveys resistance to PARPis by inhibiting 53BP1 expression; combined TRIM28/ERG targeting and PARPi therapy may improve outcomes for ERG-positive CRPC patients.

Article.Title: Auditory cortical coding of spectrotemporal modulations is sufficient to support perceptual categorization of speech and music
Article.Authors: Ginzburg J.; Gotti C.; Debaque É.; Borderie A.; Morillon B.; Martineau L.; Bonaventure P.; Zatorre R.; Albouy P.
Article.Abstract: Auditory processing is typically described as hierarchical, culminating in neural representation of abstract categories. Here, we test whether cortical coding of spectrotemporal modulation (STM) features is sufficient to support speech-music categorization by combining human intracranial recordings with continuous behavioral judgments of a naturalistic soundtrack in which speech and music occur both separately and simultaneously. We show that temporal and spectral modulation patterns largely characterize speech and music, respectively, and that cortical auditory regions robustly track these features over time, with distinct oscillatory frequency bands preferentially encoding temporal and spectral modulations. Last, speech- and music-related STM representations showed stronger tracking of category-specific acoustical features in left versus right cortical auditory regions, respectively. These findings indicate that the efficient neural coding of acoustical features provides a sufficient basis for the categorical distinction between speech and music and that the temporal and spectral components of this representation are implemented through distinct oscillatory mechanisms.

Article.Title: Unblockable communication with gravity
Article.Authors: Groszek A.; Woffinden C.; Harvey M.; White A.; Davis M.
Article.Abstract: All modern wireless communication technologies are based on electromagnetism. However, electromagnetic signals are readily susceptible to screening and blocking, so their availability cannot be guaranteed in adverse environments. This raises a fundamental question: Can information be transmitted through an unblockable channel? Here, we show that gravity, under physically realistic conditions, offers such a path. We propose and implement a wireless communication protocol in which a broadcaster encodes a binary message by moving a mass, while a receiver detects the resulting gravitational signal with a gravimeter. We validate this scheme experimentally, successfully transmitting a gravitational message a distance of ≈0.7 meters through a brick wall at a rate of 1 bit per minute. These results establish gravity as a viable platform for practically unblockable communication.

Article.Authors: Xie W.; Cui W.; Tang K.; Xi S.; Shen Z.; Zhang L.; Wu D.; Xu Z.
Article.Abstract: Spinel oxides have emerged as promising catalysts for polysulfide conversion, yet a comprehensive design strategy that elucidates the underlying structure–property relationship across diverse spinel oxides remains elusive. The complex multistep conversion processes make single descriptors insufficient to capture the full catalytic behavior, whereas identifying cooperative descriptors introduces additional complexity that challenges manual analysis. Here, we employ a machine-learning–assisted approach to uncover universal cooperative descriptors and accelerate the discovery of high-performance spinel catalysts. We reveal that the intrinsic polysulfide conversion efficiency of spinel oxides is cooperatively governed by two structural features. Further screening of promising catalysts is conducted using the extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) algorithm, achieving rapid and accurate prediction of these features on spinel oxides. The model identifies Fe 2 CoO 4 and Fe 2 NiO 4 as superior catalysts, which are experimentally validated to exhibit excellent performance. This work provides deep mechanistic insights and a powerful data-driven framework for the rational design of spinel catalysts, with potential extension to other applications.

Article.Abstract: Differentiated cells of the intestinal villus are not a monolith of equivalent cell types, but an exquisitely patterned continuum of transdifferentiated cells with evolving functions. Article.Title: Cortical population codes for embedding sensory inputs into the prior context
Article.Authors: Hachen I.; Reinartz S.; Stroligo A.; Pequeno-Zurro A.; Diamond M.
Article.Abstract: According to theories of the brain as a predictive network, perceptual decisions result from integrating incoming sensory inputs with prior experience. A neuronal population implementing this form of computation must not only retain information about past events but also combine this information with current sensory evidence. To examine how this integration occurs, we recorded extracellular activity from both primary sensory cortex and a target frontal region in rats performing stimulus categorization. Psychophysical analysis showed that judgments were history dependent. Sensory cortex represented the current stimulus largely independently of prior stimuli and failed to account for the history dependence seen in behavior. In contrast, frontal cortex embedded current input within a representation of prior sensory information, with the two variables aligned along partially overlapping coding dimensions. This mechanism predicted choice bias in the behavioral data and involved a disproportionate contribution from putative fast-spiking units. These findings suggest distinct contributions of sensory and frontal cortical regions to predictive processing and point to frontal cortex as a potential site where sensory history may be integrated with incoming evidence to influence perceptual decisions.

Article.Authors: Liu H.; Aouizerate Y.; Liu X.; Zhang Z.; Hervada C.; Zhu Y.; Vincent M.; Cascales E.; Hu B.; Doan T.
Article.Abstract: Various bacteria move on solid surfaces through a process known as gliding motility. Article.Title: Seasonal effects of simulated marine heatwaves on temperature-dependent growth performance
Article.Authors: Evans R.; Harvey B.; Russell B.
Article.Abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasingly longer and more frequent globally, but the cumulative impacts of multiple events on organism performance remain poorly understood. Simulations suggested that winter MHWs could generally benefit growth, while summer MHWs produced generally negative impacts, especially at higher latitudes where species experience summer growth periods. These simulations suggest that temperature-dependent growth may be closely linked to the seasonal timing and frequency of extreme events, with multi-season MHWs posing potential challenges for mariculture species in the future. Our simulations highlight the importance of considering multi-season impacts in climate adaptation strategies.

Article.Title: Small and large earthquakes driven by inelastic deformation in weak fault zones
Article.Authors: Zhai P.; Huang Y.; Ampuero J.
Article.Abstract: Earthquakes manifest across a wide range of magnitudes, corresponding to a diversity of rupture sizes and amounts of slip. Classical earthquake models consider rupture processes solely on the fault plane, but the surrounding fault zone rocks can host inelastic deformation. Here, we show, via a dynamic seismic cycle model incorporating spontaneous fault zone evolution through damage and healing, that both small and large earthquakes on a single fault emerge naturally from the interplay of fault slip and fault zone inelastic deformation. Our simulations reproduce key observations: frequency-magnitude distribution consistent with the Gutenberg-Richter law, magnitude-invariant static stress drop, and the dual-regime scaling of fracture energy density with earthquake magnitude. The results underscore the coevolution of earthquakes and fault zone damage as a fundamental mechanism governing earthquake behavior in nature. Article.Abstract: Vertebrate genomes contain six somatostatin (SST) gene family members, of which only SST1 and cortistatin (CORT or SST2) are present in mammalian genomes. Article.Abstract: Pediatric brain tumors are the leading cause of disease-related death in children, yet effective treatment remains a major clinical challenge. Article.Title: Discovery of volatile- and Fe-rich melts from low-velocity zones above the mantle transition zone
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Zeng G.; Chen L.; Huang Z.; Han Z.; Liu J.; Wang X.; Yu J.
Article.Abstract: Low-velocity layers atop the mantle transition zone (MTZ) are commonly observed and predicted to comprise volatile- and iron (Fe)–rich melts, yet direct evidence from natural samples remains lacking. Nephelinites from eastern China may preserve such signatures. They contain ultradeep peridotite fragments and show anomalously low potassium (K)/uranium (U) and barium (Ba)/thorium (Th) ratios, indicating derivation from recycled crustal materials in the MTZ, with high-pressure liebermannite residues retaining K-Ba. This study investigates Wuxi nephelinites, eastern China, where seismic tomography images a slab fragment in the MTZ (high-velocity anomalies) and an overlying low-velocity layer. Volatile- and Fe-rich melt inclusions [maximum FeO T content and Cl (chlorine)/K ratio of 21.8 weight % and 0.15, respectively] are identified in these rocks, consistent with predicted compositions of low-velocity zone melts. Phlogopite in unhomogenized inclusions further confirms their volatile-rich nature. Calculated densities of these inclusions exceed that of ambient mantle, thus stabilizing melts atop the MTZ. Sustained volatile influx or melt-rock reaction reduces melt density and triggers upward melt migration, forming nephelinites, providing key petrological record verifying the geophysically detected MTZ molten layer.

Article.Title: An integrative single-cell long noncoding RNA atlas reveals regulatory programs in the pan-cancer tumor microenvironment
Article.Authors: Wang S.; Qian Q.; Liu Y.; Ding Y.; Yang D.; Zheng X.; Cheng S.; Huang G.; Gao G.; Xiao J.; Zhang Z.; Jiang S.
Article.Abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) have been shown as critical components in cancer genomics, yet their functionality and regulation remain elusive. Here, we present an integrative lncRNA atlas covering more than 370,000 cells from 18 cancer types. In addition to multiple lineage- and cellular state transition–associated lncRNAs, we identify a set of lncRNAs that are embedded within cell type–specific regulons, suggesting associations between lncRNA expression and cell type–enriched transcriptional programs. By integrating CRISPR-based functional genomic screens and clinical data, we further prioritize not only CRISPR-supported candidate lncRNAs linked to tumor cell fitness and immune cell state features but also specific lncRNA signatures correlated with patient survival and immunotherapy response.

Article.Title: Steering nanometric reductive-oxidative Fenton-like cycle for PFAS mineralization
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Zheng J.; Ye X.; Zhou T.; Li T.; Feng M.; Huang D.; Weon S.; Elimelech M.; Wang X.; Zhang S.
Article.Abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs), known as “forever chemicals,” have highly stable C─F bonds that render them resistant to destruction by conventional water treatment processes. Here, we developed a destructive technology that does not require external photo-, electro-, or heat energy input, relying simply on Fenton-like cycles (peroxymonosulfate activation) under nanometric spatial confinement. Unlike the ordinary activation process, confinement shielded peroxymonosulfate radicals ( S O 5 • − ) from external quenching and enabled them to remain active for reductive defluorination. Coupled with oxidative sulfate radicals ( S O 4 • − ), this process unlocked a synergistic “reduction-oxidation” destruction pathway. Specifically, the catalyst was designed by planting single-atom cobalt on MXene nanosheets, whose interlaminar confinement directed efficient PFAS mineralization via alternating α-carbon defluorination (by S O 5 • − ) and decarbonization (by S O 4 • − ). We further constructed a Fenton bed that allowed highly efficient and cost-effective treatment of PFASs in complex water matrices. Our findings underscore the promising potential of nanoconfinement in driving reductive-oxidative Fenton-like cycles toward efficient PFAS mineralization.

Article.Title: Chromatin loci move coherently due to spatially correlated fluctuations
Article.Authors: Harju J.; Ubertini M.; Kailash D.; Chen P.; Ronceray P.; Giorgetti L.; Gregor T.; Brückner D.
Article.Abstract: From enhancer-promoter communication to DNA repair, essential genome functions require chromosomal loci to encounter each other. While live-cell imaging enables direct measurement of pairwise locus dynamics, a quantitative framework for interpreting them is lacking. Here, using imaging data from Drosophila embryos and mouse stem cells, we show that nearby loci diffuse relative to each other far more slowly than expected from polymer chain–mediated effects. We propose that this slowdown is caused by spatially correlated fluctuations (SCFs) which couple loci via the nucleoplasm. We theoretically predict how these fluctuations scale with space, time, and genomic separation and confirm these predictions using live-cell imaging. Using polymer simulations, we demonstrate that while spatially correlated equilibrium noise fails to reproduce the observed SCF scalings, coupling the polymer to actively driven flows recapitulates the experimental statistics. Consistently, we experimentally show that SCFs couple locus motion across chromosomes and that their magnitude depends on adenosine 5′-triphosphate (ATP)–dependent activity and cohesin-mediated loop extrusion. By reducing encounter frequencies while prolonging encounter durations, SCFs generate a trade-off with direct implications for gene regulation. Our results provide a quantitative framework for chromatin dynamics, revealing how nuclear activity governs chromatin encounters in living cells.

Article.Title: Beyond metabolites: A wearable biointerface integrating antibody and aptamer probes for the real-time tracking of proteins in vivo
Article.Authors: Zheng H.; Shafique F.; Qian A.; Garg M.; Gessler F.; L’Heureux Hache J.; Quach Q.; Trigatti B.; Poudineh M.; Soleymani L.
Article.Abstract: Continuous monitoring of protein biomarkers could transform the management of acute and chronic diseases. Despite tremendous potential, wearable health monitors have remained largely limited to metabolites and small molecules. A key challenge is the limited availability of biointerfaces that reversibly track low-abundance proteins in vivo without user intervention. Here, we present the Differential Aptalyzer, a minimally invasive hydrogel microneedle platform for continuous monitoring of proteins in skin interstitial fluid. The platform combines high-affinity antibodies for selective target capture with aptamers for reversible electrochemical signal transduction. When integrated into a differential electrochemical chip and pulse-assisted sensor regeneration, this approach enables continuous monitoring of proteins in a wearable format. Using cardiac troponin I (cTnI) as a clinically relevant model analyte, Differential Aptalyzer offers a broad dynamic range (0.003 to 0.640 nanograms per milliliter) and strong specificity against interfering proteins. This platform reliably tracks both rising and falling exogenous cTnI levels injected into healthy mice, as well as endogenously elevated cTnI in a double-knockout mouse model of coronary artery disease, demonstrating its capability in continuous protein monitoring and identifying coronary artery disease cohorts.

Article.Title: The interferon-gamma response pathway is a targetable driver of FSHD muscular dystrophy progression
Article.Authors: Biferali B.; Del Prete F.; Salomè M.; Garcia Manteiga J.; Alemohammad R.; Mombellardo M.; Pannese M.; Mocciaro E.; Torri F.; Eren İ.; Ferraro E.; Ballikaya D.; Ciurli B.; Votta A.; Campolungo D.; Turner D.; Canepari M.; Bottinelli R.; Siciliano G.; Eraslan S.; Ricci G.; Gabellini D.
Article.Abstract: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) is a leading neuromuscular disorder caused by the aberrant expression of the transcription factor double homeobox 4 (DUX4) in skeletal muscle. While DUX4 is normally restricted to early embryonic development, its reactivation in FSHD triggers chronic inflammation and progressive muscle degeneration. However, the precise molecular links between DUX4 and persistent immune activation remain poorly understood. Here, we show that DUX4 induces a viral mimicry-like pathway that is fundamentally uncoupled from canonical type I interferon (IFN) activation. Instead, DUX4 establishes a non-canonical innate immune state dominated by IFN-γ signaling, providing a mechanistic explanation for the non-resolving inflammation characteristic of the disease. We demonstrate that while IFN-γ treatment alone is sufficient to recapitulate key DUX4 pathogenic effects, its inhibition rescues muscle inflammation and halts disease progression in FSHD models. These findings define a “skewed viral mimicry” process driven by a disease-specific transcription factor and identify IFN-γ as a primary therapeutic target for tissue-informed immunomodulation in muscular dystrophy.

Article.Title: GenNA: Conditional generation of nucleotide sequences guided by natural language annotations
Article.Authors: Shen Y.; Cao G.; Wu J.; Chen D.; Feng C.; Chen M.
Article.Abstract: Deciphering the mapping between biomolecular sequences and complex biological functions is a central challenge in genomics. While existing generative nucleotide models capture sequence distributions, they lack explicit access to gene-associated biological semantics, limiting semantics-guided design. Here, we present GenNA, a generative nucleotide foundation model guided by natural language annotations. Pretrained on a multimodal nucleotide-text corpus spanning 2221 eukaryotic species (∼416 billion characters), GenNA internalizes relationships between sequence syntax and functional semantics within a unified autoregressive framework. Without explicit rule-based supervision, GenNA yields distinguishable perplexity responses to sequence-annotation mismatches, mutational variants, and species-label perturbations. Furthermore, across diverse generation tasks, GenNA produces statistically plausible nucleotide sequences consistent with target semantics, structural constraints, and species contexts. Overall, GenNA provides a versatile framework for controllable nucleotide generation, establishing a practical route to integrate functional descriptions with sequence design.

Article.Title: Interband connectivity and climate shaped Neanderthal extinction and Homo sapiens ’ dispersal
Article.Authors: Vidal-Cordasco M.; Rodríguez-Gómez G.; Marín-Arroyo A.
Article.Abstract: To what extent Neanderthal extinction was triggered by climate change or the arrival of Homo sapiens , and by which mechanisms, remains unresolved. Here, on the basis of climate-driven changes in habitat favorability for primary and secondary consumers and in net primary productivity, we estimate carrying capacity, herbivore biomass, and intraguild predation pressure during the time Neanderthals and H. sapiens lived in Europe. These spatially explicit estimates were incorporated into an agent-based model simulating human demographic dynamics under various scenarios. Results indicate that carrying capacity changes cannot explain Neanderthal extinction at a continental scale, though they are essential to understanding spatiotemporal distribution patterns of both human species. Conversely, the arrival of H. sapiens remarkably increased Neanderthal extinction likelihood. Because of the successive demographic expansions and contractions, group connectivity emerges as the key factor shaping population stability in both species. These findings support that Neanderthal disappearance and H. sapiens dispersals were interconnected demographic processes.

Article.Title: Cross-domain encoding models reveal shared and domain-specific neural representations across language and mathematics
Article.Authors: Nakai T.; Kubo R.; Nishimoto S.
Article.Abstract: Whether language and mathematics rely on shared or distinct neural representations remains unresolved in cognitive neuroscience. Here, we combined latent features from a large language model with functional magnetic resonance imaging encoding models to test cross-domain generalization in 32 participants performing sentence comprehension and calculation tasks. Cross-domain prediction identified cortical regions showing partially shared representations, most consistently in the left area 55b, while control analyses suggested that these effects could not be fully explained by low-level visual or task-general factors. Domain-specificity contrasts revealed stronger language-related prediction in the left superior temporal sulcus and angular gyrus and math-related prediction in the left precentral sulcus and bilateral intraparietal sulci. Model-weight analyses revealed distinct weight profiles associated with shared and domain-specific prediction patterns. Cross-domain regions also exhibited task-dependent functional coupling with language- and math-related networks. Together, these findings suggest that language and mathematics involve partially shared neural representations alongside domain-specific cortical organization, helping reconcile previous contrasting views on their neural basis.

Article.Title: Bionic skin with hair follicle regeneration capability from acoustic fluids-mediated 3D printing
Article.Authors: Cao X.; He R.; Wu Z.; Zhao Y.
Article.Abstract: Tissue engineering holds substantial potential for constructing normal skin with appendages such as hair follicles, directly restoring skin’s complete physiological functions. The current challenge lies in recreating biomimetic hair follicle organs with high-level cell density and architecture. Here, we developed an acoustofluidic-assisted 3D bioprinting platform to fabricate bionic skins with efficient hair follicle regeneration capability. Pre-formed hair follicle germs, derived from co-cultured epidermal and dermal mesenchymal stem cells, were encapsulated within a hydrogel bioink. Controlled acoustic fields generated flow vortices that directed cell migration and promoted organized cellular assembly from initially disordered states. Guided cell aggregates were then patterned through bioprinting to construct a grid-structured bionic skin. This architecture provided stable 3D support while maintaining high porosity, enabling efficient gas exchange. The printed bionic skin exhibited well-organized spatial cell distribution, high cellular viability, and promising differentiation potential. Further in vivo experiments demonstrated the efficiency of the bionic skin in accelerating mature hair regeneration, showing promise for clinical alopecia treatment.

Article.Title: Hierarchical interfacial anchoring for durable perovskite solar cells
Article.Authors: Wu J.; Wu H.; Zhang Z.; Guan X.; Zhao J.; Guo Y.; Li Z.; Li Z.; Ma T.; Tang Y.; Li Z.; Zuo W.; Pascual J.; Hou B.; Yang F.; Pan X.; Wang Y.; Wang L.; Deng L.; Li G.; Sapienza L.; Abate A.; Li M.
Article.Abstract: Although inverted perovskite solar cells now deliver certified efficiencies approaching their single-junction limits, their practical deployment remains constrained by the thermo-mechanical fragility of buried interfaces under realistic temperature fluctuations. Here, we identify thermo-mechanically driven, stress-accumulation-dominated adhesion failure at self-assembled monolayer-based buried interfaces as a critical failure mode in inverted perovskite solar cells. To address this issue, we propose an interfacial robustness design strategy based on a homometallic halide pretreatment, which constructs a chemically compatible and highly anchorable interfacial environment on transparent conductive oxides to guide the ordered assembly of SAMs. This interfacial treatment increases the density of surface hydroxyl species and enables hierarchical multipoint interfacial anchoring dominated by metal-oxygen coordination, with Cl − induced hydrogen-bonding interactions acting cooperatively, thereby enhancing anchoring robustness and improving tolerance to thermo-mechanical stress accumulation. With this interfacial strategy, the devices achieve a power conversion efficiency of 27.3% (26.9% certified) and retain 94% of their initial efficiency after 400 temperature cycles between −40 and 85°C (ISOS-T-3). These results demonstrate that rational regulation of buried interfacial anchoring architectures can simultaneously enhance device efficiency and long-term operational reliability, offering a viable pathway toward high-efficiency and durable perovskite photovoltaics.

Article.Title: Hydrogen radical-participating spatiotemporal sequential therapy via hypoxia aggravation for hypoxia-amplified immunotherapy
Article.Authors: Peng J.; Wang H.; Li Z.; Xu J.; Du Z.; Cheng N.; Li W.; Na Y.; Hou D.; Xu Y.; Yang X.; Tan Y.; Sun D.; Cheng H.; Tao W.
Article.Abstract: The hypoxic characteristics of the tumor microenvironment and endogenous antioxidant defenses compromise the efficacy of oxygen-consuming oxidative therapy, positioning oxygen-free reductive stress as a new paradigm in tumor treatment. Nevertheless, the immunosuppressive characteristics of hypoxia and reductive stress pose significant challenges for advancing reductive stress-induced immunotherapy. Here, we constructed a hydrogen radical (H•) generator synergistically activated by near-infrared light and thiols, and first elucidated that photocatalytic H•-mediated reductive stress can elicit a robust antitumor immune response via the H•-featured mechanism. Nanoplatform HA@UFTL was engineered using lactate oxidase as an ideal H• partner, with the synergistic contribution enabling cross-amplified antitumor immunotherapy. The H•-participating spatiotemporal sequential strategy highlights a triple spatiotemporal sequential cascade, including dual sequential hypoxia exacerbation, sequential oxidative-reductive stress, and sequential organelle damage. By aggravating rather than alleviating hypoxia, HA@UFTL overcomes immunosuppression induced by hypoxia and reductive stress with H• as a universal building block, providing new insights for hypoxia-based immunotherapy.

Article.Title: Non-invasive, high-precision, and independently controllable neuromodulation via optimized multiple temporal interference stimulation
Article.Authors: Jo K.; Kim Y.; Son Y.; Won J.; Jeon W.; Kwon J.; Choi H.; Park Y.; Kim J.; Park S.
Article.Abstract: Non-invasive neuromodulation is an important approach in clinical and translational neuroscience, yet existing techniques remain limited in precisely and flexibly targeting spatially distributed brain regions. Temporal interference stimulation (TIS) enabled non-invasive selective targeting; however, conventional implementations lack sufficient spatial focality, steerability, and scalability for network-level modulation. Here, we introduce optimized multiple temporal interference stimulation (omTIS), a computationally optimized framework that achieves high spatial focality, flexible steerability, and scalable control for distributed neuromodulation. Using a multi-electrode architecture, finite element analysis (FEA)–based optimization, and carefully selected multiple carrier frequencies, omTIS generates focal interference envelopes that can be positioned across multiple brain targets, enabling simultaneous and independently controllable multi-focal stimulation with minimal mutual interference. Across simulations, tissue-mimicking phantom experiments, and in vivo mouse studies, omTIS outperformed conventional TIS in spatial selectivity, steering flexibility, and cross-talk-free multi-focal modulation. These results establish omTIS as a scalable platform for precise, non-invasive control of distributed brain networks.

Article.Title: Phonon-assisted endothermic triplet sensitization enables record NIR-II-to-visible-light photon upconversion
Article.Authors: Chang K.; Wong P.; Gong S.; Sergeev A.; Li K.; Wong K.; Chen X.; Lu H.
Article.Abstract: Near-infrared-to-visible triplet−triplet annihilation photon upconversion (TTA-UC) enables harvesting low-energy photons; however, extending nanocrystal-sensitized TTA-UC into the second near-infrared window (NIR-II) remains challenging because triplet sensitization is thermodynamically disfavored under sub-triplet excitation. Here, we demonstrate that lead-free AgBiS 2 nanocrystals facilitate phonon-assisted endothermic triplet sensitization, enabling efficient NIR-II-to-visible upconversion. Under the sub-bandgap single-photon excitation, AgBiS 2 nanocrystals exhibit anti-Stokes photoluminescence, suggesting strong exciton−phonon coupling mediated by surface states. When coupled with 5-tetracene carboxylic acid transmitters and rubrene annihilators, AgBiS 2 achieves 980 nm-to-visible upconversion with a record quantum yield of 6.22% (normalized to 100%) and an anti-Stokes shift of 0.95 eV. Time-resolved photoluminescence and ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy support a surface-state-mediated uphill energy-transfer pathway coupled to low-frequency vibrational modes. Our work establishes phonon-assisted triplet sensitization as a strategy to overcome the NIR-II red wall for lead-free photon upconversion.

Article.Title: Environment-adaptive molecular neural networks enabled by heterogeneous threshold DNA neuron
Article.Authors: Xiong X.; Xu W.; Li N.; Xing S.; Huang Z.; Chen J.; Li L.; Zhu T.; Pei H.
Article.Abstract: Molecular neural networks enable autonomous information processing in biochemical environments, yet most existing DNA-based implementations operate with fixed connectivity after assembly, limiting their ability to adapt network topology to changing environments. Here, we report an environment-adaptive molecular neural network enabled by DNA neurons with sequence-programmed, heterogeneous activation thresholds. These neurons incorporate triplex-based proton-gated DNA switches with tunable pH-response windows, which regulate the accessibility of toehold and recognition domains to switch pre-encoded weighted connections between inactive and signal-propagating states, thereby reconfiguring network connectivity without changing molecular composition. We demonstrate this principle in a DNA neural network that processes 64-bit inputs, where environmental acidification activates dormant neurons and reconfigures the computational topology from a sparse convolutional neural network for coarse two-class categorization into a fully connected neural network for fine-grained discrimination among four distinct patterns. Our results establish DNA-based neural circuits capable of adapting their computational architecture to environmental cues, offering a framework for molecular information processing in fluctuating biochemical environments.

Article.Title: Recovery and resurrection of chiral homogeneous catalysts for closed-loop recycling
Article.Authors: Liu S.; Arafah N.; Huang J.; LaPierre E.; Curtis D.; Li J.; Reid J.; Bregent T.; Arseniyadis S.; Leitch D.
Article.Abstract: Homogeneous catalysis by transition metal complexes is essential for chemical synthesis; however, these processes remain unsustainable because the catalysts are generally not recovered. We address this problem with a framework for closed-loop catalyst recycling. This approach centers on two chemical processes: stasis, where catalytic activity is selectively halted while retaining molecular integrity; and anastasis, where full catalytic function is restored. We apply this framework to recycle chiral palladium catalysts used for asymmetric allylic alkylation. ortho -Quinone oxidants drive the catalyst to converge on a discrete Pd II complex that is readily recovered, while mild reductants regenerate active Pd 0 precatalysts in a subsequent step. By rendering catalyst deactivation, isolation, and reactivation chemically addressable, this work is an important step toward circular, resource-efficient synthesis.

Article.Title: SeqA-mediated sister loci cohesion regulates the efficiency and fidelity of DNA double-strand break repair across the E. coli genome
Article.Authors: Singh D.; Faraz A.; Khan N.; Babu J.; Sankar T.; Bates D.; Joshi M.
Article.Abstract: In Escherichia coli , SeqA-mediated cohesion at snap loci on the right replichore persists longer, but its role in DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair remains untested. Here, we show that site-specific DSBs at snap loci confer higher cell survival than nonsnap loci. With perturbations affecting sister cohesion [Δ seqA , topoisomerase IV overexpression (T4-OE)], this survival advantage was progressively reduced, with the combined Δ seqA T4-OE strain retaining only a transient advantage. The increased survival correlates with faster repair, reflected by rapid restoration of locus copy number and shorter-lived, thinner RecA–green fluorescent protein filaments. Consistent with more accurate repair, snap loci exhibited lower mutation accumulation under normal and antibiotic stress conditions. Comparative genome analysis of E. coli strains revealed higher GATC motif counts and higher sequence conservation. Together, these findings suggest that the chromosomal organization associated with prolonged sister cohesion at snap loci promotes efficient homologous recombination–mediated DSB repair and contributes to genome conservation.

Article.Title: Evolution of MEIS transcription factor activity during metazoan neural development—born to be wild
Article.Authors: Fedarenchik P.; Polevoy H.; Volovik Y.; Aamar E.; Mahroum M.; Barshad G.; Salzberg A.; Frank D.
Article.Abstract: Meis TALE-class proteins pattern vertebrate neural tissue, inducing hindbrain and neural crest in Xenopus laevis embryos. Meis orthologs have two conserved regions: (i) Meis-specific domain and (ii) Meis-specific TALE homeodomain. Meis homeodomain proteins are present in “ancient” metazoans-eucaryotes like cnidarians, placozoans, and protozoans. We asked: When during metazoan evolution did Meis proteins acquire functionality to induce neural pattern? Using structure-function analysis in Xenopus , we show that the Meis-specific and Meis homeodomains suffice to induce the spinal cord but not the hindbrain. Meis proteins share a functionally conserved carboxyl-terminal transcription activation domain inducing the hindbrain. Ancient Meis proteins from Trichoplax and chlorophyte algae have a conserved Meis homeodomain, but lack the Meis-specific domain. Unexpectedly, these ancestral proteins robustly induce hindbrain and neural crest in Xenopus , unlike metazoan proteins requiring the Meis-specific domain. Thus, in early eukaryotes, Meis prototypes were “born to be wild,” having the intrinsic capacity to induce vertebrate structures like hindbrain and neural crest, despite predating them.

Article.Title: Structural basis of Anopheles mosquito salivary protein complexes implicated in malaria transmission
Article.Authors: Su T.; Liu S.; Williams A.; Calvo E.; Zhou Z.
Article.Abstract: Successful malaria transmission by Anopheles mosquitoes depends on Plasmodium development within the mosquito midgut and subsequent sporozoite invasion of its salivary glands. Salivary proteins, notably Saglin and likely salivary gland surface proteins (SGS4 and SGS5), were suggested to play roles in these processes, but the lack of their structures has hindered our understanding of the underlying molecular mechanisms. In this study, we carried out biochemical and mass spectrometry analyses of salivary gland extracts and demonstrate that Anopheles gambiae SGS4 and SGS5 bind Saglin and other SG1 (salivary gland 1) proteins. Cryo-EM structure of the Saglin-SGS4 complex reveals that Saglin homodimerizes through coiled-coil interactions and disulfide bonds and engages longitudinally with SGS4. Comparisons among SG1-SGS complexes show that SG1 proteins share a conserved architecture, and SGS proteins adapt conformationally to bind different SG1 partners of varying lengths. Article.Title: Psychedelics shift decision strategies and reconfigure orbitofrontal dynamics
Article.Authors: Delgado-Sallent C.; Ahmed S.; Khawaja-Lopez A.; Lee B.; Mishra U.; Senne R.; Ramirez S.; Scott B.
Article.Abstract: Psychedelics such as psilocybin and ketamine are attracting renewed attention as rapid-acting therapeutics, yet how they reshape cognitive computations remains poorly understood. Calcium imaging showed that OFC population dynamics were reorganized under psychedelic conditions, with preserved task selectivity but altered temporal structure and shifted population correlations. Article.Title: Self-assembly of bacterial volumetric patterns directed by a synthetic reaction-diffusion circuit
Article.Authors: Wu F.; He C.; Bayakhmetov S.; Harris D.; Fang X.; Baez J.; Ohnmacht S.; Zhang Q.; Chen X.; Allison K.; Kuang Y.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Reaction-diffusion (RD) has long been proposed as a mechanism underlying biological pattern formation. Here, we engineered a synthetic gene circuit, MINPAC, that couples gene expression regulation (reaction) with bacterial colony expansion and quorum sensing (diffusion) to guide bacterial cells to self-organize into periodic volumetric patterns across multiple scales, from single cells to three-dimensional colonies. Mathematical modeling supports a clock-and-wavefront mechanism, where oscillatory gene expression interacts with outward expanding diffusions to generate these periodic spatial structures. Guided by model predictions, we further show that pattern complexity can be systematically tuned by gene dosage, with lower expression levels favoring multiple rings through faster dynamics. Article.Title: Dynamic nuclear pores dictate the emergence of lamina-associated domains and UV protection during embryogenesis
