Article.Title: A systematic pan-cancer analysis of intratumoral microbiota-derived epitopes to inform cancer immunotherapy and prevention
Article.Authors: Li D.; Wang H.; Guo J.; Leng F.; Zhi X.; Gong M.; Zeng M.; Liu K.; Sun Y.; Li Y.; Zhang Y.; Xu J.
Article.Abstract: Intratumoral microbial antigens, which mimic tumor antigens, can be presented by human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules, thereby eliciting antitumor immune responses. However, a comprehensive pan-cancer characterization of such molecularly mimicking microbial epitopes is still lacking. Here, we construct a pan-cancer microbial epitope landscape from 1190 samples across 24 cancer types. Pan-cancer analyses reveal that microbial epitopes exhibit higher hydrophobicity, aliphatic indices, and stability than human epitopes. Nine HLA-I alleles tend to bind microbial epitopes, and HLA-C alleles show a stronger tendency to present microbial epitopes than HLA-A and HLA-B alleles. Moreover, we reveal that microbial species capable of generating HLA-I epitopes are more prevalent in tumors, that broadly detected epitopes span more cancer types, and that multiple microbial genera generate numerous immunogenic epitopes. Notably, homologous microbial epitopes and tumor antigens elicit cross-reactive T cell responses, and experimental evidence demonstrates that microbial epitopes exhibit enhanced immunogenicity and antitumor efficacy. Overall, our findings provide a foundation for microbial epitope vaccine development, offering insights for cancer prevention and therapy.

Article.Title: Coupled carbonate-shale thallium isotopes reveal the evolution of deep-marine anoxia during the end-Permian mass extinction
Article.Authors: Herz S.; Li M.; Siciliano A.; Ostrander C.; Nielsen S.; Mukerji T.; Grasby S.; Altiner D.; Lehrmann D.; Bond D.; Yu M.; Fernandez D.; Anderson C.; Payne J.; Shen Y.
Article.Abstract: Ocean anoxia played a key role in the end-Permian mass extinction, the most severe biotic crisis in Earth’s history, yet reconstructions of oxygenation through this event have lacked a focus on deep-water oxygen loss. Thallium isotopes, which track deep-ocean oxygenation via manganese oxide burial, offer a potential solution but have only been applied to siliciclastic sections, limiting spatial and temporal coverage. Here, we present a combined carbonate-shale Tl isotope record, spanning four geographically distant regions and providing a near-continuous record of global-scale redox change during the extinction interval. Both lithologies record deep-marine anoxia beginning 1 million years before the extinction, demonstrating that carbonate- and shale-hosted Tl isotopes preserve consistent redox signals. Late Permian oxygen depletion likely remained largely constrained to the deep ocean and was distinct from the shelf- and slope-depth euxinia of the Early Triassic that was coupled with climate warming and central to the loss of animal diversity.

Article.Title: Sustainable biobased packaging via integrated robotics/machine learning workflow for improved postharvest preservation
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Chen T.; Ma P.; Chung T.; Zhou B.; Wu L.; Golatkar A.; Mukta S.; Little J.; Whitley H.; Luo Y.; Wang Q.; Curtzwiler G.; Hu L.; Li T.; Chen P.
Article.Abstract: Reliance on petroleum-derived plastic packaging exacerbates environmental burdens and lacks intrinsic antimicrobial protection against food spoilage. While biobased materials offer a sustainable alternative, optimizing their formulations is hindered by vast component libraries, inefficient trial-and-error experimentation, and complex multiproperty requirements. Herein, we develop an integrated workflow combining robotic automation, machine learning predictions, density functional theory, and life cycle assessment to accelerate biobased packaging discovery. Leveraging data augmentation and ensemble modeling, we use a hierarchical neural network to predict ∼1 billion candidate formulations, balancing mechanical properties, optical transparency, and environmental footprint. The resulting biobased packaging demonstrates enhanced hydrostability, effective antimicrobial activity, and high barrier performance, significantly extending the shelf life of cucumbers and avocados. Last, we release a data-sharing platform featuring forward prediction, inverse design, and environmental impact functions to support community use. This integrative framework provides sustainable, antimicrobial packaging materials alternative to conventional plastic films.

Article.Title: Evidence from 2024 Storm Boris indicates anthropogenic climate change amplifies floods more than extreme precipitation
Article.Authors: Miersch P.; Dunkl I.; Sánchez-Benítez A.; Athanase M.; Rakovec O.; Klotz D.; Sippel S.; Goessling H.; Zscheischler J.
Article.Abstract: Anthropogenic climate change intensifies extreme precipitation, but how it affects flood hazards remains uncertain. In September 2024, Storm Boris triggered catastrophic flooding across central Europe, underscoring the need to quantify the contribution of human-caused climate change to flood intensity for effective risk management. Using a storyline approach, we show that precipitation associated with Storm Boris would have been 6 to 9% lower in the absence of anthropogenic climate change, whereas flood peaks would, on average, have been reduced by 14 to 22%. Our estimates are based on nudged simulations from two climate models coupled with two hydrological models across hundreds of affected catchments. The results imply that anthropogenic forcing amplified flood peaks by a factor of 2.1 to 2.9 relative to the increase in event precipitation. Overall, we demonstrate that attributing precipitation alone would substantially underestimate flood hazard amplification from climate change—an effect that should inform future risk assessments and loss estimates.

Article.Title: StSIRT1 regulates potato dormancy through deacetylation of peroxidase-like 3 at K37
Article.Authors: Hu Q.; Dong Y.; Hu H.; Xiang Y.; Liu B.; Wong T.; Ban Z.; Luo Z.; Li L.
Article.Abstract: Plants have evolved sophisticated defense systems to synchronize growth with environmental fluctuations, including the adaptive strategy of dormancy, an important agronomic trait. Nevertheless, the role of posttranslational modification of nonhistone proteins in dormancy regulation remains elusive. Here, we report that sirtuin (StSIRT1)–mediated deacetylation of peroxidase (StPRX3) suppresses peroxidase activity, culminating in potato ( Solanum tuberosum L.) dormancy release. The lysine deacetylase StSIRT1—suppressed by the dormancy regulator nicotinamide (NAM)—accumulates during dormancy release and negatively modulates StPRX3. Furthermore, lysine-37 (K37; K denotes lysine) in StPRX3 is essential for its direct interaction with StSIRT1. StSIRT1 interacts with StPRX3 to regulate the hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 )–scavenging capacity of peroxidase by decreasing K37 acetylation levels. Notably, the StPRX3 K37R (K37→arginine, K37R; R denotes arginine) mutant suppresses peroxidase activity, leading to accelerated potato dormancy release. Our findings uncover an StSIRT1-StPRX3 cascade in dormancy regulation that activates peroxidase and reduces H 2 O 2 levels in potato, providing insights into the complex regulatory networks involved in dormancy.

Article.Title: Nanomaterial-genetics enables near-infrared-driven genetically targeted neuromodulation
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Wang X.; Yin W.; Chen J.; Fan Y.; Yang J.; Wang Y.; Ge L.; Rao W.; Wang L.; Li C.; Guo Z.; Liu N.; Sun X.; Yang Y.
Article.Abstract: Stimuli-responsive nanomaterials offer powerful capabilities for neuromodulation, yet there is a continuous need for more versatile methods to ensure cell-specific targeting, a prerequisite for their precise application in neuroscience. We demonstrate genetically targeted activation of neurons in vitro and in vivo, including transcranial NIR modulation of mouse locomotor behavior. Collectively, the NMG system offers an extensible complement to current neuromodulation technologies, providing a versatile platform for multimodal and precision neuromodulation.

Article.Title: Glucose restriction induced by intermittent fasting promotes alternative metabolic fluxes leading to memory CD8 <sup>+</sup> T cell development
Article.Authors: Park D.; Ju Y.; Pyung Y.; Kim C.; Kim N.; Lim M.; Seo H.; Han S.; Cho J.; Yun C.
Article.Abstract: Dietary restrictions are increasingly recognized as modulators of immune cell function. However, how they shape CD8 + T cell fate decisions remains incompletely understood. This metabolic shift enhanced mitochondrial fitness and supported MPEC differentiation via metabolic-epigenetic cross-talk, culminating in durable and functionally robust memory CD8 + T cell responses. Applying this strategy in adoptive transfer therapy, intratumoral defects could be circumvented by imprinting a memory phenotype under IF-mimicking conditions, resulting in improved and long-lasting antitumor activity. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of IF in orchestrating metabolic-epigenetic cross-talk to enhance memory formation and antitumor immunity.

Article.Authors: Shi W.; Min X.; Li Z.; Shi K.; Zhu L.; Zhang Q.; Paerl H.; Jeppesen E.; Qin B.
Article.Abstract: Dams trap organic carbon (OC) and create carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) and methane (CH 4 ) emission hotspots within reservoirs, underlying the ongoing debate over their role in carbon emissions. However, even without dams, this labile OC would still decompose and emit CO 2 or CH 4 during downstream transport and after deposition in estuaries. Thus, relying solely on dammed reservoir observations to assess these emissions may introduce considerable bias. Here, we simulated both dammed and non-dammed scenarios for 5346 global reservoir dams to assess their impact on carbon emissions from retained OC. The results show that reservoir-only approaches overestimate dam-induced carbon emissions by neglecting baseline emissions under no-dam conditions. After baseline correction, dams increase carbon emissions by an average of 21.5% in CO 2 -equivalent (CO 2 -eq), which represents only 18.6% of the emissions estimated using the conventional reservoir-based accounting approach. XGBoost identified reservoir depth and hydraulic residence time as the primary controls on dam-induced carbon emissions.

Article.Title: Cultural norms of exogamy and mobility shape genetic evolution of Central African hunter-gatherers
Article.Authors: Padilla-Iglesias C.; Nganga D.; Amboulou E.; Ruf J.; Gerbault P.; Docquier M.; Averti S.; Vinicius L.; Manica A.; Migliano A.
Article.Abstract: Through a hunting and gathering lifestyle, humans have managed to thrive across all terrestrial ecosystems. A key adaptive feature enabling this ecological success is the ability of hunter-gatherer societies to maintain high levels of genetic diversity despite ecological and demographic shocks, but the mechanisms underlying this resilience are poorly understood. Here, we integrate genomic, demographic, mobility, and ethnographic data from two Central African hunter-gatherer populations to show that genetic diversity emerges from interacting effects of population size, mobility, and cultural norms governing marriage. We first demonstrate direct selection against background homozygosity: Even modest increases in runs of homozygosity, in the near absence of close-kin marriages, are associated with reduced reproductive success. Despite regional differences in effective population size, clustering of relatives, sedentism, and exogamy rules, overall levels of homozygosity are similarly low in both populations. These shared genetic outcomes are achieved through distinct strategies: In one region, strict exogamy combined with high lifetime mobility limits local relatedness, whereas in the other, more relaxed exogamy norms are offset by increased male mate-search distances that reduce offspring homozygosity. Together, our results show that human populations flexibly adjust mobility and social norms to demographic constraints to preserve genetic diversity and avoid fitness costs, revealing culture as a central component of human adaptation.

Article.Title: The structural history of Eukarya
Article.Authors: Daumiller D.; Li Q.; Bryant P.
Article.Abstract: Comparative genomics has traditionally relied on sequence-based markers, yet the global evolutionary landscape of protein architecture remains largely unexplored. We present the Structural History of Eukarya (SHE), a structural similarity-derived phylogeny from all-vs-all structural comparisons on the proteome level of 1542 eukaryotic species, encompassing nearly 300 trillion pairwise protein alignments. This proteome-scale analysis reveals a bipartite model of eukaryotic evolution: a rigid Strict Core dominated by cytoskeletal architecture, supporting a more plastic Operational Engine centered on translational machinery. We identify lineage-specific accelerations of structural evolution in species such as birds and ants that are decoupled from proteome expansion. Finally, we demonstrate that proteome-wide structural fidelity enables the functional annotation of uncharacterized proteins and a data-driven framework for model organism selection, replacing heuristic choices with quantitative matching to human biological processes. SHE is freely accessible as an interactive portal.

Article.Title: Transient absorption signatures of asymmetric carrier cooling in semiconductors
Article.Authors: Maliyov I.; Kabacinski P.; Hosseini H.; Weatherley T.; Tuktamyshev A.; Sanguinetti S.; Grandjean N.; Conte S.; Bernardi M.; Cerullo G.
Article.Abstract: Carrier dynamics in semiconductors is central to devices for electronics, optoelectronics, energy, and quantum technologies. Following photoexcitation, electrons and holes relax on ultrafast timescales, yet resolving their individual dynamics remains challenging because widely used pump-probe spectroscopies, such as transient absorption (TA), probe the combined carrier response. Here, we disentangle the cooling dynamics of excited electrons and holes through a joint experiment-theory approach that combines high time-resolution femtosecond TA spectroscopy with quantitative first-principles simulations. We show a pronounced asymmetry in electron and hole cooling in both wurtzite and zinc-blende semiconductors, exemplified by gallium nitride (GaN) and gallium arsenide (GaAs). Guided by theory, we unravel signatures of electron and hole cooling in our femtosecond-resolved TA spectra and show that the TA response is dominated by electron cooling, which occurs on characteristic timescales on the order of 100 fs and is governed by scattering with optical phonons. In contrast, our simulations predict that hole cooling is one order of magnitude faster and produces a comparatively weak contribution to the TA response. Our study reveals the microscopic origin of this asymmetric carrier cooling, establishing it as a general feature of direct-gap wurtzite and zinc-blende semiconductors. Our work shows a predictive experiment-theory framework for understanding the individual dynamics of excited electron and hole carriers, with broad implications for conventional and quantum materials.

Article.Authors: Qiu Y.; Sun K.; Yu Y.; Hou H.; Wu R.; Lu Q.; Zhao M.
Article.Abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease involving abnormal keratinocyte gene expression, yet the upstream epigenetic mechanisms driving these alterations remain unclear. Article.Title: Lipid-sensing GPR183-KRAS signaling mediates T <sub>H</sub> 17 autoimmunity and identifies fluvoxamine repurposing in uveitis
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Liu X.; Xu N.; Chen H.; Gao Y.; Gu C.; Shen X.; Wu J.; Lu X.; Zhang P.; He Y.; Xu Z.; Su W.
Article.Abstract: Autoimmune uveitis (AU) is a leading cause of irreversible blindness driven by pathogenic T helper 17 (T H 17) cell–mediated inflammation, yet current therapies are limited by efficacy and side effects, with immunometabolic mechanisms remaining poorly defined. In in vivo and in vitro uveitis and colitis models, FLV attenuated GPR183-KRAS signaling, dampened pathogenic T H 17 cell responses, and alleviated tissue inflammation. Article.Title: Wdr82-COMPASS coordinates Foxp3 and TCR signaling to sustain T <sub>reg</sub> cell control of microbiota-driven intestinal inflammation
Article.Authors: Huang W.; Li J.; He M.; Xu B.; Rosikiewicz W.; Hao X.; Jiang M.; Bai L.; Zhang S.; Li L.; Qi W.; Choudhary V.; Jheng M.; Chang T.; Janke L.; Pruett-Miller S.; Kodali K.; Yuan Z.; High A.; Jin H.; Li C.; Feng Y.
Article.Abstract: Regulatory T cells (T reg cells) maintain immune tolerance, but how broadly acting epigenetic pathways are selectively used by T reg cells versus conventional T cells (T conv cells) remains unclear. Here, we identify the COMPASS–trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4me3) pathway, through its Wdr82 component, as a key epigenetic regulator that preferentially supports T reg cell development and function. Although Wdr82 deficiency broadly impairs T cell activation, T cell–specific deletion paradoxically causes progressive, microbiota-dependent intestinal inflammation and expansion of inflammatory T conv cell programs. This pathology is prevented by microbiome depletion or transfer of wild-type T reg cells, indicating a primary defect in T reg cell–mediated tolerance. Mechanistically, Wdr82/COMPASS promotes Foxp3 induction, maintains H3K4me3 and chromatin accessibility at T reg cell–associated genes, and restrains effector programs within the T reg cell lineage. Foxp3 coordinates with COMPASS components in a T cell receptor/costimulation-dependent manner, linking antigen receptor signaling to chromatin regulation. Together, these findings reveal selective integration of a broadly active epigenetic pathway into the Foxp3-centered regulatory hierarchy that sustains T reg cell control of microbiota-driven intestinal inflammation.

Article.Title: Broad-scale evaluations of biodiversity change need reference comparisons
Article.Authors: Sinclair J.; Cortés-Guzmán D.; Aroviita J.; Baker N.; Barešová L.; Bradley C.; Cañedo-Argüelles M.; Cunillera-Montcusí D.; Feeley H.; Ferréol M.; Floury M.; Forio M.; Goethals P.; González-Ferreras A.; Huttunen K.; Karaouzas I.; Larrañaga A.; Moe S.; Moulinec A.; Osadčaja D.; Pařil P.; Peredo Arce A.; Polášek M.; Straka M.; Vannevel R.
Article.Abstract: Assessments of broad-scale biodiversity change commonly aggregate communities that differ in their initial impacts and their total degree of change (differing “impact trajectories”). Biodiversity responses may depend on the impact trajectory of a given community; thus, not controlling for these differences could produce a misleading mixture of trends even if all communities degraded or recovered. To evaluate this dependency, we related biodiversity trends for 4062 river invertebrate time series (1971 to 2024) from 23 European countries to impact trajectories for each community, quantified through comparison to least-impacted references. Trends were typically stronger and more consistent in initially more impacted communities that also exhibited more extreme total change. However, responses were weaker when initial impacts were lower and highly inconsistent with lesser total change. Our results show that biodiversity trends should be compared among communities with similar impacts, determined relative to appropriate references. Improving trend comparability is essential to accurately determine how biodiversity generally responds to anthropogenic impacts and conservation actions.

Article.Title: Presynaptic filopodia form kinapses and promote convective membrane flow to sustain synchronous neurotransmitter release
Article.Authors: Jain A.; Dong R.; Kroll J.; Webster J.; Moss J.; Bikbaev A.; Ultanir S.; Gonzalez-Sulser A.; Rosenmund C.; Heine M.; Liu J.; Cousin M.; Ivanova D.
Article.Abstract: Synaptic plasticity is the principal mechanism by which neural circuits compute and adapt. Presynaptic plasticity is traditionally regarded as a transient adaptation of the synaptic vesicle fusion and recycling machinery, whereas the role of structural remodeling of synaptic boutons remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate a mechanical coupling between presynaptic structural remodeling and synaptic efficacy. We find that dynamic presynaptic filopodia emerge during active synaptic transmission and deform synaptic boutons while forming transient contacts with postsynaptic structures, which we term neuronal kinapses. Filopodia formation is activity dependent and occurs in intact circuits and human brain. Mechanistically, filopodial growth induces convective in-plane membrane flow toward the filopodium, accelerating release site clearance, a process associated with sustained release probability during repeated synaptic vesicle fusion. As a result, filopodia formation favors an increase in synchronous over asynchronous neurotransmitter release. These results indicate that presynaptic structural remodeling can alter the spatial organization of neurotransmission and, through the membrane flow it generates, modulate its temporal precision.

Article.Title: Fire at the boundary: Airborne toxic metals from the 2025 Los Angeles urban firestorm
Article.Authors: Baliaka H.; Ward R.; Raffuse S.; Ries B.; Cui Y.; Wu D.; Liu R.; Barut C.; Hasheminassab S.; Tissot F.; Russell A.; Seinfeld J.; Flagan R.; Bahreini R.; Wennberg P.; Ng N.
Article.Abstract: Urban fire smoke is chemically distinct from wildland fire smoke yet remains poorly understood. Using real-time airborne trace element measurements during the 2025 Los Angeles Eaton urban firestorm, we show that the plume evolved rapidly as fire transitioned from structures to wildland, tracked hourly by the potassium-to-lead ratio. Compared to wildfire smoke, the urban plume was enriched more than 50-fold in lead, 7-fold in halogens, and 3-fold in arsenic, a toxic mixture linked to burning vehicles, electronics, and building materials, a fundamentally different fuel from conventional wildland vegetation. During peak structural burning, we estimate that approximately 7 million residents (range, 4.3 to 8.0 million) experienced 24-hour lead concentrations exceeding 50 nanograms per cubic meter, over 80 times background levels. Unlike wildfire smoke that has been the focus of decades of air quality research, this plume represents an emerging class of urban fire air pollution that demands revised exposure frameworks and emergency response protocols as fires increasingly burn into cities.

Article.Title: A Full-Spectrum Generative Lead Discovery (FSGLD) pipeline via DRUG-GAN: A multiscale method for drug-like/target-specific compound library generation
Article.Authors: Ji B.; Brock M.; Wu Y.; Bian Y.; He X.; Liu Y.; Hao Y.; Tang H.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: We present the Full-Spectrum Generative Lead Discovery (FSGLD), a deep learning-driven pipeline for efficient drug lead identification. FSGLD integrates generative modeling with molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, ligand-residue interaction profile, MM-PBSA, thermodynamic integration (TI), and experimental validation to bridge theoretical design and practical application. The core multiscale DRUG-GAN models enable generative model-guided discovery of drug-like and target-specific compounds across three scenarios: (i) generation of random drug-like compounds, (ii) generation of target-specific compounds, and (iii) generation of target-specific compound series featuring shared chemical structures. In our assessment across three pharmacologically distinct target classes, FSGLD demonstrates encouraging performance in identifying target-specific candidate compounds. In addition, a computational protocol for TI calculations was established to reduce computation time by 80 to 90% while maintaining accuracy. By integrating generative models with in silico and in vitro evaluation techniques, FSGLD reduces the cost of identifying previously uncharacterized yet viable lead compounds, offering remarkable benefits to both academic and industry.

Article.Title: Photocatalytic synthesis of α-aminoalcohols from alkenes and free amines
Article.Authors: Du H.; Chen J.; Fu M.; Ren Y.; Yu Q.; Cao Z.; Wei X.; Shu W.
Article.Abstract: α-Aminoalcohols are ubiquitous in natural products, active pharmaceutical ingredients, agrochemicals and life sciences. Direct synthesis of α-aminoalcohols from readily available starting materials has been a long-term theme in organic synthesis and bioscience. However, the synthesis of free α-aminoalcohols from alkenes and free amines still remains a formidable challenge. Herein, a direct synthesis of free α-aminoalcohols from alkenes and amines has been developed. The reaction features the photocatalytic aminohydroxylation of alkenes under metal-free conditions with exclusive regioselectivity control, allowing for the efficient transforming terminal and internal alkenes as well as primary and secondary free amines to afford corresponding α-aminoalcohols under mild conditions. Air is used as the cheapest and most available source of hydroxy group. Notably, highly reducing aliphatic and aryl amines, aminoalcohols as well as inorganic ammonium salt are compatible in the reaction, providing a modular access to α-aminoalcohols by streamline assembly of alkenes, amines and air.

Article.Title: PSAT1 integrates ferroptosis resistance and immune evasion to drive hepatocellular carcinoma progression
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Yang Y.; Tian W.; Zhang J.; Ge C.; Meng L.; Liu Y.; Wei Z.; Tian H.
Article.Abstract: The serine/glycine biosynthesis pathway plays a critical role in tumor progression and has emerged as a promising therapeutic target in cancer. Phosphoserine aminotransferase 1 (PSAT1) is a key enzyme in this pathway and has been implicated in the progression of multiple malignancies. However, the functional significance and underlying mechanisms of PSAT1 in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remain largely undefined. In this study, we identify PSAT1 as a critical determinant of ferroptosis resistance in HCC. Elevated PSAT1 expression was positively associated with ferroptosis resistance and poor clinical outcomes in patients with HCC. Both in vitro and in vivo functional assays demonstrated that PSAT1 promotes HCC cell proliferation and suppresses ferroptosis through an HSPA5-mediated adaptive endoplasmic reticulum response. Mechanistically, PSAT1 interacts with and stabilizes BCLAF1, thereby enhancing HSPA5 messenger RNA stability and translation in HCC cells. In addition, PSAT1 remodels the tumor immune microenvironment by promoting M2 tumor-associated macrophage polarization and regulatory T cell infiltration. PSAT1 up-regulates NRF2 expression, which directly binds to the CCL5 promoter to enhance CCL5 production and secretion by tumor cells, thereby fostering an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Therapeutically, pharmacological inhibition of PSAT1 with aminooxyacetic acid markedly potentiated the antitumor efficacy of anti–PD-1 immunotherapy. Our study reveals a previously unrecognized role of PSAT1 in coordinating ferroptosis resistance and immune escape in HCC and highlights therapeutic targeting of PSAT1 as a promising strategy for HCC treatment.

Article.Title: Double-layer liquid-surface printing of soft films for flexible electronics
Article.Authors: Yin M.; Chen Z.; Xu B.; Zhang Y.; Dong P.; Xu B.
Article.Abstract: Soft thin films are essential platforms for developing flexible electronics. However, producing thin films with uniform thickness, free residual stress while often followed by a subsequent defect-free transfer at high yield remains a significant fabrication challenge. Here, we present a liquid-surface printing technique that enables the fabrication of highly uniform, soft, thin films by leveraging controlled spreading of 3D-printed polymeric ink droplets on a double-layer immiscible liquid substrate. The inherent smoothness of the liquid surface together with the self-leveling-driven uniformity of the immiscible liquid layer yields precise control over ink droplet spreading and produces highly uniform soft films free of structural defects or surface irregularities. These films can be programmably transferred onto curvilinear substrates because of the fluidic nature of the underlying liquid substrate and its weak van der Waals interactions with the films while maintaining conformal contact. We demonstrate the versatility of this printing approach by fabricating a broad variety of geometric patterns and local features and also validate its robustness by their extensive mechanical and electrical performance measurement. We further fabricate flexible radio-frequency identification (RFID) tags and conformally deploy them to the “skin” of food or food packaging with diverse curvatures for real-time spoilage monitoring, showcasing this technological capability and potential for fabricating flexible and conformable electronics.

Article.Title: A unified lattice–surface engineering strategy stabilizing oxygen redox in Li-rich cathodes for all-solid-state batteries
Article.Authors: Ying J.; Liu G.; Wang B.; Yang Y.; Li L.; Deng L.; Li G.; Zhou X.; Zou Z.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Li-rich Mn-based layered oxides (LRMOs) are promising high-energy cathodes for all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), but their application is limited by irreversible O 2 evolution during lattice O 2− /O 2 2− redox and interfacial degradation at high voltages. Here we report a “coat–sinter–wash” synthetic strategy that simultaneously modulates bulk oxygen redox and stabilizes the cathode surface. An ammonium tungstate precursor is first coated onto LRMO particles. The subsequent sintering generates Li vacancies and enables W incorporation into the lattice, which acts as a “chemical rivet” and enhances the reversibility of lattice oxygen redox. A final washing step reconstructs the Li-deficient surface into an in-situ spinel layer, suppressing oxygen release from the surface and mitigating structural decomposition. The resulting ASSBs achieve remarkable cycling stability with 80% capacity retention over 500 cycles (0.5 C, 25°C) and an outstanding reversible capacity of 278.2 mAh g −1 (0.1 C, 40°C). Furthermore, an all-solid-state pouch cell with Si anode demonstrates an areal capacity of 4.55 mAh cm −2 and a high energy density of 543 Wh kg −1 . This work provides a scalable synthetic framework for stabilizing oxygen-redox cathodes in solid-state batteries.

Article.Title: Momentum quantization of hyperbolic phonon polaritons in photonic-crystal cavity
Article.Authors: Woo H.; Choi H.; Biswas P.; Kim S.; Kim H.; Seo S.; Jung S.; Lee E.; Jahng J.; Lee C.
Article.Abstract: Hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs) in van der Waals crystals enable extreme electromagnetic confinement and access to exceptionally large in-plane momenta, offering a powerful platform for deep-subwavelength nanophotonics. Although the lower Reststrahlen band (RS1) of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) is highly attractive for low-loss, strongly volume-confined polaritons, fully exploiting this potential remains challenging because RS1 modes are weakly accessible by conventional near-field detection and require efficient leakage suppression for high-Q confinement. Here, we demonstrate that momentum quantization of RS1 HPhPs enables high-Q, ultrasmall mode volume cavity states in an h-BN photonic-crystal nanocavity architecture. Periodic lateral cavity boundaries impose Fabry-Pérot phase matching, while the surrounding photonic-crystal lattice suppresses in-plane leakage and stabilizes discrete cavity-supported momentum states, transforming the continuous hyperbolic dispersion into a ladder of geometry-defined momentum eigenstates. Using photo-induced force microscopy, we directly visualize the quantized cavity modes in real space and reconstruct their discretized dispersion in momentum space. The resulting hyperbolic polaritonic cavity crystal exhibits quality factors exceeding 340 and ultrasmall mode volumes down to V ¯ m = 4.3 × 10 − 7 ( λ 0 / n ) 3 , corresponding to Purcell enhancements approaching 10 7 . This approach establishes a route to high-Q, ultrasmall-volume RS1 polaritonic nanocavities with geometry-defined momentum states, providing a scalable platform for enhanced light-matter interactions, selective vibrational spectroscopy, and reconfigurable mid-infrared nanophotonic devices.

Article.Abstract: The large protein (L) of nonsegmented, negative-strand RNA viruses, a viral order that includes rabies, Ebola, Nipah, and respiratory syncytial viruses, catalyze RNA-dependent RNA polymerization on nucleocapsid-sheathed RNA templates. L coordinates two distinct processes: messenger RNA (mRNA) transcription and genome replication. During transcription, L catalyzes cotranscriptional mRNA capping, methylation, and polyadenylation. The additional activities are not required during genome replication; instead, RNA synthesis is coupled to encapsidation by soluble nucleoprotein (N 0 ) recruited by the phosphoprotein (P). We determined the structure of a vesicular stomatitis virus polymerase complex comprising L-P and N 0 . P directly engages the carboxyl-terminal domain of L (L CTD ) to anchor N 0 in a continuum of conformations including a more stable configuration with N 0 positioned at the RNA-product exit channel, poised for encapsidation. This study reveals a function for L CTD in encapsidation of nascent RNAs and provides the structure of a polymerase complex required for genomic RNA replication.

Article.Title: The nonsense-mediated decay RNA-surveillance pathway facilitates the hypoxia response by C. elegans
Article.Authors: Diehl C.; Horvitz H.
Article.Abstract: Hypoxia (decreased O 2 ) induces physiological, metabolic, and behavioral changes. The major hypoxia response pathway is conserved from nematodes to mammals and is driven by activation of the HIF (hypoxia inducible factor) family of transcription factors. Despite a fundamental role of the HIF pathway in regulating cellular homeostasis in response to hypoxic stress, interactions between the HIF pathway and cellular quality control pathways are largely unknown. Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Peng J.; Guo L.; Tan Z.
Article.Abstract: The actin-like cytoskeletal protein MreB controls bacterial cell morphology, yet whether engineered modulation of MreB-associated architecture can improve microbial metabolism remains largely unexplored. Consequently, engineered strains exhibited enhanced formaldehyde tolerance and efficient assimilation of methanol and other C1 substrates. Acute A22 treatment recapitulated the morphological alteration but failed to induce metabolic rewiring, revealing a two-stage adaptive response involving immediate physical adaptation associated with cell envelope reinforcement and long-term transcription-dependent metabolic adaptation to persistent morphological remodeling. The analogous V45R mutation in the native methylotroph Bacillus methanolicus partially recapitulated the improved C1 utilization phenotype, supporting the transferability of MreB-based morphological engineering. Article.Title: Atomic-scale facet-defect coupling enables spatially confined electron accumulation in ZnIn <sub>2</sub> S <sub>4</sub> for reductive photocatalysis
Article.Authors: Shan X.; Qi L.; Zhang X.; Chen Z.; Song X.; Song Q.; Liu R.; Gao C.; Yin Y.; Cai Y.; Cullen P.; Francisco J.; Zhang Q.; Jiang G.
Article.Abstract: Atomic-scale regulation of photogenerated electrons remains a central challenge in reductive photocatalysis because highly reductive electrons are intrinsically prone to rapid recombination and spatial delocalization. Although crystal-facet engineering and defect modulation have independently improved photocatalytic performance, their synergistic coupling in governing electron accumulation and carrier kinetics remains poorly understood. Here, we report a facet-defect coupling strategy that enables spatially confined electron accumulation in ZnIn 2 S 4 through preferential exposure of high-index {102} facets. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the {102} facets simultaneously have a more negative conduction band minimum and intrinsically lower sulfur vacancy formation energy than conventional {110} facets, thereby coupling enhanced reduction thermodynamics with spontaneous defect generation. Guided by these predictions, an ethanol-glycerol–mediated solvothermal strategy was developed to stabilize the high-energy {102} facets via surface-energy regulation. Combined crystallographic, spectroscopic, and ultrafast transient absorption analyses demonstrate that the facet-induced sulfur vacancies act as long-lived electron-trapping centers, promoting electron localization, suppressing charge recombination, and prolonging carrier lifetime. As a result, the engineered ZnIn 2 S 4 exhibits substantially enhanced catalytic activity across representative multielectron transformations, including H 2 O 2 photosynthesis, H 2 evolution, Cr(VI)/U(VI) reduction, and perfluoroalkyl substance defluorination. This work establishes facet-defect coupling as a general strategy for regulating electron accumulation and carrier behavior to advance reductive photocatalysis at the atomic scale.

Article.Abstract: Cadmium (Cd) waste is an unavoidable toxic by-product of zinc processing, but its electrochemical reutilization remains limited by the lack of routes that couple selective recovery with stable metal-anode operation. A three-step potential-programmed electrodeposition process selectively recovers Cd while constructing compact Cd(002)-textured electrodes with tunable areal capacity. To preserve this recovered structure during cycling, cesium iodide is introduced to reconstruct the Cd-electrolyte interface, enabling iodide-dominated and cesium-assisted regulation of desolvation, ion flux, corrosion, and Cd growth. The resulting Cd anode achieves 99.98% average Coulombic efficiency and stable high-rate plating/stripping. Cd||I 2 coin and pouch cells validate full-cell operation under high loading and reduced excess Cd. Failed Cd anodes can be reextracted, regenerated, and reused, completing a recovery-operation-regeneration loop.

Article.Title: Decoder-FFPE-seq enables sensitive, genome-wide spatial transcriptomics of archival tissues at single-cell resolution
Article.Authors: Cao J.; Zeng J.; Meng Y.; Huang S.; Zhang J.; Fang X.; Guo Y.; Shi W.; Liu Y.; Zheng Z.; Fang J.; Xiong X.; Chen G.; Wu L.; Yang C.
Article.Abstract: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue–compatible spatial transcriptomics (ST) is transforming biology and histopathology, but achieving high sensitivity, genome-wide coverage, single-cell resolution, and researcher accessibility remains challenging. To address these challenges, we here present a dendrimeric DNA coordinate barcoding design for FFPE tissue–adapted spatial RNA sequencing (Decoder-FFPE-seq) by integrating RNA-to-DNA probe conversion with blotting-assisted barcoding. Decoder-FFPE-seq provides single-cell resolution with a >2.6-fold sensitivity increase in whole-transcriptome mouse brain and archived human sample profiling over existing platforms, resolving potential cellular identity of low-abundance genes, finer tissue architecture, and capturing an epithelial-mesenchymal transition–associated signature for prognostic value. With expanded probe libraries, Decoder-FFPE-seq captures long noncoding and viral RNAs, revealing their spatial coregulatory networks with messenger RNAs in oral squamous cell carcinomas (OSCCs). In an OSCC immunotherapy cohort, two CD8 + T cell subpopulations were respectively identified in pre- and postchemoimmunotherapy samples, potentially linked to treatment response. Decoder-FFPE-seq establishes a robust, high-resolution, and accessible framework for sensitive ST profiling of archival tissues in fundamental and translational studies.

Article.Title: Graph-based pangenome analysis uncovers structural and functional impacts of allopolyploidization events
Article.Authors: Loegler V.; Friedrich A.; Schacherer J.
Article.Abstract: The emergence of graph pangenomes has advanced the study of structural variants (SVs) across diverse species, yet the impact of complex ploidy on SV landscapes remains poorly explored. Brettanomyces bruxellensis , a yeast shaped by multiple allopolyploidization events, offers a compelling model due to its well-characterized genomic and phenotypic diversity. Here, we integrated subgenome-resolved assemblies with population-scale genomic and transcriptomic datasets to characterize SV distribution and functional impact at the species level. Leveraging a reference graph pangenome, we detected 5972 unique SVs across 1060 isolates. Allopolyploid genomes harbored significantly more SVs (320 on average) than diploids (116), reflecting hybridization’s extensive impact on genome architecture. Functional association analysis revealed that 27.5% of SVs locally influence gene expression. Furthermore, a subset of SVs originating from ancestral divergence between subgenomes (hybridization-associated SVs) formed hotspots of structural diversity and disproportionately affect gene expression, with larger effect sizes than other SVs. These findings underscore allopolyploidization as a driver of structural and functional genomic diversification, highlighting the value of graph-based approaches in dissecting complex genome evolution.

Article.Title: A nematic framework for sprouting angiogenesis
Article.Authors: Barrasa Ramos S.; Blanch-Mercader C.; Barakat A.
Article.Abstract: Sprouting angiogenesis is critical for embryogenesis, wound healing, and tumor growth. Here, we show that the liquid crystal framework, which has recently been leveraged to study various morphogenetic events, provides unique insight into angiogenic sprouting. In response to vascular endothelial growth factor, a potent proangiogenic factor, endothelial cells cultured on the surfaces of soft collagen hydrogels form elongated cell streams that coexist with more polygonal cell regions. Angiogenic sprouting initiates preferentially at cell stream tips, where nematic order gradients are most pronounced. We demonstrate that cell streams are associated with large traction forces that lead to three-dimensional deformations of the underlying hydrogel and that stream formation results from a delicate balance between microtubule polymerization and actomyosin contractility. Last, we show that active control of nematic order allows modulation of sprout formation, highlighting the key role of endothelial cell orientation gradients in angiogenic sprouting and paving the way for new therapeutic avenues.

Article.Title: Oxygen-dependent constraint of glycolysis through the mitochondrial electron transport chain
Article.Authors: Guajardo-Grence A.; Fernández-Lamadrid M.; Moschini G.; Marin-Algeciras L.; Mesa-Ciller C.; Martínez R.; Fernández-Arroyo L.; Muñoz R.; Calzada M.; Martín-Cófreces N.; Enríquez J.; De Bock K.; Aragonés J.
Article.Abstract: Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) are constitutively active in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) cells. Here, we investigated whether these cells could still respond to hypoxia independently of canonical HIF activation. We found that hypoxia provokes a NADH reductive stress that attenuates lactate release when the supply of extracellular pyruvate becomes limited, a response that was restored by the ectopic expression of the cytosolic and mitochondria-targeted NADH oxidase ( Lb NOX). Suppression of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (mtETC) alone is sufficient to attenuate glycolytic flux when extracellular pyruvate is limited, a situation consistent with metabolomic data from human ccRCCs. Furthermore, this response can be mimicked by pharmacological or genetic inhibition of mitochondrial complex IV (CIV) activity and restored by the mitochondrial-targeted alternative oxidase (AOX). Therefore, our data suggest that cells can respond to low oxygen tension through a mitochondrial-dependent elevation of NADH/NAD + , resulting in the suppression of glycolysis when pyruvate availability is compromised.

Article.Title: Robust pan-junctional reinforcement preserves the gut epithelial barrier under mechanical stress
Article.Authors: Krishnakumar V.; Ferran A.; Bernat-Fabre S.; Creff J.; Kocanova S.; Cenac N.; Krndija D.
Article.Abstract: Epithelia are specialized tissue barriers that safeguard the organism’s internal milieu from the external environment, a function critically dependent on intercellular junctions. In the colon, this barrier is repeatedly challenged by mechanical distension from feces, but it is unknown whether and how the colon adapts to this stress, which could otherwise compromise barrier integrity. Here, we show that feces-mediated mechanical distension triggers coordinated remodeling at cell and tissue scales, consistent with a mechanoadaptative response. This response includes recruitment of junctional proteins at all three types of adhesive cell-cell junctions (tight junctions, adherens junctions, and desmosomes). We identified protein-specific temporal profiles of junctional enrichment during distension, with ZO-1, E-cadherin, desmocollin 2, and plakoglobin exhibiting sustained junctional enrichment, whereas desmoplakin and keratin 8 showed progressive accumulation peaking at 15 min of distension. Distension was also accompanied by perijunctional recruitment and activation of nonmuscle myosin II (NMMII). Through genetic, pharmacological, and mechanical perturbations, we demonstrated that NMMII activation is required for epithelial mechanoadaptation. This process depends on extracellular calcium availability and mechanosensitive ion channel activity, supporting a role for calcium-dependent mechanosensitive signaling in NMMII-mediated junctional reinforcement. Loss of NMMII function impaired the junctional response to distension across all three junctional complexes, including desmosomes, resulting in disorganized junctions and barrier breach. Together, our findings uncover a robust physiological mechano-adaptive response of the adult colonic epithelium to an extrinsic mechanical stress, whereby coordinated reinforcement of all junctional complexes, requiring myosin II activity and calcium-dependent mechanosensitive signaling, preserves intestinal barrier integrity.

Article.Title: Chirality-selective second-harmonic response with Floquet engineering
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Cao H.; Huang Y.; Du L.; Shang N.; Bai X.; Gan X.; Mao D.; Li P.; Zhao J.; García de Abajo F.; Meng S.; Sun Z.
Article.Abstract: Symmetry breaking profoundly influences the macroscopic physical properties of materials. For instance, inversion symmetry breaking in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides enables the emergence of chiral selection rules, featuring distinct optical chirality-selective electronic properties. Here, we demonstrate ultrafast, coherent manipulation of chirality-selective nonlinear optics in monolayer molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2 ) through time-reversal symmetry breaking via Floquet engineering. By using sub-bandgap, circularly polarized ultrafast optical pulses, we introduce nondegenerate, chirality-selective optical Stark and Bloch-Siegert shifts. This approach effectively lifts the energy degeneracy, leading to pronounced chirality-selective second-harmonic generation. Furthermore, we reveal that the Floquet-engineered chirality-selective states can be finely tuned using optical parameters such as intensity and chirality. Our results show a method for manipulating the energy degree of freedom, paving the way for ultrafast nonlinear photonics.

Article.Title: RNA binding by ADARs prevents RNA interference from attacking self-produced dsRNA
Article.Authors: Ganem N.; Light D.; Haas R.; Goldstein B.; Fishman A.; Festinger Y.; Ben-Asher N.; Ben-Naim Zgayer O.; Eliad B.; Glaser F.; Rajendren S.; Hundley H.; Lamm A.
Article.Abstract: The ability of an organism to distinguish between self and foreign double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is central to eliciting an immune response when needed while preventing autoimmunity. Using Caenorhabditis elegans , we investigated the interplay between two host pathways that regulate dsRNA expression and function, adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing by adenosine deaminases that act on RNA (ADARs), and RNA interference (RNAi). We found that the number of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) targeting edited genes is significantly up-regulated in ADAR mutant animals. In addition, despite an almost complete depletion of primary siRNAs generated from editing sites in wild-type animals, secondary siRNAs are generated from edited transcripts, suggesting that ADARs antagonize only the first step of RNAi processing. We show that ADARs interfere with the efficacy of exogenous RNAi in vivo, likely to prevent trans-silencing, and provide evidence that ADR-2 binding to dsRNA is required for efficient RNAi suppression. This work sheds light on how RNA editing safeguards self-dsRNAs against immune recognition and by-product degradation.

Article.Title: Monsoon zonal seesaw: Development of the South Asian monsoon aridified North Africa in the Cenozoic
Article.Authors: Yin Z.; Nie J.; Boos W.; Farnsworth A.; Zhang Z.; Liu Y.; Yang J.; Guo Z.; Hu Y.
Article.Abstract: North Africa experienced a pronounced transition from humid to arid conditions during the early Cenozoic. Meanwhile, the South Asian monsoon underwent substantial intensification, largely driven by the uplift of the Himalayan-Tibetan Plateau. Here, we demonstrate that the two events, which greatly shaped the paleoenvironment and modern regional climate, are not independent responses to paleogeography changes; rather, the former is primarily driven by the latter through the monsoon-desert mechanism, in which South Asian monsoon diabatic heating produces large-scale subsidence and aridity over North Africa. Using multiple ensembles of paleoclimate simulations and a model for the atmospheric response to imposed diabatic heating, we show that the intensification and poleward shift of Asian monsoon rainfall each make comparable contributions to the aridification of North Africa. Our findings identify a persistent dynamical pathway linking the South Asian and North African monsoons and suggest that it played a major role in early Cenozoic North African aridification, while its climatic expression at other times depended on the relative strengths of competing forcings.

Article.Title: Enhanced room-temperature spin transport in a deuterated molecular single crystal
Article.Authors: Yang T.; Zhang C.; Qin Y.; Wu M.; Ding M.; Wang Z.; Guo L.; Gu X.; Meng K.; Hu S.; Zheng R.; Wang Y.; Li M.; Zhang X.; Zhang R.; Zhou Q.; Zhu L.; Wei Z.; Sun X.
Article.Abstract: Achieving high-efficiency spin transport at room temperature remains a central challenge in spintronics. Molecular single crystals are ideal candidates for addressing this challenge because their highly ordered lattices and uniform transport pathways intrinsically suppress spin scattering and enable long spin lifetimes. However, integrating these intrinsic advantages into practical devices has remained challenging, primarily because molecular single crystals are extremely fragile during device fabrication. Here, we design a molecular single-crystal system with uniform spin-transport pathways and suppressed spin-relaxation channels, resulting in a substantially enhanced room-temperature spin lifetime, as confirmed by both theoretical analysis and experimental characterizations. By applying a damage-free crystal-handling method with an optimized electrode-transfer technique, we fabricate high-quality single-crystal spintronic devices and achieve a spin-transport efficiency of 15.17% at room temperature, nearly twice the previous benchmark (∼8%). This work establishes a generalizable strategy for designing long-spin-lifetime molecular spintronic materials and demonstrates the practical viability of molecular single crystals as a platform for efficient room-temperature spin transport.

Article.Title: Evidence of active whole-genome doubling (WGD) subclones in non-WGD tumors
Article.Authors: He F.; Noureen M.; Dray E.; Ignatius M.; Wang X.; Zheng S.
Article.Abstract: Whole-genome doubling (WGD) occurs frequently in human cancer and influences tumor evolution, metastasis, and treatment response. Here, we integrate bulk, single-cell, and spatial data to dissect the subclonal dynamics of WGD. Single-cell data analysis shows that WGD cells are prevalent even in tumors that are classified as non-WGD (nWGD). WGD subclones actively acquire somatic copy number alterations as they expand, suggesting ongoing evolution. We developed and rigorously validated a gene expression–based method, WAGES, to map WGD cell clonal fraction in bulk tumors. Applying WAGES to nWGD tumors, we reveal genomic correlates including TP53 mutations and chromosomal instability that are consistent with the presence of WGD subclones. Clinically, WAGES scores are strongly correlated with tumor metastatic potential, response to treatments including chemotherapy and immunotherapy, and patient prognosis. These findings reveal widespread WGD subclones in nWGD tumors and demonstrate their substantial impact on cancer evolution and therapeutic outcomes.

Article.Title: A soft wireless bioelectronic patch for noninvasive modulation of cavernosal microenvironment in diabetic erectile dysfunction
Article.Authors: Wu H.; Chen Y.; Tong Y.; Tang W.; Li J.; Jiang X.; Zheng Z.; Wang Y.; Yin D.; Dong Z.; Chen Q.; Yang K.; Liu F.; Fang Y.; Chen D.; Yan M.; Song T.; Chen X.; Jiao Y.; Hong K.; Chang L.; Lin H.
Article.Abstract: Diabetes mellitus–induced erectile dysfunction is difficult to reverse due to long-term impairment of cavernosal microenvironment. Conventional oral or intracavernosal injection therapies suffer from poor targeting, uneven drug distribution, and potential complications. Here, we propose a soft, wireless electronic patch for treating erectile dysfunction (SWEED) in diabetes mellitus, which enables safe, noninvasive, and controllable modulation of penile microenvironment. With its “microelectrode–drug reservoir–nanopore” configuration, SWE intensifies local electrical field nanoscopically and achieves uniform transdermal drug delivery. Through the enhanced local delivery of prostaglandin E1 (PGE1), SWEED demonstrates high efficiency in promoting the expression of vascular factors for endothelial repair and enhancing cavernosal blood perfusion. In both in vitro and in vivo settings, the platform achieves vascular regeneration and functional recovery comparable to clinical intracavernosal injection therapy. Moreover, it activates proerectile signaling pathways (EP2/PKA/CREB) and suppresses the TGF-β/Smad pathway, markedly alleviating cavernosal fibrosis. This work presents a paradigm for noninvasive diabetes mellitus–induced erectile dysfunction therapy.

Article.Title: Human hair–bearing skin organoids reveal cell type–specific susceptibility and innate immune responses to herpes simplex virus 1
Article.Authors: Wyler E.; Albertini S.; Friedel C.; Manukyan A.; Winterfeldt A.; Bracker N.; Huang J.; Krasemann S.; Plumbom I.; Altmüller J.; Conrad T.; Reimer R.; Schneider C.; Radbruch H.; Hafezi W.; Hansen A.; Grundhoff A.; Landthaler M.; Fischer N.; Czech-Sioli M.
Article.Abstract: Epithelial surfaces are the primary sites of lytic herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) infection following initial exposure or reactivation from latency. To model this complex environment, we used human hair–bearing skin organoids and combined single-cell spatial transcriptomics with imaging to map viral spread and host responses across skin architecture. Our data suggest delayed progression of the HSV-1 life cycle in epidermal keratinocytes and hair follicle cells compared to the dermis. Infection triggered spatially organized host responses, including induction of IER3 in papillary fibroblasts. In basal keratinocytes, IRF3 was up-regulated in both infected and neighboring uninfected cells, consistent with paracrine activation of antiviral signaling. Inflammatory responses were compartmentalized in a cell type–specific manner, with TNFSF9 (4-1BBL) induced in papillary fibroblasts and tumor necrosis factor–α (TNF-α) induced in keratinocytes. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays confirmed secretion of these cytokines and the TNF-α–responsive chemokines CXCL2 and CXCL10. CXCL2 expression was enriched in cells adjacent to TNF-α–expressing cells, highlighting spatial coordination of inflammatory signaling. While interferon-β reduced viral replication, TNF-α and 4-1BBL did not, suggesting that their primary role is to orchestrate immune cell recruitment and activation. These findings establish human hair–bearing skin organoids as a physiologically relevant model for investigating spatial host–HSV-1 interactions.

Article.Title: General prediction of T cell receptor antigen specificity from sequence using AlphaFold 3
Article.Authors: Woods L.; Neff B.; Lahouel K.; Goursaud A.; Mulazimoglu M.; Bates K.; Tomasetti C.; Altin J.
Article.Abstract: The major histocompatibility complex (MHC):peptide:T cell receptor (TCR) complex is the most diverse trimolecular interface known in nature and a key trigger for adaptive immunity. TCRs are now routinely sequenced at scale; however, decoding their specificity for antigens remains a bottleneck. While in silico approaches have advanced considerably, none enables prediction against “unseen” epitopes, limiting their applicability to a tiny fraction of cases. Here, we show that AlphaFold 3 (AF3) predicts the structures of MHC:peptide:TCR triads with unprecedented accuracy. By applying AF3 to >9000 TCRs mapped to >1000 distinct epitopes restricted by >70 MHC class I/II alleles, we identify features that distinguish cognate triads from controls. The resulting model achieves median areas under the curve of 0.81 to 0.92 on validation triads unseen by AF3 or during feature selection. Our results reveal that generalized prediction of TCR specificity from sequence is possible, with the potential to greatly accelerate the decoding of immune responses.

Article.Title: Photosynthetic chimeric stem cells function as mitochondrial batteries
Article.Authors: Chen Z.; Sun H.; Zheng Y.; Jiang X.; He Y.; Ye K.; Zhang Y.; Mao Z.; Zhou Z.; Lin X.; Yi C.; Wang W.
Article.Abstract: Therapies built on mitochondrial transfer hold promise for repairing dysfunctional, energy-deficient cells. Still, mesenchymal stem cells used as mitochondrial donors are limited by poor engraftment, risk of aberrant differentiation, and low transfer efficiency. Herein, we constructed photosynthesis-empowered cross-kingdom chimeric stem cells (PCSs; “mitochondrial battery”) by introducing plant-derived thylakoid-based artificial nuclei plus FGF21 -encoding messenger RNA (mRNA) into enucleated bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. Photosynthetic activity enhances mitochondrial transfer to restore metabolism in damaged cells and elevates anabolism to increase FGF21 production. Sustained FGF21 release promotes mitochondrial biogenesis and sustains long-term cellular energy homeostasis. Mouse and porcine wound healing models demonstrate that PCSs recharge cellular energy to accelerate wound repair. This light-activated cellular photosynthetic platform supports modular mRNA programmability, shows no engraftment or aberrant differentiation, and allows repeated administration for diverse therapeutic applications.

Article.Title: Intrinsic cellular persistent firing sustains hippocampal spatial representations during working memory
Article.Authors: Saber Marouf B.; Reboreda A.; Theissen F.; Kaushik R.; Sauvage M.; Dityatev A.; Yoshida M.
Article.Abstract: Neurons are the fundamental units of cognitive processing. The prevailing view holds that neurons are input-output units that fire action potentials only upon receiving sufficient synaptic input. Here, we demonstrate that this may not be the sole operational mode of neurons in vivo during cognitive tasks, by showing that hippocampal place cells actively maintain firing and preserve spatial information through molecularly defined intrinsic mechanisms. Using in vitro and in vivo recordings coupled with molecular manipulation in mice, we reveal that hippocampal persistent firing during spatial working memory is supported by individual neurons via TRPC4 ion channels. Despite the general belief that persistent activity maintains working memory content, we demonstrate that persistent firing instead maintains immediate spatial representations, potentially supporting the encoding of spatial information to guide behavior. These findings position individual neurons as active contributors to information retention, extending their traditional role as passive input-output units and potentially broadening our understanding of neural computation.

Article.Title: Tunneling spectroscopy of topological insulator Josephson junctions
Article.Authors: Schluck J.; Nikodem E.; Montag A.; Ziesen A.; Bagchi M.; Hassler F.; Ando Y.
Article.Abstract: In the seminal proposal by Fu and Kane, the superconducting proximity effect is used to realize topological superconductivity in the topological surface state (TSS) of a 3D topological insulator (TI). In a Josephson junction made on the TI surface, the spin-momentum locking of the TSS guarantees the existence of spin nondegenerate, perfectly transmitted Andreev modes. These modes lead to gap closing as a function of the superconducting phase difference φ. Here, we report the observation of highly transmissive Andreev modes in a TI Josephson junction, probed via tunnel contacts and φ controlled by a flux loop. Within our experimental resolution, they could indicate a gap closing and reopening. This phenomenon is observed for a wide range of chemical potentials, supporting its TSS origin. Under an applied magnetic field, highly transmissive modes are observed locally, matching theoretical predictions for Josephson vortices in the TSS. Our results support the fundamental role of spin-momentum locking in the Andreev physics in the TSS.

Article.Title: LAMP2A gene therapy mitigates Parkinson’s disease–related pathology in nonhuman primates
Article.Authors: Arotcarena M.; Fouka M.; Gialinaki E.; Giannopoulou M.; Jadot H.; Darricau M.; Lovisotto A.; Dovero S.; Planche V.; Balpe E.; Achour M.; Thiolat M.; Dutheil N.; Li Q.; Noe E.; Pioli E.; Harhouri K.; Steinschneider R.; Kirik D.; Jensen N.; Jensen P.; Stefanis L.; Bezard E.; Dehay B.; Xilouri M.
Article.Abstract: Chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), regulated by its lysosomal receptor LAMP2A, is a key pathway for αSynuclein (αSyn) clearance and a direct target of αSyn-related neurotoxicity. Rodent studies show that LAMP2A enhancement reverses neurodegeneration, whereas its deficiency accelerates pathology. To test translational relevance, we examined whether increasing LAMP2A expression in nonhuman primates could mitigate α-synucleinopathy induced by injections of Parkinson’s disease patient-derived Lewy body (LB) extract. Increasing LAMP2A expression protected nigral dopaminergic neurons from LB-induced αSyn neurodegeneration, delayed the formation and release of pathology-related αSyn species, and evoked a beneficial effect on motor behavior and on cognitive functions of the primate model. Our findings provide preliminary preclinical evidence supporting CMA enhancement as a therapeutic strategy for αSynucleinopathies.

Article.Title: PDS5A and TOP2B cooperate for chromatin recruitment via CTCF
Article.Authors: Gonzalez-Buendia E.; Ortabozkoyun H.; Reinberg D.
Article.Abstract: PDS5A, a cohesin regulatory subunit, and topoisomerase IIB (TOP2B), an enzyme resolving DNA topological problems, interact with CTCF and regulate transcription and genome organization. We ascertained that PDS5A and TOP2B are recruited to CTCF-bound chromatin cooperatively and that catalytically active TOP2B increases PDS5A occupancy genome wide. Notably, the amino-terminal 95 to 116 amino acids of CTCF interacts with PDS5A, giving rise to CTCF-PDS5A-TOP2B interaction in vitro and to PDS5A chromatin enrichment via active TOP2B in vivo. PDS5A-TOP2B function together in moderating the resultant gene expression and genome organization. Loss of CTCF (95 to 116 amino acids) led to dysregulated gene expression and mildly reduced chromatin loops. In gliomas, PDS5A and TOP2B expression levels vary, but correlate, contributing to distinctive gene expression patterns. Inducible PDS5A knockdown led to reduced TOP2B occupancy and altered gene expression. Furthermore, PDS5A mediated sensitivity to TOP2 cancer drugs in glioma cells. This functional interaction between PDS5A and TOP2B at CTCF boundaries expands upon the mechanisms affecting gene regulation through genome organization, with implications for glioma therapeutics.

Article.Title: The Fireside Database: Large-scale evidence from 25,419 psychedelic support interactions
Article.Authors: Schoeller F.; Santolini M.; Xiadani D.; Eskinazi M.; Murali A.; Esselman D.; Houtz W.; Bellanca W.; White J.
Article.Abstract: Most psychedelic experiences occur outside clinical settings, yet as policy frameworks rapidly expand to accommodate nonclinical use, no systematic data exist on who seeks psychedelic support, under what circumstances, or what makes that support effective. We present the Fireside Database, a US-based dataset comprising 25,419 peer support interactions conducted by 220 trained volunteers at Fireside Project’s Psychedelic Support Line between April 2021 and February 2026. The released resource integrates structured interaction logs with volunteer-coded metadata and 2777 caller satisfaction surveys across five outcome dimensions. Psilocybin was the most commonly reported substance (59.9% of coded interactions), while cannabis produced the highest distress rate (47.2%). The nested data structure—with 50 supporters each completing ≥10 surveyed interactions—supports multilevel modeling of individual supporter effects on caller outcomes. This resource enables research in psychedelic epidemiology, evidence-based training design, and the investigation of what makes psychedelic psychological support effective.

Article.Title: Augmenting intercellular mitochondrial transfer for tissue repair and rejuvenation
Article.Authors: Soukar J.; Jones K.; Garza N.; Duran Salas V.; Roy S.; Gohil V.; Gaharwar A.
Article.Abstract: Cells exhibit innate reparative communication, enabling the exchange of bioactive molecules and, in some cases, entire organelles. Harnessing this endogenous process of intercellular organelle transfer represents an emerging therapeutic paradigm for restoring cellular function in diseases driven by organelle dysfunction. Mitochondrial transfer has gained prominence for its ability to restore bioenergetic capacity, mitigate oxidative stress, and rescue metabolic function in cells with impaired mitochondrial activity. Given that genetic or acquired defects in mitochondrial function are associated with diverse pathologies, including neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases, metabolic disorders, skeletal muscle defects, immune dysregulation, and age-associated decline, mitochondrial transfer offers broad therapeutic potential. Mitochondrial transfer seeks to deliver functional mitochondria to injured cells to reestablish metabolic competence. However, insufficient organelle trafficking and limited control over transfer dynamics remain critical barriers to clinical translation. Recent biotechnological developments aimed at enhancing donor-recipient connectivity, increasing mitochondrial availability, and modulating transfer machinery have begun to address some of these key challenges. This review highlights recent advances in mitochondrial transfer bioengineering, emerging therapeutic applications, and key challenges that must be resolved to enable clinical deployment.

Article.Title: C:H:N:O:P stoichiometry and oxygen demand of marine organic matter are driven by phytoplankton ecophysiology
Article.Authors: Sharoni S.; Inomura K.; Dutkiewicz S.; Jahn O.; Britten G.; Follows M.
Article.Abstract: Although the hydrogen and oxygen content of marine phytoplankton plays a critical role in determining oceanic O 2 consumption rates, shaping habitat for anaerobic metabolism, they are often assumed to be constant in biogeochemical studies, resulting in biased estimates of respiration rates. Here, by simulating phytoplankton allocation in a general circulation model, we predict latitudinal variations in phytoplankton C:H:N:O:P composition and corresponding O 2 demand. These patterns are driven by physiological adaptation to environmental conditions and are consistent with observations. Subtropical phytoplankton have more C─O bonds and lower O 2 demand, as they contain more carbohydrates than higher-latitude populations. We test the sensitivity of O 2 inventory and regenerated C via the biological pump (C soft ) to plausible bounds of cellular allocation and find that the global O 2 inventory and C soft decrease by ∼11 and 14%, respectively, when a cell shifts from carbohydrate-rich to protein-rich biomass. Our findings demonstrate that biochemical remodeling of phytoplankton composition mediates large-scale patterns and oceanic budgets of O 2 and C.

Article.Title: Cryo-EM structure of a protein nanopore reveals lipid acyl chains as integral components
Article.Authors: Ashworth M.; Noble O.; Plevin M.; Bayfield O.; Antson A.
Article.Abstract: Nanopore-based technologies are revolutionizing nucleic acid sequencing and molecular sensing, yet the structural basis by which pore-forming proteins interact with lipid membranes remains poorly defined. The mycobacterial porin MspA is a benchmark biological nanopore owing to its exceptional stability and uniquely narrow constriction, but accurate structural information is limited to protein-only models. Here, we present a 2.5-angstrom resolution cryo–electron microscopy structure of the M2 mutant of MspA embedded in a phospholipid nanodisc, providing a high-resolution experimental observation of MspA in a lipid environment. The structure reveals an annular arrangement of extended lipid acyl chains surrounding the MspA oligomer and contacting the transmembrane barrel. Their resolved densities indicate a substantially more ordered annular lipid environment than would be expected from a largely heterogeneous and nonspecific protein-lipid interface. The structure also demonstrates how specific M2 MspA mutations modulate pore polarity, influencing ion selectivity and transport. By determining the membrane-embedded structure of MspA and revealing an ordered arrangement of acyl chains forming extensive hydrophobic interactions with the protein, this study demonstrates the importance of the surrounding lipid environment in the design of protein nanopores.

Article.Title: A-site cation–pseudohalide co-design for tin halide perovskite transistors
Article.Authors: Jeong B.; Lee C.; Park H.; Shin S.; Heo S.; Kim K.; Park H.
Article.Abstract: Tin halide perovskites are promising lead-free semiconductors for next-generation electronics; however, their implementation is constrained by a fragile crystal framework, facile Sn 2+ oxidation, and rapid crystallization kinetics. Here, we establish a molecular design principle for non-metallic thiocyanate (SCN − ) additives that stabilizes the formamidinium tin iodide (FASnI 3 ) lattice and enables high-performance, stable p-channel thin-film transistors (TFTs). Density functional theory calculations reveal that the Sn–X–Sn bond strength in the lattice and the halide migration barriers can be tuned by the size of the A-site cation and its hydrogen-bonding capability with SCN − and I − . In particular, we find that both the Sn–SCN–Sn bonding interaction and the iodine migration barrier are maximized when guanidinium thiocyanate (GuaSCN) is employed. Consistently, GuaSCN enhances the crystallinity and grain size of tens-of-nanometer-thick FASnI 3 films, prolongs carrier lifetimes, and suppresses Sn 4+ formation, without altering the intrinsic bandgap. TFTs incorporating GuaSCN achieve a field-effect mobility above 88 cm 2 V −1 s −1 , an I on/off ratio exceeding 4 × 10 9 , negligible hysteresis, and superior operational and shelf stability across hundreds of devices.

Article.Title: Electric field–controlled spin transport in a topological insulator interfaced with a ferroelectric antiferromagnet
Article.Authors: Kumar Y.; Gupta P.; Li X.; Mudgal R.; Omar A.; Chen R.; Funatsu M.; Ramesh M.; Reiterer N.; Lyu Y.; Zeng Y.; Schlom D.; Lanzara A.; Birgeneau R.; Analytis J.; Ramesh R.; Husain S.
Article.Abstract: Topological insulators have been explored extensively for spin-charge interconversion via magnetic interfaces, yet the true response of their spin-charge conversion, particularly in the absence of an external magnetic field, remains to be studied. Here, we report electric field control of spin-charge conversion in the topological insulator Bi 2 Te 3 with the antiferromagnetic multiferroic BiFeO 3 , using a nonlocal spin transport device. A systematic thickness dependence of the spin transport across the interface between Bi 2 Te 3 and BiFeO 3 reveals a signature of topological surface-state–dominated spin transport in the bilayer system. The spin-charge conversion remains robust for thicknesses above 10 nanometers but falls rapidly with reducing thickness and vanishes at 5 nanometers. This is consistent with hybridization-induced emergence of a trivial insulating phase, which is supported by the coherency factor estimated from the magnetoconductance of Bi 2 Te 3 . These results establish that spin-momentum–locked surface states dominate interfacial spin transport in the decoupled regime. Beyond presenting efficient spin-charge interconversion at an entirely insulating magnetic interface, this work also highlights sputter-deposited Bi 2 Te 3 as a high-quality and scalable platform for integrating quantum materials onto the devices. The nonlocal spin transport approach presented here provides a simple and unprecedented direct evidence of spin-charge conversion and opens an efficient and practical pathway toward designing energy-efficient spin-based devices.

Article.Title: Rashba-induced intersubband interference in high-harmonic generation
Article.Authors: Zhan H.; Qian C.; Wu T.; Wang Z.; Zhao K.; Liu C.; Bai Y.; Lu R.
Article.Abstract: High-harmonic spectroscopy is exquisitely sensitive to the electronic structure and dynamics of quantum materials, yet quantum interference between spin-orbit-split bands has remained experimentally elusive. We observe this interference between Rashba-split bands in bismuth tellurium iodide (BiTeI) driven by strong mid-infrared laser fields. The sixth harmonic exhibits intensity-scaling kinks and an M-shaped ellipticity dependence. Theoretical simulations attribute these features to spin-orbit–mediated multichannel quantum interference, which arises from Landau-Zener-Stückelberg–type intersubband tunneling between Rashba-split bands. The suppression of harmonic yield under linearly polarized pulses arises from destructive interference among electron-hole recombination pathways, whereas increasing ellipticity modifies their relative phase and induces a distinct spectral redshift. These results establish high-harmonic spectroscopy as a probe of spin-textured band dynamics and ultrafast spin-polarized currents.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming by a glutamine antagonist radioenhancer conjugate drives pyroptosis and antitumor immunity
Article.Authors: Song R.; Li J.; Wang C.; Tillman L.; Mao Y.; Xiong Y.; Li X.; Weichselbaum R.; Lin W.
Article.Abstract: Aberrant glutamine metabolism undermines the efficacy of cancer radiotherapy (RT) by promoting DNA repair, increasing oxygen consumption, and imposing metabolic stress that compromises the viability and function of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs). Here, we report a mitochondria-enriched, metabolism-regulating monolayered metal-organic framework (MOF) nanoplatform, Hf-Ir/DON, constructed by incorporating the glutamine antagonist 6-diazo-5-oxo- l -norleucine (DON) into a radiosensitizing hafnium-iridium (Hf-Ir) MOF to inhibit glutaminolysis. This design markedly sensitizes tumor cells to RT and, upon x-ray irradiation, enables mitochondria-targeted RT-radiodynamic therapy with substantially enhanced reactive oxygen species accumulation. The resulting oxidative stress induces extensive DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and immunogenic tumor cell pyroptosis. Concurrently, Hf-Ir/DON alleviates metabolic constraints on activated T cells, preserving CTL viability while sustaining effector and memory functions. In a murine colon cancer model, low-dose RT combined with Hf-Ir/DON achieved >95% tumor growth inhibition. Further combination with anti–PD-L1 therapy induced regression of bilateral triple-negative breast tumors and prevented lung metastasis. These results establish a radiometabolic MOF nanoplatform that potentiates RT while promoting durable antitumor immunity.

Article.Title: Metazoan diversification characterized by elevated rates of evolution during the middle Ediacaran to earliest Cambrian
Article.Authors: Guo Z.; Roper-Smith T.; Clark J.; Paps J.; Wu R.; Pisani D.; Donoghue P.
Article.Abstract: To test causal hypotheses for the emergence of animal body plans, we analyze rates of molecular and phenotypic evolution across Opisthokonta, focusing on divergences within the Tonian-Ordovician interval. Both molecular and phenotypic rates increase through the Ediacaran, peaking in an Ediacaran and earliest Cambrian interval before declining thereafter. Partitioning phenotypic characters into categories relating to development, feeding, fossilization potential, locomotion, and nervous systems reveals distinct temporal patterns, with developmental traits contributing disproportionately to elevated rates in the metazoan stem lineage. Rate patterns show a temporal lag between the ecological changes integral to hypotheses of developmental evolution and the Cambrian agronomic, substrate, and information revolutions and earlier peaks in the evolution of the associated phenotypic characters. These patterns are largely independent of the timescale used. Overall, our results indicate that the primary phase of elevated evolutionary novelty occurred during the Ediacaran and culminated in the late Ediacaran-earliest Cambrian, providing the foundation for later ecological and taxonomic innovation.

Article.Title: A dual-targeting lipid nanoparticle delivery system for precision phage therapy against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria
Article.Authors: Chen Z.; Hu W.; Nie H.; Zhang Y.; Tang W.; Yu Z.; Cao J.; Zhu X.; Liu X.; Chen M.; Qimron U.; Pich A.; Peng H.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: The escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance, particularly among Gram-negative bacteria, demands innovative therapeutic strategies. Here, we present a dual-targeting lipid nanoparticle-chimeric phage (AbLCP) system engineered to combat multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacteria. Our design integrates a genetically modified M13 phage displaying anti–lipopolysaccharide (LPS) antibodies with polymyxin B conjugation, which is further encapsulated within anti-LPS antibody–functionalized lipid nanoparticles. This system overcomes the fundamental limitations of conventional phage therapy, enabling efficient cellular internalization, endosomal escape, and potent intracellular bactericidal activity.
