Article.Title: Short-term outcomes, longer-term disability and relapse risk in LGI1-antibody encephalitis
Article.Authors: Ramanathan S.; Soltys J.; Michael S.; Mackrill S.; Cleaver J.; Williams R.; Makuch M.; Waters P.; Ansizka Y.; Dinoto A.; Farazdaghi M.; Trewin B.; Rudnik J.; Demakakos P.; Yates S.; Thouin A.; Dilwali S.; Son H.; Dale R.; Jacob A.; Lutterotti A.; Easton A.; Handel A.; Geschwind M.; Gelfand J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Leucine-rich glioma-inactivated-1 antibody encephalitis (LGI1-Ab-E) is a common and immunotherapy-responsive form of encephalitis. However, it is not known which immunotherapy regimens improve short-term outcomes, longer-term disability and relapse risk. Further, it is not known if the widely-utilised modified Rankin Scale (mRS) accurately captures quality of life (QoL) in LGI1-Ab-E, complicating disability measurements and interpretation of immunotherapy responses. A multicentre, international, real-world comparative analysis of patients with LGI1-Ab-E. Retrospective data from patient records evaluated short-term seizure and cognitive outcomes, 1-6 year disability, and future relapse risk associations, by integrating demographics, clinical features investigations and exposures to immunotherapies and antiseizure medications (ASMs). Patient- and neurologist-rated QoL assessments were used to establish an evidence-based mRS threshold for defining clinically significant disability. Cox proportional hazard models, Anderson-Gill, and generalised linear mixed-effects models were employed. 181 patients were included, with median age at onset 63 years (range 23 - 92); 122/181 (67%) were male. Short-term outcomes, evaluated at both five and ten weeks post-treatment initiation, identified exposure to immunotherapies associated with seizure resolution (OR = 13.97, 95%CI = 6.10-32.01; p < 0.0001 and OR = 8.53, 95%CI = 4.14-17.55; p < 0.0001, respectively), notably with corticosteroids, plasma exchange and rituximab, but not ASMs, intravenous immunoglobulins or steroid sparing agents. Conversely, seizure recurrence was observed after discontinuation of oral prednisolone, but not other immunotherapies or ASMs (OR = 39.53, 95%CI = 12.70-122.20, p < 0.0001). To evaluate longer-term disability, first, mRS scores were calibrated using QoL assessments: this identified a significant increase in patient-rated disability at mRS score of 2. Hence, using mRS 0-1 as a favourable outcome, we identified worse mRS at nadir associated with greater one-year disability (OR = 2.56, 95%CI = 1.56–4.20, p = 0.0003), and each month of delayed immunotherapy associated with a 16% increased risk of disability (HR = 1.16, 95%CI = 1.06-1.35, p = 0.004). Additionally, absence of immunotherapy associated both with greater one-year disability (OR = 5.67; 95% CI 1.19-26.54, p = 0.03) and a relapsing course (OR = 7.64, 95%CI = 2.51-21.77, p = 0.0002). Both a relapsing course, observed in 38% of patients, and the number of relapses associated with step-wise worsening of disability and QoL-outcomes. Rituximab exposure was the only identified clinical factor associated with reduced future relapse risk, by 93% (HR = 0.07, 95%CI = 0.01-0.48, p = 0.002). Persistent serum LGI1-IgMs, but not LGI1-IgGs, at one-year, associated with future relapses (HR = 11.69, 95%CI = 1.58-145.80, p = 0.02). Distinctive clinical factors and select immunotherapies, particularly intravenous methylprednisolone and plasma exchange, but not ASMs, associated with favourable short-term outcomes, patient-centric longer-term disability and relapses in LGI1-Ab-E. Our findings provide evidence-based disability thresholds, highlight novel prognostic biomarkers, and pragmatically guide LGI1-Ab-E care, pending randomized clinical trials.

Article.Title: TREM2: friend or foe in glioma?
Article.Authors: Peshoff M.; Hambardzumyan D.; Wu L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a neuroimmune signaling hub involved in key cellular processes including microglial phagocytosis, chemotaxis, and inflammation. Dysregulation of TREM2 has been implicated in a variety of diseases, most notably in the innate immune response to neurodegenerative disorders and cancer. The TREM2 pathway plays a significant role in governing microglia phenotypic transitions in Alzheimer’s disease, as well as in regulating tumor-associated macrophages’ ability to modulate cytotoxic activity. However, TREM2’s role can be dependent on experimental parameters and disease contexts. Due to its intricate involvement in related disorders and the myeloid-dominated microenvironment in brain tumors, TREM2 has emerged as a vital player to better understand neuroimmune contributions to central nervous system malignancies. This review critically evaluates TREM2’s controversial function in gliomas, analyzes experimental and biological variables that may underlie divergent findings, and outlines important considerations for future investigations.

Article.Title: KCNH1 variants associated with neurodevelopmental disorders exhibit prominent gain of function
Article.Authors: Thompson C.; Simmons C.; He I.; Jairam N.; Desai R.; Cha E.; Hong A.; DeKeyser J.; Laux L.; Jinnette M.; Vanoye C.; George A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pathogenic variants in KCNH1, encoding the human ether-á-go-go voltage-gated potassium channel (EAG1, KV10.1), are associated with the neurodevelopmental disorders Temple-Baraitser syndrome (TBS), Zimmermann-Laband syndrome (ZLS), epileptic encephalopathy, and other undefined neurodevelopmental disorders. Investigating the functional consequences of KCNH1 variants can provide information about molecular and cellular pathophysiological mechanisms and help guide therapeutic directions. In this study, we determined the functional properties of 26 disease-associated KCNH1 variants including three recurrent and six that were previously unpublished. Findings were compared to the wildtype (WT) channel along with six rare population variants. Our approach used automated patch clamp recording of heterologously expressed KCNH1 variants in both the homozygous state (variant alone) and the clinically-relevant heterozygous state (variant co-expressed with WT channels). We also examined the impact of alternative splice isoforms on functional consequences of specific variants. We demonstrated that the majority of disease-associated KCNH1 variants exhibit features consistent with gain-of-function including hyperpolarized voltage-dependence of activation, accelerated activation kinetics, or both that promote hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential. By contrast, one unique variant discovered previously in an autism cohort had a depolarized voltage-dependence of activation and was associated with a depolarized resting potential in cells. Pharmacological testing of KCNH1 variants demonstrated differences in potency for channel block by imipramine and an investigational non-selective potassium channel blocker (LY97241) for specific variants. Collectively, our findings support gain-of-function as the most common, albeit not exclusive, molecular mechanism underlying KCNH1-related disorders and suggest opportunities for potential therapeutic drug repurposing strategies for these conditions.

Article.Title: Global best practice recommendations for genetic counselling and testing in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Article.Authors: Salmon K.; de Majo M.; Basak N.; Crook A.; Cummings C.; Dratch L.; França M.; Heckmann J.; Higgins P.; Knight D.; Koo A.; Nalini A.; Rouleau G.; Shahrizaila N.; Sokhi D.; Son B.; Thomas P.; Trefiak P.; Van Damme P.; N/A N/A.; Ahmad-Annuar A.; Binet M.; Cochrane T.; Dave K.; Easton A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with substantial clinical and genetic heterogeneity. Advances in ALS genomics, emerging gene-targeted therapies, and genotype-specific clinical trials have increased the importance of genetic counselling and testing for individuals with ALS and their families. However, access to these services remains highly variable globally due to disparities in healthcare infrastructure, laboratory capacity, specialist availability, and funding. Existing guidance has largely been developed in high-resource settings and may not be feasible or equitable worldwide. The International Alliance of ALS/MND Associations convened an international, multidisciplinary Genetics Task Force to develop expert consensus recommendations for genetic counselling, genetic testing, and laboratory practice in ALS across diverse geographic and resource settings. Recommendations were developed through a structured, iterative consensus process incorporating clinical expertise, lived experience perspectives, published evidence, and global representation. Final recommendations were reviewed and approved through anonymous voting at an in-person consensus meeting. The resulting recommendations establish both minimum and aspirational best practices, emphasizing equitable access, informed decision-making, culturally responsive counselling, tiered genetic testing approaches, and context-appropriate laboratory standards. These globally informed recommendations provide a pragmatic framework to support clinicians, laboratories, policymakers, and advocacy organizations in improving access to high-quality ALS genetics services worldwide.

Article.Title: Do psychiatrists have a spider-sense? Clinical impressions as violations of interpersonal Bayesian expectation
Article.Authors: Amad A.; D’Hondt F.; Gauld C.; Bertoux M.; Daoudi M.; Fovet T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Psychiatric diagnosis depends on the clinician’s ability to infer mental states from complex and dynamically evolving interpersonal signals. During the psychiatric interview, clinicians do not only collect explicit symptoms; they continuously sample a rich array of non-verbal and paralinguistic cues including gaze, prosody, affective reciprocity, and interactional timing. These signals are central to psychiatric assessment, yet their contribution to diagnostic reasoning remains poorly formalized. In this Review, we propose a computational account of clinical impressions in psychiatry. We integrate evidence from phenomenological psychopathology, social cognition, and computational neuroscience. We argue that such impressions may arise when the clinician’s generative model of social interaction is persistently disconfirmed by subtle deviations in interpersonal behaviour, generating high-level social prediction errors experienced as a sense of incongruity or failed attunement. We formalize this process as VIBE: Violation of Interpersonal Bayesian Expectation. VIBE denotes a pre-reflective epistemic signal generated when observed interpersonal cues deviate from the clinician’s expected model of social reciprocity. It is not a diagnostic criterion but orients hypothesis generation by drawing attention to disturbances in interpersonal predictability. We hypothesize that VIBE may constitute a transdiagnostic mechanism: different disorders, from schizophrenia to autism spectrum disorder and mood disorders, may disrupt distinct dimensions of interpersonal prediction. The Praecox Feeling, first described by Rümke in 1942, can be read as the earliest clinical formalization of this process and as its schizophrenia-spectrum instance, in which the profile of interpersonal violations is consistent enough to be clinically recognizable. This framework recasts the diagnostic impression as an embodied inferential process rather than an opaque subjective faculty. Teaching clinicians to articulate, examine, and recalibrate these impressions could strengthen diagnostic reasoning, reduce bias, and improve therapeutic attunement. VIBE provides a bridge between phenomenological psychopathology and computational neuroscience, and offers a tractable, empirically testable model for studying the neurocomputational basis of psychiatric clinical judgement.

Article.Title: Harnessing lattice distortion for point-defect self-healing in multi-principal element alloys
Article.Authors: Zhang B.; Xun K.; Guan P.; Ritchie R.; Ding J.
Article.Abstract: Multi-principal element alloys are promising structural materials for nuclear, aerospace, and fusion applications, yet their accelerated discovery is limited by the prohibitive cost of evaluating point-defect transport and self-healing behavior across vast compositional spaces. Here, we establish local lattice distortion (LLD), an intrinsic feature of chemically complex alloys, as a predictive and universal descriptor for vacancy–interstitial diffusivity convergence. We develop and validate a high-fidelity machine-learning interatomic potential based on the moment tensor potential formalism for body-centered-cubic Zr–Ti–Nb alloys, enabling accurate large-scale simulations of defect energetics and migration. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal a robust inverse correlation between LLD and the activation energy disparity between vacancies and interstitials. This relationship is further validated in face-centered-cubic V–Co–Ni and Ni–Pd systems, demonstrating transferability across distinct chemistries and crystal structures. LLD-induced narrowing of vacancy–interstitial mobility differences promotes Frenkel pair recombination and defect self-healing. Mechanistically, vacancy diffusion is governed by the energy barrier associated with bond-length compression at the saddle state, together with statistical sampling of low-barrier jumps mediated by oversized atoms. These findings establish lattice distortion as a powerful, physically grounded design lever that links nanoscale disorder to point-defect self-healing, offering a practical pathway for the accelerated discovery of next-generation structural materials for extreme environments.

Article.Title: Knowledge gaps and scientific progress
Article.Authors: Kedrick K.; Yang W.; Gebhart T.; Wang Y.; Funk R.
Article.Abstract: Knowledge production is often viewed as an endogenous process in which discovery arises through the recombination of existing theories, findings, and concepts. Yet not all recombinations are equally valuable, and identifying those that may prove most generative remains challenging. We propose that a crucial form of recombination occurs when linking concepts creates knowledge gaps—empty regions in the conceptual landscape that may focus scientific attention on unexplored connections. Using computational topology, we develop a method to identify knowledge gaps in science at scale. In this framework, gaps form when new connections complete cycles in evolving networks of scientific concepts. We apply the method to 34,363,623 papers in Microsoft Academic Graph spanning 1900 to 2020. The main analyses use samples ranging from 8,643,571 to 31,983,201 papers. Compared with papers that introduce novel concept pairs without opening gaps, gap-opening papers have greater long-term citation impact, are more disruptive of prior work, and exhibit greater delayed recognition. Gap-opening papers receive fewer citations within five years of publication but more over twenty years, consistent with scientific communities needing time to recognize and develop newly opened research territories. Evidence for the generative capacity of gap-opening papers—as indicated by high citation impact and disruption—replicates in five additional databases (OpenAlex, the PubMed Knowledge Graph, Dimensions, American Physical Society journals, and United States patents) and across eight concept vocabularies, including several derived directly from text. Together, these results point to a distinctive generative role for gap opening in scientific discovery.
Article.Keywords: concept networks; generative capacity; knowledge gaps; knowledge recombination; persistent homology

Article.Title: A zero-one law for one-shot system identification
Article.Authors: Boullé N.; Halikias D.; Otto S.; Townsend A.
Article.Abstract: Can a model be identified from one experiment? We study analytic systems that are linearly parameterized by a combination of prescribed dictionary terms, such as partial differential operators and dynamical systems. For a single input-response pair, recovery is possible exactly when the evaluated dictionary terms are linearly independent. We prove a sharp zero-one law: either no input uniquely determines the coefficients, or almost every random input sampled from a nondegenerate Gaussian measure does. This dichotomy reduces one-shot system identification to a question about degenerate inputs and provides an a posteriori certificate in the noiseless setting. Numerical examples recover dynamical systems, nonlinear partial differential equations, and structured matrix families from single trajectory data, while also detecting when an extra probe is necessary.

Article.Title: A genome-wide senescence synthetic lethality screen identifies PARP16 as a senolytic target
Article.Authors: Ghosh-Choudhary S.; Liu J.; Beaulieu D.; Pineda R.; Yang H.; Moturi S.; Larsen M.; Alfaras I.; Pirooznia M.; Liu S.; Alder J.; Liu Y.; Chen B.; Königshoff M.; Finkel T.
Article.Abstract: Accumulation of senescent cells is increasingly viewed as a significant contributor to aging and age-related diseases. To date, the elimination of senescent cells through small molecule senolytic agents has largely relied on a limited number of repurposed agents, often leveraged from previous oncological applications. Here, we describe a CRISPR-based, genome-wide, synthetic lethal screen for senescent cells. From this screen, we identify a number of genes whose deletion appears to be well tolerated in normal proliferating cells, but whose deletion is lethal in the context of senescence. We further characterize one promising candidate gene encoding the ER-resident protein PARP16. Knockdown of PARP16 does not affect the viability of mouse or human cells but results in the death of a wide range of senescent cells. Furthermore, two distinct small molecule PARP16 inhibitors have little effect of normal cell growth but result in the selective death of senescent cells in culture and in freshly isolated human donor lung tissue explants. Together, these results demonstrate a rational strategy to identify novel senolytic therapies that could have potential applications for a wide range of age-related conditions.

Article.Title: The microbial world of male reproduction
Article.Authors: Imchen M.; Kaur R.; Bordenstein S.
Article.Abstract: The last decade has brought renewed interest to microbial influences on host biology, yet the roles of microbes in host reproductive biology are underappreciated and often defined by a profound maternal bias. This perspective synthesizes emerging evidence across the tree of life to highlight the paternal microbiome as an overlooked driver of fitness, reproductive output, and intergenerational health, impacting epigenetic sculpting of the sperm and embryo, sexual transmission of microbes, and male gamete functions. These contributions indicate that mating can involve interactions between holobionts rather than simply the union of the maternal and paternal genomes. Thus, uniting male reproduction with the growing generalizations of microbial symbiosis guides several conceptual, theoretical, and empirical avenues for research in the life sciences.

Article.Title: Windblown dunes are born in sand at the brink of transport
Article.Authors: Marvin M.; Gleason A.; Narteau C.; Rozier O.; Lapôtre M.
Article.Abstract: Windblown dunes are found everywhere in the Solar System where a supply of loose sediment is mobilized by gas flows, from the sluggish winds of Venus to speed-of-sound sublimation flows on comets. Their abundance is nontrivial because dunes only form where grains hop ballistically (“saltate”). This implies that winds across the Solar System reach “goldilocks” speeds that are just right to initiate and maintain saltation of whatever sediment is available despite vast variations in material and fluid properties, and gravity. Based on select observations, it was proposed that dune fields may be characterized by a near-threshold transport state where dune-forming winds minimally exceed the saltation threshold on Earth. Here, we demonstrate that this is indeed the case globally. Next, we show that, unlike riverbeds—which evolve to a similar state through adjustments of channel geometry—dune fields are born in it due to the rapid decrease in wind frequency with increasing wind speed. These results imply that grain sizes in windblown dunes provide a robust record of formative winds, such that corresponding wind speeds can be estimated from aeolian sandstones and dune deposits across planets. The near-threshold state of windblown dunes thus opens a promising line of investigation for paleoenvironmental and paleoclimate reconstructions on Earth and beyond.

Article.Title: Co-translational surveillance of nascent polypeptides times circadian rhythms in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Geisseova T.; Lee H.; Bang H.; Kim J.; Oh Y.; Lim C.; Lee J.
Article.Abstract: Ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) ensures proteostasis by actively degrading aberrant translation intermediates on stalled ribosomes, yet its physiological role in gene regulation remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate that Drosophila circadian clocks employ RQC to sustain 24-h behavioral rhythms. RNA interference-mediated depletion of RQC components in circadian pacemaker neurons impaired free-running locomotor rhythms. In particular, the loss of Caliban ( Clbn ) function in clearing 60S-associated faulty polypeptides led to weak but long-period rhythms in adult locomotor activity. These behavioral phenotypes were accompanied by delayed accumulation of the core clock protein PERIOD (PER), most evidently in pigment-dispersing factor-expressing clock neurons, and dampened structural plasticity of their axons. per heterozygosity exaggerated CLBN depletion-induced period lengthening, whereas overexpression of the PER-associating factor TIMELESS blunted this effect. Clbn deficiency in Drosophila S2R+ cell cultures increased the generation of prematurely terminated PER species, particularly when PER translation is high, and sensitized full-length PER to phosphorylation-dependent decay. These findings support PER as a clock-relevant RQC substrate, providing a mechanistic link between translation flux, co-translational surveillance, and circadian timekeeping.

Article.Title: Causal dynamic resonance reduces false positives in detecting causality
Article.Authors: Lainscsek C.; Salami P.; Dräger S.; Bulsara A.; Cash S.; Sejnowski T.
Article.Abstract: Many dynamical systems in nature, such as brains and weather systems, are highly nonlinear and complex. Determining information flow among the components that make up these dynamical systems is challenging. If the components are the result of a common process or become synchronized, causality measures typically fail. We previously introduced Cross-Dynamical Delay Differential Analysis, a nonlinear method for assessing causal influence, along with a complementary approach for dynamical similarity between time series data, Dynamical Ergodicity Delay Differential Analysis. Here, we show that “Causal Dynamic Resonance (CDR)” further improves the false positive rejection rate by adding white noise to the data, without perturbing the underlying dynamical system. This is followed by a study of CDR in coupled Rössler systems, where ground truth interactions are known and in invasive intracranial electroencephalographic data from drug-resistant epilepsy patients undergoing presurgical monitoring.

Article.Title: Preemptive solving of future problems: Multitask Preplay in humans and machines
Article.Authors: Carvalho W.; Hall-McMaster S.; Lee H.; Gershman S.
Article.Abstract: Humans can pursue a near-infinite variety of tasks, but typically can only pursue a small number at the same time. We hypothesize that humans leverage experience on one task to preemptively learn solutions to other tasks that were accessible but not pursued. We formalize this idea as “Multitask Preplay”, an algorithm that replays experience on one task as the starting point for “preplay”—counterfactual simulation of an accessible but unpursued task. Preplay is used to learn a predictive representation that can support fast, adaptive task performance later on. When implemented within deep reinforcement learning, it predicts human generalization to novel tasks more accurately than traditional planning and predictive representation methods across grid-worlds and a 2D Minecraft domain. Additionally, Multitask Preplay improves an artificial agent’s ability to generalize to new environments sharing task co-occurrence structure. These findings demonstrate that Multitask Preplay is a scalable theory of human counterfactual learning and generalization; endowing artificial agents with this capacity can significantly improve their performance in challenging multitask environments.

Article.Title: Coevolving gene networks underlying a phenotypic syndrome revealed via integrating comparative genomic and microevolutionary analyses
Article.Authors: Baral S.; Halali S.; Ittonen M.; Fischer K.; Gotthard K.; Wheat C.
Article.Abstract: Complex adaptive traits often comprise interacting, coevolving phenotypes that together for a syndrome that is shaped by multiple genetic loci. While using intraspecific variation is an established approach for investigating syndromes, such polymorphism typically captures only a subset of syndrome traits. Diapause, an alternative developmental pathway that evolved independently in many species to synchronize life cycles with resource availability, exemplifies this challenge. While subsets of this essential phenotype have long been studied at a single species level, the genomic basis of the full diapause syndrome remains poorly understood. This paucity of insights has fueled a long-standing debate about how life cycle synchronization evolves and whether convergent phenotypes employ shared mechanisms. Using a comparative genomic analysis spanning diverse diapause transitions in butterflies, we identified a large network of coevolving genes unique to diapausing species. The network is composed of functional modules spanning circadian regulation, metabolism, and cell cycle control. We tested whether this macroevolutionary scale network predicts microevolutionary dynamics, hypothesizing that this network is the polygenic architecture underlying the diapause syndrome. Analyses revealed that allelic variation in the diapause network is significantly enriched in signatures of local adaptation across latitudes, but only in diapausing species. Thus, we empirically show that diapause evolves through modular, coevolving gene networks, components of which impact intraspecific variation in diapause. Using this integrative perspective on a complex phenotype opens a horizon of inquiry for understanding seasonal adaptation across evolutionary scales, while demonstrating the power of integrating comparative genomics with microevolutionary dynamics to dissect complex phenotypic syndromes.

Article.Title: Physicochemical microenvironments within biomolecular condensates govern reaction kinetics beyond mass-action effects
Article.Authors: Bae J.; Hong K.; Lee D.; Jun J.; Jung Y.
Article.Abstract: Cells utilize phase separation to compartmentalize biochemical reactions within biomolecular condensates. Although these compartments can enhance reaction rates by concentrating reactants, how they modulate kinetics beyond mass-action effects remains poorly understood. Here, using spontaneous protein ligation as a model reaction, we examined how the physicochemical microenvironment within condensates modulates reaction kinetics. We systematically analyzed condensates formed by folded PRM–SH3 scaffolds and intrinsically disordered proteins (LAF, TAF, and FUS). We designed a proximity-sensitive client probe to assess excluded-volume-driven increases in effective reactant concentration. Article.Title: Lipid-induced Caveolin1 lipid droplet trafficking is associated with lipid droplet growth

Article.Abstract: Caveolae are 50 to 100 nm sized plasma membrane invaginations involved in cellular lipid uptake and lipid accumulation. Article.Title: Morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment
Article.Authors: Alam R.; Rai T.
Article.Abstract: Modern western legal and criminal justice theories assume that punishment should deter criminalized behavior by introducing costs that reduce its expected utility, but, empirically, punishment often has weak effects on rates of crime and recidivism. We demonstrate our hypothesis across 10 correlational, experimental, and economic game studies with participants drawn from the general population as well as participants with criminal backgrounds. Studies 1 to 3 draw on federal data of over 30,000 offenders and find that participants’ estimates of moral motives for crime predict higher recidivism while estimates of material motives predict the opposite. Studies 4 to 8 use judgment studies and find that morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment across a diversity of crime types, when motives are manipulated but actions are kept constant, persist for different types of consequences, and are unique to moral motivation. Studies 9 and 10 employ economic games and find that when players take money from others for moral reasons, they are less deterred by the imposition of fines. Implications for systems of punishment, offender psychology, and restorative justice approaches are discussed.

Article.Title: Counterions, polarization, and pore hydration relay drive ion permeation through hydrophobic pore formed by the MERS coronavirus E protein
Article.Authors: Wan Z.; Hong M.; Cui Q.
Article.Abstract: Hydrophobic pores are generally expected to exclude ions because the large desolvation penalty associated with ion transfer cannot be compensated within a nonpolar environment. Rather than acting as passive spectators, counterions transiently chaperone the permeating cation before dissociating within the channel, thereby lowering the energetic cost of charge desolvation while preserving net ionic conductance. Explicit electronic polarization further reshapes the pore hydration landscape and cation– π interactions, leading to substantially reduced free-energy barriers and a permeation mechanism that is in substantially better agreement with experiment. These results suggest that efficient ion transport through hydrophobic pores arises from the cooperative interplay between electrostatics, polarization, and hydration rather than complete pore wetting, providing both a mechanistic framework for MERS E protein function and a general physical principle for ion transport through biological and synthetic hydrophobic nanopores.

Article.Title: Four phases and temporal threshold of population calcium response during locomotion in cortical astrocytes
Article.Authors: Fedotova A.; Brazhe A.; Semyanov A.
Article.Abstract: Calcium activity is a major form of astrocyte excitability. Astrocytic calcium events arise spontaneously and in response to behavior, but how unitary events shape population-level activity remains unclear. Using two-photon imaging in the primary somatosensory cortex of awake mice running on a freely rotating disk, we analyzed calcium dynamics during quiescence and locomotion. During quiescence, population fluctuations were driven mainly by the co-occurrence of new events rather than by their enlargement. During locomotion, responses progressed through four phases: emergence of new events, their merging into a superevent, fragmentation, and an afterburst. These responses combined the progressive recruitment of active regions with amplification of a reproducible spatial calcium pattern. New events emerged within the first seconds after locomotion onset, indicating a rapid astrocytic response. A full population response required about 5 s of locomotion: Shorter episodes failed to develop the superevent and produced markedly smaller responses. In suprathreshold episodes, the superevent displayed a reproducible ΔF/F pattern. Hotspots within this pattern had shorter latencies and were also more active during quiescence. A dynamic mode decomposition with control model driven by synthetic or real locomotion inputs reproduced the response phases, temporal threshold, and superevent pattern. These findings show that locomotion-evoked astrocytic calcium activity is an ordered, threshold-dependent population process with reproducible spatiotemporal structure that can be approximated by a low-dimensional dynamical system.

Article.Title: Language model teams as distributed systems
Article.Authors: Mieczkowski E.; Collins K.; Sucholutsky I.; Vélez N.; Griffiths T.
Article.Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are growing increasingly powerful. Yet, fundamental constraints on the reasoning, memory, and performance of individual models has sparked recent interest in scaling abilities using LLM teams. With growing deployment of LLM teams at scale, there is a need for principled guidelines for when teams help, how many agents to use, and how structure impacts performance. Rather than building these teams through trial-and-error, we propose using distributed systems as a formal foundation for designing and evaluating LLM teams. Under this formal framework, we derive predictions about how task structure and team architecture should shape performance. Empirical evidence supports these predictions: LLM team scaling follows classical distributed computing laws based on the structure of a task, and centralized and decentralized architectures exhibit the asymmetric vulnerabilities predicted by distributed systems theory. These results establish distributed computing as a generative framework that yields testable, quantitative predictions about LLM team behavior and informs the construction of more efficient and capable teams.

Article.Title: Neuronal IL-34 programs microglial activity via the TGF-β–MEF2C axis to constrain neuroinflammation following brain ischemia
Article.Authors: Li M.; Zhou X.; Li R.; Liu H.; Qi C.; Zhang W.; Han Y.; Yin T.; Wu S.; Pan Y.; Tian D.; Yan T.; Zhou J.; Chen X.; Liu Q.
Article.Abstract: Brain ischemia induces robust neuroinflammation driven by microglial activation, yet whether ischemic neurons actively reprogram microglial phenotypes to limit inflammation remains elusive. Here, we identify neuronal interleukin-34 (IL-34) as a critical immunomodulatory signal that maintains microglial homeostasis after cerebral ischemia. We demonstrate that ischemic injury augments IL-34-CSF1R signaling between neurons and microglia. Neuron-specific overexpression of Il34 (Syn1- Il34 tg mice) attenuated infarct volume and neurodeficits after middle cerebral artery occlusion, whereas neuronal Il34 knockdown exacerbated brain injury. Microglial depletion abolished IL-34-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting microglia as essential effectors. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that neuronal IL-34 preserved homeostatic microglial signatures ( P2ry12, Cx3cr1, Tgfbr1 ), while suppressing inflammatory activities ( Il1b, Tnf, Cxcl2 ) through upregulation of the transcription factor MEF2C. Mechanistically, IL-34 activated TGF-β signaling in microglia and inhibition of TGF-β signaling abolished the protective effects of IL-34, whereas microglia-specific Mef2c overexpression rescued neuroprotection despite TGF-β blockade. Thus, ischemic neurons deploy IL-34 to orchestrate the immunoregulatory activity of microglia via the TGF-β–MEF2C axis, representing a previously unrecognized endogenous mechanism counteracting neuroinflammation. Our study reveals neuronal IL-34 as a potential therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

Article.Title: Local influenza forecasts outperform state-level forecasts in the United States
Article.Authors: Kim D.; Pasco R.; Johnson K.; Fox S.; Reich N.; Meyers L.
Article.Abstract: Accurate outbreak forecasts are critical for timely and effective public health response. In the United States, however, most forecasts are produced at the state level, which can mask substantial substate heterogeneity and limit their utility for local planning. We generated and evaluated forecasts of the percentage of Emergency Department visits attributable to influenza across 173 large metropolitan Health Service Areas (HSAs) using a gradient boosting quantile regression model and compared their accuracy to forecasts derived from state-level data alone. At a 1-wk, 2-wk, and 3-wk horizon, local forecasts outperformed state-based forecasts in 98.8%, 90.8%, and 78.6% of HSAs, respectively, achieving mean weighted interval scores that were on average a 39.2% lower (95% range: 5.9 to 76.7%), 19.6% lower (−6.3 to 59.5%), and 11.4% lower (−11.7 to 44.9%), respectively. The performance advantage of local forecasting was strongest in HSAs representing a smaller share of their state’s population and increased with the proportion of the HSA population living in urban areas and the number of metropolitan areas within a state. These results, based on an analysis of HSAs with populations greater than 250,000, demonstrate that fine-scale modeling can substantially improve forecast accuracy and highlight the potential value of local forecasts for outbreak preparedness and response.

Article.Title: Niche constraints drive differences between mycorrhizal fungal guilds in future range shifts
Article.Authors: Edwards J.; van den Hoogen J.; Hawkes C.; Anthony M.; Delavaux C.; Stewart J.; Treseder K.; Feng X.; Papeş M.; Muscarella R.; Baldrian P.; Kohout P.; Kiers E.; Lauber T.; Matheny P.; Crowther T.; Van Nuland M.; Qin C.; Averill C.; Kivlin S.
Article.Abstract: Mycorrhizal fungi are a diverse and ubiquitous group of plant symbionts whose distribution strongly influences ecosystem function across the globe. Yet, until now, we do not have quantitative data on the range sizes of different mycorrhizal fungal taxa, limiting our capacity to forecast future shifts in community composition and function. Here, we use 115,924 DNA sequence-derived observations to map the distribution of 651 common mycorrhizal fungal taxa and forecast future changes to their range sizes. We demonstrate that climate, plant cover, and soil factors, particularly mean annual temperature, net primary productivity, and soil organic carbon, exert major control over mycorrhizal fungal distributions. Based on these drivers, the ecological niches of mycorrhizal fungi consistently differ between arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal functional guilds. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal taxa generally occupy a wider niche breadth than ectomycorrhizal fungi, occurring across larger ranges of climate, soil, plant cover, topography, and disturbance conditions. Our models also predict widespread decreases in the suitable range size of mycorrhizal fungal taxa under projected future global climates, with average ranges decreasing by 13.8% or ~2.2 million km 2 under high emissions scenarios (ssp5-8.5). This decrease in projected range size will be most pronounced for ectomycorrhizal fungi, strongly linked to constraints from their smaller overall niches. By generating a global atlas of common mycorrhizal fungi and their associated environmental niche, we establish a critical baseline for widely suspected declines in global fungal biodiversity.

Article.Title: Competing capillary pathways govern buckling in drying porous microcapsules
Article.Authors: Feng L.; Wang Y.; Fang R.; Fan J.; Zhang S.; Weitz D.
Article.Abstract: Capillary forces are fundamental in nature, lifting water in plants and supporting insects on ponds. Here, we show that capillary force can also buckle porous microcapsules as they dry. As water evaporates through the polymeric shell, an asymmetric air–polymer–water interface emerges and expands, where concave menisci at interfacial nanopores generate capillary (Laplace) pressure that deforms the shell. Optical imaging and accompanying phase-field modeling show that buckling initiates once the capillary pressure spreads over a critical surface area, then proceeds quasi-statically: Dimples nucleate, deepen, and ultimately evolve into a nested, double-shelled morphology, with each step rate-limited by water drainage through the porous shell. If the air–water front penetrates the microcapsule interior before buckling starts, the capillary loading area collapses and buckling is prevented. Drying therefore follows two competing capillary pathways: One drives buckling by sustaining distributed capillary loading on the shell, whereas the other suppresses buckling through early interior air invasion. Inspired by this insight, we preintroduce an internal air bubble into each microcapsule to act as a capillary sink and bias drying toward the air-invasion pathway. Our findings provide a mechanics-based blueprint guiding the design of robust, dry-stable microcapsules for pharmaceuticals, agriculture, and beyond.

Article.Title: Localized end-on heating for hot spot ignition in precompressed isochoric plasmas
Article.Authors: Jiang B.; Xu H.; Xu Z.; Zeng B.; Wu F.; Zhou G.; Yang X.; Zhang Q.; Song H.; Fang K.; Zhang Y.; Yuan X.; Zhang Z.; Yuan D.; Zhang C.; Shi C.; Qiu Z.; Wang W.; Li X.; Li Y.; Liu J.; Zheng J.; Zhu J.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: In fast ignition inertial confinement fusion, a “heating cone” is employed to shorten the transport distance of the relativistic electron beam (REB) to the high-density plasma core, thereby mitigating energy losses at the plasma edge. However, its insertion depth and survival time are constrained by the sustained pressure from the large-scale plasma edge during the implosion process. Our whole-process simulations demonstrated that, in the double-cone ignition scheme, the head-on collision of two deuterium-tritium plasma jets not only forms a high-density plateau with a small-scale edge, but also substantially reduces the interaction time between the heating cone and the colliding plasma to approximately 0.1 ns . This shortened interaction time enables the heating cone to remain intact after the peak compression, even when placed directly at the small-scale edge of the colliding plasma. The small-scale edge is compatible with the range of the soft-spectrum REB generated by the heating lasers. Such a REB efficiently heats a localized end-on hot spot adjacent to the high-density plateau, guided by a kT-level magnetic field amplified from a seed field during the collision process. Ignited by the localized hot spot, the high-density plateau can undergo sufficient burning and achieve a fusion energy gain of 6.8 using 60 kJ heating lasers.

Article.Title: Chaperone modulation and the structural basis for sRNA recognition by the conserved ribonuclease YicC
Article.Authors: Katsuya-Gaviria K.; Paris G.; Luisi B.; Lulla A.
Article.Abstract: The broadly conserved bacterial endoribonuclease YicC represents a widespread but enigmatic family of RNA processing enzymes with poorly defined substrate selectivity. Here, we show that Escherichia coli YicC displays a distinct selectivity, cleaving small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) such as RyhB and RprA but not when they are in complexes with cognate mRNA targets or RNA sponges. Furthermore, we demonstrate that RyhB processing is modulated, but not abolished, by the RNA chaperone Hfq. Our cryo-EM structures of E. coli YicC in apo form and in complexes with substrate and nonsubstrate RNA species capture marked quaternary and tertiary structural switches triggered by sRNA stem-loop binding that engulf and ratchet the RNA into an internal catalytic channel. Structural comparison of cleavable (RyhB) and noncleavable (MicA) sRNA-bound complexes reveal a near-identical ground-state binding mode, proving that cavity docking is sequence-tolerant and decoupled from catalytic execution. Together, our findings suggest that YicC may be a state-selective endoribonuclease and reveal a framework for selective RNA clearance in bacterial posttranscriptional regulation.

Article.Title: CD49f identifies stem-like memory T cells with enhanced therapeutic potency
Article.Authors: Lineburg K.; Panikkar A.; Khaledi P.; Leung C.; Solomon M.; Martins P.; Le T.; Khanna R.; Smith C.
Article.Abstract: The efficacy of adoptive cell therapies depends on the presence of T cells with durable self-renewal, proliferative capacity, and differentiation potential, yet heterogeneity within starting cell populations remains a major barrier to consistent clinical outcomes. Here, we identify CD49f as a marker of a unique subset of human memory T cells with stem-like characteristics. CD49f Hi memory CD8 + and CD4 + T cells exhibited transcriptional and phenotypic features associated with T cell stemness, including elevated LEF1, TCF1, CCR7, CD27, and CD28, while CD49f Lo cells exhibited effector-like transcriptional programs. Clinical evaluation of solid-organ transplant recipients treated with virus-specific T cells for cytomegalovirus complications demonstrated that autologous T cell therapies manufactured from CD49f Hi -enriched T cells were associated with superior immune reconstitution and greater in vivo expansion of CMV-specific T cells. Functional assays further revealed that CD49f Hi memory T cells possessed enhanced proliferative capacity and transcriptional plasticity following activation. Consistent with these findings, CD19 CAR T cells engineered from CD49f Hi memory T cells demonstrated improved persistence and conferred superior survival in a preclinical lymphoma model. Together, these findings establish CD49f as a marker of a stem-like memory T cell subset with enhanced therapeutic potential and identify CD49f Hi enrichment as a practical strategy to improve the consistency, durability, and clinical efficacy of both virus-specific and CAR T cell therapies.

Article.Title: Galectin-3 links microglial neuroinflammation to Aβ aggregation and lysosomal processing
Article.Authors: Camprubí-Ferrer L.; Soldán-Hidalgo J.; Axell E.; Dell’Eva M.; García-Cruzado M.; García-Revilla J.; Yang Y.; Fernández-Calle R.; Larlham L.; Chouhan B.; Talaverón R.; Paulus A.; Danielson L.; Gomez-Arboledas A.; Klementieva O.; Gutierrez A.; Vitorica J.; Wennström M.; Gouras G.; Frontiñán-Rubio J.; Boza-Serrano A.; Rabinovich G.; Venero J.; Deierborg T.
Article.Abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet the molecular mechanisms linking microglial dysfunction to amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify galectin-3 (Gal3) as a regulator of plaque-associated microglial responses, linking Aβ aggregation, lysosomal function, and neuritic pathology. Using postmortem brain tissue from AD patients, we found that Gal3 + microglia preferentially associate with cored plaques and correlate with increased LAMP1 + dystrophic neurites. Gal3 was also detected in microglial lysosomal compartments, extramicroglial dystrophic structures, and in association with extracellular amyloid fibrils, suggesting roles in both intracellular and extracellular Aβ processing. In APP mice, Gal3 deficiency reduced plaque burden and neuritic dystrophy, increased plaque compaction, and enhanced TREM2 coverage around amyloid plaques. Mechanistically, in vitro microglial experiments showed that Gal3 modulates Aβ uptake and lysosomal processing, whereas lysosomal dysfunction promoted the accumulation of fibrillar Aβ from initially monomeric species, particularly in Gal3-deficient cells. Cell-free assays demonstrated that Gal3 preferentially binds fibrillar Aβ, inhibits secondary nucleation, and alters fibril morphology, while Gal3-modified fibrillar Aβ reduces N2a neuronal cell number. Finally, in silico structural analyses identified candidate Gal3 interactors enriched in leucine-rich-repeat and immunoglobulin-like proteins, supporting a role for this lectin in immune receptor regulation. Complementary in vivo transcriptomic profiling showed that Gal3 deletion suppresses type I interferon and microglial neurodegenerative transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings position Gal3 at the interface between Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and plaque-associated microglial responses in AD.

Article.Title: Structural basis for the selective inhibition of the PI3KC3-C2 complex by Rubicon in endolysosome maturation and mitophagy
Article.Authors: Chen M.; Bishnu A.; Duan Y.; Riley J.; Ni Q.; Joiner A.; Allen I.; Holzbaur E.; Ganley I.; Hurley J.
Article.Abstract: Rubicon is a negative regulator of autophagy and the endolysosomal network (ELN) and an antagonist of the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex II (PI3KC3-C2). Inhibition of Rubicon is considered a potential means to therapeutically upregulate autophagy and the ELN to treat Parkinson’s disease and other conditions characterized by autophagic and ELN dysfunction. Rubicon is specific for the UV radiation resistance-associated gene protein (UVRAG)-containing PI3KC3-C2 over the purely autophagic ATG14-containing PI3KC3-C1 complex. Here, we determined the high-resolution cryoelectron microscopy structure of PI3KC3-C2 in complex with the PI3KC3-binding domain of Rubicon and compared it to cryo-EM structures of unbound PI3KC3-C2 and PI3KC3-C1. Rubicon binds directly to PI3KC3-C2 only via the BARA domain of the BECN1 subunit, which is common to both C1 and C2. The selectivity of Rubicon for the PI3KC3-C2 complex over the PI3KC3-C1 complex is attributed to a conformation of the BECN1 BARA domain induced by UVRAG, rather than to direct contact with UVRAG or direct antagonism by the ATG14 subunit of PI3KC3-C1. Targeted disruption of the Rubicon:PI3K3-C2 structural interface by site-directed mutations enhances mitophagic activity in human epithelial cells to levels comparable to those observed in Rubicon knockout cells. Similarly, disruption of the interaction in Rubicon-overexpressing hippocampal neurons restored lysosomal flux to wild-type levels. These data show that suppressing the function of PI3K3-C2 can fully account for the negative regulatory effects of Rubicon in the autophagy and ELN pathways.

Article.Title: A periplasmic regulator establishes adaptive impermeability to control carbapenem entry
Article.Authors: Ducret V.; Gonçalves Milho C.; Gonzalez D.; Perron K.
Article.Abstract: Outer-membrane permeability is a major determinant of antibiotic susceptibility in Gram-negative bacteria and is generally thought to be controlled through transcriptional regulation of porin expression. Here we identify the small periplasmic protein PtrA as a regulator of OprD-dependent carbapenem permeability in Pseudomonas aeruginosa . PtrA promotes imipenem resistance without altering OprD abundance, associates with OprD-containing membrane complexes and reduces intracellular imipenem entry. Using zinc and copper as complementary physiological signals, we show that PtrA-mediated permeability control is mechanistically distinct from CzcRS-dependent repression of oprD and precedes transcriptional porin depletion. These findings define a two-phase mechanism in which rapid periplasmic regulation provides an immediate adaptive response before transcriptional remodeling of the outer membrane. Our work identifies adaptive impermeability as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking environmental sensing to dynamic control of bacterial outer-membrane permeability.

Article.Title: Paul R. Ehrlich: Visionary pioneer and public scientist for nature and humanity
Article.Authors: Daily G.; Dirzo R.; Folke C.; Holdren J.; Levin S.
Article.Abstract: Paul R. Ehrlich is legendary for his scientific insight and impact—and even more so for bringing science to the public through writing, speaking, and, most famously, twenty-some appearances on the Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson. He was quick-witted—he would readily add quick-tempered, with chagrin—and could bring down a house. Paul cherished deep friendships and nature. He loved collaborating with his wife of 71 years, Anne H. Ehrlich, and with innumerable students and colleagues all over the world. He made transformative contributions of astonishing range, including in ecology and evolution, biodiversity and conservation, human population and overconsumption, and the integration of ecology and economics. He was deeply committed to racial and social justice, reflected in his actions and writing.

Article.Title: Sleep pressure is increased by protein fragments and decreased by processive proteolysis
Article.Authors: Cho A.; Chen S.; Varshavsky A.; Prober D.
Article.Abstract: Sleep is universal among animals, yet the molecular-level causes and functions of sleep are incompletely understood. The fragment generation hypothesis (FGH) posits that sleep, at least in part, is an adaptive response to protein fragments, many of them protein-sized, that accumulate during wakefulness owing to cleavages by proteases, including caspases and Ca 2+ -activated calpains. According to the FGH, these fragments are a source of homeostatic sleep pressure that increases during wakefulness, and one function of sleep is to decrease protein fragment levels through their slower production and faster degradation during sleep. Predictions of the FGH have not previously been tested. Using zebrafish, we show that pharmacological inhibition of caspases decreases sleep, in agreement with the prediction of the FGH that a slower production of protein fragments would decrease sleep pressure. Pharmacological inhibition of the proteasome is shown to have the opposite effect, an increased sleep, in agreement with another prediction of the FGH, that sleep pressure would increase if fragments are protected from their proteasome-mediated degradation. Consistent with this prediction, a caspase-generated subunit of the activated caspase-3 is strongly upregulated by a sleep-increasing inhibition of the proteasome. The increase of sleep by proteasome inhibitors was found to be reduced by inhibition of calpains, suggesting that calpain-generated, proteasome-degradable protein fragments contribute to sleep pressure. Pharmacological inhibition of calpains also causes a decrease in rebound sleep after sleep deprivation, as predicted by the FGH. Together, these results suggest that the FGH may provide a molecular-level explanation of a cause and function of sleep.

Article.Title: SCN1B intron 3 retention results in a nonsense-mediated decay–sensitive mRNA linked to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
Article.Authors: Bakshi S.; Catalfio A.; Chen C.; Yuan Y.; Lopez-Santiago L.; Moore C.; Seagull D.; Macedo S.; Hussein A.; Verma I.; Stokes K.; Minton J.; Dang L.; Achkar C.; Poduri A.; Parent J.; Isom L.
Article.Abstract: Biallelic variants in the voltage-gated sodium channel (VGSC) gene SCN1B are linked to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy type 52 (DEE52). SCN1B encodes two isoforms: transmembrane β1, generated by all 6 coding exons, and β1B, generated by exons 1 to 3 followed by retention of intron 3 ( SCN1B -IR). Transmembrane β1 subunits are multifunctional proteins that regulate sodium current and channel cell-surface expression, participate in cell–cell and cell–matrix adhesion, and modulate transcription. Several DEE52 variants in the transmembrane β1 coding region have been shown to result in mixed loss-of-function. DEE52 variants are also identified in SCN1B -IR, yet their functional impacts remain unknown. Here, we provide evidence that SCN1B -IR is a cell type–specific, nonsense-mediated decay (NMD)–sensitive transcript. We investigate a severe biallelic DEE52 patient variant in intron 3, SCN1B c.449-2A>G, which results in expression of SCN1B -IR, but not transmembrane β1 transcripts. A transgenic mouse model that expresses SCN1B -IR, but not transmembrane β1, transcript phenocopies Scn1b null mice with seizures and early death. Thus, SCN1B -IR functions as an NMD-sensitive transcript that cannot compensate for the loss of transmembrane β1. We propose that future work may reveal SCN1B -IR to be a therapeutic target similar to other NMD-targeted transcripts.

Article.Title: Molecular interactions underlying selective partitioning of clients into MED1 and FUS condensates
Article.Authors: Yasuda I.; Yamamoto E.; Yasuoka K.; Lindorff-Larsen K.
Article.Abstract: Biomolecular condensates selectively recruit and exclude proteins, and this partitioning is sometimes dictated by their intrinsically disordered regions. Factors that determine partitioning include client–scaffold interactions and stabilization of the scaffold network within the condensate, yet a molecular and predictive understanding has not been fully achieved. Here, we used coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate molecular interactions between two types of nuclear proteins as scaffolds: the charge-rich disordered region of Mediator 1 (MED1) and the aromatic-rich disordered region of Fused in Sarcoma (FUS), in mixtures with client intrinsically disordered regions from six different proteins. We show distinct partitioning into the MED1 and FUS condensates, while the presence of RNA in both dilute and dense phases modulated client partitioning. Favorable client–scaffold interaction energies within condensates were associated with client partitioning, while client–scaffold interactions competed with scaffold self-interactions. Analysis of interaction energies of individual residues revealed that the interactions were localized to specific sequence regions: charged blocks for interactions with MED1, and dispersed aromatic residues for interactions with FUS. Using residue–resolved interaction energies from our molecular dynamics simulations, we developed sequence-based predictors of client partitioning into MED1 and FUS condensates. Our prediction approach for partitioning can be extended to other biomolecules, offering a framework to analyze their partitioning in cellular environments.

Article.Title: Intranasal delivery of a ROS-activatable myeloperoxidase inhibitor alleviates Alzheimer’s-like symptoms and pathology
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Cong P.; Feng E.; Zeller M.; Zhang B.; Lv Y.; Motlagh N.; Linnoila J.; Wang H.; Wang C.; Xu Z.; Gao K.; Chen Q.; Luo Y.; Wang H.; Ni D.; Xiong L.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Chronic neuroinflammation and oxidative stress are important contributors to Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Myeloperoxidase (MPO), a key driver of oxidative inflammation released mainly by activated microglia in the neurodegenerative brain, is a potential therapeutic target to inhibit the neuroinflammatory cascade and oxidative damage in AD, but the underlying mechanisms remain unexplored, and achieving targeted brain delivery of an MPO inhibitor and minimizing systemic effects remain significant challenges. We addressed these limitations by first establishing that genetic deletion of MPO in the 5XFAD mouse model improved memory performance and reduced amyloid deposition, validating MPO as a therapeutic target. We then developed a liposome-encapsulated reactive oxygen species (ROS)-activatable MPO inhibitor (LERAMI). LERAMI uniquely combines targeted delivery with on-demand drug release, utilizing a ROS-sensitive linker to selectively release MPO inhibitors in ROS-rich regions within the AD microenvironment, minimizing off-target effects and systemic toxicity. In the 5XFAD mouse model. By reducing MPO expression and activity, LERAMI significantly improved cognitive performance, accompanied by decreased microglial activation, attenuated oxidative DNA damage, improved synaptic and neuronal density, and reduced amyloid burden. RNA sequencing revealed a robust hippocampal transcriptomic reprogramming, with upregulation of pathways critical for synaptic plasticity, calcium signaling, axon guidance, and neuroprotection, along with downregulation of inflammatory and immune response pathways. These findings demonstrate that targeted ROS-activatable MPO inhibition with LERAMI represents a promising therapeutic strategy for AD and potentially other neuroinflammatory diseases, offering a unique approach to mitigate neuroinflammation, preserve synaptic integrity, and restore cognitive function.

Article.Title: The debt burden of tropical cyclones and climate change
Article.Authors: Choi J.; Jing R.; Callahan C.; Burke M.; Diffenbaugh N.
Article.Abstract: Addressing climate change through mitigation and adaptation is expected to require more than $6 trillion in global investment annually by 2035. Yet many countries face significant barriers to accessing this finance, including low or absent credit ratings, large debt burdens, and high borrowing costs. Climate change may further amplify these barriers, creating a “vicious cycle” in which mounting economic losses reduce the capacity of countries to invest in adaptation and mitigation. We provide evidence that the cost and availability of capital for many countries have already been shaped by both historical exposure to naturally-occurring tropical cyclones (TCs) and anthropogenic warming. Our empirical estimates suggest that, on average across TC-exposed countries, 20% of debt-to-GDP ratios are attributable to TCs from 1980 to 2019. Across all countries, GDP levels are on average 12% lower due to the combined impacts of baseline naturally-occurring TCs and anthropogenic warming. In a separate correlational machine-learning analysis, we estimate that these macroeconomic impacts are associated with an increased likelihood of hotter countries receiving credit ratings below investment grade ( < BBB–), as well as persistent credit risk premiums of at least 1 basis point in 64 countries and 5 basis points in highly exposed countries. We provide estimates for 181 countries, including many TC-affected and/or hot countries that do not have bond yield data. Future increases in temperature and TC activity may further worsen sovereign credit conditions, potentially undermining climate resilience and long-run development prospects.

Article.Title: Intrinsically disordered ligands for the control of receptor uptake by endocytosis
Article.Authors: Park S.; Sarro I.; Nguyen T.; Kamatar A.; Wang L.; Lafer E.; Rangamani P.; Stachowiak J.
Article.Abstract: Endocytosis plays a crucial role in signaling, recycling, and degradation of receptors. Controlling endocytosis of specific receptors is therefore a major goal for both basic science and medicine. While antibody-induced dimerization can drive signaling-induced uptake of some receptors, the steric bulk of antibodies generally inhibits endocytosis, such that control over receptor uptake remains an unmet need. Recent work has demonstrated that attractive interactions between intrinsically disordered proteins drive inward membrane curvature, a key step in endocytosis. To harness this phenomenon for the control of receptor uptake, we designed chimeras that consisted of disordered domains fused to ligands for specific receptors. These chimeras condensed on membrane surfaces, in agreement with computational modeling, driving receptor clustering and uptake via clathrin-mediated endocytosis. In contrast, chimeras that repelled one another resisted condensation, helping receptors escape endocytosis and remain on the cell surface. Taken together, these results suggest that by modulating the amino acid sequence of intrinsically disordered ligands, we can promote or hinder the internalization of specific receptors by endocytic pathways. More broadly, these findings suggest a generalizable strategy for controlling the plasma membrane lifetime of diverse receptors, opening up new pathways for modulating cellular behavior and delivering therapeutics.

Article.Title: Evolution, information content, and optimality of gene regulatory architectures
Article.Authors: Barton N.; Tkačik G.
Article.Abstract: Evolution of genetic regulatory sequences is shaped by their genotype–phenotype map, but this map itself can evolve via changes in the molecular machinery that reads out the regulatory sequences. Using population genetics theory, we derive a maximization principle, which implies that genotype–phenotype maps will evolve to associate fit phenotypes with larger numbers of possible genotypes. Mathematically, this builds on analogies between population genetics and statistical physics, as well as optimal coding in information theory. The results are particularly interesting in the context of transcriptional regulation, where optimal values of certain parameters that determine the gene regulatory architecture can be derived even without a complete knowledge of the molecular mechanisms involved. We illustrate the theory using a simplified model of transcription factor (TF) binding to cis-regulatory elements (CREs): the fraction of possible CREs across the entire genotype space that bind a given TF evolves to match the fraction of CREs under selection to bind that TF. Similar “frequency matching” results are expected to emerge generically, because selection implicitly moves the entire regulatory architecture toward a fitness maximum, determining the “replicated genotype–phenotype map” for all CREs, while it simultaneously adapts toward individually fit CREs on that map. We discuss the subtleties and limitations of the theory related to biophysical constraints and the need for mutational robustness. Last, our theory suggests a possible mathematical definition for evolvability with predictive power that can be tested in evolutionary simulations and, ultimately, in comparative genetics studies.

Article.Title: A circuit mechanism for psychosis vulnerability during perimenopause
Article.Authors: Perez S.; Boley A.; Reiley H.; Yang O.; Lilly K.; Lodge D.
Article.Abstract: The transition to menopause is a period of profound physiological change that encompasses nearly one-third of a woman’s lifespan and is associated with a distinct rise in the incidence of psychosis. Despite the clinical burden of menopause-associated psychosis, the circuit-level mechanisms linking reproductive aging to psychiatric vulnerability remain poorly defined. Current understanding is limited by rodent models that utilize abrupt surgical hormone loss, which fail to capture the progressive endocrine fluctuations and follicular depletion characteristic of the natural menopausal transition. Here, we investigate how the gradual transition from perimenopause to postmenopause regulates the ventral hippocampus-mesolimbic dopamine circuit, a pathway centrally implicated in the development of psychotic symptoms. Specifically, we show that the perimenopausal transition induces a transient state of ventral hippocampal hyperactivity that selectively drives dopamine system dysfunction, whereas this modulatory control is absent in the postmenopausal state. These findings reveal that psychosis-related circuit instability is precipitated specifically by the hormonal transition itself, rather than the persistent state of estrogen deficiency that follows. This contrasts with the long-standing “estrogen protection hypothesis,” which posits that low hormone levels are the primary driver of symptoms and explains why standard hormone replacement and antipsychotic therapies often yield inconsistent results. Our results establish that perimenopause is a mechanistically distinct neurobiological window characterized by a unique failure of hippocampal-dopamine circuit regulation. By identifying this specific period of circuit instability, this work provides a framework for stage-specific psychiatric interventions and reframes reproductive aging as a series of distinct transitions in brain function.

Article.Title: Unconventional modulation of Na <sub>v</sub> 1.4 by a scorpion toxin through cooperative binding to voltage sensor and the pore domain
Article.Authors: Zhou X.; Wang H.; Lu M.; Cong Y.; Zhang J.; Chen M.; Cai J.; Zhang J.; Liu Q.; Huang J.; Yan N.; Jin X.; Liu Z.
Article.Abstract: Voltage-gated sodium (Na v ) channels are targeted by animal peptide toxins, which serve as powerful molecular probes for dissecting channel structure-function relationships and lead molecules for drug discovery. β-scorpion toxins trap voltage sensor domains to remodel Na v channel gating, yet high-resolution structural evidence defining this process remains elusive. MD simulations recapitulate step-wise VSD II conformational transitions and demonstrate that toxin-driven rearrangements tighten the intracellular pore gate. Mutagenesis combined with electrophysiology confirm that VSD II trapping remodels the activation and inactivation gating, whereas ECL III engagement contributes both to inhibition and activation. Subtype-specific sequence variations in the ECL III region underlie the prominent species- and isoform-dependent activities of the toxin toward insect and mammalian Na v channels. Article.Title: Neurovascular protein half-lives in health and aging
Article.Authors: Gastfriend B.; Pintarić L.; Baig I.; Gonzalez D.; Daneman R.
Article.Abstract: Specializations of blood vasculature in the central nervous system (CNS), including the blood–brain barrier (BBB), neurovascular coupling, and perivascular spaces, maintain CNS homeostasis and become dysfunctional in disease and aging. Protein turnover, the process by which proteins are continually degraded and replaced, profoundly influences cell and tissue function and is dysregulated in aging and disease. Understanding the turnover of neurovascular proteins could provide insight into how the vasculature achieves both long-term structural stability and dynamic regulation. Vascular proteins, however, are underrepresented in previous studies of in vivo brain protein turnover. In this work, we used stable isotope labeling, nonenzymatic blood vessel enrichment, and high-resolution mass spectrometry-based proteomics to quantify the half-lives of brain vascular proteins in young adult and aged mice. We report half-life estimates for 1,358 proteins, including components of endothelial junctions, BBB transporters, astrocyte endfoot proteins, and vascular basement membrane proteins. We found that certain classes of proteins with related functions had similar half-lives, including BBB junctional proteins (~3 d), BBB transporters (~2 to 6 d), and most basement membrane components (>30 d). We also identified peptide motifs enriched in proteins with short and long half-lives and found differences in half-life distributions for cell type–specific proteomes. Finally, although we did not observe a global age-related shift in vascular protein turnover, we did identify specific proteins with increased or decreased half-lives in aging. This work establishes a high-quality database of neurovascular protein half-lives and provides a foundation for understanding how protein turnover contributes to neurovascular function and age-associated dysfunction.

Article.Title: The sound of persuasion: Using generative AI to identify gender gaps in political influence
Article.Authors: Busby E.; Argyle L.; Davis P.; Gubler J.; Hepner B.; Karpowitz C.; Lyman A.; Olcott J.; Preece J.; Wingate D.
Article.Abstract: Women often experience a deficit in persuasive influence, particularly in contexts like politics, where expectations about women’s behavior may conflict with gendered expectations about the domain and role. In spite of this widespread pattern, the mechanisms behind the gender gap in persuasion are difficult to isolate and test in dynamic political conversations. Women may be less persuasive simply because role-based expectations prompt others to afford women less authority when speaking about politics generally or about some political topics. Alternatively, women may be less persuasive because they tend to use linguistic patterns or rhetorical strategies that are less effective. Using an original AI-based approach, we put 4,300 human subjects into realistic, real-time phone conversations with an AI agent. These agents were randomly assigned either a masculine or feminine gendered conversation topic and a male- or female-sounding voice, allowing us to manipulate topic and perceptions of speakers’ gender while holding constant other elements of rhetorical content and strategy. After validating the experimental treatments, we find no direct effects of perceived gender of the AI agent, as cued by voice. However, gender affects other important aspects of the persuasive interaction. Research subjects were more likely to be persuaded about the masculine topic (defense spending) than the feminine topic (aid to the poor). Additionally, women research subjects were, on average, more persuaded than men. To the extent that men and women emphasize different topics in political conversations and have different discussion partners, these dynamics are likely to shape women’s political persuasive influence.

Article.Title: Domain-encoded DNA barcodes for combinatorial multiplexed protein imaging via stepwise displacement
Article.Authors: Xiao H.; Cui W.; Chen Y.; Guo Z.; Cheng W.; Guo Q.; Yang X.; Wang K.; Huang J.
Article.Abstract: Multiplexed protein imaging via DNA barcoding faces a fundamental scaling constraint: Each target requires a distinct DNA identity, making barcode capacity grow only linearly with the number of validated sequences. Combinatorial encoding in RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization achieves exponential scaling by distributing shared readout sequences across dozens of probes per transcript, but antibody-based protein labeling lacks this multiprobe architecture. Here, we report domain-encoded DNA barcodes (DEDBs), which embed combinatorial identity within the internal domain organization of a single-stranded DNA scaffold. Three orthogonal encoding units arranged across three encoding domains define a theoretical design space of 27 barcodes. Sequence reuse does not compromise readout specificity: Each read strand spans two adjacent domains, so a mismatched read strand inevitably contains a continuous stretch of noncomplementary bases and forms a thermodynamically disfavored intermediate that is subsequently displaced by the perfectly matched strand. We term this self-correcting behavior thermodynamic proofreading, and a three-process kinetic model shows that specificity arises not from initial binding discrimination but from cognate-driven correction at the product level. Coupled with signal-amplified antibody labeling, DEDBs enable quantitatively decoded nine-target intracellular protein imaging in fixed cells. The same barcode library supports Polychrome trajectory decoding for combinatorial identification and Monochrome cycle-resolved visualization for direct single-target inspection through reconfiguration of read-strand labeling. By generating combinatorial identities through the positional arrangement of reusable sequences within a single DNA strand, DEDBs reframe DNA barcode design from sequence enumeration to positional encoding.

Here, we develop a biophysical theory of interacting branched cells and show that coupling their growth to neighbor repulsion drives efficient tissue tiling with minimal territorial overlap. Strikingly, our model predicts that the same local mechanism progressively suppresses long-range density fluctuations during development, driving the system toward a large-scale order called hyperuniformity. We confirm these theoretical predictions on microglial patterning in the developing retina and show that in perturbation experiments with limited arbor growth, both tiling and fluctuation suppression are disrupted. Our results reveal that two seemingly distinct features of tissue organization, efficient space-filling and large-scale order, share a single dynamical origin, suggesting a general principle for robust tissue patterning.

Article.Title: Diffusive and advective transport in structurally anisotropic fibrous hydrogels
Article.Authors: Huang Y.; Yin J.; He X.; Ramachandran A.; Naguib H.; Kumacheva E.
Article.Abstract: Changes in fiber orientation in structurally anisotropic fibrous extracellular matrices govern transport, distribution, and accumulation of biologically active molecules and therapeutic nanoparticles in tissues. Fundamental studies of advection-driven transport in such matrices are challenging because changes in network anisotropy are generally coupled with variation in fiber dimensions, density, and surface chemistry. Here, a fibrous hydrogel was engineered in which the type and degree of fiber orientation were decoupled from these structural characteristics. Advection of charge-neutral nanoparticle probes under physiologically relevant pressure gradients was studied in a channel geometry that imposed spatially nonuniform flow across the fibrous network. The probe advection was quantified by the time of probe permeation through the gel along the fastest flow path and the time of probe distribution within the gel. We show that the permeation timescale was governed by advection along the pressure gradient, whereas the distribution timescale transitioned between advection- and diffusion-limited behavior depending on fiber orientation and probe dimension. The decoupling between these timescales became more pronounced with stronger alignment along the pressure gradient and with increasing probe dimension. Scaling analysis and a fluid dynamics simulation model further provided mechanistic insight into these experimental findings. Together, these results identify the key structural factors governing advection in anisotropic fibrous networks and provide a platform for future studies of the role of fiber orientation in tissues in regulating the transport, distribution, and dissemination of biologically active molecules, exosomes, and nanoparticle therapeutics under interstitial fluid flow.

Article.Title: Activation of ROPGEFs by a malectin-like receptor kinase is involved in tip growth regulation in Physcomitrium patens
Article.Authors: Lyu R.; Ruan J.; Chen Y.; Tian H.; Yi P.
Article.Abstract: Rho-type GTPases of plants (ROPs) play essential roles in polarized cell growth, cell division, and organogenesis. Their activation depends on two types of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs): the plant-specific PRONE-domain-containing ROPGEFs and DOCK-type SPKGEFs. While ROPGEFs have been proposed to be autoinhibited in pollen and activated by receptor-like kinases (RLKs), the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using the moss Physcomitrium patens , we show that moss ROPGEF4 and ROPGEF6 exhibit low intrinsic GEF activity and are not autoinhibited by non-PRONE regions, whereas the catalytic domain of SPK1 and SPK6 is highly active. Through a candidate screen, we identified MLRK1, a malectin-like receptor kinase, as a ROPGEF-interacting protein. MLRK1 directly phosphorylates ROPGEF4 and ROPGEF6 and stimulates their GEF activities in vitro. These effects are attenuated by substituting key phosphosites (Ser231 in ROPGEF4 and Ser524/Thr526 in ROPGEF6) with nonphosphorylatable residues. Structural modeling, pull-down assays, and functional analyses indicate that phosphorylation enhances ROPGEF-ROP interactions and promotes the membrane localization of ROPGEF4/6. Furthermore, ROPGEFs are not essential for polarized cell growth on their own but act redundantly with SPK2. At the apical membrane, ROPGEFs appear to activate ROPs, reduce their diffusion, promote actin filament assembly and vesicle secretion, and ultimately facilitate cell expansion and growth.
