Article.Title: Resilient j = 3/2 superconductivity in topological semimetal YPtBi
Article.Authors: Saraf P.; Crombie N.; Sharma R.; Dans J.; Sokratov D.; Mueller C.; Kumar R.; Kim H.; Roncaioli C.; Weiss W.; Carlton-Jones A.; Zavalij P.; Graf D.; Shekhar C.; Anlage S.; Felser C.; Paglione J.
Article.Abstract: Cooper pairing in most of the known fermionic superfluids occurs via spin-1/2 quasiparticle interactions that lead to spin-singlet or spin-triplet pairing. In the topological semimetal YPtBi, strong spin–orbit coupling results in a band inversion between highly symmetric s - and p -like electronic bands and a degeneracy at the Γ point that ensures the manifold of j = 3/2 quasiparticle states thrive near the Fermi level, where superconducting pairing occurs. Here we study the effects of magnetic and nonmagnetic disorder and carrier density on this exotic superconducting pairing state. By varying levels of disorder and carrier densities by nearly two and three orders of magnitude, respectively, we show that the superconducting critical temperature of YPtBi has a remarkable robustness, with little variation across this span. Our results suggest that superconductivity in YPtBi may reside in a regime where phase stiffness, rather than pair formation, governs the transition temperature. The insensitivity of Cooper pairing to dramatic changes in quasiparticle environment in a j = 3/2 superconductor highlights a form of protection realized in topological high-spin superconductors.

Article.Title: Anomeric configuration encodes mesophase preference of glucosylceramides in phospholipid membranes
Article.Authors: Biswas S.; Rohokale R.; Kundu S.; Zhou M.; Islam M.; Guo J.; Mane R.; Dessain S.; Fanucci G.; Guo Z.
Article.Abstract: Glycosphingolipids are key components of the cell glycocalyx, yet the extent to which their anomeric configuration affects their membrane organization remains unclear. EPR spectral simulations and complementary analyses showed that α-GlcCer predominantly partitioned into the lamellar phospholipid phase, whereas β-GlcCer was strongly enriched in the segregated GlcCer-rich phase. Importantly, analogous anomer-dependent EPR behavior was also observed for aqueous GlcCer dispersions in the absence of phospholipids, indicating that the distinct assembly propensities are intrinsic to the glycolipids and are modulated, rather than created, by the phospholipids. These findings support a two-mesophase model in which anomeric configuration acts as a stereochemical switch that biases GlcCer between phospholipid lamellae and segregated glycolipid nano-assemblies. Article.Title: Single-molecule FRET at 30: Toward conformational sequencing
Article.Authors: Hua B.; Ha T.
Article.Abstract: Single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) turned 30 this year. We argue that three advances usually treated as separate endeavors, i.e., high-information-content per-molecule readout, sequence-linked massive parallelism, and automated trajectory decoding, are in fact one convergence that is turning smFRET from a one-molecule-at-a-time measurement into a high-throughput conformational sequencer, a platform that measures dynamic conformational phenotypes across sequence space at scale. This perspective traces the 30-y arc, forecasts which advances will prove most transformative over the next decade, states the conditions on which that forecast depends, and identifies the bottlenecks that still remain.

Article.Authors: Rossi T.; Perrot A.; Huber A.; Poulain B.; Doussau F.; Valera A.; Isope P.
Article.Abstract: Sensorimotor processing relies on high-frequency signaling across widespread neuronal networks, during which synapses undergo rapid short-term plasticity (STP) that transiently enhances or depresses synaptic strength. We showed that along single axons, glutamate transients were detected at nearly all boutons, and displayed a high diversity of STP profiles. At individual boutons, initial synaptic weight and STP were regulated separately. Synaptic weight was primarily driven by release probability ( P r ) and the apparent number of functional release sites ( N ), whereas STP was mainly supported by rapid mobilization of synaptic vesicles. At the molecular level, we show that Synapsin II contributes to bouton-specific heterogeneity in release properties. These findings reveal that STP is regulated at the level of individual boutons by specific molecular determinants, enabling fine-tuned control of information flow in cerebellar circuits. A single granule cell could therefore translate an identical presynaptic spike pattern into distinct release dynamics at each of its boutons, thus diversifying the temporal structure of the information delivered to Purkinje cells.

Article.Title: Nutritional niches reveal mutualism resilience in urban fungus-farming ants
Article.Authors: Shik J.; Ditlevsen M.; Posma A.; O’Brien A.; Ottesen K.; Schougaard O.; Larsen R.; Rødsgaard-Jørgensen A.; Michelsen A.; Rinnan R.; Morimoto J.
Article.Abstract: Maintaining optimized nutrient exchange between partnered species across changing environments presents a fundamental challenge for nutritional mutualisms. Yet quantitative approaches linking nutrient acquisition by one partner with the nutritional requirements of the other have been lacking. Here we extend the Nutritional Geometry Framework from organisms and colonies to interspecific mutualisms by linking realized nutritional niches (RNNs) with nutritional performance landscapes to quantify nutritional homeostasis between interacting species. Nutritional analyses of thousands of DNA-barcoded plant fragments collected by free-ranging Panamanian leafcutter ants revealed that RNNs for fungal cultivar provisioning diverged between degraded urban and intact rainforest habitats. Despite this, colonies converged on similar nutritional intake targets that were similarly positioned relative to regions of high fungal performance, while fungal nutritional yield remained stable across habitats. These findings demonstrate that correspondence between colony nutritional intake and fungal nutritional performance provides a quantitative means of assessing nutritional homeostasis across interacting species and establishes a foundation for comparative analyses of nutrient exchange across mutualisms experiencing environmental change.

Article.Abstract: Despite highly efficacious antiretroviral therapy (ART), durable ART-free remission remains a central objective of HIV-1 cure strategies. Sustained CD8 T cell–dependent suppression lasting nearly 300 wk developed in every evaluable animal receiving the FcγR-engaging variant but arose in only one of eight recipients of the FcγR-null variant. FcγR-driven immunomodulation imprinted a CD8 T cell response characterized by enhanced antigen-specific effector function, early clonal focusing with sustained clonotype persistence, and distinct cellular-state transcriptional signatures. Article.Title: No evidence for a universal effect of writing on language use or the evolution of syntax
Article.Authors: Meloni C.; Ivani J.; Zakharko T.; You G.; van Dam K.; Cathcart C.; Bickel B.
Article.Abstract: The acquisition of writing has a lasting effect on how languages are processed in the brain, raising the possibility that it also affects how they are used and evolve over time. A popular hypothesis is that writing specifically leads to the increased use and evolution of complex hierarchical structures in language. While most case studies on individual languages have supported this, it remains unclear whether results scale to larger and more diverse sets of languages. Here we test this prediction in two ways: 1) synchronically, by modeling the effect of modality (written vs. nonwritten) on syntactic complexity, operationalized via hierarchy depth and clause count inside sentences, in corpora from 30 languages; and 2) diachronically, by modeling whether the development of writing affected the phylogenetic dynamics of hierarchy in clause combinations across 59 languages from three families. We found no effect of writing on the response variables in either analysis. Hierarchy depth and clause count inside sentences do not demonstrably differ between spoken and written use of language, and the introduction of writing had no discernible effect on the evolution of clause combinations in grammar. There is weak evidence for a decrease in variance in structural asymmetry after the introduction of writing in one family, possibly reflecting the impact of increased normativity. Our findings challenge popular beliefs about the relationship between writing and hierarchy and suggest that the evolution of syntax is more driven by culturally variable ideas about style in linguistic expression than by the evolution of writing.

Article.Title: Transoceanic dispersals and island extinctions shape global snipe and woodcock diversity
Article.Authors: Zhao M.; Capurucho J.; Stucky B.; Steadman D.; Bates J.; LeFebvre M.; Guralnick R.; Allen J.; Oswald J.
Article.Abstract: Island colonization through transoceanic dispersal has been central in shaping insular biodiversity. Following colonization, island populations often undergo morphological shifts, which may promote ecological specialization and endemism, but often increase vulnerability to extinction. Most species in the shorebird family Scolopacidae are highly migratory, which likely underpins their propensity for long-distance dispersal. Notably, snipes ( Gallinago , Coenocorypha ) and woodcocks ( Scolopax ) have colonized diverse island regions, including the southwest Pacific, Malay Archipelago, Japan’s Amami, and the Caribbean, although none of the extant island endemics are migratory. The southwest Pacific and Caribbean taxa have suffered substantial recent extinction driven by human impacts. Here, we investigate avian evolutionary and biogeographic dynamics using a combination of morphology and phylogenomic data from target capture sequencing of key extant and extinct snipes and woodcocks. Our results reveal four independent dispersals from the Eastern to Western Hemisphere and a trans-Pacific dispersal from South America to the southwest Pacific islands. Comparative analyses of migratory behavior and morphology demonstrate pronounced changes in insular groups. For example, the small Austral snipes Coenocorypha are nested within Gallinago , sister to a group of much larger, continental South American snipes. Another case is the extinct Scolopax brachycarpa of Hispaniola which osteologically more resembles Scolopax , but genetically belongs to Gallinago . Gallinago brachycarpa and other extinct Caribbean snipes may represent a radiation that is lost forever. Our findings shed light on the processes that generate and erase avian diversity on islands, highlighting the dynamic interplay of dispersal, adaptation to novel conditions, and risk for extinction.

Article.Title: China’s energy transition strategy favoring both coal and renewables: Economic risks and global implications
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Cui X.; Kammen D.
Article.Abstract: China’s energy strategy is navigating a complex policy landscape: While leading the world in renewable energy manufacturing and deployment, it is simultaneously pursuing a continued expansion of its coal-fired power fleet. This paper examines this dual trajectory by building an integrated analytical framework that combines domestic and international perspectives to analyze the social, economic, climate, and geopolitical impacts of China’s new coal-power plant investments. Combining historical trends, government planning, and projections from influential policy teams, we find that a tripling of renewable capacity by 2030, a pace China is on track to meet, is sufficient to satisfy all projected electricity demand scenarios when considered alongside the evolving generation mix and planned storage deployment. We further show that additional coal capacity is not required to ensure adequate electricity supply under these scenarios. The coal pathway could expose up to $223.6 billion of stranded assets from new projects and add an additional 327,000 workers in a declining industry. Furthermore, this trajectory may weaken the alignment between China’s domestic energy investment and its international clean energy leadership. We conclude that a clean-energy-led pathway that halts new coal construction is lower-cost, better for job growth, and more consistent with China’s role as a leader in the global clean energy transition.

Article.Title: Automating inequality? Gender bias in AI-mediated labor markets
Article.Authors: Elass K.; Gauthier G.; Nozza D.; Profeta P.
Article.Abstract: Generative AI is rapidly entering labor markets, with large language models (LLMs) now used to help write CVs and evaluate applicants. We study the risks this creates in a series of audit experiments in which applicant gender is randomly assigned while all other information is held constant. We find that LLMs generate gender-stereotypical CVs and exhibit gender bias in screening scores and wage recommendations. Screening scores track occupational gender segregation, penalizing women in male-dominated occupations and favoring them in female-dominated ones. Wage recommendations track occupational gender wage gaps when gender is explicit in the prompt, though this gradient weakens under name-based gender signaling and is sensitive to the LLMs being used. These disparities arise through two channels: evaluation bias, when identical CV content is evaluated differently by gender, and generation bias, when gendered content produced by the model affects later evaluation. Because the same systems shape both CV content and its subsequent assessment, these channels can reinforce one another. Taken together, our findings identify measurable risks of algorithmic amplification in AI-mediated job search.

Dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) translated from the mutant allele can be detected in postmortem brains of afflicted individuals. The arginine containing peptides, poly proline-arginine (poly-PR) and poly glycine-arginine (poly-GR), are particularly noxious to cells. Both can undergo cell-to-cell transmission, but underlying mechanisms are not understood. We found rapid internalization and nucleolar localization of bath-applied hemagglutinin (HA) tagged poly-PR with twenty repeats (HA-PR 20 ) in cell lines and neurons. Small molecule and RNAi approaches implicated a temperature-dependent, fluid phase endocytosis mechanism for HA-PR 20 . DPR–iridium conjugates identified candidate cell-surface proteins which were interrogated in a secondary RNAi screen. Focusing on our strongest candidate, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 (CSPG4), we showed cellular uptake of HA-PR 20 is reduced by inhibition of glycosaminoglycan chain synthesis and knockdown or ablation of CSPG4. Knockdown of CSPG4 protected PR 20 -induced neuronal toxicity. Using a dual reporter system to interrogate in vitro neuron-to-neuron transmission of PR 50, we found PR 50 synthesized by one neuron readily spread to neighboring cells. Transmission was significantly reduced with CSPG4 knockdown. Similarly conditioned media from PR 50 or GR 50 expressing neurons contained transmissible protein that was internalized into neurons in a CSPG4-dependent manner. Article.Title: Music illuminates sociocultural dimensions of autobiographical memory
Article.Authors: Turnbull C.; Kubit B.; Jakubowski K.; Margulis E.
Article.Abstract: Researchers have long theorized that autobiographical memory relies on sociocultural structures, such as life scripts and event schemas. The potency of music as a marker of social and personal identity, combined with its ubiquity in everyday life, allows us to connect these everyday scripts to larger patterns of socially and culturally shaped behavior. We collected free-response descriptions of autobiographical memories evoked by short clips of familiar songs from university undergraduates (n = 233). The songs spanned three popular genres and aligned with two significant periods of listeners’ lives. We analyzed the similarities and differences in the content of memories for particular songs using natural language processing. Memories cued by songs from the same category displayed striking similarities, suggesting that particular types of music cue memories that are similar between listeners but that vary according to characteristics such as music genre and release date. Two control conditions, in which a new set of participants reported memories evoked by key words from the lyrics (n = 121) and short narrative summaries of the lyrics (n = 129), indicate that these results cannot be explained by within-category similarities in the songs’ lyrical content. Instead, we suggest that the intersubjective structure of music-evoked autobiographical memories reflects socioculturally-defined scripts tied to song characteristics such as genre and release date. Thus, while memories may feel idiosyncratic and personal, there are also substantial similarities in life experiences between individuals with broadly similar backgrounds, and these shared experiences can be spontaneously called to mind through the seemingly innocuous act of turning on the radio.

Article.Title: Supercritical snapping and controlled launching via dual-latch gels
Article.Authors: Xu X.; Wang A.; Miller N.; Wu N.; Grason G.; Crosby A.
Article.Abstract: Natural organisms have evolved integrated Latch-Mediated Spring Actuation systems (LaMSA) that consist of multiple latches and springs to enhance power output and adapt to diverse environmental conditions. Similar designs are appealing yet largely unexplored in engineered materials due to the complexity of integrating multiple components into a single material platform. Here, we report a dual-latch magneto-elastic shell device capable of selectively activating the latches to regulate snapping pathways and energy output based on specific actuation requirements. Differential deswelling across the thickness acts as the “motor” to load the elastic energy into the shell, which is then released via the snap-through instability once the loading reaches the critical threshold, constituting an intrinsic mechanical latch. Activation of the external magnetic latch delays snapping onset beyond the threshold of the intrinsic latch, leading to a power-amplified supercritical snap-through instability as well as a bifurcation instability. The combined function of both latches allows for flexible control over energy storage and release. Additionally, this integrated LaMSA system possesses an untethered anchoring mechanism, enabling the device to launch in arbitrary directions from the substrate, driven by the energy released during snapping. We envision that the design principles of dual-latch LaMSA systems will create opportunities for power-dense actuation in engineered materials and robotic devices.

Article.Title: Localization mechanisms and function of postsynaptic K <sub>v</sub> 7 (KCNQ) channels and their reduction in KCNQ2 epileptic encephalopathy
Article.Authors: Malpotra S.; Zhao H.; Tracy G.; Wilton A.; Lau G.; Zhang J.; Keum K.; Silzer L.; Selvin P.; Tzingounis A.; Chung H.
Article.Abstract: K v 7 channels composed of K v 7.2 and K v 7.3 subunits are enriched in neuronal axons where their hyperpolarizing potassium current suppresses repetitive and burst firing of action potentials. Mutations in their genes, KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 , cause neonatal epilepsy, underscoring their critical role in regulating neuronal excitability. In this study, we provide evidence that K v 7 channels are present at and near the postsynaptic density within dendritic spines of hippocampal neurons, where their current decreases calcium influx through NMDA receptors. This spine localization is promoted by heteromerization of K v 7.2 and K v 7.3 and their binding to AnkyrinG-190, which is the only AnkyrinG isoform present in dendritic spines. Lastly, spine localization of K v 7 channels and their ability to suppress NMDA receptor activity are markedly reduced by select variants of KCNQ2 that cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). These findings reveal a subcellular population of K v 7 channels that can dampen excitatory synaptic transmission and implicate their dysregulation in KCNQ2 -associated DEE.

Article.Title: Stature reveals changing patterns of the biological standard of living in Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 y
Article.Authors: Baten J.; Stephan M.; Wang Q.; Berger E.; Brooke J.; Chen Z.; Myagmar E.; Halcrow S.; Hou K.; Hudson M.; Larsen C.; Padgett B.; Ranaweera L.; Roberts C.; Seguchi N.; Steckel R.; Sun X.; Wangthongchaicharoen N.; Wang W.; Woo E.; Zhang Q.; Zhang Q.; Zancan C.; Wang Q.
Article.Abstract: Human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health. Reconstructing this indicator allows insights into which types of societies were providing better health and nutrition—also termed the “biological standard of living” in the literature. Yet, archaeological evidence has not previously been assembled on a scale large enough for systematic comparison across premodern Eurasia. We present a dataset of 18,457 stature observations based on 783 sites from Asia and Europe, roughly spanning the 7,000 y before the twentieth century. Using harmonized estimates derived from long bones, we document broad regional variation in stature over time and examine how these patterns relate to population density and historical indicators of technological development. We observe marked declines in stature in most regions during the 500–1900 CE period, in both Asia and Europe. To interpret these patterns, we combine our stature series with estimates of population density, technological advancement, and related controls. As [Q. Ashraf, O. Galor, Am. Econ. Rev. 101 , 2003–2041 (2011)] predicted, higher technology levels were associated with higher population density, but not correlated with higher stature before the modern era. This relationship also holds after controlling for other potentially confounding factors such as latitude or transport access. By assembling the largest archaeological stature dataset for Eurasia to date and linking it to long-term demographic and historical indicators, this study provides an empirical basis for comparative research on premodern health, nutrition, and population pressure.

Article.Title: Global lake synchrony signals rising planetary-scale ecological coupling
Article.Authors: Zhang K.; Han Y.; Gillson L.; Zhang X.; McGowan S.; Meadows M.; Jin Y.; Subehi L.; Dearing J.; Hamilton D.; Zhao Y.; Pin Koh L.; Taylor D.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how localized ecosystem dynamics scale up to influence Earth-system stability remains a major challenge. Lakes, though covering less than 2% of Earth’s surface, play a disproportionate role in regulating global carbon, nutrient, and biodiversity dynamics, making them a critical nexus for assessing emerging large-scale environmental coupling. By integrating satellite observations with century-scale sedimentary archives from ~2,000 lakes, we reveal a marked acceleration in global lake synchrony since 2000. This synchronization, coinciding with converging climatic and socioeconomic pressures, signals a widespread erosion of the spatial heterogeneity and regional distinctiveness that historically characterized inland waters. We propose that increasing lake synchrony represents an emergent property of the Anthropocene, transforming lakes from regionally structured, asynchronous waterscapes into dynamically coupled planetary commons. By temporally aligning carbon and nutrient dynamics across broad spatial scales, this synchronization modifies the timing and amplitude of aggregate biophysical fluxes, altering how inland waters interact with larger-scale environmental cycles. Ultimately, this finding motivates a macroscale monitoring framework that jointly tracks synchrony, modularity, and their functional consequences, demanding a shift in governance toward preserving the ecological heterogeneity essential for maintaining long-term environmental stability.

Article.Title: Impact pathways of a jurisdictional approach to slowing deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon
Article.Authors: Caviglia-Harris J.; West T.; Harris D.; Sills E.; Mullan K.
Article.Abstract: Governance of many of the world’s largest remaining tropical forests is shared across multiple levels of government, giving subnational jurisdictions a central role in forest management. This has motivated growing interest in jurisdictional approaches (JAs) to control deforestation. For JAs to deliver on national and international conservation priorities, those priorities must be translated into incentives that reduce deforestation at the jurisdictional level. Brazil’s Priority List (PL), launched in 2008, creates such incentives by identifying high-deforestation municipalities, subjecting them to intensified monitoring, enforcement, and credit restrictions, and establishing jurisdiction-wide criteria for exit that make municipalities accountable for deforestation within their borders. While prior studies show that the PL reduces deforestation, it remains unclear where these reductions occur and whether there is displacement across land tenure types or into neighboring municipalities. We assemble a municipality-level panel dataset for the Brazilian Legal Amazon (2000–2024) that combines PL designations with annual deforestation disaggregated by land tenure. Using a heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences estimator, we estimate effects within and across municipalities. We find large and statistically significant reductions concentrated on private lands, including agrarian reform settlements and other private properties. Within listed municipalities, we find no evidence of decreased or increased clearing in Protected Areas, Indigenous Territories, or undesignated public lands. Total deforestation also declines in neighboring municipalities, with reductions concentrated on private lands. These findings are consistent with the PL translating national conservation priorities into local land-use change while limiting displacement, offering insights for the design of jurisdictional approaches aimed at forest conservation.

Article.Title: Distinct nanoscale architectures of GABAergic inhibitory synapses predict diverse synaptic output
Article.Authors: Stewart A.; Gookin S.; Garcia J.; Zent K.; Crosby K.; Smith K.
Article.Abstract: GABAergic synaptic inhibition is heterogenous across neuronal compartments, and plays a critical role in shaping local, cellular, and circuit excitability. In pyramidal neurons, inhibition is mediated by GABA A receptors (GABA A Rs) clustered at the inhibitory postsynaptic domain (iPSD). Synaptic strength depends not only on the number of GABA A Rs within the iPSD, but also on their precise nanoscale organization into discrete subsynaptic domains (SSDs). These SSDs often align with presynaptic GABA release sites to form nanocolumn structures that enhance synaptic efficacy. While nanocolumn organization is increasingly recognized as a key determinant of synaptic function, most studies of GABAergic synapses have focused on archetypal dendritic synapses, which control the plasticity and integration of excitatory inputs. Nonetheless, it remains unclear whether somatic synapses—which deliver robust inhibition to suppress neuronal output—share a similar nanoarchitecture. Here, we used complementary superresolution imaging approaches to directly compare inhibitory synapses in somatic and dendritic compartments. We found that somatic synapses are larger and exhibit greater structural diversity and nanoscale complexity than dendritic synapses. Dendritic synapses display relatively compact architectures with GABA A R SSDs frequently arranged into nanocolumns. In contrast, somatic synapses show a broader range of organizations, including aligned nanocolumns as well as more disorganized configurations with misaligned release sites or receptor SSDs, arrangements that likely exhibit input-specificity. Computational modeling revealed that these structural differences produce distinct functional outcomes, including increased inhibitory postsynaptic current amplitude and altered kinetics at somatic synapses. Together, our findings demonstrate that nanoscale organization differentially shapes inhibitory strength and signaling properties across neuronal compartments.

Third, we characterize the RumI c 1 immunity protein of the RumC1 biosynthetic cluster as a peptidase acting at the cell surface to protect the cells by trimming the stem peptide crucial for cell-wall assembly. As such, RumI c 1 provides cross-protection against vancomycin, while RumC1 is demonstrated to act differently from this glycopeptide antibiotic. Collectively, these findings establish RumC1 as a toxin targeting a key peptidoglycan intermediate of cell wall maturation, which defines a distinct mode of action among the large and highly diverse repertoire of bacteriocins characterized so far.

Article.Authors: Franz H.; Webster C.; Flesch G.; Mahaffy P.; Raaen E.; Kahre M.; Prats B.; Ehlmann B.; Atreya S.; Burtt D.; House C.; Lo D.; Stern J.; Trainer M.; Archer P.; Juarez M.; Guzewich S.; Martinez G.; Malespin C.; Pla-Garcia J.; Rafkin S.; Steele A.; Vasavada A.; Víudez-Moreiras D.; Wong M.
Article.Abstract: This work represents the first long-term record of the isotopic composition of martian atmospheric CO 2 , acquired in situ by the Curiosity rover at Gale crater during Mars Years (MY) 31–38 (2012–2025). Lesser 18 O enrichment near aphelion may reflect less favorable conditions for oxygen isotope exchange at lower temperatures. Observed seasonal variations in CO 2 carbon isotopic composition are less pronounced, consistent with less carbon isotope exchange with surface reservoirs than seen for oxygen. Article.Title: Gaplinc regulates myeloid metabolic pathways in trans in endotoxic shock
Article.Authors: Smaliy V.; Escalona D.; Liang S.; Sudek L.; Vollmers A.; Katzman S.; Smith-Berdan S.; Malekos E.; Aguilar-Pimentel J.; Rathkolb B.; Fuchs H.; Gailus-Durner V.; Hrabe de Angelis M.; Mozqueda A.; Boyd D.; Hellman J.; Forsberg E.; Carpenter S.

Article.Authors: Zhao M.; Cao D.; Cheng Z.; Hu Y.; He Y.; Wang S.; Wei X.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: The demand for three-dimensional reconstruction of membrane proteins in native lipid environments has grown substantially in recent years. Both single-particle analysis and tomographic techniques have enabled structural studies across diverse vesicular samples; however, these methods remain limited in either efficiency or resolution. Given that some vesicles exhibit anisotropic shapes in solution and adopt near-spherical or ellipsoidal geometries, we trained an AI model to estimate membrane geometric parameters and compute normal vectors based on the fitted ellipsoidal surface. This information facilitates post hoc filtering of particles picked using the isSPA framework based on the angular difference between their orientations and the membrane normals, and also enables the exclusion of particles outside the vesicles. Article.Title: A hybrid ultrafast phase transition in a chemically complex alloy under extreme conditions
Article.Authors: Zhang F.; Takagi S.; Ichiyanagi K.; Xu L.; Wu Y.; Li Z.; Tian Y.; Xu J.; Zeng Q.; Yin S.; Liu Y.; Kawai N.; Kishimura H.; Miyanishi K.; Sueda K.; Togashi T.; Nakamura H.; Ozaki N.; Amouretti A.; Yabuuchi T.; Wang L.; Cai H.; Sheng H.; Cheng X.; Chen M.
Article.Abstract: The face-centered cubic to hexagonal close-packed (FCC–HCP) phase transition is ubiquitous in static high-pressure experiments of conventional FCC metals and alloys, yet its conspicuous absence under laser shock compression (LSC) has remained a puzzle. Here we show that this transition can be realized and directly observed in the prototypical CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy under LSC at pressures exceeding ~114 GPa and Hugoniot temperatures above ~1,800 K. Time-resolved X-ray diffraction reveals that the transformation occurs on a timescale at least as fast as 1 to 2 ns, orders of magnitude faster than diffusion-controlled nucleation-growth processes, yet reversible upon pressure release, unlike classical FCC–HCP martensitic transformations. We hypothesize that the high Hugoniot temperature may provide the atomic mobility for reversibility, while the extreme deviatoric stress likely promotes rapid, displacive atomic motion. This fusion of athermal speed and thermal reversibility is difficult to classify within the classical dichotomy of phase transitions as either purely martensitic or purely thermally activated and may represent a class of stress-assisted, thermally reversible transformation accessible only under extreme pressure–temperature ( P-T ) conditions. First-principles Gibbs free-energy calculations show that the HCP phase is thermodynamically favored at low temperature over the pressure range 50 to 142 GPa, and that the computed FCC–HCP phase boundary places the laser-shock P-T state on the HCP-stable side, making it accessible to the transient LSC path. Our findings are consistent with chemical complexity acting as a powerful parameter for controlling phase transformation pathways under extreme P-T conditions, and reveal a distinct class of ultrafast, reversible transformations.

Article.Title: Sustainability of violence prevention after a randomized vacant lot greening intervention in Philadelphia: A 10-y follow-up
Article.Authors: Asa N.; Zewdie H.; Omidvar Tehrani S.; Beverly M.; Carroll-Scott A.; Rowhani-Rahbar A.; Rundle A.; Kondo M.; Clougherty J.; Godwin J.; Branas C.; Mooney S.

We measured lot greening by treatment assignment from the original 2013 cluster RCT and a longitudinal greening score to assess the sustainability of the treatment assignment from 2012 through 2023. Lots randomized to the full greening intervention remained greener over time compared to other lots. In intent-to-treat analyses, compared to lots that received no intervention, lots that received any intervention had a 9% decrease in density of any crime (estimate = 0.91, 95%CI = 0.86, 0.96) and a 9% decrease in violent crime (estimate = 0.91, 95%CI = 0.86, 0.97) per square mile per year. In contamination-adjusted analyses, compared to lots without sustained greening treatment, lots with sustained greening treatment had a 12% decrease in density of any crime (estimate = 0.88, 95%CI = 0.83, 0.93) and an 11% decrease in density of violent crime (estimate = 0.89, 95%CI = 0.83, 0.95) per square mile per year. Article.Title: Calculated residue protonation states find functional, conserved E-channel proton-loading sites in Complex I from bacteria to mammals
Article.Authors: Uddin M.; Sookhai K.; Mao J.; Ranepura G.; Chenal C.; Wei R.; Ortiz-Soto J.; Ibrahim H.; Burnap R.; Gunner M.
Article.Abstract: Bioenergetic proton pumps take protons from one side of a membrane, transiently binding them at a loading site within the protein matrix, and then release them to the other side against an electrochemical gradient. The E channel of Complex I, from bacteria to mammals, contains a conserved proton-loading region whose function is distributed among several interacting residues. Noting extensive sequence divergence across homologous Complex I structures, we asked how this function is conserved during evolution despite many amino acid changes. Multi-Conformation Continuum Electrostatics (MCCE) calculations were performed on the five E-channel subunits from 41 experimental structures from bacteria, cyanobacteria, insects, and mammals. A Monte Carlo sampling identified five to seven residues in each species that function as a proton-loading cluster. Structures with a closed E-channel have ~1 more proton in the cluster than those with open conformations. Proton binding represents ensemble averages across thousands of accessible microstates, each with an integer protonation state. A mean-field analysis showed that the proton affinity depends on both titrating residues and the surrounding protein electrostatic environment. Closely related proteins use nearly the same cluster of residues, whereas more divergent proteins substitute alternative proton-handling residues and modify electrostatically important fixed-charge groups to preserve cluster proton affinity. Thus, E-channel reversible proton-loading is preserved during sequence evolution by maintaining a local “electrostatic architecture,” often involving quite different evolutionary solutions. Thus, conservation of E-channel proton loading depends more strongly on the local electrostatic environment than on conservation of the individual residues that create it.

Article.Title: Short-term flexibility and long-term stability in models of mind perception
Article.Authors: Held R.; Hortensius R.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how people decide whether someone or something possesses a mind is central to a myriad of psychological, biological, and philosophical questions. It shapes fundamental processes at the individual (e.g., social interaction) and societal level (e.g., morality and ethics). While mind perception has been studied, it remains unclear which internal model people use when ascribing mental capacities to entities. Across four experiments (total N = 256), we explored what model people hold and its flexibility when ascribing agency and experience to entities encountered in everyday life and which differ in animacy and socialness (e.g., humans, pets, robots, voice assistants, tools). Using representational similarity analysis combined with lab-based experiments, a 6-wk long social interaction intervention, and longitudinal real-life exposure, we tested which model people use to ascribe agency and experience by comparing observed rating data to theoretical models. We demonstrated that an animacy distinction underlies the representational structure of experience attributions, while internal models for agency attributions are more idiosyncratic and flexible. When receiving explicit information on one entity, the internal model of agency changes. People update their model by incorporating this information, generalizing across the entire category of entities. We found no evidence that extended exposure to or ownership of inanimate technology, such as robots or voice assistants, or pets leads to restructuring of the models for experience or agency. Overall, these results provide insight into the internal models people hold when perceiving minds, the flexibility thereof, and offer ways to understand the roots and consequences of mind perception.

Article.Title: Peak water: Trends in decoupling regional and global water use
Article.Authors: Gleick P.; Liu J.; Al-Zu’bi A.; Berhanu B.; Tang G.; Wada Y.
Article.Abstract: Water use for human activities, including food and fiber production, energy generation, and residential, commercial, and industrial supply, has grown significantly over the past century, driven by rising populations, expanding economic activity, and changes in technologies and consumer demands. Traditional water planning has long assumed that the demand for water, like other resource demands, will grow in perpetuity, shaping infrastructure development, land-use decisions, and water-system investments. However, recent data and analysis challenge this assumption, suggesting that total water use in certain regions and sectors has peaked or even begun to decline, despite continued population and economic growth. This paper’s primary contribution is to reevaluate the status of “peak water” and decoupling based on observational and statistical data, as well as multimodel simulations. Data on global, national, and regional water withdrawals indicate that certain peak water-use levels are being reached and the paper discusses past, current, and projected demand estimates; potential drivers of observed water use reductions; and different strategies for managing and modeling water use in the future. These findings indicate that the long-presumed correlation between water-resource use, economic development, and human well-being can be decoupled and that models of water use should reflect this. Decoupling solutions must focus on efficiency technologies, regulatory water-use caps, environmental flow protections, and enhanced monitoring networks.

Article.Title: Direct CO <sub>2</sub> splitting using light-based catalysis and an oxygen reservoir
Article.Authors: Deneen S.; Fabiano C.; Ahrens A.; Barbosa M.; Kay L.; Sánchez-Alvarado A.; Craft N.; Nordlander P.; Halas N.
Article.Abstract: As the dominant anthropogenic greenhouse gas, the conversion of CO 2 into value-added products is vital for achieving a circular economy. CO 2 activation typically requires coreactants, high temperatures, or significant electrical input, any of which increases cost or limits scalability. Here we demonstrate a straightforward way to split CO 2 directly into carbon monoxide and oxygen using light. By combining a light-driven antenna-reactor photocatalyst with a material that acts as an oxygen reservoir, CO 2 can be decomposed directly into CO and oxygen with light only. Under illumination, photoexcited carriers induce CO 2 bond dissociation, while cerium oxide adsorbs the released oxygen into vacancy sites, preventing recombination. The oxygen can then be released from the ceria by flowing nitrogen under white light illumination, a process that can be repeated multiple times, restoring full photocatalytic activity. Article.Title: Leptin Receptor <sup>+</sup> cells create a perisinusoidal niche for thrombopoiesis in the bone marrow by synthesizing CXCL14
Article.Authors: Xue Y.; Zhang R.; Luo M.; Reyes A.; Merchant S.; Tippetts T.; Grabowski G.; Ngo T.; Zhang Y.; Shang Z.; Jiang N.; Tjahjono N.; Jeffery E.; Li Y.; Wei T.; Gu W.; Du L.; DeBerardinis R.; Dean K.; Schmidtke D.; Mathews T.; Lucas D.; Zhao Z.; Morrison S.
Article.Abstract: Leptin Receptor-expressing (LepR + ) stromal cells in the bone marrow are a critical source of growth factors for the maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and most restricted hematopoietic progenitors. An important unresolved question is whether they also regulate terminal differentiation in some hematopoietic cells. We found that bone marrow LepR + cells promote thrombopoiesis by synthesizing the chemokine CXCL14. Cxcl14 -expressing LepR + cells extend fine processes that wrap around perisinusoidal megakaryocytes. Deletion of Cxcl14 from LepR + cells did not significantly alter HSC function or most aspects of bone marrow hematopoiesis, including megakaryocyte generation; however, it significantly reduced the numbers of proplatelet-forming megakaryocytes in the bone marrow and platelets in the blood, as well as platelet quality. Megakaryocytes from Lepr-cre; Cxcl14 fl/fl mice expressed lower levels of genes that encode granule proteins as compared to control mice, leading to the release of platelets with fewer α-granules and defective thrombus formation/growth. CXCL14 promoted platelet formation by remodeling lipid metabolism in megakaryocytes, increasing fatty acid transporter expression and enabling megakaryocytes to take up more polyunsaturated fatty acids from circulation. A high fat diet rescued the formation of proplatelet-forming megakaryocytes and platelets, as well as platelet function, in Lepr-cre; Cxcl14 fl/fl mice. CXCL14 protein was sufficient to promote platelet formation by megakaryocytes in vitro and in vivo. LepR + cells thus create a perisinusoidal niche for thrombopoiesis by producing CXCL14, which regulates lipid metabolism and terminal differentiation in megakaryocytes.

Article.Title: The evolution and function of eukaryote-to-cyanobacteria horizontal gene transfer
Article.Authors: Cao X.; Liu C.; Liu D.; Wang Y.; Steenwyk J.; Zhong X.; Wang Y.; Liu H.; Zhang Q.; Shen X.; Qu Z.; Shao C.; Li S.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Prokaryote-to-eukaryote horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has emerged as a driver of eukaryotic evolution. In contrast, eukaryote-to-prokaryote HGT remains poorly characterized, limiting insight into how eukaryote-derived genes influence prokaryotic evolution and function. Here, we reconstructed a comprehensive and well-resolved phylogeny of 469 high-quality Cyanobacteria genomes spanning all orders. Leveraging this framework, we identified 204 candidate functionally diverse genes of eukaryotic origin in cyanobacteria, likely representing 59 putative transfer events, including 197 genes not previously documented. All 204 candidates were intronless, consistent with intron loss during their evolutionary history. Transcriptomics reveal that HGT-acquired genes are expressed at significantly higher levels than both genome-wide and functionally matched non-HGT-acquired genes, suggesting functional importance. Notably, 138 genes exhibited functional annotations absent from the host cyanobacteria. We further characterized a granule-bound starch synthase (GBSS) putatively acquired by Crocosphaera from an ancestral archaeplastid lineage, enabling starch synthesis that may facilitate energy storage for nocturnal nitrogen fixation. These findings reveal that eukaryote-to-prokaryote gene transfer is an underappreciated driver of cyanobacterial evolution and function, with broad implications for microbial ecology, functional adaptation, and cross-domain genetic exchange.

Article.Title: Vessel noise pollution offsets marine mammal energy budgets
Article.Authors: Rojano-Doñate L.; Johnson M.; Teilmann J.; Wisniewska D.; Findlay C.; Tougaard J.; Nachtsheim D.; von Benda-Beckmann A.; Schnitzler J.; Ladegaard M.; de Jong C.; Siebert U.; Madsen P.
Article.Abstract: Shipping is a major global source of underwater noise pollution and is frequently reported to alter the behavior of marine mammals. However, the energetic consequences of these noise-induced behavioral disruptions and their implications for population fitness remain poorly quantified. Using behavioral proxies of energy acquisition and expenditure derived from high-resolution sound and movement tags on 28 wild harbor porpoises, we estimate that porpoises decrease energy acquisition by 20% (range: 1 to 36%) during high-noise vessel exposures, while maintaining constant energy expenditure. With a median of 11 high-noise vessel exposures per day, these disruptions may result in an average daily shortfall of 4.6% of their net energy budget. Sustained over time, such noise-induced energetic deficits have the potential to compromise individual fitness, ultimately affecting the dynamics of harbor porpoise populations in industrialized coastal areas worldwide and reducing their functional carrying capacity. This framework establishes a direct mechanistic link between behavioral disruption and fitness-relevant impacts, providing a biologically grounded metric for predicting population-level outcomes of noise pollution and an objective basis for defining acceptable exposure levels of vessel noise for wild marine mammal populations. Moreover, it is scalable across species and ecosystems and offers a common currency for assessing the cumulative effects of multiple stressors in the Anthropocene oceans. As vessel traffic and its associated noise outputs continue to increase globally, our results offer timely insights for evidence-based management, and support efforts to balance the societal demand for low-cost maritime transport with the responsibility to ensure the sustainable use and conservation of marine biodiversity.

Article.Title: Coupled human–cattle mobility shaped the socioeconomic landscapes of the Holocene Middle Nile Valley
Article.Authors: Osypińska M.; Osypiński P.; Belka Z.; Chaix L.; Chiquet P.; Gourichon L.; Jesse F.; Langlois O.; Magnavita C.; Magnavita S.; Pöllath N.
Article.Abstract: We present a synthesis of strontium isotope data ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) from human and cattle dental enamel across Middle Nile. This dataset, which combines newly acquired and published measurements, reveals a complex history of human and cattle mobility linked to ecological gradients and sociocultural changes in this part of the continent. During the early Holocene (8,000 to 4,000 BCE), isotopic unanimity in human and cattle remains supports early, correlated mobility of humans and Bos , extending beyond Nile floodplains to adjacent uplands. In the mid-Holocene (4,000 to 1,000 BCE), isotopic data from Wadi Howar suggest bidirectional corridors for mobility of both species linking the Middle Nile and the Western Desert. This pattern correlates with the emergence of the Middle Nile civilizations in which cattle played a central cultural and economic role. From the first millennium BCE onward, a radical change can be observed, correlated with the progressive desertification processes in the Sahel. Although cattle import routes continued to follow wadi systems, they shifted south of the now desiccated Saharan lakes toward Kordofan. The long-term perspective emphasizes the continuous adaptation of societies in the Middle Nile of what is now Sudan and adjacent regions to environmental changes, aimed at maintaining sustained access to cattle, a resource that remained crucial for Middle Nile communities throughout the Holocene.

Article.Title: A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans
Article.Authors: Zeberg H.; Pääbo S.
Article.Abstract: Neandertal crania were less globular than those of modern humans, suggesting differences in the relative volumes of brain regions, including the frontal and occipital lobes. Here, we show that a common genetic variant influencing occipital brain volume in present-day people was inherited from Neandertals. The variant lies in predicted transcription-factor recognition motifs near DAAM1 , a gene that is known to be involved in brain development. Carriers of the Neandertal variant have altered DAAM1 expression and occipital lobe volumes that are about 0.85 cm³ smaller per gene copy. The variant is associated with reduced schizophrenia risk by almost 10% in homozygous carriers, while Neandertal ancestry as a whole does not show such a tendency. Any association with cognition or schooling is small or nonexistent, amounting to at most two weeks of education per allele against an average of about 15 y. Thus, this Neandertal-derived variant is linked to altered brain anatomy in present-day humans and lower schizophrenia risk while having little or no association with general cognitive ability.

Article.Title: ChREBP drives diabetic kidney disease, and its inhibition confers renal protection
Article.Authors: Nguyen T.; Suzuki S.; Okamoto K.; Ito R.; Mizuno H.; Fujita S.; Kouketsu T.; Teshima K.; Sawatsubashi S.; Takemoto T.; Yamakoshi H.; Takahashi M.; Kuroda M.; Sasano Y.; Yoshizaki Y.; Matsumoto Y.; Ohsawa K.; Kudo G.; Hirokawa T.; Kato S.; Konno T.; Doi T.; Iwabuchi Y.; Sugawara A.; Yokoyama A.

Article.Title: Emergent long-tailed dynamics in spin ice
Article.Authors: Guo C.; Zhao H.; Cai Z.
Article.Abstract: In this study, we reveal long-tail dynamics spontaneously arising from a magnetic system. Specifically, we consider a classical spin system and demonstrate the emergence of a spin-ice physics when drive-induced heating is well suppressed. We show that at high driving frequencies, magnetic monopole excitations exhibit nonergodic stochastic dynamics characterized by power-law-distributed trapping times with long tails—a behavior that persists even in the absence of driving. At intermediate driving frequencies, the system eventually heats up to an infinite-temperature state. However, contrary to conventional wisdom of Floquet heating, the heating time in our model is extremely sensitive to different initial-state realizations and also follows a long-tailed power-law distribution, which arise specifically due to periodic driving. We show that an effective short-range attractive interaction between monopoles is responsible for the long-tailed distributions observed in both monopole and heating dynamics.

Article.Title: People know who to ask for favors despite underestimating compliance
Article.Authors: Belinda C.; Solomon B.
Article.Abstract: Whether and how people approach social interactions hinges on how they expect others to respond. Extensive social psychology research suggests that people are inaccurate interpersonal perceivers, overestimating negative responses (e.g., discomfort) and underestimating positive responses (e.g., appreciation) across a variety of social situations. However, this conclusion is based almost exclusively on mean-level bias analyses that obscure the dyadic nature of interpersonal judgment and rely on a narrow conceptualization of interpersonal accuracy. Leveraging research on favor-asking and anticipated compliance as an exemplar, we demonstrate that interpersonal accuracy takes multiple theoretically distinct forms, and that the prevailing conclusion that people misunderstand their influence over others—because they tend to underestimate compliance—is likely overgeneralized. Across four studies (13,196 directed dyadic ratings), we show that people accurately differentiate between who will comply with their favor requests (dyadic meta-accuracy) despite the average tendency to underestimate compliance (mean-level bias). This pattern emerged for specific and general favor requests, among well- and newly-acquainted individuals, and beyond what could be expected due to self-projection. Through this dyadic lens, people are highly adept judges of their influence over others, as they are able to target their requests toward individuals who are uniquely likely to acquiesce to them—and can avoid wasting time on those who are not. Thus, our research refines existing implications for how people approach asking for favors. More broadly, by aligning theory, measurement, and level of analysis, our studies elucidate the need for greater theoretical precision and empirical breadth in interpersonal accuracy research.

Article.Title: Dynamical geometric modes in non-Euclidean plates
Article.Authors: Roback J.; Moguel-Lehmer C.; Fransen K.; Santangelo C.; Hayward R.
Article.Abstract: Continuum elastic shells with residual stresses can exhibit complex motions that require vanishing elastic energy to excite, also called geometric zero modes, enabling them to be driven by weak and generic energy inputs. Despite recent interest in these modes, we understand very little about their dynamical properties. Plates with a curved, rather than flat, in-plane geometry, also called non-Euclidean plates, are one example in which residual stresses and geometry combine to produce a continuum of ground states. The plate can explore these states through a geometric zero mode when it has the shape of a minimal surface—a surface with zero mean curvature. We demonstrate that a non-Euclidean plate with the shape of a saddle minimal surface exhibits the predicted continuous stability, but this degeneracy is ultimately lifted by aging. Despite developing a preferred configuration, the zero mode remains the softest mode. Using a combination of analytical theory and experiments, we show that the elastodynamics of this soft mode is captured by the dynamics of a damped pendulum. A periodic driving uncovers resonance phenomena in this pendulum mode, such as small oscillations and steady rotations, but mixes with an additional flapping mode at high frequencies.

Article.Title: Selectively disrupting lysine acetyltransferase p300 and ZEB1 interaction prevents tumor progression while enhancing antitumor immunity
Article.Authors: Luo J.; Ren B.; Zang C.; Min W.; Wang S.; Cheng R.; Tang Z.; Zhu L.; Shu C.; Weiss S.; Yang P.; Fu R.; Wu Z.
Article.Abstract: Both p300 acetyltransferase inhibitors and bromodomain inhibitors show therapeutic promise in cancer, but they mostly exhibit limited efficacy and may elicit severe adverse effects due to their lack of targeting selectivity. Thus, selectively disrupting p300 interactions with specific pro-oncogenic targets that are specifically expressed in neoplastic cells could serve as a safe and effective strategy for cancer treatment. Here, we demonstrate that p300 interacts with the pro-oncogenic transcription factor, ZEB1, and catalyzes its acetylation at an evolutionarily conserved K80 residue, stabilizing its expression in aggressive cancer cells. Ectopic expression of wild-type ZEB1 (mostly in acetylated status) but not the acetylation-deficient ZEB1 mutant modulates cytokinome of cancer cells, creating an immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment to support cancer progression. Underlining the importance of ZEB1 posttranslational processing, the K80-acetylated transcription factor is highly expressed in human cancers where its high-level expression is associated with poor prognosis. Importantly, we identify a small molecule compound, WY6, that undergoes high-affinity binding to p300 TAZ2 domain (a domain critical for ZEB1 binding) and consequently disrupts ZEB1 binding to p300, thereby suppressing K80 acetylation. WY6 treatment of tumor cells effectively represses p300-mediated ZEB1 acetylation, promoting its ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Moreover, in vivo, WY6 potently suppresses orthotopic tumor growth without eliciting obvious toxic side effects and exhibits a synergetic effect when combined with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade immunotherapy. Article.Title: Elastic interactions of mechanically polarizable cells
Article.Authors: Zemel A.
Article.Abstract: Cells mechanically interact through the deformations they generate in their surrounding extracellular matrix. We present an analytical theory of the elastic interactions between cells that actively adapt their forces in response to local deformations of their environment. Cells are represented as localized contractile force generators, modeled as polarizable point force dipoles, whose adaptive forces are determined self-consistently with those of surrounding cells. Analysis of the associated elastic interaction energy identifies a generic short-ranged interaction arising from the mutual adaptation of cellular forces. This induced-dipole interaction is analogous to the van der Waals interaction between molecules and likewise is shown to be generally attractive for cells that enhance contractility in response to stretch. Furthermore, unlike the long-ranged elastic interaction between nonpolarizable force-dipoles, that peaks at intermediate matrix stiffness and then weakens as the matrix softens, the induced-dipole interaction strengthens monotonically as the matrix softens and can reverse the interaction from being repulsive at long cell distances to being attractive at short separations. Analytical calculations are presented to illustrate the mutual polarization of forces in pairs of interacting cells on a substrate. The identification of a generic, short-range cohesive elastic interaction between cells is important for understanding cell behavior at short separations and provides a physical mechanism driving cell accumulation on soft substrates.

Article.Title: Physical distancing to prevent influenza-like illness on a college campus: The eX-FLU trial
Article.Authors: Richardson B.; Aiello A.; Hudgens M.
Article.Abstract: Public health recommendations often advise people to isolate when infected with influenza-like illness (ILI) with the goal of promoting physical distancing and limiting face-to-face interactions when risk of transmission is highest. Because isolation may have negative consequences, it is important to carefully assess whether encouragement to physically distance actually prevents cases of ILI. College campuses can be especially vulnerable to outbreaks of ILI and are ideal environments for assessing the impact of encouragement-to-physically-distance interventions. The eX-FLU cluster-randomized trial followed 579 students on a college campus over a ten-week period during flu season to evaluate such an intervention. Students in the trial were randomized to receive the intervention—encouragement to isolate in their dorm room when symptomatic for ILI—or control. Evaluating the effect of this intervention is challenging because of dependence between students in the trial and an anticipated spillover effect of the intervention. Moreover, while the intervention was designed to affect both face-to-face interactions and ILI infections, the effect on ILI infections is of primary public health interest. In this paper, a randomization-based testing procedure is proposed to assess the intervention effect specifically on ILI infections in the presence of dependent data and spillover effects. The testing procedure is shown theoretically and empirically to control the type I error rate and have good statistical power to detect an intervention effect in trials similar to eX-FLU. When applied to the eX-FLU data, this testing procedure gives moderate evidence that the intervention reduced ILI infections.

Article.Title: Two-phase NEUROD1 pioneer activity synchronizes sensory neuronal differentiation and subtype specification
Article.Authors: Lebrón-Mora L.; Bohuslavova R.; Gmiterkova L.; Merc V.; Yamoah E.; Fritzsch B.; Pavlinkova G.
Article.Abstract: Temporal control of neuronal differentiation is essential for establishing stable neuronal identities, yet the transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. To bypass early neuronal loss in germline Neurod1 deletion mutants, we generated a delayed, self-terminating conditional knockout mouse ( Neurod1ST ) that permits analysis of later differentiation stages. Integration of NEUROD1 chromatin binding and histone profiling at embryonic day (E) 11.5 with transcriptomic analyses across E11.5, E14.5, and E18.5 reveals a two-phase regulatory program during auditory neuron development that parallels dynamic Neurod1 expression. Loss of Neurod1 disrupts these epigenomic transitions, resulting in persistence of progenitor-like states with premature activation of differentiation and axonogenesis programs. This dysregulation is accompanied by activation of alternative regulatory networks, leading to defective neuronal migration and innervation, progressive identity instability, and apoptosis. In the second phase, marked by reexpression of Neurod1 in developing Type Ib/Ic precursors, Neurod1 deletion selectively impairs Type Ic specification while promoting a Type Ib-like identity. These findings identify NEUROD1 as a temporal regulator that coordinates developmental progression and stabilizes auditory neuron identity through phased regulatory activity, providing a mechanistic framework for how pioneer transcription factors couple chromatin remodeling to developmental timing.

Article.Title: Quantifying the hierarchical topological decay of fluid knots
Article.Authors: Liu X.; Ricca R.; Zhuo Y.
Article.Abstract: In this paper we analyze the hierarchical topological cascade of knotted and linked filaments associated with the natural decay of superfluid vortex tangles. This is done by using an algebraic reformulation of knot polynomial invariants to quantify the topological states of the cascade process. By interpreting the evolutionary paths associated with vortex knot dynamics as geodesic flows in an appropriate knot polynomial space defined by adapted Jones polynomials [X. Liu, R. L. Ricca, J. Phys. A Math. Theor. 45 , 205501 (2012).], we introduce an entanglement index to quantify the probability density of occurrence of each topological state. By this method we analyze all prime knots, links, and composites up to 8 crossings, and show that this measure detects accurately the decreasing topological complexity observed in simulations and laboratory experiments. By a comparative analysis carried out with data based on an alternative measure (complexity degree), we show that this entanglement index proves to be a more robust and reliable quantifier. The theoretical framework proposed here can be applied to other types of physical systems, where networks of filamentary structures are subject to continuous topological change and reorganization.

Article.Title: The quantum agreement theorem
Article.Authors: Díaz M.; Brandenburger A.; Scarpa G.
Article.Abstract: Intersubjective consistency asks when different observers of a physical system, reasoning from a shared theory, will agree on their probability assessments. Classical probability theory provides a benchmark in the form of the Agreement Theorem [R. J. Aumann, Ann. Stat. 4 , 1236–1239 (1976)]. We study the quantum mechanics (QM) analog to the classical Agreement Theorem in a finite-dimensional tripartite setting in which two observers obtain information via local projective measurements. We represent their mutual awareness by common certainty, which is formally an infinite hierarchy of certainty operators concerning the probability of an event of interest. We first prove that if the observers’ measurements commute with one another and with the property of interest, common certainty forces their probability assessments to coincide, thereby recovering a QM analog to the classical Agreement Theorem. We then construct a one-parameter family of qutrit–qubit–qubit models in which one observer’s measurement does not commute with the property and common certainty of disagreement occurs—a distinctively QM phenomenon. The mechanism is coherence between branches distinguished by one but not the other observer’s measurement. When measurement outcomes are stored in a classical register, the resulting dephasing removes this coherence and restores agreement. Finally, we prove that QM does not permit the extreme 0 - 1 configuration in which Alice is certain of a property and is also certain that Bob is certain of its negation. These results aim to turn debate in QM about observer-dependent facts into precise mathematical conditions for when intersubjective agreement or disagreement in QM can be sustained.

Article.Title: The p38α MAPK–MK2 axis drives chemotherapy-mediated nuclear actin remodeling to promote ovarian cancer progression
Article.Authors: Xing X.; Zhang Z.; Li L.; Shen Z.; Xi B.; Yang Y.; Diao M.; Ye L.; Chen J.; Zhuang G.; Zhou X.; Ahmed A.; Gong H.; Zang R.; Zheng Y.
Article.Abstract: Nuclear F-actin facilitates DNA damage repair and contributes to cancer chemoresistance. However, the regulatory mechanisms controlling its dynamic polymerization in response to genotoxic stress remain poorly defined. A major barrier in nuclear actin research is the lack of tools for precise, high-throughput analysis. To systematically investigate nuclear F-actin assembly in DNA damage response, we developed a deep learning pipeline, named nFANet, for high-throughput detection and analysis of nuclear F-actin. Here, using ovarian cancer—a malignancy where chemoresistance is a major clinical obstacle—as a model, we showed that platinum-based chemotherapy robustly induces nuclear F-actin assembly. A subsequent kinome screening, in combination with the application of nFANet, identified the kinase p38α MAPK as a critical upstream regulator of platinum-induced nuclear F-actin assembly. Mechanistically, the p38α MAPK–MK2 signaling pathway promotes formin-mediated nuclear F-actin assembly in response to chemotherapy. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition or genetic knockout of the p38α MAPK–MK2 pathway sensitized ovarian cancer cells to platinum-based therapy. Our work uncovers a key mechanism governing nuclear actin remodeling under genotoxic stress and lays the foundation for identifying a patient subgroup likely to benefit from therapeutic targeting of this pathway.

Article.Title: Diffusional depth profiling using electrochemiluminescence microscopy
Article.Authors: Nortz S.; Layman B.; Hill M.; Rana A.; Dick J.
Article.Abstract: Electrochemiluminescence (ECL) microscopy has emerged as a powerful 2D imaging technique with exceptional spatial resolution, enabling visualization of biological entities, nanomaterials, and multiphase systems. Conventional ECL experiments rely on coreactant concentrations in large excess of the luminophore to generate a bright signal in the vicinity of the electrode. While effective for surface interrogation, this confinement limits resolution in the z-dimension, making 3D imaging challenging. Here, we show that introducing an excess of luminophore enables access to 3D information through diffusion of the emission layer away from the electrode. By tuning the concentration ratio of tris(2,2’-bipyridine)ruthenium(II) ([Ru(bpy) 3 ] 2+ ) to tri-n-propylamine (TPrA), we control emission layer diffusivity. Initially, ECL arises from heterogeneous oxidation of both species at the electrode. As TPrA is depleted, the mechanism shifts to chemiluminescence, where [Ru(bpy) 3 ] 3+ oxidizes TPrA, generating a diffusing emissive layer that extends in the z-direction over time. Simulations and scanning electrochemical microscopy capture these diffusion profiles and highlight the role of concentration ratios. We apply this “diffusional depth profiling” to spirulina algae and spheroid cell models, insulating bodies that block light coming from the evolving emissive layer, revealing 3D morphology. This work uncovers the important influence of time and concentration on ECL emission layer expansion for depth profiling micro-to-mesoscale entities across biology and materials science.

Article.Title: Synergy between Gq and Gi proteins for the antipsychotic-like effects of mGlu2 receptors
Article.Authors: Ding H.; Liu J.; Zhang C.; Li W.; Fan Z.; Wang F.; Li H.; Rondard P.; Pin J.; Zhu Y.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: The capacity of one G protein–coupled receptor (GPCR) to modulate signaling outputs of another is a phenomenon with potential implications for neuron function and therapeutic action. Notably, Gi/o-coupled receptors have been shown to generate calcium signals after costimulation of Gq-coupled receptors, an effect resulting from a crosstalk between signaling cascades. But the relevance for brain function and for therapeutic applications remains largely unclear. Here we show that Gi/o-coupled metabotropic glutamate 2 (mGlu2) receptors can generate calcium signals in neurons. It results from either agonist activation or constitutive activity of a Gq-coupled receptor endogenously coexpressed with mGlu2, independently of dimerization. Specifically, the constitutively active platelet-activating factor receptor (PAFR) plays an essential role in mGlu2-calcium signaling in hippocampal neurons, an effect largely inhibited by PAFR inverse agonists and genetic variants. This mGlu2-PAFR crosstalk is required for the cognitive and behavioral rescue produced by mGlu2 agonists in a mouse model of NMDA receptor hypofunction. These data highlight the complexity of GPCR signaling and provide key insights on therapeutic strategies for psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Linear scaling reveals low-dimensional structure in observable microbial dynamics
Article.Authors: Zhou Z.; Chen X.; Baig Y.; Wang W.; Şimşek E.; Hamrick G.; Holmes Z.; Du Z.; Karig D.; You L.
Article.Abstract: Microbial communities often exhibit apparently complex dynamics driven by myriad interactions among community members and with their environments. Yet, practical modeling and control are often based on a limited number of observables, raising fundamental questions: are these observed dynamics low-dimensional? If so, how does the low dimensionality enable predictions with limited information? Here, we report an emergent simplicity that the temporal dynamics of observable microbial populations can be captured by low-dimensional representations. Using variational autoencoders, we define a critical latent dimension ( E c ) that operationally quantifies the smallest latent dimension required for high-fidelity reconstruction of observable microbial dynamics under a specified criterion. Despite the complexity of unobserved background dynamics, we find E c to be drastically lower than the community’s apparent degrees of freedom. E c scales linearly with the number of observables, providing an empirical principle for determining representation complexity. This principle holds across simulations of pairwise interacting communities, consumer–resource dynamics, spatially distributed microbial patches, and plasmid transfer, experiments with engineered and environment-derived communities, and human microbiomes. Our findings establish a scaling law for microbial community dynamics and demonstrate that low-dimensional representations of observable dynamics retain information useful for selected prediction tasks without direct measurement of the complete community.

Article.Title: Dynamic supercoiling sponsors transcription amplification by MYC
Article.Authors: Jha R.; Kouzine F.; Wang B.; Phelan J.; Das S.; Lewis B.; Levens D.
Article.Abstract: Dysregulated MYC provokes profound changes in cancer gene expression. Although usually considered an E-box-dependent transcription activator, an alternate model is that MYC is a universal amplifier of transcription. Although MYC participates in pause release, its full role in the transcription cycle remains poorly illuminated. MYC also stimulates topoisomerases to resolve DNA topological issues complicating its transactions; how this stimulation is coordinated with its transcriptional role has not been examined. We have developed a system that discriminates between MYC-driven activation versus amplification in any cell. This system enables the interrogation of genes, cofactors, and compounds that execute or modulate MYC activity. Using a combination of biochemical and cellular assays, we reveal dynamic interplay between MYC-driven transcription amplification and DNA supercoiling. Because the early stages of transcription are sensitive to DNA supercoiling, Reducing TOP1 activity 1 either through genetic knockdown or low-dose inhibition, potentiates transcription amplification by MYC. By increasing promoter melting and RNA polymerase loading, negative supercoiling provides the early transcription complexes upon which MYC acts to increase output.

Article.Title: Principles of use of tensile J-curve materials in antagonistic arrangements
Article.Authors: Cheng L.; Eom W.; Wang Q.; Kim H.; Guzman R.; Kim J.; Solis M.; Malladi S.; Tsai S.; Kersh M.; Tawfick S.
Article.Abstract: Natural ligaments are soft connective tissues that provide high stretchability for dexterous flexibility but switch to high stiffness to protect the musculoskeletal system from excessive deformation. These two functions cannot be independently tuned in conventional engineering materials with linear or hyperelasticity. Biological materials achieve this tailored behavior through a highly nonlinear tensile response characterized by a J-shaped curve, featuring an extended “toe region” of low force up to intermediate strains followed by an inflection, called the “heel region” which marks the onset of nonlinear stiffening. Here, we aim to study the characteristics of J-curves to establish principles for their use in robotic mechanisms. We define and measure the J-curve features responsible for protectiveness and mobility, describe the effective stiffness and the level of nonlinearity as a function of pre-stretch, and elucidate how the J-curve decouples flexibility from damage protection. Experimental measurements reveal the performance advantages of twisted and coiled elastomeric J-curve materials in engineered antagonistic arrangements and highlight their unique design space compared with linear elastic systems. Furthermore, we present a conceptual analysis of exploiting J-curve materials in energy-efficient running as an outlook toward their use in bioinspired robots.

Article.Title: Chromatin dynamics secondary to dexamethasone exposure identifies 67 genes linked to elevated IOP and primary open-angle glaucoma
Article.Authors: Singh N.; Batz Z.; Advani J.; English M.; Maddala R.; Rao P.; Swaroop A.
Article.Abstract: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder, and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) represents its only modifiable risk factor. We modeled increased IOP by treating three primary human trabecular meshwork cell strains with dexamethasone and generated a high-resolution map of promoter-centered chromatin contacts and regulatory modules. We identify dynamic changes in chromatin compartments and looping, cis-regulatory elements, and transcription factor hubs corresponding to altered expression profile. By integrating Genomewide association studies associated variants with dexamethasone induced chromatin landscape, we ascertain 29 target genes linked to 23 lead IOP variants and 57 genes for 46 POAG variants, with 19 shared between the two. Pathway analysis of 67 IOP- and POAG-associated genes reveals enrichment in vesicle transport, TLR, MAPK, and hippo-YAP signaling pathways. We also uncover transcriptional regulatory role of 103 noncoding lead variants. Our studies provide a mechanistic framework of genetic complexity accompanying steroid-induced IOP and related POAG pathology.

Article.Title: PPP1R1B differentially modulates alcohol intake and emotional comorbidity through distinct prefrontal circuits
Article.Authors: Li F.; Chen M.; Li X.; Zhang Z.; Luo H.; Zhu M.; Wang H.; Xu Y.; Chen F.; Wang K.
Article.Abstract: Excessive alcohol consumption frequently co-occurs with anxiety and depression in alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet the specific neural circuits and molecular mechanisms coordinating these comorbid conditions remain poorly defined. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), particularly its prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) subregions, projects to key reward and emotion centers like the nucleus accumbens (Nac) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but the functional heterogeneity of these projections is unclear. Using chemogenetics, retrograde tracing, electrophysiology, spatial proteomics, and cell-type-specific gene editing in mice subjected to a 4-wk intermittent access to alcohol (IAA) paradigm, we selectively manipulated glutamatergic projections from the PL and IL to the Nac core, Nac shell, and BLA and assessed alcohol intake, anxiety-like, and depression-like behaviors. Chemogenetic activation of PL-Nac core projections reduced short-term alcohol intake, anxiety-, and depression-like behaviors, while IL-BLA activation decreased alcohol consumption and anxiety-like behaviors only. Retrograde tracing revealed mirror-image anatomical segregation of projection-defined neuronal subpopulations within PL/IL linking spatial organization to functional divergence. IAA induced pathway-specific synaptic adaptations. Spatial proteomics nominated protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 1B (PPP1R1B) as a candidate molecule in PL-Nac core neurons. Independent immunostaining confirmed PPP1R1B downregulation, and circuit-specific knockout recapitulated alcohol-related and affective phenotypes, whereas overexpression reversed them. In IL-BLA neurons, PPP1R1B manipulation modulated alcohol intake and anxiety, but not depression. These findings define a subregion- and projection-specific organizational logic in the mPFC for differentially regulating alcohol consumption and emotional comorbidity, with PPP1R1B as a key molecular determinant. This provides a neural pathway–molecule framework for targeted intervention in AUD.
