Article.Title: Ancient genomes reveal an extinct bovine species from mid-latitude Asia
Article.Authors: Oppenheimer J.; Gilardet A.; Kozlikin M.; Kosintsev P.; Vasiliev S.; Shunkov M.; Xenikoudakis G.; Ford S.; Douka K.; Heintzman P.; Shapiro B.; Dalén L.
Article.Abstract: A previously undescribed bovine mitochondrial clade, termed yak X, was recently discovered in Pleistocene Asia.1 However, the genome-wide relationships of this lineage to other bovines remain unclear. Here, we present 20 Middle and Late Pleistocene yak X nuclear genomes that were recovered from Denisova Cave and other sites in mid-latitude Asia and have a temporal span of over 200,000 years. Phylogenetic and population genomic approaches show that yak X was a separate species that began diverging from extant yaks at least 400,000 years ago. We also document a demographic decline in yak X over the Mid-to-Late Pleistocene, along with potential population turnover accompanied by a decrease in genetic diversity around the Last Interglacial (∼130,000 to ∼115,000 years ago). Unlike divergent hominin lineages within Pleistocene Asia,2 we find negligible evidence for gene flow between yak X and other bovine species, including steppe bison (Bison priscus) and aurochs (Bos primigenius), despite their geographic and temporal co-occurrence.1 Our results show that yak X was a distinct species whose disappearance may have previously gone unrecognized during the Late Quaternary megafaunal extinctions, and highlight the broader Altai-Sayan region as a hotspot of diversity during the Pleistocene.

Article.Title: PAK-family kinases promote cell fusion irreversibility by preventing cell-wall repair
Article.Authors: Coronas-Serna J.; Saha S.; Pérez-Berná A.; Martin S.
Article.Abstract: Cell-cell fusion is critical for the sexual life cycle, as it drives the unidirectional transition between haploid and diploid phases. In fungi, fusion requires not only plasma membrane merging but also local cell-wall removal. However, the integrity of the cell wall, which resists internal turgor pressure and is essential for survival, is normally monitored by a cell-wall integrity pathway (CIP) involving Rho1 GTPase, protein kinase C (PKC), and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling, which promotes damage repair. How the CIP allows localized cell-wall degradation is not known. In the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, we previously identified pak2Δ mutants that exhibit transient fusion: cells briefly fuse and exchange cytoplasmic contents, which signal catastrophic haploid meiosis, but then reseal their fusion pore. Here, we show that the kinase activity of p21-activated kinases (PAK) is essential for cell-cell fusion, with major and minor contributions from Pak2 and the essential Pak1, respectively. Strikingly, osmotic stabilization largely suppresses all PAK-associated fusion defects, pointing to a role in cell-wall remodeling. Pak2 accumulates at the fusion site, where it promotes fusion pore opening and expansion. In its absence, Rho1-GTP, PKC, and beta-glucan synthase Bgs4 show elevated levels at the fusion site, and their partial loss of function rescues fusion. Pak1 mutants have elevated MAPK activity. Thus, Pak2 and Pak1 both antagonize the CIP. Furthermore, correlative light and cryo-soft-X-ray tomography reveals that resealed pores in PAK mutants rebuilt an intact cell wall. We conclude that PAKs enforce fusion directionality by antagonizing cell-wall repair mechanisms that otherwise restore separation between mating partners.

Article.Title: Cold sensing by a glutamate receptor drives avoidance behavior in Drosophila larvae
Article.Authors: Xu L.; Son H.; Bai X.; Sui J.; Li R.; Ronan E.; Kim G.; Ye B.
Article.Abstract: The ability to sense and avoid noxious environments is essential for animal survival. While the mechanisms of heat and cool sensation are well studied, those underlying the sensation of cold are relatively less understood. By implementing custom-built thermoelectric devices capable of delivering rapid and precise thermal stimuli, we find that cold delivered to the larval head evokes robust escape behavioral responses. We identify anterior C3da (aC3da), a group of head-located cold-sensitive neurons, as necessary and sufficient for such avoidance responses. We further demonstrate that the kainate-type glutamate receptor Clumsy acts as a novel cold sensor required for head cold sensitivity. Knockdown of Clumsy in head cold-sensing neurons suppresses their cold sensitivity. Heterologous expression of Clumsy confers cold sensitivity. Article.Title: Multiple evolutionary routes to cytoskeletal arborization revealed by the rhizarian amoeba Filoreta ramosa
Article.Authors: Guest S.; Dawson S.
Article.Abstract: The eukaryotic cytoskeleton generates remarkable diversity in cellular architecture despite being built from conserved actin and tubulin polymers. Diversification of cytoskeletal regulators, motors, and filament-organizing proteins produces varied morphologies, yet certain architectures repeatedly emerge in distantly related lineages. One notable example is cytoskeletal arborization, occurring in metazoan neurons and amoeboid lineages throughout the eukaryotic tree. Whether these similar branched architectures arise through conserved cytoskeletal organization, shared molecular reuse, or convergence driven by common physical constraints remains unresolved. Here, we investigate the rhizarian amoeba Filoreta ramosa, which forms a multinucleate reticulated network through branching and anastomosis. Using live imaging, immunofluorescence, morphometric analyses, and cytoskeletal drugs, we define how actin and microtubule systems organize branch formation, intracellular transport, and large-scale network architecture. Actin-rich protrusions initiate exploratory branchlets that become selectively stabilized through microtubule incorporation. Longitudinal microtubule arrays reinforce mature branches and support rapid bidirectional organelle transport, while branch nodes function as distributed sites of microtubule nucleation. These cytoskeletal features parallel key mechanisms underlying neuronal arborization, yet unlike neurons, Filoreta develops a decentralized reticulated network through repeated anastomosis and distributed microtubule organization, thereby scaling transport capacity and structural support with network growth. Our findings suggest that shared cytoskeletal mechanisms repeatedly support branching architectures, while distinct topologies and modes of organization allow evolution to reach arborization through different routes as increasing cellular scale imposes common demands on transport and structural integrity. Filoreta therefore provides a tractable model for investigating how conserved cytoskeletal systems generate arborized architectures that scale with cellular size.

Article.Title: Representation of fear memory features in the ventral hippocampus
Article.Authors: Milentijevic A.; Cerquetella C.; Nevian T.; Ciocchi S.; Forro T.
Article.Abstract: Fear memories are essential for adaptive behavior, as they encode salient and emotionally valenced information that enables organisms to anticipate and avoid future threats. Fearful events are experienced as unified representations, even though they consist of multiple features with distributed sensory inputs across space and time that are integrated and imbued with emotional valence. Whether these features are jointly or separately represented by the memory networks in the brain and how such memories guide behavior during novel experiences remains unclear. Here, we use a virtual reality paradigm to disentangle spatial, temporal, and emotional memory features in the mouse ventral CA1 hippocampus. We show that distinct spatial and temporal representations emerge for context- and cue-related features, with temporal features transferring to novel experiences. The preservation of neural geometry, but not of individual neural identities, is prominent in pyramidal neurons and may, alongside dynamic modulation of interneuron activity, reflect a general principle by which selective memory features are maintained and adaptively exploited.

Article.Title: Endosome motility controls light-responsive reproductive development and secondary metabolite production in Aspergillus
Article.Authors: Kumar G.; Allen J.; Oster L.; Rawa M.; Aguilar-Ramírez E.; Bok J.; Suen P.; Driscoll B.; Salogiannis J.; Keller N.; Reck-Peterson S.
Article.Abstract: Filamentous fungi, such as Aspergillus species, use microtubule transport to move early endosomes. Other cargos, such as peroxisomes and mRNAs, "hitchhike" on early endosomes to move throughout the long hyphae of these organisms. In Aspergillus nidulans, peroxisomes hitchhike on early endosomes using the endosomal protein PxdA and the peroxisomal protein AcbdA. The HookA adaptor protein links endosomes to microtubule motors. Here, we set out to explore the physiological functions of peroxisome hitchhiking and endosome motility. A. nidulans has a complex life cycle that includes asexual and sexual reproduction. A. nidulans and other fungi within the Pezizomycotina subphylum are also notable for the vast number of secondary metabolites they produce. Light and other environmental conditions influence developmental decisions and secondary metabolite production. Here, we found that sexual reproduction is favored in the absence of endosome motility, even in the light, which normally promotes asexual reproduction. RNA sequencing of strains lacking PxdA-marked motile early endosomes showed altered expression of genes involved in development. Unexpectedly, we also observed altered expression of genes involved in secondary metabolism in strains lacking endosome motility and peroxisome hitchhiking. Using mass spectrometry, we found that the loss of endosome motility affected the biosynthesis of secondary metabolites, including sterigmatocystin, a carcinogenic mycotoxin that is a food contaminant. Finally, in a pathogenic species, Aspergillus fumigatus, we found that deletion of its pxdA homolog significantly altered secondary metabolite production. Our work uncovers an unexpected link between organelle motility, developmental decisions in response to light, and secondary metabolite production in filamentous fungi.

Article.Title: Mosasaur tail morphology reveals burst swimming performance and ecological diversity
Article.Authors: Formoso K.; Hebdon N.; Fish F.; Cieri R.; Habib M.
Article.Abstract: Reconstructing locomotor performance of extinct animals is fundamental to understanding paleoecology, yet the soft tissues that control movement rarely fossilize, leaving performance poorly constrained for extinct taxa1. Burst locomotion is a key determinant of predatory and escape success2,3 and is governed by well-established fluid dynamics and kinematic principles, meaning it can be modeled from skeletal morphology alone. Here, we apply a drag-based fast-start framework, which we term a "slam-start," to estimate lunge velocity in four mosasaurs, dominant seagoing predators of Late Cretaceous oceans,4 spanning Mosasaurinae and Russellosaurina, using skeletal and caudal muscle reconstructions to parameterize tail excursion amplitude, muscle power output, and hydrodynamic drag across a range of plausible parameters. Across all modeled conditions, lunge velocity increases with tail curl amplitude and power output, while increasing drag coefficient produces only modest reductions in performance. Russellosaurine mosasaurids (Platecarpus tympaniticus and Tylosaurus proriger), which have longer tail displacement areas, exhibit higher normalized lunge velocities than mosasaurines (Mosasaurus sp. and Plotosaurus bennisoni), and these relative differences are consistent across a wide range of drag regimes. These results support distinct hunting strategies within Mosasauridae: the faster-lunging russellosaurines were likely ambush predators, whereas the slower mosasaurines were likely pelagic cruisers. As a case study, this work demonstrates that physics-based biomechanical modeling can generate quantitative, directly comparable locomotor estimates for extinct taxa using preserved morphology as input, offering a transferable protocol for studying burst performance across marine reptiles, taxa with no living analogs, and through deep evolutionary time.

Article.Title: Temporal heterogeneity in the animal fossil record driven by proliferation of microbial collagenases
Article.Authors: Vixseboxse P.; Moody E.; Donoghue P.; McMahon S.; Liu A.
Article.Abstract: The animal fossil record is a non-uniform archive of evolutionary history in which exceptional preservation diminishes toward the present,1,2,3 with biomineralized skeletal elements constituting the majority of the fossil record. Preservation of soft tissues requires rare combinations of chemical, biological, and physical conditions that preclude or delay decay until biological substrates can be geologically stabilized via mineralization or maturation.4 However, during the late Ediacaran Period (∼579-539 mya) fossilization of soft-bodied macroorganisms was common across a wide range of depositional settings.5,6 Taphonomic models seeking to explain Ediacaran exceptionalism typically appeal to unusual mineralogical and geochemical conditions or microbiological influence (e.g., Gehling,7 Tarhan et al.,8 Bykova et al.,9 and Bobrovskiy et al.10), and the Paleozoic decline in exceptional preservation has invariably been explained in terms of expansion of the oxic zone through metazoan bioturbation (though see Cribb et al.11) and enhanced scavenging.12 We explore the hypothesis that temporal heterogeneity in metazoan exceptional preservation is a consequence of the origin and/or proliferation of microbial collagenases.13 Collagenase gene trees reconciled with a time-calibrated phylogeny show that collagenases arose and were produced by obligate anaerobes billions of years before proliferating by lateral gene transfer, approximately coincident with the diversification of early animals. These results support a link between the evolution of collagenases, animals, and the non-uniformity of the fossil record. Proliferation of collagenase-producing microbial lineages occurred in concert with early animal evolution. Evidence also indicates a shift in the locus of collagen degradation within the sediment redox profile, coincident with the decline of exceptional soft-tissue preservation in the marine realm.

Article.Title: A hidden archaeal lineage with an ultra-reduced genome retaining only its replicative core
Article.Authors: Harada R.; Nishimura Y.; Nomura M.; Yabuki A.; Shiba K.; Inaba K.; Allers T.; Inagaki Y.; Nakayama T.
Article.Abstract: Host-associated prokaryotes can undergo extreme genome reduction, but the most reduced genomes belong to mutualistic endosymbionts whose hosts compensate for lost functions, eroding the symbiont's identity as an autonomous cell. Whether comparable reduction can occur while preserving the informational autonomy of a cell remains unclear. Here, we report the discovery of Candidatus Sukunaarchaeum mirabile, an archaeon with a genome of only 238 kbp (less than half the size of the smallest known archaeal genome) obtained by single-cell genomics from a dinoflagellate cell. Phylogenetic analyses reveal Sukunaarchaeum as an extremely divergent lineage that cannot be placed within any recognized archaeal phylum, although its precise branching position remains unresolved; environmental surveys indicate a diverse, geographically dispersed, and previously overlooked clade. Its genome lacks virtually all recognizable metabolic pathways yet retains the catalytic cores of the machinery for DNA replication, transcription, and translation, with losses largely confined to auxiliary and regulatory subunits. This profile contrasts with that of highly reduced mutualistic endosymbionts, in which informational genes are lost alongside metabolic ones, eroding autonomous cellular identity: Sukunaarchaeum encodes no recognizable metabolic pathway that could benefit a host, and instead dedicates ∼25% of its genome to large membrane proteins of unknown function, a feature paralleled by host-invasion proteins in parasitic archaea. These observations argue against a mutualistic mode of host dependence and reveal a second, distinct endpoint of cellular reduction: the informational core may represent the practical lower bound for a cell that retains the capacity to replicate and express its own genome.

Article.Title: Functional recomposition of excitatory synaptic inputs to individual neurons in ferret visual cortex after the onset of visual experience
Article.Authors: Jaepel J.; Tepohl C.; Satterfield R.; Fitzpatrick D.
Article.Abstract: During early visual cortex development, the onset of visual experience initiates a period of rapid dendritic growth and excitatory synapse formation that coincides with the functional maturation of visually driven neuronal response properties. How this surge in the number of excitatory synaptic inputs refines the initial functional network structure to generate coherent, yet adaptable, single-neuron responses remains unclear. To address this issue, we examined the functional properties and spatial organization of individual dendritic spines of layer 2/3 neurons in ferret visual cortex before and after the onset of visual experience. Our findings indicate that this initial period of visual experience is marked by a dramatic and selective functional and spatial recomposition of the visually naive excitatory synaptic network. This reorganization leads to an increase in the proportion and tuning strength of orientation- and direction-selective inputs and markedly expands the population of binocular inputs, particularly those with highly aligned responses across both eyes. This refinement follows distinct developmental trajectories of contralateral vs. ipsilateral inputs, as well as monocular vs. binocular inputs, that reshape the functional organization of excitatory synaptic inputs to individual neurons. In parallel, synaptic inputs are spatially reorganized, with co-tuned inputs becoming locally clustered along dendrites as a coarser branch-level organization present at eye opening is remodeled. Together, these rapid changes appear to be organized as a scaffold-and-integration process through which visual experience expands and reorganizes the excitatory synaptic network. This process enhances tuning selectivity and supports the emergence of a robust binocular representation while maintaining functional input diversity.

Article.Title: Individual identification of brown bears using pose-aware metric learning
Article.Authors: Rosenberg B.; Zhou M.; Wolf N.; Mathis M.; Harris B.; Mathis A.
Article.Abstract: # Individual identification of brown bears sing pose-aware metric learning Multi-year re-identification for brown bears collected at McNeil River, Alaska USA (2017–2022). Identifying individuals within a species is a cornerstone of ecological and biological research, holding the key to understanding behavior, population dynamics, and conservation needs. However, conventional identification methods such as genetic sampling and physical tags come with significant trade-offs, including invasiveness, high costs, and limited scalability. Despite remarkable advances in computer vision that have transformed the identification of patterned species, reliably distinguishing individuals in unmarked species remains an open challenge. Here, we curate a novel dataset of visually identified individual Alaskan coastal brown bears (Ursus arctos). This 72K image dataset contains high-resolution images of 109 known individuals from multiple seasons and in varied conditions (e.g., fur shed, substantial weight gain). Identification of these bears is notoriously difficult, yet our new pose-aware metric-learning-based AI model is able to leverage biometric information that enables individual re-identification (ReID) with promising accuracy for future research and conservation efforts. Our findings indicate that it is possible to reidentify individual brown bears across years and to detect unknown individuals in a 'real-world' open dataset. PoseSwin presents a promising approach to the challenge of non-invasive ReID of other unmarked species, as well, and points toward an expanded range of possible questions in wildlife and ecological research. > ⚠️ Data can be found at [https://zenodo.org/records/xxx](https://zenodo.org/records/xxx) ## General information * **Authors**: Beth Rosenberg, Mu Zhou, Nathan Wolf, Mackenzie W. Article.Title: Dual-mode dynamics in hippocampal populations enable rapid and precise spatial coding
Article.Authors: Ren M.; Feng S.; Chen Q.; Lin L.; Xu J.
Article.Abstract: Hippocampal spatial representations emerge within minutes of first exposure to novel environments, challenging models based solely on gradual synaptic plasticity. Here, we show that CA1 spatial coding is organized according to a dual-mode architecture comprising a pre-organized backbone and an experience-dependent component. Backbone cells expressing immediately emerging place fields form a stable spatial scaffold and dominate positional decoding from the first traversal, whereas experience-dependent cells bearing gradually emerging fields are progressively incorporated to refine spatial representations. Analyses of ensemble activity further reveal that offline dynamics prospectively organize future spatial coding. In backbone cells, latent tuning aligns with their future place fields prior to task engagement, while in experience-dependent cells this alignment strengthens before overt place-field expression. Together, these findings identify a dual-mode organization of hippocampal populations in which offline dynamics pre-organize network activity to enable rapid and precise spatial coding in novel environments.

Article.Title: The chytrid fungus threatens the last epidemiologically naive Neotropical montane amphibian biodiversity hotspot
Article.Authors: Plewnia A.; Pasmans F.; Hildwein T.; Mulder K.; Henn J.; Crawford A.; Rueda Solano L.; Fuhrmann N.; Lühmann A.; Erens J.; Flechas S.; Catenazzi A.; Rivera Jaimes L.; Araújo V.; Lansac C.; Heine C.; Salas R.; Barros-Granados A.; Barrios Yepes A.; Rengifo-Saavedra L.; Savage A.; Vásquez V.; Culebras J.; Barros Castañeda J.; Pérez-González J.
Article.Abstract: The amphibian chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (B. dendrobatidis) has caused catastrophic biodiversity loss worldwide.1,2,3 Although B. dendrobatidis is now widespread across environmentally suitable regions,4 the absence of amphibian declines in some high-suitability areas suggests the existence of refuges supporting epidemiologically naive communities. Epidemiologically naive refuges have not experienced past B. dendrobatidis epizootics despite suitable environmental conditions and may be B. dendrobatidis-free, harbor less virulent B. dendrobatidis lineages, or contain resistant host communities. As eradication of virulent B. dendrobatidis lineages is rarely successful after establishment, identifying epidemiologically naive refuges is imperative.5,6 Here, following extensive multi-year disease surveillance, we report a major epidemiologically naive refuge in the Neotropical highlands, the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (SNSM) in northern Colombia. We found no evidence for contemporary B. dendrobatidis presence, despite detecting the hypervirulent Global Panzootic Lineage in a neighboring Andean mountain range. Population genomic analyses in SNSM-endemic harlequin toads found no demographic signatures indicative of cryptic epizootic decline. Niche modeling predicted high suitability for B. dendrobatidis occurrence and B. dendrobatidis-induced declines throughout the SNSM, with climatic conditions in lowland regions surrounding the SNSM likely acting as a dispersal barrier and preventing B. dendrobatidis invasion, creating a "sky island." Infection trials using three SNSM-endemic amphibian species revealed tolerant and susceptible species. Together, our results indicate that the SNSM is an epidemiologically naive refuge at risk of invasion by hypervirulent B. dendrobatidis, which could result in the loss of 25 endemic amphibian species. We highlight the urgent need for proactive conservation action and the strict implementation of biosecurity to safeguard the unique and vast amphibian diversity of the SNSM.

Article.Title: A North American mycorrhizal fungus displays zinc tolerance intraspecific variation and protects pines from zinc toxicity
Article.Authors: Fletcher J.; Wang H.; Zhang K.; Chen X.; Barry K.; Kuo A.; Lipzen A.; Steindorff A.; Peterson D.; Guo J.; Grigoriev I.; Chen F.; Liao H.; Branco S.
Article.Abstract: Soil zinc (Zn) pollution, largely caused by anthropogenic activities such as mining and metal processing, can disrupt metabolism and reproduction, often leading to death. Some fungi can tolerate elevated Zn concentrations, but the mechanisms of Zn tolerance and if and how they affect symbionts are still unclear. To fill these gaps in knowledge, we investigated Zn tolerance in the ectomycorrhizal fungus Suillus tomentosus and its host pine Pinus contorta, two widespread symbiotic partners in American Western forests. Using a combination of whole-genome resequencing, in vitro Zn fungal assays, fungal-pine partner bioassays, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, we found an absence of S. tomentosus population structure based on Zn tolerance, and that the trait is highly polygenic, constitutive, and associated with Zn exclusion and antioxidant responses to mitigate toxicity. We also found that S. tomentosus protects P. contorta from Zn toxicity by increasing seedling performance under Zn stress, with Zn-tolerant S. tomentosus providing slightly more benefit compared with Zn-sensitive S. tomentosus. Our results illustrate that fungal metal tolerance is a complex trait, and that intraspecific variation should be considered for understanding the impacts of environmental stress on biodiversity, as well as for designing effective biotechnological tools and conservation/reforestation strategies.

Article.Title: A premitotic polarity program patterns the grass leaf epidermis
Article.Authors: Korosteleva A.; Janssen K.; Zhang D.; Ruiz Duarte P.; Polat I.; Goršek N.; Jesenofsky B.; Baç E.; Lindner H.; Raissig M.
Article.Abstract: Transverse asymmetric cell divisions (ACDs) in grass leaf epidermal development produce large basal pavement cells and small apical specialized cells. These "patterning divisions" generate the long-short epidermal cell pattern that is distinctive of grasses. Here, we show that patterning divisions require premitotic basal polarization of BdPOLAR-LIKE1 (BdPL1) in the model grass Brachypodium distachyon. Loss of BdPL1 disrupted division-plane orientation and postmitotic cell-size asymmetry in all cell files, which resulted in epidermal patterning defects. Ectopic expression analyses demonstrated that BdPL1 polarization was independent of cellular context and sufficient to promote supernumerary transverse divisions. Furthermore, the developmental regulators BdBREVIS RADIX-solo and BdYODA1 formed a post-division polarity domain that enforced cell fate asymmetry independently of BdPL1. We propose that the premitotic BdPL1 module enforces physical cell division asymmetry contributing to medio-lateral patterning of cell types, whereas the postmitotic BdBRX-solo/BdYDA1 module enforces within-file cell fate asymmetry. Together, they robustly pattern the grass leaf epidermis.

Article.Title: Mucoromycotina fine root endophyte engages in a nutritionally mutualistic symbiosis with Arabidopsis thaliana
Article.Authors: Prout J.; Burgess J.; Williams A.; Rodríguez-Morelos V.; Pressel S.; Ton J.; Field K.
Article.Abstract: Arabidopsis thaliana, a widely used genetic model species, is considered incapable of forming mycorrhizal associations, which support nutrient acquisition in most other land plants. Mucoromycotina "fine root endophytes" (MFREs) are a recently characterized group of mycorrhizal fungi capable of forming nutritional mutualisms with a wide range of plants, supplying nitrogen and phosphorus to host plants and gaining access to photosynthetically derived carbon. Here, we demonstrate that a wild-isolated MFRE strain, Lyc-1, successfully colonizes Arabidopsis roots under monoaxenic conditions without affecting plant growth. Using a combination of conventional light and epifluorescence microscopy, we demonstrate extensive extra- and intraradical colonization of the root cortex. Stable- and radio-isotope tracing further revealed bidirectional nutrient exchange between the host plant and the fungus. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a functional, mycorrhiza-like nutritional mutualism in Arabidopsis. As Arabidopsis lacks a complete set of common symbiosis signaling pathway genes, our findings suggest that Arabidopsis-Lyc-1 symbiosis may be controlled by an alternative, so far uncharacterized, symbiotic pathway. Thus, our study not only supports the existence of multiple evolutionary routes to plant-fungal nutritional mutualisms but also establishes Arabidopsis as a genetically tractable model to study plant-fungal symbiosis, thereby opening new opportunities to dissect the molecular basis and evolution of mycorrhizal symbioses.

Article.Title: Neural coordination of wing and leg movements during a terrestrial threat display
Article.Authors: Cao S.; Anderson D.
Article.Abstract: In most flying species, legs and wings mediate earthbound vs. aerial locomotion, respectively. During terrestrial social displays such as threat or courtship, however, species-typical movements of these appendages are coordinated in a stereotyped manner. How such appendicular control is integrated is poorly understood. Threat behavior in Drosophila consists of four types of leg and wing actions, which can be performed singly or in combination. Using a large-scale functional screen, we previously identified a cluster of 4-5 AIP (CL062) neurons whose optogenetic activation can evoke all threat actions and which are essential for natural threat displays. To understand how this threat command module functions, we have mapped AIP neurons into the male fly connectome and identified split-GAL4 drivers for four major downstream targets, whose functional connectivity and behavioral roles we have tested. Surprisingly, we find that distinct threat-specific actions are not controlled by parallel connections from different subsets of AIP cells to different action-specific descending neurons (DNs), a parsimonious circuit architecture. Rather, AIP neurons collectively activate two parallel downstream modules comprising pairs of neurons that control wing vs. leg movements, respectively. Wing movements are controlled via direct projections to two specialist DNs that act synergistically, while leg movements are controlled indirectly via two interneurons that act antagonistically to pattern the activity of multiple DNs, which are likely used in other locomotor contexts. These data elucidate a hierarchical circuit for appendicular coordination during a terrestrial social display and provide insight into how the brain has repurposed appendage-specific locomotor control for social communication, a form of exaptation.

Article.Title: Longitudinal study of Toba/Qom communities reveals delay and shortening of sleep in real time
Article.Authors: Casiraghi L.; Spiousas I.; Trebucq L.; Coldeira M.; Godoy Peirone C.; Zhang V.; Moyano M.; Golombek D.; de la Iglesia H.
Article.Abstract: While artificial light and digital technologies are widely assumed to delay and curtail sleep, direct, longitudinal evidence documenting these changes is remarkably scarce. From 2012 to 2024, we conducted a longitudinal study of native Toba/Qom communities in northern Argentina, including rural groups newly introduced to electricity and semi-urban groups with earlier access to electricity. Using linear mixed-effects models on a dataset of over 12,000 actigraphically recorded sleep events from 156 participants at different times, we observed striking shifts in sleep dynamics. Remarkably, both groups showed delays of close to 1 h in sleep timing, and participants from rural communities lost 35 min of sleep within the course of a decade. These changes occurred across a period that included, first, the introduction of electricity to rural communities after 2016, and, in more recent years, the spread of the internet and smartphone use among the Toba/Qom. While previous work in these and other populations has shown that both factors are associated with changes in sleep habits, our analyses suggest that they cannot fully explain the reported shifts in sleep timing across time by themselves, which may therefore be consistent with concurrent broader processes of modernization and acculturation. These transformations highlight the rapid changes that can take place in communities going through the early stages of the adoption of modern technologies, offering a contemporary parallel to the shifts in human sleep hypothesized to have accompanied global industrialization.

Article.Title: An ancient polymorphism in myosin I a/b determines chiral variation in Japanese Euhadra snails
Article.Authors: Lewis A.; Ishii Y.; Ito S.; Kimura K.; Johansen M.; Hume A.; Moore C.; Hartman T.; Jackson D.; Chiba S.; Hirano T.; Davison A.
Article.Abstract: Left-right (LR) asymmetry is a fundamental feature of animal development, yet progress in understanding its establishment has been limited by the fact that almost all animals do not ordinarily vary in the direction of their asymmetry. Snails are an exception because some wild-living species show abundant variation-externally visible in the shell coiling direction or "chirality"-yet the existing knowledge is from species, including the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis, in which the sinistral mutation is rare and causes pathology. Here, we show that chiral polymorphism in Japanese Euhadra snails is due to functional variation in an unconventional myosin I a/b, a myosin family member not previously implicated in LR specification in any animal. Both the sinistral and dextral gene variants are ancient, impart minimal transcriptional differences in the single-cell embryo, and are not associated with pathology. Analyses show that relaxed selection enabled dominant-acting amino acid substitutions in the sinistral version of the Euhadra myosin motor domain and motor-lever junction, potentially affecting actomyosin interactions. For comparison, in the pond snail, we found that thousands of genes are differentially expressed between dextral and sinistral embryos due to the frameshift mutation in a formin gene. Overall, these results reinforce the role of myosin and actin-driven processes in LR symmetry breaking, broaden the known molecular repertoire, and highlight key mutations and positions in myosins that should be explored further, including in other animals. Article.Title: Hunger recruits a parallel circuit encoding alcohol reward
Article.Authors: Nuñez K.; Sherer L.; Walley A.; Salamon S.; Chan V.; Talay M.; Barnea G.; Stowers R.; Kaun K.
Article.Abstract: Internal states like hunger, pain, thirst, and arousal can bias behavior by affecting sensory and memory processing. Internal states are critical to understand in the context of alcohol addiction because they influence cravings, reinstatement, and relapse. Norepinephrine plays a key role in both hunger and alcohol-induced arousal and preference, but the circuit-level mechanisms through which it modulates the influence of hunger on alcohol preference are not well understood. We sought to address this using intersectional genetic tools for manipulating neurons expressing octopamine, the invertebrate analog of vertebrate norepinephrine. We identified a single octopamine neuron required for ethanol seeking only when Drosophila are food deprived. Hunger increased baseline activity in this neuron, thus making it more responsive to an odor cue previously paired with ethanol. A combination of genetic and connectome analyses revealed that the synaptic partners of this octopaminergic neuron form a functional module that acts on Drosophila memory circuitry. Thus, we show that hunger recruits a parallel circuit that drives learned ethanol preference, providing a neuronal framework through which internal state influences the expression of memory for ethanol-associated cues. Article.Title: Electrical synapses mediate visual orientation behavior
Article.Authors: Frighetto G.; Dombrovski M.; Palacios Castillo L.; Meera P.; Mirshahidi P.; Mirshahidi P.; Sanfilippo P.; Vaccari A.; Kandimalla P.; Hartenstein V.; Kurmangaliyev Y.; Zipursky S.; Frye M.
Article.Abstract: Animals constantly detect and orient toward salient visual objects, but the neural circuits underlying this process remain poorly understood. We previously showed that T3 neurons, a visual columnar cell type in Drosophila melanogaster, drive saccadic orientation toward visual landmarks during flight. Here, we identify LC17 neurons, a visual projection cell type, as T3 downstream partners for saccadic visual orientation. Using in vivo optical physiology and virtual reality behavior, we demonstrate that LC17 neurons are broadly tuned to visual objects and necessary for object tracking during flight. Notably, this tracking behavior depends on electrical synapses. We show that the innexin Shaking B (ShakB), which forms gap junctions in the fly brain, is highly expressed in LC17 dendrites. Additionally, LC17-specific knockdown of shakB perturbs the cell physiological visual response and impairs the behavioral readout of object motion vision for saccadic orientation. Our findings reveal the mechanisms underlying visual orientation and highlight the interplay between electrical and chemical neurotransmission for object detection and rapid action selection.

Article.Title: Functional roles of abyssal benthos in sustaining polymetallic nodule fields
Article.Authors: Van Audenhaege L.; Jones D.; Durden J.; Fleming B.; Mejía-Saenz A.; Sweetman A.; Simon-Lledó E.
Article.Abstract: Polymetallic nodules form a critical habitat in the abyssal plain ecosystems where they occur, supporting high benthic biodiversity.1 They form over millions of years in areas of extremely low sediment accumulation rates,2,3 but it is unclear how the nodules remain on the surface, and hence are available for benthic biota. Here, we use seabed time-lapse photography to explore the potential role of benthic faunal behavior in the maintenance of polymetallic nodules on the seabed surface. We observed several species directly removing sediment from the nodule surface, mainly holothurians and gastropods, and infauna activity causing nodule uplift. Derived estimates of the area covered by animal movements, as a proxy for benthic activity,4,5 indicated that yearly to decadal timescales are needed to remove sediment from and uplift all nodules within the field of view. If these behaviors significantly counteract nodule burial over the long term, then benthic activity may be a key mechanism in nodule maintenance,6,7 as hypothesized for over 40 years.8 This essential function for the maintenance of abyssal biodiversity in nodule-field seascapes has been largely overlooked, highlighting that substantial gaps in knowledge remain in our understanding of the functioning of nodule-field ecosystems. Improving the assessment of habitat engineers may enhance predictions of ecosystem resilience if commercial mining activities occur. However, this study opens new opportunities for monitoring benthic ecosystem functioning to provide a more holistic understanding of abyssal ecosystem status and dynamics.

Article.Title: Interbacterial competition triggers stress-induced CRISPR immunity against bacteriophages
Article.Authors: Custodio R.; Martignoni M.; Zhu W.; Kuske R.; Alseth E.; Moura-Alves P.; Brown S.; Westra E.
Article.Abstract: Bacteria-phage interactions are often studied in relatively simple experimental systems involving a single bacterial strain infected by a single phage.1 In natural environments, however, bacteria typically inhabit complex multispecies communities where species compete for limited resources and ecological niches.2,3,4 Recent studies show that the microbial community context can have profound effects on the evolution of phage resistance.5 For example, Pseudomonas aeruginosa evolves phage resistance primarily through receptor loss when grown in isolation but switches to CRISPR-based immunity in the presence of bacterial competitors.6,7 Previous work showed that interspecies competition can favor CRISPR-immune bacteria over surface mutants after phage resistance has evolved.6 However, it remains unknown whether competition also alters the initial generation of CRISPR immunity by changing CRISPR-Cas expression and spacer acquisition before selection among resistance phenotypes occurs. Here, we show that interbacterial competition can trigger CRISPR-Cas activation and adaptation in P. aeruginosa. When co-cultured with Acinetobacter baumannii, P. aeruginosa exhibited markedly increased expression of CRISPR-Cas genes and a higher frequency of new spacer acquisition, whereas no such induction occurred in monoculture or mixed communities lacking A. baumannii. This upregulation was associated with markers of DNA damage and stress signaling, indicating that competition-induced stress primes the bacterial adaptive immune response. These findings identify interbacterial antagonism as an ecological and physiological trigger for CRISPR activation, linking competitive interactions to enhanced antiphage defense. More broadly, our results suggest that bacteria sense and respond to competitive stress in complex microbial communities by increasing the generation of more adapted genotypes.

Article.Title: Dynamic roles of embryonic glial cells in octopus brain development
Article.Authors: Lassnig M.; Geslain E.; Nguyen B.; Abaffyová D.; Styfhals R.; Spanier K.; Patel A.; Gattamraju A.; Poovathingal S.; Wojno M.; Van Dijck M.; Almansa E.; Rogers T.; Simakov O.; Accorsi A.; Seuntjens E.
Article.Abstract: Coleoid cephalopods, such as octopus, squid, and cuttlefish, have evolved remarkably large nervous systems with neuron numbers comparable to those of small mammals. Despite this, little is known about how these nervous systems develop, which genetic programs drive the formation and diversification of their neural cells, and what factors contribute to evolutionary brain expansion. This study combined single-cell multi-omics with spatial expression analysis to uncover the cell types and the regulatory mechanisms underlying nervous system development and evolution in Octopus vulgaris. We discovered an early embryonic glial cell population that is distinct from neurogenic progenitors and defined by orphan nuclear receptor 4a (nr4a), distal-less homeobox (dlx), and prospero homeobox (pros) regulons. Their spatial distribution and dynamic transcriptional profile during embryogenesis indicated that these cells might orchestrate cell migration, axon guidance, and brain patterning before expressing neuronal markers or differentiating into mature glia. Comparison of embryonic glial transcriptional signatures across two cephalopods, a gastropod, and Drosophila revealed shared expression of nr4a, dlx, and pros in mollusks, while embryonic glia in Drosophila expressed pros, dlx, repo, ttk, and gcm but not nr4a. Intriguingly, the overall gene expression profile of cephalopod embryonic glia has diverged from that of Pomacea canaliculata (golden apple snail), whose glia do not express guidance or patterning genes. Together, these findings identified a conserved embryonic glial cell type in mollusks that might have acquired new functions in coleoid cephalopods to organize neuronal migration and wiring in their expanded brain.

Article.Title: Integration of hydrogen peroxide sensing and detoxification by the C. elegans nervous system
Article.Authors: Xu Y.; Gangadharan S.; Seyedolmohadesin M.; Gebeyaw E.; Flack M.; Fulton A.; Ashih C.; Duncan M.; Zelich M.; Liu J.; Torkashvand M.; Shaw D.; Gusarova K.; Macwan M.; Kelly A.; Beslic I.; Sood A.; Liu O.; Scholz M.; Venkatachalam V.; Apfeld J.
Article.Abstract: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is the most common reactive chemical threat organisms face. Here, we map the neural circuit that drives chemotactic escape from environmental H2O2 in the nematode C. elegans. Twenty-four neuron classes with sensory endings at the mouth and nose respond to H2O2, with dynamics encoding stimulus intensity and exposure history. Sensing begins when H2O2 oxidizes the peroxidatic and resolving cysteines of the cytosolic peroxiredoxin PRDX-2, which relays this oxidative signal to cysteines on the LITE-1 and GUR-3 ion channels, triggering calcium influx in sensory neurons that drive escape. Most of these neurons release glutamate to drive H2O2-dependent excitation of AIA interneurons, whereas others signal through non-glutamatergic routes. Thus, the C. elegans nervous system monitors H2O2-induced changes in the intracellular H2O2-detoxification machinery and relays them to interneurons driving organism-wide escape. This raises the possibility that changes in neuronal activity in aging and neurodegenerative diseases arise from altered peroxiredoxin-mediated H2O2 signaling rather than primarily from direct macromolecular damage by H2O2.

Article.Title: Selective control of course correction over long timescales in the Drosophila central complex
Article.Authors: Crown A.; Wu A.; Hofflander L.; Barnea G.
Article.Abstract: The insect central complex governs intricate navigational behaviors. One key region of the central complex, the fan-shaped body (FB), is where movement decisions are computed during goal-directed behaviors. However, our knowledge of when FB circuits are deployed is limited, and the FB has only been directly implicated in a few, narrowly defined behaviors. Here, we demonstrate that FB circuits affect course-correcting movements that, over long timescales, align the fly's heading with the perceived direction of optic flow. Silencing a major input neuronal population to the FB, the PFNd neurons, abolishes this behavior while leaving certain reflexive turning behaviors intact. Further, introduction of a fictive error signal in either the PFNd or PFNa neurons via optogenetic activation reveals that they are sufficient to affect the forward movement of the fly while slightly biasing its heading direction. We propose a model whereby the fly recruits the circuitry of the central complex to selectively influence features of movement that emerge over long timescales.

Article.Title: Top-down inferior colliculus signals engage unipolar brush cell circuits in the dorsal cochlear nucleus of the mouse auditory system
Article.Authors: Candler C.; Peña G.; Witteveen I.; Murphy S.; Whittaker K.; Poole O.; Balmer T.
Article.Abstract: Sensory systems comprise ascending pathways that convey information from the sense organs and descending pathways that provide feedback and contextual signals to guide sensory processing. How top-down signals are integrated at early stages to improve sensory function remains poorly understood. The dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN) is a cerebellum-like circuit proposed to perform adaptive filtering, including suppression of self-generated sounds. A major question is how sound-frequency-specific top-down information is processed by the DCN, since many top-down inputs target granule cells whose axons span the tonotopic axis and are unlikely to maintain frequency-specific signals. Here, we characterize neurons in the inferior colliculus that provide descending input to DCN. We show that among their targets are unipolar brush cells (UBCs) that distribute and transform descending signals directly to principal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in a circuit that bypasses granule cells. In vivo activation of UBCs attenuated auditory responses in awake mice. Together, these findings identify a circuit through which top-down signals from IC could influence early auditory processing and potentially guide adaptive filtering in the DCN.

Article.Title: Females shape hunting of vertebrates in wild bonobos
Article.Authors: Hohmann G.; Bessone M.; Balduccio N.; Decina F.; Deville T.; Pashchevskaya S.; Soliday V.; Stewart K.; Fruth B.
Article.Abstract: Hunting and meat consumption are widely considered key drivers of human evolution, and hypotheses about their origins draw on comparisons with our closest living relatives, chimpanzees and bonobos. These comparisons typically set up a behavioral dichotomy in which chimpanzees are characterized by cooperative hunting of arboreal primates by male-dominated parties, whereas bonobo hunts are thought to involve the opportunistic targeting of terrestrial ungulates, primarily by individual females.1,2,3 Observations from two habituated bonobo communities at LuiKotale covering 10 years challenge this dichotomy. LuiKotale bonobos hunted both terrestrial ungulates (42%) and arboreal primates (43% of vertebrate prey), with red colobus monkeys comprising the majority of primate prey (77%). Males and females hunted arboreal primates at similar rates, and females accounted for most non-primate captures. Female age affected the hunting frequency of primates and ungulates, with the former being biased to younger and the latter to older females. The prominent role of female bonobos in hunting supports predictions that relate hunting activity to intersexual dominance relations rather than risk aversion, with the dominant sex being more active. Comparing data from neighboring communities revealed differences and suggests that social and environmental parameters affect prey choice by each community in different ways. Together, these findings challenge the assumption that chimpanzee-like, male-biased hunting represents the ancestral condition. They highlight the contribution of females to obtaining vertebrate prey, call for a reassessment of the role of females in hunting and meat sharing, and by extension, the framing of models of early hominin subsistence and social organization.

Article.Title: A language-model approach to species distribution reveals alternative stable states
Article.Authors: Coulon N.; Servajean M.; Thomazo J.; Flandrin U.; Hautecoeur C.; Stuart-Smith R.; Joly A.; Mouillot D.
Article.Abstract: Ecological communities are reorganizing rapidly under accelerating global change, yet predicting how species assemble, persist, or collapse remains a major challenge.1,2,3,4 Most species distribution models treat species as independent entities, overlooking the dependencies that structure ecological communities. Here, we introduce a language-model-inspired approach5,6 to species distribution that generates ecological communities sequentially, predicting each species and its biomass conditional on previously assembled species. Trained on ∼27,000 reef fish surveys,7 the generative framework reveals multiple coherent community configurations emerging under identical environmental conditions.8,9 For instance, the model can generate both coral-associated and macroalgal-associated fish communities, consistent with alternative ecological regimes described in these ecosystems. The model also uncovers a hierarchy of emergent species positions within the learned dependency structure, including core species strongly associated with particular environmental conditions, bridging species linking alternative configurations, and satellite species occupying more peripheral positions. Despite this richer representation of ecological communities, the model also improves predictions of species occurrence and biomass relative to a species-by-species machine-learning baseline (XGBoost10) and a multispecies deep-learning baseline (MLP11). Together, these results show that ecological communities can be learned and generated as a structured syntax, from which multistability, directional assembly patterns, and hierarchical species positions naturally emerge.

Article.Title: Plant synergid embryonic potential is unlocked following egg cell collapse
Article.Authors: Xiong H.; Wang W.; Sun M.
Article.Abstract: Cell-cell communication is indispensable for cell specification and differentiation throughout plant reproduction. The egg cell and its sister synergid cell have long been considered closely coordinated partners during fertilization, yet the nature of this interplay and their specific roles remain unclear. Here, we show that synergid cells could acquire the competence to initiate cell division for embryogenesis following egg cell collapse. Unlike the traditional view, synergid cells appear to take over the egg cell role without undergoing fate conversion to adopt the egg cell identity. These findings suggest that synergid cells possess an intrinsic embryogenic potential, which is specifically unlocked upon egg cell collapse, thus enabling embryogenic initiation in the absence of a functional egg cell. Building on this discovery, we established an in planta haploid-induction system independent of conventional haploid-inducing genes. Importantly, this system also functions in tomato, a distantly related dicotyledonous crop, thus offering a broad conceptual framework for engineering haploid production across diverse plant species.

Article.Title: Dorsal forerunner cells couple epiboly movements to zebrafish notochord extension
Article.Authors: Small C.; Williams M.
Article.Abstract: Convergence and extension (C&E) cell movements promote anteroposterior axis extension and narrow both neuroectodermal and mesodermal tissues during gastrulation. Mediolateral cell intercalation is largely responsible for this morphogenetic process in vertebrates, but evidence suggests that additional cell-extrinsic forces generated by surrounding tissues contribute to the shaping of many structures. In zebrafish, for example, mechanical forces generated by the anteriorly migrating prechordal plate cooperate with tissue-autonomous cell intercalations to promote extension of the notochord. Here, we propose a novel model for notochord morphogenesis by which epiboly forces within the enveloping layer are transmitted to the posterior end of the notochord via a cluster of dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs) that physically links the two. We found that scattering or absence of DFCs caused by loss of crb2a or sox32, respectively, reduces notochord C&E and exacerbates axis extension defects in planar cell polarity signaling-deficient embryos. Using an automated image segmentation and cell shape analysis pipeline, we show that cells within the posterior notochord fail to properly elongate when DFCs are scattered or absent. Finally, we demonstrate that the loss of crb2a and sox32 fails to disrupt C&E of zebrafish embryonic explants in which no epiboly occurs and all extension is driven by cell-intrinsic behaviors. Together, these findings support a model in which DFCs facilitate mechanical coupling of the enveloping layer to the posterior notochord during epiboly to ensure its robust morphogenesis during gastrulation.

Article.Title: Allelic variation in OsATG3 enhances nitrogen-responsive tillering to sustain rice productivity
Article.Authors: Hu Z.; Li C.; Shen H.; Guo Y.; Xing R.; Gao X.; Yuan Y.; Li H.; Liu H.; Han X.; Cheng M.; Wang Y.; Shen Z.; Xue Y.; Zhong C.; Guo M.; Li Y.; Chen R.; Yang Y.; Sun S.; Zhou Y.; Liang G.; Gu M.; Fu X.; Yan C.
Article.Abstract: Nitrogen (N) deficiency constrains crop productivity by limiting shoot growth, yet the adaptive mechanisms that reprogram shoot development under low N conditions remain largely elusive. Here, we identify a major locus, OsATG3 (autophagy-related protein 3), controlling tillering in response to N deficiency through a genome-wide association study in rice. OsATG3 functions as an essential autophagy component and promotes selective degradation of IDEAL PLANT ARCHITECTURE1 (IPA1) via OsATG8d-mediated autophagy in shoot apices, thereby enhancing N-responsive tillering. Natural variation in the promoter of OsATG3 modulates its transcriptional activity and underlies the adaptive range of tiller number under low N conditions. The elite haplotype OsATG3-H enhances both tillering and grain yield under N-limited supply and appears to contribute to geographical adaptation both in O. sativa and O. glaberrima. Our findings uncover a genetic and molecular mechanism that couples N deficiency to shoot developmental plasticity, providing a promising target for sustainable rice breeding with reduced fertilizer input.

Article.Title: The antimicrobial peptide pileup promotes enterocyte shedding to maintain gut homeostasis in aging Drosophila
Article.Authors: Lee J.; Kim S.; Kim E.; Lee K.; Bhin J.; Hwang D.; Lee D.; Bahn Y.; Lee W.
Article.Abstract: Cellular turnover is a fundamental biological process that counteracts aging by activating stem cells to replace aging cells. This process is especially critical for maintaining the intestinal epithelium, one of the most rapidly renewing tissues in the body. However, the replacement of aging enterocytes cannot be explained solely by the generation of new cells from intestinal stem cells (ISCs); it also requires the complementary process of physically removing aging enterocytes through shedding. Compared with the well-characterized regulation of ISCs, the mechanisms governing enterocyte shedding remain poorly understood. Here, we identify pileup, a novel age-associated antimicrobial peptide (AMP) in Drosophila, as both a genetic marker and a key regulator of enterocyte shedding. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated through age-related mitochondrial dysfunction, a process facilitated by Autophagy-related gene 1 (ATG1) kinase, activate hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, which induces pileup expression specifically in aging enterocytes. Pileup then compromises the membrane of these cells and triggers c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) activation, which we propose promotes their shedding. Notably, pileup has three homologs, and loss of all four genes leads to tumorous cell accumulation, gut barrier dysfunction, microbiome dysbiosis, and premature death. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for AMPs in the turnover of aging host cells, extending their classical function beyond microbial defense. This work provides new mechanistic insights into enterocyte shedding and underscores its essential role in preserving gut homeostasis during aging.

Article.Title: Avian germline-restricted chromosomes are reservoirs for active and expressed long-terminal-repeat retroviruses
Article.Authors: Fang B.; Edwards S.
Article.Abstract: Germline-restricted chromosomes (GRCs) occur only in germ cells and are absent from somatic cells in songbirds, but their contents and evolutionary mechanisms remain poorly understood. We performed comparative genomics on long-read GRC assemblies from male house finch (HF) (Haemorhous mexicanus), common rosefinch (RF) (Carpodacus erythrinus), and blue tit (Cyanistes caeruleus), the first two of which are newly assembled and annotated. The assemblies vary widely in size (6.5-168.4 Mb) and gene content; whereas most GRC-linked genes are species specific, a small conserved set predates the diversification of passerine birds 47 mya. Despite genic variability, GRCs are consistently repeat rich (63.7%-79.5%) and accumulate intact endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) with long terminal repeats (LTRs). This ERV proliferation peaked during the passerine radiation. In contrast, regular chromosomes purge ERVs to generate solo LTRs. Transcriptomic data reveal significantly higher ERV transcription on GRCs than on regular chromosomes in HF testis. We propose that GRCs act as reservoirs of active ERVs, potentially promoting germline transposition and accelerating speciation.

Article.Title: Environment-specific virtual head direction representation in the human anteroventral thalamus during memory-guided spatial orientation
Article.Authors: Lv P.; Chen D.; Zhang C.; Zhang K.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: Knowing which way you are facing is essential for navigation. In animals, a dedicated set of neurons-head direction cells-acts as an internal compass: each cell fires most strongly when the animal faces a particular direction. The anterior thalamus is a key hub for this system. In humans, however, direct electrophysiological evidence for a comparable head direction signal remains limited. To address this gap, we recorded intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) from the anteroventral thalamus (AVT) in patients with epilepsy while they performed a virtual navigation task. We analyzed neural activity during in-place rotation to isolate virtual head direction (vHD) information. Using inverted encoding models applied to multi-band neural activity, we reconstructed continuous vHD within two distinct virtual environments. Critically, the decoders failed to generalize across environments, indicating that the AVT vHD representation is environment specific rather than a fixed, universal map. This encoding was observed in the AVT and was temporally specific to rotation epochs; no significant encoding was detected in the pulvinar, another thalamic subregion not part of the classic head direction network in rodents. Together, these findings suggest that the human AVT carries environment-specific vHD information, bridging a gap between animal models and human navigation and highlighting a potential link to spatial disorientation disorders.

Article.Title: Effector-triggered immunity in oilseed crops is expanded despite the restricted specificity of the receptor ZAR1
Article.Authors: Breit-McNally C.; Lai Y.; Xiao R.; Mazzurco O.; Lyons C.; Singh R.; Martel A.; Seto D.; Parkin I.; Desveaux D.; Guttman D.
Article.Abstract: Effector-triggered immunity (ETI), mediated by nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat immune receptors (NLRs), plays a critical role in protecting plants from pathogens. While the scope of ETI elicited by Pseudomonas syringae type III effectors on Arabidopsis thaliana has been characterized, no equivalent study has been performed on related oilseed crops, limiting our ability to translate fundamental plant immunity research into crop protection strategies. Here, we present a comprehensive screen of the ETI landscapes in Brassicaceous oilseeds Brassica napus (canola) and Camelina sativa (false flax) using 529 P. syringae effectors. We found that 44.6% and 55.4% of the 65 effector families contained alleles that elicited ETI in B. napus and C. sativa, respectively. Mapping ETI-elicitor homologs onto a P. syringae phylogeny revealed that 79% and 88% of strains carry three or more predicted ETI elicitors in B. napus and C. sativa, suggesting a significant ETI load against P. syringae in oilseeds. Oilseed ETI landscapes are expanded relative to A. thaliana, and the number of ETI responses is correlated with the species' NLR repertoire size and ploidy. Interestingly, while the A. thaliana ETI profile is smaller than the two oilseed crops, A. thaliana ETI responses are generally stronger. Further, the A. thaliana ZAR1 NLR has a broader effector recognition spectrum than ZAR1 in B. napus or C. sativa, supporting a role for convergent evolution in expanding immunodiversity. Overall, our findings reveal an expanded functional diversity of crop immune systems compared with a wild relative and highlight both ETI conservation and the divergence of recognition mechanisms.

Article.Title: Welwitschia leaf senescence is orchestrated via ERF113-ERF115-mediated antagonism between hormone signaling pathways
Article.Authors: Xu H.; Song Q.; Mamo W.; Tolosa L.; Zhang J.; Aboushanab A.; Wang Q.; Wan T.
Article.Abstract: Phytohormone crosstalk is fundamental to plant development and adaptation. While the coordinated actions of different hormones are well recognized, the underlying molecular mechanisms in specific biological processes remain largely elusive. Here, we identified the WmERF113-WmERF115 module as a central hub that mediated jasmonic acid (JA)/abscisic acid (ABA)-gibberellins (GA) antagonism to regulate leaf senescence in Welwitschia, a desert plant with only two leaves that grow continuously over an exceptionally long lifespan. We revealed that the JA/ABA-inducible transcription factor (TF) WmERF113 directly activated senescence-associated genes (SAGs), promoting senescence and chlorophyll degradation, whereas the GA-responsive WmERF115 repressed the same targets to mitigate senescence. Notably, WmERF113 and WmERF115 physically interacted to form a heterodimer, mutually inhibiting each other's binding to target promoters. Furthermore, these two TFs acted as reciprocal trans-acting factors, repressing each other's expression through promoter cross-binding. This multiple-layer regulatory circuit ensured that leaf senescence of Welwitschia progressed in a temporally and spatially restricted manner. Our study provided an important conceptual framework in which phytohormone crosstalk was translated into TF antagonism for fine-tuning senescence, offering new insights into the adaptive strategies that enable plant survival in extreme environments.

Article.Title: Reduced dosage of phytochrome F engages SELF-PRUNING 6A to confer heat-resilient tuberization in potato
Article.Authors: Jing S.; Li X.; Jiang P.; Chen H.; Li C.; Qin J.; Zhu B.; Zeng Z.; Song B.
Article.Abstract: Natural variation at the earliness locus, or potato CDF1, enabled cultivated potato to overcome strict photoperiodic control of wild andigena landraces and tuberize under long days. Yet long-day conditions (LDs) are often associated with warm temperatures, which strongly suppress tuberization at night. With the rising ambient temperatures due to global warming, uncovering genetic factors that enable tuber formation under elevated temperatures has become a priority for breeding new cultivars with improved heat tolerance. Here we report that heat-resilient tuberization in potato can be unlocked by inactivating the photoreceptor phytochrome F (phyF) and optimized by exploiting its haploinsufficiency. Knockdown of phyF activates the SELF-PRUNING 6A (SP6A) tuberization-inducing signal and facilitates tuber formation under heat-stress conditions. Unexpectedly, loss of function of both SP6A and phyF still leads to early tuberization and heat escape, although it reduces the resilience of phyF mutants. Intriguingly, we show that haplotype-specific phyF editing in the 5' UTR or exonic regions leads to haploinsufficiency phenotypes enabling tuberization under heat-stress conditions, without other phytochrome-related penalties. Our results suggest that derepressing SP6A by a reduction of phyF dosage provides a key to unlock heat-resilient tuberization and highlight haploinsufficiency as a strategy for generating dominant alleles to enable rapid improvement of crops.

Article.Title: A putative structural transition underlies reliable formation of skeletal muscle
Article.Authors: Mendieta-Serrano M.; Hou Y.; Theis S.; Hall T.; Taylor S.; Verd B.; Parton R.; Saunders T.
Article.Abstract: During organ development cells undergo significant morphological and positional changes. Yet by the end of organogenesis, internal organ structure is typically reliably defined. It remains an open question how the internal structure of an organ emerges, particularly in the presence of dynamic boundary constraints. Here, we utilize live imaging and morphological measures of the developing zebrafish to unravel how early muscle organization materializes. We observed that myocytes undergo an ordered chiral twist according to their position within the myotome. Cell movement undergoes a rapid speed reduction once the cells span the myotome segment. Biophysical perturbation reveals cells are mechanically plastic and can adapt to changes in boundaries and environment. Combining these results, we propose that the early myotome may be undergoing a structural transition from a fluid-like to a solid-like state, which resembles a frozen system. Cell shape plasticity combined with structural changes in the material behavior could be a general mechanism for organ morphogenesis in dense tissues.

Article.Title: Evidence for diurnal habits in an exceptionally preserved Eocene owl
Article.Authors: Mayr G.; Šmídová L.; Richter A.; Wedmann S.
Article.Abstract: It is poorly understood when owls (Strigiformes) became nocturnal, which impedes considerations of the evolutionary reasons behind this distinctive behavior.1,2 Here, we report an extraordinary owl skeleton from the middle Eocene of Germany, which preserves remains of an iridescent cockroach as stomach contents-the first identifiable insect remains ever found as the last meal of a fossil bird. Because iridescence is correlated with diurnal habits in cockroaches,3 the fossil provides the strongest evidence to date for diurnality in archaic Strigiformes. Further support for a diurnal ecology comes from the absence of barred flight feathers as well as the lack of frayed leading edges of the primaries; the presence of these features is associated with nocturnality in extant owls.4,5 The humerus is much stouter than in extant owls, indicating that the wings were less adapted to silent flight. Conversely, a slenderer humerus suggests that late Eocene owls had shifted toward a nocturnal ecology. This timeframe rules out previously suggested factors for nocturnality in owls2 and constrains the origin of an ecological hallmark of these birds.

Article.Title: Neuropeptidergic-glutamatergic circuit regulates selective forgetting of olfactory learning
Article.Authors: Onishi Y.; Arai M.; Sato N.; Takamatsu M.; Teo J.; Kitazono T.; Ishihara T.
Article.Abstract: Forgetting is an active and essential process for adapting to constantly changing environments, yet the molecular and circuit mechanisms underlying selective forgetting remain poorly understood. Our previous studies in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans suggested that non-cell-autonomous neurosecretory signals accelerate forgetting of olfactory memory for diacetyl, an attractive odorant, by erasing its memory trace, which can be detected as changes in odor-evoked Ca2+ responses in sensory neurons. However, the identity of the forgetting signal, the circuit through which it acts to erase the sensory memory trace, and the time window in which forgetting occurs have remained elusive. Here, we identify a neuropeptidergic-glutamatergic circuit in C. elegans that drives the selective forgetting of olfactory memory. Our genetic and imaging analyses revealed that the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)-related neuropeptide NLP-47, secreted from AWC neurons, acts on its receptor GNRR-1 in AIZ interneurons. Glutamatergic neurotransmission from AIZ interneurons then erases the sensory memory trace in AWA neurons via GLR-4, an AMPA-type receptor expressed in AWA. Optogenetic silencing of AWC and AIZ showed that this circuit acts during the recovery phase following conditioning, defining a critical temporal window for active forgetting. This neuropeptidergic-glutamatergic pathway selectively promotes forgetting of a specific odorant memory without affecting another formed simultaneously. Together, our findings demonstrate that neuropeptidergic signaling promotes selective forgetting via a glutamatergic circuit, highlighting that active forgetting is regulated within a critical temporal window and with remarkable specificity.

Article.Title: Army ant raids connect terrestrial and aquatic food webs in mangroves
Article.Authors: Domínguez-Castanedo O.; García-Calva L.; Chiappa-Carrara X.
Article.Abstract: Army ant raids by Eciton burchellii parvispinum are iconic spectacles of Neotropical forests, driving ant-following birds and intense predation on leaf-litter arthropods1,2,3,4. However, whether these terrestrial predators influence energy flows across ecosystem boundaries remains unknown. Apart from isolated natural history anecdotes, evidence for such interactions is lacking despite recognition that cross-ecosystem subsidies strongly affect food-web dynamics5,6,7. Here, we report a previously undescribed cross-ecosystem interaction in the mangroves of Yucatán, Mexico, where army ant raids trigger localized feeding aggregations among aquatic vertebrates. Stomach-content analyses of fishes attending raids at four independent Eciton colonies, complemented by observations across six colonies, show that prey escaping army ant predation can become a substantial terrestrial subsidy for resident fishes. This pulse was associated with marked shifts in fish diet and recurrent higher-order predator aggregations, revealing a pathway through which terrestrial predator effects can extend across ecosystem boundaries.

Article.Title: Hypothalamic cell-type differences associated with selection for tameness in the silver fox
Article.Authors: Klein J.; Shepeleva D.; Vladimirova A.; Kharlamova A.; Miller A.; Kukekova A.; Markenscoff-Papadimitriou E.
Article.Abstract: The hypothalamus is a highly heterogeneous brain region that regulates fundamental physiological processes and behaviors, including innate social behaviors such as aggression, mating, and parenting1. Distinct cell types within hypothalamic nuclei have been linked to social behaviors, a principle established most clearly in mice, where manipulation of defined hypothalamic neuronal subtypes can initiate or suppress behaviors including attack, mounting, and parenting1,2,3,4. Whether hypothalamic cell types are modified as a result of selection during the evolution of social behavior remains unknown. Silver foxes (Vulpes vulpes) have been selectively bred for tame or aggressive behaviors and we have studied whether there are differences relating to these behaviors in the cellular makeup of the hypothalamus. We report here that tame foxes have fewer estrogen receptor-expressing neurons in the ventrolateral subdivision of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMHvl) than aggressive foxes, and that this reduction is specific to a neuronal subtype linked to aggressive states in mice5. We have thus identified a candidate hypothalamic neuronal subtype associated with selection on social behavior during animal domestication.

Article.Title: Hippocampal–prefrontal cortical interactions and neural representations of memory
Article.Authors: Morales-Rodriguez D.; Frank L.
Article.Abstract: The ability to store memories and access past experiences when making decisions in the present is fundamental to cognition. The hippocampus is critical for these processes and has been a primary site of investigation in the learning and memory field for the last several decades. However, it is also clear that the hippocampus must work in concert with cortical brain regions to store and recall memories. Findings that demonstrate the necessity of hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) communication in these processes, as well as findings that link the mPFC to memory storage, retrieval, and decision-making, have contributed to this growing area of study. Here, we review our current understanding of three questions related to this communication. What information is represented in the hippocampus and the mPFC? What are the underlying neural activity patterns and brain states that facilitate communication of those representations? What impact do these patterns have on the ability to learn and remember in new and familiar settings? We highlight evidence for bidirectional communication both during and after experience, and we discuss areas of active investigation to further uncover the role of bidirectional hippocampal-cortical interactions in the formation and maintenance of neural representations of memory.

Article.Title: Fungal–bacterial interactions
Article.Authors: Uehling J.; Gohar D.; Johnson H.
Article.Abstract: The study of fungal-bacterial interactions is an emerging field of biology with relevance for environmental health, medicine, and agriculture, among other sectors. The frequent co-occurrence of fungi and bacteria in many habitats has facilitated the evolution of their symbioses. Both groups are key players in host-associated microbiomes and in nutrient cycling, and these roles often intersect in dynamic ways. Interactions between fungi and bacteria can be mutualistic, commensal, or pathogenic, and they can vary in a context-dependent manner. In mutualistic interactions, fungi and bacteria can exchange nutrients, ameliorate each other's stress, enhance growth, enable dispersal, and facilitate novel niche exploration via metabolite exchange. In contrast, antagonistic interactions frequently involve competition for limited nutrients, such as iron, and active chemical warfare with secreted and bioactive compounds. Bacteria associated with fungi can occur inside of fungal cells (endosymbiotic) or on the surface of fungal hyphae (exosymbiotic). Endosymbiotic bacteria can be further differentiated into facultative symbionts, which retain the ability to enter fungal hyphae but also live independently, and obligate endosymbionts, which are always intracellular and not capable of independent life outside of hyphae. Whereas free-living bacteria can be pathogenic or mutualistic, endosymbiotic bacteria are often regarded as commensals or mutualists, although some can exhibit parasitic attributes in some conditions. A combination of molecular genetics, genomics, and microscopy has been used to study free-living bacteria. In addition to these approaches, fluorescence and electron microscopy have been used as the gold standards to study and differentiate endosymbiotic bacteria based on their intracellular location. More recently, researchers have started using systems-biology approaches to study fungal-bacterial interactions including high-throughput -omics assays. These methods produce expansive datasets that are ideally suited to artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches to tackle long-standing questions about the basic biology and evolution of fungal-bacterial interactions. In this primer we give an overview of fungal-bacterial interactions, including their diversity, community structure, and symbiotic evolution. We highlight two research systems in particular: the intracellular endosymbionts of Mucoromycota fungi and the free-living bacteria associated with edible fungi. We focus on these systems because fungi remain understudied relative to other groups, and only a handful of fungal taxa with their bacterial symbionts are backed by large enough data sets to explore these concepts in detail. Our aim here is not to be comprehensive, but instead to use the most well-understood systems to illustrate emerging principles. We then discuss advances in using AI to infer new aspects of microbial biology and provide suggestions for how these technologies could advance research on fungal-bacterial interactions utilizing existing genomic datasets.
