Article.Title: The importance of genes does not predict their mutation rate
Article.Authors: Radrizzani S.; Hurst L.
Article.Abstract: The convention that mutation is a random process has been challenged by suggestions that selection has acted on between-gene variation in the mutation rate, with claims that more important genes are protected from mutation in part, in prokaryotes, by being on the leading strand, while those required for rapid adaptive evolution have higher mutation rates, in part by being on the lagging strand. The original selectionist claims have proven contentious with several replication failures. However, none of the replication attempts fully allow for covariates and many employ data from mismatch repair (MMR) knockout strains. To address these limitations, we consider amassed mutation accumulation data for wild-type Escherichia coli , the focal species for adaptive claims, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae , in a multiple parameter-controlled analysis to predict between-gene variation in mutational density (mutations per base pair). Along with covariates, we consider putative selectively relevant parameters: protein level and essentiality to capture genic “importance”, and, in E. coli , strand with respect to DNA replication. We consider deviation of correlation and partial correlation values from those expected under trinucleotide-controlled simulations. While in E. coli more highly transcribed genes may have slightly lower mutation rates, potentially consistent with a selectionist model, the same is not seen in yeast, and in neither species do genes for more abundant or essential proteins have lower mutation rates. In E. coli there is no difference in mutation rate between genes on different strands, a lack of difference replicated in other prokaryotes. The degree of purifying selection is also not predictive of mutation density. We additionally highlight a strong artefact seen using the standard off-the-shelf statistical approach and note that results from MMR-deficient strains are discordant. We conclude that as trends are nearly uniformly unsupportive, not consistent between species and of miniscule effect size, they present no challenge to convention.

Article.Title: Virus-like particles enable highly efficient gene editing across porcine and avian in vitro, ex vivo, and in ovo models

Article.Abstract: Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology. Its externally developing embryo offers exceptional accessibility for experimental manipulation. Recent advances in genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, have further expanded the potential of these species for functional genomic studies, although the efficient delivery of such tools remains a major challenge. Here, we overcome this delivery limitation by using virus-like particles (VLPs). We evaluated VLPs as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools in porcine and avian cultures, two key livestock species at the human–animal interface. VLP-mediated delivery enabled efficient Cre recombination and high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates in porcine cells, organoids, and oocytes, particularly when multiplexed. In chickens, VLPs supported robust Cre recombination and Cas9-mediated editing in cell culture, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo . Reporter VLPs and dCas9 VLPs further demonstrated the versatility of this platform across porcine and avian systems. Together, these findings establish VLPs as an efficient and time-saving strategy for gene editing in livestock cultures across in vitro , ex vivo and in ovo systems, with potential future applications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and translational One Health research.

Article.Title: The single Cryptosporidium rhoptry sequentially drives invasion and host-parasite interface formation
Article.Authors: Cohen A.; Bergner T.; Guérin A.; Lebrun M.; Laue M.; Klotz C.; Striepen B.
Article.Abstract: The apicomplexan parasite Cryptosporidium is a leading cause of diarrheal disease in young children. Within the intestinal epithelium, Cryptosporidium establishes a unique intracellular niche in the apical brush border of enterocytes. A structurally complex interface between host and parasite acts as a holdfast and enables protein and metabolite transport. How the parasite invades its host cell and builds the interface is poorly understood. Here, we reveal parasite invasion with high temporal and spatial resolution using rigorous molecular markers. We find that sequential discharge of specialized secretory organelles anchors the parasite within the host prior to internalization. The single Cryptosporidium rhoptry persists beyond its initial pre-invasion discharge, acting as a conduit for the secretion of multiple waves of effector proteins. Ultimately, the rhoptry membrane gives rise to the feeder organelle that separates host from parasite cytoplasm. These findings lead us to propose a mechanistic model of Cryptosporidium invasion and intracellular parasitism.

Article.Title: Vertebrate paired fins are specified by an ancient dorso-ventral patterning system
Article.Authors: Dale R.; Berger S.; Alaei S.; Davis M.; Tulenko F.; Currie P.
Article.Abstract: The origin of paired fins was a major event in early vertebrate history that fueled the adaptive radiation of the gnathostome clade. Evidence for the conservation of ancient regulatory systems between paired and median fins supports a model in which appendage-patterning mechanisms first evolved in the midline and were later redeployed to a new embryonic context, the flank. However, while paired fins and limbs are asymmetric along the dorsoventral (DV) axis, the equivalent axis does not exist in median fins, which are symmetric across the midline, raising questions of how DV patterning evolved. Here, we combine genetic tools in zebrafish with comparative expression analyses in representative ray-finned and cartilaginous fishes to show that a subset of limb DV patterning genes are expressed during median fin development. Using genetic lineage tracing of the canonical limb dorsalizing factor lmx1bb , we further demonstrate that, although lmx1bb -derived cells occupy distinct spatial domains across fin types, a subset of this lineage is fated to differentiate into fin ray osteoblasts in both paired and median fins. To test the potential conservation of regulatory modules across fin types, we generated a series of deletion mutants for two known lmx1b mouse limb enhancers, LARM1 and LARM2, that we show are partially conserved upstream of zebrafish lmx1bb . These experiments revealed that LARM function is essential for dorsoventral patterning of the paired pectoral and pelvic fins of zebrafish but is dispensable for formation of the unpaired dorsal and anal fins. Collectively, these data support the conservation of an ancient LARM -Lmx1b dorsal determination system in the paired fins of osteichthyans, challenge models proposing simple co-option of a pre-existing median fin gene regulatory network and suggest that the acquisition of this regulatory module may have been a key early step in the evolution of the paired fin DV patterning axis.

Article.Title: Sperm phospholipase C signaling via PLCζ1 and PLCδ4 is essential for Ca2+ oscillations and fertility in mice
Article.Authors: Gupta N.; Zhang L.; Akizawa H.; Gervasi M.; Tourzani D.; Visconti P.; Romarowski A.; Buffone M.; Cui W.; Fissore R.
Article.Abstract: Fertilization-induced calcium (Ca 2+ ) oscillations are essential for egg activation and embryonic development in mammals. The sperm-specific phospholipase C isoform, PLCζ1, is the primary trigger of these oscillations. Functional and clinical studies have linked mutations or reduced expression of PLCζ1 to male infertility. However, whether PLCζ1 alone accounts for Ca 2+ release at fertilization in all mammals remains uncertain. Male mice lacking Plc ζ 1 exhibit subfertility and reduced litter sizes; their sperm induce delayed, low-frequency Ca 2+ oscillations, indicating a compensatory mechanism. Notably, mouse sperm express high levels of PLCδ4, essential for completing the acrosome reaction (AR). In Plc ζ 1 -null sperm, PLCδ4 is upregulated and retained post-AR. These observations suggest a secondary functional role for PLCδ4. Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, we generated Plc δ 4 knockout (KO) mice. Plc δ 4 -null sperm trigger attenuated, delayed Ca 2+ oscillations and significantly reduced fertilization rates, indicating that PLCδ4 contributes to but does not independently drive Ca 2+ signaling. We therefore generated a Double Knockout (DKO) mouse line lacking both sperm-enriched PLCs. DKO males were sterile, with sperm failing to induce Ca 2+ oscillations, and the isolated residual Ca 2+ rise was insufficient to activate eggs. These findings reveal that PLCζ1, the primary oscillator, and PLCδ4, a compensatory factor, work cooperatively within a complex, multi-component PLC system that ensures robust fertilization. This work reveals molecular specialization among mammals in initiating the fertilization Ca 2+ signals. It has implications for understanding male infertility, improving assisted reproductive technologies, and developing contraceptive strategies.

Article.Title: Phylogenetic evidence that migratory behavior increases ungulate extinction rates
Article.Authors: Abraham J.; O’Brien K.; Upham N.; Jesmer B.; Bibi F.; Faith J.
Article.Abstract: Widespread instances of migratory collapse have been documented within the past several decades, indicating that migration may be a fragile strategy in the Anthropocene. Yet the fragility of migration as a strategy for navigating seasonally variable resource availability may extend deeper into evolutionary time. We used phylogenetic imputation to infer the migratory habits of 51 ungulate species that went extinct during the late Quaternary and evaluated whether migration enhances extinction rates on macroevolutionary timescales. We found that ~80% (41 of 51) of recently extinct species were migratory, whereas only 46% (95 of 207) of extant ungulates are migratory. Furthermore, Hidden State Speciation and Extinction modeling indicated that migratory species likely experienced higher speciation and extinction rates compared to nonmigratory species, resulting in elevated lineage turnover for migratory ungulates, though diversification parameter estimates depended strongly upon whether extinct species were included in analyses. The extinctions of these ungulates led to negligible declines in global ungulate functional richness (0.8%) but more substantial declines (2.7%) across Africa. Altogether, our findings indicate that migration has complex macroevolutionary consequences, enhancing both speciation and extinction rates, which may render migration an evolutionarily fragile strategy, particularly as increasingly widespread and intensive anthropogenic activity cause gradients of resource availability to become severed ( e.g ., via human infrastructure) and more unpredictable ( e.g ., via climate change).

Article.Title: Can the exposome help solve the alcohol and cancer mystery?
Article.Authors: Vasiliou V.; Stem A.; Thompson D.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol consumption is a preventable driver of many cancers, yet a central biological question remains unresolved: by what mechanisms does ethanol promote malignancy? We propose that alcohol in the context of the exposome (i.e., the network of chemical, biological, and social determinants that interact with ethanol across the life span) provides a unifying framework for understanding alcohol-related carcinogenesis. Viewed through the lens of the exposome, alcohol is not only as a direct carcinogen but also as a systemic amplifier of environmental risk acting across multiple levels of biological organization, from molecular damage to whole-body physiology. This reframing has important implications for mechanistic research, precision prevention, and public-health policy.

Article.Title: Two parallel lateral hypothalamic GABAergic projections differentially modulate pain and anxiety in mice
Article.Authors: Sun Y.; Peng Y.; Zhang X.; Yin C.; Xiao C.; Chen J.; Zhou C.
Article.Abstract: The lateral hypothalamus (LH) is fundamentally involved in motivated behaviors, yet the precise functional segregation of its GABAergic projections in modulating pain and its affective dimensions remains poorly understood. Here, using male and female mice, we revealed that LH GABAergic neurons sent parallel projections to two pivotal pain and affect processing centers: the lateral parabrachial nucleus (LPB) and the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT). In vivo fiber photometry revealed that LH GABAergic terminals in both the PVT and LPB are robustly activated by noxious, aversive, and rewarding stimuli, indicating their roles in encoding salient and affective information. Critically, we uncovered a remarkable functional segregation of these LH GABAergic pathways. Optogenetic activation of the LH-PVT projection exerted anxiogenic effects without altering pain sensitivity in both naïve and neuropathic pain mice; whereas optogenetic inhibition of this pathway exerted significant analgesic and anxiolytic effects specifically in neuropathic pain, highlighting a context-dependent modulation of pain and affect. In contrast, optogenetic activation of the LH-LPB projection induced contralateral pronociception without impacting affective behaviors, conversely, inhibition of this pathway significantly elevated contralateral pain thresholds in both physiological and neuropathic pain conditions. We also demonstrated that stimulation of the LH-LPB projection acted via a disinhibitory mechanism involving local LPB GABAergic interneurons to enhance activity of LPB glutamatergic neurons. Collectively, our findings delineate two parallel and functionally segregated LH GABAergic output pathways that differentially control distinct aspects of pain experience, thereby offering novel circuit-specific targets for the treatment of chronic pain and its debilitating emotional comorbidities.

Article.Title: Saccadic suppression enhances saliency of ecologically relevant stimuli in the zebrafish optic tectum
Article.Authors: Soto G.; Thomas C.; Funk L.; Hladnik T.; Dehmelt F.; Hafed Z.; Arrenberg A.
Article.Abstract: Saccadic suppression, a reduction in visual sensitivity around the time of rapid eye movements, is well-documented in primate psychophysics, but its mechanisms and functions remain debated. Here, we use zebrafish to trace the origins of saccadic suppression, and we demonstrate how saccadic suppression selectively enhances the visual salience of ecologically relevant stimuli. Saccadic suppression thus contributes to more than just compensation for rapid saccade-induced image shifts. We first established a behavioral correlate of saccadic suppression in larval zebrafish escape behavior. Then, using electrophysiology, we show that retinal ganglion cells jumpstart saccadic suppression in a spatial frequency-dependent manner. Calcium imaging, combined with 360° visual stimulation and behavioral tracking, revealed that motor signals enhance peri-saccadic suppression strength in the optic tectum, where suppression lasts for more than 3,000 ms. Notably, saccadic suppression is much weaker and more short-lived for stimuli related to hunting or escape behavior than for behaviorally less relevant global flashes. This unequal attenuation effectively increases the salience of the ecologically relevant stimuli in the optic tectum after saccades. Our results demonstrate that saccadic suppression integrates visual and motor signals to optimize sensory processing within neural constraints, and they provide insights into evolutionarily conserved visual strategies.

Article.Title: Infant presence and mother-infant conflict predict fetal loss in wild mandrills
Article.Authors: Smit N.; Roura-Torres B.; Delaunay A.; Baniel A.; Huchard E.; Charpentier M.
Article.Abstract: Female fitness depends on reproductive pace and offspring survival, both of which are determined by the ability to balance resource allocation between current and future reproduction. Using 11 years of data on 356 pregnancies (52 of which resulted in fetal loss) from 117 wild female mandrills, we show that females who conceive while still caring for a young infant experience a greater probability of fetal loss as well as increased mother-infant behavioral conflict in the form of maternal rejection. In addition, females whose infants throw more tantrums show a greater probability of fetal loss, consistent with observations from other species where living offspring can interfere in parental reproduction. Finally, females who lose a fetus show greater subsequent reproductive success (produce more surviving infants and show shorter inter-birth intervals) than females who give birth but their infants die soon after birth. These findings suggest that fetal loss may represent an adaptive physiological response to the energetic constraints imposed by overlapping gestation and maternal care, potentially limiting the fitness costs associated with short inter-birth intervals and concurrent investment in multiple dependent offspring.

Article.Authors: Bierenbroodspot M.; Kunz C.; Goldbecker E.; Lorenz M.; Irisarri I.; Pröschold T.; Darienko T.; de Vries J.
Article.Abstract: Discerning the nature of the last common ancestor of land plants (embryophytes) and algae allows to retrace the adaptations that ushered in the conquest of land by plants. For this, the closest streptophyte algal relatives of embryophytes hold key information. Albeit initially coming as a surprise due to their plain body plans, all major phylogenomic efforts have concluded that the Zygnematophyceae are the algal sisters to land plants. The Zygnematophyceae are the streptophyte algal class with the greatest species richness and while we now have ample genome information on a few select members of zygnematophytes, our understanding of the genomic divergence as well as genetic potential for key traits is limited by a lack of phylodiverse data that accounts for this diversity and integrates it into a phylogenomic framework. We here sequenced 43 new transcriptome datasets for the Zygnematophyceae and built a phylogenomic tree based on a total of 104 zygnematophyceaen transcriptomes and 2243 loci. We recover a deep genetic structure for the Zygnematophyceae: Despite the deep split between Spirogyrales and their unicellular sister group Desmidiales, most Spirogyrales emerged after pronounced genetic divergence, accommodating the attainment of multicellularity and divergent traits such as unique cell and plastid division. Overall, our data capture signatures of massive ancient radiations that could only be revealed thanks to a phylodiverse sampling. Recognizing the deep genetic divergences and a vast evolutionary history of the Zygnematophyceae are key to illuminate the nature of the algal progenitors of land plants.

Article.Title: A split nozzle and two-protein chain-like fibers define the tail architecture of Pseudomonas aeruginosa podophage A1002
Article.Authors: Pang H.; Chen Y.; Peng Z.; Xiao H.; Chen W.; Li X.; Chen P.; Zheng J.; Liu H.
Article.Abstract: Phage therapy offers unique advantages against antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Based on density maps combined with AlphaFold3 predictions, we identified 11 structural protein components from the head to the tail. Phage A1002 exhibits a distinctly elongated tail morphology distinct from other reported podophages. Notably, the A1002 nozzle employs a distinct assembly strategy, featuring the unique nozzle-rope protein and nozzle-base protein, which may have evolved through modular evolution and horizontal gene transfer. Furthermore, the nozzle-rope protein provides 11 adsorption sites for fiber dimers, and these dimers are assembled from two proteins, giving rise to two types of dimers: dimers 1–7 correspond to fiber I (gp40), and dimers 8–11 correspond to fiber II (gp41). The nozzle-rope protein and these dimers combine to form a chain-like fiber. The tail tube comprises a double-layered, elongated tube structure that functions to simultaneously increase tail length and provide docking sites for six chain-like fibers. These distinctive structural features provide the molecular basis for A1002’s broad-spectrum infection of drug-resistant P. aeruginosa and offer a novel molecular blueprint for rational design of structure-guided phage therapeutics.

Article.Title: The human hippocampus supports auditory coding and multisensory integration
Article.Authors: Raccah O.; Agarwal A.; Zhu Y.; Turk-Browne N.
Article.Abstract: The hippocampus receives convergent input from multiple sensory systems, yet in humans it has been studied almost exclusively through vision. Here we examine how the hippocampus contributes to sensory processing beyond the visual modality and to the multisensory integration of visual information with these other modalities. Participants were exposed to multiple repetitions of short naturalistic movie clips, each presented in four formats: auditory-only, visual-only, congruent audiovisual, and incongruent audiovisual (audio and video from different movies). Using high-resolution fMRI, we measured univariate activation and multivariate representations across the longitudinal axis and subfields of the human hippocampus. Whereas univariate analyses detected only visual responses across hippocampal subregions, with no activation for auditory stimuli and no benefit of congruent stimuli, multivariate analyses revealed robust representations of both auditory and visual scenes. The posterior hippocampus showed enhanced pattern similarity for congruent stimuli relative to unisensory stimuli, especially in the left hemisphere, demonstrating multisensory facilitation. The anterior hippocampus showed crossmodal decoding between auditory and visual versions of the same clip, driven by the right hemisphere, suggesting a more abstract representation. Finally, whole-brain searchlight analyses revealed parallel effects in cortical regions known to support multisensory integration. These findings advance understanding of auditory and multisensory coding in the human hippocampus, revealing specialization and lateralization along its longitudinal axis.

Article.Title: An open-source eye-tracking system adaptable to diverse terrestrial vertebrates reveals state-dependent visual acquisition in lizards
Article.Authors: Leberstein N.; Remenick T.; Becker M.; Shein-Idelson M.
Article.Abstract: Gaze shifts are fundamental to visual exploration and processing, yet empirical knowledge is largely confined to a small number of model species, limiting our understanding of general principles of visual acquisition across animals. Here, we introduce a versatile, low-cost, and open-source framework design for eye-tracking in small, freely moving animals. Leveraging photogrammetry, 3D modeling, and 3D-printing, we produce headmounts adaptable to diverse head-eye geometries, as we demonstrate for lizards, turtles, and mice. Detailed recordings in Pogona vitticeps, a laterally eyed ectotherm with a high-acuity retina, reveal a rich oculomotor repertoire with kinematics closely resembling the saccadic main sequence in primates. We found both movement-coupled large binocular saccades, which exhibited a strong axial bias as well as small, isotropic, and monocular saccades suggesting a capacity for visual exploration of local details. Visual acquisition strategies were strongly tied to behavioral states with periods of active sampling (3–5 Hz saccades) separated by periods of ocular stillness lasting many seconds and suggesting a visual acquisition strategy distinct from those commonly described in endothermic model species. Furthermore, active states were correlated with pupil constriction in contrast to mammals and similarly to birds. Our results demonstrate the utility of our experimental approach for understanding visual acquisition across terrestrial vertebrates. Such a multi-perspective view on natural visual acquisition across species will be essential for developing a generalized understanding of vision, its ecological functions, and its evolutionary trajectory.

Article.Title: LEM-3/ANKLE1 nuclease prevents the formation of abnormal syncytium to safeguard neuronal differentiation
Article.Authors: Deng S.; Zheng C.
Article.Abstract: In animal development, cells exit the cell cycle after a final round of cell division to differentiate into specialized cell types. However, the impact of failed cytokinesis on the fate specification of postmitotic cells, especially neurons, remains poorly understood. We analyzed the Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking the midbody-tethered endonuclease LEM-3/ANKLE1, which resolves chromatin bridges during cytokinesis. Using genetic analysis, fluorescence microscopy, and RNA visualization, we found that unresolved DNA bridges lead to the formation of stable intercellular bridges, creating binucleate syncytia between touch receptor neurons and sister cells, which allows thorough cytoplasmic mixing despite independent nuclear transcription. In some cases, the cytoplasmic linkage between sister cells also led to the suppression of neuronal fates and prevention of apoptotic fates. Thus, LEM-3 prevents syncytium formation to ensure proper cellular differentiation.

Article.Title: Emotion knowledge is structured in a grid-like coordinate system in the human ventromedial prefrontal cortex
Article.Authors: Ma Y.; Kragel P.
Article.Abstract: Human emotional experiences vary widely in everyday life, yet they are systematically organized within a continuous affective space defined by valence and arousal. Although this circumplex organization has shaped decades of research, its neural implementation remains unclear. Here, we asked whether abstract emotion concepts are encoded using grid-like coordinate principles in the human brain. During fMRI, participants tracked trajectories through affective space conveyed through morphs of facial expressions and sequences of phrases. We found that ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) encoded affective space with robust hexadirectional modulation characteristic of grid-like coding. This coordinate representation generalized across stimulus modalities, indicating abstraction beyond perceptual features. The grid-like signal reflected a metric organization of emotion concepts independent of overt behavior, whereas distance-related signals in vmPFC predicted trial-by-trial affective judgements. Together, these findings suggest that emotion knowledge is structured by a grid-like coordinate system in the human brain that can support predictive inference and flexible decision-making.

Article.Title: Fungal suppression by bacterial metabolite-activated human intestinal γδT-cells is disrupted in Crohn’s disease
Article.Authors: Mathew L.; Carlson S.; Savage M.; Pardieu C.; O’Brien M.; Crawley E.; Harrow P.; Kaune A.; Devlin E.; Priest E.; Crescente M.; Martinod K.; Boot J.; Ngan S.; Gasparetto M.; Kok K.; Lindsay J.; Richardson J.; Naglik J.; Stagg A.; Eberl M.; Sze S.; Munro C.; McCarthy N.
Article.Abstract: Gut symbionts condition mucosal immunity to resist infection by enteropathogens, but the specific microbes and mechanisms involved differ significantly between host species. In higher primates, bacterial metabolite HMB-PP is sensed by a specialized population of Vγ9Vδ2+T-cells, which we now report can potently suppress growth of endogenous fungi in human intestinal organ cultures. In healthy intestine, HMB-PP-stimulated Vδ2+ T-cells restricted outgrowth of keystone fungus Candida albicans via a mechanism that required IL-22. In Crohn’s disease (CD), Vδ2+ T-cells were poorly responsive to HMB-PP and permitted outgrowth of C. albicans strains that formed toxin-producing filaments, triggered neutrophil extracellular traps, and induced macrophage IL-1β release ex vivo . Genomic and proteomic analysis of the Candida isolates suggested increased tissue adhesion of CD-derived strains, which rapidly invaded the gut barrier in an ‘intestine-on-a-chip’ model. These data reveal that bacterial activation of Vδ2+ T-cells suppresses fungal pathobionts in human gut via an IL-22-dependent mechanism that is dysregulated in CD.

Article.Title: CFL1-dependency of discrete cell behaviours driving mouse spinal zippering
Article.Authors: Marshall A.; Krstevski A.; Crosswell H.; Shah R.; Maniou E.; Greene N.; Copp A.; Galea G.
Article.Abstract: Epithelial fusion is critical for formation of many embryonic tissues. The developing mammalian spinal cord fuses by zippering, through cell behaviours dependent on F-actin turnover. We propose a caudal-to-rostral sequence of surface ectoderm cell behaviours which drive zippering progression in mice, and test the requirement for the F-actin severing protein CFL1 in this process. Key zipper-advancing behaviours are: (i) constriction of supracellular actomyosin cables; (ii) extension of filopodial/lamellipodial protrusions at periodic intervals; (iii) constriction of leading-edge cell borders bringing together protrusions which establish ‘pioneering’ contacts across the midline; (iv) cell-cell and ( v) cell-ECM adhesion remodelling; (vi) zipper advancement through cell partner exchange. In wild-type embryos, CFL1 is enriched at the leading edge of surface ectoderm cells adjacent to the zippering point, and localised within some protrusions. Conditional Cfl1 deletion in the surface ectoderm produces denser F-actin stress fibres, makes filopodial protrusions excessively stable, diminishes their exploratory movements which may establish nascent contacts, and impairs junctional constriction of cells at the point of fusion. Zippering speed is reduced ~30% in conditional Cfl1 -deleted embryos and ~30% develop spina bifida. We therefore propose that impaired filopodial dynamicity and junctional constriction limits the sequence of behaviours driving spinal zippering, predisposing to spina bifida.

Article.Title: Resistance mutation supply modulates the benefit of CRISPR immunity against virulent phages in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Article.Authors: Wright R.; Lovell S.; Richmond A.; Harrison C.; Ashworth E.; Kadioglu A.; Fothergill J.; Friman V.; Westra E.; Brockhurst M.
Article.Abstract: Only a fraction of bacterial genomes encode CRISPR-Cas systems, but the selective causes of this variation are unexplained. How naturally virulent bacteriophages (phages) select for CRISPR immunity has rarely been tested experimentally. Here, we show against a panel of genetically and functionally diverse virulent phages that CRISPR immunity was not universally beneficial to Pseudomonas aeruginosa , and its fitness effect varied strongly between phages in predictable ways. In addition to mechanisms known to alter the effectiveness of CRISPR immunity, such as encoding a matching spacer or a protective nuclear shell, we show that the fitness effect of CRISPR immunity negatively associated with the probability of evolving receptor-based resistance to the phage via spontaneous mutation. The supply of resistance mutations differed strongly between very closely related lipopolysaccharide-binding phages and was associated with variation at the C-terminus of the tail fibre protein altering residues involved in hydrogen bonding and the predicted binding site. Our results show that CRISPR immunity is more beneficial against virulent phages that are harder to evolve resistance to via receptor mutations, suggesting that virulent phage community composition and diversity will be important drivers of the prevalence of CRISPR immunity.

Article.Title: Transient feedforward communication between somatosensory and premotor cortex supports goal-directed behavior
Article.Authors: Ranjbar-Slamloo Y.; Kamigaki T.
Article.Abstract: Goal-directed behavior requires sensory information to be transformed into motor commands, yet the precise temporal structure of communication between sensory and motor cortices during this process remains poorly understood. By simultaneously recording spiking activity from primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and secondary motor cortex (M2) in mice performing a tactile delayed go/no-go task, we identified a brief, stimulus-triggered communication window that predicted behavioral success. Time-shifted canonical correlation analysis revealed a sharp, feedforward surge in S1 → M2 coupling peaking at a short latency, as expected for a potentially direct transmission pathway. This transient interaction conveyed stimulus-selective information such that the S1 → M2 communication subspace aligned with stimulus-coding axes in both regions. In contrast, M2 → S1 feedback interactions were weaker and delayed. Brief optogenetic suppression of S1 reduced both M2 stimulus selectivity and behavioral discriminability, consistent with a functional role of the transient S1 → M2 coupling. These findings demonstrate that sensorimotor transformation is supported not by sustained linear coupling along the stimulus- or choice- axis, but by a short-lived and highly selective feedforward communication channel that rapidly transmits reliable sensory representations into motor-planning circuits.

Article.Title: Full-length genomes evolve in parallel in a long-term evolution experiment with phage φX174
Article.Authors: Bons E.; Chabas H.; MacDonald H.; Escalera Ledermann A.; Ösze S.; Dunstan J.; Ochsner N.; Angst D.; Bonhoeffer S.; Regoes R.
Article.Abstract: The study of evolution in organisms with high mutation rates requires detailed data on the genomic composition of the population. Here we report on an innovative use of high-throughput sequencing technology combined with rapid experimental evolution that allowed us to follow the genetic diversification of four independent bacteriophage populations for 412 generations in extraordinary detail. One of our goals was to assess phylodynamic methods that use genetic information to infer key parameters of the population history. Because phylodynamic methods assume neutral evolution, we did not actively impose any selection pressures in our evolution experiment (in addition to those inherent in the bacterial cell environment). Tracing over 80′000 bacteriophage genomes, representing 884 distinct genotypes, we find that the patterns of viral diversification result in largely non-congruent genotype distributions, but also document multiple instances of parallel evolution. Unlike previous observations of parallelism in viral evolution, we do not just see the parallel evolution of mutations at single sites, but on the level of full-length genomes. Computer simulations that recapitulate our experiments in great detail show that this degree of parallelism is inconsistent with neutral evolution. We further show that the observed extent of parallel evolution biases phylodynamic analysis of migration rates, and wrongly estimates significant migration between the independent evolution lines. Our approach is applicable to many other viruses and paves the way to advanced population genetic investigations that aim to shed light on phenomena that relate to genetic linkage across the genome.

Article.Title: Viral disease outcomes are indistinguishable between experimentally infected bats and rodents
Article.Authors: Farrell M.; Tucker S.; Mollentze N.; Streicker D.
Article.Abstract: A common explanation for bats being a conspicuous source of zoonotic viruses is their purported ability to coexist with viruses without suffering overt disease. Widespread acceptance of the idea that bats have unusual antiviral traits has catalyzed the discovery of unique features of bat immune systems which may have translational value as broad-spectrum antivirals, particularly if they evolved as a byproduct of bats’ unique life history rather than through conventional co-evolutionary processes. Surprisingly, whether bats compared to other host groups suffer less disease from co-evolved viruses or from viruses generally has not been formally assessed. Here, synthesizing 86 years of experimental infections, involving 54 viruses, 85 host species, and over 5,600 animals, we document disease in bats following inoculation by taxonomically diverse viruses, including ones that are relatively benign in humans. The occurrence of overt disease, the likelihood of mortality, and the severity of disease in bats were indistinguishable from those experienced by rodents, another group associated with many zoonotic viruses. These patterns were consistent when considering only bat-associated viruses inoculated into bats and rodent-associated viruses inoculated into rodents and among inoculations which lacked shared co-evolutionary history. Instead, disease outcomes following infection were shaped by experimental design, viral host range, and evolutionary context. Unexceptional disease in bats from novel or co-evolved infections suggests that order-level host life history traits such as flight have inconsistent consequences for antiviral immunity and highlights the need to evaluate the functional properties of putatively unique features of bat immunity in vivo. While these results do not exclude the possibility of developing broader-acting or more potent antivirals from bat immune systems or diminish the potential value of mechanistic insights into bat immunity, they suggest that bat immune systems were shaped by conventional co-evolutionary processes rather than through unique circumstances that endow exceptional antiviral defenses.

Article.Title: Structural basis for inhibition of the lipid flippase MurJ by phage lysis protein SglPP7 suggests convergent evolution with other Sgl peptides
Article.Authors: Hosoda K.; Kohga H.; Wu S.; Tanaka H.; Shigematsu H.; Miyazaki R.; Chek M.; Tsukazaki T.
Article.Abstract: Some bacteriophages encode lysis proteins that inhibit essential bacterial processes, and elucidating their mechanisms is valuable for developing antibacterial strategies against drug-resistant pathogens. We determined the cryo-EM structure of the complex between the essential Escherichia coli lipid II flippase MurJ and the phage lysis protein Sgl PP7 . Structural, mutational, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation analyses revealed that Sgl PP7 binds along the intramembrane cleft of MurJ and inserts its C-terminal tail into the internal cavity, stabilizing MurJ in an outward-facing conformation. Structural comparison with Lys M (Sgl M ) and Sgl CJ3 showed that these sequence-divergent Sgl proteins stabilize MurJ in the outward-facing conformation through distinct binding modes, consistent with the possibility of convergent evolution toward MurJ inhibition.

Article.Title: fruitless is essential for male Aedes aegypti mosquito attraction to female flight sounds
Article.Authors: Loh Y.; Thornton A.; Loh W.; Lee T.; Chen W.; Xu Y.; Yap J.; Tsuchiya Y.; Eberl D.; Su M.; Kamikouchi A.
Article.Abstract: Male mosquitoes locate females through strong and innate attraction to female flight sounds, the basis of mating in the world’s deadliest animal. In contrast, females do not show any sound attraction behaviors. Despite being documented for almost a century, the molecular underpinnings of these behavioral dimorphisms remain unknown. Here, we found that by disrupting the male-specific isoform of fruitless (referred to as fruM ) in Aedes aegypti , fruM mutant males show complete abolition of sound attraction behaviors, resulting in failure of mutant males to locate females for mating. We identified strong fruitless expression in control male ears, with the loss of FruM severely disrupting mutant male ability to amplify female flight sounds. fruM mutant male ears also propagate frequency-specific, sound-evoked electrical signals at about one-sixth the magnitude of control males, significantly reducing the amount of auditory information relayed to the brain. fruitless thus plays a significant role in determining proper male peripheral hearing function underlying mating. Transcriptomic analyses of mosquito ears identified essential hearing genes under the transcriptional influence of FruM via direct or indirect actions, thus shaping male-specific hearing cellular machineries that support male attraction to female flight sounds. Our work demonstrates that FruM commands male-specific hearing behaviors involved in mating by directly controlling the earliest stages of auditory organ performance, sound amplification and acoustic signal detection. Our findings show that FruM is essential for male-specific reproductive behaviors in mosquitoes.

Article.Title: Pollinator abundance shapes sexual selection in an angiosperm
Article.Authors: Barbot E.; Dufaÿ M.; Janicke T.; Lapeyre B.; Orcel D.; Rousset F.; Tonnabel J.
Article.Abstract: Sexual selection is a central force in evolutionary biology that has been shown to shape phenotypes and population dynamics in animals. While this selective force is increasingly recognized in flowering plants, theory predicts that anisogamy generates sex differences in the fitness benefits of acquiring additional mates—a pattern well supported in animals but with limited tests in plants. Plant studies rely solely on genetic parentage analyses to estimate mate numbers, thereby conflating performance in accessing mates with success in gamete fertilization. Pollinators add an ecological layer, as their behavior and abundance can influence competition for access to mates and their gametes. Here, we disentangle consecutive episodes of sexual selection in the hermaphroditic plant Brassica rapa by combining direct observations of Bombus terrestris movements with genetic paternity analyses in experimental populations, thus providing independent estimates of the observational number of mates acquired and realized fertilization success. Our approach identifies pollen competition for ovules as the primary arena for sexual selection in B. rapa . Competition for access to mates constitutes a secondary force and was found to be stronger in the male compared to the female sex function, as predicted by classic theory. Experimentally reduced pollinator abundance modulated the balance between pre- and post-pollination sexual selection, increasing the opportunity for selection on mate acquisition. Ignoring pollinator movements led to biased estimates of pre-pollination sexual selection. Our findings demonstrate that sexual selection in plants unfolds across multiple, sequential episodes shaped by ecological context.

Article.Title: Tolerance measured at one developmental stage mispredicts climate resilience in an animal with a complex life cycle
Article.Authors: Song H.; Shi T.; Yang M.; Liu X.; Li Z.; Shi P.; Wu Y.; Allam B.; Jeffs A.; Skelton B.; Zhang T.
Article.Abstract: Forecasts of whether marine species can evolve fast enough to survive climate change rely largely on single-stage tolerance assays, tacitly assuming that tolerance measured at one developmental stage reflects adaptive capacity across the organism’s life cycle. We test this assumption in a common marine bivalve ( Mercenaria mercenaria ) and find that it fails in sign, not degree: larval and post-metamorphic tolerance to end-century ocean acidification are strongly negatively correlated ( r = −0.53, 95% CI [−0.69, −0.33]) across family-level, pedigree-conditioned and animal model estimates, with pervasive rank reversals among the top performers of each stage. A multivariate analysis of the among-family covariance matrix G shows why: under acidification, 57% of the among-family variance collapses onto a single dominant axis that loads positively on every larval trait and negatively on every post-metamorphic trait, whereas under ambient conditions the same families show no cross-stage covariance at all. Acidification therefore does not merely depress performance—it reorganizes the genetic architecture into a cross-stage conflict. Under ramping RCP 8.5 forcing this conflict geometry dictates the direction—not merely the magnitude—of adaptation: only balanced multi-stage selection preserves family diversity, whereas single-stage selection systematically erodes the opposite axis. In complex life cycles, resilience is a geometric property of ontogeny that forecasts cannot compress into a single-stage without inverting the sign of the answer.

Article.Title: Profiling of i6A37 and ms2i6A37 tRNA modifications across eukaryotes by isopentenyl-tRNA-seq
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Wang Z.; Yuan Y.; Chen S.; Xue J.; Tan J.; Chai Z.; Fang Z.; Yang G.; Xiao L.; Zhou M.; Yin Q.; Wang R.; Chen M.; Zhou X.; Zhou Z.
Article.Abstract: N6-isopentenyladenosine (i6A) and its derivative 2-methylthio-N6-isopentenyladenosine (ms2i6A) at position 37 are conserved modifications of cytosolic and mitochondrial tRNAs that typically contain the A36-A37-A38 motif. However, their distribution and function are poorly defined due to the lack of methods capable of distinguishing these closely related modifications. Here, we developed isopentenyl-tRNA sequencing (isopentenyl-tRNA-seq), an approach that simultaneously detects and discriminates i6A37 and ms2i6A37 at single-nucleotide resolution. Applying isopentenyl-tRNA-seq to twelve representative eukaryotes, we uncovered extensive species-specific diversity and dynamic regulation of these modifications. Unexpectedly, we identified i6A37 in tRNAs lacking the canonical A36-A37-A38 motif and detected both modifications in chloroplast tRNAs. Moreover, integrative analyses identifed conserved and lineage-specific pathways enriched in genes with high usage of codons decoded by i6A37-modified tRNAs. Together, this work establishes isopentenyl-tRNA-seq as a platform for high-resolution analysis of isopentenylated tRNA modifications and provides a framework for understanding their evolutionary distribution and potential functional roles in eukaryotes.

Article.Title: TCR-induced Lck SUMOylation promotes centrosome polarization via the SENP1-Lck∼SUMO1-CEP83-SCLT1/CEP89 axis
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Xiao Z.; Gong B.; Du Y.; Su Z.; Mu S.; Ye W.; Xiang S.; Zhao X.; Zhao C.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Centrosome polarization is essential for T cell activation and immune responses, and Lck plays a critical role. However, how Lck regulates centrosome polarization remains unclear. Here, we show that in resting T cells, SENP1 colocalizes with Lck at the centrosome. Upon T cell receptor (TCR) stimulation, Lck dissociates from SENP1 and interacts with small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) E3 ligases, promoting Lck SUMOylation. We map Lys228 and Lys231 as major SUMO1 modification sites that regulate Lck kinase activity and CEP83 binding. SUMOylated Lck binds and phosphorylates CEP83, facilitating SCLT1/CEP89 recruitment to promote distal appendage assembly, thereby mediating centrosome polarization and docking. Senp1-/- mice exhibit elevated Lck SUMOylation and Y394 phosphorylation in resting T cells, indicating that SENP1 negatively regulates active Lck abundance. Moreover, SENP1 deficiency enhances cytotoxicity and promotes apoptosis of CD8+ T cells. Collectively, our findings establish a role for SENP1 in modulating Lck activation and define a TCR-induced, SUMOylation-dependent Lck∼SUMO1-CEP83-SCLT1/CEP89 axis regulating centrosome polarization.

Article.Abstract: The retrosplenial cortex (RSP) supports spatial cognition, memory, and brain-wide information integration, yet its output architecture remains poorly resolved at single-neuron resolution. Article.Abstract: Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) regulates inflammation and immunity and is frequently dysregulated in autoimmune diseases, inflammatory disorders, and cancers. Article.Authors: Ge X.; Jiang F.; De La Fuente C.; Rajkhowa T.; Chen C.; Viswanathan R.; Husain A.; Bennett E.
Article.Abstract: E3 ligases confer substrate specificity within ubiquitin-dependent pathways. However, the pleiotropic HECT-type E3 ligase HUWE1 targets a biochemically and structurally diverse set of substrates through mechanisms that remain largely unknown. We develop a combinatorial cell-based system integrating global proteomics, proximity labeling, and reporter assays to systematically interrogate HUWE1 sequence features that enable substrate targeting. We define a robust HUWE1 activity signature consisting of putative substrates that accumulate upon HUWE1 impairment across multiple cell lines. By re-expressing a panel of HUWE1 deletion mutants, we find that both the largest intrinsically disordered region and the conserved ubiquitin-binding motifs contribute to substrate targeting. Structural modeling and domain analysis further suggest that HUWE1 achieves targeting plasticity through multivalent interactions, engaging both disordered and structured regions within its substrates. Together, our findings establish a framework for understanding how large, modular E3 ligases exploit intrinsic disorder and multivalency to shape their substrate repertoires.

Article.Abstract: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) drives antibody diversification through class switch recombination (CSR) and somatic hypermutation (SHM). To model this putative separation-of-function mutation, we generated an AicdaR190X knock-in mouse. These mice show a severe CSR defect and a moderately reduced but ongoing SHM. Mechanistically, the severe CSR defect correlates with defective recombination of double-strand breaks in immunoglobulin switch regions. Strikingly, fusion of AIDR190X to a catalytically inactive AID restores CSR, indicating that the C terminus mediates a non-catalytic function for recombination. Article.Abstract: Chronic itch represents a significant clinical challenge that substantially impairs patients' quality of life, yet its underlying neural circuit and molecular mechanisms remain elusive. Article.Authors: Wang W.; Wang F.; He Y.; Zhang Y.; Li C.; Chen X.; Xia X.; Liu Y.; Zhou L.; Hu Z.; Li Z.; Wang J.; Li L.; Zeng C.; Wu G.
Article.Abstract: Loss of cardiomyocytes drives cardiac remodeling and ultimately leads to heart failure, highlighting the need to promote cardiac regeneration. Article.Abstract: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) maintain their function through interactions with niche cells in the bone marrow. Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Zhang X.; Chen R.; Xiang Y.; Gong E.; Tong H.; Sun X.; Yin H.; Qi H.

Article.Title: Arbitrium crosstalk enables shared signaling among phages
Article.Authors: Lomeli-Ortega C.; Balcázar J.
Article.Abstract: The arbitrium system has transformed our understanding of phage biology by demonstrating that temperate phages communicate through extracellular peptides to coordinate lysis-lysogeny decisions. Initially considered a highly specific signaling pathway restricted to individual phage lineages, arbitrium communication has now been shown to extend beyond lineage boundaries in some phage systems. Recent studies have shown that non-cognate arbitrium peptides can interact with heterologous receptors, providing evidence of inter-phage crosstalk. Here, we synthesize current knowledge of the molecular basis of arbitrium signaling, the structural determinants of peptide-receptor specificity, and the potential ecological and evolutionary consequences of inter-phage communication. We suggest that arbitrium crosstalk may shape phage ecology by mediating competitive and potentially cooperative interactions within shared signaling environments. We also discuss its potential uses in engineered phage systems, synthetic biology, and microbiome engineering. Collectively, the available evidence broadens the concept of viral communication beyond lineage-specific signaling, while the ecological significance and practical applications of arbitrium crosstalk remain to be established.

Article.Authors: Wang B.; Kuo Y.; Dasdemir E.; Xiao W.; Rebboah E.; Tang G.; Wang W.; Abbas H.
Article.Abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains highly lethal, with treatment failure and relapse driven by dynamic cellular states and evolving interactions within the leukemic ecosystem. Article.Title: Self-amplifying RNA vaccines encoding chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinins confer immunity against phylogenetically diverse influenza A viruses
Article.Authors: Abbad A.; Yellin T.; Carreño J.; McPartlan J.; Talukder P.; Puente-Massaguer E.; González-Domínguez I.; Scherm M.; Bielak D.; Lerman B.; Mandl C.; Chahal J.; Krammer F.

Passive serum transfer confirms antibody-mediated protection independent of cellular immunity. Article.Title: Chronotherapy leveraging dietary context overcomes circadian rhythm influence on cancer cell response to PPAR antagonists
Article.Authors: Bruno P.; Özkan K.; Renoult O.; Giolito M.; Ibanez S.; Srhir S.; Guilbaud C.; Laloux F.; Leclercq I.; Bouzin C.; Serafimov K.; Dessy C.; Aubert L.; Feron O.

Article.Title: Lineage-specific metabolic transcription across environmental gradients in geothermal microbial communities
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Xie Q.; Qu Y.; Tang Q.; Cai C.; Chen L.; Hua Z.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how environmental heterogeneity shapes microbial metabolism remains a central challenge. These findings reveal how microbial functional programs and their lineage associations reflect environmental heterogeneity across geothermal habitats.

Article.Title: Life course trajectories of musculoskeletal pain
Article.Authors: Ahacic K.; Raices Cruz I.; Kåreholt I.; Bartels S.; Oksanen A.; Wicksell R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A life course perspective can help identify critical periods and high-risk groups for musculoskeletal pain. However, how musculoskeletal pain develops over the adult life course and the extent to which this development varies among individuals remain largely unexplored. This Swedish population-representative survey followed a sample of 6328 individuals over 7 waves and 42 years, from ages 15 to 101 years, including about 25,000 observations. Reported musculoskeletal pain in the joints, back, or shoulders over the past year was categorized as follows: no pain (0), light pain in 1 to 3 sites (1), severe pain in one site (2), and severe pain in 2 to 3 sites (3). Age-related pain trajectories were identified through a sex-stratified latent class growth analysis. For both women and men, 2 distinct trajectories emerged. In the high-risk group, pain increased consistently throughout working age before declining postretirement. In the other group, pain levels were generally low, surpassing light pain only after retirement age. Although the trajectory patterns were similar for women and men, the high-risk group was twice as large among women (20%) as among men (9%). The general increase in pain towards the end of the life course likely reflects normal ageing processes, including disease onset and frailty, while the trajectory of the high-risk group may indicate the cumulative effect of risk factors associated with working life. Average trends across the entire sample mask the unique experience of this high-risk group and obscure the distinct effects of ageing on the development of musculoskeletal pain.

Article.Title: The neuropathic chameleon: we are hot on the scent
Article.Authors: Kersebaum D.; Forstenpointner J.; Sachau J.; Hüllemann P.; Baron R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A common chronic pain condition, neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory or neural tissue and is characterized by a combination of negative (eg, numbness) and positive (eg, burning pain) sensory symptoms that significantly affect the quality of life. Common comorbidities such as depression and sleep disruption contribute to a substantial disease burden, which is further exacerbated by the apparent lack of effective therapeutic options. Current treatment options frequently achieve only partial, insufficient pain relief or may be completely ineffective in a considerable number of patients. The development of new drugs has thus far achieved moderate success, with many clinical trials failing to meet their primary endpoints; thus, a substantial unmet clinical need persists. One reason for this therapeutic deadlock is the considerable heterogeneity of neuropathic pain, driven by diverse pathophysiological mechanisms that vary between patients regardless of the underlying disease etiology. Accordingly, reclassification efforts follow a mechanism-based approach that reflects pathophysiological pain generators rather than disease etiology. Although diagnosis remains anchored in lesion- or disease-based criteria and structured clinical assessment, treatment development increasingly benefits from mechanism-informed phenotyping. A priori stratification based on individual mechanisms may help identify treatment responders, but implementation requires surrogate markers, as no biomarkers for pain mechanisms currently exist. In this article, we discuss candidate predictive markers and surrogate markers, focusing on sensory symptoms and signs assessed through patient-reported outcome measures and sensory testing, and their integration into future clinical trials.

Article.Title: Trustworthiness in pain research is essential. Developing and implementing the ENTRUST-PE framework
Article.Authors: O'Connell N.; Belton J.; Cashin A.; Eccleston C.; Ferraro M.; Keefe F.; Knaggs R.; Norris E.; Pogatzki-Zahn E.; Palermo T.; Pickering G.; Rice A.; Segelcke D.; Sharma S.; Smart K.; Soliman N.; Toelle T.; Stewart G.; Vollert J.; Wainwright E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Trustworthy pain research is essential for developing a deeper understanding of the phenomena, how it is experienced, its many impacts and how it might be reduced, prevented or managed to improve the lives of those who live with pain. Recognising multiple critical challenges that undermine trust in health research, an international, interdisciplinary network was convened to create an integrated framework for enhancing the trustworthiness of research in pain. The ENTRUST-PE framework was launched in 2024 with a call to action, proposing that trustworthiness in pain research is multidimensional and underpinned by 7 Core Values: Integrity and Governance; Equity, Diversity and Inclusivity; Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement; Methodological Rigour; Openness and Transparency; Balanced Communication and Data Authenticity. The framework includes specific recommendations for a range of interest holders and resources to support those recommendations. In this paper, we summarise the framework, reflect on the response to the framework from the pain research community, consider challenges and opportunities in the evolving research landscape and suggest how we might move towards deeper implementation to enhance the trustworthiness of pain research.

Article.Title: Exercise therapy for chronic pain: an updated perspective on mesocorticolimbic system function
Article.Authors: Senba E.; Minami K.; Habata S.; Kami T.; Kouda K.; Tajima F.; Kami K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Patients with chronic pain often experience behavioral issues linked to pain, depression, and other emotional disorders. These problems stem from dysfunction in the mesocorticolimbic system, and exercise offers a safe, accessible, and effective alternative. It not only reduces pain but also activates multiple neural pathways, helping restore normal function. First, in the periphery, exercise promotes the release of myokines, which are essential for the body-brain connection and influence neural activity. IGF-1, released from muscles during exercise, can cross the blood-brain barrier and affect the brain. IGF-1 specifically targets orexin neurons in the hypothalamus, which then stimulate dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area, triggering the reward system. Second, exercise can reshape neural circuits and restore mesocorticolimbic function, reducing chronic pain and related issues. We showed that exercise activates neurons in the basal nucleus of the amygdala that project to the nucleus accumbens, supporting patients' goal-directed behavior. Moreover, inhibiting GABAergic neurons in the central nucleus of the amygdala decreases freezing behavior. Third, chronic pain often leads to depression, mainly due to reduced activity of serotonin (5-HT) neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus, which impairs the brain’s reward system. Exercise boosts activity of 5-HT neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus. Furthermore, exercise can modify gene expression through epigenetic mechanisms, leading to long-lasting improvements in brain function and behavior. Overall, exercise can restore brain function, helping individuals overcome chronic pain and lead healthier lives. These findings support exercise therapy as a key component of chronic pain management and suggest mesocorticolimbic mechanisms underlying its effects.

Article.Title: Under pressure: lessons from and beyond entrapment neuropathies
Article.Authors: Schmid A.; Chang P.; Camerone E.; Sierra-Silvestre E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Entrapment neuropathies are the most prevalent focal neuropathic pain conditions globally and impose a substantial individual and socioeconomic burden. Traditionally conceptualised as purely mechanical compression syndromes, this view is increasingly challenged by converging evidence from human tissue analyses, advanced neuroimaging, and deep clinical phenotyping. Entrapment neuropathies are now recognised as biologically dynamic disorders shaped to different extents by microvascular compromise, demyelination, axonal degeneration, immune dysregulation, neuroinflammation, central nervous system adaptations, and psychosocial influences. Varying combinations and dominance of biopsychosocial processes give rise to marked clinical heterogeneity even within the same diagnostic label. This mechanistic diversity helps explain common diagnostic discordances, including extraterritorial symptom spread, normal electrodiagnostic findings despite clinical symptoms indicative of entrapment neuropathies, and imaging–clinical presentation mismatch. It also challenges one-size-fits-all treatment approaches, which have largely failed in entrapment neuropathies. Uniquely, entrapment neuropathies provide a natural human model of focal nerve injury in the context of neuropathic pain. Surgical decompression allows integration of tissue-level biology with precise clinical phenotypes and offers time-locked insights into recovery. Lessons derived from this model extend beyond entrapment neuropathies and can inform broader understanding of neuropathic and nerve-related musculoskeletal pain conditions. Here, we synthesise contemporary mechanistic insights, examine how biological heterogeneity translates into distinct clinical phenotypes, and discuss potential implications for mechanism-informed management.

Article.Title: Brain sites involved in endogenous analgesia
Article.Authors: Henderson L.; Crawford L.; Kang J.; Keay K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pain modulation is a fundamental survival mechanism that prioritises, shapes, and suppresses nociceptive inputs to optimise behaviour. Although acute pain signals potential or actual tissue damage, sustained pain can impair essential behaviours, necessitating modulatory circuits that dynamically regulate nociception according to context and motivational state. These systems are deeply conserved, embedded within primitive spinal and brainstem structures, and capable of powerful modulation independent of cortical input, although higher regions such as the prefrontal cortex can influence their function. Decades of work have sought to identify these core modulatory circuits to advance basic understanding and develop strategies for clinically meaningful hypoalgesia. More recently, dysfunction within these circuits has been implicated in chronic pain, driving efforts to characterise how their organisation and function change during persistent pain states. Although most mechanistic insights come from animal studies, human neuroimaging, particularly since the advent of functional magnetic resonance imaging, has begun to map their location and engagement during pain modulation. Early work focused on forebrain regions due to the limited spatial resolution of standard MRI, but ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging now enables mm 3 -scale investigation of brainstem nuclei. This review synthesises evidence from animal and human studies to outline the best-characterised modulatory pathway, consisting of projections from the midbrain periaqueductal gray to the rostral ventromedial medulla and onward to the dorsal horn/spinal trigeminal nucleus, and highlights recent work detailing its organization.

Article.Title: Advances in research on combination therapy for the management of pain
Article.Authors: Gilron I.; Peterson C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pharmacotherapy remains an important component of multidisciplinary, multimodal pain treatment. Based on a well-established understanding of multiple concurrent mechanisms of nociceptive transmission and modulation, the demonstrated potential for synergistic interactions of drug combinations seen in preclinical studies supports the hypothesis of superior analgesia, and possibly also, fewer side-effects as compared with monotherapy. Likely related to this hypothesis and rationale, real-world evidence shows that approximately half of all patients with chronic pain, and even more with acute pain, concurrently receive 2 or more drugs from different mechanistic classes. To date, many dozens of randomized controlled trials have evaluated various analgesic combinations for the treatment of postoperative, neuropathic, back, arthritis, fibromyalgia, pelvic, and cancer-related pain conditions. Despite this growing area of research, most analgesic drug combinations are currently administered without rigorous evidence, thus exposing patients to the added cost or risk of some combinations that are not necessarily superior to monotherapy. As such, we propose future efforts to more efficiently exploit the potential benefits of combination therapy including: (1) expansion and coordination of translational collaborations to prioritize the most beneficial and clinically relevant combinations; (2) ensuring that preclinical combination studies evaluate multiple drug dosages and multiple relevant adverse effects; (3) ensuring that clinical trials include comparisons with each and every monotherapy component of the combination; (4) conducting further real-world studies of clinically beneficial combinations to ensure safety and efficacy in broader clinical settings; and (5) the application of these principles also to the evaluation of nonpharmacological treatment combinations.

Article.Title: Molecular histochemical analysis of neuroplasticity-related gene expression in pain pathway
Article.Authors: Noguchi K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract I am deeply honored to receive the 2026 John Bonica Prize for distinguished lifetime achievement in the basic science of pain. Reflecting on 40 years of research, this review paper will summarize my key findings to date. For the past four decades, my research has focused on elucidating the molecular mechanisms of pain using animal models. By integrating morphological techniques with molecular biology, behavioral analysis, and electrophysiological recordings, I have sought to clarify how pain signals are modulated and sustained under chronic pain conditions. Since the early stages of my career, I have been particularly interested in the diverse molecular dynamics within pain pathways and their functional significance. This long-term research has been driven by the conviction that a detailed analysis of gene expression changes within pain pathways—particularly those associated with neuroplasticity—is essential to understanding the mechanisms underlying intractable pain. This review provides a comprehensive overview of our investigation into the molecular and cellular mechanisms of chronic pain, focusing on gene expression analyses related mainly to dorsal root ganglion and spinal cord plasticity, alongside historically significant contributions from the global pain research community. Finally, I will also discuss recent methodological advances and their applications, as well as the challenges and future directions facing basic pain research.

Article.Title: Prediction and prevention of pain after surgery
Article.Authors: Pogatzki-Zahn E.; Pradier B.; Segelcke D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Postoperative pain is common and has substantial clinical consequences for patients, their families, and society. Acute pain is not the only problem: a meaningful subset of patients develops chronic postsurgical pain, which is associated with considerable functional and psychosocial burden. Because established chronic postsurgical pain is difficult to treat, prevention is a key clinical objective, but it depends on the early identification of vulnerable patients and timely mechanism-informed interventions. This review examines mechanisms of postsurgical pain, as well as the prediction and prevention of unfavorable outcomes, from a translational perspective that integrates clinical evidence with mechanistic insights from preclinical models. After briefly summarizing recent developments, we outline current challenges and argue that progress requires alignment of outcome constructs across species, rigorous selection and reporting of experimental models, and identification of shared intermediate phenotypes linking mechanisms to patient trajectories. We then summarize the perioperative risk architecture underlying the transition from acute to chronic postsurgical pain, focusing on bio-psycho-social patient-related and surgical factors. Because current risk assessment tools do not yet provide sufficiently precise, reliable, and generalizable prediction, we discuss emerging evidence, including biological signatures that may refine prediction and risk stratification. We further argue that risk emerges dynamically through interactions across pre-, intra- and postsurgical phases. Building on this multi-stage, interactive framework, we propose a strategy integrating bio-psycho-social factors into clinically relevant prognostic models. Finally, we outline how this may not only help identify patients at risk, but also support mechanism-based, personalized prevention in vulnerable patients.

Article.Title: Chloride dysregulation: the next target for chronic pain therapeutics
Article.Authors: De Koninck Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chronic pain affects a substantial fraction of the population, yet pharmacological management remains deeply inadequate. This failure likely reflects the focus on developing analgesics suppressing normal nociceptive signalling rather than correcting the pathological substrates distinguishing chronic from acute pain. Here we review how the identification of injury-induced downregulation of the potassium-chloride cotransporter KCC2 in spinal dorsal horn neurons represents a landmark. It first provided a mechanistic, long-term substrate for spinal inhibitory failure. This form of disinhibition had the potential to explain several cardinal symptoms of neuropathic pain; not just hyperalgesia, through spinal hyperexcitability, and tactile allodynia, through cross-talk between sensory modalities, but also spontaneous pain, through enabling spontaneous bursts of activity in spinal nociceptive output to emerge. A second landmark is that chloride dysregulation as a substrate of disinhibition yields non-linear, non-intuitive predictions of neural circuit behaviours that shed light on several features of chronic pain and its therapeutic challenges. One is paradoxical pro-excitatory actions of tapping into normally endogenous inhibitory neurotransmission, potentially explaining failures of benzodiazepines analgesia and of conditional pain modulation. Others include degradation of sensory processing, possibly explaining diffuse pain, and leaky plasticity, predisposing to catastrophic sensitization. In turn, mechanisms regulating KCC2 itself emerge as substrates of chronification, as well as substrates of opioid-induced maladaptive paradoxical hyperalgesia. Finally, divergent yet convergent signaling cascades underlying KCC2-downregulation reveal a form of pathway degeneracy across sexes with lessons for therapeutics. All-in-all, these findings position KCC2 as a key novel target, not just for analgesia, but also for disease modification.

Article.Title: An integrative view of human nociceptor diversity: from microneurography to molecular identity
Article.Authors: Lampert A.; Tigerholm J.; Stiehl T.; Kurth I.; Haag N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neuropathic pain arises from dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system and affects up to 10% of the population worldwide. Aberrant activity in injured sensory nerve fibers, particularly spontaneous firing and altered conduction properties of nociceptors, is tightly linked to pain, yet its molecular underpinnings in humans have long remained elusive. Over recent years, major technological advances have transformed both functional and molecular analyses of sensory neurons. High-resolution single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have produced detailed atlases of sensory neuron diversity, while traditional electrophysiological approaches such as patch-clamp and microneurography have provided unparalleled insight into nerve fiber properties. Despite their individual strengths, molecular and functional classifications of sensory neurons have largely evolved in parallel. This review focuses on emerging strategies that bridge these approaches to achieve an integrated, mechanistic understanding of neuropathic pain. We discuss how microneurography-defined biophysical hallmarks, such as activity-dependent slowing, recovery cycle signatures, and following frequency, can be transferred into in vitro patch-clamp paradigms, enabling direct functional comparison with dissociated human and large-animal sensory neurons. The incorporation of Patch-seq approaches has further enabled the assignment of molecular identity to functionally defined nociceptor subtypes, exemplified by the characterization of the mechano-insensitive “sleeping” nociceptors. Finally, we highlight how multimodal datasets combining electrophysiology, transcriptomics, and computational modeling provide new opportunities to unravel the ion channel mechanisms, particularly sodium channel subtypes, that shape pathological firing states. By directly linking human nerve fiber function to molecular programs, this integrative framework paves the way toward stratified, mechanism-based therapies for neuropathic pain.

Article.Title: Toward precision pediatric pain care: integrating mechanistic science, real-world measurement, and patient partnership
Article.Authors: Simons L.; Aghaeepour N.; Cashman C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pediatric pain science is at an inflection point. Advances in neuroscience, behavioral science, digital health technologies, and patient engagement are rapidly expanding how chronic pain in youth can be understood, measured, and treated. Yet despite these advances, many children and adolescents continue to experience persistent pain-related disability and limited access to effective care, reflecting a gap between scientific discovery and real-world clinical practice. In this perspective, we propose the BRIDGE framework (Biobehavioral Research Integrated with Digital Monitoring and Guided Engagement) as a model for advancing pediatric pain research and care. Mechanistic science is increasingly identifying neural, behavioral, and contextual processes that contribute to pain persistence and recovery, creating opportunities to target modifiable mechanisms underlying pain-related disability. At the same time, digital health technologies including wearable sensors and ecological momentary assessment enable continuous measurement of activity, physiology, and patient-reported experiences in daily life, offering new insights into the dynamic nature of pain and the potential to develop digital biomarkers of risk, recovery, and treatment response. Central to this framework is meaningful partnership with youth and families, ensuring that innovations in measurement and intervention remain aligned with patient priorities and lived experience. Integrating these domains can support precision behavioral interventions, adaptive treatment strategies, and scalable models of care that expand access to evidence-based pediatric pain treatment.

Article.Title: Spontaneous neuropathic pain
Article.Authors: Zeng X.; Woolf C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Spontaneous pain is a highly prevalent and disabling consequence of neuropathic disorders, yet it remains mechanistically underdefined and therapeutically underserved. Historically, preclinical animal models and clinical trials have been overwhelmingly biased toward stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity, relegating spontaneous pain to a secondary manifestation. Emerging evidence now challenges this view. Converging data from pharmacology, neural recordings, and systems-level causal manipulations indicate that spontaneous and stimulus-evoked pain arise from substantially dissociable molecular, cellular, and circuit substrates. Injured-fiber–derived ectopic activity within specific sensory neuron subtypes serves as a dominant peripheral generator of spontaneous pain, whereas cellularly distinct, intact spared-fiber pathways mediate stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity. At spinal and supraspinal levels, spontaneous pain preferentially engages affective–salience networks during pain chronification and may ultimately become stabilized within higher-order circuitry—while remaining dynamically coupled to afferent input. This mechanistic delineation carries critical translational implications. Current diagnostic and treatment guidelines rarely differentiate symptom domains, and most therapies have been validated primarily using stimulus-evoked or overall pain intensity endpoints—potentially contributing to a mechanism–therapy mismatch and variable efficacy. We argue that spontaneous neuropathic pain should be defined as a separate symptom domain rather than considered as a spontaneous manifestation of evoked pain mechanisms. This recognition demands longitudinal, biomarker-informed phenotyping to capture its persistent and fluctuating nature, and thereby enable robust mechanistic dissection at peripheral, spinal, and cortical nodes. Reframing spontaneous neuropathic pain along these lines will provide a foundation for precision therapeutics that target defined cell types, specific molecular drivers, and maladaptive network states—enabling mechanism-based, symptom-aligned treatments.
