Article.Title: Advancing equitable pain care worldwide requires progress in low- and middle-income settings: priorities for practice, research, and policy
Article.Authors: Sharma S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Equitable, high-value pain care remains out of reach for many populations worldwide, particularly for people living in low- and middle-income countries and cultural minority groups in high-income settings. Despite carrying a disproportionate burden of chronic pain, these populations remain underrepresented in high-quality pain research, underserved by existing health systems, and constrained by social, political, environmental, and commercial determinants of health. The lack of locally generated evidence forces clinicians and policymakers to rely on externally produced research that may not translate to local cultural, linguistic, or health-system contexts. This invited viewpoint synthesizes key contributors to pain inequity—including limited prioritization of chronic pain in low- and middle-income countries, underdeveloped rehabilitation capacity, poor access to essential treatments, commercial exploitation, and misalignment between culturally shaped pain beliefs and Western-derived assessment and treatment models. I highlight opportunities to strengthen equity in clinical care through improved education of health professionals and the public, culturally and linguistically responsive assessment, and contextually adapted self-management and treatment strategies. Equitable research requires standardized collection of sociodemographic variables, deliberate inclusion of underrepresented groups, and global partnerships that avoid colonizing practices. I propose principles for fair and impactful North–South collaborations focused on co-creation of research agendas, shared leadership, sustainable capacity building, and transparent governance. Advancing equitable global pain care and research will require collective action from clinicians, researchers, institutions, policymakers, journals, funders, and communities. A coordinated shift toward culturally grounded, contextually adaptable, and ethically collaborative approaches is essential to meaningfully reduce global pain disparities and ensure all individuals benefit from scientific progress.

Article.Title: Fatigue links sociodemographic risk to pain intensity and spread in 2 surgical cohorts
Article.Authors: Sun M.; Ansari B.; Clauw D.; Harris R.; Sluka K.; Kaplan C.; Brummet C.; Lindquist M.; Wager T.; N/A N/A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Why some surgical patients develop pain that extends beyond the original site of injury while others do not remains poorly understood. The recently proposed Risk of Pain Spread (ROPS) framework integrates multiple psychosocial risk factors associated with widespread pain, but its generalizability to surgical populations has not been established. Using 2 large presurgical cohorts of participants undergoing total knee arthroplasty or thoracic surgery, we evaluated the generalizability of the ROPS framework and examined relationships among psychosocial and sociodemographic factors, surgical-site pain, nonsurgical-site pain, and widespread pain using complementary latent-variable, regression, Bayesian network, and mediation analyses. Across cohorts and analytical approaches, fatigue emerged as the most consistent correlate of pain outcomes, independent of other measured risk factors. Fatigue also occupied a central position within the conditional dependency structure of psychosocial and pain variables and accounted for substantial shared variance linking sleep disturbance, depressive symptoms, neuroticism, adverse childhood experiences, and socioeconomic disadvantage with pain intensity. Nonsurgical-site pain consistently occupied a position linking pain intensity with widespread pain across complementary analyses. Together, these findings externally validate the ROPS framework in clinically relevant surgical populations and identify fatigue as a central correlate linking biopsychosocial vulnerability with pain burden.

Article.Title: Astrocyte Orai1 signaling promotes spinal excitatory synaptic potentiation and neuropathic pain after nerve injury in male mice
Article.Authors: Tsujikawa S.; Shetti A.; Grant R.; Novakovic M.; Prakriya M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neuropathic pain after peripheral nerve injury is a multifactorial condition mediated partly by inflammation in the spinal cord that results in potentiation of excitatory synaptic transmission in nociceptive circuits. Glial cells including astrocytes are key mediators of the underlying inflammation, but the signaling checkpoints that regulate astrocyte-driven spinal cord inflammation and sensitization of nociceptive circuits are not well understood. Here, we identify Orai1-mediated store-operated Ca 2+ entry (SOCE) as an important regulator of spinal astrocyte cytokine production, metabolic reprogramming, and pain hypersensitivity in mice. Conditional deletion of Orai1 in astrocytes attenuated mechanical allodynia after nerve injury in male but not female mice, despite comparable SOCE suppression in both sexes. Orai1 deficiency also attenuated production of proinflammatory cytokines after SOCE activation, including TNFα, IL-6, and IL-33, both in vivo and in vitro. Electrophysiological recordings revealed that astrocyte Orai1 deletion prevented injury-induced enhancement of glutamatergic synaptic transmission in dorsal horn neurons, linking astrocytic Ca 2+ signaling to central sensitization. Metabolomic profiling showed that Orai1 loss disrupted glycolysis and TCA cycle intermediates while promoting accumulation of immunomodulatory metabolites such as itaconate, consistent with a less inflammatory astrocyte metabolic state. These findings identify Orai1 channels as integrators of astrocyte Ca 2+ signaling, immunometabolism, and excitatory synaptic potentiation after nerve injury, and identify a sexually dimorphic astrocyte mechanism governing neuropathic pain pathogenesis. Targeting astrocyte Orai1 channels may provide a selective therapeutic strategy for male-predominant chronic pain.

Article.Title: Mineralocorticoid receptor signaling reduces somatostatin expression in developing sensory neurons and drives neonatal pain after early-life stress
Article.Authors: Eid F.; Serafin E.; Muniz M.; Woodke S.; Booher J.; Zhang J.; Baccei M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Early-life stress (ELS) causes pain hypersensitivity in neonatal mice and alters the transcriptional profile of the immature dorsal root ganglia (DRG), highlighted by a marked reduction in the expression of a neuropeptide, somatostatin (Sst), which is known to constitutively suppress peripheral nociceptive transmission during adulthood. However, the mechanisms that drive plasticity in gene expression within the developing DRG and neonatal pain after ELS remain unclear. Here, we investigated the degree to which ELS-induced neonatal pain was mediated by corticosterone signaling onto sensory neurons and potential changes in peripheral Sst transmission. The conditional knockout of the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR), but not the glucocorticoid receptor, from immature DRG neurons prevented ELS-evoked neonatal pain. In contrast, the systemic administration of the selective MR antagonist eplerenone failed to acutely influence pain after ELS, thus suggesting that MR activation enhances pain during the neonatal period via canonical effects on gene transcription. Meanwhile, hind paw injection of the Sst receptor antagonist cyclo-somatostatin increased spontaneous nocifensive behaviors in control pups, but not in pups previously subjected to ELS, raising the possibility that a disruption in tonic antinociception mediated by peripheral Sst contributes to neonatal pain after ELS. Furthermore, administration of the peripherally restricted Sst analog octreotide reversed noxious cold and pressure hypersensitivity in neonatal mice after ELS. Finally, the selective deletion of MR from sensory neurons prevented the ELS-induced decrease in Sst expression. Collectively, these results provide novel mechanistic insight into the effects of chronic early-life adversity on nociceptive processing in the developing nervous system.

Article.Title: Regulatory architecture shapes how historical contingency affects the resilience of evolutionary potential in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Article.Authors: Castillo Moro G.; Martino R.; Pasolli P.; Tenaglia A.; Tobares R.; Häussler S.; Nikel P.; Smania A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract How biological systems maintain evolutionary potential as mutations accumulate remains poorly understood. Here, we used a Pseudomonas aeruginosa strain in which all 32 diguanylate cyclases were disrupted, abolishing biofilm formation and severely constraining recovery routes. Experimental evolution nevertheless repeatedly restored biofilm formation, resulting almost exclusively in one adaptive solution: restoring YfiN function. The predominant allele reinstated diguanylate cyclase activity while weakening YfiR-mediated repression, providing a one-shot recovery route. Representing regulatory systems in terms of information flow enabled comparisons across alternative mutational histories, showing that regulatory architecture shapes how historical contingency affects a system’s capacity to preserve its ability to generate adaptive phenotypes as mutations accumulate, a property we define as resilience of evolutionary potential . Stochastic and statistical-physics modeling further identified resilience as an entropy-driven property of the logic of regulatory interactions. Together, our findings establish a framework for understanding how evolutionary potential is preserved during adaptation in this opportunistic pathogen.

Article.Title: DNA methylation profiling of immune cells identified large-scaled methylation changes associated with ITP in CVID
Article.Authors: Dubrowinskaja N.; Anim M.; Turmanov A.; Franke A.; Wittig M.; Witte T.; Sogkas G.; Atschekzei F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID) is the most frequent primary antibody deficiency in adults. It is characterized by recurrent infections and immune dysregulation, including autoimmune conditions such as immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). While genetic defects explain up to 30% of cases, most patients lack a clear monogenic cause, suggesting that epigenetic changes may contribute to disease development. Here, we present what is, to our knowledge, the first comprehensive genome-wide methylation profiling of B cells and CD4 + T cells from CVID patients with ITP but no known genetic defect. Using the Illumina EPIC 850 K array, we identify distinct methylation signatures in these patients compared to CVID patients with infection-only phenotypes and healthy controls. Our results reveal global hypomethylation, large-scale differentially methylated regions, and abnormalities in coding and non-coding genomic areas. Some changes affect immune regulation genes, potentially implicating epigenetic mechanisms in the development of autoimmunity. These findings suggest a link between extensive epigenetic alterations and CVID and ITP. Our work provides a foundation for understanding autoimmune mechanisms in CVID and reveals epigenetic markers that could represent potential diagnostic tools or therapeutic targets.

Article.Title: Vocal divergence accompanies auditory and neural changes in urban Eurasian tree sparrows
Article.Authors: Liu X.; Peng X.; Zhang T.; Zhuang C.; Wang Y.; Zhang G.; Liu J.; Zuo L.; Zhou J.; Liu J.; Sun Y.; Wang J.; Lei F.; Wang L.; Li D.
Article.Abstract: Urbanization elevates chronic anthropogenic noise that can mask acoustic communication, yet changes in vocal signals, auditory reception, and neural processing are rarely examined together. Here, we compared urban and rural populations of Eurasian tree sparrows ( Passer montanus ) in Shijiazhuang, China, integrating vocal acoustics, auditory brainstem responses (ABRs), external and inner-ear morphology, adult neurogenesis, and proteomic profiles of the caudomedial nidopallium (NCM). Urban and rural birds differed markedly in syllable composition, with only a subset of syllable types shared between habitats. Shared syllable types also showed syllable-specific acoustic differences between habitats, including higher peak frequencies and intensities in several urban syllable types. In parallel, urban birds exhibited selective reductions in ABR amplitudes, smaller ear apertures, and altered cochlear hair cell organization. At the neural level, urban birds showed evidence of reduced adult neurogenesis in both the lateral ventricle and NCM, alongside proteomic changes associated with stress responses, synaptic organization, and neuronal development. Together, these co-occurring patterns suggest that potential vocal compensation may be accompanied by sensory and neural constraints, although their consequences for signal perception and communication success remain untested. These findings highlight the importance of examining signal production, auditory reception, and neural processing together when evaluating responses to urban environments.

Article.Title: Structural and functional characterization of hemagglutinin E190D and Q226H minor variants in human H5N1 A/British Columbia/PHL-2032/2024
Article.Authors: Lin T.; Zhu X.; Santos J.; Wang S.; Babarinde S.; Yu W.; McBride R.; Paulson J.; Hensley S.; Wilson I.
Article.Abstract: In late 2024, an avian H5N1 influenza virus derived from clade 2.3.4.4b was isolated from a severe human infection in British Columbia (A/British Columbia/PHL-2032/2024), revealing a rare combination of substitutions E190D and Q226H as minor variants in the receptor-binding site (RBS). We recombinantly produced hemagglutinins (HA) harboring these mutations and conducted receptor-binding and structural analyses. The wild-type HA with hallmark residues E190 and Q226 retained strong binding to α2-3 N-linked glycans, whereas E190D and Q226H abolished binding to α2-3 N- and O-linked glycans and no switch to α2-6 sialosides. The bulkier H226 caused steric clashes within the RBS, whereas E190D eliminated a conserved hydrogen bond with Sia-1, disrupting receptor engagement. Although D190 and H226 in this isolate are deleterious to engagement with known glycan receptors and not compatible with human-to-human transmission, continued surveillance is essential to monitor any changes in key RBS residues in circulating H5N1 viruses.

Article.Title: CDK4-dependent phosphorylation of USP35 promotes the growth of ER+ breast cancer through the mTOR-SOX2 axis
Article.Authors: Wu T.; Huang J.; Liang S.; Shi D.; Chen J.; Lai J.; Chen J.; Shao J.; Lin R.; Wu G.; He L.; Gu H.; Cao J.
Article.Abstract: The majority of estrogen receptor-positive (ER + ) breast cancers are treated with endocrine therapy plus CDK4/6 or mTOR inhibitors, but resistance persists. Deubiquitinase USP35 overexpression promotes tumor growth, yet its regulation by post-translational modifications remains unknown. We showed that CDK4 phosphorylated USP35 at Ser982, which was critical for ER+ breast cancer cell growth in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, USP35 interacted with TSC2, Ser982 contributed to USP35-mediated reduction of TSC2 protein and its association with TSC1, thereby activating mTOR signaling. Elevated signaling upregulated SOX2, driving oncogenic effects. Importantly, the CDK4/6 or mTOR inhibitor effectively suppressed the growth of USP35-high ER+ breast cancer cells and tumors. Furthermore, the phospho-USP35 Ser982 was positively correlated with the phospho-4E-BP1 level in ER+ breast cancer tissues. Our findings uncover that CDK4/USP35/mTOR/SOX2 signaling axis promotes ER+ breast cancer progression. ER+ breast cancer with high phospho-USP35 S982 level might benefit from CDK4/6 or mTOR inhibitor-based therapies.

Article.Title: Mapping cellular senescence, cellular plasticity, and alveolar niche heterogeneity in human lung development
Article.Authors: Shaikh S.; Colon L.; Purkerson J.; Becker J.; Kaur G.; Misra R.; Jehrio M.; Huyck H.; Li D.; Königshoff M.; Mora A.; Rojas M.; Eickelberg O.; Ma Q.; Bar-Joseph Z.; Lugo-Martinez J.; Finkel T.; Pryhuber G.; Rahman I.
Article.Abstract: The lung undergoes extensive structural, cellular, and functional remodeling during postnatal development. While cellular senescence is increasingly recognized as a critical regulator of tissue homeostasis, injury responses, and repair, its role in normal human lung development and neonatal lung disease is not known. Here, we combined single-nucleus RNA sequencing with spatial multiplex protein profiling (Phenocycler/CODEX) to characterize senescence-associated features in pediatric lungs. We identified spatially restricted niches enriched for GLB1, p21, and GDF15 protein abundance. Despite the presence of these senescence-associated proteins, corresponding transcriptional senescence signatures were largely absent, suggesting a non-canonical, protein-dominant state consistent with physiological developmental senescence rather than classical stress-induced senescence. These niches are associated with disrupted alveolar development and reside within inflammatory and fibrotic microenvironments. Pseudotime trajectory and pathway enrichment analyses reveal altered epithelial fate progression, along with activation of stress- and SASP-associated signaling pathways. We propose that these senescence-associated niches function as spatially confined regulatory checkpoints that are transient during normal development but become aberrantly sustained in disease. Our findings establish a framework for understanding senescence as a spatially restricted, developmentally regulated process that shapes epithelial plasticity, and contributes to impaired alveolar maturation in bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Collectively, these results highlight the dual role of senescence in orchestrating normal lung development while promoting pathological remodeling when persistence of these programs is not properly resolved.

Article.Title: Physiologically realistic gamma activity produced in silico by weakening the PING attractor state
Article.Authors: Rich S.; Shriram T.; Prescott S.
Article.Abstract: Gamma frequency network oscillations produced in silico by the Pyramidal Interneuron Network Gamma (PING) mechanism are associated with a strongly attracting limit cycle. However, these rhythms are stronger and more stable than the transient gamma activity driven by sparse spiking observed in vivo. Here we describe biophysically motivated changes degenerately driving PING-motivated networks to produce more realistic gamma activity. Increased heterogeneity, synapse-like noise, and a depolarized chloride reversal potential each weaken the attractor represented by PING-driven activity, allowing instead for spontaneous and transient increases in gamma-band oscillatory power with weakly entrained excitatory cells. These features mirror an oscillatory return to a stable focus following noise-induced perturbations. Dynamical systems with both a stable focus and limit cycle are associated with Hopf bifurcations, which are present in PING-motivated models of reciprocally connected excitatory and inhibitory populations. We therefore propose a revised explanation for physiologically-realistic gamma activity retaining a key element of PING—strong reciprocal connections between excitatory and inhibitory neurons—but where biophysical phenomena bias the system towards damped oscillations rather than a stable limit cycle.

Article.Title: Mechanically-guided mesenchymal stem cell differentiation: a promising biophysical strategy for orthopedic regeneration
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Wang G.; Zhang Y.; Zheng J.; Cui H.
Article.Abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders often leave bone and cartilage incompletely restored. Mesenchymal stem cells offer regenerative potential, but their fate is strongly shaped by mechanical context. In this Review, we examine how tensile strain, compression, fluid shear, hydrostatic pressure and matrix mechanics are converted into signals that influence bone- and cartilage-forming programmes. We highlight how cell source, donor variability, loading dose and timing, three-dimensional culture and scaffold properties shape these responses, and discuss the barriers to translating mechanically guided strategies into reproducible, safe approaches for bone and cartilage regeneration.

Article.Title: Ascorbate availability shapes inflammatory and metabolic trajectories during endotoxemia
Article.Authors: Osaki T.; Yamada S.; Soma Y.; Togashi S.; Miyata S.; Yamada K.; Fujii J.; Sekine H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Ascorbate is widely regarded as an antioxidant modulator of inflammation, yet its role in determining systemic inflammatory fate remains unclear. Here we show that reduced physiological ascorbate availability reshapes lethal trajectories during endotoxemia. Using Akr1a- deficient mice, which have limited endogenous ascorbate biosynthesis, together with ex vivo–differentiated macrophages, we found that ascorbate availability during differentiation programs inflammatory responses. Akr1a- deficient mice exhibited markedly reduced survival and segregated into two distinct patterns: an early cytokine-driven collapse and a delayed metabolic failure characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and progressive organ injury. Multi-omics analyses revealed disrupted tricarboxylic acid cycle activity, impaired anaplerosis, and polyamine accumulation, particularly spermine. In macrophages, spermine suppressed nitric oxide production, whereas enhanced spermine oxidation was associated with acrolein-modified proteins in tissues and plasma. Ascorbate supplementation improved cytokine balance, metabolic resilience, and survival. These findings identify dysregulated polyamine oxidation as a candidate pathway associated with inflammatory and metabolic dysfunction, while impaired AKR1A-mediated aldehyde detoxification may also contribute to the observed aldehyde stress.

Article.Title: Age-associated structural decline is linked to arterial flow territories in the brain
Article.Authors: Hanford L.; Eshghi M.; Du J.; Buckner R.; Mair R.; Ge T.; Juttukonda M.; Salat D.
Article.Abstract: The effect of biological aging on brain structure is widespread and apparent. However, little is understood regarding which regions exhibit similarities in vulnerability, and what biological processes drive regional patterns of senescence-associated atrophy. Here, we investigate whether associations between age and brain structure exhibit distinct patterns of regional vulnerability, and if so, whether they are related to patterns of cerebral physiology which also show age-related decline. Using both data-driven and hypothesis-driven approaches, we identify recurring patterns of accelerated and delayed decline across the lifespan. Notably, the results mapped using unsupervised clustering methods mirror the organization of major arterial flow territories, supporting the idea that vascular architecture may contribute to the spatial organization of brain aging. These results provide support for future research to further link patterns of structural deterioration to physiological processes that may be useful for identifying ‘at risk’ individuals and developing novel therapeutics for neurodegenerative disorders.

Article.Title: Structural basis of the lobster carapace blue colour mediated by an HPR protein
Article.Authors: Cedri M.; Bansia H.; Amici A.; Ortore M.; McCarthy A.; Mueller-Dieckmann C.; Lingas R.; Durbeej B.; Raffaelli N.; Wang T.; des Georges A.; Cianci M.
Article.Abstract: The chemical basis underlying the dark blue colour of live H. americanus , known as the American lobster, is studied in evolutionary biology and in polyene physical chemistry. Carapace colouration is generated by the antioxidant astaxanthin bound within the carotenoprotein crustacyanin complexes. Here, we present the ex vivo structure of the most abundant α-crustacyanin and β-crustacyanin forms, determined respectively by cryo-electron microscopy and X-ray crystallography to a resolution of 2.75 Å. Our structural analysis reveals α-crustacyanin as an elongated arrangement of β-crustacyanin heterodimers tethered by a heptatricopeptide repeat (HPR) protein. In vitro complex formation between the β-crustacyanin unit and synthetic heptatricopeptides identifies the HPR protein, in concert with crustacyanins, as a contributor in tuning carapace colour. Overall, these results explain how nature adjusts the colour from one end of the visible spectrum to the other by exploiting the bathochromic shift of astaxanthin from its unbound red form (λ max = 478 nm) firstly to the β-crustacyanin vivid blue bound form (λ max = 591 nm), and then to the α-crustacyanin bound dark blue form (λ max = 631 nm).

Article.Title: Dynamic visualization of cell adhesion molecule interactions using reversible split-HaloTag labeling in living cells
Article.Authors: Allen J.; Zhao E.; Pandey A.; Chalkley O.; Sando R.; Zhou Q.
Article.Abstract: Critical for diverse cellular functions, cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) interact to transduce information from the external environment to drive coordinated intracellular responses. However, direct visualization of CAM interactions in living cells and organisms remains a major challenge. Recent developments in split-HaloTag technology present a promising strategy for chemical labeling of protein-protein interactions. Here, we apply this method to dynamically monitor CAM interactions in living HEK293T cells using split-HaloTag-CAM fusion proteins. With high specificity, we visualized trans-cellular interactions between known adhesion pairs natively found in neuronal and immunological synapses. To expand the system's versatility, we adapted a modified split-HaloTag component (cpHaloΔN272H) that enables reversible dye exchange and facilitates rapid time-lapse imaging of CAM interactions. Leveraging fluorogenic HaloTag dyes, split-HaloTag-CAMs measured the real-time disassembly and reassembly of Ca2+-dependent CAM junctions in live cells. These tools enabled imaging long-term changes in surface contacts mediated by CAM binding, thus providing a robust platform for dissecting the spatiotemporal dynamics of CAM interactions in cellular and organismal contexts.

Article.Title: Sympathetic beta adrenergic signaling supports macrophage recruitment through the tibia muscle vascular axis during regeneration
Article.Authors: Ouchi R.; Nishimura S.; Honda A.; Yoshimoto Y.; Koike H.; Oishi Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Macrophage recruitment is essential for skeletal muscle regeneration, yet the cellular sources that replenish macrophages in regenerating muscle remain incompletely understood. Here we show, in a mouse cardiotoxin-induced tibialis anterior muscle injury model, that adjacent tibial bone marrow contributes myeloid cells to regenerating muscle in association with a vascular route at the tibia-muscle interface. Congenic parabiosis showed that most leukocytes entering injured muscle were host-derived despite shared blood circulation. Local fluorescent labeling of tibial bone marrow cells, together with three-dimensional vascular imaging and fluorescent dextran perfusion, supported movement of tibial bone marrow-derived myeloid cells toward regenerating muscle through a vascular network. Single-cell transcriptomic and in vivo analyses identified early endothelial changes involving endothelial nitric oxide synthase and beta 2 adrenergic receptor. Beta-adrenergic blockade or sympathetic denervation reduced vascular dilation, macrophage recruitment, and muscle regeneration, supporting a role for sympathetic adrenergic signaling in this vascular response during muscle repair.

Article.Title: Multi-omics profiling reveals AR7 ameliorates rotenone-induced Parkinson’s disease via gut-serum-brain axis modulation
Article.Authors: Chen J.; Xie Z.; Zhang H.; Lin X.; Xing L.; Yasen A.; Rexiati M.; Yang Y.; Wang L.; Fu C.; Liu X.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder associated with metabolic disturbances and gut microbiota dysbiosis. However, the underlying molecular networks and therapeutic implications remain unclear. This study investigated rotenone-induced PD and the therapeutic potential of AR7 using an integrated multi-omics approach. Colon tissue, serum, and intestinal contents were analyzed by transcriptomics, metabolomics, and metagenomics, respectively. Transcriptomics showed upregulation of mitochondrial and oxidative stress-related genes ( Sod , Cox5 , Cox6 , Vdac1 , Sdhc ) and downregulation of Slc18a1 , indicating impaired oxidative phosphorylation and dopamine transport. Metabolomics revealed decreased trigonelline and isopentenyl pyrophosphate and increased hydroquinone and methylpicolinate, reflecting disrupted energy metabolism and oxidative stress. Metagenomic analysis revealed enrichment of Lactobacillus acidophilus and depletion of Akkermansia muciniphila . AR7 treatment altered microbial community composition, increasing the abundance of Streptomyces viridochromogenes , Prevotella salivae , and Paenibacillus algorifonticola . Integrated multi-omics analysis identified mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress as key processes associated with rotenone-induced PD, while oxidative phosphorylation and glutathione metabolism emerged as major pathways altered by AR7 treatment. AR7 treatment was also associated with improved metabolic homeostasis and changes in gut microbial composition. These findings provide insights into the potential involvement of the gut–serum–brain axis in rotenone-induced PD and support further investigation of AR7 as a potential therapeutic candidate.

Article.Title: Declining juvenile survival of Adélie penguins in Antarctica
Article.Authors: Barracho T.; Bardon G.; Choquet R.; Houstin A.; Winterl A.; Beaulieu M.; Blanchard P.; Cornet C.; Cristofari R.; Raclot T.; Richter S.; Chatelain N.; Courtecuisse J.; Brucker M.; Zitterbart D.; Lecomte N.; Le Bohec C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract As summer sea ice around Antarctica reaches record lows for the satellite era, quantifying the demographic response of polar species to such environmental changes becomes critical. To achieve this, synthesizing results across species’ ranges and elucidating the environmental factors driving population dynamics are key. Adélie penguins ( Pygoscelis adeliae ) are considered reliable indicators of changes in Antarctica, but the processes through which sea ice and other environmental factors shape their population dynamics are still unclear, especially for critical age groups such as juveniles. Using a 17-year dataset of Adélie penguins electronically tagged in Adélie Land (Antarctica), we found that juvenile survival probability (from fledging to age 2) was most strongly associated with sea ice concentration near the natal colony during the first months at sea, with lower ice concentrations corresponding to reduced survival. Importantly, we found that juvenile survival declined by 32% from 2007 to 2020, mirroring the declining trends already observed at other distant colonies. The emergence of similar patterns at opposite ends of the continent may be an early signal for shifts in population trends expected from climate change and should prompt an extensive demographic synthesis for this emblematic Antarctic species.

Article.Title: Serotype-dependent fusion loop and pr antibody profiles in primary dengue virus infections
Article.Authors: Duarte E.; Chapa M.; Bal A.; Lee N.; Sánchez San Martin C.; Verdolin Jr M.; Graber A.; Mercado-Hernandez R.; Zambrana J.; Kuan G.; Balmaseda Á.; Bos S.; Harris E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Dengue viruses (DENV1-4) are a leading cause of arboviral disease worldwide. Antibodies to pr and FL have been linked to antibody-dependent enhancement, yet their contribution to the cross-reactive response in polyclonal serum remains undefined. Here using recombinant antigens and a multiplexed serological assay with sera from the Nicaraguan Pediatric Dengue Cohort Study, we show that anti-pr responses are serotype-dependent in magnitude yet broadly cross-reactive among DENV1–4, with very limited ZIKV recognition. All primary DENV infections generated FL-reactive antibodies, but the E-FL fraction varied by infecting serotype and detection antigen, revealing asymmetric serotype-dependent shaping of cross-reactive responses. Interestingly, the greater the magnitude of cross-reactive E binding, the lower the proportion of FL-sensitive binding. These findings show that primary infection imprints serotype-specific patterns on cross-reactive antibody landscapes to dengue and Zika viruses that may influence subsequent infection outcomes.

Article.Title: Mechanical strength is a conserved SMC complex feature
Article.Authors: Richeldi M.; Tang M.; Bouchoux C.; Sakata R.; Kinoshita Y.; Nishiyama T.; Uhlmann F.; Molodtsov M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cohesin and condensin are members of the Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes (SMC) complex family, ring-shaped protein architects of higher-order eukaryotic chromatin structure. Cohesin rings encircle two replicated DNAs to counteract mitotic spindle forces during cell divisions. In the case of fission yeast cohesin, one ring withstands forces of ~20 pN before it breaks at its ‘hinge’ interface. Here, we investigate whether the strength of the ring is conserved amongst cohesins from different species, and between different members of the SMC family. We find that DNA-DNA interactions generated by fission yeast condensin withstand the same forces as fission yeast cohesin. Thus, their physical strength is a conserved feature amongst SMC complexes. Human cohesin in turn can withstand significantly greater forces than its fission yeast counterpart. Our results emphasise the importance of considering mechanical forces when studying the role of SMC complexes in chromosome organisation.

Article.Title: Anxiety phenotypes accompany reduced Htr2a expression in prelimbic parvalbumin neurons following chronic heat exposure
Article.Authors: Qi H.; Wang Y.; Wang Y.; Chen Y.; Dai A.; Yang S.; Li J.; Zeng Y.
Article.Abstract: Extreme heat is an increasingly important environmental stressor, but the neural alterations associated with sustained heat exposure remain poorly understood. Here we show that chronic heat exposure (36 °C, 4 h/day for 60 consecutive days) is associated with anxiety-like behaviors and altered local field potential and single-unit activity in the prelimbic cortex of male C57BL/6 mice. Optogenetic activation of parvalbumin-preferentially targeted prelimbic neurons ameliorates several behavioral alterations. Exploratory transcriptomic profiling indicates reduced Htr2a expression. Fiber photometry reveals altered local serotonin-related sensor responses and calcium responses in parvalbumin-preferentially targeted neurons. Htr2a overexpression in these targeted neurons shifts several behavioral and electrophysiological measures toward control levels. Together, these findings associate chronic heat exposure with altered prelimbic circuit activity, reduced Htr2a messenger RNA expression, and reduced serotonin 2A receptor immunoreactivity in parvalbumin-positive neurons, supporting a functional contribution of serotonin 2A receptor signaling to heat-associated anxiety-like behaviors.

Article.Title: Parallel ZNF598 and GIGYF2 pathways mediate conserved collision dependent mRNA decay with divergent endonucleolytic features
Article.Authors: Hashimoto S.; Sauerland J.; Zeng J.; Kikuguchi C.; Inada T.
Article.Abstract: Quality control of aberrant mRNAs is essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis, and ribosome collisions caused by translational stalling trigger surveillance pathways that eliminate faulty transcripts. In yeast, two major collision-responsive pathways, the Hel2-Cue2 pathway and the Syh1–Xrn1 pathway, act in parallel to degrade aberrant mRNAs. However, whether analogous mechanisms operate in mammals has remained unclear. Here we show that ZNF598 and GIGYF2 function in parallel to promote degradation of collision-inducing mRNAs in mammalian cells, with GIGYF2 making a stronger contribution. In contrast, N4BP2, the proposed mammalian counterpart of the yeast endonuclease Cue2, is dispensable for this decay. In yeast, we further reveal that distinct cleavage modes of Cue2 contribute differently to mRNA decay. Together, these findings uncover both conserved and divergent features of collision-dependent mRNA surveillance across species.

Article.Title: A phosphorylation-gated C-tail YxxΦ motif drives β-arrestin–independent parathyroid hormone receptor-1 internalization through AP2
Article.Authors: Höppner J.; Dean T.; Jüppner H.; Gardella T.
Article.Abstract: G protein–coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling is tightly regulated by intracellular trafficking, which shapes the timing, location, and magnitude of downstream responses. Although GPCR internalization is classically mediated by β-arrestins, evidence for alternative, β-arrestin–independent mechanisms has emerged. Here, we define β-arrestin–dependent as well as phosphorylation-gated, β-arrestin–independent pathways for internalization of the parathyroid hormone receptor-1 (PTH1R), a prototypical class B1 GPCR. Both pathways depend on adaptor protein 2 (AP2). In the absence of β-arrestins, PTH1R internalization requires a phosphorylated C-terminal tail, as disruption of GRK activity or mutation of C-tail phosphorylation clusters impairs this β-arrestin–independent pathway. We further identify a conserved tyrosine-based YxxΦ motif within the PTH1R C-tail that mediates phosphorylation-dependent AP2 recruitment. Mutation of this motif markedly impairs AP2 recruitment and delays receptor internalization. Notably, disruption of either the β-arrestin-dependent or independent pathway increases the dependence of receptor internalization on the other, revealing a compensatory relationship between the two mechanisms. Together, these findings support an internalization paradigm for PTH1R in which C-tail phosphorylation drives PTH1R endocytosis through either a canonical β-arrestin-mediated pathway or an alternative β-arrestin–independent, AP2-mediated pathway.

Article.Title: Insulin-independent glucose uptake into mouse skeletal muscle by a sodium/glucose linked transporter
Article.Authors: Norman N.; Radzyukevich T.; Chomczynski P.; Rymaszewski M.; Fokt I.; Priebe W.; Schmidt L.; Zhu T.; Mackenzie B.; Landero J.; Heiny J.
Article.Abstract: Exercise is a cornerstone therapy for diabetes because working skeletal muscles take up glucose at dramatically greater rates than postprandial uptake and, notably, do so without a requirement for insulin. Insulin-independent glucose uptake operates normally during exercise and other conditions when adrenergic stimulation inhibits pancreatic insulin release, and it provides a means of glucose disposal in insulin resistant conditions. However, the mechanisms of insulin-independent glucose uptake are not fully understood. Here, we describe a previously unrecognized glucose uptake pathway in muscle, which we refer to as mSGLT based on shared properties with the sodium/glucose cotransporter family (SGLT/Slc5a). Skeletal muscles do not express a full-length transcript of Slc5a2, and mSGLT shows weak affinity for SGLT2-specific inhibitors. mSGLT may be a muscle SGLT isoform. mSGLT and its regulation offer potential muscle-specific targets for treating hyperglycemia and conditions when insulin-stimulated glucose disposal into muscle is impaired.

Article.Title: Shared and distinct neural pathways of aversive and appetitive pain-related learning
Article.Authors: Li J.; Busch L.; Forkmann K.; Spisak T.; Kaur J.; Schlitt-Nguyen F.; Wiech K.; Schmidt K.; Bingel U.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Aversive and appetitive learning are central to adaptive behaviour, and pain and avoidance are powerful examples of such forces shaping human behaviour. Alterations in learning are thought to contribute to the development and maintenance of chronic pain, yet their neural underpinnings remain unclear. In this registered within-subject fMRI study (German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS-ID: DRKS00027448), we examined both aversive and appetitive pain learning during acquisition and extinction in 68 healthy individuals. Ratings confirm successful learning, with exploratory analyses suggesting stronger aversive acquisition and incomplete extinction. Both conditions engage the visual cortex during acquisition, with increased connectivity to the right operculum. Aversive acquisition further elicits stronger mediodorsal thalamus activity and heightened connectivity with the locus coeruleus, alongside sustained parahippocampal activation during extinction. Incomplete aversive extinction is linked to ongoing visual cortex activity during pain anticipation. Findings suggest shared neural substrates, but stronger aversive recruitment of rapid encoding and persistent memory systems.

Article.Abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-mediated type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling axis plays an essential role in antiviral defense, inflammation, autoimmunity, and cancer. Article.Title: Bomb-radiocarbon validated otoliths reveal 130-year lifespans and declining recruitment for blue sucker Cycleptus elongatus of the Upper Missouri River, Montana, USA
Article.Authors: Lackmann A.; Andrews A.; Holmquist L.; Haghipour N.; Grisak G.; Webb M.; Clark M.; Shattuck Z.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Validated age-based life history traits are crucial towards understanding the biological complexity of the natural world. The blue sucker Cycleptus elongatus is a migratory freshwater fish of the family Catostomidae native to North America. For decades, there has been conservation concern for the species across much of its range, including populations with skewed size distributions indicative of recruitment bottlenecks. Nonetheless, no validated age-based life history information exists for the species, which is a major knowledge gap. Using thin-sectioned otoliths validated by bomb radiocarbon dating we found that individual blue sucker often live more than 100 years, exhibit sexually-size dimorphic growth, increased fecundity with size, and spot-pigmentation with age. Across 42 individuals from the Upper Missouri River, Montana, we observed a maximum lifespan of 131 years, which is 70 years older than previously reported. Furthermore, 64–76% of individuals were from hatch years that pre-date the completion of Fort Peck Dam (1940), Canyon Ferry Dam (1954), and Tiber Dam (1956), which suggests recruitment failure is more likely in the post-dam era. Article.Title: Priming parallel fiber signals drive plasticity in the in vivo cerebellum
Article.Authors: Lin T.; Hansel C.
Article.Abstract: The cerebellar role in motor adaptation rests – according to the foundational theories of Marr and Albus – on the detection of (near)coincident activity between parallel fiber (PF) and climbing fiber (CF) inputs onto Purkinje cells. Supported by numerous in vitro studies, these theories predict synaptic adaptation based on temporal precision detected in time windows of ≤ 150 ms. These predictions have not been tested in intact animals. Using two-photon imaging from cerebellar Crus I in intact, awake mice, and dendritic calcium signals as a measure of PF response strength, we show here that coincident stimulation of PF and CF inputs does not readily initiate plasticity. Rather, long-term depression (LTD) is reliably evoked by prolonged constant or ramping PF activity that precedes a CF burst by 400 ms. Article.Authors: Yang Y.; Zhao Y.; Xie K.; Song C.; Huang Y.; Kong A.; Huang S.; Xing Z.; Wang W.; Muhlert N.; Elliott R.; Tan S.; He Z.; Zhang D.

Article.Authors: Li W.; Zhou X.; Zhang F.; Zhang L.; Wang S.; Shen W.; Xu H.; Ou X.; Sun Q.; Zhang W.; Zhao M.

Article.Title: Amyloid pathology compresses dynamic range and degrades spatial coding in an Alzheimer’s mouse model
Article.Authors: Go M.; Clarke K.; Li Y.; Prado S.; Teixeira B.; Gao M.; Yu J.; Schultz S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) disrupts neural circuits vital for memory and cognition. Using two-photon calcium imaging in behaving 5xFAD mice, we examined how amyloid pathology alters hippocampal CA1 activity and spatial coding. We found elevated baseline activity but reduced locomotion-driven firing, leading to a diminished neuronal dynamic range. To our knowledge, this is the first direct experimental evidence for reduced dynamic range in an AD model. These abnormalities were strongest near amyloid plaques and became more widespread with age. We also observed altered network synchrony, degraded spatial coding, and increased neuronal response variability. Furthermore, place fields emerged more slowly in both familiar and novel environments, indicating impaired recall and learning. By showing a link between local plaque pathology and impaired flexible modulation of CA1 activity and progressive deficits in spatial memory coding, our study offers new insights into the circuit basis of cognitive decline in AD.

Article.Title: Artificial skyglow at night disrupts chronobiology and physiology in Crassostrea gigas
Article.Authors: Botté A.; Payton L.; Geerebaert Y.; Tran D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Artificial skyglow at night (ASAN) is widespread in coastal environments, with consequences beginning to be highlighted but still understudied. Long-term ASAN field studies are needed to better understand the real challenge that nocturnal light poses to coastal organisms. To fill this gap, we investigated during one year in Arcachon Bay (France), ASAN’s impact on the oysters’ biological rhythms and major physiological parameters: behavior, growth, and gametogenesis. Results show that ASAN affects oysters’ behavioral valve activity rhythms, whether they are directly driven by light cycles (daily, lunar, and annual) or not (tidal and semi-lunar), suggesting a disruption of the oyster’s internal clock functioning. Our study also reveals that ASAN affects oyster physiology at the annual scale by inducing a phase advance in body weight and shell length growth, and gametogenetic cycle. These chronobiological and physiological effects of ASAN could lead to a disruption of the oyster’s fitness.

Article.Title: In planta-specific transcriptional regulatory circuit regulates expression of MoHTR1, a nuclear effector gene of Magnaporthe oryzae
Article.Authors: Yoon Y.; Lee H.; Kim S.; Chung H.; Khang C.; Lim Y.; Lee Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract During host-pathogen interactions, fungal pathogens secrete effectors into host cells to manipulate the host immune system and facilitate infection. Although many effector genes are highly expressed during infection stages, there is limited information on the mechanisms regulating their in planta expression. Here, we characterize the promoter of MoHTR1 , a nuclear effector gene of the rice blast pathogen, to elucidate its in planta -specific expression. Using promoter deletion and mutation analyses, we identified a core cis -element (TATTTCGT) within the MoHTR1 promoter, designated the in planta inducible (IPI) element, which is crucial for in planta -specific expression. The IPI element is responsible for the expression of not only MoHTR1 , but also Slp1 , a known effector gene. Furthermore, the IPI element enables the in planta expression of MobZIP14 , a gene specifically expressed during vegetative growth. The IPI element plays a critical role in fungal virulence by enabling MoHTR1 expression. Bioinformatic and DNA-protein interaction analyses revealed that RGS1, a transcription factor containing a winged-helix binding domain, acts as a transcriptional regulator of MoHTR1 by directly binding to the IPI element. Our findings provide insights into the regulatory mechanisms driving the in planta -specific expression of fungal effector genes.

Article.Title: Pesticide-exposed bees fail to thermoregulate leading to cold colonies with consequences for offspring development
Article.Authors: Storer K.; Hawthorne S.; Lovell C.; Mahmood F.; Kenna D.; Zhu T.; Graystock P.; Gill R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract For many organisms, effective thermoregulation is needed to cope with changing environmental temperatures. But if exposure to pesticides in the environment were to impair this homoeostatic process, reproduction and population viability could be at risk. Focusing on an important insect pollinator, we conducted three complementary experiments exposing bumblebees to a pesticide under different temperature challenges and measuring the impacts on thermoregulatory ability and brood development. First, we reveal that pesticide-exposed individuals (food spiked with a neonicotinoid insecticide) cannot maintain a stable thorax temperature, especially at lower temperatures. Second, that reductions in body temperature are accompanied by behavioural changes with pesticide-exposed colonies failing to maintain the brood temperatures that control bees achieved. Third, that such collective impairment of brood thermoregulation (not the pesticide toxicity to offspring per se) leads to delayed pupal development and reduced adult population growth. Our study provides a plausible mechanistic pathway for why terrestrial insects requiring brood thermoregulation may be vulnerable to decline. With frequent extreme weather events forecasted, our findings have concerning implications for how populations will adequately persist and grow under current pesticide-use regimes with ramifications for pollination services.

Article.Title: Hippocampal somatostatin neurons gate context generalization during fear memory updating
Article.Authors: Cano-Adamuz N.; de la Vega-Ruiz R.; Caro Martín A.; Montes-Mellado A.; Redondo Alañón C.; Hernández-Vivanco A.; Méndez P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Freezing is used as a readout of fear memory in rodents, but it remains unclear how distinct freezing features reflect discrimination and generalization of threatening and neutral contexts. Using pose-tracking and unsupervised analysis in male and female mice undergoing contextual fear conditioning, we show that fear in neutral a context is expressed through fragmented freezing that resist experience-dependent updating, in contrast with more sustained, uninterrupted, and adaptable freezing in a threatening context. Neuronal recordings revealed that recalling neutral context fear is associated with increased activity of dentate gyrus somatostatin inhibitory neurons (SST INs). Chemogenetic suppression of SST INs during fear memory updating selectively facilitated neutral context freezing adaptation while activation prevented generalization of contextual information by restricting long-term fear reduction in contexts that differed from the updating context. These findings identify DG SST INs as context-specific modulators of fear memory updating and suggest that freezing dynamics serve as a behavioral signature of generalization.

Article.Title: Loss of confidence in commercial antibody validation threatens biomedical research integrity
Article.Authors: Lim T.
Article.Abstract: Recent independent investigations conducted have identified thousands of apparently manipulated validation images across the online catalogues of more than a dozen commercial antibody suppliers. This points to a problem embedded in the antibody supply chain rather than at any single company. This represents a previously unaddressed entry point for unreliable data into biomedical research, upstream of the peer-review and image-integrity safeguards journals have put in place for manuscripts. This revelation has a profound impact on research data integrity and implications for data reproducibility across fields dependent on antibody specificity. This incident has put the spotlight on antibody suppliers to improve their processes to ensure properly validated products are being supplied to research labs.

Article.Title: E2F7 and E2F8 attenuate diabetic kidney disease by suppressing E2F1-induced tubular senescence
Article.Authors: Li Z.; Dai Y.; Liang D.; Xiao Y.; Hu L.; Wu X.; Feng Z.; Chen J.; Chen S.; Yuan Z.; Shi M.; Wang Y.; Liu L.; Chen P.; Jiang S.; Guo B.; Xiao Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Targeting cellular senescence represents a critical frontier for mitigating diabetic kidney disease (DKD), yet the transcriptional hierarchies governing renal senescence remain incompletely defined. Accordingly, in vivo knockdown of E2f1 significantly ameliorates DKD pathology. Mechanistically, resveratrol induces the expression of the atypical repressors E2f7 and E2f8. These repressors directly bind to the E2F1 promoter region to repress its transcription, thereby abrogating E2f1-mediated cellular senescence. Article.Title: A covariance-aware variational generative model preserving gene correlation structure in single-cell transcriptomic data
Article.Authors: Lomas Redondo A.; Sánchez Velázquez J.; JSánchez-Arévalo Lobo V.
Article.Abstract: Measuring gene activity in individual cells reveals the diversity within tumors but is costly, technically noisy, and often captures too few rare cells. Explicitly modeling correlations within the model’s compressed description of each cell does not improve preservation of gene-gene relationships over a simpler matched model, which appears to capture this structure implicitly. Nevertheless, the model’s sampling strategy yields cells that faithfully reproduce gene activity patterns, cell-type markers, and cellular organization and compare favorably with established methods. The model trains 100 to 1,000 times faster than a diffusion-based alternative. Synthetic cells blend with real data and support standard analyses, including reconstruction of a precancerous transition. These findings support using synthetic cells to enrich rare populations, benchmark methods, and simulate transitional states in tumors.

Article.Title: Membrane-coupled conformational switching of VISTA regulates CC′ loop accessibility and immune checkpoint signaling
Article.Authors: Ganesan A.; Reddy V.; Ly N.
Article.Abstract: V-domain immunoglobulin suppressor of T-cell activation (VISTA) is an immune checkpoint that suppresses T-cell responses and has emerged as a promising target for cancer immunotherapy. Principal component analysis and conformational clustering reveal a recurrent rotational motion of the extracellular domain relative to the membrane, producing two conformational states: an “Up” state with a solvent-exposed CC′ loop and a “Down” state in which the loop transiently associates with the membrane. These transitions are coupled to proline-mediated bending of the transmembrane helix. We propose that this membrane-coupled Up/Down switching regulates CC′ loop accessibility, providing a structural mechanism that may influence VISTA-mediated immune checkpoint signaling.

Article.Title: Multi-omics analyses reveal dynamic interactions between DNA methylation and transcriptional regulation during black raspberry ripening
Article.Authors: Hsieh W.; Hung Y.; Zhang J.; Cui Q.; Chen H.; Lin L.; He M.; Wang Y.; Ho Y.; Ballington J.; Fernandez G.; Perkins-Veazie P.; H. Le B.; Li X.; Hsieh T.; Lin J.

Elevated non-CG methylation in heterochromatin coincides with increased transcription of histone variants mediating chromatin compaction, suggesting chromatin remodelers fine-tune accessibility for methyltransferases. Article.Title: Isofalcarintriol ameliorates gestational diabetes mellitus-induced β-cell dysfunction by targeting MIF to enhance mitophagy
Article.Authors: Wang N.; Liu X.; Gao Z.
Article.Abstract: Insulin resistance and pancreatic β-cell dysfunction are closely associated with impaired mitophagy, forming a core pathological mechanism in gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Mechanistically, IFT promotes the dissociation of macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) from ubiquitin-specific protease 7 (USP7) through its C224 residue, and induces MIF ubiquitination through F50/L59 residues, thereby driving the phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN)-induced kinase 1 (PINK1)/Parkin-mediated mitophagy and pancreatic injury recovery. A mitophagy inhibitor eliminates the beneficial effects of IFT, while PINK1 knockdown reverses the mitophagy-promoting effect induced by MIF knockdown. Article.Title: Interpreting NADH fluorescence lifetime across timescales
Article.Authors: Ferri G.; Cardarelli F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract NADH fluorescence lifetime imaging is a widely used, label-free way to visualize cell metabolism, typically read as a balance between glycolysis and oxidative respiration. This reading assumes that the effective NADH-binding landscape remains sufficiently stable during the experiment. This assumption is generally best protected during brief perturbations, but can fail in two ways: slowly, as prolonged treatments or differentiation reshape the identity and abundance of NADH-binding enzymes over hours to days; and rapidly, as metabolites can transiently alter their engagement with NADH even without changes in protein abundance. In this Perspective, we outline when each concern applies and offer practical guidance for experimental design and interpretation.

Article.Authors: Luo S.; Angrick M.; Coogan C.; Candrea D.; Wyse-Sookoo K.; Schippers A.; Ganji R.; Milsap G.; Anderson W.; Gordon C.; Tippett D.; Maragakis N.; Clawson L.; Vansteensel M.; Tenore F.; Hermansky H.; Fifer M.; Ramsey N.; Crone N.

Article.Authors: Yoshimoto R.; Sakurai L.; Florece A.; Yoshitane H.; Horie K.; Kitagawa H.; Sakurai T.
Article.Abstract: Aging alters daily physiology, but how these changes relate to remodeling of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) remains incompletely understood. Article.Title: Altered developmental profile of the head-direction signal in a rat model of fragile X syndrome
Article.Authors: Moore N.; Duszkiewicz A.; Asiminas A.; Dudchenko P.; Peyrache A.; Wood E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Fragile X Syndrome is a common inherited, monogenic cause of intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder, but the altered neural mechanisms underlying it remain unclear. Article.Authors: Yoshimura T.; Nakayama K.; Asato K.; Noda Y.; Fujimoto H.; Nakagawa Y.; Legrand J.; Ikeda M.; Sasaki T.
Article.Abstract: Direct empirical evidence regarding the reproductive biology and trophic strategies of ancient freshwater invertebrates remains scarce due to the typical loss of internal anatomical and dietary records. Here, we report an exceptionally preserved assemblage of the freshwater snail 'Viviparus' sp. from the Lower Cretaceous (c. 120 Ma) Kitadani Formation, central Japan. High-resolution X-ray micro-computed tomography and microfossil extraction reveal key ecological adaptations: obligate ovoviviparity with up to 16 embryonic shells showing an axial developmental size gradient within the maternal body whorl, female-biased sexual size dimorphism, and continuous indeterminate growth. This high-fidelity preservation-retaining delicate embryonic shells, intact protoconchs, and organic residues-is linked to a distinctive taphonomic window, wherein alkaline ash from palaeo-wildfires is inferred to have buffered ambient freshwater acidity, mitigating post-mortem carbonate dissolution. Our findings demonstrate that modern-type viviparid reproductive and feeding adaptations were already established by the Early Cretaceous, illustrating how wildfire-mediated geochemical buffering can preserve rare biological records in Mesozoic limnic ecosystems.

Article.Abstract: Eco-evolutionary feedbacks can alter species traits and reshape ecological networks, influencing network resilience to disturbance. We find that weak trait directionality, high functional turnover and variability, and strong resilience are tightly linked. Coupled ecological and evolutionary processes favour trait matching and generate both nested and modular network structures. Article.Title: Dynamic climate and ecological expansion drive body morphology evolution in fossil and extant neocoleoid cephalopods
Article.Authors: Wang C.; Fang Z.; Liu B.; Ding Z.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: Cephalopods originated in the Cambrian approximately 500 million years ago, evolving from externally shelled ancestors to forms with diverse morphologies. Article.Abstract: Breast cancer often returns or spreads after treatment, and therapies that can destroy tumors while also engaging the immune system are urgently needed. Article.Abstract: Discrete data are prevalent across biology, from nucleotide base pairs to mating systems or petal count on a flower. Here, using an impinging flow device compatible with videomicroscopy, we demonstrate that exposure of two EC types to SSG causes an immediate and sustained two-fold decrease in migration speed, accompanied by enhanced coordination of collective motion and directional migration against the flow. Mechanistically, FAK-mediated mechanotransduction governs flow-opposed migration, whereas the time-dependent increase in traction depends on TGF-β1 signaling and actomyosin contractility. Together, these findings identify SSG as key regulators of EC mechanics, collective dynamics, and signaling, with important implications for vascular disease diagnostics and therapeutics.

Article.Title: Transcriptomic and proteomic analysis of quiescent epimastigotes as a resource for investigating Trypanosoma cruzi persistence
Article.Authors: Olmo F.; Hesketh A.; Hage H.; Monneuse J.; Taylor M.; Costa F.; Da Silva C.; Bequet F.; Escudié F.; Mercer D.; Saliou A.; Chatelain E.; Kelly J.; Abi-Ghanem J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chagas disease is caused by infection with the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi . Despite triggering a strong immune response, infections are typically life-long and can result in severe cardiac and/or digestive tract pathology. Current drugs have limited efficacy, and treatment failure is a common outcome. Eliminating a non-replicating T. cruzi sub-population that can persist after therapy has been a key challenge for the drug-development community. Here, we describe the transcriptome and proteome profiles of a low-proliferative sub-population of epimastigote forms of the parasite isolated from exponentially growing cultures on the basis of reduced turnover of transiently-induced red fluorescent protein. This partially quiescent sub-population was characterised by down-regulation of genes/proteins involved in translation, transcription, metabolism, mitochondrial function and DNA replication, and by up-regulation of proteins that promote exit from the cell cycle in other organisms. These data provide a resource that can be exploited to dissect the mechanistic basis of quiescence, as a step towards refining the drug-development screening cascade.

Article.Title: Mathematical and experimental models of interactions among subclones and immunity in melanoma
Article.Authors: Hirsch M.; Ergun J.; Chin S.; Graff C.; Yee D.; Perez-Guijarro E.; Merlino G.; Day C.; Przytycka T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Melanoma tumors often contain heterogeneous subclones, typically with proliferative or invasive phenotypes. These subclones interact with each other and the immune system to shape tumor progression. In the experimental models, admixtures of proliferative and invasive subclones of varying proportions were implanted into immunocompromised and immunocompetent mice. Tumor growth and subclone composition were tracked over time. In parallel, we built a computational model to capture the system dynamics. By estimating parameter values of our mathematical model using experimental measurements, we found that, while the proliferative subclone outgrew the invasive subclone, T cell activities selected for the invasive subclone. Initial subclonal proportion in this dynamic system determines the overall tumor sensitivity to immune response. The key interactions identified in this study provide insights into how intratumor heterogeneity and immune pressure influence melanoma progression, suggesting strategies for optimizing individualized therapy.

Article.Authors: Huang R.; Jiang J.; Liu J.; Zhang C.; Wang H.; Zhang X.; Wang H.; Liu Y.
Article.Abstract: Individuals often rely on friends’ advice when making mate-choice decisions under uncertainty, yet how such advice is integrated into decision-making remains unclear. Both conditions elicited enhanced interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), linked to risk evaluation, and in the left superior and middle temporal gyri (l-STG, l-MTG), associated with semantic processing and value transformation. Machine learning analyses showed that task-level INS robustly forecasted overall advice influence. Article.Authors: Bai B.; Ge G.; Qiu R.; Bao J.; Liu M.; Zhao M.; Ma W.; Sheng P.; Jia Y.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: In this study, to address the problems of poor silage fermentation quality and difficulty degrading lignocellulose interfering with resource utilization of Caragana korshinskii biomass, the effects of extrusion pretreatment (temperature 140°C and screw speed of 400 rpm) on its ensiling process were investigated. Article.Authors: Sun I.; Gregory D.; Abd-Elmoniem N.; Patel M.; Casalvera A.; Gura H.; Rodriguez C.; Brighter G.; Rueda Mora S.; Chandrashekar S.; Makhoul W.; Lynch K.; Oathes D.; Sheline Y.; Balderston N.

Whole-brain analyses revealed significant session-dependent attenuation of bilateral putamen deactivation during the retention interval in both stimulation groups, with greater putamen deactivation at baseline correlating negatively with working memory accuracy. These results demonstrate that individualized task-based fMRI targeting can link TBS to circuit-level behavioral change, and that downstream subcortical responses may be more sensitive indices of TBS effects than activation at the stimulation site. Article.Authors: Mandino F.; Shen X.; Horien C.; Papademetris X.; Strittmatter S.; Keilholz S.; Xu N.; Lake E.
Article.Abstract: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) captures whole-brain activity fluctuations non-invasively in humans and animals. Beyond task/stimuli-locked responses, fMRI measures large-scale patterned activity during rest. Among these, quasi-periodic patterns (QPPs) represent recurring waves of activity that unfold over seconds and exhibit consistent spatiotemporal characteristics. Notably, certain fMRI-QPPs are well-preserved across species and altered in various neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases. Yet, our collective understanding of their neural underpinnings is limited given the indirect nature of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) fMRI signal. Simultaneous measures of local field potentials have provided some affirmation that fMRI-QPPs have neural origins, but these point-measurements are limited to a handful of sites. Here, we use a unique multimodal implementation of simultaneous wide-field calcium (WF-Ca 2+ ) imaging and fMRI to investigate the neural origins of fMRI-based QPPs. We uncover a robust time-locked correlation between QPPs detected by cortex-wide fluorescent WF-Ca 2+ imaging of neural activity and QPPs of BOLD-fMRI. These data validate the hypothesis that BOLD-fMRI QPPs derive from preceding slow waves of neural activity with regional and temporal precision.

These durable, pathway-specific imprints persist in the absence of active task engagement, suggesting a reorganization of the brain’s memory circuitry.

Article.Abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are a leading cause of mortality worldwide and heart failure remains an end-stage disease with no other treatment than transplantation. Skeletal muscle progenitors have been extensively studied as a source of cardiac cells, due to their cellular and functional similarities. We consistently found that stem cells from masticatory muscles are unable to differentiate into cardiac cells under any tested cardiogenic environment. Furthermore, pharmacological erasing of repressive epigenetic marks did not activate cardiogenic potential, suggesting that barriers restraining lineage plasticity are profound and unlikely to be reversed by simple exposure to cardiogenic environments.

Article.Authors: Liu W.; Tao X.; Fan S.; Li X.; Liu Z.; Zhang H.; Li J.; He W.; Zhang D.; Zhang T.; Zhang T.; Pang X.; Yang Z.; Ma B.; Xiang H.; Yu L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Aglycones, the bioactive metabolites of C– glycosides, can be obtained through the deglycosylation of naturally abundant C– glycosides. However, C– glycosides are more resistant to enzymatic and chemical degradation. Gut microbiota and its enzymes are known to cleave the C–C glycosidic bond, but only a limited number of active strains and functional enzymes have been identified. Here we show that a new C– deglycosylation gene cluster encoding the g lycoside- m etabolizing e nzyme from La chnospiraceae (LaGME), an enzyme complex consisting of a C – g lycoside o xidoreductase (LaCGO1) and a C – g lycoside e limination enzyme complex (LaCGE), was discovered using the DUF6379 domain-containing protein as a probe. LaGME demonstrates significant activities toward xanthone-type and flavone-type C– glycosides. After investigation into heterologous expression, structural determination and catalytic mechanism, a LaGME-mediated one-pot cascade enzymatic reaction system was developed for green production of aglycones. This research provides an approach to uncover C– glycoside-metabolizing enzymes in nature, as well as a preliminary basis for the sustainable production of value-added bioactive aglycones from glycosides.

Article.Title: Analysis of 515 human proteomes defines plasma extracellular vesicle core composition, corona and coisolated networks

Article.Abstract: Abstract Plasma extracellular vesicles (EVs) are promising liquid biopsy biomarkers, yet their proteomic profiling remains confounded by massive co-isolation. Here, we resolve this heterogeneity through a meta-analysis of 515 human plasma EV proteomes. We demonstrate that the reproducible core proteome is overwhelmingly governed by predictable, surface-charge-driven mass-action that dynamically mirrors synthetic nanoparticle corona formation. By quantitatively decomposing the core isolate against pan-synthetic coronas and agonist-induced platelet EVs, we trace the core isolate to three main mechanistic origins: an electrostatic plasma corona, ex vivo platelet vesiculation and biological macromolecular co-isolates. Crucially, the residual vesicular cargo strongly correlates with thrombin-induced platelet degranulation, indicating that phlebotomy-induced trauma contribute to the bulk signal. We provide a modular atlas that mathematically distinguishes biophysical coronas from these cellular co-isolates, establishing a new framework for interpreting biological origin in plasma EV proteomics.

Article.Title: Tamoxifen targets Wisp2 to impair subcutaneous adipocyte progenitor self-renewal and adipogenic differentiation

Article.Abstract: Breast cancer endocrine therapy, including tamoxifen, systemically disrupts estrogen receptor signaling and increases type 2 diabetes (T2D) risk in women. Hyperplastic adipose tissue expansion, especially in subcutaneous depots, facilitates nutrient storage and attenuates inflammation during a chronic positive energy balance and is impaired in the absence of estrogen. Adipocyte progenitors are renewed through Wnt signaling pathway activation, however the the mechanisms that explain the depletion of these cells during endocrine therapy are not defined. Here we show the direct impact of tamoxifen on proliferation, renewal, and differentiation in subcutaneous adipose stromal cells from humans and adult mice. In obesity, the Wnt1 inducible signaling pathway protein 2 (Wisp2) was lost in adipocyte progenitors following endocrine therapy. Wisp2 gain and loss of function studies defined the link between estrogen signaling and adipocyte progenitor maintenance. Article.Title: Assessing whole-cortex excitability from electromagnetic brain signals
Article.Authors: Pellegrino G.; Duma G.; Schuler A.; Daub M.; Marinazzo D.; Arcara G.; Soddu A.; Rasero J.
Article.Abstract: Cortical excitability is a core feature of brain function shaped by microcircuitry, large-scale networks, and neurochemistry. In humans, it can be inferred from indirect electrophysiological measures, yet it remains unclear whether these capture a single construct or multiple processes. We systematically compared established excitability metrics using whole-head magneto-encephalography (MEG) recorded at rest and during 40 Hz auditory stimulation in a large sample of healthy adults. These measures included stimulus-driven synchronization, spectral power, aperiodic (1/f) activity, signal complexity, long-range temporal correlations, and phase–gamma synchronization. Hierarchical clustering identified six distinct excitability dimensions with limited redundancy, indicating that cortical excitability is inherently multidimensional. Aperiodic and alpha-band measures were strongly coupled and most spatially aligned with stimulus responses, while temporal, complexity, and synchronization metrics were largely independent. Regional differences were most pronounced in integrative and internally oriented areas. Each dimension also related differently to cortical morphology and neurotransmitter receptor density, highlighting diverse neurobiological substrates and supporting multimodal approaches to studying excitability.

Article.Abstract: Homologous recombination (HR) is a critical repair pathway involving numerous proteins that ensure error-free DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) repair. This study presents a comprehensive biophysical analysis of the RAD51–BRC repeats interaction, integrating computational and experimental approaches. Starting with assessing the correlation between the binding affinities of individual BRC repeats and their impact on RAD51 disassembly, our investigation extends to larger BRCA2 truncations, offering unprecedented insights into the molecular determinants of RAD51 recognition. Article.Abstract: Wnt signaling is essential for embryonic development and adult tissue homeostasis, and its dysregulation contributes to cancer and other human diseases. Article.Authors: Jiao Y.; Zhang H.; Xie X.; Pi M.; Fu Q.; Zhu W.; Song J.; Bo J.; Zhang T.; Chen M.; Gu X.; Ma Z.
Article.Abstract: Sepsis often leads to multiple organ failure, but how injury in one organ propagates to another remains poorly understood. Article.Abstract: Abstract Complex ecological and evolutionary patterns shaped the rich biodiversity of the Neotropics. Article.Authors: Zhu Q.; Fan L.; Wu Y.; An S.; Li Y.; Wang H.; Yao N.; Li Y.; Huang Z.

The cortical expression of LC structure-function tethering exhibits a network-level hierarchy and aligns with a behavioral axis. The second phase introduces health-associated Lactobacillus species selected for their acidification capacity, competitive fitness, and ability to stabilize the mucosal environment. Supported by the Galaxy and global microbiology communities, this platform integrates over 315 tool suites and 115 curated workflows, enabling comprehensive metabarcoding, (meta)genomic, (meta)transcriptomic, and (meta)proteomic data analysis within a FAIR-aligned environment. It also supports research in the health and infectious disease sectors, as well as in environmental microbiology. The platform’s utility is exemplified through various use cases, including antimicrobial resistance tracking, biomarker prediction, microbiome classification, and functional annotation of key microbes. Built on reproducibility and community engagement, it supports the creation, sharing, and updating of best-practice workflows. Over 35 tutorials and learning paths empower scientists, fostering an ecosystem that keeps resources at the forefront of microbiological data analysis. The MGL enables collective analysis, democratising research, thereby accelerating discovery across the global microbiology community ( microbiology.usegalaxy.org , .eu , .org.au , . fr ).

Genetic disruption of BdCDPK5 caused long-term growth arrest and pronounced morphological defects, whereas its ectopic expression promoted parasite replication. Localization analyses further revealed BdCDPK5 to be diffusely distributed throughout the parasite cytoplasm and associated with vesicle-like structures within infected erythrocytes. Article.Title: Developmental and genetic modulation of evidence integration dynamics in zebrafish sensorimotor decision-making
Article.Authors: Garza R.; El Hady A.; Bahl A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Animals integrate information over time and maintain persistent internal representations of cues to guide decision-making. How the underlying behavioral algorithms of individual animals depend on factors such as experience, developmental stage, or genotype remains poorly understood. Drift-diffusion models provide a powerful theoretical framework to describe and predict performance metrics across a wide range of species. The stochastic nature of these models and the typically limited throughput of most experimental designs challenge the automatic inference of latent variables. Here, we combine high-throughput behavioral assays in larval zebrafish with drift-diffusion modeling, revealing that larvae progressively develop more persistent, self-reinforcing integration dynamics during early development. This effect is reduced in fish carrying mutations in genes linked to human epilepsy and schizophrenia. Our results show that behavior-based drift-diffusion modeling can offer a scalable, automated approach to generate experimentally testable hypotheses about the algorithmic implementation of sensorimotor integration in health and disease.

Article.Title: Mercury contamination impairs the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis of a neotropical caiman
Article.Authors: Lemaire J.; Mangione R.; Loveland J.; Fusani L.; Canoine V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The capacity to regulate corticosterone release following a stressful event is an essential component of the physiological flexibility required to maintain homeostasis and ensure adaptive responses to environmental change. We show that wild smooth-fronted caimans with elevated blood mercury (Hg) concentrations exhibited reduced peak corticosterone levels during standardized stress tests, indicating a dampened maximal stress response. Hg blood concentrations were negatively correlated with corticosterone responsiveness, suggesting impairment of hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis function. These results demonstrate that environmental Hg contamination is associated with reduced stress responsiveness and physiological flexibility, which likely limits the ability of Hg-contaminated individuals to cope with novel environmental stressors. We found that a methylmercury-sensitive cysteine in the glucocorticoid receptor is highly conserved across vertebrates, suggesting a shared molecular mechanism for mercury effects on glucocorticoid signaling. Article.Title: PDE10A identified by cross-hemisphere visual cortex proteomics restores adult ocular dominance plasticity involving cAMP/CREB signaling
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Zhu Z.; Xu J.; Dong S.; Mo E.; Li Q.; Li Z.; Zhao Y.; Chang P.

Article.Title: Crocin alleviates renal fibrosis through inhibiting mitochondrial dysfunction via regulating HOXD8/PGC‑1α pathways
Article.Authors: Li X.; Ma T.; Han X.; Hai S.; Yin L.; Wang L.; Wang J.; Li H.; Yang Q.; Guan X.; Li Y.; Ding H.
