We show in 450,000 3D axon reconstructions from male rats that—despite this individual variation—axon bundles possess stable radius distributions at the ensemble level. These distributions are faithfully captured by 2D cross-sections and yield robust conduction velocity predictions, as along-axon variability has only a modest effect. Conduction in large axons is particularly stable, supporting time-critical signaling. Article.Authors: Aceves V.; Xu Z.; Zhang C.; Kim J.; Ito J.; Mathers K.; Lassar A.; Liu Z.; Gray R.

EC-to-SMC-like transitions were more prominent in females, whereas EC-to-adipocyte-like transitions were more prominent in males. Regulatory network analysis using pySCENIC implicated Klf2 and Creb5 in EC fate decisions. These findings reveal sex-specific EC-lineage trajectories associated with distinct plaque phenotypes and nominate candidates for sex-informed therapeutic investigation.

Article.Title: Quantitative imaging supports that endoskeletal mineralization in sharks is an adaptive trait
Article.Authors: Winkel E.; Hansen K.; Krøjer Westh C.; Nielsen J.; Rask Møller P.; Lauridsen H.
Article.Abstract: Modern sharks (Selachimorpha) exhibit a broad suite of adaptations that enable them to inhabit diverse marine environments. Notably, their cartilaginous endoskeleton displays varying degrees of mineralization, potentially reflecting adaptations for buoyancy, locomotion, and feeding. Here, quantitative computed tomography was applied to assess endoskeletal mineralization in representatives from all nine orders of sharks spanning 26 out of 35 families. Our findings reveal that skeletal mineralization is highly variable between species and is more closely associated with ecological factors such as depth distribution, than with phylogenetic relationship. We find that deeper-dwelling species generally exhibit lower degrees of mineralization, suggesting adaptations for buoyancy regulation and energy conservation. Our study provides insight into the variation of skeletal mineralization in the ecology and evolution of sharks.

Article.Title: Directed differentiation with mechanical simulation enhances alveolar-like features in human pluripotent stem cell-derived lung epithelium
Article.Authors: Song Y.; Newton J.; Abedi K.; Toukan S.; Zhang J.; Lam T.; Yang S.; Yang J.; Salih R.; Kanagarajah K.; Young E.; Wong A.
Article.Abstract: Human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived lung models remain limited by inefficient progenitor specification and incomplete alveolar maturation. Here, we present a robust and scalable differentiation strategy that reproducibly generates high-purity ( > 85%) fetal lung progenitors without cell sorting. These cells form distal bud tip organoids that recapitulate human fetal late tip and late stalk epithelial populations with multilineage potential. We show that direct co-culture with human lung fibroblasts, combined with Notch inhibition, promotes efficient differentiation toward fetal AT1- and AT2-like epithelial states, supported by transcriptional, protein, and ultrastructural analyses. Importantly, paracrine signaling alone is insufficient, highlighting a requirement for direct epithelial–mesenchymal interaction. We further integrated a microfluidic air-liquid interface culture system incorporating cyclic stretch. Under these conditions, we observed activation of mechanotransduction-associated and developmental signaling programs together with structural and transcriptional changes consistent with more mature alveolar-like epithelial states. This platform establishes a physiologically relevant model for human alveologenesis and provides a foundation for disease modeling and regenerative applications.

Article.Title: Targeting central thalamus with transcranial ultrasound reduces arousal in healthy volunteers
Article.Authors: Hopkins A.; Cain J.; White E.; Abakians S.; Monti M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Using low-intensity focused transcranial ultrasound stimulation, we test the causal roles of the central thalamus in arousal and the pulvinar in visuospatial attention in the healthy human brain. In a within-subjects, counterbalanced design, 27 healthy volunteers (two females) complete a vigilance task (Psychomotor Vigilance Task) and a visuospatial attention task (Egly-Driver Task) before and after sham, central thalamic, and pulvinar sonication. Targeting the central thalamus slows responses and increases lapses in attention during the vigilance task, indicating reduced arousal. Pulvinar sonication reduces (and slows) responses to visual stimuli presented contralaterally, suggesting a disruption of contralateral visuospatial attention. These results provide causal evidence linking the pulvinar to visuospatial attention and the central thalamus to arousal in the healthy human brain and demonstrate that ultrasound can elicit distinct behavioral changes in healthy volunteers when delivered to close but functionally distinct thalamic regions, underscoring its potential as a tool for noninvasive brain mapping.

Article.Title: Whole brain modeling reveals subtype specific regulation for adolescent major depressive disorder
Article.Authors: Zeng X.; Zhang G.; Wang F.; Xiong Y.; Zhang T.; Zhou C.; Biswal B.; Yao D.; Guo D.
Article.Abstract: Adolescent major depressive disorder exhibits substantial intrinsic subtype heterogeneity, necessitating the development of subtype-specific therapeutic strategies. Using the Boston Adolescent Neuroimaging of Depression and Anxiety dataset, we identified two subtypes with distinct clinical features. For each subtype, we constructed a whole-brain model and performed virtual stimulation to assess regulatory effects at global (whole-brain) and regional (classical depression-related targets) levels. Here we show that the two subtypes require different but stable stimulation modalities, excitatory or inhibitory, to normalize brain activity. Optimal stimulation intensities for restoring static and dynamic features vary across targets and subtypes, whereas the stimulation modality remains consistent within each subtype. Notably, localized stimulation of subtype-specific targets within classical depression-related regions produces more effective and stable outcomes than whole-brain stimulation. These findings provide a computational framework for identifying subtype-specific regulatory strategies in adolescent major depressive disorder, bridging whole-brain modeling with potential clinical translation.

Article.Title: A glutamatergic projection from the central medial thalamic nucleus to the red nucleus regulates states of consciousness during sevoflurane anesthesia in mice
Article.Authors: Dai X.; Wu J.; Liu L.; Song W.; Wu H.; Gao S.; Zhang L.; Liu D.; Zhou Y.; Tian B.; Zhang P.; Chen S.; Chen D.; Zhang P.; Mei W.; Tang Z.
Article.Abstract: General anesthetics like sevoflurane are clinically essential, yet the neural circuits governing their induction of unconsciousness and recovery remain incompletely defined. Here, we show the potential involvement of the vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (Vglut2)-expressing glutamatergic neurons in the central medial thalamus (CMT Vglut2 neurons) in modulation states of consciousness under sevoflurane anesthesia. Results show that CMT Vglut2 neuron activity revealed a reduction during the loss of consciousness and a subsequent elevation upon recovery of consciousness under sevoflurane anesthesia. Chemogenetic activation of CMT Vglut2 neurons delays induction and hastened recovery from sevoflurane anesthesia. Moreover, during sustained sevoflurane anesthesia at steady state, optogenetic activation of CMT Vglut2 neurons facilitates cortical activation and behavioral recovery. During burst suppression under sevoflurane, this stimulation elicits cortical arousal and declines the burst-suppression ratio. Conversely, inhibiting CMT Vglut2 neurons via chemogenetic or optogenetic methods produces greater sensitivity to sevoflurane anesthesia and deepens cortical suppression, respectively. Monosynaptic connections from CMT Vglut2 neurons to red nucleus glutamatergic neurons (RN Vglut2 neurons) are identified using combined retrograde and anterograde tracing. During sevoflurane anesthesia, optogenetic activation of CMT Vglut2 -RN terminals triggers cortical activation. Overall, these findings identify the CMT Vglut2 -RN pathway as a neural circuit regulating cortical activation and behavioral arousal under various stages of sevoflurane-induced anesthesia.

Article.Title: Efficient structural information integration into protein language models with implicit mixture-of-experts ProBEiT
Article.Authors: Li M.; He S.; Sang T.; Li R.; Jiang Y.; Ren Y.; Zhao Y.; Yao S.; Yang G.; Wang X.; Lu H.
Article.Abstract: Protein language models can now predict function and mutational effects directly from sequence, yet only a few incorporate function-deciding structural information with minimal additional effort. We introduce ProBEiT, a multimodal architecture that jointly encodes amino-acid sequences and discrete, tokenized structures via a parameter-efficient implicit mixture-of-experts scheme with deterministic routing. Trained on 1.7 million AlphaFoldDB proteins, the 400 million-parameter model surpasses larger baselines across six tasks of fitness prediction and functional annotation, demonstrating enhanced understanding of sequence-structure-function relationships. Unlike existing billion-scale models, ProBEiT attains strong accuracy early in continual training period, reducing computational cost. In an experimental thermostability engineering task on glycerol-3-phosphate oxidase, it correctly identifies optimized variants with positive epistatic effects. These results show that tightly coupling structural context with sequence modeling in a modality-specialized framework enables efficient, high-performance protein engineering.

Article.Title: Hierarchical distortions in structure-function coupling linked to multiscale neurobiological characteristics in autism
Article.Authors: Kim T.; Namgung J.; Park Y.; Kim C.; Yoo K.; Satterthwaite T.; Di Martino A.; Bernhardt B.; Park B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder is associated with widespread alterations in brain connectivity, but how structural and functional networks are jointly reorganized remains unclear. Here, we show that autism is associated with altered structure-function coupling, particularly in the hierarchical organization of sensory and association systems. Using brain imaging data from 91 individuals with autism and 67 typically developing controls, we model functional connectivity from structural networks using Riemannian optimization and examine communication across multiple steps. In the resulting simulated networks, hierarchical organization is comparable between groups at lower communication steps but becomes less differentiated in autism as communication extends across multiple steps. These alterations are associated with excitation/inhibition alterations, neurotransmitter distributions, gene expression, and multisensory processing. We also identify atypical connectivity involving the thalamus and putamen. Importantly, greater hierarchical distortion predicts more severe autistic symptoms, linking macroscale network organization with neurobiology and behavior. These findings highlight hierarchical structure-function coupling as a potential framework for understanding biological and behavioral characteristics in autism.

Article.Title: Single-cell transcriptomic insights into conserved and divergent oligodendrocyte lineage programs across species
Article.Authors: Han X.; Zuo L.; Zhang Z.; Yu Y.; Hu J.; Long Q.; Tian X.; Wei J.; Zhang R.; Luo F.
Article.Abstract: Oligodendrocyte lineage cells (OLLCs) are essential for myelination and neuronal homeostasis, yet the evolutionary conservation of their transcriptional programs remains unclear. Here, we integrated approximately one million hippocampal single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomes from humans, rhesus macaques, cynomolgus macaques, and mice. OLLCs emerged as among the most evolutionarily conserved neural cell populations, with oligodendrocyte precursor cells exhibiting highly conserved transcriptional identities, whereas mature oligodendrocytes displayed greater species-specific diversification We identified evolutionarily divergent genes, including the primate-specific gene CNDP1, and uncovered a species-specific temporal shift of the transcription factor ETV1 during oligodendrocyte differentiation. Cross-species analysis of aging revealed conserved chromatin-regulatory programs together with species-specific aging signatures, including coordinated remodeling of a primate-specific Wnt regulatory network in primate OPCs, whereas aged mouse OPCs were enriched for ribosome biogenesis. Disease-risk signatures further underscore the involvement of OLLCs in neurological disorders. Together, these findings provide a comparative framework for understanding mammalian myelin biology, brain aging, and disease.

Article.Title: A role for the BBSome in restricting the entry of non-ciliary proteins into cilia
Article.Authors: Cevik S.; Yenisert F.; Kantarci H.; Pucak D.; Gallrein C.; Stöckl S.; Dünninger X.; Cakici O.; Stigloher C.; Kirstein J.; Kaplan O.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cilia possess the inherent ability to restrict the entry of non-ciliary components through the ciliary gate. Mutations in genes encoding components of the ciliary gate result in various cilia-related diseases known as ciliopathies. Yet, how non-ciliary residents are prevented from accumulating in cilia remains unclear. Here, we observe ciliary accumulation of non-ciliary proteins in BBSome-deficient mutants (Bardet-Biedl syndrome), a phenotype reminiscent of ciliary gate-defective mutants such as mks-5 and nphp-4 . Time-lapse imaging shows that these non-ciliary proteins move bidirectionally along cilia at IFT velocities, and bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) reveals that the non-ciliary protein ELMD-1 associates with the IFT component IFT-43 in BBSome-deficient mutants, indicating that they are mis-loaded onto IFT trains. This misloading allows them to bypass the ciliary gate. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) suggests the gate remains largely functional, supporting a potential two-step model of ciliary composition control: cargo selection/loading and ciliary gating. We propose that defects in cargo selection/loading (and potentially export) alter ciliary composition, allowing unintended protein entry.

Article.Title: Inhibition of spinal astrocytic GPR177 attenuates neuropathic pain by modulating C3/C3aR signaling in male rats
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Yang M.; Li A.; Liu Y.; Guo K.; Yang Y.; Yao Y.
Article.Abstract: Neuropathic pain (NP) remains refractory to conventional therapy partly because its pathogenesis is incompletely understood. G protein-coupled receptor 177 (GPR177), a multi-pass transmembrane protein, regulates Wnt trafficking and secretion. Here, we use a chronic constriction injury model in male rats and find GPR177 predominantly expresses in spinal astrocytes and co-localizes with complement component 3 (C3). During NP development, astrocytic GPR177 expression increases, accompanied by activation of C3/C3a receptor (C3aR) signaling in the spinal dorsal horn. Gpr177 silencing with siRNA alleviates nerve injury-associated hypersensitivity and reduces the increases in GPR177, glial fibrillary acidic protein, C3, and C3aR. Intrathecal administration of the C3 inhibitor compstatin and the C3aR antagonist SB290157 reduces hypersensitivity and suppresses C3/C3aR activation, supporting the involvement of C3/C3aR signaling in NP development. These findings demonstrate that spinal GPR177 contributes to NP by activating astrocytes and regulating the C3/C3aR signaling pathway, suggesting the GPR177/C3/C3aR axis as a potential therapeutic target for NP.

Article.Title: Anatomical differences in the brain organization between Australopithecus and early Homo based on computational neuroanatomy
Article.Authors: Amano H.; Tanabe H.; Bruner E.; Ogihara N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Encephalization is a hallmark of human evolution, but how regional brain morphology changed during early hominin evolution remains unclear. Here, we show regional brain morphological differences between sampled Australopithecus and early Homo specimens. Using computed tomography and endocranial casts, we generated brain models for Australopithecus africanus , Homo habilis , and Homo ergaster using an anatomically homogeneous cross-species interpolation technique. Our reconstructions suggest that the posterior cerebellum was enlarged in early Homo compared with the sampled A. africanus specimens. In contrast, relative frontal lobe volume remains largely unchanged among the sampled fossils. We also identify enlargement of temporoparietal regions that, in modern humans, are associated with functions including social communication and tool use. By integrating fossil endocranial morphology with comparative neuroanatomical information from extant primates, the present approach provides a quantitative framework for generating and testing hypotheses about regional brain evolution in extinct hominins.

Article.Title: Serum albumin maintains Wnt3a water solubility and activity
Article.Authors: Yeo J.; Chae J.; Kwon S.; Han J.; Kusen I.; Lim J.; Lee H.; Kim H.; Haam S.; Cheong J.; Kim T.; Moon S.; Jung Y.; Lee J.; Kim C.
Article.Abstract: Wnt proteins regulate adult tissue homeostasis and repair by driving stem cell self-renewal and differentiation. High-performance Wnt preparations have enormous therapeutic potential, especially alongside various stem cell technologies. Currently, a major limitation of most Wnt preparations is that they inevitably require fetal bovine serum (FBS) or detergents to maintain Wnt solubility and activity. Recently, afamin (AFM) was identified as a serum factor that solubilizes Wnt3a in conditioned media (CM), obviating the requirement for animal sera. Here, we show that serum albumin (SA) helps maintain the activity and stability of AFM-solubilized Wnt3a in CM, likely through a stabilizing effect. We further demonstrate, using test-tube assays, that SA alone efficiently solubilizes purified Wnt3a (pWnt3a) independently of AFM. This approach enables the conversion of conventional detergent-solubilized pWnt3a (CHAPS-pWnt3a) into SA-pWnt3a through dialysis-mediated detergent removal. Together, these findings define a simple and robust SA-based strategy for preserving Wnt3a activity, addressing a long-standing challenge in both experimental and therapeutic settings.

Article.Title: The Lysosomal Cation Channel <scp>TRPML1</scp> Regulates the Oligodendrocyte Cytoskeleton During Development
Article.Authors: Festa L.; Pachon N.; Anderson R.; Chen S.; Sciutto A.; Grinspan J.; Jordan‐Sciutto K.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Differentiating oligodendrocytes undergo morphologic alterations to transition from progenitors to mature oligodendrocytes that synthesize myelin, the lipid‐rich membrane that coats axons. Actin dynamics underpin the morphologic shifts in oligodendrocyte maturation; however, the origin of such regulation during oligodendrocyte differentiation remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that the endolysosomal cation channel, transient potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1), is a regulator of oligodendrocyte morphology during differentiation and initial myelination. Activation of TRPML1 increased actin filament content and is driven by the small GTPase Rac1. Actin‐associated changes in morphology are accompanied by the presence of endolysosomal‐derived calcium transients in oligodendrocyte processes. Lastly, adolescent mice with TRPML1 deletion had a reduction in staining for phosphorylated PAK1 in the motor cortex and corpus callosum, demonstrating impaired TRPML1/Rac1/PAK1 signaling. Together, our work reveals endolysosomal TRPML1 activity as a central regulator of oligodendrocyte morphology independent of myelin protein expression and may provide mechanistic insight into the distinct but coordinated pathways that lead to oligodendrocyte differentiation.

Article.Title: <scp>TRIB3</scp> Aggravates Neuroinflammatory Responses and Promotes <scp>M1</scp> Microglial Polarization After Spinal Cord Injury via the <scp>CEBPB</scp> / <scp>PTPRO</scp> Axis
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Zhou X.; Zheng L.; Yu H.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Microglial M1 polarization‐induced neuroinflammation drives spinal cord injury (SCI) secondary injury and progression; targeting this process effectively mitigates SCI damage and impedes disease advancement. As a molecular scaffold, tribbles pseudokinase 3 (TRIB3) engages diverse regulators to mediate downstream gene transcription and protein stability, coordinating neurological disease‐associated cellular processes. GEO analysis confirmed significant TRIB3 upregulation in the T10 spinal cord of SCI rats (log 2 FC > 2, p < 0.001). A moderate SCI model was established in C57BL/6 mice via T10 vertebral impact. TRIB3 was upregulated in injured spinal cord tissues of C57BL/6 mice, with specific upregulation in microglia. Lentivirus‐mediated TRIB3 knockdown restored motor function, ameliorated tissue injury, enhanced neuronal survival, reduced M1 polarization, and promoted M2 polarization. In vitro, TRIB3 was upregulated in LPS/IFN‐γ‐induced M1 microglia but downregulated in IL‐4‐induced M2 microglia. TRIB3 knockdown suppressed M1 polarization (decreased iNOS, CD16, CD86, TNF‐α, IL‐6), while its overexpression inhibited M2 polarization (decreased Arg‐1, CD206, IL‐10). Mechanistically, GST pull‐down and co‐immunoprecipitation assays revealed that TRIB3 directly interacts with transcription factor CCAAT enhancer binding protein beta (CEBPB) and suppresses its ubiquitination, thereby stabilizing the CEBPB protein. This stabilized CEBPB in turn binds to the promoter of the protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) promoter and drives its transcription. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that TRIB3 promotes M1 polarization and accelerates SCI pathogenesis via the CEBPB/PTPRO axis, highlighting this pathway as a promising therapeutic target for SCI intervention.

Article.Title: Astrocytic Gq Signaling in Mice Enhances Glial Engagement With Amyloid Plaques and Promotes Plaque Clearance In Vivo
Article.Authors: Crooks A.; Hogan‐Cann A.; Schmidt S.; Schmitz T.; Prado M.; Prado V.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the progressive accumulation of extracellular amyloid‐β (Aβ) plaques, aberrant tau phosphorylation and aggregation, neuroinflammation, and cognitive decline, with growing evidence implicating glial dysfunction as a key driver of disease progression. While astrocytes and microglia accumulate around Aβ plaques and influence their clearance, the intracellular signaling pathways that regulate these glial responses in vivo remain poorly defined. We investigated whether sustained activation of Gq‐coupled signaling in astrocytes or microglia modulates amyloid pathology in humanized amyloid precursor protein ( App ) knock‐in mouse models of AD. Amyloid mouse models were crossed with tamoxifen‐inducible transgenic lines expressing the hM3Dq designer receptor in either astrocytes or microglia to enable cell‐type‐specific activation of Gq signaling, to avoid the confound of viral expression in glial cells. Sustained astrocytic Gq signaling significantly increased astrocyte accumulation around plaques and reduced plaque burden in both the cortex and hippocampus. Astrocytic Gq signaling was further associated with Aβ reactivity within both astrocytic and microglial compartments, along with enhanced microglial recruitment and elevated expression of lysosomal/phagocytic markers. In contrast, chronic activation of microglial Gq signaling alone did not measurably alter Aβ plaque burden under the experimental conditions tested. Together, these findings demonstrate that astrocytic Gq signaling is sufficient to reprogram plaque‐associated glial interactions toward a clearance‐associated phenotype in vivo. Our results identify astrocytic Gq signaling as an important regulator of the multicellular plaque environment and a potential pathway for modulating glial responses in Alzheimer's disease.

Article.Title: Liver Kinase <scp>B1</scp> Depletion Disrupts the Pantothenic Acid: Coenzyme A Pathway in Astrocytes
Article.Authors: Alemani R.; Kalinin S.; Feinstein D.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Previous studies showed conditional knockout of Liver Kinase B1 (LKB1) from astrocytes exacerbated disease severity and glial cell activation in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis (MS). A major function of LKB1 is to maintain energy supplies under conditions of metabolic stress, suggesting that loss of LKB1 could alter astrocytic metabolic processes. Following siRNA mediated knockdown (KD) of LKB1 from primary mouse astrocytes, untargeted metabolomic screening identified significant increases in Pantothenic Acid (PA) and related metabolites; and pathway analysis showed that the PA:Coenzyme A (PA:CoA) pathway was significantly modified. This pathway was also identified by bulk RNA sequencing. In LKB1 KD cells, relative mRNA levels of enzymes in the PA:CoA pathway were reduced, and PA Kinase 2 (Pank2, which converts PA to phosphoPA) expression was reduced. Deficiencies in Pank2 are known to cause iron accumulation, which we confirmed occurs in LKB1 KD astrocytes. The KD cells also showed increased sensitivity to induction of ferroptosis. Measurement of serum PA levels in a small cohort of relapsing remitting MS patients revealed a positive correlation with age at diagnosis in those patients harboring a variant in the gene encoding LKB1. Together, these results suggest that metabolic disturbances, in this case due to LKB1 depletion, can lead to dysregulation of the PA:CoA pathway in astrocytes.

Article.Title: Microglial Transmembrane 119 (Tmem119) is Protective in Ischemic Stroke
Article.Authors: Misrani A.; Xu Y.; Wang J.; Tanifum E.; McCullough L.; Liu F.; Ngwa C.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Microglial responses to cerebral ischemia are tightly regulated by inhibitory pathways that limit excessive post‐stroke inflammation. Transmembrane protein 119 (Tmem119) has emerged as an important regulator of microglial activation and neuroinflammatory signaling. We investigated the role of microglial Tmem119 during acute ischemic stroke using primary microglia and a young adult mouse model. Primary microglia were transfected with Tmem119‐siRNA and subjected to oxygen–glucose deprivation (OGD) alone or combined with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation. In vivo, young adult male mice received stereotaxic injection of lenti‐Tmem119 or lenti‐GFP for 4 weeks before 60 min of transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO). Tmem119 expression and inflammatory responses were assessed by qPCR, Western blotting, and ELISA at 1 and 3 days after stroke. Infarct volume and neurobehavioral outcomes were also evaluated. Tmem119 silencing significantly increased IRAK4, IRF5, and CD68 mRNA expression in primary microglia. Ischemic injury reduced microglial Tmem119 protein expression and increased IRAK4 signaling in vivo. In contrast, lenti‐Tmem119 treatment before MCAO decreased phosphorylated IRAK4 protein expression and increased IL‐10 levels in both plasma and ischemic brain tissue compared with lenti‐GFP controls. Tmem119 overexpression also significantly reduced infarct volume and improved neurobehavioral outcomes. These findings demonstrate that microglial Tmem119 exerts a protective anti‐inflammatory role during the acute phase of ischemic stroke by suppressing IRAK4‐mediated inflammatory signaling and enhancing IL‐10 production. Collectively, Tmem119 limits microglial activation, reduces ischemic brain injury, and improves functional recovery, identifying Tmem119 as a promising therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

Article.Title: Plcg2 Deficiency Leads to Sex‐Associated Divergent Effects on Glial Transcriptomes
Article.Authors: Hartigan K.; Dabin L.; Kersey H.; Jury‐Garfe N.; Sharify A.; Kim B.; Lamb B.; Bissel S.; Lasagna‐Reeves C.; Kim J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Plcg2 encodes an intracellular phospholipase C signaling enzyme expressed predominately in microglia in the brain. Genome‐wide association studies implicate PLCG2 in Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk and loss of Plcg2 alters amyloid pathology in mouse models. However, the physiological impact of Plcg2 loss remains unclear. To address this gap, we performed single‐cell RNA sequencing (scRNA‐seq) of wild‐type, heterozygous, and homozygous Plcg2 ‐deficient mouse brains in the absence of amyloid or tau pathology. Our analyses generated a comprehensive, publicly available atlas of glial transcriptomic states across genotypes and sexes. Genotype‐associated changes in microglia and astrocytes were enriched in neurodegenerative disease‐related pathways, as well as oxidative phosphorylation and proteostasis pathways. Genotype‐by‐sex interaction and sex‐stratified analyses revealed divergent regulation of many of these pathways in males and females, while co‐expression and cell–cell communication analyses identified additional sex‐associated differences in glial signaling networks. Overall, these data provide a framework for understanding how variation in PLCG2 function may shape glial biology and modify pathways relevant to neurodegenerative disease in a sex‐associated manner.

Article.Title: Reactive Astrocyte‐Associated IL‐33 Signaling Contributes to a Protective Neuroimmune State During Chronic Toxoplasma gondii – Plasmodium berghei Coinfection
Article.Authors: Leleu I.; Keswani T.; Herbert F.; Picavet C.; Arnaud M.; Marion S.; Glineur C.; Pied S.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Cerebral malaria (CM) is a lethal neuroinflammatory syndrome characterized by blood–brain barrier disruption and excessive immune‐mediated neuronal damage. Astrocytes are emerging as key regulators of CNS homeostasis, yet their contribution to disease tolerance during polymicrobial infections remains poorly understood. Here, we show that chronic Toxoplasma gondii ( Tg ) infection protects against experimental cerebral malaria (ECM) induced by Plasmodium berghei ANKA ( Pb A) by establishing a regulated neuroimmune environment rather than reducing cerebral parasite burden. This protective phenotype required chronic cerebral T. gondii infection and was associated with a distinct neuroinflammatory transcriptional profile characterized by enhanced TGF‐β and IL‐33/ST2 expression. At the cellular level, chronic Tg infection remodeled the astrocyte compartment, generating reactive astrocytes displaying an intermediate inflammatory phenotype characterized by the co‐expression of inflammatory (CXCL‐10, MHC‐I) and regulatory (TGF‐β) markers. Reactive astrocytes represented one of the major IL‐33‐expressing cell populations in the brains of Tg ‐infected and coinfected mice and were associated with recruitment of ST2‐expressing group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s), which expressed IL‐5 and IL‐13 in the brain. In IL‐33‐deficient mice, cerebral ILC2 recruitment was markedly reduced and protection against ECM was only partially maintained, indicating that the IL‐33/ST2 axis contributes to, but is not solely responsible for, disease tolerance during coinfection. Our findings identify reactive astrocytes as key components of a regulated neuroimmune environment associated with protection against ECM during chronic T. gondii coinfection. These results highlight astrocyte‐associated IL‐33/ST2 signaling and ILC2 recruitment as components of a multicellular neuroimmune network that contribute to disease tolerance during polymicrobial CNS infections.

Article.Title: Spatial Coordination of Ca <sup>2+</sup> Signaling by Astrocyte Morphology
Article.Authors: Xu J.; Wang H.; Yang S.; Zhang K.; Liao X.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Astrocytes exhibit spatially heterogeneous Ca 2+ signaling, yet how this activity is organized across subcellular compartments and branch domains remains unclear. Events were assigned to manually delineated GCaMP‐positive masks representing the soma, primary branches, fine processes, and branch domains. Ca 2+ event features exhibited compartment‐dependent gradients extending from the soma through primary branches to fine processes, while coordination was strongest in primary branches, followed by fine processes and the soma. Within branch domains, intermediate‐sized events (10–100 μm 2 ) showed greater within‐domain than cross‐domain coordination in both primary and secondary branch domains and were relatively enriched within primary branch domains. Article.Title: Progressive Lineage Restriction of Bergmann Glia‐Like Progenitors During Postnatal Cerebellar Development
Article.Authors: Adachi T.; Suyama K.; Ito S.; Isogai E.; Sone M.; Hoshino M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Bergmann glia‐like progenitors (BGLPs) are transient progenitors in the postnatal cerebellum, but how their lineage potential changes during development remains incompletely understood. Our previous electroporation‐based study suggested that P0 BGLPs possess broader lineage potential than P6 BGLPs. Here, we performed recombination‐based lineage tracing by cerebellar surface application of tamoxifen to Ai9/+; Glast CreERT2/+ mice and temporally analyzed the progeny of BGLPs labeled at P0, P3, P6, and P8. We found that BGLPs undergo progressive lineage restriction during postnatal development. P0 BGLPs gave rise to Bergmann glial cells (BGs), inner granule cell layer astrocytes (IGL astrocytes), white matter astrocytes (WM astrocytes), and molecular layer inhibitory neurons (ML‐INs), confirming our previous electroporation‐based findings. In contrast, P3 BGLPs generated BGs, IGL astrocytes, and WM astrocytes, whereas P6 BGLPs generated BGs and IGL astrocytes, and P8 BGLPs generated predominantly BGs. Thus, BGLP lineage output was progressively restricted from four progeny categories at P0 to a predominantly BG‐restricted output by P8, suggesting that BGLPs dynamically adjust their cellular output during postnatal cerebellar maturation. Additional temporal analyses were consistent with a stepwise pathway from P0 BGLPs to ML‐INs, in which astrocyte‐like progenitors (AsLPs) appear first among BGLP descendants, some of which may subsequently transition into committed inhibitory neuron progenitors (INPs) that give rise to ML‐INs. These findings identify postnatal BGLPs as a useful in vivo model for studying progressive lineage restriction and stage‐specific cellular supply during cerebellar development.

Article.Title: A Glial Interplay Regulates Junctional Architecture at the Blood–Brain Barrier of Drosophila
Article.Authors: Contreras E.; Naffin E.; Collins‐Ramírez M.; Surina N.; Rothermel M.; Salazar‐Tirado J.; Schirmeier S.; Klämbt C.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Neurons require a tightly controlled ion and metabolite homeostasis, which is maintained by an effective blood–brain barrier (BBB). Since the integrity of the BBB is essential for brain function, its maintenance during development represents a significant challenge. The Drosophila BBB is formed by two glial layers. Subperineurial glia (SPG) establish pleated septate junctions (pSJs) to generate the primary diffusion barrier. Abutting the SPG lies the mitotically active perineurial glia (PG). Only a small number of PG cells are specified during embryogenesis. The FGF8‐like signal Pyramus presented by the SPG subsequently triggers proliferation of the PG, which ultimately covers the entire nervous system. To investigate the role of PG in the development and physiology of the BBB, we genetically ablated them. In these animals, glucose influx into SPG is unchanged following acute glucose perfusion. However, adult PG‐ablated flies show increased sensitivity to glucose‐only diet, indicating that while baseline carbohydrate transport can be maintained in the absence of most PG, the system fails under metabolic stress. SPG morphology and pSJ organization are largely preserved during larval stages upon PG ablation. In contrast, in PG‐ablated pupae, moody expression is impaired in SPG and pSJs progressively split, producing ectopic junctional strands. Together, these results reveal the necessity of PG for the maturation and function of SPG, as well as the mutual interdependence between the two BBB glial layers.

Article.Title: Amygdala Oligodendrocyte <scp>MDH1</scp> Dysregulation and Mitochondrial Dysfunction in High Urea‐Induced Anxiety‐Like Behavior
Article.Authors: Hu J.; Zhang M.; Jiang S.; Bi H.; Tu B.; Zhang S.; Wan G.; Wang Q.; Liu Y.; Leng J.; Chen X.; Li J.; Chen D.; Li G.; Gui J.; Huang B.; Ran J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The high incidence and mortality rates of anxiety disorders in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have drawn attention. Prior studies identified urea as an independent risk factor for mental disorders in CKD. While urea accumulation is known to impair synaptic plasticity, its effects on glial cells remain unclear. How urea influences oligodendrocyte lineage differentiation may represent a critical node in neuron–glia interactions. Previous studies have shown that OL‐lineage cells may be underrepresented in scRNA‐seq datasets. Dlat and MDH1, genes associated with TCA cycle‐related metabolism, were downregulated alongside alterations in mitochondrial and oxidative phosphorylation‐related transcriptional programs. Urea dose‐dependently decreased MDH1 expression, mitochondrial membrane potential, and intracellular ATP content in MO3.13 cells. Regulatory analyses linked MDH1 to energy metabolism and neurodegenerative pathways. Trajectory reconstruction suggested altered differentiation‐ and myelination‐related transcriptional programs in mitochondria‐related oligodendrocytes (MitOLs). The cytoplasmic concentration and fate of oxaloacetic acid (OAA) are regulated by the reversible catalysis of MDH1. OAA supplementation partially restored amygdalar MDH1 expression and alleviated anxiety‐like behaviors in UT‐B − / − mice, while improving mitochondrial bioenergetics in urea‐exposed MO3.13 cells. These findings support a candidate metabolic–glial model linking elevated urea, MDH1 dysregulation, oligodendrocyte bioenergetic dysfunction, and anxiety‐like behavior, with potential relevance to CKD‐associated anxiety.

Article.Title: Brain PDGFR β + Cells Exhibit Diverse Reactive Phenotypes After Stroke Without Requiring KLF4
Article.Authors: Manrique‐Castano D.; ElAli A.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The pathobiology of ischemic stroke is associated with the activation of brain platelet‐derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR) β + perivascular cells. While Krüppel‐like factor (KLF)4 is a well‐established mediator of peripheral PDGFR β + cell activation, its role in brain PDGFR β + cells remains elusive. Herein, we aimed to characterize the spatiotemporal reactivity of brain PDGFR β + cells, while assessing KLF4 contribution upon experimental ischemic stroke using transgenic mice that enable tracking PDGFR β + cells or conditionally depleting KLF4 in PDGFR β + cells. Moving beyond the qualitative descriptors, we sought to develop point pattern analysis (PPA) and topological data analysis (TDA) workflows to generate robust and reusable mathematical models to assess spatial cell responses and tissue scar topological changes. First, we report the emergence of phenotypically distinct reactive parenchymal PDGFR β + cells, which cannot be causally and exclusively linked, as it is currently proposed, to local cell proliferation or adjacent vascular detachment. Furthermore, we show that KLF4 is barely expressed in brain PDGFR β + cells under normal conditions and that it is only marginally induced in reactive PDGFR β + cells at the injured brain. Notably, the conditional attenuation of KLF4 expression specifically in reactive PDGFR β + cells does not alter spatial cellular distribution nor scar organization. This suggests that, in contrast to peripheral PDGFR β + cells upon ischemic insults, KLF4 is not a main regulator of the reactivity of brain cells in response to ischemic stroke. Ultimately, our findings supported by open‐source spatiotemporal models indicate that the reactivity of brain PDGFR β + perivascular cells is highly heterogeneous and fundamentally distinct from peripheral PDGFR β + cells.

Article.Title: sox17 Mutagenesis Reveals Compounding Effects ofMaternal and Zygotic Contribution on Microglia Abundance
Article.Authors: Spring C.; Dennen J.; Gan D.; Li J.; Smith C.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Embryonic development is shaped by maternal and zygotic factors but how the interplay between these factors contributes to phenotypic variability and impacts specific populations of brain cells, and subsequently neurodevelopment, remains largely unknown. Here, we reveal a double hit phenomenon that impacts microglia and microglia precursors during development. Using zebrafish, we identified a mutation in sry‐related HMG box gene‐17 (sox17) that exhibits a maternal effect phenotype presenting as a reduction of microglia in the brain and precursors in the yolk sac. We demonstrate that microglia deficits are exacerbated in homozygous offspring from homozygous parents compared to homozygous offspring from heterozygous parents, suggesting a compounding effect of maternal and zygotic sox17 mutation on microglia abundance. We observe that sox17 is expressed in microglia and yolk sac precursors and is maternally contributed. Injections of sox17 RNA during embryogenesis are sufficient to rescue microglia and yolk sac cell abundance. To identify additional genes interacting with sox17 , we perform a genetic screen using CRISPR mutagenesis and identify f11r.1, gas6 , and mpp1 as microglia regulators, which we demonstrate are expressed in zebrafish microglia. Transcriptional and mutant analyses with these genes suggest sox17 positively regulates mpp1 transcription. These results demonstrate that microglia are susceptible to additive effects of maternal and zygotic sox17 mutation, and that offspring greatly differ in their susceptibility to microglia deficits depending on the mother's genotype. Our findings highlight that both the maternal and offspring genotype should be considered when examining neurodevelopmental disorders that could arise from microglia dysfunction.

Article.Title: Retro-2 Enhances Tumor-Cell MHC-I Antigen Presentation and CD8+ T Cell-Dependent Antitumor Immunity
Article.Authors: Xu Z.; Zhou X.; Zhang Q.; Jiang K.; Ruan Z.; Hu M.
Article.Abstract: Defective major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) antigen presentation enables tumor immune evasion and limits programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockade efficacy. We tested whether pharmacological enhancement of tumor-cell MHC-I presentation could restore immunogenicity and sensitize tumors to checkpoint therapy. Retro-2, a cyclic inhibitor of retrograde toxin trafficking, increased MHC-I transcripts, surface MHC-I/HLA-ABC, and peptide–MHC-I presentation in murine B16-F10 melanoma and Panc02 pancreatic cancer cells and in human A375 melanoma and BxPC-3 pancreatic cancer cells. These changes enhanced antigen-specific CD8+ T cell killing and IFN-γ/TNF-α release, and increased human tumor-cell susceptibility to tumor-lysate-primed CD8+ T cells. In syngeneic mouse models of B16-F10 melanoma and Panc02 pancreatic cancer, Retro-2 delayed tumor growth, reduced tumor burden, and prolonged survival, accompanied by increased intratumoral CD8+ T cell abundance, proliferation, effector function, and progenitor-exhausted cells. CD8+ T cell depletion largely abolished Retro-2 activity. Combining Retro-2 with PD-1 blockade produced greater tumor control than either monotherapy in both models. Retro-2 was well tolerated, with no detectable changes in body weight, hematological indices, or major-organ histology. These findings identify Retro-2 as a pharmacological enhancer of tumor MHC-I presentation that promotes CD8+ T cell-dependent antitumor immunity and improves PD-1 blockade efficacy.

Article.Title: Machine Learning–Based Classification of Molecularly Defined α-Globin Genotypes Using Routine Hematological Parameters
Article.Authors: Uçucu S.
Article.Abstract: Alpha-thalassemia is a genetically heterogeneous hemoglobinopathy caused by reduced or absent α-globin chain production. Its phenotypic presentation may overlap with other microcytic disorders, and routine hematological parameters alone may not reliably permit identification of the underlying α-globin genotype. Although molecular analysis provides definitive genotype characterization, its availability may be limited in routine screening settings. Machine learning approaches offer a potential strategy for identifying complex patterns within routinely available hematological data and may facilitate the preliminary classification of α-thalassemia molecular subtypes.This study investigated whether molecularly defined α-thalassemia groups could be classified using routinely available hematological parameters. A dataset of 599 individuals aged 18–64 years was analyzed, including 229 genotype-negative reference individuals and 370 individuals with molecularly characterized α-thalassemia genotypes. Participants were classified into five molecular groups, including individuals carrying the −α3.7 deletion, hemoglobin Constant Spring (HbCS), the --SEA deletion, and HbH/compound α-globin genotypes. Age, sex, red blood cell count (RBC), hemoglobin concentration (Hb), hematocrit (HCT), mean corpuscular volume (MCV), mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC), and red cell distribution width (RDW) were used as predictor variables. Five supervised machine learning algorithms were trained and compared, including Decision Tree, Naive Bayes, Random Forest, k-nearest neighbors, and artificial neural network models. Model development and evaluation were performed using stratified five-fold cross-validation, with data-dependent preprocessing performed within the training folds to minimize information leakage. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, balanced accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC, together with class-specific sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1 score. Calibration was evaluated using the Brier score and log loss. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals were estimated for the principal performance measures. SHAP-based analysis was subsequently performed to assess the relative contribution of individual hematological variables to model predictions.The evaluated machine learning models demonstrated meaningful discriminatory performance for classifying molecularly defined α-thalassemia groups using routine hematological parameters. Naive Bayes achieved the highest overall accuracy (78.8%), while Random Forest showed the highest macro-ROC-AUC (0.916) and macro-PR-AUC (0.743), together with the most favorable comparative calibration performance. SHAP-based analysis identified MCH, MCV, and RDW as the most influential predictors of model decisions. Classification performance varied across molecular subgroups, with lower sensitivity observed for the Hb Constant Spring group. Routine hematological parameters contain informative patterns associated with molecularly defined α-thalassemia groups. In this cohort, machine learning models were able to distinguish individuals with α-thalassemia from genotype-negative reference individuals and to discriminate among different molecular α-globin gene patterns, although performance varied across subgroups. These findings support the potential use of machine learning as a complementary, non-invasive, and readily accessible approach for the preliminary classification and screening of α-thalassemia. However, molecular analysis remains essential for definitive genotype characterization, and external validation in independent and ethnically diverse cohorts is required before clinical implementation.

Article.Title: Ion Dynamics in Membrane Channels Under Weak Electromagnetic Fields: A Comparison of IFO–VGIC and Electrostatically Confined Ion Oscillator Models
Article.Authors: Matronchik A.; Belyaev I.
Article.Abstract: We examine how weak radiofrequency (RF) electromagnetic fields could act on ions in membrane channels. The ion forced-oscillation–voltage-gated ion channel (IFO–VGIC) model describes forced ion motion and gives an inverse-frequency response, with emphasis on low-frequency modulation and pulsation. Biological effects have also been reported for unmodulated RF and millimeter-wave fields, with responses depending on carrier frequency, intensity, polarization, modulation, cell interactions, and background static and ELF magnetic fields. Here we introduce an Electrostatically Confined Ion Oscillator (ECIO) model that adds the electrostatic channel potential. For sodium ions, about 6.9 GHz is an upper estimate of the characteristic frequency at the maximal assumed field, not a fixed frequency or predicted resonance; lower fields give lower frequencies, including the approximate 0.85–1.9 GHz range and below. With the damping used in the IFO framework, single-ion motion is strongly overdamped (Q ≈ 2.6 × 10−4), with a relaxation crossover near 1.78 MHz. In this limit, ECIO reduces to the IFO 1/ω law. Neither single-ion model explains narrow frequency windows, power-dependent resonance width, polarization, modulation, cooperative responses, or magnetic-background effects. These findings motivate collective nonequilibrium models; coherence is one possible hypothesis, but it is not derived or established by the present analysis.

Article.Title: Chemical Composition and the Antioxidant and Antibacterial Activities of Clove Essential Oil and Its Application in Strawberry Preservation
Article.Authors: Zhang D.; Du Z.; Xu X.; Jia W.; Dong X.
Article.Abstract: Clove essential oil is a potential natural preservative because of its antioxidant and antibacterial properties. However, its additional effects when incorporated into edible coatings need to be evaluated in actual food systems. In this study, clove essential oil was extracted from clove buds using ultrasound-assisted hydrodistillation, and its extraction yield, chemical composition, and biological activities were evaluated. Its application in chitosan-based coatings for strawberry preservation was also investigated at 25 °C and 4 °C, with particular attention to the effects of clove essential oil compared with the chitosan-based coating alone. The extraction yield of clove essential oil was 15.55% (w/w). Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) analysis identified eugenol (70.04%), β-caryophyllene (15.14%), and eugenyl acetate (9.37%) as the major volatile constituents. The essential oil showed DPPH and ABTS radical-scavenging activities of 61.60% and 81.18%, respectively, and inhibited the growth of Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella Enteritidis, and Escherichia coli in vitro, with inhibition zones of 12.0, 15.0, and 11.0 mm, respectively. During strawberry storage, chitosan (CH) and chitosan–clove essential oil (CH-CEO) coatings reduced decay incidence compared with the untreated control. The coatings also helped maintain reducing sugar and vitamin C contents. However, their effects varied between quality attributes: the CH coating was more effective in reducing weight loss, whereas the CH-CEO coating showed better vitamin C retention after 7 days of storage under both temperature conditions. The differences in decay incidence between the two coatings were not statistically significant. Overall, the CH-CEO formulation showed potential for maintaining selected quality attributes of strawberries, particularly vitamin C content, although it did not provide additional benefits in decay control. Further studies are needed to clarify the contribution of clove essential oil to these effects, particularly considering its retention and activity after coating preparation.

Article.Title: Homologous Recombination Deficiency (HRD) Testing in Ovarian Cancer: Clinical Utility and Limitations
Article.Authors: Ratka Z.; Woźniak M.
Article.Abstract: Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) is an important biomarker in ovarian cancer, but available assays interrogate different biological features and are not fully interchangeable. This structured narrative review examines HRD biology, testing strategies, clinical utility, and limitations using PubMed and Scopus, with emphasis on the past decade and older seminal studies. The clinical synthesis focuses predominantly on advanced high-grade epithelial ovarian cancer, particularly high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, and first-line poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor maintenance. Homologous recombination repair (HRR) gene alterations, genomic scars, and functional RAD51 assays represent distinct layers of repair biology. Genomic-scar assays have treatment-specific clinical validation, whereas RAD51 testing offers a functional readout whose clinical utility remains under investigation. Assay thresholds, specimen quality, tumor heterogeneity, and treatment history influence classification; an inconclusive result must be distinguished from a negative result. Progression-free survival benefit should also be separated from overall-survival benefit and from prognostic association. Emerging circulating, computational, epigenetic, and metabolomic biomarkers may provide complementary information but lack sufficient validation to replace established testing. Prospective studies should establish whether integrated genomic and functional assessment improves treatment decisions and patient outcomes beyond current approaches.

Article.Title: Network Organization, Null-Model Assessment, and Robustness of a Published Mycobacterium tuberculosis Candidate Drug-Resistance Gene Panel
Article.Authors: Küçükoğlu M.; Öztan G.; İşsever H.; Önal A.; Sayılı U.
Article.Abstract: Drug-resistant tuberculosis remains a major challenge, but resistance-associated genes are commonly interpreted as separate drug-specific lists. We reorganized a previously published TBProfiler Tier 1/Tier 2 candidate-gene panel into a reproducible bipartite network and quantified connected components, bipartite density, centrality, Jaccard similarity, the Szymkiewicz–Simpson overlap coefficient, evidence-tier sensitivity, degree-preserving null expectations, and leave-one-edge/gene-out robustness. The full network contained 14 drug/drug-class nodes, 49 genes, 71 edges, six disconnected components, and a bipartite density of 0.1035. In the full network, rrs had the highest number (four) of linked drugs, whereas Rv1258c had the highest full-network betweenness (0.203) but fell to zero in the Tier 1-only network. In 10,000 degree-preserving randomizations, however, Rv1258c betweenness did not exceed the null expectation (empirical p = 0.205), indicating that this ranking is compatible with the panel’s degree structure. Pairwise drug similarity, as expressed by the Jaccard coefficient, highlighted bedaquiline-clofazimine (0.833), amikacin-capreomycin (0.625), amikacin-kanamycin (0.429), and isoniazid-ethionamide (0.300); corresponding Szymkiewicz–Simpson overlap coefficients were 1.000, 0.833, 1.000, and 0.500, respectively. In the primary analysis encompassing all 91 drug-pair comparisons, three overlaps—bedaquiline–clofazimine, amikacin–capreomycin, and amikacin–kanamycin—exceeded degree-preserving null expectations after BH-FDR correction (q = 0.0046, 0.0046, and 0.0243, respectively). The separate analysis restricted to the 12 pairs with non-zero observed Jaccard similarity was considered exploratory and did not inform the primary conclusions. The amikacin–capreomycin Jaccard value fell to 0.250 under Tier 1 restriction, showing dependence on Tier 2 assignments. Collapsing amikacin, kanamycin, and capreomycin into a single second-line-injectable node preserved six components and broadly retained gene-centrality ranks (Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient, ρ= 0.851). Published CRyPTIC co-resistance patterns remained concordant with the bedaquiline–clofazimine and amikacin–kanamycin overlaps. The framework therefore quantifies the organization, evidence-tier dependence, and robustness of existing candidate-resistance associations; it does not establish novel resistance mechanisms, diagnostic accuracy, or patient-level clinical predictions.

Article.Title: Autophagy in Alveolar Epithelial Cells: Molecular Effect of Environmental Pollutants and Pathological Implications
Article.Authors: Bodega F.; Garavaglia M.; Porta C.; Dalle-Donne I.
Article.Abstract: The alveolar epithelium is continuously exposed to inhaled environmental pollutants. Particulate matter, heavy metals, inorganic gases, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), persistent organic pollutants (POPs), and cigarette smoke can induce oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, lysosomal impairment, inflammation, and proteostasis imbalance, which, in turn, affect autophagy and cellular homeostasis. The dysregulation of autophagy is related to the pathogenesis of several respiratory diseases, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), acute lung injury (ALI), and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). In this review, we discuss the physiological function and the pathological consequences of autophagy alteration in alveolar epithelial cells and examine the current literature that correlates environmental pollutants with autophagy dysregulation. The impairment of autophagy represents a common mechanism linking environmental pollution to alveolar epithelial injury. While in the early stages, autophagy acts as an adaptive response, prolonged or severe exposure may lead to defective autophagic clearance, accumulation of damaged cellular components, epithelial dysfunction, senescence, apoptosis, and fibrotic remodeling. A better understanding of the molecular interactions between pollutants and autophagic pathways may facilitate the identification of novel biomarkers and the development of therapeutic strategies to preserve the homeostasis of the alveolar tissue and prevent chronic lung disease.

Article.Title: A Conserved Xanthomonas Type III Effector, XopAZ, Encodes a Putative Peptidyl-Prolyl Isomerase and Promotes Rapid Cell Death in Tomato
Article.Authors: Sharma A.; Minsavage G.; Kara S.; Poudel M.; Vinson A.; Tran N.; Bendure H.; Timilsina S.; Vallad G.; Hurlbert J.; Jones J.
Article.Abstract: Type III effectors are major host-range determinants in phytopathogenic Xanthomonas. X. hortorum pv. gardneri is a pathogen of tomato, but the closely related X. hortorum pv. cynarae is unable to induce disease symptoms. In this study, we aimed to identify and characterize the genetic basis of X. hortorum pv. cynarae avirulence. We prepared a genomic cosmid library of X. hortorum pv. cynarae CFBP 4188, and following subcloning, identified a 510 bp gene responsible for the differential response. The X. hortorum pv. gardneri homolog of this gene contains an early frameshift resulting in translation of a shorter protein. The protein was translocated into the host cell by the type III secretion system and was named Xanthomonas outer protein AZ (XopAZ). When expressed in X. hortorum pv. gardneri, X. hortorum pv. cynarae XopAZ elicited an oxidative burst and rapid cell death in tomato leaflets, but unlike a hypersensitive response, it did not reduce in planta bacterial growth. XopAZ showed structural homology to Sensitive to Lysis D (SlyD) chaperones that function as peptidyl-prolyl isomerases. In silico docking studies indicate that XopAZ has binding affinity for similar peptide substrates as SlyD proteins, and X. hortorum pv. gardneri expressing Escherichia coli SlyD elicited similar response in tomato as XopAZ. Orthologs of XopAZ are widely distributed across Xanthomonas, with three major variants roughly corresponding to the Xanthomonas phylogeny; however, they are frequently disrupted in tomato-pathogenic strains. XopAZ is a novel Xanthomonas type III effector predicted to function as a promiscuous PPIase that enhances cell death in tomato.

Article.Title: Oxidative Stress Biomarkers Analysis in Adolescents with Positive Family History of Age-Related Diseases, a Cross-Sectional Study
Article.Authors: Zia M.; Kamps R.; Baig G.; Ahmad I.; Benish Ali S.; Ajmal M.; Qamar R.; Azam M.
Article.Abstract: Oxidative stress (OS), characterized by an imbalance between free radicals and antioxidants, is a key mediator of age-related diseases. This research analyzed serum OS biomarkers, malondialdehyde (MDA), total oxidant status (TOS), and total antioxidant status (TAS) in adolescents with a positive family history (PFH) of cardiovascular disease (CVD), hypertension (HT), and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Venous blood (5 mL) from all the adolescents in serum tubes was collected and centrifuged (4000 rpm = 3000× g, 5 min, 4 °C) for serum extraction, and a written consent was obtained before sample collection. A total of 440 teenagers, including 110 individuals with a PFH in each category and 110 controls without a PFH of any disease, were analyzed. The enzyme-linked immunosorbent test (ELISA) kits were used to assess TOS, TAS, and MDA levels. Significantly elevated TOS (CVD: p < 0.0001; HT: p < 0.0002; T2DM: p < 0.037) and decreased MDA (CVD: p < 0.0001; HT: p < 0.0001; T2DM: p < 0.0001) levels were observed in adolescents with PFH. However, higher significant TAS levels (p = 0.0001) were observed only in adolescents with PFH of HT. Analyses of parental consanguinity and lifestyle looked into their relationships with the studied outcomes; nevertheless, the results did not show independent predictive impacts. Our results recommend that the family history of teenagers with higher OS and PFH may have high susceptibility to age-related diseases later in their life. Longitudinal investigations are needed to establish if these indicators predict subsequent illnesses.

Article.Title: Helodermatid Venom Exendins: Evolutionary Diversification, Receptor Pharmacology, and Biomedical Translation
Article.Authors: Zatarain-Palacios R.; Rolon-Valencia T.; Lino-Lopez G.; Dagnino-Acosta A.; Perea-Ruiz D.; Vazquez-Vuelvas O.; Valdez-Velazquez L.
Article.Abstract: Helodermatid exendins provide a framework for examining how venom peptide diversification relates to receptor recognition and biomedical potential. This narrative review integrates published evolutionary models with sequence, structural, and pharmacological evidence for helospectins, helodermin, and exendins-3 and -4. Helospectins exhibit species-dependent receptor preferences, while comparisons between exendin-3 and exendin-4 associate limited N-terminal variation with distinct pharmacological profiles in historical pancreatic assays. These observations connect molecular diversity with experimental pharmacology while keeping sequence relationships distinct from receptor selectivity and biological function. Exendin-4-derived therapeutics and imaging agents illustrate the biomedical development of a venom peptide scaffold. Together, the literature synthesis and comparative sequence analysis provide a clearer basis for investigating how exendin variation influences receptor activity and guides the development of venom-derived peptides.

Article.Title: Multi-Omics Analysis of the Transcriptome and Metabolome as a Key to Understanding the Mechanisms Underlying Maize Yield
Article.Authors: Lenort M.; Tomkowiak A.; Bocianowski J.; Przybylska-Balcerek A.; Jarzyniak K.; Olejnik P.; Gawrysiak P.
Article.Abstract: Maize (Zea mays L.) grain yield is a complex trait shaped by genetic, physiological, and environmental variation. Principal component analysis showed substantial transcriptional and metabolomic variation but no complete separation by yield potential. These findings identify coordinated transcriptional and biochemical patterns and prioritize G32 for functional validation; however, they demonstrate associations, not causality.

Article.Title: Selective HSP90β Inhibition Disrupts SREBP1-Associated Metabolic Signaling and Suppresses Ovarian Cancer Progression: A Pilot Study
Article.Authors: Wang W.; Strasiotto B.; Cronberger E.; Wikenheiser G.; Crotzer E.; Breslin C.; Yang J.; Oh M.; Kerker T.; Dominique G.; Johnson J.; D’Amico T.; Mishra S.; Blagg B.; Stack M.
Article.Abstract: Ovarian cancer progression is supported by metabolic interactions between tumor cells and the adipocyte-rich peritoneal microenvironment, which can be further altered by obesity. Sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1), a master regulator of lipid metabolism, represents a potential therapeutic target in this setting. Analysis of gene expression data from human ovarian tumors further demonstrated a positive association between HSP90AB1 expression and SREBP1-associated lipogenic signaling. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that selective HSP90β inhibition suppresses ovarian cancer progression across lean and obese host environments and induces broad transcriptional remodeling of metabolic and tumor-associated pathways, including SREBP1-associated lipid metabolism, supporting HSP90β as a potential therapeutic target for metabolically adapted ovarian cancer.

Article.Title: Menopausal Status as an Effect Modifier of the Association Between Adiposity, Insulin Resistance, and Bone Mineral Density: A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Gursky V.; Sopova J.; Isaenko A.; Krasnova O.; Shmidt E.; Lesnyak O.; Neganova I.
Article.Abstract: Osteoporosis is a major health burden, with estrogen deficiency after menopause as its primary cause. Whether obesity, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) relate to bone mineral density (BMD) similarly before and after menopause remains unclear. Because “obesity” encompasses distinct exposures, we distinguished general, central/visceral, subcutaneous/fat distribution, and lean-mass phenotypes. We searched PubMed (2016–2026) for studies analyzing women with obesity, insulin resistance, or T2DM; assessing BMD, osteoporosis, or fracture risk; and including both pre- and postmenopausal women as subgroups or comparing results by menopausal status. From 1884 records obtained by the database search, 14 studies met the criteria, including approximately 2.55 million women, with pre- and postmenopausal women split almost equally. In premenopausal women, visceral adipose tissue, body fat percentage, elevated HOMA-IR, and central obesity were associated with low BMD. In postmenopausal women, lean mass loss (sarcopenia), subcutaneous adipose tissue dis-tribution, metabolic syndrome components, and adipokine dysregulation were among the factors associated with low BMD. Regional fat deports showed differing associations with BMD across menopause, although these findings derive largely from single studies or small subgroups. Metabolic disorder–BMD relationships are modified by menopausal status: visceral adiposity is consistently associated with lower premenopausal BMD, whereas sarcopenic obesity and adipokine imbalance are associated with postmenopausal bone loss. These findings require confirmation by longitudinal and interventional studies but provide a biologically plausible basis for menopausal-specific risk-assessment hypotheses.

Article.Title: Protective Effects of Curcumin and Quercetin Against Vancomycin-Induced Acute Kidney Injury in Rats
Article.Authors: Basiouny M.; Abd Elbadee A.; Aly A.; Sherif A.; Mohamed G.; Amr D.; Osama H.; Tarek H.; Hassan J.; Abuelhaded K.; Alam-ElDein K.; Damiati L.; Gadelmawla M.

CUR and QUR (100 mg/kg each) were administered orally by gavage in 0.2 mL of olive oil for 14 consecutive days, while VCM (400 mg/kg, i.p.) was administered from days 8 to 14. Renal Nrf2 immunoreactivity and histopathological alterations were also examined. VCM significantly impaired renal function, increased renal MDA, NO, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, Bax, and caspase-3, and decreased GSH, SOD, CAT, Bcl-2, and Nrf2 immunoreactivity. These biochemical and molecular disturbances were accompanied by marked tubular degeneration, vacuolation, luminal dilation, and vascular congestion. CUR and QUR significantly attenuated these alterations, while their combined administration produced the most pronounced improvement across renal biomarkers, oxidative/antioxidant status, inflammatory and apoptotic markers, Nrf2 expression, and renal architecture. CUR and QUR exerted significant protective effects against VCM-induced AKI, potentially through coordinated restoration of antioxidant defense, attenuation of inflammation and apoptosis, and preservation of renal tissue integrity. Their combined administration demonstrated higher renoprotective activity, supporting further investigation of this combination as a potential strategy for mitigating VCM-associated nephrotoxicity.

Article.Title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Restores Obesity-Induced Impairment of Taste-Guided Appetitive Behaviors Through Striatum Gi Signaling
Article.Authors: Inoko J.; Rattanajearakul N.; Watanabe H.; Kaibuchi K.; Nakajima K.

However, this effect was not reproduced by pair-feeding or dietary restriction, indicating that recovery of taste-guided behavior was not solely because of calorie restriction. Specifically, Gi signaling in the striatum may contribute to this restoration.

Article.Title: Serum Levels of Heat Shock Protein 70 in Pre-Eclampsia: A Systematic Review of Current Evidence
Article.Authors: Samara A.; Janho M.; Floros T.; Zacharouli K.; Ioannou M.; Messini C.; Ziogas A.; Garas A.; Daponte A.; Sotitiou S.
Article.Abstract: Heat shock protein 70 (HSP70) is a stress-responsive molecular chaperone involved in cellular homeostasis and immune regulation during pregnancy. The late-onset analysis also demonstrated a non-significant pooled effect (SMD: 0.37; 95% CI: −1.75 to 2.49; p = 0.730). Considerable heterogeneity was observed in both analyses (I2 = 97.1% and 97.9%, respectively). Although most study-specific estimates suggested elevated circulating HSP70 concentrations in pre-eclampsia, particularly in early-onset disease, neither pooled analysis reached statistical significance. The current evidence does not demonstrate a consistent association between maternal circulating HSP70 and pre-eclampsia. Prospective studies using standardized onset definitions, sampling schedules, and laboratory methods are needed before HSP70 can be considered a biomarker.

Article.Title: Protein Lactylation in Sepsis-Associated Acute Lung Injury: Evidence and Controversies
Article.Authors: Sun X.; Zhang S.; Wang G.; Bao H.; Mao Z.
Article.Abstract: Sepsis-associated acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome (SA-ALI/ARDS) is an important complication of sepsis involving disruption of the alveolar–capillary barrier and immunometabolic dysregulation. Lysine lactylation (Kla) may link metabolic states to transcriptional regulation and protein function. However, blood lactate, global Kla abundance, and the function of lactylation at specific sites are not interchangeable. This review organizes the evidence by cell type, histone and non-histone substrate, and modification site, and separately evaluates modification identification, functional perturbation, lung injury phenotypes in animal models, and observations in patients. Current studies do not show a uniform direction of effect: some lactylation events have been associated with glycocalyx degradation, ferroptosis, inflammatory amplification, and intercellular injury signaling, whereas other studies report protective feedback. Differences in models and levels of intervention limit direct comparisons. Evidence for context dependence is emerging, but dependencies on time, concentration, and disease stage have not been adequately validated. Histone H3 lysine 18 lactylation (H3K18la) in patient samples provides a candidate biomarker signal; its independent clinical value and the efficacy of lactylation-targeted interventions remain to be established. Future work should prioritize cell- and site-specific causal validation and connect these studies with standardized assays in patient samples and external clinical validation.

FAPI provided additional lesion characterization in medullary thyroid carcinoma, although a newly identified parapharyngeal lesion remained unconfirmed, and the muscular focus was indeterminate. Discordance with FDG and DOTATATE findings was also observed. 68Ga-FAPI PET/CT may provide complementary information in selected thyroid cancer cases but requires cautious interpretation alongside other imaging, histopathology, and follow-up.

Article.Title: Molecular Mechanisms Knowledge and Phenotypic Screening Should Be Complementary Approaches for Effective Not Risky Antibiofilm Research
Article.Authors: Alfei S.; Schito G.; Reggio C.; Zuccari G.
Article.Abstract: Biofilms (BFs) bacteria are rapidly developing tolerance to conventional antibiotics, which may no longer be effective. Therefore, there has been a proliferation of studies into new antibiofilm (ABF) compounds. In this regard, intriguing questions are raised and the tension “between efficacy and understanding” has been highlighted. Questions raised include the following: (i) Are BF mechanistic studies indispensable and strictly required, especially in academic institutions, where economic support may be scarce? (ii) Is a purely phenotypic approach still pertinent given relevant journals requirements? (iii) Is empirical efficacy alone sufficient for a study to be of relevance in effective ABF research? (iv) Are the issues of high costs, long-term mechanistic insights, and associated environmental issues key to defeating BFs and do they represent benchmarks for determining the scientific value and usefulness of a study? In order to meet the needs of readers less familiar with the field, the state of the art of the global challenge against BF, with respect to difficult-to-treat and even lethal chronic infection is provided. The available armamentarium of functioning antibiotics/combinations against BF is discussed, modern ABF compounds classification is reported, and relevant investigations required to investigate ABF mechanisms is clarified. A total of 126 studies on ABF activity are considered, represented in summary tables and discussed. Unexpectedly, experimentally validated causal molecular mechanisms were found in only 27of the studies examined. A total of 99 out of the 126 papers considered only phenotypic screenings or descriptive clues. This approach represents the main trend in the most recent literature, reflecting the limited resources of most academic laboratories but with progressive publication growth over time. Although phenotypic studies are the most abundant in the literature, these should be complemented by mechanistic insights that would enhance ABF research, avoiding risks such as poor rational lead optimisation, risk of false-positive phenotypic results, limited inter study reproducibility and major translational barriers. This review is simultaneously a conceptual/explorative review, integrating mechanistic and bibliometric perspectives to critically examine how antibiofilm research may balance phenotypic efficacy and mechanistic understanding.

Article.Title: Age-Stratified Homologous Recombination Repair Alterations in Prostate Cancer: A Single-Center Retrospective Tumor NGS Study from Türkiye
Article.Authors: Erdogdu S.; Cirak-Balta M.; Ekinci B.; Orenay-Boyacioglu S.; Boyacioglu O.; Erdogdu I.; Culhaci N.
Article.Abstract: The relationship between age and homologous recombination repair (HRR) and DNA damage response (DDR) pathway alterations in prostate cancer (PCa) remains incompletely understood. This study evaluated age-stratified HRR/DDR alteration patterns and recurrent genomic co-alterations using tumor-based targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS). In this single-center retrospective study, 101 patients with PCa were stratified into <65 (n = 25) and ≥65 (n = 76) age groups and analyzed using a 93-gene tumor-based NGS panel. Within the predefined 93-gene analytical set, 83 of 101 patients (82.2%) had at least one historically recorded pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) alteration. Core HRR alterations were more frequent in the <65-year group than in the ≥65-year group (36.0% vs. 15.8%; p = 0.0455). A comparable effect estimate was observed after adjustment for Grade Group (aOR = 2.94; 95% CI: 1.04–8.34; p = 0.0425), although the association did not meet the conventional significance threshold after FDR correction (q = 0.0627). When age was analyzed as a continuous variable, no statistically significant association with Core HRR alterations was observed (OR per 5-year increase = 0.83; 95% CI: 0.64–1.08; p = 0.162). Expanded DDR alterations (p = 0.251), total genomic alteration burden, and individual gene frequencies showed no significant differences between age groups. Post hoc sensitivity analyses excluding low-VAF Core HRR records or additionally excluding records with unavailable VAF/depth information yielded nonsignificant age-group comparisons (p = 0.0656 and p = 0.1044, respectively), indicating uncertainty regarding the robustness of the observed association. Exploratory co-detection analysis identified statistically significant but nested associations involving BLM, ATR, RAD50, and HERC1. These patterns were also observed in a fixed-margin sensitivity analysis; however, they do not establish functional cooperation or age-specific co-alteration architecture. Core HRR alterations were more frequently reported in patients aged <65 years; however, this association did not remain statistically significant after FDR correction and was not supported by a significant continuous-age association. Given the historical clinical P/LP classifications, limited clinical annotation, and incomplete retrospective technical validation, these findings should be considered exploratory and require confirmation in independently characterized cohorts.
