Article.Title: Degradation of Perovskite Solar Cells at the Molecular Level Under Terrestrial and Space Conditions: From Bond Chemistry and Defect Dynamics to Device Failure
Article.Authors: Akylbayeva A.; Nussupov Y.; Aldiyarov A.; Lesbayev A.; Yerezhep D.
Article.Abstract: Metal halide perovskite solar cells now rival crystalline silicon in efficiency, but their lifetime remains the main obstacle to deployment, on Earth and in space. Most reviews treat each stressor separately. Here, following a PRISMA 2020-guided search of Scopus (5123 records screened, 254 reports included), we organize the evidence as a molecular degradation cascade: bond and cation vulnerability, point-defect formation and migration, phase and stoichiometry change, interfacial and electrode reactions, and loss of device performance. Mapping moisture, oxygen, heat, light, bias, particle and ionizing radiation, vacuum, low temperature and thermal cycling onto this cascade shows that chemically distinct stressors converge on a few shared events: halide-defect migration, deprotonation of the organic cation, iodide oxidation with lead reduction, and phase change. Their reversal appears to depend on whether their products are retained, on whether an irreversible chemical branch is reached, and on temperature. Vacuum and reactive contacts push degradation toward irreversibility, and cold is expected to slow the healing reactions. We link stabilization strategies to the events they interrupt, report measured activation-energy increases of up to about 0.4 eV, and identify gaps in operando, combined-stressor, low-temperature and flight data. A roadmap outlines how molecular understanding can guide the design of durable photovoltaics.

Article.Abstract: Sepsis is characterized by dysregulated host immunity. We integrated single-cell transcriptomes from five adult peripheral blood mononuclear cell cohorts, comprising 1,503,982 cells after quality control, to characterize peroxisome-related transcriptional states. Disease-control comparisons included 114 participants and 1,087,108 cells. Peroxisome-related scores were generally elevated across multiple cell populations in sepsis. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells exhibited a continuous score gradient, with distinct high- and low-scoring states associated with inferred differentiation potential, pseudotime, and ligand–receptor communication. Participant-level modeling evaluated a three-gene signature comprising LYL1, PIM1, and RPS7 across 113 machine-learning strategies. The glmBoost-random forest model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.982 in the training cohort and 1.000 in GSE290679. These findings delineate peroxisome-related immune states in adult sepsis and nominate an exploratory computational three-gene signature.

Article.Title: IL-1β Inhibition Is Associated with Reduced Tumor Growth and Changes in Anti-Tumor Immunity and the Colonic Microbiome
Article.Authors: Machluf-Katz N.; Barsky G.; Stalin S.; Moadi L.; Weiner A.; Goldstein O.; Krishnamohan M.; Kaplanov I.; Fishman D.; Bersudsky M.; Braiman A.; Levin L.; Cooks T.; Turjeman S.; Koren O.; Osyntsov A.; Voronov E.
Article.Abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide. Interleukin-1β (IL-1β) is a pro-inflammatory cytokine upregulated in many tumors, including CRC. In the tumor microenvironment (TME) it promotes angiogenesis, immunosuppression, and resistance to chemotherapy. We aimed to elucidate the correlation between TME IL-1β and colon microbiotic changes during CRC progression and approach inhibition of IL-1β in combination with standard chemotherapy as a therapeutic strategy. Using an orthotopic mouse model of CRC, we compared tumor growth, metastatic spread, immune infiltration and microbiome composition in control and IL-1β knockout mice. We studied the effects of IL-1β neutralization in combination with FOLFOX chemotherapy on CRC progression. IL-1β promotes CRC progression by enhancing pro-inflammatory signaling, associated with recruiting myeloid cells and microbiome dysbiosis. Its deficiency delayed tumor growth and reduced metastasis that was accompanied by increased infiltration of antigen-presenting cells and changes in gut microbiota. FOLFOX chemotherapy exacerbated systemic and local inflammation, facilitating liver metastasis, where the addition of anti-IL-1β antibodies significantly reduced FOLFOX-induced inflammation and enhanced anti-tumor immunity. IL-1β from the TME links microbiome dysbiosis, tumor-promoting inflammation and poor chemotherapy outcomes in CRC. Combining IL-1β inhibition with standard FOLFOX chemotherapy represents a promising therapeutic approach to CRC treatment.

Article.Title: Integrative Multi-Omics Analysis Suggests a Candidate Gut Microbiota–Butyrate–AP-1 Regulatory Axis in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Article.Authors: Cai Y.; Li H.; Qiu B.; Cai Y.; Zhang J.; Chen Z.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is molecularly heterogeneous and associated with an inflammatory tumor microenvironment. Gut microbial metabolites can regulate host transcriptional and immune programs, but their links to ESCC remain unclear. We investigated whether microbiota-related metabolic signals converge on disease-associated transcriptional regulators in ESCC. We integrated paired tumor and normal transcriptomes from two ESCC datasets with differential expression, functional enrichment, protein–protein interaction, and transcription factor activity analyses. Bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) evaluated associations between gut microbial traits and ESCC. MR findings were integrated with gutMDisorder and gutMGene to construct a microbiota–metabolite–transcription factor network. Molecular docking and a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation explored potential contacts between butyrate and the activator protein-1 (AP-1)–DNA complex. Across both datasets, 159 shared differentially expressed genes were enriched in inflammatory, immune, cytokine/chemokine, and extracellular-matrix pathways, while JUN, FOS, and AP-1 showed concordantly increased inferred activity. Seven microbial traits showed nominal associations with ESCC, but none passed FDR correction. Database integration prioritized Eubacterium rectale and butyrate; metabolite-target intersection identified JUN and FOS. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations supported a relatively stable, energetically favorable interaction of butyrate at the AP-1–DNA interface. These integrative findings support a candidate E. rectale–butyrate–JUN/FOS–AP-1 axis in ESCC and provide a hypothesis-generating framework linking gut microbial metabolism to tumor transcriptional regulation.

Article.Title: Pentagalloyl Glucose Nanoparticles Attenuate Neutrophil Extracellular Trap-Associated Inflammation in Experimental Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
Article.Authors: Madukwe D.; Arora S.; Nazar V.; Zimmerman H.; Vyavahare N.
Article.Abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is characterized by chronic inflammation, vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) dysfunction, and extracellular matrix degradation. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) contribute to vascular injury, but their involvement in aneurysm progression and their potential as therapeutic targets remain incompletely understood. This study investigated NET-associated inflammation and evaluated elastin-targeted pentagalloyl glucose nanoparticles (PGG-NPs) as an immunomodulatory therapy.Anti-elastin antibody-functionalized PGG-loaded albumin nanoparticles were synthesized and characterized. AAA was induced in apolipoprotein E-deficient (ApoE−/−) mice using angiotensin II (Ang II) and β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN), with AAA evaluated at 14 and 28 days. NET formation, Padi4 and Elane expression, inflammatory cytokines, and elastin integrity were assessed. Primary mouse neutrophils and human aortic smooth muscle cells (HASMCs) were used to investigate in vitro NET formation and PGG-mediated protection. Ang II treatment induced NET formation in primary neutrophils, increasing citrullinated histone H3 (CitH3), myeloperoxidase and neutrophil elastase, which were significantly reduced by PGG. In vivo, inflammatory cytokines were elevated at day 14, whereas Padi4 and Elane expression increased markedly by day 28 alongside greater NET-associated markers and elastin degradation. PGG-NPs reduced Padi4 and Elane expression, aortic CitH3, circulating extracellular DNA and inflammatory mediators while preserving elastic lamellar architecture. Isolated NETs reduced α-smooth muscle actin expression in HASMCs, an effect attenuated by PGG. These findings suggest that NET-associated inflammation evolves during aneurysm development, with increased expression of NET-related genes accompanying advanced vascular injury. PGG-NPs attenuated this inflammatory response while protecting the aortic extracellular matrix, supporting an immunomodulatory role beyond their established elastin-stabilizing properties. Elastin-targeted PGG-NPs attenuate NET-associated inflammation and vascular injury in experimental AAA, supporting their potential as a therapeutic strategy combining neutrophil immunomodulation and extracellular matrix preservation.

Article.Title: Dynamic Cell and Organelle Architecture in Homeostasis and Cancer
Article.Authors: Wu Y.; Kang J.; Pan K.; Fang X.; Feng J.; Chen P.
Article.Abstract: Cellular function depends on the regulated size, shape, and spatial organization of cells and their organelles. This review examines cell-size control and the architectural regulation of the plasma membrane, cell–matrix adhesions, cytoskeleton, nucleus, mitochondria, endomembrane system, and biomolecular condensates. We relate these regulatory mechanisms to their functional consequences in physiological and disease contexts. Particular attention is given to cytoskeleton–nucleus coupling and the roles of the nuclear envelope and chromatin in mechanical responses, nucleocytoplasmic transport, transcription, and genome stability. Cancer serves as the principal disease context, while selected non-malignant disorders provide comparisons. Physiological adaptation supports tissue homeostasis, whereas pathological remodeling contributes to tissue dysfunction or disease progression, even when it benefits individual cells. Our contribution is a comparative structure–function framework that connects these systems through recurring constraints involving geometry, limiting molecular pools, intercompartmental connectivity, and quality control. This framework guides the interpretation of structural changes as potential drivers, adaptive responses, or downstream markers. Building on this synthesis, we hypothesize that mechanical and biochemical coupling between cellular compartments can buffer or amplify the functional impact of a given architectural perturbation. This perspective links structural observations to functional measurements and helps identify context-dependent disease mechanisms and potential therapeutic vulnerabilities.

Article.Title: A Lead-Anchored, Mixture-Aware Multi-Layer Bioinformatics Framework for Prenatal Metal Exposure at the Placental Interface
Article.Authors: Kesin M.; Öztan G.; İşsever T.; İşsever H.
Article.Abstract: Prenatal lead (Pb) exposure may perturb the maternal–fetal interface, while real-world exposure frequently involves multiple metals. We integrated a 308-record Pb-centered bibliometric corpus; 25 placental-interface studies; a 29-gene literature-derived candidate panel whose source attributions were verified against the primary publications; and human placental epigenomic, transcriptomic, miRNA–mRNA, toxicogenomic and protein-interaction resources. In the Rhode Island Child Health Study (RICHS) cohort, higher maternal Pb exposure, assessed as toenail Pb concentration, was associated with reduced placental 5-methylcytosine (5mC) at GLI2 cg05403744 (estimate = −0.004067 per log2 exposure; source epigenome-wide association study [EWAS] q = 0.02765). A candidate-probe enrichment sensitivity analysis did not show enrichment of the 29-gene probe set over the source Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC (EPIC) background (P ≈ 0.57; the result was insensitive to the choice of EPIC denominator). In the Extremely Low Gestational Age Newborns (ELGAN) cohort, 16 of the 29 candidates were expressed within the source 11,402-transcript analysis universe and were therefore testable for differential expression. No candidate overlapped the 191 Pb-associated differentially expressed genes (DEGs), an outcome compatible with chance (expected 0.27; lower-tail P = 0.763). RAB5A was the sole candidate among 657 principal component 2 (PC2)/multi-metal-associated DEGs, also compatible with chance (expected 0.92; P[X ≥ 1] = 0.613). Expression-matched permutation against the primary count data reproduced both results (empirical P = 0.83–0.88 and 0.54–0.64), so RAB5A is treated as hypothesis-generating mixture-level evidence rather than statistical convergence. Three experimentally supported miRNA–mRNA pairs showed modest inverse placental correlations (ρ = −0.145 to −0.203) that persisted after adjustment for clinical and histological covariates and in singleton pregnancies, but were abolished by removal of the dominant axis of expression variation (37.5% of variance) and were not distinguishable from randomly paired miRNA–mRNA controls (empirical P = 0.22–0.38). PIK3R1 and WNT3A were therefore removed from the prioritized exposure-linked follow-up set, and the miRNA strand of evidence for RAB5A was downgraded to exploratory context. The prespecified 12-protein core physical protein–protein interaction (PPI) network (CORE12) retained only CASP1–NLRP3 (STRING score = 0.998; enrichment p = 0.103). Overall, the integrated evidence supports a branched, Pb-anchored and mixture-aware hypothesis framed within the adverse outcome pathway (AOP) concept, rather than a demonstrated causal sequence or a statistically enriched gene set. The study contributes a systematic placental-interface map of the Pb-centred developmental literature and an explicit calibration of a literature-derived candidate set against chance expectation, showing how readily overlaps of the size often reported as cross-layer convergence arise under the null.

No inferred metabolic module passed donor-level false discovery rate correction. Three patient-derived models showed inconsistent score changes two days after irradiation. These findings support reproducible associations with transcriptional programs, not measurements of oxygenation, metabolic flux or radiation survival. The candidate remains exploratory, and clinical radioresistance or prediction of radiotherapy benefit has not been established.

Article.Title: A Pectin Methylesterase Inhibitor GhPMEI58 Enhances Susceptibility to Botrytis cinerea in Arabidopsis
Article.Authors: Situ S.; Shan Q.; Wu Y.; Xiao N.; Huang Y.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Plant cell walls contain large amounts of pectin, whose degree of methylesterification is essential for cell wall integrity and plant resistance to pathogens. PMEIs (pectin methylesterase inhibitors) suppress pectin methylesterase activity and thereby regulate the degree of pectin methylesterification. Thus, PMEIs engage in the plant response to fungal pathogens like Botrytis cinerea. However, whether the PMEI genes in Gerbera hybrida respond to B. cinerea remains unknown. In our study, it was demonstrated that GhPMEI58, a pectin methylesterase inhibitory protein isolated from gerbera, acts as an inhibitory regulator of gray mold resistance in Arabidopsis thaliana. The expression level of GhPMEI58 was downregulated after B. cinerea infection in gerbera. Additionally, GhPMEI58 was specifically detected during the vegetative growth stage in transgenic Arabidopsis. Overexpression of GhPMEI58 in Arabidopsis reduced the enzymatic activity of pectin methylesterase in leaves and enhanced susceptibility to B. cinerea. Furthermore, multiple genes linked to plant defense showed obvious expression differences in leaves of transgenic Arabidopsis versus wild-type after infection. This study provides possible insight into how GhPMEI58 modulates plant–pathogen interactions through the modulation of pectin methylesterification and downstream defense responses.

Article.Title: FN14 Promotes the Progression of Hepatocellular Carcinoma by Up-Regulating KRT7 and CXCL8
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Shang Z.; Xing X.; Tong X.; Qi D.; Ye X.
Article.Abstract: We identified that fibroblast growth factor inducible 14 (FN14) was upregulated in HBV transgenic HCC cells. Overexpression of FN14 promotes the proliferation, migration, and invasion of hepatoma cells, while knockdown of FN14 causes the opposite effect. The data from orthotopic tumor formation in mice showed that the tumor weight in mice injected with FN14-overexpressing Hepa1-6 cells was higher than that with the control cells, while FN14-knockout Hepa1-6 cells were unable to form tumors. The results from DEN-induced liver cancer in mice indicate that overexpression of FN14 enhances tumor formation, while knockout of FN14 reduces liver cancer. Further studies uncover that FN14 upregulates the transcription of KRT7 and CXCL8. Knockdown of KRT7 reduces the proliferation, migration, and invasion of FN14-overexpressing cells. The data from the TCGA-LIHC cohort indicate that the transcription level of FN14 is positively correlated with that of KRT7 and CXCL8, as well as the relative amount of immunosuppressive MDSCs in HCC. These results indicate that FN14 promotes cell proliferation/migration by up-regulating KRT7 and facilitates MDSC recruitment in the liver by enhancing the expression of CXCL8, which consequently facilitates the development of HCC.

Article.Abstract: Bladder cancer is the 10th most common cancer worldwide, with high recurrence rates and limited therapeutic options for chemoresistant cases. Brazilin, a natural homoisoflavonoid from Caesalpinia sappan L., exhibits antitumor activity, but its mechanism in bladder cancer remains largely unknown. This study aimed to investigate whether brazilin exerts anti-bladder cancer effects through mitotic catastrophe and to identify the key molecular target involved. KIF20A overexpression promoted cell proliferation and migration, while knockout suppressed these effects. Brazilin showed the strongest inhibitory effects in KIF20A-overexpressing cells, and in vivo, it inhibited tumor growth most effectively in KIF20A-overexpressing tumors. These findings demonstrate that brazilin suppresses bladder cancer growth by downregulating KIF20A and inducing mitotic catastrophe, establishing KIF20A as a critical functional mediator and providing a mechanistic rationale for targeting the mitotic pathway in bladder cancer therapy.

Article.Title: Recipient CCL5 −403G>A (rs2107538) Polymorphism and Acute Graft-Versus-Host Disease in Pediatric Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation
Article.Authors: Ozdilli K.; Senturk Ciftci H.; Oztan G.; Ogret Y.; Kıvanç D.; Oguz R.; Odaman Al I.; Yaman Y.; Elli M.; Anak S.; Oğuz F.

In particular, CCL5 mediates the recruitment of CCR1-, CCR3-, and CCR5-expressing immune cells, suggesting that regulatory polymorphisms in the CCL5 gene may influence inflammatory cell trafficking and recipient susceptibility to aGvHD. Genotypes were determined by polymerase chain reaction–restriction fragment length polymorphism (PCR-RFLP) and analyzed according to aGvHD status. Acute GvHD occurred in 25 patients (40.3%). Patients without aGvHD were classified as grade 0; grade 0–I and grade II–IV groups comprised 40 (64.5%) and 22 (35.5%) patients, respectively. The CCL5 rs2107538 variant showed a significant association with aGvHD, with enrichment of the GA genotype and A allele among affected patients, whereas the GG genotype was more frequent in patients without aGvHD. No significant associations were detected for recipient CCR9 rs12721497 or CXCL12 rs1801157. This pattern suggests that a promoter-region CCL5 variant, rather than the evaluated CCR9 or CXCL12 loci, may be the most relevant chemokine-related susceptibility signal in this pediatric cohort. Article.Title: From Blisters on Vipers to Nanobubbles in Vessels: A Review of Biological Decompression Bubbles
Article.Authors: Wang L.; Yu J.; Liu X.; Zhao N.; Huang G.; Zhao H.; Fang Y.
Article.Abstract: Decompression sickness (DCS) is an occupational health problem fundamentally driven by the formation of gas bubbles in the human body, which could be a threat to the life of divers, astronauts and hyperbaric workers. The phenomenon of bubble formation in organisms after decompression provided the earliest experimental evidence for decompression theory. Since then, researchers across different eras have conducted extensive work on biological decompression bubbles, which brought about the establishment of gas nuclei theory. While Yount’s quantitatively calculable Varying Permeability Model (VPM) has been successfully applied to decompression algorithms, its core assumption—the “surface-active skin”—remains experimentally unverified. But recent developments in research on nanobubbles and the Active Hydrophobic Spots (AHS) hypothesis have provided new physicochemical perspectives. This review critically evaluates the theoretical evolution and experimental progress in this field, integrating recent advances in molecular dynamics and interfacial physics. To contribute to shedding light on the unresolved paradox of biological decompression bubbles in vivo, we highlight the significance of the paradigm shift from macroscopic gas dissolution to interfacial mechanics, which may help identify the missing links in current DCS research and outline a new multidisciplinary path forward.

Article.Title: In Utero Gene Therapies Using CRISPR-Cas9 Technology: A Narrative Review of Current Research and Translational Perspectives
Article.Authors: Oczkowska W.; Pelczar A.; Głodek K.; Kimber-Trojnar Ż.
Article.Abstract: Gene therapy has emerged as a promising approach for the treatment and prevention of genetic disorders through targeted modification of cellular DNA. The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats-CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR-Cas9) system, in particular, has enabled precise correction of disease-causing mutations. Recently, increasing interest has been directed toward in utero gene therapy, which offers a unique therapeutic window to prevent irreversible pathological changes before birth. This narrative review explores the current preclinical landscape of in utero CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing. A literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar databases to identify relevant studies, focusing primarily on delivery strategies, temporal considerations, therapeutic efficacy, and safety outcomes. Preclinical evidence demonstrates that prenatal delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 components in animal models can achieve durable genome editing in multiple fetal tissues, leading to phenotypic improvements in metabolic and early-onset lethal disorders. However, significant challenges remain, including off-target effects, mosaicism, maternal–fetal immune interactions, and the risk of unintended germline transmission. Ultimately, while in utero CRISPR-Cas9 gene therapy holds substantial therapeutic potential for severe congenital pathologies, rigorous safety evaluation, delivery optimization, and resolution of ethical and regulatory dilemmas are strictly required before clinical translation can be considered.

Article.Title: Regional Differences in Mutational Processes and Molecular Timing in Microsatellite-Stable Colorectal Cancer Cohorts from Northern and Southern China
Article.Authors: Liu K.; Liu X.; Deng L.; Liu Y.; Quan F.; Zhang X.; Zhang B.; Lan Y.; Zhang X.; Xiao Y.
Article.Abstract: Geographic variation in colorectal cancer (CRC) incidence and mutational spectra has been well described, whereas the extent to which regional context is associated with tumor evolutionary timing remains unclear. We first examined the association between CRC incidence and mean annual temperature and then analyzed whole-exome sequencing data from 688 microsatellite-stable (MSS) CRCs across four Chinese cohorts, classifying tumors from Harbin and Beijing (n = 65) as the cold-region group and those from Guangzhou (n = 623) as the non-cold-region group. Comparative analyses revealed differences in mutational processes and evolutionary timing between the two groups. Specifically, cold-region tumors exhibited higher estimated contributions from mutational signature SBS93, a more polarized distribution of copy-number gain timing, and later inferred molecular timing of whole-genome doubling. Patients in the cold-region group were also diagnosed at younger ages, and higher SBS93 exposure was associated with younger age at diagnosis. In contrast, no widespread differences were detected in driver gene mutation frequencies, copy-number alterations, genomic instability metrics, or most immune-related features. Together, these findings suggest distinct mutational processes and evolutionary timing patterns in MSS CRCs from cold-region and non-cold-region cohorts, providing new insights into the geographic heterogeneity of colorectal cancer evolution.

Article.Title: MiR-93 Attenuates CALR Mutant-Driven Oncogenic Activity in Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Tang W.; Chen Y.; Huang C.; Chen Y.; Wu Y.; Yang Y.; Wu C.; Tsai W.; Tsou H.; Chen C.
Article.Abstract: High Mobility Group AT-hook 2 (HMGA2), a recognized oncogene in myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN), is regulated by dozens of microRNAs (miRNAs), notably, let-7a. We hypothesize that other miRNAs might influence HMGA2-associated phenotypic characteristics in MPN, as well. To explore further, we applied a miRNA library screening system to identify potential HMGA2 mRNA 3′-untranslated region (3′UTR)-targeting candidates and evaluated their functional effects in MPN cell models. MicroRNA-93 (miR-93) was among the few HMGA2 3′UTR-targeting miRNAs differentially expressed in MPN cells, being downregulated in CALR-mutated cells but not in JAK2V617F-mutated cells. Correspondingly, HMGA2 overexpression was observed in CALR-mutated cells. Luciferase reporter assays confirmed that miR-93 could target a highly conserved sequence within the HMGA2 3′UTR region. Upregulation of miR-93 in CALR-mutated cells significantly impeded cellular growth and increased apoptosis in vitro. Rapid development of myelofibrosis phenotypes was observed in immune-deficient mice transplanted with CALR-mutated cells. Ectopic expression of miR-93 in these cells attenuated myelofibrosis-like phenotypes in vivo and prolonged the survival of these mice. Clinically, higher miR-93 expression was associated with features suggesting a more indolent disease course in a small cohort of CALR-mutated MPN patients, although these observations were exploratory. Collectively, our experimental findings support a potential tumor-suppressive role for miR-93 in CALR-mutated MPN, while the clinical associations require further validation in larger patient cohorts.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification of bHLH Transcription Factors in Alfalfa (Medicago sativa) Reveals Anther Development-Associated Subfamilies and Tapetum-Specific Promoters
Article.Authors: Meng X.; Li C.; Zhou J.; Yi D.; Ma L.; Xie K.; Wang X.; Tang J.
Article.Abstract: Alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) is an important perennial leguminous forage crop, and the development of male-sterile lines is valuable for the exploitation of heterosis. Functional characterization of basic helix–loop–helix (bHLH) transcription factors associated with tapetum development may provide insights into the molecular basis of male sterility in alfalfa. To address this gap, this study aimed to systematically identify anther development-associated bHLH genes and explore their potential roles in tapetum development by integrating genome-wide characterization, expression profiling, and promoter activity analysis. In this study, 634 bHLH members were identified in the genome of the alfalfa cultivar Zhongmu No. 4, with a particular focus on 40 candidate genes belonging to the anther development-associated subfamilies II and III(a + c). Phylogenetic analysis, gene structure and conserved motif characterization, chromosomal localization, synteny analysis, protein–protein interaction network prediction, and promoter cis-regulatory element analysis revealed patterns of evolutionary conservation and potential functional divergence among these genes. Tissue-specific expression profiling and expression analyses under salt, abscisic acid (ABA), and jasmonic acid (JA) treatments revealed distinct tissue-dependent and temporal expression patterns among MsbHLH genes, suggesting potential roles in integrating reproductive development with hormonal and environmental stress responses. Comparative transcriptomic analysis across tissues further identified MsbHLH2 and MsbHLH30 as candidate genes preferentially expressed in anthers. Promoter-driven GFP reporter assays showed that both genes exhibited strong promoter activity in the anther wall, particularly in the tapetal region, during the meiotic and microspore stages, whereas promoter activity markedly declined at the late microspore stage. These results support tapetum-associated expression of MsbHLH2 and MsbHLH30 and identify them as promising candidate regulators of tapetum development in alfalfa. By combining genome-wide analysis with spatial and developmental promoter activity characterization, this study provides new insights into the potential regulatory roles of bHLH genes in alfalfa anther development. Their promoters may also serve as useful tools for targeted gene expression in the tapetum, facilitating functional studies of anther development and providing candidate genetic resources for the development of male-sterile alfalfa germplasm.

Article.Title: Beyond Canonical ABA Signaling: The Expanding SnRK2 Network in Plant Growth, Stress Adaptation, and Immunity
Article.Authors: Meena V.; Renu N/A.; Pełelska M.; Sip A.; Bennewitz B.; Klösgen R.; Park E.; Ludwików A.
Article.Abstract: SNF1-related protein kinase 2 (SnRK2) belongs to the sucrose non-fermenting-1-related protein kinase family and takes part in a number of different physiological processes. These kinases play a key role in the abscisic acid-dependent stress signaling and are involved in metabolism, systemic immunity, and interactions with other phytohormone pathways. In this review, we focus on the recent progress concerning the role and function of this family in ABA-mediated stress responses, its interactions with other phytohormone pathways, and its newly assigned functions in biotic stress, retrograde signaling, and stress tolerance. We also examine the regulatory mechanisms that govern SnRK2 kinase activity, such as post-translational modifications and protein–protein interactions. Lastly, we summarize what is currently known about the role of the SnRK2 family in plant acclimation and stress tolerance as well as the related regulatory mechanisms. The wide range of functions shown by this group among different plant species, from model organisms to crops and to non-model plants, suggests that it has the potential to improve crop stress tolerance and thus contribute to global food security in the face of climate change.

Article.Title: Multi-Omics Integration Identifies G6PD as a Candidate Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarker for Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Suggests Its Immunoregulatory Role
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Tian M.; Zhuang W.; Hu Y.; Yu X.; Jia X.; Gong A.
Article.Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has an insidious onset and poor prognosis, and the limited diagnostic accuracy of alpha-fetoprotein necessitates novel biomarkers. This study aims to construct an analytical framework for integrating multi-omics data from tumor tissues and single-cell transcriptomes. By integrating and analyzing the transcriptomic and clinical data of HCC, we confirmed that glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is significantly upregulated in tumor tissues and consistently overexpressed across multiple independent cohorts, with a diagnostic area under the curve of 0.906. High G6PD expression was associated with shorter overall survival and remained an independent adverse prognostic factor. To explore the potential mechanism, a virtual knockout of G6PD was simulated on single-cell transcriptomic data, which indicated that G6PD knockout significantly perturbs immune-related pathways, including antigen processing and presentation and phagocytosis. These findings not only highlight the potential of G6PD as a candidate diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for HCC but also suggest its involvement in the tumor immune microenvironment, offering new directions for further research on the diagnosis and treatment of HCC.

Article.Title: Astrocyte Developmental Timing in Neurodevelopmental Disorders: A Stage × Module Framework
Article.Authors: Kwon K.; Mabunga D.; Kim R.; Lee K.; Kim D.; Kim J.; Park E.; Kim H.; Jeon S.; Shin C.
Article.Abstract: Astrocytes play essential roles in neural circuit assembly, stabilization, and refinement, yet their contributions to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) have largely been considered within static or disorder-specific frameworks. Converging evidence indicates that astrocytes acquire distinct functional capacities across development. Here, we organize these capacities into six functional modules—synaptogenic support, excitatory–inhibitory (E/I) homeostasis, metabolic coupling, neuromodulatory regulation, inflammatory threshold setting, and neurovascular stabilization—each representing a partially separable domain of astrocyte function with a distinct developmental trajectory. We integrate these modules across three major developmental windows—fetal, early postnatal, and adolescent—to propose a stage × module framework of astrocyte involvement in NDDs. A central premise of this framework is that neurodevelopmental vulnerability may arise not solely from astrocyte dysfunction per se, but from temporal mismatches between the maturation of astrocyte functional capacity and evolving circuit demand. During early postnatal development, the convergence of synaptogenic signaling and glutamate transporter maturation defines a vulnerability window in which perturbations may preferentially destabilize circuit assembly and contribute to social, sensory, and hyperexcitability phenotypes. During adolescence, continued astrocyte remodeling, particularly in association cortices, intersects with increasing neuromodulatory and metabolic demands and may influence attentional and executive stability. Different forms of temporal mismatch—including delayed maturation, premature stabilization, and excessive gain amplification—may therefore generate distinct phenotype clusters even when the underlying molecular perturbations overlap. We further conceptualize sex as a developmental modifier that can shift the timing, amplitude, or sensitivity of astrocyte module trajectories through hormonal, chromosomal, and immune-mediated mechanisms. This dynamic perspective accommodates heterogeneity across diagnostic categories while preserving mechanistic coherence and generates testable predictions regarding stage-specific molecular signatures, phenotypic consequences, and therapeutic responses. By reframing NDDs as stage-dependent disruptions of astrocyte functional modules and their alignment with circuit demand, the proposed framework suggests that therapeutic strategies should incorporate developmental timing alongside molecular specificity, providing a conceptual basis for stage-informed intervention and developmental neuroglial precision medicine.

Article.Title: Myocardial Ischemia and Cardioprotection: From Pathophysiology to Novel Therapeutic Targets
Article.Authors: Adenawoola M.; Mouton A.; Khan M.; Zeng H.; Young M.; Stec D.
Article.Abstract: Ischemic heart disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide and is frequently complicated by myocardial ischemia–reperfusion (I/R) injury, which contributes substantially to infarct expansion, adverse ventricular remodeling, and heart failure. The pathophysiology of myocardial ischemia involves a complex interplay among energy depletion, intracellular acidosis, calcium overload, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and the activation of apoptotic, necroptotic, pyroptotic, and ferroptotic cell death pathways. Endogenous cardioprotective mechanisms, including ischemic preconditioning, postconditioning, remote ischemic conditioning, heat shock proteins, bilirubin signaling, and mitochondrial quality-control pathways, have demonstrated potent infarct-limiting effects in experimental models. These protective responses are mediated through interconnected signaling networks which converge to preserve mitochondrial integrity, maintain calcium homeostasis, reduce oxidative stress, and enhance cell survival. In addition, innate and adaptive immune responses play critical roles in post-infarction repair and remodeling, although excessive and/or prolonged inflammation can exacerbate injury. Despite strong mechanistic evidence, the translation of cardioprotective therapies into clinical practice has been challenging due to comorbidities, patient heterogeneity, and the complexity of human disease. Emerging approaches, including mitochondrial-targeted antioxidants, cell-based therapies, anti-inflammatory interventions, ferroptosis inhibitors, and SGLT2 inhibitors, offer promising opportunities for developing effective, multifaceted cardioprotective strategies.

Article.Title: Exploratory Plasma Multiomic Profiles Associated with Chronic Kidney Disease in Patients with Severe Aortic Stenosis
Article.Authors: Perales-Sánchez I.; Peralbo-Molina Á.; Sanchez-Martinez J.; Tejerina M.; Herrera-Flores C.; Sánchez P.; Padial L.; Lopez-Almodovar L.; Chicano-Gálvez E.; Mourino-Alvarez L.; Barderas M.
Article.Abstract: Calcific aortic stenosis (AS) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are progressive disorders associated with high morbidity and mortality. CKD accelerates AS progression and, when both conditions coexist, significantly worsens clinical outcomes. Therefore, characterizing circulating molecular differences associated with CKD in patients with AS may help define the molecular phenotype of this high-risk comorbidity. Plasma samples from patients with AS, with and without CKD, were analyzed through a multiomics approach using PASEF technology. Results were processed and analyzed using the bioinformatics tool Metascape to select two proteins with high potential as biomarkers: pantetheinase or vanin 1 (VNN1) and alpha 1 acid glycoprotein (A1AG1). These proteins were verified in an independent cohort of samples using immunodetection. Our findings show differences in the circulating proteomic and metabolomic profiles of patients with AS with and without CKD, suggesting that inflammation, oxidative stress and lipid metabolism are associated with CKD in this setting. These exploratory findings describe CKD-associated circulating proteomic and metabolomic differences in severe AS and provide hypotheses for validation in larger, appropriately controlled and longitudinal cohorts. These studies, which simultaneously examine multiple comorbidities, lay the groundwork for personalized medicine strategies, paving the way for more effective patient management.

Article.Title: Nebularine, a Natural Adenosine Analog, Modulates Cell Cycle Progression, Migration, and Survival in Breast Cancer Cells: Integrating In Vitro Findings with In Silico Transcriptomic Analysis
Article.Authors: Dizeci N.; Şengül G.; Kiran F.; Telkoparan-Akillilar P.; Yıldırım Ö.
Article.Abstract: Breast cancer remains a highly heterogeneous malignancy, accounting for nearly one-third of female cancers worldwide; thus, there is an urgent need for novel selective agents to overcome treatment resistance and systemic toxicities. We investigated the selective antiproliferative, antimigratory, and pro-apoptotic mechanisms of Nebularine (NEB), a natural purine nucleoside analog, across breast cancer cellular models by integrating phenotypic and transcriptional responses with structural binding dynamics and clinical prognostic correlations. Cell viability and selective indices (SIs) were evaluated in breast cancer (MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7) and non-malignant human mammary epithelial (MCF-12A) cells using MTT assays across a 0–200 μM concentration range. Cellular motility was assessed via two-dimensional wound healing assays. Cell cycle kinetics and apoptotic populations were quantified using Annexin V/PI flow cytometry. qRT-PCR was performed to profile key cell cycle (CCNA2, CDK1, CDK2, CDKN1A/p21, CDKN1B/p27, and TP53) and apoptotic (BAX, BCL2L1/Bcl-XL, CASP9, and CASP3) transcripts. Structural interactions were investigated using AutoDock Vina molecular docking models. Clinical transcript expression and prognostic relevance were evaluated using TCGA/GTEx datasets via GEPIA2 and Kaplan–Meier survival analyses. NEB exerted moderate, dose-dependent antiproliferative activity, displaying an estimated IC50 of ~100 μM in aggressive MDA-MB-231 cells and IC50 > 200 μM in MCF-7 cells (57.93% viability at 200 μM), while non-malignant MCF-12A cells retained 99.75% viability at 200 μM (IC50 > 200 μM), yielding an in vitro selectivity index (SI) > 2.0. NEB treatment impaired two-dimensional wound closure in breast cancer cells without compromising baseline non-malignant cellular motility. Flow cytometry demonstrated prominent S-phase entrapment (accumulating up to 53.23%) alongside significant execution of apoptotic cell death. Transcriptional profiling revealed profound downregulation of key replication drivers (CCNA2 and CDK1) in both cancer lines, alongside p53-independent CDKN1A (p21) upregulation in MCF-7 cells. In silico docking predicted thermodynamically favorable structural compatibility with CDK1, Casp9, Bcl-XL, and Cyclin A2 (ΔG = −6.5 to −6.6 kcal/mol). Clinically, CCNA2 and CDK1 were overexpressed in BRCA primary tumors (p < 0.05) and portended poor survival, whereas elevated CASP9 expression correlated with extended overall and progression-free survival (p < 0.05). NEB acts as a selective purine nucleoside analog that triggers S-phase cell cycle arrest and apoptotic cell death in breast cancer models while demonstrating favorable selectivity over non-tumorigenic mammary epithelium. By transcriptionally suppressing pathologically elevated clinical drivers (such as CCNA2 and CDK1), NEB provides a promising structural template for further preclinical translational development.

Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Postmortem studies have reported altered astrocyte-associated RNA in depression, but its relationship with recovered cellular composition remains unclear. Public prefrontal single-nucleus data included 71 donors; a total of 30 depression cases and 32 controls met primary analysis criteria. Exploratory KCNJ10–ATP1A2–ATP1B2 expression was also lower (−0.76; −1.19 to −0.34). Both reductions exceeded changes in the original six-marker reference and an external 50-gene astrocyte reference. The indices remained correlated after adjustment for reference expression and astrocyte nuclear fraction (r = 0.48; 0.23–0.67), although comparable correlations occurred among 10,000 abundance- and detection-matched gene set pairs. Nuclear fraction adjustment attenuated diagnosis coefficients to −0.27 and −0.41, with intervals crossing zero; estimates also changed after excluding extreme fractions. Four tissue cohorts yielded negative estimates, with imprecise pooled effects: −0.42 control SD (−0.89 to 0.04) and −0.29 (−0.71 to 0.14). These findings describe relative reductions in selected astrocytic transcripts alongside differences in nuclear representation, with covariance comparable with that of matched gene sets. Suicide, tissue source differences and missing individual postmortem covariates limit attribution to depression and the separation of cellular regulation from sampling effects.

Article.Title: Immune–Fibrosis Transcriptional Co-Variation Is a Depot-General Feature of Human Adipose Tissue: A Cross-Cohort Transcriptomic and Machine Learning Benchmark with HIV as the Probe Condition
Article.Authors: Luo H.; Wu J.
Article.Abstract: Whether immune–fibrosis coupling in adipose tissue is disease-specific molecular rewiring or a generic tissue property remains untested. We re-analyzed three publicly archived human adipose transcriptomic cohorts under an analysis plan defined a priori (not a registered protocol; archived scripts with fixed seeds document the a priori definition), scoring a 30-gene myeloid immune module and a 29-gene fibrosis module per sample. The two programs co-varied strongly in people with HIV (Spearman ρ = +0.64, p = 0.0006, n = 29) and in HIV-negative subcutaneous fat (ρ = +0.86, p = 0.024, n = 7), with no between-group difference (Fisher z difference −0.53, 95% CI −1.58 to 0.52, p = 0.32; power ≈ 17%; TOST equivalence not established, p = 0.66), and replicated across epicardial and subcutaneous depots in coronary artery disease (CAD) and control strata (ρ = +0.67 to +0.75; p = 0.78). An L2-regularized logistic regression benchmark accurately classified the fat depot (area under the curve 0.92, permutation p ≤ 0.0005) yet carried no demonstrable information on HIV status (0.52, 95% CI 0.27–0.77) or CAD (0.63–0.66). The nominal HIV-associated gene program—interferon-gamma chemokines up, lipid metabolism down—was disease-dissociated (one of 74 genes shared with 762 CAD hits; rank correlation −0.003), and immune–mitochondrial coupling was inverse (ρ = −0.36, permutation p ≤ 0.0005). These findings position immune–fibrosis transcriptional co-variation as a depot-general feature of the analyzed adipose cohorts onto which HIV superimposes expression-level shifts; co-variation of bulk-tissue modules does not demonstrate functional coupling, and the between-group equivalence is underpowered rather than established.

Article.Title: Gangliosides and Other Glycolipids as Multiple Players in the Nervous System: Their Implications for Human Disorders
Article.Authors: Mutoh T.
Article.Abstract: Gangliosides, including GM1 ganglioside (GM1), are sialic acid-containing glycosphingolipids that are involved in essential physiological roles such as cell–cell recognition, adhesion, transmembrane signaling, neuronal development, and cell fate determination. They are crucial to all phases of neuronal development. Gangliosides are enriched in the outer layer of neuronal membranes of the nervous system, where their contents are ten times higher than in other cell types. Moreover, gangliosides (especially GM1) have neuroprotective effects on neuronal cells through various pathways, although the identities of these pathways remain relatively unclear. Notably, some neurodegenerative diseases, such as Parkinson’s disease, have recently been reported to be associated with significant deficiencies of some gangliosides. Because of their location on the outer layer of the plasma membrane of neurons and immune cells, some anti-ganglioside antibodies can attack and bind to these cell-surface gangliosides. These antibodies provoke unexpected and unfavorable effects in neuronal and immune cells, as observed in Guillain–Barré syndrome with anti-GM1 antibodies. At present, however, the molecular mechanisms of these unfavorable effects remain to be explored. Here, I describe the molecular actions of gangliosides in the nervous system as both neuroprotective and neurotoxic agents.

Article.Title: Diet and Endocrine Mechanisms Linking Obesity to Cancer
Article.Authors: Maiorano P.; Shani S.; Miriello I.; Marino A.; Martinelli C.; Cortellino S.
Article.Abstract: Obesity increases the risk of several cancers through endocrine, metabolic, and inflammatory alterations. Diet influences these processes by shaping energy balance, adipose tissue function, insulin signaling, and interactions between the gut and peripheral organs. This narrative review examines how adipose tissue dysfunction supports tumor development and how nutritional interventions, physical activity, and incretin-based therapies may modify the underlying pathways. Particular attention is given to the insulin–insulin-like growth factor (IGF) axis, adipokines, nutrient sensing, and the context-dependent actions of muscle-derived interleukin-6. Evidence from human dietary studies does not establish a universal advantage of continuous restriction over intermittent regimens, and findings from animal tumor models require separate interpretation. Structured exercise has improved disease-free survival in a randomized trial after adjuvant chemotherapy for resected colon cancer. Incretin-based therapies produce substantial weight loss and selected cardiovascular benefits, whereas their effects on cancer incidence, recurrence, and survival remain incompletely established. Observational associations and experimental antitumor mechanisms should therefore inform prospective research rather than treatment claims. An integrated approach to obesity in oncology should address metabolic health while preserving nutritional adequacy, muscle mass, and treatment tolerance.

Article.Authors: Chen J.; Yu L.; Lin Y.
Article.Abstract: Long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) may influence intestinal epithelial responses to oxidative injury, but their role in ferroptosis-associated barrier dysfunction in chickens remains unclear. This study investigated whether an n-6-enriched PUFA mixture increases susceptibility to glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) inhibition and impairs epithelial barrier function in chicken apical-out enteroids. Enteroids derived from embryonic day 18 chickens were pretreated with a 200 μM mixture of arachidonic acid, eicosapentaenoic acid, and docosahexaenoic acid (n-6:n-3, 20:1) for 24 h, followed by 1 μM RSL3 for 6 or 12 h. UAMC-3203 (500 nM) was evaluated in a rescue experiment. PUFA pretreatment alone did not significantly reduce viability, but exacerbated RSL3-associated viability loss (PUFA × RSL3 interaction, p = 0.0012). UAMC-3203 partially restored viability, supporting ferroptotic involvement. PUFA pretreatment increased labile Fe2+-associated fluorescence. Lipid peroxidation showed a significant RSL3 main effect, without significant PUFA-dependent amplification. Combined treatment increased 4-kDa fluorescein isothiocyanate–dextran (FD4) permeability compared with the other treatment groups, without significant changes in CLDN1 or ZO-1 mRNA. GPX4 mRNA increased with PUFA, while SLC7A11 and PTGS2 increased under combined treatment. These findings indicate that the tested n-6-enriched PUFA mixture enhances susceptibility to GPX4-inhibitor-associated injury, with functional consequences for intestinal epithelial permeability.

Article.Title: β-Sitosterol Exerts Modest Anti-Androgenic Effects in Experimental Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: A Comparative Study with Dutasteride
Article.Authors: Buț M.; Tero-Vescan A.; Vari C.; Ősz B.; Pușcaș A.; Jîtcă G.; Bába L.; Cozac-Szőke A.; Nistor M.; Muresan X.
Article.Abstract: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is an age-related condition strongly associated with androgen signaling, chronic inflammation, and dysregulated apoptosis. Furthermore, its effects on inflammatory cytokines and apoptosis-related markers did not reach statistical significance following monotherapy. These findings support the further investigation of β-sitosterol as a potential complementary approach to BPH management, rather than as an equivalent alternative to established pharmacological treatments, including through optimized formulations or combinations with other bioactive compounds.

Article.Title: Adipose Specific Kat2a Knockdown Reveals Divergent Lipid Metabolic Regulation in an In Vivo Mouse Model and Isolated Human Adipocytes
Article.Authors: Sharma R.; Tasoula A.; Perkins C.; Barth N.; Silvis Z.; Bosron A.; Ofosu C.; Lee M.; Natarajan P.; Reddy U.; Sharma V.
Article.Abstract: Kat2a is a lysine acetyltransferase and plays an important role in metabolic regulation. Obesity-induced deregulation of metabolism predisposes to the development of insulin resistance, an underlying factor in several metabolic diseases. In this study we combined human adipocyte studies with an adipose-specific Kat2a knockout mouse model to determine whether KAT2A is required for adipose metabolic regulation in vivo. We show that in human adipocytes, small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated KAT2A knockdown altered the expression of lipid metabolism genes and impaired insulin signaling, suggesting that KAT2A contributes to the regulation of adipocyte metabolic function. In contrast, adipose-specific Kat2a deletion in a mouse model did not alter body weight, adiposity, glucose tolerance, or insulin sensitivity under physiological conditions. Moreover, the expression of genes involved in lipid metabolism, glucose uptake and insulin signaling in adipose tissue were largely preserved or slightly upregulated in adipose-specific Kat2a knockout mice, suggesting a compensatory mechanism that maintains adipose metabolic homeostasis. Together these findings indicate that murine Kat2a in adipocytes is not required for maintaining adipose metabolic homeostasis or whole-body insulin sensitivity under either physiological or diet-induced obese conditions despite exerting metabolic effects in human adipocytes. Our study identifies divergent metabolic phenotypes between cultured human adipocytes and an adipose-specific Kat2a knockout mouse model, highlighting the importance of experimental context and systemic physiological regulation in interpreting the metabolic consequences of KAT2A depletion. These findings underscore the need to validate observations from cellular models in physiologically relevant in vivo systems before considering their potential therapeutic implications.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification and Characterization of the SnRK Gene Family in Safflower (Carthamus tinctorius L.)
Article.Authors: Wang S.; Su Q.; Xiong J.; Li J.; Shi Y.; Gao Y.; Liang R.; Bai L.; Li L.; Zhou Y.; Wei J.; Xiao G.; Zhang T.; Li L.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: The sucrose non-fermenting 1 (SNF1)-related protein kinase (SnRK) family integrates metabolic, developmental, hormonal, and stress signals in plants. Transcriptome and RT-qPCR analyses further uncovered distinct tissue- and developmental-stage-specific expression patterns of CtSnRK genes during seed development from 10 to 40 days after flowering. Article.Title: HLA-DQA1*05 and HLA-DQA1*05/HLA-DQB1*02 Co-Carriage in Relation to Anti-TNF Antibody Concentrations and Response in Iraqi Patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease
Article.Authors: Kanna B.; Azeez S.
Article.Abstract: HLA-DQA1*05 has been associated with anti-TNF immunogenicity, but evidence from Iraqi patients remains limited. Article.Title: Drug Targeting MCT4 for Melanoma Treatment to Overcome Resistance to BRAF and MEK Inhibitors
Article.Authors: Spinello I.; Saulle E.; Bozzuto G.; Colone M.; Pasquini L.; Levati L.; Caporali S.; Facchiano F.; Labbaye C.
Article.Abstract: Melanoma patients harboring the BRAFV600E mutation frequently display primary or acquired resistance to BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Understanding this chemoresistant phenotype has highlighted the crucial role of metabolic plasticity, which drives a hybrid phenotype utilizing both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation. Conversely, in resistant A375/DT cells, which exhibit high oxidative stress and CD147 overexpression, AC-73 or polydatin could be used to eradicate these cells if combined with cytotoxic agents. Notably, syrosingopine, which can be used in combination with dabrafenib in parental A375 cells, demonstrated the highest efficiency in eradicating the resistant A375/DT cells. Article.Title: ER–Mitochondria–Lipid Droplet Contact Sites in MASLD and CKM Syndrome: From Hepatic Metabolic Compartmentalization to Multi-Organ Crosstalk
Article.Authors: Zhuang S.; Lin Y.; Chen X.; Chen X.; Yu J.; Yao Z.; Lin F.
Article.Abstract: Cardiovascular–kidney–metabolic (CKM) syndrome describes a multisystem continuum in which metabolic dysfunction, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular disease reinforce one another. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is common across CKM stages, but the mechanisms linking hepatic lipid handling to systemic injury remain unresolved. Hepatic metabolism depends on dynamic contacts among the endoplasmic reticulum, lipid droplets, and mitochondria, which coordinate lipid synthesis, storage, mobilization, oxidation, calcium handling, and organelle function. This review evaluates evidence that remodeling of these contacts contributes to MASLD and may amplify CKM crosstalk. We distinguish structural proximity from molecular composition and metabolic flux and propose operational criteria for a candidate “contact trap”: preserved or increased lipid droplet–mitochondria proximity accompanied by impaired adjustment of lipid droplet-derived fatty-acid handling to changing demand. This definition separates potentially maladaptive contact states from protective lipid storage and requires interface-selective perturbation and rescue to establish causality. We further examine evidence linking hepatic stress to circulating lipids, extracellular vesicles, mitochondrial danger signals, and inflammatory mediators while emphasizing that the liver is a potential metabolic amplifier rather than the sole initiator of multi-organ injury. Finally, we outline experimental and translational priorities for testing contact-dependent mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Computational Analysis of SLC15A4 Nonsynonymous Variants: Potential Implications for Immune Signaling in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
Article.Authors: Aldoseri M.; Aldoseri G.; Alwabran A.; Aldoseri G.; Mohager S.; Ahmed M.; Bedewi M.; Moglad E.; Koura H.; Kamal E.

Next, conservation analysis and 3D protein modeling were performed using ConSurf and AlphaFold-based prediction, with visualization by UCSF ChimeraX. Per-Residue Cα Coordinate Displacement was examined using bio3d methods. Population frequencies and interactions within the functional network were assessed using gnomAD and STRING analyses. Rs375529962 was the most deleterious nsSNP with the highest overall pathogenicity and instability of protein structure, followed by rs1955878827 and rs182703912, with rs202110778 being the least deleterious variant. Four pathogenic nsSNPs in the SLC15A4 gene were identified. These mutations may affect the structure and function of SLC15A4 with the potential to impair immune regulation and contribute to the aberrant innate and adaptive immune activation characteristic of SLE.

Article.Title: Targeting ANGPTL3 for Lipid Lowering in Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: A Narrative Review of Genetic, Preclinical and Clinical Evidence
Article.Authors: Blagov A.; Babayeva G.; Maksaeva A.
Article.Abstract: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide despite the widespread use of statins and proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors. A substantial fraction of treated patients retain elevated triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and remnant cholesterol after low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) targets have been met, which has been proposed to contribute to residual cardiovascular risk; however, lowering triglycerides alone has not reliably reduced cardiovascular events, and benefit appears more closely tied to the reduction in apolipoprotein B (apoB)-containing particles. Angiopoietin-like protein 3 (ANGPTL3), a hepatically secreted regulator of lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase, has emerged as a mechanistically distinct target that lowers triglycerides, LDL-C, and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) independently of the LDL receptor (LDLR). This narrative review, based on a structured PubMed/MEDLINE search, synthesizes the structural biology of ANGPTL3, compares ANGPTL3 with PCSK9, ANGPTL4, apolipoprotein C-III (APOC3) and other lipid-lowering therapies, summarizes the preclinical and clinical evidence on its pharmacological inhibition, including the effects of each agent on LDL-C, triglycerides, apoB and non-HDL-C, and discusses the limitations of that evidence and of the review itself. Loss-of-function variants in ANGPTL3 are associated with a lower risk of coronary artery disease in large population cohorts. Pharmacological inhibition has since been tested with several independent modalities, which lower atherogenic lipids but have not been shown to reduce cardiovascular events: monoclonal antibodies (evinacumab, SHR-1918), antisense oligonucleotides (vupanorsen), small interfering RNAs (zodasiran, solbinsiran), and, most recently, in vivo CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing (CTX310). In humans, the evidence for pharmacological inhibition is limited to lipid biomarkers in generally small and short trials; reductions in apoB are consistently smaller than reductions in triglycerides, and evidence of plaque regression derives from animal models only. Each modality carries a distinct efficacy and hepatic safety profile, a divergence (hepatic fat increased with the antisense agent vupanorsen but not with the siRNA agents studied) whose cause—platform chemistry, depth of knockdown, study population or ANGPTL3 biology itself—cannot be determined from the available cross-trial comparisons. We conclude with concrete recommendations for cardiovascular outcome trials, prospective hepatic-fat monitoring, and rational combination strategies with LDLR-dependent agents.

Article.Title: Oral Microbiota in Atherosclerosis and Ischemic Stroke: A Compartment-Resolved Critical Narrative Review of Immunoinflammatory Mechanisms and Clinical Evidence
Article.Authors: Miłoszewski N.; Ostrycharz-Jasek E.; Meller A.; Warias P.; Machowska-Sempruch K.; Simurda T.; Mikler J.; Masztalewicz M.; Pawlukowska W.
Article.Abstract: Periodontitis and oral microbial signals have been associated with atherosclerosis and ischemic stroke, but findings from oral samples, carotid plaques, cerebral thrombi, and clinical studies support different inferences. Detection of microbial DNA or proteins in vascular specimens does not establish oral origin, viability, or pathogenic activity. Periodontal interventions improve selected inflammatory and vascular surrogate outcomes, but evidence of fewer first or recurrent strokes remains inconclusive. The proposed framework guides appraisal and study design; it is not a validated causal model or diagnostic tool. Established periodontal care and structured post-stroke oral hygiene remain warranted, whereas microbiome-guided prediction and periodontal treatment specifically for stroke prevention remain investigational.

Article.Authors: Huang X.; Wang X.; Zhang X.; Zhong M.; Xie X.; Ren M.

Moreover, it identifies potential genetic targets for strain engineering and light-optimization strategies to enhance astaxanthin production.

Article.Title: Probiotic–Botanical Combination Modulates Neuroinflammatory and Neurochemical Pathways in an LPS-Induced In Vitro Gut–Brain Axis Model
Article.Authors: Mulè S.; Parini F.; Galla R.; Uberti F.
Article.Abstract: The gut–brain axis represents an important pathway through which intestinal and central nervous system processes may interact, particularly under inflammatory conditions. These findings provide preliminary in vitro evidence of treatment-associated changes in intestinal barrier-related properties and in inflammatory and neurochemical responses following transfer of basolateral conditioned medium to LPS-challenged organoid–microglia co-cultures. Given the involvement of related pathways in neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), these findings may provide a basis for further investigation of treatment-associated effects within experimental gut–brain axis systems, without establishing disease-specific mechanisms or therapeutic effects in neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Authors: Messina F.; Macia-Villa C.; Puche M.; Cipolloni V.; Bellomo R.; Saggini R.; Ariani A.; Conforti A.
Article.Abstract: Targeted therapies have expanded treatment options for psoriatic arthritis (PsA), but clinical response, treatment continuation, and patient-perceived recovery may diverge in routine care. Associations involving sex, obesity, disease burden, and previous treatment were context dependent. Missing original search and screening records and incomplete risk-of-bias adjudication materially limit reproducibility and confidence. The review’s contribution is an integrated interpretation of distinct treatment outcomes rather than a therapeutic hierarchy. Molecular profiling offers complementary research directions but does not establish validated treatment-selection biomarkers within this evidence base.

Article.Title: Plant-Derived Flavonoids in Ocular Diseases: Redox Signaling, Neurovascular Protection, Regulated Cell Death, and Translational Frontiers
Article.Authors: Vargas-Durazo J.; Lewis-Luján L.; Iloki-Lewis A.; Galvez-Ruiz J.; Sugich-Miranda R.; Perez-Martinez C.; Guerrero-Magaña D.; De La Torre-Othon S.; Trujillo-López S.; Iloki-Assanga S.
Article.Abstract: Flavonoids are compounds found in many plants and foods. Laboratory studies suggest that some can protect eye cells against oxidative and inflammatory injury, but these findings do not establish benefits for patients. This review examines which compounds were tested, how they act, whether they reach the eye, and how closely experimental models resemble human disease. It proposes a framework for identifying the evidence needed before selected flavonoids can be evaluated as complementary approaches to ocular care. Plant-derived flavonoids have been investigated as potential modulators of oxidative, inflammatory, and neurovascular injury in ocular diseases, but their clinical relevance remains uncertain. This narrative review critically examines the literature published from January 2016 to August 2026, supplemented by selected earlier landmark studies, to identify the evidence connecting experimental protection with plausible ocular interventions. The synthesis considers chemical identity, mechanistic support, ocular exposure, disease-model relevance, and functional outcomes. Experimental studies report modulation of antioxidant defenses, inflammatory signaling, mitochondrial homeostasis, cell survival, angiogenesis, and fibrotic remodeling. However, pathway-associated changes do not necessarily establish causal mechanisms, and protection in acute cellular or animal injury models does not establish efficacy in chronic human disease. Translation is further limited by metabolism, uncertain retinal exposure, heterogeneous preparations, and limited controlled clinical evidence. An author-proposed qualitative framework distinguishes the conclusions supported by individual findings from the additional validation required. Research priorities include standardized interventions, exposure-informed experiments, causal mechanistic studies, human-relevant models, and controlled trials with clinically meaningful outcomes. Flavonoids should therefore be regarded as candidates for further investigation as complementary interventions rather than established ocular therapeutics.

Article.Title: Multi-Modal Programmed Cell Death and Immune Microenvironment Alterations Associated with Ligamentum Flavum Hypertrophy and Ossification: An Integrative Bioinformatic Analysis with Single-Cell and m6A Profiling
Article.Authors: Zhang W.; Zha D.
Article.Abstract: Hypertrophy and ossification of the ligamentum flavum cause spinal stenosis and myelopathy, yet the roles of programmed cell death (PCD) and immune remodeling remain unclear. We profiled five PCD modalities, immune infiltration, and m6A regulators in ligamentum flavum bulk transcriptomes (GSE113212; n = 8), with validation in GSE206560 (N6-methyladenosine (m6A) MeRIP-seq) and GSE106253, and single-cell analysis of GSE294458/GSE267819 (33,817 cells) replicated in GSE271018 (51,686 cells). Ferroptosis showed the largest direction-consistent score difference (GSVA p = 0.029; GSEA NES = 1.60) and correlated with macrophage infiltration (r = 0.859, p = 0.006) and immune-checkpoint expression. Single-cell analysis localized ferroptosis activity to SPP1+ macrophages in two independent cohorts; SPP1 signaling was predicted to originate from this subset and target fibroblasts via SPP1–CD44 and SPP1–integrin pairs; macrophage ferroptosis activity increased along a computational state ordering (ρ = 0.354). More m6A peaks were detected in ossified libraries (15,102 vs. 6073 sites), with hypermethylation and downregulation of SLC7A11 (logFC = −2.81, adj. p = 0.008). A six-gene signature (five genes detectable in the external cohorts) separated disease from control samples in three cohorts (internal AUC = 1.0, exploratory). These convergent associations nominate an m6A–SLC7A11–ferroptosis–SPP1+ macrophage axis as a candidate, hypothesis-generating mechanism requiring experimental validation.

Article.Title: Multi-Omics Profiles Reveal Molecular Regulation of Ovarian Aging in Chickens
Article.Authors: Ma W.; Guo A.; Huang S.; Zhang W.; Zhang H.; Zhang H.; Zhang B.
Article.Abstract: Ovarian aging shortens the laying cycle in hens, thereby reducing egg production and posing a major constraint on the economic efficiency and sustainability of the poultry industry. This study integrates three omics approaches to investigate the molecular alterations underlying age-related ovarian functional decline. We employed an integrated approach combining RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq), and data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics, with selected targets validated by qRT-PCR and Western blotting. Ovarian tissues with follicles > 8 mm removed were collected from a total of 12 hens, including six 30-week-old hens (W30, n = 6) and six 90-week-old hens (W90, n = 6), to identify age-associated changes in gene expression, ribosome footprints (RFs), and protein abundance. A total of 18,836 genes, 17,007 RFs, and 6738 proteins were detected. Among these, 562 genes, 430 genes with altered translation efficiency (TE), and 252 proteins were differentially expressed between the two groups. Further analyses indicated that, in aged ovaries, the down-regulation of steroidogenic genes, including STAR, CYP11A1, HSD3B1, and FDX1, was associated with reduced steroid hormone synthesis. The up-regulation of matrix stiffness-related proteins, including MFAP4 and SGCE, together with the down-regulation of genes and proteins associated with matrix degradation and autophagic clearance, including ADAMTS15, MRC1, RAB7A, and CTSB, was indicative of ovarian tissue sclerosis. In summary, the multi-omics data revealed that ovarian aging in laying hens is associated with coordinated alterations across multiple molecular layers. This study identifies key genes and proteins associated with ovarian aging and provides a foundation for generating mechanistic hypotheses regarding the molecular processes involved.

Article.Title: Contemporary Approaches to Melanoma Detection and Advanced Therapeutics
Article.Authors: Spector D.; Abramchuk D.; Prokudina I.; Erofeev A.; Sviderskaya E.; Krasnovskaya O.
Article.Abstract: Cutaneous melanoma is a highly aggressive form of skin cancer, which accounts for up to 80% of skin cancer-related deaths worldwide. Despite significant advances in melanoma treatment for the past 15 years, the established therapies with BRAFi/MEKi and immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) suffer from acquired and intrinsic resistance, as well as adverse side effects. Due to the limited specificity of currently employed diagnostic probes, an urgent need exists for a new generation of molecular probes that can selectively target malignant melanoma lesions and provide adequate information on the stage and progress of the disease. This review highlights the most recent advances made in 2025–2026 in melanoma treatment and detection. In the first section, new selective PET tracers and fluorescent probes for diagnosis and staging of melanoma are discussed. The second section discusses diverse approaches to melanoma treatment, such as novel small-molecule drugs capable of overcoming resistance to BRAFi/MEKi and increased sensitivity to ICIs, multi-action nanoformulations, biocompatible microneedle patches for efficient transdermal drug delivery, and novel immunotherapy approaches. Together, this review illustrates that further research in the treatment and diagnosis of melanoma is moving toward new molecular targets, efficient drug combinations, and patient-specific therapy.

Article.Title: Biomass Concentration Determines Langmuir and Freundlich Isotherm Parameters in Biosorption by Chlorella vulgaris
Article.Authors: Koska P.; Fóris T.; Gráczer K.; Fiser B.; Vanyorek L.; Viskolcz B.
Article.Abstract: Adsorption isotherm parameters are widely used to characterize biosorbents, although their dependence on biomass concentration remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated Ni(II) and Cd(II) biosorption by Chlorella vulgaris using complete adsorption isotherms determined independently at different biomass concentrations. Increasing biomass concentration reduced specific metal uptake and altered the shape and concentration dependence of the adsorption isotherms, rather than merely changing their fitted parameters. Langmuir and Freundlich models revealed decreasing apparent adsorption capacities with increasing biomass concentration. For Ni(II), the Langmuir half-saturation concentration decreased from approximately 60.9 to 10.9 mg L−1, whereas Cd(II) exhibited substantially lower half-saturation concentrations without a consistent biomass-dependent trend. Nested F-tests comparing pooled and biomass-specific nonlinear models demonstrated significantly better fits for the latter for both metals (p < 0.01). These findings establish that biomass concentration influences the entire adsorption relationship, including its apparent saturation capacity and concentration dependence. Consequently, adsorption isotherm parameters should not be regarded as universal biosorbent constants independent of experimental biomass concentration. The results highlight the importance of biomass-specific isotherm characterization for reliable comparison of biosorption studies and the development of adsorption-based metal removal processes.

Article.Title: MetaREX: An Interactive Workflow for Quantitative Profiling of Transcriptionally Active Antimicrobial Resistance Genes from Soil Metatranscriptomes
Article.Authors: Marzec-Grządziel A.
Article.Abstract: Environmental metatranscriptomics can identify transcripts associated with antimicrobial resistance (AMR), but their analysis requires multiple bioinformatic steps. I present MetaREX, an interactive workflow integrating read quality control, rRNA screening, de novo assembly, coding sequence prediction, transcript quantification, KO-based functional profiling, CARD/RGI screening, comparative analyses, and reporting. MetaREX was technically assessed using 12 publicly available rhizosphere and bulk-soil metatranscriptomes from a single BioProject. The workflow completed the predefined analytical stages and generated the expected quantitative and annotation outputs. CARD/RGI identified nine Strict matches representing three best-hit ARO assignments across six samples. KO-based profiles provided broader functional information and were not treated as ARG-specific evidence. This assessment demonstrates workflow operation on the analyzed datasets but does not establish analytical accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, or generalizability to other environments. Evaluation on independent datasets and reference materials is needed to assess these properties.

Article.Title: Cell Crosstalk and Cell-Specific Response Contribute to Restenosis After the Implementation of Drug-Eluting Stents
Article.Authors: Chatha A.; Buenaventura G.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Restenosis, the re-narrowing of arteries after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), occurs when vascular injury activates smooth muscle cell (SMC) proliferation, leading to neointimal hyperplasia. Drug-eluting stents (DES) inhibit this process by delivering mTOR inhibitors to suppress SMC growth. However, these drugs also slow endothelial repair and cause chronic inflammation. Therefore, restenosis still occurs in patients receiving DES. This review summarizes the signaling pathways in SMCs, endothelial cells (ECs), and monocytes/macrophages that contribute to restenosis. Although cell culture experiments have investigated individual signaling pathways in different cell types, cell behavior is regulated by cell–cell and cell–microenvironment crosstalk. This review highlights the role of growth factors, cytokines, exosomes, and microparticles in multicellular crosstalk after vascular injury. Cell crosstalk and components in the extracellular matrix are not considered in most mechanistic studies and therapeutic screening efforts aimed at improving PCI outcomes. Cell culture models that incorporate multicellular crosstalk and extracellular matrix will provide a better picture of drug response, allowing cell-specific effects and potential side effects to be observed. Future studies using multicellular models and organ-on-a-chip platforms have the potential to enable high-throughput drug screening in physiologically relevant systems to support the development of therapeutics and DES following PCI.

Article.Title: Integrated Single-Cell Analysis and Network Pharmacology Reveal the Potential Mechanisms of Baicalein in Pancreatic Cancer
Article.Authors: Liu J.; Wang Y.; Xu H.; Lan W.; Zhao Y.; Lin R.; Zhao J.
Article.Abstract: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is a highly aggressive malignancy with poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options. Baicalein, a major flavonoid derived from Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi, exhibits multiple antitumor activities, but its key targets and mechanisms in PC remain unclear. This study integrated network pharmacology, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), molecular docking, and in vitro experiments to investigate the potential mechanisms of baicalein against PC. Network pharmacology identified baicalein-related targets associated with PC, which were mainly enriched in receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, PI3K–AKT, MAPK, Ras, and apoptosis-related pathways. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis revealed heterogeneous SRC expression across epithelial subpopulations, with higher expression observed in Cluster 1, and dynamic changes during epithelial cell state transitions. Molecular docking predicted favorable interactions between baicalein and key proteins, including SRC and EGFR. In vitro experiments further showed that baicalein significantly reduced PC cell viability and decreased SRC protein expression. These findings suggest that baicalein may exert antitumor effects in PC through multiple targets and pathways, with SRC representing a potential key target, providing a theoretical basis for further evaluation of baicalein as an adjuvant therapeutic candidate for PC.
