Article.Title: Metabolic and Transcriptional Profiles of A549 Lung Adenocarcinoma Cells Following Prolonged IFNγ Exposure
Article.Authors: Shi Y.; Xu T.; Li X.
Article.Abstract: Interferon-gamma (IFNγ) plays an important role in antitumor immunity; however, persistent IFNγ signaling can subject tumor cells to persistent inflammatory stress, fostering adaptive cellular responses. Here, we investigated the transcriptional and metabolic features associated with prolonged IFNγ exposure in lung adenocarcinoma cells. A549 cells were continuously treated with IFNγ (10 ng/mL) for 23 days, with a control culture passaged in parallel. RNA sequencing and untargeted LC–MS/MS metabolomics were performed. Differential expression analysis, pathway enrichment, metabolite–gene correlation analysis, and two-way orthogonal partial least squares (O2PLS) modeling were used for exploratory multi-omics integration. Selected transcripts and proteins were examined by RT-qPCR and immunoblotting. Cell migration was assessed after IFNγ withdrawal and a separate experiment examined responses to 4-octyl itaconate (4-OI). Compared with the passage-matched control, the IFNγ-exposed cells exhibited altered redox and lipid metabolite profiles, along with activation of interferon-responsive transcripts and upregulation of stress-inducible HSP70-family genes. On day 23, total and phosphorylated STAT1 levels were higher in IFNγ-treated cells, while the ratio of phosphorylated STAT1 to total STAT1 was reduced. IRG1 and HSPA8 expression also increased at day 23, although a functional relationship between them was not established. Previously exposed cells showed greater migration after IFNγ withdrawal. In separate 4-OI treatment experiments, HSPA1A and HSPA6 protein levels were elevated, together with increased cell migration. Prolonged IFNγ exposure was associated with metabolic and transcriptional differences in A549 cells, including changes in interferon-responsive and HSP70-family genes. These exploratory findings identify candidate responses to prolonged inflammatory stimulation that require validation in independently established chronic cultures and functional studies.

Article.Title: Muricholic Acid Species Regulation Networks: From Biosynthetic Pathways to Molecular Mechanisms
Article.Authors: Zhou G.; Wei L.; Han M.; Rong R.; Ni Y.
Article.Abstract: Bile acids (BAs) are pleiotropic signaling molecules. Muricholic acids (MCAs), a distinct BA subgroup with hydroxyl groups at C3, C6, and/or C7, exhibit structural diversity that underpins functional heterogeneity. This review summarizes MCA species and their derivatives, emphasizing metabolic pathway differences between rodents and humans. We explore gut microbiota-mediated MCA transformation and the associated regulatory networks. MCAs modulate key signaling receptors—farnesoid X receptor (FXR), Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5), and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α (PPARα)—as well as pathways including the gut–liver axis, ceramide metabolism, cyclic guanosine monophosphate–protein kinase G–mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (cGMP–PKG–mTORC1) signaling, and the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis. These actions implicate MCAs in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), central precocious puberty (CPP). Their potential as diagnostic, predictive, and prognostic biomarkers is also discussed. This synthesis provides a theoretical foundation for understanding MCA-driven disease mechanisms and developing novel therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Emerging Medicinal Chemistry of the YEATS4 Epigenetic Reader
Article.Authors: Lipiński P.; Dyniewicz J.
Article.Abstract: YEATS4 (GAS41) is an acyllysine reader and a component of chromatin-remodelling complexes. Its amplification or overexpression in multiple malignancies, together with functional studies, link it to tumour growth. This has prompted efforts to develop YEATS4 ligands as chemical probes and potential anticancer agents. This review examines the structural basis of histone recognition by the YEATS4 YEATS domain and surveys the discovery, synthesis, structure–activity relationships, and biological evaluation of the ligands reported so far. We compare the thiophene-based monovalent and bivalent inhibitors, bicyclic heteroaryl–piperidine carboxamides, and emerging benzimidazole and arylthiophene series. Despite progress from fragment hits to potent ligands with cellular activity, YEATS4 inhibitor development is still at an early stage, with only a few inhibitor series reported to date and key challenges remaining.

Article.Title: Multi-Target Anti-Inflammatory Mechanisms of Stachyurus praecox Leaf Extract Revealed by Metabolomics, Network Pharmacology, Molecular Docking, and Experimental Validation
Article.Authors: Le D.; Dinh T.; Dang T.; Jang S.; Ton S.; Luu H.; Yu S.; Lee M.
Article.Abstract: Inflammation is a major pathological process underlying numerous chronic diseases, highlighting the need for anti-inflammatory inhibitors from nature. This study investigated the anti-inflammatory potential of S. praecox leaf extracts and elucidated molecular mechanisms through an integrated experimental and computational approach. As a result, the 75% methanol extract (75M) inhibited tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) production in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated RAW264.7. Untargeted metabolomic analysis led to the tentative identification of 96 metabolites, predominantly flavonoids, terpenoids, ellagitannins, fatty acids, and phenolic acids. Network pharmacology analysis of overlapping targets suggested TNF and IL6 emerging as crucial hub genes. Functional enrichment analyses further revealed significant involvement of inflammatory pathways. ADMET screening suggested potentially favorable predicted ADMET characteristics. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding energies between constituents and inflammatory targets. Experimental validation showed that the 75M extract significantly inhibited NF-κB activation by suppressing IκBα and p65 phosphorylation. Furthermore, the extract attenuated MAPK signaling by inhibiting ERK1/2 and p38 phosphorylation. These findings suggest that S. praecox exerts potent anti-inflammatory activity through a multi-component, multi-target mechanism involving the coordinated regulation of the NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways, thereby providing a therapeutic basis for further investigation of S. praecox as a promising candidate for treating inflammation.

High-performance liquid chromatography determined that the monosaccharide composition of 20dBGPS consisted mainly of galactose, galacturonic acid, and glucose. However, the fructose content in the test samples was not determined in the experiment. BPSF3 significantly (p < 0.05) reduced TNF-α secretion and downregulated toll-like receptor (TLR)-2 and nuclear factor (NF)-κB mRNA expression in LPS-stimulated macrophages, as analyzed by real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction.

Article.Title: Two Decades of Dental Pulp Regeneration Research: From Tissue Formation to Functional Recovery
Article.Authors: Kang S.; Lee M.; Hwang J.; Kim G.
Article.Abstract: Over two decades, dental pulp regeneration research has broadened from supplying cells and scaffolds to regulating the tissue environment in which regeneration occurs. Drawing on literature published primarily between 2006 and August 2026, this critical narrative review asks when tissue formation after molecular or material intervention can be interpreted as partial functional recovery or restoration of normal pulp function. Molecular findings are interpreted alongside developments in cell homing, secreted signals, endogenous repair, biomaterials, and intercellular communication. Residual vital pulp repair and reconstruction after pulp loss are assessed separately, with molecular effects judged by the model, causal tests, and directly measured outcomes. Six interdependent domains guide the assessment of progress: cell origins, perfusion, infection control, immune regulation, neural guidance, and matrix remodeling. Human histological reports show that pulp-like tissue and non-pulp repair may coexist, while clinical studies report healing and, in some teeth, positive sensibility responses or improved blood-flow-related measurements. These findings distinguish tissue formation from restoration of normal pulp function. Future studies should connect molecular interventions to tissue architecture, sustained function, and patient-relevant outcomes, while distinguishing unassessed functions from functional failure.

Article.Authors: Yang P.; Jiang Y.; Li X.; Yang J.; Yu C.; Wang H.; Jiang X.; Gu L.; Wu X.
Article.Abstract: Calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) are core decoders of Ca2+ signals in plants, playing essential roles in growth, development, stress responses, and the regulation of flowering. Using transcriptome datasets from seedlings grown under short-day (SD) and long-day (LD) conditions, we identified 3341 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and screened four photoperiod-responsive candidates (ZmCDPK21, ZmCDPK38, ZmCDPK40, and ZmCDPK43). Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) validation across inbred lines with divergent genetic backgrounds confirmed that ZmCDPK21 exhibited the most pronounced and consistent photoperiodic expression pattern. Further characterization revealed evening-phased diurnal expression of ZmCDPK21, with distinct expression-peak dynamics between photoperiod-insensitive and photoperiod-sensitive germplasm. Collectively, these results support ZmCDPK21 as a photoperiod-responsive candidate gene and warrant further investigation.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Genetic Differentiation and Evaluation of Reduced SNP Subsets for Classification of Three Cultured Rainbow Trout Types
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Yang X.; Wang W.; Hu H.; Xu S.; Song H.
Article.Abstract: Genome-wide genetic differentiation among cultured rainbow trout types remains insufficiently characterized. Here, we performed whole-genome resequencing of 60 individuals representing freshwater rainbow trout (RT), golden trout (GT), and steelhead trout (ST) maintained at the same aquaculture facility. A total of 12,547,966 high-quality autosomal SNPs were identified. Population genetic analyses revealed clear genetic separation among the three groups, with pairwise FST values ranging from 0.0972 to 0.1303. Genome-wide differentiation scans identified 401 golden-associated and 207 steelhead-associated candidate genes. Functional enrichment analyses revealed receptor-mediated signaling and extracellular matrix binding in golden-associated genes, whereas steelhead-associated genes were enriched in nucleoside transport, cell adhesion, and cellular regulatory functions. These findings provide candidate genomic regions for investigating pigmentation differences and future studies on salinity adaptation. Reduced SNP sets containing 50–500 markers were further evaluated using repeated five-fold cross-validation with fold-specific marker selection. FST-prioritized and randomly selected SNP sets achieved mean classification accuracies of 96.42–97.42% and 96.75–98.67%, respectively, indicating no consistent advantage of FST-based prioritization. Overall, this study provides insights into genomic differentiation among cultured rainbow trout populations and demonstrates the potential of reduced SNP sets for germplasm identification, pending validation in independent populations.

Article.Title: Endocrine Fibroblast Growth Factors FGF19, FGF21, and FGF23 in Pregnancy and Lactation: Metabolic Regulation and Pregnancy-Related Disorders
Article.Authors: Baran K.; Skrzynska K.; Orczyk-Pawilowicz M.
Article.Abstract: Fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) represent a diverse family of proteins that are involved in signaling pathways important for normal development, the maintenance of tissue homeostasis and metabolic regulation. A specific group of endocrine FGFs comprises FGF19, FGF21 and FGF23. These proteins act as offspring. Changes in FGF concentrations are associated with disturbances in glucose and lipid hormones circulating in the blood, regulating bile acid metabolism, energy balance and mineral homeostasis. Pregnancy and lactation are characterized by changes associated with adaptive processes in glucose and lipid metabolism, mineral balance, placental function and maternal energy consumption. This review summarises the molecular mechanisms and physiological functions of endocrine FGFs and discusses their role in maternal adaptation, fetal development and pregnancy-related disorders. Abnormalities in FGF signaling are associated with pre-eclampsia (PE), gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP), and influence the metabolic regulation of the homeostasis, endothelial and oxidative stress, abnormalities in bile acid and mineral metabolism, placental dysfunction, and fetal metabolic programming. Studies conducted on dairy cows and rodents indicate that FGF21 and FGF23 play a role in lactation-related adaptations, including lipid metabolism, skeletal remodeling, mineral homeostasis and cellular responses to stress. Evidence supporting these functions in lactating women remains limited. Human studies have identified associations between circulating concentrations of the endocrine FGF and pregnancy-related disorders, which support further investigation into their potential as biomarkers. Their clinical relevance, as well as their therapeutic efficacy and safety, remain to be determined.

Article.Title: Redistribution of CD163+ CCR2+ Monocytes from Blood Circulation to the Ascites as a Potential Indicator of Progression in High-Grade Serous Ovarian Cancer
Article.Authors: Sudarskikh T.; Kalinchuk A.; Kazakova A.; Grigoryeva E.; Iamshchikova S.; Shalygina K.; Iamshchikov P.; Yatskovskyi A.; Villert A.; Kolomiets L.; Chen S.; Zhao Y.; Kzhyshkowska J.; Larionova I.
Article.Abstract: This study aimed to identify tumor-specific changes in circulating and ascites-derived monocytes from high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC) patients using flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, RNA sequencing, and in vitro experiments. Our results demonstrate that the tumor induces a decrease in the total number of circulating monocytes but an increase in the proportion of CD163+ monocytes. Notably, CD206-expressing monocytes were reduced in HGSOC patients, with extremely low CD206 levels in peripheral blood mirroring those in tumor tissues. In contrast, a marked accumulation of CD206-positive monocyte-derived macrophages was observed in malignant ascites. The presence of CCR2 on the monocyte surface further amplified the increase in CD163+ monocytes and reversed the decrease in CD206+ monocytes in cancer patients. Transcriptional levels of CD163 corresponded to protein levels and were elevated in monocytes of HGSOC patients. Moreover, the percentage of CD163+CCR2+ monocytes was decreased in peripheral blood but increased in ascites of patients with progressive disease. A functional migration assay confirmed extensive recruitment of monocytes toward malignant ascites in vitro. Collectively, our findings suggest that the redistribution of CD163+CCR2+ monocytes from blood to malignant ascites may represent a candidate indicator of disease progression in HGSOC patients.

Article.Title: Cis-Regulatory Evolution in Plants from Cis–Trans Interactions and Regulatory Grammar to Crop Improvement
Article.Authors: Guzmán P.
Article.Abstract: Cis-regulatory evolution provides a mechanism for generating phenotypic diversity and adaptive variation that can be exploited in crop improvement. In plants, changes in promoters and other cis-regulatory elements (CREs), together with variation in transcription factors and their interactions, can modify gene expression without necessarily altering protein-coding sequences. This review examines how cis–trans interactions, regulatory grammar, and genomic context shape regulatory innovation, environmental adaptation, and domestication. Case studies involving drought responses, nutrient acquisition, cotton fiber development, fruit quality, protective cuticular traits, photosynthetic specialization, and maize grain yield illustrate how regulatory changes contribute to agronomically relevant phenotypes. We further discuss how gene duplication, polyploidization, structural variation, transposable elements, and chromatin organization generate regulatory diversity. Advances in pangenomics, single-cell and spatial multiomics, precision genome editing, synthetic promoter design, and artificial intelligence are expanding opportunities to identify and test functional regulatory variants. We propose an evolution-guided framework that integrates regulatory discovery, mechanistic characterization, and experimental validation to connect naturally occurring variation with predictive regulatory engineering. Understanding how regulatory effects depend on genetic background, cellular state, and environmental conditions will be essential for translating these discoveries into improved crop performance and climate-adapted crops.

Article.Title: Integrated Bulk and Single-Cell Transcriptomic Analyses Highlight IAPP as a Molecular Feature Associated with β-Cell Identity Remodeling in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Huang Y.; Fu Y.; Wang L.; Liu Y.; Ouyang Y.; Peng X.; Chang B.; Ding Y.
Article.Abstract: β-cell identity remodeling is an important feature of β-cell dysfunction in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), but its associated molecular characteristics remain incompletely understood. This study integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, machine learning, protein–protein interaction network analysis, gene set variation analysis, and computational perturbation to characterize β-cell identity-associated molecular features. IAPP emerged as the sole overlapping candidate from the integrated machine-learning and PPI analyses and was reduced in T2DM islets. Its expression was positively correlated with INS and NKX6-1 and negatively correlated with ALDH1A3 and SOX9. Single-cell analyses localized IAPP predominantly to β cells and identified heterogeneous β-cell transcriptional states. GSVA associated IAPP expression with functional and stress-related pathways, while scTenifoldKnk-based virtual perturbation predicted changes in networks linked to insulin secretion and proteostasis. In the T2DM mouse model, reduced pancreatic IAPP protein expression was accompanied by changes in β-cell identity-associated markers. This cross-platform convergence links IAPP expression to β-cell identity-associated signatures beyond general descriptions of diabetic islet alterations. Together, these complementary observations identify IAPP as a candidate molecular feature associated with β-cell identity remodeling, without establishing a direct causal role.

Article.Title: Network Pharmacology, Molecular Modeling, and Surface Plasmon Resonance Combined with In Vitro Validation to Elucidate the Anti-Inflammatory Effects of Delphinidin in LPS-Stimulated Macrophages: Potential Relevance to Vascular Disease
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Feng L.; Li H.; Yao L.; Zheng T.; Jia S.; Yang D.
Article.Abstract: Macrophage-driven inflammation is an important contributor to the development and progression of chronic vascular diseases. Although statins substantially reduce cardiovascular risk, residual inflammatory risk and treatment-related limitations highlight the need for complementary anti-inflammatory strategies. Delphinidin (Dp), a naturally occurring anthocyanidin found in several medicinal plants used in traditional Chinese medicine, exhibits anti-inflammatory activity; however, its effects on macrophage inflammatory signaling and their potential relevance to vascular inflammation remain incompletely understood. This study integrated network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), and in vitro experiments to elucidate the mechanisms underlying Dp-mediated regulation of macrophage inflammation. Network analyses identified AKT1 as a candidate target and the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway as a potential regulatory mechanism. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations suggested a structurally plausible interaction between Dp and AKT1, and SPR analysis provided experimental evidence of direct binding between Dp and AKT1. In lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages, Dp reduced NO production and the levels of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α). Dp also decreased the phosphorylation of PI3K (p-PI3K), Akt (p-Akt), and NF-κB (p-NF-κB), while pharmacological interventions further supported the involvement of the PI3K/Akt/NF-κB signaling pathway. Collectively, these findings suggest that Dp attenuates macrophage inflammatory responses, at least in part, by modulating this signaling pathway. These findings provide a basis for further investigation of the anti-inflammatory effects of Dp in macrophages and their potential relevance to vascular inflammation.

Article.Title: Divergent Driver Mutation Frequencies and an Exploratory Prognostic Genomic Score in Colorectal Cancer: A Cohort Study from Kazakhstan
Article.Authors: Aitkulova A.; Daniyarov A.; Rakhimova S.; Yerezhepov D.; Akilzhanova A.; Sarbassov D.
Article.Abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) exhibits substantial genomic heterogeneity across populations, yet patients from Kazakhstan remain markedly underrepresented in large-scale genomic studies. Here, we characterized the somatic mutational landscape of CRC in a cohort from Kazakhstan using targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) and compared the observed genomic profile with data from the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) Project Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (GENIE) database. Tumor samples from 32 patients with CRC were profiled using the TruSight Oncology 500 (TSO500) assay, and the mutation frequencies and patterns of co-occurring alterations were compared with those in a GENIE reference cohort of 770 CRC cases. The most frequently altered genes in the Kazakhstan cohort were TP53 (53%), APC (50%), and KRAS (44%). Comparative analysis identified differences in mutation frequencies between the analyzed cohorts, including a higher frequency of GNAS alterations (19%) and a lower frequency of APC alterations in the Kazakhstan cohort compared with the GENIE reference cohort. Co-occurrence analysis revealed recurrent combinations of driver alterations, including concurrent TP53 and KRAS mutations. To explore the clinical relevance of the genomic profile, a cohort-derived 11-gene cumulative mutation score was evaluated in survival analysis. A higher score was associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) in univariable Cox regression (HR, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.02–1.50; p = 0.034), but this association was not retained after adjustment for age, sex, and pathological stage (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 0.84–1.36; p = 0.587). The score showed a moderate positive correlation with tumor mutational burden (TMB), which persisted after exclusion of the hypermutated microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) case. However, the association between TMB and PFS was not retained after exclusion of this case. Bootstrap validation of the full multivariable Cox model indicated potential overfitting, with the optimism-corrected C-index decreasing from 0.732 to 0.650. These findings provide an initial molecular characterization of CRC in a cohort of patients from Kazakhstan and identify differences in selected somatic mutation frequencies compared with an international reference dataset. However, the limited sample size and differences in clinical and technical characteristics between cohorts preclude conclusions regarding population-specific genomic features. The prognostic findings remain exploratory and require validation in larger, independent cohorts. These results highlight the importance of expanding genomic studies of CRC to historically underrepresented populations.

Article.Title: Analytical and Clinical Evaluation of the MeltArray Glioma Assay for Rapid Multiplex Detection of 18 Hotspot Mutations in FFPE Gliomas
Article.Authors: Xu B.; Lin W.; Ni W.; Hai J.; Wang Y.; Liu Z.; Huang Q.; Li Q.
Article.Abstract: Rapid hotspot mutation testing offers a practical route to integrated glioma diagnosis when tissue availability, turnaround time, or sequencing capacity is limited. We validated the MeltArray Glioma Assay, a laboratory-developed test that detects 18 hotspot mutations across IDH1, IDH2, TERT, histone H3 genes, and BRAF using only two reactions in a four-channel format. Analytical performance was assessed with respect to melting-temperature reproducibility, lowest tested detectable input, mutant allele fraction sensitivity, specificity, and the function of the RPP30 internal control. Assay calls in 168 formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded gliomas were compared with targeted next-generation sequencing. Melting temperatures were highly reproducible across three independent SLAN-96S instruments of the same model (coefficients of variation, 0.07–0.48%). All 18 mutations were detected at 10 plasmid copies per reaction; at a total input of 1 × 105 plasmid copies per reaction, four mutations were detectable at a 0.1% mutant allele fraction and the remaining mutations at 0.5%. No target-specific melting peaks were observed with 293T cell or healthy-donor genomic DNA. In clinical specimens, the MeltArray assay classified 108 specimens as positive and 60 as negative, showing 100% positive, negative, and overall percentage agreement with sequencing. The 131 mutation events comprised 66 in TERT, 45 in IDH1/2, 10 in histone H3, and 10 in BRAF. The MeltArray assay enables rapid, sensitive hotspot genotyping on a standard four-channel real-time PCR platform and is best positioned as a focused adjunct to comprehensive molecular glioma classification.

Article.Title: Polyphenolic Compounds and Bioactivities of Black Currant (Ribes nigrum L.), Blue Honeysuckle (Lonicera caerulea L.) and Viburnum Berry (Viburnum opulus L.) Fruit
Article.Authors: Yang J.; Qiao J.; Geng Y.; Xiao Z.; Sun Z.; Zhang W.; Lyu Y.; Li X.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: This work compared the phenolic composition and in vitro bioactivities of crude extracts and solid-phase extraction (SPE) fractions obtained from blue honeysuckle, black currant, and viburnum berry. LC–MS/MS analysis tentatively assigned 18 anthocyanins and 74 non-anthocyanin phenolics, covering phenolic acids, flavan-3-ols, flavonols, flavones, and related compounds. Antioxidant responses depended on both berry species and fraction type: viburnum berry crude extract showed comparatively strong 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH)-scavenging activity and ferric-reducing capacity, while the black currant anthocyanin fraction displayed greater DPPH activity. Ferric-reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) values did not differ significantly among the anthocyanin fractions. The extracts and fractions also inhibited α-amylase, α-glucosidase, and lipase to varying extents. These findings identify viburnum berry as a candidate source of antioxidant and enzyme-inhibitory constituents; the biological significance of the observed in vitro effects requires further validation.

Article.Title: Angiotensinogen Gene Expression Is Associated with Clinicopathological Data and Overall Survival in Multiple Cancers: Bioinformatics Study
Article.Authors: Osman H.; Abesher D.; Elsiddig M.; Abubakar A.; Idris E.; Adam K.; Ahmed E.; Ali E.; Abuagla H.; MohamedAhmed A.; Edris A.; Eltieb E.; Elangeeb M.; Alfaki M.
Article.Abstract: Angiotensinogen gene (AGT) has been linked to various malignancies; however, little is known about its relationship to the clinicopathological data and survival rate. This study aimed to assess the association of AGT expression with the clinicopathological data and overall survival in various malignancies. Comprehensive pan-cancer analysis was performed across 33 tumors using TIMER, GEPIA, and UALCAN databases. Then, cancers that displayed significant and concordant results in the three databases were selected for further analysis. Accordingly, our results showed significantly higher AGT expression in colorectal adenocarcinoma (COAD), rectum adenocarcinoma (READ), and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) tumors than in normal tissue (p < 0.001); however, AGT expression was significantly lower in kidney chromophobe (KICH) tumors compared with the normal (p < 0.001). The AGT expression was significantly associated with clinicopathological data in patients with COAD, READ, and STAD. Furthermore, the AGT expression was significantly correlated with immune cell recruitment in COAD and STAD. In survival analysis, upregulated AGT expression in STAD patients was significantly linked to shorter overall survival (Kaplan–Meier HR = 1.62; CI = 1.17–2.25; p < 0.001) (GEPIA: HR = 1.5, p = 0.02). In contrast, AGT overexpression was significantly associated with longer overall survival in patients with kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC) (Kaplan–Meier: HR = 0.66; CI = 0.48–0.89; p = 0.01) (GEPIA: HR = 0.66, p = 0.01). In conclusion, AGT expression is associated with the clinicopathological features in COAD, READ, and STAD. Furthermore, AGT expression is linked to the overall survival of STAD and KIRC patients. An experimental study is required to confirm our findings.

Article.Title: Frequency and Patterns of Candida auris Co-Detection with Other Candida Species in a Selected Follow-Up Surveillance Cohort—Queens, New York, January–July 2026
Article.Authors: Liu D.; Kang K.; Lui C.; James K.; Koo T.; Varghese B.; Mariano N.; Aningalan B.; Acero D.; Hartin L.; Burns J.; Rodriguez G.; Urban C.; Prasad N.; Lopresto C.; Zhou Y.; Li X.; Marathe A.; Vaidya M.; Loo F.; Schreiner A.; Chaturvedi S.; Rodgers W.
Article.Abstract: Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen that persists in health care settings, but its concurrent carriage with other Candida species is not well characterized. During January–July 2026, 46 hospitalized patients undergoing follow-up surveillance at a community hospital in Queens, New York, provided paired composite nares, axilla, and groin swabs. Specimens were tested by a C. auris-specific real-time PCR assay and by parallel culture; recovered yeasts were identified by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry. C. auris isolates also underwent Sanger sequencing of a 737-nucleotide FKS1 fragment. Of the 46 patients, 31 tested positive for C. auris; 19 of 31 (61.3%) also carried at least one other Candida species, and nine carried three or more Candida species. Twenty-seven of the 31 (87.1%) C. auris-positive patients had been admitted from nursing homes, long-term medical care facilities or a shelter. Sequencing results were concordant with PCR results, and no reliable single-nucleotide polymorphisms were detected in the shared high-quality region. Combining targeted molecular detection with culture and species-level identification revealed frequent and diverse concurrent carriage of Candida species. The conserved partial FKS1 sequence supported the assay findings but did not discriminate among the tested isolates.

Article.Title: Melatonin and GABA Improve Metabolic and Pancreatic Outcomes in Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetic Mice with Selective Benefits of Combination Therapy
Article.Authors: Parmar N.; Patel R.; Rathwa N.; Dwivedi M.; Ramachandran A.; Begum R.
Article.Abstract: Loss of functional β-cell mass is a critical factor in the pathogenesis of type 1 (T1D) and type 2 (T2D) diabetes, both characterized by chronic hyperglycemia. Melatonin (M) and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA; G) exhibit immunoregulatory properties and have shown potential to preserve or restore β-cell mass in experimental diabetic models. Thus, we aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of melatonin and GABA, alone and in combination (M+G), on β-cell regeneration and metabolic regulation in streptozotocin (STZ)-induced T1D and high-fat diet (HFD)-induced T2D mouse models. BALB/c mice received STZ (50 mg/kg/day) for five consecutive days to induce T1D, while C57BL/6J mice were fed an HFD for 30 weeks to induce insulin resistance and T2D. Both models were subsequently treated with M, G, or M+G for six weeks. In T1D mice, both monotherapies and combination therapy reduced fasting blood glucose levels, increased plasma insulin levels, improved glucose tolerance, promoted β-cell proliferation and transdifferentiation, and reduced β-cell apoptosis. In T2D mice, treatments improved metabolic parameters and glycolipid metabolism in the liver and adipose tissue, respectively, skeletal muscle mitochondrial function, peripheral insulin sensitivity and β-cell mass. Overall, M and G monotherapies demonstrated beneficial metabolic and β-cell protective effects in both models. However, combination therapy provided additional benefits for only selected endpoints, with most direct comparisons showing no significant differences and most significant melatonin × GABA interactions being consistent with sub-additive effects.

Article.Title: Under Normal Conditions, Rhau Binds the ARE-Containing Regions of fos and myc mRNAs and Functions Together with TREX-2 in Their Nuclear Export
Article.Authors: Vdovina Y.; Nikolenko J.; Glukhova A.; Zolin I.; Uvarova M.; Fet S.; Georgieva S.; Kopytova D.
Article.Abstract: In eukaryotes, mRNA export from the nucleus to the cytoplasm is predominantly mediated by the TREX-2 complex. However, certain mRNAs such as the ARE-containing mRNAs of the Fos and Myc protooncogenes are exported via the alternative HuR-Crm1-dependent pathway. The AU motif in these mRNAs is bound by the HuR protein, which in its turn interacts with the pp32 and APRIL proteins. These proteins contain the NES motif, which is bound by Crm1. The mRNAs are then exported by the thereby assembled protein complex. Since this export pathway was described for these mRNAs under stress conditions, it remained unclear how they are exported under normal conditions. In the present work, we demonstrated that under normal conditions, Crm1 has no effect on the export of kayak and myc mRNAs from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in Drosophila melanogaster. Analysis of proteins interacting with the ARE of kayak mRNA revealed the Rhau protein (hDHX36). We demonstrated that Rhau interacts with the TREX-2 mRNA export complex and is involved in the export of kayak and myc mRNAs together with it.

Article.Title: GHS-Pred: Web Application for Predicting GHS Hazard Statement and Pictogram Labels
Article.Authors: Dmitriev A.; Rudik A.; Filimonov D.; Pogodin P.; Kolodnitsky A.; Lagunin A.
Article.Abstract: The Globally Harmonized System (GHS) provides a standardized approach for chemical hazard classification. However, systematic prediction across dozens of distinct toxicity labels remains a challenge, as most published QSAR models reduce GHS classifications to either a binary “toxic/non-toxic” call, a small number of potency bands, or a five-category acute toxicity scale. To overcome this gap, we developed comprehensive in silico models using PASS (Prediction of Activity Spectra for Substances) software to simultaneously predict 52 GHS hazard statements and four hazard class pictograms (acute toxicity, corrosives, environmental hazard, and health hazard). The primary training set comprised 11,438 unique chemical structures extracted from PubChem using a data mining pipeline and annotated with GHS labels. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) models were generated using Multilevel Neighborhoods of Atoms (MNA) descriptors and a modified naïve Bayes algorithm. To evaluate data robustness and structural representation, a scaffold diversity analysis was performed using the Tool for Diversity Visualization (TDV). Additionally, the predictive ability of PASS was benchmarked via 10-times repeated 5-fold cross-validation using an adapted dataset of 445 skin irritation/corrosion compounds compiled by Kang et al. The primary models achieved high predictive robustness, confirmed by strong alignment between leave-one-out and 5-fold cross-validation metrics: the 52 hazard statement models yielded a mean invariant accuracy of prediction (IAP) of 0.784 and a balanced accuracy (BA) of 0.728, while the four pictogram models achieved a mean IAP of 0.766 and BA of 0.703. Scaffold analysis revealed a compressed diversity driven by several over-represented chemical series. In the external benchmarking on skin irritation/corrosion data, the PASS models demonstrated competitive performance, yielding balanced accuracies (e.g., Cat 1 vs. others BA = 0.780; irritant vs. non-irritant BA = 0.657) comparable to state-of-the-art machine learning models (XGBoost) and experimental in vitro test methods. The developed SAR models were implemented in the freely available GHS-Pred web application, which accepts SMILES or structural inputs to generate predicted GHS hazard profiles in a single request, offering a validated multi-label alternative to single-endpoint GHS classification tools.

Article.Title: Molecular Mechanisms of Early-Life Immunometabolic Imprinting: The Emerging Role of the Mother–Milk–Microbiome Axis
Article.Authors: Valencia Castillo S.; Rojas Quiceno J.; Múnera Benavides J.; Florián Pérez M.
Article.Abstract: Early-life immune and metabolic development is influenced by maternal physiology, human milk composition, and the developing gut microbiota. This narrative review proposes the Mother–Milk–Microbiome Axis as an integrative framework for examining how these interactions may contribute to immunometabolic imprinting. Human milk supplies bioactive components and substrates that shape microbial colonization and metabolism while also acting directly on infant tissues. Microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan-derived indoles, bile acid derivatives, lactate, and succinate, can influence epithelial integrity, immune-cell differentiation, and cellular metabolism through receptor-mediated signaling and epigenetic regulation. We examine these pathways as potential links between early nutritional exposures and subsequent immunometabolic trajectories, distinguishing evidence from human infants from mechanisms investigated in adults, animal models, and cellular systems. Although experimental studies support several individual mechanisms, direct evidence connecting milk-dependent microbial metabolism to persistent epigenetic and functional changes in human infants remains limited. The proposed axis therefore represents a conceptual framework rather than an established causal hierarchy. Longitudinal studies integrating maternal characteristics, milk composition, microbial function, and infant immune and metabolic outcomes are needed to test its connections and inform future nutritional and microbiome-targeted interventions.

Article.Title: Therapeutic Potential of Catechins in Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review of Radical Scavenging Mechanisms
Article.Authors: Gunawan R.; Setyawati L.; Novitasari D.; Rachmawati M.; Daruwati I.; Purwowidodo I.; Fakih T.; Ikram N.; Muchtaridi M.
Article.Abstract: Breast cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide, with oxidative stress recognized as a critical factor contributing to tumor initiation, progression, and therapeutic resistance. Catechins and their derivatives, a class of plant-derived flavan-3-ols, have gained increasing attention due to their potent radical-scavenging properties and their role in regulating cellular redox homeostasis that is involved in cancer. This systematic literature review aims to evaluate experimental evidence published between 2015 and 2025 regarding the radical-scavenging activity of catechins in breast cancer models and their associated biological effects. Literature searches were conducted using PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect databases following PRISMA-guided screening procedures. A total of 7 eligible studies were included after systematic filtering and eligibility assessment. The findings demonstrate that catechins, particularly epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) and its derivatives, are capable of directly neutralizing reactive oxygen species through hydrogen-donating mechanisms and electron transfer processes. In addition, these compounds modulate endogenous antioxidant systems and regulate redox-sensitive signaling pathways, including those associated with apoptosis, proliferation, and inflammation. These effects are further linked to the modulation of broader cellular processes such as autophagy and epigenetic regulation, contributing to the complex mechanistic actions of catechins in breast cancer models. Experimental evidence consistently indicates enhanced apoptotic activity, suppression of proliferative signaling, inhibition of inflammatory mediators, and a reduction in metastatic potential in breast cancer cells. Under specific cellular conditions, catechins may also exhibit selective pro-oxidant effects that increase cancer cell susceptibility to conventional treatments. These findings highlight the redox-modulating behavior of catechins in preclinical breast cancer models and support their potential as bioactive compounds. However, their clinical relevance remains to be established through well-designed clinical studies, particularly with respect to efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetic performance.

Article.Title: Lutein-Rich Extract from Gac (Momordica cochinchinensis) Fruit Peel Protects Retinal Pigment Epithelial Cells from Oxidative and Inflammatory Stress
Article.Authors: Nguyen D.; Thrimawithana T.; Piva T.; Huynh T.
Article.Abstract: Oxidative stress contributes to retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell dysfunction and is implicated in the pathogenesis of retinal diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Lutein, a naturally occurring xanthophyll carotenoid that accumulates in the macula, plays an important role in antioxidant defence and light filtration. This study investigated the antioxidant and cytoprotective effects of lutein-rich gac (Momordica cochinchinensis) peel extract (GPE) in human RPE cells subjected to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-induced oxidative stress. Cells were pre-treated with GPE (0.1–200 µg/mL), purified lutein (10 µg/mL), or the reference antioxidant Trolox (50 µg/mL) for 12–72 h before oxidative challenge. Cell viability, intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and the expression of genes associated with antioxidant defence, angiogenesis, and inflammation were evaluated. GPE at 10 and 100 µg/mL exhibited greater cytoprotective effects than purified lutein and Trolox under the tested conditions. GPE treatment significantly reduced intracellular ROS accumulation and protected RPE cells against H2O2-induced cell death. Furthermore, GPE increased the expression of antioxidant response regulators Nrf2 and HO-1, while reducing the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) and interleukin-6 (IL-6). These findings demonstrate the antioxidant and cytoprotective activity of GPE and suggest that modulation of oxidative stress-associated molecular responses may contribute to its protective effects. This study highlights GPE as a promising source of natural bioactive compounds for further investigation in retinal protection and oxidative stress-related ocular disorders.

Article.Title: KRAS/NRAS Mutation-Associated Transcriptional Dysregulation and NRL, CREM and IL6 Expression in Relation to Clinical Outcomes in Multiple Myeloma
Article.Authors: Sergeeva A.; Sidorova Y.; Chabaeva Y.; Kulikov S.; Mendeleeva L.; Solovev M.; Sudarikov A.
Article.Abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a biologically heterogeneous plasma cell malignancy with variable responses to induction therapy that are not fully explained by current risk stratification systems. Mutations in RAS family genes (KRAS and NRAS) are prevalent in MM, yet contemporary risk stratification systems do not include them despite their oncogenic potential. Our previous findings showed reduced response depth to bortezomib-containing triplet induction regimens in the presence of RAS mutations. The aim of this study is to identify RAS pathway–related molecular targets and evaluate their relationship with clinical outcomes. Forty-four patients with newly diagnosed MM received bortezomib-based induction therapy (velcade + cyclophosphamide + dexamethasone, VCD or velcade + doxorubicin + dexamethasone, PAD/VCD). Bone marrow CD138+ plasma cells were isolated for transcriptome analysis. KRAS and NRAS gene mutations were identified by Sanger sequencing, and RNA sequencing was performed on the Illumina HiSeq 3000 platform. Gene expression was analyzed using Salmon and DESeq2. The clinical endpoints were depth of response, event-free survival (EFS), and overall survival (OS). Of the 66 candidate RAS-pathway related genes examined, five—CREM, NRL, IL6, MMP14 and MEF2B—showed significantly higher expression in samples with KRAS and NRAS gene mutations (t-test, p < 0.05). Lower NRL gene expression was associated with achieving CR + VGPR (HR 10.99, 95% CI: 1.26–534.66, p = 0.01). Elevated IL6 gene expression correlated with poorer OS (HR 3.18; p = 0.05), while increased CREM gene expression was associated with shorter EFS (HR 2.62; p = 0.01). The identified association between gene expression and survival was validated using publicly available external datasets (CREM: HR 2.43, 95% CI: 1.15–5.17, p = 0.017; IL6: HR 1.8, 95% CI: 1.41–2.3, p = 0.0000014). Increased expression of NRL, CREM, and IL6 genes in bone marrow plasma cells before treatment in MM patients was associated with adverse clinical outcomes and may reflect the molecular mechanisms underlying the negative effects of KRAS and NRAS gene mutations.

Article.Title: ApoE4 and Psychosis in Neurodegenerative and Non-Neurodegenerative Disease: A Scoping Review
Article.Authors: Wasef V.; Rashidi-Ranjbar N.; Churchill N.; Fornazzari L.; De Luca V.; Graham S.; Munoz D.; Schweizer T.; Fischer C.
Article.Abstract: Psychosis is a neuropsychiatric feature found across neurodegenerative conditions including Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD). It is also a common feature in psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia. The apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 (ApoE4) allele is an established genetic risk factor for AD that may also increase the risk of psychosis. However, evidence regarding the association between ApoE4 and psychosis remains unclear. This paper evaluates the relationship between ApoE4 carrier status and psychosis in both neurodegenerative (Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease) and non-neurodegenerative disorders (schizophrenia). Additionally it explores whether sex and zygosity modulate this association. A literature review of studies identified through PubMed and Scopus was conducted. Thirty-one studies were included that investigated the relationship between ApoE4 and psychosis in select neurodegenerative and psychiatric populations. Studies were included if they assessed ApoE4 status in relation to the presence, severity, or age of onset of psychosis. Among the 16 AD-focused studies, a positive association was reported in 11 while four showed no significant association and one showed an inverse correlation. ApoE4 carriers and ApoE4 homozygotes that were female were reported to have the strongest association. The three studies examining PD resulted in inconsistent findings limited by small sample sizes. Schizophrenia studies produced findings that were predominantly null or equivocal, with no clear evidence that sex or zygosity influenced outcomes. Notably, the risk was enhanced in female carriers and ApoE4 homozygotes. Overall, ApoE4 positivity appears to be most consistent in AD, whereas evidence in PD and schizophrenia ae heterogeneous and limited, precluding direct comparison. Some studies suggest that this relationship may be modified by sex and ApoE4 zygosity, with female ApoE4 homozygotes being particularly vulnerable especially in AD cohorts. Larger studies are needed to clarify the role of ApoE4 in psychosis, particularly in non-AD cohorts.

Article.Title: Artemisinin Exerts Antifungal Activity Against Candida glabrata via Transcriptional Mediator MED15 by Modulating Lipid Biosynthesis and Biofilm Formation
Article.Authors: Zhu P.; Yuan Z.; Du S.; Sun Y.; Ran M.; Chen X.; Guo L.
Article.Abstract: Fungal infections represent a significant threat to human health, yet available antifungal agents are limited, thereby underscoring the urgent need for the development of novel therapeutic strategies. Although artemisinin has demonstrated potential antifungal properties, the precise mechanisms underlying its activity have yet to be fully elucidated. Here, we identified the transcriptional mediator MED15 as a key regulator of artemisinin’s antifungal effects through the application of drug sensitivity assays. Further, transcriptomic analyses were employed to characterize the transcriptional regulatory role of MED15 in mediating artemisinin’s antifungal activity, focusing on lipid and ergosterol biosynthetic pathways. Moreover, the regulatory function of MED15 was validated in the pathogenic fungus Candida glabrata. Our findings indicate that MED15 modulates lipid-ergosterol biosynthesis-related genes, which consequently affects biofilm development and fungal susceptibility to artemisinin. This work provides new mechanistic insights into artemisinin-mediated antifungal effects and offers a theoretical basis for developing antifungal therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Post-Translational Forms of c-Myc in Neural Degeneration and Repair
Article.Authors: Mikryukova D.; Stoyanova P.; Kalyuzhnaya Y.; Zimina V.; Kunitsyna A.; Khaitin A.; Susova O.; Demyanenko S.
Article.Abstract: c-Myc is a key regulator of neuronal proliferation, metabolism, apoptosis, and regeneration, but its contribution to the balance between neural degeneration and repair remains incompletely understood. This study investigated the roles of c-Myc post-translational forms and their interaction with FOXO transcription factors in models of neurodegeneration and nerve injury. C- and N-terminal reactive c-Myc fragments and acetylated c-Myc at lysines 148 and 323 were assessed in the cortex and hippocampus of APP/PS1 mice at different ages and after FOXO1/3a inhibition. The effects of c-Myc inhibition and K148 acetylation were further examined in primary cortical cultures, SH-SY5Y cells exposed to amyloid-β, and models of sciatic and optic nerve injury. In APP/PS1 mice, nuclear C-terminal c-Myc increased with disease progression, whereas the cytoplasmic N-terminal signal decreased. Acetylation at K148 increased at an early disease stage, while K323 acetylation increased at later stages. K148 substitution increased amyloid-β-induced apoptosis, suggesting a possible protective role for this modification. c-Myc inhibition reduced FOXO1 and its phosphorylated forms but did not affect synaptogenesis markers and produced limited effects on nerve regeneration. These findings indicate that c-Myc functions in neural degeneration and repair in a context-dependent manner, with site-specific acetylation and interaction with FOXO contributing to this balance.

Article.Title: Hippocampal Neurotopography in 3D Models of Alzheimer’s Disease
Article.Authors: Hossain M.; Lee H.; Kim H.; Kim H.
Article.Abstract: Animal models have long dominated Alzheimer’s disease (AD) research, yet they fail to recapitulate the complex structural and functional scenery of the human hippocampus. Evidence from animal studies reveals differential vulnerabilities in cornu ammonis regions, particularly CA1 and CA3. This perspective presents the concept of neurotopographic fidelity, which integrates the accurate replication of spatial, cellular, and functional characteristics of a 3D engineered hippocampal model. Emphasizing structural subdivision, cellular diversity, and synaptic connectivity, our proposed framework serves as a guide to a biologically relevant AD model. We also address the constructional complexity and propose a workflow diagram for validating 3D hippocampal AD organoids using clinical data within this integrated model. By resolving these challenges, our framework offers a proposal for developing next-generation translational models that reflect human-specific AD signatures.

Article.Title: Bacteriophages and Biosurfactants as a Novel Combined Strategy for Enhanced Control of Bacterial Skin Pathogens
Article.Authors: Hauza E.; Janek T.; Lazviashvili D.; Chanishvili N.; Roelants S.; Skaradzińska A.
Article.Abstract: Skin infections are an increasing concern due to antibiotic resistance, highlighting the need for alternative antimicrobial strategies. Bacteriophages and biosurfactants have been studied separately, but rarely in combination. We evaluated phage–biosurfactant combinations against reference strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus hyicus, and Staphylococcus epidermidis. Strain-specific phages were combined with surfactin, rhamnolipids or sophorolipids and assessed using growth assays, spot assays, fluorescence-based viability analysis, surface hydrophobicity and zeta potential. In liquid cultures, growth inhibition was strain-dependent; for S. aureus the combinations prolonged the lag phase by 3–6 h, whereas for P. aeruginosa the surfactin combination suppressed growth throughout the 14 h incubation. The phage–surfactin combination reduced S. aureus counts 24-fold relative to phage alone and 20-fold relative to surfactin alone (P. aeruginosa: 4.4- and 9-fold). At the single concentration pair tested, Bliss analysis with two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) indicated a significant departure from additivity against S. aureus and a smaller enhancement consistent with synergy against P. aeruginosa; the effect was moderate for S. hyicus and limited or absent for S. epidermidis. Enhanced activity coincided with altered surface hydrophobicity and charge. These in vitro results, obtained with reference strains rather than multidrug-resistant isolates, identify phage–surfactin combinations as candidates for further evaluation.

Article.Title: Multi-Omics Reveals MYDGF Dysregulation Associated with Synapse-Related Molecular Changes in Alzheimer’s Disease
Article.Authors: Lu Y.; Zhang J.; Dong J.
Article.Abstract: Myeloid-derived growth factor (MYDGF) is a secreted protein involved in tissue repair and cellular protection, but its expression and molecular associations in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) remain unclear. We analyzed public bulk, single-nucleus, spatial transcriptomic, and proteomic datasets, complemented by immunohistochemical images and Western blots in an AD mouse model. Bulk analyses showed lower MYDGF expression in AD fusiform gyrus and prefrontal cortex, with no significant differences in the insula or anterior cingulate cortex. Single-nucleus analyses detected MYDGF transcripts in neuronal and non-neuronal populations. In excitatory-neuron pseudobulk analyses of AD donors, MYDGF expression was positively associated with SYP and SYNGR1 in the PCC, while GSEA identified positive enrichment of synaptic vesicle cycle, cholinergic synapse, and synaptic vesicle endocytosis gene sets in the FCX. Spatial analyses revealed regional variation in MYDGF detection and associations with energy metabolism and apoptosis-related signatures. MYDGF abundance was lower in AD dorsolateral prefrontal cortex samples in the primary human proteomic cohort. Mouse Western blots showed lower MYDGF signal alongside reduced PSD-95 and synaptophysin levels. These findings indicate MYDGF downregulation in selected AD brain regions and suggest potential links with synaptic alterations. Despite lacking direct functional validation, this study provides a foundation for investigating MYDGF’s potential role in AD.

Article.Title: Morphological and Molecular Genetic Characteristics of the Colon and Faecal Microbiota Composition in Hypoxia-Tolerant and Hypoxia-Susceptible Young and Middle-Aged Male C57BL/6 Mice
Article.Authors: Dzhalilova D.; Portnova T.; Zolotova N.; Kirillova M.; Tsvetkov I.; Gladyshev N.; Fokichev N.; Mkhitarov V.; Khomyakova T.; Dobrynina M.; Makarova O.
Article.Abstract: Individual tolerance to hypoxia is associated with the severity of ulcerative colitis and colorectal cancer. Aging is accompanied by progressive tissue oxygen supply decline, which disrupts colon function and alters the microbiome. This study aimed to characterize the morphological and molecular genetic features of the colon and faecal microbiota composition in hypoxia-tolerant and hypoxia-susceptible young (4 months) and middle-aged (12 months) male C57BL/6 mice one month after sublethal hypobaric exposure equivalent to 10,000-m altitude. In comparison with tolerant mice, in hypoxia-susceptible young mice, a greater total cell number in the colon lamina propria of the mucosa (LPM) and a higher ratio of F4/80+ cells among LPM nuclei, higher Nfkb1, Il10, Hif1a, Hif3a, Cldn2 expression but lower Muc1, Muc13, Cldn7 expression, and increased proinflammatory cytokine TNF-α and anti-inflammatory IL-10 content in the distal colon were observed. In comparison with tolerant mice, susceptible middle-aged mice were characterized by a greater total cell number in the colon LPM with a higher ratio of F4/80+ cells and higher Nfkb1, Il6, Tnf, and Epas1 (encoding HIF-2α) expression, TNF-α and IL-10 content in the distal colon part, lower crypt depth, whereas Il10 mRNA level did not differ. No statistically significant differences in plasma endotoxin or serum cytokine levels (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α, IFN-γ) were detected between the groups, suggesting that the proinflammatory phenotype of hypoxia-susceptible animals may be confined to the colon. Moreover, the abundance of selected faecal bacterial taxa differed between age groups, and limited phenotype-specific differences were observed in middle-aged mice. Thus, low individual tolerance to hypoxia is associated with the proinflammatory state of the colon. The observed colon features in animals with different hypoxia tolerance may contribute to predisposition to inflammatory bowel diseases and should be considered when developing future personalized approaches to their prevention and treatment.

Article.Title: S-Scheme Bi2O2S/Rutile TiO2 Heterojunction with Photothermal Synergy for CO2 Photoreduction Under Full-Spectrum Irradiation
Article.Authors: Polskikh D.; Lyzhina K.; Fazliev T.; Solovyeva M.; Lyulyukin M.; Selishchev D.
Article.Abstract: Solar-driven photocatalytic reduction of CO2 with water vapor requires photocatalysts that combine broadband light harvesting with efficient charge separation. Herein, composites of bismuth oxysulfide (Bi2O2S) nanosheets and rutile TiO2 nanocrystals with 1–5 wt.% of Bi2O2S were prepared by a simple ultrasound-assisted suspension method and studied in gas–solid CO2 reduction under full-spectrum irradiation without sacrificial agents or cocatalysts. Rutile TiO2 with elongated nanocrystals and a specific surface area of 65.7 m2 g−1 was synthesized by low-temperature hydrolysis of TiCl4 followed by hydrothermal crystallization without calcination. The composite containing 2 wt.% of Bi2O2S exhibited the highest CH4 evolution rate of 430 μmol g−1 h−1 with a CH4 selectivity of 84%, exceeding the CH4 evolution rates of rutile TiO2 and Bi2O2S by factors of 2.7 and 108, respectively. Photoelectrochemical measurements, wavelength-dependent photocurrent polarity switching, and DFT calculations revealed the formation of an S-scheme heterojunction driven by the built-in electric field at the Bi2O2S|rutile TiO2 interface. Control experiments demonstrated a synergy between photogenerated charge carriers and thermal activation, provided by broadband light absorption of Bi2O2S, in the deep reduction of CO2 to CH4. The composite retained its activity and crystal structure over five consecutive cycles.

Article.Title: EGFR Signaling in Colorectal Cancer Metastasis: Molecular Mechanisms and Targeted Therapeutic Strategies
Article.Authors: Leiphrakpam P.; Rajappa S.; Krishnan M.; Batra R.; Are C.
Article.Abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide, with metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) accounting for most CRC-associated deaths. Despite advances in systemic therapy, mCRC remains associated with poor prognosis because of its molecular heterogeneity, metastatic potential, and the emergence of therapeutic resistance. Improved understanding of the molecular landscape of mCRC has enabled biomarker-driven treatment strategies that have advanced precision oncology. Among the key signaling pathways involved in mCRC, the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) pathway plays a central role in tumor progression and metastasis. EGFR activation triggers the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK (rat sarcoma-rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma-mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase-extracellular signal-regulated kinase) and PI3K-AKT-mTOR (phosphoinositide 3-kinase–protein kinase B–mechanistic target of rapamycin) signaling cascades, promoting cellular proliferation, survival, migration, invasion, angiogenesis, and therapeutic resistance. Genetic alterations involving KRAS (kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog), NRAS (neuroblastoma rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog), BRAF (B-Raf proto-oncogene, serine/threonine kinase), PIK3CA (phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate 3-kinase catalytic subunit alpha), HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2), and PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog) frequently dysregulate these pathways and serve as predictive biomarkers for targeted therapy. Anti-EGFR monoclonal antibodies have transformed the treatment landscape of mCRC. However, their clinical benefit is frequently limited by intrinsic and acquired resistance mechanisms driven by molecular alterations, pathway redundancy, compensatory signaling, and tumor heterogeneity. This review examines the role of EGFR signaling in CRC metastasis, the molecular alterations affecting EGFR-associated pathways, and the evolving landscape of EGFR-directed and pathway-focused targeted therapies in mCRC.

Article.Title: Gaultheria procumbens L. Fractionated Leaf Extracts and Wintergreen Essential Oil: A Direct Comparison of Their Antioxidant and Immunomodulatory Activities in Immune Cells and Human Plasma In Vitro
Article.Authors: Michel P.; Kołodziejczyk-Czepas J.; Włodarczyk M.; Krupa A.; Siwińska M.; Skrobacz K.; Tomaszewska A.; Krzyżaniak M.; Olszewska M.
Article.Abstract: Gaultheria procumbens L. leaves and wintergreen essential oil have traditionally been used to relieve pain and inflammation; however, the relative contributions of their chemically distinct non-volatile and volatile fractions to these effects remain poorly understood. This study directly compared the antioxidant and immunomodulatory activities of polyphenol-rich leaf extracts and leaf essential oil (LEO) obtained from the same batch of plant material. Fractionated extracts and LEO were chemically characterised using UHPLC-PDA-ESI-MS/MS, HPLC-PDA, GC-FID-MS, and spectrophotometric assays, and their biological effects were evaluated using human plasma and immune cell-based models, including peroxynitrite (ONOO−)-exposed plasma, stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), THP1-Blue™ NF-κB cells, and human monocyte-derived macrophages. Among the tested preparations, EAF showed the most consistent antioxidant protection of plasma components against ONOO−-induced damage. At 50 μg/mL, EAF decreased IL-6 and increased IL-10 levels in stimulated PBMCs, whereas LEO did not significantly affect either cytokine. EAF also showed the strongest inhibition of LPS-induced NF-κB activation. In resting M0 macrophages the methanol-water extract and LEO elicited a partial M1-like response, primarily reflected by increased IL-6. Overall, the results show distinct biological profiles for the volatile and non-volatile fractions of G. procumbens leaves, with broader antioxidant and immunomodulatory effects predominantly associated with non-volatile polyphenols. These findings indicate that non-volatile polyphenol-rich fractions are major contributors to the biological activity of G. procumbens leaves, although in vivo confirmation is required.

Article.Title: Spicing Up the Gut Health: Therapeutic Potential of Cinnamon in Gut Inflammation and Fibrosis
Article.Authors: Pahan K.; Wu S.; Kumar A.
Article.Abstract: Intestinal fibrosis (IF) is considered a chronic, immune-mediated, and progressive disorder associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Intestinal fibrosis is characterized by excessive extracellular matrix deposition and tissue remodeling that can result in bowel strictures, obstruction, and significant morbidity. Unlike inflammation, fibrosis is largely irreversible and remains a critical unmet clinical challenge. Currently, there are no effective antifibrotic therapies, and surgical interventions that are unable to render a cure or remission remain the primary treatment option. Furthermore, these procedures are associated with considerable risks, including postoperative recurrence and progressive bowel shortening. Therefore, effective and safer treatments for intestinal fibrosis are warranted and the key focus of the research. In this regard, cinnamon, a widely used medicinal spice, possesses anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial, and immunomodulatory properties. Recent studies show that cinnamon and its bioactive components suppress pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, modulate gut microbiota, enhance epithelial barrier integrity, and regulate extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. These effects suggest that cinnamon may attenuate intestinal fibrosis by disrupting the mechanisms underlying fibrogenesis. Therefore, this review summarizes current knowledge of intestinal fibrosis pathogenesis and highlights evidence of cinnamon as a potential therapeutic supplement to treat and/or manage intestinal fibrosis.

Article.Title: Metabolite Composition of Stem and Root Extracts of 5-Year-Old Polyscias fruticosa (L.) Harms and Insights into Their Neuroprotective Properties Using Model Systems of Alzheimer’s Disease and Neurodegeneration Induced by Toxicants
Article.Authors: Pham H.; Vu T.; Dinh M.; Leu D.; Nguyen H.; Nguyen P.; Pham T.; Phi U.; Le X.; Dang H.; Nguyen V.; Tran L.; Folk W.
Article.Abstract: Polyscias fruticosa (L.) Harms (P. fruticosa) is a nootropic plant traditionally used to enhance cognitive function; however, its neuroprotective potential and bioactive constituents remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, we evaluated aqueous (A5) and ethanolic (E5) extracts from the stems and roots of 5-year-old P. fruticosa for neuroprotective activities in transgenic Drosophila melanogaster expressing human amyloid precursor protein (hAPP), and in a trimethyltin (TMT)-induced mouse model of neurodegeneration. Both extracts dose-dependently restored memory and locomotor deficits and extended the median lifespan of hAPP flies to 42–48 days (vs. 36 days in untreated controls), with E5 showing stronger antioxidant activity. In TMT-treated mice, these extracts enhanced both short- and long-term spatial memory and attenuated anxiety-like behaviors; both extracts also preserved hippocampal pyramidal neurons and increased the number of differentiating (DCX+) and mature (NeuN+) neurons in the dentate gyrus. LC-MS/MS profiling identified putative oleanolic acid and chlorogenic acid derivatives as abundant bioactive metabolites; these were particularly enriched in E5. These findings support the traditional nootropic use of P. fruticosa plant materials and identify ethanolic extracts of stems and roots as promising, cost-effective candidates for future preclinical research into treatments for Alzheimer’s disease and toxicant-induced neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: The Challenge of Coordinating Gram-Negative Cell Envelope Biogenesis: Balancing Lipopolysaccharide and Phospholipid Biosynthesis
Article.Authors: Klein G.; Wierzchowska B.; Ayyolath A.; Raina S.
Article.Abstract: Gram-negative bacteria are endowed with an asymmetric outer membrane (OM), essential for their survival. This asymmetry arises from the unique distribution of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer leaflet and phospholipids (PLs) in the inner leaflet, which constitute the two essential components of the OM. Bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, maintain a tight balance between LPS and PL biosynthesis, which share (R)-3-hydroxymyristoyl-ACP as a common metabolic precursor. However, the mechanisms that coordinate flux between these pathways remain incompletely understood. Recent discoveries of LapB/C/D (LPS assembly proteins) have provided major insights into this regulation. LapB and LapC regulate the rate-determining step in LPS biosynthesis, mediated by LpxC. LapB also constitutes a hub for proteins involved in LPS, PL, and fatty acid biosynthesis (FAS), including LapD. LapD could regulate initiation of FAS by interaction with acetyl-CoA carboxylase and control phospholipid metabolism via modulating phosphatidylglycerol abundance, explaining pleiotropic phenotypes associated with its absence. Emerging evidence suggests that Lap proteins influence PlsB regulation. Together, these regulatory events coordinate LPS and PL biosynthesis with FAS, which provides acyl chains for both lipid A and PLs to maintain envelope homeostasis. Here, we discuss how Lap proteins participate in LPS and PL biosynthesis, with emphasis on E. coli.

Article.Title: The Balance Between Thrombotic and Haemorrhagic Risk in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation and Ischaemic Stroke
Article.Authors: Pacinella G.; Maida C.; Bona M.; Zagone A.; Daidone M.; Ciaccio A.; Miceli G.; Tuttolomondo A.
Article.Abstract: Ischaemic stroke in the setting of atrial fibrillation represents one of the most challenging interfaces between cardiovascular and cerebrovascular medicine, as the prevention of thromboembolism must be continuously weighed against the competing hazard of haemorrhagic complications. Increasing evidence has progressively challenged the traditional view of atrial fibrillation as an isolated and binary determinant of stroke risk, revealing instead a complex biological continuum shaped by arrhythmic burden, atrial cardiomyopathy, occult embolic sources, systemic comorbidities, and time-dependent changes in both thrombotic and bleeding susceptibility. Within this evolving framework, the present review critically examines the pathophysiological, diagnostic, and therapeutic dimensions of the atrial fibrillation–stroke relationship, from cardioembolic mechanisms and embolic stroke of undetermined source to acute reperfusion, anticoagulation strategies, and emerging precision-medicine approaches. The overarching aim is to provide an integrated, mechanism-oriented, and clinically actionable perspective that reconciles ischaemic protection with haemorrhagic safety across the continuum of care.

Article.Title: Co-Supplementation of Policosanol and Probiotics Exerts Metabolic and Multi-Organ Protection Against High-Cholesterol and Galactose-Induced Stress in Zebrafish: A 12-Week Consumption Study
Article.Authors: Cho K.; Bahuguna A.; Lee Y.; Lee S.; Baek S.; Kim J.
Article.Abstract: The study investigated the comparative effects of policosanol (PCO), a blend of seven probiotic bacterial strains (PB; Lactobacillus plantarum Lp-115, Bifidobacterium lactis BI-04, L. acidophilus La-14, Streptococcus thermophilus St-21, L. casei Lc-11, B. longum BI-05, B. breve Bb-03) and their combination (PCO + PB) against high-cholesterol and high-galactose (HCHG) diet-induced metabolic stress and liver, intestinal, brain and eye damage in zebrafish. 12 weeks of dietary intervention with PB, PCO, and PCO + PB substantially reduced HCHG-induced hepatomegaly and elevated body weight. All interventions improved the HCHG-disturbed blood lipid profile by reducing total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), while PCO + PB displayed a significantly greater effect than PCO or PB alone. The PCO + PB combination also showed notably higher levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) and HDL-C/glucose ratio. Furthermore, PCO + PB significantly reduced plasma malondialdehyde (MDA) levels while increasing sulfhydryl content, ferric ion reduction ability (FRA), and paraoxonase-like (PON) activity compared to individual supplementation of PCO and PB. Histopathological and biochemical analysis revealed that PCO + PB substantially attenuated HCHG-induced liver steatosis, neutrophil infiltration, hepatocyte ballooning, inflammation and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) production. Additionally, PCO + PB reduced HCHG-induced intestinal fibrosis and inhibited reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and apoptosis in the brain and eyes. Overall, these findings suggest that combined PCO + PB intake provides broader protection than either PCO or PB alone against HCHG-induced metabolic disturbances, oxidative stress, and multi-organ injury in zebrafish.

Article.Title: Astrocyte State–Dependent Remodeling of Neuron–Glia Communication in C9ORF72-Associated Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
Article.Authors: Zhao C.; Wu J.; Fan D.
Article.Abstract: Astrocyte dysfunction is an important component of non-cell-autonomous pathology in C9ORF72-associated amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (C9-ALS), yet how distinct astrocyte states contribute to altered neuron–glia communication remains unclear. Building on a previously published human single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) dataset of C9-ALS and control cortices, we reanalyzed motor-cortex samples using Seurat for preprocessing and integration, gene-set scoring for astrocyte-state characterization, and CellChat for pathway- and ligand–receptor-level communication inference. Donor-level analyses assessed astrocyte-state-specific communication differences, and an independent motor-cortex cohort was used to examine the reproducibility of key findings. CD44-high astrocytes showed stronger reactive features, whereas HPSE2-high astrocytes exhibited higher homeostasis/support scores. Although the overall number of inferred interactions was largely preserved, pooled communication strength was lower in C9-ALS. Donor-level analysis supported greater relative attenuation of HPSE2-high than CD44-high astrocyte communication with excitatory neurons. Pooled analyses showed prominent reductions in glutamate-related and neuronal adhesion/support pathways, whereas several extracellular matrix/remodeling-associated signals were relatively increased. Several altered pathways also extended into oligodendrocyte-associated two-step communication motifs. The independent cohort reproduced the astrocyte-state transcriptional profiles, with directionally consistent but statistically nonsignificant communication changes. Collectively, these findings provide a cell-state-resolved map of altered neuron–glia communication in C9-ALS and identify candidate signaling networks for further mechanistic investigation.

Article.Title: Protective Effect of Ginkgo Biloba Extract on 5-Fluorouracil-Induced Cardiotoxicity in Rats
Article.Authors: Öztürk Y.; Öztürk M.; Nicotra M.; Mariotti F.; Magi G.; Bürkek M.; Dörtbudak M.; Di Cerbo A.
Article.Abstract: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) is one of the most commonly used chemotherapeutic agents for treating solid tumors, and 5-FU-induced cardiotoxicity is the second leading cause of chemotherapeutic cardiotoxicity. This study evaluated the potential protective effect of different Ginkgo biloba extract (GBE) doses (150 and 300 mg/kg body weight/day) in rats with 5-FU-induced heart damage. Histopathological and immunohistochemical examinations were also performed to assess tissue damage/preservation associated with different GBE dose administrations. 5-FU significantly increased (p < 0.001) serum myocardial damage parameters (aspartate transferase, alanine transaminase, lactate dehydrogenase, creatine kinase-myocardial band, and Troponin-I), malondialdehyde, and Caspase-3 and significantly decreased (p < 0.001) antioxidant parameters (glutathione S-transferases, glutathione reductase, superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase). Histopathological examination revealed that 5-FU caused severe cardiotoxicity, while the use of increasing doses of GBE was associated with a more limited extent of such changes. Similarly, immunopathological analysis showed that 5-FU caused DNA oxidation (8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine) and phosphorylation (γ phosphorylated form of the histone H2AX), and that increasing GBE doses reduced levels of these DNA damage biomarkers. Taken together, these findings suggest that GBE administration may reduce markers of 5-FU-induced cardiac and oxidative damage, with the higher dose eliciting a more pronounced response. However, further experiments are needed to elucidate GBE’s potential effects on 5-FU-induced cardiac damage and the underlying mechanisms.

Article.Title: From Rehydration to Resilience: Mechanisms of Drought Stress Memory in Wheat
Article.Authors: Licaj I.; Varricchio E.; Di Meo M.; Rocco M.
Article.Abstract: Drought resilience in wheat is commonly evaluated during water deficit, whereas post-stress recovery and the influence of previous drought on subsequent responses remain less explored. This review examines wheat drought resilience from a post-stress perspective by integrating physiological recovery with drought stress memory. We distinguish responses that reset after rewatering from residual effects associated with incomplete recovery and primed responses to recurrent drought. Experimental evidence shows that physiological and biochemical recovery is generally more complete after moderate than severe drought, while field study involving numerous wheat genotypes reported enhanced antioxidant responses and reduced yield losses during subsequent drought following earlier stress exposure. We discuss the role of hormonal and redox signaling, antioxidant systems, osmolyte metabolism, transcriptional reprogramming, and epigenetic regulation, while distinguishing intergenerational effects from stable transgenerational inheritance. Importantly, persistence alterations alone do not establish stress memory; stronger evidence requires altered responses to a subsequent challenge relative to non-primed controls. We also examine how time-resolved multi-omics, high-throughput phenotyping, and AI-assisted modeling could characterize recovery dynamics and stress-history-dependent traits. Integrating recovery efficiency and primed responsiveness with conventional drought- tolerance traits may support a more comprehensive framework for improving wheat resilience under fluctuating water availability.
