Article.Title: Oral Dosage Forms of Catalase Associated with Probiotics Using Carboxymethylcellulose and Carboxymethylstarch: A Potential Approach for Intestinal Inflammation
Article.Authors: Dieye A.; Gosselin P.; Neree A.; Chorfi Y.; Mateescu M.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory bowel diseases frequently associated with oxidative stress phenomena represent an important component of intestinal inflammation. An excess of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is mucosa damaging, and its removal becomes a therapeutic strategy. The oral administration of antioxidant enzymes such as catalase remains challenging because enzyme activity can be rapidly impaired under gastric conditions. Carboxymethylcellulose (CMC)- and carboxymethylstarch (CMS)-based tablets for oral delivery of catalase were investigated. Tablets containing 30% (w/w) catalase were exposed for 2 h to simulated gastric fluid (SGF) followed by 5 h in simulated intestinal fluid (SIF). Approximately 58% of the initial catalase activity was recovered from the CMC-based tablets, and about 44% from the CMS-based tablets. Despite this partial recovery, both formulations retained sufficient functional activity to achieve near-complete degradation of 5 mM H2O2 in vitro within 240 min for CMC and 300 min for CMS. The incorporation of cross-linked starch improved the mechanical strength of the CMC-based tablets and maintained the percentage of catalase recovery. The association of catalase and probiotics within the same formulation was also examined. The co-formulated catalase–probiotics maintained bacterial viability following 2 h of gastric exposure and 5 h in SIF. The presence of catalase did not compromise the bacterial viability. It appears that such a system could provide a basis for future strategies simultaneously targeting intestinal oxidative stress and microbiota imbalance.

Article.Title: Lymphoid Architecture Across Solid Tumors: Emerging Technologies, Bioinformatics Approaches and Translational Applications
Article.Authors: Zou B.; Guan A.; Quek C.
Article.Abstract: Tumor-associated lymphoid architecture encompasses a spectrum of immune organization within the tumor microenvironment, ranging from loosely organized lymphoid aggregates to mature tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) with distinct cellular compartments and germinal center activity. These structures are found across multiple solid tumor types and have been associated with prognosis and therapeutic outcomes, particularly responses to immunotherapy. Advances in high-dimensional tissue profiling, single-cell and spatial technologies have enabled increasingly detailed characterization of their cellular composition, functional states, and spatial organization. However, variation in terminology, detection criteria and analytical strategies continues to limit comparisons across studies and the development of reproducible clinical biomarkers based on lymphoid architecture. In this narrative review, we summarized the features and clinical relevance of lymphoid architecture across solid tumors, including melanoma, lung cancer, renal cell carcinoma, breast cancer, colorectal cancer and ovarian cancer. We further discuss the evolution of technologies used to study these structures and the bioinformatics approaches used to identify and characterize them across complementary data modalities. Finally, we discuss current challenges and future directions for standardizing lymphoid architecture assessment and applying biological and computational insights to the development of clinically relevant biomarkers and therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Circulating Stress-, Cardiovascular-, and Inflammation-Related Biomarker Responses to Exhaustive Exercise Under Moderate Normobaric Hypoxia in Trained and Non-Trained Men
Article.Authors: Płoszczyca K.; Czuba M.; Niemaszyk A.; Kaczmarczyk K.; Grzebisz-Zatońska N.; Chalimoniuk M.
Article.Abstract: Hypoxia is assumed to amplify the systemic response to strenuous exercise. We examined whether moderate normobaric hypoxia augments circulating stress-, cardiovascular-, and inflammation-related biomarker responses to exhaustive exercise, and whether these responses differ between trained and untrained individuals. Eleven endurance-trained cyclists (VO2max 64.0 ± 3.0 mL∙kg−1∙min−1) and eleven non-trained men (45.4 ± 7.9) completed, in randomized order, three series in a normobaric hypoxic chamber: normoxia (N; FiO2 20.9%), 2000 m (H2000; 16.5%) and 3000 m (H3000; 14.4%). Each comprised a graded exercise test to exhaustion, 10 min of active recovery, then a constant-workload test at the lactate threshold to exhaustion. Blood was drawn before and immediately, 2, 6 and 24 h after exercise. GDF-15, sST2, MCP-1/CCL2, SDF-1/CXCL12, VEGF-A and HIF-1α were measured by ELISA and analyzed by mixed-design repeated-measures ANOVA. GDF-15 (F = 26.38), sST2 (F = 25.11) and MCP-1 (F = 14.19) showed main effects of Time (all p < 0.001), rising immediately after exercise or in early recovery and returning to baseline by 24 h. Hypoxia modified the temporal profile only for VEGF-A (Time × Condition, F = 3.24, p < 0.01), which rose after exercise under H3000 alone (p < 0.001; +25.0% trained, +12.0% non-trained). sST2, MCP-1 and SDF-1 were higher in non-trained than trained participants throughout (Group effects, p < 0.05 to p < 0.001). SDF-1 and HIF-1α did not change over time. In conclusion, exhaustive exercise induced transient changes in GDF-15, sST2, and MCP-1. Under the conditions investigated, no consistent additional biomarker response to moderate normobaric hypoxia was detected compared with normoxia. VEGF-A was the only biomarker showing a greater early post-exercise response under H3000 than under normoxia; however, a graded effect of hypoxia severity was not established.

Article.Authors: Juan C.; Wu I.; Chou C.; Wang H.; Lin Y.; Way T.
Article.Abstract: Citrus depressa Hayata peel is a source of polymethoxyflavones, but the anti-melanogenic activity of its differently prepared extracts remains incompletely characterized. CDE was selected for subsequent mechanistic, zebrafish, and phytochemical studies because it showed the strongest overall reduction in melanin accumulation and cellular tyrosinase activity within a largely non-cytotoxic concentration range (≤200 μg/mL). Representative immunoblots suggested changes in melanogenesis-associated proteins and signaling, and pharmacological inhibitor experiments revealed pathway interactions without establishing a unique causal target. CDE also decreased zebrafish embryo pigmentation. Targeted high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) detected nobiletin at 3.34 ± 0.06 μg/mL in a 1 mg/mL CDE solution; this corresponds to approximately 1.66 μM at 200 μg/mL CDE, below the purified-nobiletin concentrations associated with a clear anti-melanogenic effect. These findings support further evaluation of CDE as a candidate anti-pigmentation preparation, while comprehensive constituent characterization, extract standardization, embryo toxicity assessment, and quantitative pathway validation remain necessary.

Article.Title: Distribution and Cytotoxic Potential of NK Cell Subsets in Conventional and Immune-Protective Anesthetic Strategies: A Randomized Study in Colorectal Cancer Patients
Article.Authors: de Knijff P.; Vulcano T.; Jongman R.; Olthof C.; Struys M.; Abdulahad W.; Bosch D.
Article.Abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that anesthesia can modulate natural killer (NK) cell activity, potentially influencing anti-tumor immunity. CD56+CD16+ NK-cell subsets were characterized by flow cytometry based on NKG2A, NKG2C, and KIR expression. Cytotoxic potential was assessed by intracellular perforin and granzyme B, and CD107a expression as a degranulation marker. Significant decreases from 0 to 48 h were observed in the conventional group for NKG2A+KIR+ double-positive (DP) NK cells (−0.69 percentage points, p = 0.02) and terminally differentiated (NKG2A−NKG2C−) NK cells (−2.22 percentage points, p = 0.02). CD107a expression in DP NK cells increased at 48 h versus baseline (+44.9% MFI, p = 0.04) only in the conventional group. Intracellular granzyme B (−3.38 percentage points; p = 0.02) and perforin levels (−4.56 percentage points, p = 0.04) decreased from 0 to 48 h in the conventional group. These findings suggest that an immune-protective anesthetic strategy may better preserve NK cell subset distribution and cytotoxic potential. However, given the modest magnitude of changes, these results should be interpreted as exploratory.

Article.Title: Quercetin Alleviates Menstrual Disorders and Uterine Inflammation via Regulating PRLR/GHR and the JAK2-STAT Pathway: Evidence from Network Pharmacology Combined with Proteomics
Article.Authors: Zhao J.; Zhu A.; Wen X.; Su T.; Liu Y.; Chen J.; Che Y.; Liu H.
Article.Abstract: This study investigated the effects of quercetin (QU) on reproductive endocrine and uterine parameters in a rat model of reproductive endocrine disturbance and explored potential mechanisms. The model was established by co-administering hydrocortisone and thyroxine, with model status assessed by general health indicators. Rats were divided into normal, model, Dingkundan, QU high-dose, and QU low-dose groups. Network pharmacology predicted overlapping targets/pathways between QU and irregular menstruation, and the model was used to mimic this clinical condition, followed by KEGG enrichment. Uterine proteomics identified candidate differential pathways for comparison with network predictions. ELISA measured hypothalamic GnRH, pituitary FSH, ovarian E2, inflammatory and immunoregulatory cytokines (TGF-β, IL-10, IL-6, IL-1β), and uterine COX-2, MPO, GSH, HO-1, and total NRF2. Both network pharmacology and proteomic KEGG enrichment analyses highlighted pathways associated with hormones and with JAK/STAT signaling. Compared with the model group, QU significantly increased GnRH, FSH, and E2. In addition, QU reduced IL-6 and IL-1β, with concomitant decreases in IL-10 and TGF-β. QU also reduced COX-2 and MPO while elevating GSH, HO-1, and total NRF2. Moreover, QU attenuated PRLR and enhanced GHR fluorescence. Finally, QU significantly downregulated STAT3/STAT5 phosphorylation, with a non-significant trend for p-JAK2. Histopathological damage was alleviated. QU treatment was associated with improved reproductive hormone levels and attenuated uterine histopathological damage, inflammation, and oxidative stress markers. These effects were accompanied by PRLR downregulation, GHR upregulation, and reduced STAT3/STAT5 phosphorylation.

Article.Title: Development of a High-Quality Tag-Free Ubiquitin Production Platform for Preclinical Applications
Article.Authors: Vargas-Coto J.; Vallejo-Castillo L.; Elizarrarás-Rodríguez L.; Fragozo A.; Vázquez-Leyva S.; Gómez-Castellano K.; Mendoza-Salazar I.; Pérez-Tapia S.; Almagro J.
Article.Abstract: Monomeric ubiquitin (Ub1−76) has shown immunomodulatory properties in a herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1)-infected mouse model when administered orally, positioning it as a promising biotherapeutic agent. Accordingly, preclinical research requires sufficient, high-quality Ub1−76 material. This study focuses on developing an expression and purification platform for Tag-Free Ub1−76 and its variant Ub1−74. Ubs were expressed in Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) cells, released by sonication, and precipitated in pH 4.5 glacial acetic acid. The pH was set to 5.1, and Ubs were purified by Size-Exclusion Chromatography (SEC); the buffer was exchanged via SEC desalting. Then, a polishing step using cation-exchange chromatography (CEX) was applied, which finalized purification with a second buffer exchange via SEC desalting. We independently produced six batches of Ub1−76 and three batches of Ub1−74 using the proposed platform, yielding 109.07 mg/L for each protein. The Quality Control (QC) of the Ubs met the predefined acceptance criteria: purity by SE-UHPLC (>95.0%), concentration by Bicinchoninic Acid (>1.0 mg/mL), endotoxin content by LAL (<10 EU/mg), integrity by SDS-PAGE (single band), mean deconvoluted intact-mass centroid values (8564.40 Da for Ub1−76 and 8451.73 Da for Ub1−74). The Ubs obtained in this study were similar to a commercial Ub1−76 (Ub1−76 com), which was used as an identity reference. We also used circular dichroism (CD) to compare the secondary structure of Ub1−76 com, Ub1−76, and Ub1−74; all showed similar structures. The expression platform described here provides Tag-Free ubiquitin suitable for preclinical feasibility research and a framework for producing peptide and small-protein biotherapeutic candidates.

Article.Title: Beyond Inflammation Control in Atopic Dermatitis: Barrier Recovery, Cellular Crosstalk and Tissue Memory
Article.Authors: Galińska N.
Article.Abstract: Barrier improvement, residual inflammation and tissue memory describe different aspects of atopic dermatitis (AD). This focused narrative review asks which cellular interactions are linked to measured barrier improvement and what evidence would connect them to durable recovery. A purposive map of 23 peer-reviewed primary publications compares human physiology, epithelial–stromal or epithelial–immune communication, and experiments separating initial exposure from later challenge. Human interleukin-4 receptor alpha blockade studies show improved water-barrier function and epidermal composition during treatment, with incomplete normalization in some domains. Reciprocal organotypic cultures and conditioned medium experiments support fibroblast regulation of epidermal differentiation and keratinocyte cohesion. These endpoints do not establish treatment-free recovery of human water-barrier function. Periostin, chemokine and niche studies identify additional communication routes, while separate tissue analyses show residual immune populations despite clinical or transcriptional improvement. Mouse memory studies reveal model-dependent regenerative or inflammatory recall, and intervention timing can distinguish establishment of later susceptibility from its expression. Across separate human studies, treatment-associated barrier improvement and the persistence of selected immune states are complementary observations. Whether a defined stromal program determines durable functional recovery in human AD remains unresolved.

Article.Title: Pan-Cancer Genomic and Clinical Landscape of Human Deubiquitinases Identifies Recurrent Cancer-Associated DUBs and Candidate Substrate Networks
Article.Authors: Abdulsalam S.; Choudhary N.; Marate S.; Nayak V.; Akbar K.; Modi P.; Najar M.
Article.Abstract: Deubiquitinases (DUBs) are key regulators of ubiquitin-mediated signaling and control essential cellular processes such as protein turnover, DNA repair, apoptosis, and immune responses. Despite their importance in cancer, a comprehensive multi-omics characterization of DUBs across malignancies remains limited. Here, we performed an integrated pan-cancer analysis using transcriptomic, genomic, and clinical data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), combined with experimentally validated DUB–substrate interactions and public proteomic datasets from gastric cancer, esophageal cancer, and glioma. Our analysis revealed substantial heterogeneity in DUB expression across cancers, with distinctive relative expression profiles of DUBs including USP7, USP10, USP11, USP14, USP22, OTUB1, and BAP1. Comparative analysis of ESCA and STAD identified eighteen shared cancer-enriched DUBs, suggesting overlap in their relative expression patterns in upper gastrointestinal cancers. Genomic profiling showed frequent copy-number amplifications (USP13, OTUD7B, EIF3H, USP21, USP36) and deletions (OTUD7A, USP2, USP28, USP19, BAP1), while mutation analysis highlighted USP34, USP9X, USP29, USP24, and USP26 as genes with high observed mutation counts. Survival analysis identified several prognostic DUBs, including USP1, USP4, OTUD7A, DESI2, PSMD14, and UCHL1. Integration of public proteomic datasets with curated DUB–substrate interactions highlighted candidate associations with pathways related to NF-κB signaling, apoptosis, cell-cycle regulation, and DNA damage response. Several DUBs, including USP7, USP10, USP11, USP14, and USP22, showed high connectivity within the constructed networks, prioritizing them for further functional investigation. Overall, this study provides a comprehensive pan-cancer atlas of DUB alterations and highlights candidate DUBs and pathways with potential diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic relevance.

Article.Title: Integrative Small RNA and Degradome Sequencing Reveals Salt-Responsive microRNA–Target Interactions in Soybean Roots
Article.Authors: Zhuang Y.; Wang C.; Han Y.; Chen B.; Zhang J.; Zhang D.; Li X.
Article.Abstract: Soybean (Glycine max) is a leading source of plant protein and vegetable oil. However, soil salinization adversely affects its planting area and yield. The salt-responsive microRNA (miRNA) layer is uncharacterized, particularly in roots, where stress originates. We generated 24 small RNA and two degradome libraries from roots of a salt-tolerant (QH34) and salt-sensitive (DN50) cultivar sampled before and 2, 4, and 8 h after NaCl treatment. These findings were integrated with published transcriptome data from the same cultivars and time points. In total, 117 high-confidence miRNA loci (90 conserved; 27 candidate novel) were annotated, of which 56 mature miRNAs (45 conserved; 11 novel) were differentially expressed in at least one within-cultivar contrast. Degradome sequencing identified 441 degradome-supported miRNA–target pairs (84 miRNAs; 422 target genes). Conserved miRNAs were mostly down-regulated, whereas novel miRNAs varied more significantly and were predominantly up-regulated in QH34. Salt also altered miRNA processing: 149 significant isomiR switches occurred across 24 loci, and shifted variants were predicted to recognize transcripts that canonical forms did not. The loci encoding gma-miR319p and gma-miR160e also showed haplotype associations with salt tolerance across 172 accessions. Overexpression of Glyma.08G301200, a degradome-supported gma-miR2109 target in a network module associated with gma-miR160e, increased root elongation and survival under 150 mM NaCl. These results link natural variation at miRNA loci to a salt-responsive regulatory network, and identify Glyma.08G301200 as a candidate for improving soybean salt tolerance. More broadly, the combination of cleavage-supported targets, haplotype-associated loci, and a validated target gene offers starting points for improving salt tolerance in this crop, pending validation in independent populations.

Article.Title: Time-Resolved DPPH Response During Aqueous Extraction of Cannabis sativa L. Flowers and Leaves: A Unified Rational Model for Monotonic and Overshoot Kinetics
Article.Authors: Postnikov E.; Bartoszek M.; Sycheva A.; Polak J.; Zieliński M.; Nawrot K.; Chorążewski M.
Article.Abstract: Understanding extraction kinetics is essential for the characterization and optimization of the release of bioactive compounds from plant materials. Conventional pseudo-second-order and Peleg-type models were unable to describe the complete kinetic profile of leaf extracts. Therefore, a generalized rational-function model was proposed to describe both monotonic and non-monotonic extraction behaviour within a single framework. The characteristic kinetic profiles obtained by UV–Vis were qualitatively confirmed using EPR spectroscopy. The proposed approach provides a framework for modelling complex extraction kinetics in heterogeneous plant materials.

Article.Title: Exploring Potential Molecular Interactions of Melittin in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OSCC): A Multi-Tiered In Silico and Preliminary In Vitro Analysis
Article.Authors: Zakaria N.; Nor Hashim N.; Sharifuddin Y.; Abu I.; Syed Abdul Rahman S.; Bin Mohamad S.; Othman R.; Inche Zainal Abidin S.; Kamarul T.; Md Kasim A.; Abdul Majid N.
Article.Abstract: Melittin (MEL), the primary peptide constituent in honey bee venom, exhibits potent anticancer properties, yet its functional role and potential molecular targets in OSCC remain poorly characterised. Analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) derived from GEO and TCGA databases via protein–protein interaction network (PPIN) identified 14 candidate hub genes associated with focal adhesion and PI3K/Akt signalling pathways. Article.Title: Kidney Architecture Changes in a MASH High-Fat Diet Ob/Ob Mouse Model: Protection by FXR Agonists OCA and INT-787
Article.Authors: Palladini G.; Cavallo M.; Milanesi G.; Croce A.; Perlini S.; Adorini L.; Ferrigno A.; Vairetti M.; Di Pasqua L.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) frequently induces renal injury, and current therapies primarily target hepatic lesions. In this work, we examined liver-induced kidney alterations in an ob/ob mouse model of MASH also through in situ autofluorescence (AF) imaging of renal tissue, and the effects of FXR agonists, Obeticholic acid (OCA) and INT-787. Lep ob/ob mice with diet-induced MASH received either a high-fat diet (HFD) or control diet (CD) for 9 weeks (wks), followed by treatment with OCA or INT-787 (0.05% mixed into HFD; 30 mg/kg/day) for an additional 12 wks. HFD-fed mice developed marked liver dysfunction without biochemical evidence of kidney injury, as indicated by stable serum renal markers. No significant differences were detected in MMP activities across groups. AF scattered-light imaging revealed a clear disruption of the fibrillar collagen network: quantitative analysis of collagen fiber orientation showed that HFD 21-wk kidneys exhibited a substantial increase in fiber misalignment. Treatment with INT-787 or OCA significantly reduced angular dispersion, preserving collagen organization to values comparable to CD mice. AF imaging proved highly informative, serving not only to enhance structural visualization but also as an early indicator of kidney alterations. Given that collagen fiber orientation reflects underlying fibrotic remodeling, our findings demonstrate that diet-induced MASH compromises renal tissue architecture, and that FXR agonists effectively counteract these early structural abnormalities.

Article.Title: Mechanistic Insights into CO2 Hydrogenation to Methanol on Mo and MoP Catalysts
Article.Authors: Almithn A.
Article.Abstract: Molybdenum phosphide (MoP) catalyzes methanol synthesis from CO2 while resisting the formate poisoning that limits Cu-based catalysts. However, an atomistic understanding of how phosphorus alters the branching between direct C–O dissociation and sequential hydrogenation is still lacking. Here, periodic density functional theory calculations were used to map the CO2 hydrogenation network on Mo(110) and Mo-terminated MoP(001), which represent metallic Mo and P-deficient MoP, respectively. All intermediates bind more strongly on MoP(001), and formate is selectively over-stabilized while retaining a bidentate geometry. On both surfaces, hydrogenation of CO2 at carbon to formate is preferred over carboxyl formation by at least 90 kJ mol−1. The P-modified Mo lattice raises the barrier for direct C–O scission from 22 to 48 kJ mol−1. It also widens the effective separation between the hydrogenation and dissociation transition states from 13 to 56 kJ mol−1, directing carbon into the formate pathway. Methanol then forms via H2COO*, H2COOH*, CH2O*, and CH3O*. However, methoxy hydrogenation and the removal of surface O* and OH* are prohibitive, and secondary CO hydrogenation offers no route around this bottleneck. Phosphorus thus improves the selectivity of CO2 activation, but Mo-terminated sites cannot sustain a methanol cycle and act instead as sites for side reactions and oxygen uptake. These results, together with previous studies of P-containing MoP surfaces, suggest that methanol formation on MoP catalysts requires sites with exposed surface phosphorus.

Article.Authors: Ortiz-Hernández O.; Estrada-López E.; Vargas-Zuniga J.; Velásquez-Tinoco D.; Díaz-Reyes G.; Rodríguez-Cantarero R.; Hernández-Rivera D.; Godoy-Andrade R.; Elvir-Alvarez C.; Cuevas-Martínez A.; Pineda-Maldonado O.

Docking placed PCA outside the catalytic pocket (−4.71 kcal·mol−1, relative score). In three independent 1000 ns MD replicas per system, PCA did not maintain this pose and formed transient hydrogen bonds with different surface residues. As copper ions were modeled as non-bonded and left the active site, the simulations describe only PCA–surface interactions, not the catalytic center or inhibition mechanism. MT–PCA showed lower root-mean-square deviation than free MT (0.24 ± 0.03 vs. 0.42 ± 0.08 nm; n = 3, not significant). The kinetic data are consistent with possible inhibition by PCA, whereas its binding site and mechanism require experimental validation. With commercial PCA and no food tests, its presence in coffee pulp only motivates exploring residues.

Article.Title: PCSK9 Inhibition in Transition: From Established Treatments to Emerging Therapeutic Approaches
Article.Authors: Papagiannidou A.; Pantos C.; Mourouzis I.; Kounatidis D.
Article.Abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a secreted proprotein convertase that promotes lysosomal degradation of the hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR), thereby reducing the clearance of circulating low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). Its validation as a therapeutic target is supported by human genetic evidence demonstrating that loss-of-function variants are associated with lifelong reductions in LDL-C and protection against cardiovascular disease. This review examines the biology of PCSK9 and the expanding range of strategies for its pharmacological inhibition, integrating evidence from human genetic studies, clinical trials, and preclinical models, with particular emphasis on translational relevance. The monoclonal antibodies evolocumab and alirocumab substantially reduce LDL-C levels and cardiovascular risk, whereas inclisiran, a small interfering RNA (siRNA), achieves sustained suppression of hepatic PCSK9 synthesis with infrequent dosing. Recent therapeutic advances include the FDA approvals of lerodalcibep, a third-generation injectable PCSK9 inhibitor, and enlicitide decanoate, an orally administered macrocyclic peptide inhibitor. In parallel, nanoparticle-based delivery systems, active PCSK9 vaccination, and CRISPR-based genome editing represent emerging therapeutic strategies that remain largely in preclinical development. Beyond cardiovascular disease, PCSK9 has been implicated in sepsis, cancer, and neurodegenerative, pulmonary, and autoimmune disorders, although the supporting evidence remains heterogeneous and predominantly preclinical. In oncology, experimental findings implicating PCSK9 in tumor immune evasion and modulation of responses to immune checkpoint blockade have prompted its clinical evaluation as a potential adjunct to anticancer therapy. Further prospective clinical studies are required to establish the efficacy and long-term safety of novel PCSK9-targeted approaches and determine whether their therapeutic potential translates into meaningful clinical benefits.

Article.Title: Transcriptome-Wide Profiling of lncRNAs and mRNAs Provides an Exploratory Interaction Catalogue for Skeletal Muscle Development and Fat-Tail Deposition in Bashibay and Argali × Bashibay Crossbred Sheep
Article.Authors: Sulayman A.; Huang X.; Zhu M.; Wufuer G.; Zhang X.; Ma Y.; Sulaiman Y.; Tian Y.

Putative cis- and trans-target prediction coupled with Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway enrichment identified that candidate lncRNA targets—including ALOX15B, FBP2, HSPA8, IDH1, LTF, LAMA1, PTK2B, and STEAP4—overlapped with differentially expressed mRNAs and converged on lipid metabolic processes, the MAPK cascade, and insulin signalling. In skeletal muscle, DKK2 and SLC27A6 are predicted to have potential involvement in Wnt and PPAR signalling, respectively. qRT-PCR validation of fifteen lncRNAs and six mRNAs confirmed the sequencing results. These findings expand the ovine lncRNA catalogue and provide an exploratory transcriptomic resource and candidate interaction set for future functional dissection of the molecular crosstalk between myogenesis and fat-tail adipogenesis in sheep.

Article.Title: Green Synthesis of Silver Nanoparticles Using Plant Extracts and Their Immobilization on Sorbent Materials for Wound Dressings: A Review
Article.Authors: Amzeyeva U.; Nurlybek A.; Zhapekova A.; Rakhimova B.; Kantureyeva A.; Aknazarov S.; Varol E.; Mirzaliyeva D.; Azat S.
Article.Abstract: The rising prevalence of chronic and infected wounds and the spread of antimicrobial resistance have intensified the search for wound dressings that prevent infection, manage exudate, and promote tissue regeneration. Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) offer broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, and their “green” synthesis using plant extracts is a sustainable alternative to chemical and physical methods, providing better biocompatibility and a lower environmental impact. This review examines plant-mediated synthesis of AgNPs and their immobilization on sorbents for wound dressings. It discusses phytochemicals as reducing and stabilizing agents, the influence of synthesis parameters on nanoparticle size, morphology, crystallinity, and stability, characterization techniques, and antimicrobial mechanisms and activity against clinically relevant bacteria and fungi. Particular attention is given to mineral, carbon-based, and biopolymeric sorbents as multifunctional matrices for AgNPs. Sorbent–nanoparticle interactions, immobilization strategies, and controlled silver ion release are analyzed regarding the structural integrity, antimicrobial performance, exudate management, and biocompatibility of nanocomposite dressings. Combining sorbents with AgNPs yields multifunctional wound care materials with enhanced therapeutic efficacy. Challenges related to synthesis reproducibility, standardization of plant extracts, cytotoxicity assessment, controlled silver release, scale-up, and regulatory translation are discussed. Future directions include multifunctional sorbent-based nanocomposites, smart dressings, and clinically translatable biomaterials with improved safety and performance.

Article.Authors: Dsouza R.; Sekhar P.; Gopalakrishnan V.; Dcunha L.; Mahin A.; Vaz C.; Anil Kumar A.; Raju R.; Soman S.
Article.Abstract: Cyclin L is the subfamily of non-canonical cyclins characterized by the presence of the RS domain on the C-terminal and the cyclin box on the N-terminal. Based on the frequency of occurrence and differential regulation of phosphosites across diverse phosphoproteomics datasets, S352, S335, S338, and S342 were detected as the predominant phosphosites of CCNL1. These phosphosites showed conservation across species, while S352 and S335 phosphosites showed conservation between CCNL1 and CCNL2 proteins, highlighting their functional relevance. Further, co-occurrence analysis uncovered the co-ordinated phosphorylation patterns among CCNL1 phosphosites, and several phosphosite associations were attributed to the shared peptide localization. The functional enrichment analysis revealed that CCNL1_S352 co-regulated proteins were enriched in RNA splicing, supporting the robustness of our approach. CDK12_T893 was found to be the top co-regulated kinase of CCNL1_S352, which exhibited consistent co-regulation across diverse experimental conditions. In addition, the motif analysis showed that the consensus sequence of CCNL1_S352 aligns with the reported substrate recognition motif of CDK12, suggesting a potential kinase–substrate interaction. The cancer-specific phosphoproteomics analysis revealed upregulation of CCNL1_S352 across multiple tumour types, underscoring its clinical significance. Based on our meta-phosphoproteomics data analysis, we propose CCNL1_S352 as a potential regulatory phosphosite and suggest that cyclin L1 may have a regulatory association with CDK12.

Article.Title: Comparative Efficacy of Biologic Therapies for Psoriasis: Insights from Head-to-Head Studies
Article.Authors: Rafałowicz A.; Nowowiejska-Purpurowicz J.; Flisiak I.
Article.Abstract: Biologic therapies have substantially transformed the management of moderate-to-severe psoriasis, but differences in efficacy, speed of response, durability, and safety reflect the distinct immunological pathways targeted by individual agents. The aim of this review is the analysis and comparison of particular biological agents in terms of efficacy and safety. Head-to-head trials consistently demonstrate that IL-17 and IL-23 inhibitors achieve greater skin clearance than first-generation TNF-α inhibitors. IL-17 blockade, particularly with agents targeting IL-17A, produces rapid clinical improvement by directly suppressing keratinocyte-driven inflammation. Dual IL-17A/IL-17F inhibition with bimekizumab may provide even greater clearance, although broader IL-17 inhibition is associated with a higher frequency of mucosal candidiasis. In contrast, selective IL-23 inhibition acts upstream by suppressing the differentiation and maintenance of pathogenic Th17 cells and appears to provide particularly durable disease control. Selective IL-23 inhibitors may also preserve potentially protective IL-12 signaling, distinguishing them from ustekinumab, which targets the shared p40 subunit. Safety profiles are generally favorable across biologic classes, although mechanism-specific risks include tuberculosis reactivation with TNF-α inhibitors, candidiasis with IL-17 inhibitors, and inflammatory bowel disease concerns with IL-17 blockade. Therefore, biologic selection should be individualized according to disease severity, required speed and durability of response, comorbidities, affected anatomical sites, safety considerations, dosing frequency, patient preferences and adherence goals. Current comparative evidence supports increasingly targeted approaches within the IL-23/IL-17 axis.

Article.Title: Regulatory Roles of the Gut Microbiota in Hematological Malignancies
Article.Authors: Liu X.; Guo Z.
Article.Abstract: Relying on the proposed gut–bone marrow bidirectional regulatory axis, the gut microbiota may influence systemic immune homeostasis and the bone marrow hematopoietic microenvironment through maintenance of the mucosal barrier and signaling molecules such as short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites, and may thereby contribute to the pathobiology of hematological malignancies. Patients with hematological malignancies often exhibit dysbiosis, including decreased gut microbial diversity, the depletion of butyrate-producing beneficial bacteria, and the overproliferation of opportunistic pathogens, although patterns vary across cohorts. This dysbiosis may contribute to malignant clonal expansion and disease progression and has been associated with variation in the response to chemotherapy and cellular therapy and with the risk of graft-versus-host disease, severe infections, and intestinal mucositis following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. This narrative review summarizes interactions between the gut microbiota and hematological malignancies, disease-associated microbiota profiles, treatment-related associations, and barriers to clinical translation. Because much of the human evidence is observational, microbiota-directed interventions require prospective validation before routine clinical use.

Article.Title: SDS3 Deletion Reduces the Competitive Advantage of Deletion-Bearing mtDNA in Heteroplasmic Yeast
Article.Authors: Burlaka A.; Potapenko E.; Surikova E.; Epremyan K.; Kashko N.; Knorre D.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy is the coexistence of two different mtDNA molecules within a eukaryotic cell. Here, we used baker’s yeast to screen for nuclear gene deletions that help cells preserve wild-type (rho+) mtDNA in the presence of mutant (rho−) mtDNA with large deletions. We crossed a pool of the yeast knockout collection with a rho− strain and used barcode sequencing to compare knockout-strain abundance among all diploids and among those that retained respiratory function. Although no individual deletion remained significant after multiple-testing correction, gene set enrichment analysis and gene ranking yielded candidates that may affect suppressivity—the inheritance bias favouring rho− mtDNA—with invasive growth as the most enriched GO term. Testing candidates, we found that deletion of SDS3, which encodes a component of the Rpd3L histone deacetylase complex, in the rho+ parent reduced the apparent suppressivity of rho− mtDNA in an independent genetic background, protecting wild-type mtDNA from displacement. This effect was not attributable to higher mtDNA copy number or to a growth defect of Δsds3 rho− strains. These results suggest that SDS3 deletion either shifts intracellular competition between mtDNA variants in favour of wild-type mtDNA or alters mating efficiency in favour of crosses more likely to eliminate mutant mtDNA.

Article.Authors: Sornard W.; Limsuwan S.; Thamsatit P.; Panya A.; Phonsatta N.; Thangvichien S.; Tansakul N.
Article.Abstract: Dietary lipids may influence circulating fatty acid profiles, but the responses to formulations containing hemp seed-derived ingredients in canine nutrition remain insufficiently characterized. FO showed a greater baseline-to-Day-90 increase in α-linolenic acid relative to FC (q = 0.035); eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) showed an overall interaction but no significant Day-90 group contrast after FDR correction. Article.Title: From Nanoframe Architecture to Trace Ambroxol Sensing: PtNiRu–Carbon Black Interfaces in Complex Matrices
Article.Authors: Suchanek M.; Gruzeł G.; Łukowiec D.; Zambrzycki M.; Piech R.
Article.Abstract: Sensitive monitoring of ambroxol hydrochloride molecules (AMB) in samples of different origin requires analytical approaches capable of providing reliable responses despite complex matrix compositions. Ten replicate measurements performed at 0.5 µM yielded an RSD of 1.5%, demonstrating good precision. The analytical performance of the platform was further examined in pharmaceutical formulations, artificial urine, human plasma, river water and untreated wastewater. Recoveries of 94.7–108.5% were obtained across these matrices. Together with its satisfactory stability and simple preparation, these results support the applicability of PtNiRu-CB/GCE for sensitive AMB determination in pharmaceutical, biological and environmental analysis.

Article.Authors: Katsaran J.; Maluchenko A.; Danilova M.; Onyanov N.; Maksimov D.; Zalivako A.; Emelin A.; Feidorov I.; Salimgereeva D.; Karnaukhov N.; Voloshin M.; Bodunova N.; Volchkov P.; Krupinova J.

PanNET tissue samples, including insulinomas and metastatic samples, as well as a duodenal neuroendocrine tumor (DNET) sample, were subjected to enzymatic dissociation using different enzyme mixes. Samples yielding a high cell viability were selected for scRNA-seq, and the resulting data were compared with snRNA-seq data obtained from cryopreserved portions of the same tumors to investigate potential dissociation-related biases. In addition, morphological assessment of tissue blocks was performed to explore potential associations between tissue characteristics and dissociation outcomes. Collagenase I-based dissociation resulted in relatively high cell viability (>70%) in both PanNET and DNET samples, whereas alternative enzyme combinations were associated with lower viability. ScRNA-seq and snRNA-seq revealed differences between the two approaches, reflecting potential assay-related differences in the representation of cellular gene expression. Our findings highlight the importance of balancing efficient tissue dissociation with the preservation of cell viability and suggest that morphological and clinical characteristics should be considered when developing protocols for the single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis of PanNETs.

Article.Title: Chemotherapy-Induced Remodeling of the Collagen Matrix Differs Between Colorectal Cancer Models with Different Drug Sensitivity
Article.Authors: Druzhkova I.; Plekhanov A.; Dudenkova V.; Lisitsa U.; Kuzmin D.; Sovetsky A.; Bureev P.; Monicheva V.; Spashchanskii R.; Kiseleva E.; Mozherov A.; Ignatova N.; Gladkova N.; Shirmanova M.; Zagaynova E.
Article.Abstract: The role of the tumor extracellular matrix (ECM) in the development of chemoresistance is well known. However, there is little data on how it changes during treatment and its association with drug resistance, particularly in colorectal cancer. Here, we assessed chemotherapy-induced remodeling of fibrillar collagen in models based on chemosensitive HCT116 and more resistant HT29 cells treated with FOLFOX or FOLFIRI, using second harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy and cross-polarization optical coherence tomography (CP-OCT). This study was performed in vitro in collagen-based co-cultures with fibroblasts and in vivo in tumor xenografts and was complemented by immunofluorescence analysis of lysyl oxidase-like 1 (LOXL1), RT-qPCR of collagen genes, and analysis of public transcriptomic datasets from patients treated with FOLFOX. In sensitive HCT116 tumors, both regimens increased the SHG signal of fibrillar collagen and the CP-OCT depolarization ratio (DR), accompanied by increased LOXL1 immunoreactivity. In resistant HT29 tumors, the SHG signal did not change after FOLFOX and decreased after FOLFIRI treatment. FOLFIRI reduced the orientational order of collagen fibers in both models. DR correlated with the SHG mean intensity (r = 0.61) and energy (r = 0.57). In open-access transcriptomic datasets, pretreatment collagen gene expression did not differ between subsequent responders and non-responders to FOLFOX, whereas post-treatment tumors of responders showed higher COL1A2 and COL3A1 expression than those of non-responders. Thus, in the two models studied, chemotherapy-associated increases in collagen-related optical signals were observed in the more chemosensitive tumors, and label-free SHG and CP-OCT warrant further investigation as tools for assessing matrix changes during treatment.

Article.Title: Receptors and Receptor Heteromers in Atherosclerosis
Article.Authors: Tan J.; Belhoul-Fakir H.; Pfleger K.; Johnstone E.
Article.Abstract: Atherosclerosis, a chronic inflammatory disease characterised by plaque formation in the arterial wall, remains a leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. It is a complex disease, underscored by myriad receptors and receptor-mediated processes that collectively regulate inflammation, cell survival, and plaque formation and stability. Of interest are receptor heteromers—macromolecular complexes made of two or more distinct receptor units (protomers). Receptor heteromers composed of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) have received particular interest, due to their broad physiological and clinical relevance. Interestingly, emerging evidence suggests that GPCRs may also form receptor heteromers with receptors from other families, such as the receptor tyrosine kinases and scavenger receptors. This review outlines the roles of receptors and receptor heteromers across atherosclerosis pathogenesis and appraises the evidence for proposed complexes against established criteria for heteromer identification. Heteromer-specific properties are demonstrated for several receptor pairs relevant to lesion initiation and inflammatory amplification, whereas evidence pertaining to advanced plaque processes remains largely inferential. Answering the question of where such receptor heteromers form, and with what functional consequences, is an important prerequisite for evaluating these complexes as therapeutic targets in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

Article.Title: Gut Microbiota-Derived Metabolites in Oligozoospermia and Asthenozoospermia: Exploring Molecular Mechanisms Through Network Pharmacology and Molecular Docking
Article.Authors: Su Q.; Bi Y.; Wang K.; Fan W.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: This study explored the potential molecular associations of gut microbiota-derived metabolites with oligozoospermia and asthenozoospermia and identified key candidate targets, pathways, and microbiota–substrate–metabolite–target relationships. Human gut microbiota, substrates, metabolites, and host genes were obtained from gutMGene. Metabolite targets were predicted using SwissTargetPrediction and SEA, while disease-related targets were collected from GeneCards, OMIM, and CTD. Candidate targets were identified by intersection analysis. Protein–protein interaction networks were constructed to prioritize highly connected candidate targets, followed by GO and KEGG enrichment analyses. SwissADME and ADMETlab were used to characterize physicochemical properties and predict toxicity, respectively. An M-S-M-T network was constructed, and molecular docking was performed to assess potential metabolite–target interactions. In total, 1518 gut microbiota metabolite-related targets were obtained, yielding 22 candidate targets for oligozoospermia and 17 for asthenozoospermia. CXCL8, IL6, TNF, and TP53 were identified as shared highly connected candidate targets. GO analysis indicated enrichment in responses to bacterial-origin molecules, lipopolysaccharide response, inflammation, cytokine activity, and redox homeostasis. KEGG analysis highlighted MAPK, PI3K-Akt, TNF, HIF-1, and cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction pathways. The M-S-M-T network suggested a potential association involving Clostridium sporogenes, tyrosine/phenylalanine-derived aromatic metabolites, and CXCL8, based on the integration of reported microbial metabolic relationships and predicted metabolite–target interactions. Molecular docking yielded predicted binding scores for 3-phenylpropionic acid and 4-hydroxyphenylacetic acid with CXCL8. This network pharmacology study identified CXCL8, IL6, TNF, and TP53 as candidate targets potentially linking gut microbiota-derived metabolites with oligozoospermia and asthenozoospermia. The predicted associations involving aromatic metabolites and CXCL8 provide hypotheses for further investigation. Experimental and clinical validation is required to determine whether these associations have biological relevance in male reproductive dysfunction.

Article.Title: GABAergic and Glutamatergic Deficits in Schizophrenia: Pathophysiological Mechanisms Underlying Negative Symptoms and Cognitive Impairment
Article.Authors: Zakrzewska A.; Gabryelska A.; Strzelecki D.
Article.Abstract: Schizophrenia is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms. While classical dopaminergic models explain psychotic features, they fail to address the debilitating negative and cognitive deficits that dictate long-term disability. We aim to synthesize contemporary evidence on the impairment of the excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance within cortical microcircuits as a central pathophysiological hypothesis of the disorder. The cascade is hypothesized to be driven by N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor hypofunction, which impairs parvalbumin-positive (PV+) interneurons and consequently downregulates glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD67)-mediated gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) synthesis. Weakened PV+ interneuron function disrupts Pyramidal-Interneuron Network Gamma (PING) dynamics, reducing gamma-band synchronization and fronto-temporo-thalamic connectivity. At the macroscopic and cellular levels, the E/I imbalance is linked to reduced neuropil volume and aberrant synaptic pruning that disturbs dendritic architecture. Clinically, this triggers severe working memory dysfunction, cognitive rigidity, avolition, and anhedonia. This paper presents emerging glutamatergic and GABAergic pharmacological strategies, including glycine, D-serine, and metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR) modulators. We highlight key directions for future research, emphasizing the use of translational biomarkers (e.g., mismatch negativity (MMN), magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), and gamma oscillations) to normalize PV+ interneuron function and network-level synchronization.

Article.Title: Epithelial Ion Channels at Environmental Interfaces: Shared Mechanisms and Tissue-Specific Roles in Health and Disease
Article.Authors: Koza J.; Kopoń M.; Lewandowski K.; Hołyńska-Iwan I.
Article.Abstract: The airways, gastrointestinal tract, and skin are continuously exposed to the external environment, yet each has developed distinct mechanisms for preserving its epithelial barrier. Many of these mechanisms rely on a shared set of ion channels whose functions change with cellular location and tissue architecture. This narrative review examines epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), calcium-activated chloride channels, and selected potassium and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels, together with the transport proteins that sustain their activity. In the airways, coordinated ion transport maintains surface hydration and supports mucociliary clearance. Along the gastrointestinal tract, region-specific transport pathways regulate gastric acid secretion, nutrient absorption, and intestinal fluid balance. In the skin, related proteins participate in sweat electrolyte reabsorption, epidermal homeostasis, and repair. Disruption of these pathways produces quite different clinical problems. CFTR mutations cause cystic fibrosis, whereas intestinal inflammation may secondarily suppress sodium absorption and alter potassium transport, aggravating diarrhea in inflammatory bowel disease. Experimental studies also implicate ion channels in keratinocyte migration and cutaneous sensory responses, although their clinical significance is less firmly established. Comparing these epithelial systems helps distinguish common molecular principles from organ-specific adaptations and highlights both established treatments and unresolved therapeutic questions.

Article.Title: Development and Validation of a Four-Plex PCR Assay for Rapid Screening of Transferable Oxazolidinone Resistance Determinants: cfr, cfr(D), optrA, and a poxtA/poxtA2-Associated Target Region
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Xie J.; Li R.; Wang Z.; Chen S.; Liu K.; Zhang W.; Liu Y.; Mo F.; Niu S.; Liu M.
Article.Abstract: Oxazolidinones are last-resort agents for treating multidrug-resistant Gram-positive bacterial infections, and the dissemination of transferable oxazolidinone resistance genes across human, animal, food, and environmental settings highlights the need for efficient multi-target screening. This study developed a single-tube multiplex PCR assay for simultaneous screening of four primer-defined targets: cfr, cfr(D), optrA, and a poxtA/poxtA2-associated target region. In silico analysis indicated that the poxtA2 primer pair may also recognize poxtA, and the corresponding 586-bp amplicon could not distinguish these variants. After optimization of primer concentrations and cycling conditions, the assay generated distinct amplicons of 287 bp for cfr(D), 389 bp for optrA, 586 bp for the poxtA/poxtA2-associated target region, and 725 bp for cfr. No amplification was observed in the eight target-negative control strains. The operational analytical detection threshold for simultaneous amplification of all four targets was 10 pg/μL (2 pg/reaction), based on three replicate reactions using genomic DNA from Enterococcus faecalis QZ076. The assay was further evaluated using 161 laboratory-preserved animal-derived isolates from eight bacterial species, comprising 113 chicken-derived, 40 dairy cow-derived, and 8 dog-derived isolates. Six chicken-derived isolates were positive, whereas the remaining 155 isolates were negative for all four targets. The gene profiles detected by the four-plex PCR assay were concordant with those obtained by singleplex PCR, and Sanger sequencing supported the identification of cfr, cfr(D), and optrA, while the poxtA/poxtA2 variants in two isolates remained unresolved. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed that all six target-gene-positive isolates were resistant to both linezolid and florfenicol. Overall, the developed assay provides a practical approach for simultaneous screening of transferable oxazolidinone resistance genes in cultured bacterial isolates and may support antimicrobial resistance surveillance, although its applicability to direct clinical, veterinary, food, or environmental specimens remains to be evaluated.

Article.Title: Evaluation of Clomipramine Against Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis in an hSOD1-G93A Mouse Study
Article.Authors: Armida M.; Bullitta S.; Liguori F.; Zanfini L.; Lauricella A.; Amadio S.; Potenza R.; Volonté C.
Article.Abstract: By exploiting network medicine and drug repurposing strategies, we previously identified and prioritized clomipramine as one among a subset of suitable non-customary compounds to be tested against amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). We then investigated the chronic administration of clomipramine in vivo, in the hSOD1-A4V and hSOD1-G85R Drosophila melanogaster ALS models, demonstrating significant efficacy in ameliorating lifespan, improving motor abilities, and mitigating genomic instability and inflammation. The aim of the present work is now to test clomipramine against ALS in the hSOD1-G93A mouse, which remains today among the premier and most exploited and validated preclinical models for studying the disease. Our work demonstrates that the effects of clomipramine are not consistently reproduced across different preclinical models of ALS. In particular, clomipramine emerges as a context-dependent drug in ALS mice. Intraperitoneal administration of clomipramine does not improve overall survival at 10 mg/Kg, but it significantly worsens body weight, motor performance and neuroscore predominantly in male mice. At 20 mg/Kg, clomipramine elicits a clinically meaningful increase in survival time only in the male subgroup, despite a statistically non-significant p-value. Our study reveals the complex profile of clomipramine’s effects, rather than a clear therapeutic action. We trust that further insights and fine tuning through cross-model validation and context-dependent modulation by clomipramine might reveal a novel route for better understanding ALS and exploring clinical outcomes.

Article.Title: Effect of Antifreeze Protein Supplementation on the Quality of Cryopreserved Sperm in Yangtze Sturgeon (Acipenser dabryanus)
Article.Authors: Yue H.; Zhu S.; Luo J.; Xiong W.; Shen L.; Li C.; Du H.; Ye H.
Article.Abstract: Sperm cryobanking is essential for conserving the genetic diversity of the endangered Yangtze sturgeon (Acipenser dabryanus), but freeze–thaw injury lowers the quality of frozen sperm. In every group, approximately 99% of viable sperm were acrosome-intact, so the latter increase reflected a larger proportion of viable sperm, nearly all with an intact acrosome. Fertilization with 0.1 µg/mL AFP III exceeded the control by 8.57 percentage points (male-level p = 0.051; dish-level odds ratio 1.46) but remained numerically below fresh sperm. At 100 µg/mL, both AFPs reduced PMI and fertilization. Low-concentration AFP III is therefore a candidate additive for Yangtze sturgeon sperm cryobanking that requires validation with more males and hatching data.

Article.Title: Ivermectin and Pharmacological Ascorbate in Cancer: Mechanistic Insights, Translational Challenges, and the Rationale for Future Combination Studies
Article.Authors: Codini M.; Manuali E.; Beccari T.; Ceccarini M.
Article.Abstract: The need for more effective cancer treatments has led to growing interest in drug repurposing and therapeutic approaches targeting cancer metabolism. Ivermectin and high-dose vitamin C have both been investigated for their possible anticancer effects. Ivermectin is an established antiparasitic drug, while vitamin C is an essential nutrient. Studies in experimental cancer models suggest that these compounds can affect cell survival through changes in oxidative stress, mitochondrial activity, metabolism and cell-death pathways. High-dose intravenous vitamin C differs from ordinary supplementation because it can reach millimolar concentrations in the blood. At these levels, ascorbate can promote hydrogen peroxide formation outside cells, increasing oxidative stress in susceptible cancer cells. Vitamin C also supports the activity of certain enzymes that depend on iron and 2-oxoglutarate. These enzymes are involved in the control of gene activity, cell development, and the way cells respond to oxygen levels. Although ivermectin and pharmacological ascorbate act through different mechanisms, some of their effects involve similar biological processes. Both have been associated with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, mitochondrial dysfunction, activation of programmed cell death and changes in signalling pathways involved in cancer progression. This narrative review examines the molecular mechanisms, preclinical evidence, pharmacological limitations, and clinical experience associated with each compound. No direct preclinical or clinical cancer studies evaluating ivermectin and pharmacological ascorbate together were identified in the literature reviewed.

Article.Title: Understanding Periodontitis: A Narrative Review of Microbiota–Immune–Brain Interactions
Article.Authors: Breivik T.; Gjermo P.; Opstad P.; Murison R.; Fristad I.
Article.Abstract: Current models of immunoinflammatory diseases, including periodontitis, do not fully account for brain-regulated neuroimmune mechanisms contributing to mucosal immune homeostasis. We propose an integrative conceptual framework that combines current knowledge of periodontal immunology with brain-regulated neuroimmune mechanisms to improve our understanding of the etiology and progression of periodontitis. This narrative review integrates evidence from human clinical studies, experimental animal models, and mechanistic neuroimmunological research on microbiota–immune–brain interactions to develop a biologically integrated framework for periodontitis pathogenesis. Available evidence indicates that the brain continuously receives information via sensory nerves and the circulation regarding the oral microbiota, including dental biofilm at the gingival margin, together with associated immunoinflammatory signals. Through neural and hormonal pathways of the stress system, the brain regulates immune cell activity and the balance between pathogen-protective pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory responses. Factors associated with periodontitis may over-activate these homeostatic mechanisms, impair immune control of invasive pathobionts, and trigger compensatory innate immune responses that hinder microbial invasion while contributing to periodontal soft-tissue destruction and alveolar bone loss. In gingivitis, in contrast, the stress system may be under-activated, with pathobiont-protective pro-inflammatory activity stronger than normal, but with reduced defense against benign symbionts. Brain-regulated neuroimmune mechanisms may contribute importantly to gingival immune homeostasis. Integrating these mechanisms with current concepts of host–microbiota interactions provides a conceptual framework for re-evaluating the pathogenesis, prevention, and management of periodontitis and for guiding future experimental, translational, and prospective clinical research.

Article.Title: Disease-Modifying Therapeutics for Huntington’s Disease: State of the Art
Article.Authors: Ros G.; Bon C.; Smělá D.; Espinoza S.; Sanges R.; Gustincich S.; Persichetti F.
Article.Abstract: Huntington’s disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in HTT. Despite its well-defined genetic cause, developing safe and effective disease-modifying therapies has remained challenging. By September 2026, the therapeutic landscape included regulatory submissions for the adeno-associated virus serotype 5 (AAV5)-delivered RNA interference therapy ifezuntirgene inilparvovec (AMT-130) and the discontinuation of tominersen after the GENERATION HD2 trial, in which target engagement and biomarker responses were achieved without clinical benefit. These contrasting developments highlight both the progress achieved and the challenges of translating molecular interventions into clinical benefit. Here, we review five complementary therapeutic strategies grounded in current understanding of HD pathogenesis: editing the HTT sequence or modifying its epigenetic regulation; suppressing somatic CAG expansion by modulating DNA repair; lowering huntingtin expression with antisense oligonucleotides, AAV-delivered RNA interference and oral splicing modulators; modifying mutant huntingtin aggregation and proteostasis; and targeting downstream pathological processes. Together, these advances support combination approaches targeting multiple pathogenic mechanisms, although their efficacy and safety remain to be established. More than three decades after the identification of the causative mutation, a deeper understanding of HD biology and expanding therapeutic approaches provide grounds for cautious optimism about meaningful improvements for people with HD.

Article.Title: Synergistic Surface Biofunctionalization of PLA Fibers Using Plasma Activation and Exosome Immobilization for Biomedical Applications
Article.Authors: Bulanda W.; Kluska S.; Sokołowski K.; Ścisłowska-Czarnecka A.; Różycka A.; Zych Ł.; Stodolak-Zych E.
Article.Abstract: Electrospun poly(lactic acid) fibrous scaffolds are promising extracellular matrix-mimicking platforms for wound healing; however, their intrinsic hydrophobicity limits bioactivity and tissue regeneration. Nitrogen plasma-treated scaffolds preferentially supported macrophage viability and protein-associated activity, indicating macrophage activation, while exosome incorporation enhanced keratinocyte proliferative responses at later culture stages. Nitric oxide secretion and cytotoxicity assays indicated that these effects resulted from functional cellular modulation rather than stress-induced toxicity. Quantitative analyses confirmed significant differences between surface chemistries and functionalization states. Article.Title: Redox Adaptation in Osteosarcoma Chemoresistance: Antioxidant Dependencies, Ferroptotic Vulnerabilities, and Translational Challenges
Article.Authors: Pant V.; Bartusik-Aebisher D.; Smolak B.; Dynarowicz K.; Aebisher D.
Article.Abstract: Osteosarcoma chemoresistance remains a fundamental barrier to durable disease control. Survival following conventional chemotherapy with agents such as doxorubicin and cisplatin may require osteosarcoma cells to adapt to oxidative and electrophilic stress. This review evaluates how adaptive redox remodeling, primarily coordinated through the NRF2 regulatory hub, can promote stress tolerance while creating potential therapeutic vulnerabilities. Osteosarcoma-specific evidence linking SLC7A11-mediated cystine uptake, glutathione metabolism, and GPX4-regulated lipid peroxide defense to ferroptosis-related vulnerabilities is synthesized. Direct functional evidence from chemotherapy-resistant osteosarcoma models is distinguished from osteosarcoma-specific findings obtained in other experimental contexts and mechanistic extrapolations from other cancer types, highlighting that ferroptotic susceptibility is context-dependent and dynamically regulated rather than an established feature of all resistant tumors. Because disruption of lipid peroxide defenses can trigger secondary compensatory responses, therapeutic strategies cannot rely on indiscriminate reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation alone. Exploiting potential vulnerabilities will require a precision-medicine framework supported by functionally validated predictive biomarkers, physiologically relevant models, and tumor-selective delivery platforms.

Article.Title: Physical Activity and Exercise in Age-Related Eye Diseases: A Structure-Specific Review of Ocular Protection Mechanisms
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Zhao X.; Zhao C.; Gong L.; Zhang F.; Yan Y.
Article.Abstract: Age-related eye diseases (AEDs), including cataract, age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, and diabetic retinopathy, are rising in prevalence with global population aging, imposing significant health and socioeconomic burdens. Current pharmacological and surgical interventions often face limitations in invasiveness, efficacy, and accessibility, underscoring an urgent need for effective, less invasive preventive strategies. Exercise represents a viable, non-invasive and multi-targeted strategy to slow AEDs progression. This review adopts a structure-specific framework to systematically investigate the protective benefits and underlying mechanisms of exercise against AEDs. We summarize human evidence for disease occurrence and progression, and evidence demonstrating how exercise influences four key ocular components directly implicated in AEDs pathogenesis: (1) aqueous humor dynamics and intraocular pressure, where exercise reduces intraocular pressure via plasma osmolarity elevation, lactate/pH changes, sympathetic activation and β-adrenergic signaling; (2) ocular vasculature, where exercise promotes endothelial progenitor cell mobilization, AMPK-dependent vascular repair, and suppression of pathological neovascularization; (3) the crystalline lens, where exercise preserves transparency through antioxidant and metabolic regulation; and (4) the retina, where exercise confers neuroprotection via BDNF/TrkB signaling, anti-apoptotic AKT/Bcl-2 pathways, and Nrf2-mediated antioxidant defense in retinal pigment epithelium. Together, this structure-specific, multi-targeted approach highlights the potential of exercise to mitigate the pathological processes underlying AEDs across distinct ocular tissues. Future research should prioritize rigorous clinical trials, refined exercise prescriptions, and integration with conventional treatments to better define the role of exercise in preserving vision in an aging world.

Article.Abstract: Genomic datasets generated using hg19 and hg38 are frequently integrated by coordinate liftover, but the correctability of associated discrepancies remains uncertain. We evaluated reciprocal liftover using experimentally validated allele pairs derived from homozygote hydatidiform mole DNA, heterozygote blood DNA, and seven physical dilution mixtures. Identical whole-exome sequencing FASTQ datasets were independently analyzed against hg19 and hg38 using DRAGEN v4.3, followed by reciprocal liftover and allele-pair comparison. Discordance occurred in 789/20,038 (3.94%) and 524/19,771 (2.65%) allele pairs for hg38→19 and hg19→38, respectively. Comprehensive reanalysis incorporating intronic variants identified 304 and 156 exon-to-intronic functional shifts, substantially reducing apparent null-null (N-N) shifts. Genotype flipping and functional-region shifts accounted for 722 (91.51%) and 404 (77.10%) of discordant allele pairs in the hg38→19 and hg19→38 comparisons, respectively, and were considered potentially correctable. Residual uncorrectable discrepancies comprised 67 and 120 allele pairs (0.33% and 0.61% of all informative allele pairs, respectively), including 35 and 83 N-N shifts. BAM-level inspection revealed heterogeneous discrepancies potentially involving reference-dependent alignment, local sequence representation, and variant-calling differences. These findings demonstrate that comprehensive variant harmonization can resolve many apparent cross-assembly discrepancies, although some remain unresolved. Reanalysis against a common reference assembly remains preferable when raw sequencing data are available.

Article.Title: Integrated Multi-Omics Analysis Reveals Tissue-Specific m6A Associated Transcriptional Responses to Low-Temperature Stress in Large Yellow Croaker
Article.Authors: Wu T.; Ji Q.; Xu H.; Wu L.; Huang S.; Song W.
Article.Abstract: Low-temperature stress induces tissue-specific responses in fish, but the role of m6A modification and its association with DNA methylation remain poorly understood in large yellow croaker (Larimichthys crocea). This study integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic analyses to characterize responses in the brain and liver. Fish were gradually cooled from 20 °C to 8 °C (1.5 °C/d) and maintained at 8 °C for 24 h, with 20 °C fish serving as controls. Brain and liver samples were subjected to RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS), and N6-methyladenosine RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (MeRIP-seq). DNA methylation–transcriptome and m6A–transcriptome associations were analyzed separately in both tissues, followed by three-omics integration in the liver. Brain differentially expressed genes were mainly associated with neural signaling and signal transduction, whereas liver genes were primarily involved in carbohydrate and energy metabolism. Associations between DNA methylation changes and gene expression differed between tissues. The overlap between differentially m6A-modified genes and differentially expressed genes was greater in the liver than in the brain. Hepatic integration identified 27 candidate genes showing changes across all three omics layers, implicating cell adhesion and metabolic processes and suggesting potential involvement of cadherin–β-catenin-associated signaling. Reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) results generally supported the RNA-seq expression trends of selected genes. These findings reveal tissue-specific molecular responses to low-temperature stress and identify candidate genes for further investigation of potential epigenetic regulation in large yellow croaker. They may also provide insights into the molecular basis underlying cold-tolerance traits and inform the development of strategies to enhance stress resilience in aquaculture under low-temperature conditions.

Article.Title: Alpha Mangostin Induced Hemorrhagic Ascites and Nephrotoxicity Following Multiple Intraperitoneal Injections in Sprague Dawley Rats
Article.Authors: Setyawati L.; Mat Zin A.; Amalia R.; Holik H.; Shamsuddin S.; Mohd Fuad W.; Muchtaridi M.
Article.Abstract: Alpha mangostin (AM) is a natural substance that is thoroughly studied for its pharmacological effects as a potential treatment. Consequently, the safety aspects of AM are important in the development of new pharmaceutical candidates. Despite a comprehensive study of its pharmacological properties, there is limited evidence regarding the safety profile of pure AM administration, particularly by parenteral injection. This study assessed the subchronic intraperitoneal (i.p.) toxicity of AM in Sprague-Dawley rats to determine the No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL). The subchronic investigation was conducted on both male and female rats by providing varying doses of AM—25, 50, and 100 mg/kg, or DMSO (control)—for a duration of 48 days (terminated early). The subchronic investigation unexpectedly demonstrated significant indicators of toxicity. All AM-treated groups exhibited hemorrhagic ascites, a phenomenon that has not been previously seen following repeated administration of AM. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels in male and female rats showed a slight increase that was not statistically significant compared with the control group. The blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels in female rats administered 50 mg/kg were considerably elevated compared to the control group. Histological examination revealed significant damage to the livers and kidneys of all AM-treated rats, regardless of sex. These findings indicate that the daily intraperitoneal injection of AM may induce toxicity in rats, and no NOAEL was identified within the tested dose range. The present finding may serve as a reference for AM’s safety profile. Additional research is required to determine the optimal dosage for recurrent intraperitoneal injection of AM.

Article.Title: Early Gastrointestinal Dysfunction Precedes Colonic Inflammation in a Rat Model of Lipopolysaccharide-Induced Sepsis
Article.Authors: Silván-Ros B.; López-Gómez L.; López-Tofiño Y.; Vera G.; Uranga J.; Castro M.; Valero M.; Martín-Fontelles M.; Abalo R.
Article.Abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition characterized by a dysregulated host response to infection, with gastrointestinal dysfunction contributing to morbidity and mortality, but its initial manifestations remain poorly defined. This study aimed to characterize the very early gastrointestinal effects of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced sepsis in rats, focusing on nausea-like behavior, visceral nociception, and colonic motility. Male Wistar rats received an intraperitoneal injection of LPS (5 mg/kg) or saline. Bedding intake, food and water consumption, and body temperature were recorded within 2 h post-injection (T2). Afterwards, visceral sensitivity was assessed using tonic colorectal distension. Four hours after treatment (T4), macroscopic gastrointestinal evaluation, enteropooling measurement, and assessment of whole-colon motor activity in an organ bath were performed. Different inflammatory markers were analyzed at T4 in both plasma and distal colon. LPS-treated rats exhibited increased bedding intake and drinking events, reduced body temperature, and unchanged visceral sensitivity during tonic stimulation, whereas phasic stimulation increased it. LPS also increased gastric and caecal weights and small intestinal fluid accumulation and induced more intense and organized colonic peristaltic activity. These functional changes occurred alongside elevated circulating TNF and IL-1β. In contrast, distal colonic TNF, IL-1β, and COX-2 expression, distal colonic histological damage, COX-2 immunoreactivity, and macrophage and mast cell abundance remained unchanged. Together, these findings identify acute systemic cytokine release as a rapid trigger of gastrointestinal dysfunction preceding detectable colonic inflammatory responses, thereby providing new insights into the early gastrointestinal manifestations of sepsis.

Article.Title: Co-Occurrence of an Activating AVPR2 Variant and a Pathogenic ACVRL1 Variant in an Infant with Nephrogenic Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuresis
Article.Authors: Vasiliu I.; Spoială E.; Butnariu L.; Trandafir L.
Article.Abstract: Nephrogenic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (NSIAD) is a rare disorder of water homeostasis caused by constitutive activation of the renal vasopressin V2 receptor and may closely mimic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIAD). Recognition in infancy is challenging because severe hyponatremia may remain clinically silent and conventional biochemical findings may overlap with other disorders of water balance. We report the clinical, biochemical, and molecular characterization of a 7-month-old male infant with severe hypotonic hyponatremia incidentally identified during evaluation for bronchiolitis, which persisted after resolution of the acute respiratory illness. Serum sodium was 112 mmol/L and serum osmolality was 231 mOsm/kg (calculated), with preserved renal and hepatic function. Adrenal insufficiency was excluded by ACTH stimulation testing, while a low copeptin concentration (2 pmol/L) supported appropriately suppressed vasopressin secretion. Whole-exome sequencing identified the pathogenic activating hemizygous AVPR2 c.409C>T, p.(Arg137Cys) variant, confirming NSIAD, together with a pathogenic heterozygous ACVRL1 c.270C>A, p.(Cys90*) variant associated with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. The co-occurrence of these two pathogenic variants is clinically relevant for surveillance and genetic counselling but is not proposed as a mechanistic explanation of the water-balance disorder. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first reported case of genetically confirmed NSIAD in Romania and the first documented coexistence of these two pathogenic variants in a single patient. Although mechanistically unrelated, their coexistence highlights the clinical relevance of comprehensive genetic testing in identifying additional actionable diagnoses. Fluid restriction and oral urea were followed by an improvement in serum sodium to 130 mmol/L. This case illustrates the diagnostic value of integrating copeptin assessment with genomic testing in severe unexplained hypotonic hyponatremia in infancy, and highlights the need for independent surveillance of concomitant pathogenic findings identified by broad genomic testing.

Article.Title: Exploring Potential Links Among Gut Microbiota, Butyrate, and JUN in Lung Adenocarcinoma: A Bioinformatics-Based Integrative Multi-Omics Analysis
Article.Authors: Qiu B.; Cai Y.; Cai Y.; Li H.; Zhang J.; Huang X.; Wang Z.; Wang H.; Chen Z.
Article.Abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is highly heterogeneous, and the mechanisms linking gut microbiota-derived metabolites to tumor-associated transcriptional regulation remain unclear. We integrated two paired LUAD transcriptomic datasets, GSE40419 and GSE32863, to perform differential expression, functional enrichment, protein–protein interaction, and transcription factor activity analyses. Candidate microbial metabolites and targets were obtained from gutMGene, Similarity Ensemble Approach, and SwissTargetPrediction, while Mendelian randomization (MR) was used to evaluate associations between genetically predicted gut microbial abundance and LUAD risk. Molecular docking and a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation were conducted to assess interactions between candidate metabolites and Jun Proto-Oncogene (JUN)-containing DNA-bound complexes. We identified 1271 and 2519 differentially expressed genes in GSE40419 and GSE32863, respectively, including 912 overlapping genes. These genes were enriched mainly in cell cycle, immune and inflammatory, angiogenic, and tumor microenvironment-related pathways. Fifteen robust transcription factors were identified, with consistent suppression of the JUN-regulated transcriptional program. MR analysis revealed 10 microbial taxa associated with LUAD after false discovery rate correction. A genetically predicted higher abundance of Roseburia inulinivorans was associated with a lower LUAD risk (OR = 0.843, 95% CI: 0.756–0.940). Database integration linked R. inulinivorans to butyrate and JUN. Butyrate showed the most favorable docking score with the c-Jun–DNA complex (−4.5 kcal/mol), and molecular dynamics simulation indicated a relatively stable interaction. Collectively, these findings support a putative R. inulinivorans–butyrate–JUN regulatory axis that links gut microbial metabolism to transcriptional dysregulation in LUAD.
