Article.Title: Beyond the Barrier: Critical Role of IgA Subclasses in Health and Disease
Article.Authors: Basile V.; Pignalosa S.; D’Ambrosio F.; Tartaglione S.; Tagliaferro M.; Natali P.; Marino M.; Basile U.
Article.Abstract: Human immunoglobulin A (IgA) exists as two subclasses, IgA1 and IgA2, which differ mainly in the hinge region: IgA1 has an extended, O-glycosylated hinge that confers conformational flexibility but is cleaved by IgA1-specific bacterial proteases, whereas the short hinge of IgA2 resists proteolysis. The subclasses also differ in their distribution between serum and mucosal secretions, in their preference for protein or polysaccharide antigens, and in the glycosylation of the Fc region, which modulates binding to the Fcα receptor (FcαRI/CD89) and, consequently, the balance between anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory effects. Drawing on a narrative review of the literature indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, we summarize the structural and functional features of IgA1 and IgA2 and discuss how subclass biology relates to selective IgA deficiency, IgA nephropathy, IgA vasculitis, celiac disease, linear IgA bullous dermatosis, dermatitis herpetiformis, IgA monoclonal gammopathies, and bacterial evasion of mucosal immunity. We also consider recent advances in genetics, biomarkers, and targeted therapies, including agents directed at the APRIL/BAFF pathway and at complement, and outline how an approach that takes subclasses and glycoforms into account may improve diagnosis and treatment.

Article.Title: Polysaccharide-Modified Gold Nanoparticles: Synthesis, Catalytic and Biological Properties
Article.Authors: Alibaeva E.; Gil’fanova G.; Gubaidullin R.; Mescheryakova E.; Khalilov L.; Tsvetkova A.; Sergeev S.; Penkov N.; Sharafutdinova L.; Parfenova L.
Article.Abstract: Gold nanoparticles (AuNP) stabilized by sulfur-modified polysaccharides are of interest as multifunctional materials combining colloidal and catalytic properties, yet the influence of the polysaccharide backbone structure on nanoparticle composition and downstream bioactivity remains insufficiently understood. This study reports the synthesis of AuNP using a novel SH derivative of heparin (Hep-SH), and its comparison with previously described thiolated alginate and hyaluronic acid analogs. Reaction of Hep-SH with HAuCl4 afforded stable Hep-AuNP, confirmed by a surface plasmon resonance band at 566 nm, a spherical bimodal particle morphology (37 ± 12 and 113 ± 12 nm fractions) with a polysaccharide shell of 8–25 nm observed via SEM/BF-STEM, and colloidal stability over 14 days observed via PCCS. XPS revealed coexisting Au0/Au1+ species, and NMR spectroscopy indicated oxidation of the thiol group to a sulfonate moiety; a high negative ζ-potential (−44.7 ± 3.8 mV) is consistent with electrostatic stabilization by the polyanionic heparin shell. All three polysaccharide-modified AuNP (PS-AuNP) catalyzed the model A3-coupling reaction in a 98–99% yield at 100 °C after 8 h, whereas under milder conditions (60 °C, 4 h) the yields ranged from 25 ± 3% to 38 ± 4%, with HA-AuNP giving a significantly higher yield than Hep-AuNP and AA-AuNP. Biological evaluation on HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells showed that PS-AuNP caused concentration-dependent decreases in viability, which were least pronounced for HA-AuNP. These results show that the properties of the resulting AuNP depend on the nature of the sulfur-modified polysaccharide used in their synthesis. The proposed synthetic approach and the obtained materials may serve as a basis for the development of new catalysts and materials for biomedical applications.

Article.Title: ConGEE: A Statistically Based Approach to the Concordant Gene Expression Evaluation Inside Genome Domains
Article.Authors: Kravatsky Y.; Chechetkin V.; Stepovoi K.; Tchurikov N.; Diatlova A.; Klushevskaya E.; Kravatskaya G.
Article.Abstract: Unraveling the interrelation between the domain organization of eukaryotic genomes and global transcriptional output remains a challenging problem in genomics and is actively under study. Assessing whether genes within specific domain structures are transcriptionally co-expressed necessitates the development of robust analytical tools that retain the inherent clustering of genomic features. Therefore, we developed the ConGEE (Concordance of Gene Expression Evaluation) method, which preserves local expression patterns by shifting expression values along the ordered gene list while randomizing their domain association. The derived statistical criteria quantify the homogeneity and mean expression level for the given genome domain structure. Extensive simulations confirmed that the proposed method reliably reveals true domain-specific expression concordance: it accurately estimates expression concordance and intra-domain dispersion using calibration appropriate to the particular domain architecture. Applying the developed method to transcriptomic datasets revealed significant changes in transcriptional organization, including a distinct shift toward domain-concordant gene expression in MDA-MB-231 cells transferred to a 3D collagen matrix (which induced a vasculogenic mimicry phenotype), and differential TAD-associated transcriptional patterns in HEK293T cells under different treatment conditions. In conclusion, the developed method provides a reliable approach for assessing domain expression concordance relative to a specified domain annotation, and the relevant tools are freely available at Github.

Article.Title: Lipid Metabolic Rewiring in Cancer Drug Resistance: Pathways, Networks, and Therapeutic Strategies
Article.Authors: Chang S.; Raggi C.; Exil V.
Article.Abstract: Drug resistance limits cancer therapy, and metabolic reprogramming helps tumor cells adapt to therapeutic stress. This review examines how altered lipid uptake, synthesis, storage, and oxidation support survival by changing signaling, membrane composition, energy production, redox balance, and tumor-microenvironment interactions. The SCAP/SREBP axis is a key transcriptional regulator; oncogenic and nutrient signaling (EGFR, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, mutant p53) controls SREBP abundance and activation, and sustained SREBP activity during treatment distinguishes resistant from sensitive cells in several models, including gefitinib-resistant lung cancer and sorafenib/lenvatinib-resistant hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). MicroRNAs regulate these pathways post-transcriptionally, including ferroptosis-related targets (ACSL4, SLC7A11, GPX4). Inhibitors of lipogenesis, SCAP/SREBP, cholesterol metabolism, fatty-acid oxidation, lipid uptake and storage, phospholipid and sphingolipid signaling, and ferroptosis have improved drug sensitivity in preclinical models. However, many studies show only an association with resistance rather than that modulating a pathway restores sensitivity; findings vary between tumor types; and compensatory rewiring, toxicity, and limited tumor selectivity constrain single-target approaches, while miRNA-based therapeutics remain early-stage. Rational combinations guided by lipidomic and transcriptomic profiling are a priority.

Article.Title: A Cancer-Specific Anti-Podocalyxin Monoclonal Antibody-Drug Conjugate Exerted Antitumor Activity in a Pancreatic Cancer Xenograft Model
Article.Authors: Nakamura T.; Ohishi T.; Kaneko M.; Suzuki H.; Kato Y.
Article.Abstract: Podocalyxin (PODXL) is a potential diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target in various tumors. Development of anti-PODXL mAbs has been limited by concerns about potential reactivity with normal tissues. Furthermore, humPcMab-60 was internalized into MIA PaCa-2 and inhibited cell proliferation in vitro. In the MIA PaCa-2 xenograft model, humPcMab-60-DXd showed superior antitumor efficacy compared with humPcMab-60. Moreover, humPcMab-60-DXd exhibited dose-dependent antitumor activity without reducing mice body weight. Histological analyses revealed the collapse of the intratumoral structure and a reduction in PODXL expression in the humPcMab-60-DXd-treated xenograft. These results provide the first observation of antitumor efficacy for an anti-PODXL CasMab–drug conjugate, which could facilitate the clinical development of CasMabs for tumor therapy.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification and Gonadal Expression Profiling of the Sox Gene Family During Gonadal Differentiation in Blotched Snakehead (Channa maculata)
Article.Authors: Deng Y.; Luo Q.; Liu L.; Zou Y.; Yang T.; Huang Z.; Huang Z.; Zhao J.; Liu H.; Fei S.; Sun Y.; Ou M.
Article.Abstract: Blotched snakehead (Channa maculata) is an economically important freshwater aquaculture species with sexually dimorphic growth, necessitating a thorough understanding of gonadal development for reproductive biology and breeding. Sox transcription factors, characterized by a conserved high-mobility group box (HMG-box) domain, are key regulators of gonadal differentiation and gametogenesis, yet their genomic repertoire and expression dynamics in C. maculata remain unexplored. In this study, a genome-wide identification of the Sox gene family was conducted, encompassing phylogenetic analysis, chromosomal mapping, duplication assessment, and structural annotation. Gonadal transcriptomes from 60 to 180 days post-fertilization (dpf) were interrogated for sex- or stage-specific expression, with candidate genes validated by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) and in situ hybridization (ISH). As a result, a total of 26 Sox genes were identified in C. maculata and phylogenetically distributed across seven subfamilies (B1, B2, C, D, E, F, and K), with uneven localization on 17 chromosomes. Multiple retained paralogous pairs suggest a potential origin from the teleost-specific whole-genome duplication (TSGD) event. Expression profiling revealed discrete patterns: Sox3 and Sox11b showed ovarian enrichment and potential roles in oogenesis, Sox9a and Sox9b were testis-enriched but differentially localized to spermatocytes and Sertoli cells, respectively, and Sox8b and Sox11a displayed dynamic expression, with Sox11a shifting from early male-biased to later female-biased expression. These findings link specific Sox genes to gonadal differentiation and gametogenesis, illustrating stage- and cell-type-specific divergence among paralogs. The candidate genes provide a valuable resource for future functional studies of gonadal development in C. maculata, although their causative roles await genetic and hormonal validation.

Article.Title: NDUFV2P1, a Schizophrenia-Associated Pseudogene, Regulates Mitochondrial and Neuronal Function: Implications for Schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Lapiro Y.; Karry R.; Binah O.; Ben-Shachar D.
Article.Abstract: Schizophrenia (SZ) is a severe mental disorder affecting emotion, cognitive and social functioning. Mitochondria, which are dysfunctional in the disease, are essential for neuronal function, synaptic plasticity and behavior, all impaired in SZ. A major driver of mitochondrial dysfunction in SZ is Complex I, particularly its NDUFV2 core subunit. We showed that NDUFV2 pseudogene (NDUFV2P1; PG) is upregulated in brain and peripheral cells of SZ patients and inversely correlates with NDUFV2 expression in brain specimens and with mitochondrial respiration in Epstein–Barr-virus-transformed lymphocyte cell lines (LCLs). Recently, we reported that PG competes with NDUFV2 mRNA for binding to RNA-binding proteins. We hypothesized that PG is a biologically functional pseudogene that regulates NDUFV2 expression, thereby affecting mitochondrial function and neuronal activity. Accordingly, we modulated PG abundance in LCLs and rat primary cortical neurons. PG overexpression in healthy-derived LCLs impaired mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), network dynamics, and oxygen consumption, while PG downregulation in SZ-derived LCLs normalized these parameters. In rat cortical neurons, PG overexpression induced comparable mitochondrial disruptions alongside impaired synapse formation and reduced spontaneous neuronal firing. This study provides evidence for a cellular pathway through which PG interference with NDUFV2 leads to SZ-related mitochondrial and neuronal deficits and suggests therapeutic potential for PG downregulation in diseases with bioenergetic impairments such as SZ.

Article.Authors: Patricio-Liébana M.; Ramos N.; Gabaldón A.; Castañeda Z.; Bermejo S.; León-Román J.; Toapanta N.; Azancot M.; Núñez S.; López M.; Agraz I.; Bestard O.; Soler M.

Among histologic variables, global glomerulosclerosis showed the best discrimination (AUC 0.725; cutoff ≥ 8%), whereas other TMA-associated lesions had limited prognostic value. In multivariable analysis, both peak sCr (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.16–2.62; p = 0.008) and global glomerulosclerosis ≥ 8% (OR 8.76, 95% CI 1.23–62.40; p = 0.030) were independently associated with 12-month RRT dependence. Adding global glomerulosclerosis ≥ 8% significantly improved model fit compared with peak sCr alone (likelihood-ratio test, p = 0.016), increasing the apparent AUC from 0.815 to 0.868.

Article.Title: Long Non-Coding RNAs in Metastatic Dormancy and Drug-Tolerant Persistence: Regulators of Residual-Cell Plasticity
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Huang Y.; Zhu Z.; Deng L.; Shi Y.; Yang X.
Article.Abstract: Cancer can recur when cells that survive dissemination or treatment resume growth. A smaller metastatic burden can reflect slower proliferation, greater immune clearance or fewer viable residual cells. We review long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) perturbation studies that separate these effects. In breast cancer models, NR2F1-AS1 increases NR2F1 translation. This favors dissemination but limits proliferation in the lung. BORG promotes outgrowth from latency through tripartite motif-containing protein 28 (TRIM28), while MALAT1 helps emerging metastases survive immune attack. These experiments illustrate why a change in lesion burden can point to different interventions. The same question arises in drug-tolerant persistence (DTP). Drug-response studies identify candidate RNAs, but few test whether the RNA is needed once reversibly tolerant cells have formed. For relapse prevention, experiments need to count viable residual cells separately from growing lesions and establish when the RNA interaction matters.

Article.Title: Machine Learning-Guided Design of Peptide-Targeted CRISPR Vectors for Tissue-Specific Non-Coding RNA Knockdown
Article.Authors: Abdullah S.; Smail S.; Salihi A.
Article.Abstract: CRISPR-based genome/epigenome editing and RNA-targeted therapeutics offer unprecedented precision for correcting disease-causing mutations, yet clinical translation remains constrained by two unresolved bottlenecks: suboptimal guide RNA (gRNA) design limiting editing efficiency and specificity, and the absence of safe, tissue-selective delivery platforms. While machine learning (ML)-driven gRNA design and peptide-mediated delivery have each advanced substantially in isolation, to our knowledge, no existing framework jointly optimizes predictive guide-design models and delivery-vector design within a single pipeline a disconnect that likely underlies persistent efficacy–safety trade-offs in clinical translation. This review addresses that gap by critically synthesizing ML-driven guide design and peptide-engineered delivery within a single mechanistic and computational framework. We first outline the structural basis of peptide-derived vectors, emphasizing how charge, hydrophobicity, secondary structure, and receptor-targeting functionalization govern organ- and cell-type specificity. We then critically appraise ML methods for predicting on-target activity, off-target propensity, and specificity across CRISPR platforms, alongside computational approaches for non-coding RNA target identification, focusing on training-data limitations, feature representation, and cross-platform generalizability that constrain predictive reliability. We synthesize design principles for tissue-specific delivery, including nanocarrier integration, and highlight preclinical cases where ML-guided peptide engineering enabled targeted delivery of mRNA, antisense oligonucleotides, and CRISPR ribonucleoproteins. Finally, we assess persistent barriers data sparsity, limited model transferability, off-target genotoxicity, immunogenicity, and delivery constraints and propose emerging directions: multi-omics integration, AI-enabled de novo peptide design, and translational frameworks. This review establishes a convergent paradigm in which joint ML-guided optimization of guide and delivery design enhances the specificity, efficiency, and safety of next-generation precision genetic medicines.

Article.Title: Cellular Localization of IPF-Associated Candidate Genes and Effects of Licochalcone B on Human Pulmonary Microvascular Endothelial Cells
Article.Authors: Cai L.; Wang L.; Liu W.; Zhou X.; Li M.
Article.Abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) involves epithelial injury, vascular alterations and extracellular matrix deposition. We integrated human lung transcriptomics with the experimental evaluation of licochalcone B (LCB), a constituent of Glycyrrhiza uralensis. Seventy-four candidates from the HERB database of traditional Chinese medicine were assessed in one discovery and two validation cohorts, with robust multiarray average preprocessing of the discovery cohort, followed by single-cell and spatial localization. LCB was tested in human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells treated with transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGF-β1) using Western blotting and Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assays. Eight of 59 measurable candidates were differentially expressed in the discovery cohort and remained significant after demographic adjustment; of these, VCAM1, SLC6A4, BCHE and ESM1 showed concordant changes in both validation cohorts. Candidate-set enrichment was nonsignificant against a matched background (empirical p = 0.48). VCAM1 and BCHE remained significantly upregulated across all three cohorts after adjustment for deconvolution-estimated endothelial proportions. Two single-cell atlases showed concordant compartment-level localization, and spatial analyses supported endothelial enrichment. LCB reduced TGF-β1-induced VCAM1, alpha-smooth muscle actin and collagen type I alpha 1 chain expression, and increased vascular endothelial cadherin. With TGF-β1 and 0.7 μM LCB, CCK-8 signal averaged 92.4% of control with medium blank correction and 89.9% with LCB-matched blank correction. These findings provide preliminary evidence that LCB alters the abundance of proteins associated with endothelial activation and endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition in TGF-β1-treated pulmonary endothelial cells.

Article.Title: The Phytochemical Ensemble: A Falsifiable Framework for Complex Botanicals
Article.Authors: Qu Y.; Liu H.; Zhao X.; Ren R.; Qu W.; Cao X.; Ma G.
Article.Abstract: Whole-plant extracts are often treated as phytochemical ensembles whose effects may exceed those of single constituents, yet the field lacks a framework specifying what evidence would confirm or refute ensemble action. Portulaca oleracea L. illustrates this gap: its chemistry is well cataloged, but no study has compared whole extract with purified constituents at matched target-tissue exposure, so whether the whole outperforms its parts remains untested. We define the phytochemical ensemble by three criteria that distinguish it from additive, pairwise-synergistic, trace-compound, and batch-variation explanations, and we propose convergence, pharmacokinetic complementarity, and emergence as its three pillars. Three propositions follow, each with explicit falsification criteria and a critical experiment. Proposition 1 (stoichiometric balance and multi-node convergence) is foundational and is the only framework-refuting proposition: the framework is falsified if a perturbed ratio nonetheless matches the native activity profile, if single-node ablation abolishes efficacy, or if a single constituent reproduces the extract’s effect at matched exposure. Proposition 2 is mechanistic and is subdivided into Proposition 2a (pharmacokinetic complementarity) and Proposition 2b (microbiome mediation); failure of either weakens, but does not falsify, the framework. Proposition 3 (whole-extract superiority via physiological integration) is indication-specific. We propose an Ensemble Fidelity Score (EFS), a prototype metric that jointly requires chemical and functional fidelity, together with a clinical design comparing whole extract with a purified constituent at matched exposure. The framework is designed to be falsifiable; either outcome advances the field.

Article.Title: A Stability-Weighted Combined Map for Cell Painting Across Regular and Prolonged Incubation
Article.Authors: Lavrinenko V.; Donskaya I.; Popov V.; Litau E.; Petrova V.; Valetdinova K.; Trofimov M.; Shurova A.; Danilenko D.; Lioznov D.; Tyazhelnikov S.
Article.Abstract: Cell Painting screens usually profile compounds at a single fixed endpoint. Many drug responses, however, develop over days, and compounds whose phenotypes are weak or still forming at the chosen endpoint give unstable profiles that move between clusters in repeated experiments and blur the phenotypic map. We profiled 53 small molecules in HCT116 cells after 48 h and 8 days of exposure, each in two independent iterations, and represented every compound by the window in which its replicate profiles were more stable. The resulting stability-weighted Combined map separated phenotypic groups more clearly than either single window (silhouette score of the modal partition 0.360 versus 0.227 and 0.292). This gain exceeded random window assignment (p = 0.002), also under analysis parameters chosen without the Combined dataset (p = 0.001). The number of compounds with inconsistent cluster assignment between iterations decreased (6 versus 16 and 13 of 53), although less consistently across analysis settings. The approach distinguishes compounds whose phenotypes are captured reproducibly at 48 h, compounds captured more reproducibly at 8 days, and a convergent group for which both windows give similar profiles. It offers a practical way to add a prolonged exposure window to phenotypic screens and to prioritize compounds for follow-up.

Article.Title: Genome Evolution in Diploid Aegilops Species Assessed Using FISH with pTa-713, pTa-k566 and Oligo-45 Satellite DNA Families
Article.Authors: Badaeva E.; Ulyanov D.; Razumova O.; Kotseruba V.; Yurkina A.; Maida Jazmin G.; Kuznetsova V.; Belousova M.; Chikida N.; Tereshchenko N.; Amosova A.; Surzhikov S.; Divashuk M.
Article.Abstract: Repetitive DNAs are key drivers of genome evolution, but their dynamics accompanying the divergence of Aegilops genomes remain incompletely understood. Tandem repeats often serve as FISH markers in phylogenetic studies, however, few families have been used for evaluating relationships among Aegilops species. In this study, we employed three recently discovered satellite repeats, pTa-713, pTa-k566 and oligo-45, to analyze diploid Aegilops taxa to gain a deeper insight into the chromosomal mechanisms of genome evolution. We analyzed 121 accessions representing 11 diploid Aegilops species using these three probes and showed that they are effective for chromosome and genome identification in Aegilops. For each species, we established a generalized karyotype and assessed intra- and interspecific polymorphisms. Diploid genomes varied in repeat content and distribution; Ae. speltoides had the highest pTa-713 content, whereas D-, M- and N-genomes were highly abundant in oligo-45. The specific labelling patterns allowed us to subdivide Aegilops into six groups, mostly consistent with the taxonomic classification of the genus. FISH results showed that Ae. tauschii is karyotypically distinct from species of the Sitopsis group, which contradicts the affinity established via the analysis of low-copy DNA sequences. This discrepancy could be due to different evolutionary pathways between coding- and non-coding DNA fractions, introgressive hybridization and incomplete lineage sorting.

Article.Title: Prot2motif: Prediction of Transcription Factor DNA-Binding Motifs from Amino Acid Sequences Using a Generative LSTM Model with Attention
Article.Authors: Sheludyakov N.; Ivanisenko V.; Demenkov P.
Article.Abstract: The binding of transcription factors (TFs) to specific DNA sites plays a key role in regulating gene expression. Although experimental methods characterize binding motifs, their computational prediction directly from protein amino acid sequences remains an underexplored challenge. We developed prot2motif, a generative LSTM encoder–decoder model with additive attention that predicts a position probability matrix of the TF binding motif directly from the amino acid sequence and also generates an explicit “no motif” signal for non-TF proteins. The model was trained and evaluated on 3110 protein–motif pairs (1518 HOCOMOCO v13 TFs and 1592 length-matched non-TF proteins) partitioned using MMseqs2 clustering. Prot2motif successfully reconstructs binding motifs, substantially outperforming uniform baselines (SWscore 0.832 versus 0.625 on the TF subset); its generated output also enables reliable discrimination between TFs and non-TF proteins (F1 = 0.924), while shuffling amino acid residues within protein sequences reduced the classification F1-score to 0.647. Negative-control experiments confirmed that the model relies on the linear order of amino acid residues rather than composition alone, and that the learned motif signal strictly depends on correct protein–motif associations. Ablation analysis showed that the attention mechanism makes an important contribution to prediction quality, while non-autoregressive decoding is a viable alternative. Thus, in its current form, prot2motif provides reliable TF detection and motif generation for TFs.

Article.Title: RegenaCare: The Smart Bandage from Lab to Skin and Its Applications
Article.Authors: Tham J.; Au J.; Wong P.; Qureshi M.; Mahmoud M.; Ashok Kumar S.
Article.Abstract: Chronic wounds, including diabetic foot ulcers and trauma injuries, require frequent monitoring to detect early infection, but conventional dressings provide only passive protection. The purpose of this paper is to propose a solution for these patients by presenting RegenaCare, a low-cost, proof-of-concept NFC-powered smart bandage with a web-hosted interface displaying preliminary colourimetric and physiological-sensing data. The hydrogel is a polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)-gelatin membrane incorporating aloe vera and roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa) extract to explore roselle’s potential for pH-responsive colour change in infection monitoring, with an electronic subsystem comprising an STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller, MAX30100 heart-rate sensor, and ST25DV16K NFC module. Membranes were freeze- or oven-dried and evaluated through swelling, tensile and Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy tests. Freeze-dried samples had higher swelling ratios. Oven-dried aloe vera-gelatin membranes achieved the highest tensile strength (6.34 MPa), exceeding the 0.5–1.5 MPa target, and FTIR confirmed gelatin-associated amide bands with differences between roselle-containing and control formulations. UV-Vis absorbance likely exceeded the spectrophotometer’s upper limit, and the pH colourimetric response was non-monotonic. These results suggest the feasibility of a low-cost (approximately RM51.50 per unit), NFC-enabled smart bandage for exploratory wound monitoring, although its limitations, alongside power delivery and communication performance, require further development before real-world deployment.

Article.Title: CD40 Agonists in Pancreatic Cancer: From Immune Priming to Clinical Translation
Article.Authors: Kang M.; Go S.; Lee W.
Article.Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a highly desmoplastic and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) that limits immune-cell infiltration, impairs antigen presentation, and promotes tumor-supportive myeloid responses. CD40 agonism offers a distinct immunotherapeutic strategy by activating macrophages and antigen-presenting cells (APCs), enhancing antigen presentation, and promoting innate and adaptive antitumor immunity. Preclinical studies have demonstrated macrophage-dependent tumor regression and stromal remodeling, while combination with chemotherapy can enhance antigen release and subsequent immune priming. Clinical studies of CD40 agonists, including sotigalimab, mitazalimab, and selicrelumab, have demonstrated immune and TME remodeling, but consistent survival benefit has not been established in unselected patients. Differences in treatment context, chemotherapy backbone, treatment sequence, and antibody architecture may contribute to variable clinical outcomes. Emerging evidence indicates that limited therapeutic activity may reflect multiple factors, including APC deficiency, persistent immunosuppression, inadequate effector responses, stromal and spatial immune exclusion, and pharmacologic limitations related to Fcγ receptor engagement and systemic toxicity. Future development should therefore emphasize biomarker-guided patient selection, rational treatment sequencing, spatially controlled CD40 activation, and mechanistically matched combination strategies. Integration of immune, molecular, and pharmacodynamic biomarkers, together with next-generation CD40 agonists, may help translate CD40-mediated immune remodeling into more durable clinical benefit in PDAC.

Article.Title: Mechanisms of PARP Inhibitor Resistance and Potential Therapeutic Strategies in Breast Cancer
Article.Authors: Zhou C.; Qian X.; Liu J.; Zhu Z.
Article.Abstract: Breast cancer constitutes one of the most commonly diagnosed malignancies among the female population globally, and its development and progression are intimately connected with functional anomalies in the DNA damage response (DDR) pathway. A synthetic lethality basis for the clinical use of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) is provided by homologous recombination deficiency (HRD). Several PARPi, such as olaparib and talazoparib, are approved as monotherapies for specific populations of patients with germline BRCA-mutated, HER2-negative breast cancer. They exert considerable efficacy by blocking PARP catalytic activity, interfering with liquid–liquid phase separation, and causing PARP-DNA entrapment. Nevertheless, sustained therapeutic benefits from PARPi are markedly diminished once acquired resistance develops. The underlying resistance mechanisms, which include BRCA1/2 reversion mutations, upregulation of the homologous recombination (HR) pathway, replication fork stabilization, clearance of trapped PARP1, and increased drug efflux, are intricate and varied. In recent years, combination therapy strategies have received considerable attention, as they can overcome treatment resistance and increase the number of patients benefiting from treatment. Preclinical and early-phase clinical studies have revealed synergistic interactions of PARPi with DNA-damaging agents, immune checkpoint inhibitors, cell cycle checkpoint inhibitors, and radiotherapy. Meanwhile, the discovery of prospective targets such as SCRN2, FGFR, and USP37 opens fresh options for reversing resistance. In order to optimize clinical treatment regimens and improve patient prognosis, this study will methodically explain the mechanism of action, resistance routes, and intervention techniques of PARPi in breast cancer.

Article.Title: Evaluation of Blood–Brain Barrier-Related Tight Junction Proteins in Children Diagnosed with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
Article.Authors: Şenel M.; Usta M.; Avcı B.; Taflan F.
Article.Abstract: The potential role of blood–brain barrier (BBB)-associated tight junction proteins in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) has not yet been fully elucidated. This cross-sectional case–control study aimed to evaluate serum claudin-5, claudin-11, claudin-12, and claudin-25 levels in children with ADHD, investigate their associations with symptom severity, and assess their diagnostic performance. The study included 40 children diagnosed with ADHD according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria and 40 age-matched healthy controls. Diagnostic assessment was performed using the Turkish adaptation of the Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children—Present and Lifetime Version for DSM-5 (K-SADS-PL-DSM-5), and ADHD symptom severity was evaluated using the teacher form of the Turgay DSM-IV-Based Child and Adolescent Behavior Disorders Screening and Rating Scale. Serum claudin levels were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Serum claudin-12 and claudin-25 levels were higher in the ADHD group than in controls (both p < 0.001), whereas claudin-5 and claudin-11 levels did not differ significantly between groups. Within the ADHD group, serum claudin levels were not significantly correlated with teacher-reported symptom severity, except for a weak negative correlation between claudin-25 and hyperactivity/impulsivity (rs = −0.330, p = 0.037) that did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons. After adjustment for age, sex, and body mass index (BMI), higher claudin-12 (adjusted odds ratio [OR] = 1.006, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.003–1.010; p < 0.001) and claudin-25 levels (adjusted OR = 1.002, 95% CI: 1.001–1.004; p = 0.010) remained associated with ADHD status. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.817 for claudin-12 and 0.782 for claudin-25. In this limited study, serum claudin-12 and claudin-25 concentrations were higher in children with ADHD than in healthy controls. However, these findings do not establish blood–brain barrier dysfunction or the clinical diagnostic utility of these proteins. Their tissue origin, biological significance, and diagnostic performance require further investigation and independent validation.

Article.Title: Coenzyme Q10 Modulates Stress Responses to Simulated Galactic Cosmic Radiation in Human Retinal Organoids
Article.Authors: Bodi N.; Shahul Hameed S.; Rout G.; Stanbouly S.; Mao X.; Sharma T.
Article.Abstract: Long-duration space travel is anticipated to be associated with vision changes. The retina is responsible for relaying visual cues to the brain. Retinal neurons are especially vulnerable to changes in the space environment due to their susceptibility to increases in oxidative stress and inflammation. There are knowledge gaps on the changes that occur when human retinal neurons are exposed to space stressors, specifically galactic cosmic radiation (GCR). GCR is highly relevant to long-duration missions. To ameliorate the effects of GCR, we utilized Coenzyme Q10, which has been demonstrated to be useful in neurodegeneration. We developed retinal organoids and exposed them to 0.5 Gy of simulated GCR at Brookhaven National Laboratory. At 48 h and eight days post irradiation, RNA, protein, and conditioned media were collected to investigate changes to the retinal organoids. Through this exploratory study, we identified differential expression of a retinal ganglion cell marker and inflammatory signaling in the Coenzyme Q10-treated organoids after GCR. Further, we found single nucleotide polymorphism differences between our donors.

Article.Title: Individual and Combined Gastroprotective Effects of Ficus carica Latex and Lithium Tetraborate Against Indomethacin-Induced Gastric Ulceration in Rats
Article.Authors: Öztürk E.; Koc K.; Simsek Ozek N.; Aysin F.
Article.Abstract: This study evaluated and compared the gastroprotective effects of Ficus carica (fig) latex and lithium tetraborate (LTB), administered individually or in combination, against indomethacin-induced gastric ulceration in rats across six experimental groups. The groups were control; ulcer (indomethacin (Indo), 30 mg/kg); healthy control receiving fig latex (750 mg/kg) + LTB (40 mg/kg); fig latex (750 mg/kg) + Indo; LTB (40 mg/kg) + Indo; and combination + Indo. The phytochemical composition of fig latex was characterised by Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. Caspase-3 expression was assessed by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). Inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), interleukin-6 (IL-6), superoxide dismutase (SOD), reduced glutathione (GSH), malondialdehyde (MDA), acid phosphatase (AP), prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), and trefoil factor 3 (TFF-3) were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA). Indomethacin significantly decreased gastric SOD and GSH levels, increased AP, iNOS, and IL-6 levels, suppressed PGE2 and TFF-3, and upregulated caspase-3 expression. All treatment regimens significantly increased SOD levels and reduced AP activity and caspase-3 expression. iNOS levels were reduced by all treatments, with the greatest reduction observed following combined administration. IL-6 was significantly reduced by LTB and the combination, whereas fig latex alone showed no statistically significant effect. Fig latex and the combination restored TFF-3 and PGE2 levels, while LTB alone further suppressed PGE2 relative to the Indo group. Fig latex and LTB confer gastroprotection against indomethacin-induced gastric ulceration through complementary antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, lysosomal-membrane-stabilising, cytoprotective and anti-apoptotic mechanisms, supporting the prophylactic potential of their combined administration.

Article.Title: Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio, Platelet-to-Lymphocyte Ratio, and C-Reactive Protein as Risk Markers in Thyroid Autoimmunity, Hypothyroidism, and Hyperthyroidism: A Cross-Sectional Study
Article.Authors: Vargas-Uricoechea H.; Castellanos-Pinedo A.; Vargas-Sierra H.; Meza-Cabrera I.; Pinzón-Fernández M.
Article.Abstract: Autoimmune thyroid disease is common, and low-grade systemic inflammation has been proposed as a contributing mechanism. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) are inexpensive, widely available inflammatory markers whose value as risk indicators for thyroid autoimmunity and thyroid dysfunction remains incompletely defined. In the present study, we aimed to evaluate whether NLR, PLR, and CRP—alone, combined, and adjusted for sociodemographic, clinical, habit-related, and laboratory covariates—are associated with thyroid autoimmunity and with alterations in thyroid status. A cross-sectional analysis was conducted in 3406 adults; participants were measured with TSH, FT4, thyroid antibodies (TRAb, TPOAb, and TgAb), complete blood count, and high-sensitivity CRP values, inter alia. In this referral-based cohort, the observed sample proportion of any thyroid status alteration was 52.2%, and of thyroid autoimmunity, 39.2%; because participants were recruited from a referral population with suspected thyroid disease, these figures reflect this selected sample and should not be interpreted as general-population prevalence estimates. In multivariable analysis, NLR and PLR were strongly and independently associated with thyroid autoimmunity (both p < 0.001); CRP showed a more modest association (p = 0.033). NLR achieved an AUC of 0.752 for autoimmunity. None of the three markers showed strong discrimination for thyroid status alteration overall; CRP showed limited but statistically significant discrimination (AUC = 0.620), whereas NLR and PLR did not. CRP remained independently associated with thyroid status alteration, with a numerically larger odds ratio in the antibody-positive subgroup than in the overall cohort; however, no formal interaction term was tested, and this subgroup comparison should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as evidence of a statistical interaction. In conclusion, NLR and PLR are robust, independent correlates of thyroid autoimmunity but not of thyroid status alteration per se, whereas CRP shows a modest but consistent association with both outcomes, including in antibody-positive patients, albeit without formal interaction testing. These low-cost markers may complement antibody testing for risk stratification in autoimmune thyroid disease.

Article.Title: Three Pathogenic Axes Underlying Prurigo Nodularis and Its Systemic Comorbidities
Article.Authors: Hara R.; Nguyen T.; Saito-Sasaki N.; Sawada Y.
Article.Abstract: Prurigo nodularis (PN) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by severe pruritus and hyperkeratotic nodules. Growing epidemiological evidence indicates that PN is associated with a broad spectrum of systemic comorbidities, including cardiovascular, thyroid, renal, hepatic, psychiatric, pulmonary, and skeletal disorders. However, the biological mechanisms underlying these associations remain incompletely understood. In this review, we propose a framework comprising three interconnected pathogenic axes underlying PN: immune dysregulation, neural dysregulation, and tissue remodeling. Type 2 and type 17 inflammatory pathways, neuroimmune interactions, and fibroblast-mediated extracellular matrix remodeling contribute to PN pathogenesis, while selected immune-inflammatory and remodeling pathways may also have extracutaneous relevance. In particular, IL-4, IL-13, IL-17, and IL-31 may participate in inflammatory and remodeling processes across multiple organs. Although current evidence does not establish a causal relationship between PN and its systemic comorbidities, integration of epidemiological and mechanistic findings supports a broader view of PN beyond the skin. This three-axis framework may provide a conceptual basis for future studies aimed at identifying biomarkers, clarifying systemic disease risk, and defining the clinical relevance of shared pathogenic pathways in PN-associated comorbidities.

Article.Title: The Mechanisms of CD8+ T Cells in Kidney Injury
Article.Authors: An J.; Liu F.; Lu J.; Xu C.; Zhai N.; Lv R.; Chen Y.; Li W.; Zhao Y.; Zhong Y.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Kidney injury encompasses a range of pathological conditions including acute kidney injury (AKI), chronic kidney disease (CKD), and the transition from AKI to CKD. Given its multifactorial pathogenesis, dismal clinical outcomes, and the paucity of effective targeted therapies, renal injury constitutes a substantial global public health burden. As a core effector of adaptive immunity, CD8+ T cells not only participate in the body’s anti-infection and anti-tumor immune responses, but are also involved throughout the process of kidney injury. Emerging technologies such as single-cell sequencing and immune gene editing are now revealing the bidirectional roles and subset diversity of CD8+ T cells in renal injury. Accumulating evidence suggests that CD8+ T cells may contribute to kidney injury progression in specific experimental and clinical contexts via diverse mechanisms, including direct cytotoxicity against renal parenchymal cells, secretion of pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic mediators, remodeling of the local immune microenvironment, and induction of microvascular damage. Meanwhile, their regulatory subsets curb overt inflammation, retard fibrosis, and preserve renal function. This review surveys the biology and subset heterogeneity of CD8+ T cells, recapitulates their involvement in AKI, CKD, and disease transition, evaluates targeted immunotherapies and translational progress, and highlights unresolved issues and future priorities, with the goal of informing mechanistic studies and precision management of renal injury.

Article.Title: Integrated Multi-Omics and Experimental Validation Identify a Spermidine-Responsive FREM1 Remodeling Program in Ischemic Heart Failure
Article.Authors: Li D.; Xiong Y.; Ren C.; Luo J.; Zhou L.; Xu M.; Zhou B.; Xu B.; Ding L.; Zheng L.; Yao Y.
Article.Abstract: Ischemic injury drives a sustained myocardial response in which metabolic stress, fibroblast activation, and extracellular-matrix remodeling converge to cause heart failure, yet the cell-resolved programs linking polyamine homeostasis to post-ischemic remodeling and the response to spermidine remain unclear. In this study, we integrated disease-burden estimates with bulk and single-nucleus myocardial transcriptomics, prioritizing polyamine-related genes by differential-expression analysis, gene-set scoring, and machine learning, followed by pathway, immune, cell–cell communication, and regulatory-network analyses, and evaluated spermidine in a post-myocardial-infarction mouse model using 8-week-old male C57BL/6J mice, with fibroblast-directed FREM1 activation to test whether FREM1 modifies the treatment response. Cross-platform analysis identified FREM1, MYH6, ARRDC3, and XAF1 as reproducible components of the ischemic-failing-heart signature, with FREM1 showing the strongest discrimination in the independent cohort; the program localized predominantly to fibroblasts and was linked to extracellular-matrix, inflammatory, and intercellular-signaling states. In mice, spermidine improved systolic function, reduced collagen deposition, shifted MTA and ornithine signals toward the sham pattern, and lowered myocardial FREM1; FREM1 activation weakened these effects, though residual benefit remained. These findings identify a fibroblast-enriched, spermidine-responsive FREM1 remodeling program linking polyamine-associated stress to post-ischemic fibrosis, positioning FREM1 as a candidate regulator of the cardiac response to spermidine and a potential entry point for therapeutic stratification in ischemic heart failure.

Article.Title: X-Linked Disorders as Dynamic Systems: Rethinking Phenotypic Expression Through a Multifactorial Framework
Article.Authors: Machluf Y.; Chaiter Y.; Dekel Y.
Article.Abstract: X-linked disorders have traditionally been viewed as Mendelian conditions in which pathogenic variants determine phenotype through relatively linear mechanisms. However, marked variability among individuals carrying the same variant challenges this genotype-centered view. We present a context-dependent framework in which phenotypic expression emerges from interactions among variant-specific molecular effects, X-chromosome dosage regulation, genetic and epigenetic background, cellular and tissue context, developmental processes, environmental influences, and stochastic variation. X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) generates cellular mosaicism in heterozygous females. Variation in escape from XCI, skewing, tissue-specific regulation, and cellular selection can further shape the representation and function of cells expressing pathogenic or normal alleles. We distinguish stable XCI within established cell lineages from changes in tissue-level distributions over time. Environmental influences may also modulate clinical expression, although direct evidence linking specific exposures to outcomes in defined X-linked disorders remains limited. Selected disorders and complementary examples illustrate how these factors may contribute to variation in penetrance, expressivity, severity, tissue involvement, and disease trajectories. This framework supports disease-specific interpretation of genotype–phenotype variability and the development of testable research questions; it is not intended to predict clinical outcomes through a universal quantitative model. By integrating genetic, epigenetic, cellular, developmental, and environmental influences, it may inform more comprehensive and precise approaches to disease characterization, diagnosis, risk assessment, and management.

Article.Title: Substrate Requirements and Mechanistic Constraints of Direct-to-Proteasome Degraders: Controls and Testable Limits for Ubiquitin-Independent Degradation
Article.Authors: Kułaga D.
Article.Abstract: Direct-to-proteasome degraders recruit target proteins to the 26S proteasome without recruiting an E3 ubiquitin ligase. We assessed which substrate properties are required for degradation after direct recruitment and how strongly published studies support independence from ubiquitination. We identified four conditions for substrate degradation. Three act in series on every substrate: a binding signal, an accessible initiation region, and enough grip to unfold the folded part. The fourth, bilayer extraction, applies only to membrane-embedded substrates. Direct recruitment changes how the first condition is met and leaves the rest in place. Four anchor points have been liganded in the peer-reviewed literature: RPN1/PSMD2, Rpn13/ADRM1, the deubiquitinase USP14, and midnolin; a fifth, the lid deubiquitinase Rpn11/PSMD14, is disclosed only in a granted patent. Nine studies report degrader-induced loss of 21 targets or tagged constructs: one only weakly, one cleared only at micromolar concentrations, and one a construct that already carries a ubiquitin-independent targeting element; two boundary reports add four. None was degraded in a membrane-embedded form. The control sets differ more than the biology does: only two of the nine show that their ubiquitin-activating-enzyme inhibitor suppressed conjugation, and in the series with the broadest target range the receiving subunit is not established. We derive substrate-eligibility criteria along four axes with the confidence each carries, and propose an evidence standard, graded by the strength of the claim being made, for reports of ubiquitin-independent degradation.

Article.Title: Chronovaccinology: Molecular Clock Regulation of Vaccine Timing, Immunogenicity, and Durable Immune Memory
Article.Authors: Mahajan S.; Mahajan S.; Choudhary D.
Article.Abstract: Chronovaccinology represents an emerging interface between vaccinology, chronobiology, and immunology, proposing that circadian timing may constitute an underappreciated determinant of vaccine responsiveness. Increasing evidence indicates that molecular clock machinery coordinates immune-cell function, antigen processing, lymphocyte trafficking, and the development of adaptive immune responses, thereby creating temporal windows in which vaccination may elicit distinct immunological outcomes. This review encompasses the molecular and cellular mechanisms linking circadian clocks with vaccine-induced immunity, with particular emphasis on BMAL1/CLOCK-mediated regulation of antigen presentation and the circadian regulation of individual immune-cell populations. We further discuss circadian control of lymphocyte trafficking, T and B cell responses, and the establishment of durable humoral immune memory, focusing on the circadian regulation of germinal-centre formation, affinity maturation, and the overarching immunoregulatory mechanisms that sustain immunological memory. Finally, we critically evaluate the challenges associated with translating experimental evidence into clinical chronovaccination strategies, including interindividual circadian variation, vaccine type, age, sex, disease status, and logistical constraints. Understanding these temporal mechanisms may facilitate the development of biologically informed vaccination schedules, provide a framework for optimizing vaccine immunogenicity and long-term immune protection along with actionable insights for integrating circadian principles into future clinical trial designs and public health immunization programs.

Article.Title: A Loop Within the MRG Domain of Drosophila MSL3 Interacts with C2H2 Proteins and Is Involved in Dosage Compensation
Article.Authors: Ryzhkova V.; Babosha V.; Revel-Muroz A.; Vasileva Y.; Kozlov E.; Tikhonova E.; Arkova O.; Tvorogova A.; Georgiev P.; Maksimenko O.
Article.Abstract: Dosage compensation in Drosophila melanogaster is mediated by the male-specific lethal (MSL) complex, which includes an MSL1–MSL3–MOF sub-complex with acetyltransferase activity and an MSL2–MLE subcomplex organized by roX RNAs. The N-terminal coiled-coil domain of MSL1 forms a dimer and interacts with MSL2, while the C-terminal PEHE domain of MSL1 interacts with MOF and MSL3. Inactivation of MSL3 significantly disrupts the specific binding of MSL1–MSL2–MLE to the X chromosome in embryos, suggesting that MSL3 is involved in the recruitment of the entire MSL complex. In this study, using an msl-3 gene deletion, we confirmed that complete inactivation of MSL3 results in a severe reduction in MSL1 and restricts MSL1–MSL2 recruitment to only a small number of X-chromosome sites in larvae and adults. Furthermore, we identified DNA-binding transcription factors that predominantly interact with the MRG (MORF4-related gene) domain of MSL3. This MRG domain contains a disordered loop; deleting this loop (MSL3ΔL) did not affect the MSL3–MSL1 interaction, but disrupted MSL3 binding to the majority of the identified transcription factors. Males expressing the MSL3ΔL variant exhibited reduced viability, indicating partially impaired dosage compensation, although binding of the MSL complex to the X chromosome remained largely unaffected. In contrast, when the MSL complex was formed in females via ectopic MSL2 and roX2 expression, wild-type MSL3 effectively bound the X chromosome at both the larval and imaginal stages. However, under these conditions, the MSL3ΔL variant lost the ability to interact effectively with MSL1, resulting in a near-complete absence of MSL complex binding to the X chromosome. Together, these results demonstrate the intricate regulation of MSL complex formation, the mechanisms of which are not yet fully understood.

Article.Title: An Integrated Multi-Ontology Approach for Prioritizing Candidate Neurodevelopmental Disorder Genes
Article.Authors: Rivi C.; Turina M.; Capriotti E.
Article.Abstract: Rare neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are clinically and genetically heterogeneous conditions affecting brain function, and a comprehensive set of NDD-associated genes is still lacking. We integrated gene lists from Orphanet, SFARI Gene, GeneTrek, and a large-scale genomic study, and classified 19,354 human protein-coding genes into 2639 high-confidence genes, 6856 candidate genes, and 9859 genes with no NDD evidence. Enrichment analysis of the high-confidence set highlighted nervous system development, synaptic processes, tRNA aminoacylation, and cancer-related pathways, and Monarch Disease Ontology (MONDO) enrichment confirmed its association with NDDs. We then prioritized candidate genes with a Multi-Ontology Enrichment (MOE) score, which counts the annotation resources in which a gene shares enriched terms with the high-confidence set. Higher MOE scores were associated with stronger loss-of-function constraint in the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) a larger fraction of genes with pathogenic ClinVar variants (10.7% to 44.0%), and more frequent gene-level association in NDD sequencing cohorts (2.8% to 8.3%), and SysNDD scores provided further support. Part of this signal reflects how well genes are annotated, which we discuss as a limitation. Overall, this work provides a harmonized NDD gene resource and a transparent prioritization of candidate genes for diagnostic and functional studies.

Article.Title: Technical Robustness of Transcriptomic Senescence Classification in Human Microglia: An Evaluation of SenFlag and ICE
Article.Authors: Yuksel B.; Aydin L.
Article.Abstract: The dependence of senescence labels on technical choices becomes apparent when they are used with sparse data from the human brain. We have assessed the SenFlag rules together with five different ICE initialisations in publicly available microglial single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets. The discovery cohort included 12,220 nuclei obtained from 17 donors; the full ICE perturbation analyses were carried out on a fixed subset of 1823 nuclei. The external cohort consisted of 9371 nuclei from ten donors. All 85 complete-pipeline donor-removal fits were carried out. The median positive-label Jaccard agreement for SenMayo-initialised ICE was 95.3%, as compared with 80.0%, 29.4%, 17.6% and 1.7% for the ATF3, CDKN1A, CDKN2A and MX1 initialisations, respectively. Out of 40 attempts, 39 estimable chains were obtained under six matched molecule-thinning conditions and two MAGIC initialisation controls. The median agreement for SenMayo-initialised ICE was 95.5% at 50% count retention and 0.0% at 25%. The positive labels from the discovery cohort differed when using example constants as opposed to population-relative thresholds (91 versus 12) and decreased following thinning. In the external cohort, three ICE chains completed before depth filtering and one afterwards; no initialisation completed in both conditions. Technical stability, estimability and biological validity are separate concepts. Before biological interpretation, senescence-associated labels must have explicit operational definitions and robustness reporting.

Article.Title: Autophagy in Sepsis-Induced Immunothrombosis: Cell-Specific Mechanisms and Autophagy-Targeted Therapies
Article.Authors: Zhang S.; Li Y.; Shen X.; Zhan Q.
Article.Abstract: Sepsis-induced immunothrombosis is a principal driver of organ failure. It arises when innate antimicrobial defenses escalate into systemic thromboinflammatory injury. Autophagy, a conserved lysosomal degradation pathway, dynamically calibrates the procoagulant potential of macrophages, neutrophils, platelets and endothelial cells. This study reviews how distinct autophagic processes, including macroautophagy, mitophagy, chaperone-mediated autophagy and LC3-associated phagocytosis and xenophagy, govern the procoagulant behavior of these cells during sepsis. We propose a conceptual biphasic framework that processes stages from early compensatory autophagy to late-phase autophagic flux collapse and relate this temporal evolution to the clinical spectrum of sepsis-induced coagulopathy. Finally, we evaluate autophagy-targeted therapeutic strategies, including classic regulators, cell-specific nanodelivery systems and emerging gene-/RNA-targeted approaches, while emphasizing that most evidence remains mechanistic or preclinical. By integrating cellular heterogeneity with temporal dynamics, this review provides a mechanistic rationale for cell-targeted approaches to sepsis-induced coagulopathy.

Article.Title: From Endothelial Survival to Lung Protection: Calycosin Attenuates Ischemia–Reperfusion Injury
Article.Authors: Zhao H.; Chen Z.; Wang C.; Li Y.; Lin Y.; Wang H.; Li M.; Feng J.; Zhang G.
Article.Abstract: Lung ischemia–reperfusion injury (LIRI) contributes to early graft dysfunction after lung transplantation, yet effective pharmacological interventions remain limited. Calycosin (CA), an isoflavone sourced from Astragali Radix, has shown protective effects in experimental ischemic injury, but its effects on LIRI remain insufficiently characterized. We integrated network analysis and molecular docking with experiments in human umbilical vein endothelial cells subjected to oxygen–glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) and male Sprague–Dawley rats undergoing left pulmonary hilar occlusion and reperfusion. Computational analyses highlighted inflammatory signaling, redox regulation, and cell survival, with CA improving endothelial viability and reducing oxidative stress, apoptosis, and inflammatory cytokine levels. In rats, CA reduced histological injury, edema, inflammatory cell accumulation, and lipid peroxidation while improving arterial oxygenation, superoxide dismutase activity, and tissue ATP content. Protection was accompanied by changes in candidate gene expression and PPARγ, COX-2, BAX, and BCL2 protein abundance. In endothelial cells, the PPARγ antagonist GW9662 attenuated the protective effects of CA and its reduction of NF-κB p65 nuclear accumulation. These findings support CA’s potential as a candidate intervention for LIRI and identify PPARγ as a contributor to its endothelial–protective effects, providing a rationale for further evaluation in lung preservation and transplantation models.

Article.Title: Matrix Vesicles in Bone Mineralization: Mechanistic Processes
Article.Authors: Zhang M.; Wu X.; Yang X.; Sun L.
Article.Abstract: Matrix vesicles (MtVs) play a central role in initiating skeletal mineralization by providing a confined microenvironment for calcium phosphate formation. However, how MtV-mediated mineral initiation transitions to subsequent collagen mineralization remains incompletely understood. This review critically integrates current insights into the sequential stages of this process: from the molecular regulation of Ca2+ and phosphate/pyrophosphate (Pi/PPi) homeostasis that drives intravesicular mineral nucleation and maturation, to membrane disruption, extracellular mineral propagation, and ultimately, the interactions between MtVs and the mineralizing collagenous matrix. Building on this mechanistic foundation, we examine how MtV-derived minerals dictate mineral organization within the extracellular matrix, specifically evaluating precursor–matrix interactions as the potential bridge linking intravesicular nucleation to intrafibrillar and extrafibrillar collagen mineralization. Finally, by carefully distinguishing evidence derived from native MtVs, biomimetic membrane systems, and in vitro collagen mineralization models, this review establishes a unified framework connecting MtV dynamics to hierarchical bone mineralization.

Article.Title: Exacerbation of Allergic Diseases After COVID-19 Vaccination: A Multicenter Observational Study
Article.Authors: Ban G.; Jin H.; Lee J.; Nam Y.; Rhyou H.; Choi G.; Hur G.; Choi J.; Kim J.; Jung C.; Woo S.; Lee H.; Kim M.; Lee Y.; Kim S.; Lee H.; Ye Y.
Article.Abstract: Concerns about worsening allergic disease may contribute to vaccine hesitancy. We evaluated the frequency, severity, and factors associated with self-reported exacerbations after COVID-19 vaccination and described findings after influenza vaccination. In this multicenter observational survey, adults with physician-diagnosed allergic diseases were prospectively enrolled at 14 Korean allergy centers, while vaccination history and post-vaccination outcomes were retrospectively ascertained. Severe exacerbation was defined as requiring emergency department care or hospitalization. Among 1626 COVID-19-vaccinated patients, 281 (17.3%) reported exacerbation; 36 (12.8% of exacerbators; and 2.2% of all vaccinated patients) were severe. Female sex, chronic urticaria, and atopic dermatitis were independently associated with any exacerbation, whereas increasing age and allergic rhinitis were associated with lower odds. Bronchial asthma was independently associated with severe exacerbation (adjusted OR, 3.07; 95% CI, 1.10–8.51). No factor was associated with multiple exacerbations. Biologic therapy and allergen immunotherapy were not associated with increased risk. Exacerbations were reported in 16 of 786 influenza-vaccinated patients (2.0%) and were generally mild. Although self-reported symptom worsening after COVID-19 vaccination was relatively common, severe events were uncommon. COVID-19 vaccination was generally well tolerated, including among patients receiving biologics or allergen immunotherapy.

Article.Title: The Load That Is Missing: Load Deprivation as a Candidate Contributor to Fracture Nonunion—Mechanobiology, Assessment and a Research Agenda
Article.Authors: Sun S.; Li H.; Li T.; Wang Y.; Wang W.
Article.Abstract: Fracture nonunion is classified along two axes: the biological activity of the fracture ends and the mechanical stability of the construct. Both are necessary, and we argue that together they remain insufficient, because neither records whether the injured limb has actually transmitted load. A rigidly fixed lower-limb fracture that is kept non-weight-bearing can fail to unite while its radiographs resemble atrophic nonunion. We examine the mechanobiological evidence that load deprivation is a distinct exposure rather than the mere absence of a stimulus. Mechanotransduction at the fracture site is instructive rather than permissive: Piezo1, polycystin-1, connexin 43 hemichannels, YAP/TAZ and the osteocyte sclerostin–Wnt axis convert strain into osteogenic and angiogenic signalling, and in mice unloading delays the cartilage-to-bone transition through a chondrocyte Piezo1–ApoE–senescence route. That evidence is nonetheless largely preclinical, and no study has yet shown that a separable human phenotype can be identified reproducibly or that its management differs from current practice. We therefore treat load deprivation as a candidate phenotype requiring prospective validation, propose an assessment framework that separates baseline case definition from treatment response, and set out six testable propositions.

Article.Title: Anticancer Evaluation and Cellular-Stress Analyses of a Flavonol–Ruthenium(II) Complex Against Aggressive Breast Cancer Cells
Article.Authors: Lin G.; Chang J.; Lai Y.; Lien T.; Sun D.; Cheng C.; Yang L.; Tseng R.; Su Y.; Wu H.; Shih T.; Chang H.
Article.Abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer remains refractory to conventional chemotherapy, driving demand for selective metallopharmaceuticals that trigger immunogenic cell death and convert immune-desert “cold” tumors into immune-vulnerable “hot” tumors. Here, we delineate the in vitro efficacy and regulated cell death (RCD) landscape of compound 2 [RuCl(p-cymene)(4′-methoxyflavonol)], a half-sandwich Ru(II)–arene flavonol complex assembled from 3-hydroxy-4′-methoxyflavone and dichloro(p-cymene)ruthenium(II) dimer. Under 24 h CCK-8 assays, compound 2 potently inhibited aggressive breast cancer models—human MDA-MB-231 IC50 37.6 μM and murine 4T1 IC50 26.1 μM—while sparing non-malignant human mammary epithelial H184B5F5/M10 (IC50 72.6 μM, SI 1.9) and mouse embryonic fibroblasts (IC50 41.3 μM, SI 1.6), showing activity comparable to cisplatin (IC50 41.2 μM in MDA-MB-231) and superior to free ligand + Ru-dimer mixture (IC50 108.9 μM). Compound 2 exhibited favorable physiological stability and enhanced stability under mildly acidic, tumor-mimetic conditions, supporting a tumor-retentive prodrug behavior. CTS-RCDP multiparametric flow cytometry revealed a multimodal death network predominantly driven by pyroptosis (51.7% in MDA-MB-231, 40.1% in 4T1), accompanied by apoptosis, validated by caspase-1/-3 colorimetric assays (3.2-fold/2.4-fold increase, p < 0.01). This was coupled with pronounced elevation of mitochondrial mass and mtROS. Collectively, compound 2 emerges as a selective Ru-flavonol complex that drives pyroptosis-dominant cell death, a lytic, pro-inflammatory modality recognized to reprogram immunologically “cold” tumors into immune-vulnerable “hot” lesions.

Article.Title: TGF-β-Associated Telocyte Degeneration and Profibrotic Reprogramming in Deep Fascia Fibrosis
Article.Authors: Chen W.; Li Z.; Tang H.; Zhao W.; Wang D.
Article.Abstract: Deep fascia fibrosis is a pathological feature of multiple musculoskeletal disorders, including gluteal muscle contracture (GMC), Dupuytren’s disease, myofascial pain syndrome, and plantar fasciitis. However, the stromal cell mechanisms that maintain fascial homeostasis and drive pathological remodeling remain poorly understood. Telocytes (TCs) are specialized interstitial stromal cells characterized by exceptionally long, moniliform cellular processes termed telopodes, which form extensive intercellular networks within connective tissues. Despite their presence in deep fascia, their involvement in fascial fibrosis remains unknown. We integrated ultrastructural analysis and single-cell transcriptomics profiling of human GMC-associated fibrotic deep fascia, with validation in a rat model of GMC and functional studies using primary fascia-derived cells. Transmission electron microscopy revealed increased near-somatic telopode discontinuities in human GMC fascia compared with controls (1.53 ± 0.30 vs. 0.43 ± 0.23 per TC; GMC, n = 4; control, n = 3; p < 0.05), with a similar increase in GMC rats (1.67 ± 0.15 vs. 0.08 ± 0.03 per TC; n = 4 per group; p < 0.0001). Immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated a 94% reduction in continuously connected telopode length in fibrotic fascia (3.19 ± 1.13 vs. 58.84 ± 9.48 μm; p < 0.01). Single-cell RNA sequencing showed that TCs were largely preserved in abundance but exhibited an altered transcriptional state characterized by enhanced TGF-β signaling and acquisition of a profibrotic extracellular matrix remodeling program. In primary fascia-derived cells exhibiting TC-like characteristics (n = 3 independent isolations), TGF-β1 increased the proportion of cells with fragmented telopodes from 26.29 ± 4.98% to 92.56 ± 1.68% (p < 0.0001). Treatment with the TGF-β receptor inhibitor SB431542 reduced this proportion to 22.00 ± 5.18%, representing a 76% relative reduction compared with TGF-β1 treatment alone (p < 0.0001). Our findings identify TGF-β-associated telocyte pathological reprogramming and TGF-β-driven telocyte degeneration as a previously unrecognized feature of deep fascia fibrosis. We propose that aberrant TGF-β signaling promotes a pathological telocyte state characterized by loss of telopode integrity and enhanced ECM-remodeling potential, thereby contributing to remodeling of the fibrotic fascial microenvironment.

Article.Title: Integrative Transcriptomics Reveals Coordinated Remodeling-Associated and Ciliated-Lineage Dysregulation in Severe Asthma
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Chen X.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: Severe asthma is accompanied by increased epithelial repair/remodeling activity and reduced ciliated-cell identity, but whether these abnormalities form a coordinated pattern across clinical and experimental contexts is unclear. We integrated seven public human airway epithelial transcriptomic datasets using a staged design. Two discovery cohorts defined fixed remodeling-associated and ciliated-lineage programs, which were evaluated without refitting in an independent severity cohort and then examined in single-cell, normal differentiation, IL-13 stimulation, and in vivo allergen-challenge datasets. Article.Title: Chrysin Inhibits Telomerase and Induces Senescence in Two Cancer Cell Lines: Insights from In Vitro Analysis, Molecular Docking, DFT, and ADMET
Article.Authors: Porika M.; Tippani R.; Kalam S.; Banothu D.; Rekulapally S.; Poonuru R.; Abbagani S.; Saretzki G.
Article.Abstract: Telomerase activity (TA) is crucial for preserving telomeres and preventing senescence, while telomerase inhibition can cause cellular senescence in cancer cells for therapeutic applications. Certain phytochemical substances act as telomerase inhibitors, but understanding their impact on lung and cervical cancer cells is limited. A density functional theory (DFT) experiment revealed critical insights into molecular characteristics like net charge, orbital geometries (HOMO and LUMO), energy gap (ΔE), and dipole moment. Quantum parameters and ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination, and toxicity) properties of chrysin suggest pharmacological properties and safety. Our findings underscore the intricate interplay between telomerase inhibition, anti-proliferative activity, and senescence, offering valuable insights for future development of novel telomerase-based therapies.

Article.Title: Pulmonary and Systemic Safety Assessment of Two Bacillus thuringiensis Biopesticides After Oral, Intranasal, and Subcutaneous Exposure in BALB/c Mice
Article.Authors: Yildiz I.; Yigit E.; Zihni H.; Tekatli S.; Yenilmez E.; Sezen K.
Article.Abstract: Microbial biopesticides may contain viable microorganisms, requiring safety assessments that address infectivity, pathogenicity, host clearance, and toxicity. However, integrated evaluations of native isolates remain limited. Two microbial biopesticides, Eca9/Mm2 and Eca9/Xd3, formulated using combinations of Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. kurstaki (Eca9) and B. thuringiensis subsp. tenebrionis (Mm2 or Xd3) isolates, were evaluated in female BALB/c mice. Each preparation was administered by oral gavage (100 µL), intranasal instillation (10 µL), and subcutaneous injection (100 µL), with active, heat-inactivated, and shared control groups. Animals were monitored for mortality, clinical signs, and body weight until their designated sampling time points, with a maximum follow-up of 21 days. Microbiological recovery was assessed by heat-selected culturable spore counts in fecal and blood samples following oral and subcutaneous administration and in lung tissue following intranasal administration on days 7, 14, and 21. In intranasally exposed animals, pulmonary TNF-α, MPO, CC16, and ACE2 and serum CRP and PCT were measured by ELISA, while serum ALT, AST activities, and BUN level were determined using an autoanalyzer. Lung histopathology was evaluated by blinded semiquantitative scoring. Each preparation was analyzed separately against the shared control group, without direct statistical comparisons between preparations. No exposure-related mortality or overt clinical signs of toxicity were observed, and percentage body weight gain did not differ from control in any treatment group. Following intranasal administration, pulmonary bacterial load no longer differed significantly from control on day 21 in the Eca9/Mm2 group, whereas it remained significantly elevated in the Eca9/Xd3 group. However, histopathological responses did not parallel bacterial recovery. Active Eca9/Mm2 exhibited significant alveolar septal thickening and interstitial inflammation on day 21 despite pulmonary bacterial recovery no longer differing significantly from control. In contrast, active Eca9/Xd3 produced no significant histopathological changes relative to control; the significant alterations in this preparation were confined to the heat-inactivated form on day 7. These findings indicate that pulmonary bacterial recovery alone is insufficient to establish infection or predict histopathological alterations and that heat-inactivated preparations can elicit biological responses. The results support strain and formulation-specific safety assessments integrating microbiological, biochemical, histopathological, and clinical endpoints.

Article.Title: Electrostatic Self-Assembly of Nanosheets of Layered Perovskite-like Oxides HA2Ta3O10 (A = Ca, Sr) and Ni-Al and Co-Al Layered Double Hydroxides for Photocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution
Article.Authors: Minich I.; Smirnova T.; Ustinova A.; Kurnosenko S.; Zhuravlev E.; Silyukov O.
Article.Abstract: Developing efficient photocatalysts for solar energy conversion remains a key challenge in sustainable hydrogen production. Herein, we report a family of 2D/2D nanocomposite photocatalysts fabricated via the electrostatic self-assembly of oppositely charged nanosheets. The fabrication process involves the sequential protonation and organic modification (intercalation of ethylamine and tetrabutylammonium hydroxide) of solid-state synthesized Dion–Jacobson perovskites, CsA2Ta3O10 (A = Ca, Sr), followed by ultrasonic exfoliation into negatively charged nanosheets. Concurrently, hydrothermally prepared Ni-Al and Co-Al layered double hydroxides (LDHs) were converted into highly dispersible acetate forms to yield positively charged nanoplates. Finally, the intimate mixing of these oppositely charged colloidal suspensions drives their immediate electrostatic self-assembly into structured 2D/2D heterojunctions. Activity was also evaluated following the photodeposition of platinum onto the composites (under UV–vis, simulated solar, and visible light λ = 425 nm). While the pristine perovskite nanosheets absorb only ultraviolet light (Eg = 4.29–4.40 eV), a composite with LDHs successfully extends the optical response into the visible spectrum. The choice of the divalent transition metal in the LDH determines the resulting band alignment. In accordance with the band edge calculations, it was proposed that Ni-Al forms a type-II heterojunction that promotes spatial charge separation, whereas Co-Al establishes a type-I junction that suppresses activity. Under UV–vis irradiation, the HSr2Ta3O10/NiAl-LDH composite achieves a superior H2 evolution rate of 291 μmol h−1 (φ = 15.2%), outperforming pristine exfoliated HSr2Ta3O10. Crucially, the HSr2Ta3O10/NiAl-LDH/Pt composite demonstrates distinct photocatalytic activity under visible light (0.63 μmol h−1), while both individual components remain completely inert under the same conditions. This work highlights sheet-by-sheet electrostatic assembly as a viable strategy to extend the photoresponse of wide-bandgap perovskites.

Article.Title: Plant-Derived Bioactive Compounds in Cancer Therapy: Molecular Mechanisms, Preclinical Evidence, and Translational Perspectives
Article.Authors: Alharbi H.; Anwar S.; Almerdasi S.; Rahmani A.
Article.Abstract: Cancer remains one of the leading causes of death and is driven by complex interactions among oxidative stress, inflammation, and dysregulated cellular signaling. Over the past few years, plant-derived antioxidants have shown exciting anticancer potential in preclinical trials. However, translating these findings into effective clinical therapies remains a challenge. Moreover, their safety profile depends on the individual compound, dosage, formulation, and duration of exposure. This review provides a comprehensive overview of plant-derived antioxidants and their therapeutic potential in cancer prevention and treatment, with particular emphasis on their molecular mechanisms, biological activities, and translational relevance. Plant-derived compounds exhibit significant anticancer potential through the regulation of signaling pathways such as NF-κB, PI3K/Akt, MAPK, and Nrf2, thereby influencing cell proliferation, apoptosis, angiogenesis, inflammation, and metastasis. Despite this promising therapeutic potential, their clinical application remains challenging. Recent advances in drug delivery systems have shown their considerable promise in overcoming these limitations and enhancing their therapeutic efficacy. Consequently, natural antioxidants may represent a multi-targeted and biologically relevant strategy for cancer management. However, further mechanistic studies and well-designed clinical trials are needed to validate their therapeutic potential and support their integration into modern oncology, ultimately contributing to the development of safer and more effective anticancer therapies.
