Article.Title: A Review of Tooth-Related Bone Regeneration Research Based on Occlusion Using Bioactive Glass and Piezoelectric Ceramics
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Liu Y.; Shao B.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: The functional regeneration of alveolar bone defects, which encompasses alveolar bone resorption and the destruction of periodontal supporting bone structures, is a research hotspot in the fields of oral and maxillofacial rehabilitation as well as periodontitis treatment. It also represents a core technical challenge for achieving periodontal tissue reconstruction in clinical practice. Commonly used traditional bone repair materials generally have insufficient bioactivity, limited osteoinductive efficacy, and poor mismatch with the physiological microenvironment of natural bone, making it difficult to meet the demands for efficient repair and long-term functional healing of complex alveolar bone defects. Bioactive glass (BG) combines excellent biocompatibility, osteoconductive properties, and intrinsic bone-inductive potential. It can regulate bone metabolic remodeling processes through the sustained release of bioactive ions and has become one of the most promising core functional materials in the field of bone regeneration and repair. Piezoelectric ceramics (PCs) possess a unique direct piezoelectric effect, capable of converting external mechanical loads into endogenous electrical signals, achieving precise coupling and transformation between mechanical energy and bioelectric signals. With the stimulation provided by physiological masticatory stress, piezoelectric ceramics can create a bioelectric microenvironment similar to natural bone tissue, thereby regulating the proliferation, differentiation, and mineralization of osteoblasts and promoting bone tissue regeneration and repair. This article systematically reviews the bioactive glass–piezoelectric ceramic composite system, focusing on the core mechanisms by which occlusal mechanical stress-mediated piezoelectric effects regulate alveolar bone regeneration. It provides an in-depth analysis of the osteogenic and angiogenic promoting effects of this composite material, summarizes the structural advantages, performance characteristics, and clinical application potential of the composite system, and aims to provide a systematic theoretical basis and technical reference for the iterative development of oral bone regeneration materials and precise clinical restorative applications.

Article.Title: Multi-Omics Integrative and Functional Analysis of Glia Maturation Factor-γ: Associations with Malignant Phenotypes and Immune Microenvironment Features in Glioblastoma
Article.Authors: Deng H.; Zhang T.; Song P.; Han N.; Qiu Q.; Bu J.; Zhang M.
Article.Abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary malignant brain tumor in adults. Therapeutic outcomes are severely limited by temozolomide (TMZ) chemoresistance and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Glia maturation factor-γ (GMFG) is linked to cytoskeletal and myeloid remodeling in other cancers, yet its roles in glioma remain poorly explored. At single-cell resolution, Chemo_TAM dominated the GMFG-high myeloid population; CellChat predicted prominent signaling pathways underlying tumor–Chemo_TAM crosstalk. GMFG expression positively correlated with immunosuppressive markers and several immune checkpoint molecules; OncoPredict identified candidate drugs with lower predicted IC50 in GMFG-high tumors. Article.Authors: Cuccaro M.; Sicuranza A.; Santoni A.; Marconi G.; Malchiodi M.; Rondoni M.; Cartocci A.; Palombo K.; Monti S.; Marzano C.; Turriziani C.; Miracapillo T.; Zannetti B.; Rocchi S.; Lanza F.; Bocchia M.

Article.Title: Selected Botanical and Plant-Derived Agents in Clinical Toxicology: Mechanisms, Preclinical Evidence, and Toxicovigilance—A Systematic Review
Article.Authors: Elgharabawy R.; Emara A.
Article.Abstract: Botanical preparations and plant-derived constituents have been investigated for their potential to mitigate toxicant-induced organ injury. However, substantial variability in chemical composition, formulation, dosage, and bioavailability complicates the translation of experimental findings into clinical toxicology. This systematic review critically evaluates the mechanistic, experimental, clinical, and toxicovigilance evidence concerning selected botanical preparations and plant-derived constituents, emphasizing antidotal specificity, methodological reliability, pharmacokinetic plausibility, and safety. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through 31 July 2026, supplemented by additional identification methods. Evidence was narratively synthesized according to study design, toxicological indication, intervention characteristics, and clinical applicability. The reported search identified 802 records; 116 duplicates were removed, 686 records were screened, and 222 full-text reports were assessed. A provisional register contains 195 candidate study/report records, although their original eligibility decisions and unique-study identities remain incompletely reconciled. Four supplementary evidence matrices contain 131 potentially overlapping entries: 22 clinical, six pharmacovigilance/utilization, 44 animal, and 59 in-vitro/ex-vivo. Experimental findings implicated Nrf2/Keap1, NF-κB, PI3K/Akt, and mitochondrial pathways, but these mechanistic effects did not establish clinical antidotal efficacy. Intravenous silibinin had the most direct clinical relevance in amatoxin poisoning, although evidence of its independent therapeutic effect remains predominantly observational and confounded by concurrent treatments. Important safety concerns included herb–drug interactions, licorice-associated pseudoaldosteronism, botanical-associated hepatotoxicity, and formulation-dependent toxicity. Botanical-derived interventions demonstrate promising toxicant-specific experimental effects, but clinical translation remains constrained by formulation heterogeneity, uncertain human exposure, limited controlled clinical evidence, and methodological weaknesses. Intravenous silibinin should be distinguished from oral silymarin and other botanical products. Definitive conclusions require standardized preparations, clinically relevant dosing, rigorous safety evaluation, and completion of study-level reconciliation and independent risk-of-bias assessments.

Article.Title: From Molecular Mechanisms to Management: Advances in Diabetic Retinopathy and Diabetic Macular Edema
Article.Authors: Baiturova Y.; Sarria-Santamera A.; Semenova Y.
Article.Abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a major microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus (DM) and a leading cause of vision loss worldwide. Several risk factors have been implicated in the development and progression of DR, such as longer duration of diabetes, poor glycemic control, hypertension, dyslipidemia, renal impairment, and smoking. Diabetic macular edema is the main cause of visual impairment in patients with diabetic retinopathy. It is defined by retinal thickening from fluid leakage into the retina and can be visualized with optical coherence tomography (OCT). At the molecular level, chronic hyperglycemia triggers several pathogenic mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, advanced glycation end product formation, protein kinase C activation, and dysregulated vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, leading to blood–retinal barrier breakdown, microvascular dysfunction, and retinal neurodegeneration. Current therapeutic approaches include laser photocoagulation, intravitreal anti-VEGF agents, and corticosteroids, with ongoing research into novel interventions targeting senolytic agents, integrin antagonists, inhibitors of vascular adhesion protein-1, anti-inflammatory therapies targeting interleukin-6 (IL-6) signaling, and plasma kallikrein inhibitors. This review synthesizes the recent evidence on DR epidemiology, risk factors, pathophysiology, and treatment, highlighting the need for comprehensive risk-based screening and multidisciplinary management to mitigate the growing burden of diabetic eye disease.

Article.Title: “Where Should I Look for Vessels?” A Systematic Review of Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers in Peripheral Artery Disease Involving the Lower Limbs
Article.Authors: Bichescu M.; Sitar-Tăut A.; Țîpcu A.; Kacso T.; Lucaciu R.; Hangan A.; Procopciuc L.
Article.Abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is a progressive atherosclerotic condition associated with high morbidity and mortality. Serum biomarkers may improve diagnostic accuracy and prognostic risk stratification beyond traditional clinical tools. High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) was also associated with the presence of PAD in some studies. Biomarkers associated in individual cohorts with amputation, mortality or chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) included NLR (OR 1.28 per unit for 30-day death or amputation in acute limb ischaemia; HR 1.14 for amputation in CLTI), growth-differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15) (adjusted HR 1.57–1.70 per ln-unit), suPAR (HR 3.1–3.5), triglyceride–glucose (TyG) index (OR 5.80 for CLTI and OR 3.92 for lower-extremity arterial disease in diabetic patients, both cross-sectional), calprotectin (HR 2.5), and lower high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (low HDL-c; HR 0.38 for MACE, normal vs. low HDL-c). Novel markers such as lipocalin-2 and urinary vanin-1 were associated with outcomes in single studies. However, the evidence comes mainly from observational cohorts at moderate-to-high risk of bias, without external validation or demonstrated incremental value over the ABI. These biomarkers are candidates for future risk stratification rather than tools for routine clinical use.

These findings suggest that smoking-related carotid plaque remodeling is more strongly reflected in local TIMP and inflammatory profiles than in total MMP concentrations. Article.Title: The Role of Ubiquitination and Ubiquitin-like Modifications in the Oncogenic Fusion Protein BCR-ABL
Article.Authors: Shammas T.; Donoghue D.
Article.Abstract: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is driven by the BCR-ABL fusion oncoprotein, a constitutively active tyrosine kinase whose inhibition by tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) transformed disease management. However, kinase-domain mutations, persistent leukemic stem cells (LSCs), and kinase-independent survival mechanisms still limit durable treatment-free remission. Increasing evidence indicates that BCR-ABL is regulated not only by kinase activity but also by post-translational modifications (PTMs) determining protein stability, turnover, interactions, and degradation. Ubiquitin-dependent regulation involves opposing activities of E3 ligases and deubiquitinating enzymes, while TRIM28-mediated SUMOylation and RAPSYN-mediated NEDDylation stabilize BCR-ABL by limiting p62-dependent autophagic and c-CBL-mediated degradation, respectively. Crosstalk among these pathways suggests an integrated PTM network governs BCR-ABL fate rather than independent modifications. These mechanisms may impact persistent CML populations, though direct evidence linking specific PTMs to LSC maintenance remains limited. Therapeutically, manipulating PTM-dependent proteostasis via deubiquitinase inhibition, SUMO/NEDD8 modulation, chaperone disruption, and targeted protein degradation can complement conventional kinase inhibition. Notably, BCR-ABL-directed proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) demonstrate the feasibility of eliminating the fusion protein rather than solely suppressing its catalytic activity. Ultimately, PTM-dependent proteostasis represents a critical regulatory dimension and therapeutic vulnerability in CML. Defining the spatial, temporal, and disease-specific PTM landscape of BCR-ABL is essential to determine if selective stability manipulation can overcome resistance and deepen therapeutic responses.

Article.Title: Tumor-Derived Extracellular Vesicles in Cancer–Nerve Crosstalk
Article.Authors: Loukopoulou M.; Kottorou A.; Koutras A.; Dimitrakopoulos F.
Article.Abstract: Communication between tumors and the nervous system influences tumor growth, invasion, pain and immune regulation. This mini-review critically examines extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated cancer–nerve communication in peripheral solid tumors, selected central nervous system tumors and neuroblastoma. Direct functional evidence is concentrated in a small number of mechanisms and tumor models, with the strongest support for EV-associated neurite outgrowth and tumor innervation in head and neck cancer and more limited supportive evidence in cervical cancer. We organize the evidence by biological process: neurite outgrowth and axon guidance, neuronal reprogramming, microenvironment remodeling and reciprocal neuron–tumor signaling. EV-associated effects on neuronal phenotype, activity, Schwann cells and perineural invasion extend this framework, but do not establish a universal mechanism of EV-driven innervation. Neurite outgrowth, nerve recruitment, neuronal reprogramming and perineural invasion are therefore evaluated as distinct outcomes. Future progress requires tracing tumor-innervating neurons, integrating single-cell and spatial mapping with EV profiling and testing candidate cargo through selective perturbation and rescue. These approaches may identify context-specific therapeutic opportunities, although clinical biomarkers and EV-directed interventions remain investigational.

Article.Title: Fluorescent Calcium-Activated Potassium Channel KCa3.1 and its Interactions with Peptide Blockers
Article.Authors: Korabeynikova V.; Shmatin I.; Kirpichnikov M.; Nekrasova O.; Feofanov A.
Article.Abstract: The intermediate-conductance Ca2+-activated potassium channel KCa3.1 plays a crucial role in various cellular processes and is implicated in the pathogenesis of neuroimmune, inflammatory, cardiovascular, and oncological diseases. Pore blockers of KCa3.1 are promising therapeutic candidates and valuable tools for studying the structure and function of the channel. However, little data is available on the activity of potassium channel blockers against the KCa3.1 channel. To address this issue, a fluorescent cellular system was created to search for and study blockers that bind to the outer vestibule of the KCa3.1 pore. It comprises mammalian cells expressing mKate2-tagged KCa3.1 channels, a fluorescent ligand (charybdotoxin conjugated with Atto488), and a competitive binding procedure to measure the affinity of non-fluorescent compounds for KCa3.1 using confocal microscopy. For KCa3.1, Atto488-charybdotoxin has a dissociation constant of 1.7 ± 0.3 nM, which is just slightly larger than the apparent dissociation constant of charybdotoxin (Kap = 1.09 ± 0.14 nM). Applying this cellular system, eight peptides were studied that were not previously characterized or tested only at low concentrations in relation to KCa3.1: Moka1, MeKTx11-1, hongotoxin 1, Ce1, Ce4, Ce5, scyllatoxin, and agitoxin 2. MeKTx11-1, Moka1, and hongotoxin 1 were found to bind (Kap of 13 ± 4, 21 ± 7, and 51 ± 9 nM, respectively) and block the KCa3.1 channel. No (or very weak) binding to KCa3.1 was observed for the other studied peptides, which, in particular, highlights the recently found high selectivity of Ce1 and Ce4 for the voltage-gated potassium Kv1.2 channel.

Article.Title: CSF Proteomic Profiling of Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Phenotypes Highlights Lipid Remodeling, Heme Handling, and Neuroglial Injury
Article.Authors: Otto-Ślusarczyk D.; Alster P.; Wiercińska-Drapało A.; Struga M.; Madetko-Alster N.
Article.Abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a clinically heterogeneous four-repeat tauopathy, but the molecular links between redox biology, lipid remodeling, heme and iron handling, and neurodegeneration remain poorly defined. We performed untargeted LC-MS/MS proteomic profiling of cerebrospinal fluid from 12 patients with PSP-Richardson’s syndrome (PSP-RS), 12 with PSP-parkinsonism (PSP-P), and 12 controls. In the primary analysis, without adjustment for age and sex, 67 of the 2445 quantified protein groups showed significant differences in PSP-RS versus controls and 18 in PSP-P versus controls after FDR correction, with seven proteins shared between the two comparisons. No protein remained significant in the direct PSP-RS versus PSP-P comparison. In PSP-RS, functional enrichment highlighted lipid and lipoprotein remodeling, cholesterol transport, and accompanying complement-related pathways. No significant functional enrichment was detected in PSP-P using the experimental proteomic background. The prioritized protein panel revealed abundance changes associated with redox-related processes in PSP-RS. Increased CP and HPX were linked to iron and heme handling. Increased PON1, APOA1, APOM, and AFM were associated with lipid transport and antioxidant-related processes. Increased GFAP and SERPINA3 reflected astroglial and stress/injury responses, whereas decreased NPTX2 was consistent with synaptic and neuronal network involvement. AFM, GFAP, and SERPINA3 were also increased in PSP-P. Together, these protein-level and pathway-level findings suggest associations between lipid homeostasis, redox-related processes, and neuroglial injury in PSP. However, these findings do not establish molecular differences between PSP phenotypes, as no proteins remained significant in their direct comparison after FDR correction. In the age- and sex-adjusted sensitivity analysis, no protein groups remained significant after FDR correction in the disease-versus-control comparisons. These exploratory findings require confirmation in larger, age-matched cohorts with independent validation.

Article.Title: Antiviral Activity and Chemical Profiling of Dendronephthya hemprichi Soft Coral Extract Against Human Viruses
Article.Authors: Hussein M.; Manni E.; Alsahli S.; Alrayes Z.; Alhajouj S.; El-Ossaily Y.; Alzayed R.; Salim M.; Fouad A.; Elian A.; Abdelkarem F.
Article.Abstract: Marine soft corals represent a promising source of bioactive compounds with potential antiviral applications. In this study, the crude extract of Dendronephthya hemprichi soft coral was evaluated for its antiviral activity against herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2 (HSV-1 and HSV-2), coxsackievirus B4 (CVB4), and human adenovirus 40 (HAdV-40) using in vitro assays. The extract exhibited marked antiviral activity, particularly against HSV-1, with an IC50 of 12.99 ± 0.47 µg/mL (SI = 11.44). In the virucidal protocol, the IC50 was 11.12 ± 0.52 µg/mL, with an SI of 13.35. Relative to the reference drug acyclovir, the extract demonstrated lower potency against both HSV-1 and HSV-2. Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) analysis revealed a diverse chemical profile dominated by fatty acids, fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs), terpenoids and sterol derivatives, including oleic acid, 13-Docosenoic acid methyl ester, 9-Octadecenoic acid methyl ester, ethyl isoallocholate, ergosta-5,22-dien-3β-ol acetate, and geranyl isovalerate. Exploratory DFT descriptors and molecular docking of selected metabolites are reported. These analyses are descriptive only and do not explain the measured antiviral activity. The chemical profiling identifies constituents as FAMEs, steroids and terpenoids that may contribute to the observed activity and supports further investigation of D. hemprichi through isolation and mechanistic studies.

Article.Title: Network Toxicology and Machine Learning Prioritise a Seven-Gene Signature of Liver Injury Associated with Particle-Bound Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons
Article.Authors: Liang J.; Yan R.
Article.Abstract: As a major toxic component of environmental fine particulate matter (PM2.5), polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) pose a significant risk to human health, particularly for liver damage, following inhalation or ingestion. However, their comprehensive molecular mechanisms underlying this hepatotoxicity have long remained unclear. In this study, we developed an integrative framework that combines network toxicology, batch-corrected two-stage machine learning, gene set variation analysis, immune-signature analysis and molecular docking. We retrieved 479 overlapping candidates from 570 PAH-related targets and 12,072 liver-injury-associated genes; the intersection of network hubs (MCC top-30 and MCODE modules) with differentially expressed genes across three merged hepatic cohorts (n = 174) yielded 32 candidates, from which three complementary algorithms (LASSO, SVM-RFE and permutation-calibrated random forest) distilled a seven-gene signature (CYP2C19, MYC, EGR1, HMMR, ICAM1, MAPK3 and NFE2L2). An eight-classifier comparison selected a support vector machine, exact Shapley values quantified each gene’s contribution, and a logistic risk score built on the seven genes discriminated metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.953 in the training set, 0.828 in a held-out test set and 0.978 in an independent 216-biopsy validation cohort (10 controls and 206 MASLD cases), in which the score was discriminative but its probabilities were not well calibrated. GSVA and immune-signature analyses positioned the signature within a three-layer working model: collapse of metabolic and antioxidant capacity (CYP2C19, NFE2L2), imbalance of stress signalling (elevated MAPK3 with attenuated MYC and EGR1), and cell-behaviour remodelling (HMMR-linked proliferation programmes and ICAM1-linked immune remodelling), consistent with a state of heightened susceptibility to chemical stressors such as PAHs. In summary, this study provides a prioritised, hypothesis-generating target set and a reusable, batch-corrected analytical workflow for environmentally associated liver injury, with experimental validation of the prioritised targets as the necessary next step.

Article.Title: Systems Biology and Network Modeling of Lipid Metabolism in Brassica juncea: A Roadmap for Precision Oil Engineering
Article.Authors: Akram S.; Ahlawat Y.; Keerthi M.; Seth M.; Panda S.; Rajput C.; Kumar N.; Gupta S.; Yang T.
Article.Abstract: Brassica juncea (Indian mustard) is an economically important oilseed crop, but high erucic acid in traditional seed oils and elevated glucosinolates in seed meal remain important quality-improvement targets. Its allotetraploid genome, developmental regulation, and environmental responses complicate the prediction and engineering of lipid-related traits. This narrative review synthesizes experimentally supported findings on fatty acid biosynthesis, triacylglycerol assembly, and genetic regulation in B. juncea, and distinguishes these findings from evidence transferred from Arabidopsis thaliana, Brassica napus, and soybean. We examine available genomic and multi-omics resources, gene co-expression and regulatory network inference, constraint-based metabolic modeling, and strategies for combining these approaches with genome editing and genomic prediction. Although individual lipid-associated genes and seed traits have been characterized, a comprehensively validated, seed-specific, genome-scale lipid metabolic model for B. juncea remains unavailable. We therefore propose a staged roadmap encompassing developmental multi-omics sampling, homoeolog-aware network reconstruction, model calibration, independent validation, targeted perturbation, and multi-environment field testing. This evidence-led framework could help prioritize robust targets for improving fatty acid composition and seed oil performance without assuming that computationally inferred interactions are experimentally established.

Article.Title: Inhibition of VEGFR1 Tyrosine Kinase Signaling Attenuates Renal Fibrosis and Macrophage Accumulation After Unilateral Ureteral Obstruction in Mice
Article.Authors: Yamazaki T.; Ito Y.; Hosono K.; Kamata M.; Wada Y.; Takeuchi Y.; Shibuya M.; Amano H.
Article.Abstract: Chronic kidney disease progresses through sustained inflammation and tubulointerstitial fibrosis, processes in which infiltrating macrophages play a central role. Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-1 (VEGFR1) is abundantly expressed in monocytes/macrophages; however, the contribution of its tyrosine kinase (TK) signaling to renal fibrogenesis remains unclear. We therefore examined how VEGFR1 TK signaling participates in macrophage-mediated renal fibrosis induced by unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) using wild-type (WT) mice and mice lacking the VEGFR1 TK domain (TK−/− mice). Renal inflammation and fibrosis were assessed 7–10 days post-UUO. TK−/− mice exhibited reduced fibrosis and inflammation, accompanied by reduced macrophage accumulation and decreased numbers of both Ly6Chigh inflammatory monocytes/macrophages and Ly6Clow/F4/80high macrophages in the injured kidney. Reconstitution of WT mice with TK−/− bone marrow (BM) and transfer of TK−/− BM-derived macrophages also attenuated fibrosis and inflammation after UUO. Furthermore, immunoreactivity of platelet-derived growth factor-B (PDGF-B) was observed in close association with F4/80+ macrophages, and the number of PDGF-B+ Ly6Clow/F4/80high macrophages was reduced in TK−/− UUO kidneys. In vitro, IL-4-induced Pdgfb expression was attenuated in TK−/− BM-derived macrophages. Pharmacological inhibition of PDGFR reduced renal fibrosis and macrophage accumulation after UUO. In addition, placental growth factor (PlGF) neutralization attenuated renal fibrosis, macrophage accumulation, and inflammatory responses. These findings support the involvement of VEGFR1 TK signaling in macrophage-associated renal fibrogenesis and identify PDGF-B as a possible mediator of this process. Targeting the VEGFR1 TK signaling in macrophages could offer a strategy for mitigating renal fibrosis.

Article.Title: Molecular Mechanisms of Radioresistance in Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer: Integrating MicroRNA Regulation and Extracellular Vesicle-Mediated Communication
Article.Authors: Ishikawa M.; Chiba M.
Article.Abstract: Radioresistance limits the efficacy of radiotherapy in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Its development reflects interactions among DNA damage repair, cell cycle regulation, cell death avoidance, metabolic adaptation, cellular plasticity, and the tumor microenvironment. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate these processes through multiple targets, whereas extracellular vesicles (EVs) may connect intracellular responses with intercellular communication. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms and experimental models of NSCLC radioresistance, emphasizing miRNA regulation and EV-mediated interactions among cancer, stromal, and immune cells. We distinguish intrinsic resistance from resistance arising through selection and adaptation during repeated irradiation and assess evidence linking miRNA alterations to functional radiation responses. We also evaluate EV-associated extracellular RNA pathways and pathways reported as non-exosomal, separating cargo detection and cellular uptake from functional delivery and sustained resistance. Potential applications include radiosensitization through molecular targeting, circulating biomarkers, and therapeutic delivery. However, clinical translation requires standardized irradiation models, rigorous EV characterization, quantitative assessment of miRNA transfer, and independent clinical validation. Integrating intracellular mechanisms with intercellular signaling may clarify how radioresistance develops and persists, providing a framework for biomarker development and strategies tailored to tumor molecular characteristics. Clinical interpretation also depends on fractionation, molecular background and combined systemic treatments.

Article.Title: Evaluation of the Anti-Inflammatory Potential of Red Mustard, Red Cabbage, and Red Radish Sprout Extracts in an In Vitro Model of Human Macrophage-like Cells
Article.Authors: Martínez Pérez-Munar P.; García-Ibáñez P.; Oliva-Bolarín A.; Ramos-Molina B.; Moreno D.; Ruiz-Alcaraz A.; Núñez-Sánchez M.
Article.Abstract: Inflammation is a complex physiological process, crucial in the onset and progression of major non-communicable diseases. In view of the limitations of current therapeutic interventions, there is an increasing interest in the identification of natural compounds that possess effective anti-inflammatory properties. Cruciferous vegetables belonging to the Brassicaceae family, which are abundant in phenolics, glucosinolates and anthocyanins, are particularly noteworthy. However, further research is required to elucidate the molecular mechanisms mediating their biological activities. In this study, the anti-inflammatory properties of extracts derived from red mustard, red cabbage, and red radish sprouts were evaluated using an in vitro HL-60 derived macrophage-like cell model, which was employed to simulate a low-degree inflammatory state in response to lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Notably, treatment with the three Brassica extracts reduced IL-6 production, whereas a significant reduction in TNFα levels was observed only following treatment with red radish extract, as measured by ELISA. These findings were further corroborated by RT-qPCR analysis, which revealed a decrease in the IL6 gene expression following treatment with red radish extract. The esults of the present study highlight the potential of Brassica extracts as effective modulators of inflammation, providing a strong foundation for the development of future therapeutic strategies based on these natural bioactive compounds.

Article.Title: Isoform Switching as a Regulatory Mechanism of Glycolytic Reprogramming in Cancer
Article.Authors: Procopciuc L.; Lucaciu R.; Hangan A.
Article.Abstract: Cancer-associated metabolic reprogramming is a dynamic process that supports tumor growth, adaptation, and therapeutic resistance. Among the post-transcriptional mechanisms contributing to this plasticity, alternative splicing has emerged as an important regulator of glycolytic metabolism by generating transcript and protein isoforms with distinct biochemical and regulatory properties. This review examines the molecular mechanisms linking alternative splicing to cancer glycolysis, with particular emphasis on pyruvate kinase M1/pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM1/PKM2) isoform regulation as the best-characterized, but context-dependent, model of splice-associated metabolic control rather than as a universal tumor-specific switch. Additional splice-dependent mechanisms affecting glycolysis-related enzymes, transporters, receptors, and regulatory proteins further illustrate that the metabolic impact of alternative splicing extends beyond PKM and may influence glucose uptake, glycolytic enzyme activity, pyruvate fate, and lactate metabolism. The review further highlights the regulatory roles of key RNA-binding proteins and splicing factors, together with upstream oncogenic signaling pathways, in establishing cancer-associated splicing programs. Hypoxia, glucose and energy stress, lactate-dependent protein lactylation, and oxidative stress can modify spliceosomal activity and splicing-factor function, whereas extracellular acidosis is better regarded as a potential modulatory input whose independent role in splice-site selection remains less firmly established. Functionally, splicing-driven glycolytic remodeling contributes to tumor growth, metabolic adaptation, invasion, metastasis, cancer stemness, and therapy resistance. Therapeutically, the splicing–glycolysis axis may be exploited through modulation of the splicing machinery, antisense oligonucleotide-mediated splice switching, isoform-directed strategies, and combined or synthetic-lethal approaches targeting splice-induced metabolic dependencies. Future studies integrating isoform-resolved transcriptomics with proteomics, metabolomics, spatial and single-cell approaches, and metabolic flux analysis will be essential for distinguishing functionally relevant splice variants from non-functional transcript diversity and for identifying clinically actionable metabolic vulnerabilities.

Article.Title: Translational Study on the Effects of Janus Kinase Inhibitors on Interstitial Lung Disease Complicated with Rheumatoid Arthritis
Article.Authors: Kojima H.; Nakamura H.; Maeda K.; Sakurai K.; Tanioka T.; Miyatani M.; Wakabayashi K.; Miwa Y.; Iyoda M.; Isozaki T.
Article.Abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. This study evaluated the 1-year retention rates of Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors in patients with RA-ILD and investigated their effects in experimental pulmonary fibrosis and human lung fibroblasts. Pulmonary fibrosis was induced by bleomycin (BLM) in C57BL/6J mice, followed by treatment with BAR, PEF, or FIL. STAT1, STAT3, and STAT5 phosphorylation and the production of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), transforming growth factor-β1, and fractalkine were assessed. JAK inhibitor 1-year retention rates did not differ significantly between patients with and without RA-ILD. In the BLM model, BAR attenuated pulmonary inflammation, preserved body weight, and improved survival compared with PEF and FIL. In NHLFs, BAR most effectively suppressed IL-6-induced STAT3 phosphorylation and VEGF production. These findings suggest that BAR may exert protective effects in experimental pulmonary fibrosis through suppression of the IL-6/STAT3/VEGF axis.

Article.Title: Bioinformatic Analysis of Brain Region Proteomes in a Mice Model of Affective Disorders Annotated Using Panther GO
Article.Authors: Smirnova L.; Smirnova K.; Zavialova M.; Ermakov E.; Seregin A.; Epimakhova E.; Brzhozovskiy A.; Amstislavskaya T.; Ivanova S.
Article.Abstract: The proteomic approach to studying the pathogenesis of affective disorders is becoming increasingly effective, thanks to bioinformatics tools. However, investigating changes occurring in the brain is primarily possible only through animal models. In all brain structures examined in mice with a model of affective disorders, specific signaling pathways were identified that primarily involve neurotransmitter and neuroendocrine systems and participate in immune and inflammatory responses, as well as in processes regulating oxidative stress and vesicular transport. Thus, for the first time, qualitative changes in the brain proteome have been identified in the Q31L mice model of affective disorders, compared to wild-type mice. These preliminary results will serve as a foundation for further investigation into the mechanisms underlying disorders associated with the dysfunction of the Disc1 gene.

Article.Abstract: Mucopolysaccharidosis IVA (MPS IVA; Morquio A syndrome) is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfate sulfatase (GALNS), in which current therapies incompletely correct skeletal disease because enzyme delivery to avascular cartilage is limited. Irradiated REC-MSC feeder layers supported 2.59-fold mHSPCAAVS1 expansion and a 1.96-fold higher proportion of EGFP-positive cells. Article.Title: The Post-Translational Modification-Mediated Regulation of Oxidative Stress in Bone Metabolism
Article.Authors: Zou Y.; Weng Y.; Yan Y.; Wu S.; Ye X.; Yan H.; Ma D.
Article.Abstract: Bone remodeling depends on the dynamic equilibrium between osteogenic and osteoclastic processes, and its imbalance is considered one of the important foundations for the occurrence of bone metabolic diseases such as osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and inflammation-related bone destruction, and may contribute to promoting their development. Oxidative stress can disrupt intracellular redox homeostasis through excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), inhibit osteoblast differentiation and promote osteoclast activation, driving bone metabolism from a homeostatic toward a pathological state. In recent years, the roles of protein post-translational modifications (PTMs) in the regulation of oxidative stress have attracted increasing attention. By modulating the activity and stability of oxidative stress-related proteins, PTMs constitute an upstream regulatory tier of oxidative stress at multiple levels, including ROS generation, antioxidant defense, and mitochondrial function, and subsequently influence the differentiation and function of osteoblasts and osteoclasts. This review systematically summarizes the mechanisms by which major PTMs, including O-GlcNAcylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, phosphorylation, methylation, SUMOylation, and succinylation, participate in bone metabolism through the regulation of oxidative stress, and outlines recent advances in small-molecule compounds targeting PTM-mediated regulation of oxidative stress for bone protection. This review concludes that although different PTMs act on distinct targets, they largely converge on a common pathway whereby altered protein modification status regulates cellular redox levels and modulates bone metabolic phenotypes. It also emphasizes that elucidating the molecular mechanisms of bone metabolic abnormalities from the perspective of PTM-mediated regulation of oxidative stress may provide novel insights into the mechanistic understanding and targeted intervention of bone metabolic diseases.

Article.Authors: Baeza M.; Gomez M.; Veloso C.; Alcaino J.
Article.Abstract: Fungal communities inhabiting high-altitude environments are exposed to multiple environmental constraints, yet their diversity and genomic characteristics remain poorly characterized. Here, we investigated fungal diversity across 10 high-altitude localities in the Chilean Altiplano and Central Mountain region using ITS amplicon sequencing, complemented by comparative genomic analyses of 11 yeast isolates. Fungal communities were evaluated based on taxonomic composition, alpha diversity, co-occurrence patterns, and relationships among sampling localities. Yeast isolates were analyzed using genomic similarity, synteny, functional profiles, stress-associated proteins, enzyme homologs, and mitochondrial genome characteristics. Ascomycota was the dominant phylum, but fungal community composition and alpha diversity varied among localities, with geographic structuring evident at the genus level. Genome-scale analyses supported the classification of three isolates as Sporobolomyces salmonicolor and eight as Naganishia spp., highlighting the value of genome-based approaches for resolving taxonomic relationships. Functional profiles were broadly conserved, but differences in GPI-anchor biosynthesis, galactose metabolism, steroid biosynthesis, and mitophagy were detected between isolates. In addition, stress-related and potentially biotechnologically relevant enzyme homologs were identified. Initial characterization of the putative mitochondrial genome assemblies revealed a conserved core of oxidative phosphorylation genes, alongside apparent variation in intron content and ORF repertoire, suggesting potential mitochondrial genomic diversity. Together, these findings demonstrate substantial ecological and genomic diversity among fungi from high-altitude environments in Chile and reveal functional and genomic features that may be relevant to environmental adaptation and biotechnology.

Article.Title: LAT1 Inhibition with JPH203 Modifies Early Cellular Responses to X-Ray Irradiation in TPC-1 Thyroid Cancer Cells
Article.Authors: Kotani A.; Monzen S.; Tatara M.; Wojcik A.; Mariya Y.
Article.Abstract: The L-type amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1), encoded by the SLC7A5 gene, supports cancer-cell growth and nutrient-sensitive signaling. Although LAT1 inhibition has been reported to enhance radiosensitivity in some cancer models, its role in thyroid cancer radiation responses remains unclear. We investigated the association of SLC7A5 with thyroid differentiation and examined whether JPH203 treatment modifies X-ray responses in TPC-1 thyroid cancer cells. SLC7A5 expression, thyroid differentiation score (TDS), and progression-free interval (PFI) were analyzed using The Cancer Genome Atlas thyroid carcinoma dataset. TPC-1 cells were treated with JPH203 and X-ray irradiation. Clonogenic survival and senescence-associated β-galactosidase signal were assessed as longer-term outcomes, whereas cell-cycle distribution, apoptosis, and ribosomal protein S6 (RPS6) phosphorylation were evaluated during the early post-irradiation period. SLC7A5 expression was inversely correlated with TDS but was not significantly associated with PFI in either the overall cohort or the lower-TDS subgroup. JPH203 reduced clonogenic growth in a concentration-dependent manner but did not enhance X-ray-induced loss of clonogenic survival or senescence-associated β-galactosidase signal. In contrast, JPH203 modified early radiation responses, including G2/M accumulation and apoptotic responses. Combined JPH203 and X-ray treatment also altered total and phosphorylated RPS6 signals. JPH203 treatment modifies early cellular responses to X-ray irradiation in TPC-1 cells, but these changes did not translate into enhanced clonogenic radiosensitivity. These findings highlight a temporal dissociation between early radiation-response phenotypes and long-term reproductive cell survival.

Article.Title: REV-ERBα/β Disruption Drives Environmental Tobacco Smoke-Induced Cellular Senescence Associated with cGAS-STING Signaling Promoting Lung Remodeling
Article.Authors: Shaikh S.; Faizan M.; Islam K.; Lin K.; Wang Q.; Becker J.; Rahman M.; Panda K.; Chinnapaiyan S.; Li D.; Unwalla H.; Rahman I.
Article.Abstract: Cellular senescence and DNA damage are recognized contributors to smoke-induced lung injury. However, how these processes integrate with circadian regulation and innate immune sensing in response to environmental stressors remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify a conserved multi-lineage transcriptional program in murine lungs that we define as the SCPS axis, characterized by Suppressed Clock, Primed Senescence (SCPS), fibrinolytic Shutdown, and cGAS–STING activation. We show that environmental cigarette/tobacco smoke (ETS) exposure induces senescence and SASP factor production in both epithelial and fibroblast populations, even in the presence of an intact molecular clock. Spatial transcriptomic analysis of smoker lungs demonstrates parallel alterations marked by increased expression of senescence-associated genes, activation of DNA damage and innate immune sensors, and repression of core clock genes, particularly within AT2 cells and fibroblasts. Similarly, REVα/β-deficient mice reveal altered lung circadian, cGAS–STING, senescence, and transcriptional programs. Pharmacological clearance of senescent cells effectively reverses these molecular and cellular phenotypes. Together, these findings reveal early epithelial remodeling and fibrotic priming during environmental tobacco smoke exposure and establish a mechanistic link between senescence, circadian disruption, and innate immune activation associated with the cGAS-STING pathway as the SCPS axis for early checkpoint of fibrotic susceptibility.

Article.Title: 5-Azacytidine Reprograms Colorectal Cancer Cells Toward Senolytic Vulnerability and Enhanced T-Cell-Mediated Cytotoxicity
Article.Authors: Lisitsa D.; Kolosova E.; Budkina N.; Petrova V.; Demidov O.; Bogdanova D.
Article.Abstract: Aberrant DNA methylation is a hallmark of colorectal cancer (CRC) and represents a potential therapeutic target. DNA methyltransferase inhibitors can induce sustained transcriptional and phenotypic reprogramming of tumor cells; however, the therapeutic vulnerabilities created by this reprogramming are not completely understood. Here, we investigated the effects of 5-azacitidine (5-AZA) in the human CRC cell lines HT-29 and DLD-1 and assessed whether epigenetic priming could subsequently be exploited using senolytic or immunotherapeutic approaches. Treatment with 5-AZA reduced cell proliferation and induced a senescent phenotype accompanied by increased expression of the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors CDKN1A and CDKN2B and anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins as well as p16 expression on protein level. These changes were most pronounced in HT-29 cells. Pretreatment with 5-AZA sensitized HT-29 cells to navitoclax, a broad-spectrum BH3 mimetic, whereas the selective BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax was less effective. In DLD-1 cells, both the senescent phenotype and sensitization to navitoclax were less pronounced, indicating that the response to epigenetic priming is dependent on tumor-cell context. By contrast, in an in vitro immunotherapy model using DLD-1 tumor cells, lymphocytes and a bispecific CD19 × CD3 T-cell engager (BiTE), pretreatment of tumor cells with 5-AZA enhanced T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity and increased IFN-γ production. Thus, 5-AZA induces therapeutically relevant reprogramming of CRC cells, sensitizing them to navitoclax while simultaneously increasing their susceptibility to T-cell-mediated elimination. These findings provide a rationale for further investigation of sequential treatment strategies combining epigenetic priming with senolytic or immunotherapeutic approaches.

Article.Title: Integrative Review on Tripterygium wilfordii Hook. f.: Chemical Constituents, Pharmacology, Toxicology, and Efficacy–Toxicity Modulation Strategies
Article.Authors: Zhao J.; Li C.; Mou L.; Rao J.; Cao W.
Article.Abstract: Tripterygium wilfordii Hook. f. (TwHF) is a traditional Chinese medicinal herb, mainly used for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Recent pharmacological investigations have revealed that TwHF has a variety of pharmacological activities and therapeutic effects on various diseases. However, TwHF has certain toxicity, which limits its clinical application. Numerous previous reviews have separately summarized the chemical constituents, pharmacological functions, or toxic manifestations of TwHF. However, most published studies lack a systematic vertical correlation analysis linking chemical components, pharmacokinetic characteristics, pharmacological mechanisms, and toxicological profiles. Importantly, few reviews have focused on the core scientific issue of efficacy–toxicity balance, nor have they systematically explored the internal restrictive relationship between its therapeutic advantages and toxic side effects. Differing from previous generalized summaries, the present review takes the efficacy–toxicity relationship and its regulatory strategy as the unified core thread throughout the full text. This review systematically integrates the latest research progress on TwHF chemical composition, pharmacokinetic characteristics, multi-target pharmacological mechanisms, and toxicity mechanisms, and further focuses on analyzing the inherent causes of its efficacy–toxicity duality. Meanwhile, we comprehensively summarize current optimized efficacy-enhancing and detoxification strategies, including structural modification, carrier delivery optimization, and synergistic compatibility regulation, and clarify the technical bottlenecks and future optimization directions of existing detoxification technologies. This review may also provide a reference for the in-depth study of subsequent pharmacological mechanisms and the innovation of detoxification technologies.

Article.Title: Body Color, Nutritional Composition, and Metabolism of Two Color Morphs of Lugworm Perinereis aibuhitensis
Article.Authors: Shen C.; Zhu J.; Sun Q.; Ge Q.; Huang Y.; Cao C.; Zhao H.; Yang D.
Article.Abstract: Two distinct body color morphs of marine polychaete Perinereis aibuhitensis are commonly observed; however, the differences in pigmentation-related characteristics and energy metabolism between those two color morphs remain poorly understood. This study aimed to compare the histological characteristics, pigment content, pigment-related gene expression, nutritional composition, and metabolic responses of the two color morphs. The results showed that the green morph exhibited a higher density of pigment-containing cells in the epidermis, along with higher content of melanin together with high expression levels of tyrosinase (TYR) and C-type lectin, whereas the transcript of β-carotene 15 and carotene content was more highly expressed in the red morph. The red morph had higher crude protein and total amino acid contents, as well as higher levels of certain fatty acids, including docosahexaenoic acid. Oxygen consumption and ammonia excretion rates varied with temperature in both morphs, with the red morph exhibiting higher overall oxygen consumption and ammonia excretion rate from 12 to 25 °C. These findings demonstrate differences in pigmentation-related characteristics, nutritional composition, and metabolic responses between the two color morphs, providing a basis for further investigation of their underlying mechanisms and ecological significance.

Article.Title: Network Toxicology Combined with Multi-Omics Identifies GNMT and LGALS3 as Key Genes Linking PM2.5 Exposure to Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease
Article.Authors: Diao Y.; Hu H.; Liu X.; Wang L.; Xiang C.; Zhao J.; Kang B.; Peng D.
Article.Abstract: This study aimed to identify candidate molecular links bridging PM2.5 exposure and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and to elucidate their potential roles. A multifaceted approach was adopted in this study, integrating network toxicology, Mendelian randomization (MR), summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), multi-cohort transcriptomic validation, immune infiltration analysis, single-cell RNA sequencing, and molecular docking. PM2.5 targets and MASLD genes were collected from public databases. The eQTL data were used to assess potential causal associations via MR and SMR. Candidate genes were validated in three GEO datasets. Immune infiltration was analyzed with xCell, and single-cell transcriptomics assessed gene expression in immune subsets. Molecular docking was performed for PM2.5 components with target proteins. A total of 187 overlapping genes were identified, from which 10 hub genes were determined by protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis. MR and SMR analyses narrowed down the overlapping genes to GNMT and LGALS3, with GNMT showing a protective association (OR = 0.869, 95% CI: 0.794–0.951) and LGALS3 a risk association (OR = 1.773, 95% CI: 1.217–2.583). Immune infiltration analysis revealed increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells, B cells, and M2 macrophages in MASLD, and GNMT expression was found to be negatively correlated with CD4+ T cell infiltration. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding of selected organic compounds and metal ions to both GNMT and LGALS3. GNMT showed a protective role in PM2.5-associated MASLD, whereas LGALS3 showed a risk association. The differential expression patterns of these two genes in immune cells, together with their predicted interactions with PM2.5 components, point to a potential dual mechanism. Together, these findings provide novel insights into PM2.5-associated MASLD and identify potential molecular targets.

Article.Title: Dietary Interventions and Disease Outcomes in Finfish Feeding Trials Incorporating Host Transcriptomics: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Khang L.; Islam S.; Sutthakiet O.; Dinh-Hung N.; Permpoonpattana P.; Linh N.
Article.Abstract: Feed additives are widely used to enhance disease resistance in farmed fish, and transcriptomics is often used to explain their effects. However, whether feeding trials reporting diet-induced transcriptomic responses also show improved outcomes after infection remains unclear. We systematically reviewed finfish feeding trials combining host transcriptome-wide profiling with infectious challenge (PubMed and Scopus to 30 September 2026; protocol deposited retrospectively in Zenodo, 10.5281/zenodo.23934438). Disease outcomes and transcriptomic pathways were synthesized separately. Fifty-nine reports (54 trials, 24 species) were included. Meta-analysis of 36 comparisons from 35 trials (3280 fish) showed lower odds of post-challenge mortality with dietary interventions (odds ratio [OR] 0.24, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.16–0.35), but heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 78%) and the 95% prediction interval (0.03–1.75) included no effect. A three-level model (53 arms) gave a similar estimate (OR 0.30), and no moderator was significant. Bias-adjusted estimates from selection models and precision-effect testing included no effect. Pathogen burden favored the diet in 13 of 15 studies, and pathology in all 16 with a clear direction (one of 17 was mixed). Cytokine–chemokine, antigen presentation, NF-κB, MAPK and JAK–STAT pathways were reported most often, with no significant differences among diet categories. Randomization and allocation concealment were unclear in all studies; 17 were at high overall and 15 at high mortality-specific risk of bias, mainly owing to lack of tank replication. Dietary interventions may reduce post-challenge mortality, but the certainty of evidence is very low, and whether these transcriptomic responses contribute to protection remains untested.

Article.Title: Analyzing Globin Gene Variation in gnomAD: Implications for Variant Interpretation in Hemoglobinopathies
Article.Authors: Kontopoulou M.; Xenophontos M.; Lederer C.; Stephanou C.; Kountouris P.
Article.Abstract: Given the augmented sampling and ancestry stratification of the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) v4.1 compared with v2.1.1, population evidence for globin gene variants was assessed for changes in fulfillment of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology (ACMG/AMP) criteria, which can alter downstream variant interpretation. Variants and constraint metrics for α-globin locus genes HBA1, HBA2, and HBZ, and β-globin locus genes HBB, HBD, HBG1, HBG2, and HBE1, were extracted from gnomAD v2.1.1 and v4.1 callsets, harmonized, matched to ClinVar annotations, and evaluated for BA1, BS1, BS2, BS2_Supporting, and PM2_Supporting ACMG/AMP criteria fulfillment using Clinical Genome Resource Hemoglobinopathy Variant Curation Expert Panel thresholds. Globin gene variants increased fourfold between gnomAD releases, with HBB accounting for the largest share. In v4.1, 68.7% of quality-passing variants were ancestry-specific, 14.4% overlapped ClinVar and PM2_Supporting fulfillment rose from 81.5% to 93.5%. Among variants present in both releases, ACMG/AMP population-criterion assessments were largely concordant, with conflicting combinations in fewer than 1%. Leveraging augmented sampling and improved ancestry representation, gnomAD v4.1 increased globin gene variant discovery, particularly for rare variants, improving allele frequency estimation and assessment of BA1, BS1, and PM2_Supporting, although criterion fulfillment remains release- and callset-specific.

Article.Title: Network-Based Analysis Nominates Glucocorticoid Receptor Signaling as a Candidate Pathway in Mutant Androgen Receptor-Responsive SBMA Biology
Article.Authors: Pai T.; Hsiung C.; Lin W.; Liu Y.; Johnson K.; Grunseich C.; Chan Y.
Article.Abstract: Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA) is caused by polyglutamine expansion in the androgen receptor (AR), but the network-level organization linking AR dysfunction to downstream molecular abnormalities remains incompletely defined. Here, we used Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) to construct and compare two SBMA-related molecular networks: a canonical AR/SBMA network derived from IPA-curated SBMA-associated molecules and biomarker-derived nodes, and a mutant AR (mAR)-responsive network derived from published SBMA-relevant gene sets. The canonical AR/SBMA network was visually organized into endocrine, metabolic/mitochondrial, and structural/sarcomere-associated groups, with remaining nodes classified as uncategorized. The mAR-responsive network also contained descriptive groups, including mitochondrial metabolism, Wnt/neuromuscular junction (NMJ) organization, synaptic/G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling, redox stress, and proteostasis/chaperone response, with seven nodes classified as uncategorized. Expansion of these seven mAR-responsive nodes using IPA Grow and Connect functions highlighted glucocorticoid receptor (GR) signaling as the pathway with the largest molecular overlap in the expanded network (38 entities). Random-set sensitivity analyses assessed the AR/SBMA connectivity comparison. Complementary gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of public motor-neuron data showed enrichment of several GR-related gene sets toward higher expression in controls, providing exploratory support for further investigation of GR-related transcription. None of these signals reached significance with sample-label permutation. These findings nominate GR signaling as a network-derived candidate pathway for further investigation. This work provides a curated framework for prioritizing regulatory pathways associated with mAR-responsive molecular changes in SBMA. The analysis is hypothesis-generating, and input-selection bias requires cautious interpretation. Experimental studies are needed to determine whether GR contributes to SBMA.

Article.Title: Interaction Mechanism Between Grass Carp (Ctenopharyngodon idella) Fish Maw Collagen and Heavy-Metal Ions
Article.Authors: Feng Q.; Xu W.; Yan X.; Ramaswamy H.; Azarakhsh N.; Wang C.
Article.Abstract: Heavy-metal residues in fish maw are closely associated with its collagen fraction, yet the binding behavior and molecular mechanism of grass carp (Ctenopharyngodon idella) fish maw collagen toward common metal ions remain poorly characterized. To address this, hot-water-soluble collagen (HSC) and acetic acid soluble collagen (ASC) were extracted and characterized via SDS-PAGE, UV spectroscopy, zeta-potential measurement and amino acid analysis. Adsorption isotherms, fluorescence, CD and SEM-EDX were used to probe binding with Cu(II), Hg(II), Cd(II), and Cr(III). Dried fish maw contained 56.907 ± 0.319 g/100 g of protein and 25.01% collagen. In the four-ion mixed competitive system containing Cu(II), Hg(II), Cd(II) and Cr(III), the Langmuir and Freundlich models were applied only as empirical fitting tools, and the fitted parameters are apparent values under competition. Cd(II) showed the highest apparent adsorption capacity, while Cu(II), Cr(III) and Hg(II) exhibited stronger apparent affinity; Cu(II), Hg(II) and Cd(II) were better described by the Langmuir model, whereas Cr(III) was better described by the Freundlich model. Cu(II), Cr(III), and Hg(II) triggered static fluorescence quenching. The binding of Cr(III) and Hg(II) may involve hydrophobic interactions, while the binding of Cu(II) may involve hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces, and it may also result from the non-specific intermolecular aggregation of collagen induced by Cu(II). Low-concentration Cr(III) disrupted collagen ellipticity bands and induced disordered conformations. This work deepens the mechanistic understanding of heavy-metal binding to fish maw collagen and offers fundamental insights for future relevant research.

Article.Title: Prioritizing Sarcopenia-Related Genes from Cross-Trait Candidate Regions: Regulatory Variant Mapping and Phenome-Wide Mendelian Randomization
Article.Authors: Wang L.; Zhang L.; Zhang S.
Article.Abstract: Sarcopenia involves declines in muscle mass, muscle strength, and physical function. Identifying effector genes, their favourable expression directions, and broader phenotypic associations from genome-wide association study (GWAS) signals remains challenging. We integrated GWAS summary statistics for hand grip strength (HGS) and appendicular lean mass (ALM) with H3K27ac annotation, AlphaGenome variant effect predictions, and skeletal muscle expression data. We then applied cis-eQTL Mendelian randomization (MR) and colocalization across HGS, ALM, low hand grip strength (LHGS), and usual walking pace. Across 59 HGS–ALM cross-trait candidate regions, AlphaGenome predicted 2288 regulatory variants among 16,245 candidate enhancer SNPs and nominated 135 protein-coding effector genes. Four-trait MR identified 30 genes with significant causal effects, including 13 with concordant effect directions across multiple traits. FGF6, CCND2, and HOXB3 also received strong colocalization support. Phenome-wide MR across 784 UK Biobank disease phenotypes revealed distinct benefit–risk profiles for 7 genes. Higher CCND2 expression improved sarcopenia-related traits and reduced type 2 diabetes risk but increased the risks of parathyroid disease and atrial fibrillation and flutter. Higher HOXB3 expression increased HGS and reduced the risks of LHGS and diverticular disease. Lower FGF6 expression increased ALM, with no risk-increasing effect detected. This workflow prioritizes skeletal muscle effector genes and their favourable expression directions for sarcopenia-related traits to guide functional validation and translation.

Article.Title: An Umbrella Review on Psychological Stress and Infertility
Article.Authors: Pantos K.; Trypidi A.; Papadogkonas G.; Maziotis E.; Tsagkaraki D.; Androutsopoulou M.; Ashiku K.; Pantou A.; Chronopoulou M.; Griva T.; Simopoulou M.; Sfakianoudis K.
Article.Abstract: This umbrella review reports on biological mechanisms and synthesizes evidence from 88 systematic reviews and meta-analyses on stress, infertility, medically assisted reproduction (MAR) outcomes and management. Stress-induced activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis predominantly suppresses reproductive function in animal models; nonetheless, human data remain heterogeneous. Infertility was consistently associated with substantial psychological burden, with pooled prevalence of depression and anxiety in infertile women ranging between 31.6 and 48.8% and 36.2 and 41%, respectively, with higher levels in women than men. Psychological burden increases during MAR as well as after unsuccessful treatment. Psychological stress adversely affects semen parameters and menstrual regularity, while evidence on MAR outcomes was inconsistent. Despite reducing depression and anxiety, stress cognitive–behavioral therapy and mindfulness’s impact on pregnancy rates remains uncertain. Overall confidence was critically low, with substantial heterogeneity and overlap. This analysis highlights a biologically plausible but methodologically not validated bidirectional association, underlining the need for standardized stress assessment, longitudinal designs, and a multidisciplinary approach to elucidate causality. This leaves both the MAR specialist and the infertile patient in unchartered territory. Future studies should focus on how to navigate this zone by addressing the anticipated impact of psychological stress on infertility or, ideally, alleviating it as part of preconception care.

Article.Title: Mapping Human Tissue-Enriched Genes Across Multiple Normal Tissues Using a One-Versus-All DESeq2 Framework
Article.Authors: Kulski J.; Koks S.
Article.Abstract: Tissue-enriched gene expression programs contribute to organ identity and provide foundational reference profiles for interpreting tissue-of-origin molecular signatures. In this study, we re-analysed the dataset E-MTAB-2836 RNA-seq archive, comprising 205 samples from 32 tissues and 122 donors, using a one-versus-all DESeq2 analysis. Genes meeting a false discovery rate (FDR) F < 0.05 were considered statistically significant irrespective of the direction of the fold change. To characterise the positive tissue-enrichment spectrum, 23,639 genes with positive log2FC values were subsequently identified and ranked according to effect size and tissue-enrichment recurrence, with recurrence ranging from one to seven tissues. The number of positively tissue-enriched genes varied substantially among tissues, revealing marked differences in the extent of tissue-associated gene expression across the human body. Cross-dataset concordance was assessed using the independent GTEx v11 dataset, comprising 19,616 samples across 30 tissues. Only 22 of the 30 GTEx tissues examined overlapped with the E-MTAB-2836 tissues. However, genes identified as positively tissue-enriched in these 22 E-MTAB-2836 tissues generally showed concordant tissue-associated expression patterns in the overlapping GTEx tissues, with significant positive correlations between corresponding log2 fold-change values. As a complementary analysis, conventional expression-based Tau scores were calculated from tissue-level mean expression values to describe the relative distribution of 27,958 genes across the 32 tissues, with a median score of 0.84. Together, these analyses provide a practical framework for comparative mapping of tissue-enriched genes and a reference resource for tissue-informed investigations of gene expression and potential disease-associated molecular signatures.

Article.Title: Suppression-Associated Immune Programs in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Beyond Effector Enrichment: A Multi-Cohort Transcriptomic Analysis
Article.Authors: Al Omair S.; Almsned F.
Article.Abstract: High immune-cell infiltration does not guarantee effective anti-tumor immunity. Suppression of anti-tumor immunity may explain the variable prognosis and immunotherapy response of immune-inflamed triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). We asked whether suppression-associated transcriptional signals merely accompanied effector-rich infiltration or retained a distinct association with TNBC across cohorts. Across TCGA-BRCA (discovery, n = 728), METABRIC (replication, n = 1980), and a Saudi exploratory cohort (n = 38), we evaluated a predefined effector immunity composite, an immunoregulatory cell-enrichment composite, and a six-gene suppressive myeloid-associated transcriptional score (CSF3R, OLR1, C5AR1, CLEC4E, ARG2, S100A8). In TCGA-BRCA, the effector immunity composite and six-gene score were both elevated and co-varied strongly (Spearman ρ = 0.66). Notably, the six-gene score remained associated with TNBC after adjustment for effector enrichment and age. The immunoregulatory cell-enrichment composite showed no significant difference, with opposing shifts among its components. In METABRIC, the main findings replicated and all three programs were elevated; the Saudi cohort showed concordant elevation. In a post hoc joint model with all three programs and age, the six-gene score remained positively associated with TNBC in TCGA-BRCA (OR 2.37) and METABRIC (OR 1.27). The six-gene score thus captured reproducible TNBC-associated variation beyond effector enrichment. Our findings motivate investigating whether this myeloid–effector interplay relates to TNBC prognosis and therapy response.

Article.Title: Recent Advances in the Structure and Transduction Mechanisms of PIEZO Channels
Article.Authors: Feng Z.; Song H.; Huang J.; Hu Y.; He J.; Yi L.; Liu X.; Yu R.
Article.Abstract: The PIEZO channel is a mechanically sensitive ion channel that plays a crucial role in converting mechanical stimuli into biological signals. The discovery of the mechanically gated ion channel PIEZO represents a milestone breakthrough in the field of cellular mechanical signal transduction. As a mechanically sensitive channel, PIEZO1/2 can directly respond to changes in biomembrane tension, mediate cation influx, and regulate various physiological and pathological processes. Structural analysis reveals that the PIEZO protein has a unique “three bladed propeller” homotrimeric structure. The mechanical sensing domain and ion pore in its transmembrane topology work in concert, laying the foundation for force transmission. In terms of transduction mechanisms, the PIEZO channel senses mechanical force through dual mechanisms of “lipid bilayer gating” and “cytoskeletal traction”. The curvature sensitivity of the blade domain enables it to sense changes in membrane tension and trigger conformational changes in the pore to achieve ion flow. This article reviews the discovery process, structural features, and research progress in the transduction mechanism of the PIEZO channel, providing a theoretical reference for a deeper understanding of mechanical signal transduction and related disease treatment strategies.

Article.Title: Dopamine Transporter Deficiency and Altered Glucose Homeostasis: Insights from DAT-Heterozygous Rats and Public Transcriptomic Data Analysis
Article.Authors: Kanov E.; Fomicheva A.; Fesenko Z.; Sylko P.; Gainetdinov R.; Volnova A.; Vaganova A.
Article.Abstract: Dopamine regulates pleiotropic physiological processes, and its multifunctional nature is hypothesized to underlie the comorbidity between systemic disorders. For instance, neurodevelopmental conditions, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), are frequently accompanied by metabolic diseases that cannot be explained solely by lifestyle factors. We performed a secondary analysis of dopaminergic gene co-expression networks using large (N > 20) public RNA-seq datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) repository to explore the potential links between the islet dopaminergic system and secretory activity. Additionally, pancreatic islet hormone levels and carbohydrate metabolism parameters were evaluated in an animal model of dopamine system dysfunction: heterozygous dopamine transporter gene knockout (DAT-Het) rats. No significant differences were observed in baseline serum glucose, insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin levels between DAT-Het rats and wild-type (WT) littermates. However, during a glucose tolerance test, DAT-Het rats exhibited a slight but significant decrease in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) serum levels and relative glucose levels 15 min after a glucose load. These findings indicate more active tissue glucose uptake in DAT-Het rats, potentially linking dopamine system dysfunction to both a neurodevelopmental phenotype and metabolic susceptibility. However, the precise role of pancreatic islets in this identified shift in glucose tolerance warrants further investigation.

Article.Title: Integrative Analysis of Whole-Exome Sequencing and Machine Learning Reveals Rare Genetic Signatures Associated with Chronic Insomnia Disorder
Article.Authors: Xie X.; Chen Y.; Wu C.; Lyu H.; Gong L.
Article.Abstract: Chronic insomnia disorder (CID) is a prevalent condition with a substantial public health burden, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. In this study, we performed whole-exome sequencing in a Chinese cohort comprising 51 patients with CID and 51 healthy controls to characterize single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), insertions/deletions (Indels), and copy number variants (CNVs). We observed differences in variant distributions between the groups and identified several candidate genes through rare functional variant screening and gene-level analyses. The functional annotation and enrichment analyses highlighted biological processes involving sensory perception, steroid and lipid metabolism, and xenobiotic responses. The exploratory CNV analyses identified several recurrent genomic regions, including a chromosome 22 interval involving GSTT1 and related genes. Furthermore, the machine learning analysis identified a panel of 145 rare SNPs mapping to 68 genes, including 42 exploratory candidates. The support vector machine classifier achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.737 in the held-out test set. In summary, these findings characterize candidate genetic features associated with CID in this cohort and provide a basis for future functional investigation and independent evaluation of multi-variant genetic classification approaches.

Article.Title: Time-Dependent Transcriptional Programs During Odontogenic Induction of Human Dental Pulp Cells
Article.Authors: Uslu Tekce A.; Akman A.; Sucularli C.
Article.Abstract: Odontogenic differentiation of human dental pulp cells involves coordinated molecular changes; however, temporal transcriptional programs remain incompletely characterized. This study investigated time-dependent transcriptional responses to odontogenic induction and performed an exploratory cross-dataset consistency assessment. In GSE112144, RNA from three donors was pooled per condition and analyzed on two technical arrays. Condition-level log2 expression differences were used for descriptive pre-ranked gene set enrichment analysis. Day 14-derived gene sets and signatures were evaluated in GSE244057, comparing Day 9 induced cells with Day 0 baseline cells without a time-matched non-induced control. Early induction showed enrichment of zinc-homeostasis and detoxification gene sets, whereas later induction showed enrichment of chromosome-segregation, cell-cycle, and DNA-replication programs. Technical-array sensitivity analyses showed stable enrichment directions but could not assess biological reproducibility. Excluding metallothionein genes weakened zinc-homeostasis enrichment and rendered two related gene sets untestable, demonstrating substantial MT contributions. Cross-dataset analysis revealed limited gene set-level concordance (Spearman ρ = −0.135), although nine of ten signatures changed in the discovery-expected direction; the cell-cycle signature showed the opposite direction. Five shared metallothionein genes showed positive induction-associated expression differences at Day 1 and Day 14, while MT1E, MT1M, and MT1X showed significantly higher expression in Day 9 induced samples than Day 0 baseline samples in GSE244057. In conclusion, odontogenic induction was associated with distinct time-dependent transcriptional programs.

Article.Title: XLOS-Observed P151L MID1 Mutation Resulted in a Gain of E3 Ligase Activity Due to a Difference in Interaction with the Ube2D1 E2 Enzyme
Article.Authors: Kaur A.; Wright K.; Karuaho J.; Lahtela-Kakkonen M.; Massiah M.
Article.Abstract: The human midline-1 (MID1) protein is an important E3 ubiquitin ligase that regulates cellular homeostasis by catalyzing the ubiquitination of protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A), alpha4 (α4), and Fu kinase. The E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of MID1 is mediated by its N-terminal zinc-binding RING and B-box1 domains. In contrast to the RING domain, which promotes poly-ubiquitination, the B-box1 domain predominantly catalyzes auto-mono-ubiquitination. Our current study provides insights into the molecular basis of enhanced mono- and poly-auto-ubiquitination associated with the X-linked Opitz syndrome (XLOS)-observed P151L mutation in the MID1 B-box1 domain compared with the wild-type (WT) protein. Structural studies revealed that this gain of activity is likely due to a different binding mechanism with the Ube2D1 E2 enzyme compared with the WT B-box1. NMR spectroscopy and predictive modeling revealed that while the overall global fold remains intact, the P151L mutation results in its central α-helix extending at its C-terminus and alters the dynamic properties of residues of loop 2, a critical region for interacting with the E2 enzyme. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations confirm the structural stability of P151L mutant and additionally revealed altered backbone conformations, indicating structural reorganization around the E2-interaction surface. These changes may provide an explanation for the altered Ube2D1 binding mode and impact the P151L mutant binding the Ube2D1 E2 enzyme on the opposite side to where the WT B-box1 binds and adjacent to the canonical RING:E2 interface. The binding interaction may also provide a rationale for why P151L MID1 is unable to polyubiquitinate α4.

Article.Title: FOXP3+ Cell Infiltration in Canine Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Clinicopathological Associations and Prognostic Significance
Article.Authors: Espíndula C.; Garcez F.; Monteiro L.; Delgado L.
Article.Abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are an important component of the tumor microenvironment (TME) but their role in canine oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains uncertain. We aimed to characterize the spatial distribution of cells expressing the Treg-associated marker forkhead box P3 (FOXP3) and investigate its relationship with clinical and histopathological parameters. Higher mean peritumoral and intratumoral FOXP3+ cell densities were associated with marked lymphoplasmacytic infiltration (p < 0.001 and p = 0.005, respectively), stronger lymphocytic host response (p = 0.002 and p = 0.009, respectively), higher mitotic scores (p < 0.001 and p = 0.001, respectively), and higher worst pattern of invasion categories (p < 0.001 and p = 0.002, respectively). Higher median peritumoral FOXP3+ cell density was associated with improved cancer-specific survival (p = 0.010), although only in univariate analysis. These findings highlight the importance of the spatial distribution of FOXP3+ cells in canine OSCC and suggest that their prognostic relevance may depend on their location within the tumor microenvironment, warranting further investigation of their potential as prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

Article.Title: Free-Living Amoebae in the Lower Gastrointestinal Tract and Feces of Vertebrates and the Usefulness of Traditional and Molecular Methods for Their Isolation and Identification
Article.Authors: Adamska M.
Article.Abstract: Free-living amoebae (FLA) are common in the environment, and some of them are pathogenic to animals and humans. The presence of FLA in the lower gastrointestinal tract and feces of vertebrates, and their role in the host organism, is a young field that requires further investigation. It is particularly important to determine how FLA enters the lower gastrointestinal tract of vertebrates and how it interacts with the host and other microorganisms that compose the gut microbiome. To this end, appropriate methods are needed. Earlier studies employed traditional methods, such as culture and microscopic observation, whereas more recent studies focus on molecular methods. This narrative review summarizes heterogeneous data on FLA occurrence in the lower gastrointestinal tract and feces of vertebrates, FLA genus and species composition, genetic diversity, and taxonomic classification. It also reviews the methods used in the analyzed papers to detect and identify FLA.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide CRISPR Screening Identifies NAPRT as a Key Regulator of Human Adipogenesis
Article.Authors: Liang R.; Fan S.; Ma S.; Ma W.; Zuo Z.; Zhong C.; Fei T.
Article.Abstract: Adipocyte differentiation is central to adipose-tissue homeostasis, but its regulatory landscape remains incompletely defined in human cells. Here, we perform a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen in oleic acid-differentiated human SW872 preadipocytes to identify functional regulators of white adipogenesis. The screens nominate hundreds of adipogenesis-regulating genes, and integration with human genetic evidence prioritizes nicotinate phosphoribosyltransferase (NAPRT) as a prominent player. NAPRT loss increases lipid accumulation and PPARγ abundance, reduces intracellular nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), and diminishes cytosolic β-catenin. Supplementation with nicotinamide mononucleotide restored NAD+ and partially reversed the signaling and adipogenic phenotypes, linking NAPRT-dependent NAD+ biosynthesis to WNT/β-catenin activity. Finally, deep learning-guided virtual screening nominates quinacrine as a candidate NAPRT inhibitor, and a lysate-based thermal shift assay shows quinacrine-dependent destabilization of NAPRT. These findings identify NAPRT as a metabolic regulator of human adipogenesis and connect NAD+ availability to WNT-dependent adipocyte fate control.
