Article.Title: Identification of the HD-ZIP Transcription Factor Family and Functional Analysis of CmHB40 in Castanea mollissima
Article.Authors: Cheng Y.; Cheng L.; Hu G.; Yang Q.; Lan Y.
Article.Abstract: Evidence has increasingly shown that the HB53/40/21 clade within HD-ZIP I plays an important role in floral organ development in plants. In this study, we performed genome-wide identification of HD-ZIP family members in Chinese chestnut Castanea mollissima using bioinformatics analysis, cloned the HB53/40/21 homologous gene CmHB40, and analyzed its expression pattern and subcellular localization. Using DAP-seq technology and yeast one-hybrid and dual-luciferase assays, we identified the DNA sequences bound by CmHB40 and its downstream target genes. We also verified the biological function of CmHB40 through heterologous overexpression. Our results demonstrate that CmHB40 shares a conserved molecular structure and DNA-binding capacity with HB53/40/21 homologs from other species. However, in Chinese chestnut, CmHB40 is predominantly expressed in male flowers, where it directly binds to the promoters of pollen exine and cuticular wax biosynthesis genes CmCER1 and CmABCG11, and upregulates their expression. However, overexpression of CmHB40 in Arabidopsisthaliana inhibited petal and stamen development. The expression of GA-related genes AtJUB1 and AtGA2ox2 was upregulated in transgenic individuals. From the above results, we infer that CmHB40 shares a conserved molecular structure with HB53/40/21 homologs from other species. We propose a regulatory model in which CmHB40 participates in flower development by upregulating the expression of CmCER1 and CmABCG11. This inference awaits verification once a genetic transformation system for Chinese chestnut has been established.

Article.Title: IgG-Mediated Hydrolysis of Neuregulin-1-Derived Peptides in 5xFAD Mice During the Development of Alzheimer’s Disease-like Pathology
Article.Authors: Tolmacheva A.; Aulova K.; Ermakov E.; Chicherina G.; Melamud M.; Timofeeva A.; Nevinsky G.
Article.Abstract: Synaptic dysfunction and neurodegeneration in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) are accompanied by neuroinflammation and peripheral immune activation. Activation of humoral immunity is known to be associated with the formation of catalytic antibodies capable of catalytically degrading various antigens. Given the key role of neuregulin-1 (NRG1) in synaptic function and inflammation, and the possible involvement of catalytic antibodies in AD pathogenesis, we investigated IgG-mediated hydrolysis of three NRG1 peptides corresponding to the linker region cleaved during NRG1 maturation (C22), a conserved segment of the EGF-like domain (EGF23), and a fragment of the EGF-like domain mediating integrin binding (Int22). The study was performed on a transgenic mouse model of AD, the 5xFAD line. Individual IgG preparations were isolated from blood and subsequently tested for peptidase activity against fluorescently labeled peptides using thin-layer chromatography and MALDI-TOF MS. During development of AD-like pathology, IgG from transgenic mice, unlike controls (C57BL/6 line), hydrolyzed all three peptides with increased efficiency. The relative activity of hydrolysis of C22 and EGF23 continuously increased with disease progression and reached a maximum at advanced stages, whereas the activity toward Int22 changed only slightly. At the onset of pathology, antibodies hydrolyzed C22 and EGF23 at two and one sites, respectively, whereas by the stage of advanced pathology, the number of cleavage sites for both peptides increased to eight, indicating a qualitative restructuring of the catalytic potential of IgG during the progression of AD.

Article.Abstract: This study aims to advance the development of metal-based antimicrobial materials by exploring the correlation between synthesis parameters and functional characteristics of sol–gel-derived TiO2/CuO/ZnO powders. The examined sample has a nominal composition of 80TiO2/10CuO/10ZnO. Following gel drying, the material was subjected to thermal treatment at 400 °C and 600 °C for 2 h. Structural and optical properties were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD), UV–Vis spectroscopy, infrared (IR) spectroscopy, DTA-TG and TEM-EDS. Antimicrobial activity against Escherichia coli ATCC 25922 and Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 25923 was evaluated through minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) assays and spot tests. The obtained results demonstrated strong antibacterial activity against the tested strain, indicating that the synthesized TiO2/CuO/ZnO materials are promising candidates for application as effective antimicrobial agents. The effect of the new materials on free-radical oxidation reactions was tested by the chemiluminescent method. At pH 8.5 (optimal), the nanomaterials demonstrated pronounced inhibitory activity against superoxide radical generation. At pH 7.4 (physiological), TiO2/CuO/ZnO (600 °C) can significantly stimulate the oxidation by H2O2, which can be attributed to its composition. Such opposing activities controlled by pH enable various applications. Acute toxicity tests with Daphnia magna (OECD 202) showed that the sample calcined at 600 °C was the most toxic after 48 h, consistent with its higher redox activity.

Article.Title: The Role of Autophagy in Aging and Longevity: A Comprehensive Review of Therapeutic Strategies to Modulate Autophagy and Promote Healthy Aging
Article.Authors: Theekshana K.; Gunawardane D.; Kodikara C.; Karunathilake N.; Senerath I.; Seneviratne T.; Rathnayake M.; Ediriweera M.; Peiris D.
Article.Abstract: Aging is associated with alterations in cellular homeostasis, including age-related dysregulation of autophagic capacity and flux. Autophagy is an essential catabolic process that clears damaged organelles and aggregated proteins; however, with age, changes in this process, including alterations in autophagosome formation, lysosomal degradation, selective autophagy, or the capacity to maintain autophagic flux under stress, may occur. These changes are implicated in the pathogenesis of diseases like Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and cancer. Autophagy is highly regulated by nutrition-sensing pathways, principally through the inhibitory action of mTORC1 (Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin Complex 1) and the activating role of AMPK (AMP-activated Protein Kinase). Consequently, strategies aimed at boosting autophagy hold significant potential, ranging from lifestyle modifications such as caloric restriction and exercise to pharmacological agents like rapamycin and metformin. Additionally, other natural compounds, such as spermidine and resveratrol, exhibit similar effects. By synthesizing the molecular mechanisms, regulatory networks, and therapeutic strategies, we highlight the critical importance of modulating autophagy to extend healthspan and develop targeted therapies against age-related decline.

Article.Title: Beyond PVR: A Dual-Branch Parallel-Resistance Model Integrating Intrapulmonary Arteriovenous Anastomoses and Gas Exchange
Article.Authors: Vanni R.
Article.Abstract: Evaluating drug efficacy in pulmonary hypertension (PH) relies on decreased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), which can be misleading if the role of intrapulmonary arteriovenous anastomoses (IPAVA) is neglected. In this secondary, cross-cohort computational reanalysis of experimental data from healthy subjects, pulmonary circulation with open IPAVA was modeled as a parallel circuit featuring model-derived branch resistance—exchanging pathway resistance (RQ˙p) and IPAVA resistance (RQ˙IPAVA)—to establish a dual-branch parallel framework. This model was evaluated against acetazolamide (ACZ) vs placebo experimental data during hypoxia (FIO2 = 0.125) at rest and during heavy exercise under normoxia. Under resting hypoxia, ACZ decreased PVR (−0.25 WU vs. placebo), but there was a marked concomitant decrease in RQ˙IPAVA (−21.47 WU), which masked an underlying increase in RQ˙p (+ 0.15 WU) and a reduction in capillary flow (Q˙p = −1.08 L/min). Despite the lower expired V˙CO2, the microvascular CO2 extraction efficiency (ϵ =V˙CO2/Q˙p) increased by 16.8% under ACZ. During heavy normoxic exercise, ACZ increased the shunt fraction (Q˙IPAVA/Q˙T) from 2.4% to ~15% of cardiac output (Q˙T), reducing Q˙p by 11.3% and V˙CO2 by 8.7%, whereas ϵ remained stable (+ 3.0% under ACZ). The stability or increase in ϵ supports the hypothesis that reduced expired V˙CO2 is driven by microvascular flow diversion (Q˙p ↓, Q˙IPAVA ↑) rather than enzymatic carbonic anhydrase inhibition. Evaluating drug efficacy solely on the basis of PVR may provide an incomplete assessment of microvascular flow perfusion. Integrating hemodynamic parameters with Lavoisier’s mass balance offers a testable computational model to distinguish functional capillary perfusion from bypass recruitment in pulmonary vascular research.

Article.Title: Identification of Senescence-Associated RNA Editing as a Potential Biomarker for Senescence and Aging
Article.Authors: Kim H.; Paidimukkala N.; Kummerfeld E.; Robbins P.; Aliferis C.; Niedernhofer L.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: RNA editing is a post-transcriptional process that alters RNA nucleotide sequences, potentially affecting protein coding and RNA function. Approximately 92% of these sites were located within Alu elements, predominantly in 3’ untranslated regions (3’ UTRs), suggesting widespread post-transcriptional regulatory remodeling during senescence. Numerous senescence-associated editing events exhibited elevated editing levels in tissues from older individuals in the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project. Among these events, F11 receptor (F11R) mRNA editing was observed across multiple tissues and exhibited higher editing levels in older individuals, showing a more consistent association with aging than F11R gene expression in human tissues. These findings reveal transcriptome-wide RNA editing patterns associated with cellular senescence and suggest that RNA editing may provide a complementary layer of molecular information for studying aging and senescence-related molecular changes.

Article.Title: Artificial Intelligence in Drug-Safety and Toxicity Assessment: Molecular Determinants and Bridging Preclinical Signals to Patient Safety
Article.Authors: Madipally D.; Pathi J.; Burgener M.; Bhagurkar P.
Article.Abstract: The accurate prediction of drug-safety risks remains a major challenge in drug development, particularly for biologics and advanced therapeutic modalities, for which complex molecular and cellular interactions can contribute to immune and toxicological responses. Preclinical approaches have limitations in predicting human safety outcomes because of species-specific differences, incomplete characterization of molecular mechanisms, and limited integration of heterogeneous data. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) provide computational approaches for analyzing molecular, preclinical, bioanalytical, clinical, and real-world safety data. This review critically examines AI/ML applications across the drug-safety continuum, with particular emphasis on immunogenicity as a molecularly driven safety consideration for biologic therapeutics. Applications in peptide–HLA-binding and antigen-presentation modeling, anti-drug antibody-risk assessment, hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, systems toxicology, and pharmacovigilance are evaluated with attention to biological endpoint, validation strategy, and translational relevance. We further examine sources of failure in translating molecular and preclinical predictions to human outcomes, the role of multimodal and hybrid mechanistic–AI approaches, and the evidentiary requirements for increasingly consequential applications. Finally, we discuss regulatory considerations and emerging patient-specific frameworks, including digital safety twins, while distinguishing currently feasible supportive applications from approaches that remain preliminary or conceptual. Collectively, the evidence indicates that progress toward clinically useful AI-enabled safety assessment will depend not only on predictive performance but also on mechanistic relevance, independent and prospective validation, uncertainty characterization, and clearly defined contexts of use.

Article.Title: Urinary Biomarkers in Traumatic Brain Injury: A Systematic Review
Article.Authors: Ding X.; Deng Y.; Gao G.; Wu L.
Article.Abstract: An accurate diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring of traumatic brain injury (TBI) require non-invasive, objective metrics. This systematic review evaluates the clinical utility of urinary biomarkers across the TBI spectrum. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed and Web of Science and identified 25 empirical human studies after applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria. The included studies fell into four categories as follows: central nervous system structural and glial proteins, metabolomic and volatile signatures, peptidomic and systemic indicators, and emerging targets. Urinary S100B was associated with injury severity and, in one severe-TBI cohort, with one-month mortality at an area under the curve of 0.778, yet its discriminative value in mild TBI was limited by delayed renal excretion and pre-analytical confounders. Metabolomic and peptidomic panels showed promising classification accuracy in small cohorts, and early urinary liver-type fatty acid-binding protein and a depressed urine-to-serum osmolality ratio signaled secondary renal and neuroendocrine complications. Evidence for microRNAs, glycans, and the p75 neurotrophin receptor remains preliminary. Heterogeneity in sampling timing, normalization, and cohort composition, together with single-center designs and risk of bias, precludes clinical implementation. Standardized pre-analytical protocols and multicenter validation of multiplexed panels are required before urinary testing can support clinical decision-making.

Article.Title: Endogenous Neuronal-like Phenotypic Remodeling of Astrocyte-Associated Cells in the Ischemic Cortex After Stroke
Article.Authors: Li J.; Cai Z.; Yang C.; Tang X.; Zhou H.
Article.Abstract: Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) induces complex cellular responses in the injured brain, yet the phenotypic plasticity of resident glial cells during post-ischemic repair remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated neuronal-like phenotypic remodeling of resident cells in the peri-ischemic cortex and its potential pharmacological modulation by salvianolic acid A (SAA). A bilateral primary motor cortex photothrombotic ischemia model was established in Male C57BL/6 mice, followed immediately by local injection of RV-EF1α-eGFP to label proliferative cells or an adeno-associated virus expressing mCherry under the astrocyte-associated gfaABC1D promoter. At 30 days after AIS, virus-labeled cells were analyzed by morphology and NeuN/GFAP immunofluorescence, while whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed at 10 days to assess electrophysiological properties. AIS was associated with the emergence of virus-labeled cells exhibiting neuronal-like morphology, and some gfaABC1D-mCherry-positive cells showed reduced or undetectable GFAP expression. These cells generated action potentials and exhibited excitatory postsynaptic currents, indicating partial neuronal-like electrophysiological properties. A single acute dose of SAA increased the proportion of mCherry/NeuN double-positive cells without significantly changing the overall proportions of mCherry-positive or NeuN-positive cells. These findings suggest that ischemic injury is associated with endogenous neuronal-like phenotypic remodeling of astrocyte-associated cells and that this process may be pharmacologically modulated by SAA.

Article.Title: Unraveling the Radiobiology of Extreme Hypofractionation Doses in Head and Neck Cancer Cells In Vitro
Article.Authors: Oliveira Dias J.; de Camargo A.; da Cunha Silveira Alves da Silva D.; Sampaio Fagundes I.; Faria Gomes I.; Bueno da Silva Murra L.; Bisio M.; Giglioli M.; Vital P.; da Silva Oliveira R.; Jacinto A.; Altei W.
Article.Abstract: Head and neck cancer (HNC) has high recurrence rates, and radiotherapy remains fundamental to treatment. Although extreme hypofractionation delivers higher doses per fraction than normofractionated regimens (≥5 Gy vs. 2 Gy/fraction), with clinical benefits shown in selected settings, its radiobiological effects in HNC are insufficiently characterized. Here, we investigated the responses of HPV-positive and HPV-negative HNC cells to 8 Gy and 2 Gy irradiation. Radiosensitivity, cell cycle redistribution, and DNA damage repair were evaluated using clonogenic and real-time proliferation assays, microscopy, and flow cytometry. HPV-positive UM-SCC-47 cells were more radiosensitive than HPV-negative 93-VU-120T cells, showing greater alterations in cell death, cellular area, G2/M accumulation, DNA double-strand breaks, and micronucleus formation, particularly after 8 Gy. Real-time proliferation assays revealed transient proliferative recovery of UM-SCC-47 during repeated 8 Gy exposure, although this was not observed to a comparable extent in other HNC cell lines. In silico analysis revealed distinct temporal transcriptional responses according to HPV status, with greater preservation of proliferation- and cell cycle-associated programs in HPV-positive cells. These findings indicate that radiation responses may differ not only in radiosensitivity but also in the trajectories of surviving cells following repeated high-dose exposure, highlighting the need to further elucidate the radiobiological mechanisms underlying extreme hypofractionation in HNC.

Article.Title: Telomeres, Aging and Neurodegenerative Diseases: Molecular Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence and Therapeutic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Grasso M.; Mascali C.; L’Episcopo F.
Article.Abstract: Telomeres are regions located at the ends of chromosomes, consisting of tandemly repeated nucleotide sequences. Their primary functions are to protect chromosome ends, prevent the recognition of natural chromosome termini as DNA double-strand breaks and contribute to the regulation of cellular replicative capacity. Indeed, with each cell division cycle, they shorten until reaching a critical threshold that signals the cell to stop replicating, a process known as “cellular senescence”. Telomere shortening also occurs in response to oxidative stress and DNA damage; several studies have reported an association between shorter telomere length and neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson’s disease (PD), Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and dementia-related outcomes. However, findings are heterogeneous, and the relationship between telomere length and cognitive or functional decline remains incompletely understood. Telomere dysfunction may also affect glial cell function, potentially contributing to chronic neuroinflammation and the release of pro-inflammatory molecules. This process increases neuronal vulnerability. Several studies suggest that telomere damage may influence the neurotoxicity caused by β-amyloid oligomers and accelerate neurodegenerative processes. Furthermore, in experimental models, interventions targeting telomerase, the enzyme that preserves DNA integrity by lengthening lost telomere repeats, have shown potential therapeutic promise. However, the relationship between telomere shortening and disease progression is still unclear, and telomere length cannot even be considered a clinically applicable predictive biomarker. Although telomere shortening is a marker of biological aging and a potential factor in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases, large-scale longitudinal studies and interventional trials are needed to consider telomeres as biomarkers and therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases.

Article.Title: Cross-Environment Single-Cell Transcriptomics Reveals Conserved Programs of Trypanosoma brucei Differentiation
Article.Authors: Jakimovska Ozdemir M.; López-Escobar L.; M. Figueiredo L.; Sezerman O.
Article.Abstract: The eukaryotic parasite Trypanosoma brucei undergoes a developmental transition from the proliferative “slender” form to the cell-cycle-arrested “stumpy” form, a process that is essential for parasite transmission competence. While this differentiation pathway has been extensively studied, accurately resolving the intermediate cellular states and establishing their equivalence across experimental environments has remained challenging. Here, we integrated publicly available scRNA-seq datasets from in vitro and in vivo conditions to reconstruct a conserved differentiation landscape across environments. Dataset-specific quality control and separate normalization accommodated differences in transcript recovery, supporting the joint analysis of slender-associated, intermediate and stumpy-associated transcriptional profiles. Using higher-resolution trajectory analysis, we identified the gene expression dynamics within the transition compartment into early and late intermediate states, defined by temporally ordered gene activation and silencing programs. Moreover, we derived a four-stage model (slender, transition slender, transition stumpy, and stumpy) with reproducible gene signatures that provide distinct transcriptomic profiles for intermediate cells. The observed transcriptional sequence suggests that intracellular reprogramming begins before visible phenotypic changes emerge, previously reported during early stumpy development. We further validated this framework in an independent dataset, demonstrating that this model resolves intermediate populations that are not distinguished by existing approaches and thereby supporting its robustness across different experimental contexts.

Article.Title: Target-Specific Benchmarking of Potency Prediction on Activity-Cliff Compounds Across 33 Human Protein Targets Using Inhibition Constants
Article.Authors: Alamri M.; Bhowmick S.; Bhole R.; Chikhale R.; Kute P.; Islam M.
Article.Abstract: Activity cliffs are pairs of closely related compounds whose potencies differ far more than their structures suggest, and the compounds involved in them remain a leading cause of local failure in ligand-based potency prediction. The MoleculeACE benchmark established that models predict these compounds poorly and that the gap differs between datasets. What has been missing is a panel built on one activity endpoint, a per-target account of how large the gap is, and a measurement of how far it depends on the way the model is chosen. We curated inhibition constant (Ki) data for 33 human protein targets from ChEMBL release 37 and BindingDB and annotated activity cliffs using the MoleculeACE criteria. Sixteen descriptor and algorithm combinations per target were trained to predict potency and scored separately on cliff compounds, with the winner chosen by five-fold cross-validation inside the training set. Cliff frequency ranged from 3.95% to 61.34%. Error on cliff compounds exceeded global error for 26 of 33 targets, by 12.8% on average (Wilcoxon p = 3.4 × 10−5), with a range from an 8.0% reduction to a 122.0% increase. Choosing the model on the test set instead inflated apparent cliff accuracy by 0.119 pKi units and the number of targets that showed lower cliff-specific error than global error fell from 14 to seven once selection was corrected. Cliff-specific error has to be measured per target and quoted with the size of the subset it rests on.

Article.Title: Hepatoprotective Activity of Thunbergia laurifolia Water Extract in a Thioacetamide-Induced Liver Injury Model
Article.Authors: Kunnaja P.; Intatham S.; Khonsung P.; Jaijoy K.; Yimsoo T.; Rojsanga P.; Sireeratawong S.
Article.Abstract: Thunbergia laurifolia Lindl. has long been used in Thai traditional medicine as a detoxifying herb and for the management of liver disorders. However, evidence regarding chemically standardized extracts and their hepatoprotective effects remains limited. This study characterized a standardized water extract of T. laurifolia using caffeic acid and rosmarinic acid as marker compounds and evaluated its hepatoprotective activity in a thioacetamide (TAA)-induced liver injury model. Male Wistar rats were administered TAA and treated with the standardized extract. Hepatoprotective activity was assessed using oxidative stress biomarkers, hematological parameters, serum biochemical markers, and histopathological examination. TAA administration induced liver injury characterized by increased malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, reduced superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity and glutathione (GSH) levels, elevated serum liver injury markers, inflammatory responses, and histopathological alterations. Treatment with the standardized T. laurifolia extract significantly reduced MDA levels, restored SOD activity and GSH levels, attenuated serum aspartate aminotransferase elevation, and improved liver histopathology. Collectively, these findings suggest that the standardized T. laurifolia water extract has hepatoprotective potential against TAA-induced early-stage liver injury as evidenced by improvements in oxidative stress biomarkers, serum AST levels, and hepatic histopathological features.

Article.Title: Formulation and Characterization of Coenzyme Q10-Loaded Emulsions Based on Natural Gums
Article.Authors: Veskov J.; Krstonošić V.; Nemeš T.; Ćirin D.; Mikulić M.; Kladar N.; Krstonošić M.
Article.Abstract: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) is a highly lipophilic antioxidant with poor aqueous solubility, making its incorporation into delivery systems challenging. Oil-in-water emulsions containing 0.4% CoQ10, 10% olive oil, 0.5% tragacanth gum (TG) and gum arabic (GA) (0–3.0%) were formulated. Their physicochemical characteristics, CoQ10 content, antioxidant activity, rheological properties, and physical stability were investigated. The Sauter mean diameter D (3,2) ranged from 5.22 to 7.15 µm, with the smallest droplets observed in formulations containing 0.25–1% GA. CoQ10 content ranged from 84.07% to 95.93% of the theoretical amount throughout 14 days, without significant changes. DPPH radical inhibition ranged from 57.55% to 66.17%, with no significant differences among formulations. Increasing GA decreased apparent viscosity and consistency index, increased the flow behaviour index, and reduced the hysteresis loop area, indicating less pronounced shear-thinning and thixotropic behaviour. Physical stability decreased at higher GA concentrations, as evidenced by greater creaming and separation under centrifugation. The 3% GA formulation exhibited the greatest instability. These findings show that GA concentration influences rheological behaviour and physical stability, and that increasing GA does not necessarily improve emulsion stability. Overall, the results provide a basis for the design and optimization of TG/GA-based emulsions for pharmaceutical, cosmetic, and food applications.

Article.Title: Transmembrane Domain-Mediated Dimerization Regulates Matrix Metalloproteinase-7-Dependent Shedding of Syndecan-2
Article.Authors: Jang Y.; Hwang J.; Yang H.; Cho S.; Un Y.; Oh E.
Article.Abstract: Syndecan-2 (SDC-2) is a cell surface heparan sulfate proteoglycan whose transmembrane domain (TMD)-mediated dimerization regulates colon cancer cell behavior. In addition to functioning as a membrane receptor, SDC-2 undergoes matrix metalloproteinase-7 (MMP-7)-mediated ectodomain shedding, producing soluble fragments that promote angiogenesis and tumor progression. However, the mechanistic link between TMD-mediated dimerization and ectodomain shedding has remained unclear. Here, we show that different SDC family members exhibit distinct propensities for SDS-resistant dimer formation, which correlate with their susceptibility to MMP-7-mediated cleavage. Notably, the dimeric forms of both SDC-2 and SDC-4 were cleaved more rapidly by MMP-7, whereas dimerization-defective mutants of SDC-2 (S2GL) and SDC-4 (S4GL) displayed significantly reduced proteolytic cleavage in vitro. Conditioned media from cells expressing wild-type SDC-2 (HT29-S2W) contained elevated levels of shed SDC-2 and promoted increased migration of HT29 colon cancer cells and macrophages. In contrast, this effect was diminished in media from cells expressing the dimerization-defective S2GL mutant. Furthermore, a TMD mutant of SDC-2 identified in colon cancer patients showed impaired dimerization and decreased ectodomain shedding. Together, these findings demonstrate that TMD-mediated dimerization is required for MMP-7-dependent shedding of SDC-2 and drives tumor progression by enhancing cancer cell migration and immune cell recruitment.

Article.Title: Plant ER Proteostasis Through a Framework of Protein Load, Processing Capacity and Clearance
Article.Authors: Yoo J.; Ko K.; Lee K.
Article.Abstract: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) must coordinate protein entry, maturation and removal to sustain plant growth and stress adaptation. Although unfolded protein response (UPR) signaling and quality control pathways are well characterized, their activation alone does not reveal which process limits ER function. Here, we propose a Load, Capacity and Clearance (LCC) framework that organizes these mechanisms by their effects on protein flux. The Load module regulates protein influx, Capacity supports productive folding, maturation, assembly and export, and Clearance removes misfolded proteins and selected portions of the ER. We examine transcriptional remodeling, translational regulation, regulated RNA decay, ER-associated degradation and selective autophagy, distinguishing mechanisms demonstrated during plant ER stress from those established in other stress responses. How these processes are coordinated, and how much each contributes to ER recovery, remain to be quantified. We outline testable predictions and experimental approaches to determine which processes limit recovery, how the timing of influx restoration affects recovery, and whether combined measurements of influx, processing and clearance explain or predict stress outcomes better than UPR markers alone. This framework may guide strategies to improve plant stress resilience and recombinant protein production.

Article.Title: 5-HT7–TrkB Heteroreceptor Complexes: A Novel Molecular Pathway May Contribute to the Antidepressant-like Effects of 5-HT7 Receptor Activation
Article.Authors: Ilchibaeva T.; Tsybko A.; Eremin D.; Shalagina M.; Naumenko V.
Article.Abstract: Serotonin receptor 5-HT7 and tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) are both key regulators of neuroplasticity implicated in the pathophysiology and treatment of depression. Although functional crosstalk between these receptors has been suggested, the underlying molecular mechanism remains unknown. Here, we investigated the physical and functional interaction between 5-HT7 and TrkB receptors at behavioral, biochemical, and molecular levels. Using males of the antidepressant-sensitive cataleptic (ASC) mouse model of depressive-like behavior, we demonstrated that repeated (9 days) activation of 5-HT7 receptors with the selective agonist LP-211 produced antidepressant-like effects in the sucrose preference test. These behavioral effects were dependent on TrkB signaling, as it was prevented by pretreatment with the TrkB antagonist ANA12. Both acute and repeated 5-HT7 receptor activation increased TrkB phosphorylation in the mouse brain, although this long-term effect was brain region- and amino acid residue-specific. To determine if these functional interactions were mediated by a direct physical association, we used co-immunoprecipitation and FRET assays. We found that 5-HT7 and TrkB form heteroreceptor complexes in vitro in neuroblastoma cells and in vivo in the mouse frontal cortex, hippocampus, and midbrain. Collectively, our findings support an oligomerization between 5-HT7 and TrkB receptors and suggest that this association may contribute to the antidepressant-like effects of 5-HT7 receptor activation.

Article.Title: Exploratory Metabolomic Characterization of HbA1c-Defined Glycemic Groups in the Qatar Biobank Cohort
Article.Authors: Bacha R.; Al Saady R.; Sumon M.; Chowdhury M.; Al-Mansoori L.; Pedersen S.
Article.Abstract: Glycemic status is commonly defined using glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), classifying individuals as normoglycemic, prediabetic, or diabetic. However, these categories may not fully capture the underlying metabolic complexity associated with early dysglycemia and disease progression. This study aimed to investigate metabolomic alterations across HbA1c-defined glycemic groups using a bioinformatics-guided approach. Targeted metabolomic profiling of EDTA plasma samples from 1752 Qatar Biobank participants was performed using ultra-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS). Participants were classified as normoglycemic (NG), prediabetic (PD), or diabetic (DM) according to established HbA1c criteria. Metabolite data were integrated with clinical variables and analyzed using multivariate modeling, ROC analysis, and pathway enrichment to identify discriminatory metabolic features across glycemic states. Distinct metabolomic profiles were observed across the glycemic spectrum. The NG–PD comparison showed modest discrimination (AUC 0.64–0.69), with alterations primarily involving steroid-conjugated, lipid-related, and amino acid-associated metabolites, indicating early metabolic alterations beyond glucose metabolism. In contrast, the PD–DM comparison demonstrated stronger discrimination (AUC ~0.90), driven predominantly by carbohydrate-related metabolites, including meta_glucose, mannose, mannonate, fructose, and reduced 1,5-anhydroglucitol (1,5-AG), reflecting progressive glucose-centric metabolic dysregulation. Metabolomic profiling revealed distinct patterns of metabolic alterations across HbA1c-defined glycemic groups, with modest differences between normoglycemia and prediabetes involving steroid-, lipid-, and amino acid-related metabolites, and more pronounced carbohydrate-related differences in diabetes. These findings provide exploratory insights into the metabolic heterogeneity associated with early dysglycemia and warrant further investigation in independent and longitudinal cohorts.

Article.Title: Fungicidal Activity of N-Chlorotaurine Against Candidozyma auris
Article.Authors: Grimus T.; Coraça-Huber D.; Lass-Flörl C.; Nagl M.
Article.Abstract: N-chlorotaurine (NCT) is a well-tolerated antiseptic and anti-infective that originates from innate immunity and can be applied for topical treatment of infections of different body areas. The aim of this study was to investigate its fungicidal activity in vitro against the emerging pathogen Candidozyma auris. Five representative strains of C. auris were grown overnight in broth culture and subjected to quantitative killing assays in NCT solution. Fungal biofilms were cultivated on metal discs (A2-steel) for 1–2 weeks and incubated in NCT solution, followed by quantitative cultures and scanning electron microscopy. All strains in planktonic form were killed by NCT. At standard test conditions (1% NCT at 37 °C) at pH 7, there was a more than 3 log10 reduction in colony-forming units after 4–5 h, whereas at pH 5 the same reduction was achieved after just 2 h, with a more than 2 log10 reduction after 1 h. The addition of 5% peptone further reduced the killing time to less than 15 min (>3 log10 reduction). The viability of biofilms of C. auris was impaired in a similar way, with a 2 log10 reduction of colony-forming units after 4 h incubation time and up to 3 log10 after 6 h. At these times, no morphological changes in fungal cells were visible in electron microscopy. NCT has demonstrated fungicidal activity against C. auris similar to other yeasts. Topical application of NCT for the treatment of infections by these species, too, is conceivable, above all for wound and complicated urinary tract infections.

Article.Title: CytoLight Labeling as a Practical Extracellular Vesicle Analysis Platform for Quantitation, Phenotyping and Tracking Across In-Vitro and In-Vivo Models
Article.Authors: Rosen I.; Itzhaki E.; Gover-Proaktor A.; Shapira S.; Partouche S.; Qassim L.; Grinshpan-Langman S.; Qasim A.; Erez D.; John F.; Porat Z.; Moskovits N.; Zemel R.; Zur T.; Raanani P.; Offen D.; Granot G.; Samara A.
Article.Abstract: Reliable fluorescent labeling of extracellular vesicles (EVs) requires efficient discrimination of bona fide EVs from non-vesicular noise while avoiding dye-associated artifacts. We evaluated CytoLight Rapid Red, a commercially available luminal dye developed for live-cell imaging, as an artifact-minimizing strategy for EV labeling, surface-marker phenotyping, uptake analysis and in vivo tracking, benchmarking its performance against PKH26, carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE) and ExoBrite across multiple analytical platforms. CytoLight generated stable, EV-associated fluorescence with no detectable aggregation or measurable change in EV size or scatter characteristics under the conditions tested. By fluorescence-mode nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) and nano-flow cytometry, CytoLight yielded robust and reproducible staining across EV preparations, while CFSE showed a bimodal distribution consistent with esterase-dependent activation, and PKH26 generated particles of unidentified origin. Gating on CytoLight-positive events increased tetraspanin-positive frequencies 1.97–2.42-fold in HEK293FT-derived EVs and 1.25–1.43-fold in natural killer cell-derived EVs. In uptake assays, CytoLight yielded EV-associated signals exceeding labeled phosphate-buffered saline and protein-matched EV-depleted serum controls. In vivo, CytoLight-labeled EVs produced significantly higher organ-level fluorescence accumulation than controls, consistent with commonly reported EV-biodistribution patterns. Our findings support the feasibility of CytoLight as a practical, aggregation-resistant strategy for EV-labeling and as a positive-selection gate for fluorescence-based EV analysis. CytoLight enabled reliable particle quantification, surface-marker phenotyping, EV-associated uptake analysis and in vivo fluorescence biodistribution studies across multiple analytical platforms, offering a practical, scalable alternative to established EV dyes for standardized and reproducible EV research.

Furthermore, subcellular localization assays demonstrated the plasma membrane targeting of HvLysM2 and HvLysM3 and the extracellular localization of HvLysM8. Article.Title: A Proposed Sulfur-Redox Adaptive Reserve in Type 2 Diabetes and Obesity: From Metabolic Perturbation to Endothelial and Tissue Responses—A Critical Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework
Article.Authors: Munteanu C.; Bembea V.; Manolaki Y.; Onose G.; Turnea M.; Rotariu M.; Blendea C.
Article.Abstract: Type 2 diabetes and obesity are associated with metabolic stress and heterogeneous endothelial and tissue dysfunction. Baseline measurements of analytically specified sulfur species, thiol–disulfide couples, and operational sulfide pools provide limited information about dynamic pathway turnover or the capacity to respond to metabolic demand. This critical narrative review evaluated human and experimental evidence, published in the last twenty years, linking sulfur metabolism, redox regulation and functional responses, and developed a conceptual framework for sulfur-redox adaptive reserve. Human studies report divergent assay-defined circulating sulfide signals, impaired erythrocyte glutathione synthesis, and weight loss accompanied by lower measured sulfide fractions and sulfur metabolites. Experimental findings support sulfur-sensitive regulation of mitochondrial, endothelial, and tissue function, but do not establish a uniform direction of benefit or clinical mediation. We therefore propose sulfur-redox adaptive reserve as the context-dependent, challenge-evoked capacity of endogenous sulfide generation, mitochondrial sulfide oxidation, persulfide turnover, thiol replenishment, and linked redox systems to support preservation or recovery of independently measured endothelial and tissue function during and after a defined metabolic perturbation. Unlike metabolic flexibility, redox homeostasis, or mitochondrial reserve capacity considered separately, the construct requires coordinated sulfur-network responses to a specified perturbation and linkage to independently measured functional outcomes. Its evaluation requires serial analyte-specific measurements, characterization of the achieved internal metabolic response—such as post-challenge glucose, insulin, and triglyceride trajectories or relative exercise intensity—and an independent functional endpoint. Repeated challenge studies must establish reproducibility, incremental information beyond baseline measures, and mechanistic specificity. The framework generates testable hypotheses, but its prognostic value, mechanistic specificity and clinical utility remain to be established.

Article.Authors: Slushchev A.; Kochurova A.; Antonets J.; Mikhaylova V.; Roman S.; Kleymenov S.; Yampolskaya D.; Koubassova N.; Kopylova G.; Ryabkova N.; Katrukha I.; Bershitsky S.; Tsaturyan A.; Matyushenko A.; Levitsky D.; Shchepkin D.

Article.Title: Integrated Multilevel Experimental Assessment of Heart Support Oil Phytocompounds Across Molecular Motor Proteins, β2-Adrenergic Signalling, Mitochondrial Stress, and Cardiomyocyte Contractile Function
Article.Authors: Dunjic M.; Turini S.; Novakovic T.; Sulovic L.; Jing Z.; Nejkovic L.; Dunjic M.; Dunjic K.
Article.Abstract: Heart Support Oil (HSO) is a multicomponent botanical formulation derived from Juglans regia, Lycium barbarum, Citrus × paradisi, and Origanum vulgare. This study addressed two related but analytically distinct questions: whether selected analytically detectable HSO phytocompounds show direct target-engagement signals at molecular motor proteins and the β2-adrenergic receptor (β2-AR), and whether the complete standardised formulation modifies oxidative- and adrenergic-stress phenotypes in cardiomyocyte models. Selected constituents were examined by target-specific biophysical/biochemical assays, whereas complete HSO was evaluated in human induced-pluripotent-stem-cell-derived cardiomyocytes and AC16 cells using membrane-injury, oxidative-stress, mitochondrial, calcium-transient, electrophysiological, contractile, qRT-PCR, and immunoblot endpoints. HSO produced concentration-dependent improvements under the tested stress conditions. At 20 µg/mL, CellTiter-Glo signal reached 91.0 ± 1.4% of control, reactive oxygen species decreased to 1.29 ± 0.04-fold, and mitochondrial membrane potential and cellular ATP recovered to 89.8 ± 1.6% and 87.3 ± 1.3% of control, respectively. HSO also moderated isoproterenol-associated abnormalities in cAMP signalling, beat rate, calcium handling, and contractility and shifted stress-, inflammatory-, apoptotic-, and antioxidant-response markers toward control values. Direct target assays demonstrated measurable binding and enzymatic changes for selected constituents, but these molecular observations were not interpreted as proving that the same targets caused the formulation-level cardiomyocyte phenotype. The findings support further independently replicated, pharmacokinetic, mechanistic loss-of-function, and in vivo studies; they do not establish a unique causal mechanism or clinical efficacy.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction Is Induced by Cardiac Pressure Overload
Article.Authors: Correa F.; Bautista-Pérez R.; Santamaría J.; Gonzalez-Pacheco H.; Franco M.
Article.Abstract: Pressure overload induced by ascending transaortic constriction was examined to evaluate cytoprotection with cytidine-5´-diphosphatecoline (CDP-choline) targeting oxidative stress and mitochondrial function. Male Wistar rats pre-treated with citicoline or a vehicle showed a decrease in mean arterial pressure (56.16 ± 10.08 vs. 60.55 ± 8.70 mmHg, respectively) with ascending transaortic constriction (AAC). After 60 min of hypotension, arterial blood gases, hepatic, renal, and inflammatory markers were measured together with oxidative stress, oxygen consumption, and the activity of the respiratory chain. Pressure-overloaded animals developed a marked elevation in blood lactate with a fall in pH values and a significant increase in urea nitrogen, creatinine, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH); no changes were seen in hepatic transaminases, interleukins IL-1β, IL-6, and tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα), whereas IL-10 increased. In contrast, under a 60.55 ± 8.70 mmHg fall in blood pressure, preconditioning induced a moderate lactate elevation with a minor decrease in pH compared to the group without preconditioning. Urea nitrogen, creatinine, and LDH were elevated, whereas aspartate aminotransferase (AST)increased only in the pre-treated group; IL-1β, IL-6, and TNFα did not change, and IL-10 increased. Oxidative stress in the heart, liver, and kidney mitochondria was related to dysregulation of oxidative phosphorylation, associated with a loss of complex III and complex IV activity. Thus, CDP-choline attenuated the heart damage caused by pressure overload by reducing oxidative stress and maintaining mitochondrial function.

Article.Title: Conditioned Medium from miR-29a-3p-Overexpressing Mesenchymal Stem Cells Attenuates TGF-β1-Induced Transcriptomic Dysregulation in Renal Proximal Tubular Epithelial Cells
Article.Authors: Lee M.; Lee H.; Jang Y.; Seo D.; Suh N.
Article.Abstract: Proximal tubule (PT) injury drives renal fibrogenesis, necessitating targeted therapeutic strategies. Here, we explored whether conditioned medium (CM) from human adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) overexpressing miR-29a-3p could attenuate transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1)-induced injury in human renal proximal tubular epithelial cells (RPTECs). MSCs were transfected with a miR-29a-3p mimic or control, and the resulting CM was applied to RPTECs during sustained TGF-β1 exposure. Cellular responses were evaluated using bulk RNA-sequencing, mitochondrial membrane potential assays, and immunofluorescence. Furthermore, a 12-gene, three-axis score was constructed to quantify injury and recovery. miR-29a-3p MSC-CM effectively reduced profibrotic activation and induced a broad reversal of approximately half of the TGF-β1-induced transcriptional shifts. Notably, this CM reactivated suppressed metabolic pathways, such as oxidative phosphorylation, attenuated epithelial–mesenchymal transition and cadherin remodeling, and restored mitochondrial membrane potential. Additionally, the 12-gene, three-axis score quantified a 47.6% recovery in vitro and successfully captured progressive adaptive and failed-repair PT injury states in human kidney single-cell/nucleus datasets, including an independent validation cohort. In conclusion, miR-29a-3p MSC-CM drives a selective but robust transcriptional and functional recovery in injured RPTECs. The novel 12-gene, three-axis score provides a quantifiable, cross-dataset metric for evaluating PT injury states.

Article.Title: Positive Allosteric Modulation of mGluR5 by VU0409551 Attenuates Clinical Severity, Anxiety-like Behavior, and Persistent Neuroinflammation in Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis
Article.Authors: Goulart M.; Fahel J.; Cardozo P.; Fantin J.; Maciel E.; Oliveira J.; Silva E.; Rezende-Ribeiro J.; Silva N.; Santos L.; Mello T.; Gorshkov V.; Kjeldsen F.; Verano-Braga T.; Vieira L.; Ribeiro F.
Article.Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune, inflammatory, demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and disability. Current disease-modifying therapies primarily target peripheral immune cells and show limited efficacy in halting relapse-independent long-term progression and the resulting neurodegeneration. The type 5 metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR5) has emerged as a promising therapeutic target due to its role in regulating neuroinflammation and cell survival. This study evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of VU0409551, a selective mGluR5 positive allosteric modulator (PAM), in the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) mouse model, the most widely studied animal model of MS. Daily treatment with VU0409551 (10 mg/kg, intraperitoneally) significantly attenuated clinical disease severity and prevented characteristic body weight loss. Proteomic analyses revealed that VU0409551 treatment attenuated molecular signatures associated with immune responses. During remission, VU0409551 ameliorated EAE-associated anxiety-like behavior and attenuated persistent cortical neuroinflammatory alterations, including astrogliosis, microglial accumulation, and increased TNF expression. Notably, treatment also reduced signatures associated with astrocyte and oligodendrocyte reactivity, including C3, C4b, Serpina3n, and H2-D1. These findings demonstrate that VU0409551 exerts robust therapeutic effects, positioning it as a promising and novel disease-modifying candidate for MS.

Article.Title: ATP-Binding Cassette Transporter Expression and Methylation Profiles as Potential Biomarkers in Glioma
Article.Authors: Pilotto Heming C.; Meireles Y.; Moura-Neto V.; Aran V.
Article.Abstract: Gliomas are malignant central nervous system tumors characterized by poor prognosis and therapy failure. Adenosine triphosphate-binding cassette (ABC) transporters mediate multidrug resistance via chemotherapeutic efflux, yet their roles as biomarkers across glioma subtypes remain unclear. We analyzed adult diffuse glioma mRNA expression (n = 693; n = 325) and DNA methylation (n = 159) datasets from the Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas in silico, stratifying samples according to the 2021 World Health Organization molecular criteria. ABC transporter profiles, patient-matched methylation–expression correlations (n = 26 overlapping patients; 78 paired gene–sample observations), and prognostic values were evaluated using non-parametric tests with false discovery rate (FDR) correction, Kaplan–Meier curves, and multivariable Cox proportional-hazards regression analyses. Transporter expression and methylation varied significantly by histology and grade. ABCC1 expression increased with malignancy, predicting worse overall survival in univariable analysis (p < 0.0001). Meanwhile, strongly correlated ABCB1 and ABCG2 expressions (Spearman’s ρ = 0.80 in grade 4 tumors) were higher in lower-grade gliomas. Progressive hypomethylation occurred with increasing grade, with significant differential methylation in ABCB1 (FDR p < 0.0001) and ABCG2 (FDR p < 0.0001). In patient-matched integrative analyses, only ABCC1 exhibited a significant inverse association between methylation and expression (Spearman’s ρ = −0.58, p = 0.0019). Baseline clinical multivariable Cox regression (n = 139) suggested that higher ABCB1 and ABCG2 methylation (HR = 0.11, p = 0.03; HR = 0.12, p = 0.04 per 1.0-unit β increase, corresponding to HR = 0.80 and 0.81 per 0.1-unit β increase) may act as protective factors independent of age and grade (though attenuated upon IDH adjustment), whereas higher grade and ABCG2 expression (n = 542; HR = 1.03, p = 0.001) emerged as independent risk factors. Specific ABC transporter profiles could serve as candidate prognostic biomarkers in glioma, warranting external and translational validation.

Article.Title: FP7 and FP12, Two Synthetic Toll-like Receptor Antagonists, Do Not Cause Adverse Effects in Mice
Article.Authors: Alqallaf J.; Alqallaf A.; Parnell A.; Alonso V.; AL-Asady M.; Michael N.; Romerio A.; Shaik M.; Leake D.; Pirianov G.; Peri F.; Patel K.; Vaiyapuri S.
Article.Abstract: Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) is a pattern-recognition receptor that detects lipopolysaccharides (LPSs) from Gram-negative bacteria, triggering innate immune and inflammatory responses. Research into TLR4 antagonists and agonists is crucial for developing novel therapies to modulate immune responses in infectious, inflammatory, and autoimmune diseases. Accordingly, some authors of this study developed synthetic TLR4 antagonists, including FP7 and FP12, and demonstrated their efficacy in inhibiting TLR4-mediated effects. This study specifically assesses the safety profile of these two novel TLR4 antagonists in mice following intraperitoneal administration. Clinical signs, body weights, and biochemical and haematological parameters in mice were assessed over four weeks after intraperitoneal administration of these molecules. No mortality or adverse effects were observed after administration of FP molecules. Key circulating biomarkers were also unaffected by these molecules. Preliminary LC–MS analysis detected both compounds in mouse plasma one hour after administration. Overall, this study demonstrates that FP7 and FP12 were well tolerated in mice, with no significant toxicological effects at the tested dose. These findings are an initial step toward further preclinical and clinical development of these molecules.

Article.Title: Impaired Mitochondrial Quality Control in Vitiligo: An Emerging Mechanistic Hypothesis and Perspective on Therapeutic Innovation
Article.Authors: Banda-Lesole R.; Kgosiemang-Xaba I.; Makhafola T.
Article.Abstract: Vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune pigmentary disorder characterized by selective melanocyte loss. While oxidative stress and immune dysregulation are well-established contributors, the upstream mechanisms that initiate melanocyte vulnerability remain incompletely understood. In this narrative review, we propose impaired mitochondrial quality control (MQC) as an emerging mechanistic hypothesis that may link key pathogenic events in vitiligo. MQC, encompassing mitophagy, mitochondrial dynamics, and biogenesis, is essential for maintaining melanocyte bioenergetics, redox homeostasis, and survival under ultraviolet (UV) and environmental stress. We summarize current evidence suggesting that abnormalities in PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, dysregulated fission/fusion dynamics, and impaired PGC-1α/NRF1-driven biogenesis are associated with the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria in vitiligo melanocytes. These mitochondrial perturbations may contribute to metabolic adaptation, augmented reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, cytosolic mtDNA release, and downstream innate and adaptive immune activation reported in vitiligo, subsequently driving the characteristic features of vitiligo lesions. However, whether MQC abnormalities represent a primary pathogenic driver, a secondary consequence of chronic oxidative stress, or a bidirectional relationship remains to be established. Thus, we critically discuss the perspective that phytochemicals may act as potential modulators of MQC. Unlike general antioxidants, specific plant-derived compounds such as quercetin, sulforaphane, epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), and ginkgolides have been reported in preclinical models to modulate mitophagy, rebalance mitochondrial dynamics, and promote biogenesis, thereby targeting mitochondrial homeostasis rather than only its downstream consequences. By repositioning impaired MQC as an attractive, yet to be validated, hypothesis that may offer new insight into vitiligo pathogenesis, this review provides a framework for future investigation and highlights phytochemical-mediated restoration of mitochondrial homeostasis as a potential therapeutic avenue that warrants further experimental validation.

Article.Title: Insights into Multiple Myeloma: Immune Microenvironment, Disease Mechanisms, and Therapeutic Innovations
Article.Authors: Miyama T.; Mihara K.
Article.Abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) remains a hematologic malignancy characterized by progressive immune dysfunction and the emergence of therapeutic resistance despite substantial recent advances in treatment. The transition from monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) to symptomatic MM is associated with coordinated immune dysfunction across innate and adaptive immune compartments. Single-cell and spatial profiling technologies reveal that immune abnormalities emerge at precursor stages and intensify during progression, including T-cell exhaustion, expansion of regulatory T cells, natural killer cell dysfunction, and impaired antigen presentation by dendritic cells. The cancer immunoediting framework, encompassing elimination, equilibrium, and escape phases, provides a unifying paradigm for understanding tumor-immune coevolution in MM. Disease complexity is further compounded by pronounced spatial and temporal heterogeneity. Multi-region sequencing studies demonstrate anatomically distinct clonal architectures and immune microenvironments within individual patients, contributing to variable therapeutic responses and facilitating immune escape. Current immunotherapies, including immunomodulatory drugs, proteasome inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies, and bispecific antibodies, have transformed the therapeutic landscape of MM. Nevertheless, durable disease control remains limited by convergent resistance mechanisms, including antigen modulation, T-cell dysfunction, and persistent microenvironmental immunosuppression. A comprehensive understanding of the immune-mediated resistance mechanisms, extending beyond tumor-intrinsic genetic alterations, is essential for the rational design of next-generation therapies. Accumulating evidence suggests that immune dysfunction is closely associated with disease evolution and treatment resistance in MM and may represent a potentially targetable contributor to these processes.

Article.Title: The Discovery of Benzothiophene Derivatives as LasB Inhibitors Against Pseudomonas aeruginosa Infections
Article.Authors: Zhao S.; Lian D.; Chen Q.; Dai S.; Sun P.; Zhang W.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a clinically prevalent multidrug-resistant pathogen that poses a major therapeutic challenge. Targeting the crucial virulence factor elastase LasB has emerged as a promising strategy with which to reduce pathogenicity without imposing strong selective pressure for resistance. Here, we synthesized 19 benzoheterocyclic compounds through virtual screening and identified the benzothiophene derivative C5 as a potent LasB inhibitor (52.99 ± 0.87%). Further studies showed that C5 inhibited lasB expression in a concentration-dependent manner (IC50 = 5.80 ± 2.55 μM), thereby significantly inhibiting elastase production in Pseudomonas aeruginosa reference strain PAO1, the hypervirulent strain PA14, and the clinically resistant strains PA921 and PA929. Notably, the combination of C5 with tobramycin and ciprofloxacin significantly suppressed the development of antibiotic resistance, indicating its potential for antibacterial synergistic activity with these antibiotics. Furthermore, C5 inhibited bacterial swarming without significant cytotoxicity, demonstrating a favorable safety profile and potent activity. In summary, these results suggest that targeting LasB offers a potential strategy for treating Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections, and compound C5 has the potential to be developed as a candidate for LasB inhibitors.

Article.Title: The Molecular Potassium Code: Extracellular K+ Sensing, Allosteric Ion Selectivity, KCC2 Thermodynamics, and the Dynamic Control of Neural Inhibition
Article.Authors: Dumitrescu D.; Dumitru A.; Fulina M.; Dobrin N.; Tulin A.; Șerban M.; Covache-Busuioc R.; Toader C.; Rădoi M.
Article.Abstract: Neuronal excitability can be controlled by the level of potassium (K+) outside a neuron through both its effects on the cell membrane’s electrical properties and its influence on ion transport across the membrane. Recent studies have also shown that certain ligand-gated ion-channel receptors can be modulated by the levels of K+ outside the neuron. Therefore, understanding how each mechanism contributes to the generation of inhibitory signals requires the ability to differentiate between them. This study represents a review that integrates evidence using various methods, including electrophysiology, structural studies, thermodynamics, and optical measurements, to propose a framework called the molecular potassium code that explains how neurons respond to varying levels of K+ in their environment. The framework describes three ways that neurons interact with changing levels of K+: how these changes shift their K+ equilibrium potential and membrane voltage; how they alter the thermodynamic driving force for KCC2-mediated cotransport of K+ and Cl−; and how receptor-dependent modulation occurs at specific receptors when documented. Changes in activation, desensitization, pharmacological sensitivity, and permeation characteristics have been measured in Drosophila DmAlka channels; however, the atomic details of K+ recognition by these channels remain unclear. Human GlyRα2 variants engineered or edited to allow for assessment of K+-associated responses under elevated K+ conditions did not provide sufficient evidence for physiological recruitment of these receptors in mammals. Additionally, the presence and function of astrocytes, as well as geometric factors such as size, shape, and orientation, affect local concentrations of K+. Therefore, the framework described here provides multiple approaches that scientists can use to measure and interpret different mechanisms contributing to the generation of inhibitory signals in the nervous system.

Article.Title: Comparative Analysis of Macrophage Infiltration in Different Types of Nevi and Normal Skin: The Role of CD163+ and CD68+ Cell Populations
Article.Authors: Demyashkin G.; Filippov A.; Sazonova M.; Piskunov A.; Kazhuro D.; Holdeenko V.; Mironova D.; Chernyshev H.; Tsomartova E.; Petrosyan L.; Mingazov A.
Article.Abstract: Melanocytic nevi are common benign skin neoplasms, but the quantitative characteristics of CD68+ and CD163+ immunopositive cells within their microenvironment remain incompletely understood. The present study aimed to compare the density and distribution of CD68+ and CD163+ cells, as well as the CD68+/CD163+ cell density ratio, in benign nevi (BN), dysplastic nevi (DN), halo nevi (HN) with and without histological regression, and normal skin. This retrospective study included 141 patients: 79 with BN, 24 with DN, 12 with HN without regression, 9 with HN with regression, and 17 normal skin controls. Immunohistochemical staining for CD68 and CD163 was evaluated using digital morphometric analysis with QuPath software. DN exhibited the highest median density of CD163+ cells (659.60 cells/mm2), whereas HN without regression showed the lowest densities of both CD68+ and CD163+ cells (109.34 and 93.55 cells/mm2, respectively). In contrast, HN with regression exhibited the highest CD68+ cell density (1343.62 cells/mm2) and CD68+/CD163+ cell density ratio (3.345), both significantly exceeding those in HN without regression (p < 0.001). Normal skin specimens showed lower densities of both markers compared with BN (p < 0.001). These findings demonstrate distinct patterns of CD68+ and CD163+ cell accumulation associated with nevus type and histological regression in HN. They provide a morphometric basis for further investigation of local immune processes and potential applications in histopathological assessment, although their clinical significance requires further validation.

Article.Title: Nrf2 Inhibits CXCL2-Dependent Neutrophil Recruitment to Alleviate Airway Inflammation and Epithelial Barrier Injury in House Dust Mite-Induced Murine Asthma
Article.Authors: Ren Y.; Zhang W.; Ma C.; Wang Y.; Zhang Y.; Li S.; Han S.
Article.Abstract: Neutrophilic asthma represents a severe, often corticosteroid-insensitive asthma subtype with an unmet clinical need for new therapeutic targets. This study aimed to identify key molecular mediators and regulatory pathways involved in neutrophilic airway inflammation through unbiased bioinformatic analysis of public human asthma transcriptomic datasets. Among the identified hub genes, C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CXCL2), a critical driver of neutrophil recruitment and pulmonary inflammation, was prioritized for mechanistic follow-up. We combined HDM-induced murine asthma models, dual-luciferase reporter assays and ChIP-qPCR to characterize the transcriptional regulation of CXCL2. Our results demonstrate that transcription factor Nrf2 directly binds the CXCL2 promoter and suppresses CXCL2 transcription. Genetic deletion of Nrf2 exacerbates neutrophil infiltration, airway inflammation and epithelial barrier disruption accompanied by increased CXCL2 expression, whereas pharmacological Nrf2 activation by MOTS-c downregulates CXCL2 and alleviates neutrophilic airway inflammation. Collectively, this work identifies the Nrf2/CXCL2 axis as a candidate regulatory pathway in experimental neutrophilic asthma, providing a potential target for further translational investigation.

Article.Title: An Integrated Single-Cell Atlas Reveals Shared Stromal Activation States and Divergent Myeloid Remodelling in Periodontitis and Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Article.Authors: Isgandarov I.; Abilbayeva A.; Tarabayeva A.; Shamekova M.; Bitanova E.; Yessenkulova S.; Kulmanbetov R.; Zhubanturliyeva A.; Nurmukhanbetova A.; Tulepbergenova A.; Tulepbergenova L.
Article.Abstract: Periodontitis is epidemiologically associated with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), but the tissue-cell states shared by the two diseases are unknown. We integrated seven public droplet-based scRNA-seq datasets into an atlas of 498,185 cells from 111 oral mucosal samples using scVI/scANVI, benchmarked with scIB. Each disease was compared only with matched control tissue, using patient-level analyses. Both diseases expanded activated inflammatory and matrix fibroblast states. Activated and resting fibroblasts differed in a similar way in both diseases (ρ = 0.53; patient-bootstrap 95% CI 0.42–0.57), also within lesional tissue (ρ = 0.51). Disease-versus-control fibroblast responses, however, were only weakly shared (ρ = 0.24) and not within the oral cavity, so this similarity reflects a generic activated-stroma phenotype rather than a disease-specific fibroblast programme. Endothelial and mural responses were shared more strongly, whereas immune responses diverged. B/plasma-cell expansion was the only abundance change credible in both diseases. Periodontitis showed classical-monocyte influx and a lower share of C1Q+ macrophages. TREM2+ lipid-associated macrophages rose from leukoplakia to carcinoma, but their gain over tumour-adjacent tissue appeared in only one of two cohorts. SPP1–CD44 signalling passed significance thresholds only in OSCC. This cross-sectional study is hypothesis-generating and does not show causation.

Article.Title: Changes in Serum Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor Concentrations Following Tuberculosis Preventive Therapy in Adults with Type 2 Diabetes
Article.Authors: Cheng Y.; Sheu M.; Li Y.; Wu J.; Liu S.; Huang W.; Lee I.
Article.Abstract: Latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) is prevalent among patients with type 2 diabetes, and aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) has been reported to be associated with LTBI. This observational study aimed to determine whether serum AhR levels decrease after tuberculosis prevention therapy (TPT). Patients with type 2 diabetes were enrolled for LTBI screening, and serum AhR levels were measured for those with a positive QuantiFERON-TB result. The patients received TPT, according to clinical practice: either weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid for 3 months (3HP) or daily isoniazid for 9 months (9H). Serum AhR levels were measured during a follow-up assessment at 36 weeks after enrollment in the patients who underwent continuous TPT for >3 months. Among 88 patients who completed the follow-up assessment, 47 (53.4%) received the 3HP regimen, and 41 (46.6%) received the 9H regimen. Serum AhR levels significantly decreased after TPT in the 3HP (45.4 [24.8, 55.44] to 13.4 [6.4, 23.8] pg/mL, p < 0.001) and 9H groups (43.4 [27.2, 60.8] to 14.6 [7.3, 21.3] pg/mL, p < 0.001). However, there was no statistically significant difference in the reduction in serum AhR levels between the 3HP and 9H groups (p = 0.286). In conclusion, serum AhR levels significantly decreased following TPT with the 3HP or 9H regimens.

Article.Title: Multi-Omics Analysis Reveals That lpl-a Deletion Reshapes Muscle Lipid Metabolism in Zebrafish: From Storage Limitation to Oxidative Bottleneck
Article.Authors: Liu T.; Xiao H.; Lu C.; Sun Z.; Zhang K.; Kuang Y.; Zheng X.
Article.Abstract: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) regulates tissue lipid partitioning, but its role in fish muscle lipid metabolism remains unclear. Here, a homozygous lpl-a knockout zebrafish line (lpl-a−/−) was constructed using CRISPR/Cas9 and fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 8 weeks. Muscle physiology, biochemistry, transcriptomics, and metabolomics were analyzed in female zebrafish. Muscle lpl-a expression and LPL content were significantly lower in knockout (KO) than wild-type (WT) fish. After HFD, WT fish showed significantly higher body weight, muscle TG and T-CHO contents, and abdominal fat than WT_LF, whereas KO_HF fish had significantly lower body weight than WT_HF, with muscle TG and T-CHO comparable to KO_LF. Multi-omics revealed reduced G3P and downregulated glycogen synthesis genes, consistent with storage limitation; upregulated acsl5 and downregulated acot15/acot17, consistent with enhanced fatty acid (FA) mobilization toward β-oxidation; downregulated ppara and pgc-1α, accumulated long-chain acylcarnitines, and decreased TCA intermediates, consistent with an oxidative bottleneck; and elevated AMP, increased AMPK protein content, accumulated DAG, increased PKC protein content, decreased SOD activity, and upregulated TLR/NF-κB inflammatory genes, consistent with energy stress and inflammation. Thus, lpl-a deletion reshapes muscle lipid metabolism from a storage-dominant mode toward storage limitation, oxidative mobilization, oxidative bottleneck, and energy stress with inflammation, and is associated with reduced HFD-induced lipid accumulation. lpl-a is a key node determining lipid storage versus oxidation, offering a potential target for improving fish muscle quality.

Article.Title: Form and Function in Flux: Molecular Ensembles from Structure to Therapy
Article.Authors: Patarca R.; Haseltine W.
Article.Abstract: Molecular structure, revealed by crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, imaging, and prediction, remains foundational to biology and drug design, yet function also depends on how structures flex, adapt, and interact. Proteins and RNA populate alternative conformations and binding states, while chromatin, membranes, glycans, metabolites, water, ions, and biominerals vary in composition and organization. This narrative review treats form and function as interdependent properties of molecular ensembles: structure constrains which states are accessible, whereas regulatory inputs, partners, and cellular environments determine which states are occupied, exchanged, and used. Without assuming a shared physical mechanism, we compare these systems and propose a cross-class evidence map that links each claimed state variable to its regulatory input, matched measurement, causal test, and organismal or clinical outcome. Examples from cancer, neurodegeneration, infection, and metabolic disease show how specific states become dysregulated, and why restored binding, assembly, or imaging readouts need not indicate functional recovery. Therapies are compared by primary mode of action—direct state modulation, target-abundance reduction, or genetic and RNA-level correction—with clinical successes, failures, and safety limits reported separately. The synthesis identifies where measurement methods must advance to resolve interrelated ensembles in native contexts and to determine when targeting them yields meaningful patient benefit.

Article.Title: Post-Treatment Molecular Biomarker Reassessment in Advanced Endometrial Cancer: An Evidence-Aware Framework for Precision Therapy
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Fei F.; Kong L.; Ye M.; Jin X.
Article.Abstract: Molecular classification has transformed treatment selection in endometrial cancer (EC), but most biomarkers are defined at diagnosis and may not represent the biological state of tumors after therapeutic exposure. In advanced, recurrent, or metastatic EC, treatment can reshape target expression, hormone dependence, immune context, signaling pathways, and DNA damage response (DDR), raising an important clinical question: which treatment-relevant features should be reassessed after progression, and how should the results inform subsequent therapy? This review synthesizes evidence across immune, endocrine, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) and pathway-directed, DDR-directed, and platinum–taxane treatment contexts. We focus on biomarkers that can be evaluated through repeat tissue biopsy, circulating tumor DNA, functional assays, and clinical treatment history, and distinguish biological plausibility from clinical actionability. The evidence is uneven. HER2 evolution and clinical measures of platinum sensitivity have comparatively direct EC-specific human support, whereas hormone receptor dynamics, estrogen receptor 1 (ESR1) evolution, and selected immune features remain clinically emerging, and pathway-rebound and functional DNA repair readouts are largely investigational. We therefore propose an evidence-aware framework for post-treatment biomarker reassessment that prioritizes whether the biological rationale for a previous therapy remains valid, has been weakened, or has been replaced by an alternative dependency. Prospective longitudinal studies are needed to determine when reassessment improves treatment selection and patient outcomes.

Article.Title: Lipotoxic Palmitate Hyperpolarises Mitochondria and Converts Nuclear 5mC to 5hmC: 8-Oxo-dG, 5mC and 5hmC Read on the Same Native DNA Molecules of Human Adipose-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cells
Article.Authors: Gospodinova A.; Velichkov A.; Dimitrov N.; Todorova K.; Hayrabedyan S.
Article.Abstract: Lipotoxic stress from saturated fatty acids compromises the mitochondria of human adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (hAdMSCs) and, with them, their regenerative capacity. We exposed hAdMSCs to sodium palmitate at 250 and 500 µM for 24 h and combined live-cell confocal imaging with long-read nanopore sequencing of native DNA, reading 8-oxo-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-oxo-dG), 5-methylcytosine (5mC) and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) directly from the raw signal of the same molecules. Surprisingly, palmitate hyperpolarised mitochondria at both concentrations instead of depolarising them; the lower, obesity-range concentration fragmented the mitochondrial network over 24 h, and both raised mitophagy-associated and lysosomal puncta without preventing a concentration-dependent rise in senescence-associated β-galactosidase positivity. Mitochondrial DNA copy number fell to 56% of untreated, while the remaining mitochondrial genomes tended to carry more 8-oxo-dG (27%) and nuclear 8-oxo-dG tended to be lower (20%), neither contrast reaching significance at this depth. Nuclear CpG methylation fell from 29.87% to 26.84%, uniformly across the genome; the loss of 5mC was matched by an equal gain of 5hmC, consistent with oxidation of the methyl group rather than its loss. Methylation was depressed beside oxidised guanines in untreated cells, and less so under palmitate. In a thirteen-gene adipokine panel, promoter demethylation reached transcript and secreted protein only for IL6. Ribosomal DNA retained its methylation and was neither less oxidised nor exempt from conversion, its 5hmC rising with the genome. Palmitate thus remodels two genomes under one metabolic condition; in the adipose progenitor, lipotoxic stress pairs mitochondrial depletion with a rewritten nuclear methylome, a route by which obesity may compromise the fate and regenerative capacity of the progenitor pool.

Article.Title: Targeting MAOA to Improve Enzalutamide Responsiveness and Enhance Immunotherapy Through YAP1-Associated Signaling in Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer
Article.Authors: Ma Y.; Chen H.; Xing Y.; Huang M.; Li M.; Hu Y.; Zhao J.; Zhang C.; Shi C.
Article.Abstract: Castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) represents a significant clinical challenge, characterized by resistance to androgen receptor antagonists such as enzalutamide (ENZ) and by immune tolerance mechanisms. Although monoamine oxidase A (MAOA) has been implicated in prostate cancer progression, its role in CRPC drug resistance and immune suppression remains underexplored. We investigated the role of MAOA in CRPC drug resistance and immune evasion using a series of in vitro and in vivo models, including ENZ-resistant cell lines, patient-derived organoid (PDO) models, patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models, and humanized mouse models. Our findings revealed that MAOA was significantly upregulated in ENZ-resistant CRPC models. Yes-associated protein 1 (YAP1) may link MAOA-associated drug resistance and immune evasion. In tumor cells, MAOA-associated YAP1 signaling is linked to alterations in reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and NF-κB-related signaling, potentially contributing to ENZ resistance. Furthermore, MAOA-associated YAP1 signaling regulates tumor-cell PD-L1 expression and may contribute to immune evasion. In preclinical models, the combination of ENZ, MAOA inhibition, and PD-1 blockade exhibited enhanced antitumor efficacy compared with the other ENZ-containing treatment regimens. These findings suggest potential therapeutic benefits of targeting MAOA in CRPC. Combining MAOA inhibitors with ICIs could improve patient outcomes by addressing both intrinsic drug resistance and extrinsic immune evasion.

Article.Title: Application GenOA (Gene Optimiser Assistant) Is an Easy Way to Create Genes for a Particular Expression Level
Article.Authors: Zaytsev K.; Plekhanova N.; Makarova A.; Bogatyreva N.; Fedorov A.
Article.Abstract: Accurate expression prediction and rational gene design for specific expression levels are central challenges in synthetic biology and recombinant protein production. Here, we present GenOA, a software toolbox with a graphical user interface that predicts protein expression levels in Escherichia coli from the gene coding sequences with a correlation coefficient of 0.7, and conversely designs novel coding sequences that achieve a user-specified expression level while preserving the encoded amino acid sequence. This tool accepts either nucleotide or amino acid sequences as an input and enables users to specify target expression levels along with additional constraints, including GC content, codon usage irregularity, and the position of the sequence within the E. coli genome subspace. Beyond E. coli, GenOA allows for model training for other species by uploading custom training data for other host organisms. By integrating accurate expression prediction with sequence optimisation under multiple user-defined constraints, GenOA provides a versatile platform for the design of genetic constructs tuned for specific expression levels.
