Article.Title: A Computational Investigation of Curcumin Glucoside in α-Synuclein Aggregation: DFT Characterization, Molecular Docking, and Secondary Data Analysis
Article.Authors: Emani L.; Jalapally P.; Samudio-Ríos G.; Rao J.; Izudheen S.; Lakey-Beitia J.; Rao K.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the aggregation of α-synuclein into oligomers and amyloid fibrils. Curcumin glucoside has been investigated as a potential inhibitor of α-synuclein aggregation; however, understanding its electronic properties and predicted interactions with α-synuclein fibrils may provide additional insights into its potential molecular behavior. This study integrates density functional theory (DFT) calculations, molecular docking, and quantitative analysis of previously published Thioflavin-T (ThT) fluorescence data to investigate the physicochemical properties and potential anti-aggregation effects of curcumin glucoside. DFT calculations were performed on isolated curcumin and curcumin monoglucoside molecules using the B3LYP-D3(BJ)/def2-SVP level of theory with implicit aqueous solvation. The HOMO–LUMO energy gaps were 3.626 eV for curcumin and 3.372 eV for curcumin monoglucoside, while their dipole moments were 7.53 D and 11.19 D, respectively. These differences indicate changes in the electronic structure and molecular polarity associated with glucosylation. Molecular docking against selected α-synuclein fibril structures representing different disease stages showed docking scores ranging from −5.1 to −6.7 kcal/mol for curcumin and from −6.2 to −6.6 kcal/mol for curcumin glucoside. Previously published ThT fluorescence data related to curcumin glucoside were analyzed using a four-parameter logistic (4PL) model to characterize the reported aggregation-response profiles over time. The combined findings provide complementary electronic-structure, docking, and aggregation-kinetic perspectives on curcumin glucoside. Importantly, the DFT calculations were restricted to isolated molecules and did not evaluate electron redistribution, charge-transfer pathways, or reaction energetics within protein–ligand complexes. The docking scores are computational estimates from a scoring function and are not experimentally measured binding affinities. The 4PL analysis is a secondary re-examination of previously published ThT fluorescence data and does not constitute new experimental validation of aggregation inhibition. Collectively, these results supply a computational and quantitative descriptive basis that can guide further experimental and higher-level quantum-chemical investigation of curcumin glucoside as a potential modulator of α-synuclein aggregation; they do not, by themselves, establish a quantum-mechanical mechanism of action.

Article.Title: A Guide to Human Microbiome Data Repositories
Article.Authors: Mora-Flores L.; Alva Torres S.; Hernández-Lemus E.; Anda-Jáuregui G.
Article.Abstract: This review chronicles the evolution of human microbiome research, tracing its trajectory from early descriptive studies to the current era of large multi-omics repositories. Technological advancements, such as high-throughput 16S rRNA sequencing and whole metagenome shotgun sequencing, have shifted the field from cataloguing microbial inhabitants to understanding their functional roles and interactions with the human host. The primary aim of this document is to offer researchers a concise and accessible guide to the major human microbiome projects and the repositories that store their data, outlining the data flow starting from sample collection, in a simple, comprehensive way. We synthesize the contributions of key international projects that have shaped the field and provide a full overview of the repositories that store human microbiome data, clarifying their scope, structure, and utility for different research needs. Looking ahead, the field is moving toward multi-omics integration, AI-driven analysis, and globally inclusive sampling. Future progress will require advancing sequencing technologies while building infrastructures that are capable of handling increasingly complex data.

Article.Title: Placental Origins of Preeclampsia and Fetal Growth Restriction: A Mechanism-to-Model Roadmap for Human Experimental Systems
Article.Authors: Liu L.; Guo D.; Chen S.; Zheng L.; Ma X.
Article.Abstract: Placental dysfunction contributes to preeclampsia (PE) and fetal growth restriction (FGR), yet similar placental abnormalities can accompany different maternal and fetal outcomes. Understanding these outcomes requires experiments that connect specific cellular processes to placental function. This structured narrative review integrates clinical and developmental evidence with experiments using primary tissues, trophoblast stem cells, organoids, reconstructed interfaces, and placental perfusion. The synthesis examines trophoblast differentiation and invasion, decidual–immune–vascular interactions, syncytiotrophoblast dysfunction and maternal signaling, and nutrient transport in FGR. Comparative experiments distinguish culture-associated states from disease-associated differentiation defects, and invasion from vascular interaction. Secretory and extracellular-vesicle studies identify endothelial effects while separating placental output, systemic exposure, and recipient susceptibility. In FGR-derived trophoblasts, restoration of mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR)-regulated amino acid uptake identifies a recoverable cellular defect, although directional placental transfer remains untested. Partial rescue, negative findings, derivation effects, and the distinction between independent donors and repeated cultures qualify these interpretations. The resulting mechanism-to-model roadmap links biological uncertainties to cellular targets, interventions, and functional measurements. Traceable specimen–model linkage and assay-specific analytical evaluation can strengthen these comparisons and support testable mechanistic and treatment hypotheses without treating any isolated culture phenotype as the complete PE or FGR syndrome.

Article.Title: Integrative Phosphoproteomic Mapping of WEE1 Kinase Reveals Site-Specific Regulatory Networks Modulating Cell-Cycle Checkpoint
Article.Authors: Vaz C.; Dcunha L.; George M.; Suresh M.; Raju R.; Kanekar S.
Article.Abstract: WEE1 is a nuclear kinase that inhibits CDK1 at Tyr15, gating G2/M progression, and coordinating DNA replication with mitotic entry. We mapped the known and predicted upstream kinases, substrates, and interactors, and examined tumor–tissue correlations using CPTAC breast cancer data. Among the 33 Class I sites, Ser165, Thr173, Ser139, and Thr190 were the most frequently identified sites. Ser165-Thr173 and Ser139-Thr190 were significantly co-regulated in independent datasets. The co-regulated networks of all four sites were enriched for cell cycle processes with overlapping terms (DNA damage response, replication, and mitosis). Thr173 and Thr190 were co-regulated by CDK2 Tyr15. WEE1 phosphorylation was most strongly elevated in breast tumors, where WEE1_Thr190 correlated with RBL1_Ser1041, ESCO2_Ser75, TPX2_Ser738, and ORC2_Thr226. This hypothesis-generating framework nominates candidate phosphosites; however, no treatment-response data were analyzed, and the proposed functions require further validation.

Article.Title: Mesenchymal Stem Cells, Characterization of Biological Properties, Interactions with the Extracellular Matrix and Natural Polymer-Based Matrices
Article.Authors: Bačenková D.; Trebuňová M.; Čajková J.; Findrik-Balogová A.; Živčák J.
Article.Abstract: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are widely used in biomedical engineering due to their self-renewal capacity, potential to differentiate into multiple cell lineages, and ability to secrete bioactive factors and extracellular vesicles. Their behavior is strongly regulated by the extracellular matrix (ECM), which provides a specialized microenvironment, or niche, that plays a key role in maintaining stemness, proliferation, and differentiation. MSC membrane receptors participate in a wide range of metabolic pathways and interactions, either by binding to specific ECM molecules or by functioning as enzymes. Endoglin acts as a co-receptor for TGF-beta. Ecto-5′-nucleotidase is a key enzyme in purine metabolism. The Thy-1 receptor interacts with integrins and syndecan, influencing migration and adhesion. CD44 is characterized by its binding to hyaluronic acid. This review focuses on characterizing the physiological properties of MSCs and on culturing MSCs in three-dimensional environments. Culture of MSCs in natural ECM-derived biomaterials such as collagen, gelatin, hyaluronic acid, and others supports the maintenance of stemness and differentiation potential of the cells. Furthermore, natural macroporous scaffolds provide mechanical support while facilitating cell attachment, nutrient diffusion, and cell proliferation. Culturing MSCs in a supportive, biocompatible 3D environment expands the possibilities for tissue engineering applications.

Under microfluidic conditions, the most consistent reductions in co-localization were observed for carboxylate-modified FluoSpheres, particularly following exposure to ¼× MIC of CLR, whereas LEV at ¼× MIC significantly increased co-localization with amine-modified particles at specific time points. In both models, sulfate-modified FluoSpheres showed generally lower interaction, delayed antibiotic-dependent effects, and pronounced surface autoaggregation. Z-stack analysis revealed carboxylate-modified particle signals mainly in the middle biofilm layers, amine-modified signals in deeper layers, and sulfate-modified signals predominantly at the surface. Article.Title: Structure-Dependent Mechanistic Divergence in Male Reproductive Toxicity Between Bisphenol A and Its Analog Bisphenol S: Integration of Network Toxicology and Molecular Docking
Article.Authors: Zhang N.; Wang S.; Li J.; Ma B.; Zhang Q.
Article.Abstract: Bisphenol A (BPA), a widespread endocrine-disrupting chemical, has been associated with male reproductive health, yet its structural analog bisphenol S (BPS), selected as a primary alternative, may also pose similar risks. Immune infiltration analysis linked BPA-related genes inversely to NK cell abundance. Transcription factor analysis identified MYCN and PGR as hub nodes with distinct downstream networks. Molecular docking predicted generally favorable binding of both chemicals to key targets, with target-dependent differences in predicted affinity. These in silico results suggest that BPA and BPS may affect male reproductive health through partly distinct mechanisms, with BPA more closely associated with immune-related pathways and BPS with metabolic-oxidative stress pathways.

Article.Title: Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen-Targeted Phototherapy for Prostate Cancer: A Systematic Review of Preclinical Evidence and Translational Readiness
Article.Authors: Oisakede E.; Adegbenro A.; Olawade D.; Boussios S.
Article.Abstract: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is an established diagnostic and therapeutic target in prostate cancer. PSMA-targeted phototherapy comprises mechanistically distinct full-antibody near-infrared photoimmunotherapy (NIR-PIT), antibody-fragment photoimmunotherapy, ligand-targeted photodynamic therapy (PDT), and nanoparticle or multimodal systems. This systematic review evaluated their preclinical efficacy, safety, and translational readiness. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, the Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for studies published from 1 January 2010 to 20 August 2026. Studies were classified into four carrier–mechanism groups before comparison across a seven-domain translational-readiness framework with explicit Early, Developing and Advanced anchors. Owing to substantial heterogeneity in targeting platforms, photoactive agents, models, illumination parameters and outcomes, meta-analysis was inappropriate; synthesis followed SWiM guidance. Animal studies were assessed using SYRCLE, and in vitro or ex vivo studies using an adapted ToxRTool with a decision-relevant reporting overlay. No numerical result used in the synthesis was obtained by figure digitisation. Thirty-three studies were included: 10 were confined to in vitro experiments, 19 combined in vitro and in vivo work, and four were in vivo only; one of the 19 combined studies also assessed fresh human prostate tissue ex vivo. Platforms were analysed as full-antibody NIR-PIT or photoimmunotherapy, antibody-fragment photoimmunotherapy, ligand-targeted PDT, and nanoparticle or multimodal systems. Within these classes, reports generally demonstrated preferential PSMA-dependent uptake and light-induced cytotoxicity, with multiple murine studies reporting tumour-growth inhibition and longer time to humane endpoints. Durable tumour-free responses occurred in selected small cohorts, particularly after repeated or combination treatment. Translational evidence remained limited: one study evaluated orthotopic prostate treatment in four dogs, while another demonstrated treatment-induced apoptosis in fresh prostate cancer tissue from 17 prostatectomy patients. No included full report described therapeutic treatment in patients. The decision-relevant in vitro/ex vivo appraisal classified 17 reports as higher, eight as moderate and four as lower reliability; animal studies frequently lacked sufficient reporting of randomisation, allocation concealment and blinding. Major translational barriers were heterogeneous PSMA expression, non-standardised light delivery, limited long-term safety data and insufficient validation in anatomically and immunologically representative models. PSMA-targeted phototherapy shows preclinical activity but remains clinically immature. Translation should proceed within mechanistically defined therapeutic classes and prioritise clinically realistic light dosimetry, PSMA heterogeneity, pharmacokinetic optimisation, functional safety, independent validation, and staged human evaluation. Article.Title: Gene Expression Signatures in Endometriosis: Molecular Insights and Potential Clinical Applications
Article.Authors: Murawski M.; Bania J.; Łaczmańska I.
Article.Abstract: Endometriosis (EM) is a chronic disease affecting approximately 190 million women worldwide. Despite its high prevalence and substantial impact on quality of life and fertility, diagnosis remains challenging because of heterogeneous clinical presentation and the lack of validated molecular biomarkers. Altered gene expression provides valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms and biological heterogeneity of EM and may facilitate the identification of candidate biomarkers. However, molecular signatures derived from surgically collected lesions must be distinguished from markers measurable in minimally invasive specimens, as their potential clinical applications differ substantially. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on gene-expression alterations with potential diagnostic and clinical relevance in EM, including differentially expressed genes (DEGs), transcription factors (TFs), genes involved in major pathogenic pathways, and multigene diagnostic models. Among individual candidates, AEBP1, KLF2, HOXB6, and RORB have demonstrated promising discriminatory performance, while HOXB6 may also contribute to distinguishing stages of disease. Distinct expression profiles have also been associated with EM-related infertility. Multigene approaches appear particularly promising, as integrated expression signatures may provide more robust discriminatory performance than individual markers. However, most proposed biomarkers remain at the candidate stage, and methodological and clinical heterogeneity limits comparability across studies. Future research should prioritize independent validation in large, well-characterized cohorts, standardized analytical procedures, and evaluation of multigene signatures in minimally invasive samples to support their clinical translation.

Article.Title: Structural Biology of the SARS-CoV-2 Proteome: Experimental Context, Functional Interpretation, and Intervention Research
Article.Authors: Xia Y.; Liu S.; Luo Z.; Tao Y.; Sang P.; Liu S.
Article.Abstract: Structural biology has defined key features of the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) proteome, although structural coverage and functional support remain uneven. This review connects representative structures of structural, nonstructural, and accessory proteins with evidence from biochemical, cellular, computational, and intervention studies. We ask when structural observations support biological interpretations and what additional evidence connects those interpretations to intervention outcomes. Structural coverage, experimental context, and functional support are recorded as separate dimensions across selected proteins, complexes, virions, replication organelles, and variant studies. Selected cases show that resolved structures can coexist with disputed functions; where the evidence compared here allows, we state which interpretations we regard as adequately supported and which remain candidate explanations. Differences between studies can also reflect complementary observations at different scales. Antiviral, antibody, and vaccine studies show how structures contribute to design and mechanistic interpretation, whereas clinical outcomes concern specific products, populations, and endpoints. Major gaps concern native assemblies, the physiological relevance of some accessory-protein findings, and the translation of molecular recognition into antiviral efficacy or protective immunity.

Article.Title: A Multimodal Nano-Vehicle for the Transport of Biologically Active Amine Oxidase as a Therapeutic Enzyme
Article.Authors: Bortoluzzi M.; Rutigliano L.; Tonolo F.; Rilievo G.; Cecconello A.; Cencini A.; Macone A.; Fino P.; Agostinelli E.; Magro M.; Vianello F.
Article.Abstract: A high polyamine (PA) concentration due to altered metabolism represents an Achilles’ heel in targeting PA-rich cancerous cells. This is due to the possibility of generating toxic by-products via the amine oxidase (AO)-catalyzed oxidation of PA. Nevertheless, AO intracellular delivery remains an open challenge. Recently, an extensive study on Caco-2 cells showed the applicability of a new magnetic and fluorescent nanoparticle (SAMN@TA) as a bovine serum amino oxidase (BSAO) carrier. Here, a SAMN@TA@BSAO multimodal nano-device was tested on two different human colorectal adenocarcinoma cell lines (LoVo WT and DX), confirming remarkable cell association along with a dose-dependent loss of cell viability, reaching 43% and 60% per single treatment, respectively. This contribution stimulates further investigation on SAMN@TA@BSAO use as a potential anticancer tool.

Article.Title: Phloretin Inhibits Post-Entry CCoV Replication and Attenuates TNF-α/NF-κB-Mediated Inflammation
Article.Authors: Liu G.; Li Z.; Zhang S.; Guo X.; Wang H.; Qin T.
Article.Abstract: Canine coronavirus (CCoV) triggers severe gastroenteritis in canine hosts, and no specific antiviral drug is currently available for clinical treatment. Phloretin, a naturally occurring dihydrochalcone isolated from apples, possesses extensive anti-inflammatory properties, whereas its potential against CCoV infection has not yet been characterized. The anti-CCoV efficacy of phloretin was assessed in the CRFK cell line via CPE-based IC50 measurement, time-of-addition test and quantitative PCR assays. Transcriptome profiling, network pharmacology, molecular docking, ELISA and Western blot (p-p65, IκB-α) were further performed to dissect its underlying anti-inflammatory molecular mechanism. Phloretin suppressed CCoV proliferation with an IC50 value of 63.33 µM and mainly functioned at the post-entry replication phase. This was evidenced by a 2.32 log10 copies/µL decrease in viral load and a 2.48 log10 TCID50/0.1 mL reduction in viral titer. Negligible direct virucidal activity and mild anti-adsorption activity (0.43 log10 TCID50/0.1 mL reduction) were detected. Transcriptomic profiling of CCoV-infected cells revealed remarkable activation of the TNF-α/NF-κB signaling pathway upon viral challenge. Based on this observation, network pharmacology was employed to predict the anti-inflammatory targets of phloretin, identifying TNF, IL-6, and JAK2 as hub targets. Molecular docking further predicted stable binding affinities between phloretin and essential intracellular signaling mediators, including JAK2, p38 MAPK, and p65. Consistently, experimental validation demonstrated that phloretin markedly decreased the transcription and protein production of pro-inflammatory mediators (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-18, TNF-α), lowered p-p65 abundance by 25.14%, and restored IκB-α expression to significantly above the control baseline.

Article.Title: Disulfidptosis-Related Genes Comprise Two Functionally Distinct, Transcriptionally Uncoupled Subsets with Complementary Prognostic Associations: An Integrated Pan-Cancer Analysis of TCGA Data
Article.Authors: Kus Z.; Eslamkhah S.; Gulmez H.; Yavas C.; Arvas Y.; Yilmaz I.
Article.Abstract: Disulfidptosis is a regulated form of cell death that arises from NADPH depletion and disulfide stress on the actin cytoskeleton in cells with high SLC7A11. Scores built from disulfidptosis-related genes (DRGs) are increasingly put forward as prognostic markers, yet their internal structure and metabolic context have remained poorly defined. We examined 24 DRGs across 10,242 primary tumours (33 TCGA cancer types) and 722 normal tissues, drawing on survival, purity and genomic data. SLC7A11 was up-regulated in 14 of 18 cancers, while the majority of cytoskeletal DRGs sat at lower levels in tumours. The DRG score showed a heterogeneous pooled link to shorter overall survival (HR per SD 1.15, 95% CI 1.06–1.25; prediction interval 0.78–1.70) and stayed associated after adjustment for available clinical covariates and purity in six cancers (FDR < 0.05): adverse in five, among them lower-grade glioma (HR 1.68; attenuated to 1.24, p = 0.046, after adjustment for IDH and 1p/19q status, grade and purity) and mesothelioma, and protective in clear-cell renal carcinoma. The predefined core and cytoskeleton subsets were almost uncorrelated (median ρ = −0.04): SLC7A11 expression tracked pentose phosphate/NADPH genes independently of purity (median ρ = 0.32), whereas the cytoskeleton subset ran opposite to oxidative phosphorylation genes. After adjustment for NRF2 target expression, however, SLC7A11 was not more strongly coupled to core PPP enzyme genes than expression-matched random genes. In joint models, each subset proved independently prognostic, but in different cancers. The composite score was prognostic in more cancer types than random gene sets of equal size (9 vs. 3; p = 0.04), whereas in the four cancers with robust models, DRG-based LASSO-Cox models performed no better than models built from random 24-gene sets. DRG scores are better decomposed than read as a single disulfidptosis axis.

Article.Title: Preventive Supplementation with Taif Black Mulberry (Morus nigra) Attenuates Systemic Inflammation, Hepatic Oxidative Stress and Liver Alterations in Rats with Collagen-Induced Rheumatoid Arthritis
Article.Authors: Baz L.; Alkhattabi N.; Tarbiah N.; Al Doghaither H.; Alkhudaydi M.; Abuahamil S.; Almutairi A.; Al-Thepyani M.
Article.Abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis involves systemic inflammation, immune dysregulation, and oxidative stress, which may contribute to hepatic injury. This study investigated the effects of preventive oral supplementation with Taif black mulberry (Morus nigra) fruit powder on systemic inflammatory, serological, oxidative, and hepatic alterations in rats immunized with type II collagen (collagen-induced arthritis, CIA, model). Thirty-two male Wistar rats were randomly assigned to four groups (n = 8 per group): healthy controls, untreated collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) controls, and two CIA groups receiving freeze-dried Morus nigra fruit powder at doses of 100 and 200 mg/kg/day, respectively. Treatment was initiated on the day of the first immunization (day 0) and continued for eight weeks as part of a preventive experimental design. Immunization was induced with bovine type II collagen emulsified in incomplete Freund’s adjuvant. Serum cytokines, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies, and liver enzymes were assessed. Hepatic malondialdehyde and antioxidant enzyme activities were measured, and liver histopathology was examined using hematoxylin and eosin and Masson’s trichrome staining. Compared with the healthy controls, the CIA model rats showed higher TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17, anti-CCP, lower IL-10, increased hepatic MDA and serum ALT, AST, and ALP, reduced hepatic superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase (GPx) activities, and hepatic histological alterations. Both doses of Morus nigra lowered TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17, anti-CCp, ALT, and ALP and increased antioxidant enzyme activities relative to the untreated CIA rats, whereas significant reductions in hepatic MDA and serum AST were observed only with a higher dose. The higher dose also lowered IL-2, whereas neither dose restored IL-10. Anti-CCP and GPx responses were greater at 200 mg/kg/day than at 100 mg/kg/day. Preventive Morus nigra supplementation attenuated systemic inflammatory, autoimmune, oxidative, and hepatic alterations in the CIA rats. These preclinical findings support the protective effect on systemic and hepatic outcomes. However, further mechanistic investigations and clinical studies are required to establish its efficacy and underlying mechanisms of action.

Article.Title: Integrated Comparative Analysis Reveals Structural Diversification and Functional Associations of Arabidopsis DEAD-Box RNA Helicases
Article.Authors: Fontcuberta-Cervera S.; Ponce M.
Article.Abstract: DEAD-box RNA helicases (RHs) constitute one of the largest and most conserved families of RNA metabolism factors in eukaryotes, yet the evolutionary relationships and functions of many plant members remain unresolved. We present an integrated comparative analysis of the Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis) DEAD-box RH family by combining structural curation, orthology inference, comparative analyses of protein features, and cross-species comparisons of biological pathway enrichment among co-expressed genes. Structural curation established a reference set of 53 intact genes and four putative pseudogenes (RH43, RH44, RH45, and RH55) for subsequent analyses. Orthology inference using the DRSC Integrative Ortholog Prediction Tool (DIOPT) identified high- and moderate-confidence orthologous relationships, revealed conserved helicase lineages and putative lineage-specific expansions, and enabled systematic comparisons with Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast) and Homo sapiens (humans). Comparative analyses of protein features revealed that non-canonical DExD-box motif variants occur in 10 of the 57 Arabidopsis, three of the 26 yeast, and five of the 38 human DEAD-box RHs. Although the DECD variant appears to be shared across plant, fungal, and metazoan lineages, other variants show restricted or patchy distributions, as exemplified by the DEVD variant, whose distribution is consistent with its independent emergence in several lineages, indicating that the canonical DEAD sequence is not universally conserved. Annotated accessory motifs and domains were identified in only a small subset of proteins, although annotation-based counts probably underestimate their frequency, and the helicase core architecture was broadly conserved. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses of genes co-expressed with Arabidopsis DEAD-box RHs and their orthologs provided a basis for generating functional hypotheses for previously uncharacterized proteins, even in the absence of prior experimental evidence of ortholog function. Although these hypotheses require further investigation and experimental validation, the findings provide an integrated framework for investigating the structural and functional diversification of the Arabidopsis DEAD-box RH family. This approach may also be extended to other poorly characterized multigene families.

Article.Title: Pharmacological Insights into Capparis spinosa L.: Comparative Phytochemical Profiling and In Vitro Evaluation of Leaf and Stem Extracts
Article.Authors: Aziz I.; Farrag M.; Almuqrin A.; Marraiki N.
Article.Abstract: Capparis spinosa L. is a medicinal plant with diverse pharmacological potential; however, comparative characterization of the phytochemical profiles and multiple biological activities of its leaves and stems remains limited, particularly for plants collected in Saudi Arabia. This study provides an integrated comparison of methanolic leaf (CSLE) and stem (CSSE) extracts, combining volatile and semi-volatile GC-MS profiling with antioxidant, antibacterial, enzyme-inhibitory, cytotoxicity, and apoptosis-associated gene-expression analyses. CSLE exhibited higher extraction yield (13.31 ± 2.14%), total phenolic content (125.15 ± 1.21 mg GAE/g), and total flavonoid content (78.13 ± 1.14 mg QE/g) than CSSE. GC–MS tentatively identified 43 constituents in CSLE and 28 in CSSE, with differences in their relative GC-MS peak-area profiles. In the DPPH assay, CSLE showed stronger antioxidant activity, with DPPH and ABTS IC50 values of 129.69 µg/mL (95% CI: 96.52–145.28) and 47.25 µg/mL (95% CI: 45.46–51.89), respectively, compared with 162.45 µg/mL (95% CI: 157.42–172.21) and 68.46 µg/mL (95% CI: 64.70–72.12) for CSSE. CSLE also exhibited greater antibacterial activity (MIC = 7.81–62.50 µg/mL) and α-glucosidase inhibition (IC50 93.62 µg/mL (95% CI: 70.46–124.00) versus1 22.44 µg/mL (95% CI: 88.55–177.00) for CSSE). Both extracts inhibited α-amylase and reduced MCF-7 and HepG2 cell viability and were associated with changes in apoptosis-related gene expression; however, apoptosis was not functionally confirmed. The novelty of this study lies in its comprehensive comparison of the biochemistry of a Saudi C. spinosa L. plant accession using volatile/semi-volatile GC-MS analysis, TPC/TFC, antioxidant, six bacterial strains, two digestive enzyme inhibition, cytotoxicity, and apoptosis gene expression assessments all within a single experimental set-up; however, it does not claim to be the first leaf-stem comparison. These findings provide a basis for further investigation of their bioactive constituents and mechanisms of action.

Article.Title: Targeting UFMylation in Cancer: Emerging Roles in Cancer Stem Cell Regulation and Therapeutic Targeting
Article.Authors: Vukovic Derfi K.; Matijevic Glavan T.
Article.Abstract: UFMylation is an emerging ubiquitin-like post-translational modification involved in protein quality control, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) homeostasis, and cellular responses to stress. Increasing evidence links UFMylation to cancer development and progression, revealing tumor-promoting and tumor-suppressive functions that depend on tumor type, cellular context, and the substrates involved. Recent discoveries also implicated UFMylation in cancer stem cell (CSC) maintenance, particularly through its effects on stemness-associated signaling pathways, transcription factors, tumor sphere formation, and therapeutic resistance. This review outlines the molecular mechanisms and regulation of UFMylation and examines its context-dependent functions in cancer, with particular emphasis on CSC biology. We discuss how alterations in the UFMylation pathway may influence stem-like properties and treatment responses. We also examine therapeutic strategies for targeting the UFMylation pathway, including pharmacological inhibitors, modulation of transcription factors, and combination approaches aimed at improving treatment responses. Particular attention is given to the potential of inducing ferroptosis through UFMylation inhibition as a strategy for targeting CSCs. Finally, this review highlights principal knowledge gaps and future research directions, emphasizing the need to characterize novel relevant substrates, validate observations in physiologically accurate settings, and implement in vivo tumor models to better understand the role of UFMylation in cancer stemness.

Article.Title: Intergenerational Effects of Early-Life Arsenic Exposure on Sperm Quality and Epididymal Transcriptome: Integrative Analysis of Large and Small RNAs
Article.Authors: Cortes-Ramirez S.; Tam N.; McDonald A.; Ying J.; Leung Y.; Ho S.
Article.Abstract: Inorganic arsenic (iAs) is a widespread environmental toxicant associated with male reproductive dysfunction, yet the epididymal molecular responses to developmental exposure and their potential intergenerational consequences remain poorly understood. We investigated sperm quality and epididymal large- and small RNA profiles in directly exposed male offspring (F1) and their unexposed sons (F2). Pregnant C57BL/6J dams received 1.15 ppm iAs in drinking water throughout gestation and lactation. Adult F1 and F2 males underwent sperm-quality assessment and epididymal transcriptomic profiling, followed by differential-expression and pathway enrichment analyses. Developmental iAs exposure significantly reduced sperm concentration, total sperm count, and motility in F1 males, whereas reduced sperm concentration and total sperm count were also observed in unexposed F2 males. In F1 epididymides, large-RNA analysis identified enrichment of epithelial remodeling, inflammatory, and stress-response pathways, together with suppression of oxidative phosphorylation and metabolic pathways. Small RNA profiling revealed a downward trend in mitochondrial tRNA abundance. In contrast, F2 epididymides exhibited suppression of spermatogenesis- and cell cycle-related pathways and differential expression of 56 small RNAs, including spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs, small nucleolar RNAs, and microRNAs. An independent transcriptomic comparison with Occludin-knockout (Ocln−/−) mice, a genetic model of epididymal infertility, demonstrated concordant enrichment directions for 18 of 21 F1-associated Hallmark pathways, providing additional pathway-level support for the F1 findings. Comparable concordance was not observed in F2. To our knowledge, this is the first integrated analysis of epididymal large- and small RNA responses to developmental iAs exposure across two generations. These findings identify distinct epididymal molecular signatures associated with persistent and intergenerational reproductive abnormalities and highlight the epididymis as a potentially important site of developmental environmental responses.

Article.Title: A Parasite-Rich Microeukaryome Shows Tribe-Structured Covariation with the Bacteriome in Non-Urban Mosquitoes (Culicinae) from Colombia
Article.Authors: Cuervo-Tinjacá G.; Marín-Suárez J.; Uribe-Soto S.; Gómez-Palacio A.
Article.Abstract: The eukaryotic component of the mosquito microbiota, which includes parasites, remains poorly characterized, partly because amplicon surveys suffer from host co-amplification and primer bias. To describe their microeukaryome, we re-analysed total-RNA sequencing libraries from non-urban Culicinae collected in Antioquia, Colombia, whose virome and bacteriome were previously characterized. Ribosomal 18S and 28S reads were mined from 26 pooled samples representing 18 morphotypes and four tribes. The curated 18S matrix comprised 1350 reads across 45 taxonomic features, and a rank-aware inventory retained 29 non-redundant lineages. Stramenopiles (Gyrista and Bigyra) accounted for 43.0% of curated 18S reads and Microsporidia for 20.0%. Seven features with best-hit labels of insect parasites occurred in 15 samples; Amblyospora was supported at the genus level, whereas a Coelomomyces-labelled signal was corroborated by 28S evidence only at the order Blastocladiales. Community composition differed among tribes after rarefaction; in non-rarefied data, this difference depended mainly on an Aspergillus-labelled feature of uncertain provenance. In 21 matched samples, microeukaryome and bacteriome ordinations were concordant (Procrustes correlation = 0.507; p = 0.0047), but not within tribes, and no concordance with the virome was detected. These results provide a baseline for the microeukaryome of non-urban Neotropical Culicinae and its tribe-structured covariation with the bacteriome.

Article.Title: GPCR and Insulin Signaling: Friends or Foes in Insulin Resistance?
Article.Authors: Rueda A.; Arias-Montaño J.; Olivares-Reyes J.
Article.Abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are a diverse family of cell surface receptors that transmit signals from external molecules, such as hormones and neurotransmitters, to the interior of cells and are the most widely distributed membrane receptors in living beings. Their actions are not limited to mediating rapid effects in the cell but also regulate cell proliferation, differentiation, and gene expression. GPCRs have also been recognized for their important role in regulating metabolic actions and their association with diseases and metabolic disorders, such as type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), metabolic syndrome, and insulin resistance. A significant number of reports have demonstrated the strong relationship between insulin actions and GPCRs, such as those for adrenaline/noradrenaline, angiotensin, vasopressin, and corticotropin-releasing factor, ranging from sensitization (positive actions) to negative regulation of insulin actions. This raises the question: Are GPCRs and insulin signaling friends or foes in the development and progression of insulin resistance? This review aims to explore the complex interplay between GPCRs and insulin signaling and how their interactions contribute to the development of insulin resistance.

Article.Title: Dual Modification of Bioengineered Bacillus caldovelox Arginase Achieves Long-Lasting and Sustained Arginine Depletion for Gastric Cancer Treatment
Article.Authors: Chung S.; Tam S.; Choi M.; So P.; Kim C.; Tu Y.; Wong K.; Lee L.; Leung Y.
Article.Abstract: We have previously reported a mono-PEGylated thermostable Bacillus caldovelox arginase mutant (BCA-M-PEG20, also named as Mn-BCA-M-PEG20L), a Mn2+-enriched enzyme shown to be effective against gastric cancer xenograft mouse models. To further enhance the pharmacodynamics and efficacy of the drug, in this study, we applied a dual approach to modify the protein drug molecule. We introduced a V20P mutation (change of Val20 to Pro20) together with a metal substitution process (replacement of Mn2+ by Ni2+/Co2+), resulting in a novel enzyme drug named Ni/Co-V20P-PEG20L with high catalytic efficiency and excellent pharmacodynamic properties. Both Ni-V20P-PEG20L and Co-V20P-PEG20L demonstrated remarkable anti-cancer effects on gastric and lung cancer cell lines. Particularly, one injection of Co-V20P-PEG20L maintained a sustained arginine depletion for two weeks, outperforming Ni-V20P-PEG20L, and was therefore chosen for further anti-tumor in vivo studies. We found that the biweekly administration of Co-V20P-PEG20L at a dosage of 20 mg/kg resulted in over 50% suppression in tumor mass in a human MKN-45 gastric cancer xenograft mouse model. Although Co-V20P-PEG20L is a bacterial enzyme, mono-PEGylation technology could protect the drug molecule from anti-drug antibodies. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that Co-V20P-PEG20L is a promising new arginine-depleting enzyme for the treatment of various cancer types.

Article.Title: Myo-Inositol Versus Inactive Control in Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Garzon S.; Casprini C.; Mantovani M.; Porcari I.; Zorzato P.; Bosco M.; Laterza R.; Paladini D.; Uccella S.
Article.Abstract: This systematic review aimed to estimate the effects attributable to myo-inositol (MI) compared with inactive comparators across metabolic, endocrine, clinical, and reproductive outcomes in women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), and to assess the certainty of evidence. Scopus, PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 31 July 2026. Studies evaluating MI, alone or with nonpharmacological components, were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and ROBINS-I, research integrity using RIGID/TRACT, and certainty of evidence using GRADE. Thirty-one studies were included (20 RCTs and 11 observational studies). Quantitative synthesis was restricted to low-integrity-risk RCTs comparing MI-containing interventions with inactive comparators. Participant totals varied across outcomes, with pooled analyses including between 70 and 376 participants. MI reduced LH levels (MD, −3.217 mIU/mL; 95% CI, −5.076 to −1.359; high certainty), likely reduced the LH/FSH ratio, and likely increased SHBG levels (moderate certainty). MI may also reduce free testosterone and irregular menses (low certainty). MI likely reduced HOMA-IR (MD, −0.972; 95% CI, −1.538 to −0.405; moderate certainty). When using assisted reproductive technology, MI likely increased clinical pregnancy (OR, 2.767; 95% CI, 1.151–6.651; moderate certainty). Across outcomes, certainty of evidence was frequently limited by small sample sizes, imprecision, and heterogeneity. Effects on several other outcomes remained insufficiently explored, and phenotype-stratified analyses were not feasible because studies did not report outcomes by PMOS phenotype. In conclusion, MI is associated with metabolic, endocrine, and reproductive benefits in PMOS, with certainty varying substantially across outcomes. Larger, phenotype-stratified RCTs with standardized dosing and adequate treatment duration are needed to confirm these findings.

Article.Title: Targeted Quantitative Phenolic Profiling and In Vitro Biological Activities of Onosma erecta Sm. Extracts Obtained by Ultrasound-Assisted Extraction
Article.Authors: Sarikurkcu C.; Nar B.
Article.Abstract: Onosma erecta remains insufficiently characterized in terms of quantitative phenolic composition and solvent-dependent bioactivity. This study compared ultrasound-assisted water and methanol extracts of its aerial parts using targeted liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS), antioxidant assays, enzyme inhibition tests, and the water-soluble tetrazolium-1 (WST-1) cell viability assay in A549 human lung carcinoma cells. Of 30 targeted phenolic compounds, 21 were quantified. The methanol extract was enriched in chlorogenic acid (16,430 µg/g extract) and rosmarinic acid (2474 µg/g extract), whereas selected hydroxybenzoic acids and flavonoid aglycones were more abundant in the water extract. The methanol extract exhibited higher total phenolic and flavonoid contents and stronger responses in four of six antioxidant assays. It also showed lower half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50) against all five tested enzymes. Notably, its α-glucosidase IC50 (1.12 mg/mL) was lower than that of acarbose (1.26 mg/mL) under the assay conditions. Both extracts produced elevated WST-1 signals at intermediate concentrations, which do not establish enhanced proliferation or safety. As results derive from technical triplicates of single extract preparations, further independent replication and mechanistic and toxicological validation are warranted.

Article.Title: Transcriptomic Response of Tomato Leaves to Root-Applied Phyto-Courier
Article.Authors: Guerriero G.; Sutera F.; Gutsch A.; Berni R.; Renaut J.; Torabi-Pour N.; Quinn S.; Dehsorkhi A.; Saffie-Siebert S.
Article.Abstract: The application of nanotechnology in plant science is opening new opportunities to improve the delivery, stability and efficacy of bioactive compounds in agricultural systems. In particular, the use of nanocarriers to enhance the bioavailability of plant secondary metabolites, such as flavonoids, is gaining increasing attention due to their well-known roles in plant physiology and stress responses. Building upon previous developments of silicon-based nanoparticle delivery platforms (referred to as phyto-couriers), this study provides a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis to investigate the molecular responses induced in tomato leaves following root amendment of a rutin-loaded phyto-courier system (GS3-R; comprising silicon nanoparticles, lipids, amino acids and trehalose). Initial targeted qPCR analysis of nineteen genes comparing GS3-R with free rutin, the unloaded carrier and an empty hydrolysable polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) bag (B) used as the application control, under both non-stress and NaCl conditions, revealed treatment-dependent differences in gene expression and additional responses to salinity. To investigate the broader transcriptional response to GS3-R, RNA-Seq analysis was performed on leaves from GS3-R- and B-treated plants under non-stress conditions. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using two analytical approaches to assess the robustness of the findings. The first analysis, based on Reads Per Kilobase Million—RPKM, identified 862 DEGs, while a count-based reanalysis using DESeq2 identified 1644 DEGs, of which 670 were shared and displayed concordant directions of differential expression. Functional enrichment analysis highlighted broadly consistent patterns across both analyses, involving phenylpropanoid and flavonoid biosynthesis, redox homeostasis, membrane transport, photosynthesis, phytohormone-associated pathways and cell wall organisation. These findings show that root application of the GS3-R phyto-courier is associated with molecular responses in aerial tissues and offer a transcriptome-wide overview of the biological processes responsive to the complete formulation. The study identifies candidate molecular pathways associated with the plant response to this formulation and establishes a robust molecular foundation for future investigations aimed at elucidating the physiological significance of these pathways under stress conditions.

Article.Title: FViT: A Foundation-Tokenized Vision Transformer with Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Scale Ensembling for Deep Learning-Based Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathology
Article.Authors: Sumon R.; Park D.; Islam M.; Kim H.
Article.Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics links gene expression to tissue morphology but is too costly for routine clinical use, motivating prediction of expression from hematoxylin-and-eosin (H&E) images. FViT (Foundation-tokenized Vision Transformer) tokenizes a spot and its k nearest neighbours with the frozen foundation model Phikon, fuses the tokens with a small trainable Transformer with a relative-position embedding, predicts expression directly and by k-nearest-neighbour retrieval of measured training expression, and combines three neighbourhood sizes (k = 8, 16, 24) in a weighted ensemble. We evaluated FViT on two public cohorts, Her2ST (HER2-positive breast cancer, eight patients) and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC, four patients), with leave-one-patient-out validation in which the gene panel, the retrieval parameters and the ensemble weights are selected without the evaluated patient. The ensemble reached a Pearson correlation of 0.180 (Her2ST) and 0.213 (cSCC) on the 50 most highly expressed genes (HEGs), but only 0.067 and 0.059 over all 1000 panel genes. Controls showed that neighbourhood fusion with relative position raised the HEG of direct prediction by +0.038 (Her2ST) and +0.045 (cSCC) over a centre-only model, that retrieval changed it by +0.002 to +0.004 on Her2ST and +0.007 to +0.010 on cSCC, and that the multi-scale ensemble differed from an ensemble of three seeds of a single neighbourhood size by −0.003 to +0.008. Under the same folds and panels, the released mclSTExp model (one seed, released settings) reached 0.141 and 0.177. In a section-level protocol, 99% of the retrieved weight came from other sections of the query’s own patient, and the ensemble’s retrieval gain fell from +0.013 to −0.002 when these sections were masked. Published results use section-level protocols and other gene panels, so they are not directly comparable. With eight and four patients, the findings are exploratory.

Article.Title: Epigenetic Adaptation as a Possible Component of Plant Breeding
Article.Authors: Roumeliotis E.; Kapazoglou A.; Dalakouras A.; Tsaballa A.; Xanthopoulou A.; Ganopoulos I.
Article.Abstract: Epigenetic regulation provides a mechanistic interface between genotype and environment and is increasingly considered a complementary component of plant breeding during climate- and policy-driven transitions toward low-input agriculture. This review summarizes major epigenetic mechanisms in plants, including DNA methylation through RNA-directed DNA methylation (RdDM), maintenance and demethylation pathways, and histone modifications, and evaluates their relevance to heritable phenotypic variation and crop improvement. We discuss the extent and context dependence of epigenetic inheritance, distinguishing intergenerational from transgenerational effects, and highlight approaches for identifying functional epialleles, including epigenetic quantitative trait locus (epiQTL) mapping and epigenome-wide association studies (EWASs). We then synthesize evidence linking epigenetic reprogramming to adaptation to water deficit, salinity, heat, and nutrient limitation, emphasizing the potential and limitations of epigenetic memory for breeding. Finally, we review agronomic and biotechnological approaches for inducing or engineering epigenetic variation, including grafting and mobile RNAs, chemical priming, in vitro propagation, exogenous RNA-triggered RdDM (exo-RdDM), and biopriming. We conclude by outlining the principal challenges for integration into breeding pipelines, particularly the stability, predictability, heritability, and causal attribution of epigenetic variants across environments and generations.

Article.Title: Obesity Attenuates Fasting-Induced Upregulation of Renal Peroxisomal Fatty Acid Oxidation Gene Expression
Article.Authors: Balugo J.; Ahmad S.; Brett A.; DeCuzzi C.; Konduru G.; Kumar P.; Harris T.; Siragy H.; Culver S.
Article.Abstract: Increased kidney lipid content during obesity contributes to obesity-related kidney injury but mechanisms of renal lipid accumulation during obesity are incompletely understood. Lean mice also accumulate renal lipid during fasting but how kidney lipid metabolism responds to fasting during obesity is not clear. Mice fed a normal diet (ND) or a high-fat diet (HFD) for 17 weeks underwent either ad libitum feeding (NDfd and HFDfd) or an overnight 16 h fast (NDfa and HFDfa) before measurement of renal lipid and kidney transcriptomics by RNA-seq. Renal triglyceride was increased in NDfa mice compared to NDfd mice and also increased in HFDfd mice compared to NDfd. However HFDfa mice did not have greater renal triglyceride than HFDfd mice. RNA-seq demonstrated increased fatty acid metabolism gene expression in NDfa and HFDfa mice compared to the fed controls, but was significantly greater in NDfa than HFDfa mice. Peroxisomal gene expression was also enriched in NDfa compared to HFDfa mice. Expression of peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation genes Acox1 and Ehhadh, increased in NDfa compared to NDfd, while expression of these genes was not changed in HFDfa compared to HFDfd. These results indicate that obesity blunts fasting-induced peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation gene expression.

Article.Title: CD117 as a Lineage-Associated Biomarker in Acute Leukemia: A Favorable Prognostic Marker in AML and an Adverse Predictor in ALL
Article.Authors: Ashour D.; Abbas M.; Halahleh K.; Sughayer M.
Article.Abstract: Acute leukemia comprises heterogeneous hematologic malignancies. CD117 (c-KIT), encoded by the KIT proto-oncogene, is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in hematopoietic cell survival, proliferation, and differentiation. CD117 expression was assessed in 118 acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and 106 acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cases and correlated with clinical, immunophenotypic, molecular, and survival parameters. CD117 was expressed in 82.2% of AML and 17.9% of ALL cases. In AML, CD117 positivity was associated with AML-M2 (p < 0.001), core-binding factor (CBF) abnormalities (p = 0.010), and favorable European LeukemiaNet (ELN) 2022 risk (p = 0.041). CD117 independently predicted improved overall survival (OS) in CBF-adjusted (aHR = 0.450, 95% CI: 0.219–0.924, p = 0.030) and ELN-adjusted models (aHR = 0.295, 95% CI: 0.127–0.684, p = 0.004). CD117 was associated with improved event-free survival (EFS) only in the ELN-adjusted model (aHR = 0.374, 95% CI: 0.159–0.882, p = 0.025). In ALL, CD117 was associated with T-cell lineage (p < 0.001) and independently predicted inferior OS (aHR = 4.171, 95% CI: 1.375–12.656, p = 0.012) and EFS (aHR = 3.145, 95% CI: 1.153–8.576, p = 0.025). In T-ALL, it predicted poorer OS (aHR = 3.316, 95% CI: 1.043–10.537, p = 0.042). In conclusion, CD117 has disease-specific prognostic significance, predicting favorable outcomes in AML but adverse outcomes in ALL, particularly T-ALL.

Article.Title: Arctigenin Attenuates Hepatic Ischemia/Reperfusion Injury by Enhancing NRF2-GST/GPX4 Antioxidant Response
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Liang R.; Xu M.; Shao Y.; Li L.; Ni Z.; Wang Y.; Chen A.
Article.Abstract: Hepatic ischemia/reperfusion injury (IRI) remains a major cause of graft dysfunction and postoperative liver failure, and no specific pharmacological therapy is available. Oxidative stress plays a key role in hepatic IRI, making arctigenin (AG), a compound with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities, a potential therapeutic candidate. We evaluated AG using a 70% hepatic ischemia/reperfusion model in male C57BL/6 mice and cellular injury models induced by hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) or H2O2 exposure in AML12 cells. AG dose-dependently attenuated hepatic injury, reduced serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) activities, and decreased hepatic necrosis. AG also reduced inflammatory macrophage abundance and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in the liver after IRI. In AML12 cells, AG improved viability and reduced ROS accumulation and lipid peroxidation. Transcriptomic analysis identified glutathione metabolism, glutathione transferase activity, and cellular detoxification as major AG-responsive processes. AG promoted nuclear accumulation of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2), increased the expression of multiple glutathione S-transferases (GSTs) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), and enhanced GST and GSH-Px activities. Pharmacological inhibition of NRF2, GPX4, or GSTs attenuated AG-mediated cytoprotection. NRF2 knockdown also weakened AG-associated improvements in cell viability, apoptosis, ROS levels, and antioxidant enzyme activities after H/R. In mice, ML385 attenuated AG-associated antioxidant responses and hepatoprotection. These findings support a role for NRF2 in AG-mediated protection and implicate GST- and GPX4-associated antioxidant defenses in its effects against hepatic IRI.

Article.Title: COQ4 and COQ8A Primary Deficiencies: A Review of Proposed Therapeutic Strategies
Article.Authors: Mantle D.; Heaton R.; Hargreaves I.
Article.Abstract: In this article we have reviewed potential therapeutic strategies relating to two of the primary coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) deficiencies, COQ4 and COQ8A; these disorders have been grouped together because of their complimentary roles in stabilising the CoQ10 enzyme complex, Complex Q, as well as the difficulty in treating either of these disorders using conventional oral supplementation, as exemplified by two previously unreported case histories. Alternative strategies reviewed include methods to potentially improve blood-brain barrier access, including the identification of suitable inhibitors or activators of LRP1 or SRB1 transporters respectively. Other potential therapeutic strategies include the potential stabilisation of Complex Q using agents such as cardiolipin, targeted gene therapy using CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing or AAV vector gene delivery, or mitochondrial transplantation. All of the strategies outlined above are at an early preclinical stage with regard to their potential application in primary CoQ10 deficiency, and remain areas for ongoing research.

Article.Title: The Need for Variant-Specific Splicing Assessment in Developing Antisense Oligonucleotide Therapies for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: Lessons from the DMD c.4675−2A>G Variant
Article.Authors: Sunami A.; Horiguchi T.; Takeuchi A.; Ishikawa Y.; Kataoka N.; Komai K.; Nishio H.; Matsuo M.
Article.Abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by pathogenic variants in the DMD gene. Splice-site variants can generate aberrant transcripts whose consequences cannot always be predicted by the classical reading-frame rule. Here, we characterized the c.4675−2A>G variant at the exon 34 splice acceptor site for the development of an exon-skipping therapy. A minigene analysis demonstrated that c.4675−2A>G activated a cryptic splice acceptor within exon 34 rather than inducing skipping of the entire exon, resulting in deletion of the first 7 nucleotides, a frameshift, and a premature termination codon. To restore the reading frame by promoting skipping of the entire exon 34, we used antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting distinct splice-regulatory regions. Among the ASO treatments tested, including individual ASOs and ASO combinations, A1&E4&D1 produced the highest exon exclusion and consistently promoted exon 34 skipping across the examined −2A mutant genotypes. A1&E4&D1 consists of ASOs A1, E4, and D1. A1 targeted the cryptic 3′ splice acceptor region, E4 targeted a predicted exonic splicing enhancer region, and D1 targeted the 5′ splice donor region. These findings illustrate a stepwise, variant-directed strategy in which characterization of aberrant splicing guides the design of a tailor-made ASO intervention.

Article.Title: A Raman Spectroscopic Case Study of Ceramide- and Sulfur-Enriched Microdomains in Human Alzheimer’s Brain: Localized Molecular Signatures Resembling Bacterial Outer Membrane Vesicles
Article.Authors: Pezzotti G.; Murakami A.; Ikegami S.; Son A.; Matsuo Y.; Zavan B.; Franceschini D.; Koutsikos K.; Rigon L.; Pinton P.; Kawada-Matsuo M.; Komatsuzawa H.; Yakushiji Y.
Article.Abstract: We report a high-resolution Raman microspectroscopic case study comparing post-mortem human brain tissue from one Alzheimer’s disease subject and one neurologically healthy subject. Low-wavenumber Raman imaging revealed discrete, micron-sized protuberant microdomains present exclusively in the Alzheimer’s tissue, exhibiting intense ceramide-associated bands and characteristic oxysulfur vibrational features. These localized structures showed spectral similarity to previously reported spectra of outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) from Porphyromonas gingivalis. However, genomic analysis of bulk tissue from the same specimen detected no bacterial DNA. This discrepancy likely reflects differing spatial resolutions between the two methods, as Raman spectroscopy probes micron-scale domains while genomic assays average signals across much larger tissue volumes. Although this single-case study cannot confirm bacterial OMV presence or a causal link to Alzheimer’s disease, it identifies an unusual molecular microenvironment warranting further investigation through spatially correlated spectroscopic, genomic, and histopathological analyses. Beyond these localized structures, Raman spectroscopy also revealed biochemical signatures consistent with Alzheimer’s-associated lipid remodeling, including decreased cholesterol relative to oxysulfur compounds, reduced cholesteryl ester relative to total cholesterol, and altered phospholipid composition marked by phosphatidylserine depletion and elevated phosphatidylinositol signals. These findings demonstrate the Raman microspectroscopy’s capability to detect localized biochemical heterogeneity in diseased brain tissue.

Article.Authors: Hirata A.; Choque P.; Silva R.; Ferreira M.; De Angelis K.; Giannocco G.; Dellê H.; Camacho C.
Article.Abstract: Extra-olfactory receptors (ORs) are expressed in multiple tissues and implicated in cardiovascular regulation and placental biology. Thyroid hormones influence olfactory function, but their role in tissue-specific OR expression during pregnancy remains unclear. Methods: Pregnant Wistar rats were assigned to control, gestational hypothyroid, and levothyroxine (LT4)-treated hypothyroid groups. Hypothyroidism was induced by administering methimazole and an iodine-deficient diet; LT4 was administered at 5.0 μg/100 g body weight. Or5t5, Or10j5, Agtr1a, Oprm1, and Pgf mRNA expressions were quantified by RT-qPCR in blood, kidney, heart, and placenta on gestational day 14. Results: No OR expression was detected in the heart, and Pgf was undetectable in the LT4-treated group. Hypothyroidism reduced renal Or10j5 expression. Placental LT4 treatment increased Or5t5 and Agtr1a and reduced Oprm1 expression compared with hypothyroid animals. Correlation analyses showed that circulating ORs correlate with each other (except in controls) and with circulating Agtr1a in all samples and subgroups. The circulating ORs correlate with placental Or10j5 in the hypothyroidism group and with kidney Or10j5 in LT4-treated animals. Conclusions: Gestational thyroid dysfunction modified OR expression in the kidney and placenta. LT4 alters placental transcriptional profiles, suggesting hormone sensitivity of extra-olfactory receptor transcripts. The small sample size and ANN-imputed TSH warrant cautious interpretation.

Article.Title: High-Altitude Exposure Is Associated with Sustained Inflammation and Hyperinsulinemia in Healthy Individuals: An Investigative Study on Human Expedition
Article.Authors: Sentinelli F.; Verratti V.; Lucarelli A.; Iacobini C.; Tienforti D.; Moretto C.; Cavallo M.; Bondi D.; Barbonetti A.; Baroni M.
Article.Abstract: This study aimed to investigate the integrated in vivo impact of progressive high altitude on metabolic, inflammatory, and vascular adaptation pathways and to assess their modulation by biological sex and anthropometric profile. A Himalayan expedition was conducted with fifteen volunteers (nine men, six women; age 43 ± 15 years; body mass index (BMI) of 24.2 ± 3.70 kg/m2). Participants received acetazolamide (250 mg/day). Blood samples were collected before (50 m above sea level), during (1400 m and 5000 m), and after the Himalayan trip (return to 1400 m). Serum concentrations of Adipocyte Complement-Related Protein of 30 kDa (Adiponectin/Acrp30), C-Reactive Protein (CRP), Plasminogen Activator Inhibitor-1 (Serpin E1/PAI-1), Monocyte Chemoattractant Protein-1/chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 2 (MCP-1/CCL2), basic Fibroblast Growth Factor (bFGF), Insulin, Leptin, Macrophage Migration Inhibitory Factor (MIF) and Tumor Necrosis Factor alpha (TNF-α) were measured. Progressive exposure to high altitude induced significant activation of inflammatory pathways, documented by progressively increased serum levels, compared to baseline, of CRP, MCP-1, PAI-1, and TNF-α (all p < 0.05). Insulin increased significantly at maximum altitude (p = 0.032), with persistence during descent (p = 0.042). bFGF showed a biphasic trend. Leptin, adiponectin, and MIF changes did not reach statistical significance. A mixed repeated-measures ANOVA confirmed a significant main effect of altitude on insulin concentration (p = 0.005), on CRP (p = 0.009), on MCP-1 (p = 0.004), and on TNF-α levels (p < 0.001). However, no significant interaction of sex and BMI (Body Mass Index) with altitude was observed. Elevated CRP, MCP-1, PAI-1, and TNF-α persisted during descent, suggesting delayed resolution of the high-altitude-induced inflammatory response. These results show that progressive high altitude induces systemic inflammation and hyperinsulinemia, which persist during descent, providing new insights into the relationship between altitude-induced inflammatory pathways and insulin dynamics.

Article.Authors: Sánchez-Padilla A.; Escorcia-Barrera A.; Tafoya-Olvera M.; Valencia-Cruz A.; García-Meza J.; Alarcón-Sánchez B.; Idelfonso-García O.; Márquez-Quiroga L.; Torres-Mena J.; Fuentes-Hernández S.; Valderrama-Cervantes L.; Herrera-López E.; Aguirre-Maldonado I.; Martínez-Magaña J.; Resendis-Antonio O.; Muciño-Olmos E.; Aparicio-Bautista D.; Basurto-Islas G.; Román-González S.; Gutiérrez-Nava M.; Mendoza-Vargas A.; Jiménez-García M.; Pacheco-Rivera R.; Gutiérrez-Reyes G.; Pérez-Hernández J.

Ten IPA-predicted causal signaling networks were associated with HCC progression. The expression of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1a (Cdkn1a) gene, commonly known as P21, was the most dysregulated, and its total (CDN1A/P21) and phosphorylated protein level was increased from early to late stages. P21 was also increased and released into the bloodstream of ALD and MASLD models, both based on multiple hepatotoxins linked to HCC development, as well as in the bloodstream of ALD patients. In conclusion, P21 is altered from early stages of liver diseases leading to HCC, which betrays the onset of liver cancer before developing malignant traits; thus, P21 offers a critical therapeutic window for timely detection of high-risk patients.

Article.Title: Immune Checkpoint-Related Gene Prognostic Signature Characterizes the Immunosuppressive Microenvironment and Predicts Immunotherapy Response in Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma
Article.Authors: Dai L.; Zheng L.; Yuan H.; Li J.; Pang J.; Yue F.
Article.Abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) shows heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). We aimed to develop an immune checkpoint-related gene (ICRG) signature for risk stratification, tumor microenvironment characterization, and immunotherapy prediction. Risk score correlated with reduced benefit from combined immunotherapy and targeted therapy (p < 0.01) and shorter progression-free survival (p = 0.0035). LIPA overexpression suppressed proliferation, migration, and invasion in CAKI-1 and CAKI-2 renal carcinoma cells. This ICRG signature serves as a potential prognostic biomarker and may aid in predicting immunotherapy response. Furthermore, LIPA showed tumor-suppressive potential, providing a rationale for future personalized treatment strategies.

Article.Title: Advances and Application Potential of Functional and Stimuli-Responsive Hydrogels in Diabetic Bone Repair
Article.Authors: Jin Y.; Wang J.; Hu W.; Zhao H.
Article.Abstract: Impaired bone healing in diabetes continues to present a major challenge in orthopedic and regenerative medicine. The compromised osseous regeneration typically stems from a complex pathological cascade—namely, persistent local hyperglycemia, excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), impaired neurovascular coupling, sustained low-grade inflammation, altered insulin signaling, and the deleterious deposition of advanced glycation end products. Together, these systemic and microenvironmental anomalies impede endogenous repair, potentially culminating in delayed union or frank non-union. To overcome these limitations, functional and stimuli-responsive (smart) hydrogel networks have emerged as a versatile therapeutic platform. These matrices provide sustained local delivery, while selected responsive chemistries couple release or degradation to glucose, ROS, proteases, pH, or externally applied light. Temperature-dependent gelation, antioxidant activity, and electrical conductivity are distinguished from pathological-signal-triggered release. In this review, we summarize current progress in the rational design and implementation of functional and stimuli-responsive hydrogels for diabetic bone repair. We evaluate their biological mechanisms together with responsive chemistry, tested trigger levels, release and degradation kinetics, mechanical properties, and the relevance of each experimental model, concluding with prospective strategies to guide subsequent biomaterial innovation and clinical translation in this domain.

Article.Title: G Protein-Coupled Receptors Across Diverse Astrocyte Functions and Cellular Crosstalk
Article.Authors: Yang Y.; Lin Y.; Mah S.; Tang L.; Xu J.
Article.Abstract: Astrocytes are the most abundant and functionally versatile glial cells in the central nervous system, where they maintain homeostasis, regulate metabolic function, and communicate extensively with neurons, microglia and other CNS cell types. To mediate these interactions, astrocytes use G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) to receive diverse extracellular signals, such as neurotransmitters, secreted signals and inflammatory factors. GPCRs translate extracellular signals into intracellular signaling cascades in astrocytes and are essential for intercellular communication. Despite decades of investigation, however, astrocytic GPCR signaling remains difficult to explain within a unified framework, as receptor activation does not necessarily produce predictable outcomes based on receptor identity or G-protein signaling alone. To address this gap, we critically examine representative studies of canonical and noncanonical GPCR signaling and astrocyte-centered cellular crosstalk, considering astrocyte state and the cellular position of receptors within communication pathways. We compare receptor-specific manipulations, functional outcomes, and methodological limitations to distinguish experimentally supported causal relationships from unresolved interpretations. This evidence-oriented approach identifies testable questions and experimental priorities for investigating astrocytic GPCR signaling in physiology and disease.

Article.Title: Comprehensive Search for Channels in African Swine Fever Virus
Article.Authors: Yadav M.; Arkin I.
Article.Abstract: African swine fever virus (ASFV) is arguably the most critical threat to global food security. With a mortality rate approaching 100%, it threatens pork production, a cornerstone of human nutrition that accounts for more than 35% of all meat consumed worldwide. ASFV is also one of the most structurally complex and largest pathogenic viruses, harboring a genome of 170–190 kbp. Consequently, to better understand this pathogen, we exhaustively screened the genome of the HK_NT_202103 strain for encoded ion channels using three complementary bacteria-based assays. Out of 196 genes screened, 24 candidates exhibited transmembrane potential, and their successful expression and integration were verified using maltose-binding protein fusions and Western blotting. Fourteen of these candidates scored positively across all three assays, confirming their status as potential viroporins. This functionally redundant set of 14 viroporins enables the virus to modulate host potassium levels and proton flux across membranes. Beyond identifying general channels, we mapped specific proton-selective pores. By applying kinetic modeling and ternary clustering, we moved beyond qualitative screening to categorize these viroporins into distinct functional zones based on their specific ion-movement dynamics. Genomic comparisons across eleven diverse global genotypes revealed that these key channels have remained virtually unchanged for over a century. The combination of structural stability and functional critical mass establishes these channels as premier vulnerabilities for therapeutic exploitation. Ultimately, this study provides the first validated functional atlas of ASFV ion channels, offering a detailed roadmap for designing broad-spectrum antivirals targeting the viral metabolic core.

Article.Title: Identification of Hypoxia- and Circadian Rhythm-Related Prognostic Genes in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Through Integrative Transcriptomic and Single-Cell Analysis
Article.Authors: Zu X.; Sun G.
Article.Abstract: Hypoxia perturbs circadian rhythm gene expression in hepatocellular carcinoma, yet prognostic genes associated with both processes remain insufficiently characterized. Data from the liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) cohort in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were analyzed. Candidate genes were identified by intersecting differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with 27 hypoxia- and circadian rhythm-related genes and were further refined using univariate Cox regression and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression; a random survival forest (RSF) risk model was then constructed and validated. Independent prognostic and functional enrichment analyses, immune infiltration profiling, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and immunohistochemistry (IHC) were subsequently performed. Four prognostic genes (ADM, PFKFB3, SERPINE1, and RORA) were identified through integrative computational analysis. The RSF model stratified LIHC patients into the high-risk group (HRG) and the low-risk group (LRG), which had significantly different survival outcomes, and the risk score and tumor stage were combined in a nomogram. The four genes were co-enriched in four pathways; eight immune cell types, including natural killer T (NKT) cells, differed between the risk groups. scRNA-seq identified stem-like/hypoxic malignant cells whose differentiation trajectory showed distinct expression dynamics of the four genes. IHC confirmed significantly higher ADM and PFKFB3 protein expression in LIHC tissues, whereas protein-level evidence for SERPINE1 and RORA was inconclusive. These findings support further prognostic evaluation of LIHC and investigation of the links among hypoxia, metabolic reprogramming, and stemness.

Article.Title: Monogenic Diseases: A View Through the Landscape–Attractor Framework
Article.Authors: Damante G.; Faletra F.
Article.Abstract: Monogenic diseases are traditionally interpreted through a linear causal model linking pathogenic variants to molecular dysfunction and clinical phenotypes. However, this model does not fully explain incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, and heterogeneous disease progression. This review aims to explore the applicability of the landscape–attractor framework, originally developed in evolutionary and developmental biology and subsequently extended to gene regulatory networks, to the interpretation of monogenic diseases. We propose that pathogenic variants act as persistent perturbations of interconnected molecular networks, modifying the stability and accessibility of physiological and pathological states. Within this framework, phenotypic variability emerges from interactions between the causal variant and genetic modifiers, epigenetic regulation, environmental influences, stochastic processes, and compensatory mechanisms. We further extend this perspective across molecular, cellular, tissue, and organismal levels, introducing the concept of functional fitness to describe disease-related physiological performance. Finally, we discuss how therapeutic interventions may redirect biological systems toward more favorable functional states without necessarily correcting the underlying genetic defect. This framework offers a complementary systems-level perspective on genotype–phenotype relationships and suggests experimentally testable hypotheses for understanding and modifying disease expression.

Article.Title: Expression and Membranous Localization of CD44 Define Distinct Cellular and Spatial Phenotypes Associated with Glioma Aggressiveness
Article.Authors: Jaunecker C.; Kerschbaumer L.; Quinot V.; Freund J.; Mager L.; Machreich S.; Pacher L.; Bruckner K.; Marosits L.; Robl B.; Lang A.; Gabler-Pamer L.; Kirchhofer D.; Pirker C.; Rössler K.; Berghoff A.; Kiesel B.; Widhalm G.; Roetzer-Pejrimovsky T.; Berger W.; Lötsch D.
Article.Abstract: Adult-type diffuse gliomas comprise, amongst others, biologically distinct isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant (IDH-MUT) astrocytomas and IDH-wildtype (IDH-WT) glioblastoma (GB). Although IDH-MUT astrocytomas generally have a more favorable prognosis, they frequently recur and progress. Despite extensive molecular characterization, key drivers of glioma progression remain elusive. CD44, a hyaluronic acid receptor, has been implicated in glioma invasion and progression. We investigated CD44 expression, localization, and spatial organization across IDH-WT GB and IDH-MUT astrocytomas and their association with tumor progression and cellular states. CD44 expression and localization were assessed in IDH-WT (n = 15) and IDH-MUT (n = 17) diffuse gliomas across WHO grades by immunohistochemistry (IHC). Multiplex IHC combined with AI-assisted digital pathology (HALO) evaluated associations between CD44, GFAP-positive astrocytic, and NeuN/RBFOX3-positive neuronal regions. Findings were validated using independent snRNA-seq data. IDH-WT GB exhibited significantly higher CD44 expression with prominent membranous localization. Lower-grade IDH-MUT astrocytomas showed reduced, diffuse staining, whereas higher-grade tumors acquired a membranous CD44 localization, resembling IDH-WT GB. CD44 was strongly associated with GFAP-positive astrocytic regions and inversely correlated with NeuN/RBFOX3-positive neuronal areas in IDH-MUT tumors. AI-assisted spatial analyses confirmed distinct CD44-positive astrocytic and NeuN-positive neuronal niches, supported by snRNA-seq demonstrating positive CD44-GFAP correlations. This association was strongest in astrocytic (AC-like) metaprograms of WHO grade 2, while in higher-grade tumors it was more pronounced in mesenchymal (MES-like) states. CD44 exhibits IDH- and grade-dependent spatial patterns marking glioma progression and astrocytic/mesenchymal tumor states. Membranous CD44 acquisition accompanies progression to higher grades in IDH-MUT astrocytomas, suggesting CD44 as a marker of glioma aggressiveness.
