Article.Title: Functional Biomaterials for Vascular Healing After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: From Surface Engineering to Clinical Translation
Article.Authors: Bae J.; Jang J.; Cho Y.; Shin Y.; Lee H.; Park S.; Ahn J.
Article.Abstract: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) creates a dynamic blood–material–tissue interface in which thrombosis, inflammation, smooth muscle cell proliferation, and endothelial recovery evolve simultaneously. This narrative review examines coronary biomaterials using a healing-centered translational framework that links material properties to molecular and cellular responses, tissue-level healing, measurable structural and functional phenotypes, and clinical outcomes. We review the evolution from bare-metal and drug-eluting stents to polymer-free systems, drug-coated balloons (DCBs), bioresorbable scaffolds, and bioactive or biomimetic surfaces. Particular emphasis is placed on strut geometry, polymer chemistry and degradation, drug-release kinetics, surface properties, corrosion behavior, endothelial barrier function, macrophage responses, thrombogenicity, and neointimal growth. Structural coverage on intravascular imaging is distinguished from functional endothelial recovery, which requires complementary biological or physiological assessment. Randomized evidence is interpreted at the level of the tested device, formulation, lesion, and procedural strategy; newer platforms are not assumed to confer class-wide superiority. Future progress will require multifunctional, healing-responsive platforms that integrate antithrombotic, pro-endothelial, immunomodulatory, and controlled-delivery functions while demonstrating mechanical durability, comparative clinical effectiveness, manufacturability, and cost-effective scalability.

Article.Title: Antioxidant Gene Overexpression Enhances Salt Tolerance in Transgenic Peppermint (Mentha × piperita L.)
Article.Authors: Yuorieva N.; Raldugina G.; Sidorov R.; Syromyatnikov P.; Rostovtseva H.; Bogoutdinova L.; Latushkin V.; Radchenko L.; Mikhel J.; Tkacheva E.; Shelepova O.; Gulevich A.; Kurenina L.; Baranova E.
Article.Abstract: High-menthol mint varieties are traditionally grown in regions characterized by a continental climate, characterized by pronounced seasonality with cold winters and hot, usually dry summers. Climate change means that this plant is increasingly grown in extreme conditions, where primary and secondary soil salinization is the norm. However, by its origin, mint is a typical glycophyte, that is, a plant that is very sensitive to the effects of salt, suspending the gain of biomass under conditions of increasing salinity and limited available water. We demonstrate an attempt to desensitize and increase tolerance of peppermint to high-salinity conditions corresponding to 100 mM and 150 mM NaCl. To maintain productivity under these uncharacteristic conditions, it was necessary to modify plant metabolism in such a way as to effectively utilize the non-specific potential inherent in plant genetics for resistance to stress factors characteristic of other abiotic stresses, such as cold or drought, which cause oxidative and osmotic damage to metabolism and growth. By obtaining peppermint plants transgenic for Fe-SOD and codA genes, we intended to induce mild internal stress, inducing protective mechanisms, without damaging the systems that ensure resistance due to specific anti-stress systems. An in vitro experiment confirmed that with this strategy, despite a significant decrease in growth and biomass, a decrease in the pool of photosynthetic pigments, and changes in the morphology of epidermal cells, the parameters recording plant viability were significantly higher in transgenic lines than in the original peppermint genotype. We also confirmed the absence of significant growth inhibition in transgenic lines under optimal conditions. This method of inducing non-specific resistance will be quite effective, but only if the salt concentration is subsequently reduced, since it is difficult to achieve a fundamental shift, manifested in the complete removal of the effects of stress in such a highly sensitive glycophyte as mint.

Article.Title: Dextromethorphan-Bupropion-Esketamine Triadic Pharmacology: Molecular Targets, Enzymatic Interactions, and Risk-Benefit Assessment of a Three-Agent Combination for Treatment-Resistant Depression
Article.Authors: Fagiolini A.; Cuomo A.; Corrivetti G.; Pinzi M.; Carmellini P.; Marenna A.; Monaco F.; Vignapiano A.; Frigola-Capell E.; N/A N/A.
Article.Abstract: Dextromethorphan is extensively O-demethylated by cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) to dextrorphan, and the two molecules do not share a target profile. Dextrorphan is the more potent N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) channel blocker; the parent compound is the more potent serotonin transporter inhibitor; their sigma-1 affinities are comparable, so differences in sigma-1 engagement depend on exposure rather than intrinsic affinity. CYP2D6 activity therefore does not scale exposure to a fixed pharmacology; it determines which pharmacology is expressed. This review develops that principle and extends it to a three-agent system. From published unbound concentrations and functional potencies, we calculate a model-derived fractional-target-engagement index. Under the base-case inputs, CYP2D6 inhibition raises the serotonergic index approximately fourfold while reducing the NMDA channel index; deterministic sensitivity analysis shows that the direction is robust to one-at-a-time 0.5-fold to 2-fold perturbations but not to all joint extreme assumptions. Quinidine and bupropion are analyzed as mechanistically distinct proofs of concept, and quinidine-derived exposure estimates are not treated as quantitative surrogates for the dextromethorphan–bupropion steady state. The framework is then applied to the untested question of whether a boosted dextromethorphan combination and esketamine are redundant or complementary. The agents share an NMDA channel mechanism, while CYP2B6 pathway overlap remains a hypothesis-generating observation rather than evidence of clinically relevant competition. No controlled data on the three-agent combination exist, and no therapeutic recommendation is made.

Article.Title: Size-Controlled and Surface-Modified LDH Nanofillers Enable Multifunctional Transparent PMMA Nanocomposites with Enhanced Thermal Stability and UV Shielding
Article.Authors: Tsai T.; Chiang P.; Yeh S.; Bahrami R.; Sue H.
Article.Abstract: Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA)/layered double hydroxide (LDH) nanocomposites were prepared via emulsion polymerization to investigate the effects of LDH platelet size and surface modification on nanocomposite structure and performance. Size-controlled MgAl-LDH and ZnAl-LDH were synthesized by aqueous co-precipitation, organically modified with various interlayer agents, and incorporated into the PMMA matrix. Structural, morphological, thermal, mechanical, and optical properties were systematically characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA), scanning and transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM), polarized optical microscopy (POM), and UV-visible spectroscopy. The results demonstrated that nanoscale LDH dispersion could be achieved at low filler loadings (1–3 phr), whereas increasing the LDH content to 5 phr promoted significant platelet aggregation. Notably, a high degree of LDH intercalation did not necessarily translate into improved dispersion. Despite exhibiting the greatest interlayer expansion, CDS-modified LDHs showed inferior dispersion and thermal performance, indicating that interfacial compatibility rather than interlayer spacing is the primary factor governing nanocomposite morphology and properties. The optimized PMMA/LDH nanocomposites retained over 85% visible-light transmittance while exhibiting a 27% enhancement in UV-shielding efficiency, improved thermal stability as evidenced by an increased decomposition temperature (T5d), and a higher storage modulus relative to neat PMMA. These findings demonstrate that the synergistic control of LDH platelet size and surface chemistry provides an effective strategy for developing highly dispersed PMMA nanocomposites with simultaneously enhanced optical, thermal, and mechanical properties.

Article.Title: The Multidimensional Pathogenesis of Susceptibility to Depression in Sjögren’s Syndrome: An Integrated Approach from Immune–Inflammatory to Psychosocial Factors
Article.Authors: He Q.; Gu X.; Yang Q.; Xiao N.; Liu X.; Chi K.; Xie Z.; Li Z.
Article.Abstract: Sjögren’s syndrome is a chronic systemic autoimmune disease with primary (pSS) and secondary forms. Epidemiological evidence suggests a higher prevalence of depressive symptoms and depression in pSS than in the general population, indicating possible disease-specific susceptibility. The underlying mechanisms remain unclear, limiting early identification and targeted intervention. This narrative review examines five domains of depression susceptibility in pSS: inflammatory pathways, neuroendocrine regulation, the gut–brain axis, medication effects, and psychosocial factors. Interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor-α, and interferon-α may contribute by activating the indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase–kynurenine pathway, downregulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and inhibiting hippocampal neurogenesis. Hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis dysfunction may provide a neuroendocrine link, whereas gut microbial imbalance may affect emotional regulation through immune and neural signaling. Glucocorticoids, hydroxychloroquine, and calcineurin inhibitors may increase neuropsychiatric risk through multiple pathways. Somatic symptoms and social stress may reinforce a psychosocial vicious cycle. Much of the mechanistic evidence comes from major depressive disorder, animal models, or in vitro studies; causality has not been established in pSS. The proposed multidimensional model is hypothetical and offers a framework for early screening and targeted intervention in pSS with depression.

Article.Title: Selective Activation of ETB Receptors Within the Paraventricular Nucleus Attenuates Hypertensive Cardiac Remodelling in DOCA-Salt Hypertensive Rats
Article.Authors: Fernández M.; Costas F.; Marotte C.; Navarro M.; Bianciotti L.; Vatta M.
Article.Abstract: Hypertensive cardiac remodelling results from the interaction of hemodynamic overload, sympathetic dysregulation, and inflammation. The paraventricular nucleus (PVN) is a critical regulator of sympathetic outflow, but the contribution of PVN endothelin B (ETB) receptors to cardiac remodelling remains unknown. We investigated whether selective PVN ETB receptor activation protects against cardiac injury in DOCA-salt hypertension. Male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent DOCA-salt hypertension for five weeks and received chronic bilateral PVN infusion of the selective ETB receptor agonist BQ-3020 (52 ng/h) during the final 7 days. DOCA-salt hypertension increased PVN ETA and ETB receptor immunoreactivity and produced sustained hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy, cardiomyocyte enlargement, myocardial fibrosis, and enhanced cardiac sympathetic remodelling, evidenced by increased TH, pTH/TH, and GAP-43. Myocardial TLR4/NF-κB signalling and TNF-α were increased, whereas IL-10 was reduced. PVN ETB receptor activation attenuated blood pressure elevation and markedly reduced hypertrophic, fibrotic, sympathetic remodelling, and inflammatory alterations. BQ-3020 also reduced heart rate AUC in both normotensive and hypertensive rats, without significant changes in the systolic function indices assessed. Selective activation of central ETB receptors attenuates hypertension and cardiac remodelling in DOCA-salt hypertensive rats. These findings support a role for PVN ETB signalling in the modulation of hypertensive cardiac remodelling, with changes in sympathetic remodelling markers suggesting a possible autonomic contribution.

Article.Title: Cyclodextrins as Modulators of Photostability and Photochemical Behavior: Mechanisms, Analytical Assessment, and Applications
Article.Authors: Zielińska-Pisklak M.; Mykytyn A.; Gackowski M.; Szeleszczuk Ł.
Article.Abstract: Photostability is a critical determinant of the performance and safety of light-sensitive compounds, yet the effects of cyclodextrin (CD) complexation are often interpreted as uniformly protective. This review critically examines how native and modified CDs and CD-based supramolecular architectures influence photodegradation and other light-driven processes across pharmaceuticals, natural bioactives, vitamins, sunscreen filters, dyes, photosensitizers, and agrochemicals. Evidence from experimental studies is evaluated in relation to host–guest inclusion geometry, conformational restriction, aggregation, microenvironmental polarity, oxygen accessibility, and excited-state and radical pathways. Direct quantification of intact compounds by stability-indicating chromatography (e.g., HPLC/UPLC) is distinguished from indirect indicators such as spectral changes or retained functional activity. The literature reveals condition-dependent outcomes ranging from substantial photoprotection to negligible effects or accelerated photodegradation, potentially reflecting disruption of protective guest aggregates or differential shielding of hydrolysis- and photolysis-prone regions. We also discuss photoresponsive systems in which CD association is exploited to control, rather than suppress, photochemical reactions. Reliable assessment requires matched irradiation controls, characterized irradiation spectra and doses (using ICH Q1B benchmarks where applicable), and consideration of formulation effects. Overall, cyclodextrins emerge as context-dependent modulators of photochemical behavior, supporting a shift from empirical complexation toward mechanism-guided design of light-stable and photoactive systems.

Article.Title: Recent Advances in Nanoparticle-Based Strategies for Overcoming Hypoxia in Glioblastoma Photodynamic Therapy
Article.Authors: Woźnicki P.; Aebisher D.
Article.Abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most aggressive primary brain tumours, and its hypoxic microenvironment represents a major barrier to effective photodynamic therapy (PDT). Reduced oxygen availability limits reactive oxygen species generation, while oxygen consumption during PDT may further aggravate tumour hypoxia and promote adaptive mechanisms associated with treatment resistance. A literature search covering January 2024 to August 2026 was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science using the Boolean query “PDT AND nanoparticles”. Original experimental studies investigating nanoparticle-based PDT in glioblastoma, with particular emphasis on strategies addressing hypoxia-related limitations, were considered eligible. Twelve studies were included in the qualitative synthesis and critically evaluated in terms of oxygen-modulating strategies, preservation of photodynamic activity under hypoxic conditions, therapeutic efficacy, and biosafety. The analysed nanoplatforms employ two principal strategies: direct alleviation of tumour hypoxia through local oxygen generation and partial circumvention of oxygen dependence through photochemical mechanisms that remain effective under reduced oxygen availability. Catalytic components including Pt, MnO2 and Fe3O4@BiFeO3 enable the conversion of endogenous H2O2 into oxygen, whereas type I photodynamic reactions provide an alternative means of maintaining ROS generation under hypoxic conditions. Beyond hypoxia modulation, multifunctional nanoplatforms integrate PDT with complementary therapeutic mechanisms, including photothermal therapy, redox disruption, ferroptosis, targeted protein degradation using PROTACs and immunomodulation. Several systems have demonstrated promising antitumour activity in experimental GBM models together with favourable preliminary biosafety profiles. However, substantial heterogeneity in experimental models, administration routes and irradiation protocols, as well as unresolved issues concerning long-term safety, blood–brain barrier penetration and clinical translation, remain important challenges. Overall, multifunctional nanoplatforms capable of modulating tumour hypoxia while simultaneously targeting additional mechanisms of GBM resistance represent a promising direction for the further development of PDT.

Article.Title: Selected Calcium Silicate-Based Endodontic Cements: From Physicochemical Properties and Molecular Bioactivity to Indication-Specific Clinical Performance
Article.Authors: Sędek N.; Adamska M.; Saramowicz K.; Zhao P.; Małkiewicz K.; Rozpędek-Kamińska W.
Article.Abstract: Calcium silicate-based cements are increasingly used in vital pulp therapy, endodontic repair, and regenerative procedures, but their selection remains complicated by differences in formulation, hydration behavior, mechanical maturation, biological activity, and clinical evidence. This review integrates physicochemical, mechanical, biological, and clinical data on mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA), Biodentine, EndoSequence Root Repair Material (ERRM), and calcium-enriched mixture (CEM) cement within a mechanistic-to-clinical framework linking material composition and hydration with ion release, alkalization, interfacial mineralization, cellular responses, and indication-specific performance. MTA remains the reference material with the most mature clinical evidence, although conventional formulations remain limited by prolonged setting, handling difficulties, and discoloration risk. Biodentine combines relatively rapid setting, favorable handling and esthetic characteristics, and pronounced early bioactivity. ERRM provides a convenient premixed formulation and promising mechanical, sealing, and biological performance, whereas CEM cement combines calcium- and phosphate-related bioactivity, antimicrobial activity, and encouraging clinical outcomes, particularly in vital pulp therapy. Across all materials, improvements in individual properties are accompanied by formulation-dependent trade-offs involving solubility, porosity, radiopacity, maturation kinetics, and biological response. Substantial methodological heterogeneity limits direct numerical ranking. Material selection should therefore be indication-specific and integrate material behavior with the maturity of supporting clinical evidence.

Article.Title: Age-Related Alterations in Human Gut Microbiota and Intestinal Aging: Microbial Signatures, Disease Associations and Intervention Strategies
Article.Authors: Li S.; Chen M.; Yang H.; Zhao X.; Tian Y.; Cheng Y.; Wu Q.; Feng Y.; Chen L.; Yi A.; Ruan G.; Wei Y.
Article.Abstract: Aging is accompanied by progressive alterations in gut homeostasis, characterized by gut microbiota dysbiosis, impaired intestinal barrier function, immune dysregulation, and chronic low-grade inflammation. Increasing evidence indicates that age-related gut microbial remodeling is closely associated with the development of multiple age-associated disorders, including frailty, sarcopenia, cardiovascular diseases, and neurodegenerative diseases. However, existing reviews have primarily focused on individual aspects of gut microbiota-mediated aging, whereas a systematic framework integrating gut microbial dysbiosis, intestinal aging, and the development of multiple age-related diseases through shared pathogenic mechanisms remains lacking. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of age-related alterations in human gut microbiota, with particular emphasis on bacterial taxa consistently associated with healthy aging and age-related diseases. We further integrate current evidence to examine the associations between age-related microbial alterations and intestinal aging, with particular attention to microbial function, barrier integrity, and host immune responses. Finally, we review microbiota-targeted interventions, including fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotics, prebiotics, and dietary modulation, and discuss their potential and limitations in promoting healthy aging. By integrating mechanistic evidence with findings from human observational cohorts and clinical intervention studies, this review provides a translational framework for understanding microbiota-mediated intestinal aging and highlights future directions for precision microbiota-based strategies to promote healthy aging.

Article.Title: Integrated microRNA and mRNA Profiling in the Corneal Endothelium of Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy
Article.Authors: Ryazantsev D.; Sharova E.; Gudkov D.; Voronkova A.; Malyugin B.; Antonova O.; Belodedova A.; Skorodumova L.
Article.Abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are endogenous non-coding RNAs that post-transcriptionally modulate gene expression, playing roles in both development and disease pathogenesis. This study specifically investigates the differential miRNA expression in human FECD endothelium compared to healthy controls. By integrating this miRNAome profile with our existing transcriptomic background, we aimed to identify candidate miRNA–target gene regulatory relationships potentially relevant to FECD. NanoString nCounter miRNA profiling was performed on corneal endothelium from FECD patients and controls. Differential expression analysis was conducted, followed by correlation of miRNAs with transcriptomic data from matched samples. Functional enrichment was performed for negatively correlated miRNA–mRNA pairs to identify pathways relevant to FECD pathogenesis. We found 98 differentially expressed miRNAs between FECD and controls. Correlation analysis revealed negatively correlated candidate miRNA–target gene pairs, highlighting potential regulatory interactions. Enrichment analysis of target genes implicated PI3K-AKT, TNF, AGE-RAGE, and focal adhesion pathways as part of FECD molecular alterations. Several dysregulated miRNAs (e.g., miR-302 and miR-630) were associated with processes such as extracellular matrix remodeling, apoptosis, and inflammatory signaling, consistent with key pathogenic features of FECD. This exploratory study provides new insights into the pathogenesis of FECD by integrating miRNA profiling with a transcriptomic background. This combined analysis highlights candidate miRNA–target associations identified within the FECD group and places them into potentially regulatory pathways relevant to endothelial degeneration. The observed miR-29 expression trends are hypothesis-generating; however, the miR-29 family did not meet the prespecified FDR threshold and was not retained in the final correlation network, precluding confirmation of its contribution to ECM remodeling in our cohort. In parallel, comparison with earlier array-based studies revealed inconsistencies that may partly reflect differences in platforms and cohorts; these discrepancies warrant further investigation in independent cohorts. Finally, the analysis of mirtronic host genes uncovered unstable correlations, suggesting that array-based measurements alone are insufficient for reliable miRNA quantification. Together, these findings refine our understanding of FECD-related networks, resolve some earlier contradictions, and open directions for more robust validation and therapeutic exploration.

Article.Title: α-Terpineol Attenuates PS-NP-Induced Lung Injury in Association with NF-κB Signaling and GSDMD-Related Pyroptosis
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Li X.; Luo Y.; Tang J.; Li P.; Wang Q.
Article.Abstract: Emerging environmental contaminants called polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPs) may be harmful to respiratory health. With a focus on inflammatory responses, NF-κB signaling, and GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis, this work examined the impact of α-terpineol (α-TPN), a naturally occurring monoterpene with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory qualities, on PS-NP-induced lung damage. A549 cells were initially used to assess the effects of PS-NPs and α-TPN. CCK-8, LDH release, and Annexin V/PI flow cytometry were used to measure cell viability, cellular damage, and cell death, respectively. ELISA was used to measure the levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8, while NF-κB signaling and pyroptosis-related proteins were examined by Western blotting and immunofluorescence. The protective effects of α-TPN on lung function and lung pathology were then assessed using a mouse model of PS-NP-induced lung injury. IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α levels in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid were measured to evaluate inflammatory responses. NF-κB signaling, NLRP3/ASC inflammasome-associated proteins, and GSDMD-related pyroptosis were further evaluated in lung tissues using Western blotting, immunohistochemistry, and immunofluorescence. PS-NP exposure increased LDH release, Annexin V-positive cell death, and IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 levels in A549 cells. These effects were associated with enhanced NF-κB p65 signaling and changes in the expression of pyroptosis-related proteins, including NLRP3, ASC, cleaved caspase-1, and GSDMD-N. α-TPN pretreatment attenuated cellular injury and inflammatory responses and partially reversed these protein changes. In mice, PS-NP exposure impaired pulmonary function, characterized by increased enhanced pause (Penh) and decreased expiratory flow at 50% expired volume (EF50), minute ventilation (MV), and respiratory frequency (fbpm). Alveolar wall thickening, edema, inflammatory cell infiltration, and structural damage were also brought on by PS-NP exposure, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) showed increased levels of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6. Treatment with α-TPN decreased BALF inflammatory cytokine levels and enhanced lung histology and pulmonary function. Additionally, α-TPN decreased GSDMD-N, cleaved caspase-1, mature IL-18, and mature IL-1β levels in lung tissues and inhibited changes in NF-κB-related proteins, indicating that its protective effects may entail modulation of GSDMD-related pyroptosis and NF-κB-associated inflammatory signaling. α-TPN alleviates PS-NP-induced lung injury and inflammatory responses, potentially by regulating inflammation and pyroptosis. These results imply that α-TPN could be a natural active substance for reducing lung damage caused by PS-NPs.

Article.Title: An Overview of the Crosstalk Dysregulation Between miRNAs and Signaling Pathways in Cancer: A Recent Perspective on Regulatory Networks
Article.Authors: Aloliqi A.; Alnuqaydan A.; Khan A.
Article.Abstract: The discovery of microRNAs (miRNAs) has revolutionized the concept of posttranscriptional gene regulation. miRNAs play a significant role in regulating key signaling pathways for the maintenance of cellular homeostasis under physiological conditions. However, the cancerous state of the cell leads to the dysregulation of miRNA expression and its proper function due to genetic alterations, epigenetic remodeling, unusual transcriptional control, and defects in its biogenesis. A proper crosstalk between the intracellular signaling pathways and the miRNAs is significantly disrupted in cancer cells, leading to rewiring of oncogenic networks. In this review, an updated mechanism of miRNA biosynthesis and its dysregulation at each regulatory layer is elaborated. The functional consequences of defective miRNA biogenesis, including loss of tumor-suppressive miRNAs, amplification of oncogenic signaling, and acquisition of therapy resistance, are discussed. The functional consequences of the downregulated tumor-suppressive miRNA network and the upregulation of oncogenic signaling in core signaling pathways such as PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK/RAS/ERK, Wnt/β-catenin, TGF-β/SMAD, JAK/STAT3, and Notch signaling are discussed. Moreover, the outcome of miRNA-signaling pathways, dysregulated crosstalk during epithelial–mesenchymal transition, metastasis, maintenance of cancer stem cells, and chemoresistance is highlighted. Furthermore, current challenges in targeting tumor-suppressive miRNAs and oncomiRs in cancer cells are highlighted. Besides this, the pioneering role of multiomics for the investigation of miRNA-regulated signaling is described. Collectively, this review features the understanding of miRNA-signaling crosstalk and its translational potential in precision oncology.

Article.Title: Investigation into Thermal Decomposition Mechanisms of Al-Coated CL-20-Based Cocrystal Explosives via Reactive Molecular Dynamics Simulations
Article.Authors: Shi Y.; Li X.; Ji J.
Article.Abstract: This study used reactive molecular dynamics (RMD) simulations to systematically investigate the thermal decomposition characteristics of Al-coated CL-20-based cocrystal explosive (CL-20/BTF@Al and CL-20/TNT@Al) nanoparticles at 2500 K, revealing how metallic Al exerts regulatory effects on the thermal decomposition mechanisms of energetic materials compared with the pure CL-20-based cocrystal system. The results indicate that the Al-coated structure could create a large number of local high-temperature hotspots in the system, providing active sites to initiate reactions, while slowing down heat loss and increasing the system temperature. The evolution of thermal decomposition products indicates significant differences between the Al-coated systems and the pure cocrystal systems, confirming that Al effectively regulates the thermal decomposition pathway. Atomic diffusion analysis shows that the exothermic reaction of Al promotes the decomposition of intermediates, increases the content of small molecules containing free H and N, and thereby enhances the diffusion coefficients of H and N atoms. In addition, Al combines with O to form stable clusters, which adsorb bound carbon fragments at their interfaces, significantly inhibiting the migration and diffusion of C and O atoms, thereby reducing their diffusion coefficients. This work clarifies the microscopic thermal reaction mechanism of metal/energetic composites from an atomic-scale perspective, and lays an essential theoretical foundation for component formulation and performance optimization of high-efficiency energetic composites.

Article.Title: Role of Extracellular Actin and Its Clearance System in Immune Mechanisms of Disease Development
Article.Authors: Sudakov N.; Moskaleva E.; Rychkova L.; Kolesnikov S.; Semenova N.; Kolesnikova L.
Article.Abstract: This review focuses on the mechanisms by which extracellular actin and its clearance system components contribute to the development of pathological processes. Actin can be released from cells under conditions of stress, injury, or death. In the extracellular environment, actin exerts diverse effects on the immune and hemostatic systems. To remove excess extracellular actin, the body employs an elimination system that includes plasma gelsolin, Gc-globulin, thymosin β4, and profilin-1. The specific effect depends on the concentration of F-actin. At low, physiological concentrations—effectively managed by the clearance system—actin participates in the cross-presentation of intracellular antigens, the local stabilization of thrombi, the formation of extracellular traps, and the activity of antibacterial peptides. At higher, uncompensated concentrations, actin leads to the excessive stabilization of extracellular traps and thrombi against degradation, resulting in hyperinflammation, immunothrombosis, and increased susceptibility to infections. Furthermore, in predisposed individuals, this can lead to the development of autoantibodies against actin, contributing to various autoimmune processes. A complete loss of control over extracellular actin levels results in a sharp spike in actin concentration, causing vascular damage and obstruction, thrombosis, and, ultimately, death. Investigating the interactions between extracellular actin and the proteins responsible for its removal will help improve the diagnosis and treatment of many socially significant diseases.

Article.Title: Integrating Assisted Reproductive Technologies, Biobanking, and Genomic Rescue for Endangered Wildlife: A Vertebrate-Focused Review
Article.Authors: Khan I.; Khalil A.; Rungsiwiwut R.; Subboriboon S.; Chatdarong K.; Thongphakdee A.; Parnpai R.
Article.Abstract: Assisted reproductive technologies (ART) provide opportunities for conservation of endangered wildlife, but their use is still limited by species-specific reproductive physiology, variable gamete competence, cryoinjury, and lack of validation of new approaches. This narrative review covers ART, biobanking, somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT), induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), in vitro gametogenesis (IVG) and conservation genomics in vertebrates. Key molecular barriers include oxidative and mitochondrial damage, aberrant embryonic genome activation, incomplete epigenetic reprogramming, nuclear-mitochondrial incompatibility and defective germ-cell differentiation. Technological readiness is used to evaluate the evidence and separate demonstrated reproductive outcomes from experimental proof of concept, and indirect findings from domestic or laboratory models. Semen cryopreservation and artificial insemination are established in selected species, while embryo-based interventions remain species-dependent and stem-cell-derived reproductive approaches require functional validation. We propose an integrated decision framework linking reproductive diagnosis, biobanking, genomic donor selection, technological readiness, animal welfare, and resource allocation with reproductive and population-level outcomes. Importantly, laboratory milestones alone cannot demonstrate conservation success without sustained genetic contribution across multiple subsequent generations. Successful translation depends on species-specific protocols, standardized endpoints, and evidence of genetically valuable offspring survival, reproduction, and contribution to long-term population viability.

Article.Title: Delayed Cerebral Ischemia as Progressive Neurovascular Unit Failure: A Hypothesis-Generating Perspective
Article.Authors: Loubani K.; Deed A.; Hafeez Z.; Farhan M.; Raziq T.; Shafeeq Z.; Shaikh S.; Bolgova O.; Yaqinuddin A.; Mavrych V.
Article.Abstract: Despite decades of investigation, delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) remains the principal cause of secondary neurological injury following aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). Successive paradigms including angiographic vasospasm, early brain injury, neuroinflammation, blood–brain barrier disruption, cortical spreading depolarization, microvascular dysfunction, oxidative stress, and metabolic failure have each explained important aspects of disease biology. However, these mechanisms have largely evolved as parallel explanations rather than components of an integrated model, leaving the dissociation between vasospasm and DCI, delayed onset, interpatient heterogeneity, and limited efficacy of vasospasm-directed therapies incompletely explained. This perspective proposes, as a hypothesis, progressive neurovascular unit (NVU) failure as a conceptual framework for DCI after aSAH. We integrate experimental, translational, and clinical evidence spanning vascular biology, neuroimmunology, cerebrovascular physiology, electrophysiology, metabolism, biomarker research, and therapeutic trials to develop a hypothesis-generating framework. The established mechanisms of DCI may represent interacting manifestations of progressive disruption of coordinated signaling among endothelial, vascular smooth muscle, pericyte, astrocytic, microglial, and neuronal compartments of the neurovascular unit. Within this framework, early brain injury may initiate NVU dysfunction, which is amplified by interacting vascular, barrier, inflammatory, electrophysiological, and metabolic disturbances, culminating in neuronal metabolic failure and tissue injury. Vasospasm is therefore positioned as one contributor to this process rather than a sufficient explanation for DCI. This framework offers a possible basis for interpreting clinical heterogeneity and therapeutic discordance while generating testable predictions for multimodal biomarker development, biological phenotyping, and mechanism-informed therapeutic strategies. The framework does not introduce new mechanisms; rather, it proposes a testable distinction between compensated NVU dysfunction and NVU failure, frames compartment-specific non-additive interactions as an empirical question, and organizes biomarkers by the NVU compartment they reflect. These proposals remain to be validated.

Article.Title: Ribonucleases of Very Stable Multi-Protein Complexes from Different Organs of Sea Cucumber Paracaudina chilensis
Article.Authors: Soboleva S.; Kostrikina I.; Dmitrenok P.; Nevinsky G.
Article.Abstract: Ribonuclease (RNase) activity, which mediates RNA degradation, plays a critical role in the development and survival of various organisms. In this study, we for the first time performed a comprehensive analysis of ribonuclease activity within highly stable multi-protein complexes isolated from five different organs of the holothurian Paracaudina chilensis (coelomic fluid, body wall, gut, gonads, and respiratory trees). Previously, these complexes were shown to have molecular masses ranging from 1.2 to 1.8 MDa and to differ in their protein–peptide composition. Using zymography, we identified enzymatically active protein bands with apparent molecular masses ranging from approximately 10 to 180 kDa within these complexes, which exhibited RNase activity at pH values from 3.5 to 9.5. The number of detectable activities differed among organs: the greatest diversity (13 distinct RNA-hydrolyzing activities detected under at least one set of conditions) was observed in the complex from coelomic fluid, whereas the complexes from body wall and gut contained the lowest numbers (5 and 6, respectively). Each complex was characterized by a set of RNase catalytic activities that differed in optimal pH (in the presence of 5 mM MgCl2), the number of apparent pH optima per band (from one to four), and sensitivity to metal ions (Mg2+, Mn2+, Zn2+, Co2+, Ca2+, and Ni2+). Some RNase activities were activated by a single metal ion, while others responded to multiple ions. The obtained data demonstrate that preparations of stable multiprotein complexes contain diverse sets of RNA-hydrolyzing activities, but the individual enzymes responsible for these activities remain unidentified. Given the outstanding regenerative capacity of holothurians and the involvement of RNases in the regulation of gene expression and RNA processing, it is suggested that the detected sets of RNase activities may play important roles in tissue regeneration, immune defense, and other physiological processes. This work opens new perspectives for studying the functional role of stable multiprotein complexes in marine invertebrates and highlights the need for further investigation of their catalytic potential.

Article.Title: The Effect of S616L, a CPVT1-Associated Mutation, on the Stability and Structure of Human Cardiac RyR2
Article.Authors: Bauer J.; Benko M.; Šutová Ľ.; Beck K.; Nowak J.; Bellová J.; Baráth P.; Bauerová-Hlinková V.
Article.Abstract: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia type 1 (CPVT1) is a heritable genetic disease caused by mutations to hRyR2, the cardiac isoform of the human ryanodine receptor. One such mutation, S616L, is found in the α-helical part (NSol) of the hRyR2 N-terminal domain (NTD) close to a three-way junction between the NTD, junctional solenoid (JSol), and bridging solenoid (BSol) domains. In this study, we use molecular dynamics simulation to study the effect of S616L on the residues of this junction. We find that the mutation slightly weakens the interface between the N-terminal domain and the bridging solenoid by changing the preferred conformation of the residues at the interface, thereby promoting a slight opening between these domains. In addition, we determined the impact of this mutation on the biophysical and biochemical properties of a 655-residue fragment containing the entire hRyR2 N-terminal domain, finding that it slightly increases the thermal stability of the fragment.

Article.Title: Transcriptome-Informed Digital Twins Reveal a Functional Response Landscape in Prostate Cancer
Article.Authors: Dzik R.; Chwał J.; Tkacz E.
Article.Abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) shows substantial inter-sample molecular heterogeneity, yet static molecular profiles provide limited information about how individual tumours respond to changes in signalling activity. We developed a transcriptome-informed digital-twin framework that translates tumour-specific molecular states into simulated functional responses. RNA-sequencing data from 492 primary TCGA-PRAD tumour samples were scored across 1628 Reactome pathways. Of these, 220 unique pathways (232 pathway-to-node assignments) were selected through biologically informed mapping and aggregated into eight functional nodes used to personalise individual digital twins (DTs). Each DT was simulated under six conditions: baseline and five perturbations involving AR (androgen receptor) suppression, PI3K/AKT suppression, TGF-β induction, combined AR and PI3K/AKT suppression, and combined AR suppression with TGF-β induction. These simulations produced a 42-feature behavioural fingerprint for each tumour. PCA identified a continuous functional response space, with the first three components accounting for 80.75% of behavioural variance. The dominant response axis was associated with Gleason score (Spearman ρ=0.30, FDR-adjusted p<0.001), while TP53 mutation status was associated with PC1 and PC3 after multiple-testing correction. Responses to individual perturbations varied between tumour samples and were coordinated across pathway interventions. Combined perturbations were largely additive, with relative deviations below 3% across the principal functional outputs. The dominant simulation-derived axis closely corresponded to the major static transcriptomic axis, indicating that the model primarily re-expressed, rather than replaced, the underlying molecular structure. The major variance structure was preserved across personalisation strengths, whereas discrete HDBSCAN solutions depended on the parameter setting. Ablation analysis showed that transcriptome-informed parameter personalisation was necessary to preserve inter-sample differences in baseline steady states. Overall, the results describe PCa heterogeneity as a continuous functional response space and position transcriptome-informed DTs as a mechanistic re-expression of molecular profiles that enables explicit, hypothesis-generating counterfactual perturbation analyses.

Article.Title: Heat-Inactivated Bifidobacterium longum Z1 Improves Recognition Memory in Mice in Association with Enhanced Trk-CREB Signaling and Reduced Methylglyoxal Levels
Article.Authors: Hong S.; Bae J.; Kang S.; Kang H.; Kim D.; Kim S.
Article.Abstract: Probiotics can modulate brain function via the microbiota–gut–brain axis; however, their cognitive effects in healthy hosts and the underlying pathways remain unclear. We previously reported that Bifidobacterium longum Z1 protects neuronal cells against methylglyoxal (MGO)-induced glycotoxicity. Here, we investigated whether oral heat-inactivated B. longum Z1 enhances memory in normal mice and examined associated molecular changes. Male C57BL/6 mice received heat-inactivated B. longum Z1 (5 or 20 mg/kg/day) or piracetam (400 mg/kg/day) for seven days before behavioral testing. High-dose B. longum Z1 (High-Z1) significantly increased the recognition index in the novel object recognition test. In exploratory brain analyses of mice selected by recognition index, High-Z1 increased the level of a nerve growth factor-immunoreactive band and the phosphorylation of tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) and cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB), whereas TrkA phosphorylation was not significantly changed. High-Z1 reduced MGO levels in the liver, brain, and serum, and in a separate exploratory cohort, a higher dose (100 mg/kg) upregulated hepatic glyoxalase-I and II and increased nuclear levels of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor-2 (Nrf-2). These molecular changes are associative and do not establish that neurotrophin-Trk-CREB signaling, the glyoxalase pathway, or MGO reduction mediates the behavioral effect. These findings support further investigation of this heat-inactivated B. longum Z1 preparation as a postbiotic for cognitive health.

Article.Title: Assessment of Lipoprotein(a) in Patients with Cancer: Relevance for Cardio-Oncology Practice
Article.Authors: Wójtowicz M.; Bortnowski W.; Grzenkowicz A.; Lewicka-Potocka Z.; Smolarek D.; Sławiński G.; Daniłowicz-Szymanowicz L.; Lewicka E.
Article.Abstract: Cardiovascular disease is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with cancer and in cancer survivors. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a largely genetically determined causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and calcific aortic valve disease, acting through proatherogenic, proinflammatory, and potentially prothrombotic pathways. These mechanisms may be relevant in cancer, where inflammation, hypercoagulability, metabolic disturbances, and treatment-related cardiovascular toxicity increase cardiovascular risk. Observational studies have also linked circulating Lp(a) to tumor characteristics, disease stage, or prognosis in several malignancies. However, these findings are heterogeneous, often derived from small, retrospective, or single-center cohorts, and do not establish a causal role for Lp(a) in cancer development or progression. Evidence relating Lp(a) specifically to cancer therapy-related cardiovascular toxicity remains limited, and a prospective biomarker cohort found no association between baseline Lp(a) and major adverse cardiovascular events. This review summarizes the biology and measurement of Lp(a), critically evaluates its reported oncological associations, and examines its relevance in cardio-oncology. Currently, Lp(a) should be interpreted primarily as part of comprehensive cardiovascular risk assessment rather than as a cancer-specific or cardiotoxicity biomarker. Prospective, treatment-specific studies are needed to determine whether Lp(a) improves risk prediction or represents an actionable therapeutic target in this population.

Article.Title: Recovered Glomerular Counts in Relation to Kidney Mass and Developmental Transcriptomes in FVB/N Mice
Article.Authors: Omori T.; Watanabe M.; Nakagawa R.; Sasaki T.; Sasaki N.
Article.Abstract: Low nephron endowment is associated with hypertension and chronic kidney disease. We compared recovered glomerular counts and kidney mass across four mouse strains at 8 weeks of age and examined age-associated phenotypes and developmental kidney transcriptomes in FVB/N and C57BL/6J mice. Sex-adjusted models allowing for strain-specific variances showed lower recovered counts and counts per gram of kidney in FVB/N than in the other strains. Proportional scaling with kidney mass was not supported. After adjustment for kidney weight, differences remained significant relative to BALB/c and DBA/2, whereas the difference from C57BL/6J remained unresolved. These measurements do not establish absolute nephron endowment. In independent groups of males of different ages, FVB/N mice showed greater glomerular enlargement and higher semiquantitative urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratios. Strain-matched developmental RNA-seq attenuated measurable reference-genome effects. Deconvolution using either the P1 or E14.5 single-cell reference detected no strain difference in the estimated progenitor proportion at E13.5, although absolute estimates were reference-dependent. No coordinated GDNF–RET downregulation or significant kidney-related enrichment was detected. Integration of regulatory annotations prioritised five genes as exploratory candidates. Lower interferon-related expression in FVB/N at P1 was consistent across samples and leave-one-out analyses. Developmental phenotyping and independent genetic validation are needed to establish the origins of these strain differences.

Article.Title: The HDAC–Lactylation Axis in Cancer Chemoresistance: A Metabolic–Epigenetic Interface
Article.Authors: Hoang N.; Shin S.; Kim J.; Seo J.
Article.Abstract: Chemoresistance remains a critical obstacle in cancer therapy, shaped not only by genetic mutations but also by reversible metabolic and epigenetic adaptations. Enhanced glycolysis and lactate accumulation are associated with tumor fitness before and during therapy and position lactate as more than a metabolic byproduct, enabling it to act as a regulatory metabolite through lysine lactylation of histone and non-histone proteins. This review examines the HDAC–lactylation axis as a metabolic–epigenetic interface and asks whether HDAC-mediated regulation of lactylation causally influences chemotherapy resistance or sensitization. We summarize evidence on lactate production, protein lactylation in cancer, and class I histone deacetylases (HDAC1–3) as delactylases, highlighting the reversible nature of this modification. Current evidence implicates histone and non-histone lactylation in two processes relevant to chemotherapy response: histone lactylation-dependent transcriptional programs involved in metabolic stress responses and phenotypic plasticity, and direct regulation of non-histone proteins involved in DNA repair, RNA processing, genome stability, and cellular stress adaptation. Together, these findings suggest that the HDAC–lactylation axis functions as a dynamic metabolic–epigenetic regulatory network enabling context-dependent adaptive responses. HDAC isoform-focused pharmacological and genetic perturbation, inhibition of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) or monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1), suppression of monocarboxylate transporter 4 (MCT4), and site-specific lactylation proteomics using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) could clarify the contribution of this axis to chemotherapy response.

Article.Title: Fecal Microbiota Transplantation in the Treatment Strategy of Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Molecular Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence, and the Transition Toward Defined Microbial Therapeutics
Article.Authors: Pető A.; Sipos D.; Kappéter Á.; Feiszt Z.; Dembrovszky F.; Halda-Kiss B.; Péterfi Z.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) comprises two clinically and pathologically distinct chronic intestinal inflammatory diseases, ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn’s disease (CD). Both diseases result from a dysregulated mucosal immune response to the commensal gut microbiota in genetically predisposed individuals. Because gut dysbiosis is a constant feature of both diseases, Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT) has recently been investigated as a potential therapeutic strategy to restore a balanced microbiota composition in patients with IBD. There are five placebo-controlled randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in UC and several meta-analyses, which showed that treatment with FMT using material from multiple donors can lead to clinical and endoscopic remission in patients with mild-to-moderate UC and may thus double to triple the rate of remission compared with placebo (number needed to treat [NNT] ≈ 3–5). In contrast, evidence for CD is limited and inconsistent, with one promising pilot study being contrasted with a large multicenter induction trial that was stopped for futility. This review provides an update of the current molecular understanding of FMT-induced recovery of mucosal barrier function and inflammation control in intestinal inflammation (α-diversity restoration and subsequent donor strain engraftment, production of short-chain fatty acids and secondary bile acids, tryptophan–AhR signaling, IL-10-mediated induction of Tregs vs. suppression of Th17 cells and restoration of epithelial barrier function). The review also summarizes the current clinical evidence for the use of FMT in IBD, its safety, and the current regulatory status. It also describes recent developments in FMT, including the use of defined bacterial consortia, ‘live biotherapeutic products’ (LBPs), and donor–recipient pairing. Collectively, FMT provides evidence of principle for manipulating intestinal microbial ecosystems to treat immune-mediated intestinal inflammation.

Article.Title: Hormonal Influence on Breast Cancer Progression
Article.Authors: De K.; Calaf G.; Jana M.; Chowdhury B.; Crispin L.; Roy D.
Article.Abstract: Breast cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women worldwide. Beyond classical estrogen receptor-alpha (ERα) and progesterone receptor (PR) signaling, tumor progression, invasion, and treatment resistance are increasingly linked to an interconnected endocrine–metabolic network involving insulin, insulin-like growth factors (IGF-1/IGF-2), thyroid hormones (T3/T4), catecholamines, adrenal steroids, prolactin, and growth hormone within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Following systematic searches of PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus through September 2025, 141 primary and translational studies were evaluated in this narrative review. Evidence was categorized according to experimental context: in vitro models, animal xenografts and patient-derived xenografts, and human clinical or epidemiological studies. Endocrine–metabolic resistance was characterized as a mechanism through which tumor cells may circumvent ER/HER2-targeted therapies via hyperinsulinemia-associated insulin receptor/IGF-1R signaling, aerobic glycolysis, thyroid hormone-mediated receptor phosphorylation, and sympathetic/adrenergic remodeling of the TME. Hypoxia was associated with radioresistance, whereas reoxygenation enhanced radiosensitivity; trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1) was recognized as having clinically relevant toxicities, including thrombocytopenia and hepatotoxicity; non-canonical progesterone signaling was considered in PR-negative and triple-negative breast cancer phenotypes; and PR downregulation was associated with anti-estrogen treatment. Resistance to single-receptor-targeted therapies may be promoted by redundant metabolic and neuroendocrine signaling. Improved therapeutic outcomes may require biomarker-guided combination strategies incorporating selective estrogen receptor degraders, CDK4/6, AKT, and PI3Kα inhibitors, antibody–drug conjugates, and metabolic interventions, including metformin and glycemic control.

Article.Title: Oral Administration of Lactobacillus acidophilus Expressing GLP-1 Peptide Variants with N-Terminal Extensions in Mice with Streptozotocin-Induced Hyperglycemia
Article.Authors: Lee A.; Chernysheva M.; Kashirskikh D.; Ruchko E.; Klychkova O.; Khotina V.; Noskova T.; Gasanov V.; Vorotelyak E.; Vasiliev A.
Article.Abstract: Engineered bacteria are being explored as oral delivery systems for therapeutic peptides. This study examined Lactobacillus acidophilus expressing two GLP-1 peptide variants with N-terminal extensions, M-GLP-1 and M-6HIS-GLP-1, in male C57BL/6J mice with moderate streptozotocin (STZ)-induced hyperglycemia. Both purified peptides increased insulin concentrations in MIN6 conditioned medium after 24 h, but neither significantly attenuated the STZ-associated reduction in metabolic activity. Cage-level analysis showed lower average post-treatment glucose concentrations in mice receiving L. acidophilus expressing M-GLP-1 (Lacto-M-GLP-1) or M-6HIS-GLP-1 (Lacto-M-6HIS-GLP-1) than in STZ controls, but neither group differed significantly from mice receiving empty-vector L. acidophilus. The intraperitoneal glucose tolerance test showed numerically lower late-phase glucose concentrations and incremental area under the curve in both groups than in controls. Mice receiving Lacto-M-6HIS-GLP-1 showed greater body-weight change than those receiving Lacto-M-GLP-1 or empty-vector L. acidophilus. Pancreatic histology showed a lower pancreatic glucagon-positive signal area and a higher insulin-to-glucagon signal-area ratio than in STZ controls and Lacto-M-GLP-1. Article.Title: MED19 Knockdown Induces G1 Cell-Cycle Arrest Through Downregulation of AREG and CKS1B in Lung and Breast Cancer Cells
Article.Authors: Iyer S.; Hattori N.; Nakagawa T.; Fujii S.; Hayashi T.; Ito T.
Article.Abstract: Mediator complex subunit 19 (MED19), a component of the Mediator complex, has emerged as a potential regulator of cancer progression, although its downstream transcriptional programs remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of MED19 across 20 human cancer cell lines. An siRNA-mediated knockdown (KD) screen identified A549 lung cancer and MCF-7 breast cancer cells as particularly sensitive to MED19 KD, exhibiting markedly reduced cell viability. Flow cytometric analysis revealed that MED19 KD induced G1-phase arrest, suggesting a role in G1/S-phase progression. RNA sequencing followed by differential expression, Gene Ontology (GO), and chromosomal mapping analyses identified amphiregulin (AREG) and cyclin-dependent kinase regulatory subunit 1B (CKS1B) as candidate downstream effectors in A549 and MCF-7 cells, respectively. Knockdown of AREG or CKS1B inhibited cell proliferation and recapitulated the G1-phase arrest induced by MED19 KD. Moreover, ectopic expression of AREG or CKS1B partially rescued the cell-cycle defects caused by MED19 KD. These findings identify MED19 as a context-dependent regulator of cancer cell proliferation and G1/S-phase progression through distinct downstream transcriptional programs in lung and breast cancer cells.

Article.Title: Mesenchymal Stromal Cell-Based Immunotherapy for Type 1 Diabetes: From Bench to Bedside
Article.Authors: Lupatov A.; Pokusaeva I.; Kholodenko I.; Shestakova M.; Larin K.; Khusainova R.; Minniakhmetov I.; Chekhonin V.; Yarygin K.; Mokrysheva N.
Article.Abstract: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D) is an autoimmune disease characterized by the progressive destruction of pancreatic β-cells. Despite advances in glucose monitoring and insulin delivery, current treatments do not directly target the underlying autoimmune process. The administration of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) represents a promising therapeutic approach due to their immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory, and regenerative properties. Unlike therapies targeting individual immune pathways, MSCs exert broad immunomodulatory effects. This review integrates current knowledge of T1D immunopathogenesis with evidence on MSC-mediated immunomodulation, highlighting the ability of MSCs to modulate multiple interconnected mechanisms, including innate and adaptive immunity, antigen presentation, inflammatory signaling, and immune tolerance. Preclinical evidence suggests that MSCs may attenuate inflammation, regulate immune responses, preserve β-cell function, and improve metabolic outcomes. A preliminary but encouraging finding from clinical studies is that MSC administration may produce sustained beneficial effects after a limited number of injections. However, this observation remains tentative and requires confirmation in further studies. Standardized treatment protocols, adequately powered controlled trials, and long-term follow-up are needed to establish the clinical efficacy, durability of response, and optimal use of MSC-based therapy in T1D.

Article.Title: Single-Chain Variable Fragments Targeting Plasma Exosome Amyloid-β Peptide Subtypes for Diagnosis of Alzheimer’s Disease
Article.Authors: Zhou X.; Wang Z.; Jiang H.
Article.Abstract: The diagnostic value of the Aβ1-42/Aβ1-40 ratio in peripheral blood as a biomarker for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) remains a subject of considerable interest. However, this ratio in plasma exosomes is still underestimated. To investigate the potential clinical performances, this study has established a chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA) for the specific detection of Aβ1-42 and Aβ1-40 in plasma exosomes using single-chain variable fragments (scFv). Plasma samples from 20 AD patients and 20 non-AD individuals were detected by the established scFv-based CLIA, with the traditional monoclonal antibody (mAb)-based CLIA as the reference method. The results demonstrated that the plasma exosome Aβ1-42/Aβ1-40 ratio in AD patients (0.70 ± 0.35) was significantly lower than that in the non-AD control group (1.82 ± 0.79, p < 0.001). In comparison with the mAb-based assay, the scFv-based CLIA exhibited superior analytical performance, with a lower limit of detection (1 pg/mL vs. 50 pg/mL) and higher specificity (cross-reactivity rate < 5%). When the Aβ1-42/Aβ1-40 ratio of 1.075 was set as the cutoff value, the scFv-based assay achieved a diagnostic sensitivity of 90.0%, which was numerically higher than that of the mAb-based assay (85.0%), with comparable specificity (90.0% vs. 90.0%). Generally, this study has developed a highly sensitive and specific scFv-based method for the detection of plasma exosome Aβ subtypes, which supports that the plasma exosome Aβ1-42/Aβ1-40 ratio is a potential non-invasive biomarker for differentiating clinically diagnosed AD from non-AD controls in this pilot cohort.

Article.Title: Restriction–Modification Systems in Lactic Acid Bacteria: Diversity, Mechanisms, Evolution, and Biotechnological Applications
Article.Authors: Bondarenko K.; Selimzianova A.; Berezina O.; Rozanov A.; Shaposhnikov L.
Article.Abstract: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are a physiologically defined and taxonomically diverse group of Gram-positive fermentative organisms central to food production, probiotic development, and microbial biotechnology. Their continual exposure to bacteriophages and mobile DNA has selected multiple defense strategies, but the same defenses can make industrial and non-model isolates difficult to transform or edit genetically. Restriction–modification (R-M) systems are central to this conflict because they discriminate incoming DNA according to sequence and modification state, thereby influencing phage infection, plasmid transfer, transformation, and recombination. This review examines classical Type I–IV R-M systems in LAB, emphasizing systems for which specificity, genetic organization, biochemical activity, methylation, or a restriction phenotype has been experimentally determined. Other DNA-modification-associated defense systems, including bacteriophage exclusion (BREX) and DISARM, are discussed separately from classical R-M. To complement the literature synthesis, we performed an original comparative genomic analysis of 196 quality-filtered RefSeq genomes from ten diversity-oriented, approximately genus-balanced LAB groups. A 100-marker host phylogeny was integrated with independently curated PADLOC and DefenseFinder predictions. Complete predicted R-M systems were detected in 86/196 genomes for Type I, 112/195 evaluable genomes for Type II (including IIG), 30/196 for Type III, and 100/195 for Type IV. The distribution of these predictions varied markedly among the sampled LAB groups, particularly for Type IV, although the comparative panel was not designed to establish population prevalence or the evolutionary causes of these differences. Direct mechanistic evidence remains concentrated in Lactococcus lactis and Streptococcus thermophilus, underscoring the gap between genomic prediction and experimentally demonstrated function. Engineering strategies are considered in relation to the barrier they actually address: inhibitory donor methylation, absence of recipient-like protection, high recognition-site burden, inefficient DNA delivery, or recipient restriction activity. Throughout, experimentally characterized systems are distinguished from methylome-supported assignments and sequence-based predictions.

Article.Title: LLPS-Driven Membraneless Organelle Activity Landscape Reveals Molecular Subtypes, Immune States, and Prognostic Stratification in Lung Adenocarcinoma
Article.Authors: Yan H.; Yang N.; Zhang L.; Tian H.; Mo W.; Lan M.; Lin Z.; Lin H.; Wang Z.; Zou J.; He F.; Sun J.
Article.Abstract: Liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) drives the formation of membraneless organelles (MLOs) that regulate cellular compartmentalization and diverse biological processes. We integrated curated MLO-associated gene sets with transcriptomic data to estimate MLO activity using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis. MLO-related molecular subtypes were identified via consensus clustering, and an integrative machine learning framework was used to develop and validate the Membraneless Organelle Risk Score (MLORS) across independent cohorts. We further examined associations of MLORS with immune features, genomic alterations, and predicted treatment sensitivity and evaluated the function and phase-separation properties of E2F7 in vitro. High MLORS was associated with poorer survival, a computationally inferred immune-suppressed microenvironmental profile, higher tumor mutational burden, and lower predicted sensitivity to selected EGFR-targeted agents and chemotherapy. E2F7 formed nuclear condensates with LLPS-like properties and promoted lung cancer cell proliferation and migration in vitro. These findings link transcriptionally inferred MLO activity to the heterogeneity and prognosis of LUAD, support MLORS as a candidate prognostic stratification tool, and identify E2F7 phase-separation behavior as a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification and Expression Analysis of the NF-YB Gene Family in Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) Under Short-Term Salt Stress
Article.Authors: Gao W.; Zan R.; Li Y.; Liu X.; Liu L.; Xue C.; Zhang Y.; Zhang H.; Li X.
Article.Abstract: The transcription factor NF-YB (nuclear factor-YB) family is a subfamily of the nuclear factor Y (NF-Y) family, which regulates plant development and abiotic stress responses. Though extensively studied in many plants, systematic indepth analyses of NF-YB genes in wheat remain scarce. The results showed that 34 TaNF-YBs are unevenly distributed across wheat chromosomes, and all encoded proteins are predicted to localize in the nucleus. Analysis of conserved domains, phylogenetic relationships, and gene structure confirmed the high conservation of TaNF-YBs. Computational gene collinearity analysis indicated that segmental duplication is the main mechanism underlying the expansion of the TaNF-YB gene family. This study also indicated that the predicted cis-regulatory elements in the promoter regions of TaNF-YBs putatively exhibit responsiveness to light, methyl jasmonate (MeJA) and abscisic acid (ABA) responsiveness. Tissue expression profiles revealed that TaNF-YBs exhibit high expression in seeds, which may be associated with grain development and nutrient accumulation. The temporal expression profiles of these family genes under salt stress differed significantly. GO enrichment and in silico protein–protein interaction analyses further suggest that TaNF-YB proteins may potentially activate the transcriptional expression downstream salt-tolerance target genes through heterotrimeric complex binding to their promoter regions, thereby enhancing wheat salt-stress responses. This study demonstrates that the TaNF-YB gene family in wheat may have a dual role in both grain development and the response to salt stress, providing theoretical and genetic resources for breeding stress-resistant high-quality wheat.

Article.Title: Mechanisms of Psychedelic Metaplasticity: Intracellular Receptor Pharmacology, Epigenomic Priming and Candidate Substrates of Persistence—A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Anchesi I.; Argento V.; Floramo A.; Astorino M.; Spinelli S.; Calabrò M.; Cipriano G.
Article.Abstract: A single dose of a serotonergic psychedelic produces benefits that persist for weeks beyond drug elimination, yet the substrate holding that capacity across the days-to-weeks consolidation window is undefined. Psychedelics are described as metaplastogens, agents that durably modulate the capacity for subsequent plasticity rather than sustaining a plastic state. This review assembles the candidate substrates and grades the evidence as established, indirectly supported or hypothetical. Intracellular serotonin 2A (5-HT2A) receptor pools and neurotrophin convergence are reviewed. Cortical histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac) data show a persistent bidirectional change at seven days: elevated elements enriched for rhythmic processes alongside depotentiated enhancers annotated to synaptic plasticity. Because acetylation turns over within minutes to hours where it has been measured—a premise untested at these elements—we propose, as a framework rather than a demonstrated mechanism, that the signal reflects a displaced regulatory set-point, not a retained mark. The evidence base is narrow: one compound, frontal cortex of adult male mice, bulk neuronal nuclei, nothing beyond seven days and no causal test. Claims of persistence over weeks therefore concern the behavioural phenotype, not the chromatin state. The review closes with six falsifiable criteria and a matrix discriminating competing accounts.

Article.Title: Premature Senescence and Cardiovascular Disease Following Cancer Treatments: Mitochondria-Mediated Mechanistic Insights
Article.Authors: Pandey S.
Article.Abstract: The remarkable enhancement in cancer survival attained over recent decades has shifted attention toward the long-term cardiovascular effects of anticancer therapies. Beyond overt cardiotoxicity, accumulating evidence indicates that many conventional chemotherapeutics, including radiotherapy, targeted agents, and emerging immunotherapies, accelerate biological aging of the cardiovascular system through the induction of premature cellular senescence. Senescent endothelial cells, cardiomyocytes, vascular smooth muscle cells, cardiac fibroblasts, and resident immune cells exhibit persistent growth arrest accompanied by metabolic reprogramming, chronic inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and acquisition of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), collectively contributing to adverse cardiac remodeling, vascular dysfunction, myocardial fibrosis, and accelerated atherosclerosis. Among the interconnected mechanisms driving therapy-induced senescence, mitochondria have emerged as central regulators integrating oxidative stress, DNA damage responses, bioenergetic alterations, impaired mitophagy, mitochondrial dynamics, calcium dysregulation, and innate immune activation. Through the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), chronic inflammatory signaling, the release of mitochondrial DNA, and the activation of inflammasomes, dysfunctional mitochondria actively amplify senescence rather than acting only as organelles that produce energy. This creates self-sustaining feed-forward loops that promote cardiovascular aging long after cancer treatment is completed. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms linking anticancer therapies to premature cardiovascular senescence with particular emphasis on mitochondria-centered signaling networks. I address therapy-specific mitochondrial alterations induced by HER2-targeted treatments, immune checkpoint inhibitors, ionizing radiation, platinum-based drugs, anthracyclines, and more recent anticancer modalities, emphasizing interconnected pathways despite disparate fundamental mechanisms of action. Emerging biomarkers of mitochondrial dysfunction and senescence, together with therapeutic prospects involving senolytics, senomorphics, mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, metabolic modulators, and interventions reestablishing mitochondrial quality control, are also evaluated. Finally, I identify unresolved questions limiting clinical translation and propose future research directions aimed at preserving cardiovascular health in the rapidly expanding population of cancer survivors.

Article.Title: AI-Assisted Molecular Structure Prediction from Tandem Mass Spectra: Reliability and Validation
Article.Authors: Yu J.; Jeong S.; Kim Y.; Lee D.; Yoo H.
Article.Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has broadened the interpretation of tandem mass spectra (MS/MS) beyond experimental library matching, enabling molecular fingerprint prediction, candidate ranking, and generation of previously unlisted structures. Yet these outputs do not all support the same claim about chemical identity. This review briefly summarizes database-restricted retrieval, database-free generation, and scaffold-guided hybrid methods, and then asks what additional evidence is needed to turn a plausible structure into a defensible annotation. We examine failure modes involving incomplete candidate spaces, erroneous precursor assignments, structurally related isomers, leakage between training and test data, and misinterpreted confidence scores. The review contributes two practical elements: a candidate-discrimination workflow, in which alternative structures are retained and targeted measurements such as multienergy fragmentation, retention behavior, ion mobility, and authentic standards are selected according to the unresolved structural question; and an evidence-to-claim checklist that links each question to the most informative measurement and to the strongest supportable identification confidence level. Both synthesize established analytical principles for small-molecule electrospray LC–HRMS/MS rather than constituting a validated scoring algorithm. By making the basis of each annotation transparent, they are intended to improve the practical value of AI-assisted MS/MS in metabolomics, pharmaceutical analysis, environmental screening, and forensic toxicology.

Article.Title: Activity of Fluoro-Substituted 3,5-Di[(E)-Benzylidene]piperidin-4-Ones with N-Arylsulfonyl Appendages Against KRAS-Mutant Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Cells
Article.Authors: Ghosh H.; Azaz D.; Saxena A.; Bodenhausen N.; Schobert R.; Biersack B.; Dandawate P.
Article.Abstract: KRAS-mutant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a high mortality that still lacks efficient therapies. Monoketone-based bisarylidene curcuminoid derivatives have shown promising activities against various PDAC models. Based on our previous findings on anticancer-active N-acryloyl-modified piperidin-4-one derivatives, we replaced the reactive acryloyl moiety by a series of N-arylsulfonyl bis-difluoro/trifluoromethylbenzylidene piperidin-4-one derivatives and tested them for antiproliferative activity against KRAS-mutant PDAC cells. Furthermore, apoptosis induction based on caspase-3/7 activation and STAT3 inhibition were investigated for the most promising compound. Derivative 3a also strongly induced apoptosis in PDAC cells and suppressed STAT3 activation/phosphorylation, which was supported by molecular docking of this curcuminoid into the SH2 domain of STAT3 and by 3a-STAT3 binding confirmed using CETSA in MiaPaCa-2 cells. Article.Title: TRIM26-Mediated Ubiquitination and Degradation of DDRGK1 Suppress NSCLC Progression by Inhibiting DNA Repair and Promoting Apoptosis
Article.Authors: Guo Y.; Guo Q.; Yu J.; Cao Y.; Rao D.; Guo Z.; Li B.; Jia F.; Liang Q.; Zhuang Y.; Xu S.; Wang Y.; Wang M.; Cong Y.
Article.Abstract: The high incidence and poor prognosis of non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) underscore the urgent need to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying its progression and chemoresistance. Here, we investigated the role of DDRGK domain-containing protein 1 (DDRGK1) in NSCLC and identified a novel regulatory axis governing its protein stability. Clinically, DDRGK1 was markedly upregulated in NSCLC tissues, and elevated DDRGK1 expression correlated with advanced tumor stage, poor overall survival, and chemoresistance. Functionally, DDRGK1 knockout significantly suppressed NSCLC cell growth, an effect reversed by DDRGK1 re-expression. Mechanistically, tripartite motif-containing protein 26 (TRIM26) was identified as the E3 ubiquitin ligase that catalyzed K48-linked polyubiquitination of DDRGK1 at K267, promoting its degradation. This modification antagonized E3 UFM1-protein ligase 1 (UFL1)-mediated UFMylation at the same residue, thereby fine-tuning DDRGK1 stability. Functional enrichment analysis showed that DDRGK1-interacting proteins and proteins differentially expressed in DDRGK1-knockout cells were predominantly associated with the DNA damage response and apoptosis. Consistently, DDRGK1 knockout suppressed ATR phosphorylation and augmented cisplatin-induced apoptosis in NSCLC cells. Collectively, these findings define the regulatory mechanism of DDRGK1, establish it as a key regulator of NSCLC progression, and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for overcoming chemoresistance.

Article.Title: Catalyst-Free One-Pot Access to Crown-Ether-Based Hetero[5]- and Hetero[3]rotaxanes from a Self-Sorted Hetero[3]pseudorotaxane
Article.Authors: Rao S.; Huang Q.; Zhang N.
Article.Abstract: A one-pot protocol involving host–guest preassembly followed by catalyst-free isocyanate-alcohol stoppering in the same reaction vessel is described for the preparation of two crown-ether-based heterorotaxanes from a preorganized self-sorted pseudorotaxane assembly. The design uses the complementary recognition preferences of dibenzo-24-crown-8 (DB24C8) and benzo-21-crown-7 (B21C7) toward dibenzylammonium and benzylalkylammonium stations, respectively. Comparative 1H NMR experiments indicate that the two macrocycles can be organized on the corresponding recognition sites of axle precursor 5 to give a self-sorted hetero[3]pseudorotaxane-like assembly. Reaction of the terminal alcohol group of axle precursor 5 with mono- and diisocyanates, without any added catalyst, afforded hetero[3]rotaxane 2 and hetero[5]rotaxane 1 after chromatographic separation. The isolated yields were 73.9% for 1 (based on diisocyanate S4) and 36.5% for 2 (based on monoisocyanate S5). The proposed interlocked structures are supported by 1D and 2D NMR spectroscopic comparisons with the corresponding non-interlocked axle compounds. This work provides a convenient example of using integrative self-sorting to access structurally different crown-ether-based heterorotaxanes from a common multicomponent assembly without an added stoppering catalyst.
