Article.Title: Carpobrotus edulis Flower Extract Exerts Cytotoxic and Apoptotic Effects on A-549 Lung Cancer Cells: Phytochemical Profiling and In Silico EGFR Interaction Screening
Article.Authors: Huwaimel B.; Abouzied A.; Abd Rabo M.; Said M.; Alqarni S.; Alghubayshi A.; Alsaab H.; Alzhrani R.; Alshehri W.; Alrashidi N.; Alwahdani L.; Younes K.; Refaey M.
Article.Abstract: Medicinal plants serve as critical reservoirs of bioactive scaffolds for targeted cancer therapeutics. This study evaluated the antiproliferative potential of Carpobrotus edulis methanolic flower extract across a panel of human cancer cell lines, including pancreatic (Panc-1), breast (MCF-7), liver (HepG-2), and lung (A-549) malignancies. Screening assays revealed potent, dose-dependent cytotoxicity in an MTT-based viability assay, with A-549 lung cancer cells being the most sensitive of the four tested cancer cell lines (IC50 = 3.62 ± 0.34 μg/mL). Selectivity over non-malignant cells was not assessed. Flow cytometry showed an increase in the S-phase fraction and in Annexin V-positive cells, and ELISA showed higher Bax and p53 and lower Bcl-2 in extract-treated A-549 cells, consistent with apoptosis through the intrinsic pathway. The measured caspase-3 concentration was lower after treatment, and the assay does not distinguish pro-caspase-3 from cleaved caspase-3. Phytochemical profiling via GC-MS identified a diverse array of bioactive metabolites, predominantly triterpenoids, phytosterols, fatty acid derivatives, and cyclitols. To explore EGFR as a putative target, an in vitro EGFR kinase assay was combined with molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Among the profiled metabolites, the cyclitol derivative mome inositol displayed the most favorable docking score binding affinity toward the EGFR kinase domain (−7.35 kcal/mol), establishing robust hydrogen-bonding networks with key catalytic residues within the active site. Furthermore, a 100 ns MD simulation revealed the relative thermodynamic stability of the mome inositol–EGFR complex with more favorable RMSD, RMSF, hydrogen bond and radius of gyration profiles than the co-crystallized reference ligand. Collectively, these integrated in vitro, phytochemical, and in silico findings indicate that methanolic extract of C. edulis flowers exerts potent anticancer activity predominantly through mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis complemented by a computationally predicted interaction between its major cyclitol constituent and the EGFR kinase domain. These results establish the extract as a promising early-stage anticancer lead and provide a clear rationale for advancing to mechanistic studies, with in vivo validation reserved for subsequent investigations.

Article.Title: Luteolin and Naringenin from Herbal Medicines Suppress Pulmonary Arterial Smooth Muscle Cell Hyperproliferation in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension by Modulating IGF1R/PI3K/AKT Signaling
Article.Authors: Gou H.; Chen L.; He C.; Liang Q.; Liu K.; Zhu Y.; Yang X.; Peng W.
Article.Abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) remains a progressive disease with limited therapies. A compound–disease network was constructed; drug–disease intersection genes underwent functional enrichment analysis, whereas hub targets were prioritized by protein–protein interaction analysis. Article.Authors: Iaconisi G.; Murano M.; Gallo N.; Fiermonte G.; Truman A.; Vior N.; Maqbool A.; Sole R.; Li Y.; Dolce V.; Capobianco L.
Article.Abstract: Recombinant production platforms are promising approaches for producing hyaluronic acid (HA) for biomedical research. Article.Title: Aminosteroids from Buxaceae and Apocynaceae Plants as Antiprotozoal Agents: Structural Diversity and Structure–Activity Relationships
Article.Authors: Mukavi J.; Schäfer L.; Szabó L.; Nnadi C.; Althaus J.; Mäser P.; Schmidt T.

Article.Title: Recent Advances in Mitochondria-Targeted Nanoparticle Photodynamic Therapy for Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
Article.Authors: Przygórzewska A.; Bartusik-Aebisher D.
Article.Abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains a therapeutically challenging and biologically heterogeneous breast cancer subtype, prompting the development of strategies that exploit specific subcellular vulnerabilities. Mitochondria represent an attractive target for photodynamic therapy (PDT) because the short lifetime and limited diffusion range of photogenerated reactive oxygen species make their site of generation a critical determinant of cellular damage. This review critically examines recent nanoparticle-based approaches to mitochondria-targeted PDT in TNBC, with particular emphasis on nanoplatform design, experimental evidence for mitochondrial localisation, amplification of mitochondrial oxidative stress, regulated cell-death pathways, and preclinical efficacy. A structured search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science identified 3637 records, of which seven original studies ultimately fulfilled the predefined criteria for nanoparticle-mediated classical PDT in TNBC with mitochondrial targeting. The analysed platforms employed intrinsic mitochondrial affinity of photosensitisers, mitochondriotropic ligands, and multistage delivery strategies, while therapeutic amplification involved type I photochemistry, modulation of oxygen availability and consumption, glutathione depletion, metabolic interference, plasmonic enhancement, and combined PDT/PTT. Mitochondrial photodamage was associated with apoptosis, pyroptosis, immunogenic cell death, cGAS–STING signalling, and antitumour immune activation. Despite encouraging preclinical results, the evidence remains limited by the small number of studies, dominance of 4T1-based models, variable strength of mitochondrial-targeting validation, and limited translational assessment. Future development should focus on mechanistically validated targeting, clinically representative TNBC models, simplified nanoplatform design, and demonstration of a clear therapeutic advantage over less complex PDT systems.

Article.Title: Engineered Microorganisms as GLP-1-Oriented Living Therapeutics for Diabetes and Obesity: Mechanisms and Translational Challenges
Article.Authors: Lee A.; Khotina V.; Klychkova O.; Novikova V.; Kashirskikh D.; Gasanov V.
Article.Abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are established treatments for obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus, but gastrointestinal barriers constrain oral delivery of peptide therapeutics. These platforms produce GLP-1 or GLP-1-derived peptides, express modified GLP-1RAs or fusion proteins, or release effectors that stimulate endogenous GLP-1 secretion. Preclinical studies have reported improvements in glycemic measures and, in some models, reductions in body weight or weight gain. However, recombinant product expression and treatment-associated effects are more consistently demonstrated than exposure to intact biologically active products in vivo, receptor or pathway dependence, and the contribution of the engineered construct relative to the microbial chassis. Proteolysis, mucus interactions, restricted epithelial permeability, and receptor localization constrain access to intestinal and systemic targets. This review critically evaluates the preclinical evidence for GLP-1-oriented engineered microorganisms, with emphasis on intestinal target accessibility, local and systemic mechanisms, microbial chassis and genetic design, and the safety, manufacturing, and regulatory requirements for clinical translation.

Article.Title: Congenital Bilateral Cataracts Associated with CRYBA1: A Familial Case Report Highlighting Genetic Diagnosis, Surgical Management, and Lifelong Glaucoma Surveillance
Article.Authors: Ahmed M.; Akhter T.; Kabir F.; Kilby C.; Nguyen A.; Saeedi O.; Alexander J.
Article.Abstract: Congenital cataracts are an important cause of childhood visual impairment and require timely treatment to preserve visual development. Their management includes surgical removal of visually significant lens opacities, prompt optical rehabilitation, and lifelong surveillance for complications such as glaucoma and strabismus. Exome sequencing identified a heterozygous CRYBA1 variant, NM_005208.5:c.272_274del, p.(Gly91del), which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing in the proband and his affected mother. Gly91 is highly conserved, and structural modeling places the residue within a beta/gamma-crystallin Greek-key domain, where its deletion is predicted to disturb local protein folding and stability. The infant underwent sequential bilateral cataract extraction one week apart, and his aphakia was managed with contact lenses followed by spectacles. Infrequent intermittent esotropia was observed during follow-up, but no elevation of intraocular pressure or evidence of optic nerve damage was detected. At 3 years 7 months of age, best-corrected visual acuity with aphakic spectacles was 20/50 in each eye and 20/20 binocularly. The mother, who had undergone cataract surgery during infancy, subsequently developed advanced glaucoma of both eyes with marked retinal nerve fiber layer thinning. This case demonstrates the value of integrating molecular diagnosis with timely surgical treatment, optical rehabilitation, and long-term postoperative surveillance. Identification of the familial CRYBA1 variant confirmed the molecular diagnosis and supports genetic counseling, while the mother’s clinical course underscores the need for lifelong glaucoma monitoring following congenital cataract surgery.

Article.Title: IL-6-Mediated Macrophage–Fibroblast Communication in Pathological Lung Remodeling
Article.Authors: Chicherina N.; Gubernatorova E.; Namakanova O.; Sysonov F.; Gorshkova E.; Drutskaya M.
Article.Abstract: Fibrosis is a pathological form of tissue remodeling driven by excessive deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM). Unlike physiological tissue repair, fibrosis arises from persistent myofibroblast activation and unresolved inflammation. Chronic inflammation can both initiate fibrotic remodeling and be sustained by the resulting tissue alterations, supporting the view of fibrosis as an immune-mediated process. Fibrogenesis is fundamentally shaped by interactions between macrophages and fibroblasts. Polarized macrophages can modulate fibroblast activity and promote their differentiation into myofibroblasts. IL-6 is an important mediator of macrophage–fibroblast communication and has been implicated in fibrotic diseases affecting multiple organs. Notably, the effects of IL-6 are highly context-dependent. During acute injury, IL-6 can promote tissue repair by stimulating epithelial proliferation and angiogenesis, whereas persistent IL-6 signaling in chronic inflammation can become a major driver of fibrosis. IL-6 is also a prominent component of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), providing a mechanistic link between fibrosis, cellular senescence, and inflammaging. In this review, we provide an integrated overview of the role of IL-6 in macrophage–fibroblast interactions during pulmonary fibrogenesis, with particular emphasis on its context-dependent functions at the interface between tissue repair and pathological tissue remodeling. We also discuss current therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting IL-6 signaling.

Article.Title: In Vitro Models of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer of Sub-Saharan African Ancestry Suggest BLM-Centred DNA Damage Repair Dependency and Pevonedistat Sensitivity
Article.Authors: Pinto R.; Magalhães A.; Bento C.; Rosário F.; Lara Santos L.; Gonçalves E.; Pereira L.
Article.Abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is more prevalent in women of sub-Saharan African (SSA) than European (EUR) ancestry. BLM and interacting genes (RMI1, RMI2, TOP3A) showed greater essentiality in SSA than in EUR TNBC cell lines. SSA TNBC patients and cancer cell lines tended to have a lower median BLM expression than EUR counterparts, and its expression was positively correlated with structural mutations in tumour cells. Concordantly, BLM expression was higher in TNBC tumour cells than in normal cells, suggesting activation due to accumulation of mutations, particularly in cancers with a high burden of structural mutations. SSA TNBC cell lines were also more sensitive to the drug Pevonedistat. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that in the drug-exposed condition, DNA damage repair and helicase-related pathways were significantly downregulated, in several of which BLM is a significant core gene. Our findings support incorporating ancestry into oncobiology in vitro modelling and conducting further studies to assess Pevonedistat as a potential TNBC treatment.

Article.Title: Ultraconserved Elements Mark Genes Involved in Multilayered Regulation and Human Development
Article.Authors: Fedorova L.; Lebedev G.; Orlov Y.; Mulyar O.; Fedorov A.
Article.Abstract: Ultraconserved elements (UCEs) are genomic sequences exhibiting exceptional evolutionary conservation across vertebrate taxa, yet their biological functions remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the functional and expression characteristics of human protein-coding genes containing UCEs. Observed UCE distributions across Gene Ontology and manually curated, mutually exclusive functional groups of genes were compared with 1000 randomized UCE datasets that preserved natural UCE clustering. UCEs are preferentially located within genes involved in multilayered regulation, including transcription, chromatin organization, RNA processing, and ubiquitin-mediated protein regulation, whereas genes associated with membrane, extracellular, structural, transport, and metabolic functions are relatively UCE-poor. Within enriched groups, UCE accumulation is concentrated in multifunctional developmental regulators rather than in constitutive cellular machinery. Compared with length-matched UCE-free controls, UCE-rich genes showed higher and broader expression across 68 adult tissues and significantly higher prenatal expression in all seven organs examined. This expression excess was greatest in the developing brain and cerebellum and was most pronounced during early prenatal development. UCE-rich transcription factors are specifically enriched in developmental and chromatin-regulatory programs, including HOX-related embryonic patterning. These findings indicate that UCEs preferentially mark genes involved in several levels of cellular regulation and link ultraconservation to multilayered gene regulation and early human development.

Article.Title: Enzymatic Degradation of the Textile Dye Remazol Brilliant Blue R, a Model Recalcitrant Anthraquinone Dye
Article.Authors: Mahesh P.; Longhinos N.; Velmurugan N.; Gopalakrishnan Nair B.; Pal S.; Subhash S.
Article.Abstract: The massive discharge of Remazol Brilliant Blue R (RBBR), a recalcitrant anthraquinone dye, is of great environmental and public health concern due to its persistence, toxicity, and resistance to conventional wastewater treatment technologies. Enzymatic biodegradation has been developed as a sustainable alternative due to its high substrate specificity, mild operating conditions, and reduced secondary pollution. The review critically analyses the catalytic mechanisms, degradation pathways, and bioremediation potential of laccases, peroxidases, and azoreductases in degrading RBBR. Unlike azo dyes, RBBR lacks an azo (–N=N–) linkage; therefore, oxidative enzymes, particularly laccases and peroxidases, constitute the primary catalytic systems responsible for anthraquinone chromophore oxidation, whereas the contribution of azoreductases appears to be complementary and dependent on enzyme specificity and microbial metabolic interactions. Recent experimental evidence obtained using UV–Vis spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS), Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS), enzyme assays, and phytotoxicity analyses has considerably improved understanding of RBBR degradation mechanisms and intermediate metabolite formation. The review also compares the catalytic efficiencies, advantages, and limitations of the three enzyme systems. Recent advances in enzyme immobilization, protein engineering, microbial consortia, and hybrid biotechnological approaches to improve degradation efficiency and operational stability are discussed. Finally, future perspectives on omics-assisted enzyme discovery, advanced metabolomic characterization, pilot-scale validation, and integrated treatment technologies are outlined to facilitate the development of efficient, scalable, and environmentally sustainable strategies for the remediation of anthraquinone dye-contaminated wastewater.

Article.Title: Expression and Co-Expression Patterns of Selected MicroRNAs and ADAM Genes in Colorectal Cancer
Article.Authors: Kalita A.; Sikora-Skrabaka M.; Gołąbek K.; Biernacki K.; Strzelczyk J.; Waniczek D.; Nowakowska-Zajdel E.
Article.Abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide, and its molecular pathogenesis is not fully understood. This exploratory study investigated the expression of three selected microRNAs in colorectal cancer and their associations with previously characterized ADAM transcripts. RT-qPCR was used to assess miR-125b-5p, miR-338-3p, and miR-30c-5p in paired tumor and histologically tumor-free surgical margin tissues from 67 patients. No miRNA-ADAM transcript correlations remained significant after adjustment. Positive correlations among some miRNA pairs were observed within tumor and margin tissues. The reduced level of relative miR-125b-5p expression in colorectal cancers is an observational finding consistent with the tumor-suppressor functions described in the literature, but it does not constitute proof of those functions. Inter-miRNA correlations do not demonstrate shared regulatory mechanisms, and the absence of miRNA-ADAM transcript associations does not exclude post-transcriptional regulation.

Article.Title: Determinants of Plasma HDL-Cholesterol Concentrations in Prepubertal Children: Insights from Two Decades of Research in a Spanish Pediatric Cohort
Article.Authors: Pomares O.; Ortega-Senovilla H.; Soriano-Guillén L.; Garcés C.
Article.Abstract: High-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) is a well-established cardiovascular risk marker; however, its determinants in childhood remain incompletely understood. Dietary intake made only a modest contribution to HDL-C variability, yet fat intake modified the effect of the LIPC −514C>T variant on HDL-C. Article.Authors: Oyarzún V.; Liberona J.; Aguilar L.; Solis N.; Aguayo P.; González-Arriagada W.; Fernández-Cuya M.; Carrasco-Avino G.; Candia R.; Arrese M.; Díaz L.; Arab J.; Cabello-Verrugio C.; Balboa E.; Estrada L.; Llanquinao-Sandoval J.; Mezzano G.; Barrera F.; Cabrera D.

GH at 2 mg/kg/day was associated with fewer macroscopically detected hepatic surface nodules, while IGF-1 did not alter nodule burden. Article.Title: Nanoencapsulation Strategies for Stabilization and Delivery of Beetroot (Beta vulgaris) Bioactive Compounds: Current Advances and Future Perspectives
Article.Authors: Zannou O.; Tosif M.; Arslan R.; Tahergorabi R.; Goksen G.
Article.Abstract: Beetroot (Beta vulgaris) is a rich source of bioactive compounds, including betalains, phenolic compounds, and dietary nitrates, which are associated with strong antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cardioprotective properties. The practical application of these compounds in food and nutraceutical systems is significantly limited by their high sensitivity to environmental conditions such as pH, temperature, light, and oxygen, leading to rapid degradation, reduced stability, and low bioavailability. Nanoencapsulation has emerged as a promising strategy to overcome these challenges. Nanoliposomes, polymer-coated liposomes, chitosan-based nanogels, and nanoemulsions have emerged as promising nanocarrier platforms for improving the physicochemical stability and gastrointestinal fate of beetroot bioactive compounds. Nanoliposomes offer advantages in terms of nanoscale particle dimensions and relatively high loading capacities, whereas polymeric coatings can provide an additional protective barrier against premature release during gastrointestinal transit. Chitosan nanogels are particularly attractive because of their mucoadhesive properties and potential to promote prolonged and controlled release, while double nanoemulsions provide efficient dispersion of beetroot bioactive within nanosized droplets and can improve colloidal stability. Despite significant progress, challenges related to large-scale production, cost-effectiveness, regulatory approval, and long-term safety remain. Future research should focus on the development of sustainable, biopolymer-based nanocarriers, integration with green extraction technologies, and advanced delivery systems with improved targeting and responsiveness. Overall, nanoencapsulation represents a transformative approach to unlocking the full potential of beetroot bioactive compounds for industrial and health-related applications.

Article.Authors: Li J.; Li B.; Gao Y.; Zhao B.; Kasim J.; Shao N.; Gao Z.; Liu Z.; Song Z.; Yang Y.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Glycyrrhizic acid class compounds are used empirically for checkpoint inhibitor-induced liver injury (ChILI), but their effects on antitumour efficacy remain uncertain. The corresponding 18α aglycone shows no measurable inhibition of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 up to 20 µM in vitro, which does not establish clinical safety. Controlled trials should assess liver injury, corticosteroid exposure, antitumour outcomes and electrolyte safety together; routine prophylaxis is not supported.

Article.Authors: Li X.; Jiang Y.; Zhang K.; Yang F.; Yan L.; Hu Y.; Sun Y.; Zhang Y.; Du G.; Yu K.; Rao X.; Xiao W.

FMT from PPI-treated donors recapitulated healing impairment, whereas FMT from donors with prior oral microbiota depletion did not. Mechanistically, succinic acid activates SUCNR1-NF-κB signaling, upregulating pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) and MMP activities. In an exploratory clinical association analysis, high-dose PPI users exhibited elevated faecal S. anginosus and succinic acid, which correlated with serum TNF-α and IL-6. These findings caution against PPI overuse and suggest the succinic acid-SUCNR1-NF-κB axis as a potential therapeutic target.

Sigmoidal Avrami kinetics with exponents of 1.25–1.48, sharply saturating isotherms, an endothermic enthalpy of 71–90 kJ mol−1, and points of zero charge of about pH 7–9.5 supported cooperative binding through Ca2+–Cu2+ ion exchange, phosphate and hydroxyl complexation, and proposed surface nucleation of Cu–phosphate clusters; Cu(OH)2 precipitation was not expected at the pH used. After five HCl regeneration cycles, DKB retained 73.1–80.0% of its initial efficiency, and the first-order decay constant decreased from 0.078 to 0.056 cycle−1 with increasing pyrolysis temperature. DKB produced at 500 °C combined the highest capacity, fastest kinetics, and greatest regeneration stability, establishing duck bone as a low-cost, circular feedstock for Cu(II) remediation.

Article.Title: Mapping the Epigenetic Regulatory Landscape and Core Transcriptional Axes Across Cell Cycle Phases in Lung Cancer
Article.Authors: Salcedo-Tuiran I.; Payán-Gómez C.; López-Rivera J.; Patiño-Unibio L.; Arboleda-Mojica S.; Aristizábal-Guzmán C.; Álvarez-Moreno C.; Isaza-Ruget M.; Otálora-Otálora B.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Molecular Mechanisms, Primary Drivers Versus Early Amplifiers, and Emerging Mitochondria-Targeted Therapeutic Strategies
Article.Authors: Gopalakrishna P.; Vishnumukkala T.; Hein Z.; Karikalan B.; Chakravarthi S.; Hussan F.; Deoghare R.; Jagadeesan S.; Krishnasamy N.; Phyu S.; David P.; Kamaruzzaman M.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondria are critical for bioenergetics, calcium and redox homeostasis, and apoptosis in neurons. Neurons are especially susceptible to mitochondrial malfunction since they are terminally differentiated and have extraordinary energy requirements. Mechanisms such as defective oxidative phosphorylation, altered fission-fusion dynamics, defective mitophagy, impaired axonal transport and excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation are increasingly appreciated as important mechanisms in major neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) like Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Huntington’s disease (HD). The review discusses the structure and function of mitochondria with emphasis on oxidative phosphorylation, ROS and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) signalling, calcium-mediated excitotoxicity, lipid metabolism, and apoptotic and non-apoptotic cell-death mechanisms including necroptosis, ferroptosis, pyroptosis and parthanatos. In particular, disease-specific processes are highlighted, such as impaired mitophagy by amyloid β/tau in AD, PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1)/Parkin dysfunction and complex I inhibition in PD, Superoxide Dismutase 1 (SOD1)/C9orf72-associated mitochondrial defects in ALS, and bioenergetic dysfunction by mutant huntingtin in HD. Therapeutic approaches include mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, fusion and biogenesis enhancers, fission inhibitors, inflammasome modulators, Mitochondrial Permeability Transition Pore (mPTP) inhibitors and gene therapy. Also highlighted are recent advancements such as Ubiquitin-Specific Peptidase 30 (USP30) inhibition, intercellular mitochondrial transfer and regulatory approval of a mitochondria-targeted peptide, together with evidence supporting causality and hurdles underpinning clinical translation. Graded against human-genetic, patient-tissue and model-based evidence, mitochondrial dysfunction is best supported as a primary driver in PD and genetic ALS, and as an early amplifier of proteinopathic or mutant-huntingtin toxicity in sporadic AD and HD.

Article.Title: ABAT Overexpression Protects Against Doxorubicin-Induced Cardiotoxicity by Preserving Mitochondrial Homeostasis
Article.Authors: Yang P.; Yang R.; Guo J.; Yu A.; Liu X.; Zhang M.
Article.Abstract: Doxorubicin is a widely used chemotherapeutic agent whose clinical application is limited by dose-dependent cardiotoxicity, with mitochondrial dysfunction being a central pathological mechanism. Gamma-aminobutyric acid transaminase (ABAT) is a mitochondrial matrix enzyme implicated in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) maintenance through its role in the salvage synthesis of deoxyribonucleotides (dNTPs). However, whether ABAT exerts a protective role against doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity remains unknown. Here, we investigated the effect of ABAT overexpression on doxorubicin-induced cardiac injury and explored the underlying mechanisms. We found that ABAT expression and enzymatic activity were significantly reduced in the myocardium of doxorubicin-treated mice. Using cardiomyocyte-specific ABAT transgenic mice, we demonstrated that ABAT overexpression ameliorated doxorubicin-induced cardiac dysfunction, as evidenced by improved ejection fraction and fractional shortening, reduced serum levels of cardiac injury markers, and alleviated myocardial fibrosis and cardiomyocyte atrophy. Mechanistically, ABAT overexpression reversed doxorubicin-induced mtDNA depletion, restored mitochondrial respiratory chain complex activity, and improved oxygen consumption rate and ATP production, accompanied by reduced cellular and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species levels. Furthermore, doxorubicin triggered the initiation of mitophagy, as reflected by the accumulation of phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN)-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) and Parkin, but did not sustain autophagic degradation, as reflected by a markedly blunted bafilomycin A1-induced accumulation of microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 beta II (LC3B-II) so that autophagic structures containing mitochondria accumulated; ABAT overexpression attenuated these changes, partially restoring the responsiveness of LC3B-II to bafilomycin A1. Complementary in vitro experiments using ABAT-overexpressing H9c2 cells confirmed that ABAT attenuated doxorubicin-induced lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release, caspase-3 activation, and apoptosis. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that ABAT overexpression protects against doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity and is associated with preservation of mtDNA and mitochondrial function, reduced oxidative stress, and a reduced burden of damaged mitochondria. Given the reported antitumor properties of ABAT, these findings provide a basis for further investigating ABAT as a potential therapeutic target for mitigating doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity.

Article.Title: The Role of Long-Term DNA Replication Stress Induced by Hydroxyurea in Meristematic Root Cells of Allium cepa
Article.Authors: Żabka A.; Gocek-Szczurtek N.; Wróblewski M.; Cieślak K.; Polit J.
Article.Abstract: Replication stress (RS) is a process characterized by impaired DNA replication, resulting in the slowing down or arrest of replication forks (RFs) and in the activation of the DNA damage response. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of 24, 48, 72 and 96 h exposures of Allium cepa root meristematic cells to hydroxyurea (HU) at concentrations of 1, 2, 3 and 4 mM on cell nucleus morphology, DNA replication dynamics, mitotic activity and the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), including hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and superoxide anion (O2∙−). Furthermore, to assess epigenetic changes associated with DNA damage, the level of acetylation of lysine 56 of histone H3 (H3K56Ac) was analyzed. It was demonstrated that incubation of roots in 1 mM HU leads to the appearance of so-called interphase–mitotic (I-M) cells. Furthermore, as the HU concentration increased, inhibition of mitotic activity, a slowing down or partial inhibition of DNA replication, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) were observed. Furthermore, after 24 and 48 h of incubation with 1, 2 and 3 mM HU, a similar increase in the mean fluorescence intensity of H3K56Ac was observed, with the highest intensity recorded following treatment with 4 mM HU. Prolongation of the incubation time with the inhibitor to 72 and 96 h led to a further increase in fluorescence in the cell nuclei. The obtained results indicate that the increase in H3K56Ac levels may be associated with the accumulation of DNA damage under conditions of prolonged exposure to HU.

Article.Title: Schisandrin B Suppresses Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Through EGFR/AKT/mTOR Signaling and Mitochondrial Dysfunction
Article.Authors: Lee W.; Song G.; Bae H.
Article.Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly lethal cancer with poor prognosis due to chemoresistance and limited treatment options. Schisandrin B (Sch B), a bioactive compound from Schisandra chinensis, has demonstrated anticancer effects in various malignancies, but its role in PDAC remains unknown. This study explores the antitumor mechanisms of Sch B using network pharmacology, molecular docking, and in vitro and in vivo experiments, focusing on the EGFR/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway and mitochondrial dysfunction. Network pharmacology identified EGFR, CASP3, BCL2, and HSP90 as key candidate targets of Sch B, and molecular docking and MD simulation were used to explore putative interactions with these proteins. In PDAC cells, treatment Sch B for 48 h reduced cell viability. In addition, Sch B suppressed EGFR/AKT/mTOR signaling and induced mitochondrial dysfunction, characterized by loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, increased mitochondrial and cytosolic calcium levels, and elevated ROS production, accompanied by activation of apoptotic signaling. Co-treatment with gemcitabine demonstrated enhanced effects, elevating apoptosis and oxidative stress. Moreover, Sch B significantly reduced tumor growth in a PANC-1 xenograft model, accompanied by decreased protein expression of EGFR, AKT, mTOR, and HSP90 in tumor tissues. These findings suggest that Sch B exerts antitumor activity associated with modulation of EGFR/AKT/mTOR signaling and mitochondrial dysfunction, supporting further investigation of Sch B as a potential therapeutic candidate for PDAC, particularly in combination with standard chemotherapy.

Article.Title: Plasma SPARC Concentrations in Patients with Subsequent Shunt-Dependent Hydrocephalus After Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
Article.Authors: Hakozaki K.; Nakajima H.; Kitano Y.; Nishikawa H.; Kawakita F.; Yasuda R.; Suzuki H.; N/A N/A.
Article.Abstract: Shunt-dependent hydrocephalus (SDHC) is a delayed complication of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), and meningeal fibrotic remodeling may contribute to its development. We examined whether serial plasma SPARC concentrations were associated with subsequent SDHC development. Plasma SPARC was measured at days 1–3, 4–6, 7–9, and 10–12 and analyzed using log-scale linear mixed-effects models. SDHC developed in 54 patients (29.0%). Model-estimated SPARC concentrations increased across periods in both SDHC and no-SDHC groups without a significant SDHC-by-period interaction, whereas all the SDHC/no-SDHC geometric mean ratios were below 1. In a post hoc exploratory multivariable analysis, each 10 ng/mL increase in SPARC at days 4–6 was associated with lower odds of subsequent SDHC development (adjusted odds ratio, 0.91; 95% confidence interval, 0.84–0.98; p = 0.011). Lower plasma SPARC concentrations, particularly at days 4–6, were associated with subsequent SDHC development.

Article.Title: Immunotherapy: Examining Strategies to Address Cancer Complexity
Article.Authors: Povo-Retana A.; Ruiz-Navarro J.; Fernández-Frías L.; Alvarez-Lucena C.; Landauro-Vera R.; Izquierdo M.; Boscá L.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the interplay between immune and stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment is essential for developing effective cancer therapies and preventing relapses. In this review, starting with the basics of tumor immunology and a historical review from cancer chemotherapy to current immunotherapy, in the context of precision medicine, we focus on immunotherapies based on genetically modified macrophages, and chimeric T-cell antigen receptor (CAR), highlighting the similarities and differences between TCR-endogenous signaling and CART-dependent signaling at the immune synapse, presenting all the generations that have been developed briefly, followed by NK cell-dependent CAR therapeutic approaches where a comparison is established, analyzing their respective advantages and drawbacks. Targeting the tumor-immune microenvironment has become central to cancer treatment, with combinatorial therapies applied and assessed as a feasible strategy for this complex group of diverse pathologies. In this context, modulating the immune synapse, rewiring immune cell metabolism, and developing genetically engineered immune cells have emerged as promising approaches that open novel avenues for treating and managing cancer patients. This review offers a holistic, historical view of state-of-the-art molecular approaches, along with insights into future perspectives and current limitations of the technologies supporting immunotherapy in molecular oncology.

Article.Title: Blood Cell Intracellular pH Dynamics and Metabolic Biomarkers Under Simulated Postmortem Interval Conditions: An Exploratory Pilot In Vitro Study
Article.Authors: Ndunduma P.; Cordeiro C.; Faria S.; Criado M.; Coimbra S.; Monteiro M.
Article.Abstract: Intracellular pH (pHi) may provide complementary information on postmortem cellular metabolism and homeostasis, but its temporal behavior remains poorly understood. This pilot in vitro study evaluated temporal changes in platelet pHi and pHi in a mixed non-platelet blood-cell population (predominantly erythrocytes and leukocytes), together with plasma glucose, lactate, and ammonia during a simulated postmortem interval (PMI). Venous blood from eight healthy volunteers was maintained at 24 ± 3 °C and analyzed at 0, 3, 6, and 24 h. Intracellular pH was assessed by BCECF-AM flow cytometry, and metabolites were quantified enzymatically. Platelet and non-platelet-cell pHi remained stable during the first 3 h, decreased significantly at 6 h, and increased toward baseline values at 24 h. Glucose concentrations decreased over time, lactate increased progressively, and ammonia increased significantly only at 24 h. Lactate was associated with pHi in both blood-cell populations. Intracellular pH exhibited a biphasic temporal pattern and distinct relationships with metabolic biomarkers during the simulated PMI. An exploratory mixed-effects model incorporating non-platelet-cell pHi, lactate, and glucose explained a substantial proportion of temporal variability (marginal R2 = 0.907) and yielded a leave-one-donor-out cross-validation RMSE of 0.4998 on the log-transformed time scale. These findings support further investigation of multi-marker approaches for PMI estimation.

Article.Title: Hemostasis and Beyond: The Diverse Functions of Protein S in Controlling Coagulation, Inflammation, and Cancer
Article.Authors: Mehrpour-Karmakan N.; Jauquet M.; Wood J.
Article.Abstract: Protein S (ProS) is a vitamin K-dependent glycoprotein that was first described as an anticoagulant cofactor for activated protein C (APC). Since its initial discovery, studies of ProS have revealed an array of functions, spanning coagulation and inflammation, including in the context of cancer. ProS is now known to inhibit all three coagulation complexes—through interactions with APC, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and activated factor IX—and to have its anticoagulant activity modulated by multiple other plasma proteins. Beyond hemostasis, ProS also participates in complement regulation, through its interaction with complement component C4b-binding protein, and regulates inflammatory cell phenotype and function, through Tyro3 and Mer-Tyrosine Kinase, receptors which mediate efferocytosis, inflammatory resolution, and tissue repair. Emerging evidence further implicates ProS in cancer biology, where its effects are context-dependent and may either support or suppress tumor progression. In this review, we highlight these many functions of ProS and discuss their mechanistic commonalities. Collectively, these functions position ProS as a central regulatory node, with critical roles in physiology and disease.

HLA-DQA1 divergence at 12 months was hypothesis-generating (within-family n = 0.004). Exome typing resolved HLA allele groups (99.1%) but not KIR (19.0% ambiguous). How an HLA exposure is defined determines whether a signal is visible; only large effects were detectable; replication is required.

Article.Title: Myelin Changes in H-ABC Tubulinopathy Revealed by Nile Red Hyperspectral Imaging
Article.Authors: Jaramillo-Restrepo C.; Piazza V.; Eguibar J.; Cortes C.; Hernandez V.
Article.Abstract: Hypomyelination with atrophy of the basal ganglia and cerebellum (H-ABC) is a recently described tubulinopathy caused by mutations in the tubulin beta-4a isotype. It is a severe disorder characterized by progressive myelin loss and neurological impairment. The taiep rat, a spontaneous TUBB4A mutant, is a model for investigating the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying this disease. Homozygous taiep rats exhibit hallmark features of H-ABC, including early-onset hypomyelination, progressive demyelination, and microtubule accumulation in oligodendrocytes, whereas heterozygous animals appear to maintain normal myelin structure using conventional techniques. We combined hyperspectral imaging (HSI) and Nile Red (NR) staining to differentiate homozygous taiep and wild-type animals and determine whether subtle myelin alterations could be detected in heterozygous rats. Remarkably, heterozygous animals also showed changes in the Nile Red emission profile, with fluorescence shifted toward longer wavelengths compared with controls, uncovering previously unrecognized modifications in the myelin microenvironment. Using spectral phasor analysis, these alterations were localized and quantified without model assumptions, demonstrating the sensitivity of this approach for detecting subtle pathological changes. Together, our findings contribute to the characterization of myelin-associated spectral changes in this tubulinopathy and support the use of spectral microscopy to distinguish alterations in myelin properties, with potential applications in the study of other white matter disorders.

Article.Title: pH-Dependent Developmental and Behavioral Toxicity of Diethanolamine in Zebrafish (Danio rerio)
Article.Authors: Jablonski C.; Pereira F.; Oliveira J.; Bandeira L.; Pereira T.; Oliveira G.; Kist L.; Silva V.; Monteiro W.; Lautert-Dutra W.; Seferin M.; Ligabue R.; Bogo M.
Article.Abstract: Amine-based compounds are used in petroleum and gas processing for CO2 capture and gas sweetening. Diethanolamine (DEA), a water-soluble alkaline compound, can alter exposure-medium physicochemical properties. Its industrial use and potential release into aquatic environments highlight the need to characterize its aquatic toxicity. However, data on DEA developmental toxicity remain limited, particularly regarding the distinction between intrinsic chemical toxicity and pH-mediated effects. This study investigated the developmental and behavioral toxicity of DEA in zebrafish (Danio rerio) under pH-adjusted and unadjusted exposure conditions to examine the contribution of exposure-medium pH to the observed effects. Acute toxicity assays determined the median lethal concentration (LC50), followed by sublethal assessments of spontaneous tail coiling, heart rate, morphology, and larval locomotor activity. Under pH-adjusted conditions, heart rate increased, indicating a sublethal effect on cardiac function. In contrast, unadjusted exposures caused a concentration-dependent increase in medium pH associated with adverse effects on survival, development, and behavior, despite no morphological abnormalities. For statistical analyses, individual measurements were averaged within each vessel, and vessel-level means were used to assess concentration–response relationships and estimate concentration–response trend rates. Responses differed between DEA-Adj and DEA-Unadj under their respective testing conditions, highlighting the importance of considering exposure-medium pH when assessing alkaline chemical toxicity. pH alterations caused by chemical releases may also contribute to adverse effects in aquatic organisms and should be considered when evaluating the environmental implications of DEA contamination.

Collectively, these findings demonstrate sex-dependent neurological and molecular alterations persisting 12 weeks after Iso/OP, accompanied by changes in circulating EVs. The exploratory EV transfer findings warrant further investigation into the potential contribution of circulating EVs to brain inflammatory responses.

Article.Title: E3 Ligase TRIM21 Deficiency-Driven GAS2L3 Accumulation Facilitates Oncogenic Progression in Breast Cancer
Article.Authors: Li P.; Zhao C.; Ren Y.; Wei Y.; Zhang N.; Xin L.; Sun Y.; Yang J.; He J.; Liu X.; Gao X.
Article.Abstract: GAS2L3, a member of the growth arrest-specific 2 protein family, is abnormally upregulated in multiple human cancers, implying its potential oncogenic role. However, the mechanisms underlying its stabilization and accumulation during breast cancer progression remain unclear. This study aimed to clarify the regulatory mechanism and oncogenic role of GAS2L3 in breast cancer. We analyzed the expression and prognostic value of GAS2L3 and its related signaling pathways using public breast cancer databases, and conducted functional assays to assess the malignant phenotypes of breast cancer cells. Ubiquitination and cycloheximide chase assays confirmed that TRIM21 facilitates the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of GAS2L3, while immunohistochemical staining of clinical specimens and mouse tissues verified their negative correlation. Rescue experiments further validated this regulatory axis. High GAS2L3 expression predicted poor prognosis and promoted breast cancer cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Loss of TRIM21-mediated GAS2L3 degradation results in aberrant GAS2L3 accumulation, and the TRIM21–GAS2L3 axis drives breast cancer malignant progression, providing potential prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets for breast cancer.

Article.Title: Magnetic Nanoparticles in Precision Cancer Therapy: From Synthesis and Biological Interactions to Clinical Translation
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Xu S.; Hosseinikhah S.; Zhang W.; Zhang X.; Sacchetti A.
Article.Abstract: Cancer treatment increasingly relies on integrated therapeutic approaches, particularly for solid tumors that remain difficult to eradicate using a single modality. Magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) have emerged as versatile therapeutic platforms owing to their magnetic responsiveness and tunable physicochemical properties. Advances in synthesis methods enable precise control over MNP size, morphology, composition, and surface chemistry, shaping their biological behavior across multiple scales. At the cellular level, these properties regulate nanoparticle uptake, intracellular trafficking, and subcellular interactions. At the tissue and systemic levels, administration route, vascular transport, magnetic targeting, and ligand-mediated recognition influence biodistribution, tumor accumulation, and cellular selectivity. Material composition and surface functionalization further determine responsiveness to external or endogenous stimuli and mediate therapeutic effects, including heat generation, controlled drug release, catalytic activity, and reactive oxygen species production. These features allow MNP-based systems to support localized hyperthermia, drug delivery, catalytic therapies, and embolization-based interventions, making them attractive for treating deep-seated and inoperable tumors. However, heterogeneous tumor delivery, variable activation efficiency, off-target toxicity, and long-term safety concerns remain major barriers to clinical translation. Overall, this review summarizes recent advances and current limitations in MNP-based cancer therapy, providing a multiscale perspective that links material design, biological interactions, systemic delivery, therapeutic activation, and translational challenges.

Article.Title: Adjunctive Resveratrol or Omeprazole in Patients with Non-Transfusion-Dependent Thalassemia with Iron Overload: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial
Article.Authors: Chopetgool T.; Chai-adisaksopha C.; Rattarittamrong E.; Norasetthada L.; Rattanathammethee T.; Hantrakool S.; Piriyakhuntorn P.; Punnachat T.; Hantrakun N.; Srichairatanakool S.; Koonyosying P.; Srichairatanakool S.; Tantiworawit A.
Article.Abstract: Increased gastrointestinal iron absorption contributes substantially to iron overload in non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia (NTDT) patients. Resveratrol (RVT) and omeprazole (OMP) may reduce intestinal iron absorption and potentially complement iron chelation therapy. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of adjunctive RVT or OMP in adults with NTDT receiving stable iron chelation therapy. The primary outcome was the change in serum ferritin; secondary outcomes influenced serum iron (SI), transferrin saturation (TS), erythroferrone (ERFE), hepcidin, fetal hemoglobin (HbF), and safety. Participants with serum ferritin ≥ 300 ng/mL were randomized (1:1:1) to receive RVT 250 mg, OMP 20 mg, or the placebo (PLA) twice daily for 6 months. Thirty participants were randomized (RVT, n = 10; OMP, n = 11; PLA, n = 9), with a baseline median serum ferritin value of 629 ng/mL, interquartile range (IQR) 484–975. Serum ferritin decreased numerically over 6 months in the RVT and OMP groups relative to PLA; however, no significant treatment × time interactions or adjusted between-group differences in changes from the baseline were observed. Although significant within-group changes were observed for selected iron-regulatory biomarkers, including hepcidin, ERFE, and TS, these were not accompanied by significant treatment × time interactions and did not demonstrate differential treatment effects. Both interventions were generally well tolerated, and no serious adverse events were reported. In this underpowered trial, neither adjunctive RVT nor OMP demonstrated statistically significant treatment-specific effects on serum ferritin or other iron-related outcomes when compared with the placebo. The observed numerical trends warrant evaluation in larger, adequately powered trials. Trial Registration: ISRCTN73258526.

Article.Title: Paper-Mulberry-Silage-Enhanced Lipid Metabolism and Milk Polyunsaturated Fatty Acid Concentration in Dairy Cows: A Multi-Omics Study
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Tang W.; Wang Y.; Yang H.; Wang W.; Cao Z.; Wang W.; Li S.; Bai Y.; Hao Y.
Article.Abstract: Developing alternative forages that modify milk fatty acid composition is important for improving milk nutritional quality and diversifying feed resources in dairy production. Previous studies have demonstrated the potential of paper mulberry (PM, Broussonetia papyrifera) silage to partially replace conventional roughages and influence antioxidant status and milk fatty acid composition. However, its effects on milk polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and the associated ruminal microbial and metabolic mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of feeding PM silage on the concentration of polyunsaturated fatty acids in milk, the structure of the rumen microbial community, and lipid metabolic functions, as well as to analyze the associations between rumen microbial and metabolic profiles and the fatty acid composition of milk. Thirty lactating Holstein cows were randomly assigned to control and PM groups, with 15 cows per group. The PM group received diets containing 9% PM silage for the first 28 days and 18% for the subsequent 28 days on a dry matter basis. Rumen fluid, plasma, and milk were collected on day 56 for integrated analyses combining fatty acid profiling, ruminal fermentation measurements, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, metagenomics, and metabolomics. Milk PUFA concentration was significantly higher in the PM group than in controls, with no significant differences in dry matter intake or milk yield. PM feeding also altered ruminal microbial community composition and lipid-metabolism-related functional gene abundances, accompanied by increased glycerophosphocholine and glycerophosphoethanolamine levels. Integrated analyses linked these changes to fatty acid profiles in rumen fluid, plasma, and milk, supporting ruminal lipid remodeling as a candidate mechanism underlying the increase in milk PUFA concentrations. These findings provide evidence for the microbial and metabolic basis of the effects of PM silage on milk fatty acid composition and inform its development as a functional forage and the optimization of dairy cow feeding strategies.

Article.Authors: Vasilin V.; Zinovyeva A.; Gordeev M.; Petrenko E.; Tsimokha A.; Aksenov N.; Tomilin A.; Bakhmet E.
Article.Abstract: Protein degradation systems, such as auxin-inducible degron (AID) and dTAG-mediated degradation, have become essential tools in molecular biology. Their primary advantage lies in the rapid and efficient elimination of proteins, which facilitates the study of short-term molecular perturbations. Here, we employed these methods to unveil the role of Nanog during definitive endoderm specification. We demonstrate that dTAG-inducible degradation is significantly more efficient than the AID system for Nanog elimination. Using this approach, we show that Nanog is a context-dependent regulator; while it maintains pluripotency in undifferentiated ESCs, it promotes definitive endoderm maturation during spontaneous differentiation. Article.Title: Integrating Chronophysiological and Bioinformatic Perspectives on Nesfatin-1, Circadian Feeding Rhythms, and Cortisol Regulation
Article.Authors: Juliana N.; Abu I.; Azmani S.; Das S.; Abdul Hamid N.; Azzeri A.; Jaafar M.; Maluin S.; Elias M.
Article.Abstract: Nesfatin-1, a peptide derived from nucleobindin-2, regulates feeding, stress, and sleep–wake processes. To date, the available information suggests that nesfatin-1 is involved in stress regulation and colocalises with substances that influence cortisol, but the circadian interplay between nesfatin-1 and cortisol remains poorly defined. This review integrates biological timing, tissue-specific actions of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, and circadian misalignment, and is supported by in silico protein-association analysis. A structured database search retained relevant studies published from January 2006 to March 2026; heterogeneity necessitated narrative synthesis. Rodent experiments support effects of central NUCB2/nesfatin-1 on feeding and HPA-axis activation. Murine corticotroph experiments report increased POMC abundance, whereas an H295R human adrenocortical carcinoma-cell study reports reduced cortisol content and stimulated release. These findings concern different experimental systems and do not demonstrate coordinated central–adrenal regulation in vivo. The network analysis identified NPY and POMC as prominent nodes within the predefined candidate network, with enrichment of feeding- and HPA-axis-related pathways. Given the biologically targeted selection of input genes, these findings are interpreted as hypothesis-generating associations rather than independent confirmation of a regulatory mechanism. Within the literature examined in this review, direct evidence characterising the 24 h temporal profile of nesfatin-1 in humans, its phase relationship with cortisol, and potential alterations during circadian misalignment was not identified. This apparent evidence gap warrants further investigation through controlled, time-resolved human studies.

Article.Title: SRC-2 Regulates Brain Endothelial and Neuronal Metabolism in a Mouse Model of Neurodegeneration
Article.Authors: Srivastava R.; Singh P.; Jonsson E.; Saleem I.; Desales C.; Lonard D.
Article.Abstract: Cerebrovascular dysfunction and impaired brain energy metabolism are increasingly recognized as important contributors to neurodegenerative diseases, but their molecular regulators remain poorly understood. Here, we examined the roles of steroid receptor coactivator-2 (SRC-2/NCOA2) in the cerebrovascular and metabolic changes associated with neurodegeneration using ps19 mice as a model. In our study, we found a significant decrease in cortical SRC-2 expression in ps19 mice compared with wild-type (WT) controls, with no changes in SRC-1 and SRC-3 levels between the two groups. ps19 mice showed reduced cortical endothelial and blood–brain barrier-associated markers (CD31, occludin, claudin-5, total eNOS (endothelial nitric oxide synthase), and eNOS Ser1177) and increased eNOS Thr495 phosphorylation. HIF-1α, GLUT2, and GLUT4 were also reduced in ps19 mice, whereas GLUT1 and GLUT3 were unchanged between the groups. To examine the role of SRC-2, we used siRNA to reduce its expression in brain endothelial cells and primary neurons. In brain endothelial cells, SRC-2 knockdown reduced the expression of endothelial and BBB-associated markers, including CD31 and occludin, as well as GLUT3, while increasing inhibitory eNOS Thr495 phosphorylation and GLUT4 expression. In brain endothelial cells, SRC-2 knockdown significantly reduced the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) and NAD+/NADH ratio. Knockdown of SRC-2 in primary neurons (from WT and ps19 mice) significantly reduced the oxygen consumption rate (OCR), while the NAD+/NADH ratio remained unchanged. These findings identify SRC-2 as a regulator of endothelial and neuronal metabolism and support further investigation of SRC-2-dependent pathways as potential therapeutic targets in neurodegenerative diseases.

Article.Title: Angiotensin II-Induced Cardiac Fibrosis: Genomic and Molecular Drivers, Emerging Biomarkers and Therapeutic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Martínez-Rodríguez N.; Campos-González J.; López-Camarillo C.; Medina-Contreras O.
Article.Abstract: Chronically elevated angiotensin II (Ang II) drives adverse cardiac remodelling, converting a reparative response into progressive interstitial and perivascular fibrosis that stiffens the ventricle and precedes overt heart failure. Acting through the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, Ang II generates reactive oxygen species, recruits and polarises immune cells and activates resident fibroblasts, converging on transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β)-dependent and mechanotransductive programmes that drive myofibroblast differentiation and excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. The magnitude of this response varies between patients: germline variation in renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) genes, loci for heart failure and imaging-defined fibrosis, epigenomic reprogramming of the fibroblast, non-coding RNA networks and metabolic rewiring of collagen-producing cells all modulate the transition from compensated hypertrophy to fibrotic failure. This review integrates these genomic, epigenomic, transcriptomic and metabolomic layers with the signalling architecture of Ang II-induced fibrosis, and reviews the circulating biomarkers—collagen turnover peptides, matricellular and immune mediators, non-coding RNAs and cell-free DNA methylation signatures—that could detect fibrotic activity before remodelling becomes irreversible. We then consider why fibrosis regression under RAAS blockade appears heterogeneous, which emerging targets are mechanistically credible, and how genotype–biomarker–imaging phenotyping could enrich antifibrotic trials. Priorities for ancestrally diverse cohorts and standardised biomarker methodology are identified.

Article.Title: Maternal FNDC5 and ADIPOQ Genetic Variants as Potential Modulators of Susceptibility to Spontaneous Preterm Birth
Article.Authors: Kadivnik M.; Zlatunić P.; Drinić M.; Hercog R.; Kralik K.; Wagner J.
Article.Abstract: Preterm birth (PTB) is a complex and heterogeneous pregnancy outcome in which maternal metabolic and endocrine pathways may contribute to susceptibility to preterm delivery. This study investigated whether two maternal genetic variants involved in metabolic signaling, ADIPOQ rs266729 and FNDC5 rs1746661, are associated with preterm birth (PTB) in a Croatian population. This case–control study included 401 women: 200 with PTB and 201 with term delivery. Maternal genomic DNA was isolated from peripheral blood, and both variants were genotyped using TaqMan-based real-time PCR. Genotype and allele distributions, inheritance models, allelic combinations, logistic regression, and gene–gene interaction were analyzed. Neither variant was significantly associated with overall PTB, and no significant gene–gene interaction was observed (p = 0.18). The G–T allelic combination was more frequent in early PTB (13.6% vs. 4.6%; p = 0.03) but not after Benjamini–Hochberg correction (adjusted p = 0.09). No significant association between the investigated variants and PTB was demonstrated. The borderline findings in early PTB are hypothesis-generating and require replication in larger cohorts.

Article.Title: Detection of Antagonistic Interactions Between Cannabidiol and Temozolomide in Various Neuroblastoma and Glioblastoma Cell Lines in the MTT Assay by Means of Synergy Finder 3.0 Software and Log-Probit Isobolographic Analysis
Article.Authors: Załuska-Ogryzek K.; Wróblewska-Łuczka P.; Góralczyk A.; Łuszczki J.
Article.Abstract: Despite progress in experimental neuro-oncology and advances in the treatment of brain cancers, glioblastoma multiforme is still the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults. Cannabinoid-based add-on therapy is likely to be a treatment option for glioblastoma patients who have failed surgical excision and treatment with temozolomide (a classic chemotherapeutic drug). Cannabidiol is one of the naturally occurring compounds isolated from Cannabis, which displays the anti-cancer and anti-viability effects in several glioblastoma cell lines. In the MTT assay, the anti-viability effects of combined treatment with cannabidiol and temozolomide were assessed in two neuroblastoma (CHP-134, KELLY) and four glioblastoma (SF295, U-87MG, T98G, and C6) cell lines. The interactions between cannabidiol and temozolomide from the MTT assay were characterized by means of two independent methods: a classic log-probit isobolographic analysis and a Synergy Finder 3.0 web-application allowing automatic evaluation of interactions in five pharmacodynamic models, including the zero interaction potency (ZIP), Bliss, Loewe, highest single agent (HAS) and Bliss–Loewe consensus models. The impact of cannabidiol on several apoptotic-related proteins (p21, p18, cyclin D1, Bax, Bcl-2) and the cannabinoid CB1 receptor expressed on the glioblastoma SF295 and U-87MG cells was examined with the Western blot technique. Both cell migration and cell–cell interaction after treatment with cannabidiol, temozolomide and their combination were assessed in a wound healing assay. The log-probit isobolographic analysis of interactions revealed that cannabidiol combined with temozolomide exerted antagonistic interactions only in two neuroblastoma cell lines, CHP-134 and KELLY. In contrast, the combination of cannabidiol with temozolomide in all the glioblastoma cells, SF295, U-87MG, T98 and C6, produced (in the classic isobolography) additive interactions with a tendency toward antagonism in the MTT assay. With Synergy Finder 3.0 in the Bliss–Loewe model, the interactions between cannabidiol and temozolomide were antagonistic in all the tested cell lines (except for CHP-134) with synergy score values ranging from −19.64 (for T98G) to −15.07 (for U-87MG). Only the interaction between cannabidiol and temozolomide in the CHP-134 cell line was additive in the Bliss–Loewe model with a synergy score value of 0.95. This comparative study indicates that the combination of cannabidiol with temozolomide should not be recommended and used clinically because of antagonistic interactions reported in the MTT assay. The Bliss–Loewe consensus model can be recommended as a model of choice when screening and evaluating the types of interactions in in vitro studies using the Synergy Finder 3.0 free online available web-application.

Article.Title: The Fibrinolytic System of the Chacma Baboon (Papio ursinus): Implications for Non-Human Primate Haemostatic Disease Models
Article.Authors: Joubert J.; Meiring M.; Janse Van Rensburg W.
Article.Abstract: Baboon models are useful for investigating haemostatic disorders and potential novel treatments. The fibrinolytic system is an integral component of these models and an important potential therapeutic target. We investigated the fibrinolytic system of the Chacma baboon (Papio ursinus), including the effects of sex and ABO blood group. Tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA), plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1), plasminogen, plasmin-α2-antiplasmin (PAP) complexes, thrombin activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor (TAFI), α2-antiplasmin, fibrinogen levels, and clot lysis times of 40 adult Chacma baboons were assessed. Plasminogen activation using escalating concentrations of streptokinase vs. alteplase was determined and compared with normal human plasma. The results were compared between O and non-O ABO blood groups, and between males and females. PAP complexes and fibrinogen were mostly within the human reference interval, while tPA, PAI-1 and α2-antiplasmin tended towards the lower limit. Plasminogen and TAFI were virtually undetectable with the human ELISA kits used. Alteplase was a potent plasminogen activator compared with streptokinase (p < 0.0001), resulting in brisker clot lysis in baboon than in human plasma (10.8 vs. 13.4 min). Blood group O baboons had higher fibrinogen levels (p = 0.0355), while males had lower fibrinogen (p = 0.0134) but higher PAP complex concentrations (p = 0.0188). Except for plasminogen and TAFI, the Chacma baboon fibrinolytic system appears broadly similar to its human counterpart. Streptokinase does not meaningfully activate Chacma baboon fibrinolysis, but alteplase elicits greater plasminogen activation than in humans. These findings, as well as sex- and ABO-blood-group-related differences in fibrinogen, should be considered when designing future pre-clinical drug testing experiments in this species.

Article.Title: Personalized Geriatric Pharmacotherapy: Pharmacogenomics, Polypharmacy, and Age-Related Pharmacokinetic and Pharmacodynamic Changes
Article.Authors: Buianova A.; Mironenko I.; Arbatskiy M.; Churov A.
Article.Abstract: Aging induces profound physiological changes that alter drug disposition and response, narrowing therapeutic windows and increasing susceptibility to adverse drug reactions (ADRs). This review synthesizes current evidence on age-related pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic changes, with a focus on pharmacogenomic determinants of drug response in older adults. Progressive decline in renal function and hepatic metabolic capacity and alterations in body composition collectively necessitate age-appropriate dose adjustments. Polypharmacy, prevalent in community-dwelling and hospitalized older adults, compounds these challenges through drug–drug and drug–drug–gene interactions. Pharmacogenomic testing—particularly for CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, and SLCO1B1—offers a promising strategy with which to personalize therapy, while deprescribing frameworks provide practical approaches to mitigating medication-related risks. This review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the mechanistic basis of altered drug response in older adults and proposes actionable strategies for optimizing pharmacotherapy in this vulnerable population. Throughout, pharmacogenomic claims are graded across four levels: biological plausibility, measured pharmacokinetic effect, pharmacogenetic actionability, and demonstrated clinical utility. Furthermore, selected gene–drug examples are explicitly identified as either geriatric-specific evidence or extrapolations from general adult pharmacogenomics, clarifying which findings are truly modified by the aging process.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial DNA Abnormalities in Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies: Innate Immune Signaling and Therapeutic Prospects
Article.Authors: Wang G.; Wang Y.; Wang X.; McCullagh K.; Liu A.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) encodes essential components of oxidative phosphorylation and can stimulate innate immunity when released from mitochondria. Its genetic and immunological functions provide a rationale for investigating mtDNA abnormalities in idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs), where muscle dysfunction and inflammation coexist. Large-scale deletions and depletion have been documented in inclusion body myositis and polymyositis with mitochondrial pathology, while dermatomyositis studies reveal regional depletion and oxidative modifications in distinct biological compartments. These findings raise the possibility that mtDNA abnormalities contribute to both impaired mitochondrial function and inflammatory signaling. This review integrates subtype-specific findings with mechanistic studies of mtDNA release, DNA sensing, and inflammasome activation in IIM-related and non-IIM systems. It evaluates the evidence for mtDNA-based biomarkers and therapies targeting mitochondrial injury or downstream inflammation. The reported clinical benefits do not establish mtDNA-specific therapeutic effects. Defining how mitochondrial genome abnormalities and inflammatory signaling interact within each subtype is a priority for biomarker validation and therapeutic research.

Article.Title: Endophytic Bacteria as Modulators of Fragrance Biosynthesis in Plants: Mechanisms and Prospects
Article.Authors: Srivastava P.; Verma S.; Israr J.; Misra S.; Kumar M.; Paul D.
Article.Abstract: Plant fragrance is the blend of volatile terpenoids, phenylpropanoids/benzenoids, fatty acid derivatives, and nitrogen- or sulfur-containing compounds released from flowers, leaves, and fruit. It drives pollination and defence and accounts for much of the economic value of aromatic, medicinal, and ornamental crops. However, it shifts with genotype, developmental stage, tissue type, and stress, and a large share of it still comes from wild-harvested plants. Endophytic bacteria are the microorganisms that colonize internal plant tissues without causing apparent disease symptoms, may modulate these specialized metabolic pathways. Only a limited number of studies have directly investigated these interactions. In contrast, a substantially larger body of research has demonstrated the roles of endophytic bacteria in promoting plant growth and enhancing plant tolerance to environmental stresses. However, direct evidence establishing links between bacterial endophytes, specific genes within volatile-biosynthetic pathways, and the volatile compounds actually released by plants remains limited. The current review summarizes the current evidence on the regulation of major plant volatile biosynthetic routes by endophytic bacteria, including the MVA and MEP pathways for terpenoids, the shikimate-derived phenylpropanoid/benzenoid pathway, as well as the lipoxygenase pathway leading to green-leaf volatile production. The suggested mechanisms are generally grouped into several inter-related categories, such as microbial elicitation and pattern recognition, phytohormonal reprogramming, nutrient and precursor acquisition, modulation of carbon flux through the MVA/MEP and phenylpropanoid pathways, redox regulation and stress priming, and bacterial volatile-mediated signalling. More speculative mechanisms are discussed separately, such as microbial biotransformation, direct microbial biosynthesis of plant volatiles, and horizontal gene transfer. Evidence from culinary and essential oil herbs, medicinal plants, ornamental flowers, and fruit crops is evaluated using an evidence hierarchy that distinguishes phenotypic associations from experimentally validated causal mechanisms. Establishing a robust gene-to-metabolite causal framework will require targeted approaches, including gnotobiotic inoculation, volatilomic profiling, and stable-isotope tracing.

Article.Title: miR1919–MCD1 Regulation of Debneyol Biosynthesis in Nicotiana: Enzyme Organisation, Catalytic Evidence and the Limits of Substrate Channelling
Article.Authors: Labudda M.
Article.Abstract: Debneyol biosynthesis in Nicotiana is regulated by the microRNA 1919 (miR1919)–miR1919-targeted cell death factor 1 (MCD1) module, but the mechanisms linking enzyme association to defence-metabolite output remain incompletely resolved. Although MCD1-dependent protein association and catalytic effects have been demonstrated, direct preferential transfer of 5-epi-aristolochene (5-EA) has not. This critical narrative review addresses this evidential gap by distinguishing biochemical pathway reconstruction, protein-interaction assays, enzyme kinetics, transcript responses, metabolite profiles and infection phenotypes, and compares their inferential scope with independent plant metabolic systems. Farnesyl diphosphate is converted via 5-EA and its epoxide to debneyol. In yeast microsomes, MCD1 increased the reported maximum reaction velocity of 5-EA epoxidase (EAE) from 18.07 to 30.24 nM s−1, whereas a separate coupled-enzyme assay produced approximately threefold more epoxide. Plant experiments also revealed altered debneyol-to-capsidiol ratios, transcript abundance and infection responses. The novel contribution of this review is a structured appraisal of what each experimental approach establishes and where competing explanations remain unresolved. Direct substrate channelling, transcription-independent branch selection and specific allosteric mechanisms remain unresolved; controlled intermediate-tracing, quantitative interaction and enzyme-abundance studies are needed to discriminate among them.

Article.Title: Diclofenac Removal by Actinobacterial Strains and Ecotoxicological Responses
Article.Authors: Gonzalez Holc V.; Small M.; Arnau G.; Lautru S.; Pernodet J.; Aparicio J.; Polti M.
Article.Abstract: Diclofenac (DCF) is a widely detected pharmaceutical whose persistence and biologically active transformation products raise environmental concern. This study evaluated DCF tolerance and removal by actinobacterial strains and integrated chemical performance with plant- and earthworm-based ecotoxicological responses. Phenotypic screening at 1, 5, and 10 g L−1 DCF revealed strain- and concentration-dependent responses in growth, sporulation, and pigment production, with Streptomyces sp. E5N50 and Streptomyces sp. Z2 selected for further study. In liquid assays, after 5 days of incubation, only low biomass production was observed when 50 mg L−1 DCF was supplied without glucose, relative to glucose-containing controls. E5N50 showed modest DCF removal (approximately 23–26%), while Z2 achieved 90.8% in glucose-supplemented medium and about 70% when glucose and ammonium were supplied. A seven-day time-course study with Streptomyces sp. Z2 showed that DCF removal continued after biomass had reached its maximum, suggesting that the process was not exclusively growth-associated. Ecotoxicological responses were organism- and endpoint-dependent. The glucose + DCF + Z2 treatment, associated with the highest DCF removal, significantly increased tomato radicle elongation, whereas glucose + ammonium + DCF + Z2 produced the most favorable Eisenia fetida response, with significantly reduced body-mass loss and increased coelomocyte abundance despite the lower DCF removal removalobserved in this treatment. Overall, Z2 exhibited potential for DCF removal under defined laboratory liquid-culture conditions, and the combined chemical and biological assessment highlighted that parent-compound removal and ecotoxicological improvement provide complementary measures of remediation performance.

Article.Title: UHPLC-MS-Based Metabolomics of Goat Bone Waste and the Antioxidant, Hemocompatibility, and Fibrinolytic Potential of Its Aqueous Extract
Article.Authors: Alanazi A.; Bilel H.; Asran A.; Ahmed S.; Al Zbedy A.; Nassar A.
Article.Abstract: Recycling of food waste and animal by-products in order to produce valuable bioorganic products has been playing an important role in the green chemistry field. In this study, the chemical composition of goat bone wastes was analyzed through untargeted Ultra-High-Performance Liquid Chromatography-Quadrupole-Orbitrap Mass Spectrometry (UHPLC-Q-Orbitrap MS) metabolomics in dual electrospray ionization (ESI) modes. Using accurate-mass tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) database searching, it was possible to annotate various compounds present in the bone waste samples, such as collagen-derived amino acids, peptides, organic acids, nucleotides, and lipids. In parallel, we also investigated the biological activity of the aqueous extract of goat bone matrix (GBAE). The GBAE showed potent antioxidant activity since it was capable of completely neutralizing (100%) DPPH radicals at a concentration of 100 mg/mL. Moreover, the hemolytic activity of GBAE was studied and found to be very low (<1% with human erythrocytes), indicating its weak in vitro hemotoxicity. When oxidative stress was generated via lead acetate (0.625 ppm), GBAE provided a considerable protective effect, leading to 65.0%, 67.5%, and 73.7% hemolysis reduction at concentrations of 200, 400, and 800 mg/mL, respectively. Additionally, preliminary in vitro findings suggested that GBAE exhibited fibrinolytic potential and anticoagulant activities. GBAE showed dose-dependent thrombolytic and anticoagulant activity, with a significant increase in the percentage of clot lysis and coagulation time up to 36 min, compared with 13 min in the negative control.

Article.Title: Silica–Lignin Composites—Insight into Physicochemical Properties and Adsorption Mechanisms
Article.Authors: Blachnio M.; Zienkiewicz-Strzalka M.; Juchniewicz Z.; Sternik D.; Derylo-Marczewska A.
Article.Abstract: Two silica–lignin composites with varying biopolymer content were synthesized using the sol–gel method as effective adsorbents for the removal of organic dyes from aqueous solutions. The textural, structural, and surface properties of the synthesized materials were determined using nitrogen adsorption–desorption techniques, XRD, XPS, and FTIR. XPS and XRD analysis confirmed the effective modification of the silica surface with lignin. Increasing the lignin content in the composite altered its physicochemical properties. Textural analysis revealed a decrease in the porosity of the composites with increasing the amount of biopolymer incorporated into the silica. Thermal analysis with the identification of gaseous thermal destruction products allowed for the determination of the thermal stability of the composites. Dye adsorption experiments, including equilibrium and kinetic measurements, allowed the determination of adsorption capacity, adsorption rate and adsorption mechanisms. FTIR mapping enabled the identification of differences in the interactions of selected dyes with the synthesized composites and revealed preferential adsorption on surface areas of the adsorbents rich in lignin or silica. The obtained results confirmed the potential of silica–lignin materials in environmental applications as cheap and biodegradable adsorbents.

Article.Title: Psychobiotics and Trace Elements in Neurodegenerative Diseases: From Independent Modulators to Potential Interactions Within the Microbiota–Gut–Brain Axis—Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Sokólska W.; Orywal K.
Article.Abstract: The microbiota–gut–brain axis represents an important bidirectional communication network linking the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system and may contribute to processes involved in neurodegeneration. Increasing attention has been directed toward psychobiotics as potential modulators of the microbiota–gut–brain axis, while accumulating evidence also indicates that disturbed trace-element homeostasis may contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases. This review summarizes current evidence on the roles of psychobiotics and trace elements and examines their potential interplay within the microbiota–gut–brain axis. The review discusses bidirectional interactions between the gut microbiota and trace elements, the potential effects of psychobiotic interventions on trace-element homeostasis, and the possible implications of these interactions for neurodegenerative processes. Taken together, current findings indicate that the gut microbiota, psychobiotics, and trace elements may constitute an interconnected system influencing intestinal and systemic homeostasis as well as biological processes relevant to nervous system function. However, direct evidence demonstrating the clinical relevance of interactions between these components remains limited. Moreover, available evidence is largely based on experimental studies, while clinical findings remain scarce and heterogeneous. Further characterization of this interplay may improve our understanding of mechanisms underlying neurodegeneration and provide a basis for the development of more targeted and personalized approaches to supporting neurological health.
