Article.Title: Longitudinal Peripheral Immunophenotyping and Rituximab Response in Primary Membranous Nephropathy: A Prospective Cohort Study
Article.Authors: Georgopoulos C.; Dova L.; Stamellou E.; Duni A.; Vartholomatos G.; Liapis G.; Patsiogiannis V.; Siomou E.; Milionis H.; Dounousi E.
Article.Abstract: Rituximab (RTX) is a first-line option for primary membranous nephropathy (pMN), but many patients fail to respond for reasons that conventional markers only partially explain. We assessed whether longitudinal peripheral immunophenotyping could identify cellular biomarkers of response. In a prospective single-center cohort of 35 patients with pMN treated with standard two-dose RTX, flow cytometry of B-cell, T-cell and monocyte compartments, the systemic inflammation response index (SIRI) and phospholipase A2 receptor antibody were assessed at baseline and months 3, 6 and 12. Within a mean of 7.48 ± 2.4 months, 23 patients (65.7%) achieved either partial or complete remission. By month three, responders showed deeper B-cell depletion, higher CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ T cells, fewer intermediate monocytes and a lower SIRI. On multivariate analysis, month-3 depletion of total CD3−CD19+ B cells below 0.5% (odds ratio 5.8, 95% confidence interval 1.1–31.1) was associated with remission, and each 0.1-unit increase in month-3 SIRI (odds ratio 0.44, 95% confidence interval 0.22–0.91) with lower odds of remission. In a hypothesis-generating analysis, a model combining both had an apparent area under the curve of 0.87. Longitudinal immunophenotyping identifies candidate biomarkers of RTX response in pMN that require multicenter validation.

Article.Title: Dietary Responses in the Diabetic Brain: Transcriptomic Convergence and Comparison with an Alzheimer’s Disease Model
Article.Authors: Kordas B.; Juranek J.
Article.Abstract: Dietary interventions alter brain gene expression in diabetes, but the extent to which their responses agree across experiments and reduce differences from controls remains unclear. Five public transcriptomic datasets were reanalyzed, spanning human cortical fractions, rat brain regions, diabetic mouse hippocampus with intermittent fasting (IF), diabetic whole brain with ketogenic diet, and APP/PS1 and wild-type hippocampus with IF. Gene and pathway comparisons assessed agreement across experiments. Statistical tests distinguished opposing disease and dietary effects from reductions in the remaining distance from controls. IF and ketogenic diet identified 6569 and 999 genes, respectively, in diabetic mice. Their effects showed modest agreement (Pearson r = 0.205), with 447 genes significant in both experiments, including 359 with matching directions. They shared 59 pathways with a matching direction at a fixed intergene correlation of 0.01; these overlaps were not supported when correlations were estimated from the data. IF responses in diabetic and APP/PS1 hippocampus agreed poorly (r = −0.056). No human genes met a per-contrast false discovery rate < 0.05. Thirteen diabetic genes showed significant opposition of disease and IF effects; neither primary fasting experiment demonstrated contraction toward controls. The results support limited agreement between the diabetic dietary experiments and little agreement in IF responses across the examined disease contexts. They do not establish transcriptomic restoration.

Article.Title: Identification of a DNA Damage Response-Related Prognostic Signature and Functional Validation of SMC3 in Glioma
Article.Authors: Ma J.; Zhang C.; Zhang J.; Zhong C.
Article.Abstract: DNA damage response (DDR) deficiencies are linked to tumorigenesis and progression. However, the association of DDR with prognosis and therapeutic response in glioma has not been fully illustrated. TCGA and CGGA databases were used to acquire RNA-seq and clinical data about gliomas. LASSO-Cox regression was introduced to establish a DDR-based risk signature. The single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) algorithm was used to estimate immune infiltrates. The performance of the signature and nomogram in predicting survival was evaluated using ROC curves. Connectivity Map (CMap) analysis was used to nominate candidate compounds, and pRRophetic was used to predict drug sensitivity. Through LASSO-Cox regression, we developed a prognostic risk score based on five DDR-related genes (GADD45G, HDAC1, RRM2, SMC3, and WEE1). Higher risk scores were associated with shorter overall survival and remained significant in multivariable Cox analyses. A prognostic nomogram achieved 1-, 3-, and 5-year AUCs of 0.901, 0.936, and 0.903 in TCGA and 0.776, 0.816, and 0.802 in CGGA, respectively. High-risk tumors showed enrichment of TNFα signaling via NFκB and IL6/JAK/STAT3 gene sets, together with differences in inferred immune cell-associated features and immune checkpoint gene expression. Computational drug sensitivity analyses associated higher risk scores with lower predicted IC50 values for GSK269962A, pazopanib, rapamycin, and NVP-BEZ235, providing hypotheses for subsequent experimental validation. SMC3 overexpression inhibited glioma cell proliferation and migration in vitro. The DDR-related signature showed prognostic value and associations with immune-related transcriptional features in glioma, with in vitro evidence suggesting a functional role for SMC3.

Article.Title: Current Possible Newer Pharmacological Treatment Options for Alzheimer’s Disease
Article.Authors: Miziak B.; Pluta R.; Czuczwar S.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD), as a chronic neurodegenerative disorder, leads to progressive dementia. About 60–80% of dementia cases are due to AD, and their incidence increases especially after the age of 65. AD is characterized by impaired memory, abnormal behavior, and impaired thinking process, which causes limitation of daily activities and a gradual loss of independence. The costs of all dementia cases are likely to reach $2 trillion in 2030 alone. Currently available pharmacological treatment of AD is, for the most part, not causal, and does not modify the course of the disease. The data search for procognitive drugs was carried out using the PUBMED and Clinical Science databases. Among the drugs with animal data and preliminary clinical trials, the following can be distinguished: fosgonimeton, blarcamesine, bezisterim, posiphen (buntanetap) and ACD856. As a rule, promising preclinical results were not confirmed in clinical trials. Some clinical expectations may be associated with posiphen and ACD856. Based on preclinical data, the following drugs seem promising: tenuigenin, JQ1, gemfibrozil, coumarin derivatives, ponicidin, salicin, calcaratarin D, new 1,3,5-triazines or 2-aminopyrymidine carboxamide derivatives, epimedium brevicornu flavonoids, and drugs affecting the glymphatic system. In general, the above-mentioned drugs counteract the pathologies leading to the occurrence of AD.

Article.Title: A TLR4-Associated Microglia–Endothelial Inflammatory Axis in Drug-Resistant Temporal Lobe Epilepsy: Integrated Transcriptomic and Genetic Evidence
Article.Authors: Liu Z.; Yin J.
Article.Abstract: Microglia-driven neuroinflammation contributes to epileptogenesis and drug resistance in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), but the cellular organization of the neuroinflammatory hub and its coupling to the cerebrovascular endothelium remain unresolved. We performed a retrospective secondary analysis of publicly available datasets, integrating paired hippocampal bulk transcriptomics (GSE134697), an integrated temporal-lobe single-cell/nucleus RNA sequencing (sc/snRNA-seq) atlas (9 patients with drug-resistant TLE and 4 controls), two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) and summary-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), and independent hippocampal (n = 77) and peripheral blood (n = 141) cohorts. Five candidate neuroimmune hub genes (TGFB1, ICAM1, TLR4, TLR2 and CCL2) were prioritized using a prespecified, threshold-dependent workflow and mapped to a microglia–cerebrovascular endothelium–peripheral myeloid cell axis. sc/snRNA-seq identified an activated endothelial subpopulation, detected only in TLE samples, and expansion of a microglial compartment with disease-associated microglia (DAM)-like features; CellChat and MultiNicheNet prioritized microglia-derived SPP1, C1QA and MIF as candidate mediators of endothelial inflammatory activation via S1PR1/ITGB1, CD93 and CD74. Plasma kynurenine showed a nominally significant association with focal epilepsy in MR (inverse-variance weighted [IVW] OR = 1.96, 95% CI 1.10–3.52, p = 0.024), whereas SMR did not detect genetically predicted effects of TLR4 or TLR2 expression on focal epilepsy risk; these findings do not establish an acquired disease mechanism. A TGFB1 + TLR4 two-gene signature showed exploratory discrimination in an independent hippocampal cohort (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] = 0.868), and blood TLR4 was selectively elevated in drug-naïve newly diagnosed patients (AUC = 0.684). Targeted gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) and molecular docking nominated simvastatin as a repurposing candidate predicted computationally to interact with MD-2; this prediction has not been functionally validated. This multi-cohort study identifies a TLR4-associated microglia–endothelial inflammatory axis in drug-resistant TLE and generates hypotheses for prospective biomarker studies and experimental drug-repurposing research.

Article.Title: Effects of a Two-Strain Lactobacillus Formulation (Lactobacillus rhamnosus L34 and Lactobacillus paracasei B13) on Inflammatory and Oxidative Markers, Epithelial Junction Proteins, and Fecal Microbiota in Rats with DNBS-Induced Colitis
Article.Authors: Rattanachaisit P.; Lerttanatum N.; Tumwasorn S.; Chuaypen N.; Dissayabutra T.; Werawatganon D.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) involves dysregulated mucosal immunity, oxidative stress, impaired epithelial barrier integrity and gut microbial dysbiosis. We evaluated a two-strain formulation of Lactobacillus rhamnosus L34 and Lactobacillus paracasei B13 in DNBS-induced colitis. Twenty-four male Sprague Dawley rats were randomised into three groups (n = 8): control, acute colitis (AC; DNBS 35 mg/0.25 mL per rat rectally on days 0 and 1), and probiotic treated (RP; 3.6 × 109 CFU daily by gavage, days −3 to 6). Relative to AC, probiotic-treated rats showed lower TNF-α (p = 0.002) and MPO positivity (p < 0.001) and higher IL-10 (p = 0.001), occludin (p = 0.014) and claudin-1 (p = 0.001). Colonic MDA and Ameho scores were numerically lower in the RP group but these differences did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.085 and p = 0.310). Serum IL-17A was unchanged. Microbial community composition differed among groups (PERMANOVA pseudo-F = 5.798, R2 = 0.356, p = 0.0001), with the probiotic-associated community distinct from both control and colitis communities; distance-based analysis detected no convergence toward the control community. The formulation attenuated inflammatory and barrier outcomes and altered microbiota composition without restoring it.

Article.Title: Construction and Application of Testicular Organoid Models in Multi-Omics-Driven Male Reproductive Toxicity Assessment: A Review
Article.Authors: Sun Y.; Liu Y.; Xie M.
Article.Abstract: Conventional male reproductive toxicity testing relies on rodent bioassays and two-dimensional cultures, which are limited by species extrapolation, low throughput, and weak mechanistic resolution. Testicular and seminiferous-tubule organoids partially restore the Sertoli–Leydig–peritubular myoid niche and permit serial, non-terminal sampling, making them compatible with multi-omics profiling in a way earlier models were not. This review examines the field across four layers: the biological hierarchy and regulatory pathways that constrain model design; organoid construction strategies together with computational simulation of morphogenesis and mass transport; multi-omics integration algorithms and toxicity feature extraction; and retrospective validation on publicly deposited datasets. We compare cell sourcing, scaffold, and culture configuration routes against tubule formation and meiotic completion, derive critical-radius and shear-stress criteria governing construct viability, and evaluate similarity network fusion, latent factor decomposition, joint matrix factorization, and graph neural network approaches. Retrospective modeling indicates that adding epigenomic input to transcriptomic features yields the largest performance gain, that gradient-boosted trees outperform deep networks at current sample sizes, and that attribution profiles align with established mechanisms. We contribute an integration framework dimensioned for testicular organoid data, a fully open-source reproducible pipeline, and an explicit mapping between quantitative organoid descriptors and toxicity endpoints. Persistent obstacles include incomplete structural reconstitution biasing omics signal, sparse and inconsistently annotated public data, simulation parameter uncertainty, and unverified cross-species transfer. Minimum reporting standards, a shared characterization vocabulary, and an open benchmark platform are proposed as prerequisites for regulatory uptake.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification, Characterization, and Expression Profiling of the MYC Gene Family in Autotetraploid Alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.)
Article.Authors: Ren W.; Jiang G.; Wang J.; He H.; Du P.; Li H.; Shao Q.; Li H.; Xie Q.
Article.Abstract: The MYC gene family plays a central regulatory role in plant stress responses; however, its evolutionary dynamics and functional divergence in the polyploid forage legume alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) remain largely unknown. Here, through genome-wide identification and comparative genomic analysis, we systematically identified 38 MsMYC genes, which collapsed into 12 ancestral loci based on allele-aware synteny. The high number of sequences was driven mainly by the retention of homoeologous alleles within loci; in addition, one ancient segmental duplication and four tandem duplications contributed to family expansion, whereas strong purifying selection (Ka/Ks < 1 for the 12 ancient segmental paralog pairs) preserved the core functional architecture. Phylogenetic and structural analyses classified these members into five groups, with inter-group differences in motif composition and exon–intron organization suggesting potential functional divergence. Based on promoter cis-acting element prediction and phylogenetic analysis, we selected eight representative MsMYC genes for qRT-PCR analysis, which displayed three representative kinetic behaviors under salt, drought, and hormone treatments within this subset: early-peaking, late-peaking, and opposite-direction responses; subcellular localization analysis of eight representative stress-responsive members supported their nuclear localization, consistent with their roles as transcription factors and with the in silico predictions. Together, these results provide a genomic framework for the temporal and functional differentiation of the MYC gene family in polyploid alfalfa. This study provides candidate genes with distinct temporal expression dynamics for the molecular breeding of salt- and drought-tolerant alfalfa.

Article.Title: RNA-Binding Proteins in mRNA Splicing: Orchestration of Altered Phosphorylation of RNA-Binding Domains via Kinase Regulatory Networks
Article.Authors: Bangera A.; Ummar S.; Sambreena A.; Gopalakrishnan A.; Ramesh P.; Raju R.
Article.Abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are crucial regulators of post-transcriptional gene expression, orchestrating essential processes including splicing, mRNA transport, translation modulation, and mRNA decay. Phosphorylation of RBPs is crucial for regulatory mechanisms, mediating how extracellular stimuli control intracellular signaling and cellular decisions. In this study, mass spectrometry-based phosphoproteomic data were systematically integrated and harmonized, and Fisher’s exact test (p-Value < 0.05) was applied to quantify conserved co-differential phosphorylation across pairs of phosphorylation sites in comparison to a chosen set of RNA-binding proteins (HNRNPM, SLU7, and SRSF5). For each such pair, data were benchmarked across >800 phosphorylation profiling and 200 differential phosphorylation datasets, identifying predominant co-differential phosphorylation patterns that accounted for >75% of all observed phosphorylation events. Major phosphorylation hotspots were identified in HNRNPM, SLU7, and SRSF5 RNA-binding proteins. High-confidence pairs were further refined using secondary filters, yielding a focused set of functionally relevant relationships in mRNA and alternative splicing. As the RNA-binding activity is mediated by RNA-binding proteins (RBDs), co-differentially regulated phosphorylation sites were mapped to RBDs, and upstream kinases modulating such phosphorylation were derived from experimental, semi-experimental and predictive sources. Overall analysis confirmed phosphorylation of RBPs on their RBDs through the upstream kinases, modulating mRNA and alternative splicing through a conserved network of co-differential phosphorylation events. With further validation, the data imply a platform for identifying relevant targets and markers for studying mRNA splicing and RNA-binding activity, central to RNA processing.

Article.Title: Angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4) Protein and Its Relation to Lipids Challenges the Prognostic Performance of B-Type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) Transcontinentally in Patients with Suspected Coronary Chest Pain, Suggesting Their Combined Use in Risk Prediction
Article.Authors: Nilsen D.; Leon de la Fuente R.; Aarsetoey R.; Naesgaard P.; Gallo P.; Dib Ashur S.; Brugger-Andersen T.; Poenitz V.; Grundt H.; Michelsen A.; Aukrust P.; Staines H.; Ueland T.
Article.Abstract: BNP is predominantly synthesized in the ventricular myocardium in response to ventricular distension. ANGPTL4 modulates lipid metabolism, vascular integrity and angiogenesis. The purpose of this study is to compare the prognostic weighting of ANGPTL4 with BNP in a cross-continental setting and to assess the former’s association with circulating lipids in patients with suspected coronary chest pain. ANGPTL4 and BNP were independently associated with all-cause mortality in each cohort. Concentrations of ANGPTL4 and triglycerides (TG) were higher, and total cholesterol (TC), LDL-C and HDL-C were lower in ARG compared to NOR (each p < 0.001). ANGPTL4 correlated negatively with each lipid fraction and positively with C-reactive protein (CRP) but did not correlate with body mass index (BMI) in the cohorts combined. AUC for ANGPTL4 outperformed BNP in ARG, and the reverse was observed in NOR. However, AUC for ANGPTL4 in the combined cohorts was 0.718 (95%CI 0.680–0.756) and for BNP it was 0.730 (95%CI 0.691–0.769). Article.Title: GAC-BiT-CNN: A Hybrid Generative Adversarial Capsule–Transformer–CNN Model with Fused Protein Language Model Embeddings for Methyltransferase Prediction
Article.Authors: Muazzam M.; Ali F.; Alsini R.; Rajkhan N.; Alghushairy O.; Alkhalifah T.
Article.Abstract: Methyltransferases (MTs) are a functionally diverse class of enzymes that catalyse methyl group transfer from S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to DNA, RNA, and proteins, thereby regulating epigenetic programming, gene expression, and numerous disease processes. Dysregulation of these enzymes is implicated in a wide spectrum of human cancers and neurodegenerative disorders, making their accurate computational identification a priority in both basic research and drug discovery. We present GAC-BiT-CNN, a novel hybrid deep learning framework integrating Generative Adversarial Capsule Networks (GAC), Bidirectional Transformers (BiT), and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). The model leverages high-dimensional protein embeddings from four protein language models, including ProtGen, ESM-2, ProtT5-BFD, and ProtT5-XL, used individually, together with a fused feature set formed by concatenating the ProtT5-BFD and ProtT5-XL embeddings. All architectural components were optimised via systematic grid search hyperparameter tuning, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based analysis was applied to the fused embeddings to identify the most discriminative feature dimensions. GAC-BiT-CNN with the fused feature set achieved 98.34% accuracy on the training set and 95.50% accuracy on the held-out test set, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 98.70% and a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.901, surpassing all baseline models by a substantial margin. GAC-BiT-CNN provides a scalable, alignment-free framework with representation-level SHAP attribution for high-throughput methyltransferase identification, with direct applications in epigenomics, drug discovery, and cancer biology.

Article.Title: High-Fat Diet Provokes Aberrant Erythropoiesis in IRP1-Deleted Mice, Leading to Paradoxical Improvement of Glucose Tolerance
Article.Authors: You M.; Chung S.
Article.Abstract: Iron regulatory receptor 1 (IRP1) plays a key regulatory role in iron homeostasis, hypoxia sensing, and erythropoiesis. IRP1 deficiency causes polycythemia in early life, which is worsened by a low-iron diet. A high-fat (HF) diet is a prevalent metabolic insult that causes local hypoxia in adipose tissue, but little is known about the role of IRP1-mediated metabolic adjustments in preserving iron balance. In this study, we hypothesized that deletion of IRP1 fails to control HF-diet-induced hypoxia, thereby exacerbating diet-induced obesity and insulin resistance. HF feeding in IRP1-deficient mice induced a dramatic increase in EPO production, aberrant erythropoiesis, and splenomegaly through the reinstatement of the HIF2 α/EPO pathway. The deletion of IRP1 did not alter body weight gain but caused a paradoxical increase in glucose tolerance compared with WT mice. The 2-DOG uptake assay showed higher RBC-associated radioactivity in IRP1-deficient mice. RBC metabolomic analysis further demonstrated that IRP1 deficiency is associated with elevated metabolite levels generated by glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway. Collectively, our work demonstrates that IRP1 plays a critical role in preventing abnormal RBC formation under HF diet-mediated hypoxic conditions. Our work also provides an unexpected insight into RBC metabolism as a novel target against insulin resistance.

Article.Title: Smilax glabra Roxb. Flavonoids Attenuate D-Galactose-Induced Cardiac Alterations and Are Associated with Modulation of the PGC-1α/NRF1/TFAM Axis and PINK1/Parkin Signaling Pathway in an AMPK-Associated Manner
Article.Authors: Fu D.; Shi J.; Yang Q.; Zheng C.; Chen Y.
Article.Abstract: Smilax glabra Roxb. flavonoids (SGF) are the rhizome extracts of Smilax glabra Roxb. and possesses pharmacological activity, prior studies have demonstrated SGF’s cardioprotective potential, specifically its capacity to inhibit pathological cardiac hypertrophy. D-galactose was employed to induce aging-like changes in C57BL/6J mice and H9c2 cell. These effects were accompanied by increased AMPK phosphorylation and increased expression of proteins related to PGC-1α/NRF1/TFAM axis and PINK1/Parkin signaling pathway. These changes were consistent with an AMPK-associated pattern and may contribute to the cardioprotective effects of SGF via effects on mitochondrial function.

Article.Authors: Tepakhan W.; Panyasai S.; Jomoui W.; Kanjanaopas S.; Srewaradachpisal K.; Sripornsawan P.
Article.Abstract: Non-deletional hemoglobin (Hb) H and Hb H-like diseases are clinically significant forms of α-thalassemia with variable severity. Homozygous Hb Chumphae was also reported for the first time to exhibit a mild clinical phenotype. Hb Adana was detected at an allele proportion of 1.8% among screened carriers from Southern Thailand, and a multiplex AS-PCR for simultaneous detection of Hb CS, Hb Paksé, and Hb Adana was developed.

Article.Title: miR-195-5p Reduces VEGFA Expression and Angiogenesis in Colorectal Cancer
Article.Authors: Piccinno E.; Scalavino V.; Bianco G.; Mancarella S.; Grassi I.; Savino M.; Armentano R.; Giannelli G.; Serino G.
Article.Abstract: Angiogenesis is a key process in colorectal cancer (CRC) progression, with vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) being a major pro-angiogenic mediator. miR-195-5p has previously been identified by our group as a tumor-suppressive miRNA downregulated in CRC. VEGFA expression was evaluated in public CRC datasets and paired tumor/adjacent tissues of a cohort of CRC patients by quantitative real-time PCR and immunohistochemistry. miR-195-5p gain- and loss-of-function experiments were performed in CRC cells to assess VEGFA and VEGFR2 expression and extracellular VEGF-A levels by ELISA. VEGFA expression was also analyzed in an AOM/DSS-induced murine CRC model treated with a miR-195-5p mimic. VEGFA was predicted as a conserved miR-195-5p target and was enriched in miR-195-5p-associated RISCs. VEGFA was overexpressed in CRC tissues compared to normal or adjacent non-tumor tissues. miR-195-5p restoration reduced VEGFA mRNA and protein expression, extracellular VEGF-A levels, and VEGFR2 protein levels in the HCT116 CRC cell line, whereas miR-195-5p inhibition produced the opposite molecular profile. Article.Authors: Cavaleri M.; Erdogan Y.; Ardondi L.; Brunello G.; Sileo L.; Cappucci I.; Basile L.; Zalunardo F.; Stefano S.; Polat G.; Ferroni L.; Zavan B.

These findings indicate that the species with the higher phenolic accumulation also displays stronger antioxidant activity, suggesting that both species—particularly E. tanhoensis—warrant further phytochemical and biological investigation.

Article.Abstract: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common type of skin cancer. We included 30 BCC tissues and 30 noncancerous skin tissues in the study. Gene expression levels were determined by quantitative polymerase chain reaction qPCR. We performed in silico analyses to identify possible genes and signalling pathways associated with BCC. Our findings indicate that SMURF1 and miR-520d-5p are upregulated in BCC and may be associated with BCC pathogenesis. Both molecules are upregulated in BCC tissues and are implicated in the regulation of the TGF-β signalling pathway. According to in silico analysis, SMURF1, SMAD2, SMAD4, TGFBR1, SMAD7, SMURF2, RUNX2, MAPK1, and TGFB3 are key genes involved in the TGF-β signalling pathway, which may be relevant to BCC pathogenesis.

Article.Title: The Effects of the Medium’s pH Value on the Efficiency of the Enzymatic Transglycosylation Catalyzed by Escherichia coli Purine Nucleoside Phosphorylase and Lactobacillus leichmanii Nucleoside Deoxyribosyltransferase Type II
Article.Authors: Alexeev C.; Konkina M.; Oskolsky I.; Platov D.; Drenichev M.
Article.Abstract: The effect of the reaction medium pH value on the rate and yield of enzymatic transglycosylation catalyzed by Escherichia coli purine nucleoside phosphorylase (EcPNP) and Lactobacillus leichmanii type II nucleoside deoxyribosyltransferase (LlNDTII) was investigated. In the presence of EcPNP at pH 5.5, a significant reduction in the inosine formation rate was observed, compared with that of adenosine. A substituent at the purine O6 position neutralizes the negative effect of the 6-oxo group on the reaction rate. A substituent at the purine N6 position has virtually no effect on the transglycosylation rate. In reactions catalyzed by LlNDTII, the rate of nucleoside formation from 4-oxopyrimidines was higher at pH 5.5, but the yield decreased by approximately 10% compared with that at pH 7.0; an unusual dependence of the yield of the target nucleoside on the enzyme concentration used was also revealed.

Article.Title: Recent Advances in Neuronal-like Differentiation of Mesenchymal Stem/Stromal Cells
Article.Authors: Romano I.; D’angeli F.; Maugeri G.; Musumeci G.; Tamburino S.; Lombardo G.; Giuffrida R.; Mannino G.; Lo Furno D.
Article.Abstract: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) have been widely investigated in recent decades because of their multipotent differentiation abilities. In fact, MSCs are able to differentiate not only into mesodermal cell lines (adipocytes, chondrocytes, osteocytes), but also into neuronal and glial cells. MSCs can be derived from different sources, such as bone marrow, adipose tissue, peripheral blood and various neonatal birth-associated tissues. They are suitable candidates in cell-based approaches for both autologous and heterologous transplantation in the field of regenerative medicine. Unlike other types of stem cells, MSCs raise no ethical issues and feature low risks of tumorigenesis after transplantation into humans or animals. In addition, they may exert beneficial effects due to their paracrine actions which help tissue recovery. Numerous studies describe effects obtained following MSC treatments in a variety of human pathologies, including nervous system diseases. The nervous tissue is characterized by very limited recovery properties, likely because of a scarce presence of stem cell niches, which are confined to the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus and the subventricular zone of the lateral ventricles. These niches cannot be able to counteract the neuronal loss after damage or degenerative events. Many efforts have been made to obtain functional neuronal differentiated MSCs to be used for transplantation. However, evidence of complete neuronal maturation and functional integration of neuronal-like MSCs remains limited, and clinical studies have used undifferentiated MSCs rather than neuronal-like cell populations. In this review, we mainly focus on various differentiation protocols that have been adopted for in vitro studies, taking also into account the underlying pathways involved.

Article.Title: Effects of Repetitive Compressive Loading on the Expression of Autophagy-Related Factors, Autophagy Capacity and Cellular Activity in Human Subchondral Bone Osteoblasts
Article.Authors: Iwata H.; Sato S.; Somemura S.; Takemoto M.; Takahashi-Suzuki Y.; Sugishita Y.; Fujiya H.; Haraguchi N.; Yudoh K.
Article.Abstract: Bone metabolism is known to change in response to mechanical stress. In osteoarthritis (OA), the subchondral bone as well as the articular cartilage layer is damaged by mechanical stress, which adversely affects the mechanical environment and homeostatic balance of the entire joint, leading to the onset of OA. However, the impact of mechanical stress on osteoblasts in the subchondral bone, especially their defense mechanism against stress, remains unclear. We focused on the mechanical stress response capacity of subchondral bone osteoblasts, which, like chondrocytes in the cartilage layer, are routinely exposed to repetitive mechanical stress. The purpose of this study was to determine whether repetitive mechanical force (at a physiologic level of cyclic compressive loading) affects the expression of factors regulating autophagy, autophagy capacity and cellular activity in subchondral osteoblasts. Three-dimensional cultured tissue was generated from human subchondral bone osteoblasts using a collagen sponge scaffold. Repetitive compressive loading was applied to the 3D cell culture constructs. After mechanical loading on 3D cell–collagen sponge constructs, we comparatively analyzed the expression of autophagy-related factors (ATG5, Beclin-1, Parkin) in human osteoblasts. Levels of osteoblast differentiation activity (alkaline phosphatase) were also analyzed, and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was used to detect autophagy processes with or without the repetitive compressive loading. In both premature and mature osteoblasts, repetitive compressive loading decreased expression of the autophagy-related factors ATG5, Beclin-1 and Parkin in comparison with the non-loading group, suggesting that repetitive compressive loading may induce downregulation of mitophagy as well as cellular autophagy in subchondral osteoblasts. TEM analysis indicated that, in both premature and mature osteoblasts of the non-loading group, autophagy processes were progressing. In contrast, repetitive loading decreased the number of autophagosomes and autolysosomes in mature and premature osteoblasts. Our results demonstrated that repetitive mechanical loading resulted in a reduction in cellular autophagy and mitophagy in both premature and mature osteoblasts, while also inducing osteoblast differentiation. While mechanical stress promotes osteoblast differentiation, it also alters autophagy, a cellular defense mechanism, suggesting that under conditions of sustained repetitive loading, alterations in the autophagy response—which is essential for maintaining intracellular homeostasis—occur alongside the adaptive bone-forming response, potentially affecting osteoblast function in the long term. Our data demonstrate that reductions in both mitophagy and cellular autophagy in response to repetitive mechanical stress, even at a physiologic level, may lead to accumulation of defective mitochondria and abnormal cellular proteins in the cells, thus reducing osteoblast activity and affecting the homeostasis of subchondral bone tissue, and ultimately contributing to OA progression.

Article.Title: Hypoxia-Associated Glycolytic–Lipogenic Reprogramming and Impaired Antigen Presentation in SPP1+ Tumor-Associated Macrophages in Ovarian Cancer
Article.Authors: Zuo X.; Huang S.; Li Y.; Wang Z.; Xue H.; Min J.; Hong L.; Li S.
Article.Abstract: Ovarian cancer has an immunosuppressive microenvironment in which SPP1+ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are linked to poor prognosis and immune evasion, yet their molecular features and metabolic mechanisms remain unclear. We therefore set out to determine whether SPP1 marks a discrete TAM subpopulation or a functional state in treatment-naïve high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), to define the transcriptional and metabolic program that accompanies it, and to test whether local hypoxia is associated with it. Tumor-derived, treatment-naïve samples from three single-cell datasets (one lesion per patient; 47 patients) yielded 385,504 cells; Seurat v5 and Harmony were used for clustering, annotation, and batch correction. SPP1+/SPP1− macrophages were compared by differential expression, GO/KEGG/GSEA, metabolic scoring, and transcription factor inference, and the definition was retested with within-sample SPP1-high versus SPP1-low comparisons and with MSigDB Hallmark gene sets scored by two independent algorithms. Validation used Visium spatial transcriptomics (GSE263920), TCGA-OV (n = 429), CD8+ T cell exhaustion analysis, CellChat and a syngeneic ID8 model. Of 64,067 macrophages (16.62%), 82.0% were SPP1+; upregulated genes were enriched in glycolysis, monocyte migration and tissue remodeling, whereas MHC class II and neutrophil-related genes were downregulated. At the sample level, glycolysis, fatty acid synthesis and glutaminolysis scores were elevated and the cholesterol synthesis score was reduced, with no evidence of suppressed fatty acid oxidation or oxidative phosphorylation; HIF1A ranked 4th and NR1H3 3rd among 271 transcription factors. All 8 spatial sections showed positive hypoxia–SPP1 correlations, and hotspots showed elevated glycolysis, EMT, immunosuppression and macrophage scores. No robust association was found between SPP1+ TAM infiltration and CD8+ T cell exhaustion (p = 0.315). MDK–LRP1/SDC1 was the major macrophage-directed input. Immunofluorescence showed SPP1 immunoreactivity in a subset of CD68+ macrophages within HIF1α-rich areas of ID8 tumors, without CD8+PD-1+ T cell aggregation. SPP1+ TAMs therefore correspond to a hypoxic functional state with HIF1A activation, a glycolytic–lipogenic transcriptional program, reduced cholesterol synthesis gene expression and a reduced MHC class II program; protein-level and functional validation, and direct tests of HIF1A dependency, remain necessary.

Article.Title: The Molecular Mechanisms of Cold Tolerance in Brassica napus
Article.Authors: Luo W.; Zhou Y.; Shen J.; Xu L.; Du X.; Sheng F.; Geng R.; Cai G.
Article.Abstract: Brassica napus is a crucial oilseed crop in China, meeting approximately 55% of the country’s demand for vegetable oils. However, throughout its growth cycle, it frequently encounters low-temperature stress. As a key environmental factor constraining the stability of Brassica napus L. yield and quality, cold damage makes research into the cold tolerance mechanisms of Brassica napus L. highly significant for the breeding of cold-tolerant varieties. This paper focuses on the issue of low-temperature stress in Brassica napus L., synthesizing recent relevant research findings. It first clarifies the phenotypic effects of low-temperature stress on Brassica napus L. at different growth stages. Concurrently, low temperatures disrupt the integrity of the Brassica napus cell membrane and inhibit photosynthesis, in response, plants can mitigate oxidative damage by activating antioxidant enzyme systems, such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT). Based on the above, the current research progress in mining cold-tolerant germplasm resources in China and identifying cold tolerance genes in Brassica napus L. is further summarized as follows. This paper provides a theoretical reference for an in-depth analysis of the cold tolerance mechanisms in Brassica napus L. and for accelerating the breeding of cold-tolerant varieties. Future efforts should focus on the functional validation of key genes within cold tolerance pathways and the application of multi-gene pyramiding breeding technologies to break through the bottleneck in controlling cold damage in Brassica napus L.

Article.Title: Comparative Study on Coffee and Spent Coffee Grounds of Arabica and Robusta Varieties of Ugandan Origin: Bioactive Properties of Extracts as Circular Resources
Article.Authors: Dinu M.; Dumitru A.; Brezoiu A.; Isopencu G.; Iancu P.
Article.Abstract: Coffee consumption is increasing yearly, and so is the quantity of spent coffee grounds, a by-product that still contains bioactive compounds. The goal of this work is to evaluate the lipid fractions (LFs) and polyphenolic fractions (PFs) from roasted coffee grounds (RCG; two varieties of Ugandan origin: Arabica and Robusta) and from the corresponding spent coffee grounds (SCG) extracted with solvents of opposite polarities. A qualitative and quantitative analysis of the extracts was performed using GC-FID, 1H-NMR, Folin–Ciocalteu, HPLC-PDA, DPPH and antibacterial activity methods. A high-quality LF, coffee oil (91.82 g triacylglycerides/100 g LF, 49.85 mol% saturated fatty acids and 50.15 mol% unsaturated fatty acid chains, 8.98 mg GAE/g LF, 20.91% DPPH inhibition), with high extraction yield (10.34 g/100 g SCG), can be recovered from SCG of the Ugandan Arabica variety. In addition, SCG of both Ugandan Arabica and Robusta varieties are promising resources for the recovery of high-quality PF (12.30 and 7.85 mg GAE/g PF, 0.684 and 0.837 mg/g PF chlorogenic acids, 85.17% and 73.95% DPPH inhibition) with good extraction yields (9.35 and 5.63 g/100 g SCG) and with antimicrobial activities that remain after the coffee brewing step. These results highlight SCG of Ugandan origin as a promising resource of bioactive compounds for further valorization.

Article.Title: Antimicrobial Resistance and Infectious Complications in Cancer Immunotherapy: CAR-T Cells, Bispecific Antibodies and Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors
Article.Authors: Lasagna A.; Andreoni M.; Silvestris N.; Pedrazzoli P.
Article.Abstract: Cancer immunotherapies, including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies, bispecific antibodies (BsAbs), and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), have improved outcomes across hematologic and solid malignancies. Infection risk remains heterogeneous and depends on treatment platform, target antigen, lymphodepletion, immune reconstitution, concomitant immunosuppression, and supportive care. This narrative review synthesizes clinical trials, observational studies, and guidance identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, reference screening, and a targeted literature update through October 2026. It focuses on infection incidence, microbiological spectrum, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), multidrug-resistant (MDR) colonization and infection, antimicrobial exposure, prevention, and stewardship. Severe infections can be frequent with BCMA-directed BsAbs: the MagnetisMM-3 study reported grade 3–4 infections in 39.8% of elranatamab-treated patients, while a pooled global teclistamab cohort reported grade 3–4 infections in 55.3%; these estimates are study-specific and are influenced in part by COVID-19. Direct AMR evidence is concentrated in CAR-T and broader cellular-therapy cohorts, while comparable data for BsAbs and ICIs remain limited. Associations between broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, microbiome disruption, and CAR-T outcomes are clinically important but remain vulnerable to confounding. Prevention should integrate immune status, prior microbiology, antimicrobial exposure, and local resistance patterns rather than infer resistance risk from treatment platform alone. Prospective studies using harmonized outcomes are needed to improve individualized infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship.

Article.Title: Tryptophan and Its Selected Metabolites Modulate Melanoma-Cell Biology: A Preliminary In Vitro Study
Article.Authors: Michalak-Stoma A.; Walczak K.; Kowal M.; Sawa-Wejksza K.; Chojnacki M.; Lemieszek M.; Stoma F.; Krasowska D.
Article.Abstract: Tryptophan (TRP) and its metabolites are involved in numerous physiological and pathological processes within the skin. They may influence melanoma biology, but their role remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated the effects of TRP, anthranilic acid (AA), and cinnabarinic acid (CBA) in melanoma cells in vitro and their potential interaction with the B-Raf proto-oncogene, serine/threonine kinase (BRAF) inhibitor vemurafenib. A375, G361, and SK-MEL-3 melanoma cell lines and a THP-1-derived macrophage model were used. Cell proliferation and metabolic activity were assessed using the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay, migration using a scratch assay, and cell-cycle distribution by flow cytometry. Western blotting was used to analyze selected signaling proteins. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) and nitric oxide (NO) production were evaluated. Bioinformatic analyses investigated associations between BRAF and genes related to tryptophan metabolism and the kynurenine pathway. All compounds showed dose-dependent antiproliferative effects, with prolonged exposure increasing efficacy. TRP and AA increased G0/G1 cell-cycle arrest, whereas CBA increased the G2/M population. TRP also reduced A375 cell migration. All three compounds enhanced the antiproliferative effect of vemurafenib, with CBA showing the strongest effect (approximately 20%). Western blot analysis indicated modulation of p21 expression and ERK1/2 phosphorylation, suggesting implications for cell cycle and stress signaling pathways. Moreover, conditioned medium from A375 cells exposed to tested compounds affected cell viability, ROS, and NO production in THP-1-derived macrophages. TRP and its metabolites may be considered potential supportive agents for melanoma BRAF-targeted therapy. However, further in vivo studies are needed to clarify their therapeutic value and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms.

Article.Title: CASK Positively Regulates Keratinocyte Proliferation and Modulates the EGFR-ERK-p21 Signaling Axis
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Huang D.; Cheong K.; Cheng C.; Chang H.; Lin W.
Article.Abstract: CASK is a multidomain scaffold protein with diverse cellular functions, but its role in keratinocytes remains unclear. In this study, we established a CASK-silenced human HaCaT keratinocyte model to investigate its biological function. We found that CASK was localized to the plasma membrane, cytosol, and nucleus, and its silencing suppressed keratinocyte proliferation and induced G1-phase arrest. RNA sequencing revealed that CASK depletion attenuates proliferation-associated transcriptional programs. Consistent with this, CASK silencing increased p53 and p21 expression while reducing cyclin B and phosphorylated Rb levels, with elevated p53 and p21 mRNA in shCASK cells. However, CASK silencing-associated p21 upregulation is not majorly dependent on p53 activity. Mechanistically, CASK silencing enhanced serum-induced activation of EGFR and downstream ERK signaling, which were accompanied by increased expression of the EGFR ligands amphiregulin, TGF-α, and epiregulin, indicating augmented autocrine/paracrine EGFR signaling. Pharmacological inhibition studies demonstrated that activation of the EGFR–ERK signaling pathway is essential for p21 upregulation upon CASK silencing. Promoter reporter analyses further revealed that CASK deficiency enhances p21 transcription. Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized role of CASK in regulating keratinocyte growth and cell-cycle progression. CASK promotes keratinocyte proliferation by restraining autocrine/paracrine EGFR–ERK signaling and suppressing p21 expression, thereby contributing to epidermal homeostasis and growth control.

Article.Authors: Zamith Cunha R.; Zannoni A.; Biondolillo G.; Bernardini C.; Nasi L.; Di Placido C.; Chiocchetti R.

CB2R-IR showed marked staining in umbrella cells and faint staining in basal cells; it was also observed in bundles of nerve fibers, intramural neurons, detrusor smooth muscle cells, and vascular structures. CB2R-IR was significantly higher in the urothelium (p < 0.0001). These findings provide a molecular basis for studies investigating the endocannabinoid system as a potential therapeutic target in feline lower urinary tract disorders.

Article.Title: Stachydrine Hydrochloride Suppresses Hepatocellular Carcinoma Progression by Reprogramming Macrophage Polarization Through the LIF/PI3K/Akt Axis
Article.Authors: Bao X.; Zhang Y.; Sun L.; He C.; Li D.; Shi X.; Ma Y.

Mechanistically, SH suppressed LIF/PI3K/AKT activation in M2 macrophages, and LIF overexpression showed a trending capacity to partially counteract SH-mediated M2-suppressive effects. Bioinformatics linked high M2-TAM infiltration with poor HCC prognosis. In vivo, SH retarded tumor growth, decreased intratumoral M2-TAM infiltration, and reduced Ki-67 levels. Collectively, SH remodels the TIME to restrain HCC progression, and these effects are associated with inhibition of M2-TAM polarization and attenuation of LIF/PI3K/Akt signaling, revealing a novel immunotherapeutic mechanism and supporting SH as a promising natural agent for HCC immunotherapy.

Article.Title: Erythrocyte Membrane β-Adrenoreactivity as a Systemic Adrenergic Phenotype Associated with Ventricular Tachyarrhythmia in Heart Failure Patients Undergoing Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy
Article.Authors: Atabekov T.; Muslimova E.; Rebrova T.; Afanasiev S.; Batalov R.; Popov S.
Article.Abstract: Chronic hyperactivity of the sympathetic nervous system and remodeling of β-adrenergic receptors represent core pathophysiological mechanisms in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and in the emergence of ventricular arrhythmias. Nevertheless, clinically applicable functional indicators of this axis are still limited. We investigated whether erythrocyte membrane β-adrenoreactivity (EMA), an indirect functional membrane index derived from β-adrenergic antagonist-modulated hypo-osmotic hemolysis, correlates with a ventricular tachyarrhythmia (VTA) phenotype following cardiac resynchronization therapy with defibrillation capability (CRT-D). In a single-center observational cohort, 99 HFrEF patients underwent CRT-D implantation. A total of 70 patients with complete baseline and 12-month data formed the complete-case analysis (NCT03667989: n = 14; NCT05769036: n = 36; non-registry enrollment under the same institutional protocol: n = 20). Patients were categorized by the prespecified database variable “VTA preCRT and 12 m. post-CRT” into VTA-positive (n = 38) and VTA-negative (n = 32) groups. Baseline EMA was higher in VTA-positive patients (31.4% [22.8; 48.3]) than in VTA-negative patients (22.0% [15.8; 33.4]; p = 0.012). In multivariate logistic regression with stepwise selection, two variables were independently associated with the VTA-positive phenotype: EMA (odds ratio [OR] = 1.0446 per 1%; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.0092–1.0812; p = 0.013) and left ventricular end-systolic dimension (LVESD) (OR = 1.1023 per 1 mm; 95% CI 1.0102–1.2029; p = 0.029). The model was statistically significant (likelihood-ratio χ2 = 12.567; p = 0.0019) and well calibrated (Hosmer–Lemeshow χ2 = 9.70; p = 0.286), with good discrimination (AUC = 0.748; 95% CI 0.629–0.844). However, explanatory power was modest (Nagelkerke R2 = 0.220), indicating that most variance in the VTA phenotype remains unexplained by EMA and LVESD. At a cut-off of 0.5, sensitivity was 73.68%, specificity 71.87%, and overall accuracy 72.86%. Internal validation with 2000 bootstrap iterations confirmed robustness (optimism-corrected AUC = 0.727; 95% CI 0.612–0.835). EMA remained significant after adjustment for LVESD, supporting its role as an independent marker of the VTA-positive phenotype. The model outperformed all univariate models in terms of AUC, R2, and overall accuracy. EMA may therefore be associated with a systemic adrenergic membrane phenotype and an arrhythmic substrate. These findings require mechanistic validation and external replication before any clinical application. All reported cut-offs are exploratory and derived from a single center, and the analysis is based on a complete-case cohort with acknowledged potential for attrition bias.

Article.Title: Platelet miRNA-Based Signature as a Potential Non-Invasive Tool for Discriminating Patients with Secondary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis from Healthy Individuals
Article.Authors: Dziedzic A.; Karbownik M.; Arabski M.; Miller E.; Michlewska S.; Saluk J.
Article.Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) lacks minimally invasive biomarkers that reliably reflect disease-associated pathophysiological alterations, particularly during the progressive stage of the disease. Because blood platelets contribute to thrombo-inflammatory signalling and are the major vascular carriers of regulatory miRNA, we investigated whether platelet miRNA alterations are associated with platelet hyperreactivity in MS and whether these changes originate during thrombopoiesis by examining megakaryocytes. We analyzed platelets and megakaryocytes from MS patients and healthy controls by transmission electron microscopy, flow cytometry, ELISA, miRNA profiling based on microarrays, and Real-Time PCR validation. Logistic regression and bioinformatic analyses were used to evaluate the potential and biological relevance. MS platelets exhibited a hyperreactive phenotype, characterized by enhanced degranulation, microparticle release, P-selectin expression, and collagen-induced aggregation. GPVI levels were significantly elevated in platelets but remained unchanged in megakaryocytes. MiRNA profiling revealed widespread downregulation in platelets, while megakaryocytes showed selective upregulation of miR-223-3p. Following microarray screening, PCR validation of 10 selected miRNAs revealed widespread downregulation in platelets, while only miR-223-3p was significantly upregulated in megakaryocytes from MS patients. A two-miRNA model (let-7a-5p and miR-146a-5p) showed good internal discrimination (AUC = 0.89; sensitivity 89%; specificity 85%), but lower external performance (C-index = 0.66; sensitivity 50%; specificity 73%). MS is associated with a distinct platelet miRNA signature linked to acquired platelet hyperreactivity and vesiculation. Platelet-derived let-7a-5p and miR-146a-5p represent potential non-invasive biomarker candidates, although their diagnostic utility requires further validation in larger independent cohorts.

Article.Title: Biomarkers of Immune Injury in Cardiometabolic Disorders
Article.Authors: Zhou L.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Cardiometabolic disorders are accompanied by persistent immune activation that links metabolic stress to vascular and organ injury. Conventional inflammatory measures capture part of this process, but they provide limited information about tissue origin, biological mechanism and disease trajectory. This narrative review examines emerging biomarkers across genetic and epigenetic regulation, metabolic and oxidative stress, gut microbial exposure, innate immune activation, adaptive immune remodeling and circulating inflammatory responses. It integrates mechanistic studies with clinical observations to consider how these signals may inform the assessment of cardiometabolic immune injury. Particular attention is given to the distinction between inherited susceptibility and acquired responses, circulating associations and tissue mechanisms, and potentially injurious versus compensatory immune activity. The evidence supports substantial biological connectivity among these domains, while the strength of clinical validation varies widely. Most candidate markers and proposed combinations require standardized measurement, longitudinal assessment and external validation before biomarker-guided prevention can be justified. We propose a mechanism-informed framework for organizing candidate immune-metabolic phenotypes, recognizing reciprocal interactions rather than a universal temporal sequence. Future studies should determine whether these biomarkers improve prediction and clinical decisions beyond established risk factors and whether changes in biomarker profiles correspond to meaningful treatment benefits.

Article.Title: DNA Glycosylases in Noncancer Diseases: Oxidative Lesion Recognition, Repair Intermediates, and Tissue Responses
Article.Authors: Kang S.; Ko Y.; Cho S.; Jang S.
Article.Abstract: Oxidative DNA damage in noncancer tissues can perturb transcription, compromise telomere integrity, and impair mitochondrial function. DNA glycosylases initiate base excision repair (BER), but their biological consequences also depend on lesion recognition, chromatin residence, catalytic processing, and the persistence or resolution of abasic sites and strand breaks. This review integrates structural and kinetic evidence with experimental models of inflammation, telomeric senescence, cardiometabolic disease, neurodegeneration, and neural injury. Promoter-associated 8-oxoguanine DNA glycosylase 1 (OGG1) can either promote inflammatory transcription or restrict antiviral interferon expression in a locus-dependent manner. At oxidatively damaged telomeres in human fibroblasts, OGG1 and mutY DNA glycosylase (MUTYH) drive acute senescence through repair intermediates, whereas during repeated injury, OGG1 supports telomere maintenance and MUTYH-dependent arrest limits chromosome instability. Mitochondria-directed OGG1 expression improves metabolic outcomes in OGG1-deficient mice exposed to a high-fat diet. By contrast, vascular and neural phenotypes associated with Nei-like DNA glycosylase 3 (NEIL3) remain difficult to attribute to a defined initiating lesion. These findings emphasize distinguishing enzyme occupancy, catalytic processing, and completed repair. Therapeutic studies should define the relevant cell, substrate, compartment, and exposure period and assess tissue function directly alongside unresolved lesions and chromosome stability.

Article.Title: One Disorder, Two Brains: Challenges in Modeling Epilepsy and Associated Movement Disorders in Mice
Article.Authors: Travin D.; Anisimova P.; Bogovarova K.; Kustova A.; Tarabykin V.
Article.Abstract: Modeling epileptic syndromes co-occurring with movement disorders in mice often fails to fully recapitulate human phenotypes due to distinct gene-specific and anatomical mechanisms. This review categorizes these translational barriers into three primary groups. First, ortholog heterotopia and heterochrony drive spatiotemporal shifts in gene expression, causing orthologs to activate at disparate developmental stages or within different cell populations across species. Second, molecular redundancy and compensation obscure phenotypes through the upregulation of alternative proteins in response to target protein suppression, the activation of modifier genes, or neural network rewiring. Third, structural variations in striatal anatomy fundamentally alter corticostriatal loop functioning. Characterizing these divergent mechanisms is essential for improving the predictive validity of preclinical models and advancing targeted therapies.

Article.Title: Cultivar-Dependent Variation in Silicon Accumulation and Phytolith Formation Revealed by Comparative Proteomic Analysis in Rice
Article.Authors: Prakongkaew R.; Pongprayoon W.
Article.Abstract: Silicon is a key determinant of growth, productivity, and stress adaptation in rice (Oryza sativa L.). Silicon accumulation and its deposition as phytoliths contribute to plant performance and environmental resilience. However, although the physiological functions of silicon and the mechanisms governing its uptake and transport have been extensively studied, the proteomic basis underlying cultivar-dependent variation in silicon accumulation and phytolith formation remains poorly understood. In this study, silicon concentration, phytolith content, and proteomic profiles were compared in roots and shoots of three rice cultivars, Chai Nat 1 (CNT), Khao Dawk Mali 105 (KDML105), and RD51, at the flowering stage. RD51 exhibited the highest silicon concentration and phytolith accumulation in shoots, whereas CNT accumulated the highest silicon concentration in roots. Proteomic analysis identified 4086 and 4115 protein groups in roots and shoots, respectively, revealing cultivar-specific differences in protein abundance. Principal component analysis and differential abundance analysis demonstrated the greatest proteomic divergence between CNT and RD51, particularly in shoots. Functional enrichment analysis indicated that KDML105 was enriched in transport- and sulfur metabolism-related processes, whereas RD51 showed enrichment of mitochondrial respiration, energy production, and associated metabolic pathways. Protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis further revealed functional associations between silicon transporter proteins and proteins involved in transport, signaling, and respiratory metabolism. Collectively, these findings provide novel insights into the proteomic mechanisms underlying silicon accumulation and phytolith formation in rice. The superior silicon accumulation and phytolith production observed in RD51 highlight its potential as a valuable genetic resource for enhancing phytolith production, improving silicon-use efficiency, and strengthening climate resilience in rice.

Article.Title: Resistance Gene Pyramiding in Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.): From Marker-Assisted Selection to Functional Validation
Article.Authors: Kwiatek M.; Bobrowska R.; Noweiska A.; Spychała J.; Mikołajczyk S.; Tomkowiak A.
Article.Abstract: Gene pyramiding is widely used in wheat breeding to improve disease resistance; however, combining multiple resistance alleles does not necessarily provide stronger protection or long-term durability. Molecular markers, gene cloning and genome editing have greatly facilitated the tracking and pyramiding of resistance alleles. These approaches define the allelic composition of a line rather than the level of resistance it will express. This review examines why the effectiveness of resistance gene combinations remains difficult to predict despite advances in molecular tools. Evidence from leaf rust, stripe rust, stem rust, powdery mildew, eyespot and Fusarium head blight shows that the observed effects of combined resistance loci depend on the genetic background, gene interactions and environmental conditions, as well as on the methods used to assess disease development. We discuss how genetic characterization, expression analysis, functional assays and multi-environment phenotyping can provide complementary evidence for evaluating resistance gene combinations and how pathogen evolution and deployment strategies affect their durability. As genome editing expands the possibilities for combining resistance alleles, understanding their functional compatibility and their performance across genetic backgrounds remains essential for developing effective and durable resistance in wheat. The central conclusion of this review is that no marker profile, and no edited allele, is by itself evidence that a cultivar will be resistant in the field. Markers and gene editing shorten the route to a combination, but the resistance of that combination still must be validated phenotypically in the target backgrounds and environments.

Article.Title: Differential Modulation of the Ileal Bile Acid Transporter ASBT by Fatty Acids
Article.Authors: Malhotra P.; Farooqui Z.; Ticho A.; Comiskey S.; Qazi A.; Calzadilla N.; Suarez R.; Gill R.; Alrefai W.
Article.Abstract: The ileal ASBT bile acid transporter is a critical mediator of bile acid and cholesterol homeostasis and is modulated by fatty acids via S-acylation. We investigated mechanisms underlying differential regulation of ASBT by saturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids. Using a prenylation mimetic with a CAAX box at the C-terminus of ASBT, we showed that transport activity in transfected HEK293 cells increased significantly, suggesting that direct attachment of a saturated fatty acid stimulates ASBT function. Furthermore, siRNA-mediated attenuation of DHHC21 acyltransferase expression reduced ASBT S-acylation and its function, demonstrating DHHC21 as a positive regulator of ASBT function. Conversely, treatment with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFAs), like eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), reduced ASBT function in HEK293 cells. Supplementation of fish oil, as a source of n-3 PUFAs, to a high-fat, high-cholesterol diet fed to C57BL6/J mice protected them against diet-induced hepatic steatosis, along with reduced bile acid absorption consistent with the inhibition of ASBT. This was supported by increased fecal bile acids, decreased ileal bile acid-stimulated gene expression, and increased hepatic bile acid synthesis-related gene expression. Metabolic labeling with alkyne-EPA in HEK293 cells showed, for the first time, direct binding of this n-3 PUFA to ASBT. Unlike palmitate modification, EPA binding was highly resistant to hydroxylamine retrieval, indicating a mechanism distinct from S-acylation. Our data unraveled a novel role for DHHC21 in regulating ASBT and provided evidence for distinct mechanisms by which saturated palmitate and polyunsaturated EPA fatty acids bind ASBT. The direct effect on ASBT and inhibition of bile acid absorption may partly contribute to the protective effects of n-3 PUFAs on the liver.

Article.Title: Dual Targeting of Alcohol Use Disorder and Alcohol–Associated Liver Disease: Emerging Molecular Targets Along the Gut–Liver–Brain Axis
Article.Authors: Ryu T.; Chung B.; Yang K.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol–associated liver disease (ALD) is the hepatic end of alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet only abstinence and transplantation modify it, and recent liver-only programmes in alcohol–associated hepatitis have not delivered. This review asks whether the receptors, ligands and transporters setting drinking behaviour and alcohol-related liver injury are largely one set along the gut–liver–brain axis, so one molecule could lower both. Where resolved, it is cell-specific: hepatic glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor sits, in non-alcohol models, on sinusoidal endothelial and CD8+ T cells, not hepatocytes, and ethanol induces hepatocyte fibroblast growth factor 21, whose analogue acts on β-Klotho+ amygdala neurons. Organised by target, not organ, each candidate is appraised separately on both sides, negatives, terminations and non-replications counting alike. Of sixteen targets spanning incretin, hepatokine, glutamatergic and microbial or neuroimmune families, three are supported on both sides in the desired direction but only in separate experiments, three point in opposite directions, and ten have had no manipulation read out on both; for none were both organs read out in one experiment. Dual targeting changes what trials must measure: only one of 64 registered trials makes both endpoints primary, so objectively measured intake and a liver endpoint must be co-primary.

Article.Title: Mesenchymal Stem/Stromal Cell-Derived Extracellular Vesicles for Immunomodulation in Osteoarthritis
Article.Authors: Ley M.; Philippon M.; Labib R.; Fuentes-Chandia M.; Liu C.; Best T.; Somoza R.; Kouroupis D.
Article.Abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous disorder affecting multiple joint tissues, in which structural degeneration may be accompanied by varying degrees of synovial inflammation and immune–stromal dysregulation. Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) have demonstrated immunomodulatory and tissue-protective properties, increasingly linked to paracrine signaling. Comparative studies suggest that extracellular vesicles (EVs) make an important, but not exclusive, contribution to MSC paracrine activity, with soluble secretome components providing potentially complementary effects. Drawing on literature identified primarily through PubMed and Scopus and clinical trial records from ClinicalTrials.gov (updated through September 2026), this narrative review examines the immunomodulatory role of MSC-derived EVs (MSC-EVs) in OA, with emphasis on their interactions with the joint immune microenvironment and their contribution to tissue protection. Across experimental OA models, MSC-EVs have been reported to reduce synovitis, cartilage degeneration, subchondral bone alterations, and pain-related outcomes, although responses vary with MSC source, EV composition, engineering strategies, disease context, and treatment regimen. Mechanistically, the most consistent evidence supports modulation of macrophage-associated inflammatory responses, whereas effects on adaptive immune populations remain less established and are largely derived from non-OA models. Clinical evidence remains limited and currently provides mainly preliminary information on feasibility and short-term tolerability, with insufficient evidence to establish therapeutic efficacy. Overall, MSC-EVs represent a potential cell-free immunomodulatory approach for OA, but standardized manufacturing, product characterization, dosing, and rigorously controlled clinical trials are required to define their therapeutic value.

Article.Title: Intrinsic Inflammatory Signaling in Life and Death of Podocytes
Article.Authors: Bobkov D.; Konopleva S.; Osin D.; Demidov O.; Mihailovskaya V.
Article.Abstract: Podocytes are terminally differentiated components of the glomerular filtration barrier whose structural integrity depends on coordinated signaling between the slit diaphragm, actin cytoskeleton, mitochondria, and stress-response machinery. Evidence from cultured podocytes, experimental kidney disease, human tissue, and selected podocyte-specific genetic models indicates that podocytes can execute intrinsic inflammatory responses and, in defined settings, contribute to local inflammatory amplification. This review examines how NF-κB, p38 MAPK, JAK–STAT, cGAS–STING, NLRP3 inflammasome, and Rho-family GTPase signaling interact with cytoskeletal remodeling, mitochondrial dysfunction, senescence, regulated cell death, and podocyte detachment. Particular attention is given to the distinction between podocyte-specific evidence and findings obtained from whole-kidney analyses, global genetic models, or pharmacological interventions. The available evidence supports a context-dependent network in which inflammatory signaling may support adaptation but, when sustained or dysregulated, can contribute to barrier dysfunction and irreversible podocyte loss. We also assess therapeutic strategies targeting inflammatory sensors, kinases, inflammasome components, cytoskeletal regulators, and metabolic stress pathways. Most remain preclinical, emphasizing the need for podocyte-targeted delivery, rigorous cell-specific validation, and human translational studies.

Article.Authors: Figura M.; Zając W.; Otto-Ślusarczyk D.; Milanowski Ł.; Nowak J.; Antoniak A.; Kopczyński M.; Sadowski K.; Hołubiuk Ł.; Walęcik-Kot W.; Szlufik S.; Biliński J.; Struga M.; Koziorowski D.
Article.Abstract: Inflammation and gut dysbiosis are increasingly recognized as important contributors to the pathophysiology of Parkinson’s disease (PD). Broader inflammatory markers, including ferritin and leukocyte parameters, also did not differ significantly between groups. We conclude that single FMT did not induce significant changes in systemic inflammatory biomarkers in this exploratory cohort of PD patients. Larger studies with standardized inflammatory assessments are needed to clarify the immunomodulatory effects of FMT in PD.

Article.Title: Chemical Characterization and In Vitro Biological Activity of Edible Desert Truffle Tirmania pinoyi CCASU-TP-03
Article.Authors: Elhusseiny S.; Abougalambou S.; El-Dessouki A.; Aboshanab K.; El Enshasy H.; Al-Agamy M.; Alyahya K.; Ibrahim S.
Article.Abstract: Tirmania pinoyi is an edible desert truffle valued for its nutritional properties; however, information regarding its biological activity and chemical composition is still limited. Antimicrobial evaluation demonstrated inhibitory activity against several of the tested bacterial and yeast strains, whereas no activity was detected against Aspergillus niger under the tested conditions. In conclusion, the findings demonstrate measurable antioxidant capacity, inhibitory activity against several tested microorganisms, differential cytotoxic effects among the tested cancer cell lines, and inhibition of NO production accompanied by reduced iNOS protein expression. Further studies are required to isolate the respective pure metabolites followed by preclinical evaluation for potential use in humans.

Article.Title: Pantethine and Neurodegeneration: A Coenzyme A-Centered Framework Linking Metabolism, Neuroinflammation, and Mitochondrial Dysfunction
Article.Authors: Simili O.; Carvalho G.; Simões R.; Detregiachi C.; Pereira E.; Catharin V.; Silva G.; Miola V.; Bishayee A.; Valenti V.; Vécsei L.; Tanaka M.; Barbalho S.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a growing global health burden associated with aging and characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, metabolic failure, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress, and chronic neuroinflammation. Among the metabolic pathways implicated in these disorders, coenzyme A (CoA)-linked biology has emerged as a potentially important but still underexplored contributor to neuronal resilience and vulnerability. Pantethine, a disulfide derivative of pantetheine and a CoA-related metabolic precursor, has attracted attention because of its reported effects on cellular metabolism, redox balance, and inflammatory signaling. However, its relevance across neurodegenerative diseases remains unevenly defined, with direct support strongest in pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) and more limited evidence in common disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD). This narrative review critically examines the mechanistic and translational evidence linking pantethine to neurodegeneration. PKAN represents the most logical disease context for pantethine investigation because impaired CoA biosynthesis is proximal to disease pathogenesis, although pantethine remains investigational and its clinical efficacy has not been established. By contrast, proposed applications in AD and PD remain highly theoretical and hypothesis-generating. Nevertheless, research on pantethine and related CoA-restoring strategies may identify new intervention targets across neurodegenerative diseases and other disorders characterized by impaired cellular bioenergetics, including selected neuropsychiatric disorders. These possibilities require biomarker-informed, disease-specific studies that establish active-species exposure, target engagement, and clinically meaningful effects.

Article.Abstract: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE), particularly vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium, are important healthcare-associated pathogens, and vanA is a major acquired determinant of high-level glycopeptide resistance. The conventional polymerase chain reaction (PCR) method is reliable for molecular detection of vanA but requires thermal cycling and, in conventional formats, post-amplification analysis. In this study, we developed and evaluated a closed-tube colorimetric loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay using hydroxy naphthol blue (LAMP-HNB) for visual detection of vanA. A total of 130 Enterococcus isolates were tested, comprising 100 previously characterized in our published LAMP–lateral flow dipstick (LAMP-LFD) study (52 vanA-positive and 48 vanA-negative) and an additional 30 (13 vanA-positive and 17 vanA-negative), yielding 65 PCR-positive and 65 PCR-negative isolates overall. Reaction conditions were optimized sequentially, and the final LAMP-HNB protocol took place at 63 °C for 45 min with 4.0 mM MgSO4 and 5 μM HNB. The visual endpoint was confirmed by 2% agarose gel electrophoresis. LAMP-HNB correctly classified all 65 PCR-positive and all 65 PCR-negative isolates, yielding 100% sensitivity (65/65; exact 95% CI: 94.48–100%), 100% specificity (65/65; 95% CI: 94.48–100%), and 100% overall agreement (130/130; 95% CI: 97.20–100%). The limit of detection was 8.67 × 103 genome copies/µL (28.52 pg/µL) for LAMP-HNB compared with 8.67 × 104 genome copies/µL (285.2 pg/µL) for conventional PCR, representing a 10-fold lower DNA concentration endpoint under the experimental conditions employed. In the 100-isolate overlapping cohort, LAMP-HNB, the previously reported LAMP-LFD platform, and PCR were concordant. With its 45 min requirement for amplification after DNA preparation, the HNB format provides a rapid, closed-tube visual endpoint without a labeled probe, lateral flow strip, running buffer, or post-amplification hybridization step. These findings support LAMP-HNB as a promising molecular screening approach for vanA-positive enterococci, while larger, fully independent multicenter validation remains necessary before routine implementation.

Article.Title: Engineered Factor VIII: A Comprehensive Review of Molecular Biology, Design Strategies, and AAV-Mediated Gene Therapy
Article.Authors: Khairetdinova A.; Artemyev V.; Astakhova E.; Ambaryan S.; Pilagov M.; Maznina A.; Lobanova V.; Feoktistova S.; Mityaeva O.; Volchkov P.
Article.Abstract: Coagulation factor VIII (FVIII) is a key therapeutic protein for hemophilia A, an inherited bleeding disorder caused by FVIII deficiency or dysfunction. The development and production of FVIII-based therapeutics remains challenging due to the intrinsic complexity of FVIII biosynthesis, folding, secretion, and functional stability. Advances in the understanding of the FVIII life cycle, as well as studies of its natural homologs, have created opportunities to develop improved FVIII variants. In parallel, therapeutic strategies to restore FVIII activity have evolved from replacement therapy with exogenous FVIII to gene-based delivery of a functional F8 copy. Among these approaches, AAV-mediated gene therapy has emerged as a clinically viable platform with a generally favorable safety profile, prompting the development of multiple therapeutic candidates for hemophilia A. This review summarizes established and current knowledge of FVIII structure, biosynthesis, and immunology in the context of developing effective and clinically applicable AAV-mediated therapies for hemophilia A. Particular attention is given to engineered FVIII variants and the latest clinical findings in AAV gene therapy, as well as to long-term efficacy and safety.

Article.Title: Topological Data Analysis Identifies Copy Number Variation Subtypes of Bulls Associated with Fertility
Article.Authors: Bakoev S.; Ermilov A.; Sidorenko D.; Bakoev F.; Kostyunina O.; Altukhova N.; Nemkovskiy G.; Belyakov V.
Article.Abstract: Bull fertility is a polygenic trait of significant economic importance in dairy and beef cattle, controlled by multiple genetic variants, including copy number variations (CNVs). Conventional single-variant association analyses primarily evaluate marginal effects of individual loci, whereas CNV co-occurrence patterns require complementary approaches. This study applied topological data analysis (TDA) to identify groups of bulls based on genome-wide CNVR profiles and to assess their association with insemination success rate. A total of 88 bulls were included, and the presence/absence of 406 consensus CNVR was determined for each animal. TDA was performed using the Mapper algorithm with a two-dimensional UMAP projection as the lens and DBSCAN for clustering, followed by community detection using the Leiden method. Bootstrap resampling (100 iterations) was used to assess the stability of the identified communities, and their association with fertility was tested using ANOVA and permutation testing (n = 1000). TDA with bootstrap consensus identified five bull communities ranging from 10 to 30 individuals each. The identified subtypes differed in mean insemination success rates, ranging from 48.3% to 72.5%. These differences were assessed using ANOVA and permutation testing. Gene annotation of the loci distinguishing these communities using Ensembl release 110 for the ARS-UCD1.2 assembly revealed genes potentially involved in embryonic development, cellular signaling, and immune response (e.g., IGF2, INS, NOTCH1, PAEP, TRAF2). TDA provides a framework for identifying groups of bulls with distinct combinations of CNVRs and evaluating their potential association with fertility. Due to the sample size (n = 88) and unadjusted phenotypes, the findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating. The discovered candidate genomic regions require mandatory validation and independent replication in larger cohorts before being considered for implementation in breeding programs.
