Article.Title: The Role of Hypoxia-Inducible Factors (HIFs) in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Radiation Resistance
Article.Authors: Caputo C.; Dingley R.; Al-Jumaili Y.; Mageau E.; Tharmalingam S.; Tai T.
Article.Abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype lacking estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2 expression. Although ionizing radiation (IR) is widely used to treat TNBC, tumour radioresistance remains a major therapeutic barrier. Tumour hypoxia contributes to resistance by limiting IR-induced reactive oxygen species generation and activating pathways that promote tumour survival, progression, and aggressiveness. Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) are oxygen-sensitive transcription factors that regulate many of these pathways; however, the mechanisms underlying HIF-mediated radioresistance in TNBC remain incompletely characterized. This review examines the role of HIF signalling in TNBC radiation resistance and emerging strategies for overcoming hypoxia-mediated radioresistance. PubMed and Web of Science were searched for studies investigating HIFs, TNBC, and radiation response. Relevant studies were screened against the eligibility criteria and analyzed for mechanistic findings and therapeutic interventions targeting HIF-associated pathways. The literature indicates that HIF activation promotes radioresistance through multiple mechanisms, including altered ferroptosis and pH regulation. Proposed countermeasures include pharmacologic inhibition of HIF signalling, nanotechnology-based delivery systems, and alternative radiation-based modalities, including photodynamic and radiodynamic therapies. Collectively, these findings identify HIF signalling as a central mediator of TNBC radioresistance and a promising therapeutic target for improving radiotherapy outcomes.

Article.Title: Association Between Ambient PM2.5 Exposure and Leukocyte Telomere Length Among Rural Adults: Cross-Sectional Study in Northern Thailand
Article.Authors: Kohsuwan K.; Hongjaisee S.; Somsunun K.; Promkam N.; Santijitpakdee T.; Prapamontol T.
Article.Abstract: Ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure has been associated with oxidative stress, inflammation, and biological aging; however, evidence regarding its relationship with leukocyte telomere length (LTL) remains inconsistent, particularly in rural Southeast Asian populations. This study aimed to investigate the association between ambient PM2.5 exposure and LTL across multiple exposure windows and examine whether oxidative stress and systemic inflammation were associated with PM2.5 exposure and LTL. This cross-sectional study included 179 adults from rural communities in Northern Thailand affected by biomass-burning pollution. Cumulative average ambient PM2.5 exposure was estimated for lag 0–7, 0–14, 0–30, 0–60, and 0–90 days, corresponding to 8, 15, 31, 61, and 91 days, respectively, including the blood-collection date (day 0). Relative LTL was quantified using quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Serum 8-hydroxy-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), the Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index (SII), and the Systemic Inflammation Response Index (SIRI) were also assessed. Analyses included covariate-adjusted linear regression, exploratory wild cluster bootstrap inference, and sensitivity analyses. All p-values were unadjusted for multiple comparisons. Median relative LTL was 0.81 T/S units (Q1–Q3: 0.72–0.89). Adjusted models showed positive associations between PM2.5 and LTL at 0–30-, 0–60-, and 0–90-day windows, but not at 0–7- and 0–14-day windows. Per window-specific IQR increase in PM2.5 (8.13, 7.25, and 6.25 µg/m3, respectively), relative LTL was higher by 0.050 T/S units (95% CI: 0.012–0.089; nominal p = 0.011), 0.079 T/S units (95% CI: 0.035–0.123; nominal p < 0.001), and 0.094 T/S units (95% CI: 0.041–0.147; nominal p < 0.001). The reported confidence intervals and conventional p-values did not account for site–date clustering. In exploratory wild cluster bootstrap analyses using eight site-date groups, none of the five associations reached nominal significance (p = 0.247–0.787). The 0–30-day PM2.5 model explained an additional 3.8% of the variance in LTL (ΔR2 = 0.038; p = 0.011), while 8-OHdG contributed a further 2.4% (ΔR2 = 0.024; p = 0.041); SII and SIRI did not significantly improve model fit (p = 0.499 and 0.603, respectively). Sensitivity analyses showed positive longer-window associations with substantially varying magnitudes, whereas inverse shorter-window associations emerged in the NTAQHI-only analysis. Higher estimated ambient PM2.5 exposure was positively associated with higher measured LTL across the 0–30-, 0–60-, and 0–90-day windows in conventional adjusted models. However, sensitivity to sample composition and nonsignificant wild cluster bootstrap findings limit confidence in the robustness of these associations. Adding serum 8-OHdG, SII, or SIRI produced modest changes in model fit and did not establish mediation by oxidative stress or systemic inflammation. These exploratory findings should not be interpreted as evidence of within-person telomere change or a causal or protective effect of PM2.5.

Article.Title: A Complex Molecular Profile in Melanoma: Intratumoral Heterogeneity and Therapeutic Implications
Article.Authors: Tan Y.; Berardi G.; Guo T.; Seth A.; Olszanski A.; Wu H.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Complex molecular alterations in cancers influence tumor biology, therapeutic response, and resistance. We report a case of cutaneous melanoma demonstrating extensive intratumoral heterogeneity with important clinical implications. A 77-year-old man with stage IIA cutaneous melanoma developed an isolated nodal recurrence one year after resection. Comprehensive next-generation sequencing of the metastatic lesion revealed an uncommon genomic profile consisting of a class 3 BRAF Y472V mutation, two NF1 loss-of-function mutations, and two concurrent KIT mutations: a dominant, potentially targetable K642E mutation and a low-frequency D816V mutation associated with resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors. The tumor exhibited a high tumor mutational burden and microsatellite stability. The patient received neoadjuvant nivolumab plus relatlimab followed by surgical resection, achieving complete pathologic response. Repeat sequencing of the resected specimen demonstrated complete molecular clearance of all previously detected variants. This case illustrates the value of comprehensive genomic profiling in revealing biologically complex melanoma with coexisting driver and resistance-associated alterations. The presence of a treatment-naïve KIT resistance mutation suggests preexisting subclonal heterogeneity that may influence future targeted therapy, while high tumor mutational burden and NF1 loss may have contributed to the excellent response to immune checkpoint blockade.

Article.Title: The Lactate–Mitokine Axis in Exercise Adaptation: Linking Glycolytic and Mitochondrial Stress Signaling
Article.Authors: Tero-Vescan A.; Ștefănescu R.; Ősz B.; Buț M.; Pușcaș A.; Slevin M.
Article.Abstract: Exercise induces coordinated metabolic and mitochondrial stress responses that extend beyond ATP production to regulate cellular and systemic adaptation. Lactate, traditionally viewed as a glycolytic product, is now recognized as an oxidative substrate, interorgan carbon shuttle, and signaling metabolite, whereas mitochondrial stress promotes adaptive signaling and the release of mitokines and mitochondrial-derived peptides. This narrative review proposes the lactate–mitokine axis as a conceptual framework integrating these two exercise-responsive systems, while distinguishing experimentally established mechanisms from potential interactions that remain to be functionally validated. Repeated exercise promotes mitochondrial remodeling and increases oxidative capacity, which in turn reshapes the lactate response to subsequent exercise, as reflected by lower post-exercise lactate concentrations and enhanced lactate clearance after training. Conversely, increased lactate flux may influence mitochondrial adaptation through metabolic, redox, and receptor-dependent signaling, supporting a potentially bidirectional relationship between lactate handling and mitochondrial remodeling. The relative contribution of these interconnected responses appears exercise modality-dependent, with high-intensity, prolonged endurance, and resistance exercise generating distinct combinations of glycolytic and mitochondrial stress. Although lactate metabolism and mitochondrial stress signaling share several regulatory pathways, direct causal interactions between lactate signaling and mitokine expression or secretion during exercise remain insufficiently established. Thus, the proposed lactate–mitokine axis should be regarded as a hypothesis-generating framework requiring further experimental validation.

Article.Title: Therapeutic Advances in Mycobacterium avium Complex Pulmonary Disease: Current Treatments and Emerging Host-Directed Approaches
Article.Authors: Khachatourian N.; Takhmazian R.; Venketaraman V.
Article.Abstract: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is the leading cause of non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) pulmonary disease, with increasing incidence among aging and immunocompromised populations. Despite guideline-recommended multidrug therapy consisting of a macrolide, ethambutol, and a rifamycin, treatment remains prolonged and complicated by incomplete culture conversion, adverse effects, recurrence, and antimicrobial resistance. Intracellular persistence, biofilm formation, and intrinsic resistance mechanisms further challenge disease management. This review summarizes MAC pathogenesis, host immune responses, current treatments, and emerging therapeutic strategies. Promising approaches include novel antimicrobial agents, optimized multidrug regimens, drug repurposing, inhaled delivery systems, and host-directed therapies. Particular emphasis is placed on glutathione (GSH), an intracellular antioxidant with immunomodulatory properties, as a potential adjunctive therapy. Experimental studies suggest that GSH and its precursor N-acetylcysteine may influence oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and antimycobacterial activity. However, MAC-specific evidence remains primarily in vitro, and clinical efficacy in MAC pulmonary disease has not been established. Findings from related mycobacterial infections provide mechanistic insights but cannot be directly extrapolated to MAC pulmonary disease. Further preclinical and clinical studies are needed to determine whether GSH-based interventions can safely complement conventional antimicrobial therapy and improve treatment outcomes.

Article.Title: Cross-System miRNA Profiling Identifies a Clinically Recurrent miRNA Core in Colorectal Cancer
Article.Authors: Valentelyte D.; Lukosevicius R.; Steponaitiene R.; Salteniene V.; Morkunas E.; Balion Z.; Baldauskaite G.; Zemgulyte G.; Butaite G.; Kulokiene U.; Gedgaudiene G.; Kupcinskas J.; Inciuraite R.; Skieceviciene J.
Article.Abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) encompasses biologically diverse cellular phenotypes with distinct microRNA (miRNA) expression patterns. Seven of 29 prioritized cellular miRNAs met the EV selection criteria. Analysis of 11 matched TCGA tumor–non-tumor pairs reproduced reduced miR-30a-3p, miR-30c-2-3p, and miR-1271-5p and increased miR-140-5p expression. Target-based enrichment and exploratory miRNA-mRNA correlation analyses identified associations with CRC-relevant signaling and MYC-related, cell-cycle, DNA-repair, and metabolic programs. No significant associations with the evaluated clinicopathological features or overall survival were detected. Collectively, these findings identify a reproducible subset of CRC-associated miRNA alterations and highlight reduced miR-30a-3p and miR-30c-2-3p expression as a recurrent family-level pattern warranting mechanistic investigation.

Article.Title: PTBP1: A Key Hub and a Potential Therapeutic Target in High-Grade Glioma
Article.Authors: Li C.; Hao S.
Article.Abstract: High-grade gliomas (HGGs) are lethal primary brain tumors with poor prognosis despite multimodal therapy. Polypyrimidine tract-binding protein 1 (PTBP1) is an RNA-binding protein that regulates alternative splicing, mRNA stability, and translation. In HGGs, PTBP1 is overexpressed and correlates with tumor grade, IDH mutation status, and patient survival, supporting it as a candidate prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target. Structurally, PTBP1 contains four RNA recognition motifs connected by flexible linkers, conferring conformational plasticity for diverse RNA interactions. In glioma cells, upstream regulators—including non-coding RNAs and post-translational modifications—dysregulate PTBP1, converting it from a physiological regulator into a predominantly oncogenic driver. Multiple lines of evidence suggest that PTBP1 drives malignancy through three interconnected mechanisms: oncogenic splicing switching, stabilization of oncogenic mRNAs, and IRES-dependent translation. Although no selective, direct small-molecule inhibitor of PTBP1 has yet been clinically validated, repurposed compounds (e.g., venetoclax) and indirect modulators have shown preliminary antitumor activity in preclinical models. However, direct target engagement, in vivo efficacy, and blood–brain barrier penetration remain insufficiently established. This review summarizes PTBP1’s structure, upstream networks, downstream mechanisms, and therapeutic potential, highlighting the need for further validation of PTBP1-centered strategies prior to clinical translation.

Article.Title: The Deubiquitinating Enzyme UCHL1 Promotes Radiotherapy Resistance in Glioma by Stabilizing Keratin 18
Article.Authors: Wang H.; Zheng R.; Liu Q.; Ding X.; Zhao Y.; Xu J.; Tang R.; Chen L.; Chen X.; Shi H.; Zhang H.; Wang W.
Article.Abstract: Maintaining stemness in glioma stem cells (GSCs), coupled with robust DNA damage repair capacity, is a key determinant of radioresistance in glioma. Although the deubiquitinating enzyme ubiquitin carboxy-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL1) has been implicated in regulating tumor cell functions and facilitating malignant progression, its specific role in sustaining GSC stemness and in promoting radioresistance remains poorly understood. In this study, we combined secondary analyses of public datasets with in–house experimental investigations. Specifically, we first analyzed UCHL1 expression and its prognostic significance in glioma using the GEO2R, GEPIA2, and CGGA databases. Radiosensitivity, DNA repair capability, and GSC stemness were evaluated using clonogenic survival, comet, sphere formation, extreme limiting dilution assay, and Western blot analyses. To identify UCHL1–interacting proteins, co-immunoprecipitation coupled with mass spectrometry was performed, followed by deubiquitination and rescue experiments to validate its substrates and functional dependence. Our results revealed that UCHL1 was markedly overexpressed in radioresistant glioblastoma cells and glioma tissues, and its expression levels positively correlated with poor prognosis in patients with glioma. UCHL1 knockdown attenuated the sphere-forming capacity and self–renewal frequency of GSCs and impaired the cellular response to DNA damage following irradiation, thereby attenuating the radioresistant phenotype. Mechanistically, UCHL1 stabilizes keratin 18 (KRT18) protein via deubiquitination. The effects of UCHL1 on radioresistance and stemness properties were largely diminished upon KRT18 knockdown, accompanied by reduced expression of the stemness marker SOX2. Furthermore, KRT18 knockdown attenuated the radioresistant phenotype induced by UCHL1 overexpression. Collectively, these findings suggest a mechanistic axis through which UCHL1 may regulate GSC stemness and radioresistance and identify UCHL1 as a candidate therapeutic target for reversing therapeutic resistance in glioma, warranting further validation.

Article.Title: Salmonella Serovars Distribution in Poultry Meat and Genetic Characterization of Antimicrobial-Resistant Isolates: A Five-Year Monitoring in Sicily
Article.Authors: Castello A.; Alio V.; Baviera R.; Oliveri G.; Gargano V.; Schiavo M.; Zimmardi A.; Cardamone C.; Alduina R.; Costa A.
Article.Abstract: Salmonellosis is one of the most frequently reported zoonoses, and broiler meat/meat products are among its main vehicles of transmission. Continuous monitoring on Salmonella serovars and the spread of antimicrobial resistance is essential for epidemiological surveillance. From 2021 to 2025, a total of 350 poultry samples were collected in Sicily and analyzed for Salmonella spp. detection, serotyping and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) phenotyping. Overall, 101/350 samples tested positive for Salmonella spp. Eight serovars were identified with S. Infantis being the most prevalent, followed by S. Kentucky, S. Enteritidis, S. Strathcona, S. Agona, S. Corvallis, S. Toulon, S. Virchow. The following resistance percentages were revealed: 78.7% (144/183)—tetracycline, 68.9% (126/183)—trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, 51.9% (95/183)—penicillins, 35.0% (64/183)—third-generation cephalosporins, 33.3% (61/183)—aminoglycosides, 4.9% (9/183)—chloramphenicol, 2.2% (4/183)—fluoroquinolones, 0% (0/183)—imipenem. The following genetic determinants were searched in a selected subset of 46 isolates resistant/intermediate resistant (R/I) to third-generation cephalosporins or fluoroquinolones: blaCTX-M-1, blaCTX-M-2, blaCTX-M-4, blaCMY-2, blaTEM, blaOXA, blaSHV (third-generation cephalosporins); qnrA, qnrB, qnrC, qnrD, qnrS, qepA, oqxAB, aac(6′)-Ib (fluoroquinolones) and intI1. The high rate of AMR is of concern for human safety and environmental health, especially referring to the highest priority and critically important antimicrobials (hpCIAs) such as third-generation cephalosporins.

Article.Title: Mapping the MicroRNA Landscape of Arsenic Exposure: A Bibliometric and Evidence-Synthesis Analysis of Directional Consistency and Regulatory Themes
Article.Authors: Öztan G.; Kesin M.; İşsever T.; İşsever H.
Article.Abstract: Arsenic exposure has been associated with altered microRNA (miRNA) expression in human and experimental settings, yet the structure of this literature and the consistency of reported expression directions remain insufficiently characterized. This study combined a three-database bibliometric analysis with an audit of published directional evidence. Searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science on 27 August 2026 identified 1396 records, yielding 752 unique records and a 248-publication bibliometric corpus. Author-keyword analyses highlighted arsenic, microRNA regulation, carcinogenesis, and epigenetic themes, with miR-21 the most frequent individual miRNA keyword. A historical biological inventory contained 319 coded study–miRNA observations from 109 publications; its significance-conditioned selection prevents interpretation as a completed, unbiased evidence synthesis. Although legacy miR-21 directional concordance was 26/27, these codes do not establish independent biological reproducibility. Source-level adjudication of 11 of 137 previously unresolved records identified 10 exclusions and one eligible publication awaiting extraction; 126 records remain unresolved. Re-extraction of a human urinary-miRNA study recovered 18 signed arsenic-association estimates across three miRNAs, one of which (miR-423) was absent from the legacy inventory altogether. All were nonsignificant, but positive and negative estimates occurred across adjustment models, demonstrating that nonsignificance does not imply absence of effect. Aggregating the legacy miR-21 codes into senior-author units reduced the concordance to 8/9 (p = 0.039), and under a modest assumption of upward-reporting asymmetry (p0 = 0.65) the signal was no longer significant (p = 0.121). Mechanism-frequency ranking, aggregated false-discovery-rate control and mature-arm assignment are not supported by the available source data and are therefore not reported. The bibliometric mapping and source audit clarify research themes and reporting limitations, but definitive directional-consistency and biomarker-prioritization conclusions require completed source-level screening, significance-independent extraction, and verification of study independence.

Article.Title: Beyond Efficacy: Preclinical Validation and Translational Readiness of Recent Multimodal Photodynamic Nanoplatforms for Glioblastoma
Article.Authors: Woźnicki P.; Aebisher D.
Article.Abstract: Multimodal photodynamic therapy (PDT)-based nanoplatforms are increasingly being developed for glioblastoma (GBM) to improve photosensitizer delivery, overcome tumor hypoxia, and combine PDT with complementary therapeutic mechanisms. However, promising antitumor activity does not necessarily translate into adequate preclinical validation or clinical readiness. This review critically evaluates recent studies published between January 2025 and August 2026, identified through PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science. Of 3617 records screened, 35 studies met the broader eligibility criteria for nanoparticle-mediated PDT in GBM, including 19 studies incorporating in vivo evaluation. Particular attention was given to the biological relevance of experimental models, survival assessment, biodistribution, pharmacokinetics, clearance, systemic and neurological safety, and platform-specific translational limitations. Orthotopic models were used in 16 of 19 in vivo studies, whereas immunocompetent and immunodeficient hosts were represented almost equally. Nevertheless, clinically challenging settings such as post-resection disease, acquired temozolomide resistance and recurrence after standard therapy were rarely reproduced. Quantitative pharmacokinetic and elimination data were limited, and fluorescence or elemental measurements frequently reflected individual platform components rather than intact nanostructures. Safety assessments were predominantly short-term and often focused on body weight, routine blood parameters and organ histology. Overall, the current evidence demonstrates substantial therapeutic innovation but also reveals a persistent gap between antitumor efficacy and translational validation. Future studies should prioritize clinically representative models, quantitative absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME) characterization, long-term and neurological safety assessment, and comparisons with current standard-of-care treatment.

Article.Title: Genotype-Associated Molecular Phenotypes Across Brain and Gut Compartments in Male 5xFAD Mice: Shared Latent Structure and the Limits of Individual-Level Inference
Article.Authors: Sahin B.; Eken Y.; Sahin F.; Karaman T.; Sezerman O.; Ozer S.; Kaya Z.; Karagözlü M.; Serdar M.; Serteser M.; Baykal A.
Article.Abstract: Whether gut and brain molecular states covary within individual animals, rather than merely co-occurring at the group level, has rarely been tested in Alzheimer’s disease models. We profiled the hippocampus, cortex, cerebellum, intestine and feces of 18 male 5xFAD (5 familial AD mutations) (B6SJL background) mice and wild-type littermates at 3, 6 and 9 months by label-free proteomics, and feces additionally by shotgun metagenomics. The hippocampal proteome reproduced the amyloid-associated signature (App, Apoe, Hexb, Clu, Gfap), and protein-set analysis showed elevated microglial, lysosomal, astrocytic and endoplasmic reticulum chaperone proteins in the hippocampus and cortex, with no detectable difference in synaptic or mitochondrial sets. Fecal Shannon diversity was reduced, and the bile-acid-modifying genera Romboutsia and Turicibacter were nearly absent in all 5xFAD animals from 3 months (cage nested within genotype). Multi-omics factor analysis recovered a genotype-associated factor shared across brain and gut views (exact permutation p = 0.00125) that explained at most 6.3% of variance in any view and was preprocessing-dependent. After removal of group structure, correlation burden did not exceed a within-cell permutation null, and neither did same-animal positive controls. The 5xFAD genotype thus alters every compartment examined, and a modest latent structure links them; because the design excludes only strong or dense individual-level coupling, the null result bounds design resolution rather than showing that gut and brain are uncoupled.

Article.Title: Tiny Carriers, Big Impact: How Tannerella forsythia Extracellular Vesicles Drive Oral Diseases, and Beyond
Article.Authors: Shen Z.; Xu G.; Li Y.; Liu H.; Chen Z.; Chen S.; Han Q.; Wang Z.; He H.
Article.Abstract: Periodontitis influences systemic health through mechanisms that extend far beyond the periodontal pocket, yet the vehicles that mediate this dissemination remain incompletely defined. Within the “red complex” of periodontitis, Tannerella forsythia (Tf) has long been overshadowed by Porphyromonas gingivalis and Treponema denticola, and its extracellular vesicles (EVs) have been correspondingly neglected. This review synthesizes a decade of evidence to reposition Tf EVs as a distinct nanoscale virulence-delivery platform. Their biogenesis couples outer-membrane budding to the type IX secretion system (T9SS), and the crystalline surface layer (S-layer) appears to be actively reprogrammed—rather than passively shed—to accommodate vesicle curvature, a mechanism so far supported by compositional evidence. Their cargo is selectively enriched in T9SS substrates, TonB-dependent receptor/SusD-like nutrient-acquisition proteins, and extensively O-glycosylated virulence factors. Mechanistically, as demonstrated directly at the vesicle level in cellular models, Tf EVs engage Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2), autonomously prime and activate the inflammasome, and drive IL-12-dependent Th1 polarization. These properties define a “purely pro-inflammatory” immunological identity that distinguishes Tf EVs from those of P. gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum. Signature cargo, including BspA, miropin, and PepO, suggests potential links between Tf EVs and cardiovascular, articular, and pulmonary diseases; however, these systemic associations are currently inferred mainly from whole-cell, isolated-virulence-factor, or epidemiological evidence, rather than from direct Tf EV-level experiments, and are therefore presented here as testable hypotheses. We critically appraise isolation and standardization practices, delineate priority gaps such as unverified vesicle subtypes and unexplored small RNA cargo, and propose a four-step roadmap from subtype isolation to clinical cohorts. Tf EVs warrant recognition as an independent research object and a candidate druggable target for periodontitis, whereas their contribution to its systemic comorbidities awaits direct causal validation at the EV level.

Article.Title: Distinct Transcriptional Responses to 17β-Estradiol in Human Meniscal Fibrochondrocytes from a Female and a Male Donor
Article.Authors: Yu Y.; Vergis J.; Eby H.; Markho M.; Kopacz J.; Cartwright K.; Hershey M.; Liu J.; McCullumsmith R.
Article.Abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) affects women more often than men, and estrogen has been implicated in joint homeostasis, yet its effects on meniscal fibrochondrocytes (MFCs) remain poorly defined. We reanalyzed a public RNA sequencing dataset (Gene Expression Omnibus, GSE199087) of MFCs from two age-matched donors, one female and one male (both 47 years old). Cells from each donor were treated in triplicate with pulsed 17β-estradiol (E2, 240 µM for 1 h every 24 h over 72 h) or vehicle control. Differential expression was assessed with limma-voom, and pathways were identified with Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), Enrichr, and iLINCS, retaining only Gene Ontology terms supported by all three. In the female donor’s cells, E2 upregulated DNA replication and cell-cycle pathways and lowered MMP1, MMP2, IL12A, and MYD88. In the male donor’s cells, E2 upregulated chromatin remodeling and developmental signaling pathways, with NOTCH1 among the leading-edge genes, and downregulated antigen presentation pathways and mitochondrial genes. At the gene level, some changes were shared by both donors, including lower TIMP1. Because each sex was represented by one donor, these differences cannot be attributed to sex with confidence. The findings are hypothesis-generating and identify candidate pathways for validation in larger, sex-balanced cohorts.

Article.Title: Biomarkers for Cancer Immunotherapy: Advances, Challenges, and Clinical Applications
Article.Authors: Ahmed A.; Haq F.
Article.Abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has revolutionized oncology by harnessing the immune system to recognize and eliminate malignant cells. Despite remarkable clinical successes, a substantial proportion of patients fail to respond or develop resistance, highlighting the urgent need for reliable biomarkers to guide patient selection, predict therapeutic outcomes, and monitor treatment responses. This review addresses both the emerging and established biomarkers for cancer immunotherapy. These include molecular, cellular, and systemic biomarkers within tumor tissues, blood, and the tumor microenvironment. The principal ones include immune checkpoint-related biomarkers (e.g., programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression), tumor mutational burden, microsatellite instability, neoantigen profiling, circulating tumor DNA, and immune cell signatures. We grade each biomarker by analytical validity, clinical validity, clinical utility and regulatory readiness; place it in one of four evidence tiers; and outline the steps needed to bring candidate markers into the clinic. Recent developments in multi-omics technologies, artificial intelligence, and single-cell analysis are accelerating biomarker discovery, providing a clearer understanding of tumor–immune interactions. Furthermore, the integration of dynamic biomarkers is critical for optimally refining therapeutic strategies for real-time monitoring and detection of resistance mechanisms. This review aims to provide a worldwide overview of present achievements, challenges, and future opportunities in biomarker research and ultimately enable the development of more personalized and effective strategies for immunotherapy of cancer.

Article.Title: Comparison of Sonidegib and Vismodegib Efficiency in Drug-Sensitive and Resistant Ovarian Cancer Cell Lines—2D and 3D Model Study
Article.Authors: Stasiak P.; Sopel J.; Płóciennik A.; Świerczewska M.; Korbecki J.; Januchowski R.
Article.Abstract: Ovarian cancer is a leading cause of mortality among gynecological malignancies. Despite the initial effectiveness of chemotherapy, multidrug resistance (MDR), driven by ABC transporters such as P-glycoprotein, limits treatment success by reducing intracellular paclitaxel (PAC) accumulation. Abnormalities in the Cancer Stem Cells signaling pathway Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) play a role in drug resistance development and ovarian cancer progression. We evaluated two Shh pathway inhibitors, Sonidegib (LDE225) and Vismodegib (VIS), in the W1 drug-sensitive ovarian cancer cell line and PAC-resistant sublines, using the 2D monolayer model, as well as the 3D spheroid model, to better simulate conditions of the tumor microenvironment. qPCR analysis showed similar levels of Shh pathway gene expression in 2D and 3D cell culture conditions. PAC-resistant cell lines were 3- to 6-fold more sensitive to both LDE225 and VIS than the PAC-sensitive cell line. LDE225 showed a 6- to 10-fold lower IC50 than Vismodegib, indicating higher potency. Both agents inhibited proliferation and colony formation in a concentration-dependent manner. Differences in IC50 between 2D and 3D dense spheroids formed by the W1 cell line were small, suggesting that high spheroid density does not reduce the activity of LDE225 and VIS against cancer cells. In conclusion, both inhibitors present pleotropic effects against ovarian cancer cells, especially drug-resistant ones, and can be considered as a new treatment opportunity in this cancer. Nevertheless, further investigation of Hedgehog pathway inhibition in more advanced models is required to assess the potential of clinical application for these compounds.

Article.Title: Native American Ancestry Is Associated with NAT2 Haplotype and Inferred Metabolizer Phenotype Variation in Latin American Populations
Article.Authors: Acuña M.; Carrasco S.
Article.Abstract: The N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) gene contributes to drug metabolism, yet its pharmacogenetic variation in admixed populations remains incompletely characterized. We evaluated associations of estimated Native American genetic ancestry with NAT2 haplotypes defined by seven single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and inferred metabolizer phenotypes in four Admixed American (AMR) populations from the 1000 Genomes Project (n = 347). The complete Phase 3 dataset (n = 2504) provided comparative context. Haplotype distributions differed among AMR populations (χ2 = 78.61; Monte Carlo p = 1.0 × 10−5). After adjustment for sampling population, each 10-percentage-point increase in Native American ancestry was associated with lower odds of an inferred poor metabolizer phenotype (odds ratio [OR] = 0.78; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.66–0.93; p = 0.006). NAT2*4.001-compatible and NAT2*7.002-compatible haplotypes were more frequent with higher Native American ancestry. The inferred poor metabolizer proportion was 57.5% in the lowest and 26.4% in the highest ancestry quartile. Excluding four individuals with indeterminate expanded coding-variant assignments yielded a similar association (n = 343; OR = 0.80; 95% CI, 0.67–0.95; p = 0.0097). These observational associations support further genotype-based investigation but do not establish causality or replace individual NAT2 genotyping.

Article.Title: Conductive Hydrogels for Invasive Neural Interfaces: From Materials Engineering to Neural Signal Interfacing and Neurorehabilitation
Article.Authors: Chen W.; Chen X.; Shen L.; Deng J.; Wang Y.; Ran Y.; Wang Y.; Xie Y.
Article.Abstract: In invasive neural interfaces, mechanical mismatch between traditional rigid electrodes and brain tissue often leads to inflammation and signal attenuation. Conductive hydrogels have emerged as ideal alternative materials due to their tissue-matching modulus, hybrid conductive networks, and wet adhesion properties. In this paper, we provide a narrative review of research progress on conductive hydrogels in invasive neural interfaces: we elucidate electronic, ionic, and hybrid conduction mechanisms; critically compare strategies for modulus matching and interfacial adhesion (such as catechol chemistry and covalent anchoring); and summarize their applications in neural signal recording, electrical/optical modulation, and rehabilitation for spinal cord injury and stroke. Finally, we discuss current challenges regarding long-term stability, wireless integration, and intelligent closed-loop systems and outline future directions involving AI-driven design combined with 3D biomanufacturing.

Article.Authors: Pipatvoratam S.; Boorapha P.; Chinarak K.; Kumnerdsiri P.; Kitsanayanyong L.; Uchuwittayakul A.; Pongsetkul J.; Sai-ut S.; Rawdkuen S.; Kingwascharapong P.
Article.Abstract: This study aimed to optimize the synthesis of chitosan-derived carbon dots (CS-CDs) and incorporate them into gelatin capsule waste/Gum Arabic (Gel/GA) composite films for sustainable active packaging of minced fish. CS-CDs were synthesized hydrothermally at 180, 200, and 220 °C for 4, 5, and 6 h. The optimized CS-CDs were incorporated into Gel/GA films at 0–2% (w/v), significantly increasing tensile strength from 2.20 to 4.19 MPa and improving water resistance (p < 0.05). Antioxidant and antimicrobial activities increased with CS-CD concentration. Gel/GA/CD-2 exhibited the best overall performance and effectively preserved minced fish at room temperature for up to 48 h by reducing microbial growth and lipid oxidation. Overall, integrating CS-CDs with upcycled gelatin capsule waste provides a promising approach for developing multifunctional biodegradable active packaging with enhanced mechanical, antioxidant and antimicrobial properties for seafood preservation.

Article.Title: When Can a Computed Pt(II) Substitution Rate Be Trusted? A DFT Framework with Four Reliability Diagnostics Applied to Cisplatin
Article.Authors: Spiegel M.; Mączyński M.
Article.Abstract: This study presents a DFT protocol for the substitution kinetics of Pt(II) complexes, applied to cisplatin as a case study. We aim to demonstrate that a computed barrier that agrees with experiment does not, by itself, validate the kinetic model, and that further diagnostics are required to assess the reliability of the results. M06-2X/x2c-TZVPall calculations with implicit solvation, explicit treatment of one coordinating water molecule and a set of physical corrections were used to study the aquation, thiolation (with a capped cysteine-thiolate model) and guanine substitution (by 9-methylguanine) pathways. The calculated precomplex-to-transition-state barrier for the first aquation is 2.0 kcal⋅mol−1 below the Eyring barrier inferred from experiment; with the symmetry factor σ = 2 applied, the calculated observed rate constant is 56-fold higher than the experimental value. The formal low-concentration second-order coefficient for thiolation exceeds the reported glutathione rate coefficient by 1.5–1.8 log units, whereas omission of the physical corrections shifts the calculated rate predictions by about 5–8 log units. A direct selectivity descriptor (Sdirect) is introduced and shown to be governed by the precomplex term rather than by the activation step, making it vulnerable to precomplex overstabilization by the implicit solvent. Four diagnostics are proposed that should accompany any computed rate constant or selectivity: the sign of the precomplex free energy, the magnitude of Kpre, the proximity to the diffusion limit, and the decomposition of selectivity into precomplex and activation contributions. These provide a systematic basis for assessing the reliability of computed predictions.

Article.Title: scLAP: A Liver-Adapted Contrastive Shared-Latent Framework for Pseudo-Pairing Single-Cell Transcriptomes and Chromatin Accessibility Profiles
Article.Authors: Li H.; Wang J.; Yang H.
Article.Abstract: Matched single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (scATAC-seq) profiles from the same cells remain limited in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), hindering cell-resolved integration of transcriptional programs and regulatory chromatin states. To address this challenge, we developed single-cell Liver-adapted Alignment and Pseudo-pairing (scLAP), a liver-adapted contrastive shared-latent framework for cross-study RNA-ATAC pseudo-pairing. scLAP was trained on a paired liver single-nucleus multiome reference using 2000 highly variable RNA features and 697 ATAC features, including 647 transcription factor motif activity scores and 50 latent semantic indexing components. On a prespecified cell-level test partition (n = 3235), scLAP achieved an ATAC-to-RNA Top 10 exact-pair retrieval rate of 21.48% and a mean fraction of samples closer than the true match (FOSCTTM) of 0.0431. In six leave-one-sample-out folds, the corresponding macro means were 5.23% and 0.2278, respectively, indicating above-random ranking but limited exact-pair transfer to unseen samples. A validation-selected scButterfly configuration using 20,000 native ATAC peaks achieved 8.93% Top 10 retrieval and a mean FOSCTTM of 0.0811 on the same test cells; comparisons with Con-AAE and scMODAL remained study-specific adaptations. Applying reciprocal retrieval, a validation-derived cosine-similarity threshold, and greedy one-to-one assignment to independent HCC datasets yielded 4007 similarity-filtered candidate RNA-ATAC pseudo-pairs. Downstream analyses identified an NRCAM-associated accessibility candidate and separate exploratory MET-, CAV1-, and AP-1-associated observations.

Article.Authors: Belysheva T.; Nasedkina T.; Zelenova E.; Semenova V.; Sparber P.; Sharapova E.; Sofronov D.; Dorofeeva M.; Bozhko O.; Vishnevskaya Y.; Kletskaya I.; Mikhaylova S.; Valiev T.; Petenko N.; Orlova K.; Samoilenko I.; Varfolomeeva S.
Article.Abstract: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) and Cockayne syndrome (CS) are rare autosomal recessive DNA repair disorders. XP is characterized by extreme sensitivity to UV radiation and a very high risk of skin cancer. To date, little is known about the clinical characteristics and genetic basis of these diseases in Russia. Here, we present a detailed study of 14 patients (aged 6–30 years) from 11 unrelated families of diverse ethnic backgrounds. Using a multigene panel or whole-genome sequencing, we identified patients with homozygous or compound heterozygous variants in XPC (n = 8), XPA (n = 4), DDB2 (n = 1), and ERCC6 (n = 1). Skin cancer was revealed in 100% of the 13 XP patients; the median age at first manifestation was 13 years (range 5–23). Basal cell carcinoma (BCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), and melanoma developed in 10, 7, and 3 patients, respectively. All three cancer types occurred in two patients. The patients underwent surgical treatment; additionally, two patients with BCC received targeted therapy (vismodegib, sonidegib). Anti-PD-1 immunotherapy was administered successfully in three patients with multiple or advanced skin tumors.

Article.Title: HSF/HSP Networks and Environmental Memory: From Molecular Persistence to a Recovery-Associated State
Article.Authors: De Caroli M.; Perrotta C.; Rampino P.
Article.Abstract: Plants encounter environmental stresses in sequences of exposure, recovery, and subsequent challenge. Persistent molecular changes alone do not establish how previous exposure influences later responsiveness. Sustained protection may contribute to memory, whereas unresolved physiological disturbance can complicate its interpretation. The heat shock factor/heat shock protein (HSF/HSP) system links transcriptional regulation with protein folding, quality control, and recovery, providing a framework for examining these distinctions. We assess evidence for HSF/HSP-dependent environmental memory through its temporal organisation. Recurrent heat provides the strongest causal evidence, implicating HSF activity, transcriptional and chromatin regulation, chaperone persistence, and protein turnover in distinct aspects of thermomemory. Broader stress histories reveal altered subsequent responses, but causal HSF/HSP involvement remains less clearly resolved. We define experimental criteria for characterising recovery, demonstrating history-dependent functional responses, and identifying when candidate processes contribute causally. We then propose a recovery-associated state as a heuristic working model, rather than a demonstrated discrete cellular entity, to examine how previous exposure changes the configuration of regulatory and proteostatic processes during recovery. Persistent protective components, altered relationships among processes, or consequences outlasting the initiating molecular change may shape the later response. This framework guides experiments across stress sequences and species while distinguishing established thermomemory mechanisms from hypotheses about broader environmental memory.

Article.Title: Human Organoids in Radiation Research: Modeling Tissue Injury, Regeneration and Therapeutic Response
Article.Authors: Hao X.; Li Z.; Wang S.
Article.Abstract: Radiation therapy is a cornerstone in the treatment of abdominal, pelvic, thoracic, head and neck and central nervous system malignancies. However, irradiation inevitably damages adjacent normal tissues, leading to radiation-induced enteritis, lung injury, cardiac injury, salivary gland dysfunction and brain injury, which compromise both quality of life and treatment outcomes. Traditional two-dimensional cell cultures and animal models have significant limitations in mimicking human tissue radiation responses: the former lacks three-dimensional architecture and cell–cell interactions, while the latter exhibits species-specific differences. In recent years, three-dimensional organoid technology has rapidly emerged as a powerful platform in radiation biology and radiation oncology. In particular, organoids derived from patient tissues or induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) offer key advantages, including self-organization capacity and near-physiological tissue structure and function, which have greatly advanced in-depth research in the radiation field. This review comprehensively summarizes applications of human organoids in radiation injury and regeneration research across the brain, heart, lung, esophagus, salivary gland, intestine, muscle, thyroid, hematopoietic system, and tumors. Animal-derived and organotypic models are included only as comparative or supporting mechanistic evidence and are explicitly identified as such. We focus on advances in modeling radiation injury, elucidating regenerative mechanisms, screening radioprotective and radiosensitizing agents and predicting patient responses to chemoradiation. Current limitations and future directions are discussed collectively at the end.

Article.Title: Single-Cell RNA Sequencing of Human Lamina Cribrosa Fibroblasts in Glaucoma
Article.Authors: Normile C.; Irnaten M.; Cappa O.; Zhernovkov V.; O’Callaghan J.; Moran B.; Culligan E.; Feris S.; Curry S.; Clark A.; Simpson D.; O’Brien C.
Article.Abstract: The molecular mechanisms that underlie the extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling of the human lamina cribrosa (LC) in glaucoma remain obscure. This is the first study to characterise human glaucomatous LC cells using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). Our aim is to characterise transcriptional changes in human LC cells from glaucomatous and normal eyes and identify signalling pathways contributing to optic nerve head remodelling. scRNA-seq was performed on LC cells from glaucomatous and normal donor eyes. Differential gene expression was analysed using Seurat. Cell identity was assessed using SingleR and GTEx reference datasets. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), and transcription factor (TF) motif enrichment was evaluated using i-cisTarget. Validation was performed using quantitative PCR, Western blotting, immunohistochemistry, and immunofluorescence. LC cells were treated with ISRIB and 4-PBA. Analysis of 6131 LC cells using shared nearest-neighbour clustering and UMAP visualisation identified four broad transcriptional groups, which were used for subsequent transcriptional characterisation. Cell type mapping identified a fibroblast/mesenchymal cell origin. Glaucomatous LC fibroblasts demonstrated a pro-fibrotic transcriptional profile, with overexpression of multiple pro-fibrotic genes, master TF regulons involved in cell fate decisions, and TF motifs including SRF, as well as key integrated stress response (ISR) genes such as ATF4, ATF3 and CREB3L1. Enriched pathways included E2F, G2M, the Hallmark EMT gene set and MYC, while the p53 pathway was downregulated. Pharmacologic treatment with ISRIB or 4-PBA reduced expression of stress-response and ECM genes, while ISRIB attenuated the increased cellular metabolic activity observed in glaucomatous LC cells. Bioinformatic analysis of scRNA-seq of human glaucoma LC cells identified increased expression of myofibroblast genes, an EMT-associated/profibrotic transcriptional programme, and cell cycle signalling pathways, TF regulatory elements and stress response genes.

Article.Title: Effects of BL Exposure on Circadian Rhythms and Rhythm-Related Disorders
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Pei X.; Ge C.; Chen J.; Xu J.; Wu J.; Lu H.; Xu L.; Weng H.; Chen X.; Deng L.; Xu H.
Article.Abstract: Circadian rhythms represent a core physiological mechanism sustaining human physiological homeostasis and normal bodily function. Environmental light serves as a primary exogenous zeitgeber for circadian regulation. Among visible light spectral components, BL (BL) exerts a critical modulatory influence on the circadian system, with dual implications for physiological regulation and clinical intervention: excessive or inappropriately timed exposure may lead to circadian disruption, whereas appropriately timed BL interventions show potential to improve circadian alignment in selected populations. Accumulated evidence indicates that circadian disruption is associated with sleep disorders, mood disturbances, neurodegenerative disorders, as well as metabolic and immune dysfunction, and may have bidirectional relationships with disease progression. Nevertheless, most existing studies concentrate on circadian modulation by broad-spectrum light. Few efforts have synthesized the molecular mechanisms, potential disease-related pathways, and targeted intervention frameworks of BL-associated circadian disruption, and the translational potential of BL’s bidirectional effects remains under-summarized, forming a prominent research gap. To fill this gap, this narrative review centers on the “BL-circadian rhythm-disease” regulatory axis. It outlines biological pathways in which circadian disruption may be implicated in multiple neurodegenerative disorders, highlights the circadian-modulating properties of BL, describes evidence linking inappropriate BL exposure to circadian disruption and disease onset or progression, and compiles clinical findings on BL-based interventions and their potential benefits for circadian function and selected disease-related symptoms. However, much of the evidence derives from observational studies and animal experiments, and a causal pathway linking BL exposure to disease through circadian disruption has not been definitively established. This review discusses the potential adverse and beneficial effects of BL in circadian disruption-related pathologies, addresses current research limitations, and offers theoretical references and fresh insights for mechanistic investigations, clinical research, and translational development of BL-targeted interventions.

Article.Title: Prospective Proteomic Associations with Incident Type 2 Diabetes and Responses to Metabolic Stress in Women with and Without Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome
Article.Authors: Darwish R.; Sathyapalan T.; Dempsey L.; Abdalla M.; Butler A.; Atkin S.
Article.Abstract: Women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) have heterogeneous metabolic risk. We investigated whether targeted circulating proteins were associated with incident type 2 diabetes (T2D) and whether the retained proteins responded to experimentally induced lipid stress. In Cohort 1, 231 women with (n = 135) or without (n = 96) PMOS had T2D outcome data, of whom 25 developed T2D during a median follow-up of 12.7 years (range 10.2–15.1); 221 women (20 incident cases) had complete covariate data for adjusted analyses. Of 44 available proteins, 27 were prespecified from prior literature; following Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment, eight biomarkers (Adiponectin (ADIPOQ), Endocan (ESM1), Mast/stem cell growth factor receptor-Kit (KIT), Chordin Like 1 (CHRDL1), Cell Adhesion Molecule L1 Like (CHL1), Cathepsin V (CTSV), L1 Cell Adhesion Molecule (L1CAM) and Delta Like Canonical Notch Ligand 4 (DLL4)) had a statistically significant association with T2D in univariate models. However, following adjustment for group, body mass index (BMI) and age, only ADIPOQ remained statistically significant. In Firth penalised logistic regression adjusted for PMOS status, age and BMI, each 1 SD higher ADIPOQ was associated with lower odds of incident T2D (OR 0.12; 95% CI 0.04–0.31); the association persisted when events were restricted to a common 10-year follow-up horizon, after adjustment for baseline fasting glucose, and after excluding women with baseline fasting glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L. Adding ADIPOQ to PMOS status, age and BMI increased the bootstrap optimism-corrected AUC from 0.74 to 0.87. In an independent experimental cohort (PMOS, n = 11; controls, n = 9, with SOMAscan data), ADIPOQ, neural cell adhesion molecule L1-like protein (CHL1), mast/stem cell growth factor receptor-Kit (KIT), chordin-like protein 1 (CHRDL1) and neural cell adhesion molecule L1 (L1CAM) were measured at 0, 180 and 300 min of 5 h saline and Intralipid infusions and analysed using linear mixed-effects models. Relative to saline, Intralipid lowered L1CAM, CHL1 and KIT at 180 min (differences in change from baseline −0.33, −0.30 and −0.25 log2 units; FDR-adjusted p ≤ 0.029), with no evidence that responses differed between women with PMOS and controls, and no lipid-specific change in ADIPOQ was detected; only the L1CAM response persisted after excluding turbid or haemolysed samples. Lower adiponectin was the only protein independently associated with incident T2D, whereas L1CAM, and less robustly CHL1 and KIT, responded to acute lipid exposure. The small number of events, differential outcome ascertainment between groups, absence of external validation and the exploratory experimental cohort preclude claims of clinical prediction. These findings support further evaluation of prognostic and stress-responsive protein phenotypes in larger, independently validated cohorts.

Article.Title: High Temperature Triggers Systemic Necrosis and Reveals PRSV as the Primary Cause of “‘Mazi’ Watermelon”
Article.Authors: Zang Y.; Liu L.; Dou P.; Liang Z.; Geng Y.; Shi J.; Hou B.; Kang B.
Article.Abstract: Huaping County, Lijiang City, Yunnan Province, is a key production area for early-season winter watermelons. In recent years, watermelon fruits in this region have exhibited abnormal symptoms, such as protrusions and necrotic lesions on the surface, which has significantly reduced their commercial value; such fruits are known locally as “’Mazi’ watermelon”. Field symptoms included leaf mosaic, necrosis, malformation, and stem cracking, as well as epidermal protrusions and clustered necrosis. To identify the causal agents, typical diseased samples were collected from Xinzhuang Village, Huaping County, in April 2026. Systematic pathogen identification was conducted using tissue isolation, plate coating, and small RNA-seq techniques to detect fungal, bacterial, and viral pathogens. No pathogenic fungi or bacteria were isolated; however, small RNA sequencing identified the presence of papaya ringspot virus (PRSV) and zucchini tigré mosaic virus (ZTMV) in diseased plants. RT-PCR further confirmed mixed infection of PRSV and ZTMV in one sample and PRSV alone in another. Artificial inoculation experiments demonstrated that both viruses could induce mosaic and malformation symptoms in watermelon leaves, but disease manifestation was temperature-dependent. PRSV caused systemic necrosis under high temperatures (>28 °C), while ZTMV triggered mild necrosis at low temperatures (<25 °C). In greenhouse trials (22~35 °C), PRSV-inoculated plants developed stem cracking, fruit protrusions, and necrotic lesions, matching field “Mazi watermelon” symptoms. In conclusion, PRSV has been identified as the primary pathogen responsible for the “Mazi watermelon” symptoms in Huaping, and high temperature is a critical environmental factor that triggers systemic necrosis and severe fruit symptoms.

Article.Title: Pregnancy as a Stress Test for β-Cell Autoimmunity: The Autoimmune Phenotype of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
Article.Authors: Yanachkova V.; Shivarov V.; Kostadinov N.; Kirovakov Z.; Yordanov A.
Article.Abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous metabolic disorder comprising pathophysiological phenotypes that differ in their underlying mechanisms, clinical presentation and long-term outcomes. While pregnancy-induced insulin resistance remains the predominant pathogenic mechanism, a subset of women develops hyperglycemia largely because of reduced pancreatic β-cell reserve accompanied by islet autoimmunity. This autoimmune phenotype links gestational diabetes with autoimmune diabetes, but its boundaries and clinical significance remain incompletely defined. We aimed to review current knowledge of the autoimmune phenotype of GDM, with focus on immune pathophysiological mechanisms, biomarkers, clinical characteristics and implications for precision medicine, and to distinguish findings demonstrated directly in GDM from mechanisms extrapolated from type 1 diabetes (T1D). This narrative review was based on a structured PubMed/MEDLINE search from database inception through the end of October 2026, supplemented by targeted searches, manual screening of reference lists, and relevant clinical guidelines and consensus documents. Evidence obtained directly in women with GDM was considered alongside selected mechanistic literature from T1D and adult autoimmune diabetes. In some women with GDM, islet autoantibodies are associated with impaired β-cell function and an increased risk of autoimmune diabetes after delivery. The cellular mechanisms underlying these associations remain insufficiently studied in GDM. Pregnancy may act as a physiological metabolic stress test that exposes previously compensated β-cell dysfunction associated with islet autoimmunity, although its influence on the underlying autoimmune process remains uncertain. Islet autoantibodies are enriched among women with GDM, but their frequency varies widely between populations and assays and is lower after delivery than during pregnancy. The number and persistence of antibodies, particularly when combined with reduced endogenous insulin secretion, carry considerably more prognostic weight than a single positive result. Cellular immune mechanisms are well characterized in T1D but remain largely unvalidated in GDM. Recognition of the autoimmune phenotype extends the concept of GDM beyond a purely glucose-based classification. It is best viewed as a spectrum ranging from isolated seropositivity to pregnancy-unmasked autoimmune diabetes rather than as a uniform independent entity. A phenotype-oriented approach combining clinical features, autoantibody profiles and measures of β-cell function may facilitate earlier recognition of women at risk and more individualized follow-up, but universal autoantibody screening and antibody-specific treatment are not currently supported.

Article.Title: Single-Cell Transcriptomic Analysis of Rat Urethral Tissue Following Simulated Childbirth Injury and Microenergy Acoustic Pulse Therapy
Article.Authors: Lin G.; Zhao L.; Xing E.; Bai T.; Li H.; Tang Y.; Cao T.; Wang G.; Tang Y.; Lue T.
Article.Abstract: Microenergy acoustic pulse (MAP) therapy has been associated with functional and structural improvement after childbirth-related urethral injury, but its multicellular effects remain incompletely defined. We explored treatment- and injury-associated differences in the urethral microenvironment using single-cell RNA sequencing. Eight female Sprague–Dawley rats were assigned to sham, vaginal balloon dilation plus ovariectomy (VBDO), VBDO plus beta-aminopropionitrile (BAPN), or VBDO plus BAPN and MAP (MAP) groups, with one 24-week-old and one 48-week-old rat per group. Urethral tissues were analyzed for cell composition, differential gene expression, Gene Ontology enrichment, stem/progenitor features, senescence-associated secretory phenotype activity, and CellChat-inferred intercellular communication. A balanced single-cell dataset comprising 23,128 cells was used for downstream comparative analyses and resolved 19 annotated cell-type/state categories. Across the injury- and age-associated experimental conditions, epithelial, vascular, stromal, immune, and muscle compartments showed distinct transcriptional patterns, whereas MAP-treated samples showed a distinct cellular distribution; a separate histological cohort showed higher urethral muscle content. MAP-treated samples also showed differences in CellChat-inferred signaling activity in selected extracellular-matrix, adhesion, vascular, developmental, and neural/neuromuscular pathways, including fibronectin 1 (FN1), collagen (COLLAGEN), angiopoietin (ANGPT), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), Wingless/Integrated (WNT), Notch (NOTCH), reelin (RELN), Slit guidance ligand (SLIT), neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM), and neurexin (NRXN). Exploratory enrichment analysis identified treatment-associated differences in translation, oxidative metabolism, stress adaptation, synaptic-organization processes, progenitor-associated transcriptional states, and senescence-related programs. The treatment-split marker manifold approximation and projection (UMAPs) are descriptive and do not provide evidence of increased muscle-cell number; the reported difference in muscle-associated staining content derives from a separate animal-level histological analysis. Overall, the findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating and require validation in independently replicated cohorts.

Article.Title: Gut Microbiota as a Potential Modulator of Response to Biologic and Small-Molecule Therapies in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
Article.Authors: Margul K.; Krawczyk A.
Article.Abstract: The therapeutic landscape of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has expanded substantially with the development of biologic and small-molecule therapies. Nevertheless, many patients fail to respond to these treatments or experience a secondary loss of response. The mechanisms underlying treatment failure remain incompletely understood. Given the ability of gut microorganisms to modify therapeutic compounds, sustain pro-inflammatory immune activation, alter intestinal barrier function and produce bioactive metabolites, the gut microbiota may represent an important modulator of therapeutic response. To summarize current evidence on the role of the gut microbiota in response to biologic and small-molecule therapies in IBD, with particular emphasis on potential mechanisms of drug–microbiota interactions and their implications for treatment response and non-response. Accumulating evidence suggests that the gut microbiota may influence therapeutic efficacy through direct modification of drugs and indirect effects mediated by host immunity, intestinal barrier function and microbial metabolites. Microbial signatures associated with response to individual biologic therapies have been identified, although findings remain heterogeneous. Emerging evidence also indicates that non-bacterial components of the gut ecosystem may contribute to treatment response. The gut microbiota represents a biologically plausible modulator of therapeutic response in IBD. Integration of microbiome data with host genetic and immunological features may help identify biomarkers capable of predicting response to individual therapeutic agents.

Article.Title: Restoring Bioenergetics in the Traumatized Eye: The Emergence of Mitochondrial Implantation as a Treatment for Acute Ocular Injury
Article.Authors: Peveri E.; Beiner D.; Huang A.; Ma J.; Asthana A.; Atala A.; Orlando G.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: Acute ocular injuries—such as chemical burns, ischemic insults, and mechanical trauma—frequently lead to irreversible vision loss by triggering rapid intracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) depletion, mitochondrial calcium overload, severe oxidative stress, and profound mitochondrial dysfunction. Current clinical management primarily focuses on suppressing inflammation and preventing secondary infection, but it fails to address the underlying bioenergetic collapse that drives cellular degeneration. While stem cell and extracellular vesicle therapies have been widely investigated, direct mitochondrial transplantation has recently emerged as a novel strategy for metabolic rescue. This review evaluates the therapeutic potential of exogenously administered mitochondria to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and acute trauma in the eye. Emerging preclinical studies demonstrate that transplanted mitochondria can be internalized by selected ocular cell types, conferring short-term cytoprotection, preserving retinal ganglion cell viability, and accelerating corneal epithelial repair. However, robust evidence regarding long-term mitochondrial integration, functional fusion, durable metabolic rescue, and clinical efficacy remains limited. Despite critical challenges in delivery, stability, and dosing, mitochondrial transplantation represents a promising frontier in regenerative ophthalmology that directly targets bioenergetic failure to preserve vision.

Article.Title: Molecular Modeling of Isoniazid Encapsulation by β-Cyclodextrin for Drug Delivery: Molecular Dynamics, Interaction Energies, and DFT Insights
Article.Authors: Rady A.; Sidhom P.; Khanam S.; Abd El-Rahman M.; Mohamed L.; Sayed S.; Shoeib T.; Ibrahim M.
Article.Abstract: β-cyclodextrin (β-CD) plays a crucial role in advanced drug delivery processes, with potential applications in drug protection and release modulation. Therefore, the encapsulation potential of β-CD towards isoniazid (ISO) was herein comprehensively examined by performing molecular dynamics (MD) simulation with density functional theory (DFT) calculations. From an energetic perspective, the encapsulation process within the ISO⋯β-CD complex was energetically preferable, as evidenced by the negative interaction energy (Eint) values of configurations A–E. Compared to the other configurations, configuration A exhibited the most favorable Eint, reaching −41.66 kcal/mol. From FMO and TDOS analyses, a reduction in energy gap values was observed following the encapsulation process, indicating a change in the electronic structure of the ISO⋯β-CD complex. The effect of water on the encapsulation process within the ISO⋯β-CD complex was investigated. Furthermore, the potential release of ISO from β-CD was qualitatively assessed using simplified recovery-time estimates. Moreover, ISO adsorption over the β-CD surface was examined using the same approaches as the encapsulation model; however, it was energetically less favorable, with Eint values reaching only −18.42 kcal/mol. Overall, the MD-enhanced DFT results underscored the potential of β-CD as a candidate platform for ISO drug encapsulation; however, experimental validation is required to establish loading efficiency, release behavior, bioavailability, and toxicity.

Article.Title: Modulatory Effects of the Er,Cr:YSGG—Diode Laser Combination Irradiation on Human Osteoblasts—Might Be Relevant for Periapical Bone Regeneration?
Article.Authors: Ripszky A.; Kably I.; Neculau C.; Voicu Balasea B.; Melis I.; Bancu S.; Cernega A.; Radulescu R.; Pituru S.
Article.Abstract: This in vitro study evaluated how Er,Cr:YSGG irradiation at three energy levels (1, 3, and 6 J/cm2), 810 nm diode irradiation, and their combinations can influence human osteoblast viability and osteogenic activity. Human osteoblasts (hOB) were assigned to eight groups: control, diode, Er,Cr:YSGG at 1, 3, and 6 J/cm2, and each Er,Cr:YSGG dose followed immediately by diode irradiation. 24 h after irradiation, metabolic activity (MTT), membrane integrity (LDH), nitric oxide (NO) production, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity were assessed, and cell morphology was tracked by holographic live-cell imaging. Cell viability and membrane integrity were preserved across all protocols (MTT p = 0.325; LDH p = 0.057; both n.s.), and live-cell imaging showed osteoblast morphology and proliferation. Diode irradiation significantly increased ALP activity versus control (12.96 vs. 5.40 IU/L; p = 0.011), confirming a biostimulatory osteogenic effect, whereas Er,Cr:YSGG at 6 J/cm2 almost completely suppressed ALP activity (0.42 IU/L; p < 0.001 vs. diode). Both Er,Cr:YSGG 3 J + diode and 6 J + diode combinations significantly attenuated the diode-induced ALP increase and NO elevation in a dose-dependent manner. No protocol was cytotoxic. The 810 nm diode laser was the most osteogenically favorable condition, whereas higher-energy Er,Cr:YSGG irradiation suppressed ALP activity and, when combined with the diode, attenuated its osteogenic effect.

Article.Title: From Thermosensing to Reproduction: Plant Responses to Elevated Temperature
Article.Authors: He F.; Chen W.; Wu J.; Fang C.; Li S.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: High temperatures threaten plant productivity and survival worldwide. Plants respond to warming across their life cycle, but the effects of elevated temperature depend on its intensity, duration, and rate of change, and the developmental and environmental context in which it is experienced. Here, we synthesize current knowledge of temperature sensing and developmental responses from seed germination through plant architectural acclimation, floral transition, and reproduction. We distinguish thermomorphogenesis under moderately elevated ambient temperatures from heat-stress responses that protect cellular and developmental integrity under more severe conditions, while emphasizing their mechanistic overlap. Across these stages, we highlight how temperature responses are shaped by organ identity, species, genotype, and photoperiod, and discuss the trade-offs that must be resolved to translate developmental plasticity into heat-resilient crop production.

Article.Title: New Advances and Current Trends in Bioavailability of Coffee and Coffee By-Product Constituents and Their Metabolites: A Review
Article.Authors: Nemzer B.; Al-Taher F.; Abshiru N.; de Mejia E.
Article.Abstract: Coffee is one of the most widely consumed beverages worldwide, yet understanding how its bioactive compounds are absorbed and exert health effects remains incomplete. The objective and scope of this review is to critically summarize current advances in coffee bioavailability research, identify major limitations, and highlight emerging research trends. Recent research has advanced in three core areas. First, genetic stratification has moved the field beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by genotyping for key polymorphisms to explain inter-individual variability. Second, advanced metabolomics, including targeted and untargeted LC-MS/MS and multi-omics integration, has provided comprehensive views of phenolic absorption and bioavailability. Third, rigorous intervention designs, including randomized crossover trials and large prospective cohorts with detailed exposure assessment, have improved causal inference. Despite these advances, major limitations persist. Many studies lack sufficient statistical power to detect gene-treatment interactions. The clinical relevance of discovered metabolites is often not established. Observational cohorts remain susceptible to residual confounding, and the field lacks a standardized food matrix for cross-study comparisons. Key strategies to improve the bioavailability of coffee and its by-products were proposed, including novel delivery systems for coffee phytochemicals, human clinical trials involving encapsulated coffee bioactive compounds, and exploring coffee by-products as novel bioactive sources.

Article.Title: ADAM-10 Is Involved in Osteoblast Mineralization and Rheumatoid Arthritis-Associated Bone Destruction
Article.Authors: Nakamura H.; Kojima H.; Maeda K.; Sakurai K.; Tanioka T.; Ishii S.; Wakabayashi K.; Hosonuma M.; Azetsu Y.; Iyoda M.; Takami M.; Isozaki T.
Article.Abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a chronic autoimmune condition, causes irreversible bone destruction. A disintegrin and metalloprotease 10 (ADAM-10) has been implicated in inflammatory processes in RA. We investigated the potential role of ADAM-10 in osteoblast mineralization and RA-associated bone destruction. Serum ADAM-10 levels in RA patients were measured by ELISA, and ADAM-10 expression in osteoblasts was assessed by Western blotting. Collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mice were treated intraperitoneally with the ADAM-10 inhibitor GI254023X (100 mg/kg) for three weeks. Arthritis and bone destruction were evaluated by macroscopic, immunohistochemical, histological, and micro-CT analyses. The effects of ADAM-10 inhibition on primary osteoblast mineralization were also assessed by Alizarin Red S staining. Serum ADAM-10 levels in patients with RA tended to be higher at Stage III of the Steinbrocker classification. In CIA mice, ADAM-10 inhibition attenuated weight loss, paw swelling, and arthritis scores and suppressed bone destruction. ADAM-10 inhibition also significantly reduced Rankl expression in knee joints. Furthermore, the inhibition reversed the suppression of primary osteoblast mineralization induced by TNF-α. Pharmacological inhibition of ADAM-10 attenuated experimental arthritis and bone destruction and improved osteoblast mineralization, suggesting that ADAM-10 may contribute to inflammatory bone destruction in RA.

Article.Title: FOXM1 Targets TRIM59 to Activate Wnt/β-Catenin in Tumor Stemness and Hepatoblastoma Metastasis
Article.Authors: Yan H.; Liu W.; Jia W.; Huang J.; Xu W.; Fu Z.; Zheng B.; Yu H.; Chen X.; Gao Y.; Tian D.
Article.Abstract: Hepatoblastoma is the most common liver malignancy in children. Approximately 20% of patients present metastasis at diagnosis and have a dismal prognosis. However, the molecular mechanisms and targeted therapeutic strategies remain limited. Integrated analysis of GSE151347, GSE133039, GSE131329 and GSE75271 datasets, incorporating the mRNA expression-based stemness index, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, ChEA3 and TRRUST databases, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and differential expression analysis, identified forkhead box protein M1 (FOXM1) as a key transcription factor significantly correlated with metastatic hepatoblastoma and poor clinical outcomes. In HuH6 and HepG2 cells, FOXM1 promoted stem cell-like phenotype, migration, invasion and epithelial–mesenchymal transition. In vivo, FOXM1 promoted tumor growth in a subcutaneous xenograft model and lung colonization in a tail-vein injection model. The CUT&Tag sequencing revealed that FOXM1 occupied the tripartite motif containing 59 (TRIM59) promoter, and dual-luciferase reporter assays confirmed that FOXM1 transcriptionally activated TRIM59. Furthermore, FOXM1 gain- and loss-of-function were accompanied by changes in axis inhibition protein 1 (AXIN1) protein levels, β-catenin levels, and β-catenin nuclear translocation, potentially contributing to the regulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Finally, TRIM59 knockdown successfully rescued FOXM1-driven malignant phenotypes. This study identifies a novel FOXM1/TRIM59/Wnt signaling axis that drives hepatoblastoma metastasis, highlighting FOXM1 and TRIM59 as promising therapeutic targets for high-risk patients.

Article.Title: Genetic Associations with Type 2 Diabetes Differ According to Metabolic Contexts Defined by Insulin Resistance and Visceral Adiposity
Article.Authors: Shine B.; Hong K.; Choi J.; Kim B.; Kwon Y.; Jeong I.
Article.Abstract: Stratifying populations based on indicators of insulin resistance and visceral adiposity may help identify genetic associations with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) that vary across metabolic environments. This study aimed to investigate metabolic context-dependent genetic associations with T2DM using the metabolic score for insulin resistance (METS-IR) and visceral fat (METS-VF). A total of 70,583 and 70,513 participants were eligible for METS-IR and METS-VF stratification, respectively. After excluding participants with missing diabetes status, the final case–control samples comprised 40,970 and 40,944 participants, respectively. Genome-wide association studies of prevalent T2DM were conducted within metabolic tertiles, with additional evaluation of lead variants in the intermediate tertile (T2). Logistic regression under an additive genetic model was performed, followed by genotype × metabolic stratum interaction analyses and Cochran’s Q heterogeneity tests. Twelve notable loci were identified, showing both shared and varying association patterns across metabolic strata. CDKAL1 showed robust associations across metabolic strata, with progressively attenuated effect sizes from T1 to T3 and significant interaction results under both METS-VF and METS-IR stratifications. PAX4, CPEB3, and HHEX also demonstrated stronger associations in metabolically favorable groups, supported by nominally significant interaction and heterogeneity tests. CDKN2A/B showed associations across metabolic strata, with evidence of differences in genetic effects. KCNQ1 exhibited broadly consistent associations, although evidence of interaction varied by metabolic index. CNNM2, HNF1B, HNF4A, SLC30A8, and DNAJC5B–TRIM55 displayed subgroup-dependent patterns of statistical significance, which did not uniformly correspond to significant interaction effects. ALDH2 showed distinct association patterns across metabolic strata and between men and women. These findings suggest that genetic associations with T2DM may vary according to metabolic context, although subgroup-specific genome-wide significance does not necessarily establish differential genetic effects. Formal interaction and heterogeneity analyses provide additional evidence for metabolic effect modification at selected loci, suggesting that metabolic stratification may help characterize variation in genetic associations with T2DM in the Korean population.

Article.Title: Novel Chlorin Derivatives with a Modified Exocycle E: A Study of Spectral and Biological Properties
Article.Authors: Pogorilyy V.; Kartava J.; Tandare T.; Shchelkova V.; Suvorov N.; Vasil’ev Y.; Dydykin S.; Varga I.; Grin M.
Article.Abstract: For the first time, new natural chlorin derivatives containing tetrahydropyridine and thioimide exocycles have been synthesized. The spectral characteristics of the synthesized compounds were studied: for the thioimide, a bathochromic displacement of the long-wave absorption maximum (by 33 nm) is shown, and the tetrahydropyridine derivative has a hypsochromic displacement of the Q2-band (by 52 nm) compared to the original purpurinimide. For the resulting sulfur-containing derivative, an increase in the quantum yield of singlet oxygen generation with almost complete fluorescence quenching was found, while for the tetrahydropyridine, singlet oxygen generation was reduced by half, while fluorescence increased five-fold.
