Article.Title: Hypoxia Alters Polymeric Immunoglobulin Receptor Expression and Cell Differentiation in the Airway Epithelium
Article.Authors: Gerard L.; Lecocq M.; Detry B.; Bouzin C.; Hoton D.; Carlier F.; Plante-Bordeneuve T.; Gohy S.; Lacroix V.; Pilette C.
Article.Abstract: Secretion of immunoglobulin A (IgA), actively transported across the airway epithelium (AE) by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor (pIgR), represents a key defense of the lung against pathogens. Dysregulation of the IgA/pIgR system has been reported in respiratory diseases, but the underlying mechanism, and particularly the effects of hypoxia, remains poorly characterized. The effects of hypoxia were investigated using the model of human AE reconstituted in vitro upon culture in the air/liquid interface (ALI). AE was exposed to 1% O2, upon resting or inflammatory conditions. Mechanistic studies included pharmacological stabilization of HIF-1α and inhibition of TGF-β signaling. Additionally, HIF-1α and TGF-β pathways were analyzed by multiplex fluorescence immunostaining of lung tissue from patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and controls. In ALI AE cultures from 22 subjects, hypoxia significantly reduced pIgR expression (mRNA and proteic), regardless of inflammation. Hypoxia also altered AE structure and cell differentiation, leading to a loss of ciliated and goblet cells. Both hypoxia and pharmacological stabilization of HIF-1α recapitulated these effects and induced increased TGF-β2 expression. In lung tissue from ARDS patients, the AE exhibited reduced pIgR expression, associated with increased HIF-1α stabilization and TGF-β2 expression. Hypoxia induced pIgR downregulation and impaired cell differentiation, through HIF-1α stabilization and subsequent autocrine TGF-β2 signaling, providing a novel pathway underlying altered lung IgA immunity in disease.

Article.Title: Photoacoustic Brain Imaging in Mice
Article.Authors: Wang M.; Wang Z.; Li Y.; Wang Z.; Ma Q.; Xu G.; Yang S.; Tang Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Photoacoustic brain imaging (PABI) has emerged as a promising modality that partially overcomes the trade-off between spatial resolution and penetration depth in conventional neuroimaging. By integrating optical absorption contrast with ultrasonic detection, PABI enables high-resolution visualization of cerebral vasculature and supports multi-parametric analysis of vascular morphological features, as well as quantitative assessment of functional oxygenation parameters such as cerebral oxygen saturation (sO 2 ). In addition, PABI combined with exogenous tracers provides opportunities to evaluate blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability and track brain lymphatic drainage dynamics. Here, we present a standardized and reproducible workflow for PABI, covering system calibration, animal preparation, experimental procedures, image acquisition, and quantitative analysis. This protocol consists of a basic imaging procedure and several optional modules, providing a practical methodological tool for applying PABI to neuroscience research.

Article.Title: Transcriptional Patterns of Disruption in Structure–Function Coupling in First-episode, Drug-naive Major Depressive Disorder
Article.Authors: Guo M.; Zhu R.; Zhang H.; Wang W.; Huang Y.; Diao Y.; Li Z.; Zhang X.; Zhou J.; Ning Y.; Song Y.; Liu X.; Wu F.; Wu K.
Article.Abstract: First-episode major depressive disorder (FEMDD) is associated with alterations in macroscale brain organization, which may involve changes in brain structure-function coupling (SFC). Whether alterations in SFC affect the emergence of depression and how they correlate with gene expression remain unclear. Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data were collected from 95 healthy controls and 124 patients with FEMDD. We applied SFC analysis to calculate the structural decoupling index (SDI) and to quantify SFC in the two groups. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between alterations in SDI and gene expression. The FEMDD group showed a significantly lower SDI in the inferior frontal gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala, medial orbital gyrus, pregenual anterior cingulate cortex, and lateral occipital cortex (LOcC), whereas a significantly higher SDI was observed in the inferior temporal gyrus, lateral superior frontal gyrus, medial precuneus, and hypergranular insula than in the healthy control group. The speed of processing and working memory scores of the Measurement and Treatment Research to Improve Cognition in Schizophrenia (MATRICS) Consensus Cognitive Battery negatively correlated with the LOcC SDI in the FEMDD group. Additionally, changes in FEMDD-related SDI were associated with the expression of genes involved in synaptic signaling and neuronal development. These findings reveal regional- and network-level alterations in structure-function coupling in patients with FEMDD, providing new insights into the neurobiological underpinnings and promising neuroimaging markers for the prediction of FEMDD.

Article.Title: Brainstem Circuits Engaged During REM Sleep Regulate Apnea Susceptibility
Article.Authors: Li X.; Li P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Breathing is dynamically regulated across sleep–wake states. However, how brainstem circuits support respiratory output during sleep, particularly during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, remains unclear. Here, we show that neurons in the preBötzinger Complex (preBötC), a core inspiratory rhythm generator, selectively exhibit elevated calcium activity during REM sleep. Inhibition of these neurons selectively increases apnea occurrence during REM sleep. Optogenetic activation produces state-dependent effects, inducing prolonged apnea during REM sleep and increasing the breathing rate during wakefulness. We further identify an upstream lateral parabrachial nucleus (LPBN) projection to the preBötC that showed related state-dependent effects. Inhibition of these preBötC-projecting LPBN neurons increases apnea susceptibility during REM sleep, whereas activation induces prolonged apnea during REM sleep. Together, our findings identify REM-engaged preBötC neurons and LPBN–preBötC projection-defined neurons, whose perturbation preferentially disrupts breathing during REM sleep. This state-dependent vulnerability may provide insights into the mechanisms that contribute to sleep-related respiratory disorders.

Article.Title: Hearing Loss Caused by Chronic Kidney Disease: Evidence of Cochlear Metabolic Disturbances
Article.Authors: Zheng S.; Liu H.; Bai Y.; Ni G.
Article.Abstract: Hearing loss affects over 1.5 billion people worldwide. Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at an increased risk of sensorineural hearing impairment, although the mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Using an adenine-induced mouse model, we evaluated auditory function, cochlear pathology, and metabolism. The mice exhibited significant hearing loss, marked atrophy of the stria vascularis in the middle and basal turns of the cochlea, and pronounced oxidative stress. Metabolomic profiling identified substantial disruptions in cochlear amino acid and lipid metabolism, with concordant metabolic abnormalities in the serum and kidneys. Notably, the uremic toxin, p-cresyl sulfate, was significantly elevated in the cochlea. Overall, CKD induced metabolic disturbances and disrupted tight junction integrity, which may facilitate cochlear accumulation of uremic toxins, trigger oxidative stress, and contribute to hearing loss. These findings provide novel insights into CKD-associated hearing loss and identify potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

Article.Title: Genetic Susceptibility, Neurodevelopmental Abnormalities, and Neuroimmune Interactions Across Major Psychiatric Disorders
Article.Authors: Lu Z.; Gao Y.; Liu B.; Wu Y.; Li T.; Wang Q.; Qi H.; Ma X.; Yue W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Major psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, and autism spectrum disorder, share overlapping genetic, neurodevelopmental, and neuroimmune underpinnings that challenge traditional diagnostic boundaries. This review synthesizes evidence across three interconnected domains: convergent genetic risk affecting synaptic and immune pathways, neurodevelopmental vulnerabilities shaped by early-life insults, and neuroimmune crosstalk involving blood–brain barrier dysfunction, sustained inflammation, and complement-mediated pathology. We propose a multidimensional developmental–immune framework in which genetic liability, environmental exposure timing, and peripheral immune status jointly shape transdiagnostic trajectories. This framework reframes psychiatric disorders as dynamic interactions among stable trait-like susceptibilities and fluctuating biological states, offering a roadmap for biomarker-driven stratification and early immune-targeted interventions.

Article.Authors: Wang M.; Wan J.; Gong C.; Chai R.; Li X.; Bi Z.
Article.Abstract: This review centers on the transcription factor Atoh1 (Atonal homolog 1, also known as Math1) and its pivotal regulatory role in the development and regeneration of inner ear hair cells (HCs). It systematically elucidates the activation mechanisms of Atoh1, its integrated upstream and downstream regulatory networks, and the involvement of key signaling pathways. Additionally, the review comparatively analyzes the differences in regenerative capacity between cochlear and vestibular HCs and provides a comprehensive evaluation of the research progress and existing challenges associated with various Atoh1-targeted intervention strategies. Article.Title: GABAergic Neurons in the Dorsal Raphe Nucleus Modulate Emotion Discrimination in Mice
Article.Authors: Li R.; Guo J.; Wang Y.; Xu J.; Fang S.; Huang Z.; Wang Y.; Liu R.; Wang C.; Shan Q.; Qin X.; Chen P.; Zhou J.
Article.Abstract: Accurate recognition of the emotional states of others is essential for social adaptation. The dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) contains a substantial population of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic neurons that are implicated in various social and affective behaviors; however, their role in social emotion discrimination remains unclear. In this study, we used a mouse behavioral paradigm that distinguishes conspecifics under negative (restraint stress) or positive (relief from food/water deprivation) affective states, combined with in vivo calcium recordings and chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations, to investigate the function of DRN GABAergic neurons in this process. Observer mice preferentially investigated conspecifics in both negative and positive affective states compared with naive conspecifics. This preferential investigation was accompanied by increased c-Fos expression in DRN GABAergic neurons and rapid calcium transients, specifically at the onset of sniffing bouts directed toward affectively altered, but not naive, conspecifics. Chemogenetic or optogenetic inhibition of GABAergic neurons in the DRN abolished the preferential investigation of affectively altered conspecifics. In contrast, neither chemogenetic nor optogenetic activation of these neurons disrupted the emotion discrimination performance. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that DRN GABAergic neurons are necessary for discriminating conspecifics in both negative and positive affective states and suggest their critical role in valence-independent social-emotional decision-making.

Article.Title: Age and Neuroimmune Diseases
Article.Authors: Yu Z.; Huang X.; Zhang H.; Shi F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract With the aging population accelerating, age has become a core factor influencing the clinical phenotypes, treatment responses, and prognoses of neuroimmune diseases (NDs), including those affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS). This cross-disease review summarizes the shared and specific age-related characteristics of NDs, focusing on the pathological basis of immunosenescence and neurodegeneration underlying age-related ND progression. We extract the clinical manifestations, immune and neural mechanisms of elderly ND patients, and evaluate the challenges and individualized adjustment principles of therapeutic strategies for this population. We explore the age-related immune dysregulation features between NDs and other systemic autoimmune diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), type 1 diabetes (T1D)). This review aims to construct a cross-disease framework for the precision management of NDs in the aging era, identify research gaps and future directions, and emphasize age-adapted intervention strategies for optimizing the prognosis of elderly ND patients.

Article.Title: Thrombospondin 2 Promotes Neuropathic Pain by Mediating Nav1.7 Membrane Anchoring in Mouse Primary Sensory Neurons
Article.Authors: Wei J.; Wang Y.; Zhao Z.; Chen H.; Chang S.; Yang Q.; Wang H.; Liu X.; Zhou X.; Li X.; Zhang J.; Liang L.
Article.Abstract: Thrombospondin 2 (TSP2), a member of the thrombospondin family of extracellular matrix proteins, mediates critical cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions. However, its potential roles in neuropathic pain remain unclear. We demonstrate that TSP2 is specifically expressed in isolectin B4-negative dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. Following lumbar 4 (L4) spinal nerve ligation (SNL), TSP2 expression was upregulated in both injured (L4) and uninjured (L3) DRGs. Notably, siRNA-mediated TSP2 knockdown attenuated SNL-induced pain hypersensitivity during the development phase, but not during the maintenance phase, of neuropathic pain. Conversely, neuron-specific TSP2 overexpression in the DRG alone was sufficient to produce enhanced nociceptive behavior. Mechanistically, SNL enhanced the interaction between TSP2 and Nav1.7, promoting Nav1.7 membrane anchoring in the L3 and L4 DRGs and thereby increasing DRG neuronal excitability. These findings establish TSP2 as a novel Nav1.7-interacting protein and a potential therapeutic target for preventing chronic neuropathic pain.

Article.Title: Neural Stem Cell Therapies for Central Nervous System Regeneration: Advances, Challenges, and Integrative Technologies
Article.Authors: Marei H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neural stem cells (NSCs) are promising candidates for central nervous system (CNS) regeneration because they self-renew and differentiate into neural lineages. Advances in genome engineering, extracellular vesicles (EVs), biomaterials, organoids, single-cell technologies, and precision medicine have expanded approaches for characterizing, engineering, delivering, and evaluating NSC-based therapies for neurological disorders. CRISPR/Cas9 and related platforms may enable more precise modification of NSC function, while NSC-derived EVs offer potential cell-free strategies. Engineered hydrogels and three-dimensional scaffolds may improve cell survival, engraftment, migration, and integration. Organoids and single-cell omics provide increasingly detailed models of cellular heterogeneity and lineage specification. However, clinical translation remains limited by immune compatibility, tumorigenic risk, manufacturing standardization, graft survival and integration, and regulatory requirements. Rigorous preclinical validation, standardized manufacturing, appropriately designed clinical trials, long-term safety monitoring, and harmonized regulatory frameworks are required before routine clinical application.

Article.Title: Systematic Microcircuit Reconfigurations Underlie Early Experience-induced Visual Cortical Plasticity
Article.Authors: Yao L.; Shang Z.; Ji Z.; Meng M.; Wang F.; Gu X.; He M.; Wu S.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Experience-dependent reorganization of neuronal connections during the postnatal critical period is essential for the functional maturation of the developing primary visual cortex (V1). However, the systematic reconfigurations across microcircuit synapses underlying experience-dependent plasticity are poorly defined. Using paired whole-cell recordings from excitatory pyramidal cells and three other major classes of interneurons (INs) within layers 2/3 and 4 in the developing mouse V1 monocular region, we found that monocular deprivation (MD) for one day in juvenile mice transiently reconfigures local excitatory synapses onto inhibitory INs that specifically express parvalbumin (PV) or vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). In contrast, prolonged MD predominantly strengthens inhibitory synaptic transmission from somatostatin (SST)-expressing INs to PV-INs and VIP-INs across both layers. A physiologically based microcircuit model further recapitulated MD-induced activity changes in visual responses across layer 2/3 neurons in vivo. We provide a detailed microcircuit framework that contributes to the experience-dependent regulation of visual function.

Article.Title: Transcranial Evoked Potentials are Minimally Influenced by Afferent Feedback From Peripheral Muscle Contraction
Article.Authors: Marco M.; Andrea G.; Andrea F.; Carlo P.; Giorgio L.; Rocchi L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) investigates cortical reactivity, yet the contribution of sensory feedback from muscle twitches to the recorded signals remains debated. We combined M1 TMS-EEG with electromyography, accelerometry, and peripheral electrical stimulation to dissociate central and peripheral contributions. We compared EEG responses across trials yielding large versus small motor outputs, while peripheral stimulation isolated pure afferent components. Bayesian analysis revealed that larger motor outputs covaried with distinct EEG morphologies uniformly across all time windows—including those too early for peripheral feedback—indicating that spontaneous fluctuations in baseline motor cortex excitability drive both responses. Conversely, isolated muscle contraction produced delayed (> 65 ms), markedly smaller EEG responses with distinct spatiotemporal profiles. We conclude that sensory feedback from muscle twitches contributes minimally to TMS-evoked EEG responses, which instead primarily reflect the baseline excitability state of the stimulated cortex.

Article.Title: Multimodal alterations of brain structure and function after electroconvulsive therapy in psychiatric disorders: a voxel-based meta-analysis
Article.Authors: Yu J.; Xu Q.; Ma L.; Huang Y.; Zhu W.; Liang Y.; Tang W.; Zhu C.; Jiang X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Background Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is an effective treatment for various mental disorders. Imaging studies have reported ECT-induced structural and functional alterations in multiple brain regions; however, the findings have been inconsistent. We conducted a novel multimodal meta-analysis to identify spatially convergent brain changes induced by ECT. Methods PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase were searched to screen voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and resting-state voxel-based pathophysiology (VBP) studies of ECT in psychiatric disorders. Using the activation likelihood estimation (ALE) algorithm, we compared brain changes in patients with mental disorders before and after ECT treatment, analyzing the data both independently and in pooled multimodal datasets. Results A total of 45 eligible studies, comprising 55 experiments and 1395 patients with psychiatric disorders, were included in this meta-analysis, and 23 meta-analyses were conducted. Our findings revealed that ECT induced changes in brain regions, primarily in the bilateral hippocampus, bilateral amygdala, right parahippocampal gyrus, right superior temporal pole, right anterior cingulate cortex, right insula, right lateral globus pallidus, right medial globus pallidus, and right caudate body. Conclusion ECT induces widespread but spatially convergent changes in brain structure and function, which may be associated with both therapeutic efficacy and adverse cognitive effects. The right hippocampus exhibited prominent multimodal convergence, highlighting its role as a consistent site of convergent ECT-related change. This work advances the understanding of the neurobiological substrates of ECT-induced brain alterations and informs future investigations into its underlying mechanisms.

Article.Title: Effective connectivity reveals hippocampal disruptions during conditioning and extinction are associated with adolescent anxiety
Article.Authors: Tashjian S.; Cussen J.; Steward T.; Bray K.; Ganella D.; Kim J.; Schwartz O.; Simmons J.; Zwaan I.; Whittle S.
Article.Abstract: Anxiety disorders peak during adolescence alongside rapid neural development, yet the neural mechanisms underlying adolescent threat learning remain unclear. Using fMRI and dynamic causal modeling, we mapped effective connectivity during threat conditioning and extinction in 87 adolescents (ages 11-17, M = 15.66 years; 71.26% female), focusing on the amygdala, hippocampus, and posterior ventromedial prefrontal cortex (p-vmPFC) circuit. The adolescent brain showed distinct circuit strategies for threat versus safety learning. Threat learning (CS + ) initially engaged only amygdala and p-vmPFC excitatory coupling without hippocampal involvement, while early safety learning (CS-) recruited hippocampal inhibition of amygdala and p-vmPFC. By late conditioning, bidirectional inhibitory connectivity emerged between amygdala and p-vmPFC for both stimulus types, suggesting homeostatic regulation once associations consolidated. During extinction, the network transitioned from complex mutual amygdala-hippocampus inhibition during early CS+ trials to streamlined hippocampal-prefrontal pathways by late extinction, reflecting safety consolidation. Adolescents with higher trait anxiety demonstrated stronger hippocampal to p-vmPFC connectivity during early conditioning and altered hippocampal modulation during extinction, revealing temporally dynamic disruptions in directional signaling. This study provides the first effective connectivity map of adolescent threat learning. The identification of temporally dynamic vulnerabilities has direct implications for adolescent anxiety treatment.

Article.Title: Amygdala-cingulate projection neurons promote behavioral adjustments to decreasing contextual threat
Article.Authors: Zamudio F.; Smagulova Y.; Legister J.; Schamber P.; Luo E.; Slosky C.; Ahn K.; Reijmers L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Extinction of fear memories is guided by prediction error – the discrepancy between what is expected based on prior experience and what actually occurs. Information-seeking behaviors support integration of such information. The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is well positioned to integrate prediction error information to guide behavioral adjustment and support extinction learning. This function may occur through its interaction with the basolateral amygdala (BLA), a region essential for the encoding, retrieval, and extinction of fear memories. In this study we found that, compared to the expected occurrence of aversive foot-shocks, their unexpected omission increased BLA→ACC activity. Inhibition of BLA→ACC neurons prolonged freezing and impaired fear extinction, whereas BLA→ACC activation promoted head scanning and prevented spontaneous fear recovery. Moreover, head scanning during unexpected foot-shock omission correlated with more effective extinction learning. These findings highlight a role for BLA→ACC projection neurons in re-evaluating contextual threat by promoting acute and long-term behavioral adjustments. Because the ability to integrate danger and safety information across experiences is compromised in disorders of fear dysregulation, such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), studying the BLA→ACC pathway may inform new strategies for advancing treatment.

Article.Title: The use of Mendelian randomization to explore the causal consequences of childhood maltreatment: consideration of assumptions and challenges
Article.Authors: Sum K.; Hughes A.; Havdahl A.; Davey Smith G.; Howe L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants as instrumental variables to strengthen causal inference and has been applied to study the effects of childhood maltreatment on mental health outcomes. However, interpreting MR findings for complex social exposures is challenging due to the complex causal pathways, how they are reported, and potential violations of MR assumptions. Here, we assess the feasibility of applying MR to complex social traits using the association between childhood maltreatment and mental health and behavioral outcomes as an example. We explore four key concerns: confounding by population phenomena, pleiotropy, reverse causality, and selection. For each concern, we demonstrate scenarios where MR studies of childhood maltreatment may be biased using DAGs and critical appraisal of previous MR analyses. For confounding by population phenomena, we further perform within-family genetic analyses in 42,101 parent-offspring trios from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) to address bias due to confounding by parental genotype since childhood maltreatment often occurs within households. Adjusting for parental polygenic risk scores for childhood maltreatment (PRS CM ) resulted in modest same-trait attenuation (11%) for the association between children’s PRS CM and mothers’ report of children’s physical abuse, but cross-trait associations with children’s mental health and behavioral outcomes remained unchanged. The lack of cross-trait shrinkage suggests that genetic variants associated with childhood maltreatment may capture broader child- and family-level phenotypes rather than the exposure itself. Our findings highlight the challenges of interpreting MR studies of childhood maltreatment and suggest caution when using genetic instruments for complex social exposures in psychiatric research.

Article.Title: Brain-derived multi-omics prioritization of mitochondria-related genes in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depressive disorder
Article.Authors: Li N.; Chen S.; Wang J.; Li T.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly implicated in psychiatric disorders, yet the regulatory mechanisms linking brain-expressed mitochondrial genes to disease risk remain unclear. To investigate these mechanisms, we employed an integrative multi-omics approach combining brain-derived DNA methylation, gene expression, and protein abundance quantitative trait locus (QTL) datasets to evaluate genetically predicted associations of mitochondria related molecular traits with schizophrenia (SCZ), bipolar disorder (BD), major depressive disorder (MDD), cross-disorder phenotypes, and clinical subtypes. Summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), Heterogeneity in dependent instruments (HEIDI) testing, and Bayesian colocalization analyses were applied, followed by a study-specific three-tier framework to prioritize potential putative causal genes. Our analyses prioritized ACADVL and SLC25A24 as Tier 1 genes for SCZ, COX11 as a Tier 2 gene for SCZ, and DLST, ENDOG, and PDF as Tier 3 genes for SCZ. ENDOG and PDF were also prioritized for the BD-SCZ cross-disorder phenotype. Further SMR analyses across molecular layers supported ENDOG as a methylation-linked regulatory signal, whereas expression-to-protein associations for COX11 and SLC25A24 showed colocalization support but did not meet the HEIDI criterion. Single-cell analyses suggested context-dependent ENDOG effects across immune cell types. Together, these findings support the involvement of mitochondria-related genes across molecular layers in psychiatric disorders and identify genetically supported candidate genes that warrant experimental validation.

Article.Title: DNA methylation changes associated with antipsychotic serum concentrations in patients with psychosis
Article.Authors: Villar J.; Stavrum A.; Spindola L.; Zayats T.; Tesfaye M.; Bjella T.; Steen N.; Melle I.; Andreassen O.; Steen V.; Le Hellard S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Antipsychotic drugs (AP) are widely used to treat psychotic symptoms in schizophrenia (SCZ), bipolar disorder (BD), and major depressive disorder (MDD). However, despite over 70 years of clinical use, the pharmacological mechanisms underlying AP drug action remain incompletely understood. DNA methylation (DNAm) may provide insight into epigenetic changes associated with AP exposure. We investigated DNAm associated with olanzapine, quetiapine, and risperidone and examined whether these changes were observed across multiple APs or specific to individual drugs. We analysed genome-wide DNAm levels in the blood of 263 individuals receiving AP monotherapy (n = 136, olanzapine n = 89, quetiapine n = 26, risperidone n = 21) or who were medication-free (n = 127). Associations between DNAm and serum AP concentrations were assessed individually and across all three drugs. We identified 60 CpGs ( p ≤ 9.0 × 10 −8 ) and seven differentially methylated regions (DMRs) ( p < 6.1 × 10 −8 ) associated with AP serum concentrations across the three monotherapies. Two DMRs contained CpGs exhibiting significant blood-prefrontal cortex methylation correlations. One DMR was located in the promoter region of SHANK2 , involved in glutamatergic neurotransmission, and another mapped to regulatory regions of GNB1 and NADK , involved in signal transduction and NAD + /NADP metabolism, respectively. No epigenome-wide significant DNAm changes were identified for individual APs, and none of the identified CpGs overlapped with methylation differences reported in a large SCZ case-control epigenome-wide association study. Together, these findings provide evidence for shared epigenetic correlates of AP exposure that are largely distinct from SCZ-associated methylation differences and highlight candidate pathways for investigating the downstream biological consequences of AP treatment.

Article.Title: Defensive reactivity to interoceptive perturbation in panic disorder: Depressive symptom burden and panic severity dimensions
Article.Authors: Benke C.; Alius M.; Hamm A.; Melzig C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Panic disorder (PD) is characterized by exaggerated defensive responding to panic-related somatic sensations. It remains poorly understood how greater PD and depressive symptom severity are linked to dysregulated defensive functioning and how this manifests during disorder-relevant interoceptive threat. Addressing this question is critical for elucidating pathomechanisms underlying disorder maintenance and the frequent PD–depression comorbidity. We therefore examined how depressive symptom severity and PD severity dimensions uniquely and jointly relate to defensive mobilization during interoceptive perturbation. Eighty-five treatment-seeking patients with a principal diagnosis of PD with/without agoraphobia completed a standardized 3-min hyperventilation (HV) task inducing panic-related body symptoms vs. a non-symptom-provocation control condition. Potentiation of the startle eyeblink response was assessed as a cross-species index of defensive mobilization during the 10-min post-HV phase. Defensive mobilization was modeled as a function of clinician-rated and self-reported PD severity and self-reported depressive symptom severity, complemented by exploratory network analyses of PD dimensions (e.g., avoidance), depressive symptoms, and defensive mobilization. HV reliably induced respiratory perturbation, autonomic activation, and increases in panic symptoms and anxiety. Startle responses remained persistently potentiated following HV vs. the control condition. Greater startle potentiation was associated with higher patient-reported and clinician-rated PD severity and, most strongly, with depressive symptom severity. Network models identified depressive symptoms as a robust correlate of defensive mobilization and interoceptive fear. Depressive symptom burden was uniquely associated with defensive mobilization to interoceptive perturbation beyond PD severity. These findings point to mechanisms linking panic–depression comorbidity to persistent interoceptive threat responding and may inform PD treatment optimization.

Article.Title: Exploring the brain’s response to food stimuli in anorexia nervosa: a comprehensive meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies
Article.Authors: Zurlo L.; Cecchetto C.; Gentili C.; Dal Bò E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Despite growing interest in the neural mechanisms underlying Anorexia Nervosa (AN), brain-based correlates of its core symptoms remain only partially understood. This activation likelihood estimation (ALE) meta-analysis aimed to explore brain activity during food stimuli processing among individuals with AN and those who have recovered (REC). Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched APA PsycInfo, Psychology and Behavioral Sciences Collection, EMBASE, and PubMed up to August 28, 2025. Twenty-nine publications were included, encompassing data from 532 AN, 64 REC, and 555 healthy controls (HC). Data extraction followed PRISMA guidelines and included study design, participant characteristics, task and stimulus type, imaging modality, and brain coordinates. The findings indicated significant convergence in the left Inferior Parietal Lobule (IPL) for the HC > AN + REC contrast, whereas no significant cluster emerged for the reverse contrast. Sensitivity analyses confined to studies encompassing solely visual stimuli revealed the same significant cluster for the HC > AN + REC contrast and no convergence for the reverse, suggesting that the stimulation employed does not affect food stimuli processing. Notably, when analyses were limited to studies involving AN participants only, no significant convergence emerged for either contrast. This, together with a qualitative inspection of the merged sample results (HC > AN + REC contrast), suggests that REC individuals may contribute to the observed convergence, though this interpretation should be considered cautiously. These findings are discussed in light of the role of the left IPL hypoactivation in body image disturbance, diminished somatosensory-gustatory processing related to fasting, and fear of weight gain, three core symptoms of AN.

Article.Title: Metabolite profiling insights into bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, and schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Zhu Z.; Song L.; Yin X.; Hou W.; Man L.; Chen J.; Aickelin U.; Hui L.
Article.Abstract: Accurate differentiation of bipolar disorder (BD), major depressive disorder (MDD), and schizophrenia (SCZ) is hindered by symptomatic overlap and subjective clinical assessments. This study applied untargeted plasma metabolomics to a large cohort of 1609 adults (BD, n = 352; MDD, n = 506; SCZ, n = 373; healthy controls, n = 378) diagnosed per DSM-IV criteria. Following stringent pre-processing and quality control, we identified metabolic features associated with diagnostic outcomes using mutual information analysis, a non-parametric method capturing nonlinear relationships, and further evaluated their diagnostic potential. After adjustment for sex ang age, a total of 297 metabolites correction showed significant associations with psychiatric diagnosis after FDR (p < 0.01). Adjusted sex and age predictive models—including logistic regression, LASSO, random forest, and XGBoost—trained on random subsets of these metabolites consistently achieved high classification performance, with mean accuracy exceeding 0.88 across all pairwise comparisons after FDR correction. These results reveal distinct yet overlapping metabolic alterations across disorders, suggesting shared pathophysiological mechanisms. Notably, robust and reproducible predictions were attainable even with small feature subsets, underscoring the stability of metabolomic signatures. Collectively, our findings support plasma metabolomics as an objective, biologically grounded tool to complement clinical assessment and enhance diagnostic precision in major psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: A pro-inflammatory gut microbiota-metabolic axis in global developmental delay identified by integrated multi-omics
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Wan L.; Zeng Y.; Hao J.; Li M.; Huang C.
Article.Abstract: Global developmental delay (GDD) affects 1–3% of children, yet its etiology remains undetermined in 40–50% of cases despite comprehensive genetic testing. The role of the gut-brain axis in GDD is poorly defined, partly due to prior studies’ reliance on relative microbial abundance metrics. In this hypothesis-generating pilot cross-sectional study, we applied an integrated multi-omics framework combining absolute quantitative 16S rRNA gene sequencing with untargeted metabolomics to characterize the gut ecosystem in 16 young children with GDD (aged ≤3 years) and 20 age-matched healthy controls. Absolute quantification revealed significant enrichment of a pro-inflammatory consortium in the GDD gut microbiome, most notably the Ruminococcus gnavus group (2.15-fold increase, p < 0.05). Untargeted metabolomics identified Ethyl Diethanolamine as the top discriminant metabolite, markedly depleted in the GDD group (FC = 0.73, p < 0.0001). Pathway analysis pinpointed tryptophan metabolism as the most significantly perturbed pathway ( p < 0.001), characterized by a complex, multi-directional shift involving simultaneous upregulation of kynurenine, melatonin, and microbial indole metabolites. Multi-omics integration revealed strong overall microbiota-metabolome concordance alongside GDD-specific disruptions in fine-scale correlation networks. These pilot data suggest a pro-inflammatory gut microbiota–metabolite axis in GDD, potentially driven by expansion of R. gnavus and disruption of tryptophan metabolism. Ethyl Diethanolamine depletion emerges as a novel candidate biomarker, warranting future validation in larger cohorts.

Article.Title: Animal models in psychedelic research – Tripping over translation
Article.Authors: Abd El Hay M.; Cukić A.; Schölvinck M.; Havenith M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Psychedelic substances show promise for treating psychiatric disorders including depression, anxiety, and PTSD, but the neurobiological mechanisms underlying their therapeutic effects remain poorly understood. Preclinical findings have so far been inconsistent, limiting mechanistic insights. We argue this translational gap is exacerbated by systematic disconnects between conditions thought to shape therapeutic outcomes in humans and those employed in animal research. In this review, we analyse 266 rodent psychedelic studies published between 2014 and 2026 in order to generate a systematic audit of experimental conditions and behavioural assays currently applied in the field. Specifically, we first assessed adherence to welfare practices paralleling “set and setting” factors critical to human therapy. We found that most studies contained stress-inducing factors: only a minority reported active-phase testing (14%), environmental enrichment (7%), or refined handling protocols (21%), while drug administration almost universally relied on stress-inducing, restraint-requiring methods. Second, we evaluated the capacity of behavioural assays to capture experiential dynamics, revealing that most studies rely on brief, constrained testing with isolated behavioural markers that fail to capture the multidimensional, temporally evolving nature of psychedelic states. Beyond these methodological gaps, we identify a third critical factor largely absent from preclinical research: individual differences and social context. Most animal studies use group-level, cross-sectional designs that cannot characterize heterogeneous treatment responses or social mechanisms implicated in therapeutic change. We propose that improving translation requires a fundamental reorientation: from brief testing of stressed, isolated animals toward longitudinal tracking of individuals in enriched social environments using comprehensive behavioural characterization. We end by offering practical advice on how to implement some of these considerations in animal psychedelic research.

Article.Title: A reproducible structural brain axis of alcohol use severity
Article.Authors: Wiegert J.; Oweda J.; Lenz E.; Volkmer S.; Li X.; Abas A.; Mai A.; Roetzer L.; Meinert S.; Leehr E.; Hahn T.; Flinkenflügel K.; Borgers T.; Völzke H.; Dannlowski U.; Bamberg F.; Hermesdorf M.; Karch A.; Berger K.; Klinger-König J.; Grabe H.; Pischon T.; Krist L.; Keil T.; Leitzmann M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Alcohol use is linked to distributed structural brain alterations, but population-level alcohol-related neurobiology remains difficult to quantify. We tested whether deep learning–derived MRI representations capture reproducible variation in alcohol consumption severity and converge with clinical and biological markers. Representations were extracted from gray-matter volume maps in the German National Cohort (NAKO; N ≈ 28,000). Ridge-regression scores were derived from structural MRI to estimate alcohol consumption severity, measured with the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test–Consumption (AUDIT-C). Models were trained in NAKO, externally validated in UK Biobank ( N ≈ 25,000), evaluated in FOR2107 ( N ≈ 1900), and tested against ICD-10 alcohol use disorder (AUD), alcohol-related biomarkers, and cognition. In NAKO, the structural MRI-derived ridge-regression score correlated with measured AUDIT-C severity ( r = 0.11; 95% CI, 0.09–0.12; q FDR = 1.2 × 10 −70 ; MAE = 1.64). This association replicated in UK Biobank ( r = 0.09; 95% CI, 0.07–0.10; q FDR = 4.9 × 10 −41 ; MAE = 1.96) and generalized to AUD, with higher odds in the highest versus lowest brain-score quintile (OR = 2.28; 95% CI, 1.49–3.48; q FDR = 3.9 × 10 −4 ). The score was associated with gamma-glutamyl transferase ( β = 1.17 U/L; q FDR = 0.007), mean corpuscular volume ( β = 14.26 fL; q FDR = 4.4 × 10 −4 ), and slower reaction time ( β = 163.40 ms; q FDR = 3.0 × 10 −5 ). Deep learning–derived structural MRI representations capture weak but reproducible alcohol-related brain variation that converges with AUD diagnosis, peripheral biomarkers, and cognition, supporting their use in population-level addiction neuroscience while underscoring limits for individual-level prediction.

Article.Title: History of psychosis matters: deviation in age-related decline of working memory across the schizo-bipolar spectrum
Article.Authors: Barnes-Scheufler C.; Yalçın M.; Rösler L.; Schiweck C.; Shing Y.; Qubad M.; Reif A.; Bittner R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Deficits in visuospatial working memory (WM) have been consistently reported in both people with schizophrenia (PSZ) and bipolar disorder (PBD). In healthy controls (HCS), WM typically declines with age; however, it remains unclear whether a similar age-related decrease in WM performance occurs in PSZ and PBD, or whether a history of psychosis (HPS, meaning at least one psychotic episode) may significantly influence this trajectory. 189 participants, (20 to 61 years old) were separated into two groups based on HPS (HPS + , n = 90; HPS-, n = 99). Two cognitive tasks were employed to measure attentional control during WM encoding (ACE-WM) and WM capacity (WMC). Linear regression analyses were used to separately investigate ACE-WM and WMC. HPS+ stored significantly less information in both ACE-WM ( p = 0.004) and WMC ( p = 0.006) tasks compared to HPS-. The factor of age was significant in both tasks (both p < 0.001). A significant effect of psychosis ( p = 0.001) and a psychosis × age interaction ( p = 0.011) were observed only in the ACE-WM task. Although age significantly affected performance in both tasks separately, HPS appears to mainly moderate age-related WM performance of attentional control and not necessarily of WMC. This suggests different age-related patterns of cognitive functioning across these groups, with higher performance in the HPS- group. Although cross-sectional, our findings further our understanding of cognitive functioning across age and across mental disorders with psychosis.

Article.Title: Hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus: A central hub for pain-emotion comorbidity
Article.Authors: Su J.; Yang X.; Jiang H.; Xia J.; Ren Y.; Sun Y.; Yang C.; Zhang X.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Chronic pain and emotional disorders, particularly depression and anxiety, are highly comorbid and mutually reinforcing, but their shared mechanisms remain unclear. This review highlights the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN) as a key hub integrating stress, pain, and emotion, with a focus on two opposing neuropeptide systems: corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) and oxytocin (OXT). Chronic pain and stress promote sustained CRH activation and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysregulation, thereby favoring pain sensitization and negative affect, whereas OXT exerts analgesic, anxiolytic, and antidepressant effects. We propose that CRH-driven HPA hyperactivity coupled with relative OXT insufficiency is the core mechanism underlying pain-emotion comorbidity, further amplified by neuroinflammation and immune-neural crosstalk. We also summarize current pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions targeting this circuitry and discuss emerging directions, including single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, circuit-specific manipulations, brain-penetrant ligands, and stratified neuromodulation. The PVN-centered framework may facilitate the development of precise therapies for patients with chronic pain and emotional disorders.

Article.Title: Worldwide use of long-acting injectable antipsychotics in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Chen Y.; Wu Y.; Zhang L.; Lu M.; Dong J.; Wang L.; Sun H.; Jiang W.; Zhou Y.
Article.Abstract: Real-world use of long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAIs) for schizophrenia varies across health systems, but its worldwide utilization and sources of heterogeneity remain uncertain. We aimed to estimate LAI utilization and examine study-level moderators. We conducted a PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis under a registered protocol (CRD420251171257). Six databases were searched from inception to July 2026 for observational studies reporting an LAI numerator and corresponding denominator. Logit-transformed proportions were pooled using restricted maximum-likelihood random-effects models with Knapp–Hartung inference. Prediction intervals, subgroup analyses, exploratory meta-regression, leave-one-out and sampling-scope sensitivity analyses, and Egger’s test were performed. Twenty-six studies contributed 27 analytical estimates comprising 1 619 602 participants and 258 382 LAI users. The pooled utilization proportion was 18.7% (95% confidence interval, 15.3%–22.8%), with a 95% prediction interval of 6.0%–45.5% and substantial heterogeneity (I² = 99.96%). Utilization was 26.0% in Europe, 14.3% in Asia, and 15.7% in North America (P for subgroup difference = 0.016). Geographic region and study-level male proportion showed nominal univariable associations, but neither remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction across 13 moderator tests. Sensitivity analyses were stable, and Egger’s test provided no evidence of asymmetry (P = 0.578). Approximately one in five participants received an LAI, but utilization was highly setting-dependent. The pooled estimate should be interpreted as a cross-setting average rather than a treatment target, and the moderator findings as hypothesis-generating.

Article.Title: Large-Scale mapping of psychotropic weight effects: LLM-Based event detection across 222,545 deduplicated real-world patient narratives
Article.Authors: Natter J.; Yokoyama T.; Bruno M.; Javelot H.; Godet J.
Article.Abstract: Psychotropic drug-induced weight change is clinically important but remains difficult to compare across large numbers of medications. We analysed 222,545 deduplicated user-generated reviews covering 176 psychotropic medications and acetaminophen as a negative control. A fine-tuned classifier identified reviews describing weight gain, weight loss, or no change, and a Qwen3-8B language model extracted quantified weight changes in kilograms. We derived a Net Weight Effect (NWE), defined as the proportion of reviews describing weight gain minus the proportion describing weight loss (range −1 to +1), and the mean weight change in kilograms, both with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Antipsychotics had the highest class-level weight liability (NWE + 0.154; mean +12.6 kg), whereas stimulants showed the most weight-reducing profile (NWE − 0.050; mean −7.1 kg). Olanzapine, mirtazapine, and risperidone ranked highest for weight gain, whereas bupropion/naltrexone and topiramate ranked lowest. Long-term use (>6 months) was associated with a larger mean gain than medium-term use (+8.8 kg vs +2.3 kg), and females reported weight gain more frequently than males. Per-drug rankings were highly concordant across the four source platforms (Kendall’s W = 0.83). In an exploratory receptor-affinity analysis, alpha-2 adrenergic affinity was the strongest correlate of NWE (rho = 0.594; permutation FDR p = 0.006), whereas H1 histamine affinity was the strongest correlate of mean weight change (rho = 0.638; permutation FDR p = 0.042). Large-scale AI-assisted analysis of patient narratives can therefore generate clinically useful real-world rankings of psychotropic weight liability while also highlighting mechanistically plausible, though correlational, pharmacological associations.

Article.Title: The Living Lab at Home as an innovative platform for equitable and accessible study of families across a diverse developmental spectrum
Article.Authors: Boerner K.; Dudarev V.; Oberlander T.
Article.Abstract: Living lab platforms have gained increasing attention over the past two decades as an innovative approach to enhance engagement in research. These models emphasize co-development with participants, encourage knowledge exchange, and facilitate real-world data collection. Living labs have been applied to study health problems in older adults where research participation for vulnerable groups has been constrained by social, economic, or system-level barriers. Applying the living lab to children’s health is emerging as an innovative approach to foster more accessible research, which is especially important for children living with neurodevelopmental disorders, psychiatric conditions and chronic diseases, as well as social-environmental vulnerability. In this Expert Review Article we introduce the Living Lab at Home (LLAH) as an iterative, co-designed multi-method approach to developmental research. The LLAH offers an ethical, accessible, and equitable research platform for health research in underrepresented populations across a developmental spectrum. It allows for application of a variety of data collection methods such as smartphone-based microlongitudinal self-report, wearables, and non-invasive biomarkers to study everyday life in children with chronic pain and complex conditions. Co-development that supports the balance between scientific rigor and flexibility is key for capturing data that is of high quality and relevance. Based on our review we suggest that the LLAH holds potential for reducing inequities in research and health care systems, and opens new possibilities to individualize care, harness digital technology, and optimize health and well-being where children and youth live every day.

Article.Title: 2-AG as a potential biomarker for predicting response to short-term fluoxetine treatment in a mouse model of depression
Article.Authors: Rodríguez-López A.; Ibrahim E.; Gorgievski V.; Martin M.; Robledo P.; Maldonado R.; Tzavara E.; Álvarez-Pérez B.
Article.Abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a complex psychiatric condition with significant individual and social impact and marked variability in treatment response. Identifying biomarkers that predict antidepressant efficacy remains a major challenge, and metabolomic approaches offer a powerful tool to uncover biochemical changes associated with depression and treatment outcome. The prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus are key brain regions involved in the pathophysiology of MDD and antidepressant response. Fluoxetine, one of the most commonly prescribed antidepressants, influences not only serotonergic signaling but also the endocannabinoid system. Accordingly, evaluating endocannabinoid levels might provide critical insight into their contribution and the effect of fluoxetine. To identify biomarkers associated with early antidepressant response, male mice were exposed for 5 weeks to the chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) protocol, with fluoxetine treatment administered during the final week. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry analyses of hippocampal and prefrontal cortex samples revealed that behavioral improvement following short-term fluoxetine treatment was accompanied by increased hippocampal 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), along with reduced GABA and glutamate levels in the prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that increased 2-AG levels may predict early response to fluoxetine.

Article.Title: Emerging roles of the DLK1-DIO3 imprinted domain in neurodevelopment and complex neurological and psychiatric disorders
Article.Authors: Escamilla S.; Kuang R.; Figueroa C.; Krishnan N.; Hernández A.; Salas-Lucia F.
Article.Abstract: The DLK1-DIO3 genomic domain comprises a cluster of imprinted genes regulated by epigenetic mechanisms that precisely regulate their expression dosage, often in a timely and tissue-specific manner. This is particularly significant during brain development, as transcripts from the DLK1-DIO3 domain are involved in the physiology of most neural cell types, regulating fundamental processes such as neural precursor cell proliferation, neuronal and glial lineage specification, and subsequent functional maturation, as well as the establishment of neural and neuroendocrine circuits. Thus, disruption of the DLK1-DIO3 epigenome, induced not only by genetic alterations but also by neurodevelopmental exposure to environmental factors and maternal disease, may produce abnormal transcript expression within the domain, leading to broader dysregulation of brain gene expression programs during fetal and early development, ultimately influencing brain function and neurological and neuroendocrine phenotypes later in life. Here, we reviewed genetic, epigenetic, environmental, neurobiological, and behavioral studies linking dysregulation of genes within the DLK1-DIO3 imprinted domain to neurological and psychiatric outcomes, including autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, anxiety and depression, epilepsy, neurodegenerative disorders, susceptibility to drug abuse, maladaptive brain inflammatory response, and psychomotor alterations. Additional outcomes include neuroendocrine disorders and associated behavioral alterations. This narrative review covers the increasing observations in humans associating molecular signatures in this domain with neurological and psychiatric conditions, as well as studies in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neural cells and in rodents that provide compelling mechanistic insights about the neurodevelopmental processes affected, which could help interpret the unresolved etiology of these disorders, including increased prevalence, missing heritability, and phenotypical heterogeneity.

Article.Title: Cellular senescence changes and their association with brain structure in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder
Article.Authors: Okada N.; Seitz-Holland J.; Ikegame T.; Omileke F.; Kiyota M.; Shoji E.; Mori S.; Morita S.; Koshiyama D.; Satomura Y.; Koike S.; Jinde S.; Yagishita S.; Kamiya K.; Abe O.; Shenton M.; Kubicki M.; Kasai K.
Article.Abstract: Individuals with schizophrenia (SZ) and major depressive disorder (MDD) may experience accelerated biological aging, potentially linked to cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). While the SASP index, a composite biomarker-based measure, has been reported to be elevated in MDD, its status in SZ and its relationship with brain structure remain unclear. This study investigated whether the SASP index is elevated in SZ and MDD, and examined its associations with brain-predicted age difference (brain-PAD) and regional brain morphology across SZ, MDD, and healthy controls (HCs). A total of 119 subjects (29 individuals with SZ, 40 individuals with MDD, and 50 HCs) underwent both peripheral blood collection and magnetic resonance imaging scanning. First, across all subjects, the effects of diagnostic groups on SASP indices were assessed. Second, associations between age-adjusted SASP indices and brain-PAD were examined within each diagnostic group. Third, exploratory analyses tested associations between SASP indices and subcortical volumes as well as cortical thickness and surface area in each diagnostic group. We found a significant main effect of diagnostic group on SASP indices and significantly elevated SASP indices in both SZ and MDD. Although no significant associations were observed between SASP indices and brain-PAD in any diagnostic group, negative associations were identified in SZ between SASP indices and the surface area of the left transverse temporal gyrus and the right inferior frontal gyrus pars triangularis, regions that play pivotal roles in auditory and language processing alterations observed in SZ. These findings suggest that SASP-related processes may contribute to the neural underpinnings of SZ through localized, rather than global, alterations in brain structure.

Article.Title: Reduced attenuation of neural activation during fear extinction learning in patients with anxiety disorders: a delayed fear extinction fMRI study
Article.Authors: Qian Z.; Yang Y.; Richter J.; Domschke K.; Koelkebeck K.; Deckert J.; Herrmann M.; Plag J.; Ströhle A.; Wittchen H.; Pittig A.; Hamm A.; Arolt V.; Dannlowski U.; Schneider S.; Margraf J.; Rief W.; Lueken U.; Kircher T.; Ridderbusch I.; Straube B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Clarifying the patterns of neural activation during fear extinction in anxiety disorders (ADs) is essential for advancing our understanding of inhibitory learning. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly characterized in large, heterogeneous cohorts of patients. Utilizing a delayed fear extinction fMRI paradigm, this study examined neural responses in 280 patients with ADs — comprising panic disorder, agoraphobia, panic disorder with agoraphobia, social anxiety disorder, and multiple specific phobias — compared to 103 healthy controls (HC). The attenuation of neural activation to conditioned fear (CS+) and safety (CS−) stimuli from early versus late extinction was compared between groups. Subjective ratings of US-expectancy, arousal, and valence were also collected. In a whole-brain voxelwise analysis, patients showed significantly reduced attenuation of neural activation across both CS+ and CS− relative to HC from early compared to late phases of extinction learning. This pattern was observed in a broad network, encompassing the insular cortex (IC) and bilateral supplementary motor area (SMA), among other regions. No interaction between group and stimulus type was observed. Region-of-interest analysis of the left anterior insular cortex confirmed that reduced attenuation in this region represents a robust neural signature of altered extinction learning in ADs. Furthermore, patients reported persistently higher fear expectancy and arousal than HC, consistent with sustained alterations in threat-related processing following extinction training. Together, these findings highlight altered extinction-related neural attenuation as a transdiagnostic feature of ADs, offering novel insights into the neural mechanisms underlying fear extinction.

Article.Title: Effects of chronic oxytocin administration on white matter microstructure in autistic adults: a pilot pharmaco-neuroimaging DTI study
Article.Authors: Heemels R.; Deferm W.; Boets B.; Alaerts K.
Article.Abstract: Intranasal oxytocin is a promising therapeutic approach for social and stress-regulatory difficulties in autism spectrum disorder. However, there is limited understanding regarding whether chronic administration regimes can induce neuroplastic changes at the brain’s anatomical level and how such microstructural changes might underlie clinical-behavioral effects. This placebo-controlled pilot assessed the effects of a four-week oxytocin regimen (24 IU daily) on white matter microstructure in 27 young adult men with autism. Diffusion tensor imaging was performed at baseline, post-treatment, and after four-week and one-year retention periods. Tractography focused on fractional anisotropy (FA) in amygdala-centered tracts associated with socio-emotional processing: the bilateral Inferior Longitudinal Fasciculus (ILF), Inferior Fronto-Occipital Fasciculus (IFOF), and Uncinate Fasciculus (UF). Following four weeks of oxytocin administration, a spatially selective impact of intranasal oxytocin administration was demonstrated, indicating bilateral improvements in UF integrity and a hemispherically lateralized pattern of changes for the ILF and IFOF tracts, with FA increases predominantly emerging in the right hemisphere, while reductions were evident in left-sided segments. Especially for bilateral UF and right IFOF, the observed changes were clinically relevant, correlating with enhanced social responsiveness and reduced feelings of avoidant attachment. In conclusion, exploratory findings from this pilot neuroimaging trial suggest that a four-week oxytocin regimen may induce long-lasting neuroplastic changes in white-matter tracts relevant to behavioral improvements in adult men with autism. These hypothesis-generating findings may inform future confirmatory trials. Further investigation of the neuroplastic changes associated with oxytocin’s clinical and behavioral effects may help refine oxytocin-based interventions, not only for autism but also for other neuropsychiatric conditions in which oxytocin is being explored as a potential therapeutic option.

Article.Title: Control of whole-body glucose metabolism by central lactate in the presence of antipsychotics
Article.Authors: Pereira S.; d’Orchymont F.; Tong J.; Au E.; Singh R.; Wu S.; Beroncal E.; Choi J.; Li D.; Humber B.; Chaudhry T.; Alijaniaram M.; Agarwal S.; Vernon A.; Giacca A.; Andreazza A.; Vasdev N.; Hahn M.
Article.Abstract: The brain-liver axis is important in maintaining whole-body glucose homeostasis. Antipsychotics are used to treat schizophrenia, but one of their side-effects is disruption of metabolism. We previously reported that the antipsychotics olanzapine and haloperidol block the ability of central glucose to stimulate whole-body glucose metabolism and suppress glucose production by the liver (EGP, endogenous glucose production). Both effects by central glucose require the conversion of glucose to lactate centrally. In the current study, we therefore examined whether antipsychotics affect the ability of central lactate to stimulate whole-body glucose metabolism and suppress EGP. Using our previous model of central (third ventricle to target the hypothalamus) infusion, acute subcutaneous administration of antipsychotics, and the pancreatic euglycemic clamp in rats, we found that olanzapine completely inhibited the ability of central lactate to stimulate whole-body glucose metabolism and partially blocked central lactate-induced suppression of EGP. Since activation of the hypothalamus-liver axis of glycemic control requires central glucose and lactate to be metabolized, relevant pathways were also investigated. The adverse effects of olanzapine on central lactate sensing were not associated with decreased levels of citrate, a tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate, in the hypothalamus or robust alterations in hypothalamic mitochondrial complex I activity assessed with the positron emission tomography tracer [ 18 F]BCPP-EF. In summary, olanzapine impairs the ability of central lactate to control whole-body glucose metabolism and partially inhibits suppression of EGP by central lactate.

Article.Title: Impaired outcome-based decision-making in human cocaine addiction
Article.Authors: Lim T.; Cardinal R.; Mak E.; Ersche K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Despite rising global rates for cocaine addiction, treatments options are limited. Psychological treatments remain the standard option but have only modest effectiveness. One major barrier to treatment success is that patients often make disadvantageous decisions that go against recovery, highlighting the need for strategies to support decision-making. Converging evidence indicates that decision-making deficits in cocaine addiction are driven by impaired processing of outcomes and risks. We investigated how patients with cocaine addiction use explicit outcomes and risk information to guide decision-making. One-hundred-and-five patients with moderate-to-severe cocaine use disorder (CUD) and 80 healthy control volunteers completed a decision-making task in which reward, loss, and probability information were provided explicitly. A subset of participants underwent diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging to investigate the orbitofronto-striatal white matter tracts that underpin decision-making. We used generalized linear mixed-effects models to determine how rewards, losses, and probability influence decisions, and combined probabilistic tractography with principal component analysis to characterize the white matter tracts. We found that patients incorporated explicit probability information into their decisions to the same degree as control participants but showed reduced integration of outcomes. Notably, patients were less likely to integrate losses into their decisions than rewards. Although orbitofronto-striatal white matter tracts did not differ between groups, individual variability predicted the extent to which reward and loss information guided decisions, irrespective of diagnosis. Overall, these findings reveal fundamental challenges in using outcomes, particularly negative ones, to guide decision-making in patients with CUD, emphasizing the need for additional support to promote adaptive choices during recovery.

Article.Title: Temporal imprecision of the self in drug-free psychosis: Abnormal infraslow phase dynamics and brain complexity
Article.Authors: Chen I.; Ao Y.; Catal Y.; Liu C.; Hwang T.; Lin Y.; Hsieh M.; Chien Y.; Hwu H.; Lechner S.; Liu C.; Northoff G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Self-disturbance is a core feature of schizophrenia (SCZ) and may emerge during the prodromal phase. Temporal imprecision has recently been proposed as a core neural mechanism in schizophrenia, primarily demonstrated in faster EEG frequency ranges. Whether such imprecision extends to infraslow brain dynamics in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and relates to self-disturbance in early psychosis remains unknown. Here, we examined resting-state fMRI data from drug-free early psychosis patients (EP drug-free, n = 31, scanned before and after medication) and 31 healthy controls (HC). Brain dynamics were quantified using sample entropy (SampEn) and instantaneous peak frequency (PF) in regions associated with different layers of self-processing (interoceptive, exteroceptive, and mental). Compared to controls, EP drug-free showed higher SampEn and slower mean PF with greater variability than HC, particularly in the regions of the exteroceptive self. Moreover, EP drug-free exhibited a decoupling between SampEn and PF, whereas HC showed strong correlations. Both SampEn and PF significantly contributed to diagnostic classification, and increased SampEn was associated with greater severity of negative, disorganized, and anxiety/depression symptoms. Together, these findings indicate abnormal infraslow brain dynamics in early psychosis, characterized by increased neural complexity and disrupted temporal organization. This temporal imprecision, particularly within the exteroceptive self, may represent a key mechanism linking altered brain dynamics to self-disturbance and psychopathology in early psychosis.

Article.Title: Treating diagnostic frameworks as information systems: normative implications and opportunities
Article.Authors: Millroth P.
Article.Abstract: The DSM-5 and ICD-11 are not just clinical manuals; they are information architectures. Every time a clinician applies diagnostic criteria, every time a researcher aggregates symptoms into a diagnostic variable, and every time a committee drafts a revision, they operate on the same basic object: a coded system for transmitting information about mental states. Yet no one has applied information theory [ 1 ] to evaluate the architecture of diagnostic systems themselves. Existing applications of information-theoretic thinking in psychiatry — model-selection criteria such as AIC and BIC — assess how well statistical models fit covariance data; they say nothing about the efficiency of the diagnostic code itself. This Viewpoint argues that information theory (henceforth, IT) — the elsewhere highly influential mathematical framework developed by Shannon to characterize the capacity and efficiency of communication systems [ 1 ] — provides what is currently missing: a principled, quantitative basis for designing, evaluating, and reforming diagnostic frameworks and the instruments that operationalize them. The case for this reframing is not merely theoretical. Diagnostic quality, the product of validity and reliability in the DSM-5 and ICD-11 is, by available estimates, remarkably poor -essentially entailing that the majority of variability stems from measurement error or other irrelevant factors [ 2 , 3 ].

Article.Title: A precision health approach to medication management in neurodevelopmental conditions: a model development and validation study using four international cohorts
Article.Authors: Vandewouw M.; Niroomand K.; Bokadia H.; Lenz S.; Rapley J.; Arias A.; Crosbie J.; Trinari E.; Kelley E.; Nicolson R.; Schachar R.; Arnold P.; Iaboni A.; Lerch J.; Penner M.; Baribeau D.; Anagnostou E.; Kushki A.
Article.Abstract: Psychotropic medications are commonly prescribed to children with neurodevelopmental conditions, but responses vary widely, prescribing is largely off-label, and the expertise required is concentrated in specialized programs. We developed artificial intelligence models to predict prescribing patterns of stimulants, anti-depressants, and anti-psychotics. Feasibility was established in research cohorts by predicting cross-sectional medication use from the Child Behaviour Checklist, with training and internal testing in the Province of Ontario Neurodevelopmental network ( N = 598) and external testing in the Healthy Brain Network ( N = 1764) and Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development ( N = 2396) studies. Clinical evaluation used electronic medical records (EMRs) from the Psychopharmacology Program ( N = 312) at Holland Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital to predict the medication class prescribed at a follow-up visit (~3 months later). In all cohorts, the modelled outcome was the clinician’s prescribing decision, which reflects clinician judgement, family preference, tolerability, and access to care in addition to expected effectiveness, and does not directly measure treatment response or clinical benefit. In the research cohorts, internal testing achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (median [IQR]) of 0.75 [0.73,0.80] for stimulants, 0.83 [0.78,0.87] for anti-depressants, and 0.79 [0.72,0.86] for anti-psychotics, and external testing confirmed generalizability. In the EMR cohort, values were 0.84 [0.81,0.88] for stimulants, 0.82 [0.77,0.87] for anti-depressants, and 0.87 [0.83,0.91] for anti-psychotics. Findings demonstrate that AI can accurately learn expert prescribing patterns and predict medication prescribing decisions, supporting the potential of data-driven tools to guide personalized medication management for neurodevelopmental conditions.

Article.Title: Counteracting the overestimation of effect size in mass-univariate brain-wide association studies using cross-validation
Article.Authors: Goltermann J.; Winter N.; Gruber M.; Fisch L.; Richter M.; Grotegerd D.; Dohm K.; Meinert S.; Leehr E.; Böhnlein J.; Kraus A.; Thiel K.; Winter A.; Flinkenflügel K.; Leenings R.; Barkhau C.; Ernsting J.; Berger K.; Minnerup H.; Straube B.; Alexander N.; Jamalabadi H.; Stein F.; Brosch K.; Wroblewski A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Background Brain-wide association effects are commonly overestimated in psychiatric neuroimaging research, leading to low replicability and generalizability of findings, and ultimately to poor translation to clinical utility. Cross-validation is currently not standardly used in univariate neuroimaging analyses but could pose a potential counteracting measure for this problem. Methods We systematically evaluated the benefit of a cross-validation procedure to expose inflated effect size estimates in mass-univariate voxel-based analysis, using body mass index (BMI) as an example predictor for gray matter. A total of n = 3401 MRI scans from a psychiatric cohort were used to investigate the impact of applying cross-validation on effect size estimates across a range of sample sizes and across different localizations with a range of underlying pooled effect sizes. Results BMI was negatively associated with gray matter density with a maximum underlying effect size of R ² p = 0.036 (in the full sample of n = 3401). However, without cross-validation, effects were substantially overestimated in small samples, with effect sizes ranging up to R ² p = 0.535. Even with an underlying null-effect, effect size estimates up to R ² p = 0.429 were reached in samples with n = 25. Applying cross-validation revealed that these inflated effects in small samples did not generalize to novel data. A minimum sample size of n = 100 was required for largest brain-wide effects to start generalizing, while samples with n = 400 were needed for smaller effects to generalize. This ‘point of initial generalizability’ was not reached for underlying null effects, even with the maximum available sample of n = 3401. Conclusions Results suggest that cross-validation is an effective measure to expose overestimated effects in small samples and thus could help to counteract low replicability and generalizability in brain-wide mass-univariate association studies. Open-source code is provided for practical implementation.

Article.Title: Temporal cortical gray matter volume relates to symptom improvement during cognitive behavioral therapy for depression
Article.Authors: Schöniger K.; Kamrla R.; König P.; Zwiky E.; Küttner A.; Scheiwe G.; Andreev J.; Hamann J.; Brückner A.; Pletsch S.; Wittig E.; Selle J.; Gussew A.; Deistung A.; Tüscher O.; Wohlgemuth W.; Redlich R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a first-line treatment for depression, yet treatment responses vary considerably. Understanding neurobiological factors associated with symptom improvement may help elucidate mechanisms underlying therapeutic change. This study investigated whether baseline cortical gray matter volume (GMV) is associated with reductions in depressive symptom severity during CBT. Additional models included anxiety, perceived stress, and childhood trauma as predictors. Compared to controls, patients exhibited significantly higher depressive symptom severity at baseline and greater symptom reduction over time (all p < 0.001). Within patients, baseline GMV of the right middle temporal gyrus (MTG) was significantly associated with symptom reduction (baseline–follow-up; β = 0.55, p FDR = 0.033). Right MTG volume accounted for additional variance in symptom reduction beyond established clinical variables (Δ R ² = 0.15). Group differences in GMV did not remain significant following FDR correction. These findings suggest that temporal gyrus GMV is associated with symptom improvement following CBT in unipolar depression, extending the focus beyond traditionally emphasized limbic regions. Preserved temporal morphology may support cognitive and emotional processes engaged during CBT, underscoring the relevance of temporal cortical structure for understanding the neurobiological correlates of psychotherapy response.

Article.Title: Non-suicidal self-injury in adolescents and young adults: an expert review
Article.Authors: Kaess M.; Reichl C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is highly prevalent among community and clinical adolescent populations and is associated with substantial psychiatric comorbidity, psychosocial impairment, and elevated suicide risk. This review synthesizes key findings on the development and maintenance of adolescent NSSI and discusses the clinical implications of this transdiagnostic behavioural phenomenon. It examines the prevalence and developmental course of NSSI, environmental and biological risk factors, proximal mechanisms, its conceptualization as an independent diagnosis versus a transdiagnostic risk marker, and current treatment approaches including their limitations. Current evidence indicates that adolescent NSSI emerges from interacting environmental risk factors (e.g. adversity and interpersonal stress) and neurobiological mechanisms related to emotional dysregulation, stress responsivity, and altered pain processing. While NSSI prospectively predicts suicidal behaviour, associations with other psychiatric disorders remain probabilistic and diagnostically non-specific. Overall, findings support conceptualizing NSSI as a transdiagnostic risk marker and behavioural phenotype linked to emotion dysregulation rather than as a distinct diagnostic entity. Adolescent NSSI reflects a dynamic biopsychosocial process involving emotional, neurobiological, and interpersonal mechanisms. Early detection and accessible intervention are essential to reduce chronicity, relapse, and the escalation of suicidal behaviour. Future research should prioritize mechanism-informed and personalized treatment approaches, improved identification of at-risk adolescents, and integration of developmental, neurobiological, and digital methodologies to advance prevention and intervention.
