Article.Title: Integrative neuroimaging-transcriptomic analysis of neurodevelopment in adolescent-onset mental health problems
Article.Authors: Hou J.; van Wingen G.; van de Mortel L.; Smit D.; Liu S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mental health problems often emerge in childhood and adolescence, yet the neurodevelopmental and molecular processes underlying their onset remain poorly understood. Using longitudinal data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, we examined structural and functional brain cortical changes in youth who developed ADHD, conduct, anxiety, depressive, oppositional defiant, or somatic problems over a two year follow up period compared to healthy controls in five neuroimaging modalities (including structural MRI, resting-state fMRI, and task-based fMRI). We applied partial least squares (PLS) regression to link spatial patterns of neurodevelopmental changes to cortical gene expression profiles derived from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA). Pathway enrichment was assessed using spin-permutation-derived gene rankings. Significant neurodevelopmental alterations were observed in the ADHD and conduct groups only. PLS analysis further revealed significant spatial associations between their neurodevelopmental changes and gene expression distributions (Spearman rₛ >0.64). In ADHD, pathway enrichment highlighted mitochondrial respiration, oxidative phosphorylation, aerobic electron transport, ATP synthesis, and mitochondrial organization, with additional negative-end enrichment for synaptic protein interaction pathways. In conduct problems, all significant pathways were enriched among genes whose cortical expression patterns were inversely aligned with the conduct-problem imaging phenotype and involved translational machinery, ribosomal function, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial translation, protein targeting to mitochondria, and broader RNA/protein regulatory processes. These findings reveal distinct cortical transcriptomic patterns associated with adolescent-onset ADHD and conduct problems, with mitochondrial energy metabolism emerging as a prominent molecular correlate of ADHD-related cortical development and a distinct inverse transcriptional pattern characterizing conduct-related development. Together, our findings suggest that these externalizing problems are associated with neurodevelopmental alterations embedded within distinct cortical molecular contexts.

Article.Title: TCF7L2 functionally relevant genetic variation with clinical implications in bipolar disorder with impaired glucose metabolism
Article.Authors: Miola A.; Winham S.; De Filippis D.; Gardea Resendez M.; Romo-Nava F.; Bond D.; Singh B.; Veldic M.; Ozerdem A.; Pendegraft R.; Pazdernik V.; Ercis M.; Sanchez-Ruiz J.; Prieto M.; McElroy S.; Biernacka J.; Frye M.; Cuellar-Barboza A.
Article.Abstract: Impaired glucose metabolism (IGM) and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) are common in bipolar disorder (BD). Genome-wide association studies have identified variation (rs7903146) in the gene encoding transcription factor 7-like 2 ( TCF7L2 ) as a well-established risk factor for T2DM in the general population and variation (rs12772424) showing a significant association with BD when accounting for BMI. IGM was operationalized as evidence of prediabetes (fasting glucose of 100-125 mg/dL or glycated hemoglobin of 5.7%-6.4%) or T2DM. We compared sociodemographic, genetic, clinical characteristics, and course of illness measures between BD groups with and without IGM, then within BD subgroups (prediabetes, T2DM, and no IGM). Out of 850 BD patients included (mean age 49, SD = 13, 57% female, 8% non-White) 280 (33%) individuals had IGM. Compared to BD patients without IGM, those with IGM were older (p < 0.001), more likely to be non-White (p = 0.005), and obese (p < 0.001). The minor allele for the rs7903146 SNP (T2DM-associated SNP) was significantly greater in the IGM group compared to the group without IGM (11% vs. 5%, p = 0.009). There was no significant association between rs12772424 SNP (BD-associated SNP) with bipolar course of illness measures. Further investigation examining the complex interactions between functional genetic variants, molecular markers, environmental influence, and clinical phenotypes in BD is needed to better understand the mechanistic underpinnings to the high rate of T2DM bipolar comorbidity and identify early targets for treatment of both disorders.

Article.Title: Electroacupuncture alleviates chronic pain and comorbid depression through Gut-Metabolite-Brain axis remodeling to restore mPFC Glu/GABA balance
Article.Authors: Li S.; Huang J.; Lin D.; Luo D.; Fu W.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The comorbidity of chronic pain and depression is increasingly recognized as a systemic disorder involving dysregulated microbiota–gut–brain communication. Although electroacupuncture (EA) has demonstrated therapeutic efficacy for both pain and depression, the mechanisms linking peripheral microbial-metabolic remodeling to central neurotransmitter regulation remain incompletely understood. Here, we employed an integrated multi-omics approach in a spared nerve injury (SNI) rat model to investigate the gut–metabolite–brain mechanisms underlying EA’s efficacy. EA significantly alleviated mechanical hypersensitivity and depressive-like behaviors while restoring mPFC Glu/GABA balance, accompanied by normalization of the glutamate transporter EAAT2 and the GABA-synthesizing enzyme GAD67. Metagenomic analysis showed that EA remodeled the gut microbial ecosystem by increasing microbial diversity, suppressing opportunistic pathobionts, including Bacillus cereus, Alistipes onderdonkii , while enriching SCFA-associated genera, including Butyricimonas and Romboutsia . These alterations were accompanied by coordinated remodeling of amino acid and butanoate metabolism. Correlation network analysis identified Pipecolic acid as a central metabolic node linking gut microbial alterations with mPFC GABAergic neurotransmission and behavioral recovery. Although individual bacterial genera did not significantly mediate its restoration, causal mediation analysis demonstrated that the Pipecolic acid–GABA axis significantly mediated improvements in both mechanical allodynia and anhedonia, supporting Pipecolic acid as a functional metabolic hub linking peripheral metabolic remodeling to central GABAergic regulation. Collectively, these findings identify peripheral metabolic remodeling as a key mechanistic interface through which EA coordinates gut microbial ecology and central neurochemical homeostasis, providing a systems-level framework for understanding the therapeutic mechanisms of acupuncture in pain–depression comorbidity.

Article.Title: Large-scale EEG reveals shared and distinct neural oscillatory features across major psychiatric disorders
Article.Authors: Rao S.; Xie J.; Niu M.; Pan Y.; Li Y.; Yu H.; Xie J.; Zhang Y.; Zhao S.; Pan G.; Guo W.; Li T.; Jiang H.
Article.Abstract: Major psychiatric disorders are leading contributors to global disability, yet robust biomarkers to inform diagnosis and treatment remain elusive. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a scalable, noninvasive approach to capture neural dysfunction, but prior findings have been inconsistent due to small, single-disorder cohorts. Here, we report a large-scale, two-site comparative study of resting-state EEG in schizophrenia (SCZ), bipolar disorder (BD), and major depressive disorder (MDD) compared with healthy controls (HC). Across 9751 participants’ EEG recordings, standardized preprocessing and feature generation yielded spectral power and functional connectivity (FC) measures tested with both statistical and machine-learning approaches. Additional spectral differences included more pronounced delta-theta elevation in SCZ and a graded delta-theta continuum (SCZ > BD > MDD), suggesting a dimensional progression of neural dysregulation. Machine-learning models robustly distinguished individuals with psychiatric diagnoses from healthy controls within sites, but cross-site generalization and inter-disorder discrimination remained limited, underscoring challenges of heterogeneity. These findings identify reproducible EEG features that capture both shared and disorder-distinct neural alterations, advancing efforts towards early detection and individualized treatment in major psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Episodic memory-associated weighted atrophy network mapping in mild cognitive impairment and subjective cognitive decline: a multi-center study
Article.Authors: Huang A.; Jiang K.; Chi L.; Qiao M.; Yang X.; Wu H.; Chen S.; Fan J.; Wang H.; Chen Y.; Tong Z.; Lin X.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: This study localizes episodic memory-associated impaired networks in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and subjective cognitive decline (SCD) using a weighted key atrophy network mapping method, and investigates whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) can modulate them. Replicability was assessed across three independent cohorts involving 1312 subjects. First, single-subject key atrophy maps were constructed by comparing cortical thickness with cognitively normal groups and retaining regions showing significant thickness-memory correlations. Second, these maps served as seeds for functional connectivity analysis in a large normative connectome, generating atrophy networks weighted by atrophy extent. Third, group-level comparisons identified impaired networks in MCI and SCD, and methodological reliability was further validated against a memory network derived from patients with focal brain lesions. Finally, the impaired networks were experimentally modulated via a 4-week rTMS intervention (25 MCI, 13 SCD). Despite substantial individual-level heterogeneity, atrophied regions in most MCI patients were functionally connected to a common episodic memory-associated impaired network. This phenomenon was not significant in SCD patients. Both lesion-memory network mapping and cross-dataset validation confirmed consistency across cohorts. Critically, rTMS can modulate the impaired network in MCI patients, primarily reflected by enhanced functional connectivity within this network. In conclusion, this study developed a robust weighted key atrophy network mapping method, localizing common episodic memory-associated impaired networks in MCI/SCD. Modulation of this impaired network may serve as a potential therapeutic strategy to delay MCI progression.

Article.Title: Serum B-cell activating factor and delayed memory in first-episode drug-naïve schizophrenia: a case-control study
Article.Authors: Yang Q.; Jin T.; Jin S.; Jiang F.; Qiu J.; Yang X.; Wang P.; Yan Q.; Tian Q.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive impairment in schizophrenia has been linked to immune dysregulation, but the role of humoral immune regulators remains unclear. We examined serum B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and A proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL) in 90 first-episode drug-naïve schizophrenia (FES) patients and 90 matched healthy controls (HCs). Cognitive performance was assessed using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status (RBANS), and symptom severity was assessed using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). Serum BAFF and APRIL were measured using Luminex technology. After adjustment for age, sex, education, BMI, and smoking status, serum BAFF and APRIL levels were significantly lower in FES patients than in HCs (BAFF: F = 131.935, P < 0.001; APRIL: F = 59.772, P < 0.001). In the hypothesis-driven primary analytic model focusing on RBANS delayed memory, the Group × BAFF interaction was significant ( F (1,171) = 13.524, P < 0.001), with a positive BAFF slope in HCs ( B = 0.015, P = 0.017) but a negative slope in FES patients ( B = -0.022). This interaction remained robust in sensitivity analyses. Exploratory analyses suggested a nominal Group × BAFF interaction for RBANS total score ( F = 5.866, P = 0.016, FDR-adjusted q = 0.082), which was interpreted cautiously. No analogous Group × APRIL interaction was observed, and BAFF/APRIL levels were not significantly associated with PANSS symptom dimensions. These cross-sectional findings identify peripheral BAFF as a hypothesis-generating correlate of delayed memory in early untreated schizophrenia, but do not establish temporality, causality, or central immune-cognitive mechanisms.

Article.Title: Aerobic exercise prevents neuroinflammation and ameliorates depressive-like behaviors via suppression of HMGB1/NF-κB pathway-mediated reactive microglial states in mice exposed to chronic mild stress
Article.Authors: Jiang L.; Zhang C.; Yang D.; Liu S.; Liao R.; Xu E.; Yu Y.; Liu L.
Article.Abstract: Aerobic exercise is shown to have a positive effect on depressive-like symptoms; however, the associated mechanisms have not yet been fully elucidated. The role of neuroinflammation in the pathogenesis of depression is well-documented. High mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), a late mediator of inflammation, can promote the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines in various inflammation-related diseases. This study aimed to investigate the antidepressant effects of aerobic exercise by regulating hippocampal neuroinflammation via the HMGB1/NF-κB pathway-mediated microglial reactivity state. We assessed the depressive-like behaviors of the mice through behavioral tests. It was found that aerobic exercise significantly alleviated chronic mild stress (CMS)-induced depressive-like behaviors in mice. Furthermore, aerobic exercise reduced the total number of microglia and altered microglial morphology and reactive states in the hippocampus, accompanied by down-regulation of pro-inflammatory markers. These effects were observed to be regulated by HMGB1. We found a significant nuclear-to-cytoplasmic translocation of HMGB1 in the hippocampus, in the absence of apoptotic alterations (pyknotic nuclei, karyorrhexis, karyolysis), indicating an active release in the brain after CMS stimulation. Interestingly, aerobic exercise could reverse these alterations by inhibiting the HMGB1/NF-κB pathway. These findings not only enhance the understanding of the processes driving neuroinflammation in the hippocampi of mice exposed to CMS, but also highlight the potential of aerobic exercise as an anti-depression therapeutic strategy.

Article.Title: Neurobehavioral changes in fear generalization in clinical high risk for psychosis
Article.Authors: Clauss J.; Babadi B.; Tuominen L.; Deng W.; Leathem L.; Holt D.
Article.Abstract: Changes in basic associative learning processes have been identified in several psychiatric conditions. However, it remains unknown whether these findings result from ongoing psychopathology or represent an underlying transdiagnostic risk factor for multiple clinical states. In this study, 72 participants with subclinical psychopathology, 23 of whom met criteria for the Clinical High-Risk for Psychosis syndrome (CHR+) and 49 who did not meet these criteria (CHR-), completed a fear conditioning and generalization paradigm while functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data were collected. During this procedure, participants were presented with face stimuli that were either paired (CS+) or not paired (CS-) with a mild electrical shock, as well as eight face “morphs” (stages between the CS+ and CS-) tailored to each participant’s perceptual discrimination ability. Following the scan session, participants rated the likelihood that each stimulus had been previously followed by a shock. Fear generalization-related neural responses (in a subset of the sample, 16 CHR+ and 40 CHR- participants) and the memory ratings were then examined using both categorical and individual-level psychometric modeling approaches. Expected patterns of fear generalization-related responses were observed in the anterior insula and superior frontal gyrus and in the memory ratings. The psychometric modeling analysis revealed a significantly greater threshold in responses of the left anterior insula, representing a wider fear generalization curve, in the CHR+, compared to the CHR-, group. Moreover, across the whole sample, symptoms of anxiety were associated with a wider fear generalization gradient. These findings suggest that specific features of a basic associative memory process, fear generalization, may be linked to CHR status and transdiagnostic risk for psychiatric illness.

Article.Title: Association between tirzepatide use and risk of suicidal ideation among individuals with obesity and major depressive disorder
Article.Authors: Liu T.; Chu C.; Liu C.; Wu J.; Tsai Y.; Chang H.; Lai C.
Article.Abstract: Obesity and major depressive disorder (MDD) frequently co-occur and confer mutually reinforcing risks, including elevated suicidality. Tirzepatide has demonstrated substantial metabolic benefits, yet its psychiatric safety in high-risk populations with MDD remains uncertain. This study aimed to compare suicidal ideation outcomes among adults with comorbid obesity and MDD initiating tirzepatide versus non–GLP-1RA anti-obesity medications. This retrospective, propensity score–matched cohort study used deidentified electronic health record data from the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults (≥18 years) with diagnosed obesity and MDD who initiated tirzepatide or non–GLP-1RA anti-obesity medications were included. The primary outcome was suicidal ideation. Secondary outcomes included anxiety disorders, insomnia disorders, all-cause mortality, and emergency department or inpatient encounters. Among 24,103 matched pairs, tirzepatide use was associated with lower risk of suicidal ideation (HR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.42–0.93), anxiety disorders (HR, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.81–0.86), insomnia disorders (HR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.86–0.98), all-cause mortality (HR, 0.38; 95% CI, 0.25–0.58), and emergency department visits or hospitalizations (HR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.89–0.99). Risk reduction was generally consistent across prespecified subgroups. Control outcome analyses supported the internal validity of the findings. In conclusion, this study provides real-world evidence that tirzepatide initiation was associated with a lower recorded risk of suicidal ideation, as well as reduced anxiety, insomnia, all-cause mortality, emergency department visits, and hospitalizations, among adults with comorbid obesity and MDD. This observational association should not be interpreted as evidence of a direct antisuicidal effect. These findings support the potential for tirzepatide to serve as a metabolically favorable treatment option associated with a lower risk of suicidal ideation in this vulnerable, high-risk population.

Article.Title: Design strategies and anti-tumor applications of nanorobots
Article.Authors: Niu D.; Fang Y.; Dong Z.; Liu X.; Guan T.; Fu W.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: Malignant tumors remain a major global health challenge due to their heterogeneity, poor therapeutic specificity, and frequent development of multidrug resistance. Conventional treatment strategies are often hindered by limited tumor penetration, systemic toxicity, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. In recent years, nanorobots-engineered nanoscale devices with autonomous or guided navigation capabilities-have emerged as a transformative platform in precision oncology. These intelligent systems integrate active targeting, stimulus-responsive drug release, and multifunctional therapeutic modules, enabling dynamic interactions with the tumor milieu. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in nanorobot materials, modular design strategies, and propulsion mechanisms, and highlights their applications across central nervous system, breast, urological, and gastrointestinal tumors. Furthermore, we address key translational barriers, including biosafety, navigation precision, and regulatory challenges, and propose future directions leveraging artificial intelligence and clinical trial integration. By bridging materials science, robotics, and biomedicine, nanorobots hold promise to redefine minimally invasive cancer treatment paradigms.

Article.Authors: Ohmori S.; Suzuki M.; Yoshida K.; Takai J.; Shimizu R.; Katsuoka F.; Ohneda K.

Article.Authors: Prasad A.; Patel S.; Ng S.; Liu C.; Gelb B.
Article.Abstract: The lymphatic system plays an essential role in maintaining fluid homeostasis, lipid transport, and immune function. Article.Authors: Schaaf J.; Mitchell D.; Ogata J.; TaQee S.; Wilson K.; Conrads K.; Loffredo J.; Hood B.; Abulez T.; Hunt A.; Langeland A.; Mhawech-Fauceglia P.; Darcy K.; Tarney C.; Maxwell G.; Conrads T.; Bateman N.

Article.Authors: Feng L.; Wen Y.; Wang T.; Cao Y.; Zhao J.; Du S.; Wei H.; Liu Y.; Zhang W.

Article.Title: Individual differences in sequential decision-making
Article.Authors: Abbaszadeh M.; Ozanick E.; Magen N.; Darrow D.; Yan X.; Grissom N.; Herman A.; Ebitz R.
Article.Abstract: People differ widely in how they make decisions in uncertain environments. Article.Title: CASCADE is an agentic AI framework for trustworthy biomarker discovery in precision oncology
Article.Authors: Yaacov A.; Gillis R.; Pomerantz A.; Purim O.; Katz D.; Peled N.; Grinshpun A.; Asna N.
Article.Abstract: Autonomous AI agents can now run end-to-end scientific analyses, yet no general method ensures those analyses are correct, and one upstream error can propagate across hundreds of downstream results at machine speed. Article.Title: Agentic finance and sustainability: governing autonomous capital allocation for societal benefit
Article.Authors: Caldecott B.
Article.Abstract: Financial institutions are beginning to integrate autonomous artificial intelligence agents that can act independently in economic settings. The sustainability governance architecture built over the past decade, including disclosure frameworks, taxonomies, stewardship codes, and regulatory expectations, assumes human decision makers at the point of capital allocation. This perspective defines agentic finance as finance in which at least one party to the allocation, intermediation, or use of capital is an autonomous AI agent. We consider how agentic finance weakens principal-agent controls, complicates the specification of sustainability objectives, and creates channels outside regulated infrastructure, as well as the constraint imposed by its computational footprint. We then propose responses for different implementation horizons. They combine rules that machines can read and, where feasible, infrastructure can enforce, monitoring of agentic financial activity, internationally coordinated regulated infrastructure, and public agentic finance operated by central banks, development banks, and multilateral institutions. Article.Title: Biogenic zinc oxide nanocomposites from Azadirachta indica with chitosan encapsulation for antimicrobial and bioactive properties
Article.Authors: Afzal M.; Naz S.; Rasheed M.; Ahmad F.; Raman J.; Arefin S.; Hamlaoui O.; Tozan H.; Zafar M.
Article.Abstract: Zinc oxide nanoparticles are promising antimicrobial and bioactive agents for public health, but current methods involve toxic reagents and the aggregation of the nanoparticles. In this study, we developed zinc oxide nanoparticles using aqueous extracts from neem ( Azadirachta indica ) leaves and encapsulated the nanoparticles with chitosan for enhanced stability and performance. Using diffraction, spectroscopic, thermal, and microscopic techniques, we found that the resulting nanoparticles have a hexagonal wurtzite phase structure with smaller crystallite sizes (28.6–20.3 nm) and greater band-gap values (3.09–3.16 eV) and are evenly dispersed in the chitosan matrix with 54% zinc oxide loading. The encapsulated nanoparticles showed improved antibacterial and antifungal activities with a 26 mm inhibition zone against Staphylococcus aureus and lower minimum inhibitory concentration values compared to pure zinc oxide nanoparticles. They also inhibited the α-amylase enzyme (half-maximal inhibitory concentration [IC 50 ] = 34.37 μg/mL) and were strong antioxidants (IC 50 = 52.34 μg/mL).

Article.Title: Neural dynamics of naturalistic body motion processing in humans
Article.Authors: Chesley J.; Riecke L.; de Gelder B.
Article.Abstract: As a social species, body motion cues facilitate human interactions, prompting decades of research on the neural dynamics underlying visual body features. Building on recent fMRI evidence for widespread cortical networks sensitive to naturalistic body motion, the present study used electroencephalography (EEG) in human subjects to identify temporal markers of naturalistic body motion compared to faces and objects. Stimuli were naturalistic videos depicting bodies, faces, and objects, as well as scrambled videos controlling for low-level visual features. Consistent with previous research on visual body processes and biological motion, the present findings show that approximately 220 ms after stimulus onset, the cortex may already distinguish naturalistic body motion from face and object motion. Post hoc analyses indicated similar body-sensitive modulations across stimulus species, with a widespread scalp distribution and modulations of alpha- and beta-band power. These findings expand our understanding of body motion processing and support integrative models of multi-faceted body processes.

Article.Title: A habitat-pathology-clinical transformer model for precision prognostication of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy in ESCC
Article.Authors: Li W.; Cao Q.; Li Z.; Lu W.; Feng G.; He B.; Xie S.
Article.Abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) shows marked inter-patient heterogeneity in response to neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NICT), highlighting the need for reliable pre-treatment predictors. In this multicenter study, 102 patients with advanced ESCC from two institutions were enrolled. Pre-treatment contrast-enhanced CT, whole-slide histopathology images, and clinical data were collected. Habitat-based radiomics was selected as the optimal imaging approach, with a Support Vector Machine (SVM) achieving an AUC of 0.723 (95% CI: 0.580–0.866) in the test cohort. For pathomics, the ResNet50-based multi-instance learning model with logistic regression was selected, achieving an AUC of 0.766 (95% CI: 0.639–0.894). These signatures were integrated with clinical features to develop HPTrans, a transformer-based multimodal model. HPTrans outperformed all single-modality approaches, achieving AUC of 0.921 (95% CI: 0.889–0.952) in the training cohort and 0.824 (95% CI: 0.720–0.928) in the test cohort. Collectively, HPTrans may aid pretreatment NICT response prediction and treatment selection in patients with advanced ESCC.
Article.Topic: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

Article.Title: A high-throughput, systems-based predictive neutralization assay reveals compartment influences on neutralization networks
Article.Authors: Wang Q.; Levine K.; Blanc R.; McManus L.; Malca H.; Waller-Pulido A.; Nangle S.; Cabrera-Barragan D.; Lasrado N.; Barouch D.; McNamara R.
Article.Abstract: Antibodies leverage their fragment antigen-binding (Fab) and fragment crystallizable (Fc) domains to confer protection against pathogens. We sought to identify antibody features correlated with receptor binding inhibition at the systems level of influenza viruses. We developed a systems-predictive neutralizing antibody (SNAb) titer assay to simultaneously predict influenza receptor binding inhibition across multiple subtypes and isolates using specimens from H1- and H5-vaccinated non-human primates. We incorporated these results into a systems serology framework to assess contribution of antibody features to the phenotype. We find that Fcγ-receptor binding features are strongly associated with SNAb against H1 and H5 influenza in serum, while IgG, IgM, and IgA were enriched at the mucosa. These compartment-specific correlates of SNAb were further shaped by vaccination route. Collectively, we propose that influenza receptor binding inhibition can be predicted at scale and across anatomical sites using a systems-based approach.

Article.Title: Growth kinetics and defect-mediated texture evolution in electrodeposited Cu2O thin films
Article.Authors: Rahal A.; Bouchama I.; Khalladi M.; Ghebouli M.; Fatmi M.; Althagafi T.; Saidi S.; Benlakhdar F.; Smerat A.; Yaylacı M.
Article.Abstract: Electrodeposition conditions influence the structure and optical response of cuprous oxide (Cu 2 O) thin films. We examined three films prepared with jointly varied electrolyte pH, applied potential, bath temperature, and deposition time. X-ray diffraction identified predominantly cubic Cu 2 O with minor CuO-related contributions and crystallite sizes of 20.85–26.89 nm. Atomic force microscopy and cross-sectional electron microscopy revealed changes in surface morphology and thickness. Chronoamperometry provided a phenomenological description of the early growth response. Optical measurements indicated changes in the direct bandgap, while photoluminescence revealed differences in defect-related radiative emission. Because the deposition parameters changed simultaneously, individual parameter effects cannot be isolated. Furthermore, steady-state photoluminescence does not establish non-radiative recombination rates, and photovoltaic device performance was not measured. These findings correlate combined electrodeposition conditions with crystallographic texture, growth behavior, and optical characteristics of Cu 2 O films.

Article.Title: A parasympathetic pathway from the superior salivatory nucleus modulates refractive development, axial length, and choroidal thickness
Article.Authors: Ma Z.; Imanishi S.; Huang Y.; Chuai Y.; Kwok R.; Gettinger K.; Yoshida T.; Jeong H.; Hou J.; Yang Y.; Chen J.; Negishi K.; Tanaka K.; Yamanaka A.; Tsubota K.; Kurihara T.
Article.Abstract: The regulation of eye growth and refractive development has long been considered a locally driven process. Here, we identify an superior salivatory nucleus (SSN)-linked central parasympathetic pathway that modulates choroidal thickness and ocular refraction. We demonstrate that SSN cholinergic neurons bidirectionally modulate choroidal structure: their activation rapidly thickens the choroid and induces a hyperopic shift, while their inhibition thins the choroid and promotes a myopic shift. During juvenile development, this pathway also regulates vitreous chamber depth. Chemogenetic activation of SSN cholinergic neurons attenuated the development of lens-induced myopia and was associated with preserved choroidal thickness and reduced axial elongation. These findings provide mechanistic evidence that central parasympathetic activity contributes to refractive regulation in mice.

Article.Title: Electrical and chemical synapses share similar organizational principle
Article.Authors: Hoff H.; Ijaz S.; Echeverry F.; Tetenborg S.; Lin Y.; O’Brien J.; Verselis V.; Pereda A.
Article.Abstract: Electrical transmission between auditory contacts and the fish Mauthner cells is mediated by multiple co-existing gap junctions (GJs). Zebrafish contain four homologs of connexin (Cx) 36: Cx35.5, Cx35.1, Cx34.1, and Cx34.7. Using transgenic fish in which Cxs were tagged, we confirmed mutation analysis indicating that GJs are formed by heterotypic channels made of presynaptic Cx35.5 and postsynaptic Cx34.1. We additionally found that Cx34.7 is present together with Cx34.1 on the postsynaptic side at some but not all GJs at these terminals. However, despite its intrinsic ability to create functional channels with Cx35.5, Cx34.7 did not compensate for the loss of transmission in Cx34.1 null mutants. The findings reveal an unexpected postsynaptic functional organization at GJs, where Cx34.1 is obligatory and Cx34.7 accessory, possibly assembling under specific functional contexts. Thus, electrical synapses share an organizational motif with chemical synapses, akin to how they combine postsynaptic receptor types to modify synaptic function.

Article.Title: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of normal mouse early eye development and role of Pax6 in the formation of lens and olfactory placodes
Article.Authors: Camerino M.; Chang W.; Ferrena A.; Zheng D.; Cvekl A.
Article.Abstract: The bilateral ocular primordia are formed during late gastrulation-early organogenesis. In E9.5 mouse embryos, these structures are comprised from the ectoderm-derived lens placodes, neuroectoderm-derived optic vesicles, and periocular mesenchyme (POM). Here, we present single cell transcriptomic analysis (scRNA-seq) of E8.5-E9.5-E10.5 eye embryogenesis to define mechanisms of cell fate decisions that generate lens, olfactory and adenohypophyseal placodes, multipotent retinal progenitor cells (RPCs), early retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and the optic stalk. The E9.5 Pax6 −/− embryos, lacking both lens and olfactory placodes, show major dysregulation of genes encoding cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) and other proteins involved in cell-cell communications. These studies reveal for the first time the critical trajectories underlying early mouse eye morphogenesis and identify CAMs involved in cell sorting events to generate individual lens and olfactory placodes. These data provide a resource to develop comprehensive models of early organogenesis and studies of abnormal eye development in other mutant models.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial inner membrane partners of Aurora kinase A/AURKA and PHB2 shape organelle metabolic heterogeneity
Article.Authors: Caron C.; Jolivet N.; Kantar D.; Coyaud É.; Bertolin G.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondria adapt their activity to support tumor growth, but how signaling networks organize metabolic diversity within individual cells remains unclear. We investigated how Aurora kinase A (AURKA) and prohibitin-2 (PHB2), a mitophagy receptor, associate with inner mitochondrial membrane proteins involved in respiration, cristae organization, and metabolite transport. Using proximity-labeling proteomics, fluorescence lifetime imaging, and super-resolution microscopy, we identified NDUFA9, ATP5F1A, ATP5F1B, SAMM50, and SLC25A13 as candidate AURKA/PHB2-proximal partners. AURKA overexpression remodeled the proximal protein environments of NDUFA9 and ATP synthase without disrupting their nanoscale membrane proximity, whereas the AURKA/PHB2-targeting compound HMBB restored these interactomes. Depletion of SLC25A13 lowered mitochondrial ATP production and altered the spatial distribution of ATP-associated microdomains. These findings identify an inner mitochondrial membrane signaling platform associated with spatial ATP regulation and provide a framework for understanding how mitochondrial organization contributes to metabolic diversity in cancer cells.

Article.Title: Exposome-guided precision neurorehabilitation: A scoping review of biology, circuits, exposure, and recovery
Article.Authors: Calabrò R.; Calderone A.; Rossato E.; Molteni F.; Quartarone A.
Article.Abstract: Neurorehabilitation is an exposure-rich intervention in which treatment dose, behavioral practice, neuromodulation, and environmental conditions act on biologically heterogeneous patients. We conducted a scoping review of same-study evidence linking genetic, epigenetic, or molecular factors with rehabilitation, lifestyle, or exposome-related exposures and recovery outcomes. Searches identified 21 eligible studies, predominantly in stroke, with smaller multiple sclerosis and traumatic brain injury clusters. Candidate-gene analyses, especially brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) Val66Met, dominated a heterogeneous literature with domain-specific, mixed, or null findings. Current evidence does not support routine genotype-based treatment selection. We propose a four-level research architecture linking biological state, measurable exposures, circuit engagement, and recovery phenotypes. This framework is not a validated clinical decision tool. Its nearer-term purpose is to guide exposure measurement and mechanistic trial design, with prospective interaction testing and external validation required before clinical use.

Article.Title: Institutional thresholds in the climate and food availability nexus in South Asia
Article.Authors: Azimi M.; Rahman M.
Article.Abstract: Climate shocks interacting with socioeconomic and institutional conditions threaten food availability (FA; per capita dietary energy supply) in South Asia. Yet studies of climate-food security linkages rely largely on linear frameworks that overlook nonlinear responses and institutional heterogeneity. For eight South Asian countries (1995–2023), we construct an institutional quality index (IQI) with a nonlinear autoencoder and estimate generalized additive models with tensor-product interactions, cross-checked by quantile models. FA falls monotonically as climate vulnerability and agricultural land area rise, increases with per capita income, and is lowest near normal rainfall and at intermediate trade openness. IQI moderates these patterns. Below IQI values of 0.44–0.59, climate vulnerability and population growth (which has no direct association) are more strongly associated with lower FA at all quantiles; above them, income and trade gains strengthen on average. Institutional strengthening should therefore accompany climate adaptation and development policies in South Asia.

Article.Title: Evaluation of polydopamine-mediated immobilization of antimicrobial compounds on titanium surfaces
Article.Authors: Andrea A.; Modic M.; Molchanova N.; Jønsson R.; Prabhala B.; Hansen P.; Krogfelt K.; Mansell J.; Jenssen H.
Article.Abstract: Implant-associated infections remain a major clinical challenge, motivating the development of antimicrobial surface coatings that can prevent bacterial colonization while supporting tissue integration. Here, titanium surfaces were functionalized with polydopamine (PDA) and subsequently coated with three synthetic antimicrobial peptides (GN-2, GN-4, and IDR-1018) or chlorhexidine (CHLX). The antimicrobial activity of the resulting surfaces was evaluated against pathogens commonly associated with implant infections, and their biocompatibility was assessed using human osteoblasts. Although all three peptides displayed strong antimicrobial activity in solution, their efficacy was reduced following surface immobilization. In contrast, CHLX retained substantial antimicrobial activity when immobilized via PDA and outperformed the peptide-coated surfaces. PDA-functionalized surfaces and peptide coatings showed good compatibility with human osteoblasts. These findings highlight the importance of considering how surface immobilization influences antimicrobial function and provide insights for the design of infection-resistant biomaterial surfaces for medical implants.

Article.Title: Structural placement outpaces catalytic-state prediction in AlphaFold3 models of CRISPR-Cas13a
Article.Authors: Wang R.; Xue R.; Xu X.; Musso T.; Zhang Q.; Zhao Y.; Lai J.; Gaira S.; Wu L.; Sang R.; Zhang C.; Deng F.; Tang S.
Article.Abstract: CRISPR-Cas13a has been adopted for biosensing owing to its programmable RNA recognition and collateral RNA cleavage activity. Its function depends on both RNA-guided complex assembly and rearrangement of the higher eukaryotes and prokaryotes nucleotide-binding (HEPN) catalytic core. Although AlphaFold3 predicts biomolecular structures, its ability to capture active CRISPR conformations remains unclear. Here, we evaluate AlphaFold3 using Leptotrichia buccalis Cas13a (LbuCas13a) in apo, guide RNA-bound, target-bound, ion-containing, and ligand-containing states. Predicted structures are benchmarked against published experimental structures and assessed by fluorescence trans -cleavage assays. AlphaFold3 reliably reconstructs overall complex architectures and generates plausible models for target recognition, ion coordination, and ligand binding. However, it consistently failed to reproduce the HEPN catalytic conformations associated with activation. The predicted target-bound complexes retained inactive-like catalytic geometries, although the assays showed trans-cleavage activity. These findings demonstrate that structural plausibility does not reflect functional activation, highlighting the need for experimental validation and molecular simulations in AI-guided CRISPR engineering.

Article.Title: Free-form inverse design of a broadband visible-light metasurface quarter-wave plate
Article.Authors: Shin M.; Kim H.; Chung H.
Article.Abstract: Metasurface waveplates offer an ultrathin platform for polarization control, yet achieving high transmission and accurate quarter-wave retardance over a broad visible bandwidth remains challenging. Here, we present an inverse-designed all-dielectric metasurface quarter-wave plate based on a 0.6 μ m-thick free-form TiO 2 /air topology on a SiO 2 substrate. Adjoint-based topology optimization tailors the three-dimensional material distribution to convert normally incident left-circularly polarized light into transmitted +45° linear polarization across 500–600 nm. Full-wave simulations show average and minimum transmissions of 98.13% and 95.54%, with target-polarization purity above 99.97%. Independent Jones-matrix analysis verifies quarter-wave retardance with mean and maximum errors of 0.47° and 1.08°. At 550 nm, the device meets conversion-efficiency and leakage criteria up to 30° for four azimuths. Field analysis suggests wavelength-dependent redistribution of orthogonally polarized fields adjusts their effective optical-path difference, supporting broadband retardance. Comparisons with layer-constrained and parameterized nanopillar designs highlight the benefit of geometric freedom.

Article.Authors: Pulinkala G.; Sawatzki K.; Smith E.; Chang J.; Golez I.; Hansen S.; Tisoncik-Go J.; Picker L.; Gale M.; Komorowski J.
Article.Abstract: Using whole blood RNA-seq data from RhCMV/SIV-vaccinated rhesus macaques subsequently challenged with SIV, we identified 70 immune genes that distinguish protection status in these animals against persistent SIV infection. The application of a non-linear rule-based model allowed us to refine the whole blood protective signature into gene combinations and their specific expression levels related to cell death and inflammatory signaling pathways. The co-predictiveness exhibited by the model indicated that protected animals display an orchestrated immune response, whereas vaccine programming of these processes were absent in non-protected animals. Upstream regulator analysis revealed high resolution into IL-15 signaling linked with IL-23 and JNK1 enabled by the interpretable nature of the rule-based model.

Article.Authors: Kamata S.; Taguchi A.; Iuchi H.; Ikeda Y.; Maruyama R.; Nakanishi Y.; Sugi T.; Okuma Y.; Kobayashi O.; Tomita N.; Yoshimoto D.; Wang L.; Moritsugu N.; Takahashi C.; Tagami M.; Matsunaga H.; Okayama T.; Manabe R.; Kiyotani K.; Ikeo K.; Okazaki Y.; Kiyono T.; Masuda S.; Hamada M.; Takeyama H.
Article.Abstract: Human papillomavirus 18 (HPV18) preferentially infects cervical stem cell-like cells and is strongly associated with adenocarcinoma. However, the mechanisms underlying differentiation into cervical adenocarcinoma remain unclear due to the lack of appropriate experimental models. HPV18 E6/E7 were introduced into induced reserve cell-like cells (iRCs) to generate tumor models. Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell multi-omics analyses integrated histological and molecular data. Gland_A showed increased chromatin accessibility and elevated expression of FOXA1, FOXA2, and ALDH1A1. Clinical samples confirmed enrichment of ALDH1A1 in HPV-associated adenocarcinomas. This model recapitulates key adenocarcinoma-like features associated with HPV18 E6/E7 expression and provides a complementary experimental system for investigating cervical adenocarcinoma differentiation.

Article.Title: Multi-platform reassessment of human mitochondrial DNA methylation reveals signals consistent with technical artifacts
Article.Authors: Basrai S.; Bahcheli A.; Tan D.; Zuzarte P.; Bevan A.; Chan T.; Ng K.; Lam B.; Arruda A.; Das S.; Minden M.; Simpson J.; Reimand J.; Abelson S.
Article.Abstract: The existence and functional relevance of mitochondrial DNA methylation remain controversial. Here, we profiled cytosine methylation and hydroxymethylation across human brain and blood tissues spanning healthy and malignant states using sequencing approaches that avoid chemical conversion during library preparation. While nuclear DNA exhibited canonical methylation patterns, mitochondrial DNA consistently showed negligible signal, indistinguishable from background technical noise. By mapping cytosine-guanine sites between mitochondrial DNA and nuclear-embedded mitochondrial sequences, we demonstrate the potential of these nuclear counterparts to confound not only cytosine methylation but also hydroxymethylation measurements, corroborating and extending prior findings implicating nuclear contamination as a potential source of apparent mitochondrial epigenetic signals. Additional technical factors that inflate apparent mtDNA methylation signals were identified, including sequence context biases, flow cell chemistries, and coverage-dependent discrepancies between the heavy and light strands. Collectively, these findings caution against interpreting apparent mtDNA methylation signals without rigorous orthogonal validation and comprehensive consideration of technical and analytical confounding factors.

Article.Title: Long term survival with adjuvant immunotherapy after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy and esophagectomy in locally advanced ESCC
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Zheng X.; Liu H.; Zhang W.; Huang W.; Li B.; Xiao Y.; Qin Z.; Wang H.; Wang X.; Li B.; Ge H.
Article.Abstract: Postoperative adjuvant immunotherapy (aIT) represents a strategy for locally advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (LA-ESCC) treated with neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (nCIT) followed by esophagectomy. This multicenter retrospective cohort enrolled 418 Chinese LA-ESCC patients treated with nCIT followed by esophagectomy, split into aIT and surveillance groups. We balanced baseline confounders via 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) and analyzed overall survival (OS) and event-free survival (EFS). With a median 48.7-month follow-up, aIT was associated with higher 4-year OS among matched patients (78.21% vs. 65.20%, HR=0.571, p = 0.012), while EFS (64.45% vs. 59.46%, HR=0.735, p = 0.114) showed no intergroup difference. The observed OS association with aIT was limited to patients without major pathological response (non-MPR). In this retrospective cohort, postoperative aIT was associated with longer overall survival specifically among non-MPR LA-ESCC patients following nCIT.

Article.Title: Junction-referenced dual-mode scanning thermal microscopy with W-Cr ultra-thin oxide tip probes
Article.Authors: Kim Y.; Shin H.; Kwon O.
Article.Abstract: Quantitative scanning thermal microscopy (SThM) uses different temperature references for thermocouple and thermoresistive measurements, limiting comparison and cross-validation. Here, we establish the first junction-referenced dual-mode SThM methodology that calibrates and characterizes both responses of a tungsten-chromium (W-Cr) ultra-thin oxide tip (UTOT) probe against a common junction-temperature-rise reference. Vacuum null-point SThM calibrates the room temperature Seebeck coefficient, which, together with the initial voltage-power slope, determines the low-power effective thermal resistance. The high-temperature axis uses the first-order approximation T j ≈ R p P . We determine effective thermal resistance, Seebeck coefficient, thermal time constant, electrical resistance, and junction-referenced effective temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR) in air and vacuum. Practical power-sweep limits correspond to estimated junction-temperature rises of approximately 300°C in air and 400°C in vacuum. R ( T j ) maps the thermoresistive response onto the common junction-temperature axis, enabling comparison of both readouts and providing a basis for cross-validation.

Article.Title: Naringenin ameliorates PCOS-associated miscarriage by targeting C/EBPβ to suppress decidual macrophage pyroptosis
Article.Authors: Sun C.; Cheng X.; Ma S.; Meng J.; Guo C.; Mu X.; Song Q.; Kuang H.
Article.Abstract: To determine whether naringenin ameliorates PCOS-associated miscarriage by targeting C/EBPβ-dependent decidual macrophage pyroptosis. Methods: DHEA-induced PCOS mice and an in vitro macrophage pyroptosis model were used. Transcriptomic profiling, PELSA-based target identification, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, ChIP-qPCR, and gain-/loss-of-function experiments were performed. Results: Naringenin reduced embryo resorption and restored decidual homeostasis in PCOS mice. Transcriptomics identified macrophage pyroptosis via NLRP3/AIM2–caspase-1–GSDMD activation as a key pathological feature of PCOS decidua, which naringenin attenuated in vivo and in vitro. PELSA combined with structural validation identified C/EBPβ as a molecular target of naringenin. Pharmacological C/EBPβ inhibition attenuated pyroptosis, whereas C/EBPβ overexpression diminished naringenin's protection. Mechanistically, naringenin reduced C/EBPβ occupancy at Aim2, IL18, and IL1β promoters, suppressing inflammasome transcriptional activation. Article.Title: Identification of an adipogenesis gene, CEBPA, in an adipocyte subtype and network linked to insulin resistance and obesity
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Lee S.; Kar A.; Alvarez M.; Stringham H.; Gelev K.; Sukhatme M.; Heinonen S.; Saarinen T.; Vaittinen M.; Kaminska D.; Peltoniemi H.; Juuti A.; Männistö V.; Pihlajamäki J.; Kaikkonen M.; Pietiläinen K.; Laakso M.; Scott L.; Mohlke K.; Pajukanta P.
Article.Abstract: Human adipocytes are heterogeneous; however, cellular regulators linking obesity-related cardiometabolic diseases to adipocyte heterogeneity remain unknown. Leveraging subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) data from three cohorts ( n = 331), we identify an adipocyte subtype, Ad2, with 202 marker genes. The proportions of Ad2 associate with cardiometabolic traits (CMTs) and its marker genes significantly overlap with genes in an adipocyte-specific, highly preserved co-expression network, AdNetwork2, that comprises 212 CMT-associated genes. A cis -expression quantitative trait locus variant, rs8111294, of CEBPA , an adipogenesis transcription factor (TF) in AdNetwork2, has allele-specific downstream effects on other AdNetwork2 TFs in trans . We replicated these cis -linked trans effects in an independent dataset. For CEBPA target TFs, CEBPB and KLF15 , we functionally validate the presence of their target genes in AdNetwork2. Overall, we uncover cascading, multilayered effects of CEBPA , CEBPB, and KLF15 on 170 CMT genes in AdNetwork2, elucidating cell-type level mechanisms contributing to context-specific adipocyte heterogeneity.

Article.Title: Multimodal deep learning for risk stratification of imaging subtypes in pneumonia-associated sepsis
Article.Authors: Xiong Y.; Wang H.; Li L.; Chen J.; Zhang Y.; Grzegorzek M.; Li C.; Fan G.; Du T.
Article.Abstract: Pneumonia-associated sepsis shows substantial heterogeneity in lung injury and clinical outcomes. We analyzed a retrospective multicenter cohort of 1,088 patients and a next-generation sequencing (NGS) subgroup of 94 patients to evaluate pulmonary radiomic phenotypes, host body composition, and reported lower respiratory tract pathogen profiles. After ComBat harmonization, principal component analysis and K -means clustering were used to derive four imaging subtypes in the internal training cohort, which were transferred to validation cohorts and NGS subgroup. The subtypes showed distinct clinical outcome patterns and selected associations with body-composition and inflammatory measures in adjusted analyses. NGS report-derived pathogen-profile findings remained exploratory, with no pathogen-level differences surviving false discovery rate (FDR) correction. A multimodal transformer integrating clinical-laboratory, radiomic, and body-composition features showed numerically higher external-validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs) than selected conventional models. These findings provide a cross-scale framework for clinically interpretable risk stratification in pneumonia-associated sepsis.

Article.Title: Gene essentiality signatures for exploring cancer-relevant targets and mechanisms in large-scale drug sensitivity screens
Article.Authors: Wang W.; Bao J.; Zheng S.; Lei C.; Huang S.; Aldahdooh J.; Wang Y.; Eriksson J.; Tanoli Z.; Zhang X.; Li M.; Gaetani M.; Tang J.
Article.Abstract: Cancer drugs can produce phenotypic effects beyond their annotated targets, complicating mechanism-of-action (MoA) inference. We introduce gene-essentiality-derived signatures as a data-centric representation of drugs, learned by regressing cell-line drug sensitivity against genome-wide loss-of-function dependency profiles across hundreds of cancer cell lines. These interpretable vectors capture associations between drug response and gene dependencies. In supervised target prediction, the signatures outperformed chemical fingerprints and drug-perturbation transcriptomic signatures. Without target priors, top-ranked genes and their first-degree protein-protein interaction neighbors were enriched for known targets and pathway components, enabling de novo MoA exploration, including EGFR/HER2 signaling for lapatinib and DNA mismatch repair-linked compounds. We applied the framework to PRISM cancer cell-line screening data to predict cancer-relevant targets and MoAs for non-oncology drugs. Multiple predictions received orthogonal support from proteome-wide target deconvolution and structure-based docking, highlighting opportunities for oncology-focused drug repurposing. These interpretable, scalable embeddings support target and MoA hypothesis generation.

Article.Title: Discovery of Plasmodium falciparum SR12 as a GOLD-domain seven transmembrane protein regulating GPCR trafficking in mammalian cells
Article.Authors: Pereira P.; Ahrari S.; Kiyan C.; Kobayashi H.; Moraes M.; Bouvier M.; Garcia C.
Article.Abstract: Growing resistance to conventional antimalarials makes new drug targets identification essential. Since G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are readily druggable targets, we investigated serpentine receptor 12 (SR12), a GPCR-like protein in the P. falciparum genome. AlphaFold analysis and molecular dynamics simulations revealed structural similarity to the Golgi dynamics domain (GOLD)-seven transmembrane helix protein family (GOST proteins), which includes TMEM87A and orphan GPCRs GPR180, GPR107, and GPR108 and is involved in subcellular trafficking. Consistent with this, SR12 localizes mainly to the secretory pathway in mammalian cells. Co-expression with PAR1 and M3R increased their plasma membrane targeting. In HEK293 cells, SR12 conferred Gαq-dependent calcium signaling in response to thrombin, which was abolished in PAR knockout cells, supporting a chaperone-like role in receptor trafficking. Conclusively, our data suggest that P. falciparum SR12 promotes GPCR trafficking in mammalian cells, revealing a GOST protein in the parasite genome; physiological consequences remain undetermined.

Article.Title: Transcriptome derived T cell receptor repertoires reveal compartmental variation and shared CDR3 features
Article.Authors: Ntayi M.; Kyalo E.; Olweny G.; Kyamulabi D.; Ssengooba W.; Namaganda J.; Munana R.; Kirenga B.; Joloba M.; Mayanja-Kizza H.; Jjingo D.; Sande O.; Kayongo A.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive immune responses span distinct anatomical compartments, yet comparative characterization of transcriptome-derived T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires across blood and the respiratory tract remains limited. We reconstructed TCR repertoires using TRUST4 from bulk RNA sequencing of peripheral blood ( n = 24), bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL; n = 55), and induced sputum ( n = 100) from Ugandan participants with and without HIV and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Repertoire recovery differed across compartments, with sputum yielding fewer productive TCR sequences and clonotypes despite comparable sequencing depth. After sampling-depth standardization, TRB diversity was similar between BAL and blood, whereas TRBV23-1 usage differed between compartments. CDR3 sequence characteristics were broadly similar across compartments. Exact clonotype sharing across compartments and recurrence across participants were uncommon and influenced by repertoire sampling and clonotype abundance. These findings highlight compartment-dependent differences in repertoire recovery alongside shared sequence characteristics, informing interpretation of transcriptome-derived TCR repertoires across respiratory and systemic compartments.

Article.Title: The shared GATA factor grain is linked to reciprocal tumor-host regulation in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Lin S.; Loubière V.; Cavalli G.; Lan X.; Chen D.; Goto A.
Article.Abstract: Innate immunity provides the first line of defense against pathogens, but host responses to non-infectious challenges, such as oncogenic cells (OCs), remain elusive. Using Drosophila melanogaster with RasV12 OCs injected into adult hosts, we previously observed distinct transcriptional responses in OCs and host flies. Here, we identify a reciprocal expression profile (REP), in which subsets of genes show opposite regulation between OCs and host flies. Promoter analysis revealed an enrichment of GATA-family transcription factor binding sites among these genes. grain ( grn ) was strongly induced in OCs and emerged as a candidate REP-associated regulator. Grn promoted OC proliferation when expressed in OCs, but suppressed it when expressed in host flies. Accordingly, grn depletion in OCs combined with grn overexpression in host flies suppressed OC proliferation, whereas the converse condition enhanced it. Together, these findings support a role for Grn in REP and reveal compartment-dependent effects of Grn on OC proliferation.

Article.Title: Albinism in mammals: Cases, mechanisms, and conservation implications
Article.Authors: Jia F.; Sun S.; Liu Y.; Guan D.; Hu Y.; Du X.; Wei F.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: Albinism is a heritable pigmentation abnormality characterized by reduced or absent melanin, with potential consequences for mammalian physiology and ecology. This review compiles reports of albinism in 104 mammalian species across 14 orders, summarizes molecular investigations of 16 cases, and examines their physiological, behavioral, ecological, and conservation implications. Genetic alterations affecting pigmentation pathways can produce similar phenotypes through different molecular mechanisms, while the associated consequences, including visual impairment, reduced camouflage, and altered social interactions, may vary across species and environments. Integrating genetic evidence with field observations and ecological assessments provides a framework for understanding the relationships between pigmentation abnormalities and organismal fitness. These insights can guide future investigations of mammalian albinism, support wildlife monitoring and conservation management, and inform comparative research on pigmentation disorders in humans.

Article.Title: CNTs@ZIF-67 conductive composite nanoparticles enhance the electromagnetic shielding performance of tough organic hydrogels
Article.Authors: Lei Z.; Zhang D.; Hu Y.; Zhou T.; Diao K.; Liu D.; Song A.; Zou K.; Qin S.
Article.Abstract: With the widespread use of electronic devices, electromagnetic radiation pollution has become increasingly severe, posing potential threats to human health and the ecological environment. This study successfully prepared a tough, adhesive, green, and multifunctional semi-interpenetrating network organic hydrogel using a three-step method, and enhanced its electromagnetic shielding performance by incorporating CNTs@ZIF-67 composite nanoparticles. An environmentally friendly semi-interpenetrating network organic hydrogel was constructed using polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) and bio-based gelatin (Gel). Through an in situ growth method, ZIF-67 was grown on the surface of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) to prepare CNTs@ZIF-67 composite nanoparticles. Using a one-pot approach, these composite nanoparticles were dispersed in a precursor solution containing gelatin and PVA, followed by cyclic freeze-thaw processing to fabricate a novel hydrogel material that combines high toughness with outstanding electromagnetic shielding performance. When incorporating 50 mg of CNTs@ZIF-67, the organic hydrogel achieves a conductivity of 0.512 ± 0.026 S/m, a compressive modulus of 41.8 ± 2.09 kPa, a compressive deformation rate of 66.33% ± 3.01%, a moisture content of 88.99% ± 0.89%, and a water absorption rate of 265.92% ± 1.33%. The PGZC1 organic hydrogel with a thickness of 3 mm exhibits an average electromagnetic interference shielding effectiveness (EMI SE) of 33.32 ± 1.67 dB within the X-band (8.2-12.4 GHz), thus providing an innovative material solution for mitigating electromagnetic wave pollution.

Article.Title: SCML1 overexpression promotes DNA damage and improves the therapeutic efficacy of cisplatin for ovarian cancer
Article.Authors: Zhang P.; Zhang Y.; Wang M.
Article.Abstract: Ovarian cancer (OVCA) is one of the most common gynecological tumor and is the eighth most common cause of cancer death in women. Sex comb on midleg-like 1 (SCML1) plays an important role in the regulation of embryonic development, but its role in OVCA has not been detected. SCML1 was identified to be associated with cisplatin resistance in OVCA. The expression of SCML1 in OVCA tissues was verified by testing clinical samples. The effect of SCML1 on the proliferation and drug resistance of OVCA cells was investigated in vivo and in vitro. The expression of SCML1 is significantly lower in OVCA cisplatin-resistant tissues. After SCML1 knockdown, the proliferation ability and cisplatin resistance of OVCA cells were significantly enhanced. Article.Title: Chronotherapy for retinopathy: Unraveling the mystery of Rev-erbα in the circadian rhythm
Article.Authors: Qu C.; Wu H.; Huang Z.; Wang Y.; Wang K.; Li S.; Pu N.; Zhang J.; Ding S.; Zhang C.; Song Z.; Tao Y.
Article.Abstract: Disruption of the retinal circadian rhythm is a common manifestation of various retinal diseases, characterized by abnormal expression of clock genes and impaired light signaling in intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs). This review aims to elucidate the mechanisms of circadian disruption in retinal pathologies, explore the interrelationship between clock genes and ipRGCs, and delineate the therapeutic potential and directions of chronotherapy for retinopathies. Through a systematic retrieval and analysis of literature on retinal diseases and circadian rhythms from databases including PubMed and Web of Science, this review reveals that Rev-erbα and melanopsin form an antagonistic system within the retina, regulating the intraocular dopamine-melatonin rhythm and maintaining retinal homeostasis. Disruption of this rhythmic system leads to oxidative stress, inflammation, and dysregulation of emotional responses. Moreover, chronotherapy, as an intervention leveraging intrinsic temporal patterns, holds significant promise for treating retinopathies associated with circadian misalignment.

Article.Title: Decoding the role of cancer-associated fibroblasts in cisplatin resistance of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
Article.Authors: Liu D.; Yu D.; Chen M.; Dai T.; Li X.; Su D.; Zheng J.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: Cisplatin remains the primary chemotherapy drug for the treatment of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). However, acquired resistance significantly limits its clinical application, contributing to treatment failure and a poor patient prognosis. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in the tumor microenvironment influence HNSCC sensitivity to cisplatin by modulating tumor cell responsiveness to treatment via paracrine signaling. CAFs impede deep penetration into tumors by remodeling the extracellular matrix (ECM). Various subtypes of cisplatin-resistant CAFs have been identified in HNSCC. Potential compounds targeting these subtypes could enhance cisplatin sensitivity. Simulation of the dynamic tumor microenvironment remains limited in research, hindering clinical translation. Bioinformatics has shifted research into cisplatin resistance in HNSCC. Single-cell sequencing and spatiotemporal transcriptomics could analyze the molecular profiles of CAFs that promote drug resistance in greater depth, potentially facilitating the development of highly targeted drugs and effective combination therapy strategies to overcome cisplatin resistance in HNSCCs.

Article.Title: High-resolution prediction and risk mapping of Haemaphysalis longicornis habitat suitability in the Jiaodong Peninsula, China
Article.Authors: Bian X.; Chen S.; Xu J.; Xue H.; Xu A.; Song S.; Chong Y.; Wang F.; Tian N.; Ding H.; Feng J.; Lu Y.; Li L.
Article.Abstract: Ticks are vectors of numerous human pathogens, and accurate predictions of their spatial distribution are essential for the effective prevention and control of tick-borne diseases. High-resolution predictions remain scarce in China. To address this gap, a tick survey was conducted across the Jiaodong Peninsula at 2,647 points during the summer of 2024, integrating high-resolution environmental variables. Seven machine-learning algorithms were used, and ensemble learning was applied, resulting in a habitat-suitability map for Haemaphysalis longicornis at a 10-meter resolution. The ensemble model showed robust predictive accuracy (AUC = 0.8355). Summer normalized difference vegetation index was the primary environmental driver, followed by land use and land cover and winter normalized difference vegetation index. High risk villages accounted for 70.0%, 40.2%, and 16.9% of rural, urban rural fringe, and urban areas, respectively. Article.Title: Longitudinal pre-diagnostic blood samples predict osteoporosis risk
Article.Authors: Lassen J.; Nielsen K.; Hindhede L.; Mikkelsen S.; Kjerulff B.; Ostrowski S.; Sørensen E.; Mikkelsen C.; Pedersen O.; Bruun M.; Aagaard B.; Johannsen M.; Erikstrup C.; Villesen P.
Article.Abstract: Cross-sectional biomarker discovery studies for degenerative diseases are limited by selection bias, post-diagnostic confounding, and high biological variability. We analyzed 538 plasma metabolomic profiles (1-6 samples per participant, yearly intervals) from 99 pre-diagnostic osteoporosis cases and 99 matched controls in the Danish Blood Donor Study. We compared performance of cross-sectional and longitudinal modeling using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression and random forest. Longitudinal LASSO modeling of metabolite trajectories achieved area under the curve (AUC) values between 0.67 and 0.76, outperforming cross-sectional models with AUC values of 0.57-0.63. Article.Title: Impact of GCR and SPE on space radiation shielding: OLTARIS simulation and quantum optimization of material selection using quantum algorithms
Article.Authors: Lalwani K.; Sreedevi V.; Gakhar M.; Agrawal D.; Tinker D.
Article.Abstract: During long-term deep-space missions, a key challenge to the human and spacecraft is the space radiation, which is coming from the three different sources: Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs), Solar Particle Events (SPEs), and trapped particles in regions of Van Allen belts. High-energy particle radiation can have harmful effects on the spacecraft systems, sensors, electronic components, and astronauts, compromising mission reliability. This makes effective shielding a critical requirement. Traditionally, passive shielding materials such as aluminum have been used, but their limitations, especially in generating secondary radiations, necessitate the search for more efficient alternatives. In this study, the performance of various shielding materials, such as Lithium hydride (LiH), Polyethylene (C2H4), Lithium borohydride (LiBH4), Beryllium borohydride (Be(BH4)2), and Ammonia borane (NH3BH3) is systematically evaluated in the GCR and SPE environment using On-Line Tool for the Assessment of Radiation in Space (OLTARIS), a NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration)-developed simulation tool. Further, the effect of SPEs (October 1989) on the performance of shielding materials is studied and evaluated through particle flux distributions (energy spectrum) and equivalent dose distributions for these materials. The relative shielding effectiveness of these materials in the SPE environment varied from that in the GCR environment, suggesting that material performance is dependent on the radiation environment. Beryllium borohydride (Be(BH4)2) emerges as the best material in the SPE environment, while lithium hydride (LiH) gives the least dose equivalent in the GCR environment. The particle-wise dose equivalent and flux contributions reveal that, in the SPE environment, the material performance is directly linked to the hydrogen content of the material. In addition, the effect of solar modulation on dose equivalent in the GCR environment is studied. As solar modulation increases, the GCR intensity reduces and hence dose equivalent also reduces. As the space radiation environment consists of complex particle radiation of high energies, in order to validate the large sample of materials for space radiation shielding, the combinatorial complexity of possible configurations presents a major computational challenge. To address this challenge, the material selection problem is formulated as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model and is solved using the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). By mapping OLTARIS dose-equivalent data to the Ising model and utilizing the quantum-classical hybrid approaches of VQE and QAOA, optimal shielding configurations that minimize radiation dose are identified, demonstrating the potential of Quantum Algorithms in advancing space radiation protection strategies. Our results are in agreement between OLTARIS and Quantum Optimization in the SPE environment.

Article.Authors: Nishter Z.; Gang L.; Zahid A.; Naveed W.; Gul R.; Hameed A.; Khan W.; Elzein I.
Article.Abstract: The growing threat of microplastic contamination of the marine biosphere requires that monitoring technologies surpass the limitations of conventional approaches. This paper presents the development and validation of an integrated, machine learning-based framework for real-time detection and management of microplastics in coastal environments, whose primary contributions are real-time IoT-edge-cloud integration, multi-sensor fusion, and 72 h predictive modeling. We deployed a multi-sensor platform integrating hyperspectral imaging (400-2,500 nm) with IoT sensor networks at five monitoring locations over 18 months. The analytical pipeline employs a stacked ensemble of CNN, SVM, and random forest algorithms with soft-vote fusion. The framework processes samples 340% faster than traditional laboratory analysis while reducing operational costs by 67%. Through continuous real-time evaluation, this scalable solution will provide a quick instrument in a global network of coastal monitoring tools to create evidence-based policy and focused intervention approaches.

Article.Title: Spatial transcriptomics profiling across tissue boundaries in the developing mouse brain
Article.Authors: Hammer V.; Ossowski S.
Article.Abstract: Tissue boundaries preserve structural integrity and guide cell differentiation during development, despite constant stress from proliferation, cell death, and tissue deformation. Analysis of the dorsal pallium-meninges boundary showed specific regulatory patterns in outer brain and meningeal layers, with strong links to developmental processes and distance-dependent regulation in major pathways, including those involved in neurodevelopmental disease and cancer. Article.Authors: Hu C.; Bian L.; Luo L.; Zheng Z.; Chen Y.; Gao X.; Li F.; Yang D.; Liu Y.; Li G.; Xu H.; Yan C.; Jin G.
Article.Abstract: Intestinal-type gastric cancer (IGC) progresses through the Correa cascade, yet the molecular determinants of this transition remain insufficiently defined. Using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on matched normal, intestinal metaplasia, and tumor tissues from five patients, we identified eight epithelial subtypes, including a transitional enterocyte population that expanded along the disease trajectory. Article.Title: Single-nucleus transcriptomics uncovers region-specific molecular features underlying selective aging vulnerability of cholinergic neurons
Article.Authors: Li Q.; Chen J.; Liu X.; Gong H.; Li X.; Ren M.
Article.Abstract: Cholinergic neurons exhibit functional and molecular heterogeneity across the basal forebrain (BF), midbrain (MB), and brainstem (BS), while the aging-associated transcriptional features remain poorly characterized. Here, we performed single nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on 108,062 nuclei from the MS/VDB, HDB/SI, PPTG/LDTG, 7N, and 12N in adult and aged mice. BF cells showed greater age-associated transcriptomic alterations than MB and BS cells, with pronounced region-specific divergence among cholinergic neurons. These findings reveal region-specific associations between extracellular signaling and intrinsic transcriptional stress, highlighting a selective imbalance that underlies the vulnerability of BF cholinergic neurons.

Article.Title: Global epidemiological and genetic burden of rare neurological diseases in children
Article.Authors: Xie Z.; Sun C.; Liang W.; Zhao X.; Miao L.; Liu X.; Lu Y.; Liu C.; Yin Z.; Li J.; Xie Z.
Article.Abstract: We assessed the global burden of rare childhood neurological diseases from 1990 to 2021 and projected trends to 2050 using Global Burden of Disease data, alongside an analysis of the genetic burden from ClinVar. Four neurological conditions were classified as rare childhood neurological diseases: motor neuron disease, multiple sclerosis, neuroblastoma and other peripheral nervous cell tumors, and other neurological disorders. From 1990 to 2021, the global age-standardized prevalence and disability-adjusted life-year rates of rare childhood neurological diseases increased, with higher burdens among boys and in low-middle sociodemographic index countries. Our customized forecasting model projected that 110.2 thousand children would be affected by 2050, representing an 11.83% increase from 2021. Annual and cumulative increases in newly reported disease-causing genes and pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants associated with monogenic neurological diseases were observed from 1990 to 2024. The increasing and disparate burden of rare childhood neurological diseases highlights the need for targeted prevention.

Article.Title: Enabling climate action: A nexus approach for delivering co-benefits across biodiversity, water, food, and health
Article.Authors: Singh P.; Gupta H.; Díaz-José J.; McElwee P.; Tirado M.; Cherubini F.; Duchková H.; Llope M.; Vale M.; Khan S.; Ito A.; Hori M.; Eriksen S.; Tiwari L.; Phang S.; Mason-D’Croz D.; Xu X.; van Huysen T.; Herrero M.; Ricketts T.; Harrison P.; Smith P.
Article.Abstract: Climate response options rarely affect biodiversity, water, food, and health in uniform ways. This comparative analysis examines why technically viable response options generate uneven cross-nexus outcomes, and how governance and justice conditions shape whether these outcomes become durable co-benefits. Anchored in the IPBES Nexus Assessment, the analysis synthesizes evidence from fifteen response options spanning land, ocean, energy, urban, industrial, and societal transitions. Ecosystem-centered and demand-side pathways more consistently produce synergies because they work through ecological functions that connect several nexus elements. Infrastructure- and technology-centered options deliver mitigation and health gains, but their wider effects are more context-dependent and often shaped by land use, water demand, biodiversity risk, tenure, access, and benefit-sharing. These patterns do not arise from technical design alone. By integrating nexus governance with Earth System Justice, the analysis indicates how cross-sectoral coordination, distributive equity, procedural inclusion, accountable finance, and knowledge pluralism can shape legitimacy and durability. Climate action is more likely to deliver sustained system-wide benefits when institutions align ecological interdependencies with social rights and responsibilities. Otherwise, promising interventions may remain partial, contested or short-lived.

Article.Abstract: Obesity promotes chronic low-grade inflammation through metabolic stress and activation of the NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome. The effects of caloric restriction on this pathway in humans are poorly understood; therefore, we evaluated the impact of a 6-month hypocaloric dietary intervention in 45 adults with obesity by assessing the metabolic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, and inflammasome-related markers in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. These findings support caloric restriction as a strategy to mitigate obesity-associated immunometabolic dysfunction and identify the redox-inflammasome axis as a potential therapeutic target.

Article.Title: Targeting host ferroptosis in cancer cachexia: Tumor-immune triggers, tissue wasting, and the therapeutic paradox
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Chen R.; Ding S.
Article.Abstract: Cancer cachexia is a systemic wasting syndrome driven by tumor burden, chronic inflammation, disrupted nutrient handling, and neuroendocrine stress. Supportive nutrition, exercise, and symptom management rarely restore lean mass, function, or treatment tolerance once wasting is established. Ferroptosis, iron-dependent cell death caused by phospholipid peroxidation, may connect inflammatory iron redistribution, lipid remodeling, mitochondrial stress, and impaired antioxidant defenses. This review critically evaluates ferroptosis in cachexia from a tumor-host pharmacology perspective, distinguishing causal evidence from associated oxidative signatures. We highlight two experimentally supported mechanisms: neutrophil-derived lipocalin-2 in lung cancer cachexia and tumor exosomal miR-203a-3p in pancreatic cancer-associated muscle wasting. We also examine the paradox that tumor ferroptosis induction may weaken host-tissue resistance and worsen muscle and adipose loss. We propose a "split-ferroptosis" strategy combining tumor sensitization with host-protective iron modulation, lipid peroxide scavenging, endogenous defense reinforcement, and biomarker-guided patient selection to expand the tumor-host therapeutic index.

Article.Authors: Bertola A.; Wenner N.; Rocha L.; Keys T.; Diard M.
Article.Abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptible Escherichia coli cells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold).
