Article.Title: Making sense of touch: Spatial tactile cues promote efficient visuo‐somatosensory integration and restore motor accuracy under sensory conflict
Article.Authors: Vlachou M.; Lafaverges E.; Mouchnino L.; Blouin J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Effective interaction with complex environments relies on the integration of somatosensory and visual signals into coherent spatial representations of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, as during goal‐directed hand movements under mirror‐reversed visual feedback, motor performance deteriorates. Despite this conflict, the visual mapping between the hand and the environment remains preserved, and visual information typically facilitates motor performance, whereas tactile feedback impairs it. Here, we tested whether providing tactile input with explicit spatial structure renders visuo‐somatosensory integration functionally relevant and stabilizes motor behaviour under sensory conflict. Healthy adults performed a mirror‐tracing task, tracing a shape's contour with the index finger while tactile feedback conveyed either motion‐related cues alone or additional discrete spatial landmarks aligned with the outline. Spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness relative to motion‐related tactile input, indicating more effective online motor control. EEG source analyses further revealed that, when spatial tactile cues were present, somatosensory activity increased and functional connectivity was largely restricted to sensorimotor areas. In contrast, when tactile cues did not convey spatial information, sensory conflict was associated with widespread reductions in cortical activity, including in somatosensory and parietal areas, and with a diffuse functional connectivity pattern consistent with elevated sensorimotor uncertainty. Together, these findings indicate that providing spatial structure to tactile input can mitigate the detrimental effects of visuo‐somatosensory conflict on motor performance and support more efficient integration of visual and somatosensory information during action. image Key points Accurate movements depend on combining visual and somatosensory information to estimate the position of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, motor performance usually deteriorates and tactile feedback can become disruptive. We tested whether tactile feedback becomes useful for movement control when it provides explicit spatial landmarks, rather than only motion‐related information from finger–surface contact. During a tracing task under visuo‐somatosensory conflict, spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness compared with when touch conveyed motion cues alone. Spatial tactile cues were associated with increased somatosensory cortical activity and a more spatially restricted pattern of functional coupling within sensorimotor networks, whereas their absence was associated with reduced somatosensory and parietal activity and a more distributed connectivity profile. Spatial structure in touch promotes multisensory integration, helping stabilize motor control under sensory conflict and highlighting how tactile cue design may improve sensorimotor function.

Article.Title: Prolonged rod photoresponse and enhanced cone sensitivity in the transgenic mouse retina lacking arrestin and guanylate cyclase activating proteins
Article.Authors: Sato S.; Frederiksen R.; Sampath A.; Kefalov V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Light activates visual pigments and downstream G protein signalling cascades in rod and cone photoreceptor cells. Timely response inactivation requires visual pigment inactivation by arrestin and restoration of cellular cGMP by guanylate cyclase activating proteins (GCAPs). Using GCAP‐deficient mice, we previously showed that apo‐opsin produces photoresponse‐like signals. To investigate the inactivation of apo‐opsin by arrestin, we generated GCAP‐deficient mice lacking arrestin ( Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− ). Using ex vivo electroretinography, we found that the dim flash responses of Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− rods were ∼100‐fold slower than those of control Gcaps −/− rods. As a result, even brief dim light exposure during sample preparation resulted in prolonged rod saturation, so that only cone responses were initially observed in Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− retinas. In contrast, rod responses were observed immediately when Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− retinas were dissected under infrared light to avoid rod photoactivation. Microspectrophotometry showed that the rate of production and decay of the active rhodopsin photoproduct, Meta II, was comparable between Gcaps −/− and Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− rods. However, the rate of photoproduct Meta III decay was 3‐fold slower in Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− rods, supporting a role for arrestin in accelerating the decay of photoactivated rhodopsin. To evaluate the effect of rod saturation on cone responses, we compared photopic cone responses from wild‐type and Gnat1 −/− retinas lacking rod signalling. Cone photoresponses were larger and more sensitive in wild‐type retinas, suggesting the potentiation of cone function by the saturation of rod phototransduction. Together, our results demonstrate that the very slow deactivation of rod responses in Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− retinas might result in selective and potentiated cone signalling in darkness. image Key points Arrestin and guanylate cyclase activating proteins (GCAPs) play an important role in inactivation of the phototransduction cascade and termination of the light response in rod photoreceptors. The deletion of arrestin and GCAPs results in ∼100‐fold slower dim flash responses in rods so that even brief dim light exposure produces saturation of the rods for tens of minutes. The decay of the rhodopsin photoactivated intermediate Meta III was slowed down 3‐fold by the deletion of arrestin in Gcaps −/− rods, supporting a role for arrestin in accelerating the decay of photoactivated rhodopsin. Cone photoresponses were smaller and less sensitive in retinas lacking rod signalling, suggesting potentiation of cone function by the saturation of rod phototransduction. Together, these results demonstrate that the very slow deactivation of rod responses in arrestin‐ and GCAP‐deficient retinas can result in selective and potentiated cone signalling in darkness.

Article.Title: SGIP1 limits cannabinoid receptor signalling in spinal nociceptive synapses and modulates analgesia during neuroinflammation
Article.Authors: Dresslerova D.; Pontearso M.; Muzik D.; Bhattacharyya A.; Slepicka J.; Vasconcelos D.; Palecek J.; Spicarova D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The endocannabinoid system is important for pain modulation, whereas its utilization for analgesia is restricted due to the limited efficacy of cannabinoids and side effects. Cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB 1 ) in the spinal dorsal horn provides presynaptic inhibition of nociceptive neurotransmission. CB 1 regulatory protein, SH3‐containing GRB2‐like protein 3‐interacting protein 1 (SGIP1), controls its functional availability, while its role in pain modulation remains poorly understood. We examined the role of SGIP1 in nociceptive signalling under control and inflammatory conditions, using behavioural tests, patch‐clamp recordings in spinal cord slices and calcium imaging of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. SGIP1 knockout (KO) mice of both sexes showed a selective reduction in heat sensitivity, with no change in mechanical withdrawal threshold. Following carrageenan‐induced inflammation, both wild‐type (WT) and KO mice developed mechanical allodynia, whereas thermal hyperalgesia in KO mice reached only the control values of WT mice. Intrathecal application of cannabinoid agonist WIN55,212‐2 produced analgesia in both WT and KO mice, with enhanced effect of the lower dose (5 µg vs . 10 µg) in KO animals. WIN55,212‐2 (1 µM) in slices from inflamed SGIP1 KO mice induced significantly greater reduction in miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) frequency, without amplitude change, indicating enhanced presynaptic inhibition in KO mice. These enhanced inhibitory effects of WIN55,212‐2 in KO mice after inflammation were further demonstrated in DRG cultured neurons. Our results establish SGIP1 as a state‐dependent negative modulator of CB 1 function and identify SGIP1–CB 1 interaction as a candidate target for selective enhancement of cannabinoid analgesia under inflammatory pain conditions. image Key points SGIP1 deletion reduced basal heat sensitivity in mice of both sexes without altering mechanical threshold, suggesting a sex‐independent role in thermal nociception. Inflammation increased mechanical and thermal sensitivity in both SGIP1 KO and WT mice, whereas the increased thermal sensitivity of KO reached only the baseline levels of WT mice. Intrathecal cannabinoid agonist WIN55,212‐2 produced analgesia in both genotypes, with a bigger effect of the lower dose (5 vs . 10 µg) in SGIP1 KO mice. WIN55,212‐2 induced strong inhibition of miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) frequency in dorsal horn neurons that was selectively potentiated by SGIP1 deletion under inflammatory, but not control, conditions, consistent with a presynaptic locus of action. These effects were further confirmed by calcium imaging in DRG cultured neurons. SGIP1 acts as an inflammation‐dependent presynaptic CB 1 modulator of spinal nociceptive transmission, positioning the SGIP1–CB 1 interaction as a candidate target for selective enhancement of cannabinoid analgesia.

Article.Title: Non‐steady‐state modelling reveals reduced skeletal muscle protein synthesis as the primary driver of disuse‐atrophy in young, healthy females
Article.Authors: Pufahl C.; Mcleod J.; Ferguson E.; Boileau K.; Ross B.; Tripp T.; Wilkinson J.; Simpson C.; Gurd B.; McGlory C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Skeletal muscle mass reflects the balance between muscle protein synthesis (MPS) and muscle protein breakdown (MPB). In healthy humans, a decline in MPS is recognized as the primary driver of muscle disuse‐atrophy, with limited contribution from increased MPB. However, disuse‐induced declines in protein pool size directly influence the calculation of muscle protein turnover. We examined how accounting for changes in protein pool size impacted MPS and MPB rates assessed using deuterium oxide in healthy humans. Fourteen females (21 ± 2 years of age; 24.5 ± 3.0 kg/m 2 ) had one leg subjected to 10 days of unloading, whilst the contralateral leg underwent loading in the form of resistance exercise. Steady‐state and non‐steady‐state modelling approaches were used to calculate MPS and MPB rates. In response to unloading, there was a significant decline in MRI‐derived vastus lateralis volume, and thus non‐steady‐state equations were applied exclusively to this limb. Regardless of whether steady‐state or non‐steady‐state approaches were applied, mixed MPS rates were significantly reduced in response to unloading, whilst mixed MPB rates remained unchanged. Notably, unloading elicited protein fraction‐specific responses, whereby myofibrillar MPS rates declined significantly whilst sarcoplasmic MPS rates were unaltered. We also found that in response to loading, mixed, myofibrillar and sarcoplasmic MPS rates remained unchanged compared with basal rates. Our findings show that unilateral unloading in females induces muscle disuse‐atrophy driven by reductions in MPS rates, rather than by elevations in MPB rates, a response that was protein fraction specific and preserved irrespective of whether steady‐state or non‐steady‐state equations were used. image Key points In humans, short‐term muscle disuse‐atrophy is generally attributed to reduced muscle protein synthesis (MPS) rates, but integrated tracer approaches to measure protein turnover can be influenced by changes in protein pool size. We used deuterated water ( 2 H 2 O) to measure rates of MPS and muscle protein breakdown (MPB) during 10 days of unilateral unloading in young, healthy females. Steady‐state and non‐steady‐state equations were applied to account for changes in the protein pool size that occur with disuse‐atrophy. Unloading reduced muscle size and MPS rates, whereas MPB rates were unchanged. Accounting for the change in the protein pool size using non‐steady‐state equations did not alter this conclusion. These findings refine our interpretation of the mechanisms driving muscle disuse‐atrophy in healthy humans that might differ from more severe clinical or preclinical scenarios of muscle wasting.

Article.Title: K <sub>V</sub> channels contribute to thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle of humans
Article.Authors: Ruiz‐Pick Y.; Wagle‐Babb S.; Kichloo A.; Olivencia‐Yurvati A.; Dick G.; Romero S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Localized application of heat is used therapeutically to reduce skeletal muscle pain and improve mobility and recovery in various populations. The efficacy of this thermal therapy is considered to be partly a result of increased blood flow in the skeletal muscle directly exposed to heat (i.e. thermal hyperaemia). However, the mechanisms mediating thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle of humans remain poorly understood. Voltage‐dependent potassium (K V ) channels play a pivotal role linking upstream vasodilatory signals to electro‐mechanical mechanisms that mediate vascular smooth muscle relaxation. Therefore, the present study aimed to test the hypothesis that K V channel antagonism would attenuate thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle of humans. We used microdialysis to directly measure local blood flow via the ethanol washout technique at two sites in the vastus lateralis muscle of 10 healthy adults (seven women). One probe was perfused with 0.9% saline, whereas the other was perfused with the K V channel antagonist 4‐aminopyridine (26.6 m m ). Pulsed short‐wave diathermy was used to induce deep heating of the vastus lateralis for 90 min. Muscle temperature was measured midway between the microdialysis probes via a thermocouple. Baseline blood flow did not differ between probes ( P = 0.684). Pulsed short‐wave diathermy increased skeletal muscle temperature through 90 min of heating ( P < 0.001). However, the accompanying increase in blood flow at 90 min was attenuated when perfused with 4‐aminopyridine ( P = 0.0222). These data suggest that K V channels substantially contribute to thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle of humans. image Key points The efficacy of thermal therapy is considered to be partly a result of increased blood flow in the skeletal muscle directly exposed to heat (i.e. thermal hyperaemia). However, the mechanisms mediating thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle remain poorly understood. Voltage‐dependent potassium (K V ) channels play a pivotal role as downstream effectors that mediate vascular smooth muscle relaxation. Therefore, we tested the hypothesis that K V channel antagonism would attenuate thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle of humans. Using microdialysis, we found that K V channel antagonism with 4‐aminopyridine attenuated thermal hyperaemia at 90 min of localized heating, when this vasodilatory response was the greatest. We identified a critical role for K V channels in human skeletal muscle thermal hyperaemia, establishing these channels as important downstream effectors of this vasodilatory response.

Article.Title: Why and When to Adjust for Intracranial Volume in Structural Brain Imaging
Article.Authors: Fürtjes A.; Tucker-Drob E.; Deary I.; Cox S.
Article.Abstract: Structural neuroimaging research is marked by substantial methodological variability, with important implications for inference and reproducibility. A central but often under-justified source for this variability is whether intracranial volume (ICV) is included as a covariate. We argue that ICV adjustment is not a neutral analytical step, but a modeling decision that fundamentally alters the research question by redefining the variance under investigation, and it can even change the very direction of the estimated effect. We evaluate five common research questions in the literature and argue that each is underpinned by distinct assumptions about where ICV sits in the causal structure linking neuroanatomy with other complex behavioral traits. We identify contexts in which ICV adjustment is necessary to define the construct under study, as well as situations in which it removes meaningful variance or introduces interpretational and statistical complications. We argue that ICV adjustment should explicitly be justified, and we provide practical guidance for deciding when such adjustment is appropriate. We hope to stimulate debate and improve consistency, interpretability, and reproducibility of population-level neuroimaging research.

Article.Title: Computational Insights into Afferent Integration Underlying Mechanical Allodynia
Article.Authors: Lockhart A.; West C.
Article.Abstract: The somatosensory system provides the central nervous system with continuous information about the external environment and body state, enabling adaptive behavior. This feedback is crucial for detecting noxious stimuli and differentiating harmful from harmless touch to avoid injury (Saluja et al., 2024). Broadly, touch is mechanical somatosensory information detected by tactile receptors in the skin (Abraira et al., 2017). This information is processed through the spinal cord and ascends to the brain, where the somatosensory system assigns salience to the input (Kim et al., 2019). Importantly, tactile stimuli differ not only in intensity but also in their spatial and temporal structure. For example, low-intensity stimuli are perceived as gentle touch, vibration changes quickly and provides information about texture and surface properties (Weber et al., 2013), and strong sustained pressure may be perceived as painful. Likewise, tactile perception depends on the spatial pattern of receptor activation across the skin, including whether a stimulus is focal or broadly distributed. These sensory signals are encoded by patterns of activity across different afferent fiber classes (Abraira et al., 2017) and converge in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord (Abraira et al., 2017), where local circuits influence which pathways are activated and which sensory signals reach the brain. Spinal interneurons within the dorsal horn are key in regulating the transmission of nociceptive input. Inhibitory interneurons in the superficial dorsal horn release GABA onto somatosensory afferent fibers such as Aδ- and C-fibers to regulate touch and pain-related signaling (Stachowski and Dougherty, 2021). Inhibition also refines receptive fields, ensuring precise touch detection and preventing neighboring fields from triggering pain. This inhibition contributes to the processing and filtering of sensory input, helping to regulate responses to innocuous and noxious stimuli and supporting protective reflexes. Article.Title: Multidimensional dynamics of object representations in the human visual system
Article.Authors: Chen Z.; Isik L.; Bonner M.
Article.Abstract: Natural image representations are distributed across many dimensions of visual cortex activity, but little is known about how the multidimensional structure of these representations evolves over time following stimulus onset. Herewe examined the temporal dynamics and latent dimensional structure of natural object representations in large-scale EEG and MEG data from male and female human participants. We also compared these datawith leading representational models derived from large-scale human similarity judgments and deep neural networks. Our findings reveal a rapid expansion of stimulus dimensionality in the brain, which peaks within 100 milliseconds and gradually decays over hundreds of milliseconds. The dynamics of these dimensionality changes tracked the decoding accuracy for both behavioral embeddings and neural network features, suggesting that dimensionality may be a general indicator of representational expressivity. Interestingly, the dimensionality of the neural representations could not be fully explained by a leading behavior-based model or deep neural network. Follow-up experiments showed that the remaining neural variance carried additional perceptually relevant information not yet explained by leading models. Together, these findings reveal previously unrecognized complexity in measurements of dynamic human brain responses to natural objects. Significance Statement When we look at an object, our brains rapidly construct a rich internal representation of what we see. Using large-scale, time-resolved brain recordings from people viewing thousands of natural images, we find that the brain rapidly expands its representational complexity within the first 100 milliseconds, sustaining this richness for hundreds of milliseconds thereafter. A leading behavioral model and a large-scale deep neural network do not fully account for this complexity — yet the unexplained brain activity is not noise: people can reliably use these residual neural patterns to judge image similarity. These findings challenge the assumption that such brain recordings are informationally limited and reveal structure in the human visual system that future models will need to explain.

Article.Title: Phase-Structured Neuronal Recruitment in Motor Cortex during Skilled Movement Reorganized Early after Stroke
Article.Authors: Chen D.; Zhou Y.; Cao C.; Gong J.; Huang Q.; Zhuang J.; Jia F.; Guo Y.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Skilled forelimb movement engages both oscillatory and spiking activity in the motor cortex. However, how oscillatory phase organizes neuronal recruitment during behavior remains unclear. Here, we performed longitudinal bilateral recordings of local field potentials and single-unit activity in the rat (male) caudal forelimb area during a single-pellet retrieval task before and after stroke. Stroke altered spectral organization and redistributed neuronal recruitment across hemispheres. In the CFA contralateral to the reaching forelimb, which was the lesioned hemisphere, firing rates decreased and spike timing became more variable, whereas spike-LFP phase consistency increased in low-frequency bands. In contrast, the CFA ipsilateral to the reaching forelimb showed increased firing and reduced low-frequency phase consistency. These results demonstrate that early post-stroke motor cortical reorganization does not simply weaken neural activity but reshapes neuronal recruitment into a phase-structured form within ongoing oscillatory activity, providing insight into the dynamical principles underlying motor cortical reorganization during skilled movement. Significance Statement Skilled movement depends on coordinated interactions between populationlevel oscillations and neuronal spiking, but how this organization changes after cortical injury remains unclear. Using longitudinal bilateral recordings during skilled forelimb behavior, we show that early post-stroke reorganization is not characterized by a uniform loss of cortical activity. In the CFA contralateral to the reaching forelimb, firing was reduced and spike timing became more variable, yet low-frequency spike-LFP phase consistency increased. The ipsilateral CFA showed the opposite pattern, with increased firing and reduced low-frequency phase consistency. These findings demonstrate that firing output and spike–phase organization can reorganize independently after stroke, revealing a phase-structured dimension of motor cortical activity that is not captured by firing rate alone.

Article.Title: Intervening contexts reshape hippocampal-cortical retrieval states and later source attribution
Article.Authors: Hermiller M.; Davachi L.
Article.Abstract: Memories are often reactivated in one context and only later judged with respect to where they originally occurred. We tested how an intervening retrieval context shapes neural representations and later source memory. In two fMRI tasks, participants (both male and female) encoded objects within contextual backgrounds, completed an immediate retrieval test in which object cues appeared against either the original background or a different background, and subsequently judged each object’s original context on a neutral screen. Shifted cueing contexts reduced source accuracy and biased errors toward the intervening context, despite no detectable difference in immediate recognition or associative-memory performance. Representational similarity analyses showed that encoding patterns reflected original-context structure, whereas immediate-cue-period patterns were broadly organized by the cued (i.e., currently visible) context. On shifted trials, activity patterns showed greater similarity to encoding-derived templates for the cued context than for the original context. Across participants, greater differentiation of original-context similarity between consistent and shifted cueing in posterior hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex was associated with better source memory after a contextual shift. Within participants, precuneus contextual engagement and dorsal anterior cingulate context alignment predicted later source choices, with similar relationships after adjustment for immediate recognition responses. Later source attribution therefore depended on the contextual state expressed when an item was re-encountered, not simply on reinstatement of the original event. Significance statement Remembering is often described as bringing up the past, but memories are frequently reactivated in new contexts before we judge where they came from. We show that this intervening context can bias later source attribution even when that context is no longer visible at final test. Using two fMRI tasks, representational similarity analysis and trial-level source-choice models, we found that cue-period activity was organized by the context present during cueing and that specific context-state signals predicted later memory choices, whereas item reinstatement did not. Source-memory errors can therefore reflect contextual information encountered after the original event, not only failures to recover the original context.

Article.Title: RAI1 loss produces cell type-specific transcriptomic, circuit, and behavioural consequences across mPFC GABAergic interneuron subtypes
Article.Authors: Haque M.; Mahiout S.; Zhang Y.; Kowalczyk M.; Chang Y.; Chang H.; Lin Y.; Lee Y.; Zhang Q.; Huang W.
Article.Abstract: Haploinsufficiency of RAI1 ( retinoic acid–induced 1 ) causes Smith–Magenis syndrome (SMS), a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intellectual disability, maladaptive behaviours, and social deficits. RAI1 is a transcriptional regulator broadly expressed across multiple brain cell types, yet the cell type-specific transcriptional consequences of Rai1 haploinsufficiency remain unknown. Behavioural experiments used mice of both sexes. Our spatial transcriptomic assays in Rai1 +/- mice identified dysregulated genes across isocortical cell types, with synaptic organization and activity-dependent programs affected in a subtype-specific manner among GABAergic interneurons. To explore RAI1 function in these cells, we conditionally deleted Rai1 from parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (SST), and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneurons. In the social dominance tube test, PV- and SST-specific Rai1 loss reduced winning rates, whereas VIP-specific loss increased winning. Rai1 ⁺/⁻ mice showed social competition–induced PV/VIP cFos activation in the medial-prefrontal cortex. Overall mPFC cFos activity was increased in VIP mutants but was decreased in PV and SST mutants. Monosynaptic rabies tracing revealed RAI1-dependent, subtype-specific remodeling of long-range inputs onto mPFC interneurons. Chemogenetic inhibition of Rai1 -deficient mPFC PV or VIP interneurons normalized the social competition phenotypes. Together, our findings reveal that Rai1 haploinsufficiency induces cell-type-specific transcriptional and anatomical reorganization of prefrontal interneurons, which bidirectionally biases social behaviour output and is acutely reversible by targeted activity modulation. By resolving how a broadly expressed gene produces divergent consequences across interneuron classes, our work clarifies the cellular origins of social deficits in SMS and points to subtype-selective interneuron modulation as a therapeutic strategy i SMS and GABAergic disorders. Significance statement Social behavioural deficits are a prominent feature of SMS, a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by haploinsufficiency of the transcriptional regulator RAI1 . GABAergic interneuron subtypes in the medial prefrontal cortex are critical for social behaviour, but the transcriptional programs governing their functional development and maturation are largely unknown. Here we show that Rai1 loss causes subtype-specific transcriptomic and anatomical input reorganization, and altered Fos activity in PV, SST, and VIP interneurons, culminating in divergent social competitive outcomes. The net social deficit likely arises from competing cell-type-specific perturbations. Notably, acute modulation of interneuron activity normalizes social behaviour, highlighting a potential therapeutic opportunity. Our findings emphasize the need for subtype-specific interventions and provide a cell-type-resolved framework for understanding GABAergic dysfunction in neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Title: Selective and spatially biased activity remodeling following adult-onset sensory loss
Article.Authors: Song Y.; Parkins S.; Konda K.; Pham K.; Mesik L.; Lee H.; Li J.; Ewald S.; Lee H.
Article.Abstract: Cross-modal brain plasticity after sensory loss allows an organism to utilize the remaining senses to guide behavior. Two distinct mechanisms support such adaptation: cross-modal recruitment and compensatory plasticity. Cross-modal recruitment refers to the deprived sensory areas gaining responsiveness to the spared senses, while compensatory plasticity indicates enhanced functionality of the spared sensory areas. Widespread synaptic and circuit-level plasticity has been reported to support such cross-modal plasticity. Here we combined whole-brain clearing, light-sheet imaging, and activity labeling using a cFosTRAP2 mouse line to examine the spatial distribution of highly active cells across brain areas following acute sensory manipulations in adult mice of both sexes. Adult-onset vision loss led to an initial decrease in the density of activity-labeled cells in visual areas, including the primary visual cortex (V1), and a parallel increase in the spared primary auditory (A1) and somatosensory barrel (S1BF) cortices. V1 and some higher-order visual areas (HVAs), but not the visual thalamus, exhibited a partial rebound in activity after a week of vision loss. The activity rebound in visual cortices and the enhanced activity observed in A1 were spatially biased. Passively exposing adult-onset blind mice to sound did not further alter activity levels, except for a decrease in the claustrum. Conversely, adult-onset deafening significantly reduced the activity-labeled cell density in auditory and auditory-related areas without clear signs of compensatory plasticity in the spared areas. Our results indicate that adult cross-modal plasticity is largely observed in sensory cortices with rather specific within-area spatial bias, suggesting selective functional adaptations. Significance Statement This study examined the spatial profile of how the adult brain adapts when one sense is lost. In mice, vision loss caused brain activity to drop in visual areas followed by partial recovery over time, suggesting gradual recruitment of these areas by non-visual information. In parallel, the brain areas for hearing and touch became more active, a sign of compensation. Activity changes were not widespread but limited mainly to sensory areas with some local spatial bias. In contrast, the same duration of hearing loss produced much less evidence of compensation in the spared sensory areas. These findings suggest that the adult brain can reorganize after sensory loss, but this adaptation is selective and region-specific, implying targeted functional compensation.

Article.Title: Sour Suppresses Sweet, Salty, and Bitter: Implications for Signal Processing in Taste Buds
Article.Authors: Fleites I.; Pereira E.; Morales K.; Chaudhari N.; Roper S.
Article.Abstract: Taste is typically encountered as complex blends, yet how peripheral taste organs process heterogeneous mixtures remains poorly understood. Here we asked how sour stimuli influence the encoding of sweet, salty, and bitter tastes in primary gustatory sensory neurons. Using in vivo calcium imaging in mice of either sex to record neurons in geniculate ganglia during oral delivery of tastants, we compared responses to naturally occurring taste stimuli presented alone versus in binary mixtures that activate acid (sour)-sensing (Type III) taste bud cells. Adding citric acid or HCl robustly suppressed sucrose-evoked responses in geniculate ganglion neurons, even though acid itself did not activate those neurons. Acid-induced suppression generalized to bitter and salty tastes, which, like sucrose, are believed to activate Type II taste cells. Additional stimuli that activate acid-sensing taste cells (NH 4 Cl, KCl) also reduced sucrose responses, supporting a common mechanism linked to Type III cells. Manipulating levels of serotonin (a paracrine transmitter released by Type III cells) in taste buds altered taste suppression: increasing serotonin with 5-hydroxytryptophan enhanced acid-induced suppression whereas depleting serotonin with para-chlorophenylalanine weakened it. Finally, population analyses, including UMAP dimensionality reduction, indicate that taste suppression is not limited to a particular subset of gustatory sensory neurons. The findings are consistent with serotonin-dependent paracrine inhibition within taste buds as a contributor to sour-driven suppression in taste mixtures and reveal a compression of gustatory information into hedonic categories as early as at the level of primary sensory neurons. Significance Statement Foods typically present a complex mixture of tastes. However, understanding how the nervous system processes gustatory signals has traditionally relied on investigations that analyze responses to individual tastes. Our study investigates how mixtures of naturally occurring food tastes activate sensory neurons and how emergent signals arise when combinations of gustatory stimuli excite taste buds. Using in vivo imaging of primary gustatory neurons in mice, we show that sour stimuli suppress neural responses to sweet, bitter, and salty tastes. The findings reveal an early, peripheral stage of neural computation that helps explain how complex flavors are encoded.

Article.Title: Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns of Dynamic Audiovisual Social Stimuli in Autism Spectrum Disorder (Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns in Autism)
Article.Authors: Van De Water A.; Byrge L.; Kennedy D.; Kliemann D.; Traer J.
Article.Abstract: The neural basis of social difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains uncertain. Prior studies typically used static stimuli or reduced complex stimuli to only a few dimensions, obscuring real-world complexity. Here, we used videos with social content to engage brain networks and trained encoding models to predict brain activity from high-dimensional audio, visual, and more abstract socially relevant features (e.g., valence). We hypothesized that brain activity in autistic adults would be less accurately predicted and more heterogeneous within and across individuals than in neurotypical (NT) participants, particularly for socially relevant features. Participants [48 ASD (13 female), 90 NT (25 female)] viewed six videos (5–20 min). Brain activity was measured using fMRI. Cross-validated encoding models were assessed on prediction accuracy, variance, and pattern similarity. Brain activity was predicted significantly above chance across brain networks and videos with striking consistency between groups. Auditory and language networks were most accurately predicted. Within-participant predictions were equally variable between groups; however, autistic participants exhibited lower within-group encoding pattern similarity than NT participants and greater across-group than within-group similarity. Analyses using only socially relevant features showed the largest across-group differences in encoding pattern similarity. The novel application of encoding models to multiple videos in ASD suggests greater heterogeneity in neural representations of social information in ASD. Although group-averaged encoding accuracies were comparable across groups, ASD participants showed more heterogeneous regional encoding patterns. These idiosyncratic patterns underscore the need to incorporate individual variation in brain representations when developing translational neuroimaging approaches in autism. Significance statement Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) experience difficulties in social communication and interaction, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we present a novel application of encoding models to neuroimaging in ASD. Neural representations of dynamic and complex social information were more heterogeneous across autistic as compared with neurotypical individuals while encoding model prediction accuracy was similar for population averages across groups. Effects were robust across six videos and spatial scales. Variability in neural representation across individuals, rather than systemic population differences, may thus be associated with atypical brain function in complex social information processing in autism. The findings highlight the importance of accounting for individual variability when studying the neurobiology of autism and developing translational neuroimaging approaches.

Article.Title: Ventromedial hypothalamic output to the anterior hypothalamic area evokes complex escape behavior
Article.Authors: Coletta C.; Mohead A.; Krieger E.; Porter C.; Stewart J.; Laing B.
Article.Abstract: The ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) and anterior hypothalamic area (AHA) contribute to the orchestration of defensive responses to threat. We set out to test the effects of VMH to AHA (VMH→AHA) stimulation on behavior, organ-systems physiology, circulating pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, and brain activity patterns that support escape behavior. We used optogenetics in male and female SF1-Cre mice for behavioral assays, physiological measurements, and brain activity pattern mapping. For the first time, we demonstrate that VMH SF1 →AHA photostimulation increases complex escape behavior that requires three-dimensional navigation. Even in anesthetized mice, VMH→AHA photostimulation increases fractional shortening of the heart consistent with sympathetic arousal. In addition, we demonstrate that VMH→AHA photostimulation increases levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-6. In the brain, we find significant elevations of activity in the lateral habenula, anterior hypothalamic area, ventral premammillary nucleus, ventrolateral periaqueductal gray, and locus coeruleus. Significance statement We demonstrate that VMH→AHA photostimulation increases escape behavior that depends on a three dimensional route of navigation, increases levels of the cytokine IL-6, as well as increases activity in the lateral habenula, ventral premammillary nucleus, ventrolateral periaqueductal gray, and locus coeruleus. This work informs how hypothalamic circuitry drives behavioral and physiological responses that facilitate escape from threats in the environment.

Article.Title: Arousal state fluctuations destabilize speech intelligibility in older adults
Article.Authors: Smith S.; Sugai J.; Polley D.
Article.Abstract: Understanding speech in noisy, multi-talker environments is fundamental for social communication but becomes increasingly challenging as we age. Age-related hearing loss reduces audibility and degrades speech encoding, yet these deficits do not fully explain the momentary lapses in speech understanding that frustrate real-time communication. Here, we tested whether brain state fluctuations immediately before speech onset predict forthcoming speech recognition errors in older listeners. We measured the accuracy, speed, and consistency of speech recognition in 183 adults aged 18-76 years (103 female) using a brief, trial-based multi-talker listening task while tracking pupil dynamics before and during speech presentation. Prestimulus pupil-linked arousal predicted trial-level speech recognition in older, but not younger, adults, independent of hearing status, cognitive load, and task accuracy. In adults over 50 years of age, lower and higher extremes of prestimulus pupil size were associated with less accurate and slower responses, producing a striking inverted-U relationship between prestimulus arousal and forthcoming behavioral performance. Older adults exhibited lower extremes of pupil-linked arousal that were specifically associated with greater self-reported difficulty listening in everyday life. By contrast, stimulus-evoked pupil dilation during speech encoding, a measure of listening effort, did not predict trial-level performance at any age. These findings identify prestimulus pupil-linked arousal as a hidden marker of forthcoming lapses in speech intelligibility in older adults. When considered alongside conventional measures of peripheral hearing status in mixed-effects regression models, these measures provide a more complete accounting of biological changes underlying speech intelligibility deficits that frustrate social communication in older adults . Significance statement As we age, following a conversation in crowded environments becomes more difficult and frustrating, even when hearing tests appear normal. This study shows that fluctuations in arousal level (measured through prestimulus pupil size) are tightly linked to fluctuations in the speed and accuracy of speech processing in adults over 50 years of age. Changes in arousal state regulation uniquely accounted for the moment-to-moment variations in speech intelligibility and were more closely associated with self-reported listening challenges than other conventional measures. These findings highlight the contribution of brain-wide arousal systems to real-world listening challenges and identify a straightforward measure that could be used to more comprehensively assess and potentially improve speech understanding in social settings.

Article.Title: Btbd11 regulates glutamatergic synapse organization in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons
Article.Authors: Boyer M.; Zhang S.; Levy A.; Schamber P.; Hartman H.; Blanpied T.; Bygrave A.
Article.Abstract: The mechanisms that underlie glutamatergic synapse organization and function in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) are not well described, despite evidence that impaired glutamatergic excitation of INs is implicated in psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia and anxiety. Glutamatergic synapses received by INs have unique basal transmission properties and exhibit distinct synaptic plasticity compared to those received by excitatory neurons, likely due to cell-type specific differences in postsynaptic density (PSD) composition and maintenance mechanisms. In the present study, we show that the interneuron-specific protein Btbd11 regulates excitatory synapse transmission in mixed-sex primary cultured rat and mouse hippocampal interneurons through promotion of phase separation and support of postsynaptic nanoarchitecture. Btbd11 forms a phase separated protein complex with Psd-95 and TARPγ2 and impacts the stability of TARPγ2 and GluA1 within glutamatergic IN synapses in an expression- and phase separation-dependent manner. Using super resolution imaging, we show that Btbd11 displays nanoscale clustering properties within IN synapses that correlate with Psd-95 nanostructure. Furthermore, genetic deletion of Btbd11 decreases PSD protein expression, reduces synapse size, and disrupts Psd-95 nanocluster organization. These effects manifest as a drastic reduction in glutamatergic synaptic transmission onto INs when Btbd11 is deleted. Together, these data provide insights into a novel cell type-specific synaptic regulatory mechanism in an understudied synapse population. Significance Statement Although glutamatergic excitation of GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) is essential for maintenance of balanced signaling in the brain and dysregulation has been linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, the molecular mechanisms underlying IN-specific glutamatergic transmission are not well characterized. Using protein modeling, molecular biology, live-cell and super-resolution imaging, we describe a unique mechanism of glutamatergic synapse organization in INs by Btbd11, an IN-specific synaptic protein. Btbd11 promotes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and regulates PSD protein mobility, the abundance of key synaptic proteins, and nanoscale synaptic organization. Collectively, this is critical for glutamatergic synaptic transmission within INs. Understanding Btbd11’s role at the synapse highlights the importance of synaptic LLPS, providing insight into the regulatory mechanisms in an understudied synapse with psychiatric disease relevance.

Article.Title: Disentangling the Spatiotemporal Neural Dynamics of Conflict Detection and Resolution between Lexical and Sublexical Processes in Oral Word Reading: An Intracranial SEEG Study
Article.Authors: Zhao C.; Liu Y.; Zeng J.; Luo X.; Dai Z.; Zhang X.; Jiang Y.; Liu Y.; Li Z.; Shi G.; Zhang Y.; Sun W.; Guan Y.; Han Z.
Article.Abstract: Object recognition relies on correspondence between whole objects and their subcomponents. When this correspondence is disrupted, accurate recognition requires detecting conflicts and inhibiting misleading subcomponent information, yet the neural basis underlying these processes remain unclear. Written language, with sublexical components that may conflict with whole words, provides an ideal testbed. Using stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) recorded from 39 participants (both sexes) during Chinese character reading, we revealed a functional dissociation between neural systems supporting conflict detection and inhibitory control. Conflict detection was associated with β band activity in the fusiform gyrus and widespread θ and α band effects across temporal and parietal regions. Inhibitory control was associated with α and β band activity in the inferior frontal and precentral gyri. Granger causality analysis showed increased β band connectivity from conflict-processing to inhibitory-control regions under conflict conditions. These findings demonstrate that disruptions of whole-sublexical correspondence engage dissociable neural systems for conflict detection and inhibitory control, implemented through frequency- and region-specific neural oscillations and coordinated via increased information transfer from posterior to frontal regions. Significance Statement Reading often requires resolving conflicts between competing linguistic representations, yet the neural mechanisms that detect such conflicts and resolve them remain poorly understood. Using stereo-electroencephalography with millimeter-scale spatial and millisecond-scale temporal resolution, we dissociated sublexical conflict detection from inhibitory control during Chinese character reading. We show that these processes are supported by distinct low-frequency oscillatory networks and are linked through directed functional interactions. These findings move beyond traditional accounts of sublexical effects by identifying their underlying cognitive components and neural dynamics, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how cognitive control supports fluent word recognition.

Article.Title: Reelin Deficiency Alters the Directional Orientation, Apical Localization and Length of Primary Cilia in Principal Neurons in the Cerebral Cortex
Article.Authors: Akter S.; Mirhosseiniardakani S.; Takekoshi Y.; Qiu L.; Baker K.; Jiang K.; Lyon M.; Hattori M.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: The primary cilia of pyramidal neurons in inside-out laminated regions are oriented predominantly toward the pia, a pattern reflecting reverse soma movement during postnatal neurodevelopment. However, the mechanisms that regulate the directional cilia orientation remain unknown. Here we show that the primary cilia of neocortical pyramidal neurons in male and female mice are localized at the base of the apical dendrites and aligned distally and opposite to the axon initial segment (AIS). However, this pattern is not observed in atypical pyramidal neurons in the deep neocortex, excitatory neurons in non-laminated regions, or interneurons, where cilia are randomly positioned around the nuclei and lack preferred orientation. In Reelin-deficient mice ( reeler ), the directional orientation and apical location of cilia in late-born neocortical and CA1 neurons are altered. However, the initial impairments are partially corrected during early postnatal development. In contrast, Reelin deficiency disrupts the directional orientation and apical localization of primary cilia in early-born neocortical neurons and principal neurons in evolutionarily conserved laminated regions, where lack postnatal correction. Reelin deficiency also increases the cilia length in principal neurons across the cerebral cortex at a developmental stage when cilia length stabilizes in wild-type mice. In contrast, cilia elongation is not observed in interneurons, GFAP-positive astrocytes, or excitatory neurons in non-laminated regions of reeler . Together, Reelin regulates the directional orientation, apical localization, and length of primary cilia in principal neurons in the cerebral cortex. This study underscores the cilium as a key apical domain, particularly prominent in late-born pyramidal neurons. Significance Statement While primary cilia are implicated in various brain disorders, their physiological functions in the postnatal brain remain poorly understood. We show that the primary cilia in pyramidal neurons are localized at the base of the apical dendrites and aligned distally and opposite to the axon initial segment (AIS), forming a prominent "cilia-at-apical and axon-at-basal" pattern. Reelin deficiency alters the directional orientation, apical localization, and length of these cilia. Interestingly, late-born pyramidal neurons exhibit partial restoration under Reelin deficiency, whereas early-born neurons and those in evolutionarily conserved cortical regions do not. These findings identify primary cilia as a crucial apical domain and reveal an unrecognized Reelin-cilia functional crosstalk, which may enhance the polarity of pyramidal neurons.

Article.Title: Characterization of the 3D Structure of Chromatin in D1 and D2 Medium Spiny Neurons of the Nucleus Accumbens
Article.Authors: Estill M.; Teague C.; Hughes B.; Lee D.; Shen L.; Nestler E.
Article.Abstract: The 3D structure of chromatin is tightly regulated in concert with cell differentiation during development and with epigenetic regulation of gene expression throughout life. Despite extensive characterization at the transcriptional and epigenetic levels of D1-type and D2-type medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) – the ventral portion of the striatum important for reward – a 3D map of chromatin structure in these two neuronal cell types is lacking. Here, we provide a high-density map of chromatin structure from male mice in D1 and D2 MSNs including chromatin loops, topological associating domains (TADs), sub-TADs, and compartments. The data suggest broad convergence in overall 3D chromatin structure between these two closely aligned cell types, but also clear differences consistent with transcriptional divergence previously demonstrated for the two MSN types. We also demonstrate that various exposures to cocaine (acute, chronic, or chronic + acute) – which dramatically alter transcriptional patterns in NAc MSNs – produce far more subtle changes in 3D chromatin structure. Thus, while the 3D structure of chromatin in NAc MSNs appears to be an important concomitant of cell type, it is not broadly leveraged by cocaine to mediate changes in gene expression that contribute to a state of addiction. Significance Statement D1-type and D2-type subtypes of medium spiny neurons are present in the nucleus accumbens and perform different roles in drug addiction. This study maps the genome-wide 3D structure of chromatin in the neuronal subtypes and examines how chronic cocaine exposure alters the chromatin landscape of D1 and D2 MSNs.

Article.Title: Levodopa boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens generalizable rule representations in prefrontal cortex during the inference of meaning
Article.Authors: Mainetto E.; Zheng X.; Shah U.; Labancová K.; Verkes R.; Garvert M.; den Ouden H.; Cools R.
Article.Abstract: Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes and representations by which dopamine influences language processing remain unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers (n = 70, 47 females) boosts hippocampal processing and neural representations of generalizable abstract rules for successful inference of novel word meaning. We used a novel experimental paradigm that required participants to build new artificial word meanings by inferring and applying abstract affixation rules. A repetition suppression procedure was combined with multivariate representational similarity analyses to isolate the neural locus of both the abstract rules required for the compositional inference process, as well as the novel word meaning representations that were composed based on these abstract rules. Levodopa modulated not only inference-related signals in the hippocampal formation, but also abstract rule representations in the medial frontal cortex. These results support the hypothesis that dopamine boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of abstract rules when building novel meaning. Significance statement Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes by which dopamine boosts language processing have remained unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers enhances hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of generalizable abstract rules when building novel word meanings.

Article.Title: Neural Responses to Unexpected Stimulus Repetitions and Omissions in Auditory Cortex Provide Mixed Evidence for Predictive Coding
Article.Authors: Shukla B.; Shirley H.; Goodovitch L.; Fishman Y.; Cohen Y.
Article.Abstract: Humans and other animals process sensory uncertainty by integrating stimulus information with prior knowledge and expectations. Predictive coding conceptualizes perception as a form of Bayesian inference wherein hierarchical brain circuits update internal models to reconcile bottom-up sensory input with top-down predictions. Whereas predictive coding is a leading theory, the extent to which it is implemented in primary sensory cortices remains a matter of debate. To further investigate this issue, we examined single-neuron spiking activity in male macaque primary auditory cortex (A1) to expected versus unexpected stimulus repetitions and to expected versus unexpected stimulus omissions. On average, we found that A1 neurons did not show enhanced responses to unexpected stimulus repetitions, contrary to predictive-coding theory. However, they did show enhanced responses to unexpected stimulus omissions. Taken together, these mixed results place empirical constraints on how predictive coding is implemented in A1. Significance Statement Perception depends on the brain’s ability to infer the causes of sensory inputs by integrating new information with prior knowledge under uncertainty. Our results reveal nuanced evidence for predictive coding within the primary auditory cortex (A1). Specifically, spiking activity during unexpected stimuli and unexpected stimulus omissions provide conflicting and supporting data, respectively, for this Bayesian framework. These findings refine our understanding of neural mechanisms underlying perception and provide empirical constraints on the neurobiological implementation of predictive processing.

Article.Title: Thalamic Reticular Nucleus Excitability and Cholinergic Signaling are Disrupted in a Mouse Model of Alzheimer’s Disease Neuropathology
Article.Authors: Rivera-Ramirez N.; O’Malley J.; Jagirdar R.; Campbell J.; Silva-Pérez M.; Stephens G.; Chin J.; Beierlein M.
Article.Abstract: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) forms powerful GABAergic connections with thalamic nuclei that regulate sleep, attention, and sensory processing. TRN neurons receive dense cholinergic innervation from the basal forebrain and brainstem, dynamically shaping TRN function across brain states. We previously showed reduced TRN activity and sleep deficits in amyloid precursor protein transgenic mice (APP mice), implicating TRN dysfunction as an early contributor to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathophysiology. Here, using slice electrophysiology in mice of both sexes, we determined whether changes in intrinsic membrane properties or cholinergic synaptic transmission contribute to TRN hypoactivity in APP mice. We found that TRN neurons located in the inner core and outer shell regions undergo substantial increases in excitability after the first postnatal month. In mature animals, core neurons exhibited higher firing rates and diverse firing patterns, including persistent firing, whereas shell neurons fired at lower rates and displayed more homogeneous firing patterns without persistent activity. Firing diversity in core neurons was mediated in part by low-threshold T-type Ca²⁺ channels. Cholinergic synaptic activation, mediated predominantly by basal forebrain afferents, produced biphasic excitatory-inhibitory postsynaptic responses in both core and shell neurons, with the ratio of postsynaptic excitation and inhibition varying across postsynaptic targets. Overall, cholinergic activation suppressed TRN firing. In APP mice, core neurons showed reduced intrinsic excitability and cholinergic afferents evoked postsynaptic responses with a larger muscarinic receptor-mediated inhibitory component, leading to delayed TRN firing. Together, these findings identify both intrinsic and cholinergic synaptic mechanisms that may contribute to TRN dysfunction during early AD. Significance Statement Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is typically diagnosed after cognitive symptoms emerge when treatments are less effective, highlighting the need to understand preclinical disease mechanisms. Cholinergic signaling and slow-wave sleep are disrupted before symptom onset, but the mechanisms underlying these changes remain poorly understood. Because the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) receives strong cholinergic input and mediates sleep-related rhythms, it is well positioned to contribute to early AD pathophysiology. We previously found reduced TRN activity and disrupted sleep in an AD mouse model. Here, we show that intrinsic excitability and cholinergic synaptic signaling are altered in TRN neurons during preclinical AD. These changes may contribute to thalamic dysfunction and sleep disturbances, providing a potential circuit mechanism linking early AD pathology to disease progression.

Article.Title: Parallel Claustral Networks for Behavioral Control in Health and Disease
Article.Authors: Citri A.; Wulff A.; Faig C.; Atilgan H.; Negishi K.; Brown S.; Mathur B.; Augustine G.; Shaham Y.
Article.Abstract: The claustrum is among the most highly interconnected structures in the mammalian brain, with reciprocal projections spanning the cortical mantle and a growing roster of functions that range from sleep regulation to attentional control. Here we review current understanding of claustral circuit organization and function, synthesizing findings from anatomical, physiological, computational, and behavioral studies. We argue that a unifying logic underlies the apparent diversity of claustral functions: the claustrum operates through projection-defined subnetworks whose input selectivity, output targets, and local circuit interactions collectively determine their functional contribution and whose impact on cortical targets varies with arousal and ongoing brain state. Corticoclaustral connectivity is organized into matched inputoutput modules, local inhibitory circuits confer spatial filtering properties that amplify strong cortical signals while suppressing weaker ones and claustral output populations differ in their laminar targets, postsynaptic cell-type preferences, and molecular properties, producing diverse and context-dependent effects on cortical dynamics. These circuit properties translate into claustral regulation of cortical population dynamics across multiple timescales, from the moment-to-moment coordination of brain states to the consolidation of frontal control strategies. In pain and addiction, specific claustral projection populations are selectively dysregulated, and distinct subnetworks exert opposing influences on nociceptive sensitivity and drug-related behavior according to their cortical targets. Together, these findings position the claustrum as a modular subcortical hub for the selective regulation of distributed cortical networks and identify it as a candidate therapeutic target for disorders characterized by dysregulated cortical network activity, including chronic pain, addiction, and impulsivity.

Article.Title: Six Challenges for a Mechanistic Science of Human Interoception
Article.Authors: Avidan G.; Allen M.; Khalsa S.; Nord C.; Petzschner F.; Rozenkrantz L.
Article.Abstract: Human interoception has become a major focus of systems, cognitive, and clinical neuroscience. Work across the past decade has shown that signals originating within the body shape perception, emotion, cognition, behavior, and health. Despite rapid methodological and conceptual progress, which substantially expanded our understanding of how bodily signals are processed and represented, much of the field remains constrained by descriptive methods. As these approaches passively assess bodily signals or subjective awareness, they have limited ability to establish causal mechanisms or translate interoceptive findings into clinically informative frameworks. Here, we identify six challenges and corresponding methodological directions for advancing human interoception research: strengthening integration of animal and human models, developing causal perturbation paradigms, capturing interoception in ecologically valid contexts, standardizing multidimensional measurement across bodily systems, adjudicating between computational accounts, and translating mechanistic insights into clinically informative models of health and disease. These challenges are best understood as linked requirements for moving interoception research from relevance to mechanism. Together, they highlight the need to move beyond predominantly static, passive, and single-modality approaches toward studies that can test how internal bodily signals relate to neural activity, behavior, and health.

Article.Title: Beyond Transcriptomes and Dissociated Cells: Spatial Proteomics for Mechanistic Neurobiology
Article.Authors: Orr T.; Boles J.; Latimer C.; Sun X.; Dehkordi S.; Wu Z.; Young L.; Zwang T.; Hashoul D.; Keene C.; Orr M.
Article.Abstract: Single-cell transcriptomic studies have revealed remarkable molecular heterogeneity across neuronal and glial populations during development, aging, and disease. However, dissociation-based approaches disrupt tissue architecture, and RNA measures alone incompletely capture cellular function. These limitations are particularly relevant in neurodegenerative diseases, where pathology develops within cellular microenvironments and diseased cells progressively lose canonical cell-state identity markers. Spatial proteomic approaches are beginning to address this critical gap by enabling high-dimensional molecular profiling within the intact tissue, preserving the spatial relationships between vulnerable cells and their surrounding cellular environments across scales ranging from subcellular single-cell imaging to large-volume three-dimensional mapping. Here, we discuss emerging spatial proteomic technologies and their applications in aging and neurodegeneration, emphasizing how integration with complementary modalities, including transcriptomics, glycomics, three-dimensional genome architecture, and quantitative neuropathology, is providing new insight into disease biology. We further highlight how these approaches are beginning to accelerate therapeutic target validation, biomarker discovery, and treatment response monitoring. Realizing the full potential of spatial proteomics will require continued advances in cross-platform harmonization, analytical standardization, and computational methods capable of integrating increasingly complex, multimodal datasets.

Article.Title: Hidden Vision and Beyond: Multiscale Foundations of Thalamic Organization
Article.Authors: Ajina S.; Briggs F.; Schneider K.; Arcaro M.; Liu X.; Bhatla N.; Rosa M.
Article.Abstract: The subcortical visual system is traditionally described through a small number of canonical pathways, with the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) viewed primarily as a first-order relay to primary visual cortex and additional routes through the superior colliculus, pulvinar and koniocellular LGN considered secondary or residual. Here, we review recent evidence across species, methods, and scales that challenge this framework and suggest that the visual thalamus is an active, dynamically regulated component of visual processing. We first consider primary and nonprimary visual pathways, showing how thalamic inputs shape cortical responses through the timing, spatial arrangement, synaptic organization, laminar targeting, and circuit-level integration of feedforward signals. We then reconsider the first-order status of LGN itself, reviewing evidence that nonretinal subcortical inputs, local inhibition, and corticothalamic feedback can alter LGN responses and the signals routed onward to cortex. This shifts the view of LGN from a passive relay supplying a dynamic cortex to a dynamically regulated node in its own right. Next, we review advances in higher-order thalamic organization, highlighting structured thalamocortical connectivity, network-level coordination, and state-dependent dynamics. Finally, we consider how thalamic functions change in the injured brain, where emerging models disentangle acute effects of damage from chronic compensation to reveal how surviving thalamic and downstream pathways may be remodeled, reweighted, or recruited to support residual visual function and recovery. Together, these findings support a multiscale view of the thalamus as a collection of specialized, adaptive nuclei embedded within distributed cortico-subcortical networks, with implications for perception, cognition, sensory disorders, and rehabilitation.

Article.Title: Integrating Cytoskeletal Systems in Neurons and Glia: Dynamic Orchestration of Structure and Function
Article.Authors: Jahan N.; York H.; Bailey H.; Swann I.; Leterrier C.; Spiliotis E.; Aiken J.; Tymanskyj S.; Brown A.; Winckler B.; Fu M.
Article.Abstract: Neurons and glia form the circuitry of our nervous system, allowing nerve cells to communicate with each other and other cell types throughout the body in a highly specific manner to integrate sensory, motor, and cognitive functions. The ability of these cells to do this is profoundly dependent on an elaborate and dynamic cytoskeleton which allows these cells to adopt complex shapes and specialized structures such as myelin sheaths, the bloodbrain barrier, axonal growth cones, dendritic spines, nodes of Ranvier, synapses, and elaborate sensory organs. The cytoskeleton is also critical for morphogenetic movements, the migration of neuronal precursors, and axon growth, which together establish the organization and wiring pattern of the central and peripheral nervous system during development. This review provides a primer on our current understanding of the cytoskeleton of neurons and glia, with an emphasis on how the protein polymers of the cytoskeletonmicrotubules, actin filaments, intermediate filaments, and septinswork together to orchestrate the remarkable shapes and functions of these cells. We also highlight key questions and challenges for the field and technological advances that may help address them.

Article.Title: Embodied Computation: How Does Embodiment Impact Sensorimotor and Cognitive Processing?
Article.Authors: Schaffer E.; Saxena S.; Keller R.; Lazzari J.; McGill M.; Nayebi A.; Olivos-Castillo I.; Park I.; Perich M.; Pitkow X.; Turaga S.
Article.Abstract: Animals act on the world through a physical body and continually adjust behavior in response to the sensory feedback their actions produce. This closed loop between brain, body, and environment is central to motor control, but its role in other neural computations remains less clear. This review focuses on embodied computation: how the physical body shapes neural activity and behavior across functions ranging from motor control to cognitive processes. We examine the impact of embodiment in several domains, including compositional reuse, intrinsic motivation, metabolic costs, and connectome-constrained computation, with the broader aim of asking when the body can be abstracted away and when it is essential for explaining what the brain computes.

Article.Title: Hormonal Effects during the Reproductive Years on Brain and Behavior: Molecular Discovery to Promising Therapeutics for Womens Mental Health
Article.Authors: Wijtenburg S.; Shansky R.; Sacher J.; Humphreys K.; Napolitano S.; Neacsiu A.; Conradt E.; Ankudowich E.; Mandelblat-Cerf Y.; Johnson T.
Article.Abstract: Beginning at puberty and throughout the lifespan, women experience greater rates of depression, anxiety disorders, eating disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and hormone-linked mood disorders relative to men. How these disorders relate to hormonal fluctuations and associated changes in physiology and brain circuitry in women during the reproductive years is only partially understood. In this review, the molecular, structural, and functional brain changes during the reproductive years are discussed, with a specific focus on transitional changes during the perinatal period. Preclinical and clinical models of neuroplastic change are also discussed, along with neuromodulatory approaches that account for the contextual, spatial, and temporal parameters of interventions delivered during the postpartum period. Future directions may consider how hormonal fluctuations during reproductive years may improve preclinical and clinical models for womens mental health while acknowledging that greater work is needed to understand the role of a broader range of hormonal and environmental factors linked to mental health including lactation, trauma, contraceptive use, menstruation, and perimenopause.

Article.Title: The Neural Correlates of Sickness
Article.Authors: Lanovoi H.; Yang L.; Serino A.; Ryan T.; Carcea I.; Osterhout J.
Article.Abstract: The brain protects animals during infection by detecting immune activity, coordinating behavioral and physiological defenses, anticipating potential infectious threats, and limiting excessive inflammation. Collectively termed sickness, these centrally organized responses include changes in body temperature, activity, energy balance, appetite, fluid intake, social behavior, neuroendocrine function, and autonomic output. Rather than constituting a single uniform state, sickness is generated by distributed and partially dissociable neural pathways that translate immune signals into responses appropriate to the nature and stage of an infection. Work presented at a symposium at the 2026 Society for Neuroscience meeting highlights how humoral and cranial sensory pathways detect ongoing immune responses; how social cues, expectations, and prior experience prepare the organism for anticipated threats; and how endocrine and autonomic circuits constrain inflammation and promote recovery. Together, these findings establish the brain as an active regulator of immunity across the full course of illness.

Article.Title: NeuroAIs Next Steps: Balancing Computation and Embodiment
Article.Authors: Monaco J.; Brunton B.; Mineault P.
Article.Abstract: Deep neural networks trained at scale now predict neural activity across sensory cortices, raising a question that divides neuroscience: does the convergence between artificial and biological representations constitute understanding, or does understanding require models of biological processes grounded in the embodied, evolved character of natural intelligence? In this Dual Perspectives article, Bing Brunton and Patrick Mineault articulate two research programsProcess and Convergenceto engage this question about the future of NeuroAI research. The conversation is organized around four questions that probe what scaled modelbrain alignment reveals, what the brain is coupled to and evolved to do, what success beyond the lab looks like, and where the field should invest over the coming decade. Their exchanges reveal the distance between the two programs to be primarily about the level of analysis and priorities for what to build next. The conversation converges on shared ground: measure broadly, then distill to causal principles.

Article.Title: Postnatal Development of Sensory Circuits Supporting Lifelong Social Behaviors
Article.Authors: Kirchgesser M.; Clemens A.; Frank D.; Orefice L.; Pouchelon G.; Che A.
Article.Abstract: Sensory systems are essential for young animals as they interact with their environments in order to survive and grow. These environments frequently involve other animals, especially early in life. Thus, animals social interactions fundamentally shape and are shaped by their sensory circuit development. This Review and its associated Minisymposium will highlight new discoveries centered around the reciprocal relationship between sensory development and social interactions. Points of intersection range from gene expression in peripheral sensors to functional connectivity and neural coding in cortical circuits and span varied sensory systems and species. Taken together, we identify a common theme of refinement and specialization of sensory processing during limited developmental windows for species-relevant social behaviors. Consequently, early disruptions to sensory processing can have significant and long-lasting consequences for animals lifelong behavior and may even contribute to the etiology of autism and related developmental disorders. Thus, the work presented herein offers mechanistic insight into the complex interplay between early sensory and social development with potentially significant clinical implications. Many of these insights are made possible by technological advances in measuring and manipulating sensory circuit functions and behaviors in developing animals. This Review aims to highlight recent advances and outstanding questions that lie at the nexus of sensory, social, and developmental neuroscience.

Article.Title: Mu-Opioid Receptor in Habenula Circuits as a Substrate for Psychiatric Disorders and Addiction
Article.Authors: Darcq E.; Coffey K.; Ibaez-Tallon I.; Margolis E.; Maynard K.; Hnasko T.
Article.Abstract: The habenula is a critical regulator of affect, negative reinforcement, avoidance, and coping behavior. It is thus unsurprising that accumulating evidence supports pivotal roles for habenular circuits in the expression of major psychiatric illnesses including depression and addiction. Though high levels of mu-opioid receptors (MORs) were identified in the habenula more than a generation ago, the functional effects of MORs on habenular circuits remained largely unexplored due to challenges of selectively targeting this small and heterogeneous brain structure. In this SfN mini-symposium report, we highlight studies that resolve how MOR is distributed across medial and lateral habenular subnuclei and how MOR expression maps onto molecularly defined habenular cell types. We further describe some of the habenula-intersecting circuits that express MORs and how MOR signaling modulates neural activity and neurotransmission within these unique habenular circuits and cell types. Going beyond cellular-level effects of MOR signaling, we illustrate how neural activity in the habenula can influence affect and behaviors associated with opioid analgesia, opioid seeking, opioid dependence, and opioid withdrawal. Drawing on works outside the opioid field, we suggest commonalities through which drugs of abuse may influence habenula circuits to induce states of negative affect that contribute to continued drug use or relapse. Finally, we discuss how better understanding the molecular and functional properties of habenular cell types and circuits can identify new druggable targets, such as the orphan receptors GPR151 and GPR139, for the treatment of pain, mood disorders, or opioid and other substance use disorders.

Article.Title: Maternal Immune Activation and Neurodevelopmental Disorders: A Cross-Species Perspective
Article.Authors: Mukherjee A.; Bauman M.; Hill R.; Meyer U.; Sawa A.
Article.Abstract: Prenatal exposure to infection increases the likelihood of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). This association is attributed largely to the maternal inflammatory response, maternal immune activation (MIA), rather than to single pathogen. In this review, we discuss the molecular, cellular, and behavioral consequences of MIA and their contribution to NDDs in clinical cohorts and preclinical models across different species. We first trace the pathophysiology linking maternal infection to altered fetal neurodevelopment, describing how diverse immune challenges converge on shared nodes including cytokine signaling, oxidative and nutritional stress, placental dysfunction, and epigenetic modification. We then describe how these perturbations affect neural circuits and behavior, focusing on the disrupted social development. Next, we consider sources of individual variation, including gestational timing, fetal sex, and later-life second hits, that may contribute to the greater vulnerability. Finally, we discuss the translational implications of this work in terms of maternal cytokine and epigenetic signatures as candidate biomarkers for risk stratification and potential therapeutic approaches.
