Article.Title: Illuminating the Diversity of Electrical Synapse Form and Function
Article.Authors: Bhattacharya A.; Haas J.; Lee K.; Pereda A.; Sigulinsky C.; Martin E.
Article.Abstract: While the nervous system is organized by two main types of connections between neurons, electrical and chemical synapses, most studies focus upon the contribution of the molecularly complex and functionally diverse chemical synapse. Electrical synapses, in contrast, are perceived as simple, neuronal gap junction channels between contacts, often thought to be replaced in early development by more sophisticated chemical synapses. However, recent work and new tools push for the redefining of electrical synapse molecular architecture and function to allow for an updated interpretation of their ongoing contributions to neural circuit formation and function. Here, we describe fresh insight into neuronal gap junction structure, function, and molecular composition within invertebrate (nematodes, drosophila) and vertebrate (zebrafish, rabbit, rodent) model organisms across a variety of time periods and brain regions. Through molecular, genetic, connectomic, and functional explorations, our results argue for a new appreciation of electrical synapse heterogeneity. Based on these and other points of emerging new evidence, we argue for increased consideration of electrical synapses as complex and diverse structures which interact with chemical synapses to drive circuit formation and function.

Article.Title: Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation: Biophysical Mechanisms, Neural Effects, and Clinical Translation
Article.Authors: Chen L.; He B.; Kosnoff J.; Legon W.; Shoham S.
Article.Abstract: Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive neuromodulation technology capable of targeting both cortical and deep brain structures with millimeter-scale spatial precision. Recent advances in ultrasound hardware, acoustic modeling, neuronavigation, and multimodal imaging have accelerated the field from proof-of-concept demonstrations toward mechanistic investigation and early clinical translation. In parallel, growing evidence from animal and human studies has begun to clarify how ultrasound influences neural activity across cellular, circuit, and systems levels. In this review, we synthesize recent progress in understanding the biophysical mechanisms, neurophysiological effects, and network-level consequences of TUS. We discuss insights from optical imaging, electrophysiology, EEG source imaging, and functional MRI, highlighting how these complementary approaches reveal cell-type-specific responses, bidirectional modulation of neural circuits, and distributed changes in functional connectivity beyond the sonicated target. We further examine evidence that functional imaging is evolving from a simple measure of regional activation to a multidimensional biomarker of target engagement, circuit modulation, and treatment response. Despite these advances, important challenges remain. We conclude that TUS is approaching a translational inflection point in which rigorous mechanistic studies, standardized methodologies, and imaging-based biomarkers can establish ultrasound as both a powerful causal neuroscience tool and a clinically viable neuromodulation therapy for disorders involving dysfunctional brain circuits.

Article.Title: From Rapid Synaptic Events to Lasting Antidepressant States: Convergent and Divergent Mechanisms of Ketamine and Psychedelics
Article.Authors: Kim J.; Fogaca M.; Munguba H.; Pignatelli M.; Platholi J.; Woodburn S.; Ma (???) Z.
Article.Abstract: Rapid-acting antidepressants have challenged the long-standing view that therapeutic improvement in major depressive disorder requires chronic treatment with monoaminergic agents. Ketamine and classical psychedelics act through distinct proximal targets, yet both can produce rapid and persistent behavioral effects that implicate synaptic and circuit plasticity as the core mechanisms of antidepressant action. This review, based on a minisymposium presented at the 2026 Society for Neuroscience meeting, examines how brief pharmacological perturbations translate into lasting changes in mood-related networks. We first discuss hippocampal mechanisms underlying ketamine action, which include brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)/tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB)-dependent homeostatic potentiation, TrkB cross talk with metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGluR5) at CA3?CA1 synapses, extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK)-dual-specificity phosphatase 6 (DUSP6)-mediated extension of synaptic metaplasticity, and BDNF release at mossy fiber synapses and dentate gyrus neuronal maturation. We then consider how these local plasticity mechanisms interface with distributed circuits that regulate motivation, stress coping, and reward. Across brain regions, emerging work highlights the importance of cell type- and region-specific mechanisms that mediate ketamine's therapeutic actions. We expand on local prefrontal cortical inhibitory cellular signaling dynamics, including the interplay of various G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) in cortical somatostatin interneurons and input-specific adaptations in accumbal circuits. Finally, we compare ketamine with psilocybin, an emerging therapeutic classic psychedelic for treatment-resistant depression that targets the 5-hydroxytryptamine 2A (5-HT2A) receptor primarily. A recurring theme is that an interplay of GPCRs can help shape the timing, localization, and persistence of ketamine-induced neuroplasticity. Together, these studies suggest that antidepressant efficacy arises not from a single pathway or brain region but from coordinated, temporally staged plasticity across molecules, synapses, cells, and circuits.

Article.Title: Transforming Neuroscience Research through AI-Driven Data Integration and Analysis
Article.Authors: Gala R.; Solanki A.; Wang N.; Nikbakht N.; Warrell J.; He C.; Huo B.; Ghosh S.; Xu H.; Hawrylycz M.; Jim Zheng W.
Article.Abstract: Integrating multimodal data is essential to advance neuroscience as a discipline. Large-scale collaborative efforts, exemplified by the BRAIN Initiative, together with advances in single-cell and spatial omics, multimodal imaging, human genetics, behavioral phenotyping, protein structure prediction, and related technologies, are transforming neuroscience into a data-rich, highly interconnected science. As experimental resources, scientific literature, and collaborative networks continue to expand, integrating discoveries across modalities, species, and levels of biological organization has become the field's central bottleneck. This Perspective argues that artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming essential for overcoming these constraints. Using six evolving approaches we outline strategies to accelerate AI adoption through community building and pilot projects that drive AI transformation at both the organizational and technological levels. Organizational transformation cultivates broad AI awareness and a pro-AI culture while technological transformation improves the efficiency, scalability, and quality of data analysis, allowing researchers to generate insights more rapidly and effectively. Together, these advances position AI as a key driver for advancing neuroscience at scale.

Article.Title: The Noncanonical Hippocampus: Shared and Distinct Features of the CA2FCIG Hippocampal System
Article.Authors: Farrell J.; Esfahany K.; Kandemir B.; Alexander G.; Dudek S.; Incontro S.; Nguyen Q.; Vlez Gonzlez H.; Leroy F.; Alexandrou-Majaj N.; Moorman D.
Article.Abstract: The hippocampal CA2 region has received considerable interest in recent decades, earning a functional understanding beyond the previously held view as a small transitional zone. However, related hippocampal structures called the fasciola cinereum (FC) and indusium griseum (IG) have been largely neglected to date. While CA2, FC, and IG are typically presented as discontinuous structures on conventional atlases, recent work unveils a surprisingly high degree of overlapping gene expression and anatomical continuity, raising questions of their shared versus distinct functions. Here we review the molecular, anatomical, physiological, and behavioral features of each area, to begin to address whether these regions are subcomponents of a greater hippocampal structure or independent entities with distinct contributions to physiology and disease. Early evidence supports that the CA2FCIG axis is indeed a cohesive network unified by shared molecular and anatomical profiles, although regional differences in structure and function need to be taken into account. Notably, transcriptomics has revealed multiple subclusters within this complex of structures with no region-specific cell types, raising the need to understand whether cell types or anatomical subfields are the main functional units of this system. This conceptualization of these noncanonical hippocampal areas as a unified, multifaceted system raises many questions discussed here, along with the need for coordinated investigation across regions in future work.

Article.Title: Cross-Species Approaches to Understanding Human Cognition
Article.Authors: Buffalo E.; Cohen M.; Constantinidis C.; Kastner S.; Rudebeck P.; Sabri M.
Article.Abstract: Recent methodological advances including high-density intracranial recordings and population-level analytical frameworks enable deeper and more direct integration between animal models and human neuroscience. As a result, there is an increasing need for standardized behavioral paradigms and circuit-level analyses that can be used in both animals and humans. Cross-species approaches provide crucial foundations for treating neurological and psychiatric disorders. Parallel experiments validate therapeutic targets and enable development of mechanistically grounded behavioral biomarkers for early disease detection. Here, we provide a brief review of recent findings that have direct implications for attention deficits, memory impairments, and decision-making dysfunctions. By linking mechanism to behavior, these approaches guide targeted interventions and effective clinical translation. While challenges remain, these integrated approaches are advancing our understanding of the mechanistic foundation of human cognition.

Article.Title: Janus in Thermosensation: The Dual InteroceptiveExteroceptive Nature of Thermal Signals in Body Ownership
Article.Authors: Salvato G.; Bassolino M.; Whitmire C.; Poulet J.; Shokur S.
Article.Abstract: Thermosensation has traditionally been studied for its essential role in survival, enabling detection of environmental thermal stimuli and the maintenance of thermal homeostasis. Interestingly, unlike most sensory systems, thermosensation provides information about both the external world and the body's internal physiological state. In this review, we conceptualize these two dimensions as exteroceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the thermal properties of external objects and the environment, and interoceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the body's thermal state. Growing evidence suggests that this dual nature serves functions that extend beyond survival and homeostasis. Alterations in both thermal perception and thermoregulation have been associated with changes in body ownership, the experience that one's body belongs to oneself, while manipulations of thermal signals can influence ownership itself. Here, we review the physiological and neural bases of exteroceptive and interoceptive thermosensation, from peripheral encoding to central processing, and examine their relationship with body ownership in healthy and clinical populations. We discuss evidence suggesting partially distinct yet potentially convergent neural substrates for these two dimensions of thermosensation, highlighting the insular cortex and its broader connectivity network as a candidate through which thermal information may sustain body ownership. Finally, we consider how emerging neurotechnologies offer new opportunities to investigate the contribution of thermosensation to body ownership while also opening novel avenues for neurorehabilitation. We propose that thermosensation represents an underexplored contributor to body ownership, opening new avenues for future research on how bodily and environmental thermal signals are integrated to support the sense of self.

Article.Title: Capturing Habits in Humans: Neural Circuitry, Computations, and Clinical Mechanisms
Article.Authors: Gera R.; Wassum K.; Oh S.; Cockburn J.; Tadayonnejad R.; Obeso I.
Article.Abstract: Habits allow repeated behaviors to be executed efficiently, but habitual control can contribute to maladaptive inflexibility when it dominates despite changing goals or consequences. This review examines recent advances in understanding habitual control across neural circuits, computation, clinical phenotypes, and measurement. We first consider dorsomedial striatal mechanisms that support action-outcome learning and flexible goal-directed behavior and how chronic stress can alter striatal inputs to bias learning toward habitual control. Progress on what computational reinforcement-learning accounts for arbitration between goal-directed and habitual systems is described along prefrontal mechanisms guiding model-based control, action perseveration, and compulsivity in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). A wider behavioral spectrum beyond action initiation is provided, reviewing emerging work on habitual inhibition and frontostriatal circuit dynamics of avoidance in OCD. Recent laboratory paradigms aim to reveal habit formation more sensitively than traditional outcome-devaluation paradigms, whereas real-world digital approaches use smartphones, wearables, and intensive longitudinal measurement to track habit formation and expression in everyday life. Integrating these approaches can help link habits to physiology, symptoms and neural circuits across laboratory to real-world and clinical contexts.

Article.Title: PlacentalNeural Cross Talk: Biological Mechanisms Shaping Brain Architecture
Article.Authors: Penn A.; Mir I.; Bonnin A.; Vacher C.; Nichols E.; Escudero C.; Gumusoglu S.; Stevens H.
Article.Abstract: Impact of placental function on normal and pathological brain processes and supported behavior is an integrative research area dubbed neuroplacentology. Placental functional genetics, structure, and vascular function have been discovered to have links to multiple clinical outcomes: autism, schizophrenia, and developmental cognitive impairment in offspring and postpartum depression and cognition in mothers. There are significant data showing that long-term impacts of preterm birth, diseases of pregnancy (preeclampsia), and maternal stress and depression may all be mediated by placental mechanisms, providing clinical and translational insights. Here, we will provide an up-to-date introduction to this emerging field. Mechanistic links between variations in placental structure and function and features of human and animal brain development and function will be discussed, clarifying basic biological connections and highlighting new targets to prevent clinical impairments.

Article.Title: Learning to Navigate a Changing World: From Brain Systems to Novel Algorithms
Article.Authors: Lee J.; Zutshi I.; Alexander A.; Hermundstad A.
Article.Abstract: Natural organisms navigate a world in constant flux and are frequently confronted with sensory ambiguity and shifting goals. While biological systems can adapt rapidly to navigate in novel and nonstationary environments, this challenge remains a significant hurdle for artificial intelligence. In this review, we examine recent progress in understanding neurobiological systems that allow for adaptive, efficient spatial and abstract navigation in dynamic environments and how these observations have informed new developments for the same behavior in machines. We highlight how predictive learning serves as a unifying framework to describe the organization of neural activity across distributed systems for navigation, including the hippocampal formation, parietal cortex, and higher-order associative structures. Specifically, we explore how such neurobiological systems encode expected future states, dynamic target trajectories, action plans, and internal behavioral strategies. Finally, we contrast the diffuse, inefficient exploration of canonical artificial agents with the structured, efficient control policies for goal-directed navigation observed in natural organisms. By grounding learning in the interplay between action, prediction, and natural behavioral statistics, navigation provides a roadmap for building resilient, neurobiologically inspired continual learning in artificial agents.

Article.Title: Glial Regulation of Motor Circuit Formation, Function, and Regeneration
Article.Authors: Ackerman S.; Fontenas L.
Article.Abstract: From simple planaria to humans, proper assembly and maintenance of motor circuits is key to organismal survival. Each year, ~250,000500,000 individuals suffer a spinal cord injury with little hope of successful recovery. Moreover, motor circuits are a primary target of prevalent neurodegenerative conditions like ALS and Parkinson's disease. Thus, understanding the mechanisms that build, maintain, and rebuild motor circuits is of substantial clinical interest. Recent data indicate that glia, a heterogeneous group of non-neuronal cells within the nervous system, directly communicate with neurons to tune motor circuit dynamics. We now know glia are often active drivers of neural development and pathology, rather than passive bystanders. This mini-review will highlight recent advances in our understanding of how diverse glial cell types promote proper construction, function, and deconstruction of the key circuits that drive motor behavior.

Article.Title: Brain Initiative Roadmap: Building the Next Decade of NeuroAI
Article.Authors: Monaco J.; Kopsick J.; Miller R.; Hwang G.
Article.Abstract: The exchange between neuroscience and artificial intelligence has reshaped both fields over the past decade. Two perspectives now organize the conversation about what NeuroAI should build next. The “Convergence” perspective points to a methodological alignment: scaled models trained on naturalistic data can predict neural responses across sensory cortices (Yamins et al., 2014; Richards et al., 2019; Schrimpf et al., 2020) and drive or suppress responses in higher-level human language networks (Tuckute et al., 2024). The field is extending those successes into digital twins, brain foundation models, and connectome-grounded mechanistic networks (Aldarondo et al., 2024). The “Process” perspective asks what it would take for our models to capture what brains actually do as closed-loop controllers of bodies in environments, operating on time and energy budgets unmatched by silicon-based digital computing (Cisek, 2019; Brunton and Tuthill, 2025). The two views are not opposed but differ in priorities about what the field should build next (see Monaco, Brunton, and Mineault, this issue). Here, the National Institutes of Health's Brain Research through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies (BRAIN) Initiative sets out scientific goals for the next decade, building on its Research Roadmap (NIH BRAIN Initiative, 2025). Article.Title: During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex
Article.Authors: Raghavan V.; Madsen J.; Nentwich M.; Leszczynski M.; Falchier A.; Bickel S.; Russ B.; Parra L.
Article.Abstract: We sample visual scenes with short gaze fixations separated by saccades. While low-level integration is known, semantic integration of foveal vision across fixations remains unclear. We hypothesized that the brain responds to changes in semantic information from one fixation to the next, and therefore postulated a neural signal associated with semantic novelty for each saccade. Novelty was measured from different layers of a deep network on foveal vision. Only semantic, and not low- or mid-level, novelty modulated frontal and occipital fixation-related potentials in male and female human scalp EEG during natural viewing of full-length movies (3.4x10 6 saccades). Intracranial recordings in male and female humans (9.0x10 4 saccades) and female non-human primates (Macaca mulatta; 3.3x10 4 saccades) revealed broadband high-frequency activity modulations in scene-specific ventral visual and frontal brain areas only for semantic novelty. This modulation was stronger for movies than static images, and frontal modulation occurred early alongside occipital modulation, suggesting top-down effects. This modulation of fixation-related activity with novelty suggests that foveal representations are compared between consecutive fixations to construct scene representations during natural viewing in primates. Significance statement Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high-level meaning across these "snapshots" remains a mystery. By combining deep-learning models with massive electrophysiological datasets from humans and macaques, we show that the brain responds to changes in semantic content between fixations, but not low- or mid-level changes. We identified a "semantic novelty" signal that modulates neural activity across the primate cortex. These findings suggest visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process comparing consecutive foveal information at the semantic level. This work bridges biological vision and artificial intelligence, providing a new framework for understanding how the brain maintains a coherent understanding of a dynamic world.

Article.Title: Subliminal beauty engages the brain’s valuation circuits
Article.Authors: Fernandes P.; Kable J.; Almeida J.; Tusche A.; Ruff C.; Bergström F.
Article.Abstract: Neuroeconomic models propose that the anterior ventral striatum (aVS) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) are key regions for computing subjective value (SV) signals that guide choice. However, the role of conscious awareness in this process remains debated. Here we examined whether SV can be automatically computed in these regions without conscious awareness. In an fMRI experiment, human participants (24 females, 5 males) viewed faces that varied in attractiveness under three conditions: (i) suppressed from awareness via continuous flash suppression (CFS), (ii) clearly visible without suppression, or (iii) absent (background only) with CFS. Participants reported trial-wise facial identity (objective) and visibility (subjective) measures of facial awareness. In a post-fMRI session, they rated the attractiveness of each face as a measure of SV. When faces were seen, task performance (d’) exceeded chance and responses were faster than in absent trials. When faces were unseen, performance was at chance but responses were slower than absent trials. Neurally, seen and unseen faces elicited greater neural signal than absent trials and showed similar neural patterns in the fusiform face area (FFA). Critically, neural signal in vmPFC correlated with SV for both seen and unseen faces, with similar neural patterns. In aVS, SV-related signal was only observed for unseen faces. Furthermore, mean face-related signal in FFA correlated with SV-related signals in aVS and vmPFC for unseen faces. These findings demonstrate that SV can be automatically computed in aVS and vmPFC without conscious awareness, suggesting a neural pathway by which subliminal information can influence value-based choice. Significance statement A central question in consciousness research and decision neuroscience is whether the brain’s valuation circuitry – particularly the anterior ventral striatum (aVS) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) – can compute subjective value automatically without conscious awareness. This question is important because prevailing accounts often assume that cognitive functions supported by the prefrontal cortex require conscious awareness of task-relevant information. Using continuous flash suppression and neuroimaging, we found that faces reported unseen nevertheless evoked value-related signals in aVS and vmPFC that scaled with subjective attractiveness ratings. These findings demonstrate that subjective value can be computed automatically from social information in the absence of conscious awareness.

Article.Title: The nucleus of the lateral olfactory tract is required for learning odor-guided food avoidance
Article.Authors: Lawabny N.; Dhamshy A.; Kreisel T.; Licht T.; Rokni D.
Article.Abstract: Foraging animals must continually evaluate whether potential food sources are safe to consume. Such decisions rely on both innate preferences and learned associations formed through prior experience. Consumption of a food followed by malaise or sickness leads to avoidance of that food, reflecting learned associations between sensory cues that identify a food and its negative post-ingestive consequences. Although this form of learning has been studied extensively using taste cues, taste signals arise only after oral contact, at which point exposure to potential toxins has already occurred. Olfactory cues, in contrast, provide information about potential food sources prior to consumption, yet how odors acquire aversive value remains unclear. Here, using targeted chemogenetic perturbations, we identify the nucleus of the lateral olfactory tract (NLOT), which has direct bidirectional connectivity to olfactory regions and the basolateral amygdala, as a critical circuit element for odor-aversion learning in male and female mice. We find that the NLOT is required for conditioned odor aversion but is dispensable for other odor-guided behaviors and for fear conditioning driven by a non-olfactory cue. Our findings identify a selective role for the NLOT in linking olfactory cues to learned aversive outcomes, that supports odor-guided behavioral decisions. Significance statement Animals rely on smell to evaluate food safety before consuming it, yet the brain circuits that link odor cues to learned aversive outcomes remain poorly understood. Here we identify the nucleus of the lateral olfactory tract (NLOT), a largely unstudied region at the interface between olfactory and limbic circuits, as a critical and selective node for conditioned odor aversion learning. Chemogenetic perturbations of the NLOT disrupted both the acquisition and expression of odor-malaise associations, while leaving odor detection, odor discrimination, and non-olfactory fear learning intact — revealing a previously unrecognized specialization within olfactory-amygdala circuits that supports odor-guided decisions about food safety.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: basolateral amygdala; fear conditioning; food avoidance

Article.Title: Cell-type- and subregion-specific basolateral amygdala inputs to ventral CA1–subiculum
Article.Authors: Li (李明华) M.; Guo (郭婉宜) W.; Jiang (姜玉秋) Y.; Sun (孙钱) Q.
Article.Abstract: The hippocampus is essential for learning and memory and interacts extensively with cortical and subcortical regions. Although the heterogeneity of intrinsic connectivity of hippocampal neurons is well established, the diversity of its extrahippocampal connectivity remains less understood. Such differential connectivity may contribute to functional diversity of hippocampal neurons in specific positions. Ventral CA1 (vCA1) and ventral subiculum (vSub) form strong reciprocal connections with the basolateral amygdala (BLA), a region critical for emotional and social regulation. Consequently, BLA–vCA1–vSub circuits have been implicated in anxiety-related and social behaviors. However, the functional connectivity from BLA to vCA1–vSub at the cellular and circuit levels is underexplored. To address this, we combined viral tracing with Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2)–assisted slice electrophysiology to examine BLA projections to vCA1–vSub in mice of either sex. We found that BLA inputs are not uniformly distributed along the transverse axis in vCA1-vSub. Instead, BLA selectively excites pyramidal neurons in distal vCA1–vSub while largely avoiding proximal vCA1 near CA2. BLA terminals strongly excited parvalbumin-expressing interneurons but only weakly recruited a small subset of somatostatin-expressing interneurons, generating robust disynaptic inhibitory synaptic currents in pyramidal neurons. Additionally, the same distal pyramidal neurons that receive BLA excitation also project back to the BLA. These findings reveal that BLA establishes cell-type- and subregion-specific excitatory connections within vCA1–vSub, highlighting a circuit architecture that may underlie functional heterogeneity in ventral hippocampal processing. Significance statement The hippocampus interacts extensively with cortical and subcortical regions, yet how long-range extrahippocampal inputs are organized across hippocampal subregions remains poorly understood. We examined projections from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) to the ventral hippocampus and found that BLA inputs selectively excite pyramidal neurons in distal ventral CA1 and ventral subiculum while largely avoiding proximal ventral CA1. BLA projections preferentially excite parvalbumin-expressing interneurons, provide disynaptic inhibition onto pyramidal neurons, and are reciprocally connected with the same pyramidal neurons in ventral CA1 and subiculum they excite. These findings reveal a highly selective connectivity pattern of amygdala–hippocampal circuits, providing a circuit framework for understanding how emotional information is routed through distinct ventral hippocampal pathways.

Article.Title: The balance N1 attenuates but persists during self-initiated and repeated perturbations, even without active balance control
Article.Authors: Mensink L.; Jansen D.; Moraczewska M.; Leeuwis M.; Pel J.; Forbes P.
Article.Abstract: Standing balance requires rapid responses to postural disturbances, and the balance N1 has been proposed to reflect cortical involvement in corrective motor output. Our recent work shows, however, that the N1 persists even when active balance control is removed and corrective muscle activity is largely absent, suggesting it reflects sensory rather than motor processing. Because the N1 is also modulated by contextual factors such as postural threat, stability, and perturbation predictability, it may reflect uncertainty associated with perturbation-evoked sensory signals. We tested this in 11 participants (3 males and 8 females) using toes-up perturbations across three manipulations expected to alter sensorimotor uncertainty: perturbation timing through 15 unexpected perturbations before and after a block of self-initiated trials; repeated exposure through 60 self-initiated trials; and body-motion variability by comparing active balance with passive support and by imposing prerecorded whole-body motion during 60 additional self-initiated trials with passive support. Self-initiation reduced N1 amplitude by 21.3 ± 13.9% relative to unexpected perturbations, and this attenuation was equivalent across active and passive conditions. Habituation through repeated self-initiated perturbations produced a further 24.0 ± 17.7% decline, again independent of active balance. When perturbations were subsequently delivered unexpectedly, N1 amplitudes increased, confirming that attenuation was specific to the self-initiated context. Finally, imposing prerecorded whole-body motion during passive support did not change perturbation-evoked N1 amplitude, suggesting that body-motion variability does not drive the cortical response when active balance control is absent. These results indicate that the balance N1 is shaped by predictability and repetition, consistent with prediction error or surprise-based accounts of cortical responses to balance perturbations. Significance statement The balance N1, a cortical response to postural disturbances, has long been thought to reflect corrective motor output. We recently showed it instead reflects sensory processing, as it persists even without active balance control. Here we test whether this processing scales with uncertainty associated with perturbation-evoked sensory signals by manipulating perturbation timing through self-initiation, habituation through repeated exposure, and variability of ongoing whole-body motion. Self-initiation and repetition both attenuated N1, regardless of whether participants actively balanced or were passively supported. However, increasing whole-body motion variability did not modify the response, indicating that not all sources of uncertainty modulate the N1. These findings recast the balance N1 as tracking the sensory predictability of the perturbation, not balance-correcting motor output.

Article.Title: A spectral partial information decomposition framework for quantifying information about cognitive variables in oscillatory brain networks
Article.Authors: Lima V.; Marinazzo D.; Brovelli A.
Article.Abstract: Neural oscillations are thought to play a central role in encoding and transmitting cognitive information across large-scale brain networks, yet the relative contributions of phase synchrony and amplitude co-modulations to distributed coding remain unclear. A key obstacle is the absence of tools that can simultaneously quantify task-relevant information in the frequency domain and disentangle its phase and amplitude co-modulation components across pairwise and higher order interactions. Here, we introduce a spectral partial information decomposition framework (NeOPID) for quantifying information about cognitive variables in amplitude co-modulation and phase contributions, and to quantify redundant and synergistic information in brain relations, from pairwise to higher-order interactions. We validated the approach on Kuramoto and Stuart- Landau oscillator networks, including a whole-brain model constrained by macaque anatomical connectivity. NeOPID accurately recovers ground-truth encoding schemes and reveals that phase relations and amplitude co-modulations act as complementary coding channels with both redundant and synergistic components. NeOPID further extends this decomposition to higher-order functional interactions enabling the characterization of how cognitive information is collectively distributed across multiple oscillatory edges via redundant and synergistic encoding. To illustrate biological applicability, we applied NeOPID to local field potentials (LFPs) recorded from the macaque fronto-parietal network during a working memory task. In this dataset, NeOPID identified beta-band amplitude co-modulations as the primary carrier of stimulus information, and revealed that higher-order phase interactions exhibit both redundant and synergistic structure during the memory delay. These results establish NeOPID as a principled tool for dissecting the informational architecture about cognitive processes of oscillatory brain networks. Significance Statement Understanding how the brain coordinates large-scale communication to support cognition remains a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. Characterizing the distinct roles of phase synchrony and amplitude co-modulation has been hindered by a lack of computational approaches capable of separating these components across pairwise and higher-order interactions. Here, we introduce NeOPID (neural spectral Partial Information Decomposition), a framework designed to isolate phase and amplitude co-modulation contributions and quantify redundant and synergistic information contained in pair-wise and higher order functional interactions. NeOPID was validated on simulated oscillator models and on macaque local field potentials (LFPs) during a working memory task. Overall, the results establish NeOPID as a principled tool for dissecting the informational architecture underlying cognitive processes in oscillatory brain networks.

Article.Title: AgRP neurons as an integrative node linking the somatotropic and reproductive axes
Article.Authors: Alves G.; Vieira H.; de Sousa L.; List E.; Kopchick J.; Sousa L.; Silva J.; Donato J.; Frazao R.
Article.Abstract: Growth hormone (GH) signaling contributes to pubertal development and reproductive function, yet the hypothalamic circuits mediating these effects remain incompletely understood. Kisspeptin and agouti-related protein (AgRP) neurons are key integrators of metabolic and reproductive cues and exhibit GH-responsive signaling pathways. We therefore investigated their contributions to the reproductive consequences of altered somatotropic signaling. Using genetic mouse models of chronic GH excess or deficiency, we examined the impact of altered GH signaling on pubertal maturation, fertility, and hypothalamic neuroendocrine function. Pubertal onset was unaffected in female mice, whereas males with either GH excess or GH deficiency exhibited delayed puberty. In contrast, GH hypersecretion selectively disrupted estrous cyclicity and impaired fertility in females. Female reproductive dysfunction occurred despite preserved kisspeptin signaling, as evidenced by the preservation of intrinsic electrophysiological properties of kisspeptin neurons and unaltered hypothalamic Kiss1 mRNA expression. Chronic GH excess increased hypothalamic Agrp mRNA expression and reduced Pomc and Tac2 mRNA expression compared to control mice; these transcriptional changes were prevented by AgRP-specific GH receptor (GHR) deletion, which also improved ovarian function. Notably, selective deletion of the GHR in AgRP cells markedly improved fertility in GH-hypersecreting females. Together, these findings identify AgRP neurons as a critical hypothalamic target through which chronic GH excess impairs female reproductive function. Our results further demonstrate that GH-induced infertility occurs independently of canonical kisspeptin-GnRH dysfunction, revealing a sexually dimorphic mechanism linking somatotropic signaling to reproductive competence. Significance Statement Reproductive dysfunction is a common consequence of chronic alterations in growth hormone (GH) secretion, but the underlying neural mechanisms remain poorly defined. We show that chronic GH excess induces a sexually dimorphic reproductive phenotype characterized by profound impairment of female fertility despite largely preserved kisspeptin neuronal function. In contrast, GH excess altered hypothalamic AgRP-associated pathways, and the selective deletion of GH receptors in AgRP neurons significantly improved fertility in GH-hypersecreting females. These findings identify AgRP neurons as key mediators of GH-induced reproductive dysfunction and reveal a previously unrecognized sexually dimorphic neuroendocrine mechanism linking somatotropic signaling, metabolic circuits, and female fertility.

Article.Title: Learning rapidly reshapes brain microstructure: evidence from dense temporal sampling of diffusion MRI
Article.Authors: Kumral D.; Lenders A.; Schönauer M.
Article.Abstract: Learning is associated with rapid microstructural changes in the human brain, yet the precise temporal dynamics of these changes remain unclear. Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) combined with task-based fMRI, we assessed microstructural changes throughout a declarative learning paradigm and subsequent rest. Seventy-four participants (36 females) learned image-location associations across four encoding-retrieval repetitions while undergoing interleaved functional and DW-MRI acquisitions. A matched control group (N=37, 21 females) underwent a similar imaging protocol without learning. Dense sampling of DW-MRI acquisitions (2146 images across 22 time points in 127 min) revealed that learning-induced mean diffusivity (MD) decreases emerged shortly after learning onset and continued to develop during post-learning rest. The most robust change was localized to the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus, a region also showing functional activation during encoding and retrieval. Linear mixed-effects modeling further confirmed a significant group-by-time interaction, with MD reductions in the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus emerging as early as ≈7 min after learning onset, becoming robust by ≈35-40 min, and persisting throughout the extended post-learning period, while controls showed no changes. Our findings demonstrate that learning-related microstructural plasticity unfolds continuously from encoding to offline consolidation, with learning-induced structural changes emerging in functionally engaged regions. Dense temporal sampling of DW-MRI offers a powerful approach to bridge functional activation and structural remodeling, providing evidence of when and where experience-dependent plasticity occurs during memory formation. Significance Statement How quickly does the brain’s structure change when we learn? Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI; 2146 images) across more than 2 hours, we show that microstructural plasticity arises rapidly during learning and continues to develop during post-learning rest. These learning-induced changes are spatially precise and overlap with task-related functional activity. By capturing the entire progression of microstructural plasticity across the learning process, rather than just before and after a learning paradigm, our study provides insights into when and where learning-induced plasticity occurs, demonstrating that memory formation involves rapid, ongoing microstructural changes in functionally engaged regions.

Article.Title: Gaze reinstatement during working memory for natural scenes
Article.Authors: Dong Y.; Hung Y.; Gaspariani L.; Kiyonaga A.
Article.Abstract: The information we hold in mind with working memory (WM) may propagate beyond the cortex and out to the peripheral motor system. For instance, directionally biased hand and eye movements can express simple visuo-spatial features during WM maintenance. If such sensorimotor inflections are a form of WM representation, they may also express more detailed and task-adaptive information about WM content. Here, we ask whether gaze patterns carry item-specific detail about complex stimuli held in mind, and whether gaze during WM maintenance adapts to upcoming behavioral demands. To do this, we tracked male and female human eye movements during WM for naturalistic images, and we manipulated which image properties were most task-relevant (visual or semantic). In two experiments, we found that the eyes moved in item-specific spatiotemporal sequences during WM maintenance. Delay period gaze patterns retraced the scanpaths from stimulus encoding, echoing the ‘gaze reinstatement’ that has been observed during long-term memory retrieval. Therefore, gaze patterns during WM may reinstate visual encoding processes for maintenance. We also used time-resolved representational similarity analyses, guided by convolutional neural network modeling, to test the specificity of WM gaze patterns across a trial. We found that gaze representations were more distinct when the task prioritized visual detail, and they also ramped up in anticipation of the WM probe. Therefore, oculomotor WM signals are malleable to when and how the content will be used. WM may recruit the most primary structures in sensorimotor processing, where eye movements reflect flexible and future-oriented WM content information. Significance Statement The eyes are an outwardly accessible extension of the brain. They filter sensory input and enact motor output, but may also offer a rich window into underlying cognition. For instance, pupil dilation can reflect changing cognitive load, and biased eye movements can reflect basic spatial information about content held in mind with working memory (WM). WM is a critical neuro-cognitive function, but its physiological bases remain under debate. Here, we show that during WM the eyes can move in intricate patterns that read out the complex, real-world stimuli held in mind. This work shows how cognitive states influence oculomotor functions, and also advances theories of WM maintenance to include the most basic structures in sensorimotor processing.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: working memory; eye movements; representational similarity analysis; convolutional neural networks

Article.Title: Sex-Dependent Differences in Nucleus Accumbens Regulation of Aggression and Social Investigation
Article.Authors: Tremblay J.; Rego K.
Article.Abstract: Throughout the animal kingdom, dominance relationships establish stable hierarchies that are important for regulating access to limited resources, such as food, territory, and mates (Yan et al., 2024). Formation of these structured relationships requires shifts in aggressive and submissive behavior among individuals and is highly adaptive because these hierarchies allow animals to avoid conflict and conserve energy. Experience-dependent changes in behavior often occur through a process of positive reinforcement, and winning aggressive encounters is known to be rewarding. The nucleus accumbens (NAc) is a key structure in the mesolimbic dopamine system that regulates reinforcement learning, motivation, and reward processing. It contains a high density of dopamine-receptor-expressing neurons that receive input from several limbic and cortical regions, including the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC; Xu et al., 2024). The NAc plays a critical role in the rewarding aspects of aggression, as demonstrated through conditioned place preference assays in mice (Golden et al., 2016). Also, the positive reinforcing effects of aggression in hamsters are associated with phasic increases in dopamine in the NAc core (Cross et al., 2025). Nevertheless, much remains unknown about the cellular mechanisms and neural circuitry in the NAc regulating behavioral plasticity after repeated aggressive encounters. Borland et al. (2026) investigated how NAc activity regulates experience-dependent changes in aggression and social investigation. Investigating aggression in traditional rodent models can be challenging because female mice and rats do not consistently display robust aggressive behavior under standard housing conditions. In contrast, both male and female Syrian hamsters readily exhibit territorial aggression, making them a valuable model for investigating sex differences in the neurobiological mechanisms underlying changes in aggression. Initial investigations evaluated whether repeated social interactions produce behavioral changes and alter activity of NAc neurons in male and female Syrian hamsters. Article.Title: Beyond Pathology: Perivascular Spaces as Dynamic Players in Neurodevelopment and Brain Health
Article.Authors: Herting M.; Morrel J.; Levitt P.; McComb J.; Choupan J.
Article.Abstract: Perivascular spaces (PVS) have historically been viewed as radiological markers of aging and cerebrovascular pathology. However, this narrow perspective overlooks accumulating evidence that PVS likely undergo dynamic, prolonged maturation across the lifespan and may play an essential role in healthy brain development. This Viewpoint article challenges the prevailing paradigm by positioning PVS not as passive anatomical structures or mere disease indicators, but as active participants in postnatal neurodevelopment whose morphology and function evolve to meet the metabolic and waste clearance demands of the maturing brain. We integrate evidence from advanced neuroimaging, developmental neuroscience, and neurobiology studies to highlight that PVS structure and fluid dynamics may be coupled with several neurodevelopmental processes, impacted by early experiences, and mature through adolescence to facilitate healthy brain development and cognitive functioning. We advocate for longitudinal, lifespan approaches to PVS research, because understanding normative PVS development is paramount for interpreting pathological changes. This developmental reframing highlights new opportunities for early identification of at-risk individuals and preventive interventions targeting the brain's waste clearance system during sensitive developmental windows.

Article.Title: Opioid-glutamate interactions modulate intrinsically rewarded communication in European starlings
Article.Authors: Zhao C.; Fu R.; Preston G.; Riters L.
Article.Abstract: Affiliative, non-sexual vocal communication is essential for social learning and bonding, yet relatively little is known about its neural bases. Past research on songbirds demonstrates that song produced in affiliative, non-sexual flocks correlates positively with a bird's intrinsic reward state, and the link between song and reward is regulated by mu opioid receptors (MORs) in the medial preoptic area (MPOA). RNAseq studies also reveal a strong positive association between affiliative song and glutamatergic gene expression in MPOA, with NMDA receptor 1 (GRIN1) and glutamate receptor scaffolding protein (Shank2) correlating strongly with affiliative singing. In male European starlings we tested the hypothesis that MOR–glutamate interactions in the MPOA regulate affiliative communication. Peripheral administration of the MOR agonist fentanyl increased affiliative singing and calling behavior while reducing stress-related behavior, beak wiping. The effects on vocal but not stress-related behavior were prevented by administration of the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801. c-Fos mapping revealed that fentanyl increased neural activity in caudal MPOA (cMPOA) and interconnected regions implicated in social behavior, song production, and reward, and that these effects were reversed by MK-801. To identify a local site of MOR-glutamate interaction, we used AAV shRNA to downregulate Shank2 in MPOA. This manipulation prevented fentanyl from stimulating affiliative singing behavior, also without affecting stress reduction, suggesting that MOR–glutamate interactions in the MPOA facilitate social communication but not associated stress reduction. Together these findings provide the first experimental evidence that MOR–glutamate interactions within the MPOA, particularly the cMPOA, contribute to affiliative, rewarding vocal communication. Significance Statement Affiliative, non-sexual vocal communication is fundamental to social cohesion and well-being, yet its neural mechanisms are poorly understood. This study identifies a critical role for interactions between mu opioid receptors and glutamatergic signaling in promoting non-sexual, rewarding vocal communication. In a songbird experimental system, we demonstrate that NMDA receptor activity and the postsynaptic glutamate receptor scaffolding protein Shank2 are required for opioid facilitation of affiliative song. Our findings further reveal the medial preoptic area, particularly its caudal subdivision, to be an important site of this opioid-glutamate interaction. Together, these results extend opioid–glutamate interaction frameworks beyond classic reward circuits and suggest the existence of a conserved neural mechanism supporting affiliative social behavior across vertebrates.

Article.Title: Learning-dependent hippocampal–striatal reorganization during sequential decision-making in pigeons
Article.Authors: Yang L.; Xiao Y.; Li J.; Li M.; Li Z.; Ma Y.; Yang L.; Shang Z.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive sequential decision-making requires animals to learn how actions shape future states and rewards while adjusting behavioral strategies as experience accumulates. Although the hippocampus is implicated in state-structure representation and the striatum in value learning, how learning strategies evolve from exploratory sampling to efficient exploitation and how hippocampal–striatal interactions reorganize alongside this transition remain unclear. We trained six pigeons of undetermined sex to perform a probabilistic two-step decision task while simultaneously recording behavioral choices and hippocampal–striatal local field potentials. Strategy evolution was tracked using a dynamic reinforcement-learning framework in which model-based, model-free, and weighted model-based/model-free models were fitted across sliding windows. Hippocampal–striatal functional coordination was assessed using phase-locking analysis, and directed predictive influence was quantified using kernel Granger causality. The weighted model best explained choice dynamics, indicating a shift from model-based-like control during early acquisition toward model-free-like control during later stable performance. This behavioral shift was accompanied by two complementary neural changes: hippocampal–striatal phase coordination increased across learning, whereas hippocampus-to-striatum directed predictive influence decreased and covaried positively with model-based-like strategy weight. Direction-ratio analysis showed that hippocampus-to-striatum remained the predominant direction throughout learning, indicating reduced influence rather than directional reversal. After acquisition, hippocampus-to-striatum directed influence was not uniformly reduced but remained relatively preserved during rare, low-value, unrewarded, or less expected events. Together, these findings reveal a learning-dependent reorganization of hippocampal–striatal dynamics, in which increasing functional coordination is accompanied by reduced but condition-dependent hippocampal-to-striatal influence as behavior becomes more stable and efficient. Significance Statement Adaptive learning requires coordinated changes in behavioral strategy and neural interactions as animals progress from exploration to stable performance. Here, we show that pigeons gradually shifted from flexible, model-based-like control toward more stable, model-free-like behavior during sequential learning. In parallel, hippocampal–striatal interactions underwent a complementary reorganization: phase coordination progressively increased, whereas hippocampus-to-striatum directed predictive influence decreased with declining model-based-like control. Importantly, this directed influence remained relatively preserved during rare, low-value, or unrewarded events. These findings link behavioral strategy transition to the dynamic reorganization of hippocampal–striatal interactions, revealing how neural systems may simultaneously support efficient learned behavior while retaining sensitivity to behaviorally informative events.

Article.Title: Multiple combinations of GPCR activation gate the induction of NMDAR-independent LTD in mouse visual cortex
Article.Authors: Severin D.; Moreno C.; Contreras A.; Tran T.; Ramson S.; Reed M.; Contreras J.; Wesselborg C.; Xu W.; Huganir R.; Gallagher M.; Lee H.; Kirkwood A.
Article.Abstract: Activity-dependent synaptic weakening, including long-term depression (LTD), is a fundamental mechanism underlying experience-dependent circuit remodeling. At excitatory synapses, two mechanistically distinct forms of LTD have been identified: NMDAR-LTD, triggered by activation of NMDA receptors, and mGluR-LTD, mediated by group I metabotropic glutamate receptors. NMDAR-LTD is the best-characterized form and has been described in numerous brain regions. In contrast, in cortical synapses mGluR-LTD has been investigated primarily in the hippocampus, where it requires mGluR5 activation and its molecular mechanisms are well established. Although NMDAR-LTD is also well documented in the neocortex, mGluR-LTD remains comparatively poorly characterized, particularly in primary sensory cortices, despite growing evidence that mGluR signaling contributes to sensory deprivation-induced synaptic remodeling. We examined mGluR-LTD in slices of primary visual cortex of rats and mice of all sexes and found that layer II/III pyramidal neurons do express an NMDAR-independent LTD. Like in CA1, mGluR-LTD in V1 depends on mGluR5 activation and ongoing protein synthesis regulated by FMRP. Unlike CA1, however, where activation of mGluR5 alone is sufficient to induce mGluR-LTD, induction in V1 requires the co-activation of at least two neuromodulatory receptors, including mGluR5 together with muscarinic, noradrenergic, or serotonergic receptors. This more stringent gating mechanism may reflect the tighter constraints on synaptic plasticity in the neocortex, consistent with the view that the hippocampus and neocortex are specialized for rapid and gradual learning, respectively. Significance statement At excitatory synapses, two mechanistically distinct forms of long-term depression (LTD) have been identified: NMDAR-LTD and mGluR-LTD. While NMDAR-LTD is widespread, mGluR-LTD has been studied primarily in the hippocampus and remains poorly characterized in sensory cortices, despite evidence that mGluRs contribute to sensory deprivation-induced synaptic remodeling. This study shows that an NMDAR-independent form of LTD can be induced in visual cortical slices. Unlike hippocampus, where activation of mGluR5 alone is sufficient to induce mGluR-LTD, induction in visual cortex requires the co-activation of at least two neuromodulatory receptors, including mGluR5 together with muscarinic, noradrenergic, or serotonergic receptors. This stricter gating mechanism may reflect the tighter constraints on synaptic plasticity in the neocortex, consistent with its role in gradual, rather than rapid, learning.

Article.Title: Physiological Representation of Social Evaluation: Modeling Human Eye Movements, Pupillary, and Neuronal Responses to Faces
Article.Authors: Mao A.; Cao R.; Sun S.; Wang S.; Oh D.
Article.Abstract: Face-based social evaluations are ubiquitous and consequential, yet it remains unclear how these evaluations are represented in spontaneous physiological responses. Across four studies (222 participants: 142 females, 57 males, 23 unreported; 503 neurons), we used a data-driven modeling framework to examine how facial appearance shapes eye movements, pupillary responses, and neuronal activity during face viewing. We asked what these responses reveal about the underlying social evaluations. Pupillary responses and hippocampal firing during saccades were driven by facial variation associated with an integrated combination of valence and power evaluations; fixation duration on the eyes and hippocampal firing during fixations were more selectively tuned to threat-related evaluations; amygdalar firing primarily tracked approachability-related valence. A prospective validation study confirmed that novel faces synthesized along these modeled directions elicited the predicted physiological responses in new participants. We also found evidence of individual differences: social anxiety selectively heightened the sensitivity of pupillary responses to face evaluations. These findings suggest that distinct physiological responses across attention, autonomic arousal, and medial temporal lobe activity reflect distinct but related facets of face-based social evaluation. Significance Statement Everyday social decisions hinge on split-second impressions of unfamiliar faces. When we see a face, we instantly judge the person’s likely intention (positive ↔ negative valence) and social influence (high ↔ low power). Across four complementary studies, we show that these evaluative processes are reflected in physiological responses to faces across overt attention, autonomic arousal, and subcortical neuronal firing. Different physiological systems reflected partially distinct but related facets of social-evaluative meaning, including integrated valence-and-power, threat-related, and approachability-related evaluation.

Article.Title: Adult-Onset Auditory Deprivation Enhances Attenuation of Neural Responses in the Visual Cortex and Improves Peripheral Visual Acuity
Article.Authors: Pham K.; Mesik L.; Lee R.; Kim N.; Vogety S.; Seo B.; Dahl G.; Melvin L.; Kommu M.; Jeong R.; Lee H.
Article.Abstract: The ability of the brain to undergo plastic changes throughout the lifespan of an organism is essential to optimize its interactions with its environment. Adaptation to sensory loss is observed as cross-modal recruitment of the cortical areas deprived of their own sensory inputs by the spared senses and as compensatory plasticity of the spared cortical areas. The former is thought to increase the cortical resource for processing information related to the spared modalities, and the latter is thought to refine the spared senses. In animal models, synaptic plasticity and circuit-level plasticity have been observed in both the deprived primary sensory cortex and the spared primary sensory cortices. In this study, we examined how the primary visual cortex (V1) adapts to cross-modal auditory deprivation initiated in adult mice of both sexes. To do this, we recorded the stimulus-evoked neural activity in V1 layer 2/3 (L2/3) using two-photon calcium imaging and presented visual stimuli restricted to either the central or the peripheral visual field. We found that adult-onset deafening intensified the attenuation of stimulus-evoked responses to a range of stimuli, largely in the medial V1 representing the peripheral monocular visual field, without affecting the population decoding capability. Furthermore, adult-onset deaf mice exhibited selective behavioral improvement on peripheral visual acuity for detecting static gratings, without changes in contrast sensitivity for detecting moving gratings. Our findings suggest enhancement of neural attenuation may support compensatory plasticity in adult V1, which may benefit the stimulus encoding efficiency to improve detection of fine peripheral visual features.

Article.Title: High-Fat Diet Feeding Rapidly Induces Sex-Specific Neuronal Plasticity in Lateral Hypothalamic Glutamatergic Neurons
Article.Authors: Lu Y.; Rossi M.
Article.Abstract: Hypothalamic circuits play a central role in coordinating feeding and energy balance, yet how these circuits adapt to dietary excess to regulate body weight remains poorly understood. Lateral hypothalamic area glutamatergic (LHA Vglut2 ) neurons critically mediate food intake and body weight, but how they adapt their function to acute overfeeding and whether such adaptation is sexually dimorphic are unknown. Here, we examined the impact of high-fat diet (HFD) on LHA Vglut2 neurons in mice. Whole-cell recordings revealed baseline sex differences in neuronal properties: female LHA Vglut2 neurons exhibited higher basal excitability and differential synaptic input compared with males. HFD feeding produced distinct forms of neuronal plasticity between sexes within 1 d. In males, HFD increased intrinsic excitability while excitatory synaptic input was decreased. In contrast, excitability of female LHA Vglut2 neurons remained unchanged, but inhibitory synaptic strength was selectively reduced. To test the causal relationship between enhanced LHA Vglut2 neuron excitability and weight gain during overfeeding, we expressed the depolarizing sodium channel NaChBac to chronically increase LHA Vglut2 neuron excitability. Chronic elevation of LHA Vglut2 neuron excitability suppressed body weight gain during acute HFD exposure in males, whereas females displayed significant weight loss during HFD exposure. Together, these results suggest that female mice may be protected from diet-induced obesity via sexually dimorphic LHA Vglut2 neurons. In males, overfeeding rapidly induces compensatory changes in LHA Vglut2 neuron excitability that may act to limit body weight gain. Further enhancement of LHA Vglut2 neuron excitability can suppress weight gain in an obesogenic environment for both males and females.

Article.Title: Hexagonal modulation of theta rhythmic attentional sampling of visual space
Article.Authors: Kienitz R.; Moroz M.; Martini J.; Helfrich R.
Article.Abstract: Spatial attention improves visual perception by selecting behaviorally relevant sensory signals. Traditionally, attention has been conceptualized as a static spotlight, while recent evidence posited that attention operates as a moving spotlight that samples visual space sequentially in discrete snapshots that are clocked by theta rhythms (∼3-8 Hz). While theta rhythmic attentional sampling has mainly been observed in fronto-parietal and occipital areas, theta oscillations also hallmark entorhinal-hippocampal grid-cell networks, which encode physical space in hexagonal patterns that guide overt exploration and navigation. We hypothesized that visual attention might rely on the same underlying principles and sample visual space in a hexagonal, grid-like configuration. To test this hypothesis, twenty participants (10 females and 10 males) performed a cue-guided attention task that probed behavioral performance as a function of space and time. Reaction times were assessed as a function of spatial location and varying cue-target intervals, which displayed spatially-structured theta rhythms. Specifically, higher theta power occurred at spatial locations that were aligned to multiples of 60°, consistent with an underlying hexagonal organization. Participants that exhibited stronger hexagonal sampling relied less on the spatial cue to guide their attentional allocation. In sum, these findings suggest that covert visual attention is organized in a hexagonal pattern that might be consistent with the grid-like structure known from the entorhinal-hippocampal system and highlight that theta rhythms could reflect a common organizing principle for spatial cognition. Significance Statement Attention prioritizes sensory inputs to optimize behavior. But how does attention sample the environment in space and time? Here, we demonstrate that attentional sampling of visual space is not uniform, but might preferentially explore locations that are oriented along a hexagonal pattern, reminiscent of the spatial configuration of entorhinal-hippocampal grid cells. Moreover, covert attentional sampling exhibited oscillatory theta signatures (3-8 Hz). In sum, these findings suggest that spatial attention and navigation may share a common organizing principle, and indicate that theta rhythms may orchestrate sampling behaviors in space and time as a unifying principle underlying spatial cognition.

Article.Title: Bivalent habenula modulation of human monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways
Article.Authors: Hudson L.; Davey C.; Steward T.; Kung P.; Dai Y.; Unsworth L.; Jamieson A.; Moffat B.; Glarin R.; Harrison B.
Article.Abstract: The habenula is implicated in signaling negative reward prediction errors (RPE), yet direct evidence demonstrating its influence on downstream human brain circuits is limited. Using ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling across two negative RPE-inducing experimental tasks, we characterize habenula-directed connectivity with monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways in healthy adults (n = 47, 24 males and 23 females; n = 43, 23 males and 20 females). Negative feedback drove habenula inhibition of ventral tegmental area and dorsal raphe nucleus activity, while positive feedback had an excitatory effect. These core effects are replicated across reversal learning and perceptual decision uncertainty tasks, establishing a generalizable mechanism for behavioral adaptation. Task-specific modulatory effects emerged in pathways between the subcortical and cortical regions (ventral tegmental area→dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal raphe nucleus→medial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex→habenula), revealing context-dependent cortical elaboration of negative RPE-driven habenula signals. This provides the first evidence in humans, using model-based effective connectivity, for bivalent modulation of habenula function on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways, demonstrating how the brain integrates negative and positive signals to guide adaptive behavior. Significance Statement The habenula – an epithalamic brain region – plays a key role in the encoding of reward and punishment. Animal studies have demonstrated the habenula to be bivalently modulated by aversive and appetitive stimuli, resulting in the bidirectional modulation of monoaminergic brain region activity. Despite this evidence, the directional impact of bivalently modulated habenula activity on its circuitry has yet to be investigated in humans. This study leverages ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling to reveal the impact of bivalent habenula modulation on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical regions across two distinct tasks. Through these methodologies, we demonstrate the habenula to have a key role in guiding adaptive behavior.

Article.Title: Perception of Tones versus Tone Streams under Random Multi-tone Masking and Its Representation in Auditory Cortex
Article.Authors: Kistenmacher F.; Doll L.; Gutschalk A.
Article.Abstract: When repeated tones are presented among random masker tones, their perceptual organization is often variable. In some trials, they cannot be segregated from the masker tones. In other trials, often with a delay, they form coherent streams, segregated from the masker tones. A strong awareness-related negativity is evoked by each segregated tone of the stream in auditory cortex. A similar negative-going response has been observed when subtle, isolated tones are detected versus missed, raising the question of whether target tones that do not form a stream under informational masking are still perceived or not. Here a paradigm is introduced to probe this question while activity in auditory cortex was recorded with magnetoencephalography. Human listeners (13 female, 8 male) were instructed to indicate when they detected an isochronous stream of tones under multi-tone masking while listening to the stimulus. Thereafter, they indicated if a cue tone, presented subsequently to each trial, was comprised in the target and masker combination. Results confirmed that target tones could still be perceived in the subset of trials where they did not form a coherent stream, but the detectability in the cued frequency report was higher for tones forming a stream. A prominent awareness-related negativity was only observed when the tones formed a stream, suggesting that this response reflects the perceptual organization of the tones into streams and beyond the pure perception of the tones themselves. We speculate that the perceptual organization into a stream further enhances the detectability of the tones comprised in the stream.

Article.Title: Macaque Area LIP Reflects Confidence-Dependent Changes in Decision Policy
Article.Authors: Tu M.; Vivar-Lazo M.; Fetsch C.
Article.Abstract: The process of forming a decision gives rise to an estimate of its quality or likelihood of success. This graded sense of confidence is important for guiding subsequent decisions, but a neural mechanism linking subjective confidence to formation of the next decision has not been identified. We trained two male rhesus macaques to report a perceptual choice and simultaneous confidence judgment in a reaction-time (RT) motion discrimination task. Monkeys were more likely to repeat a rewarded choice when they reported low confidence on the previous trial, and showed greater changes in RT after a surprising outcome (low-confidence correct or high-confidence error). Neural activity in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) encoded the previous trial's choice and confidence more strongly after a low-confidence correct trial, and the strength of history encoding was correlated with a trial-by-trial estimate of choice bias. Ramping dynamics of the decoded decision variable also depended systematically on the conjunction of confidence and reward on the previous trial, in a manner that reflected individual differences between animals. The findings suggest that LIP not only reflects the formation of the current decision but could participate in confidence-guided learning via adjustments of the subsequent decision process. Significance statement Decision confidence is of primary interest in the study of metacognition, yet it also plays a key role in learning, serving as a graded prediction of accuracy that modulates the response to feedback. Reanalyzing data from nonhuman primates performing a reaction-time (RT) motion discrimination task with explicit confidence reports, we found that adjustments of choice bias and RT were gated by the animal’s self-reported confidence on the previous trial. The interaction of confidence and outcome (reward or punishment) was reflected in the activity of parietal (LIP) neurons on the subsequent trial, in ways largely consistent with the behavioral effects. The results and accompanying computational model suggest plausible functional links between the neuronal substrates of perceptual decision making and reinforcement learning.

Article.Title: PTPRO restricts higher-order branching of terminal arbors through TrkB dephosphorylation
Article.Authors: Li J.; Yasumura M.; Iguchi T.; Taniguchi M.; Oka Y.; Tsai C.; Sato M.
Article.Abstract: The structural complexity of axon collateral terminal arbors shapes synaptic connectivity. In corticospinal projections, individual axon collaterals exhibit distinct patterns of terminal arborization, ranging from sparse local branches to dense, highly complex arbors in target regions such as the pontine nuclei. How this complexity is controlled remains poorly understood. Here, using corticopontine projections in male and female mice, we show that protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) selectively restricts higher-order branching of terminal arbors in the pontine nuclei without affecting collateral number. This function requires the intracellular phosphatase domain of PTPRO but not its extracellular region. We demonstrate that PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), and that the excessive terminal arborization caused by acute PTPRO loss is rescued by TrkB depletion or phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibition. Together, these findings reveal that PTPRO-mediated TrkB dephosphorylation acts as a molecular brake on corticopontine terminal arbor elaboration. Significance Statement How individual axons regulate terminal branching within target regions is a fundamental question in neural circuit development. This study identifies protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO), a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase that negatively regulates signaling through tyrosine phosphorylation, as a selective regulator of higher-order branching in corticopontine terminal arbors. PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a neurotrophin receptor tyrosine kinase that promotes neuronal growth and branching, thereby restricting terminal arbor complexity without affecting collateral number from the main axon. Given that terminal arbor architecture determines the synaptic territory of each cortical input, PTPRO-dependent constraint on arbor elaboration may represent a general principle by which projection-specific arbor complexity is established across long-range circuits in the central nervous system.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: PTPRO; corticopontine projections; pontine nuclei; PI3K inhibition; protein tyrosine phosphatase; synaptic connectivity

Article.Title: State-Dependent Modulation of Corticospinal and Cortical Responses by Closed-Loop Paired-pulse TMS
Article.Authors: Choi D.; Güth M.; Ma M.; Harmon M.; Wischnewski M.; Park J.; Blenker A.; Lee S.; Opitz A.
Article.Abstract: Brain oscillations shape cortical excitability in a phase-dependent manner. Cortical excitability reflects the net output of intracortical circuits, including inhibitory and facilitatory pathways. However, whether the phase of ongoing brain rhythms differentially modulates inhibitory and facilitatory responses remains unknown. Paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (ppTMS) can selectively engage these circuits, providing a unique tool to dissociate their contributions. We combined real-time EEG-guided closed-loop TMS with single- and paired-pulse TMS in 24 healthy adults (13 female) to probe how sensorimotor mu (8–13 Hz) and beta (14–30 Hz) oscillatory phase shapes responses associated with intracortical inhibitory and facilitatory processes. Single-pulse TMS (spTMS), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and intracortical facilitation (ICF) were delivered at four phases (peak, falling, trough, rising). Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) and TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs) were recorded to assess corticospinal and cortical responses, respectively. We found that MEP amplitude was phase-dependent across all three stimulation types, with spTMS-evoked and ICF-conditioned MEPs showing the largest amplitudes at the rising phase, whereas SICI-conditioned MEPs were largest at the peak phase of the mu oscillation. TEP P60-N100 amplitude was modulated by oscillatory phase across all stimulation types, with maximal responses at the trough phase. SICI showed opposing phase patterns between the two measures, revealing a dissociation between cortical and corticospinal responses. MEP and TEP preferred phases were correlated across participants only in the ICF condition. These findings extend phase-dependent spTMS effects to paired-pulse stimulation and show that ongoing mu phase differentially shapes responses to SICI and ICF across cortical and corticospinal levels. Significance Statement Ongoing brain oscillations are known to shape cortical excitability across their phase cycle. However, whether this effect differentially influences inhibitory and facilitatory responses has remained unresolved. Here, using closed-loop EEG-guided transcranial magnetic stimulation in healthy adults, we probed how SICI- and ICF-conditioned responses vary across different phases of the sensorimotor mu and beta rhythms. We show that corticospinal and cortical responses to inhibitory and facilitatory paired-pulse protocols exhibit distinct phase-dependent patterns in the sensorimotor mu rhythm. These findings extend phase-dependent stimulation effects beyond single-pulse TMS and reveal that the relationship between cortical state and stimulation response differs across paired-pulse protocols.
