Article.Title: Cognitive mechanisms as a pathway linking schooling and protection against PTSD in contexts of armed conflict
Article.Authors: Blanchette I.; Josserand M.; Ingabire M.; Caparos S.
Article.Abstract: Schooling represents a protective factor for mental health, but this has not been investigated in populations exposed to armed conflicts, who present very high levels of post-traumatic stress disorder. Schooling is generally associated with better cognitive functioning, and cognitive functioning may serve as a protective factor for mental health. However, few studies have specifically examined whether cognition contributes to the protective effect of schooling on mental health. In this study, we examine the links between schooling, working memory and PTSD in two African samples exposed to high levels of violence: Rwanda ( n = 1,570) and North Kivu, in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo ( n = 1,633). We measured PTSD symptoms with the PCL-5 and working memory with a forward digit-span task, administered in the local language (Kinyarwanda or Swahili). Results of linear mixed models show that higher educational attainment is associated with less PTSD symptoms. This association persisted after accounting for important determinants of PTSD including age, gender, socioeconomic status and trauma exposure. Bootstrapped mediation analysis indicated that digit-span performance explained between 12 and 30% of the relationship between schooling and PTSD. These findings support the conclusion that formal education is associated with less psychopathology at least partly in relation to improvements in cognitive functioning. Results underscore the relevance of education and cognition for population mental health in high-adversity, conflict-affected settings.

Article.Title: Pilot–controller interactions: communication, conflict management, and perceived workload in relation to previous training exposure
Article.Authors: Karaoglu B.; Atan T.; Saracyakupoglu T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The interaction between pilots and Air Traffic Controllers (ATC) is essential for aviation safety. Operational demands, time pressure, and differences in perceived workload may contribute to communication difficulties and conflict during pilot–controller interactions. This study examines the relationships among communication and teamwork, conflict management, perceived workload, perceived performance, and previous relevant training exposure. A cross-sectional observational survey was conducted among pilots and ATCs. PLS-SEM was used to examine the relationships between the study variables. Communication and teamwork were significantly associated with conflict management (β = 0.461, p < .001). Perceived workload was negatively associated with perceived performance. Among participants with previous training exposure, this relationship was weaker and did not reach statistical significance. These findings suggest that communication, conflict management, workload, and perceived performance are interrelated, while previous training exposure may be associated with differences in these relationships. Further longitudinal or experimental studies are needed to examine whether specific training approaches are associated with changes in these relationships.

Article.Title: Dynamics of entrapped air pockets under transient pressure waves in pressurized pipelines: combined numerical and experimental study
Article.Authors: Kumar M.; Lambert M.; Hanmaiahgari P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Air entrapment commonly occurs in pressurized pipeline systems, where discrete air pockets form at fittings, high points, or geometric irregularities, yet are often neglected in practice. Entrapped air pockets within pressurized pipelines introduce complex fluid–air interactions that significantly alter pressure dynamics during transient events, leading to severe pressure surges and potential damage to the pipeline system. In this study, the transient pressure wave behavior in a slightly inclined pipeline containing entrapped air pockets is examined through three-dimensional Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations and laboratory experiments. The air-water interface is modelled in ANSYS Fluent using the Volume of Fluid (VOF) approach, and the effects of inlet pressure, air pocket volume, and air pocket location are systematically examined. Experimental measurements validate the CFD predictions, demonstrating good agreement in capturing pressure wave characteristics during air–water interactions. Results reveal that a large entrapped air pocket under low inlet pressure conditions produces the most severe response, with pressure drops reaching up to 105% of the initial static pressure. The study additionally provides insight into the thermodynamic behaviour of the entrapped air pocket during transients, which undergoes adiabatic compression and expansion, while the surrounding liquid remains effectively isothermal. The temperature fluctuations in the air pocket are more pronounced under higher initial flow conditions. By integrating CFD with experimental validation, this work provides insight into transient multiphase interactions and the thermodynamic evolution of entrapped air pockets, offering a physically consistent framework for interpreting the​ influence of entrapped air on hydraulic transients.

Article.Title: From traditional preservation to bioactive enrichment: ancestral khaya processing of Oxalis tuberosa (oca) elevates indole alkaloids, cytokinins and auxin
Article.Authors: Cabrerizo F.; Mirabal-Carrizo M.; Denofrio M.; De Gerónimo E.; Castañeta G.; Flores D.; Tejeda L.; Peñarrieta J.
Article.Abstract: β-carbolines (βCs) and carbazoles are bioactive indole alkaloids with reported anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective, immunomodulatory and anticancer activities in a structure-dependent manner. Traditional high-altitude Andean solar–frost dehydration processing (khaya) of Oxalis tuberosa (oca) has been reported to reduce anti-nutrients. In the present study, UHPLC-MS/MS profiling of fresh and processed oca identified four βCs in fresh tubers and a phytohormone profile consistent with a dormancy-like tuber stage (high abscisic and jasmonic acids; low gibberellic acid and cytokinins). Relative to fresh tubers, ancestral processing increased βCs levels 20-40-fold, induced carbazole formation, and elevated trans -zeatin, its riboside, and indole-3-acetic acid, consistent with a hormone profile indicative of dormancy-like breakage. The enrichment of these bioactive alkaloids and phytohormones highlights the biochemical relevance of these traditional practices and identifies processed oca as a candidate dietary source for further nutritional evaluation.

Article.Title: Re-entrant predator exclusion, strong resonances, and chaotic multistability in a noninvertible ricker predator–prey map
Article.Authors: Askar S.; Ghazi A.; Al Hajailan W.; Badawi M.; Foul A.
Article.Abstract: We study a discrete predator–prey map with Ricker prey growth, predator interference and inhibition at high prey density. The nonnegative quadrant is invariant, and every orbit enters a compact absorbing rectangle. Explicit equilibrium branches distinguish invasion of the predator-free equilibrium from the existence of positive coexistence states. The equilibrium invasion multiplier is nonmonotone, allowing re-entrant exclusion within the stability range of the prey-only equilibrium. Beyond that range, invasion depends on the transverse growth rate along the boundary orbit. Jury conditions determine the hyperbolic stability regions and spectral bifurcation loci. Representative 1 : 4 and 1 : 3 resonant coefficients are computed, and the unit-circle branch ends at a double- \(-1\) point. Refined cycle tests verify nearby attracting period-four and period-two states; they do not confirm the previously identified period-three locking region on the examined grid. Critical curves describe orientation reversal, while basin computations illustrate multistability without establishing a contact bifurcation. Numerical examples include two coexisting periodic cycles and coexistence of an interior irregular orbit with a boundary attractor. Positive finite-time Lyapunov exponents provide numerical evidence of chaos. These results clarify the distinction between local invasion, established coexistence and dependence on initial populations.

Article.Title: Joint modelling of factors associated with HIV and Tuberculosis in Malawi using a bivariate logistic regression model
Article.Authors: Mwamlima B.; Twabi H.
Article.Abstract: HIV and Tuberculosis (TB) are biologically and epidemiologically linked, yet their association is often not directly estimated when their determinants are analysed separately. This study used bivariate logistic regression to jointly assess factors associated with HIV and TB in Malawi and estimate their dependence. We analysed 22,504 adults aged 15 years and above from the 2020–2021 Malawi Population-based HIV Impact Assessment (MPHIA). A survey-weighted bivariate logistic regression model using the Palmgren/Dale odds-ratio parameterisation was fitted in R. Model fit and robustness were assessed through comparisons with separate logistic regression models and sensitivity analyses. Overall, 2,450 respondents (weighted 9.5%) were HIV-positive, 65 (0.29%) reported a recent TB diagnosis, and 25 had both. HIV and TB were positively associated after adjustment (OR 3.74, 95% CI 2.21–6.32). The association was consistent across sensitivity analyses (ORs 3.73–4.59), with no evidence of variation by sex, residence or age ( p = 0.19). HIV was more likely among women, Southern Region residents, ever-married respondents and older adults, but less likely among rural residents and those with tertiary education. Modelling dependence improved fit over independent models (likelihood-ratio χ² = 22.3, p < 0.001). HIV was strongly associated with ​ self-reported TB diagnosis among Malawian adults. Bivariate logistic regression provided a direct estimate of this association while accounting for sociodemographic factors. However, the small number of co-occurring cases and self-reported TB warrant cautious interpretation. The findings support integrated HIV and TB services.

Article.Title: Source consistency and a geometry driven no go theorem for phantom DBI regular black holes
Article.Authors: Pradhan A.; Ghaderi K.; Zeyauddin M.; Kumar A.
Article.Abstract: We examine the source consistency of an asymptotically flat regular black hole attributed to a phantom Dirac–Born–Infeld scalar. The positive radius black hole branch has one horizon, but the Einstein equations reconstruct a signed DBI factor approaching minus unity there, contradicting the principal square root of the action. Separately, the radial Einstein equation excludes ghost free support by a real, nonconstant, static radial scalar in a regular minimally coupled k essence theory within Einstein gravity, or by finitely many independent such fields. This local result uses the established connection between areal radius convexity and radial null energy condition violation; nonminimal couplings, general scalar tensor theories, and other matter sources are outside its scope. The negative kinetic sign is expected for a phantom field; the square root contradiction invalidates the proposed DBI background even when that sign is allowed. A signed continuation encounters singular scalar characteristics. The positive radius black hole branch approaches a simple terminal zero with finite nonzero one sided surface gravity, without establishing an evaporation endpoint. No nonzero mass two ended asymptotically flat continuously differentiable matching exists within this family. Geodesic and external test field observables remain properties of the prescribed metric.

Article.Title: Evaluating linear and nonlinear associations between long-term PM2.5 exposure and blood pressure in three large Korean population-based studies
Article.Authors: Han K.; Park J.; Kang D.; Kim J.; Jee S.; Lim J.; Woo H.
Article.Abstract: We evaluated associations between long-term exposure to fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) and blood pressure using data from three large-scale Korean population-based studies: KoGES, KNHANES, and KCPS-II (n = 243,952). Long-term PM 2.5 exposure was estimated using 1-year (lag 1y) and 3-year (lag 3y) moving averages. Study-specific associations with systolic (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were estimated using multivariable linear regression and combined by random-effects meta-analysis. Linear and nonlinear dose–response relationships were further evaluated using multivariate random-effects meta-regression, and potential effect modification was examined across subgroups. Pooled estimates showed positive but non-significant associations with SBP, and negative but non-significant associations with DBP, and showed substantial between-study heterogeneity (I 2 = 83.2–98.3%). In dose–response analyses, PM 2.5 showed positive linear associations with SBP and nonlinear associations with DBP at both lags, although these patterns varied after sequential exclusion of individual studies. No significant effect modification by age, sex, smoking status, or body mass index was observed after false discovery rate adjustment. Long-term PM 2.5 exposure may relate differently to SBP and DBP, with a possible positive linear pattern for SBP, while DBP showed negative pooled estimates and nonlinear patterns. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the substantial between-study heterogeneity.

Article.Title: An augmented mountain Gazelle optimizer for efficient training of transfer learning-based artificial neural networks
Article.Authors: Maddaiah P.; Narayanan P.; Dilip K.; Saini D.; Sahoo B.; Das N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are prevalent for classification and regression problems from diverse fields. Gradient-based optimization algorithms, which optimize weights and biases of the ANNs during training, have high training time and low accuracy due to the limitations that come from the gradient. Metaheuristic algorithms are alternative training algorithms for ANNs as they are efficient to explore search spaces such as multi-modal and higher-dimensional. Mountain Gazelle optimizer (MGO) is a recent metaheuristic algorithm that has notable effectiveness compared to the state-of-the-art algorithms. However, it lacks in searching potential regions, sustaining diversity in the population, and preventing local optima. To address these problems, this paper proposes an augmented mountain Gazelle optimizer (AMGO) by incorporating a strategy from a recent metaheuristic, which examines more potential regions, an empirical-based update equation, and opposition-based learning (OBL). The efficiency of the AMGO algorithm was validated by the experiments on the CEC2017 test suite benchmark functions and on training ANNs for classification and regression problems on various datasets, including potato leaf disease detection. Moreover, its performance was compared with well-known and recent metaheuristic algorithms. Further, its significance was verified with the Friedman and Wilcoxon rank-sum statistical tests. The results show that the AMGO algorithm has better performance than the MGO for 23 benchmark functions and diverse datasets. Moreover, the AMGO algorithm increases the average train and test accuracies by 2.9% and 4.4%, 1.9% and 1.8%, 3.6% and 3.8%, 10% and 9.8% compared to the MGO algorithm for the classification problems. Furthermore, it decreases the train and test RMSE values by 0.0032 and 0.0031, respectively, compared to the MGO algorithm for the regression problem. These outputs illustrate the significant improvement of the AMGO algorithm over the MGO. Experimental evaluation on the CEC2017 benchmark suite and ANN training problems demonstrates that AMGO provides competitive and generally improved optimization performance compared with the original MGO and several competitive metaheuristics. The proposed framework is particularly effective for ANN weight optimization while maintaining the computational complexity of the original MGO.

Article.Title: Integrative metabolomics and gene expression analyses reveal acetogenin-rich annona muricata leaf extract suppresses MCF-7 cell proliferation in obesogenic microenvironment
Article.Authors: Yantih N.; Tedjo A.; Fadilah F.; Mugiyanto E.
Article.Abstract: Obesity is associated with a significantly poorer prognosis in patients with Luminal A breast cancer, this investigation sought to determine the growth-inhibitory potential of Annona muricata leaf extracts against MCF-7 cells under obesogenic conditions and to identify key bioactive compounds through integrative metabolomics, gene expression analysis, and molecular docking. MCF-7 cells cultured in an obesogenic microenvironment were treated with 96, 75, and 25% ethanol extracts of A. muricata leaves. Antiproliferative assay was determined by IC₅₀ values. Expression of BAX and E2F2 was analysed to assess apoptotic and proliferative responses. Metabolomic profiling was executed via LC-MS/MS, with subsequent multivariate statistical tools—specifically PCA and PLS regression—employed to identify correlations between specific metabolites, IC₅₀ data, and gene expression patterns. Selected metabolites were evaluated by molecular docking against MDM2 (PDB ID: 1T4E). The 96% ethanol extract exhibited the strongest antiproliferative activity (IC₅₀ = 1.671 µg/mL). All extracts upregulated BAX, particularly the 75% extract, while E2F2 was downregulated in the 25 and 96% extracts. LC–MS/MS identified 339 annotated metabolites with clear PCA clustering. The PLS model showed excellent predictive performance (R²Y = 0.9897; Q²-cum = 0.9762; RMSEE = 0.0541). Metabolites at retention times 24–40 min with VIP 1 were mainly acetogenins, including muricatocin A and chatenaytrienin 1, negatively correlated with IC₅₀ and associated with increased BAX and decreased E2F2. Docking analysis showed stronger binding affinities than the native ligand. Acetogenin-rich A. muricata extract demonstrates potent antiproliferative activity under obesogenic conditions, potentially through inhibition of the MDM2–p53 interaction and modulation of apoptotic and proliferative pathways.

Article.Title: Graph foundation models for intelligent monitoring and control of renewable energy networks
Article.Authors: Kumar T.; Vashistha A.; Sharma G.; Alohali M.; Al-Wesabi F.; Alanazi R.
Article.Abstract: The rapid expansion of renewable energy resources has transformed modern power systems into highly interconnected and dynamic networks that require intelligent monitoring and adaptive control. Existing graph-based approaches mainly learn structural relationships from historical data and do not explicitly respect the electrical laws of the network. This paper proposes a physics-informed graph foundation model (PI-GFM) coupled with a digital twin (DT) for monitoring and control of renewable energy networks. PI-GFM is an impedance-aware graph encoder that is pre-trained in a self-supervised manner on pooled heterogeneous network data and then adapted through task heads for fault classification, bus-voltage estimation and one-hour-ahead DT forecasting. Electrical knowledge enters as soft penalties on nodal active and reactive power balance and on the linearised (LinDistFlow) branch voltage drop; the full nonlinear AC power flow is not enforced, and this scope is stated explicitly. The DT synchronises a latent network state over a four-hour window through a learned fusion, under explicitly defined operating limits, and its voltage estimates drive a reactive-power support controller. The framework is evaluated on a fully specified simulation of the IEEE 33-bus feeder with photovoltaic, wind and battery resources, solved with AC power flow and subjected to inverter faults, high-impedance line faults, voltage-instability events and reconfigurations, using chronological splits, 5 random seeds and DNN, LSTM, GCN, GAT and GraphSAGE baselines. On the unseen test season, PI-GFM attains a bus-voltage MAE of 3.31 × 10 −3 p.u., 17% lower than the best baseline (3.96 × 10 −3 p.u.), and a DT synchronisation accuracy of 84.9% of bus-hours within 0.005 p.u. (best baseline 75.9%). Its four-class accuracy is 96.39% (best baseline 97.12%), with a fault-detection false-alarm rate of 1.29%. Used as controller input, it keeps all buses within 0.95–1.05 p.u. in 88.2% of test hours, against 85.8% without control and 96.9% with perfect state knowledge. The ablation shows that both the physics terms and the DT reduce the estimation error, and pre-training improves low-label performance. The results are obtained on simulated data, on one feeder family, on a single CPU platform.

Article.Title: Testing predictive-state sufficiency and recursive closure in additive-manufacturing microstructure models
Article.Authors: Ji J.; Liu J.; Zavdoveev A.; Kopylov V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Most additive-manufacturing models predict final microstructure from process parameters or thermal-history descriptors. We ask a different question: how much of a material’s thermal history must be carried forward to predict what the next heat cycle will do to it? We call this compact, continuously updated information a predictive material state. In Ti–6Al–4V simulations we hid the phase fractions and inferred state coordinates from noisy total-alpha measurements. Two coordinates reduced identification RMSE by 27.1% relative to one; for held-out continuation prediction, one coordinate lay within the prespecified 0.001 RMSE margin of the best tested dimension. Transferred to a separately formulated kinetic model with only the readout recalibrated, a three-coordinate state cut median prediction error by 87.1% relative to ten conventional thermal-history descriptors with access to the entire past. Carried recursively through six unseen thermal segments with no intervening measurement, a two-coordinate state stayed 86.8% below the same descriptor baseline. A recurrent network forecast terminal phase fractions; its hidden state was not evaluated for predictive sufficiency or recursive closure. These computational results support task-dependent predictive compression within the tested input domain and tolerance.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: recursive closure; Ti-6Al-4V; microstructure prediction; additive manufacturing; phase fraction prediction; thermal history

Article.Title: Speaker Recognition as a Verification Method for Voice Control in Production Scenarios
Article.Authors: Norda M.; Bombel L.; Reuter P.; Hansen M.; Appell J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Voice control is already firmly established in the consumer sector, but its potential for flexibility and efficiency is also increasingly being discussed in industry. For a secure application, e.g. to prevent exploitation by unauthorized machine operators, user verification based on automatic speaker recognition can be used as an additional authentication measure. The aim of this work is the evaluation of a speaker recognition system regarding various influences relevant for use in production scenarios. For this purpose, a data set of typical German production voice commands was used, which was recorded with four microphone configurations at ambient noise conditions up to 84 dB(A). Error rates regarding the acceptance or rejection of a speaker served as an evaluation measure for discussing optimal conditions for use in voice-controlled production. The greatest influence was seen in the choice of microphone configuration used, while channel mismatch and Lombard effect had a lesser influence on recognition. Furthermore, large improvements in error rates were observed up to an audio length of approximately 5 s. Under optimal conditions, over 90% correct acceptances and rejections at 84 dB(A) ambient noise level could be achieved. Further research is needed on the choice of an optimal decision threshold for accepting or rejecting speakers.

Article.Title: Manganese deficiency induces root-centered oxidative and morphological reprogramming in date palm (Phoenix dactylifera L.)
Article.Authors: Ben Maachia S.; Namsi A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Manganese (Mn) deficiency is a hidden abiotic stress that compromises date palm ( Phoenix dactylifera L.) productivity and underlies brittle leaf disease (BLD). Yet, the early physiological signals that precede visible leaf degeneration remain unclear. Using a controlled in vitro model with clonal plantlets, we show that Mn deprivation strongly impaired root development, producing shortened, thickened, and browned roots, with a marked shift in biomass allocation toward structural dry matter. Despite the residual Mn present in plant tissues at the start of the experiment, Mn deprivation progressively reduced Mn accumulation in leaves while increasing its relative retention in roots, revealing altered internal partitioning rather than immediate whole-plant depletion. Leaf chlorophyll pools remained largely unaffected, highlighting their low sensitivity to early Mn stress. In contrast, oxidative responses were organ- and time-dependent: roots exhibited a transient several-fold induction of peroxidase activity, while leaves displayed a delayed but marked accumulation of hydrogen peroxide. Multivariate analyses clearly separated Mn treatments and sampling times, integrating root morphology, Mn partitioning, and oxidative markers into robust diagnostic profiles. Together, these findings reveal a temporal sequence in which root-centered alterations precede delayed foliar oxidative responses under Mn deficiency. These patterns provide a useful physiological framework for interpreting early Mn stress in date palm and may support the identification of potential biomarkers for nursery screening and Mn management.

Article.Title: Time and time–frequency domain analysis of electroretinography signals in individuals with autosomal recessive bestrophinopathy
Article.Authors: Behbahani S.; Azizi S.; Jaldian H.; Ahmadieh H.; Hatami F.; Mirzaei S.; Suri F.; Jorjani M.; Shirdel M.; Karimi A.; Amiri S.; Sabbaghi H.
Article.Abstract: Autosomal recessive bestrophinopathy (ARB) is associated with retinal dysfunction, yet its effects on electroretinographic (ERG) responses remain underexplored. This study aims to characterize the alterations in retinal function in ARB patients using time and time-frequency domain analysis. Thirty-three subjects participated: 14 patients with ARB (28 eyes) confirmed by ophthalmologic examination and genetic testing, and 19 age- and sex-matched normal vision (37 eyes). ERGs were recorded under dark-adapted 10.0 and light-adapted 3.0 conditions. Time-domain features were extracted. Continuous wavelet transform (CWT) was used to analyze the time-frequency domain. Under light- and dark-adapted conditions, individuals with ARB had significantly lower a- and b-wave amplitudes compared to people with normal vision (FDR < 0.02, effect size magnitude > 0.6). ARB subjects showed significantly prolonged b-wave implicit times in both conditions (FDR < 0.02, effect size > 0.7). Moreover, ARB individuals demonstrated a significant reduction in the first three dominant energy levels under both light- and dark-adapted conditions (FDR < 0.004, effect size magnitude > 0.5). Our results show profound retinal dysfunction in ARB, confirming photoreceptor/bipolar impairments secondary to BEST1 mutation and Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) disruption, with novel time-frequency biomarkers surpassing traditional metrics. Clinically, they enable early diagnosis, progression tracking, and intervention evaluation in this rare dystrophy. Future longitudinal studies will validate their prognostic utility.

Article.Title: Development and psychometric validation of the generative AI Educator PerspectoMeter Scale (GAIE-PM) in medical education: a descriptive scale development study
Article.Authors: Kohan N.; Ahmady S.; Hooshmandja M.; Yaseen S.; Keshavarzi M.; Rezaei P.
Article.Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into medical education, creating both opportunities and concerns for educators. Responsible implementation requires an understanding of educators’ perceptions of its limitations. This study aimed to develop and psychometrically assess the Generative AI Educator PerspectoMeter Scale (GAIE-PM) to measure medical educators’ perceptions of generative AI limitations in medical education. This descriptive scale-development study was conducted among medical educators at medical sciences universities in Iran in 2024. Following a modified Association for Medical Education in Europe (AMEE) Guide-informed approach, the scale was developed through a systematic literature review, a qualitative study with Iranian experts in three virtual focus groups, item generation, expert validation, pilot testing, and psychometric evaluation. After expert validation, 18 items were retained for pilot testing. Data were collected from 180 medical educators. Principal Factor Analysis (PCA) with Varimax Rotation was used to examine the preliminary factor structure, and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to assess the measurement model. Test–retest reliability was assessed in a subsample of 30 medical educators over a two-week interval using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Pearson correlation coefficient. To ensure a more robust assessment of internal consistency, McDonald’s omega (ω) was calculated alongside Cronbach’s alpha. The preliminary PCA supported a three-factor structure consisting of Pedagogical Limitations, Technical and Access Limitations, and Ethical and Quality Limitations, explaining 48.37% of the total variance. The final PLS-SEM measurement model retained 14 items across the three factors. Internal consistency was acceptable across the three factors, with Cronbach’s alpha values ranging from 0.69 to 0.81, a mean Cronbach’s alpha of 0.75, composite reliability values ranging from 0.81 to 0.86, and a mean McDonald’s omega of 0.81. Average variance extracted values ranged from 0.505 to 0.570, indicating acceptable convergent validity. Discriminant validity was supported using the Fornell–Larcker criterion. Test–retest reliability showed good temporal stability, with an ICC of 0.82 for the total scale score and factor-level ICC values ranging from 0.76 to 0.88. Pearson correlation coefficients between the two administrations ranged from 0.76 to 0.84 ( p < 0.001). The GAIE-PM Scale demonstrated acceptable psychometric properties for assessing medical educators’ perceptions of generative AI limitations in medical education. The scale may help identify pedagogical, technical/access, and ethical/quality-related concerns that should be considered when integrating generative AI into educational settings. Further validation in larger and more diverse samples is recommended.
Article.Topic: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

Article.Title: Energy-driven structure in coupled brain–body dynamics
Article.Authors: Lombardo D.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive function is often modeled through large-scale neural dynamics, while physiological and metabolic processes are typically treated as constraints. Here, we introduce a proof-of-concept generative computational framework that integrates neural oscillators, an autonomic-like oscillator, and a scalar energy-like variable into a unified dynamical system. The model implements bidirectional coupling between neural activity, physiological input, and the energy-like brain metabolism variable, enabling analysis of their joint influence on simulated cognition. Brain–body coupling was quantified by synchrony among global neural, cardiac, and respiratory dynamics and independently assessed with a nonparametric composite coupling index. While neural dynamics are characterized using predictability-based measures of temporal structure. Across heterogeneous network topologies and parameter regimes, direct associations between brain–body dynamic coupling and synthetic outcomes remain consistent. Predictability-based neural measures show modest associations with energy-sensitive outcomes but minimal associations with a control outcome. Mediation analyses indicate that the energy-like variable partially accounts for relationships between dynamical measures and synthetic outcomes across configurations. These effects persist under perturbations and ablation of explicit energy feedback, suggesting robustness of the coupling architecture. Given the synthetic nature of outcomes, all statistical effects reflect properties of model-internal dynamics. Rather than providing empirical evidence for biological cognition, this framework establishes a hypothesis-generating formal model of how coupled nonlinear systems generate structured dependencies among neural, physiological, and energy-like variables.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: neural oscillators; brain energy metabolism; neuronal synchronization; coupled dynamical systems; mediation analysis

Article.Title: Explainable hybrid CNN–transformer with fuzzy feature optimization for thyroid nodule malignancy classification on ultrasound
Article.Authors: Jingle I.; Paul P.; G I.; Parvin J.; U B.; R Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Thyroid nodule malignancy classification using ultrasound remains challenging owing to the differences in assessment by TI-RADS among different observers as well as the lack of interpretability in deep learning models. This study proposes a framework that is based on hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture with fuzzy feature optimization and visual explanation. This system combines convolution feature extraction, Transformer modeling, fuzzy membership feature selection, Softmax classifier, and Grad-CAM explanation. Model training was done using the TG3K+TN3K dataset, whereas DDTI, AUITD-Algerian, and micro-lesion synthetic dataset were used for testing. The performance evaluation of the model included classification metrics, cross-dataset testing, TI-RADS feature alignment, probability calibration, ablation testing, computation speed, and reader study by three radiologists. The model based on the suggested framework attained 91.8% accuracy, 89.8% sensitivity, 93.0% specificity, and 90.5% F1-score, along with an ROC-AUC of 0.932 and an inference time of 0.54 s per image. The use of Grad-CAM resulted in 82.85% mean feature alignment with TI-RADS region annotations by radiologists. Diagnostic accuracy increased by 9% points with the use of the assistance of AI. The calibration of probability led to a decrease in expected calibration error from 11.6 to 3.8%. However, factors such as disparities between the datasets used, the retrospective manner in which evaluation was done, and the use of artificial perturbations are some of the reasons why there is no immediate application of these findings into practice. This is because further prospective validation from multicenter studies is necessary to confirm clinical applicability of the results.

Article.Title: Leakage-controlled evaluation of vendor-aware three-dimensional missing-tooth localization in partially annotated multi-vendor cone-beam computed tomography
Article.Authors: Asgari H.; Zarafshan F.; Talaeipoor A.; Mazinan E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Three-dimensional missing-tooth localization in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is challenged by partial annotation and scanner-dependent acquisition differences, while the benefit of unlabeled scans remains uncertain. We therefore conducted a leakage-controlled evaluation of physical-space reconstruction, vendor-adversarial learning, dense teacher–student consistency, and reliability-gated semi-supervision under common case-level partitions. After excluding two discordantly annotated exact duplicates, 83 labeled and 73 unlabeled scans with 111 objects were eligible. Across 75 repeated-seed runs, mean pFROC was 0.890 for pure supervision, 0.899 for vendor-adversarial training, and 0.872 for gated semi-supervision. In 50 post-lock exploratory benchmark runs, conventional 3D detection achieved 0.921 versus 0.886 for confidence-only Mean-Teacher-3D; the primary fold-blocked test was not significant ( $$p=0.25$$ ). A post-lock exploratory cumulative gate ablation showed no pFROC change from uncertainty alone; full gating increased mean pseudo-label precision at confidence 0.70 to 0.826 while reducing coverage to 0.680, and modestly increased pFROC by 0.007 ( $$p=0.50$$ ). After fold-specific calibration, vendor-adversarial training achieved the strongest locked outer-test operating point: sensitivity 0.793 (95% CI 0.697–0.880) at 0.458 false positives per volume (0.301–0.639). Post-lock leave-one-vendor-out results were heterogeneous: vendor-adversarial training was numerically strongest for Meyer and Newtom but not Kavo. Semi-supervised superiority was not demonstrated. The study is therefore positioned as an auditable evaluation of acquisition control and unlabeled-data use in multi-vendor CBCT rather than as evidence for a fundamentally novel or universally superior semi-supervised algorithm. These conclusions are specific to the investigated cohort and acquisition profiles and do not establish scanner-independent generalization.

Article.Title: Machine learning models with SMOTE and GAN-based augmentation for myofascial pelvic pain syndrome classification
Article.Authors: Yu H.; Yang L.; Zhao X.
Article.Abstract: Class imbalance may distort performance estimates in clinical prediction models for myofascial pelvic pain syndrome (MPPS). To compare class weighting, categorical-aware synthetic oversampling, and constrained generative augmentation for contemporaneous classification of MPPS. The retrospective single-center dataset contained 2016 records (568 MPPS and 1448 health-examination controls) and 23 predictors. Exact duplicate predictor signatures were kept in the same partition, producing a development set of 1409 records (397 MPPS) and an untouched test set of 607 records (171 MPPS). Logistic Regression and XGBoost were evaluated with original data, class weighting, SMOTENC, and a constrained tabular GAN. Five-by-three nested cross-validation, calibration, and threshold selection were confined to the development set. Both augmentation methods balanced each fold-training subset to 1:1. Constrained-GAN XGBoost had a test ROC-AUC of 0.852 (95% CI 0.813–0.886), compared with 0.846 (0.808–0.884) for class-weighted XGBoost; the absolute difference was 0.006 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.002). Their PR-AUC estimates were 0.749 (0.694–0.801) and 0.747 (0.686–0.808), respectively. The GAN pipeline had a Brier score of 0.128 (0.111–0.144) versus 0.130 (0.116–0.144), whereas the calibration intercept was closer to zero for class weighting (− 0.013, − 0.171 to 0.172) than for GAN augmentation (− 0.174, − 0.319 to -0.006). Across five algorithmic seeds, GAN-XGBoost had slightly higher mean ROC-AUC (0.856 versus 0.849), while class-weighted XGBoost had slightly higher mean accuracy (0.779 versus 0.776). XGBoost outperformed Logistic Regression. GAN augmentation produced slightly higher discrimination point estimates, but class weighting was comparable across calibration, decision-curve, and threshold-dependent measures. These internal results do not establish overall clinical superiority and require external validation in symptomatic populations.

Article.Title: Hypothermic treatment alters the metabolic profile of newborns, mimicking or masking an inherited metabolic disorder
Article.Authors: Messina M.; Meli C.; Raudino F.; Ruggieri M.
Article.Abstract: Hypothermic treatment, initiated within the first six hours of life, is currently the main treatment capable of reducing brain damage in newborns with asphyxia and moderate or severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy. However, it is not yet clear how the treatment alters the newborn’s metabolic profile, nor whether such changes might mask or mimic a metabolic disorder, leading to false positives or false negatives in screening for inherited metabolic disorders. The present study therefore assessed changes in the metabolites routinely analysed in the Italian neonatal screening programme. A comparative analysis was conducted between full-term newborns with asphyxia/ hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy who underwent hypothermic treatment and a control group, through tandem mass spectrometry analysis. Treatment resulted in a number of changes being observed, including a decrease in glutamate, an increase in glycine, a reduction in certain short- and long-chain carnitines, and an increase in lysophosphatidylcholines. These findings suggest that hypothermic treatment may significantly alter the metabolic profile of the newborns. Consequently, the findings of our research have indicated that it is recommended to take dried blood spot samples at the conclusion of hypothermic treatment, with the aim of reducing the risk that the treatment may affect the interpretation of screening for inherited metabolic disorders. However, further studies are required to ascertain the usefulness and necessity of incorporating this second test into newborn screening protocols.

Article.Title: Multi-objective energy optimization in intelligent grids with high renewable penetration
Article.Authors: Sharma P.; Srinivasarao B.; Reddy K.; Heera M.; Sree S.; Rajendran N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract As renewable energy sources enter into smart grids, the intermittency, uncertainty, storage coordination, operational cost, carbon emissions and stability of these grids will pose significant challenges. Optimization techniques in conventional systems or rule-based energy management systems are not able to adapt to the fast changes of operating conditions continuously. This paper proposes a Multi-Objective Adaptive Deep Reinforcement Learning (MO-ADRL) framework for real-time optimization of energy in the intelligent grid with high renewable energy penetration. Energy management is formulated as a sequential decision-making problem, and an actor–critic deep reinforcement learning architecture computes continuous dispatch actions. The agent has a Temporal Transformer module which forecasts short-term electricity demand and renewable generation to make proactive decisions. The algorithm contains an adaptive multi-objective reward mechanism which dynamically balances the operational cost, carbon emission, utilization of renewable energy, renewable curtailment, peak demand, battery degradation, and energy supply reliability. Prioritized experience replay is integrated so that transitions with large temporal-difference errors, which usually correspond to critical grid events, are revisited more often during training. The proposed framework achieves real time coordination of solar PV, wind, battery energy storage, grid electricity and flexible demand. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms rule-based energy management, PSO, GA, DQN, DDPG, PPO and SAC for renewable penetration levels from 40% to 80%. At 80% penetration, MO-ADRL lowers the daily operating cost by 31.11% and CO₂ emissions by 38.09% relative to rule-based management, raises renewable utilization to 96.8%, reduces peak demand by 33.76% and keeps supply reliability at 99.6%. MO-ADRL therefore offers an adaptive and scalable route to autonomous energy management in future renewable-dominated intelligent grids.

Article.Title: Outcome ascertainment and decision-analytic performance across prediction windows for acute kidney injury: a landmark analysis in MIMIC-IV
Article.Authors: Teng S.; Liu Q.; Gao F.; Liu B.
Article.Abstract: Early warning systems for acute kidney injury are typically evaluated by discrimination, yet ranking ability does not indicate whether acting on a prediction is worthwhile, and how decision-analytic value changes with the prediction horizon has seldom been examined. This study assembled adult intensive care admissions from MIMIC-IV into a single at-risk cohort defined at a 12 h landmark, and applied four prediction windows of 6, 12, 24 and 48 h differing only in the censoring point. Discrimination, calibration and standardized net benefit were estimated for each, alongside the proportion of admissions in which the outcome could be ascertained. Ascertainment rose from 42.7% at 6 h to complete at 48 h, the latter following from the entry criteria, and varied from 14.2% to 93.4% with the hour of admission; among ascertained admissions the event proportion was similar across strata, indicating that sampling largely determined whether an outcome was observed. In the cohort ascertainable at 6 h, standardized net benefit fell by 14.9% against 5.2% for discrimination (difference 9.65% points); because the measures lack a common no-information value, this fell close to zero on a chance-corrected scale and across sensitivity analyses. Decision-analytic value is thus bounded by the measurement process rather than declining faster than discrimination.

Article.Title: Graph and dual position attention mechanism based text description generation for entities
Article.Authors: Li W.; Li Q.; Wang Z.; Ye Z.; Zhao L.
Article.Abstract: Although the sequence to sequence with attention and copy mechanism model is a mature and excellent natural language generation framework. Automatic natural language description generation for entities in the structured knowledge graph is still an open challenging task. Firstly, the sequence to sequence model takes the knowledge graph as a sequence input, so it cannot efficiently learn the structural features and the multi-relational properties of the knowledge graph. Secondly, the generated natural language descriptions should be able to correctly express the positional relationship between the attributes of the entity. In order to address the above two problems, a novel knowledge graph embedding with Dual Position Attention mechanism based Natural Language Generation model (referred to as DPANLG) is proposed. In it, we first leverage the graph attention neural network that have been proven to be efficient and effective methods for capturing the structural features and the multi-relational properties of the knowledge graph. Then, a dual position attention mechanism is employed to deal with the inter-dependency attributes of an entity. Finally, the generated text undergoes further refinement aided by large language models and elaborately designed prompts. We perform empirical experiments on two benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate that the proposed DPANLG model achieves promising results and outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

Article.Title: Effects of an expressive movement programme on lumbo-pelvic ROM and pelvic tilt patterns
Article.Authors: Vidaci A.; García-Luna M.; Cortell-Tormo J.; Vega-Ramirez L.
Article.Abstract: Lumbo-pelvic mobility plays an important role in movement efficiency, postural control, and the coordination between the trunk, pelvis, and lower limbs. However, quantitative evidence on the outcomes of expressive movement programme on lumbo-pelvic range of motion (ROM) in a field-based assessment conditions remains limited. The aim of this study was to examine the changes in lumbo-pelvic ROM following a structured expressive movement programme, as well as to explore potential differences according to sex. A quasi-experimental pre–post design was conducted in 49 physically active university students (39 males, 10 females). Lumbo-pelvic ROM, derived from anterior and posterior pelvic tilt in standing position, was assessed using three wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors. Participants completed a body expression programme incorporating mobility, flexibility, and body awareness exercises. Pre–post differences were analysed using paired t-tests, with mean differences, 95% confidence intervals (CI), and effect sizes reported. A repeated-measures ANOVA was conducted to examine the sex × time interaction for total ROM. Total lumbo-pelvic ROM increased significantly following the programme (+ 7.3°, + 29.08%; p < 0.001), indicating a significant pre–post improvement in lumbo-pelvic mobility. Females presented higher baseline ROM, likely associated with greater prior experience in artistic-sport activities. Although sex differences persisted post-test, the sex × time interaction was not significant, indicating no significant sex-related difference in pre–post change. Females exhibited higher anterior pelvic tilt, whereas males showed greater posterior pelvic tilt. These findings provide preliminary evidence that participation in an expressive movement programme is accompanied by significant changes in lumbo-pelvic mobility and pelvic tilt patterns, highlighting the potential value of the programme for movement education and lumbo-pelvic mobility training.

Article.Title: Quantitrack: a unified software to study protein dynamics in living cells
Article.Authors: Ball D.; Wagh K.; Stavreva D.; Hoang L.; Schiltz R.; Chari R.; Raziuddin R.; Mazza D.; Upadhyaya A.; Hager G.; Karpova T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Linking the spatiotemporal dynamics of proteins in live cells to biological function is a fundamental challenge in biology. Single molecule tracking (SMT) has emerged as a powerful technique to investigate protein dynamics at the single molecule level. However, SMT analysis often requires expertise in biophysical modeling and programming, and integrating results from different analyses can be challenging. To address these barriers, we developed QuantiTrack: a MATLAB-based SMT analysis software with a simple graphical user interface. This provides a much-needed end-to-end solution where a user can load a movie, detect and track single molecules, and perform complementary downstream analyses within a standardized workflow. QuantiTrack includes quantitative metrics for selecting detection and tracking parameters and troubleshooting experimental design and includes a detailed step-by-step user guide. We used simulations to demonstrate how signal intensity, labeling density, and motion blur affect detection and tracking fidelity. Using multi-state simulations, we further benchmarked complementary methods to identify distinct mobility states from heterogeneous trajectory populations. Finally, we applied QuantiTrack to real experimental data where we address how the glucocorticoid receptor (GR), a hormone-regulated transcription factor, responds to treatment and washout of its cognate hormone. Hormone washout results in rapid (in minutes) downregulation of GR target genes to basal levels. By integrating complementary analyses within QuantiTrack, we showed that hormone washout substantially reduced the bound fraction of GR, its occupancy in the mobility state associated with GR activation, and dwell times. Together, these analyses showcase QuantiTrack as an integrated platform for extracting biologically meaningful measurements from single molecule trajectories.

Article.Title: Knowledge, attitude, and practice regarding tuberculosis among university students in Aden, Yemen: a cross-sectional study with advanced statistical analysis
Article.Authors: Gubran A.; Ali N.; Mohammed H.; Kolais S.; Saeed A.; Ali A.; Dhaifulla E.; Al Radfani H.; Alamrani E.; Ali A.; Ahmad T.; Salem M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major public health threat in Yemen; however, to the best of our knowledge, no published studies have assessed knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) among university students in this context—a key population for health promotion. Therefore, this study aimed to assess the knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding tuberculosis among university students in Aden, Yemen. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 302 university students in Aden, Yemen, using a validated structured questionnaire. KAP scores were computed and categorized. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, bivariable analyses, and binary logistic regression with model diagnostics. Advanced statistical methods including ROC curve analysis (with AUC), mediation analysis, hierarchical regression, sensitivity analysis (three different cutoff points), and cluster analysis were also employed to provide comprehensive insights into the relationships between KAP domains and to identify distinct student profiles. Only 45.7% of students had good knowledge, 54.6% had positive attitudes, and 38.4% demonstrated good preventive practices. Critical gaps included lack of awareness that a cough > 2 weeks warrants medical evaluation (22.8% correct) and correct treatment duration (40.1% correct). Binary logistic regression identified male sex and non-medical college enrollment as independent predictors of poor knowledge ( p < 0.001). ROC curve analysis demonstrated excellent discriminatory ability (AUC = 0.82), with an optimal knowledge cutoff of 14/22. Mediation analysis revealed that attitude partially mediated the knowledge-practice relationship, with 40% of the total effect operating through attitude. Hierarchical regression showed that knowledge and attitude together explained 49% of the variance in practice scores, with knowledge contributing 24% of incremental variance and attitude contributing an additional 13%. Cluster analysis identified three distinct student profiles: “High KAP profile” (18.5%), “Moderate KAP profile” (54.3%), and “Low KAP profile” (27.2%). Knowledge and practices regarding TB among Yemeni university students are dangerously inadequate, particularly among males and non-medical students. The mediation and cluster findings suggest that interventions should target both knowledge transfer and attitude change simultaneously, with priority given to the “Low KAP profile” cluster.

Article.Title: Mildly reduced alpha-1 antitrypsin levels are not associated with chronic airflow limitation, emphysema, or respiratory symptoms
Article.Authors: Tanash H.; Zaigham S.; Piitulainen E.; Ekström M.; Andersson A.; Behndig A.; Blomberg A.; Bossios A.; Brandberg J.; Ström J.; Hiller A.; Janson C.; Johnsson Å.; Lindberg E.; Malinovschi A.; Mannila M.; Moberg A.; Nilsson U.; Pesonen I.; Swahn E.; Szabo Z.; Torén K.; Sköld M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Severe Alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is a risk factor for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and emphysema, but risks in mildly reduced AAT levels are unclear. We evaluated the association between mildly reduced serum-AAT levels and chronic airflow limitation (CAL), emphysema and respiratory symptoms, and risks in relation to smoking. We measured serum AAT in people aged 50–65 years in the population-based Swedish CArdioPulmonary bioImage Study (SCAPIS, n = 24,931). We carried out binary logistic regression models to assess pulmonary and cardiovascular outcomes associated with mildly reduced AAT levels. In total, 23,072 individuals had normal serum AAT concentration (≥ 0.86 g/L in men and ≥ 0.94 g/L in women), and 1,859 had mildly reduced AAT levels (0.61–0.85 g/L in men and 0.61–0.93 g/L in women). Mildly reduced AAT levels were not significantly associated with CAL, defined according to either GOLD criteria (CAL GOLD ) or the lower limit of normal (CAL LLN ), or with emphysema on computed tomography (CT): OR (95% CI) 1.01 (0.85–1.21) for CAL GOLD , 0.95 (0.80–1.13) for CAL LLN , and 0.94 (0.75–1.18) for emphysema. Mildly reduced AAT levels were associated with lower odds of DLCO < LLN (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.57–0.87) and lower odds of respiratory symptoms (0.87 (0.78–0.97) compared with normal AAT levels. In this large population-based cohort, mildly reduced AAT levels were not independently associated with CAL or CT-defined emphysema. These findings suggest that mildly reduced AAT levels alone may not represent a major risk factor for airflow limitation or emphysema in the general population.

Article.Title: Suppression of plasmid-mediated colistin resistance by major compounds of essential oils
Article.Authors: Píriz J.; Rivera-Moreno M.; Gallardo A.; Pacheco P.; González F.; Ugarte-Ruiz M.; del Rosario Sánchez-Benito M.; Quesada A.; Igeño M.; Gil-Molino M.
Article.Abstract: Many bacteria share plasmids that confer resistance to colistin, making them difficult to control with this last-resort antibiotic. Among other alternatives, major fractions of the aromatic compounds that can be distilled from cinnamon, clove, oregano and thyme extracts present strong antimicrobial activities. Going beyond, this work shows how these major essential oil compounds promote the functional suppression of colistin resistance phenotypes conferred by the two known classes of plasmid-encoded determinants in Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica isolates from human and animals. After growth in concentrations immediately below the lethality threshold of carvacrol, eugenol or thymol, or to a lesser extent cinnamaldehyde, an E. coli strain isolated from cattle and carrying the IncFII element encoding the Kluyvera -like arnT operon loss in parallel colistin resistance and its gene determinant. Similarly, carvacrol, eugenol or thymol, although not cinnamaldehyde, produce loss of phenotype and gene inactivation of the most widespread member of the mcr family, mcr-1 , in a E. coli strain from human or in a S. enterica Choleraesuis strain from swine, where colistin resistance determinants are encoded by IncX4 or IncHI2 elements, respectively. The loss of resistance was associated with disruptive mcr-1 mutations or with loss or deletion of plasmid regions carrying the resistance determinant, although direct molecular targeting was not demonstrated. This work expands the spectrum of action of these widely used major essential oil compounds, adding the suppression of colistin resistance to their previously known antimicrobial activities. Furthermore, the observed association between exposure to these compounds and loss of plasmid-mediated colistin resistance highlights the still unexplored potential of natural products for biomedical applications.

Article.Title: Development and validation of the refractive surgery-related quality-of-life questionnaire
Article.Authors: Tananuvat N.; Upaphong P.; Thabsuwan K.; Sawetwong P.; Niparak M.; Tangmonkongvoragul C.; Chaidaroon W.; Ausayakhun S.; Wongpakaran N.; Wongpakaran T.
Article.Abstract: The Refractive Surgery–Related Quality-of-Life Questionnaire (RESQ) was developed and validated to measure visual symptoms, ocular symptoms, functional impact, and satisfaction in refractive surgery candidates. Candidate items were derived from existing questionnaires and expert input, then pilot tested in 30 healthy participants. Psychometric evaluation was conducted in 168 refractive surgery candidates (mean age 33.4 years; median MRSE − 4.4 D) who completed the RESQ along with the EQ-5D-5L and NEI-VFQ-25. Test–retest reliability was assessed preoperatively and responsiveness at 3 months postoperatively. Initial testing supported a 30-item version (RESQ-30) with acceptable to good internal consistency. In the candidate sample, internal consistency was high (Cronbach’s alpha 0.81–0.93) and test–retest reliability was good for vision, impact, and total scores (ICC 0.75–0.79), with moderate reliability for ocular symptoms (ICC 0.67). Convergent validity was supported by correlations with EQ-5D-5L (ρ = −0.39 to − 0.53) and NEI-VFQ-25 (ρ = −0.43 to − 0.78) (all p < 0.001), and scores improved after surgery. Rasch modeling supported refinement to a 20-item RESQ (RESQ-20) with good fit, ordered thresholds, strong reliability (person 0.88; item 0.98), and evidence of essential unidimensionality. Further validation in independent samples is recommended.

Article.Title: Handheld volumetric capnography (Lumetry) for carbon dioxide monitoring in advanced COPD
Article.Authors: Schellenberg M.; Mbi-Etah E.; Trinkmann F.; Herth F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Regular measurements of oxygen (O 2 ) and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) are crucial for evaluation of the respiratory status in patients with moderate and advanced COPD. While O 2 monitoring is well established by pulse oximetry, there are still no established methods for non-invasive home measurements of CO 2 in patients during spontaneous breathing. Until now, patients must consult specialists or clinics for standardized procedures such as blood gas analysis (BGA) or transcutaneous capnometry (tCO 2 ). We therefore investigated a new hand-held device (Lumetry), based on volumetric and spirometric capnography with modernized algorithms for COPD patients during calm, spontaneous breathing (exclusion criterion RR > 21/min) and optimized beathing maneuvers. The aim of the study was to assess (1) the safety and usability of Lumetry and (2) agreement with well-established measurement methods BGA und tCO 2 . In this single-center prospective study, electively admitted patients with COPD GOLD 3 or 4 underwent spirometric capnography CO 2 measurements (petCO 2 ). Patients were stratified according to presence of hypercapnia as defined by a daytime paCO 2 >45 mmHg. End-tidal (petCO 2 ) values were translated to pCO 2 per device specific algorithms. Different breathing maneuvers (rested breathing, one deep exhalation, two deep in- and exhalations), were performed and the Lumetry results were compared with standardized CO 2 procedures in capillary blood gas analysis (Siemens, RAPIDpoint 500) and transcutaneous CO 2 measurement (Radiometer TCM5). Agreement between measurement methods were assessed using Bland-Altman analysis calculating mean bias and limits of agreement (LoA) 57 patients (32 women) were included in the analysis of whom 30 (52.6%) had hypercapnia. In the overall cohort, Lumetry slightly underestimated pCO 2 values compared to capillary blood gas analysis (CBG) during rested breathing (mean bias 6.1 mmHg, 95% LoA − 2.6 to 14.8 mmHg). Best agreement was observed for the deep breath mean maneuver (bias 2.1 mmHg, LoA − 8.2 to 12.4 mmHg). When stratified by hypercapnia status, the same pattern was observed. Lumetry showed similar agreement to CBG when compared to standard transcutaneous CO 2 levels (bias − 1.7 mmHg, LoA − 10.4 to 7.0 mmHg). There were no safety restrictions and the Lumetry device was easy to handle. Capnographic Lumetry measurements showed acceptable limits of agreement to capillary blood gas analysis. They furthermore proved non-inferior to transcutaneous CO 2 measurements. Results were consistent in hypercapnic and non-hypercapnic COPD patients and optimized by adapted deep breathing maneuvers. The Lumetry device was safe and easy to use. These promising results highlight its potential for home-based CO 2 monitoring and early detection of hypercapnic exacerbations.

Article.Title: Thermodynamic limit of double-junction photovoltaic cells under AM 1.5G or white LED lighting
Article.Authors: Jarosz G.; Signerski R.
Article.Abstract: The fundamental processes involved in charge carrier generation and recombination in ideal single- or double-junction photovoltaic cells are used to determine the thermodynamic efficiency limit of photovoltaic conversion. A procedure for calculating the efficiency limit for any irradiance spectrum is presented, without recourse to the Shockley diode equation and taking into account thermal radiation. Simulations were conducted for AM1.5G and selected white LED illumination. The resulting efficiency limit curves show the optimal bandgap pairs for a given irradiance spectrum. Our analysis indicates that the thermodynamic efficiency limit for AM1.5G increases from 33.8 % for a single-junction photovoltaic cell to 45.5 % for a double-junction photovoltaic cell, whereas for LED lighting this increase ranges only from 52.8 % - 54.8 % to 60.6 % - 60.9 %. Replacing single-junction cells with double-junction cells in solar panels can lead to a significant increase in cell output power if the energy gaps of both subcells are properly selected. The range of energy gaps for which the efficiency limit exceeds 40% is quite wide. On the other hand, for indoor photovoltaic cells, there is little benefit from replacing single-junction cells with double-junction cells, while optimizing single-junction cells can yield significant efficiency gains.

Article.Title: Self-targeted attacks of a virus on scale-free networks as revealed by the COVID-19 pandemic
Article.Authors: Kalda J.; Ratas M.; Kalda T.; Ramazanli A.; Herrmann H.; Belikov J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract During the first wave of the global COVID-19 pandemic, the reproduction number within a country or a county decreased approximately as inverse square root of the cumulative number of the infected population within that country; a weighted fit to the data for US counties gives the exponent 0.53, the central 95% of its bootstrap distribution lying between 0.33 and 0.66. This conclusion is based on the analysis of publicly accessible data for the spread of COVID-19. We suggest that this is a consequence of the scale-free nature of the human contact network, and results from what we call self-targeted attacks : virus finds and destroys the biggest nodes, the superspreaders, first. Our simulations with synthetic scale-free networks show that the data are consistent with a scale-free effective contact network, with the cumulative degree distribution exponent close to 2, i.e. with the degree distribution decreasing as $$k^{-\gamma }$$ , $$\gamma \approx 3$$ . We give a scaling argument for the simulation results and test its assumptions directly in the simulations. Finally, based on the number of antibodies against a certain set of viruses, we put forward and test via simulations a population screening procedure aimed to reveal potential superspreaders; according to our simulations, vaccination of the nodes revealed by the screening suppresses the spreading of the virus already at a vaccination coverage of 6%, as compared with 4% if the nodes of the highest degree are vaccinated directly.

Article.Title: Comprehensive assessment of ML-enhanced hybrid RSO–SAO for optimal PV–WT allocation in radial distribution systems
Article.Authors: Krishnamoorthy S.; Vairamani R.; Ramasamy K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The necessity for effective decentralized or distributed generation (DG) planning in contemporary power systems has expanded due to increasing grid integration of renewable energy sources, driven by rising fuel costs and environmental concerns. However, optimal DG allocation remains a challenging multi-objective problem due to its nonlinear, nonconvex nature and the high computational burden of load-flow evaluations. This study proposes a novel Machine Learning-assisted hybrid Rhinopithecus Swarm Optimization–Snow Ablation Optimizer (ML–RSO–SAO) framework to address these challenges. The proposed framework transforms conventional stochastic search into an intelligent, data-driven optimization process. A surrogate modelling approach using Artificial Neural Networks is employed to predict active and reactive power losses, significantly reducing computational cost, while a Random Forest-based decision mechanism identifies critical candidate buses, thereby simplifying the search space. The hybrid RSO–SAO algorithm effectively balances exploration and exploitation, leading to faster convergence, avoidance of premature stagnation, and improved solution quality. The method is validated on IEEE 33-bus and IEEE 69-bus test systems with solar and wind DG integration. Compared with PSO, WOA, DEO, and SMA, the proposed approach achieves lower power losses, improved voltage profiles, and enhanced economic and environmental performance, demonstrating its effectiveness for reliable DG planning under uncertainties.

Article.Title: YOLOv11-PVT: a transformer-enhanced framework for accurate multi-class brain tumor classification from MRI images
Article.Authors: Srinivasu P.; P. V. S. K. S.; Cherukumalli R.; V. H.; B. R.; Nuaim A.
Article.Abstract: Brain tumor classification and detection from Magnetic Resonance Imaging(MRI) images is critical for early diagnosis. State-of-the-art deep learning (DL) methods, such as the You Only Look Once (YOLO) family of detectors, have recently gained widespread success in analysis of medical images. In this paper, based on the state-of-the-art YOLOv11 and YOLOv8 architectures, The study has propose a brain tumor detection framework and improve the performance of brain tumor detection by replacing the conventional Cross Stage Partial(CSP)-based backbone with a Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT). The baseline YOLOv11 model is trained with a balanced and augmented Brain Tumor MRI Dataset, achieving improved Precision, Recall, F1-score, Mean Average Precision(mAP@0.5), and mAP@0.5:0.95 compared with baseline YOLOv8 and YOLOv11 models. To overcome the limitations of convolution-based feature extraction, particularly the lack of global contextual information and difficulty in detecting small or low-contrast tumors, this study proposes a hybrid YOLOv11-PVT model. The PVT backbone generates hierarchical multi-scale features and global attention representations, thereby providing richer contextual information. Results show that the proposed YOLOv11-PVT framework demonstrated improved sensitivity and stronger IoU-based localization consistency compared with the baseline YOLOv11 model. These results demonstrate that transformer-enhanced backbones can improve the robustness and localization capability of tumor detection systems.

Article.Title: Residential and workplace segregation are differently associated with gaps in ambient air pollution exposure across US metropolitan areas
Article.Authors: deSouza P.; Tan S.; Haskell-Craig Z.; Hohsfield K.; Crooks J.; Li J.; Klopp J.; Makarewicz C.; Considine E.; Kumar P.; Kinney P.; Levy J.; Josey K.; Lee J.
Article.Abstract: Structural racism contributes to health disparities partly through residential segregation and unequal environmental exposures, but workplaces may constitute a distinct geography of segregation. Using home and workplace locations for approximately 95% of the U.S. workforce across 380 metropolitan areas, we measured residential and workplace segregation at metropolitan and census tract scales for Black-White, Hispanic-non-Hispanic, and less-than-high-school vs. college contrasts and linked them to worker-weighted PM 2.5 and NO 2 concentrations in 2018. Metropolitan residential segregation was consistently associated with wider exposure gaps across all groups, pollutants, and locations. Metropolitan workplace segregation was associated with a wider Black-White workplace NO 2 gap (0.042 ppb per SD; 95% CI 0.005, 0.078), an association largely accounted for by group differences in the centrality of each group’s jobs, but with narrower or reversed workplace gaps for Hispanic and less-educated workers. Workplace segregation is therefore associated with exposure inequality in group-specific ways that are obscured by residence-only or single-contrast analyses.

Article.Title: Non-invasive blood glucose detection system using combined visible and near-infrared spectral data
Article.Authors: Bae T.; Kim B.; Kwon K.; Kim Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract This pilot study evaluated non-invasive estimation of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM)-reported glucose from fingertip visible–near-infrared (VIS–NIR) reflectance in ten adults. Optical measurements (approximately 12 per minute) were retained as separate 70-feature vectors and paired with 1-minute FreeStyle Libre 2 CGM readings checked approximately 10 min afterward using clock-based timing; multiple optical records therefore shared one CGM label. The dataset contained 6,816 optical samples. Seven regression models were compared using sample-level five-fold and subject-independent leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation. Under LOSO, Random Forest achieved MAE 11.248 mg/dL, RMSE 17.326 mg/dL, MARD 10.379%, and R² 0.767. In Clarke Error Grid analysis against CGM values, 82.40% and 85.30% of predictions were in Zones A and A + B, respectively. LOSO DNN classification accuracies were 92.74% and 92.43% for 30 and 15 mg/dL categories. These findings support feasibility but indicate inter-subject variability. The manually timed 10-minute offset was approximate and not an individually validated physiological lag correction. No independent capillary or laboratory blood glucose reference was available; thus clinical blood glucose measurement accuracy or safety was not established.

Article.Title: Characterization of cardiac fibrosis and Fosl-2 associated arrhythmias with volumetric optoacoustic spectroscopy
Article.Authors: Özsoy Ç.; Lin H.; Pancorbo L.; Nozdriukhin D.; Reiss M.; Hukara A.; Seebeck P.; Laimbacher A.; Distler O.; Kania G.; Razansky D.; Deán-Ben X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Unraveling the complex mechanisms underlying systemic sclerosis (SSc) constitutes an important challenge for clinical management of degenerative alterations caused by this autoimmune disorder. Cardiac arrhythmias as well as fibrotic buildup, namely, an excess accumulation of collagen in the myocardium, are known to represent life-threatening complications associated to SSc. This study explores the capability of volumetric multi-spectral optoacoustic tomography (vMSOT) to characterize myocardial fibrosis-related anatomical, functional, and molecular features in a transgenic Fosl-2 tg mouse model, which has been used to investigate systemic sclerosis-associated cardiac fibrotic remodeling. A vMSOT approach was developed to uniformly illuminate the isolated perfused (Langendorff) murine heart for five-dimensional (spectroscopic real-time volumetric) interrogation of the entire organ. Anatomical, functional, and molecular characteristics of Fosl-2 tg hearts were compared with those of wild-type controls (Fosl-2 wt ), including myocardial collagen deposition, wall thickness, ventricular volume, cardiac dynamics, and rhythm. Preliminary observations from limited animal cohorts further suggest differences in beat-to-beat dynamics and responses to isoproterenol stimulation between Fosl-2 tg and Fosl-2 wt hearts. In conclusion, vMSOT provides a powerful platform for comprehensive cardiac phenotyping and reveals imaging features consistent with myocardial fibrosis and associated functional alterations in the Fosl-2 tg model.

Article.Title: Age group differences in the relationships between Big Five personality traits and gait features derived from a single IMU sensor
Article.Authors: Lin G.; Wang Q.; Wang Y.; Tian Y.; Chen M.; Yu X.; Zhao Y.; Li W.; Yeung D.
Article.Abstract: Emerging literature increasingly links personality traits to observable behaviors, including walking gait. While inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor enables detection of subtle body movement, the associations between personality traits and IMU-derived gait features – and their age-related variations – remain largely underexamined. Therefore, this study explored the age group differences in the relationships between Big Five personality traits and IMU-derived gait features. One hundred Hong Kong Chinese adults ( M age = 48.50, SD = 16.35, range = 20–75 years) completed a controlled walking test with an IMU sensor and a standardized personality trait measure. Ninety normalized gait features were extracted from gait data, including 84 time-domain features and 6 kinematic features. Correlation analyses revealed that distinct features of lateral angular velocity significantly correlated with extraversion and open-mindedness. Furthermore, age group significantly moderated the gait-personality relationships for extraversion. Notably, the association between extraversion and standard deviation and variance of lateral angular velocity in middle-aged adults was stronger than that of young adults. This study highlights gait-personality relationships that are uniquely detected by an IMU sensor. By elucidating differences across young, middle-aged, and older adults, these findings establish a robust empirical framework for utilizing IMU-derived data to uncover personality-related behavioral changes throughout the lifespan.

Article.Title: First principles investigations of negative differential resistance in edge chlorinated MgO nanoribbons
Article.Authors: Sambasivarao J.; Kumar A.
Article.Abstract: MgO nanoribbons (MgONRs) are analyzed using the first-principles approach utilizing density functional theory (DFT) for potential nanoelectronic applications. Chemically edge-modified MgONRs are investigated for their electrical characteristics. The structural investigations reveal that the nanoribbons are energetically favorable, and chlorination at the edges relatively reduces the energetic favorability of the structures. Bandstructure calculations reveal that the bare MgONRs and chlorine passivated MgONRs are all metallic structures. Further, the two-probe methodology is deployed for the voltage-current ( \(V-I\) ) characteristics. The chlorine passivation is found to significantly enhance the current magnitude, and an interesting negative differential resistance (NDR) phenomenon is noticed in all the chlorine passivated structures. MgONRs having chlorine passivation at the Mg-edge (Cl-MgO-B) have a relatively higher peak-to-valley current ratio (PVCR). The observed results show that the chlorinated MgONRs have potential relevance in future nanoelectronic applications such as switching devices, oscillators, nonlinear electronic circuits, etc.

Article.Title: RGB-D SLAM in indoor dynamic environments based on adaptive triangulation-affine local consistency and semantic filtering for education and teaching
Article.Authors: Cao A.; Zheng H.; Li N.; Zhang X.; Zhou Y.
Article.Abstract: Visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) has been widely applied in indoor robotic navigation, augmented reality, and intelligent systems, with potential applications in educational robotics, interactive teaching environments, and spatially aware learning systems. However, most traditional visual SLAM systems rely on the assumption of scene rigidity, which makes them vulnerable to dynamic objects in indoor environments. To address these problems, this paper proposes an RGB-D SLAM system for indoor dynamic environments based on adaptive triangulation-affine local consistency and semantic filtering. Specifically, first, an adaptive triangulation-affine local consistency matching strategy (ATALC-matching) is designed to detect outliers and optimize the matching set. Reliable local structures are evaluated using a barycentric triangulation constraint, while degenerate regions are further verified using an affine fallback model. Second, an efficient semantic segmentation model is employed to obtain object-level regions, and dynamic objects are identified according to the ratio of outliers within each segmented region. Finally, both the outliers detected by ATALC-matching and the features located in dynamic regions are removed from the matching set before visual pose estimation. Meanwhile, map points associated with detected outliers are erased during map updating to reduce the accumulation of unreliable landmarks in the global map. Extensive evaluations are conducted on the TUM RGB-D dataset, the Bonn RGB-D Dynamic Dataset, and real-world scenarios. Compared with ORB-SLAM3, the proposed system reduces the root-mean-square-error of the absolute trajectory error by 94% and 38% on the highly and slightly dynamic TUM sequences, respectively. Evaluation on runtime shows that the complete system achieves an average processing speed of approximately 20 FPS. Real-world evaluations further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods in detecting outliers and dynamic objects.
