Article.Title: Adjunctive Multisensory Passive Immersive Virtual Reality With Synchronized Plantar Tactile Stimulation for Gait and Balance Disorders in Parkinson's Disease: An Exploratory Randomized Controlled Trial
Article.Authors: Shirolapov I.; Natalevich S.; Khivintseva E.; Komarova Y.; Romanchuk N.; Sergeeva M.; Popov N.; Kalinin V.; Zakharov A.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Postural‐locomotor disorders, particularly freezing of gait and postural instability, are among the most disabling symptoms of advanced Parkinson's disease (PD) and respond only partially to dopaminergic therapy. Evidence for virtual reality (VR) approaches in moderate to severe PD remains limited. This prospective randomized controlled open‐label exploratory trial evaluated the addition of multisensory passive immersive VR with synchronized plantar tactile stimulation to conventional rehabilitation for gait, balance, and freezing disorders in moderate‐to‐severe PD (Hoehn and Yahr Stages 2–4). In the study, 80 PD patients were randomized into an experimental group (EXP, n = 40) receiving standard pharmacotherapy and conventional rehabilitation plus 10 sessions of passive immersive VR with synchronized plantar tactile stimulation and a comparison group (COM, n = 40) receiving standard pharmacotherapy and conventional rehabilitation only. Because the VR sessions were added to an otherwise identical program, the trial evaluates the effect of adding this intervention rather than a VR‐ or tactile‐specific effect. Outcomes were assessed at baseline and after 10 days using the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), Berg Balance Scale (BBS), and Freezing of Gait Questionnaire (FoG‐Q). The EXP group showed significant improvements in the UPDRS “Gait” cluster (an eight‐item composite of UPDRS items 2.11, 2.12, 2.13, 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, and 3.13, range 0–32; median from 12.5 to 8.0 points, p < 0.001), BBS (from 38.0 to 43.5 points, p < 0.001), and FoG‐Q (from 9.0 to 6.5 points, p < 0.001). A formal group × time analysis confirmed a differential treatment effect for every outcome. For the main outcome, the UPDRS “Gait” cluster, the baseline‐adjusted between‐group difference was −2.48 points (95% CI −3.37 to −1.59; p < 0.001; Hedges' g = 1.16). Large effects also favored the EXP group for the FoG‐Q (−2.14 points, 95% CI −2.62 to −1.66; g = 1.65), the BBS (+2.20 points, 95% CI 1.31 to 3.10; g = 1.06), the UPDRS freezing subscore (items 2.13 + 3.11; −0.89 points, 95% CI −1.13 to −0.66; g = 1.32), and the UPDRS postural subscore (items 3.12 + 3.13; −0.74 points, 95% CI −1.08 to −0.41; g = 0.93). Secondary outcome p ‐values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg procedures. By contrast, in the COM group, no significant change was observed for freezing of gait ( p = 0.083), and improvements in other outcomes were smaller than in the EXP group. No serious adverse events were recorded. The trial was exploratory, so the effect estimates require confirmation rather than supporting robustness in themselves. Overall, multisensory passive immersive VR with synchronized plantar tactile stimulation was well tolerated and shows preliminary promise as an adjunct to conventional rehabilitation for gait and balance disorders in moderate‐to‐severe PD. Wider clinical implementation requires long‐term multicenter studies with standardized assessment criteria and analysis of long‐term sustainability. These findings support integrating passive VR technologies into personalized neurorehabilitation programs.

Article.Title: Region‐ and Time‐Dependent Gene Expression Responses to Siponimod, Atorvastatin and Methylprednisolone After Spinal Cord Injury
Article.Authors: Bimbova K.; Kisucka A.; Kuruc T.; Ileninova M.; Kucharova K.; Ihnatova L.; Bacova M.; Magurova M.; Lukacova N.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) triggers a secondary injury cascade in which microglia, infiltrating macrophages and astrocytes influence tissue degeneration and repair. These responses are dynamic and region‐dependent, yet the comparative effects of anti‐inflammatory therapies remain unclear. We evaluated siponimod, atorvastatin and methylprednisolone after Th9 compression injury in rats. Gene expression was assessed by quantitative RT‐PCR in rostral, lesion and caudal spinal cord segments at 2 and 6 weeks postinjury. At 2 weeks, all treatments reduced microglia/macrophage‐associated and inflammatory transcripts, particularly rostrally, as shown by reduced Iba1 and iNOS expression. Siponimod and atorvastatin also decreased IL‐1β rostrally, whereas siponimod was associated with region‐specific increases in inflammatory markers at the lesion site and caudally. Siponimod most consistently increased microglia/macrophage‐associated transcripts linked to immunoregulatory and reparative responses caudally, including IL1rn, TGF‐β, SOCS3 and IL4Rα. It also reduced selected inflammatory astrocyte‐associated markers and increased transcripts linked to repair‐related processes, while atorvastatin and methylprednisolone showed mixed effects. At 6 weeks, none of the treatments consistently suppressed pro‐inflammatory microglia/macrophage‐associated markers. Siponimod was associated with elevated transcripts linked to immunoregulatory and repair‐related processes, together with region‐dependent increases in inflammatory markers. Astrocyte‐associated reactivity markers were largely normalised, whereas remodelling‐associated transcripts were altered. Treatments induced modest changes in neuronal/axonal and myelin‐associated transcripts, predominantly rostrally, without significant functional improvement. Overall, these interventions differentially modulated microglia/macrophage‐ and astrocyte‐associated gene expression, with siponimod producing the broadest, but mixed and region‐dependent, gene‐expression pattern. These findings highlight the regional and stage‐dependent complexity of glial and inflammatory gene expression after pharmacological treatment of SCI.

Article.Title: The Causal Contribution of the Cerebellar Hemispheres in Social Mentalizing
Article.Authors: Ferrari C.; Paternò S.; Ciricugno A.; Cattaneo Z.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Mentalizing has traditionally been associated with the recruitment of cortical regions of the social brain; however, growing evidence indicates that the cerebellum also plays a significant role in social cognition and behavior. In the present study, we combined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) with the Yoni task, a well‐established measure of mentalizing, to provide causal evidence for the involvement of the cerebellar hemispheres in reasoning about others' minds. We also determined whether this contribution is specific to mentalizing or reflects domain‐general cognitive processes engaged during (but not specific to) mental inferences. We found that TMS over the right cerebellar hemisphere impaired performance in both the mentalizing condition (reasoning about Yoni's mental states) and the control condition (reasoning about Yoni's physical characteristics), indicating a domain‐general contribution of this region to cognitive processes involved in mentalizing. In turn, TMS over the left cerebellar hemisphere impaired performance only in the control condition. Together, these findings provide clear causal evidence for the involvement of the right posterior cerebellar hemisphere in mentalizing‐related tasks, shedding light on potential cerebellar mechanisms and hemispheric asymmetries underlying social cognition.

Article.Title: Nonlinear Dopaminergic Vulnerability and Incident Freezing of Gait in Parkinson Disease: Limited Incremental Value of Global Volumetric MRI
Article.Authors: Kim K.; Bhaskar S.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Freezing of gait is a disabling manifestation of Parkinson disease, but it remains uncertain how risk varies across the spectrum of nigrostriatal dopaminergic loss and whether global volumetric magnetic resonance imaging adds prognostic information. We analyzed longitudinal Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative data from participants who remained free of recorded freezing through completion of a temporally aligned multimodal imaging index. The cohort comprised 521 participants with 251 incident recorded events; 520 participants and 250 events contributed to adjusted models. Lower mean striatal specific binding ratio was associated with subsequent recorded freezing after adjustment for age, sex, and motor severity (hazard ratio per one‐standard‐deviation increase, 0.740; 95% confidence interval, 0.613–0.894; p = 0.002). Restricted cubic splines showed evidence of a nonlinear association ( p < 0.001), with risk rising disproportionately at lower binding; relative to the median, the adjusted hazard was 2.52 (95% confidence interval, 1.72–3.69) at the 5th percentile. Regional analyses localized this pattern predominantly to the putamen. Nonlinear representation improved model fit compared with linear dopaminergic modelling (likelihood‐ratio χ 2 = 13.78; 2 degrees of freedom; p = 0.001) and increased Harrell concordance from 0.627 to 0.649, although the bootstrap confidence interval for this increment included zero. Three‐year discrimination improved from 0.643 to 0.682. Adding ventricular ratio did not improve fit or discrimination, and the optimism‐corrected concordance statistic was 0.633. These findings support a cohort‐specific threshold‐like dopaminergic vulnerability pattern, predominantly putaminal, whereas global volumetric MRI added negligible incremental prognostic information, and model performance remained insufficient for individual clinical prediction. The nonlinear functional form requires external replication.

Article.Title: Neurovascular Unit Redox–Metabolic Communication in Poststroke Cognitive Impairment: Spatiotemporal Dysregulation, Cellular Crosstalk, and Precision Intervention
Article.Authors: Zhang Q.; Chen Y.; Bai M.; Zhang X.; Yin Y.; Sun K.; Li W.; Ding Y.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Poststroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is a dynamic syndrome driven by focal brain injury, pre‐existing cerebrovascular burden, metabolic comorbidities, and reduced brain resilience. Increasing evidence suggests that persistent disruption of redox–metabolic communication within the neurovascular unit (NVU), rather than neuronal loss alone, promotes the transition from acute ischemic injury to chronic cognitive decline. This review summarizes metabolic reprogramming in BMECs, pericytes, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocyte‐lineage cells, and neurons, emphasizing the intercellular transfer of metabolites, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, oxidized lipids, extracellular vesicles, and mitochondria. We propose that PSCI develops through a spatiotemporally dysregulated continuum involving vascular injury, cell‐specific metabolic remodeling, maladaptive signal propagation, impaired axonal and synaptic energy support, and progressive network disconnection. Ischemia–reperfusion triggers bioenergetic failure, NADH/NAD + imbalance, mitochondrial electron leakage, endothelial dysfunction, and capillary no‐reflow. Subsequently, blood–brain barrier disruption, immunometabolic activation, iron and lipid dysregulation, and defective organelle quality control sustain white matter and synaptic injury. Therapeutic strategies should therefore be stage‐specific: restoring microcirculatory perfusion and physiological redox signaling acutely, promoting inflammation resolution and metabolic repair subacutely, and combining vascular–metabolic modulation with neurorehabilitation chronically. Future studies should integrate cell type‐specific interventions, metabolic flux tracing, spatial multi‐omics, and longitudinal cognitive assessments to establish causal donor–carrier–recipient–stage–outcome relationships.

Article.Title: Investigating Age Group Differences and the Effect of Arousal on the Evoked Pupil Dilation Response to Transcutaneous Auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation
Article.Authors: D'Agostini M.; Teugels A.; Franssen M.; Jafari H.; Mather M.; Van Diest I.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is hypothesized to prevent cognitive ageing by increasing phasic locus coeruleus (LC) activity. Short taVNS bursts have been shown to increase phasic LC activity as measured by evoked pupil dilation in young adults. Little is known about their effects in ageing. taVNS‐evoked pupil dilation may be smaller in older adults due to age‐related increases in tonic LC activity. This study will test age group differences in taVNS‐evoked pupil dilation and evaluate whether administering taVNS bursts after slow‐paced breathing—an arousal‐reducing technique—increases pupil responses in older adults. Thirty‐three cognitively unimpaired older adults (55–75) and 33 young adults (18–35) will receive taVNS bursts at the cymba concha (left ear) after blocks of slow‐paced breathing at 0.1 Hz and spontaneous breathing on the same day in counterbalanced order. In each breathing condition, a 2.5‐min breathing block will precede a 2.5‐min stimulation block, three times. Pupil size will be measured during each stimulation block. We hypothesize that taVNS‐evoked pupil dilation is smaller in older adults compared with young adults, and it is larger following slow‐paced breathing exercises compared with spontaneous breathing in older adults. The breathing manipulation will be considered successful if the slow‐paced breathing condition (vs. spontaneous breathing) is associated with decreases in arousal ratings, respiratory rate, and prestimulus baseline pupil size (tonic LC activity index) and with an increase in vagally mediated heart rate variability from baseline. This project represents an important first step toward examining conditions that might increase the impact of taVNS in older adults.

Article.Title: Opioid Modulation of Major Neurotransmitter Systems: Acute, Chronic, and Withdrawal Effects
Article.Authors: Novakova D.; Pritulova E.; Novotny J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Opioids are widely used in clinical practice for the management of moderate‐to‐severe acute and chronic pain. However, their use is associated with the development of tolerance and physical dependence, often followed by a withdrawal syndrome upon discontinuation. The mechanisms underlying opioid dependence and withdrawal are highly complex and remain incompletely understood. These processes involve multiple regions of the central nervous system and are accompanied by widespread alterations in neuronal signaling pathways. Neurotransmitters, which are essential for communication between neurons, play a critical role in opioid addiction and withdrawal. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the major neurotransmitter systems, their involvement, and the changes that occur during acute and chronic opioid exposure. Particular attention is also given to the consequences of opioid discontinuation. Overall, this review summarizes current knowledge of the molecular mechanisms underlying both the acute and long‐term effects of opioids on key neurotransmitter systems in the brain.

Article.Title: Integrative Evolutionary and Structural Analysis of GBA1 Provides Insights Into Mutation‐Specific Effects Associated With Parkinson's Disease
Article.Authors: Mustafa S.; Abbasi A.; Mughal K.; Batool F.; Malik M.; Khalid R.; Abbasi A.; Bao Y.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT GBA1 encodes lysosomal acid β‐glucosidase (glucocerebrosidase [GCase]), a key lysosomal enzyme and one of the most important genetic factors in Parkinson's disease (PD). Yet how different GBA1 variants influence PD‐related molecular pathology remains incompletely understood. Here, we integrated phylogenetic, comparative sequence, structural, docking, and molecular dynamics analyses to identify evolutionarily constrained features of GBA1 that may influence its interaction with α‐synuclein (SNCA) and thereby contribute to PD pathogenesis. Phylogenetic reconstruction indicated that GBA1 originated early in bilaterian evolution and was maintained as a single‐copy gene in the sampled taxa, consistent with strong functional constraint. Sequence‐based analyses across sarcopterygian lineages further supported pervasive purifying selection, especially within the TIM barrel catalytic domain. Comparative structural analyses highlighted a conformationally sensitive segment spanning Residues 379–389, which includes catalytic and neighboring residues and showed recurrent involvement in both mammalian evolution and PD‐associated mutant proteins. Docking and molecular dynamics simulations of wild‐type and mutant GBA1–SNCA complexes indicated that PD‐associated substitutions can remodel hydrogen‐bond networks and influence the conformational landscape of the GBA1–SNCA complex in a mutation‐specific manner. Although no statistically significant differences in global structural or energetic properties were detected, individual variants exhibited distinct patterns of conformational deviation, flexibility, and interaction dynamics relative to wild type. In particular, Residues 387–389 emerged as part of a structurally responsive region linked to altered GBA1–SNCA association. Together, these findings highlight candidate structural determinants for future experimental studies of GBA1‐associated neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Inferior Frontal Gyrus Alterations in Freezing of Gait in Parkinson's Disease Without Evidence for Overall Hemispheric Lateralization: A Systematic Review and Activation Likelihood Estimation Meta‐Analysis
Article.Authors: Taniguchi S.; Deckmyn H.; Gilat M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Freezing of gait (FOG) is one of the most debilitating motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD). Prior studies have suggested a potential right‐hemispheric preference in the pathophysiology of FOG. Yet, there is limited evidence regarding which brain regions are most consistently associated with FOG and whether these alterations indeed show right‐hemispheric lateralization. We aimed to identify brain regions associated with FOG based on multimodal neuroimaging findings and to examine their hemispheric lateralization. A systematic review across multiple neuroimaging modalities was performed, followed by an activation likelihood estimation (ALE) coordinate‐based meta‐analysis to assess convergent brain alterations in PD patients with FOG (freezers) versus those without FOG (nonfreezers). Hemispheric lateralization was assessed using the distribution of reported stereotactic coordinates. The systematic review included 108 articles, of which 33 were included in the primary ALE meta‐analysis. We identified a significant convergent cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) pars opercularis/dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in PD freezers compared with nonfreezers. No evidence of overall hemispheric lateralization was observed based on the distribution of reported coordinates. Our findings identify the right IFG as a consistent neural correlate of FOG, potentially reflecting heightened frontal recruitment, with no clear evidence of hemispheric lateralization. The lack of further consistency in brain regions could reflect the known heterogeneity in the pathophysiology of FOG.

Article.Title: Differential Cellular Dynamics of Platelet‐Derived Growth Factor Receptor β Cells and Macrophages After Complete Spinal Cord Transection in Neonatal and Juvenile Rats
Article.Authors: Takiguchi M.; Tamaji R.; Funakoshi K.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Lesion morphology after complete spinal cord transection (CST) varies depending on the time of injury. Following CST, the stumps are connected by fibrous tissue in adult and juvenile rats, whereas they are connected by thin meningeal tissue in neonatal rats. Here, we compared the cellular dynamics after CST in neonatal and juvenile rats to investigate factors contributing to the morphologic differences between the two groups. The intensity of PDGFRβ‐positive structures associated with fibrotic scar formation at the lesion core was significantly higher in juvenile CST rats than in neonatal CST rats. In neonatal rats, the intensity gradually decreased, whereas in juvenile rats it peaked at 7 days and then decreased. Pro‐inflammatory CD11c‐positive macrophages were abundant in the lesion core 2 days after CST, then rapidly decreased in both neonatal and juvenile CST rats. Anti‐inflammatory CD163‐positive macrophages in the lesion core were significantly more abundant in neonatal CST rats than in juvenile CST rats and remained elevated until 14 days after CST. Neonatal CST rats exhibited less fibroblast accumulation and higher CD163‐positive macrophage density in the lesion core compared with juvenile CST rats. These differences may be associated with morphologic differences in the lesion core between the two groups. CD163‐positive macrophages in the neonatal CST rats may primarily promote meningeal remodeling rather than fibrous tissue proliferation leading to fibrous scar formation.

Article.Title: The Glial Firestorm: Targeting Ferroptotic Microglia–Astrocyte Crosstalk in Intracerebral Hemorrhage
Article.Authors: Guo P.; Chen H.; Li N.; Liu D.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) causes substantial mortality and disability, with secondary injury extending beyond the initial hematoma. This narrative review examines the working hypothesis that ferroptotic microglia amplify a neurotoxic astrocyte response after ICH. In the iron‐rich hemorrhagic milieu, microglial iron loading and impaired antioxidant defenses favor lipid peroxidation, whereas inflammatory astrocyte states marked by LCN2, C3, and MMP3 contribute to barrier dysfunction and neuronal injury. Findings from ICH and related experimental models suggest that oxidized lipids, extracellular vesicles, and inflammatory mediators could connect these responses. Reactive astrocytes may then reinforce myeloid oxidative stress through altered iron handling, glutamate clearance, and complement signaling. Ferroptosis must be considered alongside apoptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis, and resident microglia share erythrophagocytic and iron‐handling functions with infiltrating monocytes/macrophages. These overlapping processes limit the attribution of mixed myeloid signals to a single lineage or death pathway. The proposed bidirectional circuit remains a framework for testing rather than an established sequence in ICH. Therapeutic interception could combine early control of iron‐dependent lipid injury with later astrocyte modulation through STAT3 or PPAR‐γ, provided that beneficial hematoma clearance is preserved. High‐resolution spatiotemporal mapping, lineage‐resolved experiments, and sex‐specific analyses are needed to identify the relevant cells and treatment windows. Targeting this glial interaction may complement neuroprotection, but its therapeutic value requires direct experimental and clinical validation.

Article.Title: Rimonabant reveals reward- and anxiety-related behavioral effects of N-arachidonoyl dopamine (N-ADA) in mice
Article.Authors: Colis-Arenas O.; Navarro-Montellano K.; López-Lariz C.; Romero-Guevara R.; Marichal-Cancino B.
Article.Abstract: The endovanilloid N-arachidonoyl dopamine (N-ADA) is a lipid mediator associated with nociception and inflammation, but its effects on reward and anxiety remain unclear. We examined the behavioral impact of subacute N-ADA pre-exposure on conditioned place preference (CPP) and anxiety-like behavior in the circular open-field test (COF), assessed both under basal conditions and after acute CB1 blockade/GPR55 modulation with rimonabant. Male BALB/c mice were pre-exposed for four days to either vehicle (10% ethanol) or N-ADA (0.1 mg/kg). A counterbalanced CPP protocol was then conducted over eight days. Place preference was assessed before and after rimonabant administration (0.1 mg/kg), and anxiety-like behavior was evaluated using the COF following rimonabant. N-ADA exposure alone did not significantly modify place preference compared to baseline (p > 0.05). However, following rimonabant administration, N-ADA-exposed mice displayed a significant increase in preference for the drug-paired compartment (p < 0.05) and increased anxiety-like behavior in the COF (p < 0.05). These findings indicate that prior exposure to N-ADA can influence reward- and anxiety-related behaviors specifically under conditions of CB1 blockade/GPR55 modulation. The results support the modulatory role of N-ADA on reward- and anxiety-related behaviors at the dose tested, indicating an interaction with endocannabinoid signaling (or other rimonabant-sensitive mechanisms).

Article.Title: Anterior insular cortex neurostimulation modulates sensory hypersensitivity and pain-related emotional behaviors in a rat model of chronic neuropathic pain
Article.Authors: Acunha R.; Medeiros P.; Machado H.; Sbragia L.; Coimbra N.; Maione S.; de Freitas R.
Article.Abstract: Background and aims: Chronic neuropathic pain (NP) is frequently accompanied by anxiety- and depression-like behaviors that contribute to functional impairment. The insular cortex plays a central role in pain processing and interoceptive regulation, with the anterior insular cortex (AIC) critically involved in integrating sensory inputs with emotional and behavioral responses. However, whether direct modulation of AIC activity can simultaneously regulate sensory hypersensitivity and pain-related emotional behaviors remains unclear. This study investigated the effects of electrical neurostimulation of the AIC (eAIC) on chronic NP and associated affective disturbances. Methods: Male Wistar rats were subjected to chronic constriction injury (CCI) of the sciatic nerve to induce NP or to a Sham procedure. Twenty-one days after surgery, an independent group of animals received a single session of eAIC neurostimulation delivered via stereotaxically implanted electrodes at low-frequency deep brain stimulation parameters (20 μA, 100 Hz, 15 s). Mechanical and cold allodynia, as well as anxiety- and depression-like behaviors, were subsequently evaluated using established behavioral paradigms. Results: The eAIC significantly attenuated mechanical and cold allodynia in CCI rats. In parallel, eAIC reduced anxiety-like and depression-like behaviors without altering general locomotor activity. These effects were selectively observed in neuropathic animals and were not detected in SHAM-operated controls. Conclusion: These findings demonstrate that AIC activity regulates both sensory hypersensitivity and pain-related emotional behaviors in chronic NP. By showing concurrent modulation of nociceptive and affective dimensions, this study provides physiological evidence supporting the AIC as a key cortical node linking pain processing to emotional behavior and underscoring its relevance for integrative neuromodulatory strategies.

Article.Title: Impact of testosterone on daily wheel running in female rats
Article.Authors: Craft R.; Morgan M.
Article.Abstract: Sex differences in daily activity have been attributed to the actions of gonadal steroid hormones. We tested this hypothesis by measuring the impact of male-typical levels of testosterone (T) on female rats' daily activity. Analyses were conducted on pooled data from three studies in which adult female Sprague-Dawley rats were implanted with blank or T-filled capsules (and adult males were implanted with blank capsules); home cage wheel running activity was measured 23 h/day before and for 3 weeks after capsule implantation. Approximately 75-80% of running occurred during the dark phase of the light-dark cycle in all groups, throughout the study. Before capsule implantation, the total number of wheel revolutions was significantly higher in females than males at the end of the light phase and during most of the dark phase; running speed and duration of daily running were higher in females compared to males. During the 3 weeks after capsule implantation, dark phase (and end-of-light phase) wheel revolutions, and average and maximum running speeds increased in all groups; however, T exposure blunted females' running increases during the second half of the dark phase, such that running during that period was similar to that of males by week 3. T also decreased the duration of females' active time, primarily by shifting offset of wheel running earlier, making it comparable to that in males. T non-significantly decreased females' running speeds. These results indicate that, within 3 weeks, T defeminizes females' daily activity in multiple ways. Thus, in addition to producing myriad physiological changes, male-typical levels of T also alter females' locomotor behavior.

Article.Title: Interaction between orexinergic and opioidergic systems in the dentate gyrus on modulation of pain-related behaviors in the tail-flick test as the animal model of acute pain in male rats
Article.Authors: Karbasi H.; Habibi S.; Amirteymori H.; Ghalandari-Shamami M.; Yekta B.; Haghparast A.
Article.Abstract: The dentate gyrus (DG), as a part of the hippocampal formation, is considered one of the brain areas involved in pain perception. This area contains opioid and orexin receptors. The present study examined the hypothesis that the interaction between opioidergic and orexinergic receptors in the DG area may influence acute pain-related behaviors. Two hundred thirty-nine adult male Wistar rats received unilateral microinjections of different doses of morphine (5, 10, 25, and 50 mM/0.5µl saline) and orexin A (0.25, 0.5, 1, and 2 nM/0.5µl saline) to assess their effects as opioid and orexin receptor agonists in the DG. Following this, the rats were administered varying doses of SB334867 (3, 10, 30, and 100 nM /0.5μL DMSO), an orexin-1 receptor (OX1r) antagonist, or TCS OX2 29, (3, 10 and 30 nM/0.5μL DMSO), an orexin-2 receptor (OX2r) antagonist before an effective dose of orexin A (1 nM /0.5μL saline). They also received naloxone (1.5, 5, 15, and 45 mM/0.5μL saline) before the same effective dose of orexin A. Finally, rats received varying doses of SB334867 (10, 30, and 100 nM /0.5μL DMSO) or TCS OX2 29 (1, 3, 10, and 30 nM /0.5μL DMSO) before an effective dose of morphine (25 mM/0.5μL saline). The tail-flick test was employed to evaluate their acute pain thresholds. The findings demonstrated that the administration of morphine and orexin A within the DG resulted in antinociceptive responses. However, SB334867 and TCS OX2 29 significantly diminished the antinociceptive responses of morphine and orexin A. Naloxone also reduced the analgesic effects of orexin A. These findings suggest a role for opioidergic and orexinergic systems in the DG in modulating acute pain. A better understanding of the neural circuits regulating pain will advance the search for novel treatments.

Article.Title: Behavioral characterization of transgenic mice for renin-angiotensin and bradykinin system: Implications for neurodevelopmental disorders?
Article.Authors: Vendramini A.; de Lara M.; Suiama M.; Nering M.; Hayashi M.; Abílio V.
Article.Abstract: The high prevalence of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) and neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) is gaining increasing attention. Classically recognized for its cardiovascular role, the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) - bradykinin axis has increasingly been implicated in the pathophysiology of NDDs, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and schizophrenia. The RAS-bradykinin axis is governed by the interplay between angiotensin I - converting enzyme (ACE) activity and bradykinin B2 receptor (B2R) signaling, a relationship that modulates the shift between detrimental vasoconstrictive states and beneficial, neuroprotective vasodilation. ACE is responsible for the conversion of Ang I into the hypertensive peptide Ang II while also being able to cleave and silence the hypotensive peptide bradykinin. In this study, we used genetically modified mice for transgenic ACE (carrying either three or one functional copy of the ACE gene) and B2R null knockout mice to determine the impact on behavioral domains relevant to NDDs of increased ACE and/or B2 receptor deletion. Three-month-old transgenic mice carrying three copies of the ACE gene showed increased locomotor activity, as well as social and cognitive deficits compared to wild-type animals. B2R knockout mice displayed sensorimotor gating dysfunction. Our results further support the involvement of the RAS-bradykinin axis in neurodevelopment and in behavioral measures relevant to NDDs. Overall, our present data suggest specific alterations in these physiological systems may lead to different behavioral abnormalities in mice. These findings highlight the need for future mechanistic investigations and contribute to a clearer understanding of the comorbidity between CVDs and NDDs.

Article.Title: Impact of combined chronic stress and REM sleep deprivation on memory function and hippocampal BDNF protein content in Wistar rats
Article.Authors: Hariyanti D.; Muliadi A.; Rosyidah C.; Arsyad A.
Article.Abstract: The concurrent impact of chronic psychological stress and sleep disruption on systemic adaptation and hippocampal cytoarchitecture remains poorly understood. This study investigated the neurobiological threshold of compounded stress by exposing male Wistar rats to combined Chronic Unpredictable Mild Stress (CUMS) and Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Deprivation (RSD), specifically chosen over total sleep deprivation due to the unique role of REM sleep in emotional regulation and spatial memory consolidation over 21 days. We evaluated body weight loss, sensorimotor function Open Field Test (OFT), declarative memory Novel Object Recognition (NOR), serum corticosterone, hippocampal malondialdehyde (MDA), and Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF). Results revealed that the combined stress paradigm precipitated significant body weight loss while preserving basal locomotor activity. In contrast to motor preservation, spatial recognition memory was significantly impaired. Biochemically, serum corticosterone and hippocampal MDA levels did not show statistically significant differences across groups. Crucially, while isolated CUMS significantly suppressed hippocampal BDNF protein content and RSD exhibited a similar trend of reduction, the combined paradigm triggered a compensatory neurotrophic rebound, returning BDNF to control baseline levels. However, the localized BDNF rebound did not translate to recovery cognitive performance. These findings suggest a phenomenon of neurobiological dissociation under compounded stress exposure. The organism experiences significant body weight loss and declarative memory impairment, while simultaneously initiating a localized, yet functionally ineffective, compensatory BDNF response in the hippocampus.

Article.Title: Long lasting alterations of feeding by adolescent obesity
Article.Authors: Rougeux S.; Mukherjee D.; West R.; Peters K.; Naneix F.
Article.Abstract: The prevalence of obesity is increasing worldwide, especially amongst younger populations. As both brain and body are still under development, numerous studies have shown that adolescence is an especially sensitive period for the impact of external insults including unbalanced diets. To better understand and prevent the vulnerability to obesity and maladaptive food choice, it is crucial to explore the long-term impact of adolescent exposure to obesogenic diets on different feeding behaviours. To address this, we gave mice access to an obesogenic diet with a very high-fat content (vHFD) specifically during adolescence and investigated the long-lasting impact on feeding at adulthood months after a switch to a healthy diet. Using specific feeding tests, we found that both males and females vHFD-exposed mice exhibited an increased intake of both standard food and palatable high-fat foods, without impacting preference for non-caloric food rewards. Importantly, these alterations are not fully correlated with diet-induced weight gain. The study reveals that the chronic consumption of energy-rich obesogenic diets during adolescence leads to long-lasting dysregulation of feeding, which may support long-term vulnerability to overeating and obesity.

Article.Title: Cardiac vagal and cardiac sympathetic activity in healthy humans during and after face immersion
Article.Authors: Ackermann S.; Poppa T.; Nazif B.; Raab M.; Laborde S.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: The interaction between cardiac vagal and cardiac sympathetic activity during face immersion remains poorly understood, yet it is critical for identifying potential autonomic conflict. This study sought to disentangle the individual and synergistic contributions of breathing mode (apnea vs. snorkel breathing) and water temperature (10°C vs. 30°C) on heart rate, cardiac vagal (RMSSD), and cardiac sympathetic (PEP) indices before, during, and after exposure. Methods: In a randomized within-subjects design, 52 healthy adults completed five 30-second conditions: 1) apnea in an empty bowl, 2) apnea in cold water, 3) apnea in warm water, 4) snorkel breathing in cold water, and 5) snorkel breathing in warm water. Heart rate, RMSSD, and PEP were measured for 30 seconds before, during and after each condition. Results: Significant bradycardia occurred in all five conditions. Apnea in an empty bowl resulted in the smallest bradycardia and a decrease in RMSSD. While cold-water apnea caused the strongest bradycardia, snorkel breathing in cold water elicited the largest RMSSD increase. PEP remained stable throughout all conditions and time points. Conclusion: These results demonstrate that face immersion triggers stimulus-dependent autonomic pathways. The observed decoupling of heart rate and RMSSD during apnea questions the validity of RMSSD as an index of cardiac vagal activity during breath-holding. The stability of PEP is consistent with predominantly cardiac parasympathetic involvement in diving bradycardia. These findings highlight limitations of RMSSD interpretation during apnea and emphasize the necessity of accounting for breathing modality in autonomic assessments. Applied interventions using cold-water face immersion under safe conditions are encouraged.

Article.Title: Behavioural and neuroinflammatory characterization of mouse stress paradigms relevant to post-traumatic stress disorder
Article.Authors: Govindula A.; Nampoothiri M.; Arora D.; Mudgal J.
Article.Abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a stress-related psychiatric disorder characterized by intrusive memories, avoidance, negative mood, and hypervigilance following exposure to traumatic events. Preclinical and clinical evidence suggests that repeated or cumulative stress exposure can alter neuroimmune signalling and increase vulnerability to PTSD. This study compared three stress paradigms in male mice i.e. combined stressor early-life stress (CS-ELS), composite restress (CRS), and discrete restress (DRS), to characterize behavioural phenotypes relevant to PTSD and their associated neuroinflammatory changes. Among the paradigms evaluated, CS-ELS, which combined altered mother-pup interactions with subsequent physical and psychological stressors, exhibited a broader pattern of behavioural alterations, accompanied by elevated serum CRH and corticosterone concentrations. Molecular analyses revealed increased NLRP3 and tryptase expression and reduced TSPO expression in CS-ELS mice. IL-1β levels were numerically higher but did not differ significantly from controls, whereas CRP expression showed a significant increase in the Dunnett-adjusted comparison despite a nonsignificant overall ANOVA. These findings suggest associations between cumulative stress exposure and behavioural, neuroendocrine, and neuroinflammatory alterations relevant to stress-related neuropsychiatric disorders. The CS-ELS paradigm may provide a useful preclinical platform for further investigating stress-associated behavioural and molecular changes and evaluating potential therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Sexual experience modulates conditioned preference for morphine in female Long–Evans rats
Article.Authors: Meerts S.; Frost M.; Kresse K.; Beasley T.; Zhu H.; James C.
Article.Abstract: Sexually experienced female rats, compared to naïve rats, return to the male more quickly after receiving sexual stimulations, spend more time with the male, and display more proceptive behaviors during paced mating. Additionally, rewarding effects of mating are greater in sexually experienced relative to naïve female rats. A number of findings led to the hypothesis that experienced-induced neuroplasticity in the endogenous opioid system may be responsible for sexual experience-inducedchanges in display of paced mating behavior and mating-induced reward. To test whether reward mediated by the opioid system differed between sexually experienced and naïve female rats, we asked whether rats would exhibit a conditioned object preference (COP) for 0.5, 1, or 2 mg/kg morphine. Ovariectomized, Long-Evans female rats were primed with estradiol benzoate and progesterone and either exposed to an empty paced mating chamber for 15 min (Naïve) or received a 15-intromission test of paced mating behavior (Experienced) on four separate occasions before undergoing the COP procedure for morphine. We predicted that sexual experience would lead to a sensitized opioid system reflected by conditioned preference for lower doses of morphine in experienced vs. naïve rats. Instead, we found that naïve female rats exhibited a conditioned object preference for all three doses of morphine, whereas experienced female rats exhibited a conditioned object preference only for 2 mg/kg morphine. In addition to illustrating that the opioid system is altered by sexual experience, these findings provide insight into the involvement of endogenous opioids in experience-enhanced paced mating behavior.

Article.Title: Human milk oligosaccharide supplementation in post-weaning rats fed a high fat/sucrose diet affects glutamate receptor gene expression in the nucleus accumbens and amygdala
Article.Authors: Noye Tuplin E.; Fernandes T.; Lowry D.; Cho N.; Sales K.; Patterson R.; Reimer R.
Article.Abstract: The consumption of human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), a key component of breast milk, during early life has been shown to have long-lasting impacts on metabolic processes, immune system function, and nervous system development. The long-term effects of early-life HMO supplementation on behaviours that are associated with metabolic processes, such as food preferences and food choices, and mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, are less clear. The present study examined the effects of post-weaning supplementation with two common HMOs, 2'-fucosyllactose (2'FL) and 3'sialyllactose (3'SL), on anxiety-like behavior, sucrose consumption, food preference, and glutamate receptor gene expression in adulthood in Sprague-Dawley rats. We also assessed whether HMO supplementation could attenuate any changes in glutamate receptor gene expression or behavior associated with a high-fat/sucrose (HFS) diet. The present study demonstrated that the effects of HMO supplementation are both sex and dose-dependent, with changes in glutamate receptor gene expression in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) representing the most prominent changes. Effects on sucrose intake were modest and sex-specific, with H/HFS females consuming less sucrose than H/AIN females on the first, but not second, day of testing. This effect was most evident in females that received the high-HMO diet before the HFS challenge and was accompanied by lower GluR1 and GluR2 gene expression in the NAc. Rats fed a HFS diet displayed a preference for palatable food, regardless of early HMO exposure, which may be the result of changes to incentive salience or "wanting" for palatable foods. The findings of this study show a potential link between early-life HMO supplementation, behaviour, and the expression of genes related to synaptic plasticity.

Article.Title: The impact of postweaning food texture on swallow function in the juvenile Ts65Dn mouse model of Down syndrome
Article.Authors: Singhal G.; Sitko J.; Fisher E.; Cullins M.; Connor N.; Glass T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Children with Down syndrome (DS) often show feeding and swallowing difficulties, including prolonged reliance on soft diets. The Ts65Dn mouse model mirrors oromotor challenges in DS, yet the impacts of extended postweaning periods of soft food conditions are not well understood. We examined whether a soft food condition from postnatal day (P)21-P34 alters oral motor behaviors, weight, swallow function, and hypoglossal nucleus BDNF expression in Ts65Dn vs. euploid controls, hypothesizing that soft food would impact these outcomes. Methods: Male and female Ts65Dn and euploid littermates were assigned to hard or soft food (HF, SF) from P21-P34. Daily body weight and water intake were recorded. Videofluoroscopic swallow studies (VFSS) measured swallow rate, inter-swallow interval (ISI), jaw excursion rate (JER), and jaw cycle swallow ratio. ProBDNF and mature BDNF were quantified in hypoglossal nucleus at P35. Water consumption was analyzed at the cage level, and BDNF outcomes were analyzed using generalized linear models. Data were analyzed using mixed effects and three-way ANOVA with Sidak post hoc correction (α = 0.05). Results: Ts65Dn weighed significantly less than euploid control at P21 and P34. Mice in all genotype groups licked significantly more water in the HF condition than in the SF condition. VFSS revealed a significant genotype effect on ISI, with higher ISI in Ts65Dn than euploid mice. A sex x food texture x genotype interaction was detected for JER, with female Ts65Dn HF mice showing lower JER than female euploid HF mice. None of the overall models for proBDNF, mature BDNF, or the mature BDNF/proBDNF ratio reached statistical significance, although predictor level associations were observed for sex with proBDNF and food condition with mature BDNF. Conclusions: Soft diets did not worsen genotype specific differences in VFSS measures. Predictor level BDNF findings were exploratory because the corresponding overall models were not statistically significant.

Article.Title: Appetite responses over 24 hours before and after 12-weeks of resistance exercise in older male adults: Secondary data analysis of a randomised trial
Article.Authors: Griffen C.; Renshaw D.; Hattersley J.; Weickert M.; Duncan M.; Broom D.
Article.Abstract: Background: Despite resistance exercise (RE) being a key component of landmark recommendations for weight control, there is still a paucity of data on the effects of RE on appetite. The aim of this study was to examine the effects of 12-weeks of RE on appetite. Methods: Thirty-three older men (age: 67 ± 4 years; BMI: 25.4 ± 2.4 kg/m2) were included in this secondary pooled data analysis of a 12-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 4-arm parallel group trial. In the present analysis, RE (2x/week at 80% 1RM; n = 17) and no exercise (NE; continue habitual physical activity; n = 16) groups were pooled and compared to one another. Appetite profile was measured over 24 h inside a metabolic chamber at baseline and post 12-weeks using visual analogue scales (VAS). Area under the curve (AUC) was calculated using the trapezoidal method. Significance was set at p < 0.05. Results: No significant group-by-time (p ≥ 0.08) or group-by-time-by-time point (p ≥ 0.10) differences occurred between groups for VAS hunger, satiety, fullness, prospective food consumption, or composite appetite score. Similarly, no significant differences were observed for 24-h VAS AUC for hunger (p = 0.35), satiety (p = 0.58), fullness (p = 0.41), prospective food consumption (p = 0.21), or composite appetite score (p = 0.40). Discussion: The present study found no statistical effect on appetite following 12-weeks of RE in older adult males. RE should continue to be undertaken throughout the life course and be included as part of physical activity recommendations for optimal health in older adults due to the many physical, mental health and functional benefits.

Article.Title: Changes in food reward are associated with improvements in metabolic markers and eating behaviors after bariatric surgery
Article.Authors: Lachance A.; Toro V.; Legault M.; Gagnon P.; Pelletier M.; Biertho L.; Provencher V.; Iceta S.; Tchernof A.; Picard F.; Michaud A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Bariatric surgery improves metabolic health and eating behaviors. However, its impact on food reward, particularly liking and wanting, remains poorly understood. Objective: To characterize changes in explicit and implicit food reward following sleeve gastrectomy and to examine their associations with metabolic health and eating behaviors. Methods: Food reward was assessed before and 4 months after surgery using the Leeds Food Preference Questionnaire. Eating behaviors, assessed with the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire, and glycemic and lipid profiles were measured at both time points. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess changes in food reward and their associations with metabolic and behavioral outcomes. Results: Twenty-nine participants (8 women and 21 men, 39.2 ± 10.7 years, initial BMI: 44.0 ± 4.7 kg/m2) completed both assessments. Explicit and implicit wanting for high-fat sweet foods significantly decreased following bariatric surgery (p < 0.01 and p < 0.001, respectively), whereas explicit liking remained unchanged. Lower implicit wanting for high-fat sweet foods was significantly associated with improvements in eating behaviors and insulin-like growth factor binding protein 2 (IGFBP-2), a marker of glucose metabolism. Exploratory mediation analyses showed that implicit wanting for high-fat sweet foods accounted for 16 to 18% of the association between IGFBP-2 and changes in eating behaviors. Conclusion: Sleeve gastrectomy is associated with reduced motivational drive for high-fat sweet foods, while hedonic appreciation remains stable. These findings suggest that post-surgical metabolic adaptations may improve the control of food intake, in part by modulating implicit motivation for high-fat sweet foods.

Article.Title: Estradiol attenuates cardiac apoptosis and modulates cardiovascular remodeling in ovariectomized female rats with 6-hydroxydopamine-induced parkinsonism
Article.Authors: de Campos B.; Borges F.; Ariza D.; de Jager L.; Reginato G.; Gonçalves A.; Martins Novais Padrão A.; Fonseca H.; Pinge-Filho P.; Crestani C.; Martins-Pinge M.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and reduced striatal dopamine concentrations. In addition to its characteristic motor manifestations, PD is associated with nonmotor complications, including cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction, orthostatic and postprandial hypotension, and blood pressure instability. The lower prevalence of PD in women has prompted investigation into the potential protective effects of female sex hormones. In this study, we evaluated cardiovascular function, autonomic modulation, cardiac and vascular morphology, and apoptosis in ovariectomized female rats with 6-OHDA-induced parkinsonism treated with estradiol. Wistar rats underwent bilateral ovariectomy and received estradiol (1 mg/kg) or almond oil as the vehicle for 13 consecutive days. Seven days after ovariectomy, 6-OHDA or SHAM vehicle was infused bilaterally into the SNpc. Six days later, the animals underwent femoral artery catheterization, and mean arterial pressure (MAP) and heart rate (HR) were recorded after 24 h. The 6-OHDA lesion reduced striatal dopamine concentrations by more than 50%, confirming the induction of parkinsonism. No significant group differences were detected in MAP, HR, autonomic variability, or baroreflex sensitivity. However, parkinsonism reduced left ventricular wall thickness, increased apoptosis in both ventricles, and decreased cardiac and aortic collagen content. Estradiol increased left ventricular wall thickness and partially attenuated ventricular apoptosis and the parkinsonism-associated alteration in aortic elastin. These findings indicate that 6-OHDA-induced parkinsonism produces cardiac and aortic structural alterations that are not reflected in basal cardiovascular or autonomic measurements and, estradiol may modulate selected cardiac alterations. Although the underlying mechanisms and translational relevance require further investigation, our findings suggest potential clinical relevance for postmenopausal women with Parkinson's disease.

Article.Title: Probiotics attenuate AlCl₃-induced Alzheimer’s disease via gut–brain axis modulation and suppression of NF-κB/NLRP3 neuroinflammation
Article.Authors: Elfiky A.; Shahy E.; Mahmoud A.
Article.Abstract: Disruptions along the brain-gut-microbiota axis significantly contribute to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis. This study evaluated the therapeutic potential of a multi-strain probiotic mixture in mitigating cognitive decline, neuroinflammation, and amyloid pathology in an AD rat model. In the present study, after induction of AD in rats by oral administration of AlCl3 (50 mg/kg) for 28 days, followed by oral treatment with a probiotic mixture (109 log CFU/ml) for 42 days. Behavioral assessments were conducted during the final week. Hippocampal tissues were obtained for histopathological and gene expression analyses and fecal samples were subjected to full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing via Oxford Nanopore approach. Probiotics significantly improved AD-induced deficits in locomotor activity, exploratory behavior, and spatial recognition memory. Histological analysis revealed marked reductions in hippocampal β-amyloid deposition and substantial restoration of colonic mucosal barrier integrity. Microbiota profiling showed that probiotics reversed dysbiosis, significantly enriching beneficial genera (Blautia, Clostridium, Eubacterium). Blautia abundance was strongly negatively correlated with NF-κB expression. Mechanistically, probiotics suppressed neuroinflammation by down-regulating pro-inflammatory cascades TNF-α, NLRP3, IL-1β, and NF-κB activation. Furthermore, treatment suppressed amyloidogenic processing via decreased APP mRNA and enhanced Aβ clearance through upregulation of LRP1 and modulation of AGER. These findings provide integrative evidence that probiotics exert neuroprotective and immunomodulatory effects, supporting their translational potential as a preventive strategy against AD-related cognitive decline.

Article.Title: Functional involvement of HMGB1-related neuroinflammation in depression and its modulation by intermittent theta-burst stimulation(iTBS)
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Xin S.; Zhang K.; Zhang Y.; Wang L.; An C.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: Intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) is widely used for its rapid antidepressant efficacy in clinical practice. However, its underlying neuroimmune mechanisms and objective biomarkers of treatment response remain largely unexplored. High mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), a critical driver of neuroimmune interactions in stress-related disorders, may link peripheral inflammation to central pathological processes in depression and may serve as a potential therapeutic target. Therefore, we aimed to explore the functional involvement of HMGB1 in depression and whether HMGB1-related inflammatory signaling is modulated by iTBS. Methods: We measured circulating HMGB1 levels in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). In mice exposed to chronic restraint stress (CRS) or lipopolysaccharide (LPS), HMGB1/TLR4/NF-κB signaling and neuroinflammatory responses in the prefrontal cortex were assessed. Glycyrrhizic acid (GA), a well-established HMGB1 antagonist, was used to determine the functional relevance of HMGB1. iTBS-mediated antidepressant effects were assessed via behavioral tests and HMGB1-related inflammatory signaling analysis. Results: HMGB1 was markedly upregulated in patients and in depressive‑like mouse models, accompanied by activation of the HMGB1/TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway and increased neuroinflammation. GA alleviated depressive-like behaviors. iTBS reversed behavioral deficits and suppressed HMGB1-associated inflammatory signaling. Conclusion: HMGB1 is functionally involved in depression, and the therapeutic effects of iTBS are associated with suppression of HMGB1-related neuroinflammatory signaling. These findings suggest that HMGB1 may have potential as a biomarker for monitoring the biological effects of iTBS, warranting further investigation into its role in treatment response.

Article.Title: Central GHSR inverse agonism by a LEAP2 analog regulates thermometabolic and behavioral responses via catecholamine signaling
Article.Authors: dos Santos I.; dos Santos H.; Ribeiro J.; Leite J.; de Abreu A.; Mendonça M.; da Silva E.; Colombari E.; Pedrino G.; Gomes R.; Fajemiroye J.; Lima P.; Perelló M.; Marques S.; Xavier C.
Article.Abstract: Background: Liver-expressed antimicrobial peptide 2 (LEAP2) is an endogenous GHSR inverse agonist that antagonizes ghrelin-mediated signaling, thereby opposing several of the physiological actions elicited by ghrelin. Evidence indicates that GHSR participates in autonomic, cardiovascular, renal, and psychogenic regulation, interacts with dopaminergic signaling and interplays with adrenergic pathways during sympathetically driven hypertension. Here, we investigated whether catecholaminergic mechanisms mediate behavioral and thermometabolic effects evoked from central GHSR inverse agonism by a LEAP2 analog. Methods: Adult male Wistar rats were systemically pretreated with either the tyrosine hydroxylase inhibitor α-methyl-para-tyrosine (AMPT; 200 mg/kg) or the non-selective dopamine receptor antagonist chlorpromazine (CLP; 2 mg/kg) and then centrally pretreated with LEAP2 analog (6 nmol) or vehicle. Rats were evaluated across a range of paradigms, including anxiety- and panic-like behaviors, open-field exploration, ingestive activity, treadmill performance with VO₂ recorders and infrared thermography of caudal heat dissipation. Results: Central LEAP2 analog impaired the expression of anxiety- and panic-like responses and attenuated heat-conservation mechanisms triggered by aversion. Behavioral and food ingestive effects were largely dependent on dopaminergic receptor signaling, whereas thermoregulatory responses during exercise required the entire catecholaminergic pathways inhibited by AMPT. Conclusion: LEAP2 analog regulates specific behavioral and thermometabolic responses through neurobiological mechanisms involving catecholaminergic pathways and dopamine receptors, highlighting central GHSR as a potential pharmacological target for neuroendocrine defense mechanisms.

Article.Title: Environmental enrichment differentially suppresses anxiety-related behaviors, reduces passive avoidance learning, and upregulates hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in high- and low-avoidance Hatano rats
Article.Authors: Akaishi T.; Nakayama A.; Okawa H.; Asano H.; Tokuoka H.; Meihua Z.; Shaoxia P.; Watanabe G.; Yanagisawa R.; Ohta R.; Soga T.; Yamamoto S.; Abe K.; Kawaguchi M.
Article.Abstract: Anxiety disorder risk is influenced by both adverse environmental factors and genetic background. We previously described high-avoidance animal (HAA) and low-avoidance animal (LAA) strains of male Hatano rats that may provide robust models for assessing interactions between genetic background and environment driving anxiety disorder pathogenesis. We examined the potential of environmental enrichment (EE), a non-pharmacological approach, to suppress trait anxiety disorders by comparing anxiety-related behaviors and physiological metrics between HAA and LAA lines exposed to EE or standard housing. At 4 weeks of age, 10-12 male rats from each strain were assigned to EE or standard conditions. EE for 4-5 weeks significantly (p = 0.0002 by Tukey-Kramer's test) reduced anxiety-related behaviors in LAAs in the elevated plus maze test, but had no similar anxiolytic effect in HAAs. In contrast, EE for 11 weeks significantly (p = 0.0072 by Tukey-Kramer's test) reduced passive avoidance memory retention in HAAs, but not in LAAs. Real-time quantitative PCR revealed upregulated expression of Bdnf exons 1, 3, and 4 in the hippocampus of LAAs following EE, while the same treatment increased the expression of Bdnf exon 3 in the hippocampus of HAAs. Alternatively, EE did not alter mRNA expression levels of the BDNF receptor TrkB and the glucocorticoid receptor in hippocampus, or influence plasma corticosterone, prolactin, and testosterone concentrations. These findings have potential clinical implications for anxiety disorders, suggesting that effects of EE may vary depending on an individual's genetic background and underlying biological characteristics.

Article.Title: Distinct behavioral and electrophysiological correlates of sleep disturbance during verbal and spatial working memory tasks
Article.Authors: Wang P.; Xie C.; Chen Y.; Wang K.
Article.Abstract: Associations between sleep disturbance and working memory (WM) vary across tasks and outcome measures. This study examined behavioral and electrophysiological correlates of subjective sleep disturbance during verbal working memory (VWM) and spatial working memory (SWM) in university students. Sixty-one participants were classified using Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores into a sleep disturbance group (n = 28) and a normal sleep group (n = 33) and completed separate verbal and spatial 2-back tasks with event-related potential (ERP) recording. After adjustment for depression, anxiety, and stress, the sleep disturbance group showed lower VWM accuracy (ACC) (mean difference = -3.89 percentage points, 95% CI [-6.83, -0.96]) and discrimination sensitivity (d'). VWM false alarm rates (FAR) were also higher, although the absolute difference was small. Higher PSQI scores were associated with lower VWM ACC and d' and higher FAR. The sleep disturbance group showed lower VWM P3 amplitude averaged across the analyzed electrode sites and longer P3 peak latency at Oz. No significant group-related effects were detected for VWM median reaction time or N2 measures, or for SWM behavioral and ERP measures. These findings link subjective sleep disturbance to lower ACC and discrimination during verbal updating, accompanied by differences in later task-related electrophysiological processing. Future longitudinal and intervention studies with matched tasks and objective sleep measures could clarify the temporal and causal relationships underlying these associations.

Article.Title: Exploring the reconfiguration effects of physical fatigue on the gradient space of brain function based on EEG
Article.Authors: Yang G.; Chi P.; Zhao S.
Article.Abstract: Objective: This study examined how physical fatigue reorganizes the low-dimensional structure of EEG functional connectivity using three embedding approaches. Method: Thirty male participants completed a Bruce treadmill test to exhaustion, with resting-state EEG recorded before and after exercise. Frequency-specific wPLI connectivity matrices were analyzed using PCA, Laplacian eigenmaps, and diffusion maps with common-reference alignment. Regional G1-G3 scores, G1-G2 displacement, λ1-λ3 eigenvalues, and their associations with exercise duration were assessed. Results: PCA showed increased beta-band G1 scores over the central scalp region and decreased scores over the occipital region, together with reduced alpha-band G3 over the central region. LE showed increased theta-band G3 over the central region. PCA displacement exhibited a significant frequency band × scalp region interaction, driven by greater alpha-band occipital displacement. Theta-band λ1-λ3 increased with PCA but decreased with DM, whereas LE showed no significant eigenvalue changes. The PCA-derived beta-band central ΔG1 was positively correlated with exhaustive exercise duration (r = 0.50, p = 0.004). Conclusions: Physical fatigue induces frequency-, region-, component-, and method-specific reorganization of the low-dimensional structure of scalp-level EEG functional connectivity. PCA was particularly sensitive to spatially differentiated gradient changes, while LE and DM captured complementary aspects of fatigue-related reorganization. The association between central beta-band ΔG1 and exercise duration further suggests potential behavioral relevance of gradient.

Article.Title: The effect of positive emotions on psychophysiological recovery and performance in athletes - investigating the undoing-hypothesis
Article.Authors: Zajonz P.; Sascha Leisterer-Härtig N/A.; Sylvain Laborde N/A.; Legerlotz K.; Wolfarth B.; Franziska Lautenbach N/A.
Article.Abstract: Athletes have to cope with psychosocial and physiological stressors, requiring recovery to ensure subsequent performance. According to the undoing-hypothesis, positive emotions (PE) may enhance psychophysiological recovery. The present two studies investigated the undoing hypothesis and its benefits for athletes' cognitive (Study 1; n = 60) and motor (Study 2; n = 30) performance. After a combined psychosocial-physiological stressor, participants either completed a five-minute PE induction (music; imagination exercise) or were assigned to a resting condition. Emotions, perceived stress-recovery, and physiological parameters (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, cortisol) were assessed. In Study 1, inhibition and cognitive flexibility were measured once. In Study 2, hand force and jump height were measured using a pre-posttest design. Due to the lack of psychological stress responses and successful PE induction, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the undoing hypothesis. Nevertheless, the present study provides valuable methodological insights into the challenges of testing the undoing hypothesis in athletes. These insights can inform the design and implementation of future studies and thereby contribute to advancing research on the undoing hypothesis in athletic populations.

Article.Title: Intermittent fasting as a therapeutic strategy in Alzheimer’s disease: Understanding of brain-derived neurotrophic factor modulation
Article.Authors: Shrirame D.; Tatode A.; Dabhade D.; Taksande J.; Taksande B.; Kakade O.; Umekar M.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques, tau tangles, neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress, and it causes cognitive impairment and neuronal loss. The pharmacological treatment is of limited effectiveness, therefore the interest in novel approaches such as intermittent fasting (IF). IF, a nutritional regimen of periodic caloric restriction, has shown a potential to modulate neurodegenerative alterations by metabolic and molecular mechanisms. This review presents the implications of IF in the etiopathogenesis of AD, specifically in controlling brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). BDNF is a major neurotrophin that plays a key role in synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, and cognition. Evidence indicates that BDNF is drastically decreased in AD, therefore enhancing disease progression. IF enhances BDNF expression via mechanisms such as improved mitochondrial function, increased ketone body production, and reduced systemic inflammation. Preclinical studies indicate that IF not only upregulates BDNF but also alleviates key AD pathologies, including Aβ deposition and tau hyperphosphorylation. Additionally, clinical data highlight the cognitive benefits of IF and its role in modulating metabolic health, although studies specifically linking IF, BDNF and AD in humans remain limited. This review underscores the need for further research to determine optimal IF protocols and clarify its long-term impact on AD progression. IF's ability to modulate BDNF and other neuroprotective pathways positions it as a promising non-pharmacological intervention for AD management. By bridging metabolic health and neuroprotection, IF offers potential therapeutic synergy for mitigating AD's complex etiopathogenesis.

Article.Title: Openness to experience modulates the neural dynamics of semantic processing
Article.Authors: Li B.; Huang C.; Lin Q.; Huang H.
Article.Abstract: Personality fundamentally shapes language processing, yet the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. Openness to experience (Openness), as measured by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI), has been associated with enhanced creativity and engagement with novel semantic information. This study examined how openness modulates the neural dynamics of semantic processing using event-related potentials (ERPs) during a semantic category verification task. Participants evaluated category relatedness across the four levels of semantic structure, including high typicality (HT), low typicality (LT), related violations (RV), and nonrelated violations (NRV). Neural responses exhibited the expected graded pattern, with N400 amplitudes becoming more negative as semantic relatedness decreased. Critically, higher Openness was associated with greater N400 differentiation between related and nonrelated violations, an effect uniquely predicted by Openness beyond the remaining four personality traits. Follow-up analyses revealed that this differentiation was primarily driven by enhanced N400 responses to nonrelated violations rather than by reduced responses to related violations. This pattern is inconsistent with a simple facilitation account in which higher Openness uniformly eases semantic processing. Instead, it suggests that Openness is associated with heightened sensitivity to semantic mismatch or more sustained semantic evaluation when incoming information is incompatible with an activated context. Behavioral performance was comparable across participants; the observed neural differences were not accompanied by detectable differences in task success. Together, these findings establish that Openness is systematically related to variation in the neural dynamics of semantic processing, while highlighting the need to clarify the underlying cognitive mechanisms and contributions of other individual differences.

Article.Title: The effect of concurrent application of the deep brain stimulation of the nucleus accumbens and cannabidiol injection during extinction period on reinstatement of METH-induced conditioned place preference in extinguished rats
Article.Authors: Mohammadi M.; Zendehdel M.; Haghparast A.
Article.Abstract: Methamphetamine (METH) is a potent stimulant drug that significantly alters the function of the central nervous system (CNS). METHS's abuse may be linked with a variety of psychiatric disorders, primarily by affecting the reward system. Cannabidiol (CBD), a primary cannabinoid component of the Cannabis plant, has been shown to affect the reward system, suggesting it for modulating addictive behaviors. On the other hand, deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the nucleus accumbens (NAc), one of the most significant brain regions implicated in mediating rewards, is effective in alleviating drug-seeking behaviors. The present research aimed to evaluate the effects of low-frequency DBS, CBD, and a combination of both on the extinction and reinstatement of METH-induced conditioned place preference (CPP). CBD was injected into the lateral ventricle at doses of 2.5, 5, and 10 μg/5 μL, and low-frequency DBS (10 Hz, for 30 min) was administered to the NAc, both during the extinction phase. The results showed CBD (10 µg/5 µL) or DBS facilitated extinction. DBS decreased mean extinction latency but did not differ significantly from CBD (10 µg/5 µL) alone. The combination groups at all tested CBD doses showed reduced mean extinction latency compared with the control groups; only the 10 µg/5 µL combination group differed significantly from DBS alone. However, neither CBD (10 µg/5 µL) alone nor DBS altered the CPP score on the reinstatement day. Combination of DBS and CBD administration (at all doses) significantly decreased the CPP score on the reinstatement day. In conclusion, it can be suggested that CBD may be beneficial for alleviating METH-induced reinstatement in combination with DBS, while both alone had no effect.

Article.Title: Maternal high-fat diet and metformin treatment affect palatable diet preference and central reward system gene expression in rat offspring in a sex-specific manner
Article.Authors: Hu S.; Cui J.; Wang R.; Wang J.; Guo H.; Zhang D.; Zou L.; Song L.; Sun B.
Article.Abstract: Maternal metformin (MT) treatment improves the metabolic phenotype of high-fat (HF) diet-exposed offspring, but its effect on offspring's palatable food preference remains unclear. We assessed HF diet and sucrose preferences in adult offspring from Sprague-Dawley rat dams fed a control diet, an HF diet with or without MT treatment. Additionally, we measured the mRNA expression of sweet taste perception-related genes in taste buds and dopamine- and opioid-related genes in the central reward system. In adult males, maternal HF diet increased HF food preference and decreased dopamine-related gene expression in the reward system. Furthermore, maternal MT treatment decreased low-concentration sucrose preference, and reduced opioid-related gene expression in the reward system. Maternal HF diet elevated sweet taste perception-related gene expression in taste buds, while maternal MT treatment reversed these changes. In adult females, neither maternal HF diet nor MT treatment affected HF food preference. However, maternal HF diet decreased low-concentration sucrose preference and reduced the expression of sweet taste perception-related genes, while maternal MT treatment did not reverse it. At weaning, maternal MT treatment generally decreased dopamine- and opioid-related gene expression in the central reward system across both sexes. Notably, this early-life central reward transcriptional suppression persisted into adulthood in males but not in females. Our results indicate that maternal HF diet and MT treatment influence HF diet and low-concentration sucrose preferences in adult offspring in a sex-specific manner, which may be associated with altered gene expression in the central reward system and the peripheral taste perception pathways.

Article.Title: Food restriction and hyperactivity differentially shape microglial Iba1 immunoreactivity across feeding-, cognitive-, and reward-related circuits in the activity-based anorexia model
Article.Authors: Camoglio C.; Dedoni S.; Scherma M.; Siddi C.; Nilsson I.; Fadda P.
Article.Abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is characterized by marked metabolic, behavioral, and neurobiological alterations. Although neuroinflammation and microglial activation have been suggested to contribute to its pathophysiology, preclinical evidence remains inconsistent and appears to depend on the experimental conditions and brain regions examined. Here, we asked whether the two core components of the activity-based anorexia (ABA) paradigm, food restriction and voluntary hyperactivity, are associated with distinct regional patterns of Iba1 immunoreactivity across neural circuits involved in energy balance, cognition, and reward, and whether these alterations relate to the behavioral and metabolic severity of the model. Using the ABA rat model, we quantified the percentage of Iba1-positive area in the prefrontal cortex, dorsal and ventral hippocampus, anterior cingulate cortex, nucleus accumbens, caudate putamen, amygdala, and the arcuate and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus. ABA animals displayed an overall reduction in Iba1 immunoreactivity, with significant decreases in the hippocampus and paraventricular nucleus. Conversely, food restriction alone increased Iba1 coverage in the arcuate nucleus, whereas voluntary physical activity selectively enhanced Iba1 immunoreactivity in reward-related areas, particularly the nucleus accumbens. These findings indicate that starvation and hyperactivity induce distinct, region-specific changes in Iba1 immunoreactive coverage, potentially reflecting alterations in microglial responses that may differentially affect hypothalamic, cognitive, and reward-related circuits implicated in AN pathophysiology.

Article.Title: Gene-environment interaction in transgenic rats overexpressing human DISC1: effects of early social isolation on behavioral domains
Article.Authors: Pedroso-Fidelis G.; Avila F.; Nani J.; Porta L.; Bertagna N.; Rodolpho B.; Lee R.; Cruz F.; Hayashi M.
Article.Abstract: Early-life social isolation (SI) is a well-established environmental stressor associated with persistent behavioral alterations relevant to psychiatric disorders. Whether SI interacts with neurodevelopmental brain abnormalities to modify behavioral vulnerability remains unclear. We investigated the effects of post-weaning SI in transgenic rats overexpressing full-length human Disrupted-in-Schizophrenia 1 (tgDISC1), a model characterized by DISC1 protein aggregation, impaired dopamine homeostasis, and abnormal neuronal migration. Male wild-type (WT) and tgDISC1 rats were housed individually or in groups from postnatal day 21 for 28 consecutive days and evaluated using behavioral tests assessing stress-coping, self-care, locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, contextual fear memory, and social behavior. SI reduced grooming behavior, shortened the latency to the first immobility episode in the forced swim test, and decreased contextual freezing regardless of genotype, whereas locomotor activity and anxiety-like behavior were unaffected. Genotype-dependent differences were observed in anxiety-related measures, showing distinct performances in the Open Field and Elevated Plus Maze tests. In the social interaction test, SI selectively altered social preference, revealing a significant gene × environment interaction, indicating that neurodevelopmental brain abnormalities specifically modulated the effects of early-life SI on social behavior. Together, these findings demonstrate that early-life SI induces selective behavioral alterations, whereas DISC1-related dysfunction selectively influences the behavioral consequences of SI in the social domain rather than conferring generalized vulnerability. These results highlight the value of multidomain behavioral phenotyping in gene × environment models and identify social behavior as a sensitive marker of DISC1-related susceptibility to early-life stress, with implications for the developmental origins of psychiatric disorders.
