Article.Title: Integrative Mendelian Randomization and Single-Cell Transcriptomic Analysis of Aging-Related Genes Associated With Stroke Risk
Article.Authors: Li H.; Li J.; Chen Y.; Shen X.; Xu Y.; Bian R.; Yao Y.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: Stroke is a major cerebrovascular disease, and aging is a major risk factor associated with poorer outcomes. Identifying genetic mechanisms linking aging-related processes to stroke may help prioritize relevant genes and pathways. Aims: To identify aging-related genes associated with stroke risk and explore their molecular and cellular context. Study design: An integrated analysis combining eQTL-based Mendelian randomization and single-cell transcriptomics. Methods: eQTL data were obtained from eQTLGen, with stroke GWAS data from FinnGen as the discovery dataset and the GWAS Catalog as the validation dataset. MR, sensitivity, and colocalization analyses were used to evaluate associations between genetically predicted gene expression and stroke risk. Single-cell data (GSE174574) were analyzed using Seurat to characterize cell-type-specific expression of prioritized genes. GSEA and GSVA were used for pathway analysis, while RcisTarget, miRWalk, and DGIdb were used to explore regulatory and drug-gene interactions. Results: In 340,999 participants, 22 aging-related genes showed nominal MR associations with stroke risk. Validation in 1,039,382 participants identified LPAR3, MEOX1, VEGFA, and PRKDC. Higher genetically predicted MEOX1 and VEGFA expression was associated with lower stroke risk, whereas LPAR3 and PRKDC were associated with higher risk. VEGFA showed additional support from regional colocalization analysis, whereas LPAR3 and MEOX1 were primarily supported by MR evidence. Regulatory analysis identified 51 predicted miRNAs and 53 drug-gene interaction records involving VEGFA and LPAR3. Conclusion: LPAR3, MEOX1, VEGFA, and PRKDC were prioritized as aging-related genes associated with stroke risk. VEGFA showed additional support from regional colocalization analysis, while LPAR3, MEOX1, and PRKDC require further functional validation.
Article.Keywords: Mendelian randomization; aging-related genes; colocalization; single-cell transcriptomics; stroke

Article.Title: The Benefits of Physical Exercise on Epilepsy Treatment: Possible Mechanisms via Neurotransmitters Modulation
Article.Authors: Taherkhani S.; Bagheri Tadi F.; Amani P.; Mohajerian R.; Janzadeh A.
Article.Abstract: This narrative review aims to critically explored current preclinical and clinical evidence on the therapeutic benefits of physical exercise in epilepsy management, with particular emphasis on the underlying mechanisms mediated by modulation of key neurotransmitter systems, including GABAergic, glutamatergic, monoaminergic, and neurotrophic pathways. It seeks to reframe exercise from a historically perceived risk factor to a promising non-pharmacological adjunct capable of reducing seizure susceptibility and improving comorbid outcomes. A comprehensive narrative synthesis of the literature was conducted by searching major databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science) for peer-reviewed English-language studies examining physical exercise or activity in experimental epilepsy models and people with epilepsy. Inclusion prioritized investigations of neurotransmitter alterations (GABA, glutamate, dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline), BDNF signaling, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and related clinical endpoints such as seizure frequency, cognition, and quality of life. Accumulating evidence demonstrates that regular moderate-to-vigorous aerobic and resistance exercise reduces seizure frequency and severity in animal models and selected clinical cohorts, while concurrently ameliorating depression, anxiety, cognitive deficits, and overall quality of life. Mechanistically, exercise elevates brain GABA levels and GABAergic neurosteroids, restores excitatory-inhibitory balance by modulating glutamate, enhances monoaminergic transmission (dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline), and robustly upregulates hippocampal BDNF and downstream plasticity pathways (ERK/mTOR). Physical exercise emerges as a safe, accessible, and multifaceted complementary strategy in epilepsy treatment, exerting anticonvulsant and neuroprotective actions principally through neurotransmitter modulation and neurotrophic support. Integration of structured exercise into multidisciplinary care is warranted, although larger randomized trials are needed to optimize intensity, modality, and patient stratification, particularly in drug-resistant epilepsy. Exercise may enhance GABAergic function and attenuate pathological glutamatergic activity, particularly after repeated training in experimental epilepsy models.Exercise may modulate serotonergic, dopaminergic, and noradrenergic signaling, but the direction and functional significance of these changes depend on exercise characteristics and experimental context.Adenosine and lactate provide potential metabolic links between exercise-related energy demand and neuronal excitability, although their antiseizure relevance in humans remains uncertain.BDNF–TrkB signaling may contribute to exercise-related synaptic plasticity, neuronal resilience, and excitatory–inhibitory network organization, but is not established as a universal mediator of neurotransmitter adaptation.Exercise-related adaptations in oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial function, and neuroplasticity may contribute to greater network resilience and reduced seizure susceptibility.Mechanistic evidence remains predominantly preclinical, and direct links between exercise-induced molecular changes and seizure outcomes in people with epilepsy remain limited.

Article.Title: Multimodal based brain tumor classification using clustered federated learning in edge based IoT network
Article.Authors: C. R.; B. M.
Article.Abstract: Aim: A brain tumor is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells that causes a severe impact on the quality of life. Nowadays, various methods based on multimodal medical images are used to identify brain tumors. Meanwhile, these methods require extensive amounts of labeled information to identify disease tissues and often encounter various challenges based on privacy and accuracy. This paper establishes a Taylor-based Focal Log-cosh Entropy Network (TFLE-Net) to classify brain tumors from demographic data and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) images by utilizing clustered federated learning in an edge-based Internet of Things (IoT) network. Methods: The detection process is executed in clustered federated learning concerning two entities: server and nodes. In a local training model, an input MRI scan is pre-processed, further brain tumor areas are segmented, and then, the mining of various features is performed. Simultaneously, the normalization of input demographic data is done, and the suitable features are selected using information gain. Further, the extracted features and chosen features are subjected to TFLE-Net to classify brain tumors. Results: The TFLE-Net yielded Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.057, Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.047, True Positive Rate (TPR) of 97.789%, and accuracy of 96.987%. Conclusion: The proposed model improveds brain tumor classification through multimodal feature integration and information gain-based feature selection. The obtained results demonstrated its potential for accurate, privacy-preserving brain tumor detection in edge-based IoT healthcare environments.

Article.Title: miR-665 ameliorates neuroinflammation after intracerebral hemorrhage by modulating myeloid cell polarization via targeting STAT3
Article.Authors: Huang Z.; Yang Y.; Sun B.; Luo J.; Yang Y.; Zou D.; Cui Y.; Wang L.; Ma Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: Microglia-mediated neuroinflammation contributes to secondary injury after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), but the role of miR-665 remains unclear. Methods: An ICH rat model was established. A combination of techniques, including Neurological scoring, brain water content measurement, histology and molecular assays were employed to assess miR-665, the STAT3/NF-κB pathway, myeloid polarization and inflammation. Stereotaxic miR-665 agomir/antagomir delivery verified its function. The targeting relationship between miR-665 and STAT3 was confirmed by a dual-luciferase reporter assay. In vitro experiments were performed in Hemin-stimulated BV2 cells with miR-665 mimics/inhibitor, followed by flow cytometry detection of cell polarization and inflammatory factor analysis. Rescue experiments with STAT3 overexpression were conducted both in vivo and in vitro. Results: After ICH, miR-665 was downregulated andinduced excessive activation of the STAT3/NF-κB signaling axis in peri-hematomal tissue, accompanied by M1-like/pro-inflammatory myeloid cell polarization and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines. Upregulation of miR-665 ameliorated neurological function, reduced brain edema, promoted M2-like/repair-associated polarization, and suppressed inflammation, whereas miR-665 downregulation aggravated injury. Dual-luciferase assay confirmed that miR-665 directly targets STAT3. In vitro, miR-665 overexpression inhibited STAT3 phosphorylation and further suppressed the downstream NF-κB signaling, reversing the Hemin-induced M1-like/pro-inflammatory polarization. STAT3 overexpression counteracted the protective effects of miR-665. Conclusion: Downregulated miR-665 after ICH exacerbates neuroinflammation by promoting M1-like/pro-inflammatory myeloid cell polarization via disinhibition of STAT3 and subsequent activation of NF-κB signaling. Upregulating miR-665 exerts neuroprotection by inhibiting STAT3 phosphorylation and facilitating M2-like/repair-associated myeloid cell polarization, highlighting the miR-665/STAT3 regulatory cascade as a promising therapeutic target for post-ICH neuroinflammation.

Article.Title: Gut microbiota-derived extracellular vesicles in ischemic stroke: mechanisms of neurovascular injury and repair
Article.Authors: Li F.; Chen F.; Gu R.; Zeng J.
Article.Abstract: Objective: To examine how gut microbiota-derived extracellular vesicles (GMEVs) may link post-stroke intestinal dysbiosis and barrier dysfunction with secondary brain injury and recovery after ischemic stroke (IS). Methods: This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on GMEV biogenesis, cargo, transport, and signaling across the gut-brain axis, with emphasis on peripheral immune activation, blood-brain barrier (BBB) injury, glial responses, neurovascular dysfunction, and repair. Evidence from endogenous and engineered bacterial vesicle studies was considered separately. Results: IS disrupts intestinal homeostasis through autonomic, endocrine, hemodynamic, and immune pathways, potentially altering GMEV release, composition, and translocation. Vesicles from pathobionts may promote endothelial activation, complement and inflammasome signaling, oxidative stress, leukocyte recruitment, regulated cell death, BBB disruption, and maladaptive glial responses. In contrast, vesicles from selected commensal or probiotic bacteria may support epithelial integrity, immune resolution, and restorative neurovascular signaling. Engineered bacterial vesicles have shown promise as targeted therapeutic carriers in preclinical IS models; however, these findings do not establish equivalent effects for endogenous gut-derived vesicles. GMEV actions are likely dependent on microbial source, molecular cargo, route of exposure, dose, host state, and timing, and may be harmful or beneficial rather than intrinsically producing both effects. Conclusions: GMEVs are plausible mediators of gut-brain communication after IS and may represent both therapeutic targets and delivery platforms. Translation will require source-resolved tracing, rigorous vesicle characterization, physiologic dosing, clinically relevant models, and longitudinal human studies to define their causal and therapeutic relevance.

Article.Title: rTMS Attenuates Microglial Phagocytosis and Promotes Neurorepair in a Photothrombotic Stroke Mouse Model
Article.Authors: Han Y.; Tuerhong B.; Zhang Y.; Wu J.; Mo L.
Article.Abstract: Objective: This study investigated the effects of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) on functional recovery in photothrombotic (PT) stroke mice and whether rTMS promotes neurorepair by modulating microglial phagocytosis. Methods: Eight-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were used to establish a focal stroke model via photothrombosis (PT group). The Sham group and PT + rTMS group were included. rTMS was initiated 24 h after modeling. Neurological deficits were assessed. Microglial activation, synaptic phagocytosis, neuronal injury, and the levels of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and interleukin-1β (IL-1β) were evaluated. Differentially expressed proteins and core regulatory pathways were analyzed. Results: rTMS treatment significantly increased body weight, prolonged the latency to fall and shortened the balance beam crossing time, reduced foot faults, and improved the discrimination index in PT mice. rTMS reduced the number of Iba1-positive microglia and CD68-positive cells, attenuated microglial synaptic phagocytosis, and alleviated neuronal loss and apoptosis. rTMS significantly decreased the levels of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β in the brain. A total of 416 differentially expressed proteins were identified between the PT and PT + rTMS groups. The differentially expressed proteins were significantly enriched in microglial phagocytosis pathways and related signaling pathways. Conclusion: rTMS significantly ameliorates neurological deficits and cognitive impairment in PT stroke mice. The underlying mechanism may involve the inhibition of excessive microglial activation, attenuation of microglia-mediated synaptic phagocytosis, and alleviation of neuroinflammation. Proteomic analysis reveals that rTMS modulates the expression of proteins associated with microglial phagocytosis-related signaling pathways, which may contribute to the observed post-stroke neurorepair effects.

Article.Title: Astrocyte-derived small extracellular vesicles deliver Serpina3k to attenuate cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by restraining neuroinflammation and neuronal apoptosis
Article.Authors: Xia W.; Yin C.; Li L.; Liu F.; Fan X.; Cao Y.; Bu X.
Article.Abstract: Aim: To determine whether astrocyte-derived small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) deliver Serpina3k to recipient neural cells and protect against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI). Methods: A mouse transient middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion model was combined with pharmacological inhibition of sEV release, astrocyte-targeted Serpina3k knockdown and intrathecal delivery of astrocyte-derived sEVs. Brain sEV cargo was profiled by label-free proteomics and Transwell co-cultures were subjected to oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation. Neurological outcomes, infarct volume, apoptosis and inflammatory mediators were assessed, and Serpina3k-interacting proteins were identified by co-immunoprecipitation. Results: Blocking sEV release aggravated neurological deficits, neuronal apoptosis and inflammation. Brain-derived sEVs increased after ischemia-reperfusion and protected neurons against oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation. Serpina3k was enriched in ischemia-derived sEVs and localized predominantly to astrocytes; astrocytic Serpina3k knockdown reduced sEV-associated Serpina3k and worsened deficits, whereas Serpina3k-deficient sEVs increased neuronal apoptosis, microglial IL-1beta and IL-18 release, infarct volume and Caspase-6/NLRP3 signalling. Serpina3k co-immunoprecipitated with Caspase-6 and Omi/HtrA2. In vivo, Serpina3k-deficient astrocytic sEVs were associated with larger infarct volume, increased Omi/HtrA2 expression and reduced HAX-1 expression. Conclusion: Astrocyte-derived sEV-associated Serpina3k is an endogenous protective cargo that limits cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by restraining microglial inflammatory activation and neuronal apoptosis.

Article.Title: Pharmacological modulation of the striatal mGluR5–NR2B association attenuates L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia in 6-OHDA lesioned parkinsonian rats
Article.Authors: Zhao L.; Fu R.; Zhu X.; Qian W.; E Y.; Zheng Z.; Lin J.
Article.Abstract: Objective: The clinical utility of L-DOPA is severely limited by the development of L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). Although metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGluR5) antagonists alleviate LID, the underlying molecular mechanisms, particularly those involving striatal glutamate receptor crosstalk, remain incompletely understood. Methods: Adult female Sprague-Dawley rats with unilateral 6-OHDA lesions were randomized into Sham, PD, LID, MTEP, and MK-801 groups (n=6/group). L-DOPA/benserazide was given twice daily for 14 days, with MTEP or MK-801 30 min before each dose. AIMs, open-field activity, striatal mGluR5-NR2B co-immunoprecipitation, PKC/MEK/ERK phosphorylation, and c-fos/Pdyn mRNA were assessed. Behavioral and molecular data were analyzed by mixed models, ANOVA, or Kruskal-Wallis tests.Results: We observed aberrant elevation of the mGluR5-NR2B interactions in the striatum of 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA)-lesioned parkinsonian rats exhibiting LID. Administration of the mGluR5 antagonist MTEP or the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801 reduced the co-immunoprecipitated association, reduced the synaptic association of mGluR5 with NR2B, and markedly attenuated LID severity. Mechanistically, the decoupling of these receptors was accompanied by decreased ERK1/2 phosphorylation, reduced PKC protein expression, and decreased L-DOPA-induced c-fos and prodynorphin mRNA levels. Furthermore, abnormal involuntary movement (AIM) scores significantly correlated with the extent of NR2B-mGluR5 interaction and downstream signaling activation. These findings suggest that increased mGluR5-NR2B association is associated with LID and may contribute to its expression. Conclusion: The therapeutic efficacy of MTEP or MK-801 is likely mediated by reducing this receptor interaction and downstream signaling, highlighting a potential molecular target for LID treatment.

Article.Title: IL-17 aggravates the neuroinflammatory response in depression by regulating microglial polarization through the JAK1/STAT3 signaling pathway
Article.Authors: Wei Y.; Xiao Y.; Xu Y.; Yuan J.
Article.Abstract: Background: Microglia-mediated neuroinflammation is closely related to the development of depression. As a proinflammatory cytokine, IL-17 plays a key role in various neuroinflammatory diseases. This study aimed to investigate the potential molecular mechanisms through which IL-17 affects neuroinflammation in depression through the regulation of microglial polarization. Methods: A chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced mouse model of depression and an LPS-treated BV2 cell model were used. The depression-like behavior of the mice was evaluated using the sucrose preference test (SPT), tail suspension test (TST), and forced swim test (FST). Neuronal injury was assessed using HE staining. The levels of neurotransmitters and inflammatory cytokines were analyzed using ELISA. Microglial polarization was analyzed by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence, and the expression of IL-17A and JAK1/STAT3 pathway-related proteins was assessed using Western blotting. Results: IL-17 was highly expressed in clinical specimens from patients with depression, mice treated with CUMS and BV2 cells. The inhibition of IL-17 improved depression-like behavior in CUMS-treated mice, reduced neuronal damage, and increased the expression of the neurotransmitters 5-HT, NE, and DA. In addition, IL-17 inhibition inhibited M1 microglial polarization and inflammation. In terms of molecular mechanisms, IL-17 promoted microglial M1 polarization by activating the JAK1/STAT3 signaling pathway and aggravating neuroinflammation related to depression. The use of the JAK/STAT pathway activator RO8191 attenuated the inhibitory effect of IL-17 inhibition on microglial M1 polarization. Conclusion: IL-17 activates JAK1/STAT3 signaling, promotes M1 microglial polarization, and aggravates neuroinflammation related to depression.

Article.Title: Association of metabolic insulin resistance with white matter hyperintensity burden and plasma proteomic signatures in the UK Biobank
Article.Authors: Si X.; Qi X.
Article.Abstract: Background: Metabolic insulin resistance is closely related to cardiometabolic dysfunction and vascular injury. Its association with subclinical cerebral small vessel disease, and the circulating molecular signals that may accompany this association, remain incompletely characterised. Methods: We analysed 59,826 UK Biobank participants with brain magnetic resonance imaging to examine the association between the metabolic score for insulin resistance (METS-IR) and white matter hyperintensity (WMH) burden. Associations were evaluated using multivariable linear regression and restricted cubic spline analysis, with spline models restricted to participants with complete covariate data. Proteomic data were available for 6,790 participants. Protein-wide association analyses, functional annotation and LASSO prioritisation explored circulating protein links between METS-IR and WMH burden, followed by exploratory mediation models in 1,309 participants with complete model data. Results: Higher METS-IR was associated with greater WMH burden after adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle and vascular risk factors. Complete-case spline analysis suggested a nonlinear association, with steeper fitted slopes at higher METS-IR values. Proteomic screening identified 1,266 proteins associated with METS-IR and 122 proteins associated with WMH after false discovery rate correction, yielding 119 overlapping proteins. These proteins were enriched for immune-inflammatory processes and cell adhesion. LASSO prioritisation selected eight candidate proteins, and exploratory mediation models yielded indirect-effect estimates for selected proteins, with GAL showing the largest estimated proportion mediated. Conclusions: METS-IR was associated with WMH burden after adjustment for measured covariates in this large UK Biobank analysis. Integrated plasma proteomic analyses identified immune-inflammatory and cell-adhesion signals that may help characterise molecular correlates of metabolic insulin resistance and cerebral small vessel disease burden.

Article.Title: The diagnostic dilemma of Acute Vestibular Syndrome: why HINTS outperforms diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging?
Article.Authors: Bayar Muluk N.
Article.Abstract: Objectives: To evaluate the diagnostic approaches, specifically the comparative accuracy of bedside clinical examinations versus early neuroimaging, in differentiating central from peripheral causes of Acute Vestibular Syndrome (AVS). Methods: A comprehensive narrative literature review was conducted utilizing established scientific databases, including PubMed/Medline, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase, covering articles published up to 2024. A structured search strategy was applied using keywords such as 'Acute Vestibular Syndrome', 'Central vestibular dysfunction', 'Peripheral vestibular dysfunction', and 'HINTS protocol'. Peer-reviewed clinical trials, mechanistic studies, and authoritative guidelines were included to synthesize the current evidence regarding the diagnosis and management of acute vertigo. Results: The synthesis of the literature reveals that targeted bedside neuro-otological examinations demonstrate superior sensitivity (96.8%) and specificity (98.5%) compared to early 'Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging' in detecting posterior circulation strokes within the initial 48 h. Early neuroimaging frequently yields false-negative results in up to 14.3% of ischemic events. Conclusion: Accurate differentiation of etiologies in continuous vertigo relies heavily on structured bedside clinical assessments rather than immediate neuroimaging. Implementing these clinical protocols prevents severe neurological sequelae from missed posterior fossa strokes while simultaneously avoiding unnecessary healthcare expenditures for benign peripheral conditions.

Article.Title: Salidroside alleviates MPP <sup>+</sup> -induced injury and mitochondrial fission in PC12 cells by mediating the HDAC6/MST1/MIEF1 axis
Article.Authors: Zhao R.; Chen L.; Li X.; Mao X.; Zhou Y.; Shen J.
Article.Abstract: Objective: To investigate the protective effects of salidroside (SAL) against MPP+-induced injury and mitochondrial fission in PC12 cells and to explore the involvement of the HDAC6/MST1/MIEF1 signaling axis. Methods: NGF-differentiated PC12 cells were exposed to MPP+ to establish a cellular model of Parkinson's disease-related injury and subsequently treated with SAL. Cell viability, apoptosis, inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP production, mitochondrial morphology, and mitochondrial fission-related proteins were evaluated. HDAC6 promoter activity, the interaction between HDAC6 and MST1, and MST1 acetylation were analyzed. The mechanistic role of the HDAC6/MST1/MIEF1 axis was further examined using HDAC6 knockdown and MST1 or MIEF1 overexpression. Results: SAL significantly improved cell viability, reduced apoptotic nuclear changes and the levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α, and alleviated oxidative stress by decreasing reactive oxygen species and malondialdehyde levels while increasing superoxide dismutase activity. SAL also restored mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production, increased mitochondrial length, and decreased the expression of the mitochondrial fission-related proteins DRP1, FIS1, and MFF. Mechanistically, SAL enhanced HDAC6 promoter activity and increased HDAC6 expression, while reducing MST1 and MIEF1 expression. HDAC6 interacted with MST1 and regulated its acetylation. The protective effects of SAL were markedly attenuated by HDAC6 knockdown or MST1/MIEF1 overexpression. Conclusion: SAL alleviates MPP+-induced cellular injury, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and excessive mitochondrial fission in PC12 cells through an HDAC6-dependent mechanism involving the MST1/MIEF1 axis. These findings support further investigation of this pathway in physiologically relevant models of Parkinson's disease.
